## Front matter of the volume

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, corrected with the greatest care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they have done so.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price—and especially this collection, a single, methodical, and chronological work consisting of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete series in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# A.D. 461–462

## Pope Saint Hilary

### Prolegomena

[Column 0009]

## Life of Pope Hilary

*(From the Pontifical Book.)*

*[Note: After an interregnum of nearly seven months, on the day before the Ides of November in the year 461, the fifth year of the emperor Leo, Hilary, a Sardinian by birth, formerly a deacon and an envoy at the Council of Ephesus, was appointed in succession to Saint Leo. At the beginning of his pontificate he confirmed what had been decreed by the three ecumenical councils against the Arian, Nestorian, and Eutychian heresies. Through Victor of Aquitaine, then easily foremost in this field, and on the authority of Gennadius and Marianus Scotus, he arranged for a new paschal cycle of 542 years. Gelasius says in Letter 11 to Dardanus: “When the emperor Anthemius of the West, with the Macedonian Philotheus relying upon his intimacy with him, wished to introduce new councils of divided sects into the city, he openly compelled him before the blessed apostle Peter, in a loud voice, not to do so—so completely that the emperor promised, with an oath, that these things should not be done.”**

*In his time at Constantinople, the hand of a certain painter who attempted to depict Christ in the form of Jupiter withered; after confessing the crime and offense, Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, healed him. Cedrenus, in his Compendium. Daniel the Stylite, renowned for holiness and miracles, also flourished. According to his acts, by his prayers he obtained for the emperor Leo a male child by his wife Verina and extinguished a four-day fire in the city of Constantinople.*

*How, after completing his embassy, Hilary—who had escaped the intrigues of Dioscorus of Alexandria and the Ephesian robber council—came to Rome, and what he did there, we have related above in the notes to the letter that Hilary, while still a deacon, wrote to the empress Pulcheria concerning this matter. Severus Binius. See what we have noted concerning this letter at the foot of the next column. Editor.]*

Hilary, a Sardinian by birth, son of Crispinus [Crispinianus], held the see for six years, three months, and ten days.

*[Note: On the fourth day before the Ides of September in the year of Christ’s birth 467, the eleventh year of Leo’s reign, Hilary died in life and pontificate. He had held office for six years, ten months, less two days. What I have said will be shown to be correct if you consider the beginning and end of his pontificate. Severus Binius.]*

He issued a decretal and scattered it throughout the whole East [the Lucan manuscript reads “exsparsit”; read: “dispatched it”], and letters concerning the Catholic faith, confirming the three synods—Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—and the Tome of the holy archbishop Leo.

*[Note: The Lucan manuscript reads “or the book of the holy bishop.”]*

He condemned Eutyches and Nestorius, and all their followers and all heresies, confirming the condemnation [read: “dominion,” as in the Lucan manuscript] and primacy of the holy Catholic and apostolic see.

He issued a decree concerning the Church in the basilica of Saint Mary, in the consulship of Basiliscus and Hermenericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

*[Note: That is, a synodal decree. The decree of which the author of the Pontifical Book, Anastasius, speaks was issued at the Roman council held under Hilary in the year of our Lord 465, the fifth year of Hilary’s pontificate. Severus Binius.]*

He built three oratories in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica: one of Saint John the Baptist, one of Saint John the Evangelist, and one of the holy Cross, all of silver and precious stones.

He made the confessio of Saint John the Baptist of silver, weighing 100 pounds, and a golden cross.

*[Note: In the same manuscript, “autem” is absent, and below “fecit” is absent.]* He made the confessio of Saint John the Evangelist of silver, weighing 100 pounds, and a golden cross. In both oratories he placed bronze doors covered with silver.

In the oratory of the holy Cross he made a confessio, where he placed the Lord’s wood [the same manuscript reads “lamb”], and a golden cross with gems, weighing twenty pounds.

In the confessio he made silver doors weighing fifty pounds. Above the confessio he placed a golden arch weighing four pounds, borne by onyx columns; and there stood a golden lamb weighing two pounds.

A golden crown stood before the confessio. A beacon with dolphins weighed five pounds. Four golden lamps weighed two pounds.

He made a nymphaeum and a three-sided portico before the oratory of the holy Cross, where there are columns of extraordinary size called Hecatonpenta [the same manuscript reads “Hecatonpentaic”].

There was a basin and two citharic shells [the same manuscript reads “two decorated shells”], with porphyry columns, pierced [the manuscript reads “spread out”], pouring forth water.

In the middle of the basin was a porphyry basin with a citharic shell [read: “citharic,” though the printed form is corrupt] in its center, pouring forth water. It was enclosed on both the right and the left in the middle by bronze screens and columns, adorned on every side with pediments and architraves of mosaic, and with Aquitanian, Tripolitan, and porphyry columns.

Before the confessio of the blessed John he placed a silver crown weighing twenty pounds. A beacon-shaped vessel weighed twenty-five pounds.

Likewise, at Saint John, inside the holy font, he placed a golden lamp with ten lamp-wicks [printed *nixis*; read: *lychnis myxis*] of ten lights, weighing five pounds.

Three silver stags poured forth water; each weighed thirty pounds. A silver tower with dolphins weighed sixty pounds. A golden dove weighed two pounds.

In the Constantinian basilica he placed ten silver canthari [the same manuscript reads “phara canthara”] hanging before the altar; each weighed twenty pounds. A golden cup weighed six pounds. Another golden cup weighed five pounds.

Five golden chalices weighed one pound each [read: “two pounds each”]. Five silver cups weighed ten pounds each. Twenty ministerial chalices weighed two pounds each. Five silver pitchers weighed ten pounds each.

At the church of the blessed apostle Peter he placed a golden cup weighing five pounds. Another golden cup with green and hyacinth-colored gems weighed four pounds. Ten silver ministerial chalices weighed two pounds each. Two silver pitchers weighed eight pounds each.

Fourteen silver beacon-vessels and canthari [the same manuscript reads “twenty-four”] weighed three pounds each [the manuscript reads “five”].

At the church of the blessed apostle Paul he placed a golden cup weighing five pounds. *[Note: The same manuscript reads: “At the blessed apostle Paul, a golden cup weighing five pounds; another golden cup with gems weighing five pounds; silver cups, etc.”]* Four silver cups weighed six pounds each. Ten ministerial chalices weighed two pounds each. Two silver pitchers weighed ten pounds each.

At the church of the blessed martyr Lawrence he placed a golden cup with green and hyacinth-colored gems weighing four pounds. A golden lamp of ten lights [read: “lamps”] weighed five pounds. A most pure golden cup weighed five pounds. Two golden lamps weighed one pound each. A golden beacon-cantherus weighed two pounds.

A silver tower with dolphins weighed twenty-five pounds. Three silver cups weighed twenty-four pounds. Twelve ministerial chalices weighed two pounds. A silver altar weighed forty pounds. Ten silver lamps weighed twenty pounds. Two silver pitchers weighed ten pounds each.

In the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence he placed ten silver beacon-can­thari, weighing ten pounds [the same manuscript reads “sixty”]; twenty-six bronze canthari; silver vessels for baptism or penance, weighing ten pounds; and fifty bronze beacons.

In the city of Rome he appointed ministerial servants [the same manuscript reads “ministeria,” ‘liturgical vessels’] who were to visit the established stations.

A handled or station cup [the manuscript reads “handled,” or omits the word] weighed eight pounds. Twenty-five cups for the titles weighed ten pounds each. Twenty-five silver pitchers weighed ten pounds each [the same manuscript adds “each”]. Fifty ministerial chalices weighed two pounds each.

All these he stored in the Constantinian basilica or at Saint Mary’s.

He built monasteries at Saint Lawrence, as well as a bathhouse and a residence [the same manuscript adds “and another beneath the bronze”; in that manuscript “at Saint Lawrence” and the following text through the libraries are absent] for Saint Lawrence.

He built an oratory of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery. He also built two libraries in the same place.

At Luna he built a monastery within the city [the same manuscript reads: “Likewise, a monastery within the city of Rome at Luna”].

He held one ordination in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-five priests, five deacons [the same manuscript reads “six”], and twenty-two bishops for various places.

He too was buried at Saint Lawrence, in the crypt beside the body of the blessed Sixtus. The episcopate was vacant for ten days.

Concerning the Ephesian robber council, the factions of Dioscorus, and his flight.

[Column 0011D]

To the most glorious and most devout empress Pulcheria, Hilary the deacon.

“I was eager to …,” etc.

*(You will find this letter, which is Letter 46 among the Leonine letters, transcribed in volume 54 of our Patrology, column 837.)*

# Letter I of Pope Hilary to the bishops of Tarraco

## Concerning the synodal decree

[Column 0012D]

In the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Basiliscus and Herminericus.

### I

Since a devout assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges us to discuss with more diligent care whatever is necessary for ecclesiastical discipline [the Lucan manuscript reads: “certain things that”], let us, brothers, if it pleases you, with the Lord’s help establish permanently whatever concerns the proper conduct of ordinations, in accordance with the precepts of divine law and the decrees of the canons of Nicaea, so that no one may dare, at the peril of his own status, to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see.

For we who administer the duties of the supreme priesthood shall be held responsible for such transgressions if we are found negligent in God’s affairs. We remember how greatly the Lord threatens the negligence of priests, since the one who enjoys higher honor commits a more serious offense, and the loftiness of dignities makes sinners’ faults more grievous.

### II

First of all, therefore, care must be taken that no one aspire to the sacred ranks who has married a woman who was not a virgin, as was previously prescribed in the earlier records [the Lucan manuscript reads “proscribed”].

Anyone who has entered into a second marriage contrary to the apostolic precepts must also be rejected.

### III

Those ignorant of letters, those who have suffered some bodily impairment, and those who are penitents [printed: *ex poenitentes sunt*] must not dare to aspire to sacred orders.

Whoever becomes the consecrator of such persons will undo his own act [the Lucan manuscript reads: “he himself will dissolve it”].

### IV

Moreover, if anyone has committed something unlawfully, or has found that something was committed by his predecessors, he must condemn it if he wishes to avoid personal danger. We do not wish to exercise the severity of punishment in any matter.

But whoever has sinned in God’s affairs through stubbornness or some other excess, or has himself refused to abolish what he wrongly did, will find in himself whatever he failed to cut away from another [variant: “in another” / “has not cut away”].

So that this may thereafter be guarded more firmly, if it pleases you, commend (*commendate*; variant *commodate*, “entrust”) all your judgments, cases, and proper subscriptions, so that *aditus* (“access”; printed *auditus*, “hearing”) to unlawful matters (*illicitis*; printed *illicitus*) may be closed by synodal judgment.

The bishops and priests unanimously acclaimed:

“Hear, O Christ; life to Hilary!”—said six times.

“We both confirm these things and teach these things”—said eight times.

“These things must be held; these things must be observed”—said five times.

“We give thanks for your teaching”—said ten times.

“We ask that these things be observed forever”—said fifteen times.

“Through the holy Peter we desire that these things be observed forever”—said eight times [the Lucan manuscript: “that they be preserved in God”].

“May this presumption never occur”—said ten times.

“Whoever violates these things will find the consequence in himself”—said seven times.

And silence having been made, Bishop Hilary said:

### V

Moreover, brothers, new and unheard-of seeds of perversity are continually arising in certain places, as has reached us through letters sent from Spain containing a definite report.

Indeed, some people think that the episcopate—which is granted only on the basis of preceding merits [the Lucan manuscript: “not without”]—is not a divine gift but an hereditary advantage. They believe that, like things that are perishable and mortal, the priesthood too may be transferred by legal or testamentary right [variant: “by legacy or testamentary right”].

For many priests who are near death are said to designate others by name to be substituted in their place, so that a legitimate election is not awaited, but the favor shown by the deceased is taken [variant: “offered”] as the consent of the people.

Consider how serious this is; and therefore, if it pleases you, let us also remove this permission generally from the churches, lest—which is shameful to say—anyone think that what belongs to God is owed to a human being.

So that what has been brought before us [variant: “conveyed to us”] may also come to your knowledge, let the written reports of our Spanish brothers and fellow bishops be read.

The notary Paul read them.

*[Note: This addition is absent from the Lucan manuscript.]*

It is added in Justellus’s manuscript:

“And it was decreed that priests should presume nothing further of this kind.”

*[Note: This letter was read at the Roman council held at Rome in the year of our Lord 465, which will be mentioned below. While it was being read, the Fathers added their judgments by acclamation and interjection. For this reason it seemed appropriate here to insert it word for word from Cresconius and the Vatican manuscript, just as it had been written and sent by the bishops of Tarraco to the apostolic see. In the Roman synod it is printed together with the opposing acclamations, interjections, and judgments of the Fathers. It therefore had to be placed in both locations, so that it might easily be seen what additions it had received from the intervening judgments of the Fathers.**

*Although the barbarian fury of the Goths, who devastated nearly all the churches of Spain, had relaxed the force of ecclesiastical discipline in Spain, this letter clearly indicates that the province of Tarraco nevertheless remained the guardian of laws and canons, that it respected the Roman pontiff, and that it brought all controversies before him as the supreme judge and pastor of the Church. Severus Binius.]*

# Letter of the bishops of Tarraco to Pope Hilary

They complain before the Roman pontiff about the ordination of a bishop carried out by Silvanus, bishop of Calagurris, contrary to the rules of the Fathers and the canons of Nicaea, and ask him what they should do in this case and by what means they ought to counter abuses of this kind.

[Column 0014C]

To the most blessed Pope Hilary, whom we venerate in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius, bishop, and all the bishops of the province of Tarraco.

*[Note: Sirmond collated Hilary’s letters with three manuscripts, and the last one also with two others. They are the Pithoean, Arelatensian, Lérins, Corbie, and Reims manuscripts. Hardouin also collated them with the manuscript collection of Dionysius, from which we provide more accurate readings.]*

Even if no necessity of ecclesiastical discipline existed [variant: “dictated”], we ought in truth to have sought that privilege of your see by which, after receiving the keys of the kingdom following the Savior’s resurrection, the unique preaching of the most blessed Peter looked to the illumination of all throughout the world. The primacy of his vicar is as eminent as it is feared and loved by all.

Therefore, worshiping God completely in you—for you serve him without reproach—we have recourse to the faith praised by the apostolic voice, seeking answers from the place where nothing is commanded through error or presumption, but everything through pontifical deliberation.

Although matters stand thus, there is nevertheless among us a false brother. Just as we could not remain silent about his presumption for longer, so the necessity of the coming judgment has compelled us to speak.

A certain Silvanus, bishop established at Calagurris in the farthest part of our province, has usurped unauthorized divinations [read: “ordinations”] and driven our humility to such a point that, against his utterly empty superstition, we ask for the sole remedy of your see.

For already seven or more years ago, setting aside the rules of the Fathers and disregarding your institutions, he ordained a bishop when no people had requested one. We thought that this rash action could be cured by a fraternal and peaceful admonition, but it grew worse.

Finally, contrary to the antiquity of the canons and the decrees of the synod, inflamed only by the spirit of presumption, he made the priest of another of our brothers a bishop in the same place that had been assigned to that brother—the man upon whom he had laid hands against his will and resistance, and who had already been added to our assembly.

As a result, our brother, the bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, reported to us his most wretched rashness; his diligence and concern had taken great care, if only it had achieved some good.

For he repeatedly opposed all the bishops living in the vicinity, so that they would not join themselves to a schismatic. Yet, with damnable obstinacy, that one man alone did not blush to commit everything that was unlawful—and what we are ashamed to say.

Therefore, since these presumptions, which divide unity and create schism, must be countered quickly, we ask your see that we may be instructed by apostolic utterances concerning what you wish to be observed in this matter.

Thus, with the brotherhood assembled, the constitutions of the venerable synod brought forth publicly, and supported by your authority against the spirit of rebellion, we may, with God’s help, understand what ought to be done concerning the ordainer and the ordained.

Your triumph will surely be achieved if, during the time of your apostolate, the Catholic Church hears what the chair of Saint Peter possesses, and if the newly sown seeds of weeds have been uprooted.

And the subscription:

“May divine eternity preserve your holy apostolate, praying for us, through unending ages.”

*[Note: I have placed this letter after the earlier letter of the bishops of Tarraco, since it refers to a letter written long before and is therefore later in time. I thought it would be more agreeable and would make the truth of the affair easier to perceive if events that occurred earlier were narrated and placed earlier. In the Roman council this letter was read first and deservedly placed first. The acclamations of the bishops inserted into the reading of this letter will be indicated below in the account of that Roman council.**

*It contains two matters worthy of note. First, that only the Roman see has authority to dispense in matters undertaken contrary to the canons; second, that no provincial council has such authority that it could do this without consulting the apostolic see. Severus Binius.]*

# Letter of the bishops of Tarraco to Pope Hilary

*(C, G)*

[Column 0016]

To the most blessed Pope Hilary, whom we venerate in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraco.

We have learned from our illustrious son Vincentius, of our province, who reported it, what care your apostolate takes of the priests of its provinces. At his urging, our desire rose with willing devotion to the boldness of writing.

Therefore, offering to your crown the fitting service of a provincial written address, we ask you, most blessed father whom we venerate in Christ with apostolic reverence, to deign to keep our humility in mind in your prayers, as you do the others.

We especially ask that you deign to confirm, after weighing our assertions, the action we have taken and which is being brought to your knowledge both through the vote of nearly the entire province and through the example of antiquity.

The holy Nundinarius, bishop of the city of Barcelona, has completed the lot of human existence. He left to our venerable brother Irenaeus, whom he had previously established in his own diocese with our consent, whatever his poverty was able to possess, and by the disposition of his final will he desired that Irenaeus be substituted in his place.

The judgment of the deceased concerning his merit does not, however, waver. For all the clergy and people of that same city, as well as the best and most numerous provincials, gave their consent and hoped that he would retain the deceased’s place.

Considering the judgment of the deceased, approving Irenaeus’s life, recognizing the nobility and number of those who were petitioning, and taking into account the usefulness of the Church in question, we judged it best that a bishop of no lesser merit should be substituted for so great a priest who had departed to God—especially since it is clear that the Church of that town, in which Irenaeus had previously been ordained, had always been a diocese of the Church of this city.

Therefore, we humbly beseech your apostolate to confirm by your authority the decree of our humility, which appears to us to have been justly made.

We had already complained in our letters about the presumption of Bishop Silvanus, and we are surprised that we have received no reply from your apostolate.

Now, repeating the same representations, we ask you to deign to instruct us through apostolic words concerning what ought to be observed in these matters.

And lest perhaps, through the negligence of the bearer or the difficulty of the long journey, our humble letter concerning this matter should not have reached you, we preferred also to repeat our petition.

And the subscription:

“May divine eternity preserve your holy apostolate, praying for us, through unending ages, for all of us and for your Church, our truly [variant: ‘venerable’] lord and apostolic pope.”

# Letter II of Pope Hilary to Ascanius and the other bishops of the province of Tarraco

I. No bishop is to be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan bishop.  
II. No bishop is to leave his own Church and transfer to another.  
III. Irenaeus is to be removed from the Church of Barcelona and return to his own.  
IV. On removing bishops who have been illicitly ordained, and on there being no two bishops in one Church.  
V. On the condemnation of Irenaeus if he does not return to his own Church.

Hilary, bishop, to Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraco.

After receiving the letters of your affection, in which you asked that the presumptions of Silvanus, bishop of the Church of Calagurris, be checked, and again sought to have the excessively unlawful wishes of the people of Barcelona confirmed, we received a letter, with the subscriptions of various persons, from the civic notables and landholders of Turiaso, Calcantes, Calagurris, Virgilius, Tritium, Legio, and Civitas [the Lucan manuscript reads: “of Cascantum, Calagurris, Vareia, Tritium, Livium, and Veroviscum”; Dionysius reads: “of Vareia, Tritium, Livium, and Veroviscum”].

Through these letters they excused what your complaint had brought forward concerning Silvanus. Yet their defense was not free from equally just and entirely deserved reproach, since it became clear that, without the knowledge of the metropolitan, our brother and fellow bishop Ascanius, priests had been ordained for certain cities [the Lucan manuscript reads: “Hence”].

Therefore, since we see that whatever has been reported by either side is confused by every kind of perversity, having considered the exigencies of the times, we decree by this arrangement that what has been done belongs to pardon, provided that from now on nothing is attempted contrary to the precepts of the blessed apostle or to the constitution of the canons of Nicaea.

## I

First, in accordance with the rules of those same Fathers, we wish this to be observed: no bishop is to be consecrated in any way without the knowledge and consent of our brother Ascanius, the metropolitan.

The ancient order has maintained this; the authority of the 318 holy Fathers has defined it. Whoever stretches out his hands against it declares himself unworthy of the fellowship of those whose precepts he has resisted.

## II

In contempt of those Fathers, a further point is also disregarded through a proud spirit: it is forbidden [variant: “it is provided”] that anyone, having abandoned his own Church, should presume to transfer to another.

Bishop Irenaeus is attempting to do this, with your excessively improper acquiescence—and, more grievously, with your assertion—although you seek to have the matter confirmed by our authority, despite the fact that you chiefly profess to be stirred by great indignation against unlawful matters.

## III

After the letters concerning the ordination of bishops, in accordance with the decrees of the canons and my predecessors, had been read before the assembly of the brothers whom the festivity of my anniversary had gathered [Note: By “the anniversary of my pontificate,” understand the day of my ordination or election, on which I was elected and raised to the office of supreme pontiff. At this time it was a solemn custom for several bishops to gather in Rome each year and celebrate with great solemnity the day on which the bishop of the Roman Church had been raised to the summit of the supreme pontificate. Saint Leo delivered several sermons on his ordination, that is, on the anniversary of his elevation to the height and summit of the supreme pontificate. Relevant here are what Saint Augustine says about the birthday of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, in Sermon 32 on the Words of the Lord at the end, and about the anniversary of his ordination in Homilies 24 and 25. I do not see how some confirm this same point from Paulinus’s Letter 16 to Delphinus. For he is speaking of that solemn and very ancient custom by which the faithful used to gather, without regard for the summer heat, on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. We discussed this above in the notes to the prefatory letter of the Council of Chalcedon, which Galla Placidia wrote to the empress Pulcheria. See Baronius under the year 465, no. 17. Severus Binius.], a judgment having been pronounced, you will learn from the tenor of the proceedings, which we have sent at the same time, what has been decreed concerning the ordination of bishops in accordance with the statutes of the canons or the decrees of my predecessors.

Therefore, after Irenaeus has been removed from the Church of Barcelona and restored to his own [Note: Codex Luc., “to his own”], let the passions that, through ignorance of ecclesiastical laws, seek to obtain what is not permitted be calmed by priestly moderation; and let a bishop from the local clergy be ordained for the people of Barcelona without delay, of the sort whom you, brother Ascan, ought especially to choose and whom it is fitting for you to consecrate. For if something similar should perhaps be done [Note: Codex Luc., “otherwise”], our command would be blunted—not without a rebuke directed chiefly at your name—since we have learned that something was admitted as an insult to God, from whom the grace of priestly dignities comes in a special manner. Nor should episcopal honor be regarded as an hereditary right, since it is conferred upon us solely by the kindness of our God and Christ [absent from Codex Justinianus].

## IV.

We therefore confirm the bishops who have now been ordained—although, while you were unaware, they advanced and, together with those responsible for them [Note: Codex Luc., “they deserved”], deserved to be removed—on this condition: that none of them has been the husband of a widow [reading: “a widowed woman”], and that he has entered into the marriage and vows of one virgin, just as the legal enactments also prescribe when they say: “Let a priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated” (Leviticus 21; Ezekiel 44). In accordance with this, blessed Paul the Apostle, teacher of the nations, also did not remain silent in his specific instruction concerning those who desire to become priests, saying: “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3).

You ought indeed to be so formed by the force of this judgment, dearest brothers, that among the other things which must be avoided you strive especially to preserve what you know is commanded before all else [Note: Codex Luc., “to guard”]. Among these matters, care must also be taken that there not be two priests at the same time in one Church; that no one ignorant of letters, or lacking any part of his limbs, or even someone from among the penitents [reading: “an ex-penitent”], be allowed at all to approach the sacred ministry. Nor should you think the petitions of the people so powerful that, when you desire to comply with them, you abandon the will of our God, who forbids us to sin. His indignation is stirred more gravely by this, because his kindness is offended when unlawful things are done by those who are interpreters of reconciliation.

## V.

To ensure that everything is corrected according to what we have written, we have sent this letter with our subdeacon Trajan coming to you. But if Bishop Irenaeus, having laid aside his shameful ambition, neglects to return to his own Church—a return that will be granted to him not by judicial right but by humaneness—let him know that he must be removed from the fellowship of bishops. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers. Given on the third day before the Kalends of January (in the year of the Lord 495), in the consulship of the illustrious men Basiliscus and Herminericus.

[Note: This opening is shared by this and several other papal letters. This will readily be apparent if the first letter of Zephyrinus and the third of Fabian are compared with this third letter of Hilary; likewise, the third letter of Saint Leo with the second of Pelagius. — Sev. Binius.]

## LETTER III. OF POPE HILARY TO ASCANIUS, BISHOP OF TARRAGONA, WRITTEN PRIVATELY; IT HAS THE SAME SUBJECT AS THE PRECEDING LETTER

### To his most beloved brother Ascan, Hilary the bishop.

We must be mindful of the divine grace toward us, which by the mercy [reading: “grace”] of its favor has raised us to the priestly dignity for this purpose: that, adhering to its commands and placed, as it were, in the watchtower of its priesthood [reading: “of priests”], we may prohibit unlawful things and teach what ought to be followed.

Therefore, by a letter sent through our subdeacon Trajan, we admonish you that what has been wrongly done be corrected. And we are greatly surprised that your affection not only failed to rebuff the petitions of the people of Barcelona with any authority, but even, by sending letters to us, requested the completion [reading: “agreement”; so also Codex Justinianus] of their perverse desire, introducing in the preamble of your letters a reference to a council—as though the excesses of guilt were diminished by the multitude of the ignorant [reading: “petitioners”; perhaps “those making petitions”]. Even if each person had, under the heading [reading: “subscription”] of his own name, reported the matter along with you and had furnished his own subscriptions to each of them [reading: “brothers”], your affection would nevertheless have borne the highest responsibility for the matter that displeases us. For, on account of the position and honor owed to you, the other priests ought to have been taught, not followed.

Therefore, as I indicated in the general letter, let Irenaeus return to his own Church, and let a prelate be consecrated immediately for the people of Barcelona from its own clergy, provided that the canonical statutes and apostolic commands agree with him. And although those who were ordained priests without your affection’s knowledge and consent ought, together with those responsible for them, to have been removed, nevertheless, so that we may not decree anything harsh in so great a necessity, we wish those who have become bishops to remain—provided that they are not found liable under the apostolic commands and the statutes of the holy Fathers, and that henceforth nothing contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, as has been done up to now, is perpetrated.

It is your concern, dearest brother, to protect everything entrusted to you with the authority proper to you, and not merely to withhold consent from unlawful things, but also to restrain everything that you find has been done contrary to the rule. Above all, compel Irenaeus to return to his own Church, since this is what we decree solely for the sake of unity [reading: “humaneness”]. He ought rather to return of his own accord if he does not fear being separated from the fellowship of priests [Codex Justinianus lacks the negation, which is superfluous here]. Nor should two prelates be permitted to belong to one Church. We entrust the execution of this especially to the diligence of the aforementioned subdeacon, whom our authority has also caused to travel to Spain for the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother.

[Note: This letter was written on the following occasion. Bishop Auxanius had obtained, by underhanded means, that the province of Embrun should be subjected to his episcopate with respect to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Since this had been granted by apostolic authority to the prejudice of Ingenuus, bishop of Embrun and metropolitan of the Maritime Alps, at the petition and complaint of that same Ingenuus, he delegated to Leontius, Veranus, and Victurus the investigation of the case and the restoration of the rights of the metropolitan of Embrun. Against those who are afflicted with a mad desire to enlarge the boundaries of their diocese, he added this golden and most noteworthy judgment: “The expectation of the fruit of our ministry lies not in the extent of regions, but in the acquisition of souls.” Baronius, year 465, no. 27. — Sev. Binius.]

## LETTER IV. OF POPE HILARY TO LEONTIUS, VERANUS, AND VICTURUS, BISHOPS

He delegates to them the dispute between the bishops Ingenuus and Auxanius and decrees that the city of Cimiez and the fortress of Nice should return to the governance of one bishop.

### To his most beloved brothers Leontius, Veranus, and Victurus, bishops, Hilary the pope.

[Note: Although no mention is made here of which Church Bishop Leontius belonged to, there is nevertheless no doubt that he was bishop of Fréjus. Hilary of Arles extolled him with the highest praises in his funeral oration for Saint Honoratus, his predecessor as bishop; letters of Sidonius Apollinaris are also preserved that were written to him, and Saint Leo mentions him in Letter 89 to the bishops of Viennese Gaul. Baronius at the aforementioned place. — Sev. Binius.]

We are moved by the principle of justice. Although it ought to be observed by all who think rightly, it must especially not be rashly neglected by the priests of the Lord, whose duty it is to instruct the rest by their example and teaching.

Our brother and fellow bishop Ingenuus of Embrun, always supported by the honor of metropolitan of the province of the Maritime Alps, reports that, to his prejudice, as the attached documents make clear, we established certain measures at the request of our brother and fellow bishop Auxanius—measures that would conflict with all the defenses presented in this same case. Indeed, when the reports reviewed in our judgment are considered—reports that our brother and fellow bishop Veranus sent to my predecessor of holy memory together with the other priests of the province—and when the response of the Apostolic See that was then sent is made known, it is evident that nothing ought afterward to have been attempted, nor should anything be established by the recent underhanded maneuver to the injury of synodal rules.

[Note: From this example it is clear that the ears of supreme pontiffs are very often filled with false and malicious accusations and reports, so that at times they condemn and oppress good and innocent men on the basis of bad information. Therefore, no one should wonder that Saint Leo harshly attacked Hilary of Arles, and that Pope Hilary harshly attacked Mamertus of Vienne, bishops renowned for their holiness, since, especially in matters that are more contentious, it is very easy for each person to be deceived under the appearance of what is right. — Sev. Binius.]

For although even what was elicited from us may be considered invalid—because the person who deserved to have it carried out was unwilling to execute what had been intimated to him—nevertheless, so that we may not be moved by hatred or favor, neither of which ought to exist in the discussion of cases, we entrust to your charity the examination of the attached complaint. Whatever is shown to have been obtained from us by underhanded means shall have no force against the venerable canons or against the judgment of my predecessor of holy memory.

[Note: It was established not only by decrees that nothing should be changed concerning privileges granted to Churches in ancient times. “The privileges,” he says, “which former emperors, by general constitutions, granted to all the Churches of the orthodox religion, we decree shall be preserved forever firm and unimpaired.” We order that all sanctions obtained contrary to the ecclesiastical canons through the intervention of favor or ambition be deprived of their force and validity, and so forth. What Saint Leo thought concerning privileges that must be inviolably preserved may be learned from his Letters 53, 54, 55, 89, and 109. — Sev. Binius.]

For we do not wish, dearest brothers, the privileges of the Churches—which must always be preserved—to be confused; nor do we permit one priest to possess rights in the province of another, because by this the sanctions of the holy traditions are violated no less than the Lord himself is assailed. The expectation of the fruit of our ministry lies not in the extent of regions, but in the acquisition of souls.

Let our brother and fellow bishop Ingenuus therefore possess the episcopal authority of his province, concerning whose unlawful cession he was formerly censured by the Apostolic See. And, with everything preserved that the authority of my predecessor of holy memory determined concerning the Churches of the city of Cimiez and the fortress of Nice, as we have said, let nothing harm the rights of the Churches because a bishop was recently consecrated in one of the places mentioned by the aforesaid brother, as he stated, in order to exclude the ambition of another’s greed. Rather, let the established form of correction remain, so that the aforementioned places return to the governance of one prelate, since it was not fitting for them to be divided between two priests. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers.

[Note: This letter is circular and encyclical, sent to all the Churches according to the custom and practice followed upon the creation of a new pontiff. A letter written to Leontius with the same subject and the same wording is preserved in an old codex of the Church of Arles. Along with all those that follow, it was first brought to light by the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius. — Sev. Binius.]

## LETTER V. OF POPE HILARY TO LEONTIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

Concerning the beginnings of his episcopate.

### To his most beloved brother Leontius, Hilary the pope.

I believe it is evident to all who preserve the ancestral traditions incorruptibly how much reverence, in the Spirit of God who dwells in the priests subject to him, is owed to the blessed Apostle Peter and to his See. Since we wish them to rejoice with us over the beginnings of our ordination, we have judged that the works which the gracious kindness of God has displayed toward us should be reported to your holiness:

first, so that you may rejoice in the Lord with the affection that we have always mutually shown one another, with the Lord’s assistance; and then so that, through the arrangement of your fraternity, it may become known to all the brothers and fellow priests throughout the province that the right hand of the Lord has deigned to visit my humility, and that he has entrusted me with the governance of the Apostolic See, not on account of merit, but through the abundant generosity of his grace.

Therefore, dearest brother, you will deign to convey to the knowledge of all the brothers what we have disclosed to your holiness in this present communication, so that, as we have said, they may join their prayers to ours, entreating our Lord Jesus Christ to grant us not only the joys of exultation but also their prayers’ beneficial results for the universal Church. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February (in the year of Christ 462), in the consulship of Our Lord Severus Augustus.

## LETTER OF LEONTIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES, TO POPE HILARY (C)

[Note: This letter of Leontius was first published by Dacherius in *Spicilegium*, volume V, now volume III, page 302.]

He congratulates Hilary on his pontificate and asks him to protect the rights of the Church of Arles.

We grieve that death has taken away your most holy predecessor Leo, who watched over the struggle against heresies and, alas, uprooted the tares flourishing too abundantly in the field of the Lord; but we rejoice that God has repaired the loss through your holiness. For a son rejoices in the honor of his mother. And since the Roman Church is the mother of all, we had reason to rejoice that, amid so great a collapse of affairs and weakness of the ages, he raised you over her, so that you might judge the peoples with equity and direct the nations upon the earth.

Therefore, when that messenger, Concordius, a deacon of our Church who was then present when your holiness was raised to that lofty summit of honor, brought us the news, we gave thanks to our God and resolved to greet you as soon as possible with this letter from our humility. Thus the affection that has long grown between your holiness and us might be strengthened in the Lord and henceforth increased, with the due reverence by which sons ought to honor their father.

Blessed, then, is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Now your holiness must labor and strive vigorously so that you may bring to a definitive conclusion what Pope Leo, most holy, began. With the army of Gideon—through trumpets sounding in the mouths of strong men and through lamps carried and brandished in sturdy hands—may your holiness cause the accursed walls of Jericho, so often anathematized and shaken, to fall.

Moreover, since our Church of Arles has always been adorned by the Apostolic See with extensive favors and privileges, we ask your holiness that nothing be taken away from us through it, but rather that our rights be increased, so that we may be able to work with you in the vineyard of the Lord God of Sabaoth and break the efforts of the envious. If there were no authority to restrain them, it is certain that they would grow worse from day to day, because the malice with which they hate us continually increases. Dated in the consulship of Severus Augustus.

## LETTER VI. OF POPE HILARY TO LEONTIUS

He replies to Leontius’s letter, which Leontius had written before receiving Hilary’s preceding letter.

### To his most beloved brother Leontius, Hilary the pope.

The affection I have for the Churches of Gaul and for all the priests of the Lord in them, even those placed in a lower rank, receives a considerable increase from the fact that the beginnings of your address have been conveyed to me by our son, the distinguished man Pappolus. From this, however, I infer that the letter I sent some time ago concerning the beginnings of my episcopate had not yet been delivered to you when you wrote; otherwise you would certainly not have been silent about it, unless some circumstance delayed the bearers.

I therefore indicate that I already carried out what both custom required and charity demanded, and I wish you to know this more fully from the very copies of the letters that I sent, so that you may understand that I was in no respect negligent of my fraternal duty. Let us therefore strive in turn to increase our exchanges of address, so that the care of writing may compensate us for the absence of our common presence, dearest brother.

You have not allowed the grace of your affection to perish, since I know that you are intent upon the concern that I should desire to observe the rules of the ancestral canons. Nothing healthier can be conceived from this desire than that, in one Church—which ought to have neither spot nor wrinkle—there should be one discipline observed by all.

If anything in instruction or correction must be added to it, your diligence will provide for this most properly if, as you have deigned to write, a person so well informed is sent to us that he can fully inform our investigation about every matter. For, insofar as the grace of God grants me the ability to promise, I promise that I shall provide for the universal concord of the priests of the Lord, so that all may refrain from daring to seek their own interests and strive to obtain the things of Christ. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother.

## LETTER VII. OF POPE HILARY TO LEONTIUS

He urges him to send a report concerning Herme, who was said to have rashly usurped the episcopate of the Church of Narbonne.

### To his most beloved brother Leontius, Hilary the pope.

We are astonished that your fraternity should be so forgetful of Catholic law that, when anything unjust and contrary to the statutes of our Fathers is done in the province belonging to your metropolitan authority, you do not allow us to correct it—even if you yourself either do not wish or are unable to do so—by your silence.

For we have learned by rumor, and have investigated carefully as far as possible through the deacon John, who was brought to our attention in his letters by our son, the distinguished man Frideric, that a certain Hermes has presumed, with execrable rashness and by a most unjust usurpation, to seize the episcopate of the city of Narbonne. Your holiness ought to have reported this to us immediately.

Therefore, dearest brother, we admonish you: if the assertions are credible, setting aside every excuse, send to us a report bearing the signatures of your affection and of our brothers, either through the bearer of this letter or through someone whom you yourselves choose, so that in a responding letter you may learn what we are able to determine. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Nones of November (around the year of Christ 462).

## LETTER VIII. OF POPE HILARY TO THE BISHOPS OF THE VARIOUS PROVINCES OF GAUL

I. He permits Herme to preside over the Church of Narbonne, but without the power to ordain bishops.  
II. Councils are to be held every year from whatever provinces are able to attend, and they are to be convened by Leontius.  
III. Bishops are not to travel to another province without letters from their metropolitan. If they cannot obtain them, the bishop of Arles shall examine the case.  
IV. Concerning the parishes of the Church of Arles that Leontius was reclaiming, he refers judgment to the bishops.  
V. Ecclesiastical estates are not to be alienated unless the reason for the alienation is first presented before a council.

### To his most beloved brothers, the bishops of the provinces of Vienne, Lyons, First and Second Narbonnaise, and the Pennine Alps [reading: “Poenine Alps,” or “Pennine Alps”], Hilary the bishop.

Although your knowledge of what and how much was formerly committed in the Churches of Narbonne and Béziers is not lacking, and although the wickedness of the presumption that has reached us is certainly manifest throughout the regions of Gaul, it nevertheless belongs to apostolic vigilance not to keep silent about faults detected in our examination, lest through an inappropriate silence we appear to share in the connivance of those acting unjustly.

Long ago, therefore, the bishops of the aforementioned cities brought no less grief to my predecessor of holy memory than to us by daring to pursue unlawful petitions—something that could scarcely be softened before our patience except by the lamentation of their necessities. You yourselves also recognize the examples by which this was done, and how worthy of rebuke it is. For what could be more contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers and to the very regulations of the canons?

Our brother and fellow bishop Hermes believed that he had a legitimate right to receive the Church of Narbonne because, as he said, he was being unworthily excluded by the people of Béziers, by whom he had been ordained. If he truly grieved that this had been done to him, and if he had known how to remedy his own injury by a lawful means, he ought rather to have hoped for vengeance on behalf of those who suffered the wrong than for pardon for the wrongs committed.

Finally, if now at least he adopts the common mind of all the priests of the Lord, if he imitates the example, if he turns the eyes of his heart toward these matters that have been somewhat lulled by consideration for ecclesiastical peace, and considers, for the peace or faith of the whole Church, the many errors that have been committed, there is certainly nothing that he would not himself condemn and blush to have granted to himself which he rightly reproved in another.

For we know—and for a long time have had no uncertainty concerning the conduct of the brother mentioned—that, when we review in our minds the course of his former life and his previously adopted purpose [reading: “his entire former purpose”], we judge that he encountered rather than committed the excesses that we criticize in him.

With a large council of brothers presiding, gathered from various provinces by the grace of God for the birthday feast of the blessed Apostle Peter, and with our brothers and fellow bishops Faustus and Auxanius presiding, while many others were attending to matters relevant to the force and authority of the judgment, we established this out of love for peace: in the sentence that we issued, with Christ our Lord inspiring us, after considering both delegations sent from there, there was neither a lack of the charitable indulgence of the Gospel nor of the apostolic rod of discipline. For indulgence did not make us remit everything, nor did affection make us impose restraint.

### I.

We have taken away from the man who is now permitted to preside over the Church of Narbonne the power of ordaining bishops, because of the wrongful acts committed. We have judged that this power belongs instead to our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, prelate of the Church of Uzès, since he is said to be first in rank by seniority of honor. If he should die while Bishop Herme is still alive, this responsibility shall belong to the one whom the episcopal order finds to be first.

When Bishop Herme is no longer present, the custom of appointing bishops shall immediately be restored to the Church of Narbonne—a custom that was lost not because of the city but because of the cause of the presumption.

Therefore, let the sincere love of your fraternity in the Lord, sharing with us the concern of pastoral care apportioned among its own sees, vigilantly exercise care for the Churches entrusted to it. Let it remember what has arisen in the province of Narbonne in such a way that it detests the deed rather than adopt it as an example. We do not wish this to happen henceforth, just as we know that it did not happen before.

Accordingly, dearest brothers, you must act with necessary zeal so that the error which, with the help of Christ our Lord, we recently abolished may never again produce similar or new excesses. This cannot be guarded against in any other way than by carrying out the statutes of the venerable canons in the assemblies that definite necessity has hitherto caused to be omitted. In these assemblies, according to the need of cases as they arise, matters done contrary to the observance of ecclesiastical discipline can be corrected and what ought to be followed can be established.

### II.

Each year, therefore, an episcopal council is to be assembled from whatever provinces are able to attend. It is to be held at suitable places and times according to the arrangement of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, to whom we have delegated the responsibility of gathering the brothers, after the metropolitans have been notified by his letters.

Thus, if anything is found anywhere to have been done contrary to the apostolic commands in the ordination of bishops, the appointment of presbyters, or the making of clerics of any rank, or if anything in their conduct is disapproved, it may be cut away by the common authority of all.

Let there be a meeting especially in that solemn assembly which, with Christ our Lord presiding, is venerable to the holy and fearful to the perverse. No one shall be permitted to wander from the rules that the united fraternity, in accordance with the definitions of the canons, has established jointly for itself. Since an annual examination is impending, each person shall direct his actions in such a way that he ought rather to desire the scrutiny of judgment than fear it.

In the settlement of more serious cases, and of those that cannot be resolved there, the judgment of the Apostolic See is to be sought.

### III.

We also cannot pass over the matter that must be attended to with especially careful concern: no one should dare to travel to any province without the letters of his metropolitan. This must likewise be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual Churches.

Conversely, we provide for the matter in this way: if they have not been able to obtain such letters because of some hostility, the bishop of Arles, together with the two metropolitans of the provinces concerned, shall examine everything and establish what must be observed according to the nature of the case. He shall also order that no foreign cleric be received to the injury of another without the testimony of his own bishop, in accordance with the statutes of the canons.

Let each brother and all alike know that these present enactments must be obeyed. Our admonition also declares that the judgment of Christ our Lord will by no means be absent from those who, by proud rebellion, avoid the assemblies and thereby show, through the testimony of their own conscience, that they do not possess confidence in their priestly innocence.

### IV.

Moreover, a petition from the same brother was presented to us. In it he states that the parishes of the Church of Arles were transferred by his predecessor Hilary to others, which was not permitted, and he asks that they be restored to their former right by our authority.

But mindful of apostolic moderation, we have referred his complaint to your fraternity for examination, so that in your assembly the arguments expected by us may be presented and whatever accords with the ecclesiastical rules may be decreed.

### V.

At the same time, we wish the whole fraternity to be admonished concerning this matter: estates that are neither abandoned nor burdensome and that belong to the Church, from which the needs of many are customarily relieved, are not to be transferred to another by any right unless the reason for the alienation is first demonstrated before a council, so that what ought to be done may be considered by the common deliberation of all.

May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers. Given on the third day before the Nones of December (in the year of Christ 470 [Note: In the year of Christ 470, both Pope Hilary and Severus Augustus, who was consul in the year of Christ 462, had already departed this life]), in the consulship of the most glorious Severus Augustus.

## LETTER IX. OF POPE HILARY TO LEONTIUS

Concerning Bishop Mamertus, who had ordained a bishop for the people of Die outside his own boundaries, so that his case might be examined in a synod.

### To his most beloved brother Leontius, Hilary.

We ought to learn from a report by your affection how Bishop Mamertus of Vienne exceeded priestly moderation by acting contrary to the enactments of the Apostolic See, so that we might issue a timely judgment appropriate to such audacity and to the order of the ecclesiastical rules.

For, as was stated by our son, the illustrious man Gunduicus, master of the soldiers, the bishop mentioned above, against the will of the people of Die, seized that city—which did not at all belong to the number of Churches assigned to him by the authority of the Apostolic See, as we read in our registers—in a hostile manner in a hostile manner, as it is said, and presumed to consecrate a bishop.

If this is so, dearest brother, we could pronounce how manifold the fault is, were we not, as we have said, bound to observe both moderation and the order of judgment. Therefore, mindful of the responsibility that you know has been entrusted to your affection, you must examine in the synodal assembly—according to our statutes, it is to be gathered each year under your presidency—whatever has now been brought to our attention in a brief report. You must demand from the aforesaid man an account of his action before the entire assembly of the fraternity and then make the matter known to us in a letter signed by all, so that, with the Holy Spirit dictating what must be done, we may order measures to restrain unlawful attempts. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of October (in the year of Christ 463), in the consulship of Basil, the illustrious man.

## LETTER X. OF POPE HILARY TO THE BISHOPS OF THE VARIOUS PROVINCES OF GAUL

That no one should transgress his own boundaries, and that councils should be convened each year through the efforts of Bishop Leontius.

### To his most beloved brothers, the bishops of the provinces of Vienne, Lyons, First and Second Narbonnaise, and the Alpine province, Hilary the bishop.

Although we remember that your fraternity retains what has been established by us and does not disregard anything that we have written—namely, that for the sake of ecclesiastical discipline and of the cases that quite often arise among the priests of the Lord, synodal councils should be held every year, and that we have especially wished the chief responsibility for them to rest with our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, priest of the Church of Arles—and although we believe that nothing else can be done except what our ordinance has established for the common house of the Lord and what you will approve, nevertheless, by repeated letters we now decree again that the same matters must be observed.

This is especially necessary since the bishop of the city of Vienne is involved in a very serious offense, having consecrated a bishop for the people of Die to the injury of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius. We postponed issuing an appropriate sentence of punishment for this deed and meanwhile replied to the report of the brothers concerning what had appeared necessary.

But since such a great excess has brought us a greater cause for concern, we have sent these instructions to the entire fraternity also through our brother and fellow bishop Antonius, so that the common concern of all, once admonished, may take care that no brother, rushing to injure another, transgress the boundaries established by the venerable Fathers.

Therefore, confirming everything that was determined by us through our brothers and fellow bishops Faustus and Auxanius, we ask you to deign to hold annual assemblies, arranged by our brother and fellow bishop Leontius after the metropolitans have been notified—as must often be said—in places to which no traveler will find it difficult to come.

Care must also be taken to establish suitable times as well as suitable places, so that anyone who might think of neglecting this most necessary and salutary decree of ours may appear all the more inexcusable, dearest brothers.

We have left the confirmation of the man whom the bishop of Vienne rashly presumed to ordain, although he was foreign and did not at all belong to him, to the will of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius. We trust that he will weigh what is just without departing from humaneness. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers.

## LETTER XI. OF POPE HILARY TO THE BISHOPS WHO INVESTIGATED THE CASE OF MAMERTUS IN SYNOD

The command of Pope Hilary concerning the Church of Die, where a bishop was improperly ordained by the bishop of Vienne.

I. Through Bishop Veranus, Mamertus is to be warned to abstain in the future from improper ordinations, under threat to his rank and privileges.  
II. The man consecrated by Mamertus for the people of Die is to be confirmed at the discretion of Leontius, bishop of Arles, by whom he ought to have been consecrated.

### To his most beloved brothers Victurus, Ingenuus, Idatius, Eustasius, Fonteius, Viventius, Eulalius, Veranus, Faustus, Auxanius, Proculus, Ausonius, Paulus, Memorialis, Caelestius, Projectus, Eutropius, Avitianus, Ursus, and Leontius, Hilary.

Very greatly concerned, and suspended in eager expectation by what the recent report reliably conveyed to us, we have received the letter of your affection, delivered by our brother and fellow bishop Antonius, whom we regard as a worthy interpreter of so important an embassy. Its very opening has grieved us. For whereas we believed that our anxiety would find rest, and be relieved in large measure by the provisions established by my predecessor of holy memory concerning the bishop of Vienne, we have learned through your clear assertion—and marvel with no little sorrow—that those determinations, by which he had established the privilege of the Church, have now been overstepped by Bishop Mamertus.

[Note: Mamertus, also called Mamercus, was the bishop of Vienne, a man of most holy life and blessed death. He restored in Gaul, during the reign of the emperor Valentinian III, in the year of Christ 452, the ancient sacred practice of the litanies, which had been neglected through the relaxation of discipline and diminished worship, as Ado of Vienne writes. Three days before the Ascension, following his own example and highly beneficial experience, he celebrated those observances called Rogations, now received by the universal Church.

That these Rogations were not first instituted in Gaul by Mamertus, but merely reformed by him with great fervor in order to avert the dangers of earthquakes, fire, and other calamities, is testified after Ado by Sidonius, in Book V, Letter 4, to Aper, in these words:

“The solemnity of these Rogations was introduced first by Mamertus, father and bishop, by a most reverend example and highly beneficial experience. Previously, indeed—may this be said without offense to the faith—they were wandering, lukewarm, infrequent, and, if one may put it so, sleepy supplications, always blunted by the obstacles of the meals of those making the petitions; to which, to say no more, neither potter nor gardener ought to have been summoned. In those, however, which the aforesaid high priest both introduced and organized, people fast, pray, sing psalms, and weep,” and so forth.

Thus it is clear that Saint Mamertus did not so much institute the sacred Rogations as restore them, bringing them back into better form. Saint Augustine, who lived many years before Mamertus, mentions these three-day Rogations customarily celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension in Sermon 173, *On the Season*, for the vigil of the Ascension:

“We must know and understand, dearest brothers, that we are celebrating days of compunction and repentance,” and so forth.

And near the end:

“Let no one deliberately seek out occupations by which he may withdraw himself from the assembly of the Church. Without doubt, he loves the wounds of his sins who during these three days does not seek spiritual remedies for himself by fasting, praying, and singing psalms.”

That litanies and processions were used in the Church in the time of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus and Tertullian, in the third century, is evident from Basil’s sixty-third letter to the people of Neocaesarea and from Tertullian’s second book *To His Wife*. See also what I said above in the notes on canon 17 of the Council of Laodicea. See what Baronius writes at length on this matter in the year 475, no. 11 and following, and in the notes to the Martyrology for 25 April, under the word “Litanies.”

The people of Vienne honor this Mamertus with an annual festival on 11 May. What sort of man he was, and how great, is shown by Sidonius Apollinaris, who knew him and enjoyed his most intimate friendship, in Letter 11 of Book IV and Letter 1 of Book VII; by Alcimus Avitus, the second bishop of Vienne after him, in the homily he delivered on the Rogations; by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 34; and elsewhere.

It is therefore not surprising that Pope Hilary rose so vehemently in this letter against this Mamertus, illustrious for holiness, as though he had unlawfully usurped another’s jurisdiction. Who does not know that pontiffs’ ears are often filled with false accusations and misrepresentations, so that, while they think they are doing what appears just, they harass an innocent man? This happened to the most holy pontiff Leo in the case of Hilary of Arles, whom he attacked most sharply as an innocent man in Letter 89; the same may have happened to Pope Hilary, through misrepresentation, in the case of Mamertus. SEV. BINIUS.]

He has now been able to transgress those provisions established by my predecessor of holy memory, through which he had proved the privilege of the Church to have been acquired. This is especially astonishing because the moderation of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius ought to have offered a model of restraint to one who was seeking advancement. Or, if Mamertus, inflamed by a spirit of rivalry, thought Leontius—which he ought not to have done—could be disregarded, then, instructed at least by the example of his predecessor, he should have imitated the restraint of the one whose honor he enjoys, and should not, by transgressing, have violated what he might now lose if we did not maintain the safeguards of patience.

Who has ever benefited from a rebellious mind? Or whom has the pride of self-exaltation not brought low? Higher is the grace of humility, through which poverty of spirit opens the path of the heavenly kingdom toward the reward of promised blessedness. Nor should the transgressor think that what he has done is a trivial breach, if, instructed in ecclesiastical teaching, he recognizes what each of the two deserves: one is forbidden, according to the prophetic word, to dwell in the midst of the Lord’s house; the other is declared to be always joined to God, who, as God looks upon him, is saved by his consolation.

Many statements of venerable men of old could be recalled, demonstrably spoken according to truth; but since the same case has compelled us to speak, more recent examples should be drawn upon. For the dignity of the Church of Vienne grew through the former transgression of the bishop of Arles; and, for the correction of what had been wrongly done, the matter was afterward settled by an inviolable decree, so that one man should not be disgraced while the other was entirely stripped of his ancient honor through the fault of his predecessor.

Accordingly, as both the report of your affection and the representation of our brother and fellow bishop Antonius have disclosed, it is clear that the aforesaid man wishes to destroy privileges confined within definite limits, desiring more than he ought. He abused the moderation of our brother and fellow priest Leontius and did not fear to consecrate for the people of Die a bishop contrary to law, even if the man was otherwise worthy of the office.

In this matter, his deed ought to have been dealt with in such a way that, in proportion to the character of what had been perpetrated, he would see even the man whom he had improperly created removed from priestly fellowship, without escaping the loss of his own rank; and that he himself, convicted of having acted most unworthily, would feel that he had been corrected by a just penalty. This was necessary lest the unpunished recklessness of his conceived audacity should think that it had produced an example of license.

Nevertheless, for the peace of the Churches, remembering apostolic wisdom, we wish the wounds of so great a transgression to be treated first with soothing remedies, so that a member of our body, perhaps needing healing, may be restored to its former integrity by gentler medicines, and so that no one may suppose that what is not immediately cut away is being neglected. Gentleness always precedes the severity of healing; not every fault is at once restrained by the sword, nor is a remedy offered without investigation or without considering what may easily be beneficial. The proper time, the need of the sick person, and the method and quality of the medicine itself must now be sought, so that every effort of the healer, wisely directed toward restraining faults, may rejoice in restoring what it saves, and may not lack moderation in cutting away what must be removed.

After your Fraternity has weighed these matters carefully and prudently, do not suppose that such things can be concealed from us—things in which the man who is not unjustly summoned to account has risen up chiefly as an insult to your dignity. Nothing established by my predecessor of holy memory could be taken away from our brother Leontius by right; nothing due to his honor could be removed. For it was decreed even by the law of Christian rulers that whatever the bishop of the apostolic see, after examination, should pronounce concerning Churches and their rulers, for the peace of all the Lord’s priests and for the observance of discipline itself in removing disorders, should be received reverently and preserved faithfully. Your affection should know this together with its peoples. Such provisions could never be overturned, since they were supported both by priestly ecclesiastical authority and by royal authority.

Therefore, dearest brothers, the presumption of the aforesaid man, which proceeded to the injury of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, should for the present be tolerated without the penalty it deserves, so that if the transgressor abuses the remedies of satisfaction and pardon, and does not promise to remedy the present excess by diligent observance in the future, then, when the complaint returns, the privileges of the Church of Vienne may be transferred to the bishop of Arles by the same precedent through which they were transferred at the beginning.

[Col. 0031B] I. Accordingly, retaining the name of moderation, we have sent a letter to our brother and fellow bishop Veranus, instructing him, as our delegate, to confront the aforesaid man, so that he may learn what you have reported concerning him. For it ought not to be burdensome to rebuke a delinquent brother for his own excesses, since it is well established that we are commanded frequently to forgive them.

If we receive no indication of his correction—an undertaking which he must retain in his profession, by which he will testify that he will always preserve, without any further transgression, the definition of the apostolic see at the peril of his rank—then the same four cities, with whose ordination Bishop Mamertus was not, or will not be, content, must be restored to the Church of Arles. This must also be done if anyone should ever afterward become an imitator of this presumption, following the man whom we now correct with affection, although we trust that he will henceforth abstain from unlawful acts.

II. Concerning the man who, although improperly, is known to have been ordained for the people of Die, we have judged, in accordance with justice, that his priesthood should be confirmed at the discretion of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, by whom he ought rightly to have been consecrated.

May God preserve you, dearest brothers, for a longer life. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March [24 February], in the consulship of the illustrious Basil.

[Col. 0031]

## Decrees of Pope Hilary. (S)

### A Decree of Pope Hilary According to Gratian, Which Is Not Included in the Earlier Material

[Col. 0031B]

Each person receives the whole Body of Christ in equal portions.

Where a part of the body is present, the whole is present also. The same principle applies to the Lord’s Body as to the manna that preceded it as its figure. Of it Scripture says: “He who gathered more did not have too much, and he who had gathered less did not have too little” (Exodus 16). For in this mystery one must not assess visible quantity, but the spiritual power of the sacrament.

### Another Decree of the Same Pope, from the Code of Sixteen Books, Chapter 19, on the Contentious

“If anyone appears to be contentious,” as the Apostle says, “we have no such custom, nor the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11:16): if anyone acts in this way, let him be marked until he corrects himself.

[Note: It is also found in Burchard, Book X, chapter 55, where I read the final words as: “until he is corrected.” MANSI.]

## In the Year of Our Lord 467. Pope Simplicius

### Prologue

[Col. 0031]

## Life of Pope Simplicius

*(From the* Liber Pontificalis*)*

[Col. 0031D] [Note: After Hilary’s death the see was vacant for ten days. In the year of Christ 467, which was the eleventh year of Leo, the Eastern emperor, Simplicius, a Tiburtine, son of Castinus, was made pontiff on 20 September.

During his time nearly the entire Christian world was under the rule of heretical princes, and no Catholic king held authority even over a small province. For after the Western emperors Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, and Augustulus had been killed or banished, Odoacer, king of the Heruli, an Arian—according to the prophecy of Saint Severinus, the apostle of Noricum and the neighboring peoples, famous for his miracles—subjected Italy and the entire Western Empire to his rule. He rejected the title of emperor, the purple, and the imperial garments, and thereafter ruled while assuming only the royal name.

The Arian Goths held Gaul together with Spain. Genseric, an Arian, savage persecutor of Catholics and a tyrant, ruled all Africa. In the East, after Leo’s death, the emperor Zeno, a Eutychian, by a pretended treachery, showed himself a most bitter enemy of the Church. The impious emperor Zeno recalled from exile Peter the Fuller, an Acoemete monk, and Timothy the Cat, the sacrilegious usurper of the Church of Alexandria, whom the emperor Leo had banished, by a most just judgment, because of their heresy and sedition. He not only recalled them from exile but also, after ejecting the most holy and Catholic bishops, Martyrius of Antioch and Timothy of Alexandria, installed sacrilegious and apostate monks in their places, not without great danger and loss to the entire Church.

To these troubles was added the violent ambition of Acacius of Constantinople, by which he attempted to extort from Simplicius, through the emperor, the long-desired prerogative of the see of Constantinople—an honor he had already sought several times in vain under two preceding pontiffs.

Amid these storms at sea and turbulent agitation of the winds, amid barbarian fury and the insolence of the Arians joined to power, in these most wretched times Pope Simplicius, deprived of the support of all Christian rulers, sat in the chair of Peter with the same authority and freedom that his predecessors had always possessed.

He resisted the ambition of Bishop Acacius, as Gelasius testifies in Letter 11 to the bishops of Dardania. He expelled Timothy the Cat from the see of Alexandria.
