He opposed the emperor Zeno when he demanded a universal council, and, after Zeno had issued a confession of faith, received him into communion with the Church on the condition that he would show himself a defender of the Catholic faith and expel the most impious Fuller, the occupant of the see of Antioch.

He was informed by Acacius by letter about affairs in Alexandria, as he himself had requested out of his concern for all: namely, that Timothy the Cat, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, had brought death upon himself by drinking poison, and that the Catholic Timothy had been restored to the see from which he had been expelled.

When Pope Simplicius learned from the envoys of the Church of Alexandria, whom Bishop Timothy had sent to Rome to ask pardon because, terrified by the Eutychians, he had named Dioscorus at the altar, that Peter Mongus, formerly the usurper of the see of Alexandria, was hiding in the city after being expelled from it and was misleading many there, he instructed Acacius to press the emperor for Mongus’s banishment. He approved the penitential petition sent to him by those who had been led astray from the Catholic faith by Eutychian rulers and bishops, and, with paternal affection, granted them absolution from heresy, which was reserved to the apostolic see alone.

What else can one conclude from this except that Pope Simplicius occupied that chair which, by the authorizing will of God Most High, has been built upon a firm rock in such a way that no human or infernal power can prevail against it? The disturbances stirred up in the Church by the usurpers of the two patriarchal sees—Peter the Fuller, Timothy the Cat, and Peter Mongus—will become clear from the notes on the letters of Simplicius. The manner in which the emperor Zeno obtained the empire, and afterward recovered it after the tyranny of Basiliscus, as well as the sort of man he was toward God and religion, will be discussed there.

It is noteworthy that Nicephorus reports this event as having occurred at this time, in Book XV, chapter 12: when two bishops were disputing, one Arian and the other Catholic, the Catholic challenged the Arian to undergo the test of fire. When the Arian refused, the Catholic passed unharmed through the fire and disputed from within it. SEV. BINIUS.]

Simplicius, a Tiburtine by nationality, son of Castinus, sat for fifteen years, one month, and seven days.

[Note: That he occupied the see for fifteen years, five months, and ten days is shown by the dates of the beginning of his pontificate and of his death. For it is established from a letter of his successor Felix that he died at the beginning of March in the year of Our Lord 483. SEV. BINIUS.]

He dedicated the basilica of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill in the city of Rome,

[Note: This basilica, formerly erected on the Esquiline Hill, now lies completely ruined. At Platina’s there survives one of its inscriptions, in these words:

“In this temple I remember having read these verses, composed in mosaic work:

‘This estate your strong mind decreed for you, Christ,

to whom that testator transferred his wealth.

And Pope Simplicius, fitting it to the heavenly rites,

truly made it your gift.

So that the thresholds of the apostles might not be lacking to us,

he arranged the name of the martyr Andrew.

This church uses proper titles as its inheritance,

and, succeeding the household, establishes its sacred rights.

Come, devoted people, and learn through these exchanges

that heavenly realms are sought by earthly wealth.’”

This is from Platina. SEV. BINIUS.]

and the basilica of the blessed Apostle Andrew beside the basilica of Saint Mary; another basilica of Saint Stephen beside the basilica of Saint Lawrence; and another basilica within the city of Rome, beside the Licinian Palace, dedicated to the blessed martyr Bibiana, where her body rests.

[Col. 0034A] He established that, because of the influx of the people, priests should remain by weekly turns at the designated churches, always ready to hear confessions of sins and, as the needs of the faithful required, to administer the other sacraments.

[Note: He decreed that, because of the crowd that was arriving, priests should await the people by weekly turns in the assigned churches and should always be ready to hear confessions of sins and to administer the other sacraments as the needs of the faithful required. Those who performed this duty were called *hebdomadarii*, because one group succeeded another by turns.

From this it is evident that sacramental confession of sins, instituted by Christ the Lord, had continued to be practiced frequently in the earlier centuries down to this time. The claim of the innovators of our age that Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, abolished sacramental confession together with the penitentiary priest and his function and office is ridiculous.

Nectarius abolished or moderated nothing that pertained to the essential use of this sacrament. He merely removed or regulated the rite by which public sins were listed in a written confession by those who were about to offer penance to the priest, and by which the priest publicly recited those sins that produced the greater scandal, as he judged necessary according to his prudence.

Since the scandal reported by Socrates and Sozomen concerning a deacon and a certain woman had arisen on this occasion, Nectarius abolished this custom and rite of public penance. In this respect many other bishops perhaps followed him, although there were also those who deeply regretted that the ancient and honorable custom, so useful for restraining sinners, had been abolished. There could be diversity of judgment in this matter according to differences of places and times, without error.

Accordingly, when Socrates, in Book V, chapter 19, and Sozomen, in Book VI, chapter 16, report that each person was left to the counsel of his own mind, and so forth, if Socrates—the Novatian and enemy of penance—and Sozomen, who, according to Gregory in Book VI, Letter 195, was frequently accustomed to lie, did not maliciously omit something, the statement should be understood as referring not to the exclusion of confession but to public satisfaction and consultation with the penitentiary priest. In this way, each person was left free to confess to whichever priest possessing jurisdiction he wished, and, after performing penance according to that priest’s instruction, to approach the sacred mysteries.

So Bellarmine, Book III *On Penance*, chapter 14; Suárez, volume IV, disputation 17, section 2, no. 30 and following. The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, volume I, under the year of Our Lord 56, seems almost entirely to reject this whole story, as though it had been fabricated by Socrates, the Novatian, and the liar Sozomen. Since this cannot be maintained without serious difficulty, I prefer what I said above. See the notes on the Council of Laodicea. SEV. BINIUS.]

He established weekly stations at Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Paul the Apostle, and Saint Lawrence the Martyr, so that priests might remain there for penitents and for baptism.

[Note: Of the seven regions of the City, three were occupied by Heruli who were not in communion with the Catholic Church, since they were Arians. Hence Pope Simplicius appointed penitentiary priests—weekly priests, that is—to only four regions. In this way the authority and majesty of the Roman Church shone forth, even though the Roman emperors had disappeared from the Western world and the Arians held barbarian rule in Italy. SEV. BINIUS.]

The third region [of the first region] at Saint Lawrence, the first region at Saint Paul, and the sixth or seventh region at Saint Peter.

[Note: For a fuller account of these matters, see the notes on the letters. SEV. BINIUS.]

During his episcopate a report came from Greece from Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and stated that Peter of the city of Alexandria, an Eutychian heretic, had composed a petition in Acacius’s handwriting.

At the same time there was the First Church,

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads “the first,” that is, the first apostolic see acting as executor.]

that is, the executor of the apostolic see. Then, hearing this, Simplicius the bishop condemned Peter of Alexandria, concerning whom Acacius alleged innumerable crimes, but reserved a period for repentance.

At the same time Timothy the Catholic and Acacius wrote back, saying that Peter had also been involved in the death of Proterius the Catholic. Then Archbishop Simplicius, concealing his purpose, never wrote back to Acacius, but condemned Peter while awaiting a time for repentance.

He made in the Roman Church a golden cup weighing five pounds, and sixteen silver goblets for Saint Peter, each weighing twelve pounds.

He held three ordinations in the city of Rome, in December and February: fifty-eight priests, eleven deacons, and thirty-six [82] bishops in various places.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads seventy-eight.]

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter on 2 March, and the episcopate remained vacant for six days.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads seven.]

[Col. 0035]

## Letters of Pope Simplicius. (C)

[Note: This letter displays the great and vigilant zeal of Pope Simplicius, who, although living under the sword of the Heruli, did not neglect his concern for Churches abroad which, situated farther away, groaned under Gothic servitude.

It should be observed that, just as here he appointed Zeno of Hispalis vicar of the apostolic see for the Churches of Spain, so elsewhere he delegated his own authority to Acacius of Constantinople for the administration of the Eastern Churches. This was done so that the man to whom God had entrusted care of the whole Church might appear deficient in no part of his duty. SEV. BINIUS.]

### Letter I of Pope Simplicius to Zeno, Bishop of Spalensis [more correctly, of Hispalis]

He appointed the excellent bishop of Hispalis vicar of the apostolic see, entrusting him with the see’s authority in all the Churches of Spain.

[Col. 0035B]

[Col. 0035C] To his most beloved brother Zeno, Simplicius.

From the report of many we have learned that your affection, through the fervor of the Holy Spirit, so conducts yourself as a governor of the Church that, with God as its author, it suffers no losses from shipwreck. Rejoicing therefore in such indications, we have judged it fitting that you should be supported by the authority of our vicariate, so that, strengthened by its force, you may in no way permit the decrees of apostolic instruction or the boundaries established by the holy Fathers to be transgressed. For he deserves to be enriched with a worthy reward of honor through whom divine worship is known to increase in these regions.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

### Letter II of Pope Simplicius to John, Bishop of Ravenna

He rebukes John because he had ordained Gregory bishop by force, and orders Gregory to govern the Church of Mutina, where he is to have no case to conduct with John.

[Col. 0035D]

Simplicius, bishop, to John, bishop of Ravenna.

If you had any regard for ecclesiastical discipline, or if any measure of priestly modesty were maintained in you, such reprehensible excesses would never have been committed. If you could not restrain yourself from them by the command of the rules handed down by the Fathers, you should at least have been recalled by the example of your predecessor of holy memory. Although he had sinned less by making an unwilling man a priest, he nevertheless recognized that a judgment was deserved for such usurpation.

Where did you learn these actions, which you perpetrated against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory—not by election but by hatred? You allowed him to be dragged to you and harassed by an inexcusable exercise of force, so that you might confer honor upon him, not through peace of mind but through madness, as it must be called. Such things could not have been done with sound judgment.

We do not wish to exaggerate what deserves condemnation, lest we be compelled to pronounce the judgment that is deserved. For he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.

But one consideration leads us to a milder sentence: we preferred that you should learn this through the report of our brother and fellow bishop Projectus, rather than that we should publish it in our letters on account of the disgrace. Our moderation has restrained the scandal of which you are known to be the author in such a way that our brother and fellow bishop Gregory—who is known not to have been promoted but driven out—shall govern the Church of Mutina, as he requested, without having any case to conduct with you, and shall not refuse to accept the spiritual fellowship which he ought not to have been forced to undertake unwillingly.

If any dispute should perhaps arise for him, let our judgment be sought by him or against him.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads “from him.”]

We shall also provide for the necessities which, because of your action, he is compelled to endure, by this determination [variant: “we provide”]: after the estate which he says was given to him a year ago has been relinquished and returned to the Church of Ravenna, a property in the territory of Bologna producing an income of thirty solidi, free of charges, shall without question be transferred to him for the duration of his life, while the right of ownership remains with the Church of Ravenna, to which it shall return after his death.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads “there.”]

But if our provisions are not obeyed, you yourself can judge what awaits the obstinate person after transgression.

We announce, moreover, that if you should afterward presume anything of this kind, and should attempt to make anyone—a bishop, priest, or deacon—against his will, you must know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna and of Emilia will be taken away from you.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the consulship of Severinus, an illustrious man.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads “the fourth day before the Kalends of June.”]

### Letter III of Pope Simplicius to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, Bishops

Gaudentius, bishop of the Church of Aufinum, is deprived of priestly office and of three parts of the Church’s revenues because of unlawful ordinations.

Simplicius, bishop, to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, bishops.

Your affection’s report instructed us, and the sequence of the proceedings informed us more fully, that Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Aufinum [Burchard: Offinum], had carried out unlawful ordinations contrary to the statutes of the canons and to our commands. We order that all authority for these be completely taken away from him.

For we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Severus that, if necessary, he himself should perform this duty in the aforesaid Church, having considered the rules of the Fathers, in which Gaudentius is convicted of having abused his office. Those whom he improperly advanced are to be removed from ecclesiastical ministries.

Likewise, since he does not know what is fitting concerning the Church’s revenues or the offerings of the faithful, he is to be permitted nothing from them, except that one quarter [variant: one portion] alone is to be granted to him. Two quarters are to be administered by the priest Onager [a marginal reading: Bonager], under threat to his own rank, for the repair of ecclesiastical buildings and for distribution to pilgrims and the poor; the final quarter is to be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each.

[Note: The Lucan Codex reads: “the final portion of the clergy … divide.”]

Furthermore, the usurper is to be compelled, through the insistence of the aforesaid brother, to restore the Church’s properties which we have discovered to have been alienated.

[Note: An equally ancient hand has added in the margin words that should be restored to the text at the place I have marked: “and he shall be compelled to restore what he took away; to whom,” and so forth.]

We also specifically command the aforesaid brother to ensure that he restores those three portions which he is said to have claimed exclusively for himself for three years.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November; variant: fourteenth], in the year of Our Lord 475, after the consulship of Leo Augustus.

### Letter IV of Pope Simplicius to Zeno

He asks Zeno to restrain by royal power Timothy the Cat, who was attempting once again to seize the see of Alexandria and secretly disseminate his heresies from Constantinople.

To Zeno Augustus

[Note: In the Verdun Codex: “To Basiliscus,” not “To Zeno.” Pagius, under the year of Christ 476, no. 11 and following, argues that Simplicius wrote this letter to Basiliscus, not to Zeno.]

Simplicius, bishop.

I should wish, insofar as the judgment of my devotion permits, to offer your Piety the duties owed to it in continual conversations, since I receive Christian princes with constant reverence. But since the care of sacred religion also contributes to the advancement of this intention, a more important duty presses upon me: at once to render you honor with an eager mind and faithfully to disclose the facts. For either your clemency’s constant affection draws me to both tasks, or consideration for my rank and concern for apostolic moderation compels me.

Having therefore fulfilled the duty of greeting you, most glorious and most merciful son, Emperor Augustus, I neither ought nor can remain silent about the scandals which are said once again to be stirred up in the Churches of the East through the renewed brigandage of heretics.

For, as writings of monks fervent for the Catholic faith have reported to my knowledge,

[Note: When Simplicius had learned from the most trustworthy report of monks of the Church of Constantinople that Timothy the Cat, the most wicked usurper of the Church of Alexandria, had not only been released from exile but was also residing freely at Constantinople and devoting all his strength there to propagating heresy, he wrote this letter to the Emperor Zeno, under whose protection Timothy was secretly supported. He adds an open letter on this matter addressed to Bishop Acacius, to be presented to that same Zeno, intending that he might not be wholly led astray by heretics. Although the origin of the entire evil ought to have been attributed to the emperor alone, since he had recalled the sacrilegious usurper of the Church from exile with honor, Simplicius most prudently refrains from assigning him blame, so that, moved to repentance, he may become the destroyer of the crime he committed. An error has crept into the consular note: in place of Armatus, who, as the more correct fasti attest, held the consulship with Basiliscus in this year, the name Augustus has been inserted. SEV. BINIUS.]

I have learned that Timothy the parricide, formerly the devastator of the Church of Egypt, like Cain—as divine Scripture testifies in Genesis 4—having been driven from the face of God, that is, excluded from the dignity of the Church, and now wandering through deserts, destined to endure for a long time the torments of an evil conscience, was taken into the exile of his own error. Nevertheless, having rekindled the fires of his former madness, he gathered bands of the lost and once again seized, in a bloody state, the Church of the city of Alexandria, which he had previously stained with priestly blood, expelling its lawful bishop.

Thus the humility of exile, which ought to have driven into him, in view of his impious deeds, the goad of repentance, seems rather to have provided leisure for nurturing more savage madness. By this he is plainly shown to be far more detestable than Cain himself. Cain, after being condemned for a single crime, abstained; this man advanced to greater crimes after his punishment.

Nor was he content with this limit to his crimes. He is also said boldly to have entered the city of Constantinople, always burning with love for sound doctrine, so that the destroyer of human salvation might leave nothing undefiled. There, from associates in his wickedness, he is said gladly to have heard the voice belonging to Christ alone—a voice by which he was clearly shown not to be “blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” but the usurper of the divine height, evidently the Antichrist.

Although he had been so laudably excluded from Catholic communion, he is nevertheless said to have celebrated, in certain private houses, with hands sprinkled with human blood, not divine sacrifices but sacrileges. By this his reception was certainly not confirmed; rather, the treachery of his accomplices was exposed, since, unless they repent, they will all utterly fall from that seat of iniquity—the seat which, like his father the devil, who made himself like the Most High, he does not cease in his faithlessness to construct for himself eternally, to his own ruin.

The venerable emperor, although my spirit shudders even at the thought that such a thing could have been attempted by so great a gladiator, is nevertheless held back by the greatest astonishment—as I confess—that it could have been committed under the gaze of Your Piety. For who could be unaware of, or doubt, your mind, ever devoted to God’s clemency and dedicated to orthodox principles? Indeed, just as, by the ordering of heavenly providence, you were instructed in the virtues of the august memories of Marcian and Leo alike for the public good, so also have you been formed by their convictions in the Catholic truth. No one at all should doubt that your Piety follows the faith of those whose imperial successor you are. Since all hold this firmly and certainly concerning the mind of your Tranquillity, far be it from us to suppose that in your times the integrity of divine worship, or the sincerity of the Catholic faith strengthened from antiquity, should be disturbed.

Look, I beg you, to the divine benefits; consider what has been granted to you; and, so that these blessings may be able to endure, judge that the author of the gift must be propitiated, not offended. Amid every kind of public responsibility, a religious prince must take the greatest care of what protects his rule; and the rectitude of heavenly observance must be preferred to all things, without which nothing can stand rightly. Your Clemency has abundant documentary evidence—if you order it to be sought in the archives of your palace—together with the definitions of our predecessors. For it must not be believed that your conscience is unaware of what was circulated throughout all the provinces of the East from the citadel of your empire: namely, the writings which my predecessor Leo, of blessed memory, sent in reply to the inquiries of the august memories of Marcian and likewise of Leo, and to those of the Council of Chalcedon, of blessed remembrance. In these he explained the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation so fully and clearly that whoever does not plainly recognize there the grounds of his redemption cannot now be called not merely Catholic, but even Christian.

[Col. 0040A] Certainly, so that the necessary instruction may not be lacking to you, I have sent copies of those same letters to our brother and fellow bishop Acacius, to be presented to your understanding. If, therefore, Your Piety deigns to review them, you will assuredly see what the bishops of the entire East wrote in reply concerning their agreement with this proclamation: carefully examined, truthfully promulgated, and therefore in no way to be assailed by the convoluted arguments of destructive falsehood. For in truth, what has flowed pure, sincere, and clear from the fountain of Scripture cannot be disturbed by any arguments of obscure cunning.

This same apostolic rule of teaching persists in its successors—the rule to which the Lord entrusted care of the entire flock; to which he promised that he would in no way be absent until the end of the age; and against which he promised that the gates of hell would never prevail [Col. 0040B]. Of its judgment he testified that what was bound on earth could not be loosed even in heaven (Matthew XVI).

Therefore I beseech and implore Your Clemency—to whom my brother and fellow bishop Acacius will plead with special urgency in my place—that, having become imitators of such great and such worthy predecessors, you should reject with a Catholic heart the agents of unspeakable presumption and decree by royal authority that they be restrained. Whoever attempts to sow anything other than what we have received, as the Apostle foretold, let him be anathema (Galatians I). Let no access be opened to your ears for those who creep in with pernicious intentions [variant: “who seek to steal in”]; let no confidence be granted for retracting anything from the ancient decrees. For—as must be repeated again and again—what the apostolic hands, with the agreement of the universal Church, deserved to cut down with the edge of the evangelist’s sickle [Col. 0040C] cannot regain strength by growing again; nor can what is known to have been assigned to eternal fire return as a fruitful shoot to the Lord’s vine [variant: “a fruit-bearing”].

Finally, if the contrivances of all heresies, struck down by ecclesiastical decrees, are never permitted to restore their shattered struggles through renewed opposition, then above all I beg that the see of blessed Mark the Evangelist—that is, the Church of Alexandria—be freed from the occupation of the most bloodthirsty robber, restored to a Catholic bishop, and recover both its freedom and its peace. But let the impious parricide, who is guilty alike under divine and human laws, be led back under the same law by which he had previously been thrust out, and be kept away from the slaughter of innocent souls [Col. 0040D]. Let the poisons of that deadly head depart far from the kingdom of Your Piety. Since, with their ears stopped against the life-giving proclamation, they were unable to receive healing words, let them be removed from the destructive company of human beings and waste away in a solitude suited to their own venom. For this reason, in the voice of blessed Peter the Apostle, I entreat you—as the minister of his see, whatever that see may be—that you not allow the enemies of the ancient faith to rage with impunity, those who desire to have your subjects under their control; that you decree that all the Churches of the Lord preserve the peace of the true confession, you who desire to keep the world subject to your rule at peace; and that you suffer no part of the one hope of salvation to be violated—the hope that leads the human race to the heavenly kingdoms and to eternal life—you who desire God to be reconciled either to your rule or to your salvation.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of January (in the year of Christ 476), during the consulship of Basiliscus Augustus [with Armatus as colleague].

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Read: “the fourth day before the Nones of June,” as also in the following letter, “the fifth day before the Ides of June,” and in the seventh, “the third day before the Ides of June,” as Bollandus conjectured under 2 March, where he treats of St Simplicius. See Pagi, on the year of Christ 476, no. 14.]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] This is that letter written to Acacius which the pontiff sent to the emperor, open and not yet sealed, together with the preceding letter, with the purpose and argument mentioned above. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER V. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

He writes to Acacius that he should oppose Timothy with every effort, so that the universal council which Timothy was seeking to convene before the emperor might not take place.

**Pope Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.**

As has been revealed by the reports of priests and monks serving the Lord from various monasteries, the devil is again disturbing the Churches of the Lord, so that, after the Alexandrian priest had been expelled, a heretic condemned by the whole Church is said to have occupied the same place from which he had been driven out [Col. 0041B]. Moreover, with certain people supporting him, he is said to have dared to come to Constantinople, so that a city distinguished among the cities of Christian emperors for its devotion to the Catholic truth, and a Christian people attentive to the defense of religion, might be disturbed by the depravity of the heretics, which had already been brought to rest.

But the mercy of God, whose cause this is, was not lacking. Thus Timothy, who had rightly been separated from the universal Church by priestly judgments and imperial decrees [variant: “who was lawfully separated”], was not permitted to approach either the Church of Your Love or the thresholds of the homes of the faithful. We have learned that he threatens to convene new assemblies on his behalf, believing that what universal authority decreed concerning him can be dissolved. Since the teaching of our predecessors of holy memory stands firm, against which it is unlawful to dispute, whoever appears to think rightly does not need instruction through new assertions. Rather, everything is plain and complete by which either someone deceived by heretics may be instructed or someone may be prepared for planting in the Lord’s vineyard. Therefore, having appealed to the faith of the most merciful emperor, see to it that the proposal for a synod be rejected, and let there be no sluggish submission at the ears of the Christian emperor; for Christ is the strength of his salvation and of his kingdom.

Therefore, together with the priests and monks mentioned above, make timely supplication to his Piety also in our name, and present this mission to his Clemency on our behalf as well, so that nothing may be insinuated [variant: “stolen in”]. Let him be instructed by the prayers of all alike, so that amid public responsibilities the enemy may not contrive any ambushes against ecclesiastical peace. Let him ensure that the Church of Alexandria be restored to its integrity and drive away the enemy and parricide from the see of blessed Mark the Evangelist. Let him graciously investigate within the inner chambers of his palace how the integrity of the Catholic faith is maintained. And lest this be in any way corrupted by the fraud of rivals to the faith, although the documents can be found in the archives of your church, we have nevertheless sent copies, which you will prepare [variant: “hasten”] to present to his Piety.

[Col. 0042A] Let them recognize the writings which my predecessor Leo, of holy memory, sent in response to the consultation of Leo, of august memory, writings known and celebrated by all the authorities there, and let them recognize how reverently they were received. Thus, as we trust, he will appear to be an imitator of the faith of the man whose more worthy imperial successor he is by God’s favor; and he should regard as addressed to himself whatever was handed down before him to emperors through pious reading. For that is the permanence and the posterity to be propagated through the succession of the kingdom: that in the successor is found what descended from the predecessor.

Therefore, dearest brother, I urge that every effort be made to resist the perverse attempts to convene a synod. Such a synod has never been called except when something new has emerged in depraved minds or something ambiguous in the assertion of doctrines [Col. 0042B], so that, when the matter was considered in common, the authority of priestly deliberation might illuminate any obscurity. This was what the impiety of Arius first, then of Nestorius, and finally of Dioscorus and Eutyches compelled the Church to do.

And—may the mercy of Christ our God and Savior avert it!—it must be declared abhorrent to restore condemned offenders, to recall exiles, or to absolve those banished for a criminal conspiracy, against the judgments of all the priests of the Lord throughout the world and of the rulers of both realms. Therefore, as must often be repeated, communicate all these things humbly to the most merciful ears. God will undoubtedly come to your aid. May he recognize that, since the king’s heart is in God’s hand, the established foundation of his authority has no other source [variant: “does not know”].

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January [variant: “the sixth day before the Kalends of February”].

[Note: [Col. 0042D] He wrote this letter, and several others of the same subject, to Acacius on the occasion of the public embassy which Odoacer sent to Zeno. We have transferred it here from a Vatican manuscript, where it was first printed in volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, together with the following letters. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER VI. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

He commends Acacius because no church in Constantinople was open to Timothy Aelurus, and urges him to warn the emperor not to permit the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon to be violated.

**Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.**

When our sons, the illustrious man Latinus, patrician, and the distinguished Madusius, were being sent on a public embassy, we could not neglect what we attend to with our whole purpose. Recently, when a complaint had come from priests and monks concerning Timothy, formerly separated from the universal Church, we wrote both to the most Christian emperor and to Your Love, dearest brother, urging that every effort be made to resist any insolence by which heretics might plot against the Council of Chalcedon. In praising the steadfastness of Your Love, we declared that it greatly pleased us—or rather the Lord himself—that you had not permitted a condemned man, condemned not only on account of the faith but also on account of parricide, to enter any church in Constantinople.

We now remind you again not to cease, when these same writings reach Your Love—or even before they arrive—to act and plead humbly with the most Christian emperor, also in our name, so that what has so often and so properly been established may not be violated by any underhanded approach. For the sure and singular foundation of his kingdom is to preserve unharmed, for the true and eternal King, the council of priests assembled in the cause of the faith by the divine Spirit.

## LETTER VII. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE PRIESTS AND ARCHIMANDRITES OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He commends the steadfastness in the faith of the clergy and monks living in Constantinople, since they did not admit Timothy to communion; and he shows that, as one repeatedly condemned, Timothy must not be heard.

[Col. 0043B]

**Bishop Simplicius to the priests and archimandrites established at Constantinople.**

Through our son Epiphanius, a laudable man, we received the letters of Your Love later than you wished, and were deeply grieved that renewed fires of scandal should arise within the Church of God there, where they had been extinguished by the authority of the apostolic see and the judgment of the universal synod. For whom throughout the whole world is the condemnation of the wicked doctrines of Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus unknown? For whom is the expulsion of Timothy, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, again unknown? The earlier Council of Ephesus is witness; the recent Council of Chalcedon is witness. Whoever desires its judgment to be reconsidered declares that he is not counted among the faithful [Col. 0043C]. For the impiety of the aforesaid men, its authors and leaders, was struck down by the united judgment of Christian emperors and rulers—not only separated from the body of the Church, but banished from the assembly of all by various exiles.

There is no need now to speak of their error. After so many priests of the Lord, long before us, had defeated these heresies throughout every part of the world, our predecessor Leo, of blessed memory, asserted in many learned discourses what the integrity of Catholic truth follows and what it rejects. With this instruction established, there is no need for contention, as though these matters were still to be judged as doubtful. Rather, just as we rejoice that you are doing, stand firm against the expelled with steadfast steps. Let the adversary not frighten you, and do not suppose that victory from above will be slow to come. Whoever resists has learned how to fall.

We have written these brief words to Your Charity for consultation—or rather also for consolation—intending, as you desire, to send certain persons according to the needs of the case. Yet, for complete sufficiency, not for defending the faith—which has been firmly established [perhaps: “firmly”]—but for repelling heretics and the condemned, the writings which you remember that we sent to Flavianus, of holy memory, to the holy Council of Chalcedon, to Marcianus, of august memory, and to Leo, of blessed memory, my predecessor, should suffice. The bishops of the entire East likewise made these matters known in their replies to the emperor Leo at that time.

Thus it is beyond doubt that what so many priests of the Lord decreed when they assembled in unity cannot be dissolved, nor can what they individually established in their own Churches, nevertheless thinking alike, be dissolved—though they spoke with different voices, they spoke with one mind—when they condemned alike the abominable authors of these doctrines and their followers. Therefore, amid so many forms that have been erected for preaching, one must rely not on a new assertion but on steadfastness.

It has already been proved what your labors have accomplished, with the Lord’s help; their God-pleasing fruit has shown it. When you resisted the robber, he was not permitted to enter the Lord’s house. When certain persons came out to meet him, he exposed others perhaps still hiding who were like himself. For good things are not joined to the worst, right things to perverse ones; saving things cannot unite with harmful things. Light has no communion with darkness, nor does the believer share in the portion of the unbeliever.

Therefore, those who choose the company of such people will share the fate of the condemned, unless, with minds brought to repentance—especially those who were recently deceived—they recognize the precipices to which they have been led and, when the cloud of falsehood has been dispelled, turn themselves toward the splendor of the true faith. We desire this to come about through the mercy of the apostolic see. Since we know that life accords with the Lord’s will, we have also sent appropriate writings to the most Christian emperor and to our brother and fellow bishop Acacius. We do not think his silence should be accused, because, knowing the faith of this most approved priest, we hold it certain that what he kept silent about is not his own position.

But so that Your Love may know more fully the sequence of the letters we sent to the most Christian emperor, we have sent copies with the messenger you dispatched on his return.

Given on the third day before the Ides of January, during the consulship previously mentioned.

## LETTER VIII. SIMPLICIUS TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

[Note: [Col. 0043D] When the emperor Zeno, disregarding the requests of all Catholics and scorning the pious admonitions of the most holy pontiff Leo, had recalled the most wicked Timothy from the exile imposed upon him by the emperor Leo, and had brought him into the city against Christ the Lord himself, it happened by God’s just judgment that Basiliscus, the scourge of God and rod of the Lord’s anger for punishing Zeno, invaded the empire. After Zeno was driven into the exile from which he had recalled the execrable heretic, Basiliscus held the empire for one year and six months. When that period had elapsed, Zeno, made somewhat better by this affliction, returned to the imperial office after defeating the tyrant through the prayers and intercession of the holy protomartyr Thecla. He immediately wrote to Pope Simplicius and made an unimpaired profession of the orthodox Catholic faith. When the pontiff received it with great joy, he sent him this letter of congratulation, in which he congratulates him on recovering the empire by God’s grace and urges him, after removing the violent usurper Timothy, to restore the true bishop of the Church of Alexandria, who was living in exile, to his see. The usurper of the see, learning of the emperor’s zeal and not awaiting the judge’s sentence, “desired death for himself,” says Liberatus in chapter sixteen; and, praying for this persistently, he was released from human life by drinking poison. Thus, by God’s just judgment, the avenger of his crimes rose up against himself, although the emperors who preceded him had most unjustly forgiven him. SEV. BINIUS.]

He congratulates him on recovering the empire and urges him to restore the bishop of Alexandria to his see and ensure that the decrees of Leo and of the Council of Chalcedon are observed.

[Col. 0044D]

**Bishop Simplicius to Zeno Augustus.**

Among the works of divine providence, which are always pious and just, scarcely any human tongue is sufficient to proclaim the Lord’s power in our own times. For who could grasp even in thought or express in words what, at the very crisis when both affairs and public hopes were in distress, restored you to peace for the sake of holy religion, except that, in consideration of so great a miracle, we must cry out with the prophet: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm LXXVI)? It powerfully humbles those who exalt themselves and mercifully exalts those who humble themselves.

Even if the measure of heavenly dispensation is weighed with more perceptive judgment, it clearly appears that the destruction of the faithless was permitted to enter so that the faith of Your Clemency might be tested even amid adversity; and the more you seemed to be pressed by hostile circumstances, the more clearly your magnanimity might shine forth [Col. 0045B]. For this reason your gentleness brought about your departure from Constantinople, so that, desired and sought by everyone, you might return with greater glory, and so that from the dangers arising from opposites all might recognize what was beneficial in you.

This was plainly an example of that Davidic virtue by which, yielding for a little while with singular patience to the fury of a parricide, David was soon recalled by the prayers of the peoples and returned to the kingdom at a more eminent height of victory. Rejoice, therefore, venerable emperor, that those who proved to be your enemies were enemies of the Divinity; and rejoice that you suffered together with the Church, and that the empire was restored together with the freedom of the Catholic faith. To show in all things that your cause is shared with God, rely bravely upon his aid and persist, so that the one through whom he subdued public usurpers may also drive tyrants from the Church.

For just as Your Piety rightly and reasonably trusts that at that time we earnestly implored our God for nothing other than the return to us of rulers of the Roman Empire such as those of whom we now speak, so you see that it is expected that you demonstrate by the character of your actions that you are such rulers as those of whom we now speak. Look, I beg you, upon the steadfastness, conspicuous to the whole world, of Marcian and Leo, of august memory, in their Catholic devotion. Weigh carefully and profitably the fact that, since those who departed from their rectitude could not remain in the same position, the legitimate and divinely appointed successor to royal power will without doubt be the one who persists as an imitator of their faith.

You owe reverence, most glorious and most merciful son and emperor, to such great men, men of such distinction, of august memory; you owe the services due to God [Col. 0045D]. He led you back to their empire; you, in turn, render to God a service like theirs. And because these matters have been refuted through the teaching of the blessed Apostle Peter, as my humility recently proclaimed, may they, with God’s support, benefit those who will remain in the firmness of the kingdom, rather than those destined to fall.

Indeed, receiving the letter Your Clemency sent as an immense pledge of venerable religious devotion, I breathe again with great joy, and have no doubt at all that your mind will conduct itself in divine matters in ways far better than I could wish. Nevertheless, mindful of my duty, I urge Your Clemency at greater length on this point because, out of concern equally for your empire and your salvation, I always desire you to cleave to those causes alone by which both the stability of the present kingdom is preserved and the glory of the eternal one is obtained.

Therefore, above all I beg that Your Clemency decree that the Church of Alexandria, freed by your dispositions from the deadly as well as heretical usurper, be restored to its Catholic and legitimate bishop. Also decree that, after those whom he is said to have ordained in various Churches through diabolical presumption have been expelled, bishops of the true faith be appointed in their place. Just as you cleansed your republic of tyrannical domination, so strip the Church of God everywhere of the robberies and contagions of heretics.

Do not allow what was brought about by the iniquity of the times—and by those whom a rebellious spirit stirred up not only against your empire but also against God—to prevail over what so many and such great pontiffs, together with the distinguished orthodox bishops, established by the agreement of the universal Church. Order the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, and the teachings which Leo, my predecessor of blessed memory, fully expounded with apostolic instruction, to remain inviolate and in force. For what was settled by their definition cannot in any way be reconsidered, nor can one who has so often been condemned with a single voice everywhere be received.

This is indeed, as you have learned by experience, the Catholic faith: it deposed the powerful from their seat and preserved the humble, destined for exaltation, under its protection. Therefore Your Piety must act sufficiently so that the one who is the author of this gift to you may also be its propagator.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October [variant: seventh day before the Ides] (in the year of Christ 477), after the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus.

## LETTER OF ACACIUS TO POPE SIMPLICIUS (C)

[Note: [Col. 0045D] In the ancient manuscript of Freising of the eighth century, as I have noted elsewhere, this letter is introduced as follows: “Here begins a copy of the letter which Acacius sent to Simplicius, pope of holy memory of the city of Rome, in which he reported that Peter of Alexandria had been condemned.” [Col. 0046D]]

He informs Simplicius more fully about the condition of the Church of Alexandria, writing that, because of the death of the heretic Timothy and the flight of Peter Mog(g)us, the disturber of that Church, peace had been restored to the Church and Timothy had been restored to his see.

**Acacius to the most blessed and holy father, Archbishop [variant: patriarch-bishop] Simplicius.**

You continually exhort us, in accordance with the Apostle (II Corinthians XI), to bear the concern of all the Churches, although we are voluntarily watchful and take the lead. Yet you demonstrate your customary divine zeal [variant: “your concern through divine zeal”] by seeking more certain information about the condition of the Church of Alexandria, so that, in accordance with the paternal canons, you may undertake the labor, pouring out pious sweat on behalf of these matters, as has always been approved.

But Christ our Lord, who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans VIII), presiding over our thoughts and recognizing that we have one and the same mind in these matters for his glory, himself completed the whole victory. He made us partners with the most tranquil emperor [Col. 0047A], and removed Timothy, the deceased man, who breathed out storms and, as became evident, disturbed ecclesiastical tranquility, from human life, saying to him: “Be silent and be muzzled” (Mark IV).

He also scattered Peter, who had likewise arisen in Alexandria like a storm [variant: “a similar storm”], and, with the Holy Spirit blowing, turned him toward eternal flight—one and the same man among those who had formerly been condemned. For, as has been found in our archives [variant: “in the councils”], and as you will be able to recognize from your own archives [variant: “carefully”], if you deign to inquire, you will learn what subsequently was reported at the time concerning this same man from the bishop of Alexandria to Rome and vice versa.

Peter, being a son of night and appearing alien to the shining works of day, found darkness suitable for carrying out his robbery and an accomplice in it. In the middle of the night, while the corpse of the man who had overturned the paternal canons still lay unburied [Col. 0047B], he crept into the see [variant: “stole the see”], as he supposed, with only one person present—and that person was one who shared in his madness—so that for this reason he might be subjected to greater punishments. Yet what he hoped for did not come to pass.

That man, judging himself in even the smallest degree, disappeared completely and nowhere showed himself. Timothy, however, guardian of the paternal canons, who follows the example of David’s gentleness, submits himself and remains patient to the end; restored by Christ to his own authority, he rejoices in the honor of his own see. Receiving the voices of his spiritual children, he awaits the grace of healing, honored all the more by Christ, the chief of priests, for whose sake he has bound upon himself the crown of endurance [Col. 0047C].

Therefore, let Your Blessedness pray earnestly both for the most Christian emperor and for us ourselves. Nothing is being omitted that concerns the protection of ecclesiastical discipline. I, and those who are with me, salute all the brotherhood that is with you in Christ.

And in another hand: “May you be preserved in the Lord, most holy and most blessed father” [variant: “Pray for us, most righteous father”].

## LETTER IX. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

He congratulates him that Timothy, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, has been restored to his Church.

**Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.**

Your Love’s letter makes known how effective is the perseverance of priests who supplicate the Lord, and with what joyful affection he welcomes the zeal offered in sincere minds for the defense of the faith. After so many struggles, by which God’s mercy, placing his servants and ministers under your authority in the cause of their own religion, made them proven victors, you testify that the Church of Alexandria has at last been freed by divine judgment and, inviting us to share in its common joys, that the man who had been driven out by a heretic has returned to its see.

Therefore, with rejoicing hearts, we first beseech Christ our God for the safety of the most faithful emperor, to whom this divine favor grants, because of the devotion by which he surpasses all priests, that we may be free intercessors before heavenly omnipotence on behalf of the Christian peoples [Col. 0048A]. As, then, we rejoice at the return of our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, so, at Your Love’s admonition, we desire that he be found irreproachable. For you remember that long ago he did not possess the steadfastness of a faithful bishop, when fear compelled him to have the name of the condemned Dioscorus recited among the altars.

Given on the third day before the Ides of March (in the year of Christ 478), during the consulship of the illustrious man Illus.

## LETTER X. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

He gives thanks that Timothy has been restored to the Church of Alexandria and asks him to order that Peter, the disturber of that Church, be expelled.

[Col. 0048B] **Bishop Simplicius to Zeno Augustus.**

Through Peter, a distinguished man, count of the most noble lady Placidia, I recall that I presented the letter of my humble office amid the joy of the universal Church, while the triumphant glory of your kingdom in the Lord was enlarged by exultation in divine gifts. Nor, among all the priests of the Catholic faith, could I alone or the first remain silent concerning the works of our Lord, because, according to blessed Paul the Apostle (II Corinthians XII), bearing the care of all the Churches, I claimed for myself in a special way the highest joy over the peace restored to them through Your Clemency. Through the help of the Divinity, we have been privileged to have you victorious over the enemies of religion and of the kingdom; and in one and the same outcome, with Christ victorious everywhere in us, both the worship of the true faith [Col. 0048C] and the condition of the empire have been restored.

Both had been disturbed because the devil had temporarily intervened, so that, when the adversaries of one and the other had been scattered, the praises of the victor might be made greater. Having therefore obtained the fruit of so splendid a virtue, I now continue without ceasing, with the joy of the universal Church, to give thanks—thanks assuredly everlasting—that you have restored the Church of Alexandria to the ancient and true faith in the person of my brother and fellow bishop Timothy. His letters, recently arriving to me, stated that, after the profanation of the condemned Eutyches and Dioscorus had been expelled, he had returned to govern the orthodox in the see of blessed Peter and of Mark the Evangelist, as had previously been established. They prompted us, as we desired, to report these matters to your pious understanding.

Therefore, so that the peace of your kingdom may be perpetual and secure, guard with vigilant protection the tranquility you have granted to everyone in the Church mentioned above. Protect with more religious zeal and more attentive diligence what, with the Lord’s help, you have done for the salvation of innocent souls. For it is no lesser glory to preserve what one has founded [variant: “to preserve what one has granted”] than to grant it. All have recognized that as much divine favor has been bestowed upon you as diligence has been shown by Your Piety toward the Christian religion.

Although your Providence, intent on benefiting divine worship in every part of your kingdom, has never ceased to prefer the tranquility of the Church to public concerns, I nevertheless beg you to order, as is earnestly requested through us—or rather, as we ourselves more particularly implore—that Peter, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria and therefore rightly condemned, be transferred elsewhere by your most pious command. He is reported to be secretly plotting in the city of Alexandria against the measures established by you, so that he may not infect people of weak faith, as he is said to do, and lead them over to the instruments of his perversity.

Let pernicious contagions remain far from the innocent, so that through you there may be sincerity within the sheepfold of the Lord’s flock, which imperial authority alone can preserve.

## LETTER XI. POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

He writes that Timothy, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, had asked him for pardon because, moved by fear, he had caused the name of Dioscorus to be recited among the altars, and that he had written to the emperor so that he might keep Peter, the disturber of that Church, far away.

**Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.**
The labor of your devotion and of those who, together with you, have recently been disturbed by the devil demonstrates how many and how abundant are the fruits that steadfastness in faith and the courage of minds devoted to the Catholic religion always bear. For when the enemy of Christ and of the Christian kingdom invaded the palace, soon to fall, and by impious persecution shook the Lord’s faithful and people, he overcame the sacrilegious assaults through prayer and vigils. The heavenly victory extended so far that, upon the return of the most religious prince, a Catholic bishop was restored to the Alexandrian Church. [Col. 0049C] We immediately shared our rejoicing over this with exultation in divine grace, and caused one another to offer congratulations by letter.

Although the fullness of that joy was never lacking, our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, made more worthy by persecution, and mindful of his former undertaking, sent through our brother and fellow bishop Isaiah, and through our sons Nilus the presbyter and Martyrius the deacon, the customary official letter of the Alexandrian Church. In it he stated that he had undone what he had previously done under fear concerning the name of Dioscorus, and sought pardon for that error. He also enabled us to rejoice over the Church’s tranquillity, having learned in his own case—as your charity sees with us—that what we then censured in him did not go unpunished, and that he has now, through divine mercy, been reconciled to us.

Therefore, dearest brother, taking the opportunity afforded by the arrangements recently made in the city [Col. 0049D], and embracing the arrival of our son Peter, a most distinguished man and count, as though he were departing in accordance with the decision, we wished this same matter to reach your knowledge—both by our own purpose, and at the request of our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, and through the entreaties of his legates—so that you too might now become a participant in our common joys; so that, in the tranquillity of the aforesaid Church, you might share with us, as we have said, the fruit of your labor; and so that, when presenting our letter to the most Christian and most clement prince, you might also make this matter known, in order that he too, under God’s protection, may rejoice in the gifts of his own devotion and faith, and that, through your active charity, he may deign to strengthen the Churches by sending salutary letters with still greater zeal for the Catholic religion.

Let him make provision through the prudent ordering of his commands, lest—as we have experienced—the ancient serpent, though its head has so often been cut off, pour out its venom in any religion [perhaps “region”], and once again find an opportunity to infect anyone—God forbid. By the prudent ordering of the commands of his piety, let him make provision for the faithful and enact laws—as he has more clearly shown to be pleasing to God—so that they may not lurk in darkness and strike unawares those walking in the light, or lie in wait, as the prophet testifies, to seize those whom they find poor in faith.

Let him make particular provision concerning Peter, who is sheltered in the hiding places of certain households and of men like himself. Since, out of zeal for the faith, the prince ordered him removed from the episcopate and cast into foreign lands—as we too have written to his piety—let him decree by a special command that Peter be expelled to distant territories, for it is again asserted that he is ceaselessly plotting something against the arrangement of the faith [Col. 0050B] itself.

Since, therefore, it was appropriate for us to make these things known through a most trustworthy bearer of letters, and to offer a more particular admonition, we urge you that, when the messenger begins his return—or if some other opportunity should perhaps arise—you make us informed as soon as possible and hasten to relieve our concern.

Moreover, so that we might rejoice with perfected joy, our same brother and fellow bishop Timothy also sent us a copy of the petition of satisfaction made by those whom the two condemned men, Timothy and Peter, had led away from the truth of the Catholic faith through fear of condemnation. Timothy wished, with priestly compassion, to assist those who had fallen; in view of the mercy of God, who wills no one to perish, we do not consider this petition to be rejected.

## LETTER XIII. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

He urges him to protect Timothy, restored to the Alexandrian Church through his action, and to order Peter, the disturber of that Church, to be expelled still farther away.

[Col. 0050C]

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus.

Recently, when my brother and fellow bishop Timothy, bishop of the city of Alexandria, had sent word to the City in an unprecedented manner, I learned of the victory of your faith in his restoration. For, supported by your piety and aided by the Divinity, both the tranquillity of the empire and the splendor of the Catholic religion, once the cloud of scandals had been dispelled, recovered their integrity.

I remember having given thanks to your clemency after God for this, and even now I could not remain silent about the reverence owed to your reign. Otherwise I might seem ungrateful if, whenever an opportunity arose, I ceased praising you for so many triumphs, whether of the empire or of the Churches.

Therefore, in offering the service of due veneration, I beg you to extend your protection more diligently to all priests of the true faith, and especially to the bishop of Alexandria, whose struggle you were both witnesses and judges of. I ask you to decree by your most pious constitutions that Peter, the invader of that see—whose status even in the diaconate could not be maintained in due order [possibly “could not be established in his proper order”—the reading *orde* is uncertain]—be banished far from so distinguished a city, lest he perhaps seduce some of weaker faith and again disturb, God forbid, the scandals that you have quieted in that Church.

You have proved by your own person that he gave you the protection of his right hand, who, to the joy of the whole world and the exultation of the universal Church, preserves the Roman Empire under your clemency.

Given on 23 October [in the year of Christ 478], during the consulship of a most distinguished man.

[Note: Timothy of Alexandria, restored to his episcopal see, sent these three legates—Bishop Isaiah, Nilus the presbyter, and Martyrius the deacon—in accordance with ancient custom to the Roman pontiff, asking pardon for his offense: namely, that, compelled by the swords of the Eutychians, he had recited the name of Dioscorus at the altar, contrary to the constitutions of Pope Leo. Although he had done this under compulsion, that deed could nevertheless appear no small crime in so great a pontiff.

Through the same legation he made known that Peter Mog(g)us, the invader of the Alexandrian see, who seemed to have attempted flight, was hiding in the city and acting secretly, leading many astray and gravely bringing ruin upon that Church. It therefore seemed necessary that, in order to remove these dangers, he should be driven farther into exile.

After receiving this report, Pope Simplicius wrote to the emperor and to Bishop Acacius, earnestly requesting that care be taken to thrust the wicked man as quickly as possible into more distant exile—especially because he was acting as bishop of Alexandria, although it was established that he had not yet been ordained even a deacon. See Baronius, year 478, no. 9 and following. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XIII. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

The same subject as in the preceding letter.

Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

Recently, at the request of those who had been sent to us by our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, I announced our common joy to your affection by letter, and likewise stated that we rejoiced over the fruit of that most pious work by which the Catholic priest of the aforesaid Church had been restored. We have hastened to signify this again, so that you might recognize that joys do not love silence.

Therefore, always rejoicing and desiring that the vows of our common prayers be joined together, I urge you, dearest brother, that, now that matters have been settled under God’s direction by the most clement and most Christian prince, diligent concern not be lacking. Rather, Peter, cast down from an honor not belonging to him, must not be permitted to live in the Alexandrian region. As we also requested, ask repeatedly that he be banished far beyond the borders of his homeland, lest he seduce any of the ignorant by persuasion of his wickedness and turn them away from the path of Catholic truth.

Whatever you obtain from the most religious imperial authority, let your care cause it to reach my knowledge, and let it make us participants in actions that pertain to the preservation of evangelical doctrine.

Given on 17 October [in the year of Christ 478], during the consulship of Illus, a most distinguished man.

## LETTER XIV. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

He praises the emperor’s concern in punishing those who conspired at Antioch in the slaughter of bishops. He laments that his letters to Acacius were not carried out, and approves the election of the bishop of the Antiochene Church, although the decree of the Council of Nicaea was not observed.

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus.

I have always received with joy the venerable communications of your piety concerning the Antiochene Church. From them we have learned that, following the defense of the faith—which preserves and guards you—your inborn zeal for the Catholic religion has restrained the audacity of impiety and the crimes committed at Antioch.

We rejoice that you possess the mind of a most faithful priest and prince, so that imperial authority, joined to Christian devotion, might become more acceptable to God and its integrity become manifest, when those who engaged in the sacrilegious slaughter of bishops are ordered to perish by deserved punishments. In this you provide both for the tranquillity of the Church and for your empire, because avenging the insult against God is the grace of the one who takes vengeance, and divine favor is won by those whose care does not leave sacrilege unpunished.

But, to speak frankly to a Christian prince, if the order of my former letters had been maintained—those which I remember having written long ago to my brother and fellow bishop Acacius concerning Peter and his other accomplices—this would not have occurred, for which he has now justly deserved to exact vengeance.

I had ordered that, after a report had been made to your piety, the aforesaid man, together with the others who had seized the Churches of God through the opportunity of tyrannical domination, should be expelled beyond the boundaries of your empire. This was so that they might not pour the venom of pestilential opinions through sacrilegious speech into the minds of the more simple, or wound the more innocent souls with impious words against the orthodox faith.

The result of neglecting and treating such matters as trivial is now apparent: as you report, not only the people between the altars were destroyed by their deadly persuasions, but even bishops and preachers of the faith, priests themselves, perished by grievous swords.

Therefore, if any remnants of them are found under your empire, order them even now to be driven into foreign lands, lest thereafter any necessity or cause for punishment arise. It is better to block the entrance than to exact punishment for sin.

Since you judged that the Antiochene seditions could be suppressed by your most religious purpose in no other way than by having a bishop appointed at Constantinople for those who requested it, without prejudice to that venerable Council of Nicaea, you have stated that this was undertaken only in his person, so that thereafter, according to the definitions of the Fathers, the election of the bishop of Antioch would be reserved to the Eastern synod. You do not wish it to be regarded as an injury that this was done to remove dissension.

The blessed apostle Peter holds this pledge of your piety, and the mind of a most Christian and most faithful prince has sworn in these words: that henceforth, with the ancient custom preserved in the city of Antioch, the bishop shall be ordained by the bishops of his province. Thus what my brother and fellow bishop Acacius has now carried out at your command will not become a precedent for posterity or confuse the decrees of the Fathers, which above all you have undertaken to preserve intact.

Accordingly, what you have ordered in a holy and religious manner for the love of peace, we cannot condemn, lest the condition of the Antiochene Church appear uncertain under our hesitation—especially since the man who is said to have been ordained is supported, according to the testimony of your clemency, by such great preaching that, once the pain of these wounds has been set aside, we can glory both in him and in the Church that deserved him.

After weighing these matters, I have taken care to respond with words and the service of veneration, so that you may order the great deceits and crimes of heretics—which you repeatedly prove to be so harmful, and which must be pursued by divine and secular laws—to be removed from the memory and society of men, since, as you see, their impiety can be restrained by no authority.

Given on 22 June [in the year of Christ 479], after the consulship of Illus, a most distinguished man.

[Note: Through the agency and instigation of Peter Cnapheus, whom the emperor Zeno, after removing him from the throne itself, imprudently permitted to remain and operate in the Antiochene Church, the Eutychians repeatedly stirred up new disturbances and bloody seditions there.

When Stephen, the orthodox bishop, was solemnly celebrating the sacred assembly with his people in the great church, the Eutychian offspring of Peter Cnapheus, the most depraved of all men, entered in a formed band with swords drawn and raging. They attacked the priests of God and slaughtered them with extreme savagery. They seized the most holy bishop Stephen himself, against whom they burned with the greatest hatred and whom, inflamed with anger, they dragged away to be killed, and they put him to death after subjecting him to the most atrocious tortures.

Evagrius, drawing on John the Rhetor, the most careful writer of his age, writes the following in Book III, chapter 10: “After Peter had been expelled from the Antiochene Church, Stephen took possession of his see, which he held for three years up to this present year.” He adds: “The Antiochenes killed him with reeds sharpened to resemble spears, as John the Rhetor records.” Nicephorus, in Book XV, chapter 18, writes, again from the same John, that his body was thrown into the river Orontes.

After the emperor Zeno had sent avenging soldiers to Antioch and inflicted the deserved penalties on the sacrilegious murderers, he ordered that the future bishop of Antioch be elected at Constantinople, in order to provide for the peace and tranquillity of that city. It was feared that the scar, once covered over, would break open again as an ulcer if an election for the bishop were held at Antioch.

Stephen the Younger was elected at Constantinople. But since this had occurred contrary to ecclesiastical rules and the ancient custom of the Antiochene Church—for it was accustomed to ordain the bishop of Antioch only in a council of all the bishops of Syria—the emperor Zeno wrote to the pontiff, asking that what had been done be ratified by the Roman pontiff.

The pontiff replied that he would gladly ratify the ordination, provided that this extraordinary example caused no prejudice to posterity and that the emperor promised this by oath. Thus, by a new and wholly unheard-of example, it came about that the Antiochene bishop, who was ordinarily ordained by all the bishops of Syria, was ordained by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, through the emperor’s agency and with the Roman pontiff’s ratification.

On this occasion something else also occurred. Just as a hidden harmful moisture, when transferred by nature to the skin, produces a sharper itch through slight rubbing, so the ambition for primacy that had until then lain hidden in Acacius was inflamed more and more by this act. It implanted in him an even more violent desire for primacy, until, through hunger—or rather to satisfy his rage—he broke through the barriers guarded by the canons, shattered the bonds of Catholic communion, and cast himself and his successors headlong, as will be said below in its proper place. See Baronius, year 479, nos. 1 and 2. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XV. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ACACIUS

The same subject as in the preceding letter.

Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

Wounded and deeply afflicted by the letters of the most clement prince and by your affection concerning the sacrilegious and most grievous slaughter that took place at Antioch, I reply, asserting that, if what I had written long ago concerning Peter and his other accomplices, and what I had asked to be suggested to his piety together with the other brothers who were present, had been carried out as I had desired, the audacity of the heretics would not have advanced to so great a crime; nor would there have been any necessity for assisting the aforesaid Church in any other way than by diminishing somewhat of its own legal rights.

Although it has contributed to tranquillity that, by order of the most Christian prince and without prejudice to the canons, a bishop of Antioch was ordained through your charity, this was nevertheless not done without envy—a danger that even the one who ordered the example testifies must henceforth be avoided.

For this we ought rightly to give thanks to his piety: he moderated his power in his glory in such a way that, with most faithful devotion, he submitted what he ordered to the rules of the Fathers, and did not receive into authority what he established should be prohibited in the succeeding age. Thus, in this one person only—whom, at his command and through his concern for the tranquillity of the Antiochenes, you consecrated as bishop, not through any usurpation of your own—the act demanded by necessity was to suffice.

In this we recognize that your service was not unreasonable. Looking to the rights of the Churches, you rightly testify that you long hesitated, lest you appear to covet what, in so grave a matter and before so great a prince, you could not refuse.

Therefore, dearest brother, mindful of the ancient institutions whose observance in you has been approved, just as you see that what you know was certainly commanded to you cannot be judged pardonable, so, by honoring the Fathers yourself, strive to ensure that there is no need to do what you now desire to have cleansed through satisfaction.

## OBSERVATION OF P. ANTONIO PAGI

Regarding the year of Christ 479, no. 2 and following.

[Col. 0054]

These two letters just cited led Baronius and everyone else to believe that Stephen the Elder, bishop of Antioch, was killed by the heretics in the year 479, and that, by order of the emperor, Stephen the Younger was ordained at Constantinople by Acacius in his place.

But this common opinion is false. In the subscription of the earlier letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno, instead of “after the consulship of Illus, a most distinguished man,” one must read “after the consulship of Placidus, a most distinguished man.” Therefore that letter was given in the year 482, since Placidus held the consulship in the year 481.

Because the earlier letters of Placidus’ name had been worn away, it was easy for a scribe to err and read “Illus” instead of “Placidus,” especially since Letters 12 and 13, which precede it, were given during the consulship of Illus, a most distinguished man, namely in the year 478.

These two letters of Simplicius, therefore, in which the murder of the bishop of Antioch is mentioned without his name being given, belong to the year 482 and are to be understood not of Stephen the Elder but of Stephen the Younger. For the latter was killed by the heretics, and neither of them was ordained by Acacius; rather, Calendion was ordained, and he succeeded Stephen the Younger, as I shall show under the year 482.

As for what Binius, following Baronius, says—that the bishop of Antioch was ordained at Constantinople by a new and unusual example—it is disproved by what we said under the year 449. There we showed that Maximus, bishop of Antioch, was consecrated at Constantinople by Anatolius.

In the words of Evagrius reported by Binius after Baronius, the phrase “which he held for three years up to this present year” appears neither in the edition of Christophorson nor in that of Valesius. Those words were therefore published through an error of Baronius’s printer, who failed to distinguish them typographically from the text of Evagrius.

For Evagrius does not mention the duration of Stephen’s episcopate. Nevertheless, Binius and others attribute that entire passage to Evagrius. I have thought it necessary to point this out, lest the passage deceive anyone in the future. See Pagi under the year of Christ 482, no. 3 and following, where there is further discussion of these letters of Simplicius, the murder not of Stephen the Elder but of Stephen the Younger, and the ordination at Constantinople by Acacius of Calendion alone.

[Note: In the year of our Redemption 482, during the consulship of Severinus, Stephen the Younger, bishop of Antioch, departed this life in the third year of his episcopate. A synod of the neighboring bishops was gathered there, and Bishop Calendion was elected in his place.

As Evagrius testifies in Book III, chapter 10, Calendion persuaded all who assembled to pronounce an anathema both against Timothy the heretic and against the letters of Basiliscus written generally to everyone. With Zeno’s permission, he also transferred to Antioch the sacred relics of the great Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, concerning whom we treated above in the notes on the Council of Nicaea.

Pope Simplicius reports to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, that Bishop Anastasius had been sent to confirm Calendion in the Antiochene see, and that Anastasius had obtained from the Apostolic See confirmation of Calendion’s election.

What did Acacius do after this? He declared Calendion guilty of treason and therefore unworthy of the episcopate—first because, as Evagrius says, he had joined certain factious persons against Zeno, and also because he had removed Zeno’s name from the diptychs. Gelasius, Letter 11 to the Dardani.

Thus the man who had received the confessor Eustathius in the name of a confessor obtained the glory of confession by enduring exile.

After Calendion had been removed, Evagrius adds in chapter 16 of the aforesaid book, Peter Fullo, surnamed Cnapheus, who had been bishop of Antioch before Calendion and Stephen, wrongly recovered the see. Having seized it alternately by force and deceit, he openly promulgated the heresy of the Theopaschites, which had often been condemned, and even ascribed a cross to the most holy Trinity in the trisagion hymn, teaching by word and deed that not merely one person but the whole most holy Trinity had suffered.

Hence it will be explained below how greatly the Eastern Church was disturbed. See Baronius, year 482, nos. 2 and 3. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XVI. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE SAME

He confirms the election of Calendion, bishop of Antioch.

Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.
