Although the manner in which the beginning of the Antiochene priesthood came to be reported later than it should have been could by no means have escaped us, the man himself, or his synod, also made it known. Just as we had not wished this to happen, so we proved accommodating toward the excuse produced by necessity, because what is not voluntary cannot be called guilt.

Therefore, through our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, who was sent from the aforesaid region, and after receiving your affection’s letter, we have returned to your charity the reciprocal exchange of our correspondence. We have necessarily embraced the priesthood of our brother and fellow bishop Calendion within the bosom of the Apostolic See, and, by the grace of Christ our God, we count the bishop of so great a city among our colleagues through the unity of the college.

We are astonished, however, that you gave us no information about the condition of the Antiochene Church. We now learn that it is in such a state that wicked men are attempting, by exploiting the death of Timothy of holy memory, to keep that same Church captive.

[Note: Timothy, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, died in the year 492, after having sat for twenty-three years. Liberatus, chapter 16. The bishops of Egypt assembled and, by common agreement, John, an orthodox man, was appointed in his place.

A legation was sent to seek confirmation of the election. When the pontiff learned from the report of this legation about the state of the Antiochene Church, and that Acacius had craftily and maliciously concealed it, he wrote him the following Letter 17, rightly rebuking him for having written nothing about matters of such importance, although he ought to have done so by virtue of the office entrusted to him as vicar of the Apostolic See.]

Therefore, your affection must act with the most clement prince, lest what was obtained under the times of tyrants be overturned under his rule.

Given on the Ides of July [in the year of Christ 482], during the consulship of Severinus, a most distinguished man.

[Note: I explained above, in the notes to Letter 16, on the words “Timothy of holy memory,” the occasion on which this letter was written. Zeno the emperor, at the urging of Bishop Acacius, removed John, who had been appointed in Timothy’s place, and substituted for him that infamous heretic Peter Mog(g)us, who had previously been expelled. The pretext was that John was perjured, since he had sworn that he would never allow himself to be elected bishop of Alexandria. See Baronius, year 482, nos. 11 and 12. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XVII. OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO THE SAME

He complains that, although the emperor’s letter had reached him, he had received no letter from Acacius; and that the emperor was asking for the heretic Peter to be made bishop of Alexandria, while Simplicius himself was prepared to confirm John. Finally, he begs Acacius to warn the emperor not to favor a heretic who had already been condemned.

[Col. 0056A]

Simplicius to his most beloved brother Acacius.

We are equally astonished and grieved that concern for charity and faith lies so concealed [or “lurks”: *latitare*] in your affection’s mind that, although the Christian emperor, moved by piety and religion, sent faithful and capable messengers to address me and consult me on ecclesiastical matters, you yourself, forgetful both of reciprocal gratitude and pastoral vigilance, neither wished to address us nor thought fit to inform us about matters pertaining to the preservation of Catholic truth.

Therefore, dearest brother, recognize that what you rightly see being blamed with free affection must be repaid with greater diligence. Accordingly, diligently discharging the office entrusted to you, raise your thoughts prudently and watch with all vigor for the preservation of the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, lest through our negligence and sloth a deadly loss [Al. “suspension”] creep upon the Lord’s flocks.

Recently, a report was sent to us in the customary manner from the Egyptian synod, which was very large in number and supported by communion with the Catholic faith, and from almost the entire clergy of the Alexandrian see itself. It disclosed that our brother Timothy of holy memory [formerly, “of blessed memory”] had died, and that, by the unanimous will of the faithful, John had been appointed in his place, since everything required for the priesthood was believed to be established in him.

Nothing seemed to remain except that, while giving thanks to our God and rejoicing, we should grant, through the assent of Apostolic moderation, the desired confirmation that a Catholic bishop had succeeded the deceased without disturbance.

But suddenly, just as I was arranging such matters according to custom, I received letters from the most tranquil prince. They declared that the aforementioned man was unworthy of the priesthood as guilty of perjury—a charge that, it was said, was not unknown even to your fraternity.

I immediately withdrew my step and recalled my judgment concerning his confirmation, lest I be considered to have acted rashly against testimony so great and so weighty.

But what greatly astonished me was that, in the same letter, the emperor judged Peter fit to be advanced to the governance of the aforesaid Church. Peter had long been proved a companion and leader of the heretics; this, we remember, is not hidden from your conscience, and we trust that you know the very documents by which he was refuted. It is also beyond doubt that he continues to remain outside Catholic communion, and it is certain that we have often written about expelling him from that city.

Although he promises to agree with the definitions of the true faith, he is just as estranged from their fellowship—as I said above—as he is separated from their communion. If he now seeks to return to it, he cannot enter except through satisfaction appropriate to Christian rules, and consequently he cannot ascend to the height of priestly dignity.

Rather, once reconciled, he should desire that the aid which must consequently be applied to his soul after repentance be granted to him, not seek the rank of supreme honor. He has long been proved perverse; otherwise, under the appearance of returning, he may seek not the remedy of sincere salvation but the opportunity to spread his wickedness.

By this action we would not so much withdraw him from error as inflict destruction upon the faithful. In this way we would violate the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and, through a savage coupling, open the way into the Church for ravenous wolves to rage.

Finally, the very people with whom he was formerly divided from Catholic participation are said to be requesting him as bishop. Thus it becomes sufficiently clear that they do not desire the true faith, but seek power for their impious doctrine in their own bishop. Nor can peace between them and those who think truly arise from a source from which the deadly condemnation of heretical minds grows and the pitiable captivity of Catholics follows.

Bound, therefore, on every side by such great evils and dangers, both by the dignity of the priesthood and by concern for Catholic preaching, you must wisely resist them by whatever means you can. Your affection may not act sluggishly in a matter which you do not doubt concerns the cause of your soul and the regard owed to honor and reputation.

Therefore, finding opportunities, do not cease incessantly to plead with the most clement prince for the Catholic faith; diligently call him back from whatever is harmful to Christian doctrine; repeatedly instruct him according to what we command; and persist rather in that direction which is friendly to the truth.

And, as the venerable apostle Paul instructed holy Timothy, never cease to urge, advise, explain, and testify “in season and out of season.” Then report truthfully to us what is being done and what ought to be done, so that you may be shown a faithful servant in multiplying the talents entrusted to you by the Lord’s dispensation, if you do not refuse to persuade people everywhere you can—not only in the Church over which you preside, but wherever possible—in favor of Catholic unity and the definitions of the Fathers.

Given on the Ides of July [in the year of Christ 482], during the consulship of Severinus, a most distinguished man.

[Note: This is Pope Simplicius’ letter replying to the emperor Zeno, who had requested that Peter Mog(g)us be placed over the Alexandrian Church, left vacant by Timothy’s death, while John, whom the Alexandrian Church had elected, was rejected.

This letter had remained unknown to scholars, although they had been informed of Zeno’s request by Simplicius’ letter to Acacius. The oldest Codex Frisingensis unexpectedly supplied it to us, though not in its entirety. P. Frobenius Forster, Benedictine prior and librarian of St. Emmeram at Regensburg, consulted that manuscript for the use of this edition.

From it, however, we learn nothing beyond what was already known: namely, that Simplicius refused to comply with the emperor. JOAN. DOM. MANSI.]

## FRAGMENT OF A LETTER OF POPE SIMPLICIUS TO ZENO

Here begins the letter of Pope Simplicius of holy memory to the emperor Zeno.

[Col. 0058B]

Among other matters, and concerning the point at issue.

But now let us come to those concerning whom the letters of your Tranquillity declare that one must be excluded from the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church and the other appointed over it. First, if you please, let us examine Peter’s character and merit.

He is, without doubt, the accomplice of the parricidal Timothy [perhaps “the accomplice in Timothy’s parricide”], and, by your own command as well, wholly deserving of perpetual exile. He has always been both an ally and a teacher of those who wage war against the truth. It is beyond doubt that I have often requested by letter that he be expelled from the city of Alexandria; for if he had possessed the true faith, he would certainly have remained in Catholic communion.

If he now approaches that communion in order to be corrected, this very act convicts him of the error he has retained for so long. Yet if even now he were seeking correction with a sincere mind, he would consequently offer satisfaction. He does not seek dignity—perhaps, “does not await” dignity—who, after repentance, is worthy of indulgence, not honor.

Far be it from me to begrudge his salvation if he repents. I embrace him, exhort him, and rejoice, most glorious emperor; but for one long wounded by the injury of wickedness, the appropriate gift is the mercy of medicine, not authority.

Only then can he be called religious, if, after condemning his perversity, he chooses to return to sound faith. Otherwise it is manifest that he does not desire treatment for his own sickness but covets the height from which he may spread the venom of his perfidy among wretched souls with greater confidence and license, and from a higher position reduce Catholic freedom to slavery with much greater violence.

I ask next who are supporting his advancement. I hear that they are archimandrites and monks, or, if there are others, those who have separated themselves from Catholic communion. Is their testimony, then, to be approved, and their persons admitted—men for whom no ground of conscience in sound faith is available and who are bound by the same error as he himself [or “as him”]?

The end.

[Note: Simplicius sent these final, very brief and pointed letters to Acacius, attempting to summon him to battle against the heretics. But in vain: he had become a deserter and was serving in the enemy camp, diligently working with the emperor so that the two venomous serpents, savage beasts, and torches of the heretics—Cnapheus and Mog(g)us—might be forced upon the Antiochene and Alexandrian sees, and their lawful possessors, the bishops Calendion and John, expelled from them. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XVIII. OF SIMPLICIUS TO THE SAME

He says that he is astonished that Acacius did not at all inform him about the troubles of the Alexandrian Church; he urges him to suggest to the emperor that the desired peace be restored to that Church.

[Col. 0059A]

To his most beloved brother Acacius, Simplicius.

We have no leisure for reflection; nor does the matter permit us to rest, since, if we abandon it, we shall be answerable—perhaps unanswerable—before Christ our Lord, whose concern it is. And it is astonishing that, after so much time has elapsed and so many opportunities have arisen from it, Your Dilection has not wished to inform us at all about the Alexandrian Church, which is being shaken so grievously. Yet our admonition has never ceased to urge you, [Col. 0059B] with shared concern, to follow my letters with the Christianest and most merciful emperor by means of personal addresses from Your Dilection, and, mindful of the established custom, to labor continually with us in defense of the orthodox, lest any of us, while the Christian people perishes, incur the guilt of surrender and appear rather a hireling than a shepherd. Therefore we exhort Your Dilection not to cease, opportunely and importunately, insinuating this into pious ears, so that, once the scandals that have assailed the Alexandrian Church in renewed outbreaks have been removed, the desired peace may be restored and, difficulties being set aside, the success of your vigilance may be swiftly brought about. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Severinus; sent through Restitutus.

## LETTER OF SIMPLICIUS TO THE SAME

Published at Rome by Luca Holstenius.

[Col. 0059C]

To his most beloved brother Acacius, Simplicius.

In the letter of Your Dilection, which you sent through our son, the deacon Epiphanius, a man of approved faith, you have explained at greater length what our most religious sons, the priests and archimandrites, together with the monks, had previously written in brief; and you have reported it in a lengthy volume, but in language demanded by the matter, so that we might learn what had been done by the heretics at Constantinople and in other regions. You have set before our eyes each of the acts committed anywhere against ecclesiastical regulations and against the Catholic faith itself, so that it might be seen by what remedy assistance could also be brought to the Churches [Col. 0059D] to which, under the pretext of tyrannical domination and during the absence of the most Christian emperor, a pernicious brigand and recurrent invader had inflicted force through exiles, after his fall upon the Alexandrian Church.

Therefore, after God—who has visited the Church and the commonwealth with wondrous consolation—we have judged that we must implore the help of the most merciful emperor, even though you had made no request for this, so that, in return for all that the Lord has bestowed upon his realm, no Church of God in the world, among those which he recognizes as subject to his empire, might thereafter be violated by the contagion and depravity of heretics, but that all might be preserved from the commands of the devil’s doctrine by his own pious authority. Those who have believed that the priestly ministry could be conferred upon them through the presumption of a condemned man must, once an imperial constitution has been promulgated, be ordered to be excluded even from human society. Thus, when these men have been removed and condemned to perpetual exile in solitude, Catholic bishops may either be restored to the deceived Churches or appointed to them.

In this matter neither our prayers before the most religious ruler, nor Your Dilection’s petition, nor the supplication of so many of our brothers and priests whom we have discovered to have arrived at Constantinople, nor the entreaty of the monks will be able to fail. Indeed, whatever pertains to the integrity of the Catholic faith, upon which the security of the Churches has been established, he has restored through his return to piety, with the Lord everywhere accompanying him and anticipating the prayers of all. And in the Christian mind the grace of obtaining a request is readily available when the cause concerns religion.

Therefore, just as in our letters, so also through the petition of Your Dilection and of all the brothers who have presented themselves before the sight of the most Christian emperor as witnesses to their faith, it must again be requested that Timothy, together with his followers, be sent into irrevocable exile. With him, Paul, expelled from the Church of Ephesus, and Peter, driven from the city of Antioch, and all those who think that they were ordained bishops by him or by those whom he illicitly appointed, ought to be struck by the same sentence.

As for Antony, who, as the leader of those whom they had sent as tyrants against the Church, appeared—according to what is written, “an enemy and a defender” (Ps. VIII, 3)—[Col. 0060C] and as for a certain John of Constantinople, who, having received from the heretics the priesthood of Apamea—which he could not receive either from the man who had previously been a presbyter elsewhere or from the Catholics—declared himself a heretic and turned back upon its author the reproach of what had wrongly been done against him: having expelled Peter, the usurper of Antioch, he himself usurped that same Church. We remove him, under anathema, from the company of Christians and even from the name of Christian; nor must any opportunity for satisfaction ever be opened to such men. For just as Judas was concealed among the apostles, so these men, through the deceit of a treacherous and diabolical spirit, lay hidden among the ministers of God.

We also rejoice in the faith and devotion of the Christian people and earnestly seek its advancement and increase, continually praying to God that, persevering in the fear and love of the Lord, it may be worthy both to grow in number and to be fortified by heavenly protection. In this above all we glory and shall rejoice in pleasing our God, because he regards pastoral fruitfulness and the growth of the devout flock.

But it is not fitting for our brothers and fellow bishops to remain long at Constantinople—especially now, when, because of the upheaval of the persecution that had been stirred up, the cities in the Churches mentioned above are anxious and bewildered. Let no one, uncertain in judgment and trembling in mind, await some new reversal after the Council of Chalcedon against its definitions, for throughout the world what was established by the whole body of priests is held with inviolable observance and has appeared to be confirmed so often by the assertion of heavenly vengeance. Therefore whoever, after so many examples of divine indignation, does not follow the definitions of that venerable council resists the judgment of God.

## OBSERVATION OF P. ANTONIO PAGI ON THE YEAR OF CHRIST 477, NOS. 12 AND 13

[Col. 0061]

Holstenius published in the Roman Collection a letter of Pope Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, which lacks a date and consular year and which Labbe, in volume IV of the Councils, p. 1039, misplaced after all the letters of Simplicius. Since Simplicius wrote it shortly after receiving from Acacius an account of the violence inflicted upon the Churches under the pretext of tyrannical domination and during the absence of the most Christian emperor—and at a time when Aelurus was still alive, whom he says must be sent, together with his followers, into irreparable exile and whose removal must be requested from the emperor Zeno—it is clear that this letter should be placed immediately after Letter 8 of Simplicius to the emperor Zeno, sent on the eighth day before the Ides of October after the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus, in which Simplicius congratulates the emperor on the recovery of his empire. For in the same collection of councils there follows that letter of Acacius to Simplicius in which he announces the death of Timothy Aelurus—a fact still unknown to Simplicius when he wrote the letter published by Holstenius to Acacius.

From this we understand that Acacius had informed Simplicius about the synod he had convened at Constantinople. For Simplicius says:

“Therefore, after God, who has visited the Church and the commonwealth with wondrous consolation, even though you had made no request for this, we have judged that we must implore the help of the most merciful emperor, so that, in return for all that the Lord has bestowed upon his realm, no Church of God in the world, among those which he recognizes as subject to his empire, might thereafter be violated by the contagion and depravity of heretics, but that all might be preserved from the commands of the devil’s doctrine by his own pious authority. Those who have believed that the priestly ministry could be conferred upon them through the presumption of a condemned man must, once an imperial constitution has been promulgated, be ordered to be excluded even from human society. Thus, when these men have been removed and condemned to perpetual exile in solitude, Catholic bishops may either be restored to the deceived Churches or appointed to them. In this matter neither our prayers before the most religious ruler, nor Your Dilection’s petition, nor the supplication of so many of our brothers and priests whom we have discovered to have arrived at Constantinople, nor the entreaty of the monks will be able to fail.”

Simplicius had implored the emperor’s help in his letter to Zeno, sent on the eighth day before the Ides of October after the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus; therefore the letter published by Holstenius was sent in the earlier months of the following year. For in that letter, which Simplicius wrote on the eighth day before the Ides of October in the year 477, he says:

“Therefore, above all, I ask that you decree that the Alexandrian Church, freed by the dispositions of Your Clemency no less from its deadly than from its heretical usurper, be restored to its Catholic and legitimate bishop, and that, after those whom he is reported to have ordained in diabolical rashness have likewise been expelled, bishops of right faith be appointed in their place,” and so forth.

# In the Year of Our Lord 479. Saint Lupus of Troyes and Saint Euphronius of Autun

[Col. 0061]

## NOTICE ON SAINT LUPUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

(From the Bibliotheca of Galland.)

[Col. 0061C]

1. Saint Lupus, bishop of Tricassinum [Troyes], a truly admirable man, left to posterity great renown of his name, as we understand clearly enough from the testimonies of the ancients concerning him. For Eucherius of Lyon, speaking of the solitude of Lérins, says [Note: Eucherius, Letter to Hilary, § 42, Bibliotheca Patrum of Lyon, vol. VI, p. 866b.]:

“This place had Lupus, a man of revered name, who represented to us that wolf from the tribe of Benjamin, Paul the apostle.”

But Sidonius is to be heard above all others. Addressing the same Lupus, he writes [Note: Sidonius, book VI, letter 1, p. 995b, vol. I of the works, Sirmond’s edition, Paris.]:

“You, Father of fathers and bishop of bishops, another Jacob of your age, from a certain watchtower of charity—and not from the lower Jerusalem—look down upon all the members of the Church of our God. You are worthy to console all the weak, and rightly to be consulted by all.”

Elsewhere he calls him [Note: The same, book VII, letter 3, p. 1041c, ibid.] “easily the foremost of the Gallican pontiffs, both master of his profession and author of his dignity.” Indeed, he says [Note: The same, book VI, letter 1, p. 996b, ibid.]:

“He is the first of all the pontiffs throughout the whole world as far as it extends; his prerogative subordinates the others to him, his judgment causes even the assembled college to tremble, and in comparison with his gravity even the hearts of the very old become childish.” [Col. 0063A]

In a word, Lupus is for Sidonius [Note: Sidonius, ibid., p. 997c.] “a model of conduct, a pillar of virtues, a genuine sweetness because a holy one.” These and many other things of this kind were written about our bishop of Troyes by the bishop of Clermont.

2. The same Sidonius praises Saint Lupus not only as surpassing others in the outstanding gifts of piety and integrity that befit a bishop, but also in learning and education. First, he sent the count Arbogast, who had proposed to him various questions drawn from the Sacred Scriptures for solution, to the bishop of Troyes himself, testifying [Note: The same, book IV, letter 17, p. 953c, ibid.] that “even his consultation would not suffice to ventilate adequately the abundance of that man’s learning.” Then, writing to the same holy pontiff, he says [Note: The same, book IX, letter 11, p. 1105c, ibid.]:

“To me, the rigor of your judgment in letters is to be feared in two ways, just as it is in your character.”

But we understand above all how greatly Saint Lupus shone in the praise of wisdom from the fact that in the year 429, scarcely two years after he had assumed the episcopate, he was unanimously appointed by the Gallican Fathers assembled in a great synod as envoy to Britain against the Pelagians, together with Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.

The venerable Bede speaks at greater length about this mission [Note: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book I, chapter 17.]; Norisius follows the history of the same mission in detail [Note: Norisius, History of Pelagianism, book II, chapter 5, pp. 304 ff., vol. I of the works.], and after him Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, vol. XV, pp. 15 ff.] and others.

We have said that Lupus was sent to Britain in 429, after completing two years in the government of the Church of Troyes. For the opinion of Pagi is not accepted by learned men [Note: The same, vol. XVI, p. 123, note 1, and p. 750, note 6, on Saint Sidonius.]. Pagi, relying on Sidonius’s letter in which he says [Note: Sidonius, book VI, letter 1, p. 997a, Sirmond’s works, vol. I.] that Lupus had already completed nine five-year periods in the apostolic see, thinks that the bishop of Clermont calculated by the five-year periods of the imperial reign and therefore determines that Lupus’s ordination must be assigned to the year 428 [Note: Pagi, Prolegomena to the Dissertation on Hypatius, § 31; and on the year 428, § 23; likewise on the year 472, § 5.].

Norisius and Tillemont, therefore, following Baronius in the cited passages [Note: Baronius, on the year 472, §§ 14 and 15.], maintain that Saint Lupus was ordained in the year [Col. 0064A] 427 and sent as envoy to Britain in 429.

After he had completed fifty-two full years in the episcopate of Troyes, he finally departed from this life for heaven in the year 479, full of days [Note: Bollandus, Acta Sanctorum, vol. VII, July, commentary on Saint Lupus, nos. 45 and 82, pp. 59, 67.].

3. Of this great bishop of Troyes, who was an outstanding glory of the Gallican Church and whose immense praises Sidonius Apollinaris entrusted to memory, only two letters survive. One was published by Sirmond [Note: Sirmond, Councils of Gaul, vol. I, p. 122.] and subsequently passed into the collection of councils [Note: Councils, vol. V, p. 71, Venetian edition of Labbe.]; the other was published by Acherius in the Spicilegium [Note: Acherius, Spicilegium, vol. V, p. 579, or the new edition, vol. III, p. 302.].

The first was written after the year 443 by Saint Lupus, in his own name and that of Saint Euphronius, bishop of Autun, to Talasius, bishop of Angers, who had consulted both bishops about three matters: namely, the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, and Easter; digamists; and those who are admitted while married.

The second was addressed by our bishop of Troyes to Sidonius, congratulating him on his bishopric of Clermont. Saint Lupus is said to have written this letter toward the end of the year 471, in the forty-fifth year of his episcopate—that is, after nine five-year periods had already passed in the apostolic see, as Sidonius himself says in the letter he wrote in reply to the same holy bishop [Note: Sidonius, book VI, letter 1, pp. 997a, vol. I of Sirmond’s cited works.].

Regarding both letters, it is useful to consult Tillemont [Note: Tillemont, vol. XVI, pp. 135 ff.] and the authors of the History of French Literature [Note: History of French Literature, vol. II, pp. 490 ff.]. Concerning the latter letter, however, it is worthwhile to transcribe here the words of a learned man [Note: Bosch, on the Acta Sanctorum, vol. VII, July, p. 67, no. 82.]:

“Whoever reads this letter, I am mistaken if he will not deeply mourn with me the loss of so many others which we infer from Sidonius to have been written by him [Lupus], since Sidonius presents him as the counselor of all the Churches in doubtful matters and their comforter in adversity. Yet it is pleasing to have heard the Saint speaking even once, so that from this we may know more deeply his character and spirit.”

[Col. 0063]

## LETTERS OF SAINTS LUPUS AND EUPHRONIUS (C, G)*

## FIRST LETTER. LUPUS TO THE LORD POPE SIDONIUS

[Col. 0063D]

I give thanks to our Lord God Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit, who, in this general instability and distress of his most beloved bride, the Church, has called you, dearest brother, to the priesthood for her support and consolation, so that you may be a lamp in Israel. And just as, with the highest praise, you carried out the ambitious honors of worldly service, so, with Christ himself helping you, may you eagerly traverse the laborious duties and humble ministries of the heavenly service, without turning your eyes backward after putting your hand to the plough, like farmers who have grown sluggish.

You recently attained imperial honors through the most glorious relationships; you exercised, with honor and amid resounding applause, the trabeal vestments, splendid prefectures, and whatever an unquiet succession of desires can imagine as blessed in this world. The order has changed, and in the house of the Lord you have reached a position of eminence that must be exercised not in the overflowing brilliance of worldly pomp, but in the deepest abasement of the mind and the humble prostration of a bowed heart.

You who once strove to surpass the distinction of your birth by adding honors, and did not believe that a man had achieved enough if he were merely equal to others and did not rise above his peers, have now entered a condition in which, although you are superior to no one, you must consider yourself superior to no one. Placed beneath the least of your subjects, you will be more honored the more the humility of Christ girds you, and you kiss the feet of those above whose heads you once disdained to place your own feet.

This labor now certainly falls to you: to be the servant of all, though you seemed the master of all; to bend before others, though you trampled down the rest—not because you were proud, but because, by the majesty, or rather the vanity, of your former dignities, you had to surpass others by as much as now, more than anyone else, you must withdraw from such precedence.

Therefore transfer your talent now to divine things, since you were so capable in human affairs. Let your peoples gather from your mouth the thorns from the head of the Crucified One, whereas they formerly gathered roses from your worldly pomp; and let them receive from the speech of a priest words of heavenly discipline, whereas they formerly received from the speech of a ruler the rule of civil discipline.

I, who loved you so greatly when you were following the barrenness of the world—by what measure do you think I now love you as you follow the fruitfulness of heaven? I am already being released, and my dissolution is near; yet I shall not think myself dissolved, since, although freed, I shall live in you and leave you in the Church.

I rejoice to be stripped off, since you have put on the Church and the Church has put you on. Well done, my old friendship, but my new brotherhood! The last title suppresses the former ones; today I wish to remember nothing of our former affection, since the dignity you now possess makes our love both firmer and more enduring.

Would that God willed me to embrace you! In spirit I accomplish what I cannot in the body, and in the presence of Christ I no longer venerate and kiss the prefect of the commonwealth, but the prefect of the Church—one who is my son in age, my brother in dignity, and my father in merits.

Pray for me, that, perfected in the Lord, I may complete the work he has entrusted to me, and may finally fulfill in him the time that remains—the man who has filled so many and such great periods, alas for me, with things I ought not to have done. Yet with the Lord there is mercy. Remember me.

[Note: The date of this letter is also uncertain, except that its mention of Talasius as a new bishop, as appears likely, seems to suggest that we should believe it was sent to him not long after the Council of Angers at which he was ordained. Besides the various copies of it that have come into our hands, we have noticed that it is also mentioned in an ancient collection of canons preserved in the library of Saint-Germain of Paris. JAC. SIRMOND.

They answer the consultation of Talasius, bishop of Angers, concerning three matters. First, how the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, and Easter are to be celebrated. Then, concerning lower clerics who are permitted to marry: whether they may enter into a second marriage. On this point they teach that the Church does indeed permit doorkeepers to marry other wives and become digamists, but entirely excludes exorcists and subdeacons from second marriages. Moreover, in the Church of Troyes, exorcists and deacons, after they have been admitted to the clergy, are also barred from first marriages; in the Church of Autun, doorkeepers are barred from second marriages. Finally, subdeacons ought to exchange the peace among themselves in the sacristy, not at the altar. This letter exists in various ancient manuscripts and is cited in the very ancient collection of canons of Saint-Germain of Paris. JAC. SIRMOND.]

## SECOND LETTER OF THE HOLY BISHOPS LUPUS OF TROYES AND EUPHRONIUS OF AUTUN TO TALASIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS (C)

[Note: The memory of Lupus, bishop of Troyes, is exceedingly famous among all. That of Euphronius, bishop of Autun, is known from Sidonius, Gregory of Tours, and Hydatius, who mentions another letter of his in the Chronicle under the year 451: “In the days following Easter, certain things were seen in the sky over the regions of Gaul; a letter concerning these matters from Euphronius, bishop of Autun, to the count Agrippinus clearly demonstrates it.” Talasius of Angers has been discussed in connection with the synod of Angers, at which he was ordained. JAC. SIRMOND.]

Concerning the solemnities, clerical digamists, and those who are admitted while married.

[Col. 0066A]

To the holy lord, most blessed brother Talasius, bishop, venerable in Christian worship and honor, Lupus and Euphronius, bishops likewise appointed:

We have examined the memorandum that was sent through the subdeacon Arcontius, and, as you requested, we have taken care to answer Your Holiness. The vigil of the Nativity of the Lord is to be celebrated in a very different manner from the vigil of Easter: at the former, readings concerning the Nativity are to be read, but at the latter, those concerning the Passion. The solemnity of Epiphany also has its own special observance.

These vigils in particular should be kept either throughout the whole night or at least until the approach of morning; but the Easter vigil is rarely prolonged from evening all the way to morning. Furthermore, at the Easter vigil readings from various books are to be recited, all of which must contain something concerning the prefiguration or prophecy of the Passion. At the aforesaid vigil, however, as may seem appropriate, while psalms are being sung and readings given, anyone may undertake to read whatever he wishes, whether from the prophets or from the New Testament—not by legal obligation, but by voluntary reading.

As for clerics who are digamists, the Church permits and tolerates them up to the rank of doorkeeper; and whatever rule any priest may have adopted for the sake of greater strictness, he shall rightly observe. But it entirely excludes exorcists and subdeacons from second marriages.

It would be better, if it could be done, to prevent the begetting of children by those whom we admit while married. It is better not to admit such men than afterward to dispute about them amid differing opinions, since it is better to exclude every cause of controversy, so that he who does not wish to beget children in the clergy may not appoint married men at the altar.

These matters we have set forth in the language of this letter according to the custom of our Churches, which have one rule. If anything stricter can be added for the honor of the Lord, and if we cannot imitate it, we shall nevertheless praise it for the Lord’s honor.

For we do not permit those already attached to the services of the Church to pass to a second marriage; and after they have been admitted, we also entirely bar them from a first marriage—exorcists and subdeacons, that is. In the Church of Autun, however, even a doorkeeper in the lowest office, if he takes another wife, is completely removed from office.

Subdeacons ought to approach one another for the exchange of peace in the sacristy. At the altar they may do so only when they hand cloths to the deacon or receive what is being brought forward; they are not permitted to exchange the peace there at all. But if an exorcist, subdeacon, or even a doorkeeper—as was mentioned above—should be so insane as to bind himself to a second marriage, he is entirely excluded not only from office but also from communion.

(Several letters of Ruricius and Sidonius of Rheims written to Lupus of Troyes appear below.)

# In the Year of Our Lord 480. Ruricius

[Col. 0067]

## OBSERVATION OF JACOB BASNAGE ON RURICIUS

[Col. 0067B]

Ruricius, called the Elder to distinguish him from his namesake nephew, who was bishop of Limoges, was born of the most illustrious family of the Anicii. At first he was devoted to the world, as Faustus, his very close friend, testifies in Letter 6. Faustus exults joyfully over his conversion in these words:

“After the storms of this life, with the hand of the Most High guiding him, he turned toward the harbor of religion and the prow of salvation. After the shadows of seductive vanities and the illusions of fleeting dreams, he desired what would endure and be solid; and at last, scorning the unhappy world, he seized its great art.”

He had taken Iberia as his wife. He appears not to have had children by her. Having become a cleric, he was promoted to the bishopric of Limoges, which at that time was not held in great esteem. Nevertheless, Ruricius did not allow himself to be despised. “The lowliness of the city,” he said, “ought not to diminish our authority. For it is much better and much more distinguished to know a city from its priest than a priest from his city” (Letter 32, book II).

They say that in that episcopate he was the twenty-fourth successor after Martial. But that Martial, who is said to have been bishop both among the people of Bordeaux and among those of Limoges, must be relegated to the realm of fables. He does indeed advise his friend Celsus to come with his sister to the solemnity of the saints (Letter 114, book II); from this someone might perhaps infer that one of the saints whose solemnity was celebrated at Limoges was Martial. It is a mere conjecture! But who today would be surprised that ancient saints who never existed—or at least saints about whom many fabulous things are told—are venerated?

Of Ruricius himself, who ought to have been better known to us, they report that he built a monastery in honor of Saint Augustine in the common cemetery of Limoges and was buried there under a canonical rule. All of this is contrary to the truth.

What is entirely certain is that Ruricius was a very close friend of Faustus, Leontius, Aeonius, Sidonius, and even Caesarius himself, all bishops of Gaul who were famous in that period, as is clear from his letters.

In old age he could scarcely endure the air; in winter he was somewhat stronger, but during the summer days he could scarcely overcome his customary illness in lodgings and cool places. For this reason he was absent from the Council of Agde, which Caesarius, by whom he had been invited, took badly. Indeed, Sedatus, bishop of Nîmes, gave Caesarius a hand in this matter. Ruricius rejected the complaints or insult, explaining that Caesarius’s letters had arrived to him very late, though he nevertheless ought not to have been admonished later, since perhaps he deserved to be courted.

He died shortly after that council. The editors of the Bibliotheca Patrum say that he reached the year 499. But since the Council of Agde was convened under Caesarius in the year 506, it is clear that Ruricius lived considerably longer.

His letters were written in a polished style, as the age permitted; nevertheless, one can extract very little from them that relates either to doctrine or to the history of those times. Most are letters of courtesy, or consolatory letters, or exhortations to piety and flight from the world.

Baluzius observed that Ruricius had the habit of reading through better writers and making their words his own. He proves this by various arguments drawn from the two letters of Sulpicius Severus that he was then publishing (Miscellanies, vol. I, preface). Ruricius seems indeed to have drawn some material from them without naming the author; and in fact some passages are similar, so that he appears guilty of plagiarism, made worse by the fact that he borrowed only the words and expressions.

[Col. 0067]

# LETTERS OF RURICIUS, BISHOP (C)

## BOOK ONE

## LETTER ONE

To his particular lord in Christ, the lord patron Faustus, bishop, Ruricius.

[Col. 0067D]

Long ago, my revered lord and most blessed priest, when the most celebrated report proclaimed you, I came to know you. Long ago, once the desire of pious love had been infused into me, I beheld you with the eyes of my heart among those to whom you deigned to write; yet I hasten no less to see you also bodily, if somehow, while you are present, I might break the bonds of my sins, receive the wings of that dove (Ps. LIV, 7), fly away from the snares of hunters (Ps. XC, 3), and, placed with you, rest in the law of the Lord.

Thus I might quench the thirst that I acquired by reading your little works, drawing more abundantly from the source from which they flowed, once you yourself were present. And the little spark of charity that you kindled in the warm ashes of my sleeping soul might, through the nourishment brought forth from the dense thicket of the Scriptures, be strengthened into a living flame—a flame kindled by the eloquence of your holy mouth, which, according to its customary manner, would exercise the power of its potent nature in the breast of a sinner: warming what is cold, illuminating what is dark, and consuming the thorns of sins.

My soul has clung to you, outstanding teacher. May your prayers also help me, so that, scorning earthly actions, I may long for heavenly things. For “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15), so that it cannot incline its ear to the divine oracles (Ps. XLIV, 11), nor, obedient to the command of the one who calls, forget its father’s house and depart from its land and kindred (Gen. XII, 1), desiring instead the land that is shown to it.

For my weakness is not yet able to drive out the fear arising from my condition and to open a purified heart to perfect charity, so that, leaving present things behind, we may seek eternal ones; and, having cast out the slave woman (Gen. XXI, 10), may freely attain the paternal inheritance.

Therefore I hope, my lord, that you will pray for me without ceasing. Whenever you deign to water the dryness of my soil with the rain of your eloquence, do not, as you have done now, while still unaware of my weakness, offer me delicate and sweet foods, but harsher ones, suited to my sickness. Delicacies are not suitable for a fool.

Afterward, grant your censor’s approval to those who betray me—those who, following the tendency of the human mind and hindered by excessive affection, turn aside from sound judgment and, out of love, fall into falsehood. Indeed, let not Your Holiness fear that the hand which treats my wounds is more pleasing to me than the hand that cuts them. For, by the Lord’s gift, I already perceive both that I cannot be cured by these means and that I have nevertheless become gravely putrid.

Therefore I choose that a righteous man rebuke me with the correction of mercy rather than that the oil of a sinner fatten my head (Ps. CXL, 5). With a suppliant prayer I ask, then, that from the treasure of your inner chambers, from which you are accustomed to bring forth things new and old (Matt. XIII, 52), you, as a most skilled physician who daily, with God’s grace assisting, heal innumerable and varied illnesses of the sick, send also to my sickness the medicines that you recognize as suitable.

## LETTER TWO

To his particular lord in Christ the Lord, his patron, Bishop Faustus, Ruricius.

Thus far impious negligence and negligent impiety have possessed me, my lord, that I do not know what I should chiefly accuse in myself, nor can I find what I should first excuse. For if I attempt to offer some argument in defense of my excuses in sins (Ps. CXL, 4), I shall add sin to sin without remembering the judgment, so that I may burden myself with a double and greater offense: though guilty of delay, I shall begin to be guilty of falsehood; and I shall extend the charge from a human offense even to an eternal one, now awaiting only the sentence for the guilt of sloth, while for my falsehood I shall be subjected to divine vengeance.

Especially since true confession earns indulgence, while false excuse deserves offense, I prefer to ask pardon through a confession both simple and suppliant, rather than multiply my sins.

You have, then, excellent father and outstanding shepherd, my voluntary confession of my guilt. You have also, in the error of a disciple, something to correct, and in the sickness of a little sheep, something to heal. It belongs to your power and judgment to decide whether you wish to cut away the corruption of my ulcer with the harshness of iron or to cure it with the gentleness of medicines.

Whatever treatment you choose, I shall embrace it fearlessly, nor shall I avoid the blow of a father’s hand, provided that I may obtain a portion of the promised inheritance. I shall not consider what punishment I receive in the scourging, but what share I possess in the testament.

For it is better for me to weep over my father than to be disowned by a father who despises me. The affection of parents restrains in order to correct; it does not persist in order to punish. Nor does the arrogance of one who is proud cause him as much grief as the humility of one who confesses brings joy.

Thus that most indulgent father of the Gospel received his son, who had squandered the substance entrusted to him, in a joyful embrace, more ready to rejoice over his return than to charge him with his fall (Luke XV). In the end, no crimes are reproached—neither luxury nor poverty. The return of the convert alone compensates for all the losses [Col. 0070C], because plainly the father’s ability to restore was greater than the son’s ability to possess.

Thus his departure had made him guilty, but his return made him innocent. That mercy is enough for the heir. Indeed, the pardon of paternal clemency alone is not enough: the father embraces him, caresses him with favor, and also multiplies generous gifts.

He gives a ring so that the son may not again depart from his father, led by faithlessness. He gives shoes for his feet, so that he may more easily scorn the rough and difficult places of the arduous journey. He also gives him the first robe that he had lost, so that the one he had received back from death might be endowed with his former immortality.

The fatted calf is also given to the younger son on his return, whereas a lamb had been given to the elder son when he was departing from Egypt. For the father himself leads him out of Egypt.

Imitate the faith of so great a parent, you who are so great. Offer assistance to sinners; grant forgiveness to those who strive; bestow intercession; and, for the son who confesses, not only grant pardon yourself but also beg pardon yourself, so that the one whom you call free in a foreign land you may be able to see liberated in his own.

And let the man who lost the Lord’s generosity through himself deserve, through you, to obtain freedom; nor let him be separated from your consolation who is separated from the reward.

## LETTER THREE
To his most devoted and ever most distinguished son Hesperius, Ruricius.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] He was a young man who loved literature. Sidonius called this distinguished man “the jewel of letters and friends” [Col. 0070D–0071D], *Book IV, Letter 22*. Ruricius wrote to him frequently, as is clear from Letters 3, 4, and 5, addressed to him. BASN.]

The affection and that sovereign force of loving-kindness, through which rigid things are bent, rocky things softened, swollen things calmed, rough things gentled, gentle things made to swell, savage things made mild, mild things made savage, peaceful things kindled, dull things sharpened, barbarians brought under dominion, and monstrous things pacified, have opened for me access to write to your kindred spirit—an access that incompetence had blocked. Working its power in me as well, it has opened my tongue-tied mouth, brought me out from the safest retreat of silence into the public and fearful judgment, and compelled me to undertake something new at your invitation.

Clearly, although until now I have followed that old maxim which says, “Very often it is better to be silent than to speak,” and have preferred to read my ignorance in the silence of modesty rather than put it forth shamelessly in unpolished speech, I now wish—not so much unmindful of my customary practice as forgetful of my rusticity, and having suddenly been changed, as it were, from Arion into Orpheus—to appear to your most eloquent ears with a chattering mouth, not so much dutiful as insulting. And this while I attempt what is unfamiliar and presume upon what is unaccustomed.

But, as I think, you will grant pardon to one who comes compelled by the necessity of necessary necessity. For a heart conscious of shared suffering recognizes what affection claims for itself, by natural authority, in the minds of mortals. Therefore, lest by lingering too long over an excuse we stretch out the page so far that our less polished speech not only fails to please you but also, through its disorderly abundance, produces weariness, we now burst into the voice of affection and belch forth the words of our longing, commending to you our pledge, your deposit, whose reception has enabled you to take possession of us.

To you alone I have entrusted the hope of my posterity; to you the comfort of my present life and, if the divine will so grant, its relief in the future; to you I have entrusted all my prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] The manuscript expressly reads *elicitorem*, a novel word formed from *elicere* and not inelegant in sense, just as Jupiter was called Elicius for drawing forth thunderbolts; Ovid, *Fasti* III:

“They draw you down from heaven, Jupiter; hence even now the lesser gods celebrate you and call you Elicius.”

Unless one prefers *licitatorem*, which is not pleasing, or *elucidatorem*, which I would prefer. So Canisius.—Those verses of Ovid are wrongly cited, if I am not mistaken. Jupiter was called Elicius not because he hurled and drew forth thunderbolts, but because he allowed himself to be drawn down from heaven. When Jupiter, to oblige Numa, who wished to know how a thunderbolt could be expiated, crossed from heaven to earth, he was called Elicius. Likewise Hesperius was called the “elicitor of little stones” because he drew gems out of earth or stones. BASN.]

I have chosen you as the one who elicits and forms noble stones, who searches out gold, and who discovers hidden water. You know how to restore gems concealed in rocks to their own nobility; and surely, amid such great confusion of things, they would lose their distinction if they had no judge.

Gold too, mixed with worthless sand, cannot retain either its brilliance or its value unless an artisan’s skill washes it with water and liquefies it in the fire. Nor will the water of a spring flow unless the industry of one who seeks it carefully excavates the veins of running water that have been enclosed and the channel covered over by flowing earth. So too the perception of minds still tender, besieged by the cloud of ignorance as though by the rough thickness of encrusted rust, cannot brighten of itself unless it is cleansed by the constant file of a teacher.

[Col. 0071D]

Therefore, in all these matters it is now your task—your task—to respond both to your own opinion and equally to our judgment, lest you seem either to have presumed unlawfully or we to have chosen without due consideration.

## EPISTLE IV

To his most devoted and ever most distinguished son Hesperius, Ruricius.

[Col. 0072A]

I have received the letter of your kindred spirit, sprinkled with grace as well as eloquence, with affection no less than wit, with salt as well as honey. In it, neither sweetness nor savor lacks anything. Although it excels in every art of diction and reasoning, it nevertheless seems to differ from itself in judgment alone. For while you hasten to attribute greater worth to my little page—not suited to praise, but fitted by the ineptness of rusticity for blame—and follow either the course of declamation or the impulse of a devoted friend, you have departed from the standard of sound judgment.

I think that in this matter you descended to perfection not through the fault of ignorance but by deliberate choice, for three reasons: so that, in dealing with slight material, you might display the sharpness of your intellect, the eloquence of your mouth, and the abundance of your speech. Just as on a barren and neglected patch of ground the cultivator’s vigor is more apparent when he either subdues the resistance of stubborn clods by the repeated pressure of the plowshare or makes excessive dryness fertile by scattering manure, so that industry produces an abundance of fruit which the nature of the soil denies, so you enriched the poverty of my letter with the fertility of your eloquence. Thus, if you suppress it, it can be praiseworthy because you have spoken; but if you publish it, it will bring shame both upon me for false praise and upon you for an error of judgment.

And therefore, since you wished my incompetence to be the work of your modesty, take care that, if we fail to answer your proclamation, your choice does not become imperiled. So, if you trust me at all, if you are concerned for either of us, hide this volume—unworthy of remembrance and most worthy of oblivion—if you wish both to obtain, according to your own judgment, the reputation of an orator for me and the role of an approved judge for yourself.

## EPISTLE V

To his most devoted and ever most distinguished son Hesperius, Ruricius.

You had promised, dearest son, to send me some little blossoms from the branch which you had undertaken to transfer from bitterness into a domestic flavor and to transform, so that by their fragrance I might know what hope I ought to entertain for the hope: whether the flowers themselves would promise buds, or the buds in turn fruit of their own quality, and whether those fruits, once again, could be softened by your cooking and satisfy the hearts of their hearers with the word of sweet eloquence.

Since you have delayed doing this for some reason I do not know, I have found an opportune time to remind you: at this season, in the harmony of the world, all living creatures—both the mute and the voiceless, those that walk, fly, and crawl—burst forth in praise of their own creator, each in its own manner, with its own hisses and its own voices, though with discordant sound and different mouths, yet with equal affection, as though in a single concert; and they reveal that they perceive the power which they cannot express.

At this time the appearance of the whole world is renewed and restored. Everything in it that until now was squalid in its condition, troubled by cold, congealed in ice, deformed by nakedness, or half-dead from dryness emerges in the likeness of a resurrection, so that human frailty may learn from visible things about invisible things, and from present things about future things, and may, laying aside despair, receive hope of a better age to come.

Now too the earth, enclosed by barren cold, as though married through hidden passages and having conceived a masculine seed in this springtime, opens its veins for childbirth. From this it produces everything that is pleasant to delight, sweet to eat, useful for use, necessary for nourishment, pleasing to the sight, agreeable to smell, and soothing to touch.

For this is that temperate season which nourished the substance of the newly born world, still tender as though in its cradle, in a certain lap and embrace of the most merciful nurse, lest summer heat burn up matter hardened by no labor, winter frost extinguish it, or gusts of wind carry it away.

Your undertaking therefore has found the most fitting season, when at last the sluggishness of the mind may be laid aside and the dullness of the heart sharpened. [Note: The manuscript has *detestata* in the margin.] And if it cannot declaim among human beings, let it at least hurry to cry out among cattle or chatter among birds.

## EPISTLE VI

To the holy and most devout lord and father, the presbyter Nepotianus, Ruricius.

[Col. 0073C]

I have received the books that Your Holiness sent: distinguished by eloquence, perfect in knowledge, upright in teaching, and clear in the purity of their faith. Rich in the abundance of sacred testimonies, eminent in authority, and shining with light, they can readily illuminate the minds of the faithful and expose and refute the errors of unbelievers.

I was attracted by a very slight taste of them rather than nourished, and because of the cares of the world I could not reach satiety. For just as a stomach consumed by the heat of fever neither receives sweet foods offered to it nor asks for those taken away, so a mind worn down by worldly anxieties and cares neither desires spiritual banquets when absent, nor takes what is set before it, nor perceives what is poured into it.

Although this is how matters stand with me, you have nevertheless shown the affection of a loving father, fulfilled the service of a concerned teacher, and performed the duty of a diligent physician by sending suitable medicines to one suffering from such weariness. Yet, because of my negligence, I cannot attain health through them.

You, however, will receive your reward from the just recompense-giver, who is accustomed to return gracious thanks even for the ungrateful. Of the books mentioned above, I retained one, as you instructed, and returned another, which you should know belongs to Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Because you had ordered this, I thought it proper to inform you. You permit me to copy the one I retained; I have resolved that what we cannot commit to memory, we should at least strive to commit to pages.

## EPISTLE VII

To his own particular patron in Christ, Bishop Bassulus, Ruricius.

You prove in many ways how the holy affection and your affectionate holiness deign to love me: you send things to be read, correct what has been neglected, provoke love by loving, and teach by the examples of what you preach in words.

But since your seed makes no progress in sterile and thorny soil, which is choked as the thorns grow over it, lest the Lord of the vineyard order me, like that unfruitful fig tree which he has awaited for so long in vain, to be cut down, postpone the more severe sentence by your prayers, until through the richness of your teaching the unfruitful bitterness of the soil is sweetened. [Note: The manuscript reads *pinguine* (“with fatness”; perhaps “by the richness”).]

But since my sins are greater than my words, and I cannot atone for deeds by speech, I at least pay an epistolary duty and inform you that I have returned the book you had lent me. I hope that the other, which is not presently needed for your purposes, will likewise be returned by the bearer of this letter. Please also let me know, when you return, whether, by God’s favor, you will be leaving for the festival of the saints at Gurdon.

## EPISTLE VIII

To his particular patron in Christ the Lord, Bishop Sidonius, [Note: He was bishop of Clermont and a most celebrated man. BASN.] Ruricius.

You have often preached, and I remember hearing you say, that we can in no way be cleansed from our iniquities unless, with conscience pricking us, we confess our crimes. For who could obtain—not to say seek—forgiveness unless he joins confession of his error to lamentation? Error requires forgiveness, not forgiveness error.

Recognizing that I was very late in doing so, I did not delay informing Your Piety of the crime I had recently committed, lest what now, through my self-disclosure, pertains to forgiveness should later, through my silence, pertain to guilt.

But now I bring the very deception into the open. I declare myself guilty of theft against you, and announce that, without your knowledge, I unlawfully took possession of your deposit. Yet you gave me the opportunity to commit this deed, either by testing one who was greedy or by wishing to instruct one who was ignorant.

I confess that I copied the book which you had ordered me to receive from my brother Leontius. If you approve it, forgive me; if you charge it against me, acknowledge it. [Note: Perhaps, “If you approve it, acknowledge it; if you charge it against me, forgive me.”] For a complaint is joined to the confession.

At first, the desire to read it moved me. Then the book itself compelled me to copy it. For when I had tasted only a little of its banquets, it enticed me with the flavor of its seductive savor, so that, imitating our first parent in a certain way, I suddenly despised the Lord and strove to reach satiety; and I listened more to the counsel of the persuader than to the command of the ruler.

To reveal all the secrets of my heart, I seemed to hear the words of the book itself exhorting me:

“Why do you delay, ingrate? Why do you hesitate? You know the will of the common Lord toward you, how through various occasions he strives to polish you, and how the good shepherd is accustomed to feed you spiritual foods even against your will. Believe me: if you delay rather than copy, he will charge you with more. For he is accustomed to favor diligence, not to begrudge it.”

By such and similar silent addresses I voluntarily and yet under compulsion cast myself into his bonds. I hastened to copy him as an example. Whether I ought to return him transcribed as he is or prepared rests upon your judgment. For my part, I will gladly accept whatever fine you impose, because I believe your decree to be my remedy and regard your sentence as healing, not punishment.

## EPISTLE IX

To his particular patron in Christ the Lord, Sidonius, Ruricius.

[Col. 0075B]

Your recent preaching, together with the ancient affection of your piety, has so enticed me that I dare repeatedly to wrong your ears with my foolishness, while I desire, as far as my sterile little intellect allows, to approach your learning.

Although attaining it is great and difficult, following it is nevertheless beautiful and sublime. For in the case of supreme things, not only attainment but imitation itself is delightful. Since almost no one is entirely without some share of the thing to which he has striven to climb and attain.

Therefore, my lord, I desire—I desire, I say—to be refreshed by your foods, to drink from your fountain, to be filled with your banquets, and to be fattened at your feasts. If someone, when you distribute them, does not merely taste them with the tip of his mouth but, desiring them with all the inward parts of his soul, drinks them as a guest and afterward hides them in the deepest recesses of his heart to chew them over again, he will begin, through constant belchings, to burst forth in praise of the almighty Lord: full in heart, fasting in mouth, hungry while satisfied and satisfied while hungry, destined to be filled more fully in regeneration.

Nor can the food whose nourishment is in the word be lacking. Obtain for me, through your patronage, that I may deserve to share in these delights; come to the aid of one striving beyond the measure of his strength, and at the same time ensure that I am not found alien to the flock entrusted to you.

Pray to the Lord, and bring the wandering sheep back from the pastures of the world to the Lord’s folds; for I trust that through your intercessions I may become a lamb worthy to be your disciple.

## EPISTLE X

To his lord, dear to his heart, Lupus, [Note: He was bishop of Troyes.] Ruricius.

I have received the letter of your greatness, in which you graciously excuse the poverty of messengers for causing you to sprinkle me less often with the dew of your eloquence. At the same time, you indicate that you wonder why, although I have plenty of messengers and am not lacking a supply of polished words, I nevertheless decline to write to you more often.

I have no doubt that you made this boast ironically, in keeping with the wit of your eloquence. You have an abundance of letter-carriers, while you know that I suffer from poverty of speech and from the sterility of a slender intellect, like a stream whose channel dries up in the summer months and which sweats rather than flows.

You added that, just as Patroclus belonged with Achilles, Theseus with Hercules, or Pirithous with Theseus, so you ought to be joined with me. In these stories and deeds of our ancestors we should understand not the precedence of the persons but the comparison of affection: remembering the names of friends, let us follow their examples; transferring their names to ourselves, let us bring over their merits; and selecting from their deeds whatever is magnificent and honorable, let us suitably adapt it to our own lives. Let us serve one another in unfeigned love, not in disguised flattery.

Let us strive for the truth of our hearts to accomplish in us what the falsehood of poets invented in the friendships of those men, so that while we seem to imitate ancient things, we may leave behind things worthy of imitation; and while praising the deeds of our elders, may be praised by those who come after us.

Thus, my lord, flame of my heart, I have dictated these words briefly and hastily in response to your persuasion, which I trust more than my own conscience. If your skill and integrity take account of a friend’s modesty, they will either conceal them or take care to correct them.

## EPISTLE XI

To the sublime and ever most distinguished brother Fredar, Ruricius.

Since you wished the foolishness of our wilderness to be added to the beauty of your grove, I have sent, as you instructed, fir trees pleasing not in appearance but in height; remarkable not for their fruits but for their foreign origin; suitable not for use but delightful for beauty. When they have grown together in the density of their shade, they will provide the coolness of the Cévennes to the oceans in summer. [Note: The reading before “Cévennes” is corrupt.] [Note: The reading after “coolness” (*frigus*) is corrupt.]

Among those most splendid trees of various kinds, distinguished both in beauty and usefulness, rich in their burden, adorned with blossoms, and fragrant with scent, your industry has supplied what nature alone did not produce. To pass over the redness of roses, the whiteness of lilies, the perpetual greenness of the laurel, and other such things—for precious things often become cheap through abundance, and daily plenty creates weariness—there too are gathered foreign delights of grasses, shoots, and shrubs, blooming for sight and use.

But what should first be praised or wondered at there, where even the inclemency of the seasons is tempered? There the burning heat of summer is driven away by the coolness both of shade and of water. The harshness of winter, on the other hand, is so little felt that within the same place the warmth of the air and the song of the birds rather restore the appearance of spring.

But why do I, forgetful of my own incompetence, attempt, my lord, in impoverished speech to describe or recount the riches and delights of your countryside, in praise of which even greater intellects would falter? Grant pardon, then, to my shamelessness, which you yourselves have compelled: your esteem forced me to become verbose for your ears.

I trust that this longer letter will please you, my lords, in affection even if it displeases in expression, once you understand that it is abundant not because of the charm of eloquence but because of my love for you. I also knew that your sublimity reproaches your friends more for the modesty of silence than for the boldness of loquacious familiarity.

## EPISTLE XII

To his heart’s own lord, Celsus, Ruricius.

I tremble to open my tongue-tied mouth in your praise, knowing that even greater intellects rightly succumb to you. For what should I mention first concerning the praise of your affection or esteem? You have bestowed upon me all the delights of countryside, character, and—greater than all these—love; or certainly, if any of these were lacking, it should be attributed to circumstance, not charged to you. [Note: Perhaps *oris*, “of speech,” rather than *ruris*, “of countryside.”]

For I found with you everything that a dear heart possessed and that the world held bright. You deprived me of no pleasure whatsoever; indeed, through your proximity you made the desert of my little lodging desirable to me. And for this reason I rejoice all the more to be your neighbor, because one who is joined to good people is not wholly bad.

But lest a longer speech, foolish in itself, bring you weariness, I offer you my most abundant greetings and inform you that I have sent the glass vessel, as you instructed. Its workmanship ought to imitate brilliance, not fragility, so that the affection left to us by our parents, handed down by our teacher, and strengthened by the fellowship of life, may be polished by adversity and not be broken by any storm.

For just as the precious purity of gold and silver, if corrupted by an admixture of bronze, lead, or any other cheaper material, cannot possess its natural brilliance or sound unless it is purified by the testing of fire, so it gives neither clarity to the eye nor a ringing tone to the ear; rather, when struck, it resounds hoarsely and harshly.

Therefore, brother most excellent, contemplating and following this judgment—not mine but the Lord’s—let us regulate our life midway, with the Lord himself as helmsman, so that when calm smiles upon us, a more favorable breeze invites us, and the tranquil sea caresses us, we may nevertheless know that the level surface of the sea beneath us can suddenly rise like mountains. Let us not allow our ship to be driven out into the deep, where storm may break it or wave engulf it.

## EPISTLE XIII

To his heart’s own lord, Celsus, Ruricius.

[Col. 0077D]

I have received the letter of your brotherly affection, which brought me no small anxiety. For I fear that you have judged my letters differently from the way they were sent by me. And therefore you seem to recall a rash presumption, since you ask me to pray for you and to admonish you repeatedly.

Would I, brother most excellent, dare to correct you, when I cannot correct myself? Would I correct you, who look upon me—still fluctuating amid the storms of the world, like a little boat amid the surges of the sea—as though you were already viewing me from a higher watchtower or a more elevated hill? Would I correct you, who are approaching the harbor of forgiveness through the indulgence of repentance, with the Lord as your helmsman? [Note: A verb is missing.]

I did not write in such a way, beloved brother, as to flatter myself while biting you with a condemning tooth, nor to wound you, but to bind you to me through the familiarity of a letter. For if you consider it carefully, those words concern prayers, not deeds; they belong more to one who wishes than to one who admonishes. I explained not what we were doing but how I wished us to live.

But if you examine the deeds of my past and present life, you will be ashamed, with my most intimate and secret brother as witness, to bear what I was not ashamed, with God as witness, to promise. [Note: Perhaps “to commit.”] For my crimes I hope that you will pray to the Lord rather, so that those whom he wished to be partners in friendships and kinship in this world, he may command to be participants in good things in the future.

## EPISTLE XIV

To his heart’s own lord, Celsus, Ruricius.

I have sent the horse you ordered: gentle in its docility, strong in its limbs, firm in its vigor, outstanding in form, [Note: Perhaps *Fartura*.] well-proportioned in build, and moderate in temperament—not excessively swift in speed, nor sluggish. Its bridle and spur are subject to the rider’s will; it has both the willingness and the strength to carry a burden, so that it neither yields beneath what is placed upon it nor casts off what has been loaded.

Having thus reported these matters as was appropriate, and having first offered greetings and distributed my promises, I ask you to promise that, God being favorable, you will deign to come to us together with your sister for the festival of the saints, to honor the patrons, show affection to the brothers, and offer favor to the people.

## EPISTLE XV

To his own particular patron in Christ the Lord, Bishop Eonius, [Note: He was bishop of Arles. He had certain disputes with Hilary, the successor of Leo; later, the Roman pontiff granted him the rights of a vicarate, which he had attempted to exercise without the pontiff’s knowledge. Ruricius mentions this Leontius frequently in Book II, Letters 39 and 41, and in Letter 48. BASN.] Ruricius.

Having learned of the holy passing of my lord Leontius, your predecessor, whose memory is venerable to me, I was confused in heart and mind and grieved for a long time and deeply: both because, impeded by my sins, I had not deserved to meet so great a bishop and because I had been deprived of such a father.

Although I did not enjoy the sight of his outward person, I was nevertheless delighted by the grace of his inward self and clung to him constantly with the vision of my mind. Through him and in him, he was in a certain way present to me: seen by my gaze, heard by my affection, touched by contact, and held in an embrace.

For beloved persons see one another nowhere better than in the heart, the seat of love itself. Hence I desired all the more to see with bodily eyes one whom I thus beheld with spiritual eyes.

Yet his merits, which had previously offered me consolation, gave consolation to my grief. For I trust that the one whom he loved with fatherly devotion he also protects through diligent intercession.

I have reported these things to Your Holiness as though conversing with you and seeking from you relief from this grief, with affection dictating my words. But now, to resume what I had begun to say, once I had learned of the accession of that lord and of your ordination to the apostolate, I was considering sending something in service to you.

Yet your gifts anticipated the service of my humility. They have given me greater confidence to write, because I presume that one whom you have deemed worthy of your generosity is not alien to your hearts. And therefore, as I understood from your words, since you deign to value me so highly, I offer abundant written greetings for the preservation of your blessedness. At the same time, by a particular prayer I ask that you deal with me with such affection that I may recognize that you have sent Lord Leontius ahead and exchanged him for yourself rather than lost him.

## EPISTLE XVI

To the venerable, admirable, and saintly brother Sidonius Videnti, Ruricius.

[Col. 0079B]

Long ago, when most celebrated report proclaimed your praises, I came to know you, and in the seat of love I beheld you with those eyes of the mind by which you yourself more rightly despise earthly things and contemplate heavenly and divine things. From this I assigned you the name of the one by whose gift I saw that you had been endowed.

And therefore, while I carefully love you in the mirror of my heart and intensely admire the beauty of your inner person, you have stirred the inward parts of my soul to longing. They have been moved by the purest affection for you to such an extent that I desire to see with bodily eyes the one whom I contemplate with spiritual eyes.

For this reason I offer you my most abundant greetings in Christ the Lord, and, speaking more personally, I ask that, together with my lord the bishop, whom I trust will come to us in accordance with his graciousness, you deign to do us the honor of visiting our humility. Thus, placed together, we may each derive fruit from the other’s presence: while the attention of the questioner becomes the instruction of the respondent, and mutual progress, in a certain sense, becomes the possession both of learner and teacher.

Peace, peace, peace.

## EPISTLE XVII

To Pomerius, lord of his soul and worthy of cultivation with all the inward parts of affection in Christ the Lord, Ruricius, bishop.

It is written, as you yourselves know better: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19)

If you charge anything against me, forgive me now, for you should know that the Lord has taken vengeance. Know that we have been led along such pathless roads and into such hidden solitudes that the mind shudders to retrace them, the spirit recoils, and speech cannot describe them.

For we came upon a path blocked by branches, narrowed by confinement, rough with thorns, closed by roots, overgrown with brambles, harsh through neglect, obstructed by piles of stones, covered by interwoven roots, and deep with swallowing mud. Thus, amid evils so varied and so numerous, the form of danger was not simple: the strength of the roots held the horses’ feet, while the rotten soil could not support them.

The path was stretched upward into the mountains and plunged deeply into valleys, so that we thought we were traveling across a billowing sea, with the blasts of raging winds arousing the waves, while the day was snatched from our eyes by mists and clouds.

For although a ray of sunlight shone upon the world, its brightness and warmth could not reach us because of the density of the forest. Along the ill-starred journey the tall growth of ferns pressed upon us, and the overflowing dew drenched us so thoroughly that, contracted by cold, or driven to it, we sought the warmth of a fire for many days during the dog days.

But when we had reached the place toward which our purpose was directed, surrounded by water and soaked through, we began to perish from thirst.
