For although, as we said, there was coldness in the air, there was warmth in the spring, fragrance in the river, heat in the field, and sultriness in the fortress.

To sum up everything in a brief statement: know that we traveled by such a road that no one would desire to go by it either to paradise—not to mention exile.

Therefore, since our Lord commanded me to encounter all these things and you to escape them, distinguishing my sins from your merits even by a visible journey, he ensured that you, who spiritually proceed along the narrow and difficult way, would not fall into these hardships, while we, who walk along the broad and spacious way, always looking backward, encounter its afflictions.

Pray to the Lord, whom we confess can do all things, that although by different roads he may nevertheless bring us together in one city: a city into which mercy can bring us, and merits you.

## EPISTLE XVIII

To his sweetest and kindred son Omacius, [Note: He was the presbyter most beloved by Ruricius. Eparchius used his assistance to obtain letters of recommendation for Aprunculus. See below, Book II, Letters 27 and 56. BASN.] Ruricius, bishop.

Know that my failure to write to your sweetness through Venerius was caused neither by negligence nor by any accusation, but by being occupied. I have therefore sent this letter through Amelius, in which I offer you my most abundant greetings and remind you always to remember your purpose.

May neither the appearance of something more pleasing divert your mind, already dedicated to God, from the path you have begun; nor a more harmonious sound corrupt your hearing; nor a sweeter taste infect you; nor a softer touch entice you; nor a more alluring scent lure you, allowing death to enter the soul through the windows of the body.

Nor, while holding the plow, should you look backward contrary to the Lord’s command, so that the furrow may lose the straight line. Rather, fix all your senses upon him to whom, under his inspiration, you have vowed yourself, and cling to him with your heart so firmly that, whenever the alluring form of any of the aforementioned vices strikes you, it cannot approach a breast fortified by steadfast faith and divine meditation.

And however much you may seem to be situated amid crowds, enter the chamber of your heart, shut your door, and do not cease to pray to the Lord (Matt. 6:6), so that he who sees in secret may say to you, as he said to holy Moses when Moses cried out to him not with his voice but with his heart: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14:15)

I hope that in such prayers you will also deign to remember me, and that the desire for the sweetest and most salutary rest may soon bring you to us—even if affection itself is what brings you back among us.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0081]

## EPISTLE ONE

To the most sublime and ever most devoted brothers in Christ the Lord, Namacius and Ceraunia, [Note: If I am not mistaken, this was Namacius, the same man to whom Sidonius Apollinaris wrote while he was living in Aquitania Secunda. He was a learned man who devoted himself to literature amid the watchful cares of military camps. When free from military service and from naval battles against the Saxons who harassed those shores, he devoted himself to hunting and alone possessed hunting dogs suited to rousing boars. He was doubtless wealthy, since he both hunted and built. His wife was Ceraunia, to whom, as to him, our Ruricius frequently writes. They had a daughter, who died young, as is clear from Ruricius’s third letter. There was another Namacius who became bishop of Clermont after Rusticus’s death; he must be distinguished from our Namacius. BASN.] Ruricius.

[Col. 0081A]

The ancient sages said that two friends have one soul. I proclaim and affirm that this is entirely true. For after I departed from your brotherhood, I feel myself divided and recognize that a part of me remained with you. I do not seem to myself to be whole in your absence.

And since I do not find myself in myself, I search for myself with you, having returned to you; and there I see that, to the extent you commanded me to leave myself behind, I carried away an equal measure of you with me.

And so, even before it occurs, with the Lord’s favor, the wished-for union of our pledges—our souls’ division already made between us, [Note: Perhaps “division” should be read here.] a division which those who love ought to embrace more as divine than avoid—will bring about in their hearts a complete and sincere transfusion of love.

I rejoice that I am bound to you by its chains, and I exult to be fettered by such bonds. I desire more to be bound by their interweaving than to be released. I trust that you too are constrained by them.

I offer your returning companions my most abundant greetings, and, giving thanks for everything, I leave unsaid what belongs to our praise. I indicate that I have remained silent because, as the saying goes, boasting in one’s own praises is hateful. Your praise has become mine, and therefore, as I said, I thought it better to remain silent about your greatness; for whatever I say about you, I seem to have bestowed upon myself.

## EPISTLE II

To the most sublime and ever most devoted brothers in Christ the Lord, Namacius and Ceraunia, Ruricius.

[Col. 0081C]

[The supplied source ends here, at the beginning of the letter.]

Among the other thanks which I rightly owe you, I offer immense gratitude for the presence and sight of our common patron, Lord Postuminus, because you caused your little lodging to be illumined by his prayers. For while he displays faithfulness toward you, he bestows a blessing upon us; and although he was a most vigilant inspector, a most importunate exactor, and a most rigorous executor, we nevertheless weighed all these things as light because of your favor and his holiness. For, as it is written: “Love endures all things; love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:7), especially since we believe that what he seemed to demand from us he conferred upon us by God’s favor.

Therefore, when he returned to his own city [Note: Manuscript: *propria dicivitate*. But the syllable *di* has been erased. Should one read *propria de civitate* (“from his own city”), or *proprium in civitatem* (“his own into the city”)?], I gave him what I gave not because it was necessary, but because he wished it; and I offer my most abundant greetings to your indivisible brotherhood. I anticipate in my mind both my journey and your presence, and I declare that everything has been inspected, handed over, and secured, just as you commanded and as was worthy and proper. Nor do I fear that your spirits should be offended even slightly because you see one word removed from the little book of the dowry, since you acknowledge that what is lacking in number has not merely been compensated but even increased in value.

## EPISTLE III

To the most exalted lords and most devoted brothers in the Lord Christ, Namacius and Ceraunia, Ruricius.

How grievously I have been struck by the cruelty of the messenger’s report concerning your bereavement, you can more easily infer from our mutual love than I can disclose in writing. For my spirit, exhausted by excessive sorrow, refuses to set forth what it shudders to recall. I grieve, most devoted brothers, over your exceedingly bitter calamity, and I sympathize with you with all my heart. For although at present I am separated from you in body, I am nevertheless always joined to you in mind; and while I do not withdraw from you in spirit, I believe that I am present at your lamentations. For, according to the divine pronouncement, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it in the body.

For we are incorporated into Christ not only by faith, but are also bound together by the union of children. Therefore, if such an excess of cares had permitted it, I myself would have come to comfort you in place of a letter. But what are we to do, best of brothers? Just as we cannot resist the divine command by our strength, so neither ought we to resist it by our will. With every vigilance we must guard against this: while we bewail our dear pledges with excessive grief, we might seem blasphemous or in some way injurious toward the Lord, and the author of our soul might pierce it more grievously, upon finding an opportunity, than He struck it through the loss of our loved ones.

Therefore, in every bitterness and sorrow we must flee to Him, and refer all our calamities to Him with our whole heart—Him who heals the wounded, raises up the sorrowful, and comforts the afflicted. And that saying of holy Job must be uttered without qualification: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Accordingly, lords of my heart, I have ventured to write these things to you so that, although I knew I could not lessen our common grief by my words, I might at least moderate it in some measure by divine utterances. And truly you can draw no small consolation from Christ’s will: although premature death awaited him, He deemed him worthy to assume him as one of those to whom He said the kingdom of heaven belonged (Matt. 19:14). Thus you have a patron in your son, and you may grieve less for one whom you saw taken up by the Lord.

## EPISTLE IV

To the most exalted lords and most devoted brothers in the Lord Christ, Namacius and Ceraunia, Ruricius.

More than once, dearest brothers, I resolved to write to you or come to you because of the exceedingly bitter calamity of our common bereavement. But bodily weakness always drew me back from preparing for the journey, and excessive grief of heart drew me back from the duty of writing. For whenever I tried to direct my mind toward writing, my senses immediately shuddered and my mind recoiled; and so, instead of words, tears always came to me, so that I would first drench the page with a rain of tears before painting upon it with my pen, just as that father said, revealing his affection at the loss of his son:

> Twice he tried to depict the calamity in gold;  
> twice the hands of his country fell.

Or, rather, to put it in words of my own: “Because my soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:3). And not without cause. For I have lost a daughter whom I rejoiced to have received as my own and whom I rejoiced that you had brought forth; I have lost the consolation of life, the hope of posterity, the honor of the family, the joy of my heart, the light of my eyes. Nor have I been struck by a simple bereavement. For together with my daughter I have lost brothers, in whose affection I found consolation and in whose union I gloried.

Our bond of brotherhood has been broken, dearest brothers; the pledge of our mutual love has been taken from us. Alas for me, best of brothers: while I lose your trust, by whose entrusting you had won me, I have lost you as well. And therefore, at the loss of one relationship, I sigh that the consolations of many relationships have been taken from me. Yet I shall not lose the one homeland which was acquired for me through her, since I shall judge that land especially to be my homeland which she occupied with her body.

But where am I proceeding, driven by grief, forgetful of duty yet mindful of gratitude? Why am I reopening, through renewed recollection as though by a fresh incision, a wound that time had to some extent covered? And why, though I wished rather to console you through divine promises, do I myself receive no consolation?

Nevertheless, I shall explain to you the causes of this renewed grief. For my mind, exhausted by sorrow, had at last begun in some measure to receive consolation from the apostolic exhortation that says: “I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4:13). But when our unhappy common [relative] arrived, and I saw him without the jewel by which he had previously shone, through which he had been both more acceptable and more pleasing to me, he appeared to me disfigured, as though stripped of his own adornment.

He knows, dearest brothers, who searches the hidden things of hearts, how suddenly my grief was doubled, and how day by day my sorrow was multiplied by the excellence of that one and the desolation of this one, so that I cannot look upon the latter or remember the former without tears. Thus I shall often say that prophetic utterance: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1). But he was mourning the sins of his people; I, however, mourn my own sins, which have weighed upon both me and you by their burden and their number. I mourn so that I may lament his death and my life, her death and my survival.

You, venerable sister, had presumed something very different of me, as though on the basis of our merits, when, deceived by excessive love, you promised yourself so much from our prayers—despite my denying it—that you believed your household would be saved through our intercession and that your daughter, so to speak, would become immortal through me. But my merits soon appeared, wounding me with an incurable wound and striking you, who had believed otherwise than you ought concerning a sinner, with the bereavement of so great a pledge.

Now, at least, venerable sister in the Lord Christ, you will recognize both that you believed falsely and that I spoke truly. But for too long, forgetful of heavenly precepts, we have yielded assent to human grief. We must return to the divine commandments, lest we mourn her, dead in body, in such a way that we ourselves die in heart.

Therefore, leaving present things aside for a little while, let us think again about the future, so that what the present weakens, the future may strengthen. We, dearest brothers, must bear that condition of human frailty which the prophets, the apostles, and all the holy and righteous have borne—or, greater still, which our Lord, the Lord of all, deemed worthy to assume.

We should not lament, but rather give thanks to God and rejoice, that we possessed a daughter such as we desired, whom the God who had given her promised to us. Indeed, we have changed her place; we have not lost her. We have sent her ahead to Christ, at His command. To have children is a general blessing; to have good children is a special reward. To live is common to all; to live well and to depart well from this life belongs to few—not because of the condition of nature, but because of guilt; not by divine ordinance, but by personal will.

Therefore, let our heart not be troubled, and let us mourn our daughter not because of loss but because of longing, lest we seem unbelieving toward the Lord’s promises or forgetful of His command. Let those who cannot have the hope of resurrection mourn their children—their unbelief, not the divine decree, deprives them of it. Let the dead mourn their dead, since they believe them to have perished forever. Let those who do not believe that the dead have rest find no rest for their grief.

But for us, whose hope and portion is Christ—hope in the land of the dying, portion in the region of the living—for us, whose death is not the end of nature but of the present life, since we believe that it will be restored to something better, we must say with the Apostle: “When this corruptible body has put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:54); and with the prophet: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). For repentance must be maintained in temptation, lest it compel us to sin either in word or in heart.

Therefore, let a ready faith wipe away your tears, since we believe that our dear ones have not so much lost life as changed it. We see them leaving a world full of sorrows and hastening to the region of blessedness; leaving a painful pilgrimage and reaching the homeland of rest. Hence the prophet says: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141:8).

Believe me, dearest brothers: she is now secure in her own rest and concerned for our salvation. If she could converse with us, she would say this: “Do not weep for me, pious parents; do not, through the lamentation of excessive love, prove ungrateful toward so good a Lord. Granted that at the time of my departure your affection behaved thus; now faith ought to temper your grief with time. For although I am dead to you, I live to the living God.

“Can you love me more than the Lord, who made me; who gave me life, bought and redeemed me because He wished to; and when He wished, received me according to His goodness? Or what greater consolation for your grief can you have than that our Lord deemed it worthy to hand over His only Son to death for us? When the Son of God was willing to die according to the flesh, should a human being receive the condition of the human lot so bitterly?

“Therefore, most loving parents, mourn your own sins instead, and think about satisfaction for your crimes. Thus, if you love me in Christ—for you cannot truly love me unless you love me in the Lord—you may deserve to come into the bosom of the patriarch, where the Lord has appointed me because of my innocence [possibly: His innocence] and because of His goodness, since ‘His mercy is better than life’ (Ps. 62:4). There we may rejoice together, not in false but in true joys, not in temporal but in eternal joys.”

It is fitting that you, best of brothers, be consoled by such instructions and by similar divine promises [the text has the corrupt form *sponsibus*]. For just as future things are already present with the Lord, so the faithful Catholic ought to regard the heavenly promises—which he confidently trusts will be fulfilled in their own time—as in some sense already present: to possess them beforehand through hope and faith, and to obtain them through works.

These are the things that offer us consolation in sorrows, confidence in adversity, and moderation in prosperity, so that we are neither lifted up by good fortune, nor yield to adversity, nor consumed by grief. These things, then, dearest brothers, I have dictated for transmission to you as a common consolation, not without great sorrow of spirit. Nor did an abundance of words compel me to extend my discourse somewhat further, but rather the heat of our hearts, so that frequent remembrance might gradually soften the longing kindled by memory. In this also let us demonstrate equal gratitude toward our common daughter, and just as her life had bound us together, so may her memory preserve us in that same love.

## EPISTLE V

To the exalted lord and most devoted brother in the Lord Christ, Namacius, Ruricius.

When we seek an opportunity to write as the right of affection demands, we ought not to let an offered occasion pass us by, so that a considered message, once sent out and not lost, may return to us a portion of your presence. It is given and possessed; it seems to depart, yet does not depart; it is sent by me and received by you; written by me and read by you. Yet it is not divided, since, although apparently divided, it is held whole in the hearts of both.

For, after the manner of the divine word, it is handed over and does not go away; it is bestowed upon the needy and is not taken from its author. It is the gain of the recipient without loss to the giver, enriching the poor without impoverishing the possessor.

## EPISTLE VI

To his own lord and special patron in the Lord Christ, Cronopius, bishop, Ruricius, bishop.

In organizing or governing the Lord’s flock, there ought to be reason, not presumption, among overseers and superiors; concern for guardianship, not contention over seizure. Otherwise they may incur the charge of mercenaries, since they do not maintain the discipline of shepherds; and they may be found, as the Apostle says, to seek not the glory of Christ but their own (1 Thess. 2:6), preferring to receive praise from human beings rather than await their reward from the Lord—seekers of present gain and scorners of eternal reward.

Therefore, as that same Apostle teaches (Rom. 12), if we are united in peaceful assembly for holy work, loving without hypocrisy, serving with diligence, and members of one head, we ought unanimously to govern the body. For the folds of the Lord’s flock may be many in number, but they must not be diverse in faith.

Thus, as the Lord Himself deigned to foretell, let us not quarrel through envy and divide the Lord’s flock through dissension, so that a manifold schism proceeds from us. Rather, by the unity of doctrine, let us gather the Lord’s simple sheep, so that there may be in us “one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16). Just as He is King of kings and Lord of lords, priest of priests and high priest of high priests, so He should also be understood as shepherd of shepherds.

Therefore, out of zeal for charity, not greed, with these [letters; perhaps *cum his*], I have sent my presbyter to your Holiness concerning the diocese of Gemiliacum, about which I wrote to you some time ago, lest my silence be attributed to negligence rather than concord. You see that not a few irrational persons have yielded to reason [Note: The passage is corrupt]. If you recognize that what I say is true, or that what I repeat is just, do not allow me to endure injury any longer, nor yourselves to endure disturbance any longer.

## EPISTLE VII

To the exalted and ever magnificent brother Elafius, Ruricius [Note: He had built an altar, or rather a church, in a fortress of the Ruthenians surrounded by mountains, at a time when scarcely anyone else dared to repair ancient structures. He invited Sidonius to consecrate it, as is clear from Sidonius, Epistle 15, Book IV. Others call him Eriphius, wrongly, I believe. BASN.], bishop.

Thus, by God’s favor, the fame of your works has spread so widely that all who are engaged in labors earnestly beg to be commended to your brotherhood by every effort of prayer. For they do not doubt that their weariness will find a favorable result with you.

Accordingly, the bearer of this letter, named Ulfila, whom the presbyter Fraretrius commended to me in his own letter [Note: Or *Frasetrius*], asked for letters of recommendation to you. I gladly granted them, both because of the divine command and because of our mutual obligation. To your indivisible charity I offer my fullest greetings, and I have ventured to commend the aforesaid man out of brotherly affection, not by pontifical authority.

For in a sinner, dignity loses dignity; an honor not deserved is a burden rather than an honor. Although I trust that, because of our devotion to one another, this will please you, nevertheless, if you show us any true or vicarious love, I hope that you will grieve rather than rejoice. For so great a matter does not exalt me, unworthy and wholly undeserving as I am; it weighs me down.

## EPISTLE VIII

To the holy and apostolic lord Aenius, my patron and pope, who is to be honored above all others by me with especially devoted reverence and affection in the Lord Christ, Ruricius, bishop [Note: Read *Aeonius*, who at that time was bishop of Arles and, as they say, the Roman pontiff’s vicar throughout Gaul. BASN.].

Whenever holy or apostolic men—commended by works of mercy, by the merits of their deeds, by the life that springs from merit, and by the fame of every virtue—are compelled, weighed down by the burden of their troubles, to seek assistance, while they seek relief from the labor of writing, they confer a benefit upon our desire. And although their labor is our sorrow, their need nevertheless becomes, through the exercise of our office, in some way our charity. While we comply with their request, we satisfy our own will; and thus the poverty of the petitioner becomes the advantage of the giver.

Accordingly, I gladly granted letters of recommendation to our brother and fellow presbyter, Possessor by name [Note: The manuscript has a faulty reading, and one that is worse]. He is a possessor more by piety than by means, since he poured out what he had for the redemption of his brother and became a possessor of paradise when he ceased to be a possessor of worldly property.

If your Holiness deigns to learn his need more fully, kindly review the letter which our brother Eumerius, bishop, sent through him to my humility; and at once you will recognize how you ought both to assist him according to your custom and to sympathize with him out of mutual charity. To set his brother free from enemies, he preferred to become captive to creditors; and so that the other might not be deprived of life by a most cruel death, he himself became an exile from his homeland.

Following the saying of the holy apostle Paul [Note: The manuscript formerly read *contuenter*], in which he writes to the Romans: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I often resolved to come to you, but until now I have been prevented” (Rom. 1:13), we too are compelled, urged on by shame, to say: “We wished more often to send writings to your most sincere piety, but until now we have been prevented”—prevented, to be sure, by him who is accustomed always to oppose a good will, envying our progress and your affection, our affection and your progress; our progress and your affection.

For your instruction is our education, and our letter is the consolation of your longing. And again, your progress and our affection: our education is your reward [Note: “And always the consolation of our longing is the affection of your discourse.”]. [The text here is corrupt: “and the times, the communication of your longing, are the affection of your discourse.”]

For in the few days which your affection truly made both few and very brief for me, while our gaze could not be satisfied by contemplating you but grew more ardent through seeing you, since we desired you present and sought you placed before us for this very purpose, you watered our senses from the purest spring of your kind heart. Thus, even if afterward I received no precious gifts from your holy mouth, I nevertheless possess your presence within the hidden places of my mind, and I behold your image in the mirror of my heart—the image which your perfect charity painted there, so that no forgetfulness of age can erase it, since it is renewed at every moment by continual remembrance.

There I converse with you more secretly, according to your customary piety. There too I consider the formation of a better life. There I kiss you with the lips of my mind and embrace you with the hands of my heart. Hence true love, which is nourished alive in my inmost being by the image of your face and kindled by the spark of charity, promises me a return of your affection; and my spirit stands as guarantor to me for your spirit. When I ask the heart conscious of mutual love how much I ought to presume upon you, it answers me.

Therefore, now that your prayers have at last opened an avenue for my writing, I send this greeting and ask for your intercession on behalf of sinners. In a special prayer I ask this: that by your continual petitions you implore the mercy of our God for all my offenses and, with your customary clemency and abundant goodness assisting, beseech Him to command that we reach the same harbor of rest, even if not the same reward.

Thus, insofar as here we cannot often see one another with bodily eyes because of the distances between our lands, may we at least there rejoice in mutual presence. When the just Judge bestows upon you the crown of your merits, may forgiveness of my offenses not be denied me by the most merciful Redeemer and most perfect Advocate [Note: The manuscript reads *ommissorum*, possibly *omissorum*].

May He Himself deign to plead the sinner’s case before the judgment, lest He punish his guilt at the judgment, since the Almighty knows how neither to destroy the truth of judgment through the goodness of mercy nor to lose the goodness of mercy through the severity of judgment.

Therefore, through the ineffable working of mercy and power, may He grant you this: that those whom He has joined here in truth He may not separate there in dwelling.

Recalling your promise, I make this special request: may your Holiness not only refrain from keeping our brother Pomerium, but even compel him to come to us, and send us his share, undivided between us both. And if he comes to me, do not judge that he is departing from you, because you will find him here in me, and, with your body remaining [there], as we trust, you will come with him in your heart. You may also gain no small fruit from this, if our rusticity makes some progress in the fear of God through his teaching.

## EPISTLE IX

To Pomerium, lord of his soul and abbot, especially cherished in the inmost heart in the Lord Christ, Ruricius, bishop.

The wise men of this world said that two friends have one soul. I confirm this as true also by ecclesiastical testimony, which says: “The believers were of one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32). One, certainly, in charity, not in number; in the simplicity of faith, not in the singularity of person.

This I proclaim and prove. For ever since I departed from your unity, I feel myself divided, and I recognize that my own part has remained with you. Nor do I believe myself whole in your absence. When I do not find myself within myself, I seek myself among you, returning to you; and there I perceive that, as much of myself as I left with you, so much of you I carried away with me.

And I give thanks to almighty God for so astonishing a work of His, since He has deigned to grant, through a general dispensation, that among those whom distances of place separate, the spirit may travel freely, confined by no laws of absence; and that nothing should be so impenetrable that it would not lie open to the eyes of the mind. Through the gaze of the heart, dear ones may behold one another, by the grace passing between them, wherever charity itself resides.

Therefore, offering my fullest greeting to your piety, whose disposition toward me, as I infer from my own mind, is most full, I earnestly ask this: if you return an affection equal to ours; if you love us with a similar charity; if our love works within your inmost being; if our affection reaches to the marrow of your heart; if the sweetness of your power over me has subdued you for my sake as mine has subdued me for yours, so that you can neither resist nor wish to resist its command—then, longing for a longing brother, I shall hasten to come to you as soon as possible, both to discharge the debt of my promise through your kindness and to soothe our mutual affection.

When we are placed face to face, we shall offer you equal grace through our sight and conversation; and if you love as you are loved, as much will be rendered by me to your charity as you yourself have shown to mine. Nor need you fear the weariness of finding the journey. For, as that man said, love conquered the hard road. And according to our Apostle: “Love endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7); it neither seeks what is its own nor ever knows excess.

It is also fitting that the mildness of autumn should accord with the affection of a traveler who longs to come, provided that the heat of the summer just past kindles it and the cold of the approaching winter does not extinguish it.

## EPISTLE X

Also, a letter of Lord Ruricius.

After rereading my letters, you may perhaps wonder that I have written to you as to a brother, when this is appropriate neither to our age nor to your honor. For just as you are older than I am in years, so you are younger in rank. And therefore, if we had considered, God willing, either your long life or our respective offices, we ought to have written either to a father or to a son.

But since the holy apostle John also writes in his first epistle, chapter 1, to the same people—to fathers, young men, and children—saying: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known Him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one. I write to you, children, because you have known the Father,” by this distinction of words he assigns not the age of the outward person but the quality of the inward one.

To the extent that we advance in knowledge and love of God, we are undoubtedly called fathers. To the extent that we fight manfully against the adversary who, like a lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8), we are recognized as young men. But insofar as we give ourselves over to sluggishness and indolence, fail through weakness of faith to walk the road of the commandments, and rise more sluggishly, as though from sleep, from the preoccupation with secular activities in order to observe and carry out the divine commands, we are rightly judged to possess the levity of children.

Hence the apostle Paul admonishes the negligent in this way: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and you will touch Christ,” or, “Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

And when those standing around Him said in the Gospel, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are seeking you, wishing to see you” (Matt. 12:47), the Lord answered: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And pointing to the apostles who followed Him, He said: “Are these not the ones who do the will of my Father?”

We can be called Christ’s mother when we carry Christ in our hearts. For holy Mary, who conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin, conceived our Lord not through a man’s embrace but through faith acting as a bridegroom.

We become His brothers when we order, support, and adorn our life with every kind of virtue, so that we may be able to be “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). For who could doubt that, if we become heirs of God the Father, we may most rightly also be called Christ’s brothers, since He Himself adopts us? He fashioned us as His own, redeemed us as strangers, chose us as servants, and received us as sons.

He fashions us by His power, redeems us through His passion, and adopts us in grace through His foreknowledge. Yet we are sons by adoption, while He alone is Son by nature. To recall us to the same blessedness from which we had fallen, He, without ever ceasing to be what He was, nevertheless willed to be what He was not, so that the Word might become flesh.

And while the Creator descended into the humility of the creature, the creature ascended to the sublimity of the Creator. Thus divine things communicate themselves to humanity, and human things participate in divinity, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> Though He was in the form of God, He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted Him and granted Him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:6).

Hence the same teacher, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Accordingly, we know no one according to the flesh. Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know Him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16), because bodily weakness having ceased in Him, He is believed to be wholly in divine power.

And therefore, according to the same Apostle, since “we are all one in Christ” (Gal. 3:28), we are most rightly called brothers, because one womb—the sacred font—poured us forth, and the same breasts of Mother Church nursed us together with life-giving Spirit.

For this reason, brother, I have written to you: I have learned that, God willing, you have turned your soul from the activities of the world toward eternal blessedness, and that you have become an imitator of that merchant in the Gospel who, after selling all that he possessed, bought the most precious pearl; or of the man who, having found a treasure in a field, sold everything he had and bought the field itself in a praiseworthy desire (Matt. 13:44).

You are not an importunate coveter of another’s possession, but a prudent distributor of your own means, retaining charity, as the most sincere thing, in a perfect heart—not in order to sell more sparingly, but to lend more generously.

I rejoice over this deed and give thanks to God, who, according to the riches of His goodness and power, through His immeasurable mercy, deigns, so to speak, to come almost against His own pronouncement. For He Himself said that it is difficult for those who possess money to attain the kingdom of heaven. Behold, He has deemed you worthy of these things even in this world, and hastens to advance you in the kingdom.

Yet the same Lord immediately tempered the severity of that earlier pronouncement, which the apostles feared so greatly, by the moderation of His mercy, saying that what was impossible for human beings by nature was possible for God in them by grace.

I therefore exhort you, out of mutual affection, since you eagerly devote yourself to this work with every expenditure, to persist as a vigorous builder in the construction of that tower which the Lord commanded to be built in the Gospel, so that your adversaries may have more to grieve over its completion than to laugh over its interruption.

## EPISTLE XI

To the exalted and ever magnificent brother Praesidius, Ruricius, bishop.

Many people, trusting that I possess great influence with your indivisible exaltedness not because of the merit of my life but because of the privilege of our friendship, seek letters of recommendation from me by which they may excuse themselves before you. Because of the requirements of our office, we cannot refuse these to them—not through the audacity of presumption but through the discipline of our ministry.

We desire to provide them with the consolations of the present life and you with those of the eternal life, so that they may be reserved through your patience for repentance, and you may reach forgiveness through mercy. As Scripture says: “There will be judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13). For He who said, “Forgive, and it will be forgiven you” (Luke 6:38), will doubtless restore in the future what He sees a person doing here that He commanded.

His truth is present to us; may our faith not be absent from Him. Hence you can understand most clearly that the absolution of your wretched dependents is the forgiveness of sins, and that what you have granted to others is to be conferred upon you through your prayers, according to His saying in the Gospel: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2).

Therefore, on behalf of Urso and Lupicinus, who came to me to intercede for their crimes, as though I were bound to you by a special right of charity, as I said above, I approach you as a supplicant. First, may you deign to forgive God, and then us, what they have committed, and [*infieri*: a corrupt reading; Note: The word is corrupt]; and do not bring shame upon us because of their condemnation, since, when they were brought before my humility, they believed themselves to have been absolved.

## EPISTLE XII
I rejoice that, amid the adverse and varied storms of this world’s sea, you have at last brought your vessel into the harbor of salvation, with the Lord as pilot. Established in that secure and tranquil anchorage, you will laugh at the heat of the treacherous, wicked, and bitter sea itself. Henceforth you will not fear those things about which you formerly had little fear; rather, you will be able to possess much joy, as you look back upon them, left behind, or look down upon them from a higher watchtower, marveling that you have escaped. It remains for you, inserting your hand into the helm, always to gaze attentively at the stars and spread the sail of the voyage you have begun, lest either a more violent gust throw you into the deep or the rocks near the shores dash you to pieces.

Nor, according to the judgment of the Lord Savior, should you now hold the plow and, startled by the cries of collapsing Sodom, imitate Lot’s wife by looking back (Gen. XIX, 26). Or, having already departed from Egypt and crossed the waves of the Red Sea hanging to right and left (Exod. XVI, 4)—waves bringing you such great help while preparing destruction for your pursuers, as the Lord both prepares and illuminates your way—and having undertaken the arduous journey through the wilderness, should you remember the pots of meat or the onions, which, in the manner of bodily pleasures, are known to be corrupted by their very nature: foul, neither pleasant in use, nor sweet in odor, nor destined to endure. Such is everything in this world that delights the ear, softens the touch, charms the sight, flatters in order to ensnare, serves in order to hold, and entices in order to kill. For whatever pleasure you may wish to seize, what punishes remains, while what delights passes away; fleeting sweetness goes by, but the conscience that will condemn—or must be condemned—remains.

Hence Solomon also says: “The tongue of a prostitute drips honey; but in the final days you will find it more bitter than gall” (Prov. V, 3). Yet, although he himself had foretold this, he nevertheless fell into it. And therefore see, dearest brother, how evil is that which, while detested, is admitted; while shunned, is scarcely avoided. Hence you too, as Scripture says, “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23), and examine your conscience, lest, though you seem by outward appearance to have departed from something, you remain attached to it in affection. Rather say to the Lord with the prophet: “My soul has clung to you; but your right hand has received me” (Ps. LXII, 9). Or also: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Thus, with as much labor and perseverance as you served the world, serve God; as the Apostle says, or admonishes: “I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. But now, freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and your end is eternal life” (Rom. VI, 19).

Patience, dearest brother, must be embraced not merely in name but in practice; it must be exercised not only with the mouth but with the heart. It is true that, just as we sin through both the inner and the outer person, so we must repent through both, so that, as the same Apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Thus let our heart conceive groans as conscience pierces it, so that our mouth may pour them forth through a confession of shame.

The fiftieth psalm, dedicated alike to repentance and forgiveness, should be sung day and night with groaning and weeping, so that one may truly and beneficially say: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. XXXVII, 9). And: “I acknowledge my iniquities” (Ps. L, 5). And: “My sin is always before me” (ibid.). Or also: “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Ps. XXXVII, 19). Our sins must be before us here, so that they cannot be against us forever. For thus it is read in the prophets: “Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26). From whom, then, shall we declare or bring forward our iniquities first before the Lord, if not from the devil, who is both the instigator and the accuser of sins? He urges us to sin; he accuses us when we have sinned. Therefore, in this world, we should forestall him in confessing our crimes, lest in the future he have anything to bring against us.

## LETTER XIII

Ruricius, bishop, to the most blessed and venerable brothers in Christ, the priests Foedamius and Vilicus.

[Note: They were priests of the diocese of Limoges, who had previously been involved in disputes with their bishop Ruricius. BASN.]

Although I did not receive your brotherly letter through the subdeacon Contimtus [Note: Perhaps “the subdeacon Contimtus.”], nevertheless I sent this letter to you through him, prompted by affection, so that I might satisfy your desire and, being the elder, first open a way for writing, lest an excuse be left available in the future and the matter be said to arise from unwillingness, distrust, or embarrassment.

I therefore offer your blessedness my abundant greeting in Christ the Lord, and I hope that, as befits ecclesiastical men, you love me not with your lips but with your heart, and that in conversation you will dare to speak of your former sincere affection for me. For if it had been genuine, it would have remained; and if it had been changed [Note: That is, “otherwise”], it would not have been changed. Yet on whose side the change occurred, let our conscience know, and let the knower of consciences know without any witness asserting it. I call him as witness to my declaration: that I was not guilty of beginning the quarrel, and that nothing done or said has remained in my heart, because I know that the eternal and true Judge has told us that, unless we forgive our brothers from the heart, we ought not to be forgiven.

You have, then, my pledge; return to me your faith. For in my letter you unquestionably have the bond you choose: either that of charity, which beneficially binds and guards, or that of treachery, which culpably entangles and destroys. Nor should you charge me with anything concerning the judgment of former times, because it is my settled principle to preserve concord in assemblies and to maintain strictness in judgments.

I rejoice especially at this also: I have learned that you have returned to the complete familiarity of my lord and brother. It remains for your “insequilla” [Note: A corrupt word; perhaps “insequella.”] in the Lord to preserve what his grace has granted for your good.

## LETTER XIV

Ruricius, bishop, to the venerable and, in Christ the Lord, magnificent daughter Ceraunia, worthy of special honor and affection.

[Note: See above, Letter 1, Book I.]

[Col. 0094B]

The reason I did not previously send you a painter was this: I believed that, because of the arrival of the new judge, you were occupied and so frightened that you could not think about these matters. But when, by God’s favor, I learned from both your letters and the reports of your people that you were conducting your affairs successfully and were in good health, after first sending my greetings I dispatched the painter with his pupil, although he was busy here, because I preferred to diminish my own need in order to satisfy your request.

But because both your purpose and our duty demand it, I have ventured to admonish your reverence briefly in these few words, so that from his work you may take an example for practicing repentance and putting on the garments of the new person, by which the old Adam may more easily die within you and the one who gives life may arise. Just as he paints walls with many colors by varied skill, so may you adorn your soul, which is God’s temple, with the various kinds of virtues, so that you may truly say spiritually of your spiritual house with the prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your dwelling, and the place where the glory of your dwelling is” (Ps. XXV, 8; Acts VII, 48).

For according to the judgment of our Lord himself, “God does not dwell in things made by hand” (Acts XVII, 24), nor is he pleased by the tents of a man; rather, he is pleased with those who fear him and with the one who hopes in his mercy. Again he deigns to teach us through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what place will be my rest? Has not my hand made all these things? And upon whom else shall I look, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 1).

And the Lord himself cries out in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28), and the rest that follows. Therefore, dearest sister and daughter in Christ the Lord, having laid aside the ambition of your former way of life, you ought to put on humility of heart, lend mercy to those in need, and preserve chastity not only of body but also of soul. In order that, with the Lord’s help, you may both acquire and guard these things, you must fast frequently and pray always, because Adam was appointed both guardian and cultivator of paradise (Gen. II, 15): namely, so that freedom of choice might have material for work, and so that what diligence in prayer had obtained might be guarded by abstinence from food. But because he neglected to preserve fasting for himself, through forbidden desire he lost both life and immortality.

Under Zerubbabel [Note: “Zorobabel.”], those who had returned from captivity were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, while they were engaged in a struggle against foreigners for the restoration of those same walls; “they worked with one hand and fought with the other” (2 Esdras IV, 17). That is, with the left hand they held out the shield of faith against their adversaries, while with the right they built the walls of good works, like courses of stones fitted together. Those men who were building, together with their prophets, worked with their loins girded, as the Lord also commands us to observe in the Gospel, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII, 35). One is girded about the loins when his flesh serves chastity and not lust; and his mind shines like a burning lamp, which Christ kindles with his commandments.

For all these things, according to the Apostle, happened as a figure of us (1 Cor. X, 6). We should understand that, as long as we were occupied with the affairs of the world, we served like captives of the Babylonians and their king, led away from Judea into the land of our enemies. Therefore, returning through repentance to our homeland—that is, to heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of all the faithful—we must restore what has fallen, mend what has been torn, erase the past, beware of the present, and prepare for what is to come. Thus, by the Lord’s kindness, drawn away from our former captivity to sin, we may serve not the king of Babylon but Christ, the King of heaven, in Jerusalem, the city built for the congregation of the saints.

For this reason we ought to water our faces more with tears than with baths, so that we may say with the prophet: “For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10). We ought to subdue our body with tireless vigils and continual fasts, so that, exercising true judgment between soul and flesh, the flesh may not rule the spirit, but conquered flesh may serve the spirit.

The Lord gave us an example of this when, through an angel, he spoke to Hagar, Sarah’s slave-girl, who had preferred to abandon her mistress rather than obey her, saying to her: “Return and be subject to your mistress” (Gen. XVI, 9).

Devoted to all these labors and good works, you may be both perfect in your way of life and devout in confession, and in the kingdom of your Father—the one of whom the Lord says in the Gospel, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father” (Matt. XXIII, 9)—you may truly shine as Ceraunia, in accordance with your name, among that blessed throng, and become the maker of your own name. Concerning this splendor of works the Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify not you but your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16). His is both the giving and everything that is given.

For, according to the Apostle, “Every good gift descends from above, from the Father of lights”; from him both the will is granted and its accomplishment is provided. Repentance must not merely be obtained in name but carried out in action. Repentance is not an idle name; it acquires its laborious designation from the quality of its work. For one cannot be called repentant who commits things requiring repentance, but only the one who wipes away his former sins or stains through humility of heart, subjection of body, diligence in good works, constancy in prayer, continual groaning, bruising of the breast, and outpouring of tears, so that he may say with the prophet: “Do not remember our former iniquities” (Ps. LXXVIII, 8)—that is, not our daily ones. And: “I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed” (Ps. VI, 7). And: “I will water my couch with my tears” (ibid.). And again: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. XXXVII, 9). And again: “For I will declare my iniquities, and I will think upon my sin” (ibid., 19).

Therefore let our crimes be here before us and against us, so that they may not be able to stand against us on the day of judgment; and here, while we are placed in this condition, may we deserve to say with confidence: “I acknowledge my sin, and I have not concealed my injustices” (Ps. XXXI, 5). “I said, ‘I will declare against myself my injustices to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.”

It is certain that to the extent that your former way of life displeases you, to that extent you will please the Lord; and to the extent that you please yourself, you will without doubt displease him who says: “For he shatters the bones of those who please themselves” (Ps. CXL, 7).

Therefore, like the strictest censors, let us ourselves impose the severest penalties upon our faults, and let us in a certain sense become our own torturers and judges through various bodily sufferings. Then, at the time of that just examination, the King’s sentence will have nothing to condemn in those whom the discipline of a chastened life has already corrected here. For the just and merciful Judge does not judge twice for the same matter: he shows himself gentle to the one whom he finds here to have been harsh in satisfaction for his sins; kind to the one whom he knows in this life to have been strict with himself, according to the Gospel saying: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matt. X, 38). Or this: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Luke VI, 21).

Everything done in this world, whether good or evil, is brief, as the Lord has either promised or willed to be demonstrated by experience. Therefore we must be steadfast in enduring hardships for the love of God. For “if weeping remains until evening, joy follows in the morning” (Ps. XXIX, 6). Let us therefore now sow in tears what we shall then reap in joy (Ps. CXXV, 6).

These few words, spoken as encouragement for strengthening your faith, suffice as consolation for exhortation. Although I do not practice these things myself, I nevertheless exhort you to practice them. For I know that a reward is assigned to exhortation, since we read: “Weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII, 15). And lest you perhaps say in judgment: “I sought someone who would grieve together with me, but there was none; and someone to comfort me, but I found none” (Ps. LXVIII, 21).

But seek out in the divine Scriptures the more perfect and greater resources from which these things have been excerpted, if you wish either to complete what you have begun or to reach what has been promised. The Lord will grant you, as you seek in this way, knowledge together with strength, so that you may understand what you read and guard what you have understood. For when the Father of orphans and judge of widows discovers that you hope in him alone, he will grant your wards protection with fatherly compassion and lead you, through the reward of a judge, to your prize.

## LETTER XV

Ruricius, bishop, to the holy and apostolic lord Aeonius, bishop, patron and pope, whom I cherish above all others in Christ the Lord with special honor and affection.

[Note: He was bishop of Arles; see Letter 8. BASN.]

A short time ago I received a letter from your holiness in which you considered it appropriate to admonish me, with special affection, concerning my lack of duty, saying: “Nothing is superior to charity.” I strongly affirm that this is entirely true. In accordance with the Apostle, I call that charity perfect and sublime which proceeds from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. I, 5). According to the same Apostle, it is patient and kind; it is not inflated, does not envy, does not seek its own, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it believes all things and hopes all things (1 Cor. XIII, 4 ff.). Hence it never falls.

It is patient because, fixed upon God amid the world’s temptations and storms, it stands unmoved. It is kind because it delights in the progress of those near it. It is not inflated because it does not grow proud over the humble. It does not envy because it knows not how to envy an equal. It does not seek its own because, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, it places even the least before itself and purchases the advantages of others at the cost of its own disadvantages. It does not rejoice over iniquity because it knows no joy except in the prosperity of its brothers. It rejoices with the truth because it honors a friend with sincere, unfeigned affection; it does not mock him with false flattery but celebrates him with true honor. It believes all things because it trusts in the divine commandments and promises; and therefore it hopes all things, because it does not doubt that great things will be repaid for small, perpetual things for perishable, and eternal things for temporal.

It never falls because humility cannot have a fall, since it always has an ascent. Though it constantly meditates upon exalted things, it does not presume to dwell among the lofty. Though its way of life is regarded as being in heaven, it nevertheless appears to cling to earthly things; it possesses lofty works with a humbled mind, from which it may glory in the Lord, yet it is not exalted in the world.

Because you ordered me to write these things, I have ventured to do so, not out of confidence in my learning but out of regard for your condescension. It is yours to teach us by your words and always to summon us to this same charity by your example. For the affection that, before acquaintance, was begun and continually nourished through the exchange of letters between absent persons ought to be increased by bodily sight, and what began through speech ought to grow through personal presence.

## LETTER XVI

Ruricius, bishop, to the noble and always magnificent brother Turentius.

The affection of an anxious heart demands that the speech of one less skilled be brought forth; nor does it blush at the reproach of rusticity, provided that it fulfills the command of charity. As the holy Apostle says: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 18). For it is far better to love one’s neighbor sincerely than to preach perfectly.

Indeed, many more people in the world are found endowed with the charm of eloquence than perfected in the strength of love. For just as what is good is rare, so what is eternal is difficult. For, according to the Lord’s judgment, broad and well-trodden is the way that plunges into Gehenna; narrower and more difficult is the way that raises one to glory. Why is this, unless because many walk on the former and few on the latter?

And now, as the end of the present age approaches and the day of old age draws ever nearer—as our shorn hair also teaches us, or at least makes appropriate—let us take care not to meditate upon youthful deeds in our old years, and not to allow the desire of adolescence to reign in a worn-out body and decrepit heart. Otherwise, at the time of judgment, in that fearful examination of the eternal dispensation, when he who is the witness and judge of all mortals will weigh not only merits and deeds but also examine words and desires, and, according to his promise, will grant a reward for the offering of cold water (Matt. X, 41), while imposing punishment upon others for the frivolity of an idle word, he may establish us as guilty—not indeed of the pleasure of a deed committed, but at least of the will of desire.

For “whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). We should similarly observe this concerning all other matters, so that, after cutting away the members of this weak body that serve its various appetites, we may enter the kingdom maimed but whole, rather than being cast into eternal fire sound in body but ruined in soul.

Having profitably considered and properly examined all these matters, while time is granted us, let us turn away from evil and tirelessly do good (Gal. VI, 10). Let us forget the past, despise the present, and desire the future. Let us forget in our deeds and remember in our consciences, so that every sin may die for us in life and live in repentance. Let us now sow in weeping what we shall later reap in joy. For the time of this life is the time of work, while the day of repayment is the time of harvest, when without doubt what each person now scatters in seed will appear in his crop. As one of the saints said: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer me” (Gen. XXX, 33), calling the day of resurrection “tomorrow.”

We have ventured to write these things confidently to your fellowship, excellent brothers, not with pontifical authority but with brotherly affection, with charity dictating them; by them we wished to demonstrate toward you and concerning you not the skill of a dictator but the affection of a true brother.

Greeting you, I ask that, as you graciously promised, you send us without delay, by the bearer of this letter, Saint Augustine’s book On the City of God. While you build us up on earth through its reading, may you prepare for yourselves its city’s dwelling places in heaven. Yet we cannot reach that city in any other way than by ascending the steps of charity. For charity itself is the more excellent way, which joins you to God while you are placed here and leads you from this place to God. Concerning it the prophet also testifies: “They go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

Therefore let us sharpen here the eyes of our heart with the collyrium of good works, so that there we may be able to see God. For according to the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V, 8). Accordingly, the vision of the inner person must be prepared here, so that there its sight may not be dimmed.

## LETTER XVII

Ruricius, bishop, to the holy and most blessed lord Sedatus, bishop and pope, whom I specially cherish with particular honor and affection.

[Note: He was bishop of Nîmes, to whom Ruricius wrote frequently. BASN.]

You often reproach me and repeatedly charge me with the fact that until now I have not written to your indivisible blessedness in Christ the Lord. Would that the ability to do so were as great as the will to write, and that the affection conceived in the heart could be expressed by the mouth. But where expression is lacking, affection is silent; and within the hidden places of the breast the conscience is content with the knowledge that it is not guilty of a lack of love, even if it does not see itself equal in the repayment of services.

For it trusts that, just as a person may sense within himself the love of a brother through that brother’s reflection, so a loving brother may likewise recognize it from his own affection. Nothing measures the secrets of other hearts better than contemplation of our own hidden things. Thus great is the love we bear one another.

I therefore complied with your request and your command, so that I might send you writings woven together from whatever sort of words I could manage. If you love us simply, as I trust you do, you will either immediately destroy them, lest what is dear to you begin to be despised by others—for love and hatred do not listen with equal judgment—or else you will preserve them for rereading by yourself alone, so that whenever the fire of charity kindles in you the desire to see us, you may temper your longing through their conversation.

Indeed, so that you might more fully know the sincerity of our love toward you, we have ventured to cause you an injury. For we are certain that people do not so much desire to hear eloquent things as strong ones, nor pleasurable things as true ones. Therefore we believe that neither the length of our page will bring satiety to your piety nor our rustic speech disgust, knowing that the more you chew us over, the more ardently you will hunger.

## LETTER XVIII

Ruricius, a client, to his holy patron.

To Sedatus, obeying paternal admonitions,

he sings thanks and returns a greeting.

With gentle prayers, in fear, he asks him

lest perhaps the slight Muse displease

the judgment of so great a master.

Gladly return your eyes to these lines;

often turn them over with holy hands;

as you reread them, remember me.

May your tongue always recall me and sing of me,

may your mind hold me and sleep retain me,

may your little lips always sing me again.

Bury these words in your loving heart.

Recite them while seated beneath your roof,

while traveling along the road,

while among drinking cups, reclining in the forum,

and at frugal meals and sweet foods.

Recite them, enclosed in the cave of your breast

and the marrow of your heart,

with a singing mind,

so that we may also see one another’s faces

and that the God who grants life may permit us

to express in living words

the things that now weary the inmost heart—

God, giver of all good things,

Christ reigning eternally with the Father,

and the Holy Spirit, to whom fitting hymns are owed.

The verses end.

## LETTER XIX

Ruricius, bishop, to his ever-indivisible and always magnificent son Rusticus.

[Note: There were several men named Rusticus at that time. The author of the Annals of Marseille invented a Rusticus for himself as bishop of Marseille; he may instead have been bishop of Narbonne. The bishop of Narbonne held the second position in these Gallic provinces after the bishop of Arles. A letter of that Narbonese bishop to Eucherius was published by Sirmond. But since that man, already bishop from the year 430, had undoubtedly died by the time Ruricius was writing, when Ruricius was bishop only from about 470, there was another Ruricius, an illustrious man of Bordeaux, whom Sidonius calls Rusticus by name alone: “I see Rusticus only by name.” This was the man to whom Ruricius wrote Letters 19 and 53 of this book. BASN.]

A common friendship causes me anxiety through others, and causes you anxiety through me. For those who trust that I can do everything for you—not merely much—take refuge in our little church for their security. I cannot help but both grieve over their groans and obey their prayers, so that I may plead more earnestly with your authority both on account of their guilt and for your advancement as well.

Nor should you wonder that I said their guilt pertains to your advancement. For through your pardon their indulgence becomes forgiveness. Just as the poverty of the needy is known to be the abundance of those who give. What will be repaid to us in judgment is what we have provided in this world, as the Lord himself says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI, 38). And again: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 14).

Hence we clearly recognize that our God has placed his judgment in our own jurisdiction. He, the merciful and just hearer of our prayers, has prescribed for his authority the standard of our gentleness, so that in a certain sense he might not exercise the right of severity against those whom he has not seen here to be eager for vengeance. For he desires us to be what he is. He is merciful; he seeks the merciful, saying: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V, 48). Daily he grants forgiveness to sinners and suppliants; therefore he also asks indulgence from sinners.

Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say, following his teaching: “Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). By these words we bind ourselves with extremely harsh bonds unless we fulfill what we promise. The prophet likewise says: “A person holds anger against another person and seeks healing from the Lord” (Eccli. XXVIII, 3).

Therefore I approach as intercessor for Baxon, who has taken refuge in the church of Userca [Note: Perhaps “the bosom” or “womb” of the Church; unless one prefers to read “Usercha,” a geographical name. EDIT.], hoping that, first out of fear of God and then because of our intercession, you will deign to spare him. By absolving him, you can both remove shame from us and acquire a reward for yourselves.

## LETTER XX

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Capillutus.

Your frequent illness is unwelcome to me; it also seems to me a divine admonition by which our most gracious Lord prefers, in his great mercy, to chastise sinners rather than destroy them, so that illness may convict or correct those whom the length of their years has not corrected [Note: Perhaps “convince” or “correct.”], and they may lay aside the linen garment of the world and take up the Church’s garment, which is sackcloth, a sign of contrition. For “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L, 19).

He goes to heaven who has dashed himself against the ground. For “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 12). Hence that perfect penitent says: “My soul has clung to the pavement; Lord, revive me according to your word” (Ps. CXVIII, 25). What is “according to your word” except “according to your promise”? Whoever mourns his sins before you, pierced with remorse in this world, you bring into your kingdom, where thereafter he may sing securely: “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper. You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX, 12).

Therefore I urge your piety to carry out as soon as possible, with God’s help, what you have conceived. For death does not delay, as the Lord himself says: “Do not delay turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day” (Eccli. V, 8). For his anger comes suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.

Therefore, while we have time, let us turn to the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world. For without doubt merciful God grants his help to the one whom he sees attentive to his commandments.

## LETTER XXI

Ruricius, bishop, to Eufrasius, bishop.

[Note: He was the twelfth bishop of the Auvergne, successor of Aprunculus. He had already occupied the see of Die, where he received Quintianus humanely when Quintianus was fleeing the plots of the Goths. Apollinaris, the son of Sidonius, succeeded him in the bishopric of the Auvergne. BASN.]

[Col. 0101D] I give thanks to your most sincere brotherhood in Christ the Lord, because, when our weariness had been reported to you, you considered it important to visit us immediately by your letters. In caring for our illness, you demonstrate the health of your own heart. For, as you yourself know better, “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I, 5). And the one who visits the sick is strengthened in love.

Hence I hope especially that, while you seek me through words, you will assist me through prayers. As the bearers of the letter return, I return the reciprocal service of wishing you health; and, just as the report reached you, I indicate sufficiently that I have been afflicted according to divine mercy, not according to my merits. For he himself who feeds us with tears in scant measure (Ps. LXXIX, 6), in accordance with his kindness, has set a measure to chastisement suited to our weakness, lest our weakness fail under the correction of his hand.

Therefore, through his favorable mercy, I now report that I am somewhat better. By sending you consolation for your sorrow through this letter, I arrange that you, who out of love share in our hardships, may also share, in God’s name, in the joy of my recovered health, through reading it. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXII

Ruricius, bishop, to his most devoted and always magnificent son Verus.

Having reread your letter, I gave thanks to God that I learned from its report that you had recovered before I learned that you had fallen ill. I trust that this happens to you so frequently by the favor of God rather than through His displeasure. For “the Lord chastises the one whom He loves” (Prov. 3:12), and “He scourges every son whom He receives” (Heb. 12:6). Thus attentive admonition and gentleness show that you have been received into divine discipline. For paternal clemency prefers to correct a negligent son through manifold hardships rather than punish him for sinning; it prefers to draw the wavering and uncertain person toward His service with the reins of loving moderation rather than restrain the wanderer, stumbling down the precipices of the world, with a harsher blow.

[Col. 0102C] For He is the most indulgent master of the household, who lays down His life for His sheep. He is the good father who, anxious to carry the lost sheep back to the Lord’s folds on his own shoulders, prefers this to calling it back under the pressure of goading spurs. He is the merciful father who, when the wicked prodigal son and squanderer of his allotted inheritance returns to him, even if late, not only does not reckon his former offenses against him, but also multiplies the rewards he had lost: he cherishes him in his arms, caresses him with kisses, enriches him with gifts, and strengthens him with instruction, showing not so much anger at his departure as joy at his return (Luke 15).

For He Himself took upon Himself the effects and affections signified by all these names, so that, as the Apostle says, “in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. 1:1), He might teach us by words, instruct us through discipline, urge us on by benefits, shape us by examples, reconcile us by prayer, redeem us through suffering, give us life by death, grant us immortality, justify us by resurrection, and carry us upward by ascension. And, having reconciled us through His blood, He restored us to the Father’s favor from which we had fallen.

[Col. 0102D] For He is our propitiation with the Father (1 John 2:2), continually pleading with His mercy: “Father, I pray not only for these, but for those who are going to believe in me through their word” (John 17:9). “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (ibid. 24). “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He cries out to us daily through His apostle: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For whoever loves the world does not have the love of the Father in him. For everything that is in the world—the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of human life—is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God also remains forever” (1 John 2:16 ff.).

In the Gospel He invites us with endearments, urges us with gifts, and presses us with exhortation, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28), and the rest. Thus, as though submitting our necks to the life-giving yoke of His commands, let us be harnessed to His saving chariot of freedom and mercy, and therefore dare to follow Him when He calls us back, listen to Him when He cries out, and not despise Him when He speaks gently—lest afterward we experience Him as judge.

[Col. 0103A] What judgment? As He Himself deigned to forewarn and teach in the Gospel: “When He sits upon the throne of His majesty” (Matt. 19:28), when He will weigh and examine not only merits and deeds but also words and desires. Whoever He sees here neglecting His saving commands and proudly disregarding His most salutary admonitions, He will not only exclude from the door of the heavenly kingdom with the foolish (Matt. 25:3), but will also assign his portion with the unbelievers, so that with those with whom he has shared fellowship in this world, he may have the same portion in eternity (Luke 12:46).

## LETTER XXIII

To his son Constantius, Ruricius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0103C] Ruricius here rebukes Constantius as excessively devoted to the world; he was more occupied with Liber than with the Lord, and did not attend the temple fasting even on feast days. Sidonius often praised him. He was a man of exceptional intelligence, and by his eloquence greatly benefited the Roman party. He was an eminent poet devoted to sacred literature, but was a presbyter of Lyon and, according to Isidore, a bad bishop. He wrote the Life of Saint Germanus in an elegant style. There is another letter of Ruricius to him, number 42. BASN.]

[Col. 0103C]

Although I have learned that you are devoted to Bacchus, symphonies, various kinds of music, and also choruses of young women, nevertheless, since it is good occasionally to draw breath from these pursuits while youth is burning most intensely, and to devote yourself more to the Lord than to Liber, and to attend to your parents rather than to songs, I urge you to meet me tomorrow—which will be Wednesday—at Briva, and early at that, although I have very little belief that you will do so, fasting.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] It appears to have been written to the same Constantius.]

## LETTER XXIV

[Col. 0104A]

You had promised me something else, as God is my witness: that you ought to worship Him, not [Note: [Col. 0103D] Perhaps “Janus.”] Janus. You even want me to be an accomplice in this crime, so that I might supply delicacies for the worship of this error and pour oil upon the fire. You should know that this benefits neither of us.

But perhaps you will say, “You promised.” With what face do you demand promises from me when you have violated your sacred pledges? How will you grant pardon to my promise so long as I know that you serve this [Note: [Col. 0103D] Perhaps “portion” or “person.”] parsion? Let us not appear to confirm a pact whose deed we condemn, nor become a cause of scandal [Note: [Col. 0103D] Perhaps “for those whom.”] for which we ought to be an example.

## LETTER XXV

Ruricius sends greetings to his Apollinaris.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Apollinaris was the son of that most celebrated bishop of the Arverni. Ruricius praised him as one who followed in his father’s footsteps: “You prove yourselves to be his sons not only through the nobility of your lineage, but also through the flowering of eloquence and every kind of virtue.” His father had praised his son; nevertheless, we shall soon show that the offspring was degenerate. He followed the commander Victorius into Italy; after Victorius was killed, he was banished near Milan and returned as a fugitive to Arvernia. Afterwards he was present at the battle of Vocladum; there, Savaro asserts, he fell together with a very great multitude of the Arvernian people. But Apollinaris escaped again.
