He had a wife named Placidina. When she heard that the seat of the Arverni was vacant after the death of Euphrasius and that Quintianus had been elected, she approached Quintianus, supplicating him to allow Apollinaris to enjoy the bishopric of the Arverni. Quintianus yielded to Placidina’s prayers. Apollinaris, however, after offering gifts to the king, succeeded to the bishopric; abusing it, he departed this world four months later. Apollinaris therefore lived after the battle of Vocladum, contrary to Savaro’s assertion. He was a degenerate son who, after offering gifts to the king, held the episcopal seat occupied by his father and abused it. He had a son, Arcadius, through whose negligence Arvernia was devastated. His mother Placidina and his father’s sister Alcima were arrested at the city of Cahors, deprived of their possessions, and condemned to exile. Arcadius himself, the author of the crime, fled to Bourges (Gregory of Tours, book 3, chapter 12). Thus degenerate sons of heroes. BASN.]

Because you deign always to take care of us out of mutual affection, I inform your solicitous piety and pious solicitude that, on my return from you, I have undertaken a not inconsiderable but, with God’s favor, pleasurable task—one that could benefit me greatly if either the intention of my understanding or the understanding of my talent were to follow it. For the blind man awaits the sunrise in vain. It always rises for those who see, but for those who do not perceive its radiance, it is always covered, as though by clouds.

[Col. 0104B] I have received for reading our Sollius, our lord and common father, whom I had said that I was giving to your Sublimity to be transcribed.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] He means Sidonius, whom some call Solius.]

Although reading him restores my former affection, the obscurity of his words does not kindle my talent. Even if, after so long an interval, we sometimes rekindle the little flame of affection for him, still faintly shining amid the sparks and ashes of forgetfulness, with sighing tears, and sometimes water it with tears sweet to us, nevertheless the more it is drenched with that rain, the more it is inflamed. For through the abundance of tears the flame of longing and affection grows rather than diminishes.

If, therefore, the Lord grants this effect to your pious decision as its supporter, I hasten to review him in your presence and to become a disciple of the teacher. I am neither ashamed, even at this age, nor reluctant to undertake the diligence of a student, provided that, at an advanced age, I may attain the discipline of the art. [Col. 0105A] For everyone ought to learn before teaching. He prematurely assumes the arrogance of a teacher unless he has first undertaken the service of a disciple.

What could be more just than that you should be the interpreter of your father’s eloquence, since you can bring forth everything he wrote not so much from the parchment of a book as from the page of your heart? You prove yourselves to be his sons not only through the nobility of your lineage, but also through the flowering of eloquence and every kind of virtue—qualities bestowed upon you not so much by instruction as by nature.

For although a stream issuing from a spring gains strength by flowing and gathers fullness as it runs, it nevertheless owes both its name and its distinction to the source from which it derives them. If divine clemency had wished him to survive until this time, just as he was then already rejoicing in your imitation, so now he would rejoice in your perfection, when he saw hope reaching fulfillment; nor would he begrudge himself an equal whom he had desired to be better.

## LETTER XXVI

Although through the deacon Justus I did not deserve to receive a letter from your kind and eloquent heart—one that would both educate my intelligence and nourish my longing—I nevertheless, since I would rather be judged an affectionate rustic than an urbane impious man, did not allow the opportunity for writing to pass me by. I am one who would not wish even a single hour of the opportunity not merely to write to you, but even to see you, to be lost.

Therefore I send you my warmest greetings and ask that, without detriment to either of us and for the benefit of both, whenever opportunity permits you always deign to brighten us with your letters. For what you expend upon us in affection you do not spend wastefully; what you bestow you do not lose; and what you send us on paper you retain with yourself in your heart.

## LETTER XXVII

Ruricius sends greetings to his Ommacius.

I departed from your piety in such a way that I did not depart from you at all. I left you in that same part of the lower man in which I remained with you. I know that I remained there, from which neither the ancient plotter nor the recent adviser [conciliator] could exclude me.

From there I also admonish you with the saying of that most wise Solomon: “My son, do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him. New wine is a new friend; it will grow old, and you will drink it with pleasure” (Eccl. 9:14). Therefore let us grow old in our friendships and be renewed in affection from day to day.

And if a friend must not be abandoned, how much less a father—one who instructed you, nourished you, and, with the Lord’s help, brought you as far as the priesthood; to whom perhaps, in accordance with divine mercy, even the interest of this life is owed!

But I write these things to your blessedness not as though imputing or reproaching anything, but as to a dearest son whom I desire to walk through this world without any blemish of impiety, and to appear pure and immaculate on the day of judgment before God, His angels, and the whole congregation of flesh.

[Col. 0106A] I therefore salute your unanimity and ask that you deign to pray for me and, when it is convenient for you, to consider us worthy of a visit. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII

Ruricius sends greetings to his Euphrasius.

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Concerning him, see the note to Letter 20.]

I am astonished that, after the judgments rather than the written replies of so many such men, your Holiness sought the opinion of my ignorance. I infer that you did this more from personal attachment than from necessity, lest you appear to have omitted, in this matter, the agreement of one whom you esteem so highly and hold in special regard.

Therefore I give thanks for your indivisible brotherhood with me in Christ, because you deign to think and judge of us in such a way that we have nothing either deceitful in the simplicity of charity or counterfeit in the purity of truth.

I therefore discharge the duty owed by unanimity, and concerning the matter about which you deigned to write to me, I declare that I hold the same opinion as our brothers. But what ought to be done, or what seems most necessary to me, I faithfully made known to you verbally through your deacon, since it was . . . . m. to indicate it in writing. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXIX

Ruricius sends greetings to his Eraclianus.

Whoever knows that he is guilty in the discharge of his duty ought first to make supplication before daring to offer greetings. For just as one who is being accused is approached inopportunely, so the person who confesses is opportunely forgiven. Therefore we have brought our offense openly before you, so that we may more easily obtain pardon.

For no room is left for accusation when access has been opened to one who laments, in accordance with the saying: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.” The malice of the accuser will not prevail where the humility of the supplicant has gone before.

[Col. 0106C] Therefore, if by making excuses we have now washed away our fault, let us proceed to the matter itself. We offer your piety as much greeting as affection can understand but speech cannot express; as much as we can feel but are unable to set forth; as much as the inner mind, warmed by desire, can conceive but the outer tongue cannot affirm.

Therefore, giving thanks to the author of that very charity, who has deigned to plant it in your hearts, let us pray that He may always preserve in us and continually deign to increase His special gift of generosity [Note: [Col. 0106D] Perhaps “bestowal.”]. For, according to the Apostle, it is the more excellent way that leads to life.

For the rest, I ask especially that you daily supplicate our common patron on our behalf. For, as you read, “the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.” And as our Lord Himself says in the Gospel concerning the one who asked his friend for three loaves of bread at night—importunately indeed, but beneficially—what was granted to the persistence of the one who insisted, and what was refused to the friendship of the one who demanded it.

I entrusted the rest verbally to the bearer, since it was too lengthy to indicate in writing. Therefore, as the beginning of the letter states, I ask that you deign to grant pardon for my delay. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Capillutus.

I give thanks to your piety because you deign to consult me about the ordering of the city [Note: [Col. 0107C] This word seems to me corrupt.], although, with God’s favor, you are fully and abundantly sufficient for yourselves.

And since what pleases you and your brothers ought not to displease us, you are doing well in appointing the man whom the common consensus has chosen. But admonish him to pursue truth, not falsehood; peace, not destruction; discipline, not discord; the public good, not private greed; justice, not plunder. Let him protect the good and correct the guilty; let him not make them wretched, but defend them. Let him correct offenders and guard the innocent, so that by acting in this way he may be able to please the future judgment more than the present one.

## LETTER XXXI

To the illustrious and ever most magnificent son Agricola, Ruricius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0107C] Agricola was an illustrious man, the son of the emperor Avitus and brother of Bedicius. At that time, as count and master of the soldiers of the Arverni, he accomplished much in the defense of the city against the Goths. Sidonius Apollinaris had married his sister Papianilla, as is evident from book 2, letter 12. BASN.]

Having reread your Sublimity’s letter, I gave thanks to God because I learned that you had recovered through His ordinance before I learned that you had fallen ill; this removed anxiety from us and restored health to you. Nevertheless, I infer that this illness was mercifully imposed upon you by our Lord Himself, moved by favor rather than anger, in keeping with His customary goodness.

For thus we read: “The Lord chastises the one whom He loves,” and “He scourges every son whom He receives” (Heb. 12:6). This is also shown in your case, so far as I hear, in fact: by ordering your affections, He was making His own affection known to you; and, with your habits and mind changed, He was laying upon you the yoke of His gentleness, so that, submitting your necks to His saving chariot, while you carry the light burden of His commandments, you may lay down the heavy burden of your sins.

[Col. 0107C] For this is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High: He deigns to make the just from sinners, members of His household from strangers, and His friends from slaves.

It remains for you now to prove in your heart the conversion you have displayed in your clothing, and to let this change be found both in your garments and in your mind: just as until now he had concealed blackness beneath white garments, so now let him shine with the brightness of his deeds beneath dark clothing.

[Col. 0108A] For on the day when a sinner is converted and groans, he will then be saved—provided that, in accordance with the teaching of Saint Paul the Apostle, just as until now we have presented our bodies to serve the world and iniquity leading to iniquity, so now we present our members to serve justice for sanctification (Rom. 6:13).

Let us not be like those who fear God while displaying one thing in their speech and possessing another in their conduct; showing one thing in their clothing and proving another in their deeds. Otherwise that saying of the Lord will bite us: concealing the wolves’ ferocity beneath the clothing of sheep.

For that divine eye, as it is written, observes the good and the wicked in every place. Without doubt, whoever He sees turning toward Him with an undivided heart, He Himself will descend into that person’s heart as its perpetual dwelling, so that He may not lack a habitation for whom that person has prepared a dwelling.

[Col. 0108B] Let us therefore give common thanks to our Lord for such indescribable goodness of His. He prefers to admonish servants rather than destroy them, to correct rather than punish, and to grant everlasting kingdoms in exchange for the interest of this brief life.

For the rest, I send you my warmest greetings, and with particular affection I commend your handmaid to you—although, with your piety safe, she has no need of this—so that, since you considered it worthy to receive her with such affection, you may always cherish her. Through the indulgent generosity of divine bounty, she has made both of us indebted to herself: by her fertility she has made you grandparents and us great-grandparents.

I greet my lady daughter with the longing and honor due to her. If I had the ability to travel, my desire to visit you on her account would have been most eager, so that the one whom, because of our kinship, we behold continually with the inner eyes of our hearts, we might also see with our outer eyes. I wish you well.

## LETTER XXXII

To the holy and apostolic brother Caesarius, specially honored by me above all others with every distinction of honor and affection, Ruricius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Caesarius had written to Ruricius asking him to be present at the council convened at Agatha from the whole territory under Gothic rule. His letter is preserved among the letters of Faustus, edited above (see below). That council was highly celebrated; at the time, the bishop of Arles acted as primate of Gaul, convened councils, and presided over them. The learned Baluzius conjectures that this dignity had been entrusted and confirmed to Caesarius by papal authority. But at that time, namely in the year 506, Symmachus, bishop of the Roman see, had completely revoked the rights previously granted to Aeonius, bishop of Arles, and had confirmed the constitution of Leo the Great restored by himself, asserting that a light-minded and fickle disposition was unbecoming in a pontiff. In truth, however, Symmachus had restored those revoked rights and granted Caesarius permission to exercise them. Yet eight years elapsed between the council of Agatha and the restoration of the vicariate of Arles. Therefore, relying on his own authority and disregarding the decree of the Roman pontiff, Caesarius, when convening the council of Agatha, had written to Ruricius asking him to attend. Ruricius refused, because he was not in sufficiently sound health, but rather because he believed himself despised by Caesarius. Several men from the province of Vienne were also absent. Although subject to Alaric, they were unwilling to lower their fasces before the bishop of Arles and claimed as their own the rights recently confirmed by Symmachus. Angered by their absence, Caesarius enacted a law which provided that, if a metropolitan bishop sent letters to his comprovincials inviting them either to the ordination of the supreme pontiff or to a synod, they should not, except in the case of serious bodily illness or a royal command, postpone their attendance beyond the appointed day, setting aside all other considerations. This decree of the council, together with Caesarius’ complaint about Ruricius’ absence, occasioned this letter. BASN.]

Our brother and fellow priest Capillutus has appeared especially welcome to us on this occasion, since he himself, long desired by us, has arrived and also represents to us a certain presence of you through your letter. [Col. 0109A] Upon his return I arranged to send this letter, by which I repay the duty of affection owed to your blessedness.

As for your writing to ask why I did not come to the synod, as our conversation had arranged, illness, not unwillingness, caused this. You yourselves can recall how exhausted you saw me at Bordeaux [perhaps “at Bordeaux”], and this in winter, when I am usually stronger than usual. In summer I can scarcely endure my customary illness even in my own lodging and in cool places, to say nothing of whether I could have borne the heat [aestus] of that region had I come. Therefore I hope rather that you will deign to pray for me and that, if God grants me life, you will inform us earlier through your man of the other occasion which you mention that you wish to attend.

[Col. 0109B] I report that your letter reached me only very late. For even if we are not to be admonished on account of dignity or age, we ought not to be notified later than others who perhaps—speaking less prudently—deserved to be sought out. If the authority of cities lends standing to others, the humility of our city ought not to deprive us of authority. Indeed, it is much better and much more honorable to recognize a city through its priest than a priest through his city.

## LETTER XXXIII

To the holy and apostolic patron Sedatus, specially preferred by me to all others and honored with distinctive devotion and affection in the Lord, Ruricius, bishop.

Since every inclination of my heart, thirsting for you, frequently seeks an opportunity to write to you, at last, after long reflection, it finds a suitable bearer through whom I might both break a long silence and ask for spiritual delights, desiring to be sprinkled with the dew of your speech.

[Col. 0109C] I believe that it was of this thirst that the holy Psalmist said: “My soul is like earth without water for you” (Ps. 142:6). In sober intoxication he desired to quench the dryness of his body with that water of which our Lord deigns to cry out in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

The same Lord also offered this water to the Samaritan woman—that is, to the Church to be gathered from the Gentiles—saying: “The water that I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life” (John 4).

[Col. 0109D] If a faithful person has not merely sipped this water with the tip of his mouth, but, desiring it with all the inward parts of his soul, has drunk deeply as a guest at the feast, he immediately bursts forth in praise of the almighty Lord and begins to belch forth what he has drunk. Thus did the most blessed evangelist and disciple, who deserved to recline upon the Lord’s breast and heard the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, cry out in that utterance which no one had heard before: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1).

This was the Word, begotten by the Father outside time and, in time, created from a mother, so that He might become creator; so that He could be a certain portion of humanity and the fullness of the whole divinity; and so that this portion of humanity might redeem the fullness of humanity through His suffering.

[Col. 0110A] Thus the image of the invisible God became the form of a servant, so that the impassible one might suffer, the incomprehensible one be grasped, and the immortal one die—He who, by undergoing death, would destroy death, so that by rising again He might restore life.

But what am I doing, forgetting myself and thirsting for you, as though conversing with you about such matters and thereby burning ever more fiercely with longing for you, hastening to quench my thirst with something like a little stream of affection, attempting the inscrutable and inaccessible? I do not consider what I should say, how I should say it, or to whom I should say it. But, as I trust, your piety will grant pardon for what affection compels. For charity endures all things.

[Col. 0110B] I therefore send my warmest greetings to your heart, inseparable from mine, and ask that you deign to pray for me without ceasing. At the same time, with particular affection I commend to you the part of my body through whom I deliver this letter, so that through them you may fully prove how you love me. I think they will be dearer to you because they carry with them a portion of me.

Whatever affection you deign to bestow upon them, know that you bestow it upon us. For if, according to the holy Apostle, the lesser member shares the greater member’s pain, surely the greater also rejoices in the prosperity of the lesser (1 Cor. 12:26). Thus at last, when all the members are everywhere arranged in peace and quiet, the head—the ruler and, as it were, master of the whole body—rejoices.

In this head all the members are commanded to look, as the prophet says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). Another prophet clearly explains this, saying: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for He draws my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15). And again: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1).

[Col. 0110C] Let us therefore raise the eyes of our hearts toward Christ, and in the night of this world lift our hands to the Lord through fruitful works. May He deign to be our head, and may He cause us to cling to our head, so that we may deserve to be members of His body. Then, departing from this world, we may be able to say to our Redeemer, as at Israel’s departure from Egypt: “My soul has clung to you, but your right hand has received me” (Ps. 62:9).

When it has meditated on these things day and night in the prison of this body, it will not be put to shame in its desires. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXXIV

To the holy and apostolic patron Sedatus, specially preferred by me to all others and honored with distinctive devotion and affection in the Lord, Ruricius, bishop.

[Col. 0110D]

Through the chief physician Palladius I received a letter from a fruitful heart and eloquent mouth, which invited us, through the desire of the heart, to mutual sight. But what can we do, since the different illnesses of our bodies resist the desires of our souls? You are prevented by excessive strength, while we are worn away by the frailty of the body; in your case four feet belonging to another cannot bear your weight, while even my own two feet, because of my debility, can scarcely support me. Thus we are unable to fulfill our common wishes.

For I swear by the Lord that, had I been able, I would have come to the appointed synod with every eagerness. But although I had arranged my intention to travel, necessity arising from weakness restrained me. For I could not bear the air [aerem] of that region, especially at this time. I trust that you will believe this and will not hesitate to turn malicious people aside toward another interpretation.

[Col. 0111A] Having sufficiently indicated these matters as best I could, I sent you, together with a greeting offered from my desirous heart, a horse, if you deem it worthy, of the kind I knew you needed: gentle in tameness, strong in its limbs, firm in vigor, outstanding in appearance, well-proportioned in build, and balanced in temperament—that is, neither sluggish through slowness nor recklessly swift. Its bridle and spur are subject to the rider’s discretion; it has both the willingness and the ability to carry a burden, so that it neither yields beneath what is placed upon it nor throws down what has been loaded.

It remains for you to inform me by reply how you like it. Although I presume so much upon your heart, inseparable from mine, that even evils committed by me, not to mention those sent by me, would please you.

[Col. 0111B] For the power of undivided love is such that nothing displeases one in a friend [perhaps “a friend”], although evil ought rather to displease. Hence comes the fact that human judgments are hindered either by love or by hatred, so that what is right is not brought forth.

But you, whom neither hatred irritates nor envy inflames, gladly receive our jokes and inform us abundantly about your health and your activities, so that the longer we read you, the more richly we may be instructed. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXXV

To the holy and apostolic brother Caesarius, specially to be honored by me in the Lord Christ, Ruricius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Concerning him, see above.]

Since we seek opportunities to write to one another out of mutual affection, we ought not to neglect those that are offered, so that a mediating word, which is sent forth but not lost, may bring us a certain portion of presence; it is bestowed and possessed, seems to depart yet does not depart, is directed by me and received by you, written by me and read by you, and yet is not divided, since, although seemingly divided, it is held whole in the hearts of both.

For, in the manner of the divine word, it is handed on without departing; it is given to the needy without being taken from its author; it is the recipient’s gain without the giver’s loss, enriching the poor without diminishing the possessor.

[Col. 0111C] Therefore, when my most beloved nephew Parthemius came, I did not delay to send these letters through him, both to present my presence to you in writing and to commend him to you. Whatever affection you deign to bestow upon him, know that you present yourselves to us.

I also ask you especially to pray without ceasing for me and for these pledges of ours. Let not the distances between our regions impede the affection of our love, since those who love one another in the Lord, who is present everywhere, are not to be considered separated in body when they are joined together in mind in Him. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXXVI

Ruricius sends greetings to his beloved nephews Parthemius and Papianilla.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Parthemius was a nobleman who later lived in the favor of Theudebert, king of Austrasia. But after he had exacted taxes beyond the laws, upon the king’s death he fell into the hatred of the people and into the greatest dangers. He had Papianilla as his wife, but killed her together with his friend Ausanius. Struck by the goads of conscience, he was found by the people at Trier shut inside a chest. Smeared with spittle, beaten with fists, and with his hands bound behind his back, he was buried under stones at a pillar. There was another Papianilla at the same time, the daughter of the emperor Avitus, utterly different from the woman whom Ruricius here praises with her husband as half of his soul. Perhaps you are astonished that such a man as that Parthemius was praised by a bishop; but a bishop is a human being and considers nothing human foreign to himself. BASN.]

After your piety departed, I feel that I am half a man, because I recognize that the greatest part of me—that is, the inner man—has walked with you while my body remained here. Nevertheless, I also see that you remain in my heart, which stayed here.

I therefore salute your sweetness and urge you to remember my words, since it is certain that, with God directing you, you can advance in what is good if you treat the counsels of your elders both with affection and with appropriate practical use.

## LETTER XXXVII

Ruricius sends greetings to his brother Pet. . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0112D] In the manuscript this word is written in such a way that one cannot know whether it should be read as Petro, Petur, or Petul.]

Because obedience is preferred to sacrifices, I would rather expose my rusticity than lose charity. “Knowledge puffs up, but charity,” as you yourselves know better, “builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

Therefore, since you ordered me to keep you informed on every occasion both about my affairs and to temper your desire—which you extend toward me not because of my merit but through your general and innate affection—with conversation, I report that, by God’s favor, I am somewhat better, but alas, our entire little lodging is afflicted by various hardships.

[Col. 0112C] I ask especially that you earnestly supplicate the Lord, so that you who have restored our health through your prayers may also, through the protection of your intercession, bring the help and remedy of divine mercy to these people. Pray for me.

## LETTER XXXVIII

To the exalted and most magnificent sons Eudomius and Melantia, Ruricius, bishop.

How grievous the mourning caused me by your bereavement is, God, who knows my heart, bears witness; but I cannot express it to your lofty station. For the suffering of your grief wounded my spirit as though I had lost one of my own loved ones [perhaps: relatives], because by treating me well you made me close to you and, in a certain sense, related to you. And therefore, since on account of your esteem you frequently take upon yourselves our labors and troubles, it is right that we too, whenever they arise, should share in your sorrows. For if, according to the Apostle’s judgment (1 Cor. 12:26), the members of one body have sympathy and grieve with one another, it is fitting that we also should often experience their afflictions.

We grieve, therefore, over your misfortune, and believe that we are present at your lamentations. But what are we to do, my lordly sons? Indeed, we neither can nor ought to resist the divine will, and we must take every precaution lest, while we mourn our sweet loved ones with excessive grief, we should be found blasphemous and injurious toward the Lord, and lest the author of death should, when he finds an opportunity, pierce our souls more grievously than he struck them through the loss of those dear to us. Therefore, in every bitterness or sorrow, we must flee to God and refer all our misfortunes to him with our whole heart—he who heals the wounded, raises up the sorrowful, and comforts the afflicted.

And that saying of holy Job must be spoken without qualification: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). When he said this, he had lost ten children together with all his possessions; yet he was not compelled by loss or grief to blaspheme. As Scripture says: “In all that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips” (Job 2:21).

I have presumed to write this to your piety out of mutual affection, so that I might in some measure moderate, through divine words, the grief of your hearts, which I could not lessen through my own letters. And truly, if you trust me as one who is devoted to you, you can take no small consolation from the will of Christ the Lord: since he allowed the death to occur prematurely, he deemed him worthy to be received among those whom he teaches the kingdom of heaven to contain. Thus you have a patron in your son, and you may grieve less for one whom you saw received by the Lord.

I pray that you may fare well.

## LETTER XXXIX

To my lord, holy and apostolic patron Victurinus [Victorinus], bishop, especially to be honored in Christ the Lord with reverence and affection, Ruricius, bishop.

Our brother and fellow priest Capillutus, although he did not bring us your letters written on paper for us to reread, nevertheless displayed them—or rather, as one may suppose, their contents—as though written upon his heart. Hence neither a thief can carry them away, nor a violent man tear them out, nor rain wash them away, nor age obliterate them, while he, a most faithful sharer in your heart and your most devoted messenger, repeatedly impresses upon me, and with increasing sweetness, how and with what constant affection you think of me.

Not that there is anything in me with which you could satisfy the hunger of your charity—for you are accustomed both to receive and to give solid and never-perishing food—but when stronger nourishment is unavailable, may you sip our weakness as though it were a cup of milk, so that you may temper the longing of your devout and pure heart with the nourishment of innocence.

Yet it is no wonder that this miracle is found in your virtue: that you love those who venerate you, although you are accustomed to love those who hate you. Indeed, to increase your charity toward us, you retain our two lights—Aurelian, I mean, and Leontius. For their welfare and completion I ask you to pray unceasingly to divine mercy, as I trust you do, and always to pray with them for us; for I confidently believe that, because of your departure and their foolishness, given their present tender age, the Lord, their nourisher, will still deny them nothing.

I therefore offer your piety abundant greetings, as much as the affection of my lips can express, though not as much as the affection of my heart desires. And I ask you, in our name, to keep safe those aforementioned sweetest goads of my heart, and whenever the opportunity of a messenger presents itself, to water us with the showers of your blessing.

Pray for me.

## LETTER XL

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his own Apollinaris [Note: In the manuscript, Apollonari.]. [Note: Concerning him, see the note to Letter 25.]

The affection of your high station is a forceful exactor within my heart, compelling me to serve your love rather than my own modesty, since it does not consider in what language or on what page we obey your commands, but only that we obey them. For you compel us frequently to do violence to the ears of your learning with rustic words, while you repeatedly wish to receive our letters. I obey your will; I obey your command. For I prefer that you should trust me about myself more than I trust myself. What you command proceeds from affection, not authority. And therefore, whatever displeases you, you will doubtless correct rather than expose.

Indeed, nothing is more commanding than love. Whoever gives himself to it with his whole heart will gladly endure both the bonds it imposes and the burdens it lays upon him, since he receives the command of the one giving orders not unwillingly but devotedly fulfills it.

May divine mercy therefore grant that, amid the disturbances or necessities of this present time—whether they have been postponed forever or merely held back for a while—we may sooner be made to enjoy the fruit of our presence with you, so that the desires stirred by affection may be soothed by sight. [Note: Read “may he make you, or us, enjoy the fruit of your presence.”]

The end.

## LETTER XLI

To my most devoted lord and brother, venerable to me with every honor, Leontius [Note: He was Leontius, bishop of Arles. Although Ruricius was silent above concerning his death, this proves only that his letters were not arranged according to chronological order. There was indeed another Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, to whom Leo the Great granted the authority to convene the Gallican councils, so that he might more easily draw away the hearts of the Gauls, who were attached to Hilary of Arles. But this Leontius was already advanced in age in the year 445, as Leo himself testifies. Baronius supposed that this Leontius was the same as the one to whom the letters of Sidonius and Ruricius were addressed; but the Leontius of Fréjus had certainly died by the time of Sidonius and Ruricius. Their contemporary was Leontius of Arles, who succeeded Ravennius. Leontius of Fréjus died around the year 446; he therefore cannot have been the one whose death Ruricius, bishop from the year 470 onward, laments. Savaro is wrong in three respects when he supposed that the Leontius of Fréjus was the one to whom Sidonius and likewise Faustus wrote, and who signed Faustus’s letter to the presbyter Lucifer at the Council of Lyon. First, the man praised by Faustus was from Arles, and the vicariate of Gaul had been entrusted to him. Second, I do not know what Savaro means when he so often introduces the presbyter Lucifer. It was not Lucifer against whom Faustus hurled his weapons, but Lucidus, whose name was wrongly changed into Lucifer, an otherwise unknown man. Third, he signed the Council of Arles, which Leontius presided over; but he seems to have been absent from the Council of Lyon, the only one Savaro mentions. Leontius of Arles maintained frequent correspondence not only with the Gallican bishops but also with Pope Hilary. Those letters are found in the fourth book of the Councils. BASN.], Ruricius.

I give thanks that you have considered it worthwhile both to care for us and to refresh us with the novelty of vegetables, which you know we gladly receive; in this you show equal regard for custom and affection. And so, as your boy returns, I return the reciprocal duty of greeting and remind you to think continually, God willing, of the service you have undertaken.

For God is shown to require not the beginning but the completion of a good work, saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). His mercy, as we believe, will grant that he who has deigned to inspire you with a spirit of repentance may also, according to his compassion, grant you strength in action and complete forgiveness at the end. He alone can heal what is corrupted, restore what has fallen, erase what has been committed, hide the past, preserve the present, and grant what is to come.

The end.

## LETTER XLII

Ruricius to Lord Constantius.

I give thanks for the delicacies you sent, and I report that I have received as many of both kinds of birds as you indicated. At the same time, through the very boys who brought these things to us, I inform your piety that I have sent you a boar’s hide, so that while we feast upon the winged creatures you sent, you may be satisfied with a biped made from a quadruped.

Yet I would rather that you be caught by its flesh than by its life, because Scripture rightly compares to this animal the man who always thinks about worldly matters and continually meditates upon earthly things. For of all living creatures, only man was created exalted and made so that, always intent upon heaven, he might look upon his Creator, rather than endlessly carry out worldly works with his eyes fixed upon the ground.

## LETTER XLIII

To Lord Ambrosius [Note: Concerning him, see Sidonius, Book 9, Letter 6. Savaro suspects that he was the bishop of Sens whom Agraetius succeeded. BASN.], bishop, Ruricius, bishop.

The apostolic commands remind us that we should give earthly things to those from whom we receive divine things. Observing this, at least in this respect, in exchange for the heavenly riches that you supply us both through living speech and through the interpretations of the Fathers, we have sent sea vegetables.

By this we show that we possess nothing of our own: indeed, we are strangers to the divine goods that you bestow, and we send you things that are foreign to us. Therefore, because we recognize that we are exiles from heavenly things and dwell confined to earthly seats alone, we ask you especially to deign gladly to accept these things, foreign to us, and frequently to bestow your own upon us. Let the former be an act of affection, the latter of ministry; the former is rendered in return for teaching, the latter as a favor.

## LETTER XLIV

To Lord Hispanus, from Ruricius, bishop.

I give thanks that, while in name you send us gifts, in reality you send us spoils, thereby proving your most sincere piety toward me, by which we are delighted more than by delicacies. From the one we restrain the hunger of the body, from the other that of the heart; from the one we offer passing nourishment to the belly, from the other we provide lasting affection to the soul.

Accordingly, while returning thanks both for your love and for your gift, we offer your piety abundant reciprocal greetings. And because you deign to be concerned for our welfare, I report that I am well, in accordance with your pious wishes, and I ask you to inform me, when you will be celebrating holy Easter, by those who return.

The end.

## LETTER XLV

From Ruricius, bishop, to the presbyter Albinus.

When the rumor carried by the messenger of our common grief reached me—a fact that I nevertheless found astonishing, since I did not learn it earlier from a report sent by your brotherhood—I would immediately have come to seek you, had the reverence due to these days not held me back.

I have sent this letter, in which I hope you will deign to consider me excused, and that you will console in my place our daughter, whom I hear is grieving intensely, both according to reason and by your authority: our Lord did with his servant what he wished and when he wished.

Therefore, anyone who is displeased by the divine command will seem to act against the Lord’s will—indeed, against the divine will, since he alone can lead our soul from the body whenever he wishes, who poured it into the body. Consequently, this excessive mourning, which appears to arise from piety, comes more from the counsel of the devil than from piety, so that when grief, unable to endure consolation, reproaches God with impiety in its complaints, the soul may be lost through unbelief, even though God sent the Son beforehand through human birth.

Let the dead mourn their dead—those who do not believe that they will rise again, who think that the soul perishes together with the flesh, and who have no confidence either in the blessedness of the soul or in the restoration of the body. But we, who have hope of resurrection in Christ, and who believe, according to the promise of the Lord himself, that our souls are placed among the dwelling places of the saints, let us turn to him in heart and prayer, and draw consolation from his promise: that he will make those who believe in him live with him. No one should be judged dead before him except the unbeliever.

Let us therefore temper our mourning, as Scripture teaches us, saying: “The mourning of the wise lasts seven days, but that of the wicked all the days of his life” (Sirach 22:13). Just as we know that he is dead in body but, because of his innocence, lives to God in soul, so let us, while alive in body, die in heart.

The end.

## LETTER XLVI

From Ruricius, bishop, to Taurentius.

I give thanks for your most ready devotion in the Lord and your most sincere affection toward me. In imitation of divine goodness, it hastens, before being asked, to do what it foresees I must ask of it, and by its goodwill anticipates our duty, since it has undertaken not only to preserve but also to increase the affection it bears toward this man. It makes him joyful by anticipating him with benefits because it fears to cause him even brief sorrow.

And therefore it prefers to offer grace to one who is silent rather than grant it to one who asks, knowing undoubtedly that there is more merit in what is given through spontaneous kindness than in what is granted in response to prayers. For one of these is given to necessity only because necessity demands it; the other is often surrendered even to the persistent importunity of the petitioner (Luke 11:8).

Therefore, returning a greeting, and secure in your pious promise, I report that I have sent your girl to the place through your boys, whom I have dispatched. I trust that, according to your promise, you will grant her not only pardon but also favor in response to our intercession.

## LETTER XLVII

Ruricius to his venerable brother Joannes [Note: At that time there were two men in Gaul with this name. The first was a teacher of grammar; the other was elected bishop of Chalon by Patientius. This is the man to whom Ruricius writes and whom he calls brother. This Joannes, says Sidonius, was distinguished for his humanity. He had first been a lector and, for that reason, a minister of the altar from childhood. Then, having become archdeacon, he was retained in that office for many years because of his diligence. Finally, when he had become a priest of the second order and the bishops wished to restore the declining discipline of the Church of Chalon, he was elected bishop, although, as they say, he had no such thought himself. BASN.].

[Note: This word is contracted in such an intertwined form of the letters M and A that I despair of reading it; it must therefore be guessed. Perhaps “Amicus.”]

Our common friend, having done under compulsion what he ought to have done voluntarily, has now been driven by necessity to seek a letter of recommendation to your reverence. Through my introduction he has presented himself to your favor, although because of his negligence he was previously ungrateful, and now he ought to be treated with kindness.

I agreed to his request the more readily because I believed—and still trust—that you will gladly agree to my request. Therefore, after sending greetings, I hope you will consider it worthwhile to receive him for the sake of our intercession. And because he has repaid what he owed, may you deign to grant him the interest on those very solidi, not so much because of our prayers as because of the divine commandments.

You will certainly do this in accordance with your way of life, which, God willing, I hear you advance in day by day. For you know that the man who receives the kingdom of God with joy and thanksgiving, and ascends glorified to the mountain of the Lord, is the one who has not demanded interest on his money from his neighbor in the present age but has awaited it from the Lord in the future. He does not cast traps of insoluble debts upon those who are struggling through deceitful benefits; rather, he is a lender to and creditor of the one who says: “Give, and it will be given to you,” and “With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

He is certainly unfaithful and unjust even to himself who does not wish to possess eternally what he has chosen to desire. For although anyone may establish many things, gather much, and acquire endless wealth through various transactions, he will depart from this world a beggar unless he has sent ahead from his possessions his portion for eternal blessedness, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied. For when he dies, he will not take everything with him, nor will the glory of his house descend with him” (Ps. 48:17). And again: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

If such men were kind to their own souls, they would entrust their goods rather to the one who is both a reliable guarantor of the poor and a most generous payer of interest. Do not therefore be eager, dearest brother, to receive now twofold what the Lord promises to repay you a hundredfold; from this you will be able neither to fear destruction by moth nor to dread loss through a thief (Matt. 19:29). For our Lord himself is both the giver and the guardian of his gifts.

The end.

## LETTER XLVIII

To Aprunculus [Note: Ruricius wrote to him several times, as is clear from Letters 54, 55, and 56. Baronius said that Aper, born likewise to an Arvernian mother, belonged to him (Annals, year 484, Book 6, section 427). Did the annalist understand Aper to be the same as Aprunculus, or his brother? Neither is true. Aprunculus was not an Arvernian. He held the see of Langres among the Burgundians, but, fleeing the plots of the Arians, he was elected bishop of the Arverni after the death of Sidonius. He is wholly different from Aper, or Asper, who was not a bishop at all. His parents may be found listed in Sidonius, Book 4, Letter 21, p. 959 of Sirmond’s edition. BASN.], bishop, Ruricius, bishop.

The affection of mutual love has required me to send letters to your inseparable holiness for no other reason than this, even though no suitable opportunity has presented itself. Accordingly, I have entrusted these to the man of my son Leontius, and after offering greetings I ask how, by God’s favor, you are faring.

You yourselves know that your welfare is our joy. I hope that, when the aforementioned man returns, you will make us secure, by divine favor, concerning your affairs, since you see that we are concerned for your prosperity.

## LETTER XLIX

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to Ceraunia.

Trusting in the most sincere affection with which, out of the kindness of your heart and not because of our merits, you deign to honor us in the Lord, I have confidently sent these to your reverence. After offering abundant greetings in the Lord and in our God, I especially ask you to deign, if possible, to grant us without delay what I requested verbally through your servant Amandus. [Note: Perhaps “what I indicated.”]

This matter can relieve us and can bring you no loss; I shall count it a very great favor. Again, in whatever you command or necessity requires, I shall strive to repay it with reciprocal services.

## LETTER L

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to Censurius [Note: He was the bishop of Auxerre. Sidonius calls him Censorius. A presbyter who wrote the Life of Saint Germanus in his name has this form: “To the most blessed lord Censurius, venerable to me with apostolic honor, Constantius, sinner.” So too our Ruricius. BASN.], bishop.

I rejoice that I have received a letter from your holiness, even if by chance. For it makes no difference whether those who love one another converse out of necessity or voluntarily, provided that they do converse, and that those whom the distances between places separate in body are joined by faithful intercourse of mind and feeling.

For the virtue of long-established piety has granted us this general and greatest benefit: that although we cannot behold one another with bodily sight, we see one another with spiritual vision. Therefore, when the bearer of these letters returns, I have taken care, as you instructed, to send this reply, so that I might answer both your concern and our mutual affection.

I therefore offer abundant greetings to your apostolate. As for the matter that you wished to ascertain by the testimony of my letters—whether Sindilla lost his pigs because of the prudent Foedamius—know that I diligently inquired among my people where they had been. But, as I already knew, I learned that Sindilla had endured these things chiefly because he disturbed the peace, and that he himself had lost his pigs through his perversity, while boasting that he belonged to the opposing side. [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

As for the aforementioned Foedamius, he was in no way guilty toward him. Whatever he suffered, he ought to attribute and impute wholly to no one but himself.

In this matter, how much I labored, out of consideration for you, to have your men either released from custody or recover your pigs, you could already have learned more fully from the men themselves who reported it; for that reason it was unnecessary to mention it in a letter.

It is your responsibility justly to defend the truthful man against this accusation, while you acknowledge in your writings that my man unjustly suffers it.

## LETTER LI

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his own Stephen.

Your holiness’s piety drew me to its service in so few days that, although by God’s favor I hold you in my heart and behold you with the eyes of my mind, I nevertheless continue to seek you, urged on by affection. For everything that is sweet seems brief, and everything that is dear is insatiable.

And thanks be to almighty God for this marvelous gift of his: in an ineffable dispensation he has deigned to grant it generally to his servants, so that those separated in body may be joined in spirit, and no distance, however great, may be so difficult that it prevents the sight of the mind. Rather, those who love one another may behold each other through the contemplation of charity where charity itself abides.

Thus your bond with me, which is renewed and increased daily by continual remembrance in my heart, promises me a return of your love, while my mind serves as a guarantor to me for your minds, daring to presume as much upon your affection as it longs to bestow upon you.

I therefore offer abundant greetings to your blessedness, and I ask you unceasingly to entreat our common Lord to grant that, if in this age we cannot often see one another because of the disturbances and storms of this life and the distances between regions, he may at least bring us together in that city “which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3), to which the mercy of the Lord will be able to carry us and your merits.

## LETTER LII

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Praesidius.

[Col. 0120A]

Many people, because they trust that they have considerable influence with your inseparable highness—not through merit of life but through the privilege of friendship—seek letters of recommendation from us by which they may excuse themselves to you. We cannot refuse these to them, given the demands of our office; not through audacity or presumption, but through the discipline of our ministry, since we desire to provide them with consolation in the present life and you with provision for the eternal one.

Thus they may be granted time for repentance through your patience, and you may reach forgiveness through mercy, as Scripture says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not acted mercifully” (James 2:13). For he said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37).

Without doubt, whoever he sees doing here what he commands, he will restore to him in the future what he has promised. His truth is available to us, provided that our faith in him does not fail.

You can therefore observe most clearly that the release of your wretched dependents is the forgiveness of sins, and that you should receive through your prayers what you grant to others, according to his saying in the Gospel: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2).

I therefore come as a petitioner on behalf of Urso and Lupo, who came to me to intercede for their crimes, as though especially bound to you by the right of affection, as I said above. I ask you to deign to forgive, first for God's sake and then for ours, what they have committed, and not to bring shame upon us because of their condemnation, since they believed themselves already absolved when they were brought before my humility.

## LETTER LIII

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Rusticus [Note: Concerning him, see above, Letter 19.].

You deign to show us a customary and proven affection and humanity beyond what is usual, since you take away from your own resources what you lavish at our expense. From your boy’s report I learned that you had ordered delicacies from the inner parts of a fish to be supplied to us, in part from Visera. [The wording is uncertain.]

After offering greetings, I give you many thanks, asking divine mercy to grant you, in return for the honor you pay us out of fear of him, happiness in present things and blessedness in those to come.

The end.

## LETTER LIV

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to Aprunculus [Note: Concerning him, see above, Letter 48.], bishop.

Just as I received with joy the letter of your holiness through the venerable Elogius, so I have gladly sent this reply with the same man upon his return. In it I offer your apostolate the duty of greeting that I owe, and I ask you to deign to pray for us and especially to request from our common Lord that we may at last be worthy to come together and see one another.

Thus may the love which, according to the Lord’s saying, has grown cold in our hearts through absence because of the length of time [perhaps: “through the passage of a long period”] be rekindled through our presence among living ashes, and may the fire of our former love be restored through living voices as though by our breath. By the love and power of that fire which the Lord sent upon the earth (Luke 12:49), may he burn up the thorns of our negligence and sloth through the force of his mighty nature, and illuminate the darkness of our sleeping heart.

## LETTER LV

Another letter of Ruricius to the same bishop.

[Note: Perhaps “of supplications” or “of those supplicating.”]

The persistence of supplication supplies for us the duty of ordinary grace, so that what we ought to do out of mutual affection we do under the compulsion of an external necessity, granting another’s request when we recognize that we owe it to our own affection.

Thus this exchange of letters has been extorted by a new misfortune from one who laments, rather than made joyful by the voluntary inclination of friendship. Yet since we neglect the spontaneous grace of writing, we must at least not omit the request that has been pressed upon us.

Therefore, through our brother and fellow priest Maxentius, whom the brother bishop himself commended to us, I have sent this letter. After offering greetings, I commend him to your apostolate as he requested. He says that he has acquaintances and friends there who can make his case more fully known to your blessedness in person, and through whose testimony it may be believed that what is perhaps not believed on his own assertion.

## LETTER LVI

Likewise to the same.

Our sons Omacius and Eparchius sent me a letter full of tears and lamentation, especially begging me to act as intercessor before your holiness on behalf of our son Eparchius’s ignorance. They trusted that, because of our mutual affection, you ought to deny us nothing.

I have likewise sent our presbyter Eusebiolus to your piety in this matter. Through him I offer you abundant greetings and ask you, after sufficiently admonishing the aforementioned man as is fitting, to grant indulgence for his error in response to our entirely just supplication. [Note: The manuscript reads “our supplication iniquia,” apparently corrupt.]

Just as guilt should not be released while someone foolishly and faithlessly persists in defending his sin, until he acknowledges his offense [Note: This word is absent from the manuscript], so recognition of sin ought to bring forgiveness to the one who confesses it. For confession of an offense, when it is not feigned, is a remedy for evil; and there is no place for public punishment where the guilty person is punished by the torment of conscience.

## LETTER LVII

Another letter of Ruricius to the same.

[Col. 0121D]

The day before I received the letter of your holiness, I had sent my fellow priest to your brotherhood concerning the same matter about which you had written to me, as you will be able to learn from his own report. For not only our son Eparchius but also his brother had tearfully begged me in writing to approach your apostolate as a petitioner.

Compelled by the confession of guilt, the plea for pardon, and the affection of kinship, I granted it, since I did not believe that you would write to me about this matter. But since, out of the affection that exists between us, you have deigned to consult my humility about the justice of your severity, and to indicate it especially through your own letters, let our Lord know that I both approve and praise your action and greatly admire it.

For when, through an admonitory spiritual sword, you inflicted pain upon one who seemed beyond hope in order to restore his salvation, you brought health to many who were sick. For many in the Church who cannot be healed by a word are healed by an example.

What remains is for mercy to follow severity: receive with a father’s gentleness the man whom you rebuked with a bishop’s authority. And, following that Gospel example (Luke 15:30), let us invoke the one whom in all things we ought to follow and imitate. When his son had squandered his paternal inheritance and confessed his crime, he not only mercifully granted him pardon but also gladly restored his former favor.

Let us likewise grieve with the one who has fallen, assist the crushed, embrace the one who has returned, and rejoice over the one who has been found.

I am certain that your apostolate did this for the very purpose of excluding a slightly weakened son from his mother for a short while, so that you yourselves might soon restore him to her in health; and of grieving him temporarily, although you desire to rejoice in him eternally.

## LETTER LVIII

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Severus.

While you excuse our negligence and laziness, you reprove us, and through your benefits and services we acknowledge ourselves to be your debtors. But I know that you do this from the sincere and perfect love with which you love us, since what you give us seems little to your charity, while you desire to devote your whole self to us every day.

Yet benevolence alone would be more than sufficient for us, even if the readiness of your spirit and the constant performance of service were lacking. [Note: “Readiness of spirit, although regular service, etc.”]

After offering greetings, I give abundant thanks to your piety, because toward me you not only retain the affection of your father, of blessed memory, but have even surpassed it.

## LETTER LIX

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Sthoracius.

I give and offer abundant thanks to your piety, because you have made us aware of the negligence of our servants. While a shrewd enemy had withheld the suitable transport that was due to us, your kindly affection supplied it.

The Lord permitted him to inflict this upon us for a time so that he might prove both our patience through injury and your affection toward us through sympathy, and unquestionably bring you the profit of a good work performed from our resources through the benefit of your love.

## LETTER LX

Ruricius, bishop, to his son Vittamenus.

Your esteem makes us intimate with you, since you gratefully accept what is gladly offered by us. For that gift is proved acceptable and sweet which is commended not by its size but by affection.

This makes us eager to render you the service of spontaneous devotion, even to desire what we cannot express in words. Accordingly, after offering greetings, I report that I have presumed to send one hundred pears to your highness and another hundred to my daughter. If they should perhaps displease you in the taste of their flavor, they will, as we trust, please you through the affection of the sender.

## LETTER LXI

Ruricius, bishop, to his brother Namatius [Note: Concerning him, see the first book.].

I offer you abundant greetings, and I hope that if you cannot come to us the day after tomorrow, you will at least deign to come on the third day. For, inflamed by the longing of your affection, we too say with the prophet: “My soul longs for you like land without water. My spirit has failed. Do not turn your face away” (Ps. 142:6–7).

Do not delay your arrival, lest you extinguish the fire in our heart that you rekindled with the consolation of so brief a time.

The end.

## LETTER LXII

Ruricius, bishop, sends greetings to his son Vittamenus.

[Col. 0123B]

I give thanks to your most gracious highness for your regard toward me, because through the diligence of your letters you make us—who, as you know, by the right of friendship are concerned for your affairs and welfare, God willing—secure concerning your actions and safety.

Accordingly, I return through this letter the reciprocal duty of greeting to your nobility, and I report that I have sent it to you from Decaniacum. I also announce that, by the favor of the divinity—which I trust is pleasing to you—I am well. [Note: The manuscript reads “you,” rather than “which is pleasing to you.”]

The Lord will grant that, returning from here as soon as possible, I may be worthy to be presented to your sight, so that you may trouble with your presence the affection whose desires you have stirred through your kindness.

## LETTER LXIII

Ruricius, bishop, to his brother Clarus, bishop.

[Col. 0123C] For the charity which your Apostleship extends to me—not for my merits, but for the goodwill of your hearts—I will not say that I can repay its benefit in kind; I cannot even express in words as many thanks as you deserve. Nevertheless, by letter I perform the duty of sending greetings, and I transmit through the conversation of this page a part of my heart, in which I have received an eager affection for you. At the same time I beg you to beseech our common Lord to make us soon enjoy the fruit of our presence together; and that those whom He has joined by the impulse of His inspiration He may also unite through the mutual sight of our faces, so that the gaze may extinguish within us the longing which conversation has kindled.

As for the columns, I give thanks; and, as you ordered, since at present I cannot send vehicles there because of the approaching winter, I shall send them after holy Easter, with God’s favor. Concerning the smaller ones, as you instructed me by word, I inform you that, if they can be found, I need ten of them. But if the Lord grants prosperity in all things, before I send the vehicles I shall dispatch a man to you.

## LETTER LXIV

Ruricius, bishop, to his brother Volusianus [Note: [Col. 0123C] He was bishop of Tours, successor to Perpetuus; later he was exiled to Spain by Warig, king of the Goths, because he had incurred the suspicion of the Goths: they naturally believed that he favored the Franks. See more about him in Gregory of Tours, I, 226, book X, 31. BASN.], bishop.

[Col. 0124B]

Thus—and this is the worse thing—our ancient affection, implanted in us, will be partly erased (for it must be confessed) by our negligence, partly by the necessity of the times, and partly by bodily weakness, through a long oblivion, so that, having become completely forgetful of one another, we shall seek you neither by any services nor even by letters.

I marvel that your Nobility sends letters to me as to a son, when, without any regard for religion or kinship, you are so pleased with the injuries done to us that you do not wish to avenge them. Therefore, unless I had considered the reputation of my person or the demands of my office, I would have sent back to you as bearer of your letters a man like those whom your wife—not a matron, but an insolent and utterly unrestrained mistress—has brought upon my people. [Col. 0124C] If you have endured her character for so long, whether willingly or under compulsion, at the cost of diminishing your reputation, know that others neither wish to endure it nor are content to do so.

For as to your writing that fear of the enemy has made you dull: an outsider who is accustomed to endure an enemy within should not fear an enemy from without.

[Col. 0123]

# EPITAPH OF THE RURICII, BISHOPS OF THE CITY OF LIMOGES

(From book IV, poem 5, of Venantius Fortunatus.) (S)

[Col. 0123D]

Although, envious Death, you threaten with swift gaping jaws,

you still have no power to exercise your rights over the holy.

For after Christ, returning, subdued savage Tartarus,

you lie defeated beneath the feet of the righteous.

Here tombs cover the sacred limbs of bishops,

shining throughout the world; their spirit dwells among the stars.

Two Ruriciuses, flowers of the Anicii,

through whom Rome was joined to the height of ancestral nobility.

With rank accumulating through their name, kin by blood,

they rejoice together—here the grandfather, there the grandson.

[Col. 0124D]

Each in his own time founded pious temples for his patron:

the one built that of Augustine, the other that of Peter.

The one was upright, the other devout; the one grave, the other serene;

together they strove to see which would be the greater.

Bestowing abundant wealth upon the poor,

they sent riches to heaven for them to follow.

By redeeming the world’s sins with a scattering hand,

we believe them to be among the apostolic choirs.

Happy are those who, having thus purchased them with fleeting nobility,

possess the rights of the senate in heaven.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 481. VICTOR OF VITA

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0125]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

Joseph Bertinelli to Giovanni Minotto Othobono, archbishop and bishop of Padua.

I might appear to have acted with little prudence—not to say rashly—in the judgment of certain insufficiently just assessors of affairs, by placing before your eyes, most illustrious prelate and most humane of men, both the cruel spectacle of persecutors stripping themselves of every trace of humanity and the image of the most savage persecution.

For the mind recoils not only from looking upon, but even fears speaking of, all that our History displays: the slaughter, sufferings, wounds, racks, deaths, and intolerable forms of death inflicted upon the holiest men of every age and condition. It fears speaking of the cruelty of barbarians raging everywhere, and of the countless bishops, priests, and others who endured suffering so steadfastly and firmly for the name of Jesus that the torturer himself and the instruments of torture seemed to grow weary before those who suffered them—even though the victims were tormented to such a degree that, the less strength they had left to endure, the more keenly they felt the force of the tortures and the bitterness of their sufferings.

Yet may you, by pontifical authority, if not behold with your eyes, at least embrace in mind and thought, such and so great athletes of Christ, such founders and teachers of our religion. And as I consider proclaiming the praise of your dignity and virtue, may I consecrate to your name the memory of those whose names are written in heaven, commended to the monuments of the annals.

Although you did not see them, you nevertheless see who they are and what sort of people they are who seek your patronage. You see how worthy it is of a noble ruler to extend his right hand to the afflicted and to help those in need of assistance; how worthy it is of an excellent bishop to receive kindly bishops like himself, and priests and sacred ministers who have suffered for the faith of Christ; and finally, how worthy it is of a humane heart to pity wretched people, to come to the aid of those who labor, and to deny nothing to those who seek protection.

When you see these things, I do not set before your eyes slaughter, blows, axes, chains, or the other kinds of punishment; rather, I present the examples of mutual charity and goodwill that meet us everywhere in this History. I present them all the more willingly, not so much because everything in them is worthy of you, as because you seem to express the greater part of them in your own character.

Would that I were such a man that, while I clearly see and greatly admire who and how great you have always been, I could also adequately set forth what belongs to you—not merely by speaking of it, but by celebrating it in worthy praises! But since I cannot pursue everything—for who could pursue everything belonging to one who has attained not merely the name of honor, but honor itself?—allow me, with an even temper, deliberately to pass over many things which, placed openly before all, everyone sees and praises exceedingly.

Let others speak of the nobility of your lineage, the antiquity of your family, the distinctions of your illustrious homeland and parents, your kinships, the names of your ancestors, and the splendid deeds performed by them. Although these things belong to you and are great, you reject them as though they were another’s, and consider nothing yours except what virtue has made your own.

Let others say that you are the nephew of Alexander VIII, supreme pontiff; that you are cousin-german to the most illustrious Cardinal Pietro Othobono; that you were designated bishop by Benedict XIII, the excellent pontiff. These things are indeed great, almost unique, and thus your own; but they are not those things which no one could adequately speak of.

Let the most celebrated city of Padua, seat and teacher of the liberal arts, over which you preside, speak of all that you do; let that seminary of learning, so well suited to educating youth, speak— the institution which you have undertaken to restore to its former splendor. We consider these achievements greater and worthy of still greater praise. Yet we neither wish to present to ourselves nor to demonstrate to others everything praiseworthy in you, but only whatever is greatest.

We regard as greatest, and at the same time admirable, those virtues of the spirit which alone are yours, which you do not share with others, and which, although they cannot be commended by everyone, are nevertheless most worthy of everyone’s commendation.

First there presents itself your piety and religious devotion toward God, so dear to God and so proper to a bishop; then your lofty character, gentleness of manners and integrity, kindness toward all, and charity and beneficence suited to your nature; and, above all—though each of these virtues is great and worthy of praise—that profound modesty by which you surpass others and do not allow yourself to be praised.

As for us, therefore, who prefer to seem excessively timid rather than insufficiently prudent, lest we be accused of courting anyone’s favor through some little flattery, we defer to your supreme virtue and refrain from every kind of panegyric. Nevertheless, we do not allow any public testimony of our respect to be lacking: we offer this History to your Eminence, small indeed in bulk but great in reality and worthy of you. We ask you to approve our little gift, whatever it may be, and not to despise the intention of the giver, who, knowing that he owes you much and cannot give much, considers it sufficient if he wishes to owe you very much.

Meanwhile, excellent prelate, illustrious more through virtue and merits than through rank and praises, who seem to have been bestowed upon your Church by a divine gift, continue—as you do—to serve it well through labors and vigils, to care for the safety of your innumerable flocks, and to leave behind perpetual monuments of your clemency, for the eternal praise of Christ the Redeemer.

[Col. 0127]

# P. FR. CHIFFLET’S EXPLANATIONS OF VICTOR OF VITA

In our notes on the works of Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, more than one occasion arose to offer preliminary remarks about this Victor and his History; it is now worthwhile to pursue the matter more carefully. I shall speak first about the book, then about its author, so that we may investigate the cause from its effects.

## CHAPTER I. The title of the work

The title must be prefixed to the work before anything else. Most people conceive it insufficiently distinctly as *On the Vandal Persecution*. For there was also persecution by Geiseric outside Africa—in Spain, Italy, Dalmatia, Campania, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, Sardinia, Bruttium, Lucania, Old Epirus or Hellas—as Victor asserts at the beginning of book I. Hence there can be no doubt that he himself titled his work *History of the African Persecution*, which is the title found in the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes.

But since Trasamund also harassed the orthodox in Africa during the time of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, for us, who have survived all these calamities, this work of Victor must be bounded in time and place in such a way that it becomes *History of the African Persecution under Geiseric and Huneric, Kings of the Vandals*.

## CHAPTER II. The *Notice of the Bishops of Africa* is part of it

That Victor himself either composed the *Notice of the Bishops of Africa*—those ordered by King Huneric to assemble at Carthage, published anonymously by Sirmond—or at least copied it from a public archive and inserted it into his work is apparent first from the very nature of its subject.

For in that *Notice* not only are the names of the bishops and their sees listed, but both in the text and at the end it is recorded what happened to each one, how many fled, how many perished, and how many were exiled and where. No one will deny that this material belonged to the man who had undertaken to describe the entire history of the persecution.

It is apparent, next, from an old manuscript of Saint Mary of Laon, in which that *Notice*—as Sirmond himself reports—followed the *Statement of Faith* offered to King Huneric by Eugenius of Carthage and the other bishops; it was therefore interwoven and attached to the account of the African persecution.

Finally, it is apparent from the manuscript from which Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, repeatedly assigns to Bishop Victor the names of the African cities drawn from that same *Notice*.

## CHAPTER III. Who was the author of the *Book of Faith*?

It is uncertain by whom the *Book of Faith*, attached to the *History of the African Persecution*, was written. Most people attribute it to Victor himself, whose the remaining work is; others attribute it to Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, following Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, chapter 94, where he says:

“Eugenius, bishop of the African city of Carthage and a public confessor, when summoned by Chuneric, king of the Vandals, composed, with the agreement of all the bishops and confessors of Africa, Mauretania, Sardinia, and Corsica who remained in the Catholic Church, a book of the Faith fortified with passages from the holy Scriptures, after being asked to explain the Catholic faith and especially the proper meaning of the word *homoousion*; and through his fellow confessors he presented it.”

Moreover, at the end of book II Victor seems to attribute it to all the Catholic bishops of Africa, when he says:

“Having foreseen this, our predecessors had written a book on the Faith, composed with sufficient propriety and adequacy, saying: ‘If you desire to know our faith, this is the truth which we hold.’”

In the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of the Holy Trinity near Dijon, this book is entitled:

“Here begins the Book of the Catholic Faith against the Vandals, published by Januarius of Zerta and Villaticus of the Median Houses, bishops of Numidia; by Boniface of Foracium and Boniface of Gazaufala, bishops of Byzacena.”

Yet these were the bishops through whom that book was sent, as is noted at its end, not those by whom it was written. Having considered these matters, I would judge that the book was either prepared by Eugenius himself, primate of Carthage, or at his command by some learned man, and finally reviewed and approved by all the bishops of the kingdom. Nevertheless, whoever ultimately wrote it, it belongs to Victor’s History.

## CHAPTER IV. The year in which the History was written: A.D. 487

The time when this History was written is indicated by the author at the very beginning of the work: the sixtieth year since the Vandals had crossed over from Spain into Africa. Since Prosper records this crossing in his *Chronicle* under the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur—that is, in the year 427 of the Christian era—adding sixty to this number produces the year 487, when this work was completed.

## CHAPTER V. To whom this book was dedicated. The age of Diadochus, bishop of Photice in Old Epirus

It is possible to conjecture from Victor’s preface to whom this book was dedicated. Whoever that person was, he was planning to compose a history to which he would attach the African persecution; and he possessed such authority or dignity that Bishop Victor professed himself ready to submit his neck in obedience to his commanding order.

Since Victor was writing from Constantinople, scarcely anyone other than Acacius, the patriarch of Constantinople who was then alive, could be found to whom he either could or should have shown so much honor. Acacius held that see for seventeen years, from A.D. 471 to 488, according to the most reliable authorities on Byzantine history.
