Victor adds that, just as Timothy and Luke were disciples of the Apostle Paul, so this man was a disciple of the blessed bishop Diadochus. He says:

“You received from heaven every good gift and every perfect gift, instructed by so great a pontiff; and the blessed Diadochus, whose many memorials of Catholic doctrine shine forth like stars, is proclaimed in every form of praise. It is enough for you to equal the teaching of your teacher, for it is enough for a disciple to be like his master.”

This Diadochus was bishop of Photice in Old Epirus, as Photius testifies in the *Myriobiblon*, codex 201; he mentions him again in codex 231. His ascetic work of one hundred chapters, translated into Latin by Francisco Turriano, is contained in the *Library of the Fathers*. From this work the monk Maximus, who flourished under the emperor Heraclius, cites a chapter, calling Father Diadochus by that title as a mark of honor.

Although Diadochus’s period has until now been obscure, from this passage of Victor we can at least establish that he flourished around the middle of the fifth century after Christ. The man of outstanding dignity who used him as his teacher was therefore the one at whose command Victor wrote the *History of the African Persecution* in A.D. 487.

## CHAPTER VI. The division of the work into five books

As for the division of this History, it is uncertain whether Victor himself divided it into several books. Indeed, since no traces of such a division appear, since the text itself contains no mention of several books, no transitions, and no forms of prologues or epilogues apart from the beginning and end of the entire work, it is more probable that, in the author’s conception—as is generally the case with other ancient works—the History proceeded continuously in a single stream. The divisions were subsequently made by later editors, sometimes into fewer and sometimes into more sections, according to each one’s temperament and judgment.

Thus, although most printed editions present three books, we find six altogether in the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes. They are divided in such a way that the first book is the same in both versions, while the printed second book is subdivided into two and the third into three.

At the end of book IV, after the words “Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, at Carthage,” the following additions appear. They are not by the author but by a later copyist:

“This is the law, this is the command of the most wicked and God-hated king Huneric, son of Geiseric, which he issued against the people of the faithful, hissing like a dragon with a forked tongue. But now it is time for us to bring the narrative to an end in this fourth little book, because it is unworthy and improper for the divine word to lie beneath tyrannical speech. We therefore ask the hearers kindly to lend their ears when the beginning of the fifth book sounds in them, since we confidently intend to narrate the great and wondrous contests of the martyrs, with the assistance of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who wondrously crowns his saints with laurels. The fourth book ends. The fifth book begins.”

At the end of book V, after the words “And Maximus the monk and Septimus the monk,” the following is added:

“Although in the present work we have not been able to explain the wondrous struggles of these most glorious martyrs, because of the multitude of countless other martyrs, nevertheless at the end of this work we promise, with the Lord’s help, to narrate them. Now, therefore, let this be the end of our narrative in this fifth little book. The fifth book ends. The sixth book begins.”

[“From that time onward the Arian bishops became more cruel, etc.” At the end, finally, of book VI, after the words “perished by a similar death,” the copyist concludes as follows:]

“The sixth book ends. The Passion of the Saints previously promised, who suffered at Carthage, begins.”

“About to proclaim their triumphs, etc.”

These are the *epilogues*—*epilogoi* (ἐπίλογοι)—from the manuscript of Portes, not by the author himself but by an antiquarian, or interpolator of the Middle Ages, who placed them as boundaries around the divisions he had established in the work.

Since I am considering the proportion of the parts and the convenience of the reader, I have chosen to follow a middle course and divide this History into five books. The subject of the first will be the African persecution under Geiseric, king of the Vandals; of the second, the beginnings of the persecution under Huneric, king of the Vandals; of the third, the profession of faith offered to King Huneric by the Catholic bishops; of the fourth, the cruelty of King Huneric toward the orthodox bishops, together with their catalogue; and of the fifth, the cruelty of King Huneric toward the remaining Catholics.

As an appendix there will follow the acts of the seven monk-martyrs of the territory of Capsa. The manuscript of Portes also makes Bishop Victor their author, as does the blessed Rhenanus, a careful writer, who, in his edition of this work, marked the end of Bishop Victor’s History at the conclusion of these acts.

Indeed, since these acts follow Victor’s written *History of the African Persecution* in all the copies of Victor that we have been able to see, both printed and manuscript, it is pointless to seek another author for them. Victor, having already mentioned these martyrs briefly in the course of his History, could have devoted himself to narrating their deeds at greater length—especially since in their tortures and the cruelty of the tyrant, the immense courage of the martyrs, and the divine providence shown toward them, would have shone forth more clearly than usual.

## CHAPTER VII. Victor was bishop of Vita

Until now, many have held the opinion that Victor was bishop of Utica in the province of Proconsular Africa. We rejected this view with substantial arguments in our work on Ferrandus.

I know that Victor, bishop of Utica, is mentioned in the first Carthaginian conference, number 128, in the post-consulship of Varanes, in the year 411 after Christ. But that man has nothing to do with the period of King Huneric.

When Bishop Victor was writing the *History of the African Persecution*, in the sixtieth year since the Vandals had crossed into Africa from Spain—that is, in A.D. 487—he mentions in the *Notice* of the province of Proconsular Africa Florentinus, bishop of Utica, who had been exiled to Corsica by King Huneric three or four years earlier. He was still being detained there with forty-six other exiled bishops when Victor was writing this History.

If someone objects that Victor may by then have been appointed Florentinus’s successor, who was perhaps already dead, he will surely appear an equally discerning judge of those cruel times. The flocks of all the African Churches had been scattered in every direction; their shepherds had either been killed or sent far from their homeland; and it was scarcely possible for them to draw breath, much less to watch over their flocks or appoint successors to bishops removed by death.

But just as it is certain that this Victor was never bishop of Utica, so it is indisputable that he was bishop of Vita. Since that city of the province of Byzacena was unknown to more recent copyists, they suspected an error in the ancient copies and, deceived by the similarity of the words, substituted Utican for Vitan.

In the good-quality manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes, I read at the very beginning of the work:

“Here begins the prologue to the History of the African Persecution, published by Saint Victor, bishop of Vita by birth.”

Later I encountered a Paris edition of this History from the year 1541, printed by Galeotus Pratensis and prepared by Blessed Rhenanus. There, after the preface beginning “Formerly the ancients, etc.,” the following title appears:

“History of the Persecution of the Province of Africa in the Times of Geiseric and Huneric, Kings of the Vandals, by Saint Victor, Bishop of Vita.”

It is therefore no longer at all doubtful that he himself wrote of himself in the series of the bishops of Byzacena: “Victor of Vita is not found.” He had plainly been reserved by a sure plan of God, like that Virgilian shepherd who, from the summit of a rock,

“hearing the sound of the bloody battle,”

might commend the history of that dreadful persecution to the memory of posterity.

## CHAPTER VIII. He wrote from Constantinople

I believe that he wrote this History from Constantinople. For he could not have remained hidden in Africa for long or escaped the eyes of so many searchers who scrutinized every hiding place in order to leave no Catholic, and especially no bishop, immune from Arian savagery.

I therefore suppose that, changing his clothing, he escaped to Constantinople in the company of Uranius, the envoy of the emperor Zeno. In book V he presents Uranius as a witness to the cruelty exercised at Carthage before his eyes against the orthodox.

“But if anyone,” he says, “thinks this story fictitious, let him question Uranius, Zeno’s envoy, in whose presence these events especially took place”—namely, because, when he came to Carthage, he boasted that he had come for the defense of the Catholic Churches.

“And to show him that the tyrant feared no one, he stationed several torturers, and more savage ones, in those streets or alleys through which envoys customarily passed on their way up to the palace and on their return—plainly to the disgrace of the state itself and the dregs of our already failing age.”

A little earlier, when he had mentioned those whose tongues had been cut out by the roots but who nevertheless spoke fluently, he adds:

“But if anyone wishes to be incredulous, let him go now to Constantinople; there he will find one of them, the subdeacon Reparatus, speaking polished sentences without any impediment. For this reason he is held in very great honor in the palace of the emperor Zeno, and the empress especially venerates him with remarkable reverence.”

Behold, he invites his readers—those present, to consult Uranius the envoy in Constantinople, in the emperor’s palace; those absent, to travel to Constantinople and learn there the course of the African persecution. He could scarcely have done this, or done it for no reason, if he himself had not at that time been residing there.

Thus, when he summarizes at the end of the *Notice of the African Bishops*: “Exiled to Corsica, 46; exiled here, 302,” the latter number must be understood as referring to those sent away to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER IX. He was first bishop of the province of Byzacena

I have judged that this same Victor of Vita later became primate of his province of Byzacena. He is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* as the man by whom Fulgentius was ordered to be ordained bishop of Ruspe.

Nor are the indications groundless. For, as we explained at greater length in our work on Ferrandus, in Africa, outside the province of Proconsular Africa, whose chief city was Carthage, the first sees were mobile and shifting, and the bishops followed the senior bishop of each province. By “senior” I mean not the older in age but the one senior by promotion or ordination; for that reason he was customarily designated by the title “senior,” so that he could indiscriminately be called either the senior, the primate of his province, or the bishop of the first see.

I reason as follows. The *Notice* of Byzacena presents three bishops named Victor: the bishop of Nara in thirteenth place, the bishop of Vita in forty-sixth place, and the bishop of Gaurava in one hundred first place.

In A.D. 487, when Victor of Vita was writing, ten of the Byzacene bishops had already been removed, most probably the older and weaker ones. If these were the first ten listed by the *Notice*, then Victor of Nara held third place in the remaining sequence of bishops, Victor of Vita the thirty-sixth, and Victor of Gaurava the ninety-first.

It is sufficiently established that Fulgentius was ordained bishop for the people of Ruspe in A.D. 507, twenty years after 487, by the authority of Victor, primate of Byzacena. During those twenty years, therefore, it is far more probable that thirty-five of the Byzacene bishops died after Victor of Vita than that only two died after Victor of Nara, or ninety after Victor of Gaurava.

By this reasoning I infer that the Victor of Vita who wrote the *History of the African Persecution* was the same man who, twenty years later, became primate of Byzacena.

## CHAPTER X. The chronological period of the reigns of Geiseric and Huneric

Geiseric seized Carthage under the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus, according to Prosper and Marcellinus in their *Chronicles*—that is, in the year 439 after Christ.

Idatius reports the same event in the fifteenth year of the monarchy of Placidius Valentinian, or of Theodosius the Younger. Nor does the Augustan fragment published by Henricus Canisius after the *Chronicle of Tiro*, in volume V of the *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 161, differ from this account. It records that Carthage was occupied by Geiseric under the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus, since this formula for stating the consulship has the same meaning as the familiar formula used by Prosper and Marcellinus, as we showed in our notes on the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* by Ferrandus.

Therefore, what Victor says in book I of the *African Persecution*—that Rome was captured by Geiseric in the fifteenth year of his reign—must be understood as referring to completed years.

For Geiseric occupied Rome under the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius, that is, in A.D. 455, according to Prosper, Marcellinus, and other chroniclers; and indeed not long after Maximus was killed by his own men on the day before the Ides of June.

This was the fifteenth completed year of Geiseric’s reign and the sixteenth as it was passing. The same authorities—Prosper, Idatius, and the author of the Augustan fragment—also give the day on which Carthage was captured as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November. Marcellinus is therefore suspected of an error, since he reads “the tenth day before the Kalends.”

From that day Victor of Vita counts, to the end of book I, thirty-seven years and three months of Geiseric’s reign; the Augustan fragment adds six days. If from 19 October 439 one counts thirty-seven years, three thirty-day months, and six days, Geiseric’s death falls in the year 477, on 13 January.

Now add, with Victor of Vita, seven years and ten thirty-day months of Huneric’s reign, and, from the Augustan fragment, a further eighteen days. You will see that Huneric died in the eighth year of his reign, almost completed, in A.D. 484, on 6 December.

## CHAPTER XI. The period of Huneric’s persecution and his edicts against the Catholics; between them occurred an ominous eclipse of the sun

Victor teaches us in book II that Huneric, a bloodthirsty beast, raged for five years or more, sometimes against the Manichaeans and sometimes against his own Arians; thereafter he turned his fury against the orthodox.

In book V he describes at length the famine and pestilence that devastated Africa, at least from the summer of Huneric’s eighth year, A.D. 484. While this disaster was raging, the persecution of the Catholics by the Arians ceased, because the common calamity had made the Arians anxious for their own safety. At that time King Huneric himself, as Victor says, ordered each of them to be recalled to his provinces and homes.

Since Huneric died when the eighth year of his reign was drawing to a close, it may also be inferred from this that his persecution of the Catholics lasted little more than two full years—namely, the whole of the seventh year of his reign, together with part of the sixth and part of the eighth.

The two edicts must now be restored to their proper dates. The earlier concerned the summoning of all the bishops of Africa to Carthage on the Kalends of February in the eighth year of King Huneric, A.D. 484. The later concerned the closing of the churches and was issued in February of that same year, 484.

The earlier edict was indeed promulgated in the eighth year of Huneric’s reign, A.D. 483, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, as appears from book II. But the date subscribed to the edict must be corrected: it reads the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, that is, 20 May. For in that year Easter fell on 10 April and the Ascension on 19 May.

How, then, could the edict have been read publicly in the church on the nineteenth, if it was issued and completed only the following day, namely 20 May? We therefore think it was issued on the very day of the Ascension, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, or at any rate two days earlier, the sixteenth day before the Kalends, so that the number XIII may have entered in place of XIV or XVI through the easy alteration of V into II.

From that time until the Kalends of February in the year 484 nearly nine full months elapsed. Accordingly, we have not hesitated to restore the word “nine,” from the Cologne edition and the manuscript of Portes, in place of the later edict, which has been corrupted in the printed editions and reads as follows:

“Afterward it is clear that all were warned, a period of nine months and of renewed contention having been granted to them (if anything could be adapted to their purposes), so that on the Kalends of February of the eighth year of our reign they might assemble without any fear.”

This later edict, which is contained in book IV, was issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and therefore on the intercalary day itself of the leap year 484. Ancient opinion held that this day had an unhappy omen, as is shown by Valentinian, who was raised to imperial power at Nicaea in the year 364, immediately following a leap year, after avoiding the leap day itself as though it were ominous, as Ammianus writes in book XXVI.

During those same times Gregory of Tours also records an ominous eclipse of the sun in book II, chapter 3, of his *History of the Franks*:

“Then,” he says, “the sun also appeared dark, so that scarcely a third part of it shone forth. For I believe this happened because of such great crimes and the shedding of innocent blood.”

This eclipse at the astronomical new moon occurred midway between those two barbarous edicts, on 14 January, and could have been observed at Carthage in the morning hours, as the astronomical tables show.

## CHAPTER XII. The two envoys of the emperor Zeno to Huneric: Reginus in A.D. 483, the seventh year of Huneric; Uranius in A.D. 484, the eighth year of the same king

There is no doubt concerning Uranius. For, as Victor reports in book V, when Uranius boasted that he had come to defend the Catholic Churches, Huneric, in order to mock him and insult him more outrageously, stationed several torturers, and more savage ones, in those streets or alleys through which envoys customarily passed on their way up to the palace and on their return.

But the manuscripts do not agree so clearly concerning Reginus.

Rhenanus’s Paris edition of 1541, and nearly all the more recent editions, read as follows:

“For on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, the envoy of the emperor Zeno, with the queen present, sends an order to Bishop Eugenius to be read in the middle of the church, etc.”

But consider: how could the emperor’s envoy have thought it part of his office to send Huneric the tyrant’s edict to Bishop Eugenius, to be read in the middle of the church, when it had nothing to do with his master’s interests and indeed was entirely opposed to them?

Therefore the Cologne edition of 1535 renders the passage as follows:

“For on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, when the king was not present, he sent an order through the envoy of the emperor Zeno to Bishop Eugenius, to be read in the middle of the church, etc.”

This reading too is unstable, since it obscurely—indeed, I would say ineptly—suggests that the edict was sent both to Zeno’s envoy and to Bishop Eugenius.

We therefore restore the passage clearly from the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes:

“For on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, with Reginus, the envoy of the emperor Zeno, present, [he sent an order] to be read, etc.”

Whether this is the same Reginus to whom the deacon Ferrandus’s book *On the Seven Rules of Innocence* was addressed, I leave undecided, since I can neither confidently deny nor affirm it.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Carthaginian bishops mentioned by Victor: Quodvultdeus, Deogratias, Thomas, Eugenius
From this number Baronius excluded Thomas, following the more recent editions of Victor, which for Book I mostly read as follows:

> “The former ordainer of the aforesaid priest” (that is, of Bishop Deogratias), “named Thomas, while he was repeatedly harassed by various plots on their part, at a certain time they struck the venerable old man with the *catomi* in public.”

But in the Portas manuscript—which the Cologne edition of 1535 also agrees with in this respect—we read:

> “A certain man named Thomas was ordained to the priesthood. While he was being subjected to various…”

You see that here Thomas is reckoned as a bishop of Carthage, and not without good reason. For, if Thomas ordained Bishop Deogratias, then he himself must have been a bishop. If he was a bishop, why did Victor not call his see by name, as he usually does in other cases? Moreover, if Thomas consecrated Bishop Deogratias together with two other bishops, in accordance with the ancient canons, how could he be called his sole ordainer? Finally, since Bishop Deogratias had been ordained three years earlier, how could Thomas have remained at Carthage for so long outside his own see, contrary to the canons?

We therefore approve the reading of the Portas manuscript and of the old Cologne edition, which presents this man as a bishop of Carthage, appointed in succession to Bishop Deogratias, who had recently died. As for what Victor adds immediately afterward—“Hence it came about that after the death of the bishop of Carthage…”—we think this must be understood of Thomas’s own death, whether he breathed out his soul under the punishment of the *catomi*, or survived it for a short while.

Accordingly, Victor’s bishops of Carthage may be distinguished as four in all. The first was Quodvultdeus, banished to Naples in 439, immediately after Geiseric had captured Carthage. After he had died in exile, in the year 452, apparently, on 26 October, the emperor Valentinian prevailed upon Geiseric that a Carthaginian bishop named Deogratias should be ordained in his place. Deogratias embraced the captives whom Geiseric had carried from Italy into Africa with paternal affection; at length, worn out by old age and labor, he died while caring for the Roman captives, on 22 March 456, after having governed for three years. Thomas was ordained immediately afterward, but at the very beginning of his episcopate was put to death by the wickedness of the Arians under torture. From then on Carthage remained without a bishop for twenty-four years, until Huneric, at the request of the Augusti Zeno and Placidia, widow of Olybrius, permitted Eugenius to be ordained bishop at Carthage, apparently in the year 480. Not long afterward Eugenius endured the full weight of Huneric’s persecution and survived him for a long time.

## CHAPTER XIV. The venerable old man Thomas, struck *catomo* or *catomis*

The more recent editions of Book I have:

> “They struck the venerable old man in public with *catonis*.”

The Portas manuscript has *catomo*; the Cologne edition of 1535 has, incorrectly, *cathomos*. I would readily concede to Rosweyd, in the *Martyrology of Ado* on 15 June, and to Lacerda in the *Sacred Adversaria*, that *catomo* and *catomis* are used adverbially. But when I read in the Acts of the martyr Babylas, 24 January:

> “The enraged Numerian ordered three children to be lifted onto the *catomus*: the first was to receive twelve blows, the second nine, and the third seven,”

I understand *catomum* there as a noun, referring not to the punishment itself but to the place—or rather to the machine or instrument of punishment: for example, a column, a gallows, a beam, or a piece of wood to which those about to be beaten were accustomed to be raised or suspended, so that their shoulders might receive the blows.

Saint Eulalia of Mérida was ordered to be beaten on the shoulders (*catomari*); and in the theatre Hadrian, according to Aelius Spartianus, decreed that bankrupts should be *catomidized*. Thus *catomare*, or *catomidiare*, means κατὰ τῶν ὦμων τύπτειν, “to beat upon the shoulders.”

This is indisputable from the etymology, but the manner and the precise thing itself remain uncertain. For the aforementioned Rosweyd and Lacerda think that to be beaten or suspended *catomo* or *catomis* means to be hung head downward from someone’s shoulders and beaten. Baronius agrees in his notes to the *Roman Martyrology*, 15 June, B; and after him Bollandus, or Enschenius, in the notes to the Acts of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr of Barcelona, 12 February, C. They differ only in recognizing an upright bodily position in that form of punishment. Thus, to beat someone *catomis* would mean what schoolmasters customarily do when, with children hanging by their arms over someone’s shoulders, they inflict blows upon the children’s buttocks.

This opinion rests upon two passages in the Martyrologies, namely 15 June and 18 November, where Vitus and Barula, who are said to have been beaten or suspended *catomo* or *catomis*, are boys. But shall we also regard that bishop Thomas, already weighed down by old age, and Eulalia of Mérida, the martyr, as children, because they are said to have been *catomized*, or beaten *catomo*?

You will say that this was a more severe form of disgrace: that old men, men in positions of dignity, or even women, were sometimes beaten in the manner of children. But what of the emperor Hadrian? Would you say that he decreed that bankrupts should be suspended in the theatre, before everyone’s eyes, from other people’s shoulders by their hands or feet, and beaten on the buttocks? I cannot be brought to believe this without solid and manifest evidence from antiquity. The plainest meaning of these words, which I have stated above, is readily available, both from their etymology and from the practice of all peoples: namely, that to be beaten *catomis*, or to be *catomized* or *catomidized*, is to have blows received upon one’s shoulders or shoulder blades.

As for those who were to be beaten in this manner, when they are said to have been bound, raised, or suspended, do not imagine here someone’s shoulders to which they were attached by their hands or feet—which is done in some places for the punishment of children. Rather, imagine a column, as in Christ’s scourging; or a gallows or wooden beam, as in the martyrdom of the virgin Antonina, whom Festus, according to Metaphrastes, ordered to be suspended and beaten:

> “And when she had been taken down from the wood…”

We are astonished that learned men should introduce into the praetoria of the Roman world a practice of punishing children that was almost momentary and customary only in a few places, where martyrs, through the fury of tyrants and executioners, were beaten with rods and whips for so long and so cruelly that sometimes, although this was contrary to Roman laws, they poured out their souls together with their blood under that torture.

## CHAPTER XV. On the confessors whose tongues had been cut out at the root by Huneric’s command, yet who spoke clearly nevertheless

Victor says in Book IV:

> “King Huneric, sending a certain Count in anger, ordered him, after the whole province had been assembled in the forum, to cut out their tongues and their right hands at the root. When this had been done, through the assistance of the Holy Spirit they spoke and speak in such a way as they had spoken before. But if anyone wishes to be incredulous, let him go now to Constantinople, and there he will find one of them, the subdeacon Reparatus, speaking polished words without any impediment. For this reason he is held in exceedingly great honor in the palace of the emperor Zeno, and the queen venerates him with extraordinary reverence.”

The Greeks report in their *Menologion* and *Menaia* that these confessors numbered sixty. Victor shows that not all of them were bishops, since he places the subdeacon Reparatus among them. Aeneas of Gaza, in the *Theophrastus*, says that on the third day after the punishment this gift was divinely bestowed upon them—not so that they might recover their tongues, but so that, without tongues, they might express whatever they wished more articulately than ever before:

> “I thought,” he says, “that it was impossible for a flute-player without flutes to display any evidence of his art, or for a harpist deprived of his harp to practice the musical art. But this unprecedented spectacle compels me to change that judgment…”

He continues:

> “I myself saw you men and heard you speak; and I was astonished that a voice could be so articulate. I sought for the instrument of the voice, and, not trusting my ears, transferred the task of judgment to my eyes. With their mouths open, I saw that their entire tongues had been torn out at the root.”

Procopius likewise testifies that he saw and heard the same men at Byzantium, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*. Marcellinus also writes in his *Chronicle*, under the consuls Theodoric and Venantius—that is, in the year 484 of the Christian era:

> “Finally, I myself saw at Byzantium some exceedingly devout men from this company of the faithful, with their tongues cut out and their hands mutilated, speaking with an unimpaired voice.”

The emperor Justinian himself says in the constitution concerning the office of the prefect of the praetorium of Africa (*Code*, Book I, title 27):

> “We saw venerable men who, with their tongues cut out at the root, spoke pitifully of their punishments.”

Saint Gregory the Great, in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 32, states that they fled from Africa and came to Constantinople. He learned of the miracle from the eyewitnesses themselves when he had been sent to that metropolis of the Eastern Empire as *apocrisiarius*, which Baronius assigns to the year 583, number 12.

Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Zeno Augustus—although in a different place—writes:

> “The royal city bears witness that these confessors, although their tongues had been cut out, spoke perfectly to the very end; their bodies lie there.”

Then, at the end of his *Chronicle*, under the fortieth year of Justinian’s reign:

> “Theodore Cebarsusitanus, bishop and defender of the Three Chapters, was sent into exile to the royal city in the same month and on the same day on which Justinian died, and was buried beside the confessors whose tongues the Vandal king Huneric had cut out.”

Thus, when the *Menaia* and the *Menologion* state that these men were dispersed throughout all the regions of Roman rule, either understand this as referring to their passage, when they were traveling by land or sea before reaching Constantinople, or perhaps to some of them who carried their miracle about with them. For the authorities cited do not permit us to doubt that most of them lived at Constantinople and spent their lives there.

It has been conjectured that Vigilius of Tapsus, or Tapsitanus, was one of these sixty confessors, both because he is also mentioned last among the bishops of the province of Byzacena who were summoned by Huneric and assembled at Carthage, and because he wrote at Constantinople, as we have demonstrated; moreover, he wrote or dictated so many books, and books of such a kind, as no one, so far as we know, among all his colleagues did. Hence it is highly probable that he was one of “the most learned” (ἐκ τῶν λογιωτάτων, as the *Menaia* have) who were selected for that punishment, so that their tongues and right hands might be mutilated and they could no longer attack the heresy by word or writing. Yet, as I have said, this is a conjecture. In the profound silence of the writers, who did not state the names of the individuals, nothing beyond conjecture presents itself to me.

One of these sixty confessors was, as the *Menaia* together with the *Menologion* and Gregory the Great in the passage cited report, the man who, having fallen into sexual vice, rejected divine grace from himself, so that afterward he could not speak at all. Procopius tells the same story of two men, though not without suspicion of error or falsehood.

From this, moreover, one may estimate how arduous the virtue of chastity is, and repeat those words of Cyprian—or Origen—in the book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, near the beginning:

> “Death still advances through woman. I lie if we do not see that the destruction of very many has arisen from this. How many and what sort of bishops, clergy, and laymen alike, after having trampled down the struggles of confessions and victories, after mighty deeds and signs or miracles displayed everywhere, are known to have suffered shipwreck together with all these things, when they wish to sail in a fragile ship! How many lions has one delicate womanly weakness subdued—weakness which, although vile and wretched, makes prey of the great!”

## CHAPTER XVI. Whether Victor, bishop of Vitensis, has been vindicated as a saint

There remains a question of no small importance concerning the apotheosis of our Victor. On this point I say only that I cannot support it with any sufficiently firm testimony from antiquity. I know that in some ancient manuscripts the work on the African persecution is attributed to Saint Victor the bishop; but this title comes from scribes, who possess no authority to enroll anyone in the canon of the saints.

My own conjecture is that he lived a holy life in Sardinia while he was primate of Byzacena, and that he was buried there among so many other heroes, whether immigrants or natives, about whom Jacobus Pintus collected much material in his work *On Christ Crucified*, Book III, title 4, section 12. But at the beginning of the eighth century after Christ, and in the year 720, according to Pintus, when the Saracens were devastating Sardinia, so many tombs of the saints were thrown into confusion that no certain traces remained of the greater part of them, and consequently none of Victor of Vitensis either. Nor, so far as I know, are there any ancient Martyrologies or old church registers that attest that he was entered among the festivals of the saints.

Peter, bishop of Equilinum, says in Book IV, chapter 70, of his *Catalogue of the Saints*:

> “Victor, bishop of Carthage, flourished in the time of the emperor Anastasius. He was distinguished for virtues and learning. Against the Arians he composed one book. He wrote one book on penance, in which he established for those doing penance a rule of life according to the authority of Scripture. He also wrote one book of consolation to a certain Basil concerning death, complete in its hope of resurrection and furnished with instruction. He composed homilies as well, which are preserved arranged in books by brothers concerned for their own salvation. He paid the debt of the flesh on 12 Kalends of May.”

Peter derived these statements from Gennadius, chapter 77, but not very faithfully. For he wrote Victor as bishop of Carthage instead of bishop of Cartenna in Mauretania Caesariensis, and said that he flourished in the time of the emperor Anastasius, although he ought to be assigned to the earlier period of Geiseric, king of the Vandals. Let us hear Gennadius himself:

> “Victor, bishop of the city of Cartenna in Mauretania, wrote one long book against the Arians, which he presented to Geiseric, king of the Vandals, for reading by his own people, as I learned from the preface of the book itself. He also wrote a book on public penance, in which he established for those doing penance a rule of life according to the authority of Scripture; and he wrote a little book of consolation to a certain Basil concerning the death of his son, furnished with a complete instruction in the hope of resurrection. He also composed many homilies, which I learned are preserved arranged in books by brothers concerned for their own salvation.”

This is Gennadius. As for Peter of Equilinum’s notation of Victor’s death on 12 Kalends of May, he perhaps drew it from the records of Cagliari, which on that very day mention a certain Victor buried there.

From this turbid source—that is, from the testimony of Peter of Equilinum—various errors flowed into more recent writers. Thus the Sicilian abbot Maurolicus, on 20 April, writes in his Martyrology:

> “Likewise, Victor, bishop of Carthage, a most learned man, in the time of the emperor Anastasius.”

Peter Galesinius made this Victor out to be from Carthage but bishop of Utica. For on the same day, 20 April, he writes:

> “At Utica in Africa, Saint Victor, bishop and confessor.”

Philip Ferrarius was uncertain which position to adopt. Citing both authors in his general catalogue of saints who are not in the Roman Martyrology, he called Victor neither a Carthaginian, with Maurolicus, nor an Utican, with Galesinius, but simply a bishop in Africa, agreeing with both and subscribing to the error of neither. On 20 April he writes:

> “In Africa, Saint Victor, bishop.”

But Baronius, trying to avoid this Scylla, did not entirely escape the Charybdis. On 23 August he writes:

> “At Utica in Africa, blessed Victor, bishop.”

In his notes he asserts that Victor himself wrote the *History of the Vandalic Persecution in Africa*. Yet it is remarkable that this Victor is nowhere mentioned by Bede, Usuard, Ado, Rabanus Maurus, or the other ancients.

In Usuard’s edition published at Cologne in 1521, however, on 23 August, I read:

> “At Le Mans, Victor, bishop and confessor.”

Nevertheless, other Martyrologies mention Victor, or Victorius, of Le Mans on the Kalends of September.

In this complete silence of antiquity, therefore, we leave it to the Sacred Congregation of Rites to determine whether Victor, whether of Vitensis or of Utica, the author of the work on the African persecution under Geiseric and Huneric, kings of the Vandals, can properly be regarded as vindicated and enrolled in the canon of the saints.

## CHAPTER XVII. Several variant readings from the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portas, in Victor, bishop of Vitensis’s work on the African Persecution

*(We deliberately omit this description of the variant readings, as being of little interest to the reader, to whom we shall present in this edition the very carefully corrected text of Ruinart’s edition. — Editor.)*

[Col. 0141]

# Sirmond’s Preface to the History of the Vandalic Persecution

## I.

Among the almost innumerable barbarian nations that, as the fourth century declined or the fifth was beginning, flooded the Roman world, and especially the provinces of the Western Empire, none surpassed the nation of the Vandals in savagery and inhumanity. All the surviving ancient monuments of those times proclaim this, and—to speak especially of ecclesiastical affairs—the sacred calendars, which scarcely mention one or two martyrs who suffered under other barbarians, everywhere testify that many together, and indeed very frequently, perished under the most severe persecutions of the Vandals.

For among the Vandals native ferocity, the treachery of heresy mingled with pagan superstitions, insatiable rapacity, and other vices of the same kind converged in such a way that they showed compassion neither toward the weaker sex nor toward those of tender age, and no reverence toward sacred things or persons. But this barbarian fury, which carried many martyrs to heaven, is itself the reason why we possess almost no certain information about those same martyrs. For while they laid waste everything with sword, fire, and plunder, they left no opportunity to write about their affairs—or even to draw breath—to those who survived those storms.

Even if some happened to commit something to writing, all such records perished amid those disturbances and the frequent destruction of cities and provinces. Those who afterward published accounts of these events preferred to treat civil affairs or to commend military campaigns rather than deliberately to discuss the triumphs of the martyrs, as is clear from Procopius and certain other authors whose works have survived to us.

We possess one truly golden little work on this subject: Victor of Vitensis’s account of the African persecution raised under Genseric and Huneric. Even he, however, reports only a few things out of many, and does not conceal this, since he restricts his narrative to Africa alone, although he admits that Genseric’s persecution spread over many more provinces—thirteen in all. Yet scarcely anything else concerning those events can be learned by us apart from what this author relates.

This, however, increases the value of his work and ought to stir us to diligence in gathering those sacred remains of a holier antiquity which, the rarer they are, should be considered the more precious. It is shameful that secular authors were so concerned and diligent in recording military affairs and the renowned deeds of their heroes, while our own writers were so careless and negligent in handing down to posterity the glorious struggles of the saints for the faith—although nothing is more effective for kindling in us the fervor of divine love.

Indeed, if it is sweet and honorable to die for one’s country or republic, it is worthy of far greater praise to contend for the cause of God, or to die bravely while fighting for the defense of the true faith. It must not be tolerated that those who fought to defend the faith of Christ should be held in lower esteem among Christians than those who devoted all their efforts to acquiring or preserving an earthly kingdom.

## II.

Our purpose in this little work, therefore, is chiefly to discuss those glorious men who, harassed in the persecutions of the Vandals, a nation most deeply devoted to the errors of Arianism, either won the crown of martyrdom by shedding their blood or at least became renowned for the glory of their confession in defending the divinity of Christ the Lord.

But since civil and ecclesiastical history so assist one another that scarcely anything can be said about one without the aid of the other, we are occasionally obliged to treat, if only briefly, the changes of the Empire and those princes who ruled at that time—both so that each matter may be related in its proper place and time, and because such civil changes, which provided the occasion for the Vandal invasions, also gave rise to the persecutions that we undertake to describe and, as far as we can, illuminate.

This History embraces the entire period extending from the Vandals’ first incursion into Gaul to the extinction of their rule in Africa—that is, approximately 128 years. For in the year 406 the Vandals poured out from their homeland, and after various fortunes they held Africa until the year 534, when they were finally driven out under the emperor Justinian and his general Belisarius.

We have divided the whole little work into two parts. The first contains Victor of Vitensis’s excellent work, carefully compared with various manuscripts, together with several other monuments, which we have attempted to illuminate in the notes and observations that follow. The second presents the entire history of this persecution in a continuous narrative, although some ancient writings are occasionally inserted in such a way that they do not at all interrupt the thread of the history.

## III.

The first place in the first part, therefore, is occupied by the little work of Victor, bishop of Vitensis, *On the Vandalic Persecution*. There is scarcely any more illustrious monument in the whole of antiquity, or one more useful and effective, whether for inflaming the devotion and fervor of the Christian religion in the breasts and minds of the faithful, for confirming the dogmas of sacred doctrine, or finally for refuting heretics, both ancient and modern.

For this reason, as soon as it first came to light, it seemed especially suitable for blunting the slanders of the innovators who accused the doctrine of the Catholic Church of novelty. In this work the divine mysteries of the unbloody sacrifice and the sacred rites are praised; here one may find the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, the gift of penance, and the indulgence of reconciliation granted through the ministry of priests, to whom, by Christ’s institution, it belongs to loose sins. Here the unity of baptism is strongly commended; here the sacred blessings of the baptismal font are praised; and the solemn rites customarily used at the funerals of the faithful departed are mentioned.

Basilicas consecrated to God in honor of the saints, invocation of the saints reigning in heaven, the primacy of the Roman Church, virgins consecrated to God, and many other matters of this kind occur throughout the work. They are all the more certain as indications of ancient tradition because this author presented them without deliberate purpose and without any appearance of affectation.

The work also seemed to be of great importance for restraining the fury of those heretics, by setting before them the example of the Vandals, lest they should appear to imitate them in violating sacred things. Certainly this was the intention of Blessed Rhenanus, through whose efforts the work first came to light. He says in his preliminary admonition:

> “It will be useful to read through Victor’s African History even for this reason: scarcely any other example could be more effective in deterring people from religious sects than the dreadful and unspeakable deeds perpetrated by Christians against Christians, when the barbarians, following their hatred of the Romans, rage against them under the pretext of religion.”

Hence its editions subsequently became so numerous, both in Germany and in France, the countries in which the fury of the heretics was raging most fiercely.

## IV.

No one ever called into question that the author of this History was an African bishop named Victor; but there was no unanimity concerning his see. For some printed books give Victor of Utica, others Victor of Vitensis. Yet even among learned men the opinion of those who called him Utican seemed to prevail, since the city of Utica was better known to everyone than Vitensis, which scarcely anyone knew.

But after it became known from the *African Notitia* that a bishop Victor of Vitensis flourished in Africa during the period of the Vandalic persecution, while at that time the bishop of Utica was called not Victor but Florentinus, as the same *Notitia* makes clear, everyone then agreed that Victor, the author of this distinguished work, ought to be called Vitensis.

Nor should you say that Victor may have been substituted for Florentinus of Utica, who died in exile in Corsica, and that this Victor wrote the History. These are mere conjectures and can in no way prevail over the authority of the manuscripts, especially since it appears that no other bishops were substituted in those disturbances for bishops who had died.

Those who inserted Victor of Utica in place of Victor of Vitensis did so through ignorance of the see of Vitensis. They substituted for it the Utica familiar to them, suspecting that an error had entered the ancient copies. But they were deceived by the very similarity of the words by which they thought others had been misled.

Rightly, therefore, Peter Francis Chifflet, S.J., restored the African History to Victor, bishop of Vitensis, as its true and legitimate author. We not only embrace the learned man’s opinion, but consider that it can be defended by arguments so certain and indisputable that we believe no one in the future will ever oppose it.

The unanimous agreement of all the manuscript copies demands this of us. Not one of them, at least among those thus far seen, presents Victor of Utica as the author of this work. We have found four manuscripts in which this History is preserved complete. Three of them clearly and more than once give the name of Victor, bishop of the Vitensian territory; in the fourth, however, he is simply called Victor the bishop, with no mention of his see.

The manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portas agrees with these. It is ancient and of excellent quality, and, according to Chifflet, bears this title:

> “Prologue to the History of the African Persecution, published by Saint Victor, bishop of the Vitensian territory.”

Lucas Holstenius notes in his observations on the *Roman Martyrology*, under 10 Kalends of September, that in the manuscript of the Vatican Library the same author is expressly called Victor, bishop of Vitensis, not of Utica.

Finally, Blessed Rhenanus, who first committed this History to print in 1535—it must be acknowledged that he did so from at least one manuscript—attributed it to Victor of Vitensis. He surely would not have done this if his manuscript had been marked with the title of Victor of Utica, a city so famous in Africa.

From this it may be inferred that manuscripts from Italy, Germany, and France all agree on this one point: that this Victor should be called Vitensis, not Utican.

## V.

The first person who appears to have corrupted the genuine title of this work was Reinhardus Lorichius. In 1537 he published the same History at Cologne under the name of Victor, bishop of the Utican territory, claiming that he had rescued it, as he himself says, from the ravages of the bookworms by which it seemed to be gnawed.

Although in 1541 Rhenanus’s edition was again printed in Paris by Galeotus Pratensis, once more under the name of Victor of Vitensis, another edition of Lorichius was produced in that same year at Basel by Westhemerus under the name of Victor of Utica. Since everyone approved that attractive restoration, as it seemed to them, all subsequent editions, whether in France, Germany, or other regions, came to bear the name of Victor of Utica.

Whether Lorichius did this on his own initiative or because of an error in some manuscript, I do not know. It seems probable, however, that his manuscript was like the others. I infer this from the fact that he calls the author Victor, bishop of the Utican territory, just as our other copies call our Victor bishop of the Vitensian territory.

Indeed, the word *patriae* (“of the territory” or “homeland”) seems better suited to an entire diocese than to a very famous city such as Utica. I can readily believe that Victor was called bishop by nationality of Vitensis because, since there was no city in that diocese, he was regarded as the bishop of an entire small region.

Thus, in Marmarica one bishop presided over the entire province. Since there was no particularly famous city there deserving to be the capital of the others, the bishop, now having his see in one place and now in another, was called the bishop of the entire region.

There is no need to borrow examples of this outside Africa, since at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in session 2, among the other Byzacene Fathers, Candidus, by the grace of God bishop by nationality of Dicca, subscribed his name.

Nor should it seem surprising that bishops existed without cities, since it is certain that many of them in Africa were established in villages, estates, and rural districts, as Aurelius the Catholic and Primianus the Donatist, bishops of Carthage, reproached one another in the *Carthaginian Conference*, chapters 181 and 182, inquiry 1.

## VI.

Chifflet, however, maintains that the obscurity of the see of our Victor was compensated by the dignity of primacy. In chapter 9 of his little work he thinks that this same author was Victor, primate of the province of Byzacena, with whose permission Fulgentius was elevated to the throne of the Church of Ruspe, as the author of Fulgentius’s Life relates in chapter 16.

To prove this, the learned man observes that the *African Notitia* contains only three Victors among the Byzacene Fathers. The first, Victor, bishop of Narra, is listed in thirteenth place; Victor of Gawar, in ninety-first; and finally our Victor of Vitensis, who occupies the thirty-sixth place in that list.

Yet Chifflet regards it as equally extraordinary to assert that ninety bishops—or only twelve—died within a period of twenty years. From this he thinks it entirely plausible that Victor obtained the primacy of his own province of Byzacena.

If this is admitted, we must concede to him the title of Confessor—not only because he was persecuted with the others under Huneric, or at least because he was driven from his see by the violence of Trasamund, but also because he died in exile for the faith of Christ.

For whoever the Victor praised in the Life of Fulgentius, bishop-primate of Byzacena, may have been, it is inferred that he died in exile, since at the time when peace was restored to the Church and the bishops were permitted to return to their sees, it was not Victor but Liberatus who held the primacy of the province of Byzacena.

## VII.

To some, perhaps, another question raised by Chifflet will seem more important: namely, whether Victor, the writer of this History, was ever enrolled among the saints or honored with some public cult.

Certainly, I think no one will deny that he ought to be numbered among those holy confessors who fought for the defense of the Catholic faith under the persecution of the tyrant Huneric. Indeed, in ancient manuscripts he is often called Saint Victor. But this was the customary formula of the ancients, by which the title was attributed to ecclesiastical authors, especially bishops.

More relevant is what is read on this matter in the present *Roman Martyrology*, where under 23 August we find:

> “At Utica in Africa, blessed Victor, bishop.”

In his notes on this passage Baronius observes that this Victor is the very man who became famous for writing the history of the Vandalic persecution.

But Lucas Holstenius, in his observations on the *Roman Martyrology*, rightly complains that these words were added by more recent writers and cannot actually be found anywhere in the ancient manuscripts.

The first person who seems to have provided the occasion for entering this Victor’s name in the sacred calendars was Peter de Natalibus, as Chifflet conjectures. For on 20 April he praises Victor, bishop of Carthage, whom he says flourished in holiness and learning under the emperor Anastasius, and he attributes to him all the little works that Gennadius, in his catalogue, chapter 77, records as having been published by Victor, bishop of Cartenna.

Following Peter, Abbot Maurolicus celebrates on the same day Victor, bishop of Carthage, a most learned man who flourished under the emperor Anastasius, omitting the catalogue of his works.

Peter Galesinius gives a somewhat different account:

> “At Utica in Africa, Saint Victor, bishop and confessor.”

In his annotations he praises several African Victors to whom this eulogy might apply.

Ferrarius, however, in his general catalogue of saints who are not in the *Roman Martyrology*, has only:

> “In Africa, Saint Victor, bishop.”

Yet in his notes he observes that this man is no different from Victor of Utica, who wrote the history of the Vandalic persecution.

From all this it is clear that our Victor’s memory was obscure among the ancients, and that his name never occupied a place in the sacred calendars. The same is true of several other men distinguished for holiness and learning.

Nor may we reconcile our Victor’s name with the saints on the basis of wholly uncertain and doubtful monuments. For Victor deserves solid and genuine praise for having produced so excellent a work; and, as the Cologne scholars who prepared the edition of the *Library of the Fathers* express it, one may see in this work his outstanding virtues—piety, learning, and zeal for religion—rendered vividly and faithfully.

## VIII [Col. 0146D–0147B]

Some also ask at what time and in what region Victor composed this history. The first question is not difficult to answer, since Victor himself testifies that he wrote it in the sixtieth year after the Vandals had entered Africa. That year is plainly A.D. 487, since it is certain that the Vandals crossed from Spain into Africa in 427, during the consulship of Hierius II and Ardaburius.

The solution of the second question, however, is not so easy. Chifflet infers from two passages in the same History that Victor wrote about the Vandalic persecution at Constantinople. The first occurs in Book V, no. 7, where, after describing various tortures inflicted upon the orthodox, Victor adds:

“But whoever thinks this fabulous should ask Uranium, Zeno’s envoy, and so forth.”

The other passage is taken from the same book, no. 6. There, after speaking of the confessors of Tipasa, who spoke without tongues, he adds:

“If anyone wishes to be unbelieving, let him now proceed to Constantinople, and so forth.”

By these words, Chifflet says, Victor, residing at Constantinople, invites readers who are present to question Uranium, who was then serving at court; and those who are absent he urges to come to the city, so that they may learn the whole sequence of the persecution. From this he concludes that those bishops who are said to have been exiled at the end of the *Notitia Africana* were in exile at Constantinople.

But Cotelerius rejects this opinion in volume III of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, in his notes on the life of Saint Sabas, because it would be inaccurate to say that those bishops had been relegated to Constantinople. Huneric, king of the Vandals, he says, could relegate Catholic bishops to various places within his dominions; he could expel them from his kingdom; he could send them to Constantinople; but such a sending should in no way be considered relegation. Hence this learned man concludes that it is more probable that Victor wrote his history while in exile in Old Epirus, a region subject to the Vandals, and that this circumstance also occasioned his dedication of the work to Diadochus, who is said to have been bishop in that same province.

But if conjectures may be used, it seems more probable to me that Victor composed his history in Africa. For he repeatedly says things suggesting that, when he wrote it, he had not been living in foreign regions. The persons who are said to have been relegated here in the *Notitia* seem to me to be those of whom, according to the author of the *Life of Fulgentius*, chapter 4, the crafty malignity of Huneric, the persecutor and tyrant, had decreed that they should endure the hardship of exile near their own homeland. Such was Faustus, bishop of Praesidium, who, as the same source says, had been ordered to be relegated not far from his own see.

I would more readily believe this of our Victor than of the others, because he did not attend the conference of Carthage and therefore could more easily have escaped the hands of the Arians. Victor invites his readers to question Uranium, who perhaps was still then in Africa; but when he urges others to proceed to Constantinople, he plainly declares—as it seems to me—that he himself was not in that city.

## IX [Col. 0147C–0148A]

Chifflet’s other opinion is still less probable: he maintains that Victor, whom he first places at Constantinople, could or ought to have dedicated his history to no one other than Acacius of Constantinople.

The profound reverence that the African bishops of that time held for the Apostolic See prevents us from accepting this. On the contrary, the Roman pontiff and Acacius of Constantinople were engaged in the most serious disputes, which eventually erupted into open schism.

Certainly, at the Council of Carthage that Reparatus convened immediately after the freedom of the African Church had been restored, the Fathers of that Church declared that they would admit nothing unless either custom or a decision of the Roman Church were produced. At the very beginning of the Vandal tyranny in Africa, Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, urged the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus in a letter not to reopen, in a second disputation, errors that the authority of the Apostolic See and the united agreement of the priests had suppressed when they began to reappear.

Likewise, when the Byzacene Fathers, exiled in Sardinia, were asked by John and Venerius what should be held concerning grace and free will, they replied that this had to be learned from the chapters containing what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves.

Still more relevant to our subject is what the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* relates in chapters 12 and 13. When Fulgentius had decided, from his desire for the perfection of life, to travel to the remotest desert of the Thebaid, Eulalius of Syracuse and Rufinianus, an African bishop in exile, recalled him from his purpose because a treacherous dissension had separated the monks living there from communion with blessed Peter.

See below, note 3 on Victor of Vita, pp. 61–62.

## X [Col. 0148A–B]

Victor’s History encompasses what the Vandals did against the orthodox, from their entry into Africa until Huneric’s death. Nevertheless, many things were omitted by the author, either because they were not sufficiently known to him or because he had decided to report chiefly what he himself had witnessed during Huneric’s persecution.

He therefore often indicates that he selected only a few events from many and omitted much—not only what had happened in foreign regions, but also what the orthodox had suffered in various parts of Africa.

Victor explicitly states that a general persecution against the Catholics was raised throughout Africa under Huneric, especially in Book V. From the same author it is also clear that the disaster extended to foreign nations in Genseric’s time, for near the end of the first book he lists thirteen provinces outside Africa that had been shaken by such a terrible storm.

## XI [Col. 0148B–C]

As for the division of this History, it is uncertain whether the author himself divided it into several books. If the first book is excepted—which ends with Genseric’s death in all printed and manuscript copies—there are almost as many different divisions of the work as there are manuscript codices.

In the common editions it is divided into three books, apart from the passion of the holy monks. Manuscript codices, however, present five or six books, and these begin at different places in different copies. Chifflet, for his part, divided the entire work into five books as he thought best.

We have deliberately followed his arrangement because this division has now become the most widely accepted among learned readers.

## XII [Col. 0148C–0149A]

Some ask whether the profession of faith that constitutes the third book of Victor’s History should in fact be attributed to this author.

Gennadius, in his catalogue, makes Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, its author—either because it was genuinely published by him, or because Victor, or someone else, composed it at his command, or finally because, since Eugenius was the foremost and principal bishop of all Africa, the work was assigned to his see and dignity even though it had been produced by someone else in the name of all.

In a very ancient manuscript of the Church of Laon it is attributed to all the African bishops together, under this title:

> “Here begins the little book of the Catholic bishops delivered to Huneric, king of the Vandals.”

It then begins:

> “By royal authority,”

and continues as in Victor’s History. The *Notice of the African Church*, first published by Sirmond and later inserted by Chifflet into Victor’s History, is appended to it.

Moreover, the same profession of faith was published separately under Victor’s name in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. This gave occasion to certain writers who composed catalogues of ecclesiastical authors to introduce a new Victor as the author of this little book. Some thought that he had been Victor, bishop of Cartenna, because Gennadius records in chapter 77 of his catalogue that this man wrote a lengthy book against the Arians.

But they should have noticed that Victor of Cartenna’s book was offered to Genseric, as Gennadius himself testifies in the preface at the place cited. It must therefore be acknowledged that it was different from the profession of faith found in Victor’s History.

In any event, Victor could have inserted the profession of faith into his History in the same way that he inserted Huneric’s edicts.

## XIII [Col. 0149A–D]

It remains for us to speak of the ancient copies by which we corrected this edition of Victor.

We possessed altogether four manuscript codices containing the complete History of Victor of Vita: three from the Colbert Library, which, with his customary generosity toward letters and in accordance with his usual kindness, the distinguished Stephen Baluze supplied to us; and a fourth from the Benedictine monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs of the Cluniac order.

The oldest of the Colbert manuscripts appears to have been written in the ninth century or the century after it; the second is somewhat more recent. The third seems to be only about five hundred years old, but it was written in a careful and diligent hand, and its page margins contain variant readings from another codex, so that this manuscript rightly counts as two.

The codex of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, formerly belonging to the monastery of Crespiacum, also appears to have been written approximately five hundred years ago.

We also consulted the variant readings of a manuscript of good quality, as Chifflet states, from the Carthusian house of Portes; that same learned man supplied them to us in his notes on Victor.

Besides these codices, we had three others in which, after the first book had been omitted, the complete History of our Victor is found under the title *Passion of Saint Eugenius*. One belongs to the Reverend Fathers of the Fulian monastery of Saint Bernard in this city of Paris; another is preserved in our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Both were written approximately five hundred years ago.

The third of these codices appears to be a century more recent. It belongs to our monastery of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne.

In addition, we compared the profession of faith—that is, the third book of Victor’s History—and the *Notice of the African Church* with the very ancient and excellent manuscript of the cathedral church of Saint Mary of Laon, which was written at least eight hundred years ago.

## XIV [Col. 0149D–0150D]

The editions of the same author that we were able to consult are the following.

First, we consulted the oldest of all, prepared by the blessed Rhenanus and printed at Basel in 1535. In that year our Victor of Vita first appeared from the Frobenian press, among other authors of ecclesiastical history.

The same collection of authors was printed again at Paris in 1541 by the press of Galeotus Pratensis.

During the interval between these two editions, however, this same History of Victor was printed at Cologne in 1537 by Reinhard Lorich of Hadamar, apparently from a manuscript, since in his dedicatory letter he claims to have rescued the history from the ravages of moths by which it seemed to be gnawed.

A second edition by Lorich appeared at Basel in 1541 from the press of Bartholomew Westhemer.

In the same city, in 1555, a new collection of sacred authors appeared from the workshop of Heinrich Petri under the title *Orthodoxographia*. Among other monuments of sacred antiquity, it contains our Victor’s three books on the Vandalic Persecution, together with the passion of the seven holy monks.

In 1569, moreover, a new edition of Victor was prepared at Paris by Francis Baldwin, a distinguished jurist who had rendered great service to literature. He was the first to illuminate this History with commentaries.

Shortly afterward, in 1576, Margarinus de la Bigne published at Paris the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, which was printed again in the same city in 1589. In both editions our Victor has a place, as he does in the Cologne edition and in other similar collections of the works of the holy Fathers that appeared afterward.

All these editions were published under the name of Victor of Utica, except for the two editions of the blessed Rhenanus, in which he is called Victor, bishop of Vita. But the true title was asserted by Peter Francis Chifflet in the edition already mentioned, which he had printed at Dijon in 1664.

Furthermore, so that those ignorant of Latin would not be deprived of the opportunity to read so outstanding a work, it has been translated into the vernacular more than once.

It first appeared in French in the preceding century, namely in 1563, through the work of Francis de Belleforest, printed in Paris by Gabriel Buon. A second French translation appeared in the same city in 1664, prepared by the most illustrious Arnaud d’Andilly.

It was also published in English in 1605.

For preparing our edition of Victor’s History, we used all these editions, comparing the manuscript and printed copies with one another. We shall present their variant readings in the appropriate places.

This is what we thought should be said in advance about the History of Victor of Vita. To discuss here at greater length the other monuments contained in this volume would be unnecessary, since the prefatory notice placed before each individual work explains those matters sufficiently.

Nevertheless, so that the reader may have the entire sequence of Vandalic history, as it were, under a single glance, after the catalogue of the contents we provide a chronological index. In it we have assigned each chapter of this History to the individual years in which it is commonly thought to have occurred.

If anything—or rather, if everything—I may have done wrongly in the course of this entire History, may the reader receive it kindly and judge favorably of my effort in so excellent, yet almost neglected, a field. Let him bear in mind that I have lacked neither a sincere concern for truth nor diligence, though at times I may have lacked learning equal to the subject. We hope that this deficiency will be supplied by others more learned.

This History of the Vandalic persecution was part of a larger History of the persecutions raised by Arian emperors and barbarians, which we had prepared. If we learn that another portion of it will not displease pious and learned men, we shall publish that portion in due time, when a more suitable opportunity arises.

# Dissertation on Victor of Vita, with a New Life of Him, prepared in French by D. Liron [Col. 0151]

## First Article [Col. 0151A–0152D]

### On Victor of Vita and His History: Why the Life of This Author Has Until Now Been Unknown

Among the historians who have left posterity some account of what happened in the Church of God, very few have taught us about events more memorable than the author who wrote the history of the persecution that the Vandals raised against the Catholics of Africa in the fifth century, from the year 437 to the year 484.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] It was renewed several times afterward, but with less violence.]

Although the author of so excellent a work deserved to be extremely famous throughout all subsequent centuries, it is nevertheless true that he was not widely known. Those who composed catalogues of ecclesiastical writers—Gennadius of Marseille, who lived in his time and spoke about Saint Eugenius of Carthage; Saint Isidore of Seville; Saint Ildephonsus of Toledo; Honoratus, priest of Autun; Sigebert of Gembloux; Henry of Ghent; and Abbot Trithemius—did not mention Victor.

Thus, if those who composed martyrologies in the ninth century had not cited him on a few occasions, one might say that so serious a historian and so useful a work for the Church would have remained almost entirely unknown until the sixteenth century.

It was in 1535 that Rhenanus, a learned man, first had the History of the Vandalic persecution printed by Froben under the name of its true author—that is, Victor, bishop of Vita.

But it happened—as though people in every age had conspired to obscure the memory of this pious historian—that Lorichius published it two years later at Cologne under the name of Victor of Utica. Although Rhenanus’s edition was reprinted at Paris in 1541 under the name of Victor of Vita, Lorichius’s edition also appeared for a second time at Basel in the same year. From that time onward, everyone attributed the History of the Vandalic persecution to Victor of Utica. His name appears in all editions produced from 1541 until Father Peter Francis Chifflet finally restored it to its true author in 1664. Dom Thierry Ruinart, a Benedictine, followed him in this, and we owe most of these facts to his learning.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The theologians of Cologne, Baldwin, Vossius, and others.]

From Rhenanus’s edition until that of Father Chifflet, Victor of Vita was known only vaguely, and those who had spoken of him had said very little. Father Chifflet, however, while restoring the work to him, thought that he should also investigate matters concerning his person and undertook to clarify facts that had until then remained obscure.

No one can question Father Chifflet’s learning. Just as it is certain that his work rendered a considerable service to the public, so no one intends to deprive him of the just praise he deserves. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that he relied too heavily on his conjectures and, because he had not examined his author’s text sufficiently, made Victor a man quite different from the real Victor of Vita.

Those who wrote after him were obliged to abandon him concerning certain facts, but they have not yet purified the account sufficiently. We believe that both groups have departed so far from the truth that, when Victor’s History is compared with the Life composed for him, two men are found who scarcely resemble one another at all. This will readily be judged by comparing the work of M. Baillet, who most recently wrote on this subject, with the new Life that we are giving to the public.

If someone asks why so many able persons have been mistaken about Victor, the reasons are easy to discover.

First, we possess no ancient author who spoke about him, described his qualities, or marked out the principal circumstances of his life. Thus, having no guide for dealing with this historian, each person spoke of him as best he could and according to the attention he had devoted to reading his work.

Second, this difficulty could have been remedied by examining carefully and attentively what Victor says about himself in his History. But truth obliges us to acknowledge that people behaved with excessive negligence in a matter of such importance.

Third, the source of almost all the errors committed in Victor’s Life is that he was confused with his predecessor, who bore the same name and is mentioned in the catalogue of African bishops who came to Carthage by order of King Huneric in 484 to confer with the Arian bishops.

People failed to see that Victor’s History could not be reconciled with this catalogue. Because they did not distinguish Victor of Vita, who is mentioned in that document, from the man who composed the History of the persecution, they mixed up and confused everything, as we hope to make abundantly clear below.

## Article 2 [Col. 0153A–D]

### Statement of the Question

The question, then, is who this Victor was who wrote the History of the Vandalic persecution.

Those who examined this subject before us admit that the work was long attributed to Victor, bishop of Utica, a celebrated city of the proconsular province. Later, however, when it became known from the *Notice of the African Church* that Victor, bishop of Vita in Byzacena, was living during the Vandalic persecution, and that at the same time it was not Victor but Florentinus who governed the Church of Utica, everyone agreed that the author of the History of this persecution ought to be called Victor of Vita.

Several manuscripts also give Victor the title of bishop of Vita. From all this it was concluded that Victor mentioned in the African *Notice* and Victor the historian were the same person.

Since we intended to provide a Life of this ecclesiastical writer, we found ourselves obliged to examine the matter carefully. We recognized that the author of the History of the Vandalic persecution was indeed called Victor and that he was bishop of Vita, since all the manuscripts leave us no room to doubt it.

But for the rest we are obliged to take another path. We hope to show very clearly that Victor who wrote the History of the Vandalic persecution was not a bishop throughout the whole lifetime of King Huneric, who died in 484. Rather, if he was honored with that dignity, as we believe, he received it only under the reign of Guntabond, Huneric’s successor, apparently in 487, when Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, was restored to his church.

It follows that Victor the historian is not the bishop of whom the African *Notice* says that he was not present, or did not come, at the conference of Carthage.

We therefore differ from those who have written about this author on three important points, upon which everything else absolutely depends.

First, we maintain that everything Victor the historian did during the lifetimes of Genseric and Huneric was done while he was not yet a bishop, but only a cleric and probably a priest of the Church of Carthage.

Second, we maintain that he was not the person mentioned in the African *Notice*.

Third, we maintain that he was not exiled by Huneric.

These three points are so closely related that it is enough to prove the first in order to remove doubt about the other two. Nevertheless, we shall also demonstrate the third separately, so that no difficulty may remain concerning the whole matter.

## Article 3 [Col. 0153D–0157A]

### First Point: Victor of Vita, the Ecclesiastical Historian, Was Not Made a Bishop before 487

Since what we are about to prove is not known to everyone, it is appropriate first to establish certain evident facts. These will serve as the foundation of what we have to say and will shed considerable light on all our arguments. We therefore ask readers, especially those who wish to judge this dispute, always to keep them before their eyes.

1. Everyone agrees that among the tyrants who have afflicted the Catholic Church, there has perhaps never been one more cruel and detestable than Huneric, son of Genseric and king of the Vandals in Africa. This prince was also deceitful and crafty. Thus, when these two evil qualities were joined together, he adopted measures capable of destroying the Catholic faith throughout Africa, had God not supported it by his omnipotence.

2. From the year 437 or 439, when Genseric began openly to persecute the Catholics, until the year 484, when his son and successor Huneric died, the Church of Africa was almost continually in desolation: afflicted, oppressed, and ravaged.

There were no councils or assemblies of bishops. Successors were often prevented from being ordained to those who had died, and those who remained lived in fear and sorrow. Genseric forbade the faithful to assemble in the churches, while Huneric closed them completely and expelled all the bishops.
