3. There can be no doubt that every bishop, in such sad and deplorable times, was obliged to remain continually in his diocese. The Arian bishops and clergy, supported by the king’s entire power, were constantly circling around the flocks, seeking to devour some sheep. In addition to their Arian impiety, they rebaptized all whom they could seduce.

It follows that every bishop must have remained in his church unless he was forcibly removed, and that the people themselves would have prevented him from being absent. Victor provides evidence of this in what he says about Blessed Cyprian, bishop of Unizibira, who would gladly have joined the 4,976 confessors had he been permitted to do so.

4. Consequently, throughout Victor’s entire History one sees no bishop outside his diocese unless he had been carried away by force.

5. Victor’s History is now divided into five books. The first contains Genseric’s persecution; the other four describe that of his son Huneric. The profession of faith of the Catholic bishops presented to King Huneric at Carthage fills the entire third book. In the following books the author continues his narrative.

I assume—and this will appear evident to everyone who reads the History—that Victor followed the order of events. I do not mean that he kept a journal; rather, I mean that he did not confuse the sequence of the general events, that he did not attribute to Genseric what was done by Huneric, that he described before the conference of Carthage what occurred before that conference, and that what he reports afterward in fact happened after the conference, not before it, and so forth.

6. As for Victor personally, it will be seen that he was an eyewitness of the principal events he reports in his history and consequently took a substantial part in the affairs of the Church.

He never speaks of himself in the singular, but always in the plural, perhaps imitating Saint Luke. Thus, whenever Victor uses expressions such as “we went,” “we said,” and so forth, one should conclude that he was present. When he does not use such expressions, there is no doubt that he is reporting only what he heard and learned from others.

7. Huneric began to reign in 477. In 481 he permitted a bishop to be ordained at Carthage; this was Saint Eugenius. The ordination was soon followed by persecution.

In 483 the persecution increased in an extraordinary manner. To cause still greater harm, Huneric announced and ordered the conference of Carthage.

The conference took place in 484. Huneric continued the persecution, which spread throughout Africa, and he died miserably. Victor ends his History with his death.

With all this established, we shall now show that Victor was made a bishop only after 484, during the reign of Guntabond, successor of King Huneric.

The first proof that presents itself is drawn from Victor’s second book.

In 481, the emperor Zeno and Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III, wrote to King Huneric and asked him to permit a bishop to be ordained at Carthage. Huneric sent Alexander, Zeno’s ambassador, to the Catholic Church and had him accompanied by his secretary, named Vitarit, who publicly read the king’s permission.

This took place on June 18—or, according to some editions, May 19—in Victor’s presence. His words are as follows:

> “When this edict had been read to the entire Church in our presence, we began to groan and to say quietly that means were being sought for persecuting us. It is certain—and it is a known fact—that we spoke to the ambassador in these terms: ‘If this is so, and if such dangerous conditions are being imposed, this Church would rather have no bishop. Jesus Christ, who has deigned to govern it until now, will govern it still.’ But the ambassador refused to accept this remonstrance. At the same time the people became inflamed with the desire to have a bishop; they raised unbearable cries that could not be quieted by any reasoning.”

1. It is not clear why a bishop of Byzacena—which Victor is supposed to have been—would have come to Carthage at a time when there was no need for him there. The Church was being governed by priests, according to the ancient practice of the Church.

2. King Huneric’s permission was brought into the Church when no one was expecting it. Thus there was no particular reason to summon bishops from outside, still less from a province different from that of Carthage.

3. Victor’s narrative shows that the clergy, who understood the evil intentions of the Vandal king, preferred that the Church of Carthage remain in the condition in which it had been for twenty-four years—that is, without a bishop—rather than have one under conditions that would inevitably cause a violent persecution. That is exactly what happened immediately afterward.

But the people, incapable of such reflections, absolutely wanted a bishop, and they could not be restrained.

If Victor’s style is considered, it was he who spoke to the ambassador Alexander. This already shows that Victor was a member of the clergy of Carthage. For it seems that a particular bishop from a province different from the Proconsular province, in which Carthage was situated, would not have spoken in this way.

4. The admirable portrait Victor gives of the virtues and great qualities of Eugenius, who was elected, and the detail with which he treats the subject strongly confirm this view. Indeed, he specifies everything so exactly that it is difficult not to conclude that, in what he says about Saint Eugenius, he intended to portray his own bishop from life.

Here is a second proof.

After Victor has described Saint Eugenius’s virtues and conduct, he says that the Arian bishops, especially Cyrila, conceived a dreadful jealousy and envy of him and therefore slandered him every day.

They asked the king to forbid Eugenius to sit on the episcopal throne and to preach to the people according to custom. At the instigation of his pastors, the prince went still further: he sent word to Saint Eugenius that it was his will that Eugenius prevent all those who wore Vandal dress from entering the Catholic church.

Our author adds that the bishop replied that the house of God is open to everyone and that no one can reject those who wish to enter. Eugenius said this because a great multitude of our Catholics wore Vandal dress, since they held offices in the royal household.

The expression “our Catholics” is much more appropriate to a priest of the Church of Carthage than to a bishop from another province.

1. After this response, Huneric placed executioners at the church door. Using a specially made instrument, they tore the skin from the heads of all who entered wearing barbarian dress.

Victor says that he knew several people who had suffered this inhuman treatment and that he knew of none of them who had at that time departed from the right path.

It is obvious that a bishop of Byzacena, a province different from the Proconsular province, could not have spoken in this way under the reign of the cruel Huneric. It suits perfectly, however, a priest of Carthage who had complete knowledge of the persons involved and of the acts of apostasy that had subsequently occurred.

For the word *tunc*, “at that time,” sufficiently indicates that several later fell away. Now only an eyewitness could have known so many people in Carthage.

Below we shall explain why we judge that Victor was a priest rather than a deacon.

2. Victor, having thus marked the beginnings of Huneric’s persecution, accurately describes the cruelties that he inflicted upon his brothers and nephews, whom he undertook to put to death in order to place the crown of the Vandals upon the head of his son and his descendants. To understand this, one must know that his father, Genseric, had enacted a law that the eldest of his grandsons and descendants should always reign to the exclusion of the others. Huneric went even further: for, seeing that the patriarch of his religion, named Jocundus, was extremely loved and esteemed in the household of his brother Theodoric, he had this bishop burned alive in the midst of Carthage, [Col. 0157B] while the entire populace was present, before the steps of the great New Square. It is not only these details that show that the writer was a person from Carthage; what follows is even more remarkable. Victor was present, if not at this impious execution, at least in Carthage. Here are his words:

> “In this criminal impiety we considered the evils that were about to fall upon us, and we all said to one another: ‘Can one hope that he who is so cruel toward his own bishop will spare either our religion or our persons?’”

There, then, is Victor in Carthage, when Saint Eugenius was its bishop, and when there was no necessity or apparent reason for a bishop from another province to go there—especially if one considers that the [Col. 0157C] persecution was already sufficiently inflamed. See Facts 2, 3, and 4.

3. After Huneric had rid himself of all those whom he feared, and believed that he had thus established the Vandal kingdom within his family, he turned all his fury against the Catholic Church. God made this great persecution known before it occurred through several miraculous visions. About two years before it began, a person from Carthage saw in a vision the church of Faustus, where the Catholics assembled, with all its ornaments and in all its splendor. A moment later, the candles and lamps were extinguished, a startling darkness succeeded the light, a horrible stench was perceived, and the church no longer appeared in its former condition. This [Col. 0157D] vision was reported to Saint Eugenius in Victor’s presence. Thus we find him once again in Carthage; this is the third time that we see him there and consequently, to say no more, a strong presumption that Victor was not a bishop in a province different from the Proconsular, such as Byzacena was, but only a priest of Carthage, and that he resided in that city.

It should further be noted that, of the seven visions he reports, five were seen by Catholics of Carthage, and the other two by two bishops of the Proconsular province, of which the bishop of Carthage was the particular metropolitan.

4. The tyrant Huneric intensified the fire of the persecution [Col. 0158A] by condemning 4,976 bishops, priests, deacons, and other members of the Church to exile, sending them into the desert through the agency of the Moors. All these confessors were assembled at Sicca and Lara, cities of the Proconsular province, to be handed over to the Moors. One of these confessors was the Blessed Felix of Abbir, a city in the same province, who had been a bishop for forty-four years and was paralyzed. Victor was present; we must hear him speak:

> “After giving much thought to the fact that this good old man could not be transported on an animal, we had the king petitioned by his officials that, since Felix was soon to die, he should order that this bishop remain at least in Carthage.”

Later Victor again speaks in these terms:

> “Having tied him crosswise upon a wretched [Col. 0158B] horse, we carried him along the entire journey like a piece of wood.”

Victor, therefore, was personally present. See the sixth fact. All this took place in the Proconsular province. Who, then, could believe that a bishop of Byzacena was always found everywhere at precisely the right moment? This cannot be reconciled with the facts we have posited.

What follows must be carefully weighed. It is said that all the confessors were assembled in the cities of Sicca and Lara; that two counts came there and began addressing the confessors with gentle and ingratiating words, and so forth; that all of them cried out in a loud voice: “We are Christians, we are Catholics,” and so forth; and that they were confined [Col. 0158C] in a harsh prison where, nevertheless, they had sufficient room. “We were permitted,” Victor adds, “to enter there, exhort the brothers, and celebrate the divine mysteries.” Three important things should be inferred from this passage:

First, Victor was not among the confessors; throughout this entire narrative he clearly distinguishes himself from them. He was free. Second, Victor was a priest. Finally, it is not plausible that a bishop would have left his diocese at that time, since what Victor did on this important occasion could have been carried out by a priest or even a deacon. His freedom to act, what he did particularly for the Blessed Felix of Abbir, and the large sums of money he carried—all this [Col. 0158D] shows that Victor resided at Carthage, that he had friends at King Huneric’s court, and that Saint Eugenius had sent him with money so that he might accompany the holy confessors to the place of their exile, attend to their spiritual and bodily needs, and examine what would take place. What follows will confirm all this.

Moreover, it is not without reason that I say that a bishop could not have left his diocese then. Besides the reason we have already indicated, the number of those being led into exile was already very large and extremely detrimental to the Catholic peoples. Victor describes the complaints of the faithful as they watched the confessors pass by: they would have no one to baptize the children, bind sinners and absolve penitents, bury the dead, or offer the divine sacrifice. The example of the holy bishop Cyprian of Unizibira makes this still clearer. He consoled the confessors, showing all of them an equally devout and tender affection. He was ready to give his life for his brothers and to submit voluntarily to the same sufferings, but he was not permitted to do so. Finally, Victor, reporting the admirable faith of the old woman who joined the confessors with her grandson, who was still a child, says that he reproved her for acting at an inopportune time and contrary to prudence, by joining a company of men and uniting herself, without being obliged to do so, to the army of Jesus Christ. From all these [Col. 0159B] facts it is clear that a bishop ought not to have abandoned his diocese on this occasion; but Victor’s activities are perfectly suited to a priest of Carthage deputed by Saint Eugenius.

7. In no. 8 Victor reports what particularly concerned the Blessed Felix, bishop of Abbir, whom we have just mentioned; and in no. 9 he describes what happened in the cities of Sicca and Lara, where all the confessors were assembled to be handed over to the Moors who were to lead them into the desert. It is highly probable that what is said of Felix of Abbir in no. 8 took place at Carthage, where this bishop had initially been taken. These words of Victor—

> *Suggessimus ut a suis rex peteretur, ut saltem eum propere moriturum Carthagini esse juberet, quia ad exilium nulla posset ratione perduci.*

—“We suggested that the king be petitioned by his own men, so that he might at least order that, since Felix was soon to die, he should remain in Carthage, because he could in no way [Col. 0159C] be taken into exile”—make it sufficiently clear that Felix and Victor were in Carthage, where the king resided. For if Victor had been at Sicca or Lara, it would not have been easy for him to write to the court to obtain the favor he requested; whereas it was not difficult to have the prince addressed by certain Vandals who favored the Catholics, or by Catholics in the king’s household, in order to obtain so minor a concession. Finally, if Felix and Victor had been at Sicca or Lara, Victor would surely have reflected that the king might reply that, if Felix could be transported to Carthage, he could just as easily be transported into the desert. Thus we see Victor in Carthage for the fourth time.

[Col. 0159D] 8. Be that as it may, the 4,976 confessors were gathered from various places at Sicca and Lara, and Victor accompanied them throughout the entire journey to the desert, which was the place of their exile: *Dum iter ageremus cum Dei exercitu comitantes*—“While we were making the journey, accompanying the army of God.” But before going further, we must not omit an important observation. We said that the confessors’ prison was not so confined at the beginning, and that Victor was permitted to enter it. But when the two counts sent by the king were unable to corrupt anyone with their false caresses and promises, the saints were placed in narrow and dreadful places where they could scarcely move. They were even denied the consolation of being visited. What Victor says about this in no. 10 is terrifying. He adds:

[Col. 0160A] > “At last, nevertheless, after giving great gifts to the Moors, we were allowed to enter with difficulty and secretly, while the Vandals were asleep.”

This reveals the inexhaustible charity of Saint Eugenius, whose almsgiving, Victor says, seemed incredible.

9. As we have already said, Victor accompanied the saints as far as the desert. This is evident throughout his narrative, and especially in these words: “We could not count all those who died along the way, because their number was too great.” Having finished this subject in no. 12, he says in the following section that Huneric planned to do still worse against the Church of God, so as to destroy the whole body after having torn apart [Col. 0160B] some of its members. For on the day of the Ascension, while Count Reginon, ambassador of the Emperor Zeno, was present, he sent an edict to be read to Bishop Eugenius in the middle of the church, and at the same time couriers carried copies of it throughout Africa. In this edict Huneric ordered all Catholic bishops, setting aside every excuse based on fear, to come to Carthage on the first day of February of the following year, in order to confer there with his bishops and prove from the Scriptures the faith they defended. The edict is dated May 20, 483. Victor adds the following:

> *Cognoscentes igitur qui aderamus, simulque legentes, contritum est extemplo cor nostrum, et contenebrati sunt oculi nostri.*

> “When we who were present learned of this [Col. 0160C] and read it together, our hearts were immediately crushed and our eyes were darkened.”

And afterward: “They deliberated about what ought to be done, and found no other remedy for so pressing an evil than to present a petition,” and so forth.

It is clear from this that, after Victor had led the confessors to the place of their exile, where he could no longer serve them, he promptly returned to Carthage, and that he was there on May 20, 483. This conduct is entirely natural and suits a priest of the Church of Carthage very well, but not a bishop of Byzacena, who would at least have returned to his diocese after rendering this service to the confessors. Thus this is the fifth time we find Victor in Carthage—or rather, he always resided there, unless the orders of his bishop required him to be absent in the service of the Church.

10. Since everything we have said so far shows that Victor often spoke of himself, it would be very strange, if he had been bishop of Vite, that he never said he was a bishop; and it is virtually impossible that he would not at least have mentioned his episcopate. It would be astonishing that this author, who assures us that Huneric, after the conference of Carthage, stirred up such a general persecution in all the provinces of Africa that there was no place or house exempt from it, should not have told us a single word about what happened in his own diocese.

11. Victor reports only a few particular events [Col. 0161A] selected from everything that occurred in the different provinces of Africa, whereas he says much more about the Proconsular province, of which Carthage was the metropolis. But as regards the city of Carthage itself, our author has composed a very complete and highly accurate history of everything memorable that occurred there under the reigns of Genseric and Huneric. He gives such a fine account of the great deeds of the holy bishops Deogratias and Eugenius; all the events are described with such precise detail, the persons are named, and everything that serves to make a history authentic is so carefully marked out, that no one can fail to judge that this could only have come from an eyewitness who resided at Carthage and possessed perfect knowledge [Col. 0161B] of the places, the people, and the smallest circumstances.

12. Finally, here is a fact that by itself is sufficient to demonstrate irrefutably what we maintain. After the alleged conference, Huneric stripped all the bishops who had been assembled at Carthage of their churches, houses, and possessions; then he had everything they had brought to Carthage taken from them and drove them out of the city, so that they had nothing but the clothes covering them. Victor says that, in this deplorable condition, the holy bishops adopted a very wise course: not to withdraw. The reasons may be found in our historian, who then reports the trickery Huneric used to destroy these men of God; and [Col. 0161C] the outcome of this diabolical intrigue was that those bishops who had promised to take the oath demanded by the wicked prince received orders never again to see their cities or churches. They were banished, and were given fields to cultivate like plowmen and farmers, on condition that they perform no religious or ministerial function. As for the others who had refused to swear, they were banished to the island of Corsica to cut timber. All this was carried out with as much rigor as precision. Thus all the bishops of Africa were in exile: some on the island of Corsica, and others outside their dioceses, in rural areas, reduced to plowing and cultivating the land. Yet, amid the great fire of [Col. 0161D] this cruel persecution, when all the bishops were banished, we still find our Victor in Carthage. He himself tells us so. In Book V, no. 9, he assures us that, while Bishop Eugenius was already in the place of his exile, the Vandals attacked his clergy, consisting of 500 persons. These barbarians made all these devout ecclesiastics suffer hunger and whippings, and then sent them into exile. There is no indication that Victor shared in this persecution, probably because he was not in Carthage at that time; but he returned there shortly afterward. For he writes in no. 14 that he was a witness (*nobis videntibus*—“with us looking on”), and that he saw an act of violence the Vandals committed against a child of good family. For [Col. 0162A] they took him away from his parents at the command of their patriarch Cyrila and forcibly rebaptized him. After this testimony of Victor, whom we again find in Carthage after the exile of all the bishops of Africa, it is evident that he was not a bishop, but only a priest of the Church of Carthage. We therefore believe that we have very well proved the first point: Victor was not yet a bishop when Huneric died, after the conference of Carthage, in the year 484. Those who wish to defend the common opinion will be obliged to show that everything we have said is without foundation.

**ART. 4. Second point: that Victor the historian is different from Victor, bishop of Vite, mentioned in the African Notice.**

[Col. 0162B] We shall soon have finished the second point: namely, that our Victor the historian is not Victor, bishop of Vite, who is mentioned in the notice or catalogue of the bishops of Africa. For if Victor the historian was not a bishop in the year 484, as we believe we have demonstrated, it necessarily follows that he was not bishop of Vite and therefore is not the person recorded in the Notice. This admits of no reply.

I cannot refrain from adding an observation here: in the account of the conference, when Victor speaks of the bishops, he always uses the third-person plural—“the bishops,” “our bishops”—thereby distinguishing himself from them. After reporting the profession of faith, when he resumes [Col. 0162C] his narrative and recounts what it produced, he uses the first-person plural; from this one may infer that he was present at Carthage and at the conference. This appears all the more probable because, after reporting the king’s edict, when he describes the mistreatment this prince inflicted upon the bishops who had come to Carthage, he abandons the first person and resumes the third. Thus there can be no doubt that he distinguishes himself from them, although he was present. Now, according to the Notice, Victor of Vite did not come to Carthage. Therefore Victor the historian, who was in Carthage, is different from Victor, bishop of Vite, mentioned in the Notice.

**ART. 5. Third point: that Victor the historian was not exiled by Huneric.**

[Col. 0162D] Here the negligence of those who have written about our Victor becomes plainly evident. Let it be judged whether I am mistaken.

1. Nearly all the observations we made concerning the first point apply also to this one. We have shown that in the year 481 Victor was in Carthage on June 18, when King Huneric granted the Catholics permission to elect a bishop; that he was still there some time later, when this cruel prince had his patriarch Jocundus burned alive; and that Victor was in the same city when God made the future persecution known through visions. We found him there again when the king was petitioned on behalf of the Blessed Felix, bishop of Abbir. [Col. 0163A] At the very least, it is certain that in the year 483 he accompanied the army of confessors as far as the place of their exile, while himself remaining free and acting and laboring to assist them in all their spiritual and bodily needs. Finally, Victor was still in Carthage on May 20, 483, when Huneric sent Saint Eugenius his edict for the conference of Carthage, which he appointed for the first of February of the following year. From all these facts I conclude that Victor was not exiled before May 20, 483.

2. From May 20, 483, the day Huneric signed his edict for the conference, until the first day of February of the following year, when the Catholic bishops were all in Carthage, no bishop was sent into exile. It is likely [Col. 0163B] that the exiles were recalled and returned to their churches as a consequence of the king’s edict. At least, it cannot be denied that all the bishops, even those who had been banished, came to the conference. For:

1. By his edict Huneric orders all the Catholic bishops of Africa to come to Carthage to prove their faith from the Scriptures. He excepts no one, not even the exiles: *Omnes Carthaginem veniatis*—“You shall all come to Carthage.” And Victor speaks as follows: *Conveniunt non solum universae Africae, verum etiam insularum multarum episcopi*—“There assembled not only the bishops of all Africa, but also those of many islands.”

2. Huneric sufficiently implies through these words, *Omissa omni excusatione formidinis*—“setting aside every excuse based on fear”—that the exile had ceased.

3. Victor makes clear that Huneric’s intention was that all the bishops, without exception, should [Col. 0163C] come to Carthage, because this deceitful prince had devised the measure as a means of destroying the Catholic religion; he judged that he could accomplish this only by exterminating all the bishops: *Ut qui membra aliqua absciderat totum laniando perderet corpus*—“so that, having cut off some members, he might destroy the whole body by tearing it apart.”

4. Indeed, we see that Felix of Abbir, who was one of the 4,976 exiles, appears in the African Notice—that is, in the catalogue of the bishops who came, at the king’s order, to the conference at Carthage the following year. The same is true of Presidius of Suffetula and Donatian.

5. There were 466 Catholic bishops at this conference, or 458 if eight from Sardinia and the neighboring islands are excluded. Now, in the time of Saint [Col. 0163D] Augustine, when the Emperor Honorius permitted the great conference of Carthage against the Donatists, there were only 470 bishoprics and 406 Catholic bishops. One must therefore infer that all the bishops of Africa were present at Carthage in the year 484, since their number was as large as, and even larger than, it had been under the empire of Honorius.

It must therefore be accepted as certain that all the bishops of Africa were present at the conference of Carthage in the year 484, and that consequently those who had been exiled were recalled; that from the publication of [Col. 0164A] the edict until the assembly of the bishops Huneric exiled no one; and that, since Victor was not exiled before the edict, as we have proved, he was not exiled either before the conference or before February 1, 484.

3. Finally, as for the period during which the bishops remained in Carthage, it is impossible reasonably to doubt that Victor was also present there, so accurately does he describe all of Huneric’s acts of inhumanity. Add to this what we observed in the preceding article.

4. Once all the bishops had been stripped of their churches and possessions, and some exiled to the island of Corsica and the others to various places in Africa, with none escaping the Vandals’ cruel [Col. 0164B] thoroughness, Huneric stirred up a general persecution throughout Africa, so that in this great country there remained no place or house that was not filled with tears and groans. No age or sex was spared, except those who succumbed to the violence of the executioners. Now, during this dreadful persecution, which apparently began at the end of April [Note: [Col. 0163D] We believe that one should read “at the end of the edict of Huneric,” *sub die VI calendas Maias* (“on the sixth day before the Kalends of May”), instead of *Martias*, since the profession of faith of the Catholic bishops [Col. 0164D] that preceded this edict was dated *sub die XII calendarum Maiarum*—“on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.”] of the year 484 and lasted until Huneric’s death, Victor resided in Carthage.

We have irrefutable proof of this in Book V (no. 14) of his History, where he reports an act of violence committed in that city against a child of about seven years of age, at the command of Cyrila, and says that he witnessed it: *videntibus nobis*—“with us looking on.” This proof is so strong and evident that it is unnecessary to [Col. 0164C] dwell on it any longer.

One may also observe that, since Victor often spoke of himself in various places in his work, there is no reason to suppose that he would have wished to conceal from us the grace he would have received from God, had he been driven from his church and exiled for the faith. It is therefore evident that Victor suffered nothing in his own person during Huneric’s reign, and that God preserved him free so that he could render the persecuted faithful all the services they needed, and write down and leave to posterity the many great struggles of the holy martyrs and confessors of Africa, which without him would have remained forgotten.

Everything I have said thus far appears so clear, so well founded upon Victor’s narrative, and so closely interconnected [Col. 0164D] that I do not see how anything substantial can be opposed to it. Nevertheless, I believe it will not be useless to anticipate an objection that those who maintain that Victor wrote his History in exile might perhaps make. They will say to me: You claim that Victor was a priest of Carthage and that he was in that city during and after the conference. Yet Victor tells us that after the conference of Carthage, when Saint Eugenius, bishop of that city, was already in the place of his banishment, the Vandals also attacked all the clergy of his [Col. 0165A] church; that they had them beaten with rods and clubs, made them suffer cruel hunger, and then sent all these generous ecclesiastics into exile, to places very far away. It must therefore be concluded that Victor shared in these sufferings and in the exile.

I reply to this: first, that since everything I have advanced has been sufficiently proved, I am not obliged—and no one even has the right to demand—that I prove every circumstance that might follow from it. The reason is that one can raise difficulties against the most certain facts when those who reported them did not wish to provide a detailed account. Nevertheless, I say:

2. Victor does not use the first person when he describes the persecution suffered by [Col. 0165B] the clergy of Carthage, as he habitually does when he speaks of matters in which he participated; nor does he say anything at all that might give reason to believe that he suffered with the other ecclesiastics. We therefore have the right to suppose that he did not share in this persecution. See the sixth fact.

3. It is in fact after narrating all these events and the exile of the ecclesiastics that Victor assures us, in no. 14, that he was present in Carthage when the child mentioned above was forcibly rebaptized. See the fifth fact. Therefore, since throughout the continuation of his History we see that Victor was often employed in the Church’s most important affairs and that he made several journeys for this purpose, it is highly probable either that he followed [Col. 0165C] Saint Eugenius, his bishop, to care for him and observe what was happening—a conclusion that the manner in which he describes this holy confessor’s sufferings strongly supports—or that he was entrusted with some commission for the benefit of the churches, which were then in an unbelievable state of affliction after the loss of their pastors. Thus, Victor having been obliged to leave Carthage, could not return there until after the banishment of the clergy, when his presence there had become absolutely necessary. All this is highly probable in itself and also agrees very well with Victor’s narrative. That is sufficient to answer the objection.

**ART. 6. That the African Notice and the authority of the manuscripts cannot be reconciled with the History of [Col. 0165D] the Vandal Persecution except by admitting two bishops of Vite named Victor.**

We believe that we have well proved what we promised to establish: first, that Victor the historian was not a bishop when Huneric died toward the end of the year 484; second, that he is not the Victor, bishop of Vite, mentioned in the African Notice; and third, that he was not exiled by Huneric.

This being so, it is untrue, as has been written, that Victor the historian was made bishop of Vite toward the end of Genseric’s reign. It is untrue that he played a major part in Huneric’s persecution, which drove him from his see. It is untrue that Huneric banished him in the year 483, when he issued an [Col. 0166A] edict ordering all the Catholic bishops throughout Africa to appear at Carthage to enter into conference with those of his sect. All these claims remain without foundation.

But, it may be asked, what becomes of the authority of the African Notice, which tells us that Victor, bishop of Vite, was not present at the conference of Carthage? And what also becomes of the authority of the manuscripts, which oblige us to believe that Victor, bishop of Vite, composed the History of the Vandal Persecution?

We reply that we accept both authorities equally; we take care only not to confuse two different men, as those who wrote before us on this subject have done. For, having clearly proved from the History of the Vandal Persecution that its author Victor was not a bishop until Huneric’s death; and since, moreover, the African Notice testifies that there was a bishop of Vite in Africa during Huneric’s lifetime; and since, finally, the authority of all the manuscripts leaves us no reason to doubt that Victor, bishop of Vite in Africa, was the author of the History of the Vandal Persecution, it follows that this historian is different from Victor, bishop of Vite, mentioned in the Notice. It follows that the Notice and the History cannot be reconciled except by distinguishing two Victors, bishops of Vite.

We therefore say that there was indeed in [Col. 0166C] Africa, in the year 484, a bishop of Vite named Victor: this is what the Notice teaches us; and that, since all the bishops of Africa were obliged to come to Carthage on account of the faith, and all came except two bishops of Byzacena—Victor of Vite and Possidius of Massimane—one must infer that these two bishops died at that time or shortly afterward. Nothing other than this could have prevented them, since, as we have said, Huneric even recalled the Catholic bishops from exile so that they might come to the conference. But after the death of this barbarian king, which occurred toward the end of the year 484, when Guntabond recalled Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, from exile and granted the Church some measure of peace, one should presume [Col. 0166D] that Victor the historian was elected bishop of Vite in the year 487, since all the manuscripts agree in giving him the name Victor and the rank of bishop of Vite. We thus see that we preserve the full authority of each source, and that by this means the contradiction between the African Notice and Victor’s History disappears entirely. Under the opinion followed until now, by contrast, these two authentic sources cannot be reconciled, as follows from everything we have said in Articles 3, 4, and 5.

If anyone regards it as extraordinary that a man named Victor should have succeeded another Victor, let him know, first, that the name of [Col. 0167A] Victor was so common in Africa that there were fifty bishops bearing it in that province in the year 411, and that more than twenty appear in the Notice we are discussing—that is, men who were living in the year 484.

2. Even if the name Victor had been less common, this argument would be entirely weak and would not deserve to be raised, since we find men who bore uncommon names nevertheless succeeding one another in the same church. A great many examples could be given; here are two, which will suffice. The name Epictetus is certainly much more unusual and far less common than Victor; yet we find Epictetus, bishop of Centumcellae or Civita Vecchia, who attended the First Council of Arles [Col. 0167B] in the year 314, and another Epictetus, his successor, who distinguished himself under Constantius by his impiety, having been one of the leaders of the Arians in the West. In the city of Pudentiana in Numidia there had been a Catholic bishop named Memmianus. When he died, another bishop was ordained in his place who was also named Memmianus. This is what we learn from the acts of the great conference of Carthage. Thus, to return to our subject, the first Victor, bishop of Vite, is the one mentioned in the Notice; the second, his successor, is the pious historian of the Vandal Persecution, in accordance with the manuscripts. Let us now examine briefly whether the other facts that have been advanced in Victor’s life are better founded than those [Col. 0167C] we have just overturned.

**ART. 7. Concerning certain other facts attributed to Victor the historian without foundation.**

Since, then, the three points examined above are certain, it follows that—
1. It was therefore a mistake to say that Victor wrote his History in exile, either at Constantinople, as Father Chifflet maintains, or in ancient Epirus, according to M. Cotelier. Thus, in accordance with our third point, we must acknowledge, with the Reverend Father Ruinart, Benedictine, and M. Baillet, that Victor never left Africa; but we must part company with them in their supposition that Victor was in exile somewhere in Africa. For, besides the fact that he says nothing from which this can be inferred with any plausibility, we find that he was at Carthage after all the bishops of Africa and the clergy of Carthage had been exiled. [Col. 0167D]

2. There is no plausibility in Father Chifflet’s claim that Victor dedicated his History to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, nor in M. Cotelier’s view that this work was addressed to Diadochus, a bishop in ancient Epirus. All this is without foundation.

3. Since Victor was not ordained bishop until after the peace of the Church under Gunthamund, probably in the year 487, he cannot have been primate of the province of Byzacena twenty years later. Thus it was not our Victor who is mentioned in the Life of [Col. 0168A] Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe. And since this point is unfounded, to say nothing further, everything built upon it becomes even more uncertain: namely, that our Victor suffered greatly in the persecution of Thrasamund, Gunthamund’s successor; that this prince had him arrested in his church and brought to the prisons of Carthage; that, while on the road, Victor sent instructions to the bishops of Byzacena to consecrate Saint Fulgentius bishop of Ruspe; that after a year in prison he was exiled to the island of Sardinia, where he died as a confessor in the year 510, or, according to others, in 512. We shall believe all this when proofs have been given us. It concerns another Victor, not the Victor of Vita.

[Col. 0168B] 4. The Reverend Father Ruinart was right to reject the claim made by some that Victor was numbered among the saints. It is said that those who first inserted the name of Saint Victor of Utica into the martyrologies intended thereby to honor the memory of the author of the History. But since these authors—Galesinius, Baronius, and Ferrarius—are very recent, and since they are supported neither by the manuscripts of the martyrologies nor by any ancient author, no account should be taken of their intention. Thus the safest course on this point is to follow Father Ruinart’s observation. This is all the more necessary because Petrus Natalis, who perhaps first gave rise to the cult of Victor, intended to speak of another Victor, bishop of Cartenna in Africa.

[Col. 0168C] 5. It seems to me that M. Baillet was not right to reject what the same Benedictine says—namely, that Vita was rather a district than a city—and he should not have believed it to be a city merely because it is marked on maps drawn from the *Notice of the Churches of Africa*. For since that *Notice* does not tell us whether Vita is a region or a city, those who drew these maps should not have made Vita a city unless they possessed some other authority besides the *Notice*, of which we are told nothing. What Victor says of Saint Papinianus, whom he calls the bishop of our city, would prove the point much better; but the authority of Victor’s manuscripts, where he is described as bishop of the territory or district of Vita (*Patriae Vitensis*), leads us to believe that he is speaking of the city of his birth, not of the city over which he was bishop.

[Col. 0168D] 6. Finally, if we ask what we think of the author of the third book, which contains the profession of faith of the African bishops presented to King Huneric, we answer that Gennadius of Marseille, a contemporary author, attributes it to Saint Eugenius of Carthage; the manuscript of Laon, to all the bishops of Africa; and the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, to our Victor. Victor himself attributes it to all the bishops. But since his wording is too vague, we have reason to believe that the bishops conceived this project when they were all assembled at Carthage, and that it was carried out by Saint Eugenius, our Victor, and several other clerics of Carthage. Victor therefore calls it “our book.” And although I do not insist upon this expression, it may nevertheless plausibly be believed that his modesty led him to use it in order better to conceal the part he had in this document. After examining the difficulties concerning the person of our pious historian, it is now time to gather what he himself has taught us [Col. 0169A] about his life and to describe its course. We have had the account composed by the late M. Baillet appended to it, so that readers may see at a glance the points on which we differ from this learned critic and from the others.

[Col. 0169]

# LIFE OF VICTOR, BISHOP OF VITA IN AFRICA, ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORIAN

[Col. 0169B] Victor was an African (Book V, no. 1), but we do not know in which city or province he was born. Some have thought that they could infer from a passage in his History that he was from Peradama, a city of Byzacena. Yet they did not dare to rely firmly on Victor’s wording. Indeed, on the same grounds one might say that he was from Tamalluma in the same province (Book I, no. 1), or even from Carthage (Book I, no. 14), since he calls “our Armogastes” that holy confessor who lived at Carthage in the household of Theodoric, son of King Gaiseric, and who died there.

What is therefore probable is that Victor was born in a city that possessed the title of *civitas*, whose bishop in the year 430 was Saint Papinianus, at the time when the Vandals laid siege to the city of Hippo (Book I, no. 3). “It was then,” Victor says, “that the venerable Papinianus, bishop of our city, had his entire body burned with red-hot iron plates.” If the Council of Thelepte or Telle is not an invention, it shows that Papinianus was bishop in the province of Byzacena in the year 418 (*Councils*, vol. II, col. 157). He is therefore apparently the same man of whom Victor speaks. When Victor says that Papinianus was bishop of his city or *civitas*, we understand him to mean the city of his birth, not the city of which Papinianus was bishop. This is not to say that Victor may not already have been a bishop when he wrote these words; but since Vita, of which he was bishop, was not a *civitas*—it is mentioned as such in no monument, and Victor’s manuscripts call it [Col. 0169D] a district or small territory (*Ruin. praef.* §§ 4 and 5)—we must, and believe ourselves obliged to, understand the expression as referring to the city where he was born rather than to the one he governed as bishop.

Victor describes in such detail everything memorable that took place at Carthage after Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, seized that great city in the year 439 (*History of the Persecution of the African Church by the Vandals*, passim); he marks and names so precisely all the places where events occurred in the city and its surroundings; he is found there so often during Huneric’s reign; he knew so many people there; and finally he enters into such detail concerning everything that [Col. 0170A] happened in the Church of Carthage, that there is no reason to doubt that he spent the greater part of his life there. [Col. 0170B]

We believe that he was a priest of that celebrated Church, whose clergy consisted of five hundred persons, or even more. He learned the admirable history of the holy martyrs Martinianus, Saturianus, and their two brothers, as well as of the illustrious virgin Maxima, from the very man who had kept them in prison, and from Blessed Faustus, bishop of Buronitia. Maxima was still alive in the year 487, apparently in the Proconsular Province, where she governed a large number of virgins, and Victor knew her very well (Book II, no. 9; Book V, no. 9; Book I, nos. 10, 11, and 4).

When Gaiseric renewed the persecution, he sent [Col. 0170C] a certain Proculus into the Proconsular Province to compel the bishops to surrender the sacred vessels and the books of the Churches (Book I, no. 12). It was at this time that Saint Valerianus, bishop of Abbenza, having nobly opposed this profanation, was driven from the city, with orders forbidding anyone to give him shelter either in his house or on his land. Thus this venerable old man, more than eighty years of age, remained for a long time on the public road, stripped of everything and exposed to every hardship of the seasons. Victor says that he had the good fortune to greet him during this cruel exile. He speaks of this action with deep piety and humility. This occurred, as we believe, after the death of Saint Deogratias, bishop of [Col. 0170D] Carthage, who died in the year 457 (Book I, no. 8).

Victor had also known particularly well the illustrious confessors Armogastes, Archinimus, and Saturus, who lived at Carthage, where they confessed the Catholic faith and resisted with extraordinary courage the promises and cruelties of King Gaiseric and his sons Huneric and Theodoric (Book I, nos. 14–16). One cannot read what Victor writes about them without being compelled to acknowledge that he lived at Carthage from the time of Gaiseric onward.

Gaiseric died in the year 477, after reigning thirty-seven years and three months in Africa following the capture of Carthage, and his eldest son Huneric succeeded him. This prince, so notorious for his detestable cruelties, [Col. 0171A] initially behaved with some gentleness and moderation toward the Catholics (Book II, no. 1), going so far as to allow them to assemble publicly in the churches, which Gaiseric had forbidden. At the request of Placidia, his sister-in-law, widow of Olybrius and of the emperor Zeno, he even permitted the Church of Carthage—which had been without a bishop for twenty-four years—to elect one freely and have him ordained.

But beneath this appearance of humanity, Huneric began to reveal to the Catholics what he was plotting against them. He sent Alexander, Zeno’s ambassador, to the Church of Carthage so that the people might choose in his presence a bishop worthy of that rank. But he had Alexander accompanied by his secretary, named Vitarit, who carried an edict [Col. 0171B] to be read publicly. In this edict the king declared that he permitted the Church of Carthage to have whichever bishop it wished ordained, but on condition that the Arian bishops who were in Constantinople and the provinces of the East should, by order of Zeno, have freedom in their churches to preach and instruct the people in whatever languages they wished and to follow the Christian law—that is, the doctrines of the Arians. If this were not carried out for them, the bishop ordained at Carthage, his clergy, and the other bishops, together with their clergy, throughout all the provinces of Africa, would be sent among the Moors.

When this edict was read on June 18—or, according to some editions, on May 19—in the year 481, before the entire assembled Church, Victor, who was also present, began to groan and complain, because it appeared that pretexts were being sought to persecute and crush the Catholics. Therefore this generous minister of Jesus Christ publicly declared to the ambassador Alexander that, if matters stood thus, and if the Church of Carthage could have a bishop only on such dangerous conditions, it would rather have none at all; Jesus Christ, who had always deigned to govern it, would govern it still. Such was Victor’s generosity. As one of the principal members of the clergy, he believed that he ought to make known the true interest of the Churches of Africa, and especially of the Church of Carthage. But his remonstrance was useless: the ambassador Alexander paid no attention to it and took no concern over it. Moreover, the people, who wanted a bishop, raised intolerable cries, so that they could not be calmed by any other means. Eugenius was therefore elected. He was a holy man, pleasing to God, whose virtue was so brilliant that even the Vandals respected him.

Although his ordination filled all the faithful of the Church of Carthage with joy, his reputation soon aroused the envy of the Arian bishops, especially Cyrila, one of their leading men, so that they overwhelmed him daily with new calumnies. They induced the king to order him not to sit on the episcopal throne and not to instruct the people according to custom. The king then demanded that the holy bishop forbid entry into the church to all who wore Vandal dress. But when Eugenius replied that the house of God was open to everyone, Huneric began the persecution by attacking those who wore the dress of his nation because they held offices in his household. Their entire scalps, together with their hair, were torn away (Book II, no. 4). Many died from this; others lost both eyes. Women in this condition were dragged through all the public squares of the city so that everyone might see them, adding humiliation to cruelty. Yet despite these ill-treatment, Victor assures us that he knew a great many of them, and that not one of all these illustrious Catholics [Col. 0172B] departed in any respect from the straight path of truth.

Huneric had a vehement desire to leave the kingdom to his children (Book II, no. 5), contrary to the constitution of his father Gaiseric, who had ordered that the oldest of his grandsons and descendants should always succeed to the crown (*Procopius, History of the Vandals*, Book I). To accomplish his purpose, this cruel prince began openly persecuting his brother Theodoric and his children, as well as the children of his brother Genton. Since the first of his bishops—whom the Vandals called patriarch—named Jocundus, was highly honored and loved in the household of his brother, whose children might have obtained the kingdom through the prelate’s support and influence, Huneric had him burned alive in the middle of Carthage before the entire people. Victor witnessed this criminal impiety. Seeing in the deed the evils that were about to fall upon the Catholics, he admits that they said to one another that a prince who was so cruel toward his own bishop would not spare the Catholic religion or those who professed it. This occurred in the year 481, two years before the great fire of persecution (Book II, no. 6), which God made known through numerous visions and signs granted to several holy persons, so that his servants would not be taken by surprise and would have time to strengthen themselves against so many evils.

Victor, always attentive to the Church’s prosperity and suffering, carefully collected these visions, having learned several of them from those who had received them. The very first was reported in his presence to the holy bishop Eugenius. We shall record here the vision of Bishop Quintianus, because Victor provided its interpretation. This holy prelate was seated upon a high mountain, from which he saw in the plain a flock of sheep whose number was innumerable. In the midst of this great flock were two cauldrons upon the fire. There were also butchers who killed the sheep and threw their flesh into the boiling water; by this means the entire great flock was destroyed and consumed. Victor says that these two cauldrons signified the [Col. 0173A] two cities of Sicca and Lara, where the great multitude of confessors who were sent into exile in the deserts of Africa were first assembled; or that they signified King Huneric and Cyrila, his bishop, who, according to Victor, was the principal author of the persecution (Book II, no. 18).

Huneric attempted several very criminal means of finding an occasion to launch a public and general persecution throughout Africa (Book II, no. 7). But when he failed either to succeed or to dishonor the Church of Jesus Christ, he dropped the mask. Having had 4,976 bishops, priests, deacons, and other members of the Church gathered together, he sent them into exile in the desert. Among these holy confessors were several afflicted with gout, and others whose advanced age had deprived them of their sight. Among them stood out Blessed Felix, bishop of Abbir, a city of the Proconsular Province. Having fallen into a severe paralysis, he could no longer feel anything and could not speak at all.

Our Victor found himself greatly embarrassed by such a misfortune. Realizing that it was impossible to transport the holy old man on horseback, he appealed to several Vandals of the court. They asked the king to order that, since Felix was soon to die, he might at least remain at Carthage, since there was no way to take him to the place of exile. But the tyrant furiously replied: “If he cannot sit on a horse, let them tie him with ropes to untamed oxen and drag him wherever I have ordered.”

Victor was therefore obliged to bind the venerable bishop sideways across a wretched horse and have him carried the entire way like a piece of wood. All these holy confessors were assembled in the cities of Sicca and Lara, where the Moors had been ordered to gather, because the saints were to be handed over to them there to be taken into the desert. It was a vast wilderness, filled with such a great quantity of venomous animals and scorpions (Book II, no. 12) that what was said about it seemed incredible to those who had not witnessed it. Some of these creatures even poisoned from their breath those who were far away from them. Such was the dwelling that Huneric had prepared for the confessors.

While they were in the two cities just mentioned, the king sent two counts there (ibid., no. 9), who tried through fine words and promises to corrupt the servants of Jesus Christ. But this was entirely useless, for all these saints answered only by renewing aloud their confession of faith. They were therefore shut up in a miserable prison, though one in which they had at least some room. Victor himself—we believe that he had been deputed and sent by Saint Eugenius of Carthage, his bishop, with considerable sums of money to assist the confessors in every way possible until they reached the place of their exile—was permitted to enter, [Col. 0174A] preach and exhort the brothers there, and celebrate the divine mysteries (Book II, nos. 9–10).

Since the persecuting Vandals could corrupt no one—not even a single child—they sought out the narrowest and most dreadful places in which to confine the army of the Lord. The confessors were denied every kind of consolation, and no one was permitted to visit them. To make the guards more exacting and cruel, they were beaten with sticks and tormented severely. The confessors of Jesus Christ were thrown one upon another like locusts. Since they could not leave to attend to their natural needs, they turned their cramped dwelling into a place of horror more unbearable than the most dreadful tortures. [Col. 0174B]

In this extremity Victor did not lose courage. One day, while the Vandals were asleep, he gave generous gifts to the Moors, who barely allowed him to enter secretly into the place. There he sank into the filth up to his knees. The pious Victor has contented himself with telling us in a few words what he did for the holy confessors on this important occasion; for immediately afterward the Moors ordered them all, amid loud cries, to prepare for the journey they had to make (Book II, no. 10).

These barbarians treated the saints with extreme cruelty. They forced them to run, throwing stones at them and stabbing them with the points of their spears. When the old men and the frail could no longer walk, these pitiless men [Col. 0174C] tied them by the feet and dragged them over the stones until they gave up their spirits. The number who died in this way was so great that Victor could not count them (Book II, nos. 11–12).

Yet on this sad occasion he had a great cause for edification, which must not be omitted. During this journey, which produced so many martyrs, Victor, accompanying this great army of confessors, one day saw a poor old woman carrying a sack and some clothing. She was holding by the hand a small child whom she comforted, saying: “Run, my lord. Do you see how all these saints march joyfully and hasten to arrive at the crown?”

Victor reproached her for acting at an inappropriate time and contrary to the rules of prudence by joining a company of men and associating herself with the confessors. She replied: “Bless me, bless me, and pray for me as well as for this child, my grandson. For although I am a sinner, I am the daughter of the former bishop of the city of Zura.”

Since this city in the Proconsular Province was very far from the place where the confessors then were, Victor answered her: “Why are you traveling in such poverty, and what reason do you have for coming here from so far away?”

The pious woman replied: “I am going into exile with this little child, your servant, for fear that the enemy may find him alone and draw him from the path of truth, plunging him into [Col. 0175A] death.”

At these words Victor, his eyes filled with tears, could say nothing except that the will of God was being accomplished. When the strongest of the confessors had arrived in the desert, Victor, having fulfilled his commission and no longer able to do anything for these saints, quickly returned to Carthage to his bishop, Saint Eugenius (Book II, nos. 9, 12).

Meanwhile Huneric was plotting something more horrible against the Church than what we have just related. Having attacked some of its members, he resolved to destroy the whole body. On the day when the Church celebrates the feast of the Ascension of Our Lord, he sent Bishop Eugenius an edict to be read in the middle of the church in the presence of Count Regin, [Col. 0175B] the ambassador of the emperor Zeno. Regin was a Catholic, and we still possess the letters that Saint Fulgentius (*Epistle* 18) and Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, wrote to him much later in answer to his questions.

While the king’s edict was being carried to the church of Carthage, couriers set out in haste to deliver copies to all the Catholic bishops throughout the provinces of Africa and on the islands of Sardinia, Majorca, Minorca, and Yvica, which obeyed the Vandals. By this edict the tyrant ordered all the bishops, without exception, to come to Carthage on the first day of February of the following year to give an account of their faith, or to confer and dispute with the Arian bishops (Book II, no. 13).

[Col. 0175C] Victor, who was present when this edict was read, was heartbroken with grief and could not restrain his tears. He believed that when Huneric said he did not want there to be scandal in the provinces God had granted him, he had made it sufficiently clear that he did not want there to be any Catholics in his kingdom. They deliberated about what ought to be done and found no better remedy for so great an evil than to present a petition in the name of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage. But Huneric, who had resolved to destroy the Catholics, paid no attention to it (Book II, no. 14).

On the first day of February in the year 484, the bishops of Africa were present at Carthage, numbering approximately 466, overwhelmed with pain and grief. [Col. 0175D] Our Victor omits nothing important that occurred in this sad circumstance. Since the bishops had requested that the people be present at the conference, it is at least probable that Victor, who was at Carthage the previous year and whom we shall find there again after the conference during the persecution, also attended this assembly.

The patriarch of the Vandals, Cyrila, who had kindled this fire and did not consider himself capable of withstanding the Catholics’ attack, employed trickery, lies, calumnies, and violence to break up the conference and avoid entering into the matter. He succeeded only too well, because Huneric was guided entirely by his counsels. [Col. 0176A]

But the Catholic bishops, who had foreseen all this, had also drawn up a lengthy profession of their faith, which they sent to the king through four bishops on April 20. This book was composed at Carthage after the bishops’ arrival; thus it may be believed that it was written by Saint Eugenius, our Victor, and several others (Book II, no. 18; Book IV, no. 1).

I shall not relate here the dreadful aftermath of this so-called conference, nor the more-than-barbarous cruelty that the Vandal king exercised against so many bishops. It is enough to say that they were all finally exiled, some to the island of Corsica and others to various places in Africa, but all away from their Churches. Afterward this inhuman prince sent men like himself throughout all the [Col. 0176B] provinces, sparing only those who succumbed to their violence. No place and no house was exempt from the persecution; tears and groans were heard everywhere.

Victor, who was a priest of Carthage, remained in that city to support the faithful, for it was there that the violence of the persecution was greatest because of the presence of the king and his patriarch. The pious historian, who describes only a few particular events that occurred in the provinces, omits nothing of what took place before his eyes in the capital of Africa. He witnessed the violence that Cyrila had inflicted upon a child of about seven years, the son of a noblewoman, whom this prelate forcibly rebaptized (Book IV, no. 5; Book V, nos. 1, 4).

[Col. 0176C] After God had purified his Church through this dreadful persecution, he finally cast into the fire the rods he had used to chastise it. Not a single drop of rain fell in Africa, and the famine was so severe that this vast province was depopulated; the Vandals suffered no less than the native inhabitants. At last the wretched Huneric, after reigning seven years and ten months, went to receive the punishments due for his impiety. He died consumed by worms (Book V, no. 14).

Gunthamund, the son of his brother Genton, succeeded him in accordance with Gaiseric’s law, for he was the oldest of the princes of the royal house. Gunthamund was fairly favorable toward the Catholics. He recalled Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, from exile; and in the third year of his reign, which was the year 487, he restored to the Catholics of Carthage the cemetery of Saint Agileus the martyr. We learn this from an ancient and very exact author who continued Prosper’s chronicle.

It was at about the same time that Saint Eugenius, having returned to Carthage, ordained, as we believe, our Victor bishop of Vita, in place of another Victor who had died three years earlier. This is what we judge should be inferred from the manuscripts of Victor’s History, all of which give him the title of bishop of Vita.

The good bishop believed that God, who had permitted him to witness so cruel a persecution, had preserved him so that he might write its history for the edification [Col. 0177A] of the Church and the instruction of later ages. He undertook this work at the request of one of his friends, whose name is unknown to us, in the year 487 of Jesus Christ, sixty years after the Vandals entered Africa (*Victor*, Prologue; Book I, no. 1).

What we have just reported about Victor’s actions shows that, although he does not appear to have personally suffered anything, he nevertheless had a substantial part in everything that took place under Huneric. Perhaps there was no one in all Africa who was better informed than he about every detail of that famous persecution of the Vandals, whose memory he has left to posterity.

We have divided it into five books, although there is no proof that this division comes from the author. [Col. 0177B] It is written in a simple but deeply moving style, and its coloring is extremely vivid. It is rightly regarded as one of the most important monuments that remain to us, not only from the African Church but from all Christian antiquity.

We find nothing more concerning our Victor after the year 487, because we do not believe that what is said about him is well founded, nor that he is the Victor mentioned in the Life of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe. Those who read attentively what we have [Col. 0178A] reported about Victor will doubtless find great similarities between the life of Saint Luke and his own. He was not as well known as he deserved to be, as we observed in the Dissertation. Even the prologue that he placed at the head of his History is so corrupt that no certain fact can be drawn from it.

But the authors of the martyrologies made extensive use of his work. His name does not occur in the ancient manuscripts of the martyrologies. Peter Galesinius seems to have been the first to insert it in his, under the name Victor of Utica, and from there it passed into the Roman Martyrology. But if it is true that Petrus Natalis gave rise to this addition when, under April 20, he mentioned Victor, bishop of Carthage—although he intended to speak of Victor, bishop of Cartenna—then it is sufficiently clear that the cult of our Victor of Vita has no foundation in antiquity.

There are many other holy persons who are not recorded in the Church’s registers. And, after all, one cannot read Victor’s History without recognizing his faith, charity, singular piety, zeal for religion and the salvation of souls, humility, and other virtues, which, joined to his learning, give him a distinguished place among the great men who have edified and instructed the Church of God.

[Col. 0177]

# LIFE OF SAINT VICTOR, BISHOP OF VITA IN AFRICA, CONFESSOR

By M. Baillet, priest.

[Col. 0177C] **I.** The Roman Martyrology presents, among the saints whose memory the Church honors on August 23, a certain Victor, bishop of Utica in Africa. On this point Baronius believed that this saint was none other than the celebrated author of the *History of the Persecution of the Church in Africa under the Vandals*, because he, like nearly everyone of his time, shared the opinion of those who had made that author bishop of Utica. If it were true that Saint Victor had in fact been bishop of Utica—which was a city of the Proconsular Province, well known in antiquity—we would be obliged to acknowledge that he was entirely different from Victor, the author of the *History of the Persecution*. But since it appears that those who first inserted the name of Saint Victor of Utica into the martyrologies intended thereby to honor the memory of the man who composed the *History*, it is clear that the Victor in question was bishop not of Utica but of Vite, in the province of Byzacena. Some have written that Vite was rather the name of a district than of any city in that province. But maps drawn on the basis of the *Notitia of the Churches of Africa* clearly mark a city of [Col. 0178C] that name in Byzacena, which lay east and south of the Proconsular Province, a few leagues from Ruspe, of which Saint Fulgentius was bishop. Victor was made bishop of Vite toward the end of the reign of Genseric, the first king of the Vandals in Africa, who died in the year 477. He played a major part in the persecution that King Huneric, the son and successor of that prince, renewed against the Catholic Church. Since he became a zealous defender of the orthodox faith concerning the divinity of Jesus Christ against the Arians, he was also among those whom Huneric expelled from their sees for that reason. It appears that he was already in exile in 484, when that prince issued an edict ordering all the Catholic bishops of Africa to assemble at Carthage to enter into conference with those of his sect [Note: [Col. 0177D] *Catal. episc. Afr.*, vol. IV of the *Councils*; Schelstrate, *De Ecclesia Africana*, p. 292 and following].

It is not known with certainty where his [Col. 0178D] exile was located. Some [Note: [Col. 0177D] Chifflet, edition of Victor; G. Cave, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*] believed that it was the city of Constantinople—not because it had been assigned to him by the persecutor, but because they were persuaded that Victor had chosen it as a place of refuge where he hoped to live peacefully under the protection of the emperor Zeno. Others [Note: [Col. 0178D] Cotelier, vol. III, *Monumenta Graeca* concerning the *Life of Saint Sabas*, Ruinart’s edition of Victor] conjectured that it was somewhere in ancient Epirus. But there is no indication [Col. 0179A] that he left Africa; and, had he been far removed from it, he could not have been so precisely informed about the details of the persecution whose memory he wished to leave to posterity. He wrote its history in 487, during his exile. We possess it in five books. Its style is simple but deeply moving, and its colors are extremely vivid. We regard it as one of the most important monuments of the African Church that have survived.

**II.** Huneric had died as early as December 13 of the year 484, after putting some of the Catholic bishops to death and relegating the others to the island of Corsica. He was succeeded by his nephew Gondebaud, or Guntabond, who granted the Church a kind of peace by allowing the persecution to abate [Col. 0179B]. But it was a short-lived peace, and the respite that the indulgence of this prince allowed the Catholic prelates who had returned from exile to enjoy during the first years of his reign was often disturbed by the efforts of the Arian bishops, who continually sought to harm them. Nevertheless, Guntabond had the courage to resist the requests of those of his sect and even to recall the remaining Catholic bishops from exile. But when he seemed to be promising a good peace to the Church of Africa, he was removed from the world after twelve years of reign by an illness that left the crown to his brother Thrasamond. This new king, besieged by the bishops of his sect, brought back the sad times of his uncle Huneric; and although he was less cruel, he gave scarcely less trouble to the [Col. 0179C] Catholic bishops who were zealous to preserve the purity of the faith among their peoples. There can be no doubt that Saint Victor was among those who suffered most, especially after he had become metropolitan, or primate, of the province of Byzacena and was therefore, as it were, charged with general oversight of its pastors and flocks. Around the year 504, Thrasamond, seeking to undermine the Catholic Church at its foundations, issued an edict forbidding [Col. 0180A] the ordination of bishops to replace those who died. Since he could not secure obedience by all his authority, he had as many as two hundred gathered together and relegated them to the island of Sardinia. We do not know what induced this prince to spare Saint Victor on that occasion. But two years later, having learned that Victor had no hesitation in ordaining bishops for Catholic churches that lacked them, despite the prohibition, he became so angry with him that he had him arrested and brought as a prisoner to the prisons of Carthage. While he was on the way, the delegates from the city of Ruspe again approached him as metropolitan of the province, asking him to appoint Saint Fulgentius as their bishop. He cited neither the king’s orders nor the chains binding his hands, [Col. 0180B] nor the threatening presence of the guards who surrounded him as an excuse; nothing prevented him from granting the delegates of Ruspe the satisfaction they requested, and he secretly sent a commission to the neighboring bishops to consecrate Fulgentius. At Carthage he was regarded as the principal object of the Arian bishops’ hatred. Thrasamond, still angered by the contempt Victor had shown for his orders, banished him after a year in prison and sent him to Sardinia with many other confessors of the Catholic faith. He died in that exile, according to some around the year 510, or according to others in 512, shortly after Saint Fulgentius, banished for the same reason, had arrived in the same place.

Victor, known throughout all the ages of the Church through the *History* he wrote, long remained unknown to [Col. 0180C] the faithful who profess to know saints only through their cult. Indeed, his name appears in none of the ancient martyrologies. It is claimed that the first person to mention him was Peter Natal, who inserted him into his catalogue under April 20; others moved him to the following day, as can be seen in the German Martyrology of Canisius. We do not know what obliged the compilers of the Roman Martyrology to list him on August 23.

[Col. 0179]

# HISTORY OF THE PERSECUTION OF THE AFRICAN PROVINCE (C, S)

## [NOTE]

N.B. In Sirmond’s edition the notes were published separately after the text; for the reader’s convenience we have brought them back beneath the text. We have, however, printed the pagination of the notes, as it appears in Sirmond, in heavier type, so that an analytical index may later be reprinted with some benefit. **EDITOR.**

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0179D]

**1.** Formerly, the ancients, out of their zeal for wisdom, never ceased carefully examining and diligently investigating what events—whether favorable or adverse, and of whatever kind—had occurred in provinces, places, or regions. Concerning those events, or in the places where they had occurred, they sharpened the stylus of their intellect and, with the flower of their learning exhaling its fragrance, offered baskets of histories, presented as a freely bestowed gift, to the ignorant [Col. 0180D].

[Note: [Col. 0179D] 61. Thus the *Orthodoxographia*. Lorichius, however, has *Historiae calathos*, and so forth. Nearly all the other manuscripts and printed editions have: “sharpening the stylus of their intellect and offering to the ignorant, with the flowers of their learning exhaling their fragrance, baskets of histories,” etc. The manuscript of Saint-Martin-des-Champs has “with the flower of their learning exhaling its fragrance to the ignorant,” etc., as above. The edition of Blessed Rhenanus differs slightly: “in which they might sharpen … and offer with alacrity the flowers of history to the ignorant.”]

They took care that what had been accomplished in part should not remain wholly concealed. But, puffed up with the pride of worldly love, those men eagerly desired the glory of their self-exaltation to be spread far and wide with praise. Your reverence for learning, however, commanding you to weave a history, [Col. 0181A] inquires—with a similar ardor, but a different kind of love—[Note: [Col. 0181A] Thus the *Orthodoxographia* and Lorichius. The other manuscripts and printed editions have instead: “desiring, he inquires,” etc. If these two words are retained, this preface seems rather to be addressed by someone else to our Victor than to be Victor’s own preface to his *History*. Likewise, below the same manuscripts have “You will be able,” with “as you wished,” omitting the word “you ask.” However this passage is ultimately explained, it must be admitted that this preface is so entangled in verbal circumlocutions that it is difficult to grasp the author’s true meaning. This is why we suspect that it has been corrupted, either through the carelessness of copyists or for some other reason unknown to us.]

**2.** They do this so that they may be praised in this world; you do it so that you may appear illustrious in the future and say: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; the meek shall hear and rejoice” (Psalm 33:3). “You will be able,” you say, “to do as you wish,” because you have received from heaven every good gift and every perfect gift, having been instructed by so great a pontiff, the blessed Diadochus, who is to be proclaimed with every kind of praise [Note: [Col. 0181B] Thus, together with one of the three manuscripts of the Colbert Library against which we collated this history, the editions of Blessed Rhenanus and Chiffletius have *Diadocho*. Another Colbert manuscript has *Diacodo*. The others have *Diacono*. Chiffletius, assuming as certain that our Victor lived at Constantinople and composed the *History of the Vandal Persecution* there, immediately infers that he dedicated it to Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople: “For,” he says, “there was scarcely anyone else to whom Victor could or ought to have shown so much honor.” Then, proceeding further, he identifies the Diadochus mentioned here—whom he considers to be the same as Diadochus, bishop of Photice in ancient Epirus, praised by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*—as a teacher of Acacius of Constantinople, so that the words in this preface may be applied to him. He also says that he discovered the previously obscure date of Diadochus from this passage of Victor. But the learned man wrote all this only by conjecture. We have already said elsewhere that Victor was not living at Constantinople when he wrote the *History*.
