Nor is it at all probable that this author, who speaks so magnificently here of the authority of the Roman pontiff, dedicated his history to Acacius, who at that time was so violently opposed to the Roman Church. For this work was written in the year 487, when the most serious disputes were raging between Pope Felix and Acacius of Constantinople. Shortly afterward Acacius himself died separated from communion with the Roman Church; from this arose the schism between the two Churches, Eastern and Western, which lasted so long. It is no more certain that Acacius was a disciple of Bishop Diadochus, whom Evagrius says was elevated from being prefect of the orphanage to the see of Constantinople. Nor do I know whether the things Victor attributes in this preface to the person to whom he dedicated his work suit Acacius. “I see another Timothy,” he says, “etc., and Luke, skilled in medicine, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles,” and other matters which there is no need to repeat here. I have nevertheless pursued this point somewhat more fully in order to vindicate our Victor from the charge by which Chiffletius carelessly stained him, saying that he was polluted by communion with the schismatic Acacius. For the rest, although I would not dare affirm that the Diadochus mentioned here was the bishop of Photice, I readily admit that the possibility is far from improbable, especially since at this time we find a Diadochus, bishop in ancient Epirus, who, under the name Didacus, signed, among the other bishops of that province, the letter sent to the emperor Leo; it is preserved in the Council of Chalcedon, part III, chapter 51.]

whose sayings exist like innumerable shining stars, monuments of Catholic doctrine. And it is enough for you to equal the teacher’s doctrine, since it is enough for a disciple to be like his master. I see another Timothy [Col. 0182A], instructed in the sacred writings from the beginnings of childhood, and, among others, the eminent and ready Luke, skilled in medicine, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles.

For I, submitting the neck of obedience to the command of the one who orders me, shall attempt gradually and briefly to indicate what occurred in the regions of Africa while the Arians were raging. Like a rustic laborer, with weary arms, I shall gather gold from hidden caverns; and the ore, still dirty and confused in appearance, I shall not hesitate to hand over for testing by the craftsman’s judgment and fire—by him who is able to fashion monetary solidi [al. “to paint them”].

# BOOK ONE. THE PERSECUTION IN AFRICA BY GENSERIC, KING OF THE VANDALS

[Col. 0181]

**3. I. The Vandals’ entry into Africa.** —It is now, as is clear, the sixtieth year (A.D. 487) since that cruel and savage people of the Vandal nation reached the unhappy shores of Africa, crossing with ease through the narrow strait by which this great and spacious sea contracts itself within a narrow channel of twelve miles between Spain and Africa. Once the entire multitude had crossed, their leader Genseric, wishing to make the reputation of his nation terrifying, immediately ordered all those to be counted whom the womb of the belly had brought forth into this light up to that day [Col. 0182C]. The old, the young, the little children, slaves and masters alike, were found to number eighty thousand.

When this estimate had been spread abroad, to this day the ignorant judge the number of armed men to have been so great, although it is now small and weak [Note: [Col. 0181D] Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandal War*, observes that Genseric stationed Vandals and Alans under no fewer than eighty commanders—whom he called “leaders of thousands”—in suitable garrisons. This title deceived everyone, since all believed that those so designated had actually been placed over a thousand men. Thus, although, as that author continues, the army of both nations numbered no more than fifty thousand, the name of eighty thousand created that appearance.]

Finding the province peaceful and tranquil, and the beauty of the entire flourishing land spread in every direction, they attacked it with their impious forces [al. *impendebant*, “fell upon it”], laying waste and plundering it, destroying everything by fire and murder. They did not spare even the fruit-bearing shrubs at all [al. “in any way”], lest those whom mountain caves, precipitous places, or other secluded spots had concealed should, after their departure, be nourished by those provisions [Col. 0183A]. Thus, when they raged again and again with the same cruelty, no place remained free from their contagion.

They raged with particular savagery against churches, basilicas of the saints, cemeteries, and monasteries, so that they burned the houses of prayer and all the towns and cities in fires greater than those with which they destroyed cities. Whenever they happened to find the closed doors of a venerable sanctuary, they vied with one another in striking them with their right hands, opening an entrance, so that it could rightly then be said: “As in a forest of trees, they cut down its doors together; with axe and hatchet they demolished it. They burned your sanctuary with fire upon the earth; they profaned the dwelling-place of your name” (Psalm 75:6–7).

**4. II. Their savagery.** [Col. 0183B] —How many distinguished pontiffs and noble priests were then killed by them through various kinds of punishment, so that they might hand over whatever gold or silver they possessed, whether private or ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0183C] Notice that ecclesiastical property is distinguished here from other property, including property possessed by clerics. See the code of the canons of the African Church, chapter 32, or canon 49 of the Third Council of Carthage]! And while whatever they possessed was more readily revealed under the pressure of torture, they again pressed the informers with cruel torments, supposing that some part, not the whole, had been disclosed; and the more that was given, the more they believed the victim still possessed.

To some they opened their mouths with wooden bars; because they confessed where money was, they thrust foul mud into their throats. They tortured and tormented others by stretching their sinews and tightening them across their foreheads and shins. To many they cruelly offered seawater, to others vinegar, olive lees, fish sauce, and many other substances, as though placing them at the mouth of inflated wineskins, without mercy. Neither weakness of sex, nor consideration of nobility, nor priestly reverence softened their cruel spirits; rather, the fury of their anger was increased wherever they saw the honor of rank.

How many priests and how many illustrious [Note: [Col. 0183C] Colbert manuscript 1, together with Chiffletius, adds “men.” *Illustris* was a title of great dignity, conferred on prefects of the praetorium, quaestors, and others. On this see more in Cangius’s *Glossary*.] men they loaded with enormous burdens, like camels or other kinds of pack animals, I cannot relate. They drove them onward with iron goads, and some of them miserably surrendered their souls beneath their loads.

The maturity of old age and venerable gray hair, which had whitened the head’s locks like bright wool [Note: [Col. 0183C] We have retained the reading of several printed editions. Colbert manuscript 1 has *hostibus* (“from enemies”). The others have “could claim no mercy for themselves from their hosts,” except the second Colbert manuscript, which lacks *sibi* (“for themselves”).], secured no mercy for them from their hosts. Barbarous fury even tore little children from their mothers’ breasts and dashed innocent infancy to the ground. Others, holding them by the feet from opposite sides, tore them apart from the natural passageway all the way to the crown of the head. At that time captive Zion perhaps sang: “The enemy said, ‘I will burn up my borders, kill my infants, and dash my little ones to the ground’” (2 Kings 8:12) [Note: [Col. 0183C] Colbert manuscript 3 and Chiffletius have *aliis* (“others”). Some printed editions have “others, holding the little one by the feet” [Col. 0183D] etc. Below, instead of *forte Sion* (“perhaps Zion”), Lorichius has *porta Sion* (“the gate of Zion”).]

**III. They overthrow buildings.** —In certain buildings of great mansions or houses, where the fire had been less effective [Col. 0184B], they tore away the roofs [Colbert manuscript: “scattered,”] and leveled the beauty of the walls with the ground, so that now it is impossible to see what that ancient splendor of the cities had been. Very many cities, moreover, are inhabited either by only a few inhabitants or by none. For even today, if any remain, they are gradually deserted, as at Carthage, where, out of hatred, they utterly destroyed the theaters, the temple of Memory, and the road called Coelestis—[Note: [Col. 0183D] Three printed editions have: “just as at Carthage they destroyed an edifice worthy of the theater of Coelestis,” etc. Below, they have *Coelestis*; Colbert manuscript 2 has “which they called Coelestis.” The idol Coelestis was famous among the Africans; it is mentioned by Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, by Ambrose against Symmachus, and at greater length by Salvian, Book VIII of *The Government of God*. Augustine detests the filth of the goddess Coelestis and the temple and shrine of Memory mentioned here in Book II, chapter 26, of *The City of God*. The author of the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, part 2, promise 38, records that the Road of Coelestis was destroyed by Vandal hands; that work is printed among the works of Saint Prosper. The same author describes the Temple of Coelestis, which gave its name to the road, in these words: “In Africa, at Carthage, they said there was a very large temple of Coelestis, surrounded by the buildings of all their gods. Its paved square, decorated with a lithostrated pavement, precious columns, and walls, extended for nearly two thousand paces.” He then adds how that temple, cleansed by Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, was consecrated to the true God. The author asserts that he himself was present at this event; anyone wishing to learn more may consult his fuller account. Those various temples of the gods were destroyed under Constantius Augustus and Placidia, the parents of Valentinian III, at the insistence of the tribune Ursus; the site was converted into a field for the burial of the dead, as the author just mentioned relates.]

And, to speak of necessary things, they enslaved to their religion’s license and tyranny the great basilica [Colbert manuscript 21: “of the ancestors”] where the bodies of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, of Celerina or of the Scillitan martyrs, were buried, as well as the other churches that they had not destroyed [Note: [Col. 0184D] Colbert manuscript 2 has *Celerini*. Augustine mentions the Basilica of Celerina in Sermon 174. Cyprian discusses the martyr Celerina and her nephew Celerinus in Letter 39 of the Oxford edition, elsewhere Letter 34. We have included the acts of the Scillitan martyrs, whom Victor mentions here, among the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, under the year 200, p. 75, and the passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity under the year 202, p. 81. The Scillitan martyrs were so called from Scillitan, a city of the Proconsular Province, whose bishop Pariator signed the synodical letter of the bishops of that province, as can be seen in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, Session 2.].

Wherever there appeared to be fortifications that the hostility of barbarous fury could not assault [Col. 0184C], they gathered innumerable crowds around the camps and tormented them with savage swords, so that, when the defense of the walls prevented them from reaching the corpses, they might kill those inside through the stench of the rotting and liquefying bodies. Who could recount how many priests, and how numerous, were then tortured by them? [Col. 0185A]

At that time the venerable bishop of our own city, Papinianus [Note: [Col. 0185B] Thus four printed editions. The manuscript of Port-Royal has *Pampinius*; Colbert manuscript 1, *Pampianus*; the other Colbert manuscript, *Pampinianus*. The *Orthodoxographia*, Lorichius, the Martin manuscript, and Colbert manuscript 3 have *Pampinias*, a name that both manuscripts also display in the title prefixed to the chapter. An old calendar in the Capuan sanctuary of the monk Michael commemorates this man, whom it calls Papinus, and Bishop Mansuetus on November 28, the same day on which their feast is celebrated in the commonly used martyrologies. Among these, Usuard and Ado call the former Papinius; Florus calls him Papyrius. On that same day Ado joins together several others who are frequently praised in Victor’s history. It will be useful to quote his words here, for after recounting the martyrdom of Saints Papinius and Mansuetus in the persecution under Genseric, he writes: “At that time other holy bishops also—namely Quodvultdeus of Carthage, Valerian, Urban, Crescens, and the one called Habetdeus, as well as Eustachius, Crescentianus, Cresconius, Felix, Hortolanus, and Florentianus—condemned to the most severe exile for the same truth of their preaching, completed the course of their lives in confession of piety.” Ado says this of those holy confessors, with whom we shall deal individually in their proper places.] was burned over his entire body with plates of glowing iron.

Likewise Mansuetus of Uricita [Note: [Col. 0185C] Thus Colbert manuscript 1 together with the edition of Chiffletius, Balduinus, and others. But the other Colbert manuscript together with the Martin manuscript has *Viricitanus*; the third Colbert manuscript, the *Orthodoxographia*, Lorichius, and other editions have *Juricitanus*. It has not been possible to identify this see. *Urcitana* occurs both in the Cyprianic Index and in the African *Notitia*, in the Proconsular Province, where its bishop is said to be Quintianus. Hardouin, in his notes on Book V, chapter 4 of Pliny, believes that the reading should be *Quintianus Ucitanus*. It is certain that there were two African cities of that name, as is clear from the cited passage of Pliny, where he says: “There are two Ucitan cities, the greater and the lesser.” Bishop Octavianus of Ucimajus took part in the Carthaginian Conference, Inquiry 1, chapter 133. Tripolius, bishop of the Church of Ucita, signed the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, Session 2 of the Lateran Council. Nevertheless, in the Cyprianic Index of the Oxford edition, *Urci* is listed among the other cities of Africa, perhaps taken from this passage of the *Notitia*. This holy bishop is said to have been burned at the Fornitan Gate. In my opinion, these words designate a gate of Carthage from which the road led to the city of Furni. If, however, Victor is speaking of events that occurred before the capture of Carthage, these words must be understood of the city of Furnitana itself. Florentinus, bishop of Furni, from the Donatist sect, took part in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198. Simeon, bishop of the people of Furni, signed the Council of Carthage under Boniface; that same Boniface is said to have consecrated a church at Furni in the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 29. Finally, older than all these was Geminius of Furni, who spoke in favor of rebaptizing heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 59.] was burned at the Fornitan Gate.

At that time the city of Hippo Regius was under siege, and it was governed by the blessed Augustine, worthy of every praise, the author of many books. Then that river of eloquence which flowed abundantly through all the fields of the Church was dried up by fear, and the sweetness of the words that had been poured forth with such graciousness was turned into the bitterness of wormwood, so that David’s proclamation was fulfilled: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled, and I was still from good things” (Psalm 38:2–3).

By that time he had already completed 232 books, apart from innumerable letters, his exposition [Col. 0185B] of the entire Psalter and of the Gospels, and his popular treatises, which the Greeks call *homilies*. It is quite impossible to determine their number [Note: [Col. 0186B] In Colbert manuscript 1, which is approximately seven hundred years old, six verses are inserted here under the title *Epitaph*. Although we do not believe them to be by our Victor, we have nevertheless thought it appropriate to reproduce them here.]

### EPITAPH OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

Here the most chaste mother placed the ashes  
of you, Augustine, another light of merit.

As a priest preserving the heavenly laws of peace,  
you instructed the peoples entrusted to you in morals.

Grace awaits you and crowns you with praise for your deeds.  
The mother of virtues is happier in her offspring.

Shortly afterward, instead of the words *truces impietatis insanias* (“the savage insanities of impiety”), Colbert manuscript 1 together with one printed edition has *trucis impietates insaniae* (“the insanities of savage impieties”).]

**IV. The destruction of Carthage.** [Col. 0186A] —Why say more? After these savage insanities of impiety, Genseric seized and entered the great city of Carthage itself, reducing that ancient, freeborn, and noble liberty [Note: [Col. 0186C] Genseric captured Carthage on October 19, 439. We discuss the matter more fully below, in our historical commentary, chapter 5. Salvian, Book VII of *The Government of God*, gives further information about the power of this city and its various offices. He observes that, as at Rome, Carthage had a senate and various dignities, retaining even the same names that were in use at Rome. “It possessed,” he says, “absolutely everything by which the organization of the commonwealth throughout the world is administered or governed. There were all the instruments of public offices … there were military forces and authorities directing the army; there was proconsular honor; there was a daily judge and governor, proconsul in name but consul in power; finally, there were all the administrators of affairs and the dignities distinguished from one another both by rank and by title.”] to slavery.

He also took captive a considerable number of the city’s senators. Then he issued a decree that each person should bring whatever gold, silver, gems, and precious garments he possessed [al. “should offer”], and in this way the rapacious man, by such a method, quickly stole their ancestral and paternal wealth.

He also assigned the individual provinces: he reserved Byzacena, Abaritana, and Getulia for himself, together with part of Numidia; but he divided Zeugitania, or the Proconsular Province, among his army by a kind of inheritance, while Valentinian was still emperor and defending the remaining provinces, though they had already been devastated [Col. 0186B]. After Valentinian’s death, he gained possession of the whole circuit of Africa, as well as the great islands—Sardinia, Sicily, Corsica, [Col. 0186D] Ebusus, Majorca, Minorca, and many others [Note: [Col. 0186D] Colbert manuscript 1 and the Martin manuscript have *Efesum*. The *Orthodoxographia*, Rhenanus, and Lorichius omit this word. Ebusus is an island in the Mediterranean Sea; its bishop, Opilio of Ebusus, is listed below, last in the African *Notitia*. It is therefore evident that this island too was subject to the Vandals while they ruled in Africa, and that its omission in several editions is unjustified. See below what we observe in the notes to the African *Notitia* concerning it and the other places Victor mentions here. 65. Nothing need be said here about Odoacer, king of the Heruli, who is said here to have received Sicily from Genseric under the obligation of tribute, since his deeds are well known from the authors commonly read. He was the first of the barbarians to assume the title of king in Italy after the Western Empire had been extinguished. He was followed by Theodoric the Great, who established the kingdom of the Ostrogoths in Italy.]—and, with his customary arrogance, maintained control over them all.

One of these islands, Sicily, he later granted to Odoacer, king of Italy, under the right of tribute; and Odoacer paid him tribute at the appointed times as to a lord, while reserving a portion for himself.

Moreover, he did not hesitate to order the Vandals to drive bishops and noble laymen entirely naked from their churches [al. “and places”] and sees. If, once the choice had been offered, they delayed leaving, they were to remain slaves forever. This was also done in the case of very many, for we know that many bishops and distinguished and honored laymen became slaves of the Vandals.

## V. He Expels the Clergy

Then he ordered the bishop of the aforesaid city—that is, of Carthage—manifest before God and human beings, named Quodvultdeus, together with a very large crowd of clergy, to be put aboard ships with their timbers broken, and expelled completely naked and stripped of everything.

[Note: His memory is celebrated on 26 October. Ado joined him with the others on 28 November, as we said above (Col. 183, note a). More about him may be found below in the historical commentary, chapter 9.]

God, in the compassion of his goodness, graciously brought them by a prosperous voyage to Naples, a city of Campania. The multitude of senators and distinguished men he first crushed through a cruel exile and afterward cast into foreign lands.

[Note: “Three,” says Cangius in his Glossary. Among authors, the ranks of honorific distinction are *illustrious*, *most distinguished*, and *respectable*. See more on these matters in this author.]

After the bishop had been expelled, as we have said, together with the venerable clergy, he immediately seized for his own religion the church named Restituta, in which the bishops had always resided, and took away all the churches within the city walls, together with their wealth. He also occupied whichever churches he wished outside the walls, and especially two splendid and spacious churches of the holy martyr Cyprian: one where he shed his blood, and another where his body was buried—a place called Mappalia.

[Note: Concerning this basilica, see Baronius under the year 397. Several synods were held there, as may be seen throughout the African Church’s book of canons. Concerning the two mentioned below, erected in honor of Saint Cyprian, we spoke in the introduction to the acts of that saint, no. 17, in *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 203. Procopius gives a fuller account of how one of these, which the Arians had violated, returned to Catholic control under Belisarius, in book II of *The Vandal War*. We too shall discuss this matter below in the historical commentary, chapter 12.]

Who could endure, or recall without tears, that he ordered the bodies of our dead to be carried to burial without the solemnity of hymns, in silence? He added that the portion of the clergy that had remained should also be driven into a punitive exile [alternative: “given over to punishment/destruction”].

[Col. 0188A]

While these things were happening, the leading priests and distinguished men who remained from the aforesaid provinces, which he had allotted to the Vandals, decided to approach the king in order to make supplication. When, as was customary, he had gone out to the Maxulitan shore, which popular usage calls Lugula, they dared to appear before him, although they had already lost their churches and possessions, beseeching him to grant them at least the opportunity to live there, so that they might console the people of God while the Vandals were now ruling.

[Note: Colbertinus 2 and the Martyrum manuscript, together with Rhenanus, Lorichius, and others, read *visi sunt* (“they seemed”). The third Colbertinus reads *usi sunt supplicationibus* (“they made use of supplications”). A little farther on, where it is said that he “is reported to have answered them,” Colbertinus 1 and the first edition read *probatur* (“is proved”). The other Colbertinus, the Martyrum manuscript, and the Orthodoxographia, together with Rhenanus and Lorichius, read: “To whom the king says: ‘I have decreed,’” and so on.

Ortelius thinks that the Maxulitan shore mentioned here by Victor was so called from Maxulitana, a city of the proconsular province. He interprets *Ligula* as so named because it was a very narrow and long strip of land projecting into the sea and resembling an outstretched tongue. Caesar calls similar places *Lingulae*, or, as other editions have it, *linguae*, in book III of *The Gallic War*. Later, however, the name *ligula* became so established that Martial mocks grammarians who persisted in retaining the word *lingula*, although by that time even among senators and knights it had become so obsolete that it was pronounced or written only as *ligula*.]

It is reported that he answered them through an intermediary with savage words: “I have decreed that no one of your name and race is to be spared, and you dare to make such requests!” He also wished to drown them in the neighboring sea at that very hour, unless his own people had pleaded with him for a long time not to do so.

They therefore withdrew, exhausted by sadness and grief, and began, as they could and where they could, to celebrate the divine mysteries after their churches had been taken away. Then, as the kingdom increased in wealth, its arrogance also began to spread more widely.

## VI. Sebastian’s Faith

I shall now relate an event that took place at that very time. There was a certain count named Sebastian, son-in-law of the famous Count Boniface, keen in counsel and energetic in war. Geiseric feared his presence just as much as he valued necessary advice. Wishing to destroy him, the king sought an opportunity for his death through religion.

[Note: Lorichius, who was familiar with him. Idacius and Prosper give more information about Sebastian in their chronicles. His memory appears in a Martyrology published in French at Liège in the year 1624, as the Bollandists testify under 27 May. Nowhere else, however, is he listed among the saints—unless he is perhaps to be identified with the martyr Sivastianus, commemorated in the old Carthaginian calendar on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. But that is the feast day of the great Sebastian, whose memory has always been celebrated throughout the Catholic Church.

The comparison of baptism with bread, which Sebastian is said to have employed here, appears in a brief statement of faith against the Arians, published by Sirmond with other short works at Paris in 1630. From this one may infer that this little book was written while the Vandals ruled in Africa, so that Catholics might use it as a handbook against the Arians.

Concerning Boniface, the famous count whose son-in-law Sebastian is said to have been, we shall say more in the historical commentary, chapter 3.]

The king planned to confront Sebastian in the presence of his bishops and household. “Sebastian,” he said, “I know that you have sworn to remain faithfully attached to us; your labors and vigilance demonstrate the truth of your oath. But so that your friendship with us may always remain joined and constant, it has pleased our priests now present that you should become a worshiper of the religion that both we and our people venerate.”

Sebastian, recognizing that the matter was strange yet important to many, replied shrewdly for the occasion: “I ask you, lord king, to have one exceptionally pure, fine-grained (*similagineus*, alternative reading) loaf brought now.”

Geiseric, unaware of Sebastian’s strategy, immediately ordered one to be brought. Sebastian took the purest loaf and spoke as follows:

“This bread, in order to attain such a splendid brightness that it would be considered suitable for the royal table, has had the adulterated bran removed; kneaded from fine flour, it has passed through water and fire. For that reason it is bright in appearance and pleasant to eat.

“So too I have been ground in the mill of the Catholic mother, purified like clean flour in the sieve of examination, drenched with the water of baptism, and baked in the fire of the Holy Spirit. And just as this bread comes from the oven, so I, through the offices of the divine sacraments and with God as craftsman, came forth clean from the font.

“But let what I propose be done, if you wish. Let this bread be broken into pieces, soaked in water, kneaded again, and put into the oven. If it comes out better, I shall do what you urge.”

When Geiseric and all who were present heard this proposal, he was so bound that he could not free himself at all. Therefore [alternative reading: *quem alio*] he later killed the warlike man on a pretext of another kind.

## VII. A Severe Persecution

To return to the point from which we digressed: he terrified them with savage commands, so that our people might in no way breathe freely among the Vandals, and so that no place for prayer or sacrifice might be granted to those who groaned.

[Note: By this term is denoted the sacrifice of the Mass, in which the Catholic Church has always believed that Christ is truly offered. Lorichius reads: “anywhere at all for prayer or sacrifice.”]

[Col. 0190A]

Thus the prophecy was clearly fulfilled: “At this time there is neither prince, nor prophet, nor leader, nor place in which to offer sacrifice to your name” (Dan. 3:38).

Daily accusations of various kinds were also brought, even against those priests who lived in the regions that paid tribute to the royal palace. If perhaps someone, while admonishing the people of God—as was customary—had mentioned Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Holofernes, or anyone similar, he was accused of having spoken these things against the person of the king and was immediately driven into exile.

This type of persecution was carried out openly here and secretly elsewhere, so that the reputation of the faithful might be destroyed through such intrigues.

[Col. 0190B]

For this reason we know that very many priests were then banished, including Urbanus of Girba, Crescent, metropolitan of the city of Aquitania, who presided over 120 bishops; Habetdeus of Teudalis; Eustratius of Suffetana; and two Tripolitan bishops, Vices of Sabrata and Cresconius of Oea; as well as Felix, bishop of the city of Hadrumetum, because he had received a certain foreign monk named John—and many others, whose enumeration would take too long.

[Note: Colbertinus 2, the Saint Martin manuscript, the Portarum manuscript, and the Orthodoxographia read *Vicis Sabratenum*; the third Colbertinus reads *Bricis Sambratenum*. Perhaps *Vincen[ti]um Sabratenum* should be read. Certainly, numerous passages of the *African Register* show that in writing names of this kind the letter *n* was often omitted; thus *Cresces* for *Crescens* occurs there more than once. Ado, listing in his martyrology on 28 November the holy bishops driven into exile under Genseric, places Crescentianus—whom he may be identifying with the man mentioned here—between Eustratius, whom he calls Eustachius, and Cresconius. Victor nowhere else mentions Crescentianus; moreover, Ado lists him where Victor has Vices Sabratenus.

I have no doubt that here a bishop is designated together with his see. Victor names the other bishops with their respective sees; the word is also divided into two parts in the manuscripts. The context likewise requires this, since two bishops of Tripolitania are named: apparently one of Sabrata and one of Oea. Sabrata and Oea are well-known cities of that province, mentioned in the *African Register* and at the Carthaginian conference. Hence Baronius is not to be followed when, in his notes on 28 November in the Roman Martyrology, he calls Florentianus—whom Victor mentions below with Hortulanus in book IV, chapter 4—bishop of Vicessabrata, and distinguishes him, like Cresconius (although the latter is expressly called bishop of Oea in the *African Register*, as Baronius himself writes), from the two Tripolitan bishops listed here. Baronius takes those Tripolitans to be Crescentianus and Hortulanus, whom Ado praises here.

For *Cresconium Oensem*, the Portarum manuscript and Rhenanus’s edition read *Cresconium Eensem*. In manuscripts this city is frequently called *Eea* or *Ea*. Colbertinus 1 and the Saint Martin manuscript read *Meensem*; the other Colbertinus, *Uticensem*; Colbertinus 3, *Censoriensem*; Lorichius and several editions, *Nicensem*. Nevertheless, it is beyond doubt that Cresconius of Oea, named among the Tripolitan fathers in the *African Register*, is meant here. On both cities, Sabrata and Oea, see the notes on the *African Register*, under the Tripolitan bishops, nos. 2 and 4. Ado and the Roman Martyrology also commemorate Felix, bishop of Hadrumetum, named here by Victor, with the others on 28 November.]

[Note: Thus read all the manuscripts and printed editions. Two of the Colbertini, however, have a different reading in the margin: the first, “Bishop of Eqtame”; the other, “of Aquitana.” Christian Lupus, in his dissertation on the titles of the African Church, chapter 2, thinks that “of the Mauritanian city” should be read here. The learned Baluzius rejects this view because no city of that name appears anywhere in Africa. Baronius, under the year 443, substituted “of Azuritana” for “of Aquitana.”

Assura was in the proconsular province; but the sole metropolis of that province, both civil and ecclesiastical, was Carthage, as everyone knows. In the other provinces, the bishop senior by ordination held the primacy, without distinction among the cities. Yet he was not permitted to assume the title of primate or metropolitan; he was called the bishop of the first see, or the elder, or senior. On this matter there now seems to be no disagreement among learned men, although previously some had thought otherwise.

This ecclesiastical arrangement did not prevent the individual provinces from having their own civil metropolises. In view of these considerations, it seems unusual that Crescent should be called “metropolitan.” Did Victor, while living abroad in foreign provinces, adopt the manner of speech used by those with whom he was dealing? Certainly, at the Council of Ephesus the Fathers called Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, “metropolitan.” Ferrandus, as Chiffletius has already observed, attributed to the African primates everything that the canons of the ancient councils had established concerning metropolitans.

Nor was the title metropolitan wholly foreign among Africans. Augustine uses it at the beginning of his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, the Donatist bishop of Caesarea, where he calls Deuterius, the Catholic bishop of the same city, “the metropolitan of Caesarea.”

We do not know, however, what that see of Aquitana was. In the index of African cities prefixed to the Oxford edition of the works of Saint Cyprian, an Aquitana is mentioned, said to have belonged to an uncertain province. There were several bishops of Aquae in Africa. One of them was from Caesarean Mauretania, and the learned Stephanus Baluzius thinks that his see is designated here, in his notes on chapter 135 of the Carthaginian conference. We shall say more about it in the notes to the *African Register*, no. 23, concerning the bishops of this province.]

When these men had been placed in exile and death had come upon them, it was not permitted that other bishops be ordained for their cities. Nevertheless, the people of God, remaining steadfast in the faith, like a swarm of bees building waxen dwellings, were increasingly strengthened by the honeyed cells of faith.

[Note: Thus read Colbertinus 1 and three printed editions. The Orthodoxographia and Lorichius read *claviculis* (“with little keys”); Chiffletius reads *caliculis* (“with little cups”). A little earlier, for “as a swarm,” Lorichius has “as swarms of bees building waxen dwellings.”]

Thus was fulfilled the saying: “The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong” (Exod. 1:12).

## VIII. The Virtues of Deogratias

After this, at the supplication of the emperor Valentinian, a bishop named Deogratias was ordained for the Church of Carthage after a long period of desolating silence. If anyone should try, little by little, to investigate [alternative: “run through”] the virtues that the Lord worked through him, his words would begin to fail before he could explain even part of them.

[Col. 0191B]

Once this bishop had been installed, it happened—because sins were pressing upon the people—that in the fifteenth year of his reign Geiseric captured Rome, once that most noble and famous city, and at the same time carried away the wealth of many kings together with their peoples (A.D. 455).

When this multitude of captives reached the African shore, the Vandals and Moors divided the immense population. As is customary among barbarians, husbands were separated from wives and children from parents.

At once the man full of love for God devoted himself to selling all the gold and silver vessels of the ministry, to liberating people from barbarous slavery, to keeping married couples together, and to restoring children to their parents.

Because no places were sufficient to receive so great a multitude, he assigned two famous and spacious basilicas, Faustus and Novarum, with beds and bedding, determining how much each person should receive according to his due.

[Note: The Orthodoxographia, together with Lorichius and Belforest’s French translation, reads “Faustus and Novarum.” Colbertinus 1 has: “spacious basilicas that had been built in the name of Faustus, and Novarum.” A little farther below, instead of “with beds,” Lorichius reads “their beds.”

The church of Faustus was famous at Carthage, and several synods of the African Church were held there. Saint Augustine preached Sermon 122 there, and the most holy bishop Deogratias was also ordained there. At that time it was the primary and principal Catholic church at Carthage, since the Arians had occupied the basilica Restituta, as stated above.

The baptismal fonts were also located there, as is clear from Victor himself below, book 2, no. 17. We also learn from the ancient martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, and others that it was enriched with the relics of several holy martyrs. Under 15 July they say: “In Africa, in the city of Carthage, the feast of the holy Catolinus, deacon, and the other martyrs who rest in the basilica of Faustus.” Instead of Faustus, the old martyrology commonly attributed to Saint Jerome has “of Saint Fausta.” But, as learned men have often observed, such changes of letters frequently occur among the ancients.

The Catulinus mentioned here is undoubtedly the same person about whom Augustine preached the sermon entitled *On the Feast of Catulinus*. His memory is also celebrated in the Carthaginian calendar on 15 July.

Finally, after Africa had been recovered by the emperor Justinian, Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, restored the episcopal seat in the basilica of Faustus, as we shall say in the historical commentary, chapter 12.

The basilica of Novarum mentioned here seems to be the very one that Augustine calls the basilica of Novorum in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, third day, chapter 13, no. 15.]

Since many [variant: *mansio*, “dwelling”] had been weakened by unfamiliarity with sea travel and by the cruelty of captivity, there were quite a few sick people among them. Like a devoted nurse, that blessed bishop went around among them continually with the physicians [alternative: “in the role of a physician”], with suitable food following, so that, once the pulse had been examined, whatever each person needed might be provided in his presence.

Nor did he rest from this work of mercy during the night. He went from bed to bed, asking how each person was doing. He had devoted himself wholly [Colbertinus 1: *omni*, “to every”] to this labor, so that he spared neither his weary limbs nor his already decayed old age.

For this reason, the Arians, inflamed by envy, repeatedly sought to kill him through numerous plots. I believe that the Lord, foreseeing this, wished to rescue his little sparrow quickly from the hands of the hawks. The urban captives mourned his death so greatly that they thought they were being delivered into the hands of the barbarians precisely when he departed for heaven.

[Note: Optatus, in book I *Against Parmenian*, calls Pope Zephyrinus “the urban bishop.” The same Optatus speaks of an “urban commemoration” in book II. See Cyprian’s Letter 43, or 40 in some editions. Lorichius’ edition reads *urbis* (“of the city”) instead of *urbici* (“urban”).]

He served as bishop for three years. The people, devoted to him in love and longing, might have seized the body of so worthy a man, had they not buried him, according to custom, while the crowd was unaware and occupied in prayer.

[Note: Thus Lorichius, the Orthodoxographia, and Belforest. Chiffletius reads *dum morae vacatur* (“while time was being taken”); Rhenanus reads *dum avocatur* (“while they were distracted”). Saint Deogratias was ordained when Aetius and Studius were consuls, that is, in the year 454, in the basilica of Faustus. His feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 22 March and in the Carthaginian calendar on 5 January.]

## IX. Thomas the Confessor

Since one must not always remain silent about the impieties of heretics, and since it cannot be shameful to relate what contributes to the praise of one who suffers, a priest named Thomas, once ordained, was repeatedly harassed by various plots of theirs. At one time they struck the venerable old man publicly in the face with blows [variant: *publica*].

[Note: There is disagreement among authors as to whether the Thomas mentioned here should have a place in the catalogue of the bishops of Carthage. Since he is mentioned nowhere else, the matter must be settled from this passage of Victor. I shall therefore present the readings of all the manuscripts that I have been able to consult, so that each person may judge the matter according to what seems best.

Chiffletius and, as he himself reports, the manuscript of the Carthusian house at Portae read: “A certain man named Thomas was ordained to the priesthood, who, when …” The Orthodoxographia and Belforest’s translation read: “A certain man was ordained to the priesthood …” The editions of Rhenanus, Balduinus, and the *Bibliotheca Patrum* read: “The former ordainer of the aforesaid priest …,” a reading which Baronius defends as genuine.

In the Orthodoxographia and several printed editions, after the words “The ordainer … named Thomas,” the text resumes: “Thomas, the venerable bishop, while …” These words seem to have been transferred into the text from the margin, where they appear in Colbertinus 1 and the Martyrum manuscript.

Lorichius accordingly reads: “A certain man was ordained to the priesthood, named Thomas.” Then the title of the following chapter is “A certain man was ordained to the priesthood, named Thomas.” The chapter itself begins: “Thomas, the venerable bishop, while subjected to various …”

We have selected the reading of the two Colbertine manuscripts, to which the reading of the third Colbertinus and the manuscript of Saint Martin is almost identical: “a certain man was formerly ordained to the priesthood,” which seems more consistent with the rest of the text.

What chiefly moves me to remove Thomas’s name from the catalogue of the bishops of Carthage is that he is not mentioned at all in the very ancient Carthaginian calendar, in which all the other Carthaginian bishops of those times are carefully listed. In that calendar are recorded not only Aurelius, Capreolus, and Deogratias, who died in Africa, but also Quodvultdeus and Eugenius, who, although they died in foreign provinces, are nevertheless commemorated.

Moreover, when Ado lists the holy bishops who suffered under the persecution of Geiseric, drawing from Victor’s history, he omits this Thomas.]

He, counting this not as a disgrace but as a reward for his glory, rejoiced in the Lord.

After the bishop of Carthage had died, he forbade the ordination of bishops for the provinces of Zeugitana and Proconsularis; their number was 164. As they gradually died out, only three now seem to remain, if indeed even those survive: Vincentius Gigitanus, Paulus Sinnaritanus—Paul in truth and in name—and another, Quintianus, who is now fleeing persecution and lives as a stranger in the Macedonian city of Edessa.

[Note: The Orthodoxographia and Lorichius read “Vigitanus.” In the *African Register* there occurs Vincentius of Ziggis in the proconsular province, whom the learned Baluzius, in his notes on chapter 128 of the Carthaginian conference, thinks to be the very man mentioned here; there he is listed among the Catholic bishops. See below (Col. 288), note 41, on the bishops of the proconsular province listed in the *African Register*.

Norisius, in his critique of Garnerius’s notes on Marius Mercator, thinks that the see mentioned by Victor here was Gegetu, situated beyond Naraggara toward Numidia and represented on the Peutinger map. Hence the anonymous Ravennate, book III, no. 6, places Gegetu in Numidia. Among the bishops of Sitifensian Mauretania, no. 13 in the *African Register*, Constantius of Gegetum is listed. But there can be no doubt that Victor here indicates a bishop from the proconsular province.]

[Note: Thus Colbertinus 2, together with Rhenanus and other printed editions. The Martyrum manuscript and Colbertinus 1 read “Sitinaritanus.” The second edition has “Sitmaritanus.” The truth of our reading is confirmed by the *African Register*, where, among the bishops of the proconsular province, no. 3, Paulus of Sinnarus occurs, as we restored it from the Laudunensis manuscript. See the notes on that passage of the *Register*.]

[Note: Lorichius reads “Edessa.” Edessa is a city of Macedonia in Aemathia, commonly called Vodena. In the *African Register*, among the bishops of the proconsular province, Quintianus of Urcita is listed; he may perhaps be the same Quintianus whom our Victor praises here.]

## X. Maxima and the Other Martyrs and Confessors

But even then it is established that there were very many martyrs. There was also an immense and numerous multitude of confessors, some of whom I shall attempt to recount.

[Note: Thus Colbertinus 1. The others read: “But it is also established that there were very many martyrdoms … from which some …”]

At that time there were slaves belonging to a certain Vandal. This Vandal was one of those whom they call the Millenarians: Martinianus, Saturianus, and their two brothers. There was also among them a distinguished fellow slave, a servant of Christ named Maxima, beautiful both in body and in heart [alternative: “mind”].

[Note: The Orthodoxographia has “Maturianus”; Lorichius has “Mauritanus,” although below he consistently writes “Maturianus.” Colbertinus 1 calls him “Saturnianus.” The old martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, Florus, and others, under 16 October, have “Martianus and Satyrianus.” Concerning the Millenarians mentioned here, we spoke above, drawing on Procopius (at the foot of Col. 181, note a).]

Because Martinianus was an armor-maker and seemed especially favored by his master, while Maxima ruled the entire household, the Vandal believed that he could make these servants more faithful to him by joining Martinianus and Maxima in marriage.

Martinianus desired marriage in the manner of worldly young men; but Maxima, already consecrated to God, rejected human marriage. When the time came for them to enter the private silence of the bedchamber, Martinianus, unaware of what God had decreed for him and wishing, with marital confidence, to lie with her as with a wife, heard the servant of Christ reply aloud:

“Martiniane, brother, I have dedicated the members of my body to Christ, and I cannot enter into a human marriage, since I already have a heavenly and true bridegroom. But I shall give you advice. If you wish, you too can secure this for yourself while you have the opportunity: you can take delight in serving the one whom I have desired to marry.”

Thus, through the Lord’s providence, the young man obeyed the Virgin and gained his soul. The Vandal knew nothing of this spiritual exchange. Martinianus, however, was pierced and transformed, and he persuaded his brothers to regard the treasure he had discovered as something they should share in common, since they were brothers.

He therefore converted, together with his three brothers and accompanied by the girl of God. They secretly went out by night and joined the monastery at Tabraca, which was then governed by the distinguished shepherd Andreas.

[Note: Tabraca is a city well known to ancient authors, situated between the proconsular province and Numidia, in the present kingdom of Algeria. Its bishop Victoricus gave his sentence from Tabraca in no. 25 of the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. Rusticianus also attended the Carthaginian conference, together with Clarentius, his opponent from the Donatist party, *Cognitio* 1, chapters 125 and 187.]

She, for her part, lived not far away in a monastery for women. When the barbarian began searching and offering frequent rewards, what had happened could not remain concealed. Discovering that they were no longer his but Christ’s slaves, he threw them into chains and persecuted the servants of God with various tortures. He sought not only to force them to mingle with one another, but, what was more grievous, to defile the ornaments of their faith through the filth of rebaptization.

This matter came to the attention of King Geiseric, who ordered that the implacable master continue to afflict the slaves until they submitted to his will. He commanded that stout clubs, palm-like and with their roots, be made in the likeness of wild beasts—clubs which, as they battered [Colbertinus 1: *quatientes*, “striking”] their backs, would not merely break their bones but would also pierce them, leaving their spikes embedded inside.

As blood poured out and the flesh was torn apart so that the entrails were exposed, on the following day, with Christ healing them, they were always restored unharmed.

[Col. 0194C]

This was done repeatedly and for a long time [Saint Martin manuscript: *ut*, “so that”], and no traces of the wounds were visible, since the Holy Spirit continually healed them.

[Note: We have restored this reading from two manuscripts, one Colbertine and one Martinian, and it agrees with Belforest’s translation. Other manuscripts, as though this miracle had happened only to Maxima, read: “After this Maxima was confined under strict guard and stretched out upon a cruel spike,” followed by “when …” instead of “upon a spike.” Some have “always.”

Our reading is confirmed by Usuard, Ado, and Notker, who composed summaries of the martyrdom of the saints Maxima and her companions from Victor’s narrative in their martyrologies under 16 October. Ado’s words are these: “Of the holy martyrs Martianus and Satyrianus, with their two brothers, and of the distinguished virgin Maxima, servant of Christ. They were beaten with knotted clubs and torn as far as the bones; after enduring such things for a long time, they were always restored unharmed on the following day. Later, condemned to harsh prison custody, when they had been fastened in the stocks, by the wondrous power of God the decaying strength of the great pieces of wood was dissolved,” and so forth.]

After this they were confined under extremely harsh custody and stretched out in cruel fetters. While a frequent stream of visitors to the servants of God was not lacking, everyone saw the decaying strength of the enormous wooden beams dissolve.

This miracle is celebrated by everyone’s voice, and the man responsible for the custody testified to us under oath that it happened exactly so.

## XI. They Complete Their Martyrdom

But when the Vandal neglected to acknowledge the divine power, avenging wrath began to rage in his household. He himself and his sons died together; the best of the household and animals alike perished. Thus the mistress, left a widow and deprived of her husband, sons, and possessions, offered the servants of Christ to Sersaon, a kinsman of the king [another reading: Sesacnius], as a gift of gratitude. When he had received them with excessive rejoicing, as people given to him, the devil began to afflict his sons and household with various disturbances, on account of the saints’ merit. That kinsman reported the matter to the king in due order, as it had occurred.

The king immediately decreed that they should be sent bound to a certain Moorish king, a pagan named Capsur [another reading: Capsum]. But, confused and defeated, he released Maxima, the handmaid of Christ, to her own choice. [Note: Thus read two Colbertine manuscripts with Lorichius; the others have *propria voluntate* (“by her own will”). Our reading is confirmed by Ado, who, in the place cited in the preceding note, continues Maxima’s martyrdom from Victor as follows: “At this miracle Maxima, the handmaid of Christ, released to her freedom, afterwards became the mother of many virgins of God,” etc.] She is still alive today, a virgin and mother of many virgins of God, and is by no means unknown to us.

When they arrived, they were handed over to the aforementioned Moorish king, who lived in a part of the desert called Capra-Picta. When the disciples of Christ saw the many unlawful and sacrilegious sacrifices being performed there by the pagans, they began, through their preaching and way of life, to invite the barbarians to acknowledge the Lord our God. In this way they won a vast multitude of pagan barbarians for Christ the Lord, in a place where previously no report of a Christian had ever been spread.

Then they considered what should be done so that the field, already cultivated and furrowed by the plough of preaching, might receive the evangelical seed and be watered by the rain of holy baptism. They sent envoys along the extended roads of the desert. At last they reached the city of Rome and asked the bishop to send a priest and ministers to the people who had come to believe.

[Note: Rhenanus likewise has this reading, except that instead of *construitur* (“is built”) he has *constituitur* (“is appointed”). Colbertinus 1: “What had been requested was fulfilled with joy. A bishop is appointed,” and so approximately the other Colbertinus also reads. Lorichius: “The bishop of God is fulfilled with joy because of what had been requested. A church is built,” etc.]

The bishop whom they had requested was appointed with rejoicing; a church of God was built; at the same time a very great multitude of barbarians was baptized; and from wolves a fertile flock of lambs was multiplied. Capsur reported this to Geiseric. Envy arose from the matter, and he ordered the servants of God to be bound with their feet behind them and to perish together, dragged behind running chariots through thorny places in the forests. They were tied in such a way that, as their bodies were torn by the thorns of the woody growth, dragged forward and backward, each could see the other’s death.

[Note: Chiffletius and three other printed editions read: “When the Moors were running nearby, they looked upon one another.” Farewell, etc. Ado also seems to have read this way; in the place already cited he has: “With untamed horses running nearby, they said farewell to one another,” saying nothing about the Moors’ lamentation. Some manuscripts, however, read *plaudentibus Mauris* (“the Moors applauding”) instead of *plangentibus Mauris* (“the Moors lamenting”). Either reading can be accepted. For those barbarians, either because, as stated above, they had been converted to the faith, or because of the natural compassion common to all human beings—as often happens in the contests of martyrs—could scarcely bear to see men afflicted by so atrocious a punishment, especially since the martyrs endured it with such patience. They could also have applauded out of the joy customarily felt by people avid for bloody spectacles and contests. Moreover, the commonly used martyrologies celebrate the feast of these four brothers together with Maxima on 16 October; in some martyrologies another 270 martyrs are added, but they suffered in another persecution.]

When they were bound and were being dragged by untamed horses, while the Moors lamented, they saw one another and, in the narrow interval before their departure, each said farewell in this manner: “Brother, pray for me; God has fulfilled our desire. In this way one reaches the kingdom of heaven.” And so, praying and singing psalms, they gave up their holy souls, while the angels rejoiced.

To this day Jesus Christ our Lord does not cease to perform great miracles there. For the blessed Faustus, once bishop of Buronita, testified to us that a certain blind woman had been given sight while he himself was present.

[Note: Mart. Orth. and Lorichius read *Faustinus*. The name of the see itself is more difficult. Almost all have *Buronitanus*; perhaps *Buconitanus* should be read. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198, Donatus, bishop of Bucconia, appeared on the Donatist side. Bucconia was a city of Numidia, for among the bishops of that province the African *Notitia* lists Vitalianus Bocconiensis. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna, among the cities of Mauretania—which he calls Gaditanian Mauretania—in book III, section 11, mentions the tower of Buconis. Was a bishop called Buconitanus from this place? Colbertinus 2, Lorichius, and others instead have *Burtinitanus*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, Donatus, bishop of the people of Buritana, appeared; Morisius says in his criticism of Garnerius that this city belonged to an uncertain province, although he suspects that it belonged to the proconsular province, and that it was the same city whose bishop Cresciturus Busitanus subscribed to the synodal letter in the second session of the Council of Saint Martin. Here, however, Victor seems to have intended to indicate a bishop from Mauretania.]

## XII. The Persecution Becomes More Severe

After this, Geiseric’s hostility against the Church of God was kindled. He sent a certain Proculus into the province of Zeugitana, ordering him to compel the priests of the Lord to surrender all the divine ministries or books, first stripping them of their weapons so that, once disarmed, the enemy might more easily capture them.

[Note: Lorichius reads: “Who could fail to grieve with the priests crying out,” etc. Below, for *palliis* (“cloths”), Mart. and Chiffletius have *pallis* (“palls”). Rhenanus and several printed editions read *ipse* (“he himself”), in the singular, etc.]

When the priests cried out that they could not surrender these things, the plunderers ravaged everything with their own hands and—shameful to say—made themselves tunics and trousers from the altar cloths. Proculus, the executor of this deed, nevertheless began to eat his own tongue piece by piece and was soon consumed by a most shameful death.

At that time Saint Valerian, bishop of the city of Abbenza [another reading: Habensa], while he had fought manfully not to hand over the divine sacraments, was ordered to be expelled from the city alone. It was further commanded that no one should allow him to live either in a house or in a field. For a long time he lay naked on the public road beneath the open sky.

[Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts and printed editions that I was able to consult, except Chiffletius, who has “seventy.” Usuard, Ado, and others likewise agree with us in their martyrologies on 15 December.]

He was more than eighty years old; and although unworthy, we were granted at that time to greet him in such exile.

[Note: The manuscripts read *Habensae*. Lorichius has *Habenssae*; Colbertinus 2, *Abense*; Rhenanus, Chiffletius, and others, *Abensis*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, among the Catholic bishops Fortunatus, bishop of the people of Abbenza, is mentioned; he had no Donatist opponent. In chapter 198, Lucius, bishop of Habensa, appears among the Donatists. The feast of the Valerian mentioned here is commemorated by the commonly used martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, and others on 15 December. Ado and the Roman Martyrology also commemorate Valerian, together with other African bishops persecuted under King Geiseric, on 28 November. Baronius, in his notes for that day, thinks this was the same Valerian as the one mentioned above; this seems certain. The old calendar in the Capuan sanctuary of Michael the monk commemorates, on 15 December, Saint Valerian the bishop and Saints Eustachius and his companions. On the same day another calendar, reported by the same author, commemorates Eustratius and his fellow martyrs. This is the same Eustratius whom Victor mentioned above in section 7. The body of Valerian, brought to Italy together with the relics of Saint Augustine, as is believed, is preserved at Robbio, a town in the diocese of Vercelli, as Ferrerius observes in his *History of the Bishops of Vercelli*.]

## XIII. The Martyrdom of the Lector and Others

At a certain time the solemnity of Easter was being celebrated. In a certain place called Regia [another reading: Reia], in honor of Easter Day, our people had opened the church that had been closed to them. The Arians discovered this.

[Note: Mart., Lorichius, and three printed editions have *Reia*. In the index of cities prefixed to the works of Saint Cyprian, there are two cities called Regium. In the *Notitia of Africa*, Victor Regiensis is listed among the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania; and in Numidia there was Fortunius Regianensis.]

Immediately one of their priests, named Adduit [other readings: Andiot, Andiut, Adiut, Anduit], gathered a band of armed men and stirred them up to attack the crowd of innocent people.

[Note: Four printed editions have *Andiot*; the first has *Andiut*; Lorichius, *Adiut*; Colbertinus 1, *Anduit*. Below, Chiffletius and Lorichius likewise read: “a gathered band of armed men,” etc.]

They entered with drawn swords and seized weapons. Others also climbed onto the roofs and shot arrows through the windows of the church. At that moment, while the people of God happened to be listening and singing, a single lector stood in the pulpit singing an alleluiatic melody. An arrow struck him in the throat; the book fell from his hands, and he himself fell dead afterward.

[Note: The Roman Martyrology commemorates this lector and the others mentioned here on 5 April.]

Many others, too, were clearly killed by arrows and javelins in the middle of the altar’s steps. Those who were not killed by swords at that time were later worn down by punishments and, by order of the king, almost all put to death, especially those of more mature age.

For elsewhere, as happened at Tinuzuda [another reading: Thunazuda, Tumiruda, Tinzuda, Tinuzuda, Tunuzada], in the farmsteads of the village of Ammonia, or in other places, at the time when the sacraments of God were being distributed to the people, they entered in the greatest fury, scattered the body and blood of Christ on the pavement, and trampled it with polluted feet.

[Note: It is remarkable how much the manuscripts and printed editions vary in writing the name of this place. We have retained the reading of Colbertinus 1; it seemed worthwhile to display the alternatives here so that each reader may choose whichever seems best. Several printed editions have: “As happened at Thunazuda and Galibus, in the village of Ammonia”; Orthod. and Lorichius: “It happened at Tumiruda, at Galbis, in the village,” or similar readings; the Martinian manuscript: “It happened at Tinuzuda and Galbus, the village of Ammoe”; Carthusian-Portuguese: “It happened at Tinzuda and Galbiis, in the village of Ammonia”; another Colbertinus: “It happened at Tinuzuda, Galbus,” etc.; a third Colbertinus: “Tunuzada … the village,” etc. Pliny, book IV, chapter 5, lists the town of Thunudis; Ptolemy has Thunusada. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, the Donatist bishop Victorianus Tunusidensis appears. Thunu is also found on the Peutinger Table. But what is signified by the word *Galibus*, or *Galbus*, and the other words that follow, cannot be divined. Among the Africans, *magalia* were farmsteads, or huts of the poor and shepherds. Virgil speaks of these in *Aeneid* 1: “Aeneas marvels at the mass of what was once Magalia.”

I know of no other Ammonia except that part of Libya in which Jupiter Ammon was chiefly worshiped, but that place does not fit this passage. Perhaps we should read: “in the *magalia* of the village of Ammon.” For Ptolemy, in book IV, chapter 3, when listing the cities between the two Syrtes, includes Ammon.]

## XIV. A Remarkable Event

Geiseric himself had ordered—his bishops persuading him to do so—that within his own palace and that of his sons no one but Arians should be appointed to the various offices.

Among the others, they then came to our Armogastes. For a long time and repeatedly they bound his swollen legs by twisting them with cords, and, tearing apart his forehead—which bore the mark of Christ, who had fixed the banner of his cross upon it—making it more furrowed than ploughed, they displayed the stretched and roaring sinews. The sinews snapped like spider threads while the saint looked toward heaven.

[Note: Colbertinus 1 and the first printed edition have: “and, descending, the stretched sinews roared, making it still more scratched and furrowed,” etc. Another Colbertinus and Mart. read: “the sinews displayed a furrow, still more furrowed,” etc. Below, for *cannabinis* (“hempen cords”), Lorichius has *caballinis*.]

When the torturers saw that the cords of sinew had been torn apart, they brought increasingly stronger cords and hempen ropes. But, while he invoked nothing except the name of Christ, all those things vanished. They also hung him head downward by one foot, yet he seemed to everyone to sleep as though on a bed spread with feathers.

When Theoderic, the king’s son and Armogastes’ master, ordered him to be beheaded because punishments were ineffective, his priest Jocundus prevented him, saying: “You can kill him by various afflictions. For if you kill him with the sword, the Romans will begin to proclaim him a martyr.”

[Note: Two manuscripts have *Theudericus*. Others have *Theaerichus* or *Theodoricus*. Procopius, in book I of his *Vandalic History*, calls him *Theodorus* and says that he died without children. See below, column 205, note a. Lorichius consistently has *Thederychus*, once *Dederychus*. This name, familiar among the kings and princes of northern peoples, was said in their language, *Teuderiich*, that is, “powerful among peoples.”]

Then Theoderic condemned him to dig pits in the province of Byzacena. Later, as a greater humiliation, he ordered him, not far from Carthage, where everyone could see him, to serve as a herdsman of cows.

Meanwhile, when the Lord revealed to him that the day of his death was near, he summoned a certain Felix, a venerable Christian and steward of the king’s son’s household. Felix revered Armogastes as an apostle. Armogastes said to him:

“The time of my release has come. I beg you, by the faith which we both hold, to bury me beneath this holm oak, so that, if you do not do so, you may render an account to our God [another reading: to the Lord].”

[Note: Mart., Orthod., and Lorichius have this reading. Others have: “beneath a carob tree,” etc.]

He did not care where or how his body would be buried; rather, he wished to demonstrate what Christ had revealed to his servant.

[Another reading: God.]

Felix replied: “Far be that from us, venerable confessor. I shall bury you in one of the basilicas, with the triumph and honor that you deserve.”

Blessed Armogastes said to him: “No; you shall do what I have said.”

Fearing to grieve the man of God, Felix truthfully promised that he would do as he had ordered. Immediately, within only a few days, the companion of a good confession departed this life.

[Note: This expression gave rise to the practice of calling Armogastes “the companion” in the Roman Martyrology on 29 March, as though this holy man had once held the rank of *comes*. But I would be mistaken if the words “companion of a good confession” here meant anything other than “with” or “in” a good confession. Thus Ado, Usuard, and other ancient writers of martyrologies, who commemorate on this same day, 29 March, the feast of the same holy confessor and of the two who follow, Archinimus and Saturus, or Satyrus, say nothing about this rank of *comes*.]

Felix therefore hastened to dig the grave assigned to him beneath the tree. But when intertwined roots and the hardness of the dry earth delayed him, and he was distressed that the saint’s bodily members were being buried so slowly, he eventually cut through the roots and dug much deeper into the earth. There he saw a sarcophagus prepared from the most splendid marble, such as perhaps no king had ever possessed.

## XV. The Confessor Archinimus

Nor may I pass over a certain Archinimus by name, a native of Masculanum [various readings: Archimimus, Archimimum, Masculan, Masculum, Masculinum, Masculin].

[Note: Chiffletius has *Archimimum*, named Mascula, as though Mascula were the proper name of this confessor, who had been appointed over the theatrical profession. But the oldest of all, Colbertinus 1, together with Mart., Lorichius, and Orthod., has *Archinimum*. He is also called this in the published martyrology of Ado and in three ancient manuscripts; Florus likewise agrees. In Usuard, whose autograph is in our possession, we read *Archiminus*; this reading is also found in four other martyrologies cited by the Bollandists on 29 March. The second Colbertinus has *Archiminium*. Notker, in the martyrology published by Canisius in volume VI of *Ancient Readings*, has *Archimimus*. This is also the reading of the third manuscript of the Colbertine library, though it is the most recent of all. The Liège martyrology calls him *Arginimus*. The ancient copy cited by Baronius has *Masculanus*. The second and third Colbertine manuscripts and the editions of Rhenanus, Balduinus, Bignius, and Cologne agree with this, reading *Masculan*. The Martinian manuscript has *Masculum*. Lorichius, Orthod., and Surius: “Archinimus by name, Masculinus”; Belforest translates it as “Masculin.” From all this it is clear that the proper name of this confessor was Archinimus or Archiminus, while Mascula, a celebrated city in Numidia, was his homeland. More about this city may be found in the notes on the bishops of Numidia listed in the *Notitia*, section 94. Indeed, of all the martyrologies mentioned above that commemorate this saint together with Armogastes and Saturus on 29 March, not one calls him Mascula; on the contrary, all praise Archinimus. Evidently the writers of these calendars were persuaded that the word *Masculan* designated not the confessor himself but his homeland. Later writers, therefore, should be corrected, since they carelessly introduced into the sacred calendars “Mascula, by profession an archimime.”]

When many plots were laid against him to make him abandon the Catholic faith, the king himself later tried to win him over with flattering secular speeches, promising to heap many riches upon him if he readily yielded to the king’s will.

[Another reading: delights.]

Because he remained strong and unconquered in the faith, the king ordered him to undergo a capital sentence. Yet, in his cunning, he secretly commanded that if, at that hour, he feared the blow of the flashing sword, he should be killed outright, lest the king make him a glorious martyr; but if he appeared courageous in his confession, the sword should be spared.

But, made strong like an immovable pillar, established by Christ, he returned as a glorious confessor. Although the envious enemy did not wish to make him a martyr, he could not violate our confessor.

## XVI. The Faith of Saturus

We know of another man named Saturus who lived in that period. He was a shining member of the Church of Christ and frequently reproved the depravity of the Arians with Catholic freedom. He had been the steward of Huneric’s household.

He was summoned, accused by a certain deacon named Marivado [Mart.: *Maurivado*; Orthod. and Lorichius: *Mauridano*; perhaps *Varimado* should be read], whom the unhappy Huneric especially honored, so that Saturus might become an Arian.

[Note: Mart. has *Maurivado*; Orthod. and Lorichius, *Mauridano*. Perhaps *Varimado* should be read. See the historical commentary, chapter 4.]

Honors and great riches were promised if he complied; terrible punishments were prepared if he refused. The terms were laid down as follows: if he did not obey the royal commands, then, after an initial investigation, and after his house and property had first been confiscated and all his slaves and children sold, his wife, in his presence, would be handed over in marriage to a camel-driver.

Saturus, filled with God, did more to hasten the fulfillment of this threat by provoking the impious. For this reason, his wife appeared to have asked those carrying out the order for a delay, without her husband’s knowledge.

Another Eve came to her husband, instructed by the serpent’s counsel (Genesis 3). But he was not an Adam who would touch the alluring fruits of the forbidden tree.

[Another reading: “of the tree of life.”]

For he was not needy but was called Saturus, “sated” [another reading: *satiatus*, “satisfied”], satisfied by the abundance of the house of God and refreshed by the torrent of its delights.

The woman came to the place where her husband was praying alone, with her garments torn and her hair unbound. Her sons accompanied her, and she carried in her hands a little girl who was still nursing.

[Note: Mart. has “and one little child,” in the masculine gender. Lorichius has approximately the same: “and one infant,” etc.]

She threw the child at her unsuspecting husband’s feet and herself embraced his knees with her arms, hissing in the voice of a dragon:

“Have pity on me, sweetest husband, and at the same time on yourself; have pity on the children we share, whom you see here. Let those whom the nobility of our lineage has made illustrious not be subjected to servile status. Let me not, while my husband is alive, be subjected to a disgraceful and shameful marriage, when I have always boasted among my peers of my Saturus. God knows that you will do this unwillingly, though perhaps some have done it willingly.”

He answered her in the words of holy Job: “You speak as one of the foolish women speaks” (Job 2:10).

[Another reading: “They may drag away.”]

“Woman, I would be afraid if the bitter sweetness of this life were its sole reality. Wife, by your device you are serving the devil. If you loved your husband, you would never draw your own husband toward a second death. Let them sell off (*distrahant*) the children [another reading: *detrahant*, “drag away”], separate the wife, and take away the property. I belong to my Lord; secure in his promises, I shall hold fast to these words: ‘If anyone does not leave behind his wife, children, fields, or house, he cannot be my disciple’” (Luke 14:26).

What more is there to say? When the woman departed with the children, rejected, Saturus was strengthened for his crown. He was examined, stripped, crushed by punishments, dismissed as a beggar, and forbidden permission to appear in public. They took everything from him, but they could not take away the robe of his baptism.

## XVII. The Conclusion of Geiseric’s Persecution

After this, Geiseric ordered the church of Carthage to be closed. Since there was no bishop, the priests and ministers were scattered and dispersed among various places of exile.

It was scarcely reopened when Prince Zeno pleaded through the patrician Severus; and thus all returned from exile.

As for what happened in Spain, Italy, Dalmatia, Campania, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, Sardinia, Bruttium,

[Note: Only Orthod. and Lorichius, together with Belforest’s French translation, include Venice here. For the words that follow, Lorichius has “Old Epirus or Hellas” rather than “Old Epirus, or Hellas.” The word *Veteri* (“old”) is also omitted in Rhenanus’s edition. On Geiseric’s death, see the historical commentary, chapter 7.]

and Venice, Lucania, Old Epirus, or Hellas, those who suffered there will more fittingly recount it themselves in mournful lamentation.

But let this be the end of our persecution, carried out by Geiseric as loftily as it was cruelly. He remained in power for thirty-seven years and three months.

# BOOK TWO: THE BEGINNINGS OF HUNERIC’S PERSECUTION

## I. Huneric’s Beginnings

When Geiseric had died, Huneric, his eldest son, succeeded his father.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Cornelius of Compiègne, and the monastery of Saint Bernard of the Reverend Fathers of the Fulian Parisians have *Nundricus*. Orthod. and Lorichius have *Hunericus Nundrius*.]

At the beginning of his reign, in accordance with barbarian subtlety, he began to act more gently and moderately, especially toward our religion. Thus, where previously, under King Geiseric, it had been ruled [another reading: “proclaimed”] that spiritual assemblies should not take place, gatherings of the people began to assemble.

And to present himself as religious, he ordered that the Manichaean heretics should be sought out more diligently. He burned many of them and transported very many overseas in ships. He found almost all of them to be Manichaeans of his own religion, especially the priests and deacons of the Arian heresy. For this reason he was more deeply ashamed and burned with even greater fury against them.

One of them was found, a monk named Clementianus [another reading: Dementianus], who had written on his thigh: “Manichaean, disciple of Christ Jesus.”

Because of this, the aforementioned tyrant seemed more praiseworthy. [Note: This expression is absent from Mart., Germ., and Ful., which below read, “He saw … with what greed.” Lorichius reads: “therefore the aforementioned tyrant seemed more praiseworthy, displeasing in one respect because,” etc.] He was displeasing in one respect, because he thirsted with excessive longing for insatiable greed and burdened the provinces of his kingdom with various accusations and levies, so that this saying was applied especially to him: “A king in need of revenues is a great accuser.”

[Note: Colbertinus 2, the Saint-Germain manuscript, the Fulian manuscript, and Compiègne, together with Lorichius, read: “A king in need of revenues is a great accuser.” Mart. and Colbertinus 1 have: “He has accused great men.” Orthod. and Lorichius: “Great calamity it is.” Among authors of the Middle Ages, *calumniare* or *calumniari* means the same as to bring a lawsuit or summon someone into court to recover something. See Du Cange’s glossary.]

At the request of the emperor Zeno and Placidia, the widow of Olybrius,

[Note: This was the sister of Eudoxia, Huneric’s wife, who, together with Eudoxia and their mother, had been carried off to Africa by Geiseric after the capture of Rome. More about them may be found in the historical commentary, chapter 6. Lorichius consistently has *Placida* instead of *Placidia*.]
