he granted permission for the Church of Carthage to choose and ordain for itself whichever bishop it wished. For twenty-four years it had been deprived of this adornment.

## II. He Permits the Ordination of a Bishop

He therefore sent the distinguished Alexander to the church with a message of this kind: in his presence the Catholic people were to request a priest suitable for themselves. He also sent through his notary, named Vitarit [printed edition: Vitared], an edict to be read publicly, containing these words:

“Our lord has ordered it to be said to you that the emperor Zeno and the most noble Placidia have written through Alexander, the illustrious man, asking that the Church of Carthage have a bishop of your own religion. He has ordered this to be done, and has written back to them—or has ordered it to be said to their envoys whom they sent—that, just as they requested, you should ordain whichever bishop you wish.

“This is to be on the condition that the bishops of our religion who are at Constantinople and throughout the other provinces of the East shall, by his command, have free choice in their own churches to instruct the people in whatever languages they wish and to observe the Christian law. In the same way, here or in the other churches established in the African provinces, you have free choice [another reading: “you shall have”] in your churches to celebrate the liturgy, to instruct the people, and to do whatever belongs to your law, as you wish.

“For if this freedom is not preserved for them, both the bishop who is ordained and the clergy, as well as the other bishops with their clergy who are in the African provinces, will be ordered to be sent among the Moors.”

[Note: By this word the ancients designated instructions or exhortations to the people, which the Greeks commonly called *homilies*. Victor himself explained this above in book I, section 3, where, among other works of Saint Augustine, he mentions popular treatises that the Greeks call *homilies*.]

When this edict was read in the presence of us all, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July,

[Printed edition II: “of June.”]

we began to groan and mutter, because, while evil schemes were being devised, a persecution was being prepared for the future.

And we are reported to have said to the envoy:

“If this is so, with these dangerous conditions inserted, this church does not desire to have a bishop. Christ governs it, he who has always deigned to govern it.”

[Another reading: “Let him govern it.”]

The envoy neglected to accept this response. At the same time the people, desiring that this should happen, blazed up like fire. Their shouting was intolerable and could not be quieted by any means.

## III. The Virtues of Eugenius

When Eugenius, a holy man pleasing to God, had accordingly been ordained bishop, sublime joy arose and the Church of God’s gladness was increased.

The Catholic multitude rejoiced under barbarian rule at the restoration of a bishop. A very great number of young men and adolescent girls, rejoicing together with one another, testified that they had never seen a bishop sitting on his throne.

That man of God, the priest Eugenius, began through the practice of good works to be regarded as venerable and worthy of respect even by outsiders. He became so dear to everyone that, if it had been permitted, all would have gladly offered their lives for him.

Through him, too, the Lord deigned to perform such acts of almsgiving that it seems incredible that he could distribute so much, when the barbarians held everything and the Church is known not to have possessed even the means to give a single coin.

If anyone began to praise the humility, charity, and piety divinely granted to him, he could not adequately describe them.

Money is shown never to have remained with him, unless perhaps it was offered at such an hour that the sun, completing its daily course, was already giving night its order and place. He reserved only as much as was sufficient for the day [another reading: “there was added to him only as much”], not as much as greed might have demanded, while our God continually bestowed upon him great and still greater gifts each day.

But when his fame had become celebrated and evident everywhere, the Arian bishops began to be tormented by grave envy, attacking him daily and especially through Cyrila.

[Note: This is how the name is written most often. Others have *Gyrila* or *Cyrileas*, and some even *Cyrillus*; the same variation occurs below whenever the name appears. It is enough to mention it once here.]

What more need be said? They informed the king that Eugenius should by no means sit upon his throne or speak the customary word to God’s people. They further urged him to prohibit anyone, male or female, whom he saw in the church wearing barbarian dress.

He replied as was fitting:

“The house of God is open to everyone; no one who enters can be driven away. Especially since there has been a very large number of our Catholic people wearing their clothing because they serve the royal household.”

## IV. The Beginning of the Persecution

When he received such a reply from the man of God, Huneric ordered torturers to be stationed at the church doors. Whenever they saw a woman or man wearing the dress of their people, they immediately threw small, toothed stakes onto the person’s head, tied the hair to them, and tightened them violently, tearing away the entire skin of the head together with the hair.

Some, while this was being done, immediately lost their eyes; others died from the pain. After this punishment, the women, their heads stripped of skin, were led through the streets with a herald going before them, for the display of the whole city.

They considered what they suffered to be their greatest gain. We knew very many of them, and we do not know of a single one who, even under the pressure of punishments, then departed from the straight path.

When he was unable in this way to break the wall of faith [another reading: “any wall”],

he conceived the plan that the members of our religion who served in his palace should enjoy neither their customary rations nor their regular pay. He also added the intention of crushing them with peasant labor.

He sent freeborn and very delicate men to the Utican plain, so that under the blazing heat of the sun they might cut the clods from the fields.

There they all went with joy and rejoiced in the Lord. Among their company was a man whose hand was withered and had provided him no service for very many years. When he truthfully excused himself, saying that he could not work, he was ordered to go on all the more violently.

But when they had reached the place, and especially when everyone groaned in prayer for him, by divine mercy that withered hand was restored whole to the confessor.

From this point Huneric’s persecution of our suffering and travail took its beginning.

### V. Huneric Rages against His Own

But he himself, who for a long time had displayed leniency toward everyone, wishing to establish for his sons after his death a kingdom which did not come to pass, began to persecute cruelly Theodoric, his brother, and his sons, as well as the sons of his brother Genton.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] This had not in fact yet occurred when Victor was writing this History, namely in 487; but it happened later [Col. 0205C], when, after the deaths of Guntamund and Trasamund, Hilderic, Huneric’s son by Eudoxia, obtained the kingdom and restored peace to the African Church, as we shall explain more fully in chapter 12 of the historical Commentary.]

[Note: [Col. 0205C] Others write “Gentunis”; Orthodoxus, “Genzonis.” Procopius likewise calls him this in book I of the *Vandalic War*, where he is mentioned once and again; he was Geiseric’s second son. But that author is mistaken when, in the passage cited, he writes that Theodore—for so he calls Theodoric—the youngest of Geiseric’s sons, having left no children of either sex, ended his life before his father’s death [Col. 0205D]. For this passage of Victor makes clear that Theodoric and his sons survived Geiseric’s death, and that Huneric treated them with such cruelty.]

He would have spared none of them, unless death had taken away the opportunity to fulfill his desire.

First, knowing that the wife of his brother Theodoric was, I believe, a clever woman—and fearing that she might arm either her husband or her elder son, who seemed prudent and wise, against the tyrant with sharper counsels—he brought an accusation against her and ordered her to be killed by the sword. After she had been killed, he also killed that son, a man well educated in letters and great in learning, to whom, because he was older than all the others, the kingdom among Geiseric’s grandchildren was chiefly owed according to Geiseric’s constitution.

[Note: In his testament, Procopius says, he had ordered that the kingdom should always belong to whichever of his descendants was first in age, excluding even the sons of the one who had previously reigned, if they had older male relatives. Hence Huneric was succeeded first not by his son Hilderic but by Guntamund, and then by Trasamund, and afterward by Hilderic. Gelimer was the first to attempt to violate this law, to his own disadvantage, as we shall say in the historical Commentary; Procopius explains the matter more fully in his two books on the Vandalic War.]

He was inflamed to perpetrate something still more atrocious. While the populace stood assembled in the middle of the city before the steps of the new street, he ordered a bishop of his own religion, named Jocundus, whom they called their patriarch, to be burned alive, because he was held in the highest favor in the house of Theodoric, the king’s brother; perhaps through his support that household might have obtained the kingdom.

[Note: It was customary among these and other barbarians to call the chief bishop of their own people “patriarch.” From this arose the name “patriarch” in certain regions that they once inhabited, and their descendants, after being reconciled to the Catholic Church, retained it. On this matter see the extensive and learned discussion by Louis Thomassin, a priest of the French Oratory, *New and Ancient Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book I, part I, chapter 21 of the Latin edition.]

In this crime of impiety we foresaw that disaster was coming upon us, saying individually to one another: “If he has become so cruel toward his own priest, when will he spare our religion or us?”

Then he sent the elder son of Genton, named Godagis, into cruel exile with his wife, without the comfort of a male or female servant. He likewise banished his brother Theodoric, naked and destitute, after the killing of his wife and son. After Theodoric’s death, he cast away the surviving son, a little child, and his two grown daughters, having placed them on asses, inflicting further suffering upon them.

He also pursued many of his own countrymen, counts and nobles, with false accusations, because they favored his brother. Some he burned, others he slaughtered with the sword. He thus imitated his father Geiseric, who had drowned his brother’s wife, after tying a weight of stones to her, by throwing her into the famous Cirtean river Ampsaga, and after killing the mother had also killed her sons.

[Note: This is the reading that should be retained. Others have “Ausaga.” That river is now called in the native language Suffegmar, and it separates Africa proper from Mauretania. Perhaps because of its size, Colbert manuscript 2 and Rhenanus’s edition call it “famous”; others, however, call it “fetulosus” or “fecilosus.” Pliny, Pomponius Mela, and the other authors who mention this river never call it by that name.]

When his father Geiseric was dying, he had also entrusted many men to him under oath. Forgetful of his pledge and a violator of the oath, he killed them by various punishments and burnings. For a certain Heldicus, whom his father had appointed governor of the kingdom, already a veteran and advanced in years, he beheaded shamefully; and his wife, together with another woman named Theucaria, he burned in the middle of the city.

[Note: In the manuscripts of Martin, Germanus, and Fulvius she is called Thevarica; in Orthodoxus and Lorichius, Themaria. Some likewise call Heldicus “Heldica,” and some call his brother Camut “Gamuth.” Lorichius has “Caniut, the brother of Heldicus,” and so forth.]

He ordered their bodies to be dragged through the streets and alleys. They lay there all day, and only in the evening, after being petitioned by his bishops, did he permit them to be buried. Camut, the brother of Heldicus, he could not kill because he had taken refuge in their church. Nevertheless, he shut him up in a place used as a latrine—[Lorichius: “in a dark place”]—and decreed that he should remain there for a long time.

Afterward he condemned him, together with a certain goatherd and peasant, to dig trenches useful for vineyards. He also scattered them with cruel whippings twelve times a year, that is, every month, allowing them scarcely a little water and bread for food. They endured these things for five years or more. Such sufferings could have profited them toward an eternal reward if they had been Catholics and had borne them for the merit of their faith.

But we have been unable to keep this silent, so that the king’s impiety toward his own people also might not be left unmentioned. For he not only burned his own bishop Jocundus, as we have shown above, but also burned very many of his priests and deacons—that is, Arians—and delivered others to the beasts.

### VI. Visions before the Persecution

Thus, having quickly cut off everyone whom he feared and having, as he thought, secured for himself a kingdom that was destined to be brief and unstable, he became idle and secure on every side. He turned all the weapons of his fury against the persecutions of the Catholic Church, roaring like a lion.

Before the storm of persecution, however, the impending evil had been revealed through many preceding visions and signs. For nearly two years before it occurred, someone saw the church of Faustus shining in its customary adornment, resplendent with brightly burning candles, coverings of hangings, and lamps.

[Note: Seventy-four manuscripts—Colbert 3, Martin, Orthodoxus, Baldus, Lorichius, and Surius—read “shining”; and while he rejoiced in the brightness of such splendor, “also shining with gleaming candles, coverings of hangings, and glowing lamps,” and shortly afterward: “And that whole crowd of persons in white.” We have adopted the reading from four manuscripts: Martin, Germanus, Fulvius, and Colbert 1. But the other Colbert manuscript reads “of those making offerings” instead of “of those in white.” Chifflet, Baldus, Surius, and Rhenanus, together with the third Colbert manuscript, have “of the blessed”; Lorichius has “of the abbots.” We discussed the church of Faustus above, note 25 (Col. 0191, note b).]

As he rejoiced in the brightness of that great radiance, suddenly, he said, the splendor of that desirable light was extinguished. Darkness followed, and a foul odor, born from the nostrils of the adversary, arose. The whole crowd dressed in white was threatened and driven outside by certain Ethiopians. For this reason he lamented continually, because he never saw it restored again to its former glory. He related this vision to us while the holy Eugenius was present.

A certain presbyter also saw that same basilica of Faustus filled with crowds of innumerable people, and shortly afterward emptied and filled instead with a multitude of pigs and goats.

Another saw a threshing floor prepared for winnowing, with the grain not yet separated from the chaff by the judgment of the winnower. While he marveled at the size of the immense mass, although it was confused and mixed, suddenly a storm whirlwind came. With a resounding blast, it announced its approach as dust rose. By its force all the chaff flew away, while the grain remained.

After this there came a tall man, brilliant in appearance and shining in bright clothing. He began to purge the empty, emaciated, and rejected grains, casting them away as one casts away inferior meal. Examining the mass for a long time, he scarcely brought even its tested portion to a small heap.

Another said: “A very tall man stood upon a mountain called Ziquensis, and cried out to the right and to the left: ‘Move away, move away!’”

[Note: The city of the Ziquensians is mentioned in Africa in the letter of Constantine the Great to Probianus, as also in the *Purgation of Caecilianus*. Lorichius, however, reads: “above the mountain of the Lord, who is Ziquensis,” and so forth.]

Another saw the sky roaring and disturbed, with sulfurous clouds hurling enormous stones.

[Note: Colbert 2, Fulvius, Germanus, Martin, Rhenanus, Orthodoxus, and Surius read: “clouds that began to hurl enormous stones,” and so forth. Colbert 1 has: “sulfurous and enormous clouds,” and so forth. Lorichius reads: “disturbed sulfurous clouds that began to hurl enormous stones,” and so forth.]

When the stones fell upon the earth, they became more intensely heated and burned with greater flames. Entering into the inner parts of houses, they set fire to those whom they found there. The man who saw this said that, when he had hidden himself in a certain room, by divine mercy the flame could not reach him. I think this was to fulfill the prophetic word: “Close your door, and hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of God has passed” (Isaiah 26:20).

[Note: Manuscripts 2 and Rhenanus read: “Hide yourself for a little while,” and so forth.]

The venerable bishop Paul also saw a tree extending to the heavens with flowering branches, and by its spread casting shade over almost the whole of Africa.

[Variant: “Nearly the whole” is absent in some witnesses.]

When everyone rejoiced at its size and beauty, suddenly, he said, a violent ass came. Rubbing its neck against the strength of its roots, by its impact and with a great crash it struck that marvelous tree to the ground.

The honorable bishop Quintianus also saw himself standing upon a certain mountain, from which he looked upon a flock of innumerable sheep.

[Variant: “His sheep” is added in some witnesses.]

In the midst of the flock were two cauldrons boiling violently. Slaughterers of sheep were present, plunging their flesh into the boiling cauldrons. As this continued, the whole great flock was consumed.

[Note: Colbert 1 and the printed editions call him “Quintinianus.” Baronius thinks he was bishop of Sicca, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 23 May, where he is said to have suffered with the saints Lucius and Julian during the Vandal persecution. We shall say more about them below, when discussing the persecution under Guntamund in the historical Commentary, chapter 10.]

I think those two cauldrons were the two cities, Sicca Veneria and Lares, in which the first multitude had gathered and from which the conflagration began; or else King Huneric and his bishop Cyrila.

[Note: Colbert 2, Germanus, Portus, Martin, together with Orthodoxus and Lorichius. Colbert 1 and Fulvius, however, add “Laribus” after “Larensem.” Colbert 1, Rhenanus, Chifflet, Bignonius, Baldus, and Surius read: “the cauldrons, Sicca Veneria and Lares, two,” and so forth. Sicca Veneria and Lares were two formerly episcopal cities in proconsular Africa. The bishop of the former subscribed to the synodal letter of the fathers of that province to Paul, bishop of Constantinople, which was read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2, where Candidus is called bishop of Sicca. At the Council of Carthage in 525, Vitulus, bishop of the people of Lares, was present. Bishops from both cities, Catholic and Donatist, also attended the Carthaginian Conference. Fortunatianus, Catholic bishop of Sicca, often spoke there and subscribed chapter 139; his opponent Paulus is listed among the Donatists in chapter 198. Victorius, bishop of Lares, appeared with his opponent Honoratus in chapter 131, and Honoratus again in chapter 197. Restitutus, a Donatist bishop of Laritus, was present in chapter 208. Henry Norisius discusses the location of these cities learnedly in his *Observations against John Garnerius*, which should be consulted. Finally, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Castus of Sicca gave his opinion in favor of rebaptizing heretics, number 28. The city was made famous by the celebrated controversy between Urbanus and Apiarius. Augustine mentions the town of Hilarum and Sicca in letter 229. Whether Paul and Quintianus, whom Victor mentions here, were bishops of these cities is uncertain, since Victor does not say so and these two sees do not appear in the *Notitia* of Africa.]

But since many visions have been mentioned, let this suffice, for brevity’s sake.

### VII. A Severe Persecution

What more is there to say? First, the tyrant decreed by a terrifying command that no one should serve in his palace or perform public duties unless he made himself an Arian. A great number of them, with unconquerable firmness, abandoned temporal military service rather than lose the faith. Later he cast them out of their homes, stripped them of all their property, and banished them to the islands of Sicily and Sardinia.

[Note: Orthodoxus and Lorichius. But Martin, Germanus, and Fulvius read: “Quod etiam.” The others read: “quodam tempore statuere,” and so forth.]

He also hastened to establish throughout Africa that the treasury should claim the property of our bishops after their death. Anyone who could succeed a deceased bishop was not to be ordained unless he offered five hundred solidi to the royal treasury.

But this structure, which the devil attempted to build, Christ immediately deemed worthy of destroying. His household servants suggested to him, saying: “If your order establishes this, our bishops who are stationed in Thrace and in other regions will begin to suffer worse things.”

Then he ordered the sacred virgins to be assembled, sending Vandals with midwives of their own people to inspect and touch them in violation of the laws of modesty and honorable shame, where neither their mothers nor any Catholic matrons were present.

[Note: Colbert 1, Martin, and Orthodoxus, together with Lorichius, read “to inspect and touch, contrary to the right of modesty and shame,” and so forth. The Roman Martyrology recalls the memory of these virgins on 16 December.]

They tortured them by suspending them heavily and tying enormous weights to their feet. They placed heated iron plates upon their backs, bellies, breasts, and sides. During their torments they were told: “Say that your bishops sleep with you, and your clergy.”

We know that many of them then died from the severity of these punishments. Others who survived became bent, their skin shriveling. They were striving to find a path by whose access he might, as he did, make the persecution public. Yet, although he did so, he could by no means discover how to defile the Church of Christ.

### VIII. The Faithful Driven into Exile

With what rivers of tears shall I describe what happened when he sent bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other members of the Church—four thousand nine hundred and seventy-six in number—into exile in the desert?

[Note: Colbert 2, Martin, Germanus, Fulvius, Portus, Lorichius, and Orthodoxus, together with the martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, Notker, and others, have this number. Colbert 1, Rhenanus, Surius, Baldus, Belfort, and Baronius in the Roman Martyrology have “sixty-six.” Chifflet and Bignonius have “sixty-four.”]

Many of them suffered from gout; others, because of advanced age, had been deprived of natural eyesight. Among them was the blessed Felix, bishop of Abbir, who had already spent forty-four years in the episcopate. Struck by paralysis, he neither felt anything nor spoke at all.

[Note: Colbert 3, Orthodoxus, and Lorichius read “Abiritanus”; Martin, Fulvius, and Germanus likewise. Portus has “Harbiritanus”; the Chifflet edition has “Abderitanus”; Rhenanus, Surius, and other printed editions have “Abdiritanus.” There were two African cities called Abbir, one of which was called Abbir Major. The bishop of each attended the Carthaginian Conference: Felix, bishop of Abbir Major, in chapter 133, where it is said that no Donatist was present there; and Annibonius, Catholic bishop of Abbiritum, in chapter 215. At the Council of Carthage in 419, Candidus, bishop of Germania, subscribed; elsewhere he is simply called Abbiritanus, presumably of the city whose successor from Abbir-Germaniciana appears at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, number 16. These cities were entirely distinct from Abdera or Abzera, whose bishop Fructuosus is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128. The Felix praised here by Victor appears to be the same man who is called Abaritanus among the proconsular bishops in the African *Notitia*, number 2; on this matter see the notes on the *Notitia*. The published martyrologies commemorate him and the others praised here on 12 October, while the Greeks do so on 7 September.]

Thinking especially of him, since he could not be carried on a beast, we proposed that the king should be petitioned by his own people, so that at least he might order him to be taken quickly to Carthage, since there was no possible way to bring him into exile. The tyrant is reported to have said to them angrily: “If he cannot sit upon an animal, let untamed oxen be yoked and, after he has been tied with ropes, let them drag him wherever I have ordered.”

We carried him throughout the entire journey, bound crosswise upon a pack animal, like a log of wood.

### IX. The Astonishing Faith of a Little Woman

Everyone was gathered in the cities of Sicca and Lares, so that the Moors, arriving there, might lead those delivered to them into the desert.

Then two officials arrived and began, with blameworthy cunning and flattering words, to address the confessors of God: “What do you think you are doing, being so obstinate and refusing entirely to obey the commands of our lord? You could be honored in the king’s presence if you hastened to do his will.”

At once they cried out with a great shout, saying: “We are Christians; we are Catholics. We confess the Trinity to be one God without violation.” They were shut into a more severe, though still larger, custody, where we were allowed to enter, offer words of exhortation to the brothers, and celebrate the divine mysteries.

There were also very many little children there, whom their mothers followed with maternal affection.

[Note: Lorichius and Rhenanus omit “others sorrowful.” They also read “trying to turn them back”; Colbert 1 has “trying to make them die”; Rhenanus, Surius, Bignonius, and Baldus have “trying to make them destined to die.”]

Some mothers rejoiced, others were sad, and others tried to draw them back. Some rejoiced that they had given birth to martyrs; others, by their efforts, attempted to turn them away from confessing the faith through the flood of rebaptization. Yet neither flatteries nor natural affection overcame anyone then, nor did carnal tenderness bend anyone toward the earth.

It is pleasing to relate briefly what an old woman did at that time. As we accompanied the army of God on the journey, and perhaps advanced more during the nights because of the heat of the sun, we saw a little woman carrying a sack and other clothing, holding one infant in her hand, and comforting him with these words: “Run, my lord. Do you see how all the saints are going forward and hastening joyfully toward the crown?”

When we rebuked her, because she seemed importunate, whether in joining the men despite her sex or in attaching herself to Christ’s army, she replied: “Bless me, bless me, and pray for me and for this little grandson of mine. For although I am a sinner, I am the daughter of the former bishop of the city of Zuritana.”

[Note: Germanus, Fulvius, and Orthodoxus, together with Lorichius, read “Zuritana”; Martin has “Zurinate”; Colbert 1, “Turitana”; Surius, “Quiritana.” In the Oxford Index already cited, Zura is assigned to an uncertain province. From the Carthaginian Conference, however, we learn that it belonged to the proconsular province. When Quintus—“Qui supra,” as Baluzius has it, rather than the reading of the common editions—testified at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, that Paulinus of Zura, who did not know letters and was present, had subscribed, and Paulinus himself, a Catholic bishop, professed that he possessed unity, Habetdeus, deacon of Primianus, bishop of the Carthaginian Donatist party, said: “Our presbyter is there. It is our diocese.” In the same chapter of the Conference, as we have already said in note 39, Donatus, bishop of the people of Buritana, is also listed.]

We asked her: “Why do you walk in such a wretched state, and for what reason do you show that you are traveling here from so great a distance?”

She replied: “I am going into exile with this little servant of yours, lest the enemy find him alone and turn him from the way of truth to death.”

At these words, filled with tears, we could say nothing except that the will of God should be done.

### X. The Hardships of Prison

But when the adversary—who perhaps was already saying, “I will divide the spoils; I will fill my soul; I will kill with my sword; my hand shall rule” (Exodus 15:9)—could not seize anyone, he searched out narrow and utterly dreadful places in whose chambers he might confine the army of God.

Then even the consolation of human visitation was denied them. The guards were punished with clubs and severely afflicted. The confessors of Christ were thrown upon one another, compressed by the confinement, one upon another, like swarms of locusts—or, to speak more precisely, like the most precious grains of wheat.

In that cramped condition, no opportunity for withdrawing to perform natural functions was allowed. Necessity forced them to use the same place for excrement and urine, so that the stench and horror surpassed every kind of punishment.

[Note: Chifflet and several printed editions read: “The condition of the place did not permit this, but they made excrement,” and so forth. Colbert 2, Rhenanus, and Baldus have: “The place did not permit it, but they made excrement and urine.” Later Chifflet and others read “after a great gift had been given”; Lorichius, “by giving great gifts,” and so forth.]

On one occasion, after we had given the Moors a large gift, while the Vandals were asleep, we were scarcely admitted secretly to enter. As we entered, we began to sink up to our knees, as though in a whirlpool of mud. Then we saw fulfilled what Jeremiah had said: “Those who were brought up in scarlet embraced their dung” (Lamentations 4:5).

What more is there to say? Surrounded on every side by the din of the shouting Moors, they were ordered to prepare for the journey to the place to which they had been assigned.

### XI. The Hardships of the Journey

Accordingly, they departed on the Lord’s Day with their clothing, faces, and heads smeared with excrement. Nevertheless, while the Moors cruelly threatened them, they sang the hymn to the Lord with rejoicing: “This is the glory of all his saints” (Psalm 149:9).

The blessed pontiff Cyprian, bishop of Unzibir, was present there at that time, an outstanding comforter who cherished each person with pious and fatherly affection, not without streams of flowing tears.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “Unizibilinensis”; Lorichius has “Unzibilinensis.” This Cyprian is the same man who is listed among the bishops of Byzacena in the African *Notitia*. On that city see the notes on the Byzacene cities, number 41. The published martyrologies commemorate his feast, as well as that of the others mentioned above, on 12 October.]

He was ready to lay down his life for his brothers and, if he were released, to give himself willingly to such sufferings. Whatever he possessed he spent at that time on his needy brothers. He sought an opportunity to join the confessors, himself a confessor in mind and courage. Later, after many struggles and the squalor of prison, he proceeded joyfully into the exile he desired.

The roads and paths testify to how many crowds from different regions and cities came to see the martyrs of God. Since the roads could not contain the troops of those arriving, immeasurable crowds of the faithful descended over the mountain peaks and through the hollows of the valleys, carrying candles in their hands and throwing their little children at the footprints of the martyrs. They cried out:

“Whom are you leaving us wretched people to go to the crowns? Who will baptize these little ones for us in the fountains of living water? Who will bestow upon us the gift of penitence and release us, bound by the chains of sins, through the indulgence of reconciliation? For it has been said to you: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 18:18). Who will bury us when we die with the solemn prayers? From whom will the customary rite of the divine sacrifice be offered?

“If it were permitted, may we too go with you, so that in this way no necessity might separate children from their fathers.”

[Note: In Martin, Lorichius, and Orthodoxus, the words “in tears” are absent. In other witnesses, the words “and in praises” are absent.]

Amid these cries, tears, and praises, no comforter was any longer permitted to continue. The crowd was forced to run, so that when they reached the place where a cellar had been prepared, they might take up their arduous lodging.

[Note: Chifflet has “cannaba.” Martin, Colbert 1, Fulvius, and Germanus read: “where there was then a ship,” and so forth. Orthodoxus and Lorichius have: “where a laborious lodging had then been prepared for the Moors.” Among authors of the Middle Ages, *cannava* designates a wine cellar or a similar underground place, which in French we call *une cave*; this fits the present passage very well. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

When some of the old men gave out, and others, although young, were perhaps delicate in body, they began to be struck as they ran with the points of spears and with stones. Thus, becoming still weaker, they were exhausted all the more.

### XII. Cruelty toward the Confessors

Afterward the Moors were ordered to drag those who could not walk, with their feet tied, like the corpses of dead animals, through hard and rough places covered with stones. First their clothing was torn away, and afterward their individual limbs.

Some had their heads crushed by the sharp edges of stones; others had their sides split open. Thus, in the hands of those dragging them, they breathed out their spirits.

We could not count their number, since the multitude prevented it. Nevertheless, throughout the entire public embankment, the vile burial of the saints rose up, with the tombs speaking.

The others, who were stronger, reached the places of solitude. There they were settled and received barley to eat like beasts of burden. The multitude of poisonous creatures and scorpions there is said to be so great that it seems incredible to those who do not know it; merely by its breath it infuses venom even into those at a distance. For they say that no one struck by a scorpion has ever escaped.

Yet, although their venomous ferocity continues to the present time, Christ defending them, it is known that they have harmed none of his servants.

But while the exiles were being fed there on grains of barley, even this was later taken away—as though God, who had rained manna upon the fathers, could not now feed those committed to such an exile.

[Note: Lorichius has “even now” instead of “now”; Colbert 1 reads “feed even now his household.” After these men had been subjected to such exile, he began to consider, and so forth.]

### XIII. The King’s Edict

He considered harsher measures against the Church of God, so that, having cut off some of its members, he might destroy the entire body by tearing it apart.

On the day of the Lord’s Ascension, in the presence of the emperor’s envoy Regino, he sent Bishop Eugenius a decree to be read in the middle of the church, written in the following terms. He also sent it throughout all Africa by the couriers.

[Note: Martin, Fulvius, Germanus, together with Orthodoxus, Surius, Lorichius, and Belfort, read “with no king present.” Colbert 1 has “with our king present.” Bignonius and Baldus read “with the queen present.” Rhenanus has “the envoy … the queen being present,” and so forth. Certainly Eudoxia, daughter of Valentinian, had been captured at Rome and married to Huneric, but she had already fled to Constantinople, as Zonaras reports. Nicephorus says that she lived with her husband for sixteen years, in book XV of his *History*, chapter 12; therefore we think the common reading should be retained. The count Regino could at that time have been an envoy in Africa. That he was well known to the Africans is clear from the fact that, later, when he was stationed in the East, he proposed certain questions to the blessed Fulgentius, which Fulgentius answered in letter 18; after Fulgentius’s death, the deacon Ferrandus did so as well, as Ferrandus’s short work on this subject testifies. Chifflet published it with the other works of the same author at Dijon in 1649.]

#### Edict of King Huneric

Addressed to Eugenius of Carthage and the other Catholic bishops established throughout Africa, ordering them to come to Carthage to give an account of their faith.

“King Huneric of the Vandals and Alans, to all the Homoousian bishops.

“It is established that it has been forbidden not once but repeatedly for your priests to hold assemblies in the estates of the Vandals, lest by their deception they overthrow Christian souls. Many, despising this matter, have now been found to have celebrated Masses in the estates of the Vandals contrary to the prohibition, asserting that they possess the complete rule of the Christian and true faith.

“And because we do not wish there to be scandal in the provinces granted to us by God, therefore know that by God’s providence, with the agreement of our holy bishops, we have decreed this: that by the day of the first of the coming February, setting aside every excuse of fear, you must all come to Carthage, so that you may enter into a dispute concerning the account of the faith with our venerable bishops and properly prove from the divine Scriptures the Homoousian faith which you defend, so that it may be recognized whether you hold the complete faith.

“We have sent the text of this edict to all your fellow bishops established throughout Africa.

“Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of Huneric’s reign.”

[Note: Colbert 2, Fulvius, Germanus, Martin, Lorichius, and Orthodoxus read “of January,” although below they have “of February.” Below, instead of “the Kalends of June,” Germanus, Fulvius, and Orthodoxus have “the Kalends of July”; Martin has “the third day before the Kalends of July.”]

### XIV.

When those of us who were present learned this and read it together, our hearts were immediately crushed and our eyes darkened. Truly, our feast days were then turned into mourning and our songs into lamentation, when the wording of the edict revealed the fury of the persecution that was to come—especially where he said: “We do not wish there to be scandal in the provinces granted to us by God,” as though he were saying: “We do not want Catholics to exist in our provinces.”

[Note: As though he were saying: “We do not want Catholics in our provinces.” These words are absent from Colbert 1, Martin, Germanus, Lorichius, and Orthodoxus. Below, where we have followed Colbert 1, “unless from the holy …,” most printed editions have “unless from the holy …”; most other manuscripts, together with Orthodoxus and Lorichius, read: “Then it seemed a reasonable cause to the holy Eugenius, if the barbarian heart could be softened, by suggesting that a letter be written in the following manner.”]

It was discussed what should be done. The impending disaster offered no remedy except that a reasonable suggestion should be submitted by the holy Eugenius, if the barbarian heart might be softened. It was written in the following form.

### Response of Saint Eugenius

A suggestion delivered to King Huneric by Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, requesting that overseas bishops also be summoned to the conference concerning the common faith.

“Whenever the matter concerns souls, eternal life, or the Christian faith, it is necessary to suggest without fear whatever is appropriate, just as the royal government has promised.

“Recently the royal authority, through the notary Witarit, deigned to admonish my smallness. In the presence of the clergy and people, he read to us the king’s decree concerning the merit and religious character of the faith.

[Note: Colbert 2, Fulvius, Germanus, Martin, Portus, and Orthodoxus, together with Lorichius, read: “concerning us, by the merit of religion and faith.” The third Colbert manuscript has: “the decree concerning the merit of the religion of the faith.”]

“From its wording we learned that a royal decree had likewise gone forth to all my fellow bishops, ordering that they come on the appointed day for a discussion of the faith. We declared that we had received this reverently.

“My humility suggested to the aforesaid notary that all those from every overseas region who share with us one religion and communion should also be informed, since everywhere all obey his kingdom. This is especially fitting because the matter concerns the whole world, not merely the particular African provinces.

“And because I promised in a second response that I would submit a written suggestion, I justly and humbly ask your Magnificence to deign to carry my aforementioned suggestion to the ears of our lord, the merciful king, so that his clemency may graciously recognize that we are not at all avoiding or fleeing a disputation concerning the law, with God’s help; but that, without the consent of the whole Church, we ought not to undertake the defense of our faith.

“We ask that, in his goodness, commensurate with his greatness, and in the justice of his wisdom, he deign to grant this.

“Given by Eugenius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage.”

## XV. He Is Rejected

[Col. 0214D] When this petition was presented by the blessed Eugenius, the man who had already conceived grief was driven to bring forth iniquity more grievously; and thus he appears to have ordered Cubadus, the prefect of his kingdom, to say to the holy man Bishop Eugenius:

“Submit the whole world to me, so that the entire world may be brought under my power, and I will do, Eugenius, what you say.”

To this the blessed Eugenius replied as he was able [or: as was fitting]:

“What has no rational basis,” he said, “ought not to be said. It would be as though someone were told to be carried through the air and fly, something contrary to human nature.

“For I said: If the king’s power desires to acknowledge our faith—which is the one true faith—let him send to his friends; and I too will write to my brothers, so that my fellow bishops may come, who will be able to demonstrate to you, together with us, our common faith, and especially the Roman Church, which [Col. 0215A] is the head of all the Churches.”

[Note: Thus Cyprian formerly called the Roman Church “principal,” in Letter 59 of the Oxford edition, elsewhere numbered 55; other African Fathers followed him. Optatus, Book II Against Parmenianus, Augustine in many places, and others did likewise. See our Mabillon’s preface to the Gallican Liturgy. Moreover, Pope Julius complains in his letter to the Eastern bishops that he had not been summoned by them to the council. See Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, Book III, chapter 10. Fulgentius and the other bishops exiled in Sardinia, in Letter 15 to Venerius and John, praise the words of Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff, to show that, concerning grace, all must hold what, they say, “the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church thinks and observes.”]

To this Cubadus said:

“So, then, are you and my lord the king alike?”

Bishop Eugenius said:

“I am not like the king. Rather, I said: If he desires to know the true faith, let him write to his friends, so that they may send their catholic bishops; and I will write to my fellow bishops, since the cause of the entire catholic faith is one.”

Eugenius did this not because there were lacking [Col. 0215B] in Africa men who could refute the objections of the adversaries, but so that those might come who were independent of their domination, possessed greater confidence in their freedom, and could likewise announce throughout all lands and among all peoples the calumnies of our oppression.

## XVI. Cruelty toward the Bishops

But the man who was weaving snares refused to hear reason. By means of repeated arguments he acted so as to harass, with various attacks, whichever bishops he had heard to be learned.

He had already sent Bishop Donatianus of Vibianum Secundum into exile, after having him beaten with one hundred and fifty clubs, as well as Praesidius of Sufetula, a man of considerable intelligence.

[Note: Nearly all printed editions read “Vibianense,” except that they have “Vibianensem.” Codex Colbertinus 1 has “Vibianense secundum.” So too do the manuscripts of Martinus, Fulgentius, and Germanus. But since below they read *episcopos* rather than *episcopum*, as though the word “second” designated a certain bishop whom Victor identifies as the Donatian associated with them, Orthodoxy and Lorichius likewise read “Vinianense secundum Donatianum,” with one hundred … bishops imposed, and below “under the true, acute protection of Sufetula,” and so forth. These readings, however, are exceedingly corrupt. For it is clear that only one Donatianus is being designated here from the ancient martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and Notker, in which, on 6 September, Donatianus alone is celebrated with those listed below in these words: “The holy Donatianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fusculus, who …”; on the same day they are also commemorated in the Roman Martyrology. In the African *Notitia*, moreover, I find four bishops named Donatianus: Veselitanus and Teglanensis in Numidia, Elien­sis in Byzacena, and Uzinadensis in Caesarean Mauretania. The Praesidius praised here is the same man who is called Suffetulensis in the African *Notitia* among the bishops of Byzacena; likewise, Mansuetus is Afufeniensis and Germanus Peradamiensis, in the same province. But I have been unable to find Fusculus, unless perhaps he was Filtiosus Aggaritanus, also mentioned in the province of Byzacena. Certainly, in the autograph of Usuard, instead of *Fusculus* there is *Fulcolus*.]

Then he flogged the venerable Mansuetus, Germanus, Fusculus, and many others.

While these things were happening, he ordered that no one should share a common table with men of our religion, nor eat at all with Catholics.

This measure brought them no benefit, but conferred the greatest gain upon us. For if, as the Apostle says, their word customarily spreads like gangrene (2 Tim. 2:17), how much more might a common table of food defile us, since the same Apostle says: “Not even to eat with the wicked” (1 Cor. 5:11)? [Col. 0216A]

## XVII. A Great Miracle

But when the fire of persecution was already being kindled, and the flame of the king who attacked us was burning everywhere, our God displayed a certain miracle through his faithful servant Eugenius, which I must not pass over.

In that same city, Carthage, there was a certain blind man, well known to the citizens and to the city, named Felix. The Lord visited him, and he was told in a vision during the night—for the day of Epiphany was dawning:

“Rise, go to my servant Bishop Eugenius, and say to him: ‘I have sent you to him.’ At the hour when he blesses the font, so that those coming to the faith may be baptized, he will touch your eyes; they will open, and you will see the light.”

[Note: In Codex Colbertinus 1, approximately eight hundred years old and written in the same hand as the text itself, the following was written in the margin: “Note that among the ancients baptism was performed on the sacred day of the Epiphany.” The same statement appears in Lorichius’s edition in the title of the chapter, except for the word “note.” Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, and Saint Leo, in Letter 16 of Quesnel’s edition, to the bishops of Sicily, disapprove this custom; later pontiffs and synods in various provinces followed them. Nevertheless, another custom was observed in other provinces, as is certain of Africa. That it was also observed in the Eastern provinces is clear both from the Greek *Euchologion* and from John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 171, in Cotelerius, volume II of *Monuments of the Greek Church*. There it is reported that, each year on the feast of the Theophany, the holy font in a certain village used spontaneously to sweat, so that baptism might be administered from that water.]

Warned by such a vision, the blind man thought that, as usually happens, he was being deceived in a dream, and he refused to rise. But when he was again urged in sleep to go to Eugenius, he was compelled to do so. Again he neglected the command, and a third time he was urgently and severely rebuked.

He awakened a boy who was accustomed to offer him his hand. With swift agility he went to the Basilica of Faustus; he prayed and then came with great tears to a certain subdeacon named Peregrinus, asking him to announce him to the bishop. He indicated that he had some secret matter to disclose.

[Note: The printed editions read “deacon.” We have preferred the earlier reading, which appears more consistent with the discipline of those times. For subdeacons stood outside the sanctuary, according to the Council of Laodicea.]

When the bishop heard this, he ordered the man to enter. For, because of the solemnity of the feast, the people were singing and the nocturnal hymns were resounding throughout the entire church. [Col. 0216B]

The blind man related to the bishop the sequence of his vision and said to him:

“I will not leave you unless, as you were commanded by the Lord, you restore my eyes to me.”

Saint Eugenius said to him:

“Withdraw from me, brother. I am a sinner and unworthy, sinning more than all other men—especially since I have been preserved to these times.”

But the man held his knees and said nothing other than what he had already said:

“As you were commanded, restore my eyes to me.”

Eugenius, observing his shameless credulity and seeing that the hour was already pressing, went with him to the font, accompanied by the attendant clergy. There, kneeling and groaning profoundly, striking heaven with his sobs, he blessed the rippling basin of the font. When he had risen after completing the prayer, he answered the blind man:

“I have already told you, brother Felix, that I am a sinful man. But may the Lord, who has deigned to visit you, grant you according to your faith and open your eyes.”

At the same time he marked his eyes with the sign of the cross. Immediately the blind man received his sight, the Lord restoring it.

He kept Felix there with him until everyone had been baptized, [Col. 0217A]

[Note: Lorichius reads: “Because of this great miracle, the people, stirred up, began to restrain the man who had received his sight. Afterwards it happened …”]

so that the people, stirred by so great a miracle, would not crush the man who had received the light.

The event was subsequently made known to the whole Church. The man who had been blind went with Eugenius to the altar, as is customary, in order to offer to the Lord the offering of his salvation. The bishop received it and placed it upon the altar.

A clamor arose, and an irrepressible outburst of joy was provoked among the people.

[Note: Others read “while he was meeting” or “while he was accompanying.” Codex Colbertinus 1 has “through the agency of.” Orthodoxy and Lorichius read “provoking immeasurable joy,” and so forth.]

Immediately a messenger went to the tyrant. Felix was seized and questioned about what had happened and how he had recovered his sight.

He related everything in order, and the Arian bishops said:

“Eugenius did this by magic.”

And because, overcome by confusion, they could not cloud the light of the miracle—for Felix was known and manifest to the entire city—they nevertheless wished, if it were permitted, to kill him, just as the Jews desired to kill Lazarus after he had been raised (John 12:10).

## XVIII. Laetus the Martyr

That calumnious day of the Kalends of February, appointed by the same ruler, was now approaching. The bishops not only of all Africa but also of many islands assembled, exhausted by affliction and sorrow.

Silence prevailed for many days, while the most experienced and learned men were meanwhile separated [alternative reading: “then overcome” (*exinde superaret*)], in order that, once accusations had been added, they might be killed.

For one man from that very company of teachers, named Laetus, a vigorous and most learned man, was burned alive after the long filth of imprisonment. He believed that by instilling fear through such an example he would crush the rest.

[Note: He was bishop of Neptis in Byzacena, as is clear from the *Notitia*. Victor of Tunnuna also attests this in his *Chronicle*, as does Isidore in his brief *History of the Vandals*, under the year 501 of the Spanish era. The common martyrologies celebrate his memory together with the confessors listed above on 6 September. Victor of Tunnuna, however, asserts in the *Chronicle* just mentioned that he was crowned with glorious martyrdom on 20 September, during the consulship of Augustus Zeno. The same Isidore, under the year 560, writes that the war against the Vandals undertaken by the emperor Justinian began because of an apparition of this holy man. Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, nevertheless says that the emperor was stirred to it by the exhortations of a certain bishop who had come from the East to Constantinople at God’s command. A little below, the text reads “believing that by such an example he would instill fear, etc.” Codex Colbertinus 1 has “believing that … would arouse fear.” Martinus, Fulgentius, Germanus, Surius, Orthodoxy, and Lorichius have “which would instill fear in the rest and injury.”]

At last they came to the contest of disputation, to the place, that is, which the adversaries had chosen.

Our men therefore, avoiding the tumult of shouting, lest the Arians later say that the multitude of our people had overwhelmed them, selected ten from among themselves to answer on behalf of all.

Cyrila, with his attendants, set up for himself in an elevated place a most arrogant throne, while our men stood by [variant: “while we stood by” (*nobis*)].

Our bishops said:

“That conference is always welcome in which the proud elevation of power does not rule; rather, by common agreement we proceed so that, with the judges discerning and the parties presenting their case, what is true may be recognized. But now who will be the judge, who the examiner, to confirm by the scales of justice what has been properly stated or refute what has been wrongly asserted?” [Col. 0218B]

[Note: Others read: “That discourse must always be conducted there where …” Below, instead of *cognitoribus discernentibus*, some manuscripts and editions have *decernentibus*, “deciding.” The *cognitores* were those entrusted with reviewing the judgments of bishops. Augustine discusses them in the brief account of the conference. Morinus has more on them in Book I, chapter 20, of his *Ecclesiastical Exercises*. They are mentioned frequently in the acts of councils, from which anyone can readily discern their function. Below, instead of “confirm what has been presented,” Fulgentius and Martinus read “let them confirm” or “refute the insults brought forward.” Germanus has “let him confirm or the insults,” and Orthodoxy and Lorichius have “refute what has been wickedly asserted.”]

When such things and others had been said, the king’s notary replied:

“Patriarch Cyrila said—”

[Note: We have restored this passage from Codex Colbertinus 1 and Codex Portuensis. The Catholics interrupted when the notary pronounced the words “Patriarch Cyrila said.” For they could not tolerate his calling Cyrila “patriarch,” and therefore interrupted the thread of his speech. The other Colbertinus, Rhenanus, Chiffletius, Balduinus, and Bignonius omit one line. “Cyrila said: Let it be read,” and so forth. Surius, Orthodoxy, and Lorichius, and Balduinus in his prolegomena, read differently: “Patriarch Cyrila said: Some of you have arrogantly and unlawfully usurped for yourselves the name ‘Catholics.’” Our men protested: “Let it be read,” and so forth. But, unless I am mistaken, those who adopted this reading inserted the word “Catholics” without manuscript authority, since otherwise the sense seemed to them to be meaningless. For Fulgentius and Germanus, who have this reading, have *patriarchae* rather than *catholicorum*, while the third Colbertinus, together with the Compendianus, has neither. As we have already observed, it was common among these and other barbarians to call the chief bishop of their nation “patriarch.”]

In response, our men condemned the arrogantly and unlawfully usurped title and said:

“Let it be read to us: with whose permission did Cyrila assume this title for himself?”

From that point they raised a tumult, and the adversaries began to bring accusations.

Our men had requested that, if they were not at least permitted to examine the matter, they might be allowed to await the decision of the prudent multitude. But all the sons of the Catholic Church who were present were ordered to be beaten with one hundred clubs [or: struck].

Then the blessed Eugenius [Lorichius: Eusebius] began to cry out:

“Let God see the violence that we suffer; let him recognize the affliction and persecution that we endure at the hands of our persecutors.” [Col. 0218C]

Our men turned and said to Cyrila:

“State what you intend.”

Cyrila said:

“I do not know Latin.”

[Note: Codex Colbertinus 1 adds: “to speak.”]

Our bishops said:

“We know plainly that you have always spoken Latin. You ought not now to make excuses, especially since you yourself kindled the fire of this matter.”

And seeing that the Catholic bishops were more prepared for the contest, he wished by various evasions entirely to avoid a hearing.

[Note: Lorichius reads this way. But other manuscripts and editions have: “He entirely avoided the hearing …”]

Our men, foreseeing this in advance, had composed a written statement concerning the faith, written with sufficient propriety and completeness, saying:

“If you desire to know our faith, this is the truth that we hold.” [Col. 0220A]

# BOOK THREE

## The Confession of Faith Offered by the Catholic Bishops to King Huneric

## I. The Unity of God’s Substance

[Col. 0219] We are commanded by royal authority to give an account of the catholic faith that we hold. Therefore, supported by divine assistance, we undertake, according to the modest measure of our abilities, briefly to make known what we believe and proclaim.

[Note: The Codex Laudunensis and others read “with assistance.” Martinus, the Compendianus, Lorichius, and Orthodoxy read “the faith that we believe.”]

First, then, we understand that we must explain the unity of the substance of the Father and the Son, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον).

We therefore confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in such a unity of divinity that we faithfully acknowledge both that the Father subsists in the distinct property of his person and that the Son likewise exists in his own person, while the Holy Spirit retains the distinct property of his person.

[Note: Colbertinus 1 adds, in a later hand, “and of the Holy Spirit.”]

[Note: Martinus, Germanus, Fulgentius, and Chiffletius read “in the distinctiveness of his person.” Colbertinus 1, the Compendianus, Lorichius, and Orthodoxy have *sua* rather than *suae*. The other Colbertinus and the Laudunensis, together with Balduinus, Rhenanus, and Bignonius, read “in the person proper to his distinctiveness.” The third Colbertinus has this in the margin, while in the text it reads “in the person proper to his divinity.”]

We do not assert that the Father is the same as the Son, nor confess that the Son is the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor do we understand the Holy Spirit to be either the Father or the Son. Rather, we believe that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten from the Father [or: born], and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, and that they are of one substance [Col. 0219B] or essence.

[Note: This phrase is absent from the Laudunensis and from Rhenanus’s edition. In Colbertinus 1 it was written in another hand. It is also absent from the recapitulation below, section 21. Nevertheless, it occurs in the other manuscripts and editions.]

[Note: Lorichius adds “and.”]

For the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son, and the proceeding Holy Spirit have one divinity, but three distinct properties of person.

And because a heresy that had arisen against this catholic or apostolic faith introduced a certain innovation, asserting that the Son was not begotten [*genitum*; variant *natum*, “born”] from the substance of the Father [*de*; variant *ex*], but had come into existence from things that did not exist—that is, from nothing—the Greek term *homoousion* was introduced to refute and utterly abolish this impious confession that had emerged against the faith.

*Homoousion* means “of one substance” or “of one essence,” signifying that the Son was born not from any existing things (*ullis exstantibus*; variant *nullis exstantibus*, “non-existent things”), nor from another substance, but from the Father.

Whoever thinks that *homoousion* must be removed wishes to assert that the Son came into existence from nothing. But he is not from nothing; without doubt he is from the Father. And rightly the Son is *homoousion*, that is, of one substance with the Father.

## II. Proved from the Scriptures

That he is from the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father, is confirmed by these testimonies. The Apostle says:

“He is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance, upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3).

And again, God the Father himself rebuked the unbelief of those who refused to hear the voice of the Son, proclaimed through the prophets and remaining in his substance. He said:

“They did not hear the voice of the substance” (Jer. 9:10).

[Note: The Laudunensis adds “my.” Below, in the Compendianus and in Lorichius, the text reads: “He who is the radiance and figure of his substance, and the heretics refused to hear the substance. Another prophet said: ‘They did not hear the voice,’” and so forth. The word “heretics” is absent from the Compendianus. In the margin of one Colbertinus are the words: “In Jeremiah according to the Septuagint interpreters.” This is correct. Moreover, instead of “upon the mountains,” Lorichius and others have “upon the mountain receive lamentation,” and instead of “path,” some have “paths.”]

He rebuked them with a terrible denunciation for despising that voice of the substance, and spoke to the same prophet, saying:

“Upon the mountains receive lamentation, and upon the paths of the wilderness mourning, because they have failed, because there are no men; they did not hear the voice of the substance, from the birds of heaven to the beasts” (ibid.).

And again he rebukes those who, departing from the confession of one substance, refused to stand in that same substance of faith, saying:

“If they had stood in my substance, I would certainly have turned them away from their evil way and from their wicked thoughts” (Jer. 23:22).

And again it is shown most clearly that the Son must not be confessed as outside the substance of the Father, but contemplated within that same faithful substance, when the prophet says:

“Who stood in the substance of the Lord, and saw and heard his word?” (ibid., 18).

That the Son is the substance of the Father was therefore designated long ago by prophetic oracles, when Solomon said:

“For you were displaying your substance and sweetness, which you had for your sons” (Wis. 16:21),

which, in the figure and image of heavenly bread, was shown to have flowed down from heaven for the people of Israel.

[Note: Saint Fulgentius offers excellent explanations of this passage and of the others cited here in his book, or *Response to Ten Objections of the Arians*, specifically in his response to their fourth objection. Colbertinus 1, Martinus, Fulgentius, Germanus, and Orthodoxy, together with Lorichius, read “in the Son.” Below, instead of “which you have in,” Orthodoxy and Lorichius read “because in.” Colbertinus 1 has “who in,” so that what follows may be understood of the Son. Indeed, the sense of those Fathers seems to require that it be read “in the Son.”]

The Lord himself explained this in the Gospel, saying:

“Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you bread from heaven” (John 6:32),

clearly designating himself as the bread when he says:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (ibid., 41).

Of this the prophet David also says:

“Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

## III. The Father and the Son Are Equal

To show still more clearly the unity of the substance of the Father and the Son, and the equality of their divinity, he himself says in the Gospel:

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

And:

“I and the Father are one” (John 10:38, 30).

[Note: Rhenanus reads “and the equality of divinity.” Colbertinus 1 has “that the divinity may be shown to be equal.” Below, “I in the Father,” and so forth, Chiffletius, Bignonius, and Balduinus, together with Colbertinus 1 and Rhenanus, have only: “I and the Father are one.” The Laudunensis has: “I in the Father … For I and the Father,” and so forth.]

This does not refer merely to unity of will, but to one and the same substance, because he did not say, “I and the Father desire one thing,” but, “We are one.” The assertion of the Father’s unity is declared from what they are, not merely from what they will.

Likewise the evangelist John says:

“For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

This must in no way be referred to the Jews,

[Note: Or rather: “not so much.”]

because the evangelist truly said of the Son that he made himself equal with God.

Again, it is written in the same Gospel:

“Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (ibid., 19).

And:

“Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (ibid., 21).

Again:

“So that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (ibid., 23).

Equal honor is given only to equals.

Again, there the Son says to the Father:

“All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John 17:10).

Again:

“Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” (John 14:9).

He would not have said this unless he had been equal to the Father in every respect.

Again, the Lord himself said:

“You believe in God; believe also in me” (ibid., 1).

And, to demonstrate further the unity of equality, he said:

“No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

And just as the Son reveals the Father to whomever he wishes, so the Father reveals the Son, as he said to Peter when Peter confessed that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God:

“Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

And again the Son says:

“No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

And:

“No one comes to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him” (John 6:44).

[Note: Martinus, Colbertinus 1, Fulgentius, Germanus, Rhenanus, Lorichius, and Orthodoxy read: “From this it is clear that the equality of the Father and the Son consists in their bringing believers to one another.”]

From this the equality of the Father and the Son is clear, since they bring believers to one another.

Again he says:

“If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also; and from now on you know him and have seen him” (John 14:7).

## IV. The Two Natures in Christ

But since we confess that there are two natures in the Son—that is, true God and true man, possessing a body and a soul—we understand that whatever the Scriptures report of him concerning the excellence of sublime power must be attributed to his wondrous divinity; and whatever is narrated more humbly of him, below the dignity of heavenly power, we ascribe not to the Word of God but to the man assumed by him.

[Note: Martinus, Germanus, the Compendianus, Fulgentius, and Orthodoxy have “of excellent power.” Colbertinus 1 has “more excellent.” Lorichius reads “of excellent sublimity and power,” and so forth. Below, Martinus, Germanus, the Compendianus, Lorichius, and Fulgentius have “for the remembrance of his divinity.”]

According to his divinity, therefore, is what we said above when he declared:

“I and the Father are one”;

and:

“Whoever sees me sees the Father”;

and:

“Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise”;

as well as the other statements contained above.

Those things that are reported of him according to his humanity are these:

“The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

And:

“I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

And:

“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

Or when he said from the cross:

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46).

And again, speaking in the person of the Son, the prophet says:

“From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 21:11).

Or when he is said to have been made lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6), and many similar passages, which we have not inserted for the sake of brevity.

The Son of God, therefore, bound by no necessities of created conditions but acting through the free power of divinity, assumed what is ours with such wondrous compassion that he did not at all cease to be what is his, namely, divine. For divinity admits neither increase nor diminution.

Therefore we give thanks to the same Lord Jesus Christ, who for us and for our salvation descended from heaven, redeemed us by his passion, gave us life by his death, glorified us by his ascension, and, seated at the right hand of the Father, will come to judge the living and the dead, granting the reward of eternal life to the righteous and repaying the wicked and unbelieving with the punishments they deserve.

## V. The Generation of the Son

We therefore profess that the Father eternally and ineffably begot the Son from himself—that is, from what he himself is—and that the Son was born from God, not externally, not from nothing, and not from some underlying matter.

[Note: Or: “or.”]

He who was born from God is nothing other than what the Father is, and therefore he is of one substance, because the truth of birth does not permit diversity of kind.

For if he is of another substance than the Father, then either he is not the true Son or—what is impious to say—he was born a degenerate son.

He is indeed the true Son, as John says:

“So that we may be in his true Son” (1 John 5:20).

Nor is he degenerate, because true God was born from true God, as the same evangelist John explains when he says:

“This is the true God and eternal life” (ibid.).

And the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Therefore, if he does not have his substance from elsewhere, he has it from the Father; and if he has it from the Father, he is of one substance with the Father.

But if he is not of one substance, then he is not from the Father but from elsewhere, since it is necessary that he have his substance from wherever he comes.

Everything else is from nothing, but the Son is from the Father. Let each person choose between the two: either let him grant that the Son has his substance from the Father, or let him confess that he came into existence from nothing.

## VI. The Objection Is Resolved

But perhaps the prophetic testimony is brought forward:

“Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

I have not said: “Explain to me the manner or quality of the divine generation, and express the mystery of so great a secret in human words.” For I asked from where he was born, not how he was born.

Divine generation is indescribable, not unknowable. Indeed, it is so far from being unknowable—that is, from its origin being unknown—that the Father repeatedly declares that he begot from himself, and the Son that he was born from the Father. No Christian at all doubts this, as is shown in the Gospel, when the Son himself says:

“Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:14).

Likewise the evangelist John says:

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

We therefore conclude our confession in a brief statement.

[Note: The Laudunensis reads: “As” (*sicut*).]

If he was truly born from the Father, he is of one substance and is the true Son. But if he is not of one substance, neither is he the true Son; and if he is not the true Son, neither is he true God.

Or, if he is true God but is not from the substance of the Father, then he too is unbegotten. But since he is not unbegotten, he is therefore a created work, as is supposed (*putatur*; variant *putetur*, “as it may be supposed”), subsisting from elsewhere, if he is not from the substance of the Father.

But far be it from us to believe this.

For we profess that the Son is of one substance with the Father, rejecting the Sabellian heresy, which so confuses the holy Trinity that it says the Father is the same as the Son and likewise believes the Holy Spirit to be the same, failing to preserve three persons in unity.

## VII. The Unbegotten and the Begotten Have the Same Substance

But perhaps it is objected:

“Since the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, it is impossible for the begotten and the unbegotten to have one and the same substance. For if the Son were unbegotten, just as the Father is unbegotten, then their substance could more readily be different, since each one, subsisting from himself, would not possess a common substance with the other.”

But when the unbegotten Father, from himself—that is, from what he himself is—whatever that may be, or whatever it may be possible to call it—

[Note: Lorichius reads: “If indeed that can be said, or rather, because it cannot be said at all …” Rhenanus agrees with our edition, except that instead of “at all” he has “all things.”]

begot the Son, it is evident that the substance of the begetter and the begotten is one, because we truly confess that the Son is God from God and light from light.

For that the Father is light is testified by the apostle John, who says:

“God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:54).

Again, concerning the Son he says:

“And the life was the light of human beings, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4–5).

And below:

“There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid., 9).

From this it is evident that the Father and the Son are of one substance, since the substance of light and radiance cannot be different—namely, the substance of that which generates from itself and of that which exists from the one who generates from himself.

[Note: In most copies, *se* is absent. Lorichius has “which exists from the begetter.”]

Finally, lest anyone introduce a difference of natural light between the Father and the Son, the Apostle says of this same Son:

“He is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1:3).

In this it is taught most clearly that he is coeternal with the Father, inseparable from the Father, and of one substance with him: radiance is always coeternal with light; radiance is never separated from light; and radiance can never be different from light by nature or substance.

[Note: Colbertinus 1 has “of natural substance.” Martinus and Orthodoxy, together with Lorichius, have “by nature and substance.” The Compendianus has “radiance from light and substance.” Rhenanus has “the nature of substance.”]

For he who is the radiance of light is also the power of God the Father. He is therefore eternal because of the eternity of his power, inseparable because of the unity of his brightness.

And this is what we faithfully profess: that the Son was born from the substance of the Father, as God the Father himself gives the clearest testimony.

To show that he had begotten a proper Son from the substance of his ineffable nature, and to instruct the ignorance of our frailty by raising us from visible things to invisible realities, he applied the language of earthly birth as an example of divine generation, saying:

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

What could the Divinity deign to say more clearly or more brilliantly?

By what indications, by what examples drawn from existing things, could he make known the distinctiveness of generation more fully than by showing, through the mention of a womb, the distinctiveness of a mother who gives birth?

[Note: All manuscripts except Colbertinus 1 and Portuensis read “of generation,” as do the older editions of Rhenanus and Lorichius.]

This is not because he is composed of bodily members or distinguished by any outline of limbs. Rather, because we could not otherwise grasp the truth of divine generation through the hearing of the mind, we are prompted by the term “womb” of a human being, so that there might no longer be any uncertainty that he was born from the substance of God—he whom we know to have come forth from the Father’s womb.

### 27. VIII. The Undivided Substance of God

[Col. 0224C] Therefore, believing that God the Father generated the Son impassibly from his own substance, we do not say that the substance itself was either divided in the Son or diminished in the Father, and thereby became liable to the defect of passion. Far be it from us either to suppose, think, or believe such things about God; for we faithfully profess that the perfect Father generated the perfect Son without diminution of himself, without any derivation, and altogether without any weakness of passion.

For whoever objects to God that, if he generated from himself, he suffered the defect of division, can say that he also experienced labor when he established all things, and that for this reason he rested from all his work on the seventh day. But neither in generating from himself did he experience any passion or diminution, nor in establishing all things did he undergo any weariness.
