[Col. 0224D] For, so that the impassibility of the divine generation might be demonstrated to us more clearly [Laud., Colb. 2, Rhenanus, Lorichius, and Orth.: “might be intimated”], we have received the profession that the Son is light from God, light from light [Lorichius: “from light”].

If, then, in the production of visible and worldly light something of this kind is found—namely, that when light is taken from light and brought forth through a certain birth of generation, the source of light itself, which gave another light from itself, could neither be diminished nor suffer any loss at all of the light supplied from itself [Rhenanus: “could happen”—or “could befall”]—how much more rightly and suitably must we believe concerning the nature of the divine and ineffable light that, generating light from itself, it could not be diminished at all?

[Col. 0225A] Hence the Son is equal to the Father: he was not born in time, but is coeternal with the one who generated him, just as radiance generated from fire is shown to be coeval with the one who generates it. Let this suffice as what we have said concerning the equality of the Father and the Son, and concerning the unity of their substance, insofar as the limits of brevity have allowed.

### IX. The Holy Spirit Is Consubstantial with the Father and the Son

It remains for us to say something about the Holy Spirit, whom we believe to be consubstantial, coequal, and coeternal with the Father and the Son, and to confirm this by testimonies.

Although this venerable Trinity is distinguished by persons and names, it must not for that reason be believed to differ from itself or from its own eternity. Rather, the divinity that exists before the ages in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is truly and properly believed; nor can it be divided by our interpretations, nor again can the Trinity itself, changed into one person, be confused.

This is the fullness of our faith; this is our belief. For this reason we neither permit them to be regarded nor called gods, but confess one God in the persons and names mentioned above.

For the ineffable Divinity did not present itself within names and persons so that it could be enclosed or grasped as though by words; rather, so that we might know it to be what it was, it granted believers an understanding of itself to the extent that the narrowness of the human mind was able to receive it, as the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0225D] **Note.** This passage follows the Septuagint version, which has *οὐδὲ μὴ συνῆτε* (“nor will you understand”); the Vulgate has *non permanebitis* (“you will not remain”). For the most part, the Scriptural texts quoted here belong neither to this version nor to the Vulgate, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. The same is sometimes true of passages from the New Testament: at times they conform to the Greek text, at times to our Vulgate, and sometimes to neither. This single observation must suffice here.

The divinity of the Trinity is therefore one, and in the designation of this word there is a signification of one substance, not of one person. To confirm this matter to the faithful, the Divinity itself has always been present in its testimony through many and repeated declarations. Let us therefore, for the sake of brevity, bring forward a few from among the many, since true proof of majesty [alternative: “indeed, true proof of majesty”], although it possesses a plurality of testimonies, does not require plurality; a few things suffice for the believer.

### X. It Is Proved from the Scriptures

[Col. 0225C] First, therefore, from the books of the Old Testament and afterward also from the New, we shall teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance. The Book of Genesis begins thus:

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:1–2).

[Col. 0225D] He who is the Beginning, when the Jews asked who he was, said: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). [Alternative reading: “He who.”]

[Col. 0226A] The Spirit of God was borne over the waters as Creator, holding creation together by the power of his might, so that, being about to bring forth all living things from them, he might himself supply the unformed elements with the fuels proper to fire; and so that, even then, as the mystery of baptism shone forth, the nature of the liquid might receive the power of sanctification and first produce living bodies unto life [alternative: “and might first produce”].

**Note.** We have judged that the text should be read thus by combining the Port. and Laud. manuscripts. Laud. has *elementi signis fomenta*; Port. has *elementis propria fomenta*. All the other manuscripts and printed editions have: *ipse rudibus elementis; ignis proprii fomenta praestaret* (“he himself would supply the unformed elements with the fuels proper to fire”).

David, therefore, with God inspiring him, testifies: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6).

[Col. 0226D] See how full this brevity is, and how clearly it returns to the mystery of unity. He places the Father in “the Lord,” the Son in the designation “Word,” and names the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the mouth of the Most High.

**Note.** Colb. 1, Mart., and Orth., with Lorichius, read “in the sacrament the unity returns.” Moreover, a little earlier, instead of “full is the brevity,” Lorichius has “clear is the brevity.”

And so that a mere utterance might not be understood in the Word, he asserts that the heavens were established through him. But so that a mere condition might not be supposed in the Spirit, he demonstrated in him the fullness of heavenly power.

[Col. 0226B] **Note.** Laud., Mart., and Orth. read “might be reckoned as the Spirit.” Nevertheless, our reading should be retained. For by these three words—“Lord,” “Word,” and “Spirit”—praised in the psalm, the most holy confessors show that the three persons of the most holy Trinity are expressed.

For where there is power, there must necessarily be a subsisting person; and where the word is “all,” it signifies not something taken away from the Father and the Son, but something consummated in the Holy Spirit—not that he alone possesses what is in the Father and the Son, but that he possesses the whole together with both.

### XI. Three Persons in One Name

Again, when the Lord spoke about the calling of the nations, proclaiming the Holy Spirit within the one name of the Divinity—“the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit”—he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

[Col. 0226C] Again, when the Apostle proclaimed heavenly things to the Corinthians, he added: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (1 Corinthians 13:23).

And so that we may confess more openly the unity of substance in this Trinity, we must also observe how God, when he was ordering the creation of the world and of humankind, revealed the mystery of the Trinity, saying: “Let us make humankind according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

[Col. 0226D] When he says “our,” he plainly shows that the speaker is not one alone; but when he brings forward “image and likeness,” he indicates equality and suggests distinctions of persons.

**Note.** Several manuscripts, together with some printed editions, have “he brings forward likeness,” signifying the equality of the distinction of the persons. Below, instead of “dissenting likeness,” Laud. has “dissenting unlikeness.”

[Col. 0227A] Thus, in the same work there is an open acknowledgment of the Trinity, in which neither the plurality is empty [alternative: “the cause”] nor the likeness discordant, since the following words speak in the same way: “And God said, and God made, and God blessed” (Genesis 1).

It is necessary, moreover, that the author of the whole creation be one God. This principle of faith is finally disclosed and confirmed by the ancient blessing given through Moses, by which the people are commanded to be blessed through the sacrament of a threefold invocation. For God said to Moses:

“Thus shall you bless my people, and I shall bless them: May the Lord bless you and guard you. May the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you. May the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:23ff.).

The prophet David confirms this very thing, saying: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Psalm 66:8).

The heavenly powers of the angels venerate this unity of the Trinity in a hymn [MS 2: “in one hymn”]; and, singing three times with unceasing voice, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), they exalt his glory to the summit of one dominion.

[Col. 0227B] To impress this still more clearly upon the minds of the faithful, we bring forward Paul, who knew the heavenly mysteries. For he says:

“There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4ff.), and so forth.

And certainly he taught that these differences of divisions operate according to the quality and merit of those who participate in them, when he distributed the differences of the graces and concluded by saying:

“But all these things the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each his own as he wills” (ibid., 11).

[Col. 0227C] **Note.** Chiffl. and others read *docens* (“teaching”). Lorichius has *docuit operari* (“taught to operate”), and thus “of the graces themselves,” and so forth.

Therefore no room for doubt remains: it is clear that the Holy Spirit is both God and the author of his own will. He is shown most plainly to work all things and to bestow the gifts of divine dispensation according to the decision of his own will. For where the voluntary distribution of graces is proclaimed, a condition of servitude cannot be supposed: in a creature, servitude is to be understood; in the Trinity, dominion and freedom.

And so that we may teach still more clearly that the Holy Spirit is of one divinity with the Father and the Son, this is confirmed by the testimony of the evangelist John. For he says:

“There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one” (1 John 5:7).

[Col. 0227D] **Note.** In a manuscript of Colb. approximately seven hundred years old, the following observation appears in the margin: “Note that in the epistle of blessed John it should be read thus.” As for these words, “There are three who,” and so forth, which Saint Jerome—or whoever the author was who published the prologue to the canonical epistles under the name of this holy doctor—complains were omitted from some copies of the sacred Bibles through the unfaithfulness of translators, it is clear from this passage that they were more carefully preserved in African manuscripts, where the African Fathers assembled together used them in making a profession of faith.

We never read that the Arians, who at that time possessed royal power and could do almost anything against the Catholics, protested about this matter. Moreover, Fulgentius shortly afterward, near the end of his book *Against the Arians*, cites the same passage not only as taken from Scripture but also as one praised by blessed Cyprian, under the heading of a testimony from Scripture: “Cyprian,” he says, “inserted these testimonies from the Scriptures. The Lord says: ‘I,’ and so forth. And again: ‘It is written concerning the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: and these three are one.’”

Cyprian praised it both in his book *On the Unity of the Church* and in his letter to Jubaianus. Fulgentius again cites the same passage in his book *On the Trinity* and in another work written against Pintus, an Arian bishop, although learned men judge that the author of the latter was someone other than Fulgentius but his contemporary. See Mabillon, Appendix 2 to the *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 246.

Nevertheless, Augustine, in Book II *Against Maximinus*, chapter 22, section 3, where he discusses these words from the epistle of blessed John, “The three are one,” seems to have used a manuscript in which this testimony concerning the Father and so forth was not expressed. The same must be said of Facundus of Hermiane, Book I *In Defense of the Three Chapters*. Facundus, however, composed that work outside Africa, while residing at Constantinople.

It is remarkable that in some very ancient manuscript copies of the Bible the above-mentioned prologue to the canonical epistles is prefixed, indeed under the name of Saint Jerome, and yet that verse is omitted from the text. We leave a more careful discussion of this controversy to our colleagues who are laboring to edit the works of Jerome.

[Col. 0228A] “Are the three,” he says, “separated in differentiated equality, or divided by any degrees of difference through a long interval of separation? No: the three,” he says, “are one.”

[Col. 0228D] **Note.** Other manuscripts read “in differentiated equality.” Lorichius has “in the quality of indifference.” Rhenanus has “in undifferentiated equality.”

### XII. Creation Is Common to Them

[Col. 0228A] So that the one divinity [Lorichius: “dignity”] of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son may be demonstrated still more fully in the creation of all things, you have the Holy Spirit as Creator in the Book of Job:

“The divine Spirit,” he says, “is the one who made me, and the Spirit of the Almighty who teaches me” (Job 33:4).

And David says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:30).

If creation and renewal come through the Spirit, then without doubt the beginning of creation did not occur without the Spirit.

[Col. 0228B] After creation, therefore, let us show that the Holy Spirit also gives life, just as the Father and the Son do. Concerning the person of the Father, the Apostle says: “I testify before God, who gives life to all things” (1 Timothy 6:13).

Christ gives life. “My sheep,” he says, “hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27–28).

We are given life by the Holy Spirit, as the Lord himself says: “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6:64).

Behold, the one act of giving life by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit has been plainly demonstrated.

### XIII. Foreknowledge

Although no Christian is unaware that foreknowledge of all things and knowledge of hidden things are in God, this must nevertheless be shown from the Book of Daniel. “God,” it says, “who knows hidden things and who knows all things beforehand before they come to be” (Daniel 13:42).

This same foreknowledge is in Christ, as the Evangelist reports: “From the beginning Jesus knew who it was that would betray him, and who those were who did not believe in him” (John 6:65). [Alternative reading omits “not.”]

That he is a knower of hidden things is clear from this: when he exposed the obscure counsels of the Jews, he said, “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:4).

Similarly, he himself revealed that the Holy Spirit foreknows all things when he said to the apostles: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all things and will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 13:16).

[Col. 0229A] Whoever is said to announce what is to come is certainly not doubted to foreknow all things, because he searches the depths of God and knows everything that is in God, as Paul recalls:

“For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

And in the same passage: “For no one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him; so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (ibid., 11).

[Col. 0229D] **Note.** Colb. 1 has “He is the searcher of the depths.”

### XIV. The Power of the Holy Spirit

To understand the power of the Holy Spirit, let us bring forward a few examples of terrifying events.

A deceitful disciple had sold a possession, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 5), but concealed part of the money, placing the remainder before the feet of the apostles as though it were the whole. He offended the Holy Spirit, whom he thought he could escape notice from.

[Col. 0229B] But what did blessed Peter immediately say to him?

“Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (ibid., 3).

And below: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (ibid., 4).

Thus struck by the power of the one to whom he had wished to lie, he expired.

What does blessed Peter wish the Holy Spirit to be understood as here? It is plainly evident when he says, “You have not lied to human beings, but to God.” It is therefore manifest that whoever lies to the Holy Spirit lies to God, and whoever believes in the Holy Spirit believes in God.

The Lord showed something similar, indeed something stronger, in the Gospel, saying:

“Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matthew 12:31–32).

[Col. 0229D] **Note.** Ful., Germ., Colb. 1, Orthod., Lorichius, and others read: “Behold, a terrifying sentence! Irremissible,” and so forth.

Behold, by a terrifying sentence he declares that the sin of one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable.

[Col. 0229C] Compare this sentence with what is written in the Book of Kings:

“If a man sins against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” (1 Kings 2:25).

[Col. 0229D] **Note.** The Africans frequently gave this title to the Books of Kings, as is clear from Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion*; from blessed Augustine in various places; from the Third Council of Carthage; and elsewhere. Saint Cyprian also usually calls the Books of Kings by the Greek word *Basileiōn*. Some Fathers from other provinces do the same, although Saint Jerome seems to disapprove of this in his *Prologue Galeatus*. Lorichius here reads “Kings.”

If, then, to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit and to sin against God are similar—that is, if each is an unexpiable crime—everyone can now recognize how great the Holy Spirit is.

### XV. The Presence of God Everywhere

[Col. 0230D] That God is present everywhere and fills all things we learn from the mouth of Jeremiah:

“I am God who is near and not far away. If a human being is hidden in hidden places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:23–24).

**Note.** Several manuscripts and old printed editions have “of Isaiah.” This passage, however, is taken from Jeremiah.

What does the Savior say about his own presence everywhere in the Gospel?

[Col. 0230A] “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20).

The prophet likewise says of the Holy Spirit, that he is present everywhere, speaking in the person of God:

“I am in you, and my Spirit stands in the midst of you” (Ezekiel 36:27).

And Solomon says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice” (Wisdom 1:7).

David likewise says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take up my wings toward the sunrise and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 139:7ff.).

[Col. 0230D] **Note.** Colb. 1 and Lorichius have “to the underworld.” Below, for “if I take,” Laud. has “if I receive.” For “toward the sunrise,” Colb. 1 has “at dawn”; for “at the ends,” another Colb. manuscript has “at the end”; for “will hold me,” Ful., Germ., and Lorichius have “will sustain me.”

### XVI.

[Col. 0230B] God dwells in his saints according to the promise in which he said: “I shall dwell in them” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

The Lord Jesus says in the Gospel: “Remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). Paul proves this by saying: “Do you not know that Jesus Christ is in you?” (2 Corinthians 13:5).

All this is fulfilled through the indwelling of the Spirit, as John recalls:

“By this we know that he is in us, because he has given us of his Spirit” (1 John 4:13).

Paul likewise says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

And again he says: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

Which God? Clearly, the Holy Spirit, whose temple we appear to be.

[Col. 0230D] **Note.** Colb. 1 says “he calls him the Holy Spirit,” whose temple we ought to be.

### XVII.

That the Father reproves, the Son reproves, and the Holy Spirit reproves must be proved as follows.

[Col. 0230D] In the forty-ninth Psalm it is written:

“But to the sinner God says: Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant through your mouth?” (Psalm 50:16).

And below: “I shall reprove you and set you before your face” (ibid., 21). [Laud. adds “before.”]

David likewise, praying, says to Christ: “Lord, do not reprove me in your anger” (Psalm 6:2), because he himself is to come to reprove all flesh.

[Col. 0230C] What does the Savior say about the Holy Spirit in the Gospel?

“When he comes,” he says, “the Paraclete will reprove the world concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment” (John 16:8).

Foreseeing this, David cried out to the Lord: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Psalm 139:7).

### XVIII.

That the Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good is proved as follows.

The prophet says: “You are good, Lord, and in your goodness teach me your statutes” (Psalm 119:68).

The Only-Begotten himself says of himself: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

David likewise says to the Lord concerning the Holy Spirit: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land” (Psalm 143:10).

[Note: Laud. has “way” instead of “land.”]

### XIX.

[Col. 0230D] Who could remain silent about that dignity of the Holy Spirit?

The ancient prophets cried out: “Thus says the Lord.” When Christ came, he appropriated this voice to his own person, saying: “But I say to you” (Matthew 5:22).

[Col. 0231A] What did the new prophets cry out? [Alternative reading: “who cried out.”]

The prophet Agabus, for example, says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Thus says the Holy Spirit” (Acts 21:11). And Paul says to Timothy: “The Spirit expressly says” (1 Timothy 4:1).

This voice plainly demonstrates the undifferentiated equality of the Trinity.

Paul says that he was called and sent by God the Father and Christ: “Paul,” he says, “an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Galatians 1:1). [Laud.: “and to God the Father.”]

But in the Acts of the Apostles it is written that he was set apart and sent by the Holy Spirit. For thus it is written:

“The Holy Spirit says: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

[Col. 0231B] And shortly afterward: “They, being sent by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia” (ibid., 4).

Likewise in the same book: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Acts 20:28).

### XX. The Name “Paraclete” Is Common

[Col. 0231B] Let no one, because the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete, regard him as something contemptible.

For *Paraclete* means advocate, or rather comforter according to the Latin language; and this designation is also common to the Son of God, as John says:

“I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone sins, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

[Col. 0231D] **Note.** The Vulgate has “Advocate,” which means the same thing. The Greek text has *Παράκλητον* (*Paraklēton*), from which the word *Paraclete* may also be derived, even when pronounced briefly with the letter *i*, as they say. The distinguished Joannes Baptista Thiers proves this at length in a special dissertation on the word.

When the Lord himself says to the apostles, “The Father will send you another Paraclete” (John 14:16), by saying “another Paraclete” he undoubtedly reveals that he himself is also a Paraclete.

Nor is this name of Paraclete foreign to the Father. It is a name of beneficence, not of nature.

[Col. 0231C] Finally, Paul writes to the Corinthians:

“Blessed is God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

When the Father is called the Comforter, the Son the Comforter, and the Holy Spirit also the Comforter, nevertheless one consolation is provided for us by the Trinity, just as there is one forgiveness of sins, as the Apostle affirms:

“You have been washed, you have been justified, and you have been sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

We could still bring forward many more testimonies from the divine Scriptures, which, in accordance with the sacrament of baptism, manifest the Trinity as possessing one glory, operation, and power. But because the understanding of the wise is already full from these things, we have passed over many matters for the sake of brevity.

[Col. 0231D] **Note.** Since baptism is administered “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” these words express the unity of the Trinity.

### XXI. Recapitulation

[Col. 0231D] Let us therefore recapitulate what we have said.

If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; if he liberates; if he is Lord and sanctifies; if he creates with the Father and the Son and gives life; if he possesses foreknowledge with the Father and the Son; if he is everywhere and fills all things; if he dwells in the elect; if he reproves the world; if he judges; if he is good and upright; if it is proclaimed concerning him, “Thus says the Holy Spirit”; if he appoints prophets; if he sends apostles; if he appoints bishops; if he is the Comforter; if he dispenses all things as he wills; if he washes and justifies; if he kills those who tempt him; if the one who blasphemes him has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come—which is certainly proper to God—then, since these things are so, why is there doubt that he is God, when the greatness of his works reveals what he is?

[Col. 0232A] **Note.** Germ., Ful., Colb. 1, Lorichius, and Orthod. read: “that he is God, since the greatness of his works manifests what he himself is.” The others have: “that he is not God, since through the greatness of his works it manifests what he himself is.”

He is certainly not alien to the majesty of the Father and the Son, since he is not alien to the power of their works.

His divine name is denied in vain when his power cannot be denied. I am forbidden in vain to venerate him with the Father and the Son, when I am compelled to confess him with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0232B] If he grants me forgiveness of sins, sanctification, and everlasting life together with the Father and the Son, I am exceedingly ungrateful and impious if I do not render glory to him together with the Father and the Son.

Or, if he is not to be worshiped with the Father and the Son, then neither should he be confessed in baptism. But if he must be confessed in every way, according to the Lord’s command and the tradition of the apostles, so that faith may not be incomplete, who could prohibit me from worshiping him?

For the one in whom I am commanded to believe is also the one to whom I ought to pray. I shall therefore worship the Father, worship the Son, and worship the Holy Spirit, with one and the same veneration.

If anyone thinks this difficult, let him hear how David exhorts the faithful to worship God: “Worship his footstool” (Psalm 99:5).

[Col. 0232C] If it is a religious act to worship his footstool, how much more religious is it to worship his Spirit?

That Spirit, namely, whom blessed Peter proclaimed with such exalted language, saying: “Through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom the angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

If the angels desire to gaze upon him, how much more ought we mortal human beings not to despise him, lest perhaps it be said to us as it was said to the Jews:

“You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts 7:51).

[Col. 0232D] **Note.** Lorichius has “let us not deny him.” Below he has “You resisted the Holy Spirit.” The Scriptural text has “you resist.” Nevertheless, in the brief statement of faith apud Sirmondus, as here, it reads “you resisted”; therefore we have retained the reading found in the printed editions and manuscripts.

### XXII.

But if such great and weighty considerations do not incline the mind to venerate the Holy Spirit, receive something still stronger.

[Col. 0232D] Paul instructs the prophets of the Church in this way; and among them, and through them, the Holy Spirit was certainly speaking:

“If all prophesy, but an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, examined by all, and the secrets of his heart also become manifest; and then, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Corinthians 14:24–25).

[Col. 0233A] And certainly the Holy Spirit is in those who prophesy.

If, then, unbelievers fall on their faces and, struck with fear, worship the Holy Spirit, confessing unwillingly [Lorichius: “overcome”], how much more is it beneficial for believers to worship the Holy Spirit voluntarily and from devotion?

[Col. 0233B] The Holy Spirit is worshiped, however, not separately in the manner of the Gentiles, just as the Son is not worshiped separately, because he is at the right hand of the Father.

**Note.** Lorichius has this more briefly: “but when we worship the Father, we believe that we invoke the Holy Spirit; and when we beseech the Father, we trust that we are heard by the Son,” and so forth.

Rather, when we worship the Father, we believe that we worship the Son and the Holy Spirit also; for when we invoke the Son, we believe that we invoke the Father, and when we beseech the Father, we trust that we are heard by the Son, as the Lord himself said:

“Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I shall do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:13).

And if the Holy Spirit is worshiped, then the one whose Spirit he is is certainly worshiped.

No one is unaware that nothing can be added to or taken away from the divine majesty by human petitions [Lorichius: “But each person, according to the purpose of his will, either acquires glory for himself,” and so forth]. Rather, each person, according to the purpose of his will, either acquires glory for himself by faithfully venerating it, or awaits everlasting confusion by stubbornly resisting.

[Col. 0233B] For it is certain that pride and contempt condemn, while honor awaits the fruit of devotion.

**Note.** Mart. has “pride and contention,” but this reading seems preferable to the others, which have “contention.” Lorichius’s edition confirms our reading, for it has “contempt.”

Why, then, should the faithful not honor the Trinity in its entirety, since they trust that they belong to it, and glory in being reborn in its name and called its servants?

For just as people are called men of God from the name of God the Father—Elijah was called a man of God, and Moses was called a man of God—so we are named Christians from Christ, and we are also called spiritual people from the Spirit.

[Col. 0234A] If someone is called a man of God but is not a Christian, he is nothing; and if he is called a Christian but is not spiritual, he cannot have sufficient confidence in his salvation.

### XXIII.

Let our faith in the Trinity, therefore, be whole according to the confession of saving baptism, and let there be one devotion of piety.

Let us neither suppose differences of powers in the manner of the Gentiles nor suspect a creature in the Trinity insofar as divinity is concerned.

Nor should we be disturbed by the scandal of the Jews, who deny the Son of God and do not worship the Holy Spirit. Rather, let us worship and magnify the perfect Trinity, and let us hold in our conscience what we say with our mouth in the mysteries:

“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

[Col. 0233C] **Note.** During the solemn celebration of Mass, both Greeks and Latins have always been accustomed to sing this hymn. When some in Gaul began neglecting it outside public Masses, the Synod of Vaison in 529 decreed, in canon 3, that it should always be sung at all Masses—whether morning Masses, Lenten Masses, or those celebrated in commemoration of the dead—in the same order in which it was said at public Masses. On these various Masses, see Mabillon, Book I of *On the Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 6, or, for a fuller discussion, the late Cardinal Bona, Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 13 and following.

Take care not to confuse this hymn, which the Greeks call *epinikion* [ἐπινίκιον], that is, “triumphal,” and concerning which Isaiah speaks in chapter 6 and John in Revelation chapter 4, with the hymn that they call *trisagion* [τρισάγιον], which they often sing, while the Latins sing it once a year, namely on Good Friday: “Holy God, holy mighty one,” and so forth. On these matters consult our Hugh Menard in his notes on the Gregorian sacramentary, p. 10, where he discusses them fully and learnedly.

By saying “Holy” three times, we confess one omnipotence, because there is one worship and one glorification of the Trinity. Thus may we hear from the Apostle what the Corinthians heard:

[Col. 0234B] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

This is our faith, confirmed by evangelical and apostolic traditions and authority, and founded upon the fellowship of all the Catholic churches throughout the world.

[Col. 0234B] **Note.** These two words, “confirmed by authority,” are absent from Colb. 2, Orthod., Rhenanus, and Lorichius.

In this faith we trust and hope, by the grace of almighty God, to remain until the end of this life.

Here ends the petition presented on the date [or: the seventeenth] of the twelfth day before the Kalends of May by Januarius [Note: Most manuscripts read “Zattarensis”; Colb. 1, “Zaitarensis.” In the African Register, in the Laud manuscript, it is called “Jacterensis.” See what we observe concerning this city in the notes to the Register itself. Lorichius, moreover, has “Jenuarium” instead of “Januarium.”], bishop of Zattara, Villaticus of Casis-Medianis, bishops of Numidia, and Boniface of Foratianum, and Boniface of Gratiana [Note: Colb. 1, Rhenanus, and Balsamon read “Gatianensis.” Portius and Orthodocus, with Lorichius, read “Gazanensis.” A second Colbertinus, Martianus, Fulgentius, and Germanus also read “Gazanensis.” In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 198, Victor, bishop of Gratiana, is listed among the Donatist bishops. Although the other three bishops mentioned here are listed in the African Register, the name of this Boniface of Gratiana is missing there—a genuinely surprising omission. Unless he is the very man whose name has dropped out in the first position listed there, in which case “Gratianensis” should be read instead of “Vassinassensis,” as the Register has it. Indeed, Peter the abbot, at the Council of Carthage under Boniface, mentions Boniface, bishop of Gratiana, first see of the province of Byzacena, to whom he had turned in the absence of the bishop of Carthage, to whom his monastery was directly subject. Yet the Boniface who subscribed to this confession of faith does not seem to have been the first bishop, since he subscribed after Boniface of Foratianum; and this Boniface of Foratianum is mentioned in the African Register as the sixty-eighth among the Byzacene Fathers.]

# BOOK FOUR. HUNERIC’S SAVAGERY AGAINST THE CATHOLIC BISHOPS

[Col. 0233]

## I. The Arians’ Slander

When our little book was being read, those madmen, unable to endure with blind eyes the light of truth set before them, began to shout and to complain bitterly that we had called ourselves Catholics by our own name. At once they falsely reported to the king that we had caused a disturbance and were avoiding a hearing. He, inflamed at that very hour and believing the lie, hastened to do what he wished. Already possessing a written decree, and secretly sending his agents with that decree through the various provinces [Col. 0235A], he closed in a single day all the churches of Africa while the bishops were in Carthage, and bestowed all the property of the bishops and churches upon his own bishops as a gift.

Not knowing what he was saying, nor about what he was making assertions, they did not blush to produce against us the law that our Christian emperors had formerly issued against them and against other heretics for the honor of the Catholic Church, adding many things of their own, as suited tyrannical power. This, then, is the text of the law that was issued and brought forward.

## II. King Huneric’s Edict against the Catholics

King Huneric of the Vandals and Alans, to all peoples subject to our kingdom.

“Triumphant majesty and royal virtue are shown by turning evil counsels back upon their authors. For whoever has discovered some form of wickedness must blame himself for what he has incurred. In this matter our Clemency has followed the nod of divine judgment, since, while it causes each person to be treated according to the deserts of his deeds—whether favorably or, perhaps, in an adverse manner—it also brings about a corresponding recompense. Therefore, against those who have provoked us by believing that they ought to resist the command of the illustrious memory of our father or of our Clemency, we assume the censure of severity. [Note: 82 Lorichius and Orthodocus read: “followed, decreed contrary things for persons according to what their deeds . . . deserved. Therefore,” etc. Further below Orthodocus reads “to the command.” Colb. 1, Baldus, Rhenanus, and Bignonius read: “who believed the command . . . ought to be despised.” Chiffletius and others, corruptly, read: “who believed the command . . . retained.”]

“For we caused it to be made known to all peoples that, in the territories of the Vandals, no Homoousian priests were to hold assemblies, nor claim for themselves any of those mysteries which rather pollute them. When we saw this being disregarded, and found very many saying that they retained the complete rule of faith, it is subsequently clear that all were warned, a period of nine months having been granted [Note: Colb. 1 and Martianus read: “nine months, whatever of dispute might be adapted to their purpose.” Other manuscripts read as in the printed editions, but for “of the new” they have “of the new thing”; Orthodocus has “disputes” instead of “of dispute.” Lorichius reads: “It is clear that all were warned to preserve or retain the rule of faith, for a period of nine months. Whatever of dispute could be adapted to their purpose,” namely, up to the Kalends of February, and so forth.], and of a new dispute—if anything could be adapted to their proposals—so that by the Kalends of February in the eighth year of our reign they might assemble without any fear.

“When they were flocking to the city of Carthage for this purpose, after the appointed time had elapsed, we are known to have granted them another delay of several days. While they asserted that they were ready for the contest, on the first day our venerable bishops proposed to them that they should properly approve from the divine Scriptures the term *homoousion*—‘of the same substance’—as they had been warned to do; or else condemn what had been cut off by approximately a thousand and more bishops from all over the world at the Council of Ariminum, or at Seleucia [Note: This is a manner of speaking commonly used among Africans, as is clear from Optatus, *Against Parmenianus*, book I, and Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VII, chapter 7, where “about a thousand, or rather more” is signified. This tyrant says that the doctrine of the Catholics was condemned by approximately a thousand bishops at the Council of Ariminum or at Seleucia, although, according to Athanasius himself, no more than four hundred assembled at Ariminum and only one hundred and sixty at Seleucia. But after the Arians had inclined Catholic prelates to their side, partly by cunning arts and partly by force, they selected some of their own number who traveled through the cities and provinces and compelled the bishops who had been absent to subscribe to their doctrines. Both synods were convened in the year 359 at the command of the Emperor Constantius Augustus, who ordered the Western bishops to assemble at Ariminum and the Eastern bishops at Seleucia, a city of Isauria.].

“They were entirely unwilling to do this, recalling the whole matter to sedition by stirring up the people themselves [Note: Thus Orthodocus. The others read: “the aroused populace.”]. Indeed, on the second day also, when we ordered them to answer concerning the same faith, as had been proposed, they seemed to have adopted this course as a reckless expedient, disturbing everything with sedition and shouting so as to prevent the contest from taking place [Note: Colb. 2, Chiffletius, Balsamon, Rhenanus, and Bignonius read: “They evidently adopted this through the reckless course already taken.” Martianus, Fulgentius, Germanus, Compendius, Lorichius, and Orthodocus read: “They seem to have adopted this through the reckless course already taken.”].

“Since they had provoked us in this way, we decreed that their churches should be closed, prescribing this condition for them: that they should remain closed as long as they were unwilling to proceed to the proposed contest [Note: Chiffletius and others read: “Since they provoked us in this way.” Rhenanus reads: “Since they provoked this.”]. They chose to do this with the obstinacy that they appear to have adopted through wicked counsels.

“So it is necessary and entirely just to turn against them what is demonstrated by the content of those laws which, after bringing emperors of different periods into error with them, they then succeeded in having promulgated. The substance of these laws appears to be that no church should be open except to the bishops of its own institution; that no one should be permitted either to maintain a private congregation or to hold assemblies; that they should neither possess nor build churches in cities or even in the smallest places; but that those churches, having been claimed, should be joined to the rights of the treasury; and that their estates, joined to the churches of their faith, should pass to their own bishops. [Note: Others read “emperors of different times.” Portius reads: “which it then happened that emperors of different times, led with them into error, should promulgate.” The laws cited here are for the most part found in the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 5, in many chapters; this Vandal here gives their epitome. A little below, Orthodocus and Lorichius read *contextio* instead of *conceptio*; Rhenanus and Chiffletius read *superexceptis* instead of *exceptis*.]

“Nor should they have any permission to travel to any places whatsoever, but should be made exiles from all cities and localities. They should have no power whatsoever to baptize, nor perhaps to discuss religion, and no authority to ordain anyone—whether bishops, priests, or others who might happen to belong to the clergy. The severity of the penalty was prescribed so that both those who allowed themselves to receive such honors and the ordainers themselves would each be fined ten pounds of gold, with the added provision that no opportunity would be allowed them even to petition or plead; and even if they had deserved some special privilege, it would be of no avail [Note: We restore this passage from Lorichius and Orthodocus. Colbertinus reads: “nor of coming to,” etc.; the other manuscripts and printed editions, corruptly, read: “to call to mind whatever,” etc. Compendius reads: “If they should wish to lessen any of these penalties, they would be entirely unable to do so.” Lorichius reads: “If they should be unable to lessen anything, they would be entirely unable.”].

“If they persisted in this wickedness, they were to be removed from their native soil and sent into exile under suitable escort. The emperors mentioned above likewise persecuted the peoples, so that they had no right either to give, to make wills, to receive, or to accept anything left to them by others—not under the name of a trust, nor as a legacy, nor by gifts, nor by a bequest called a gift in contemplation of death, nor by any codicil or other writing.

“Thus even those who served in their own palaces were to be subjected to the gravest condemnation according to their rank, so that, stripped of every privilege of honor, they would incur infamy and recognize themselves as liable to a public charge of this kind. A penalty of thirty pounds of silver was also imposed upon the officials of various judges. If it happened that this penalty had to be imposed five times upon persons persisting in error, then such persons, convicted and subdued by blows, were to be sent into exile.

“Moreover, they had ordered all the books of the priests whom they were persecuting to be delivered to the flames. We command the same thing to be done with books of this kind, by which iniquity has persuaded them into the error of that name.

“For, as has been said, they had ordered these measures to be observed against each individual person [Note: 83 Colb. 2, Martianus, Fulgentius, Germanus, Lorichius, and Orthodocus omit a line: “the illustrious, fifty pounds of gold each; the spectabiles, forty pounds of gold; the commoners,” etc. Lorichius has *singuli* for *singulatim*. In the third Colbertinus, Compendius, and Lorichius, senators and merchants are not listed. Colb. 1, Rhenanus, Lorichius, and Baldus read *sacerdotales* instead of *sacerdotes*, and Rhenanus does not list merchants.], so that the illustrious would pay fifty pounds of gold each, the spectabiles forty pounds of gold, senators thirty pounds of gold, commoners twenty pounds of gold, priests thirty pounds of gold, decurions five pounds of gold [or: three times five], merchants five pounds of gold, plebeians five pounds of gold, and circumcellions ten pounds of silver [Note: Thus Colb. 1, Fulgentius, Germanus, Compendius, Lorichius, and Orthodocus. Others read “ten pounds of gold.” Our reading is better: those men would not have paid ten pounds of gold, since the preceding classes paid only five.].

“If anyone should perhaps remain in this wickedness, all his property was to be confiscated and he was to be punished with exile. The civic orders, and also the managers and tenants of estates, were ordered to inflict this penalty: if they should choose to conceal such persons and fail to make them public, and should not bring those detained [or: such persons in …] before the court, they themselves would be held liable to punishment. Tenants of royal estates were also subjected to this fine: whatever they contributed to the royal household, they would be compelled to pay an equal amount to the treasury as a penalty.

“They established that this was to be observed generally against all tenants or possessors who believed that they should persist in the same superstition. Judges, moreover, who did not press this matter with the utmost insistence were to be punished by the penalty of proscription and the punishment of death. Three chief officials were also to be punished, while the others were to be fined twenty pounds of gold.

“Therefore it is necessary that all Homoousians be bound by these enactments, since it is clear that they have held and continue to hold the substance of such evil persuasion [Note: Rhenanus reads “of evil.” Orthodocus, with Lorichius, reads “persuaded by evil things into the fire.” Colb. 2 and Compendius read “persuaded by evils into the fire.” Further below, for “by all,” Compendius, Lorichius, and Rhenanus read “by men.” Fulgentius, Germanus, Colb. 1, and Orthodocus read “by men … to possess.” For “not to have brought against different persons,” Colb. 1, Martianus, Compendius, and Orthodocus read “to have brought against adversaries.”].

“We decree that they abstain from all the matters stated above, under prosecution by the officials of all the cities; and also that the judges who are shown, by neglecting the preceding provisions, not to have inflicted the dreadful punishments upon various persons are to be dealt with accordingly.

“Therefore, all who are entangled in the errors of the aforesaid faith of the *homoousion*, which was condemned by the entire council of so great a number of priests, are commanded to abstain from all the property and transactions mentioned above, knowing that nothing has been permitted to them. Let the same penalty await and bind them all if they are not converted to the true religion, which we venerate and worship, by the day of the Kalends of June in the eighth year of our reign.

“Our Clemency established the appointed day for this reason: so that indulgence might not be denied to those who condemned their error, while punishments worthy of obstinate minds might restrain the stubborn. But those who remain in the same error—whether occupied in the military service of our household or placed in charge of various offices and necessities—shall be compelled, according to their ranks, to undergo the assessments of the fines described above, and anything that any of them may perhaps have obtained through clandestine means shall have no validity.

“Our promulgation has also ordered this to be observed with regard to private persons, or persons of whatever rank or station: namely, that such people should be subjected to suitable punishments, as was expressed above in the laws concerning them. We decree that provincial judges who neglect to carry out what has been established shall be bound by the penalty prescribed above for such persons.

“But to the true worshipers of the divine majesty—that is, to our priests—we decree that all the churches, and the entire body of the clergy of the aforesaid name, established in whatever lands and regions are possessed under the rule of our empire by the favor of the Divinity, together with the property belonging to them, ought to prosper by this decree. We do not doubt that what has been justly bestowed upon the most holy bishops will contribute more abundantly to the support of the needy [Note: Huneric misused the examples of the emperors in making this decree; Augustine repeatedly proves that similar measures were justly taken by Catholics against the Donatists, especially in *Treatise on John* 6, number 25, and *Against Petilianus* II, chapters 58 and following.].

“We therefore command this law, flowing from the fountain of justice, to be made known to all, so that no one may claim that what has been commanded was unknown to him. We wish you well.

“Given at Carthage on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.”

[Note: In Colb. manuscript 1746, written approximately seven hundred years ago, the following heading is added. Although it does not seem to us to be by our Victor, it is nevertheless worth reproducing here:

“This is the law, this is the command of the most wicked king and hateful-to-God Huneric, son of Geiseric, which he issued against the people of the godly, hissing like a dragon with a forked tongue. But now it is time for us to bring the narrative in this fourth little book to an end, because it is unworthy and indecent that divine speech should lie under tyrannical conversation. We therefore ask the hearers to lend their ears willingly when the beginning of the fifth book sounds in them, since we trust that it will narrate the great and wondrous contests of the martyrs, through Jesus Christ himself, who marvelously crowns his saints with laurels. Amen.”

Then follows: “The fifth book begins. After these things,” and so forth.]

## III. Savagery against the Catholic Bishops

After these deadly edicts, disseminated with venomous poison [Note: Several manuscripts and printed editions read “poisoned across the page.” Cyprian also calls the persecuting edicts “deadly edicts” in Letter 52 to Antonianus, now number 55 in the Oxford edition. The author of the *Passion of the Seven Monk Martyrs*, related above, likewise mentions “deadly edicts.”], he orders all the bishops who had assembled at Carthage—and whose churches, houses, and property he had already seized—to be stripped of everything in the lodgings where they were staying and, once stripped, driven outside the walls.

Not an animal, not a slave, not even the garments they were wearing and might change were left to them. He further ordered that no one should receive any of them into his lodging or provide them with food. Whoever attempted to do this out of compassion was to be burned with his entire household in a fire.

The bishops, though cast out, acted wisely at that time by not departing from the place, even though they were begging. For if they left, they would not only be forcibly recalled, but it would also be falsely said of them, as it was falsely said, that they had fled from the contest—especially since, when they returned, the churches would no longer have any property, their houses having been seized [Note: Orthodocus and Lorichius read: “they would never be recalled at all.” Further below Lorichius and others read: “especially since they would not return.” There was no longer any property belonging to the Church, since everything had been seized.].

Thus, while they lay groaning around the walls under the open sky, it happened that the impious king went out to the pools. They all preferred to meet him, saying:

“Why are we being afflicted in this way? For what crimes that we may perhaps have committed are we suffering these things? If we have been assembled for a disputation, why are we stripped, why are we paraded about, why are we delayed, and why, without our churches and houses, are we suffering from hunger and nakedness outside the city, rolling in the midst of filth?”

But he looked upon them with grim eyes and, before he had heard their petition, ordered horses and riders to be driven over them, so that by this violence they might not merely be crushed but even killed. Many of them were then crushed, especially the old and the infirm.

## IV. They Are Circumvented by Deceit

Afterward those men of God were ordered to come to a certain place called the House of Memory, unaware of the fraud prepared for them. When they had arrived, a folded document was shown to them, and with a serpent’s subtlety they were told:

“Our lord King Huneric, although he regrets that you have been contemptuous and are still slow to obey his will, so that you may become members of the religion of which he himself is a member, has nevertheless now formed a good intention concerning you. If you swear that you will do what this document contains, he will restore you to your churches and houses.”

All the bishops replied:

“We always say, and have said, and shall say: We are Christians; we are bishops; we hold the one true apostolic faith.”

After a brief silence following their confession of faith, those who had been sent by the king hastened to extract an oath from the bishops. [Note: Colb. 2 and Fulgentius read “Hortalanus”; the others, without aspiration, “Ortulanus.” He was bishop of Benefa in Byzacena, as appears from the Register. Florentianus is so called in Colb. 2, Fulgentius, Martianus, Portius, Orthodocus, Lorichius, and Belfortius, and likewise in the African Register, where he is called bishop of Midila in Numidia. The third Colbertinus, with some printed editions, has “Florentinianus.” He is counted with Hortulanus by Ado and in the Roman Martyrology, on 28 November, among the African confessors mentioned above; see notes 11 and 23 above (Coll. 185, n. a, and 190, n. c). In this place several manuscript codices and printed editions insert much material taken from Huneric’s edict related above. We have placed it in its proper location, as other codices have it and as the order of events requires.]

Then the blessed men, the bishops Hortulanus and Florentianus, spoke for all and with all:

“Are we irrational animals, that we should swear easily or rashly without knowing what the document contains?”

The men sent by the king hurried to disclose to them the contents of the writing, which had been disguised in words of this sort. For the deceptive document said:

“Swear whether, after the death of our lord the king, you desire his son Hilderic to be king, and whether none of you will send letters to the regions overseas; for if you give an oath to this effect, he will restore you to your churches.”

Then the pious simplicity of many began to consider giving the oath, even contrary to the divine prohibition, lest the people of God should later say that the churches had not been restored because of the fault of the priests who had refused to swear.

Other bishops, however, more shrewdly sensing the deceit of the fraud, absolutely refused to swear, saying that the authority of the Gospel had forbidden it, since the Lord himself said: “You shall not swear at all” (Matthew 5:34).

The king’s ministers said to them:

“Let those who intend to swear stand apart.”

When they withdrew, the notaries wrote down what each person said and from which city he came. The same was done with those who refused to swear. Immediately both groups were handed over to custody.

## V. They Are Driven into Exile

Afterward the fraud that had been concealed became apparent. To those who had sworn it was said [Note: Thus Lorichius. But Chiffletius and others read: “Why did you wish to swear contrary . . . ? The king ordered,” etc. Others read: “for which reason he ordered,” etc. Further below, Compendius and Lorichius read: “receive colonies by right for cultivating the field” instead of “receive the status of tenants for cultivating fields.”]:

“Because you wished to swear contrary to the commandment of the Gospel, the king has ordered that you shall never see your cities or churches again. Instead, having been banished, you shall receive landholding rights to cultivate fields, but on the condition that you neither sing psalms nor pray, nor carry a book in your hands for reading; that you neither baptize nor ordain, nor presume to reconcile anyone.”

Likewise they said to those who had not sworn:

“Because you do not desire the kingdom of our lord’s son, for this reason you refused to swear. Therefore you have been ordered to be banished to the island of Corsica, where you shall cut timber useful for the royal ships” [Note: Chiffletius inserted here the *Register of the African Church*, which he thought should rather be published separately later.].

# 38 BOOK FIVE. HUNERIC’S GENERAL PERSECUTION AGAINST ALL THE ORTHODOX

[Col. 0241]

## I. The General Persecution

That beast, thirsting for the blood of the innocent, therefore added the following: while the bishops had not yet been sent into exile, he dispatched the most savage torturers at one and the same time through all the provinces of African territory. No house and no place remained where there was not wailing and mourning, and no age or sex was spared except those who yielded to their will [Note: Lactantius frequently gives persecutors the name “beasts” in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Thus he calls Nero an evil beast in section 2. Concerning Diocletian and his colleagues he says in section 16: “Three most savage beasts were raging,” and so forth. The same author proves in book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 11, that this designation is especially appropriate to persecutors. Baluzius discusses the matter further in his notes to chapter 19 of the aforementioned little book.].

They beat some with clubs, hanged others, and burned still others with fire. Women—and especially women of noble birth—they tortured completely naked in public, contrary to the laws of nature. Of these I shall mention briefly and hurriedly one of our own, Dionysia.

When they saw that she was not only courageous but also more beautiful than the other matrons, they first tried to strip her and attack her with clubs [Note: Compendius reads: “When she suffered this and said, ‘I am secure concerning God,’” and so forth. Rhenanus, like the other printed editions, has “tried” where the passage here has “asked.” A little earlier, where the text has “they tried … to attack,” Lorichius reads: “they were ordered … to inflict.”].

While she endured this and said, secure in her Lord:

“Torture me as you please, but do not strip my modest limbs,”

they became still more enraged. They placed her, stripped of her garments, in a higher position, making her a spectacle for everyone.

Amid the blows of the rods, while streams of blood already flowed over her entire body, she said in a free voice:

“Ministers of the devil, what you reckon you are doing to my disgrace is itself my praise.”

And because she was filled with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, though constricted by the bonds of punishment, she was already a martyr herself and encouraged others to martyrdom.

By her holy example she nearly freed her entire homeland. When she saw her only son, still of very tender age and delicate, fearful of the punishments, she rebuked him by the gestures of her eyes and encouraged him with maternal authority, so that he became much braver than his mother.

To him, standing amid cruel blows, she said:

“Remember, my son, that we were baptized in the name of the Trinity in the mother, the Catholic Church. Let us not lose the garment of our salvation, lest the one who comes to invite us find no wedding garment and say to the servants: ‘Cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth’ (Matthew 22:13).

“That is the punishment, my son, which must be feared, because it never ends; that is the life which must be desired, because it is possessed forever.”

By such words she strengthened her son and swiftly made him a martyr. The venerable youth, Majoricus by name, gave up his spirit in the contest of confession and completed his course bearing the palm. She embraced her victim and, giving thanks to the Lord with as loud a voice as she could, chose to bury him in her own house, rejoicing in the hope of what was to come, so that whenever she poured out prayers to the Trinity over his grave she might be confident that she was never separated from her son.

How many, then, were won for God through her in that city, as we have said, would take too long to recount. For her sister also, Dativa by name; Leontia, the daughter of Saint Germanus the bishop; Dativa’s relative; the venerable Emilius, a physician; the religious Tertius, renowned for his confession of the Trinity; and Boniface of Sibida—or Sibidensis—what sufferings they endured and with what tortures they were disemboweled, whether as women or as men, who can narrate in order?

[Note: The African Register represents one Germanus, namely the bishop of Peradama in Byzacena, concerning whom mention was made above. If he is the same man who is mentioned here, we may infer that our Victor was a native of Peradama, from these words in particular: “One of our own, Dionysia,” and so forth. Indeed, he speaks of Dionysia and the other martyrs mentioned here as people who were especially well known to him. Yet below, in section 11, he calls Habetdeus “our” bishop. The common Latin martyrologies commemorate all these martyrs together on 6 December; the Greeks do so on the following day. Usuard has the following: “In Africa, the holy women Dionysia, Dativa, and Leontia, and the religious man Tertius, Emilianus, and Boniface, with three others, all of whom …” In the Roman Martyrology, after these words of Usuard, Saint Majoricus, son of Saint Dionysia, is separately added: “In the same place, Saint Majoricus, son of Saint Dionysia, who …” On the following day it has: “At Tuburbum, Saint Servus the martyr, who …” Ado, however, lists the names of the three designated by Usuard, as well as Servilius, Victrix, and Majoricus. From these words it is clear that the three whose names Usuard omitted were Majoricus, son of Saint Dionysia; Servus of Tuburbum; and Victoria, who will be mentioned below. Consequently, except for Victoria, they are commemorated twice in Baronius’s martyrology. Emilius, whom some call Emelius, is called Aemilianus by Usuard and Ado. A little below appears “Sibidensis.” We have been unable to locate this city. Perhaps “Sicilibensis” should be read. For, as Norisius observes, it looked obliquely toward both Tuburba towns and was eighteen Roman miles distant from the larger one. Its bishop on the Donatist side, Quadratianus by name, took part in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 198. There is also a city called Cilibiensis, whose bishop Tertullus, likewise a Donatist, is listed in the same Collation, chapter 206. Augustine mentions the estate of Zubedi in the territory of Fussala in *The City of God* XXII, chapter 8.]

## II. The Passion of Servus

[Note: 85 The reading of this passage varies in all the codices. We have retained Chiffletius’s reading, which Bignonius, Rhenanus, and Baldus also exhibit, except that they have *servi* for *Servus*. Portius, Fulgentius, Germanus, Orthodocus, Surius, and Lorichius read: “Servus also, of the greater city of Tuburbum, of a man of noble birth and rank,” etc. Colb. 1 reads similarly, but has *majoris* for *Majorus*; Compendius has *Majoricus*. The second Colbertinus agrees with Chiffletius, except that it has “of a man of noble birth and rank.” In the margin of the third Colbertinus, the first hand has “Majori, martyr.” There were in Africa two cities called Tuburbum, the greater and the lesser. The martyrologies cited above recognize from this passage of Victor only one martyr, named Servus; yet some modern writers, taking *majoris*, which must refer to Tuburbum, as the confessor’s name, invented another martyr named Majorus. We shall discuss in our historical commentary, chapter 6, another fabricated martyr at Tibur in Italy, created on the occasion of this same Servus.]

Servus also, of the greater city of Tuburbum, a man of noble birth and rank, endured punishments for Christ that no one could adequately describe.

After countless blows with clubs, he was repeatedly raised by pulleys. While he hung high above the whole city, they lifted him aloft and then suddenly released the hempen ropes. Falling by the weight of his body upon the paving stones of the streets, he collapsed like a stone upon stones.

They also dragged him repeatedly and rubbed him against sharp stones, so that, when the skin had been torn away, you could see the flayed skin of his body hanging from his sides and back, and from his belly [Note: Colb. 1 and two printed editions read “throughout the city.” All the others read “through the whole city,” a reading that can be supported by what follows, where the holy martyr is said to have fallen upon the stones of the streets. He was perhaps dragged from one street to another. Below, Compendius has “he was dismissed” instead of “they released him.”].

Already in the time of Geiseric he had endured things not very different from these, so as not to disclose the secrets of a certain friend of his. How much more now, in order to strengthen the sacraments of his faith? And if he faithfully displayed loyalty to a human being without reward, how much did he owe to the one who will repay faith with its reward?

## III. Victoria’s Courage

In the city of Culusita I cannot report what happened, for it is impossible for a human being even to count the number of martyrs and confessors there [Note: This is a city in the Proconsular Province; its bishop Aemilianus is listed in the Register. More information about the city may be found in the notes to the Register below.].

There a certain matron, Victoria, the author of her own name, was being burned in the sight of the crowd by prolonged suspension. Her husband, already lost to the faith, with her children present, implored her as follows:

“What are you suffering, my wife? If you despise me, at least have pity on these children whom you bore, you wicked woman. Why do you forget your womb and count for nothing those whom you brought forth with groaning? Where are the pledges of conjugal love? Where are the bonds of fellowship that the marriage tablets, written between us long ago by the law of honor, established?

“Look, I beg you, upon your children and your husband, and hasten to fulfill the command of the king, so that you may both gain the torments that still await you and be given back to me and to our children.”

But she listened neither to the weeping of her children nor to the serpent’s flatteries. Raising her spirit far above earthly affection, she despised the world and its desires [Note: Colb. 1 and Orthodocus, with Lorichius, read “raising the sight of her eyes very high.” A second Colbertinus reads “raised far higher by great affection.”].

When those who were torturing her saw that, through the prolonged suspension, her shoulders had been torn apart and that she was dead, they took her down, utterly lifeless in every part. Later she reported that a virgin had stood beside her, touched each of her limbs, and that she had immediately been healed.

## IV. The Faith of the Martyr Victorianus

How, then, I am to praise Victorianus—a citizen of the city of Hadrumetum and at that time proconsul of Carthage—I do not know, for words fail me. [Note: By this title, I think, some magistrate appointed by the king is to be understood, one who administered justice, like a kind of shadow of the Roman proconsuls in Africa. The common martyrologies commemorate Victorianus together with the two brothers mentioned below on 23 March. Galesinius inserts among them Verolus and others, of whom we shall speak below in the Historical Commentary, chapter 10. Concerning these men, see the Bollandists, 21 February and 23 March; on the same day, the ancient Capuan calendar, made publicly available by the monk Michael in the Capuan sanctuary, indicates the feast of Saint Victorianus and his fellow martyrs. The people of Liège further boast that they possess some relics of this Victorianus, as Saussayus testifies in his Gallican Martyrology on 23 March. Hadrumetum was a celebrated city in Africa, the chief city of the province of Byzacena; its bishop Felix is mentioned above by Victor in book I, section 7. It would be useless to gather more information about this city here. In the time of Saint Augustine, the monks of Hadrumetum were famous for the controversies they stirred up concerning grace and predestination, on account of which the holy Doctor published several short works. Finally, the editor of the Oxford edition of the works of Saint Cyprian observes in his notes on the Council of Carthage, no. 3, that this city was at one time called Black Sissa.] he was the proconsul of Carthage, or perhaps the governor—I do not know, for the words fail me—than whom no one in those regions of Africa was richer, and who was also regarded as completely trustworthy by the impious king in all matters entrusted to him.

The king spoke to him familiarly and is said to have told him that he would hold him dearer than all others if he would readily assent to the king’s command. But that man of God sent back this reply with great confidence:

“I am secure in Christ, God and my Lord. Say this to the king: Let him consign me to the flames, let him drive me before wild beasts, let him torment me with every kind of torture. If I should consent, I was baptized in vain in the Catholic Church. For if this present life alone existed, and we did not hope for another life, which is truly eternal, I would not act so as to glory briefly and temporally, and become ungrateful toward him who bestowed his faith upon me, the Creator [al. ‘the creditor’].”

At this the tyrant was aroused, and what length and variety of punishments he inflicted upon him no human speech could explain. Victorianus, however, rejoicing in the Lord and happily completing his course, received the martyr’s crown.

## V. Two Brothers, Confessors

Who could explain the contests of the martyrs that took place also in the city of Tambaia? [Note: Manuscripts and editions vary: *Tambadensem*, *Tambianensem*, and *Tambudensem*. In Augustine’s seventh book against the Donatists, chapter 44, a bishop Secundinus from Tamba is mentioned; in the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 80, he is called the martyr Secundianus of Thambeis. In the *Notitia Africae*, Servusdei of Tambeita is listed among the Byzacene Fathers. Concerning this city and Aquae Regiae, also mentioned here, see the notes to the *Notitia Africae*.]

There two brothers by birth, from the city of Aquae Regiae, secure in the Lord, swore to one another that they would ask their torturers to torture them under one punishment and with equal suffering. [Note: Ful., “entered”; Rhenanus, Chiffl. and other printed editions, “swore and asked.” The nature of their oath is explained shortly afterward, when one of them says to his wavering brother: “We swore upon the body and blood of Christ.” As early as the middle of the third century, the schismatic Novatian compelled his followers to swear upon the body and blood of Christ that they would never pass over to the side of Pope Cornelius.]

When, in their first suspension, stones having been tied to their feet, they hung all day, one of them asked to be taken down and given a respite. His brother, fearing that he would deny the faith, called out to him from the place of suspension:

“No, no, brother! We did not swear thus to Christ. I shall accuse you when we come before his terrible throne, because we swore upon his body and blood that we should suffer for him together.”

By saying this and much else, he strengthened his brother for the battle of suffering. The latter cried out in a loud voice:

“Apply whatever punishments you wish, and constrain Christians with cruel tortures. What my brother is going to do, I too am doing.”

How many red-hot plates burned them, with what kinds of claws they were raked, and by what torments they were tortured, the event itself shows. For the torturers themselves threw them away from their presence, saying:

“All the people imitate these men, so that no one will turn at all to our religion.”

And especially because no bruises or traces of punishment could be seen on them.

## VI. The Remarkable Faith of the People of Tipasa. A Great Miracle

Let us hasten to relate, to the praise of God, what happened in Tipasa, a city of greater Mauretania. [Note: In the *Notitia Africae*, Reparatus of Tipasa is listed among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis. There is also another Tipasa in Numidia, whose bishop Rusticus is recorded in the same *Notitia*. We discuss both in the notes to the *Notitia Africae*.]

When the whole population saw that an Arian bishop, Cyrila, had been appointed from the notary’s office to destroy souls [Note: Rhenanus and Chiffl., together with several manuscripts and editions, read “from the court notary”; Orth. and Lorichius, “from the notary Cyrila.”], the entire city at once fled by ship to nearby Spain, leaving behind only a very few who had found no opportunity to sail.

The Arian bishop first began to compel those who remained with flatteries and afterward with threats, trying to make them Arians. But remaining strong in the Lord, they not only mocked the madness of the persuader, but also began publicly to celebrate the divine mysteries, assembled in one house.

When he learned of this, he secretly sent a report against them to Carthage. When the king became aware of it, he angrily sent a certain count and ordered him, after the entire province had been assembled in the marketplace, to cut out their tongues and cut off their right hands at the roots.

When this had been done, by the favor of the Holy Spirit they spoke—and still speak—in exactly the manner in which they had spoken before. But if anyone wishes to be incredulous, let him now go to Constantinople, and there he will find one of them, the subdeacon Reparatus, speaking polished words without any impediment. [Note: We shall say more about confessors who spoke without tongues in the Historical Commentary, chapter 7.]

For this reason he is held in extraordinarily high esteem at the palace of the emperor Zeno, and especially the empress venerates him with remarkable reverence.

## VII. The Vandals Rage Against Their Own People

But who could adequately recount or heap up the varieties of punishments which, by order of their king, the Vandals themselves inflicted upon their own people? Even if a writer tried to set down individually the events that took place at Carthage, he could not, without rhetorical embellishment, name all the tortures themselves. What happened is even now displayed openly before everyone. [Note: Lorichius reads, “which is today plainly displayed before everyone.”]

You may see some without hands, others without eyes, others without feet, others mutilated in nose and ears; still others, after being suspended for a long time, with their shoulder blades torn from their bodies, had the head that normally projected above them sunk down between their shoulders. While the torturers kept them hanging in lofty buildings, they drove them to and fro through the empty air by moving the ropes with their hands.

Sometimes, when the ropes broke, many fell from that height with a powerful impact and lost the crown of the head together with their eyes. Others, their bones shattered, immediately gave up the spirit; others breathed their last a little later.

But if anyone thinks this a fable, let him question Uranium, Zeno’s envoy, [Note: Germanus, Ful., Mart., Comp., and Colbert 1 read *Anius*; Orth. and Lorichius, *Avius*.] in whose presence these things occurred above all. The reason was that, when he came to Carthage, he boasted that he had come to defend the Catholic churches. To show him that the tyrant feared no one, the tyrant stationed more and even crueler torturers in those streets and alleys through which envoys customarily passed when going up to or down from the palace—plainly to insult the commonwealth itself and to display the dregs of our already failing age.

## VIII. The Steadfastness of an Exiled Matron

At that time, therefore, the wife of a certain royal chamberlain named Dagila [Note: Colbert 1, Comp., and Port. read “of the royal chamberlain Dagilla, who”; Orth. and Lorichius, “Dagilius”; Ful., Germanus, Mart., Colbert 2, and Belfor., “Dagilium, who,” and so on.
