Thus the husband too may at some time have been a confessor.]—a noble and refined matron who had already often been a confessor during the reign of Geiseric—was utterly weakened by whips and clubs and was banished into a barren and impassable exile, where perhaps no human being could gain access to her to offer consolation. She left her house, her husband, and her children [al. “son”] with joy.

Later, it is said, she was offered a transfer to a milder desert, where she might, if she wished, enjoy the company of companions. But believing that a great joy would be hers where there was no human affection to console her, she begged that this should not happen.

## IX. The Struggles of the Carthaginian Clergy. Muritta’s Noble Deed

At that time also, when the bishop Eugenius had already been established in exile, the entire clergy of the Church of Carthage—nearly five hundred or more—was worn down by slaughter and hunger. [Note: The common martyrologies commemorate all these men, together with Eugenius and Muritta of Salutari, on 13 July. Several martyrologies also commemorate Muritta separately on 24 March.]

Among them were very many young readers, mere children, who, rejoicing in the Lord, were driven far away into cruel exile. But I must not keep silent about the greater freedom granted at that time to the deacon Muritta than to the others, when they were being beaten in the middle of the city.

There was a certain man named Elpidoforus, exceedingly cruel and savage, who had been assigned to tear apart the bodies of Christ’s confessors amid the assaults of punishment. [Note: Colbert 1 and Port. read *Helpidoforus*; Orth. and Lorichius, *Epidoforus*.] He had formerly been baptized among us in the church of Faustus, and the venerable deacon Muritta had received him from the baptismal font as one newly born.

But afterward, when he apostatized, he displayed such savagery against the Church of God that he was found to be the foremost of all the persecutors’ executioners.

What more need be said? When first the presbyters were summoned in order to be afflicted with punishments, and afterward the archdeacon Salutaris, the aforementioned Muritta was prepared for torture. He was second in the office of the ministers.

While the honorable old man was being stretched out, with Elpidoforus sitting and snarling, before he was stripped [Lorichius: “before he was tortured”], Muritta secretly carried, unknown to everyone, the *sabanum*—the linen cloth with which he had once covered Elpidoforus when receiving him from the font. [Note: This word evidently denotes linen cloth. This can be gathered from Victor’s passage here, and nearly all the writers of glossaries agree, as may be seen in the learned Cangius’s *Glossary*, where the word is said to have been borrowed from Greek. Gregory the Great also used it more than once, especially in *Dialogues* IV.55, where he says that a *sabanum* had been prepared for a man coming out of the bath. In III.17, a man wrapped in a *sabanum* was buried. In the Carthaginian conference, hearing 2, chapter 53: “and when within the folded *sabanum* …” Many other examples of this object occur throughout. See the Bollandists in the life of Saint Zosimus, 24 January.]

Having shaken these cloths out and displayed them stretched before everyone, he is said to have begun speaking in these words, moving the whole city to weeping and tears:

“These are the linen cloths, Elpidoforus, minister of error. They will accuse you when the majesty of the Judge comes. They will be preserved through my diligence as a testimony to your destruction, to plunge you into the abyss of the sulfurous pit.

“These cloths, wretched man, wrapped your spotless body when you rose from the font. These, most miserable man, will pursue you more fiercely when you begin to possess the flaming Gehenna, because you put on the curse as a garment, tearing apart and losing the sacrament of true baptism and faith.

“What will you do, wretch, when the servants of the Master of the household begin gathering the invited guests for the royal banquet? Then the king, seeing you—once summoned, but now stripped of the wedding garment—will say to you in terrible indignation: ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?’ (Matthew 22:12ff.). ‘I do not see what I bestowed; I do not recognize what I gave.

“You have lost the military cloak [Note: Lorichius reads “which I wove on the fabric of virgin members”; others, “upon the protection of virgin members.” Some add *gestatus* after *membrorum*. For *tendicula*, Sur. and Bign. have *tendiculas crucis*, “the tendrils of the cross, which he stretched out.” Colbert 1 adds *manus* after *crucis*. Below, for *cultum*, Ful., Germanus, Comp., and Orthod., with Lorichius, read *vultum*, “face.” Sur., Bign., Colbert 1, and Rhenanus read: “my eyes do not see the character.”] of my service, which I wove for ten months in the protection of virgin limbs; and, stretching out the tendrils of the cross, I washed it with water and adorned it with the purple of my blood. I do not see the garment of my sign; I do not see the mark of the Trinity.

“Such a man cannot take part in my banquets. Bind his hands and his feet with cords, because he deliberately wished to separate himself from his Catholic brothers of old. He himself stretched out the ropes into a continuous noose, by which he bound himself, and he hindered others from coming to this banquet. He placed a stumbling block along the path for many; now, with everlasting shame and perpetual disgrace, I have thrown him out of my banquet.”

While Muritta was saying these and other things, Elpidoforus, falling silent through the fire of conscience before the eternal fire, was burning.

## X. Clerics Driven into Exile

All of them, therefore, offering their backs for blows, went cheerfully into exile. [Note: Colbert 1 reads: “And so all the parents, their backs covered with blows, went cheerfully …”]

While they were still on the road, traveling a long distance, merciless and violent men were sent against them at the urging of the Arian bishops, so that whatever Christian pity had perhaps supplied them for their sustenance might be cruelly taken away. At that time each of them perhaps sang more willingly:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb” (Job 1:21);

“I must also go naked into exile, because the Lord knows how to provide food for the hungry and clothe them in the desert.”

Indeed, two Vandals who had often become confessors under Geiseric went into exile with these clerics, their mother accompanying them, having despised all their riches.

But a certain apostate reader named Theucarius, [Note: The printed editions read *ex lectore*, “from a reader”; it seems, however, that *exlectore* should be read as one word, indicating that he had once been a reader of the Church but afterward became an utterly filthy apostate. For *Theucario*, Lorichius and Orth. read *Theucorio*, Bign. *Theucariae*. Among the Bollandists, 24 March, *Theutorico*. Mart. reads *Theucario perdico*.] informing the authorities about the multitude of confessors proceeding—that is, the clergy of the Church of Carthage—said that twelve little boys whom he knew to be strong singers and skilled in musical melodies should, by his designation, be separated. When he was still a Catholic, he had taught them as his pupils.

As soon as he had made this report, a hasty order was issued, and by the violence of barbarian fury a group of twelve children was called back from the road. They were separated in body, though not in spirit, from the flock of the saints. Fearing the precipice, and sighing amid tears, they clung to the knees of their companions with their hands so that they might not be torn away. Nevertheless, heretical violence separated them with threatening swords and brought them back to Carthage.

But when the authorities dealt with them with the flatteries customarily used toward children of such an age [al. “most of them were no longer of such an age”], they proved to be more mature than their years, and, so that they would not fall asleep in death, they lit for themselves the lamp of evangelical light.

The Arians were deeply angered by this and were ashamed to have been defeated by children. Therefore, inflamed with rage, they again ordered them to be beaten with clubs. Only a very few days earlier they had scattered them with various blows. Wounds were added to wounds, and the renewed punishment grew crueler again.

But, with the Lord strengthening them, it happened that the younger age did not fail in its suffering; rather, their spirit grew stronger, fortified in faith. Carthage now honors them with extraordinary affection and sees them as a choir of twelve apostles in the form of children. They live together, eat together, sing psalms together, and together glory in the Lord.

In those days also two merchants, Frumentius and another Frumentius of the same city, were crowned with an outstanding martyrdom. [Note: Colbert 1 gives a somewhat fuller text: “and another, likewise named Frumentius, of that same city of Carthage, with one name and likewise outstanding in grace, together …” Port. also has the words “of that same city of Carthage.” The common martyrologies commemorate them on 23 March.]

Then seven brothers—not by nature but by grace—living together in a monastery, having completed the contest of confession, reached the unfading crown: Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servus the subdeacon, Rusticus the subdeacon, Rogatus the monk, Septimus the monk, and Maximus the monk. [Note: The Port. codex reads “Servius … Septiminus.” We have related the passion of these holy martyrs above, on page 99, at the end of Victor of Vita’s History (see below, column 263), where we made several observations about them, especially concerning the addition found in two manuscript codices: one in the Carthusian house of Portes and the other in the Colbert Library, no. 1746. The Colbert manuscript that we examined, after listing the names of these martyrs, reads as follows: “But although in the present work we have not been able to explain more fully the contests of these most glorious martyrs, contests worthy of imitation and admiration, because of the multitude of countless other martyrs, nevertheless, at the end of this work of ours, with the Lord’s help, we promise to narrate them. Here, then, is the end of the account of our fifth book. In that manuscript the sixth book begins as follows: ‘From that time onward, more cruelly …’”]

## XI. The Cruelty of Antonius toward Saint Eugenius

For at that time the Arian bishops, presbyters, and clerics were raging more cruelly than the king and the Vandals. They themselves, armed with swords together with their clerics, ran everywhere to persecute people. Among them was a certain bishop named Antonius, more savage than the rest, who inflicted such wicked and unbelievable things upon our people that they cannot be told.

He was in a certain city near the desert, bordering on the province of Tripolitania. Like an insatiable beast thirsting for the blood of Catholics, he ran roaring here and there to seize them. For the impious Huneric, knowing Antonius’s ferocity, wished Saint Eugenius to be banished to those regions of the desert. [Note: Eugenius is said in the African *Notitia* to have been exiled to Tamalluma. No city-name occurs in the whole *Notitia* that comes closer to this name than Tamalluma, where Habetdeus also is said below to have been exiled. There were two cities called Tamalluma, one in Byzacena and the other in Mauretania Sitifensis. There was also the Tower of Tamalluma, whose bishop attended the Carthaginian conference. The learned Baluzius considers this latter place to be the same as Tamalluma in Byzacena. We discuss these places in the notes to the African *Notitia*. From Victor’s context it is clear that Antonius was prefect of Tamalluma, one of these cities. I almost omitted mentioning that Colbert 1 here reads “the desert of Tamalbinia.”]

When Antonius accepted responsibility for guarding him, he surrounded him with such strict confinement that he permitted no one to enter to him. Moreover, he was devising various ambushes and punishments by which to destroy him.

But Saint Eugenius, while mourning the hardships of our persecution and wearing down his aged body with the harshness of a hair shirt, sleeping upon the bare ground and wetting the bed of his sackcloth with a rain of tears, eventually felt the violent disease of paralysis.

When this news was reported [al. “upon the report”], the Arian turned it into a cause for rejoicing and hurried to the bed of the exceptional man of God. When he saw the true bishop, under the pressure of the illness, producing halting words, he decided to destroy at once the man whom he did not want to survive.

He ordered harsh and exceedingly bitter vinegar to be sought. When it had been brought, he forced it into the venerable old man’s throat, though his throat resisted and refused it. For if the common Lord, who had come for this purpose, when he tasted it, refused to drink, how much more would this servant and faithful confessor have refused, unless heretical savagery had forced it upon him?

From that vinegar, which was especially harmful to his illness, the disease received an increase. But the mercy of Christ afterward came mercifully to his aid and restored him healthy. [Note: Colbert 1, no. 3119, has this in the margin: “This venerable man, after many tribulations and many crowns of patience, finally rested in peace on the third day before the Ides of July. The archdeacon Salutaris, and Muritta, second in the office of the ministers, already raised as confessors for the third time and gloriously distinguished by the title of perseverance in Christ, will be treated separately in the Historical Commentary, chapter 8.”]

## XII. Against Saint Habetdeus

How much the same Antonius could harass another of our bishops, Habetdeus, who had likewise been banished to the city of Tamalluma, where Antonius had been, the event itself demonstrates. [Note: Several manuscripts and editions read: “But when another of our bishops, Habetdeus, had been exiled … he harassed him …” Comp. has “with him” instead of Habetdeus, although below it calls him Habetdeus; for *Tamallumensi* it has *Adlumensis*. Habetdeus is called in the African *Notitia* the bishop of Tamalluma in Byzacena. He was therefore exiled from the city of Tamalluma in Byzacena to Tamalluma in Mauretania.]

For when he afflicted him with various persecutions, and could not make him an Arian, seeing that the soldier of Christ remained steadfast in confession, he had promised his followers, saying:

“Unless I make him embrace our religion, I shall not be Antonius.” [al. “I am not Antonius.”]

But when he was found inferior to his own promise, he conceived another plan at the prompting of the devil. He bound the bishop’s hands and feet with enormous chains, stopped his mouth so that his tongue could not cry out, and sprinkled water over his body as though for rebaptism—as if he could bind conscience together with the body, or as if the one who hears the groans of those in chains and searches the secrets of the heart were not present there; or as if deceptive water could overcome the purpose of so firm a will, which the man of God had already sent as an envoy to heaven amid streaming tears [Note: Colbert 1 and Port. read “flashing tears”; Mart., Comp., Lorichius, and Orth., “shedding tears.”]

He immediately removed the man’s chains and addressed him in a voice that seemed almost joyful:

“Behold, brother Habetdeus, you have now become our Christian. What more can you do except consent to the king’s will?”

Habetdeus replied:

“That is the condemnation of death, impious Antonius: when consent is extracted from the will. I, holding fast to my faith and confessing repeatedly with my voice what I believe and have believed, defended it by crying out. But after you bound me with chains and closed the door of my mouth, in the court of my heart I completed the record of my resistance, with the angels subscribing to it, and sent it on to be read by my emperor.”

## XIII. The Violence of the Arians

This violence of the tyrants was indeed widespread. The Vandals were sent everywhere for this purpose: to intercept travelers on the roads and bring them to their priests to be slaughtered. [al. “when”] After they had killed them with the sword of the deceptive water, they handed them, as Scripture bears witness, the mark of their destruction, so that they would not be dragged elsewhere by similar violence. For neither merchants nor private persons were permitted to travel anywhere unless the wretched men displayed their own death, marked by the sign of the character.

Christ had shown this long ago by revelation to his servant John, where he says:

“No one will be permitted to buy or sell anything except one who has the mark of the beast on his forehead and on his hand” (Revelation 13:16–17).

Their bishops and presbyters too, accompanied by armed men, went around villages and towns during the night. They scornfully forced open the doors and entered as plunderers of souls, carrying water and a sword. Those whom they found at home—some perhaps asleep in their beds—they sprinkled with fiery and lightning-like rain, and with demonic shouting called them their Christians, in order to display the plaything of their heresy rather than any form of religion. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts and editions read: “a plaything of their heresy rather than …” Comp. has “rather.” Lorichius reads: “the water of their heresy as a plaything rather than …”]

Those who were less capable of understanding and ignorant thought that the sacrilegious pollution had been inflicted upon them [al. “attributed it to them”]. The wiser, however, rejoiced that nothing done to them against their will and while asleep could harm them.

Many of them immediately threw ashes upon their heads; others, because the deed had been done, covered themselves with mournful haircloth; some smeared themselves with foul mud; and they tore apart the linen cloths violently imposed upon them thread by thread and threw them with their own hands into latrines and filthy places.

## XIV. The Noble Deed of a Woman

By this same violence, before our eyes, a son of a certain nobleman, about seven years old, was separated from his parents at Cyrila’s command. His mother, with her hair loosened and without the modesty proper to a matron, ran through the whole city after the abductors. The little boy cried out as best he could:

“I am a Christian! I am a Christian!” [Note: Ful., Germanus, Comp., Colbert 1, Port., and Mart. add: “By Saint Stephen I am a Christian.” Everyone knows that Saint Stephen was then especially famous in Africa because of the miracles frequently performed in that province through his holy relics brought from Palestine. Augustine often discusses them, especially in his books *On the City of God*. Port. and Colbert 1 supply the words that follow: “To whom …”; the others, together with the editions, have only: “to whom, stopping his mouth …”]

But they stopped his mouth, in these three words declaring the Trinity, and drowned the innocent child in their own abyss.

Thus, it is proved, the same thing happened to the children of the venerable physician Liberatus. [Note: Galesinius and several martyrologies commemorate this saint, his wife, and his children on 23 March; the Bollandists also treat them on that day. The passage below, beginning “For when …,” is transmitted differently in the Comp. codex, which reads: “For when, at the king’s command … the possibility of separating their little children from their parents and, through an affection of piety, overcoming their courage …”]

When he was ordered, by the king’s command, to be sent into exile with his wife and children, Arian impiety devised the separation of the little children from their parents, so that through their parents’ natural affection it might overthrow their courage as well. Thus the tender pledges, their children, were separated from their parents.

When Liberatus wished to shed tears, he was rebuked by his wife’s authority, and at the very moment of his departure his tears immediately dried. For she said to him:

“Behold, Liberatus: because of your children you are about to lose your soul? Count them as though they had never been born; for Christ himself will certainly claim them. Do you not see them crying out and saying, ‘We are Christians’?”

But what this woman did before the judges must not be left unmentioned. While she and her husband were held separately under guard in prison, so that they could not see each other at all, a message was sent to the woman and she was told:

“Relent now from your harshness. Behold, your husband has obeyed the king’s command and has become one of our Christians.”

She replied:

“Let me see him, and I will do whatever God wills.”

When she was brought out of prison, she found her husband standing, surrounded by a great crowd, bound before tribunals [al. “before the tribunal.”] Believing true what the enemies had pretended, she seized him by the edge of his clothing near the throat and strangled him before everyone, saying:

“Wretch and reprobate, unworthy of the grace of God and his mercy, why did you wish to glory for a brief time and perish forever? What will gold profit you? What will silver profit you? Will they perhaps free you from the furnace of Gehenna?”

She said much else besides.

Her husband replied:

“What are you suffering, woman? What do you think, or what perhaps have you heard about me? I remain Catholic in the name of Christ and will never be able to lose what I hold.” [Note: The name “Catholic” has always clung to the worshipers of the true faith, despite the futile resistance of heretics, as is evident from various passages in the holy Fathers and writers of ecclesiastical history: Lactantius IV.30; Augustine passim; Socrates, who likewise distinguishes the Novatians from the Catholics; and others. Augustine says in *Against the Letter of Mani*, chapter 4: “In the bosom of the Catholic Church the very name ‘Catholic’ holds me, a name which not without cause this Church has obtained among so many heresies, so that although all heretics wish to be called Catholics, nevertheless, when some stranger asks where one goes to the Catholic assembly, no heretic dares point out either his basilica or his house.”]

Then the heretics, conscious of their lie and exposed, were entirely unable to disguise their fraud.

## XV. Confessors Who Died in the Deserts

Since above we have briefly spoken of the enormity of their violence, many people, fearing it, shut themselves away—men and women alike—in caves or deserted places, with no one aware of them. There, when no supply of food came to their aid, overcome by hunger or cold, they breathed out a broken and contrite spirit amid these hardships, carrying with them the security of an inviolate faith.

Thus the presbyter Cresconius, a citizen of Mizentina, was found in a cave on Mount Ziquensis, his corpse already decomposed and detached. [Note: Some ancient martyrologies cited by the Bollandists, 23 March, commemorate him together with those mentioned above. Port. reads *Mizentanae* instead of *Mizentinae*; Colbert 2, Mart., Ful., and Germanus, *Mizeitanae*; a third Colbert manuscript, *Mitetanae*; Orth., Lorichius, and Belf., *Miritanae*. We have already discussed the city of the Ziquensians above, column 207, note a. Port., Colbert 1, Mart., Germanus, and Ful., together with the editions of Orth. and Belf., read *Quizitanae*. If this reading is correct, the place indicated here is Quiza or Quida, a city of Mauretania Caesariensis, whose bishop Tiberianus is listed second among the bishops of that province in the *Notitia*. We shall make further observations about this city below in the notes to the *Notitia*.]

## XVI

And since we have already spoken of Saint Habetdeus, he then proceeded to Carthage, resolving to approach the wicked king, so that he might make manifest even to men the conscience that he had always held as familiar and friendly to the Trinity [al. “had held and cherished”]. Nor could Antonius restrain him out of shame for himself. He offered the most impious king a written petition in words of approximately this kind:

“What, I ask, do you now have against those who have been cast out? What against those whom you fight every day after banishing them into exile? You have taken away their possessions; you have deprived them of their churches, homeland, and homes. Only the soul remains, and you are trying to take that captive.

“O times! O customs! The whole world understands these things, and even the persecutor himself sees them. If the faith you hold is called faith, why do you harass the members of the true faith with such persecutions? What have you to do with our exile? What have you to do with the poor in this world, whose life is always in Christ?

“At least let those whom you have cast away from the sight of all peoples be permitted to enjoy the company of wild beasts.”

When this bishop of God had said these and similar things, the wicked tyrant is said to have ordered him:

“Go to our bishops, and follow whatever they tell you, because they are known to possess complete authority in this matter.”

But this could not recall Antonius from his madness, since he knew that by obeying the king he could please him all the more and gain great power. Bishop Habetdeus, however, rejoicing in the goodness of his conscience, preferred to return to the place of his exile.

## XVII. Severe Famine

At that time an unbelievable famine arose and began to devastate all Africa in a single widespread destruction. No rain fell then; not a drop at all flowed down from heaven. And this was not without cause, but by the true and just judgment of God: for where, while the Arians were persecuting, the water of the muddy whirlpool was bubbling with fire and sulfur [another reading: “and fire”], the rain of heavenly mercy, which had always flowed abundantly, was denied.

The whole face of the earth remained lurid. In summer no vine was covered with shade-giving leafy branches; no sown field, sprinkled with seed, made the surface of the ground green; no ever-green olive tree, filled with leaves [another reading: “pleasant”], had its customary covering of its lovely foliage; no fruit-bearing thicket, with the earth as its spouse, had produced the buds of flowers, later to yield fruits as usual [another reading: “about to yield”]. Everything was gloomy and horrifying, and a calamity equal to pestilence had confounded all Africa.

The earth produced no green vegetation at all for human beings or animals. Long before, the channels of the rivers, whose currents had rushed in steep descent, had dried up; and the veins of the springs, whose surfaces had rippled with perpetual flow, had likewise been exhausted. Sheep and oxen alike, moreover all the livestock of the fields and the wild beasts of the forests, were nowhere to be seen, consumed by starvation.

And wherever a grassy patch, perhaps situated in a damp valley, had begun to put forth the color of newly growing hay—pale rather than green—at once a scorching, fiery wind arose, drying everything by burning it. For a dusty storm [another reading: “a cloud of dust”], boiling everything beneath the dry sky, had clouded the entire region.

No commerce was conducted at that time. No plow turned and split any clod of earth while young oxen pulled it, because neither oxen nor [Note: Ful. reads this correctly. Colb. 1 and Port. with Notker have *aratra*, “plows”; another Colbertinus manuscript has *astra*, “stars,” erroneously; others have *castra*, “camps.”] harrows remained at all.

Amid all these evils, one part of the peasants had perished, and the remnant that happened to survive was soon seeking burial. And because, under the pressure of famine, neither commerce, as we have said, was carried on in the customary manner, nor the cultivation owed to the earth performed, crowds of young men, old men, youths, girls, boys, and even little girls, together with corpses, were scattered everywhere, wherever and however they could, wandering around towns, villages, and individual cities.

For they had been turned into a crooked and perverse bow (Psalm 77:57), and, provoking God at the waters of contradiction (Psalm 106:32), they suffered hunger like dogs (Psalm 59:7, 15)—not so that they might eat bread, but so that they might feel the Trinity whom they had denied as hostile to them.

Some spread out across the fields; others sought the secrecy of the forests, looking for ancient roots of plants or any sort of refuse. Some, when they attempted to leave their homes, fell at the very threshold, and, conquered by famine, collapsed in crowds. The roads and paths, covered with corpses and filled with the stench of the dead who were breathing out their last, killed the living who walked along them on every side.

Everywhere, every day, there were also funerals of those dying, and there was no strength to provide the dead with the burial owed to compassion. The living were not sufficient to bury them, since, with famine dominant, they themselves were soon to die.

Individuals desired to reduce themselves and their children to perpetual slavery, to sell their freedom, but they could not find buyers. Mountains and hills, city streets, roads and paths had everywhere become one common grave for all whom hunger, feeding upon them, had denied nourishment.

The Vandals themselves, whom the frequent plunder of many provinces and the possession of Africa had previously made rich [Colbertinus 1: “recent plunder”], were tortured by even greater want. And the prouder they seemed to themselves because of the accumulation of slaves, the more they declined, weakened by the famine that tormented them.

No one retained a son, no one a wife, no one his own slave. Each person went out, not where he wished but where he was able, and either immediately collapsed or never returned at all.

The unhappy multitude was then also being driven to gather in the city of Carthage itself. And while those crowds of corpses still possessing life were flowing there, when the king who had inflicted the deaths saw the slaughter, he immediately ordered them all driven from the city, lest the contagion of those wasting away should also prepare a common grave for his army [Note: Lorichius reads, “lest it should prepare a grave for his own people as well.”]

He therefore ordered each person to be recalled to his own province and home. But there were none to return, since everyone already carried his own burial in his face.

And for this reason the destruction of those rebaptized may perhaps have been greater: while the Arians promised continuance of the present life, not even that came to pass, and the first death forestalled the second.

Famine thus ravaged and claimed dominion for itself so thoroughly that certain places, once very populous, now lie in deep silence, their inhabitants extinguished and only their walls remaining.

## XVIII. The Customs of the Barbarians

But why do I linger over something that I cannot explain? For even if those writers were still alive, or had been permitted to speak about such matters, the river of Ciceronian eloquence would dry up, and Sallust would remain utterly speechless.

And, to pass over foreigners unworthy of so great a subject, even if Eusebius of Caesarea arose, capable of undertaking this work, or his translator Rufinus, adorned with Greek eloquence [Lorichius: “and Latin flowers”], what more need be said? Neither Ambrose, nor Jerome, nor even our own Augustine would suffice.

Hear this, all nations; receive it with your ears, all who inhabit the world—and you earth-born and children of men, all together, rich and poor (Psalm 48:1).

Some of you love barbarians and sometimes praise them to your own condemnation. Examine the name and understand their customs. Could they have been called by any other proper name than “barbarians,” a name possessing the meaning of ferocity, cruelty, and terror?

No matter how many gifts you lavish upon them, no matter how many services you use to soothe them, they know nothing else except to envy the Romans. [Note: After the various barbarian incursions, when in many provinces of the Empire—especially the Western Empire—the barbarians and the older peoples whom the Romans had formerly subdued had become intermingled, the practice prevailed of calling the latter Romans and the former Barbarians. Thus no injury was inflicted on anyone by the name “Barbarian”; on the contrary, those who had never been subject to the Roman yoke regarded it as an honor. Hence Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, enacted laws for the Barbarians, that is, the people of his own nation, and for the Romans, namely the ancient inhabitants of Italy. For further examples, if you have leisure, see Hadrian Valesius, *Rerum Francicarum*, Book 6, about the middle; we have already said something on this subject above (Col. 199, note a).] As far as their will is concerned, they always desire to obscure the splendor and nobility of the Roman name, and they do not wish any Roman at all to remain alive.

And if they are still known to spare their subjects, they spare them in order to make use of their services; for they have never loved any Roman.

If barbarian ferocity were attempting to dispute the faith with us, Arian heresy would at least dispute rationally. But when does a doctrine possess reason that separates God the Son, the Savior, from God the Father?

Why did they act with deceit and slander, and, like a storm-spirit, seek to overturn everything with the tempest of their fury? If an episcopal disputation was necessary, why executions by hanging, why fires, why hooks together with crosses?

Why did the serpentine offspring of the Arians devise such kinds of torture against the innocent as not even Mezentius himself devised? [Note: Mezentius was a king of the Tyrrhenians, notorious for extreme impiety toward gods and men. After being driven from his kingdom by his own people, he joined Turnus in his war against Aeneas and was killed by Aeneas, as Virgil relates in Book 10 of the *Aeneid*. Pliny also mentions Mezentius, king of Etruria, in Book 14, chapter 11, reporting from Varro that he aided the Rutulians against the Latins in exchange for wine.]

The desire born of fury and the cruelty of avarice fought against innocence, in order both to destroy souls and to snatch away property. [Note: Comp. reads *arriperet*, “seize,” instead of *harpagaret*, “snatch away.” Other manuscripts have *avaritia crudelitatis*, “the avarice of cruelty.”]

If a conference was desired, why the plundering of other people’s possessions—not merely those of priests, but also those of all laypeople? Yet those who were stripped rejoiced and received the robbery of their own goods with gladness.

## XIX

Let every age, every sex, and every condition now come forward. Let the whole multitude of the Catholic name come forward, I beg: that multitude carried in a mother’s womb throughout the world, which alone knows how to offer genuine brotherly affection, which learned from Paul its teacher both to rejoice with those who rejoice and to mourn with those who mourn (Romans 12:15).

Let them gather together at the house of our sorrow, and let us pour out rivers of tears with equal eyes, because the cause of our faith is one and the same.

I do not want any heretic to come and grieve with me—one who perhaps desires to add to the pain of my wounds (Psalm 69:27) and rejoices every day at my misfortunes (Psalm 35:26). I do not want, I do not want a stranger; I seek brotherly affection.

I do not want any of the sons of foreigners, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity (Psalm 144:8), because foreign sons have always lied to me; they have grown old and have stumbled away from their paths (Psalm 18:46).

These men say to me every day, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:4), while the people purchased with the precious blood of the Lamb are being afflicted.

Amid their reproaches, I, prepared for scourges (Psalm 38:18), do not cease to sing to the Lord who scourges me: “Remove your scourges from me” (Psalm 39:11), because I have failed—not through the strength of your hand, but through the persecution of Arian heresy.

Let all who travel with me along the narrow road now come, and who, because of the words of God’s lips, guard themselves against difficult paths (Psalm 17:4). Let them see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.

For I have been harvested on the day of the Lord’s fury (Lamentations 1:12). All my enemies opened their mouths against me; they hissed and gnashed their teeth. They said, “We shall devour her. Behold, this is the day we were waiting for; we have found it, we have seen it” (Lamentations 2:16).

Be present, angels of my God, who are never absent from the ministry assigned to you for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of eternal salvation (Hebrews 1:14). See all Africa, formerly supported by the ranks of so many churches, now desolate of them all; adorned with so many orders of priests, now sitting as a widow [the text reads *duam*, apparently corrupt] and cast aside.

[Note: In these words Victor appears to designate bishops and presbyters. In earlier usage the title “priest” (*sacerdos*) was more often attributed to bishops than to presbyters, as can be seen in Cangius’s *Glossary* and frequently in ancient authors. Thus the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* expresses that this holy man was ordained presbyter by Bishop Faustus in these words: “The priest suddenly consecrates him presbyter.” Yet, especially during the earliest centuries of the Church, the title “priest” was also attributed to presbyters in Africa, as can be seen in Cyprian, Letter 67, otherwise 68. Indeed, Optatus, Book 1, says that deacons are established in the third priestly rank, placing bishops first and presbyters second. Among Africans, moreover, primates were often called “elders,” a name they sometimes also applied to other bishops, as Cangius observes in his *Glossary*. In any case, these words and nearly all that follow are taken from the Lamentations of Jeremiah.]

Her priests and elders have perished in deserted places and islands, seeking food to eat, and they do not find it (Lamentations 1:19).

Consider and see that Zion, the city of our God, has become worthless, made like something polluted by menstruation among her enemies (Lamentations 1:11, 17).

The enemy stretched out his hand to all her desirable things, because he saw the nations invading and entering her courts, though you had commanded that they should not enter your church (Lamentations 1:10).

Her roads mourn, because no one comes to the festival. All beauty and delight have departed from her presence (Lamentations 1:4, 6).

Her virgins have learned to walk on harsh paths, and her young men, educated in the halls of monasteries, have gone into captivity among the Moors. While the stones of her sanctuary are scattered [another reading: “the holy stones”], not only at the heads of all the streets (Lamentations 4:1), but also in the squalid places of the mines, speak to our God, her protector.

Trusting that you may plead, say to him that she is afflicted and that her belly is troubled by her weeping (Lamentations 1:20), because she has sat among the nations and found no rest, nor is there anyone to comfort her (Lamentations 1:2–3).

She sought from the Fathers of the East someone who would grieve together with her, and there was no one; someone to comfort her, and she found none. She ate gall in her food and was given vinegar to drink in her thirst (Psalm 69:21–22), imitating the sufferings of her Bridegroom and Lord, who suffered for her precisely so that she might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21).

[Note: Colb. 1 and Mart. read *partibus*, “regions,” which may perhaps be better. For, as we shall say below in the historical commentary, emperors—especially those of the East—often tried to rescue Africa from the hands of the barbarians, but without success until the time of Justinian. We nowhere read that the Africans requested aid from Eastern bishops.]

## XX. The Author Invokes the Saints

Pray, most holy patriarchs, from whose ancestral stock was born she who now labors upon the earth.

Pray, holy prophets, recognizing her whom you formerly sang about in prophetic proclamation when you foretold her affliction.

Be her advocates, apostles, you who, when the Lord ascended in you, raced like swiftest horses throughout the whole world in order to gather her.

And especially you, Peter: why are you silent concerning the sheep and lambs entrusted to you with great care and solicitude by the one great Lord common to all? (John 21:15 ff.)

[Note: Not only the people, but the sheep themselves—that is, the blessed pastors of the peoples—were entrusted to Peter’s care. Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, Book 10, no. 176, testifies that three orders of the faithful were entrusted to Peter: first the lambs, at the second command the little sheep, and finally the sheep. Hence some infer that in the text of John, instead of *probátia* (προβάτια), which appears in the second place, *próbata* (πρόβατα) may once have been written. This reading, however, is supported by no manuscript known to us, as is clear both from the Royal edition and from the Oxford edition. Some interpret those three degrees as peoples, presbyters, and bishops. For this reason, says Ambrose in the same work, no. 175, Peter alone of them all professes faith and is placed before them all. Bernard has more on the care of all entrusted to blessed Peter in Book 2 of *On Consideration*, chapter 8.]

You, holy Paul, teacher of the nations, who preached the Gospel of God from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Romans 15:19), recognize what the Vandals and Arians are doing, and how your children groan in captivity and mourning.

[Note: The words from this point through “all” are absent from the Colbertinus 1, Martini, Fuldensis, Germanicus, and from the printed editions of Surius, Baldi, Bignonius, Orth. and Belfort. Nevertheless, it can be inferred from the ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage that the Africans were devoted to Saint Andrew with exceptional devotion. Among the apostles, that calendar celebrates only Andrew—who is there called both apostle and martyr—together with James, apart perhaps from the chief apostles.]

You, glorious Andrew, brother of Peter and not unlike him in your passion, whose name is interpreted “manly,” because you fought manfully, consider the groaning of the African people. May it not displease you; rather, intercede for us with God.

And all of you, holy apostles, groan together for us.

[Note: Here should be referred what Salvian writes about the Africans in his books *On the Government of God*, especially Books 7 and 8, where he admirably describes and laments their most depraved customs—especially their luxury, their eagerness for spectacles, their contempt for men consecrated to God, and other vices of this kind by which they stirred up God’s vengeance against themselves.]

But we know that it is unworthy of you to pray for us, because what has happened to us was not punishment for testing us, as with the saints, but punishment owed to our evil merits.

Yet pray even now for your wicked children, because Christ also prayed even for his Jewish enemies (Luke 23:34).

Let the chastisements justly inflicted upon us suffice, and let pardon now, at last, be requested for those who are sinning. Let it be said to the destroying angel: “It is enough; now restrain your hand” (1 Chronicles 21:15).

Who does not know that the crimes of our offenses brought these things upon us, since we strayed from God’s commandments and were unwilling to walk in his law (Psalm 78:10)?

But, prostrate, we beg you not to despise your wretched sinners [Note: “Suppliants” may perhaps be read instead. Colb. 1, Port., Germ., Ful., and Chiffl. have “sinners,” so that the sense is: “that you may deign to implore him for us, who raised you humble fishermen to the apostolic summit.”] through him who raised you humble fishermen to the apostolic height.

## XXI

The most wicked Huneric held dominion over the kingdom for seven years and ten months, completing the death deserved by his deeds.

For, having putrefied and boiled with worms, he appears to have been buried not as a body but as parts of a body.

[Note: Lorichius reads “having been consumed by death.” Below, only Comp., Orth., and Lorichius read *putrefactus*, “having putrefied”; the other manuscripts and printed editions have *putrefactum*, “having putrefied,” in the neuter.]

[Note: We have restored this passage with the help of Orth. and Lorichius. In the others no meaning is apparent. It is nevertheless useful to reproduce the readings of the individual manuscripts, so that each person may form his own judgment. The editions of Rhenanus, Chiffl., Surius, Bignonius, and Baldi read as follows: “But that lawgiver and transgressor, formerly coming to them from the heresy of the Donatians, Nicasius, perished by a similar death within a short time.” Colb. 1 has “the transgressor of the law given,” and so forth. Port. has “transgressor.” The other Colbertinus and Mart. have: “the transgressor of the law given, King Ucasius, coming to them from the heresy of the Donatians,” and so forth. Ful. with Germ. likewise has *Donatistarum*, “of the Donatists,” instead of *Donatianorum*. Comp. has “the transgressor of the law given, king of the heresy of the Donatists,” and so forth, as do the others. The third Colbertinus is even more corrupt: “but he, by the law given and the transgressor, king Donatio of them,” and so forth. It should be observed that, instead of *Nicasius*, the manuscripts have *Ucasius* or *Utasius*, which favors our restoration; thus they have *ut asinus*, “like an ass.” In this passage, as we have restored it, Victor alludes to what is related in Jeremiah 22, where the prophet foretells in verse 19 to Jehoiakim, king of Judah, that, because of the crimes in which he was entangled, the burial of an ass would be his burial: he would putrefy and be cast outside the gates of Jerusalem. Victor of Tunnuna describes this ill-omened death of Huneric, and Saint Isidore, following him, relates it in his *Chronicle* under the year 501 of the Spanish era: amid the countless impieties he had inflicted upon Catholics, Huneric ended his life miserably in the eighth year of his reign, with all his internal organs poured out, like Arius his father. Gregory, bishop of Tours, appears to indicate the same thing. In Book 2, chapter 3, of *The Deeds of the Franks*, he reports that this king was seized by a demon and tore himself apart with his own bites: “In that madness,” he says, “he lost his life,” shortly after the sun had appeared entirely foul. This occurred toward the end of the year 484.]

Just as that former king, the transgressor of the law given, was buried like an ass, so this man perished within a short time by a similar death.

# FIRST APPENDIX, OR A SHORT WORK PROBABLY ATTRIBUTED TO VICTOR OF VITA

## Notice

### 1

We append this *Passion of the Blessed Monks* to Victor of Vita’s *History*, following all the manuscript and printed copies that we have been able to inspect, in all of which the two works are joined together.

In most manuscripts this *Passion* is found under the title of the fourth or fifth book of Victor’s *History*, so that there can be no doubt that those who copied these manuscripts were convinced that this *Passion* was the genuine offspring of Victor himself, the bishop who described the African persecution with such a pious and faithful pen.

Indeed, in one Colbertinus manuscript, number 905, this *Passion* is joined to Victor’s *History* without any title or mark of division, so that to readers it appears to be a continuous sequence of one and the same narrative.

They all reproduce the closing formula *Explicit*, which is customarily placed in manuscripts after each individual work, only after this *Passion*, in this or a similar form in the others: “Here ends the history of the African persecution by blessed Victor,” and so forth.

Add to this that in another Colbertinus manuscript, number 3119, in which—as we have already observed in the preface—various readings from another manuscript are represented in the margin, the *Passion* immediately follows Victor’s *History*, bearing this title: “The little book of the same author concerning the passions,” and so forth.

In a third Colbertinus manuscript, number 1746, these words are likewise added in the margin opposite the title: “The martyrdom of the seven monks continues fully, as he promised above,” and so forth.

The manuscript of the Carthusian house of Portes, however, as Peter Francis Chifflet observes, expresses the same thing in the very title of the *Passion*, in these words: “Here begins the Passion of the saints promised above, who suffered at Carthage.”

The place in which Victor promised this account of the *Passion* is none other than the passage inserted in the aforesaid third Colbertinus manuscript, which we shall reproduce in full below, in its proper place, in the notes to Victor of Vita. In the manuscript of Portes, as Chifflet likewise observes, it appears in these words:

“Although in the present work we have not been able to explain the wondrous struggles of these most glorious martyrs, because of the multitude of other innumerable martyrs, nevertheless, at the end of this work of ours, with the Lord’s help, we promise that we shall narrate them.”

This is what those manuscripts contain. Although we do not think that these words were written by Victor, we have nevertheless considered it necessary to inform the reader about them.

### 2

I had almost omitted Ado, archbishop of Vienne, and, after him, Notker, monk of Saint Gall, who likewise attributed the account of the martyrdom of these same holy monks to our Victor. This is clear from the summary of the *Passion* itself, which they excerpted word for word from the very narrative that we present here and attribute to Victor, the African bishop who described the Vandal persecution.

It will be useful to reproduce their words. In their martyrologies, under 17 August, they read as follows:

“In Africa, the birthday of the holy martyrs Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servus and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and Septimius the monks, and Maximus the boy. During the Vandal persecution, by order of the most cruel and impious king Huneric, they were dragged from the territory of the city of Capsa, from the monastery in which they lived, and brought to the city of Carthage.

“There, because of their confession of the Catholic faith and their defense of the one baptism, they were first committed to prison custody, bound with heavy iron weights, and assigned to dark places. There, after they had strengthened the Christian people day and night in constancy of faith, the tyrant, inflamed with fury, ordered a ship to be filled with bundles of wood and all of them to be bound together and burned in the open sea after fire had been placed beneath them.

“When, according to the will of the infamous king and his cruel ministers, wood had been thrust into the fire while their hands were extended and their feet raised, the fire was immediately extinguished by divine command before everyone’s eyes. Whenever the flames were repeatedly rekindled, the balls of fire were extinguished again and again.

“Therefore the tyrant, filled with fury and shame alike, ordered them to be killed with the handles of oars, and so each was put to death like a dog, with his skull crushed.

“Thus, with the Lord crowning them, they completed the glorious course of their contest. Their bodies were thrown into the sea, but at that same hour they were returned unharmed. The Christian people reverently lifted them up, and, with the clergy leading the procession, buried them amid solemn hymns in the monastery adjoining the basilica called Celerina’s.

“Blessed Victor, African bishop, writes in the history of the same Vandal persecution—which he himself endured with the others and set forth in a faithful and distinguished style—that …”

### 3

We have thought it worthwhile to report these matters at greater length as they appear in those authors, so that it may now be clear that as early as the ninth century men devoted to sacred history were persuaded that our Victor was the author of this *Passion of the Holy Monks*.

This could also be confirmed from the forms of expression that frequently occur in the same manner in both works, from the similarity of style, and from other arguments of this kind, which are evident to anyone who pays even a little attention.

But there is no time to pursue these matters more fully, especially since, even if it is not altogether certain whether the *History* and the *Passion* had precisely the same author, no one, as I think, can deny that this work was written by an ancient author—and indeed by Victor, if he himself was not the author, then by someone of equal standing. Anyone can easily detect this by reading it.

### 4

The time at which those holy martyrs received their crowns is sufficiently indicated by the author of the *Passion*, when he reports that they obtained the palm of martyrdom in the seventh year of King Huneric.

Since Huneric died in the year 484, almost at the completion of the eighth year of his reign, their death must be assigned to the preceding year, namely 483.

The authors, however, do not agree sufficiently among themselves about the day on which they completed their martyrdom. If we believe the Acts, they suffered on the sixth day before the Nones of July—that is, on 2 July. More recent and ancient martyrologies alike, however, celebrate their memory on 17 August.

The authority of the *Passion* seems preferable to that of the martyrologies. Perhaps they changed the feast day of these martyrs because of some translation of their sacred relics, as happened frequently elsewhere.

### 5

There is no need to investigate here at greater length the place where they were either apprehended or suffered death. Their *Passion* itself makes clear that they were brought from a monastery in the territory of Capsa in Byzacena, where they were living the monastic life, to Carthage, and that there they were crowned with martyrdom.

On the occasion of the city of Capsa, near which the author of the *Passion* says they lived, it occurred to me that they might perhaps be the very martyrs who are celebrated in the most ancient African calendar as the “Capitan martyrs.”

Certainly the very learned John Mabillon, who extracted this calendar from a manuscript and was the first to publish it, suspects that *Capsitanorum* should be read for *Capitanorum*. He also observes that in Cyprian’s Letter 63, where the printed editions have *Capsensem*, the manuscripts have *Capensem*.

It would indeed seem strange if these holy martyrs, who are certainly known to have been so famous at Carthage, had no place in that calendar, which the same learned man proves to have been compiled around the time of their martyrdom.

Nevertheless, we present this only as a conjecture, since there are also other cities in Africa to which the name “Capitani” might equally be applied. In the African *Notitia* we have Felix, bishop of Carpis, from the proconsular province, not to mention Primus of Capra in Mauretania.

Moreover, Tacape, a well-known city of the province of Tripolitania, is called *Cape* in various editions and manuscripts of Ptolemy, except for one Palestinian manuscript.

It should also be added that our martyrs are said in the Acts to have suffered on 2 July, whereas, as we have said, the common martyrologies commemorate them on 17 August.

But the feast of the Capitani is recorded in the African calendar on neither of these days, but on … the Ides of November.

### 6

Lorichius valued this account of the martyrs’ *Passion* so highly that he judged it should be placed before Victor’s *History*, although in the manuscript he had used it constituted the fourth book of that *History*.

He testifies that he did this chiefly for two reasons. First, these martyrs are mentioned in Victor’s *History*, so that when the reader reaches that point he will already have been informed about their glorious struggles.

Indeed, it is a brief and lucid exposition of the savagery with which the Arians raged against the Catholics. For this reason his other explanation is even more persuasive: he says that he placed it before the *History* so that, after reading even a single page, the reader might immediately receive an example of the steadfastness by which the strong martyrs of Christ, in the history that follows, preferred to meet death rather than be torn away from Christ.

We collated it with as many manuscript and printed copies as we did Victor’s *History*: namely, those in which Victor’s *History* was complete—the three Colbertinus manuscripts and one of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, besides the Carthusian manuscript of Portes.

There would be no point in discussing the ancient printed editions here, since nothing needs to be said beyond what we observed in the preface to Victor.

# PASSION OF LIBERATUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

*(Collated with manuscript copies and ancient editions.)* (C, S)

## I

About to proclaim the triumphs of the blessed martyrs, I ask divine assistance for narrating what was done, so that he who granted them victory in overcoming may extend to me, unworthy and undeserving as I am, however small an ornament of words.

For I shall then be able to indicate what is desired, if they themselves deign to plead with the Lord for me, wretched as I am.

## II. A Severe Persecution in Africa

The seventh year of the most cruel and impious king Huneric was being celebrated, and behold, the ancient enemy, that long-established serpent, brandishing the poisons of a forked tongue [another reading: “a three-pronged tongue,”] used a certain Cyrila, a bishop of the Ariomaniacs, as his agent.

He overturned and gained control of the mind of the bloodthirsty king, persuading him that he could not maintain a peaceful and long-lasting reign unless he destroyed the name of the innocent.

Yet by God’s judgment, not many days later, he was overtaken by a most shameful death and breathed his last, swarming with worms.

With bloodstained mouth he began to attack the entire multitude of Catholics, which throughout the whole African province had multiplied, as was foretold to the patriarch Abraham (Genesis 22:17), like the sand of the sea.

He sought to wound it with the sword of rebaptization and to defile with filthy, black earthly mire that robe of unique and pure baptism which Christ, cleansing it with the wine of his flesh and pressing it in the winepress of the cross, had made white.

The tyrant, accepting the serpent’s suggestion, as he was both yielding [Note: Two Colbertinus manuscripts read *docibilis*, “teachable,” a reading supported by the printed editions of the *Orthodoxographia* and Lorichius, which have *docilis*, “teachable.” The Portes manuscript has *nocibilis*, “harmful.” A little below, for *uno tempore*, “at one time,” some printed editions have *pro tempore*, “for the time being.”] and savage, began at once to stir up all Africa by savage edicts.

First he drove a very numerous and vast crowd of priests and ministers into cruel exile, to distant and remote regions.

For them he ordered as an act of mercy a kind of grain twice sharpened, permitted only to animals to eat, to be distributed—not ground by the skill of the mill, but armored by the husk that still remained around it. [Note: Colb. 1 has *bisactum*. A little below, some copies have *solum*, “only,” instead of *solis*, “of animals.”]

Later, as the madness of his impiety increased, the most cruel ruler ordered even this to be taken away.

A short time afterward he also ordered all the churches at once to be closed with enormous blocks of masonry, their venerable doors having first been condemned.

For he ordered all the monasteries of holy men and women to be given to the pagans—that is, to the Moors—together with their inhabitants.

There was one universal wailing, one wholehearted and complete desire to die for Christ. Rivers of tears flowed together, because the Lord had permitted them to eat the bread of tears and to be given tears to drink in measure—or perhaps without measure.

And although some portion of the dying crows was found leaving the ark, panting over the corpses of the dead, the number of blessed doves in honor of the Trinity is nevertheless greater.

How many noble and excellent men exchanged for heaven the land of their broad and spacious estate [Note: Rhenanus reads this way; others have *Domini*, “of the Lord.” Colb. 1 has “the Lord’s earth.”], and surrendered body and possessions together!

And how many delicate and noble women, contrary to the modesty of nature, were beaten with rods before the watching crowd and, tortured by various torments, carried away trophies of victory [another reading: “trophies of victorious deeds”]!

How many little children, mocking the deadly edicts, despised the world before entering upon its seductive path?

### III. Seven monks arrested

Then seven brothers were arrested, living together in a monastery in that concord which belongs to the Lord’s service—for “it is good and pleasant when brothers dwell together”: namely, Boniface the deacon; Servus the subdeacon; Rusticus the subdeacon; Liberatus the abbot; Rogatus the monk; Septimus the monk; and Maximus the monk. They were, of course, seven brothers of the Maccabean number, whom the one Catholic mother, the Church, had begotten and whom she had healthfully brought forth through the womb of the eternal font. They came from the territory of the city of Capsa, over which the holy Vindemialis, an outstanding priest and faithful bishop of Christ, presided.

[Note: Portus and Notker, in the martyrology, have *Servius*; the Orthodox edition, with Lorichius, has *Serus*. And below, for *Septimus*, Colbert 1 and Portus, with Notker, have *Septiminus*. Ado, however, reads *Septimius*. Further, in listing these martyrs’ names, Liberatus is named after those initiated into sacred orders, out of reverence for his rank. It was later established that abbots should be distinguished by sacred orders. Observe likewise that those distinguished by some rank are here designated, with the name *monk* omitted, by the title of their dignity—an ancient custom. Thus Saint Jerome, the Venerable Bede, and other holy men are commonly called merely priests, though they are known truly to have been monks. Hence Gennadius, ch. 59: “Leporius, still a monk, later a priest,” etc.]

[Note: This city was situated in Byzacena. Concerning it, and concerning Vindemialis, that most blessed bishop, see further the notes on the *Notitia*, below, among the bishops of Byzacena, no. 60 (col. 325).]

When they had been brought to the city of Carthage, the serpent first tried to hiss at them with seductive blandishments, promising perishable honors and riches of immense pleasures, as well as the king’s friendship and many other things with which the devil, hunting foolish souls, commonly ensnares them in the birdlime of the world. But Christ’s soldiers rejected all these things as though they were contagions, crying out with one voice:

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism. Nor, with the Lord’s help, can what was once commanded in the holy Gospel be repeated among us: ‘He who has been washed once has no need to wash again, because he is wholly clean.’ Do what you wish; inflict punishments upon our bodies. It is better to endure temporal punishments for a little while than to await and undergo eternal torments. Keep what you promise, together with the riches that will soon perish with you. But no one will be able to tear from the doorposts of our foreheads what the artisan Trinity has deigned to inscribe in the one baptism.”

[Note: Colbert 1, Lorichius, and the Orthodox edition have *whom he has united in one*, etc. Others have *what … the Trinity has deigned*, etc. Some have *who* instead of *what*.]

### IV. They are thrust into prison

Why say more? While they were divinely fortified with such steadfastness, they were ordered to be handed over to prison custody and, loaded with the weights of iron, were assigned to dark places where no mercy of gentleness smiled upon them.

[Note: Several manuscripts have *constricted*. Ado likewise reads *constricted*, and in his abridgment of this Passion has: “constricted by cruel iron weights,” etc.]

But the people of that city, always faithful in the Lord, gave a gift to the jailers and visited Christ’s martyrs day and night. They were so strengthened by their instruction and by the power of faith that they themselves also desired to endure such things with complete joy for Christ’s name and readily to offer their necks to the executioner.

This came to the tyrant’s ears. Inflamed with the drunkenness of fury, he ordered them to be subjected to unheard-of punishments and loaded with heavier chains. He commanded a ship to be filled with bundles of dry wood and, after all had been bound within it, ordered fire to be placed underneath and them all to be burned in the middle of the sea.

### V. Their courage

When they had been brought out of custody, the multitude of God’s people led the warriors of the Trinity, like innocent lambs to sacrifice, to the place of execution. They regarded the rigid weights of their chains as necklaces, because those bonds were not fetters but ornaments.

Thus they advanced confidently toward punishment, as though hastening to a banquet, singing to the Lord with one voice throughout the circuits of the streets:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. This is for us a day of celebration, more festive than every solemnity. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation, when for the faith of the Lord our God we endure the punishment prepared for us, lest we lose the garment of the faith we have acquired.”

The people also cried out publicly:

“Do not fear, O people of God, and do not dread the threats and terrors of present tribulations. Rather, let us die for Christ, just as he died for us, redeeming us by the price of his saving blood.”

[Note: Others have: “But the people also cried out publicly.”]

[Note: Lorichius has: “by the saving price of precious blood.”]

Yet with vehement effort the authors of these evils wished to separate from the company of the saints one who seemed to be a little child among them, named Maximus. They said:

“Little boy, why are you hastening to your death? Leave them; they are insane. Listen to our advice, so that you may find a remedy for life and enter the palace of so great a king.”

Then he, though a child in age yet mature with the wisdom of an old man, cried out:

“No one separates me from my holy father, Liberatus the abbot, and from my brothers, who raised me in the monastery. With them I have lived in the fear of God; with them I desire to receive martyrdom, and with them I believe that I shall find future glory. Do not suppose that you can seduce my childhood. The Lord wished us seven to be gathered together; together he will deign to crown us all with one martyrdom. Just as none of that sevenfold number of blessed Maccabees could perish, so too the sevenfold number of our community will suffer no loss.

“For if I deny him, he too will deny me, for he himself said: ‘Whoever denies me before human beings, I too will deny before my Father who is in heaven; and whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven.’”

### VI. They attain the palm

They were therefore hurried to the naval execution, according to the will of the impious king and his cruel ministers. With hands and feet extended, they are said to have been nailed rather than bound.

[Note: Colbert 1, with Chiffletius, has *they are said to have been nailed rather than bound*. Lorichius, with the Orthodox edition, has *they are said to have been raised rather than bound*. Ado has: “with hands extended and feet raised, to pieces of wood,” etc.]

When fire had been applied to the wood, it was immediately extinguished by divine command before the eyes of all. Though it was repeatedly renewed with fuel, again and again the pyre was extinguished by a mass of flames.

[Note: Two Colbert manuscripts, with Martinus, have: “the pyres were extinguished by a mass of flames.” Lorichius and the Orthodox edition have: “fiery masses of flame.” Chiffletius and others have: “the masses of flame were extinguished”; Ado has the same.]

When the tyrant was thereby filled at once with still greater fury and shame, he ordered them to be killed with the bars of oars and thus, one by one, to be extinguished like dogs with their brains crushed. By this kind of death they happily returned their indebted spirits to the Lord. They did not shrink from being killed by blows of wood, since all their hope had always been in the Wood.

But when their venerable bodies were thrown into the sea, the deep, contrary to the nature of the waters, immediately hastened at that very hour to return the unharmed bodies to the shore. It did not dare, as is customary, to keep them in the depths for three days, lest it should prove wholly disobedient to the Lord’s command. Even the tyrant himself, although unrepentant, is said to have been terrified by this kind of miracle.

The rejoicing multitude carefully committed the bodies of the holy martyrs to burial, preceded by the venerable clergy of the Church of Carthage. The deacons Salutaris and Muritta were also present there as bearers of the relics; they had already become confessors for the third time through their preaching.

### VII. Burial

The relics of the blessed saints were therefore buried with solemn hymns in the monastery of Bigua, adjoining the basilica called Celerina’s.

[Note: Ado likewise has *Bigua* in his martyrologies. Colbert 2, Portus, Lorichius, and the Orthodox edition, however, do not have *Bigua*; instead of *adjoining*, two Colbert manuscripts, Portus, and Martinus, with Bignius, Rhenanus, and Balduinus, have *immediately*. Victor likewise mentions the basilica of Celerina in book I, no. 3; concerning it, see note 10 on the same author above, col. …]

And thus, in the confession of the Trinity, the most blessed martyrs suffered and, with the Lord crowning them, completed the glorious course of their contest. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SECOND APPENDIX, OR SHORT WORKS WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO VICTOR OF VITA

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING HOMILY

The following homily on the blessed martyr Cyprian is found in two ancient manuscript codices, one belonging to the Colbert Library and the other to the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, after the Passion of the seven monks related by us. It seemed appropriate to publish it here as well. Although it may not be by our Victor, it belongs to his period and is by no means unworthy of being attributed to him.

The Africans always honored Cyprian with singular devotion. Among them the feast of this holy martyr was so celebrated that the day on which it was commemorated was simply called “the Cyprian day,” as Procopius testifies in book I of *The Vandalic War*. The sailors, as the same author states, also transferred this name to the storms that customarily arose every year around that time.

Among all the monstrous crimes committed by the Vandals after the capture of Carthage, the Catholics especially abhorred the fact that, under the rule of Huneric, the Arians had invaded the magnificent church constructed on the seashore in honor of this holy martyr. After driving out the Catholic priests, they performed their sacred rites there according to their abominable practice.

### 2

The adherents of the true faith bore this with the greatest distress. According to what Procopius had learned from public report—and what he relates in book II of *The Vandalic War*—the holy Cyprian repeatedly appeared at night in visions to those who steadfastly persevered in the orthodox faith, in order to exhort them to patience. He promised that at last, and that shortly, he would avenge himself against the enemies of the faith.

During this period, when the persecution was raging most violently, the author of the present homily delivered his discourse, as will become clear from its reading. Soon afterward the outcome of events confirmed the truth of the blessed martyr’s promises, as Procopius himself writes; he had been present at the events.

For when Belisarius, during the reign of Justinian, had landed in Africa around the time of the holy martyr’s feast, he proceeded directly to Carthage. On the very eve of Cyprian’s feast, the Arians who had adorned the temple dedicated to him with all the splendor they could command, upon hearing of the slaughter of the Vandals, immediately took up mourning. Thus the Catholics recovered the church of the blessed martyr and celebrated his feast with immense joy.

But, God willing, we shall discuss this matter more fully below in chapter 12 of our historical Commentary.

# HOMILY ON SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP AND MARTYR

### I

Today the annual feast of blessed Cyprian compels us to deliver our customary discourse. For who could remain silent about the virtues of so great a martyr, conceal his glory, or fail to recount his merits—unless perhaps those who now feel the grief of the loss of his own episcopal see?

He does not celebrate in heaven the triumphs of his victories and possess the crowns of his triumphs and the heavenly insignia in such a way that he does not also lament the great wound of the mangled people, the dispersed clergy, the banished priesthood, lost chastity, violated modesty, polluted sanctuary, and profaned altar, together with the captivity of his own inmost being.

He is the one who grieves over the fallen and the ruin of his own people with such feeling, saying:

[Note: Thus Cyprian speaks at the beginning of his book *On the Lapsed*: “Among the fallen brethren, feeling cast me down as well.”]

“And feeling cast us down together with our fallen brethren.”

[Note: Colbert reads *pariens* (“bringing forth”) for *parens* (“father”).]

The bishop seeks his people, the shepherd his flock, the father his country, and the martyr the faith—not without great sorrow. Would that the barbarian might be extinguished, since a citizen is regarded as extinguished; and would that the faithless man might not hold the altars from which the faithful man is mourned as excluded. Or at least the very solitude of the martyrs might in some measure console him, for whom one who ought to obey would surely be lacking, if the devout man did not taunt him and the sacrilegious mocker did not press upon him.

We have said this, brothers, to show that the martyr suffers again, feels tortures again, and once more endures executioners on behalf of all—he who, after so many palms of victory, had already been secure concerning himself and his own affairs. Once he was beheaded; now he is punished daily in his own members. He is now bound by the griefs of those whose service once brought him joy.

### II

But amid all these things, brothers, let us raise ourselves toward the Lord, we who lie fallen through ourselves; let us not be destroyed by the misfortune of despair, since we have been saved by the remedies of hope through Christ who gives life.

Blessed Cyprian is free in God and with God, though he is held captive in us; he reigns in the heights, though on earth he appears delivered over to his enemies. He is present to himself and is not absent from us. Before the just Judge he stands as a just patron for sinners; before the merciful King the innocent advocate pleads.

[Note: The Saint-Martin manuscript has *existit* (“stands”); Colbert has “before a merciful judge or king.”]

He says to the Lord:

“Lord, why have you delivered your house to adversaries, your inheritance to enemies? Why have you given holy things to the profane, clean things to the polluted, and lambs to wolves? Why do you hand over the flock to beasts?”

As a shepherd he boldly calls the Prince of shepherds to account. “Why,” he asks, “has the King subjected such a devoted army to hostile power?” As an energetic commander, he makes a fitting inquiry. “Why has he delivered the faithful to the faithless?” The priest, proved in martyrdom, cries out.

He also speaks of the causes concerning his own body:

“Lord, why have you allowed the members that confessed you so faithfully to be taken captive? Why have you left the witness of blood, whom you had raised to such great honor, in such great contempt? Finally, concerning us and concerning what belongs to us—for all things are yours—do as you will. Where is your name? Where is your glory? Where is your power? By saying these things, the nations that blasphemed you have invaded us as they invaded you.

“Rise up: why do you sleep, Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever. Restore your glory to yourself; restore your land to your own people; restore my bones to me, so that, when you triumph, your enemies may perish and we may rejoice in our own places and in our proper order.”

### III

The holy Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, is also present. Having suffered on this same day in such a cause, he does not abandon his companion or desert his colleague in such a petition.

# NOTICE ON THE AFRICAN LIST

### 1

The list of Catholic bishops who had gathered at Carthage by order of Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals, in order to give an account of their faith, under the title *List of the Provinces and Cities of Africa*, was first published from an ancient manuscript of the cathedral church of Laon by the illustrious priest Jacques Sirmond of the Society of Jesus, renowned for his study of sacred antiquity and his immense learning.

Since this list was appended in that codex to the profession of faith that constitutes book III of Victor of Vita’s *History*, Pierre-François Chifflet, also of the same Society, took the opportunity to insert it in its entirety into the new edition of this author that he prepared. As he himself says in chapter 2 of his *Elucidations on Victor*, he was led to do this chiefly for three reasons.

First, as we have already said, this list was appended in the Laon manuscript to the profession of faith found in Victor. Second, it did not merely list the names of bishops or cities without comment; its compiler also recorded what happened to each bishop—who perished on the journey, who remained, who escaped, and other matters of this kind—which ought to have been collected by the person who undertook to write a complete history of the persecution. Finally, Abraham Ortelius, who frequently cites this list from a manuscript in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, repeatedly attributes it to Victor of Utica.

### 2

Although we readily acknowledge that the African list, as edited by Sirmond and preserved in the Laon manuscript, belongs to the history of the Vandalic persecution, we do not think it follows immediately that Victor adopted it, especially since it is certain that other documents relating to the same subject existed which this author nevertheless did not insert into his *History*.
