He more than once admits that he omitted many distinguished deeds of martyrs and confessors.

Gregory of Tours also praises several Passions of those same martyrs in book II of his *History of the Franks*, although Victor does not possess them. I say nothing of the distinguished letter of Eugenius of Carthage, preserved for us by the same Gregory. Eugenius wrote it to his people as he was setting out into exile, to exhort them to persevere steadfastly in the faith; nothing could therefore have been more relevant to the history of the Vandalic persecution. Yet Victor omitted it. We cannot divine his reason, just as we are not obliged to account for other matters that depend upon human free will.

It is enough for us to publish this list separately from Victor’s *History*, since it is not inserted into Victor’s *History* in any manuscript codex at all, at least among those known to us so far.

Nor are we greatly influenced by the fact that Abraham Ortelius repeatedly cited this list under the name of Victor of Utica. It is likely that in Haller’s codex, from which Ortelius obtained it, the list was appended to the profession of faith, as in the Laon codex. When Ortelius discovered that this profession formed part of Victor’s *History*, he called the entire item a “Fragment of Victor.” In the same way he called Victor “of Utica,” since he had read him so named in printed editions.

### 3

Whatever the truth may be in this matter—which does not seem to me especially important—we have followed the manuscript codices and the advice of learned men. We were much more concerned to prepare a careful and accurate edition of so valuable a monument than to determine whether Victor had actually inserted it into his *History*.

Therefore, when I had set out for Campania several years ago and was passing through Laon, I was glad to find this suitable opportunity to inspect the manuscript codex itself. The most courteous canons of the distinguished church of that city granted me access to it. I carefully compared Sirmond’s edition with the manuscript, which is of excellent quality and had been copied with a diligent and accurate hand at least eight hundred years ago, and I recorded various readings, which we shall report below in the notes.

To ensure that nothing within my power was left undone, I also examined Abraham Ortelius’s *Geographical Thesaurus*, revised and enlarged by him at Antwerp in 1596. I collected the names of the African cities that are repeatedly cited in that edition from the manuscript *Fragment of Victor of Utica*. Comparing them with the list published by Sirmond, I determined where the two codices agreed or differed. I shall inform the reader of these matters in their proper place.

We frequently cite that fragment under the name of Haller’s codex because Ortelius repeatedly states that he received it from the distinguished Louis Haller of Harlesteyn, a most devoted student of sacred antiquity.

### 4

One matter remains of which I wish to inform the reader before the list is presented. After most of the names of the bishops recorded in this list, Sirmond placed the letters *per.* In the manuscript codex, however, the form is *prbt.*, or in some places *pbr.*, so that in these words a small horizontal stroke generally cuts the letter *b* through the middle.

The manuscript codex itself of Laon supports Sirmond’s restoration—or rather his conjecture. After listing separately the names of all the confessors, it explains their total number and then indicates how many of them perished, how many remained, and how many went into exile. It is therefore probable that the letters occurring after some bishops’ names signify nothing other than that these men, distinguished from the others by this abbreviation, perished on the way. Likewise, those who were deported to Corsica or escaped by flight are designated by the words *Corsica* or *fug.*

In addition, it is not probable that these letters designate priests, as I once suspected. The priests had not been ordered to come to that assembly; nor would so many have appeared to represent their bishops, and the tyrant would not have tolerated this with impunity. Moreover, the abbreviation sometimes occurs even after the names of men listed earlier.

Although all these considerations might have induced Sirmond to change the manuscript reading, it nevertheless seemed better to present the matter as it appears in the manuscript, leaving each person free to judge it as he wishes.

Indeed, I have more than once found that the same letters designated priests in several manuscripts. This is especially to be observed in manuscript Colbert 3281, written approximately eight hundred years ago, and in another manuscript of the same library, no. 401, written approximately six hundred years ago, although in the latter the word *presbyter* is more often written with the letters *prbr.*

It would be superfluous to say more about this matter. Perhaps one day a codex will appear through which this difficulty can be resolved.

### 5

Finally, the number of bishops repeated in summary at the end of the list does not agree with the number found by enumerating the same bishops individually. Here too we have preserved the manuscript reading, since it is possible that some names have fallen out of the list.

To prevent this discrepancy from troubling anyone—one number appearing in the individual enumeration and another in the total—we have retained the manuscript reading while placing Sirmond’s restorations in brackets. We have likewise prefixed to this monument the title assigned to it by the same learned man, namely *List of the Provinces*, etc., before the title found in the manuscript, *Here begin the names*, etc.

NOTES AND OBSERVATIONS ON THE DESCRIPTION OF THE AFRICAN CHURCH.

[Col. 0275C] 99 It did not seem sufficient to compare with manuscript codices the Description of the African Church that we published above, unless it were also elucidated by notes and observations, lest we present readers with nothing but the bare names of cities and towns. I therefore thought that I would do something welcome to everyone if I brought together here whatever I had been able to gather from ancient records, both sacred and secular, for the illustration of the sacred geography of Africa. I undertook this labor all the more willingly because no one had hitherto attempted such a work, although the African Description has been reprinted not merely once or twice but repeatedly since it first saw the light, after being drawn from obscurity by the most learned man Jacques Sirmond. The title of the book that the distinguished Emmanuel Schelestratus published some years ago under the name of *The African Church* had indeed led one to hope for this; but he turned his thoughts elsewhere and seems to have taken no care to elucidate the episcopal cities of Africa.

Although I had not sufficiently persuaded myself, before attempting the work, that the undertaking was difficult and beyond my strength, I certainly experienced this fully in the course of the work itself. I would therefore have abandoned the labor I had begun without hesitation, had not the commentaries of learned men [Col. 0276C] who had written about African cities lightened the burden. And since some advantage to the republic of letters always arises from disagreements among learned men, I do not deny that this happened to me through the controversy that arose between the learned Jesuit priest Jean Garnier and [Col. 0276D] Henri de Noris of the Augustinian order, recently appointed by the most blessed Pope Innocent XII prefect of the Vatican Library. For on this occasion, while Noris was subjecting Garnier’s notes on the inscriptions of the synodal letters—then numbered 90 and 91 among the Augustinian works, but now numbered 175 and 176 in the Benedictine edition—to severe scrutiny, he explained and exposed, with a pen no less learned than subtle, many matters concerning African cities that had previously been obscure and wrapped in much confusion. No less useful to me were the learned observations and notes with which the distinguished Étienne Baluze illuminated the Carthaginian Collation in the first volume of the new Collection of Councils that he edited. Other learned men who have assisted me I shall not, when a suitable opportunity arises, allow to pass without an expression of gratitude, but shall acknowledge them in their proper places.

For the rest, I wish to warn the reader that, whenever I may seem to indulge conjectures more than is appropriate, I have always taken particular care [Col. 0277A] to represent the names of cities, towns, and indeed of the persons themselves exactly as they are found in manuscript codices, or at least in printed editions. I have judged that by changing a single little letter matters can sometimes be so confused that one city is transferred from one province to another, or one city is fabricated from two, or one is divided into two, with other inconveniences of the same kind. We cannot deny that even learned men have sometimes, through carelessness, stumbled into such pitfalls. Thus, to pass over other examples, our Victor, transformed from a bishop of Vitensis, became a bishop of Utica and was transferred from the province of Byzacena to the Proconsular province; and from perhaps a humble village or town over which he presided, he was elevated to the seat of a celebrated Roman colony. Certainly, although this caution must be exercised in all matters, it must be observed with special scrupulousness in describing African cities, since, as Pliny says at the beginning of Book Five, the names of the peoples and towns of Africa are for the most part unpronounceable except in their own languages; and from similarity of pronunciation, [Col. 0277B] which occurs in a foreign language, scarcely anything certain—or hardly anything at all—can be extracted.

IN THE SIXTH YEAR. So the manuscript codex of the church of Laon reads, but incorrectly. For it is certain from Victor and the other ancient writers that the edict for the assembly of the bishops, to be held at Carthage in February of the following year, was issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June in the seventh year of Huneric’s reign. Chifflet therefore rightly emended *eighth* for *sixth*.

CONCERNING THE PROCONSULAR PROVINCE.

1. EUGENIUS OF CARTHAGE, OF TAMALLUM. You will find much about Eugenius, that most illustrious confessor of Christ, in Book II and the following books of Victor of Vita, and still more below in our historical Commentary, chapter 8. As for Carthage, which Solinus in chapter 30 of the *Polyhistor* calls the second glory of the world after Rome, it would be superfluous to gather further material. For, to use Sallust’s words in his book on the Jugurthine War, “I think it better to keep silent about Carthage than to say too little.” [Col. 0277C] Our Victor briefly describes its destruction in Book I; we shall speak more fully of it in our Commentary, chapter 5. Victor describes the location of the place called Tamallum, to which Eugenius was driven into exile, in Book V, no. 2; in the next item he indicates that it was the city of Tamallum, a city of which we shall treat more fully below, where we discuss the bishop of Tamallum among the Byzacenians, no. 55.

2. FELIX OF ABARIS. He himself seems to be the Felix whom Victor, in Book II, no. 8, calls Felix of Abbir; on that passage we made further observations about the city of Abbir in note 79 (above, col. 209, n. c). The same Victor nevertheless mentions a province of Abaris in Book I, no. 4, and indeed one distinct from the Proconsular province. For there it is said that Gaiseric retained Abaris and other provinces for himself, while leaving Zeugitana, or the Proconsular province, to his army. Pliny, in Book XVI, chapter 36, praises the fishing reed of Abaris in Africa as superior to all the others. Ortelius cites Castellum Aboritanum from Victor of Utica, as he says; but since this author mentions a city of Abaris from the same Victor, he does not by these expressions necessarily designate one and the same place. It is nevertheless not improbable that *Aboritanus* here in the *Notitia* should be read for *Abaritanus*. We certainly have in Africa the city of Abora, which unquestionably belonged to the Proconsular province, as is clear from the synodal letter of the bishops of that province to Paul, bishop of Constantinople. This letter was read at the Lateran Council against the Monothelites under Saint Martin, in action, or session, 2. Felix, bishop of the holy church of Abora, subscribed it. Moreover, at the Carthaginian Collation held in 411 in the case of the Donatists, in Inquiry 1, chapter 133, Trifolius, a Catholic bishop of Abora, was present. Finally, Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, mentions the town of Abora.

3. PAULUS OF SINNARA. This bishop is praised by Victor in Book I, no. 9, where his see is written differently in different codices, as we observed in note 30 (Col. [Col. 0278A] 194, n. [Note: [Col. 0194C] So Colb. 2, together with Rhenanus and the other printed editions. But Mart. and Colb. 1 have *Sitinaritanus*. Edition 2 has *Sitmaritanus*. The truth of our reading is confirmed by the African *Notitia*, where, among the bishops of the Proconsular province, no. 3, occurs Paulus *Sinnarensis*, as we restored it from the Laon codex. See the notes on that place in the *Notitia*.]). We restored *Sinnarensis* from the Laon codex, since the other printed editions had *Sinuarensis*. Our reading is confirmed by the Fifth Ecumenical Council, to which Victor, bishop of the municipality of Sinna in the Proconsular province, subscribed. The reading may incline either way in the passage found in the Carthaginian Collation, where in chapter 133, among the Catholic bishops, is listed Stephanus, bishop of the people of Sinnuara. Some printed editions nevertheless have *Simuaritensis*, and shortly afterward *Ad Sinuar*. Although an old codex, as the learned Étienne Baluze testifies, has *Ad Sinnar*; concerning this expression, see below among the cities of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 115.

4. PIENSIS. I was unable to find this place in Ortelius from Haller’s codex. Perhaps *Picensis* should be read. For Picus is mentioned in the Peutinger Tables. Among the bishops of the Proconsular province who subscribed the synodal letter mentioned above, no. 21, there is also Felix, bishop of Pariensis; should he be referred here? Polybius mentions a place called Prion, where Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, defeated and captured Spendius and the other rebels.

5. HIPPAZARITENSIS. It is astonishing how much authors vary in writing the name of this word—not only different authors, but sometimes one and the same author. In Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 3, it is called Ἵππον Διάῥῤυτος, *Hippon Diarrhytus*; Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, observes that the Greeks called the city by this name because of its irrigating waters. Pomponius Mela designates it by the same surname in Book I of *The Geographical Description of the World*, chapter 7; and rightly so, as Vossius proves in his notes on this passage of Pomponius, against Salmasius, who dared to deny it contrary to the testimony of nearly all writers. Antoninus, moreover, calls the same city Hippozarritus, and the Peutinger Tables call it *Ipponte Diarito*. In the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, whom our Dom Placidus Porcheron published from a manuscript of the Royal Library, it is called *Hippone Zareston* in Book III, no. 6, and *Yppone Zarestum* in Book V, no. 5. Finally, Polybius frequently mentions in Book III of his *Histories* the cities of the Uticans and Hippacritans as neighboring Carthage.

[Col. 0278C] Ecclesiastical records vary no less than secular ones. In the Carthaginian Council under Saint Cyprian, concerning the rebaptism of heretics, no. 72, the martyr Peter of Hippo Diarrhytus gave his judgment. Augustine answers his objection in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 35, where this city is designated by the same name, although in several printed editions, and in all the manuscripts, as our editors observed in the new edition of this saint’s works, it appears as *Hippo Zaritus*. Augustine himself, however, in Book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 8, calls it Hippo Diarrhytus. The synodal letter of the Proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council was subscribed by Donatus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy church of Hippozaritus. A bishop of the same place on the Donatist side, named Victor, is called simply “bishop of Hippo” in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 133, where he is appointed one of the keepers of the documents. [Col. 0278C] But in chapter 179 he is called “bishop of Hippo of the Diarryti”; and in chapter 139 he had already been called the opponent of Florentinus, bishop of the Catholic church of Hippo Zaritus—or, as the distinguished Étienne Baluze emends it, “of the Hipponians of Zaritus.”

From the varying ways in which this name is written by ancient authors, it is entirely clear—as learned men have already observed more than once—that they used the letters *z* and *d*, or *di*, interchangeably. If necessary, this could easily be demonstrated by numerous examples. On this matter, if you wish, consult Justellus on chapter 78 of the *Code of the African Church*; Noris in Book II, chapter 3, of his *Pelagian History*, and in his observations against Garnier’s notes; Baluze throughout his notes on the Carthaginian Collation, especially on chapter 139, in volume I of the *New Collection of Councils*, and on chapter 6 of Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*; Jean Hardouin in his notes on Pliny; Garnier, Chifflet, and the other authors whom it is not possible to list more fully here.

Finally, although no one is unaware that there was another Hippo, surnamed *Regius*, [Col. 0279A] over which Augustine presided, it will nevertheless not be useless to observe here that Strabo, in Book XVII, called both of these cities Hippo Regius. Solinus, in chapter 30 of the *Polyhistor*, speaks of both: “Hippo, afterward called Regius, and the other Hippo, called Diarrhytus because of the strait flowing between them, were founded by Greek knights as very famous towns.”

6. GUNELENSIS. Haller’s codex, as cited by Ortelius, has *Gunelmensis*; under either name the city is equally unknown to me.

7. UZIALENSIS. So both manuscript codices read. The printed editions, however, have *Uzalensis*, and better so. Evodius, bishop of Uzala, is famous in Augustine’s Letter 33 and elsewhere throughout; nearly all the sacred records of that age praise him. Baluze is surprised that this man was not listed among the other bishops who attended the Carthaginian Collation in 411, since, on the other hand, Felix, bishop of the same city, appears among the Donatists in chapter 204. Baluze himself restored the name of Evodius, which had been corrupted in Inquiry 3, chapter 141, [Col. 0279B] of the cited Collation, from a manuscript codex; previously it had read *Emaedio*, or *Ennodio*. Mustulus, likewise bishop of Uzala, subscribed the Carthaginian Council under Boniface. Augustine indicates the location of Uza in Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, where he testifies that the city was near the colony of Utica. Pliny calls it the Latin town of Uza in Book V, chapter 4.

8. MEMBROSITANUS. Haller’s codex, as cited by Ortelius, has *Membresitanus*. Memblosa and Membresa—or rather Membressa—are two cities in Africa bearing nearly the same name but distinct from one another, as Henri de Noris conclusively proves against Garnier in his remarks on Garnier’s notes on Marius Mercator.

In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 133, Theasius, bishop of the people of Memblosa, is mentioned; he testified that the unity of the Catholic Church existed among his people. A little earlier, Gennadius, Catholic bishop of the people of Membressa, had been listed, and in chapter 198 Restitutus is set against him on behalf of Donatus. I admit that in the common editions this Restitutus is called bishop of the people of Simingis; but this is erroneous, as the learned Baluze observed. At that point he inserted several words within brackets in order to restore two Restituti, who had been mistakenly merged into one by copyists: one a Donatist, the opponent of Gennadius of Membressa, and the other a Catholic bishop of Simingis.

That first Restitutus is none other than the Restitutus who, when the schism among the Donatists was raging, had been ordained in the place of Salvius of Membressa, as Augustine relates in Letter 108 of the new edition. That Salvius had been condemned in the famous Council of Bagai in 394; Augustine frequently discusses him in his books against the Donatists, where he describes his various fortunes.

The anonymous geographer of Ravenna, unless I am mistaken, mentions both cities—Membressa and Memblosa. In Book III, no. 3, he has *Membrisca*, and in the following number *Membrone*. I believe these are also *Membrissa* [Col. 0279D] and *Membione* in the Peutinger Tables.

Now, since Bonifacius, who is mentioned here in the *Notitia*, is called *Membrositanus* in the Laon codex and in the printed editions—a term that can be derived both from Memblosa and from Membresa, since in either case only a single letter must be changed—it remains uncertain which of the two cities that bishop governed. Baluze, in his notes on chapter 133 of the Carthaginian Collation, counts Gennadius of Membressa and, shortly afterward, Theasius of Memblosa among the bishops of the Proconsular province, on the basis, as he says, of the African *Notitia*. But since in the *Notitia* itself only one bishop of Membrositanus occurs, on this argument only one of the two ought to be assigned to the Proconsular province, although I do not deny that both cities belonged to that province.

[Col. 0280A] If, however, the sheets that Ortelius received from Haller’s codex were accurately transcribed, and if they contain *Membresitanus*, I should rather believe that Bonifacius was bishop of Membressa than of Memblosa. Nor does it count against this that some have thought Membressa belonged to Numidia, since we have Victor, bishop of the church of Membressa, who subscribed the aforementioned synodal letter among the bishops of the Proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, action 2; and Paschasius, likewise bishop of Membressa, attended the Carthaginian Council under Boniface in 525.

Moreover, Membresa, written with a single *s* as in Haller’s codex, occurs in the Carthaginian Council under Saint Cyprian, at which, concerning the rebaptism of heretics, the confessor Lucius of Membresa delivered his judgment. Procopius mentions the same city, which he calls Membrissa, in Book II of *The Vandalic War*, where he writes that it lay 350 stadia from Carthage. That it was situated on the boundaries of Numidia and the Proconsular province is clear from Antoninus.

9. BENEVENTENSIS. So the Laon manuscript codex reads, together with the common editions. [Col. 0280B] Haller’s codex, however, as cited by Ortelius, has *Benentensis*. Hence the learned Baluze, in his notes on chapter 128 of the Carthaginian Collation, suspects that the city of Beneventum, or Benentum, mentioned here in the *Notitia*, is the very city over which Adeodatus, bishop of the people of Bencenna, presided, listed among the Catholic bishops in the cited chapter of the Collation.

Garnier had already judged that *Bencennensis* should be read for *Beneventensis*; but Henri de Noris did not accept this opinion and for that reason reproved Garnier in his censure of Garnier’s notes on the inscription of the synodal letter of the Carthaginian Council. Noris maintains that Bencenna and Beneventum were two entirely different cities in Africa: the former, he says, is known from the Carthaginian Collation; the latter is mentioned not only in the *Notitia* but also in the celebrated Council of Arles held in 414. At that synod, among the other bishops who had come from Africa with Caecilianus of Carthage, Anastasius, bishop [Col. 0280C] of the city of Beneventum, subscribed.

10. UTIMMIRENSIS. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 126, Severus, bishop of the people of Utimara, is mentioned: 104 should he be referred here? The frequently cited Baluze, moreover, believes that *Utimminensis* should be read for *Utimmirensis*; he thinks that Octavius, bishop of the people of Utimma, mentioned in chapter 133 of the Collation, presided over this place. Haller’s codex supports this opinion, since, as Ortelius observed, it reads *Utimiensis* for *Utimmirensis*.

But perhaps the learned man did not notice that the city of Utimmira mentioned here in the *Notitia* had already been joined by him to Utmensis. For in chapter 126 of the Collation, where previously *Timianus, bishop of the people of Utina*, had been read, together with Felix, his opponent, he restored *Utmensis* for *Utina*, because below, in chapter 133, Isaac, Catholic bishop of Utina, was listed together with Felicianus the Donatist. In his notes on this passage he concludes that Utma belonged to the Proconsular province, because the bishop called *Utimmirensis* in the common *Notitia* appears as *Utimiensis* in Haller’s codex, which Ortelius used.

But since he expressed this almost as a matter of doubt, he seems to have intended nothing more than to put his conjectures before the public, so that anyone might afterward embrace whichever seemed better. Leo Allatius and Henri de Noris, for their part, admit two cities called Utina in Africa, one of which must be written with aspiration as *Uthina*. Furthermore, the older editions of the Collation call Octavius bishop of the people not of Utimma but of *Utinuna*; and in chapter 198 Bonifacius, his opponent on behalf of Donatus, is called bishop of Utunna. [Col. 0280D] Nevertheless, Baluze’s reading, which has *Utimmensis*, seems preferable.

11. PUPPITANUS. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 126, Pannonius, bishop of the people of Puppita, was listed among the Catholic Fathers. Fortunatus, bishop of the people of Puppitana, also attended the Carthaginian Council held under Boniface in 525. [Col. 0281A] Gulosus, bishop of Puppita, was the first of all to subscribe the synodal letter of the Proconsular bishops, already mentioned several times. Thus, in most other councils and ecclesiastical records, one repeatedly encounters a bishop of Puppita or the church of Puppita.

Antoninus, however, calls this city Putput in his *Itinerary*. It is called Pudput in the Peutinger Tables. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book V, no. 5, has *Pulpu*; our Placidus Porcheron confirms this reading from Priscian’s Book VI, *On the Parts of Speech*, where that author cites these words of Livy from Book CXIII, as Ortelius observes, a lost book: “And he himself guarded the coast around Pulpud.”

12. REPARATUS OF PUPPIANA. This is the man who dedicated a monastery in the province of Byzacena, for whose freedom Peter the abbot labored so greatly at the Carthaginian Council under Boniface. Gaudiosus, bishop of the people of Puppiana, the successor of Reparatus, subscribed that council. Bonifacius, bishop of Pappiana, should also be referred here; he subscribed the synodal letter of the Proconsular bishops read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin.

[Col. 0281B] Older than all these was the aged Victor of Puppiana, praised at the Carthaginian Council under Aurelius in 397, whose canons are reported by Justellus on page 346 in the *Code of the African Church*. At the council held in the same city under Genethlius, Victor is called *Pupputanus* in some codices, but *Puppianus* in others. See volume II of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, columns 1158 and 1828.

13. ARADITANUS. So both manuscript codices read, together with the printed editions. Ortelius suspects that he was so called from Aradus of Sardinia, which island, he says, Victor counts under the African diocese. But the learned man is mistaken. The bishops of Sardinia at that time did indeed belong to the African diocese, but they are listed separately below; nor did they ever belong to the Proconsular province.

Aemilianus, bishop of the people of Aradis, attended the Carthaginian Council held under Boniface in 525. Bishops of Aradus frequently occur in Eastern synods, but these were from Phoenicia.

[Col. 0281C] 14. THELENSIS. Bonifacius, bishop of Telis, presided over the same city; he subscribed, among the bishops of the Proconsular province, the synodal letter praised at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. Natalicus, a Donatist bishop of Telis, attended the Council of Cabarsussum. It is now agreed among all learned men that this council must be called by that name, whereas earlier editions called it *Cavernense*; on that basis some invented “Caverns of Susa,” a place near Carthage. On this matter see Baluze in the new *Collection of Canons*, columns 95 and 256, and other authors throughout.

Felix of Telis, likewise of the Donatist sect, attended the Carthaginian Collation in chapter 208. From this passage Baluze draws an argument to prove that Tela and Zela were two distinct cities in Africa. For in the same Collation, chapter 136, Natalicus the Donatist is said to be the opponent of Donatianus, Catholic bishop of the people of Zella; and again in chapter 163 the same Natalicus appears among the Donatists as bishop of Zella.

On this view, then, one must say that Felix succeeded Natalicus who subscribed the Council of Cabarsussum, and that the Natalicus mentioned here in the Collation was a different man. Finally, the Council of Telis, or Zella, is famous because controversies concerning its authenticity or falsity have arisen in this century.

15. MULLITANUS. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 133, Candorius, bishop of the people of Mullita, attended together with Marcellinus the Donatist, his opponent, who is also mentioned in chapter 198. Segetius, bishop of the same city, subscribed the Carthaginian Council held under Boniface in 525, after peace had been restored to the African Church.

16. DUASSEDEMSAI. So both manuscript codices read, together with the printed editions. Garnier reads *Duassendelmai*, but on his own authority. He was no more successful in judging that this word designated the city of Dionysiana, since Dionysiana is mentioned below among the cities of the province of Byzacena that were without bishops.

Noris, in his observations against [Col. 0282A] the same Garnier, thinks that the seat of Assenemsala is designated here. Fortunatianus, bishop on behalf of Donatus, of Assenemsala—or rather, as the edition of Baluze has it, *a Senemsalis*—attended the Carthaginian Collation in chapter 201. At the Carthaginian Council under Boniface, Patronianus of Senemsala is listed among the Proconsular bishops; and at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, Julianus of the Senepsalitani is mentioned. The learned man believes that these expressions designate the same city.

But Baluze, who after Holstenius touched the matter with true acuteness and was extraordinarily perceptive in correcting ancient records, seems to me to have handled it correctly: he says that *Duas Senemsal.* should be read here, that is, “of the two Senemsalitan cities.” Thus the Julianus mentioned above subscribed at the aforementioned Lateran Council the synodal letter of the Proconsular bishops addressed to Paul, bishop of Constantinople, under this formula: “Julianus, bishop of the holy Church of the two Senepsalitan cities,” or rather, “of the two Senemsalitan cities.”

There were therefore, it seems, two places of the same name, having one bishop, who for this reason was sometimes called *Senemsalitanus*, but at other times *of the two Senemsalitan cities*, as here in the *Notitia*, and sometimes also *a Senemsalis*, as we observed above from the Carthaginian Collation. There was, moreover, another city of almost the same name in the Proconsular province, over which Felix of Selemsela presided; he is mentioned at the Carthaginian Council under Genethlius. Gratian also speaks of him in 16 q. 1, c. *Felix*, as Baluze notes in his observations on chapter 201 of the Carthaginian Collation, on the occasion of Cresconius, bishop of Silemsila, of the Donatist sect, who is mentioned there.

17. MISSUENSIS. Antoninus in his *Itinerary* and the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book V, mention Missua. But the Peutinger Tables, Pliny in Book V, chapter 4, and other authors call this city *Misuа*, while Ptolemy calls it *Nisua*. Procopius, in Book II of *The Vandalic War*, calls Missua the naval station of the Carthaginians. Servusdei, bishop of Missua, subscribed the Carthaginian Council under Boniface in 525. The name *Muzua* also occurs below, no. 49.

[Col. 0282C] 18. LAPDENSIS. Rufinus, bishop of Labda on behalf of the Donatists, mentioned in chapter 198 of the Collation, seems to have belonged to the same place. Victor, bishop of Labda, also attended the Carthaginian Council under Boniface. Further below, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, occurs Restitutus, bishop of Lapidia, no. 61.

19. ASSURITANUS. In the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, the confessor Victor of Assures gave his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics, no. 68. The same Cyprian wrote a letter to Epictetus, his brother—that is, I believe, to the bishop—and to the people residing at Assures; in the new edition it is no. 65. Evangelus, bishop of the Church of Assures, presided over the same city; he is mentioned in the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in the code of the canons of the African Church, in Justellus, p. 346, and he also attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 120. Moreover, Praetextatus, a Donatist bishop of Assures, subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussis in 393, and the following year was deposed from his see at the Synod of Bagai. Saint Augustine mentions Rogatus, whom those same Donatists had substituted for Praetextatus, in Book III, ch. 56, Against Cresconius. After Rogatus had later converted to Catholic unity, as the same holy teacher relates in Book 9, no. 9, of On the Proceedings with Emeritus, the Circumcellions cut off his hands and tongue.

Antoninus mentions Assures more than once in his Itinerary. Ptolemy calls the city Assurus, while the Peutinger Tables call it Assures. Hardouin maintains that it is the same city as the town of Azuritanum—or, as other manuscripts read, Absuritanum—mentioned by Pliny, Book V, ch. 4. He is supported by the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin: Victorinus, bishop of the Church of Auzira, subscribed it. Yet, besides Evangelus, the Assuritan bishop whom we have said appeared among the Catholics at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 120, Victor, the Catholic bishop of Azures, spoke at ch. 187. Baluzius resolves this difficulty by observing that this Victor is called the bishop of Ajura in *Cognitio* 2, ch. 15. Indeed, since at the cited ch. 187 Victor asserts that he had a church in the city of Rotaria, he seems to have belonged to Numidia. For Felix of Rotaria, mentioned by Optatus in Book I, was from Numidia. See below, no. 67, Servius of Assures, among the bishops of the province of Byzacena.

20. URCITANUS. Haller’s manuscript, in Ortelius, reads *Uracitanus*. Victor, in Book I, no. 3, praises Mansuetus of Uricita, who, at the command of King Genseric, was burned at the gate of Fornita. On this occasion we made several observations concerning the city in the note to that passage (Col. 185, n. b). Baluzius considers Boniface of Uruga, who attended the Carthaginian Conference on the Donatist side, ch. 187, to have been the bishop of this same city.

21. TENNONENSIS. Optatus, bishop of Tonnona, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. More famous, however, was Victor, bishop of the same city and author of the *Chronicle* published under his name. In defense of the Three Chapters, he and other African bishops, under the emperor Justinian, endured exile and other severe hardships, as he himself testifies in the aforementioned *Chronicle*.

107 22. UTICENSIS. “The cities of Utica and Carthage,” says Pomponius Mela in Book I, ch. 7, “both renowned, both founded by the Phoenicians: the former famous for Cato’s fate, the latter for its own.” Florus, Book IV, ch. 2, calls Utica “a kind of gate of Africa.” Pliny, Book V, ch. 4, calls it famous for Cato’s death. From the *Itinerary* of Antoninus, the Peutinger Tables, Polybius, and other authorities, it can easily be concluded that it lay not far from Carthage.

Victor, bishop of Utica, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, together with Gedalius, a Donatist and his opponent. It would be superfluous to gather further information about this city, celebrated alike by sacred and secular writers.

23. MIGIRPENSIS. In the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Primus of Misgirpa—or rather, as the Oxford editor observes, Felix, the first of that name, of Misgirpa—gave the second judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics. For he is called nothing other than Felix of Migirpa by Augustine, especially in Book VI, ch. 6, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, where Augustine answers his objections. See what our editors observed in the notes to this passage.

Victor, the Catholic bishop of the people of Migirpa, appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, with his opponent Gloriosus. The same Gloriosus was again listed among the Donatists in ch. 198. We also have Titus—or Tutus—bishop of Migirpa, who attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 397, in Justellus’s *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, p. 346.

24. GISIPENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 233, Januarius, bishop of the Church of Greater Gisipus, was listed among the Catholic Fathers; he had no Donatist opponent. I would not dare assert that this passage proves that there were two cities in Africa, one distinguished from the other by the addition “Greater,” especially since no evidence of this appears to me in the ancient records.

Redemptus of Gisipus attended the Council of Carthage held under Boniface in 525. Mellosus, bishop of the Church of Gisipus, subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular Fathers to Paul, bishop of Constantinople, cited at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. Beware, however, of confusing Gisipus with Ginesis, as Garnerius did, thereby incurring Norisius’s severe criticism.

25. UZITENSIS. Norisius thinks that *Ucitensis* should be read here, from the city of Uci. There were two cities of that name in Africa, as we observed from Pliny in note 12 to Victor of Vita (Col. 185, n. b). There was nevertheless a town called Uzita, praised by Hirtius in his *Book on the African War* and by Dio Cassius, Book XLIII.

Norisius argues that this town belonged to Byzacena and thinks this can be demonstrated from Hirtius’s own words. There Uzita is said to have been six miles from the port of Leptis Parva. Leptis, however, was in Byzacena, eighteen miles above Hadrumetum toward Tripoli, as Antoninus testifies in his *Itinerary*. It was therefore farther from the proconsular province than to be assignable to that province as well. Ptolemy also supports this view: in Book IV, ch. 3, he lists Uzita among the cities subject to Hadrumetum. Who does not know that Hadrumetum belonged to Byzacena?

Baluzius, for his part, thinks that Paul, bishop of the people of Uzitta, presided over this city of Uzita listed in the *Notitia*. Paul appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, with the other Catholic Fathers.

26. EXITZIOSUS VERENSIS. The printed editions read *Exitiosus*. Baluzius suspects that Vitalis, bishop of Ucra, presided over this see; he is mentioned among the Donatists at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 208. Certainly, in the editions of the Conference preceding Baluzius’s, this Vitalis is called not *Ucrensis* but *Virensis*. The Peutinger Tables indeed contain *Veri*, while the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book III, no. 5, calls the place *Verim*.

Quodvultdeus, bishop of Verus, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419. Earlier still was Vitalis, bishop of the city of Verus, who came from Africa with Caecilianus and other bishops to the First Council of Arles.

27. CRESCES CICSITANUS. The printed editions read *Crescens*. At the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 209, Flavosus, bishop of Cissis, appeared among the Donatists, while shortly before, in ch. 206, Quodvultdeus, bishop of Cessis and belonging to the same sect, had been listed. In other editions preceding Baluzius’s, however, this Quodvultdeus is called *Cissitensis*, while in Labbe’s edition, ch. 207, he is called *Gessitensis*. Perhaps one or the other of these two bishops occupied the see of Cicsis mentioned here in the *Notitia*.

Whether one of them belonged to Mauritania, where a city of Cissis is also listed below, no. 107, is uncertain. Baluzius suspects that Flavosus was substituted by the Donatists in the place of Quodvultdeus, who had died on the journey. Yet even to Baluzius this seems difficult, principally because the names of both bishops were recited on the same day at the Conference, while the Catholics said nothing concerning the name of Flavosus of Cissis. Shortly before, when Quodvultdeus was listed as already dead, they had raised a serious dispute with the Donatists on that very account.

At the Council of Carthage under Gratus, Elpidophorus of Cuisis is praised. He could be referred to this entry, unless we knew from another source that *Cuiculitanus* must be read there. See below among the Numidians, no. 10.

28. BOLITANUS. Among the other cities which Ptolemy, Book IV, ch. 3, says were under Carthage, he lists Volus Secunda. Crispulus, bishop of the Church of Volus, presided over it. Crispulus attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, with Quodvultdeus, a Donatist and his opponent. Quodvultdeus also appeared in ch. 208. In that passage the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius corrects what he had said concerning the people of Volus at ch. 128, where he had inadvertently confused them with the peoples of Volus in Mauritania Tingitana.

The same learned man warns, in his note on ch. 135, that the city of Volus must be distinguished from Vallita. The reading of the *Notitia* can also be confirmed from the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, at the final chapter, where Paulinus praises Muranus as bishop of Bolus.

That the martyrs of Bolus were famous in Africa is clear from Augustine, who preached a sermon in the Basilica of Gratian on their feast day. This is Sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*. The memory of the saints of Volus is celebrated in the most ancient Carthaginian calendar on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

29. CARPITANUS. Ptolemy mentions Carpis in Book IV, ch. 3. Pliny calls this city Carpi. Optatus of Milevis mentions Carpos in Book II *Against Parmenianus*. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Secundinus of Carpis voted that heretics should be rebaptized, no. 24; Saint Augustine answers him in Book VI, ch. 31, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

Antonius, bishop of the people of Carpis, was listed at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, with his opponent on the Donatist side, Veratianus. The same Veratianus was counted among the custodians of the records from the Donatist sect in ch. 223.

Penthadius, successor to Antonius and bishop of the Church of Carpis, subscribed to the Council of Carthage held under Aurelius in 419. Venerius, likewise bishop of Carpis, attended the following century’s Council of Carthage under Boniface. Finally, among the other bishops of the proconsular province who subscribed to the synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in session 2, Bassus, bishop of the Church of Capris, is mentioned.

30. MAXULITANUS. The Peutinger Tables have *Maxula*. Ptolemy, Book IV, ch. 3, also mentions Maxula and, shortly afterward, lists Maxula Vetus first among the cities under Carthage. Pliny, Book V, ch. 4, calls Maxula a colony.

At the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, Numidius of Massyla is mentioned in ch. 6, which is ch. 8 in the code of the African Church. At the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 112, another Numidius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Maxula, appeared together with Felix, his opponent from the Donatist sect. Finally, another Numidius, bishop of the same city, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

The feast of the saints of Maxula is celebrated in the ancient Carthaginian calendar on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August. We have two sermons of Saint Augustine concerning them, entitled *On the Holy Martyrs of Massyla*.

31. BONUSTENSIS. Among the Catholic Fathers who assembled for the Carthaginian Conference, Rufinianus, bishop of Bonustus, is mentioned in ch. 133.

32. TINNISENSIS. The Peutinger Tables contain *Tumsa*, perhaps for *Tunisa*. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna mentions *Tumissa* and *Tuniza* in Book III, no. 6. Ptolemy, Book IV, ch. 3, praises *Thinissa*, and among the cities under Carthage he lists *Thernissa* and *Uthina*. In the preceding chapter he had already mentioned *Tenissa*, but in Mauritania Caesariensis.

Tunes is famous in Polybius, who describes its location in Book XIV in these words: “Tunes is about 120 stadia from Carthage . . . and can be seen from almost every part of Carthage.” It is likely that this city grew from the ruins of Carthage; even now it is the capital of the kingdom—or rather, of the republic—that bears the same name.

Sextilianus, bishop of Tunes or Tuni, acted as the representative of Primosus, bishop of Carthage, at the Fifth General Council. Baluzius suspects that Valerius, bishop of the people of Utinisa, listed at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, among the Orthodox Fathers, presided over the city of Tinnis mentioned here in the *Notitia*.

The editions preceding Baluzius’s, however, read *Utinicensis*. But this variation does not oppose the learned man’s opinion, since Haller’s manuscript of the *Notitia* also read *Tinicensis* for *Tinnisensis*, as can be inferred from Ortelius, who cites *Tinicia* from Victor’s manuscript of Haller’s codex.

Moreover, in the already mentioned Conference, ch. 180, Colonicus, bishop of Thinistus, appeared among the Donatists. Baluzius thinks *Thinissensis* should be read there. He nevertheless believes, with Baronius, that this see should be assigned to Numidia.

Finally, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, the confessor Venantius of Tinisa gave his opinion among those favoring rebaptism, no. 29. Augustine answers his objection in Book VII, ch. 13, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

33. CULSITANUS, or rather Culusitanus. Nicasius of Culusis is mentioned at the Council of Carthage under Gratus. Vincent, bishop of the Church of Culusis, was famous. He was one of the seven Catholic bishops chosen at the Carthaginian Conference to defend the cause of the Catholic Church against the Donatist schismatics, and he was also listed among the other Fathers in ch. 138.

The same bishop attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius, held in 319, as is clear both from Labbe’s edition and from the code of the canons of the African Church. He is the same man whom Paulinus praises in the final chapter of the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, although in the printed editions he is called the bishop of Colossis, contrary to the evidence of almost all the manuscripts. As our editors testify in the new edition of this holy teacher’s works, those manuscripts read *Culusitanus*; yet they themselves did not correct the text.

In the following century, Marcianus, bishop of the people of Culusis, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. Finally, Peter, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Culcisis, subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops, which was read in session 2 at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin.

Norisius nevertheless argues against Garnerius that the city of Culucis must be distinguished from Culusis. Antoninus in his *Itinerary* and the Peutinger Tables place Culucis in central Numidia, whereas all the evidence cited above makes it certain that Culusis belonged to the proconsular province. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna mentions Culucia in Book V, no. 4.

Nor is there space to refute another error of Garnerius, who confuses this same city of Culusis with Curubis. From what we shall say below concerning Curubis, no. 36, it will be clear that the two were entirely different.

Finally, Victor of Vita praises the city of Culusis in Book V, no. 3. So many martyrs and confessors flourished there under the Vandal persecution that it was impossible for any person to count them. Above all, Victor praises Victoria, an illustrious matron.

34. BULLENSIS. The confessor Therapius of Bulla gave judgment against the baptism of heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 61; Augustine answers his argument in Book VII, ch. 25, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

Victor of Bulna may perhaps also be assigned here; he subscribed to the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province mentioned so often above, as can be seen in session 2 of the Lateran Council under Saint Martin.

Procopius mentions the plain of Bulla once and again in Book I, *On the Vandalic War*; it lay on the route toward Numidia. Saint Augustine also mentions the plain of Bulla in Letter 65. See below, no. 50, *Bullensis Regiorum*.

35. NEAPOLITANUS. Last of all, Junius of Neapolis gave his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian.

Fortunatianus, bishop of Neapolis, subscribed to the Council of Carthage held under Aurelius in 419. He also attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, with Ampelius, a Donatist and his opponent. Ampelius was again listed among the bishops of the same sect in ch. 206.

Hirtius in his *Book on the African War*, Pomponius Mela, and other authors discuss this city. The Peutinger Tables place it approximately midway between Clypea and Pudput. Antoninus agrees in his *Itinerary*, where the sequence is Putput, Curubis, Neapolis, Clypea.

Ptolemy calls Neapolis a colony; Pliny calls it a free town. There were other cities called Neapolis in other provinces.

[Col. 0286D] 36. CURBITANUS. This reading is supported by the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province, already cited several times and approved at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. Benenatus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Curubis, subscribed it.

The ancients, however, more often wrote *Curubis*. At the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 198, Victor, bishop of Curubis, was listed among the Donatists. Peregrinus, bishop of the Church of Curubis, also attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

Saint Augustine calls the same city Curubis in Book XXII, ch. 8, *The City of God*. Secular writers agree with the sacred authors: Pliny, Antoninus in his *Itinerary*, and the anonymous geographer of Ravenna in Book V, no. 5. Ptolemy, however, calls it *Curobis*, or, as the Palatine manuscript reads, *Curabis*, in Book IV, ch. 3.

After Norisius’s criticism of Garnerius, I believe no one in the future will confuse this city with Culusis.

[Col. 0287A] 37. SIMMINENSIS. Haller’s manuscript reads *Simminiensis*. In the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book V, no. 5, *Siminina* occurs. Our Placidus Porcheron thinks this is the same city as *Sinuama*, mentioned in Book III, no. 5, by the same author.

Baluzius believes that *Simminensis* was written here in the *Notitia*, and below, no. 42, *Seminensis* for *Simitensis*. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, Benenatus, bishop of the Church of Simitis, attended among the Catholic Fathers. Another Benenatus, bishop of the Church of Semitis, subscribed with the other Fathers of the proconsular province to the synodical letter mentioned so often above, which was approved at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin.

Certainly, the various forms in which this city’s name is written in different places invite conjecture. Pliny, Book V, ch. 4, mentions the town of Simittium. Antoninus calls it *Simittu*. At the Carthaginian Council in Labbe’s edition, held under Aurelius in 419, Adeodatus of Simittium—or Sumitium, or Simoethium—attended. In the code of ecclesiastical canons from Dionysius Exiguus, apud Justellum, col. 169, and in the code of the canons of the African Church, col. 396, he is called Adeodatus of Simidica, or, as the Greek text has it, Σιμηδικίτης (*Simēdikítēs*).

Take care, however, not to suppose that Simittium and Simidica were one and the same city. Norisius proves in his observations against Garnerius, already often cited, that they were entirely different. This can easily be demonstrated from the Carthaginian Conference: in ch. 126, Benenatus of Simittium, already mentioned, declares that he has neither another bishop with him nor heretics as his opponents. In ch. 135, Adeodatus, bishop of the people of Simidica, was likewise listed among the Catholics, and he too enjoyed Catholic unity.

Hence conclude either that *Simidicensis* should be restored for *Simitensis* in Labbe’s subscriptions, or at least that the Adeodatus mentioned in that Carthaginian council was entirely different from Adeodatus of Simidica praised in the Conference, ch. 135, and that he succeeded Benenatus, as Norisius maintains. See below, no. 42, where we shall discuss the bishop of Semitis.

38. CLIPIENSIS. The name of Stephen, bishop of the Church of Clypea, who subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, is written in the same way. Crescens, bishop of Clypea, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

The Peutinger Tables also have *Clipeis*. The ancients, however, more often wrote *Clypea* or *Clupea*. Thus write Ptolemy, Book IV, ch. 3; Caesar, Book II, *On the Civil War*; Hirtius, *On the African War*; Pliny; Antoninus in his *Itinerary*; Pomponius Mela; Solinus; Polybius; and many other authors throughout. Silius Italicus gives the reason in Book I: it was built in the shape of a shield.

Laodicius, bishop of the people of Clypea, attended the Carthaginian Conference. In ch. 133 he is mentioned with his opponent Geminius. Geminius again appeared with the other Donatists in ch. 198.

This city was the first of all the African cities to come under Roman power, under Regulus, as Polybius observes in Book I of his *Histories* and Florus in Book II of his *Roman History*, ch. 2. The ancients believed that Hercules had fought there with Antaeus, king of the Africans, as Procopius reports in Book II, *On the Vandalic War*. The myths contain more about Antaeus, but there is no opportunity to recount it here.

39. MEGLAPOLITANUS. Norisius proves through numerous examples that this should be read *Meglapolitanus*. He criticizes Garnerius for writing *Megalopolitanus* without the authority of any manuscript. Haller’s codex, in Ortelius, reads *Megapolis*; but the 800-year-old Laon manuscript supports Norisius.

Although Labbe’s edition of the Councils, in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 133, mentions Romanus, bishop of the people of Megapolis, Albaspinei’s edition reads *Meglapolitanae*. Baluzius notes that an old manuscript supports this reading. Papirius Masson’s edition reads *Neglapolitanae*.

Our reading is also supported by the synodical letter from the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, cited so often above. Among the bishops of the proconsular province who subscribed it was Reparatus, bishop of the Church of Meglapolis.

40. TIMIDENSIS. Felix, bishop of the Church of Timida, is listed among the proconsular bishops who subscribed to the same synodical letter at that council, session 2. The memory of the martyrs of Timida was once famous in Africa, as is clear from the ancient Carthaginian calendar, in which the feast of the saints of Timida is recorded on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.

This is the same city commonly called Timida Regia. Augustine praises its bishop, the confessor Faustus, in Book VII, ch. 22, *On Baptism against the Donatists*. Long before, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Faustus had given his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics, no. 58.

Restitutus, bishop of the people of Timida Regia, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

Some learned men have thought that Januarius, bishop of the people of Tunuda, mentioned at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 120, also presided over this city. Norisius rises against them in his observations against Garnerius’s notes. He believes that the see of Tunuda should rather be derived from Thunu in the Peutinger Tables, from Tunuba in Ptolemy, or certainly from the town of Tunudisa, which Pliny, Book V, ch. 4, places in the proconsular province.

Baluzius restored *Tunudisensis* in his notes on this passage of the Conference, since Victorianus, the Donatist who is said to have been Januarius’s opponent, is called the bishop of Tunusudus in ch. 201 of the same Conference.

Ptolemy, Book IV, ch. 3, mentions Thunusda. We have said more about the city of Tunusudus in note 46 to Victor of Vita (Col. 198, n. f).

What induced the learned men to think that *Tunudensis* had been written here for *Timidensis* was the fact that the older editions of the Conference read *Tumidensis*. This error also misled the learned man who prepared the latest Oxford edition of Saint Cyprian.

41. VINCENTIUS ZIGGENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 197, Donatus, bishop of Zicis, appeared among the Donatists. The distinguished Baluzius thinks that this name designates the see of Zigga, mentioned here in the *Notitia*, and he criticizes Holstenius there for thinking that this city of Zicis was the same as Sicca, since Paul, bishop of Sicca, is mentioned among the Donatists in the following chapter.

Fortunatianus, the Catholic bishop of Sicca, declares in ch. 139 that Catholic unity was so firmly established in his city that the Donatist bishop who resided there was scarcely known by name.

Baluzius thinks that Vincent, who is called the bishop of Zigga here in the *Notitia*, is the same man who is called the bishop of Gigita by Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 9. See note 29 on that author (Col. 193, n. a).

On that assumption, however, the city of Zicis—or, as Baluzius wishes, Zigga—mentioned in the Conference would be different from the Zigga under discussion here, which he nevertheless says is the same as Gegita. For in the Conference, Quadratus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Gegita, declares in ch. 128 that there had never been any Donatist bishop in his city. Therefore Donatus of Zicis, who, as we have said, attended as a Donatist in ch. 197, could not have been his opponent.

Finally, Antoninus’s *Itinerary* places Cigisa between Carthage and Tuburbus Minor. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book III, no. 6, mentions Gegite among the cities lying on the borders of the proconsular province and Numidia.

Candidus, bishop of Sicca, subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. But perhaps he was the bishop of Sicca Veneria, which city was generally called simply Sicca, without any addition. See concerning it note 75 on Victor of Vita (Col. 207, n. e).

42. SEMINENSIS. Baluzius thinks that *Seminensis* here and *Simminensis* above were written for *Simitensis*. Nevertheless, as he himself admits, Junianus, bishop of Simina, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525; he is elsewhere also written *Simminensis*. See above, no. 37.

[Col. 0289A] 43. TAGARATENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, Lucius, bishop of the city of Tagara, is mentioned with Quintus, his opponent, who was again listed among the Donatists in ch. 208. Ortelius, from Haller’s manuscript, mentions the city of Tagara in the proconsular province. Below, among the bishops of Numidia, no. 112, we have Crescentius of Tacara.

44. ALTUBURITANUS. This is the reading of the Laon manuscript. Haller’s codex has *Altubaritanus*, while the printed editions have *Altaburitanus*. The Peutinger Tables and all the older geographers support our reading.

In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, Basilius, bishop of the people of Altibura, is listed among the Catholics, together with Augustalis from the Donatist side, who is again mentioned in ch. 197. From the same sect, Victor, bishop of Altibura, attended the Council of Cabarsussis.

Constantine, bishop of the Church of Altobura, was a Catholic; he subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. I believe the same city is mentioned in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, where *Altieuros* occurs, approximately midway between Carthage and Cirta.

45. CELLENSIS. Below, among the Fathers of Mauritania Sitifensis, no. 17, appears Cresciturus of Cella. Honorius, bishop of the people of Cella, who attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, with Castus, a Donatist also mentioned in ch. 187, must be referred to one or the other of these cities.

46. UZIPPARITANUS. The Peutinger Tables have *Uzippira*, and in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 131, Marianus, bishop of the people of Uzippira, is listed. Other ancient records nevertheless confirm our reading: Sementius of Uzippa attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

47. AUSANENSIS. Both manuscripts and the printed editions read this way. Perhaps *Ausafensis* should be read. At the Council of Cabarsussis in 393, among the other Donatists, Salvius, bishop of Ausafa, subscribed; the following year he was deposed from his see at the Synod of Bagai.

In Labbe’s edition this Salvius is called *Ausacensis*, or, as the margin has it, *Ausanensis*. It is more likely, however, that he belonged to the province of Sitifis, where Assafa was located. See below, *Sitifenses*, no. 24, concerning that city.

48. NARAGGARITANUS. This is the reading of the Laon manuscript and the printed editions. It should nevertheless unquestionably be written *Naraggaritanus*. Haller’s codex, in Ortelius, has *Naraggaritensis*, although that author carelessly assigns the city to Numidia.

Naraggara is a city known from Ptolemy, Antoninus, the Peutinger Tables, and other authorities. Its bishop Faustinus, belonging to the Donatist sect, is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 208.

Victorinus, bishop of the people of Nagargara, is said to have subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525; *Nagargaritanae* stands there for *Naraggaritanae*.

Among the other Fathers of the proconsular province who subscribed to the synodical letter mentioned so often above at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin appears Benenatus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Naraggara.

Finally, Polybius, Book XV of his *Histories*, mentions the African city πόλιν Μάργαρον, “the city Margaron.” Casaubon both translates and interprets this as *Margarum*, or *Nadagarum*. Certainly this passage of Polybius favors our reading, since otherwise we might have thought that the letter M had entered through the carelessness of copyists in place of N.

49. MUZUENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, Rufinianus, bishop of the people of Muzua, appeared and professed that he possessed Catholic unity.

This is the same Rufinianus who, as the learned Baluzius notes, attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419, although the name of his see is written in various ways in different manuscripts and printed editions.

In Labbe’s edition of the Councils, vol. II, cols. 1603 and 1605, he is called Rufinianus of Muzuta or Musta; but in col. 1670 Rufinus is called bishop of the Church of Maza. In Justellus’s first code of the canons of the African Church, col. 306, he is called Rufinianus of Muzuca. Later, in the subscriptions of the council, col. 399, he is called Rufianus of Maxa; in another codex, as the same Justellus notes, Rufinianus is called bishop of Maza. A more reliable manuscript has *Mugensis*. In Dionysius Exiguus’s *Collection* in Justellus, col. 169, he is called Rufinianus of Muzuba.

Although the genuine reading cannot easily be discerned amid such a variety of readings, the one that calls Rufinianus bishop of Muzua nevertheless seems preferable to us. It is certain that one of the proconsular bishops is being listed here. But the see of Muzuca belonged to Byzacena; we shall discuss it and Muzula below, among the bishops of that province, no. 42.

Musta belonged to Numidia, as is certain from Antoninus’s *Itinerary* and other authorities; Antonianus of Musta is listed below among the Numidians, no. 71. Although there was a city called Musta in the proconsular province, it must be distinguished from Muzua, as is certain from the Conference. Rufinianus of Muzua, as we have already said, testified there that he possessed Catholic unity. Victorianus of Musta, whom Norisius argues came from the proconsular province, had two Donatist bishops as his opponents. See below, *Numidians*, no. 71.

The cities of Maza, Maxa, or Muga, or of Muzuta or Muzuba, are not known to us from other records. We do have Madis in the *Notitia*, but it was in Numidia, no. 37.

Finally, Latinus of Muga subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussis, but we do not know to which province he belonged. Rusticianus of Mutiga, whom the sermon attributed to Saint Augustine discusses at the end of volume IX of the Benedictine edition, seems to have been from Numidia.

Finally, all the Greek manuscripts, whether in the prologue of the council or in the subscriptions, consistently read Ῥουφιανὸς Μουζουενασίανος (*Rhouphianos Mouzouenasianos*), with the single exception of one manuscript, which once has Μαξένοης (*Maxenoeis*). But perhaps this has been discussed at greater length than the matter required.

50. BULLENSIUM REGIO. *Bullensium Regiorum* must be read. The bishop of this place was sometimes simply called the bishop of Bulla, as is clear from the Carthaginian Conference, where, in ch. 208, Felix, bishop of Bulla, is listed among the Donatists. Earlier, however, in ch. 135, he had been called the opponent of Dominicus, bishop of the people of Bulla Regia.

At the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, Epigonius, bishop of Bulla Regia, is mentioned. This has been corrected from the manuscript of Luca Holstenius; previously the reading was *Bullensium Regionum*, as can be seen in vol. II of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, col. 1161, and in the appendix, col. 1830.

Antoninus in his *Itinerary*, the Peutinger Tables, and Pliny, Book V, ch. 3, mention Bulla Regia; Pliny calls it a free town. This is, I believe, the same city that Ptolemy calls Bullaria in Book IV, ch. 3, where he says that the city was established under the Third Augustan Legion.

Perhaps *Bullariensis* should be read for *Bulleriensis* in the subscriptions of the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, where Mellosus, bishop of Bullaria, appears.

### 51. TITULITANUS

Among the Donatists who appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 202, Victor, bishop of Titulus, is mentioned [Col. 0290D]. He had already been called, in chapter 126, the adversary of Cresconius, bishop of the people of Titulus. Hence we infer that this city was called Titulus. Victorinus of Castellum-Titulianum is listed below among the Numidians, no. 51.

### 52. TUBURBITENSIS

There were two cities in Africa called Tuburbium, as everyone knows; they were distinguished by the additions “Greater” or “Lesser.” Nevertheless, each was sometimes called simply Tuburbium, as is clear from the Carthaginian Conference. For in chapter 203 Maximinus is called a Donatist bishop of Tuburbium, although earlier, namely in chapter 133, he had been called the adversary of Victor, bishop of the people of Lesser Tuburbium. Likewise Rufinianus, a Donatist bishop of Tuburbium, is mentioned without an addition in chapter 201; he was the adversary of Cyprian, the Catholic bishop of the people of Greater Tuburbium, as is clear from chapter 135, where he is called Rufinus.

[Col. 0291A] Sedatus of Tuburbium, who sat among the rebaptizers at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian and spoke at no. 18, and Faustus, bishop of the city of Tuburbium, one of the African bishops who assembled with Caecilian of Carthage at the First Council of Arles, belonged to one or the other of these episcopal sees, as is clear from the subscriptions of that synod. Pliny mentions the colony of Tuburbis in book V, chapter 4. Antoninus places Tuburbominus between Bulla Regia and Cigis in his *Itinerary*. The *Peutinger Table* shows the locations of both. Ptolemy mentions Tuburbo; I omit the other authorities.

Perhaps Germanus presided over the same city. He is said to have subscribed the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, where he is called bishop of the holy Church of Ciumtuturbo—perhaps for *civitas maioris* or *minoris Tuburbii*, that is, “the city of Greater or Lesser Tuburbium.” In fact, the names of the episcopal sees in this letter are for the most part corrupt.

Our Victor praises Servus, an illustrious confessor of the city of Greater Tuburbium, in book 163, no. 2; see the note on that passage [Col. 0291B] (Col. 242, n. d.). The ancient Carthaginian calendar commemorates the martyrs of Tuburbium on 3 Kalends of August [30 July]; some have attributed this name to the famous martyrs Felicitas and Perpetua, while others have attributed it to Maxima and her companions. Our John Mabillon discusses them learnedly in his notes on the aforementioned calendar. We too treated this question in the *Admonition to the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas* in the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 81. See also p. 495.

### 53. EUDALENSIS

This is how both manuscript codices read, as do the printed editions. Nevertheless, I would prefer to read, with learned men—Stephen Baluzius in his notes on the Carthaginian Conference and Jean Hardouin in his notes on Pliny—*Theudalensis*. Certainly Victor of Vita, book I, no. 7, praises Habetdeus, bishop of Theudalis, exiled by Genseric. On him, see BYZACENI, no. 55. Urbanus, bishop of the people of Theudalis, was present at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126.

Charles of Saint Paul, however, distinguishes Eudalis from Theudalis in his *Sacred Geography*, though he derives the distinction from this passage of the *Notitia*. [Col. 0291C] Ptolemy mentions Theudale in book IV, chapter 3; Pliny, book V, chapter 4, calls it a free town.

### 54. TULANENSIS

It is not found in Ortelius. At the Council of Carthage under Gratus, Metus of Taccana was present. Should he be assigned here? In another manuscript he is called *Caunensis*. But I have no time to linger over conjectures of this sort.

In all, only fifty-four bishops are mentioned here in the proconsular province, although it is certain that there were once far more in that province. But after the populations had been scattered into various regions, very many cities, as our Victor says in book I, no. 3, were inhabited either sparsely or by no inhabitants at all. Certainly the same author asserts in no. 9 of the same book that their number had been 164, when, after the death of Deogratias, bishop of Carthage, Genseric prohibited the ordination of bishops in the provinces of Zeugitana and Proconsularis.

[Col. 0291D] In the synodical letter of the bishops of that province to Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, which was read in the Second Session of the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, sixty-eight Fathers are said to have subscribed. Yet the bishops of Carthage and of several other cities listed here in the *Notitia* are not included there.

## FOR THE PROVINCE OF NUMIDIA

### 1. BERCERITANUS

The Halleri codex reads *Becerritanus*. The distinguished Baluzius judges that Fortunatus, bishop of Vesceris, who is listed among the Donatists in chapter 187 of the Carthaginian Conference, presided over this see. Ortelius and Charles of Saint Paul, however, think that the Vesceritan city mentioned in the Conference is the one called Οὐεσκεθήρ (*Oueskethēr*) by Ptolemy, in Mauretania.

Among the cities of Numidia listed below in no. 3 of the *Notitia* of Leo the Wise occurs Κάστρον Βέδερα (*Kastron Bedera*, “Fort Bedera”), or *Castrum Bedere* (“Fort Bedera”), as rendered in the Beveregian edition; Goar’s version, however, has *Castra Vetera* (“Old Forts”).

### 2. GAZAUFULENSIS

This is how it is called by Antoninus, who has *Gazaufula*. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, the martyr Salvianus of Gazaufala pronounced a judgment against the baptism of heretics, no. 76. Augustine answers his objection in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 40. Procopius calls it *Gazophyla* in book II of the *Vandalic War* and writes that it was two days’ journey from Constantina. *Gazaupala* appears in the *Peutinger Table*.

### 3. CALAMENSIS

This city is frequently mentioned by Augustine, since it was not far from Hippo Regius, as appears from book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. The same holy doctor often praises Megalius, bishop of Calama and at that time primate of Numidia. In the Carthaginian Conference, Investigation 3, chapter 247, Augustine professed that Megalius had raised him to the summit of episcopal dignity.

Possidius likewise reports that Megalius succeeded Crescentianus in the see of Calama. He appeared among the Catholic Fathers at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 139, having already been chosen in chapter 55, together with six other bishops, to defend the Church against the Donatists. This same bishop is famous for having committed Augustine’s life to writing; for that reason he rightly obtained a place among sacred writers.

He had as an adversary Crispinus, of the Donatist sect, often mentioned by Augustine, who had died shortly before the Conference, as Petilian testified there in chapter 139, already cited. Donatus, bishop of Calama and belonging to the same sect, is listed by Optatus in book I among the traditors who had attended the council at Cirta under Secundus, primate of Tigisis.

Calama was still a celebrated city at the end of the ninth century, since it is listed first among the other cities of Numidia in the *Notitia* composed under Leo the Wise. Charles of Saint Paul was the first to publish this *Notitia* in Greek and Latin, but in mutilated form, as Guillelmus Beveregius complains. Beveregius published it complete from a manuscript in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, in the Sheldonian press, in 1672, in his notes on the canons of the Council in Trullo, volume II of the *Synodicon*, or *Pandects of the Canons of the Apostles*, etc.

Yet that otherwise learned man unjustly accuses Catholics—whom, following the custom of heretics, he calls “papists”—of unorthodox belief. He reproaches them for having either corrupted this *Notitia* in their codices or at least published it unfaithfully, supposedly in favor of the Roman pontiffs, because it enumerates far more bishoprics subject to the patriarch of Constantinople than to the Roman patriarch and assigns him boundaries by which he arrogantly claims dominion and power over the entire Christian world.

As though the prerogatives of the pontiffs of the Roman Church should be inferred from the greater or lesser number of bishops who, as they say, are subject to him by patriarchal right, rather than from the primacy granted by Christ to Peter over the other apostles—a primacy which, according to the Church’s perpetual and constant tradition, was transmitted to the successors of that see, as the Catholic Church has always believed and still believes. The holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin, taught this; and the Greeks themselves acknowledged it at the time when this *Notitia* was copied by them, for at its beginning the order of the patriarchs is arranged so that the Roman pontiff occupies the first place.

Finally, Beveregius had no reason to become so agitated against Catholics, since long before he wrote, the same *Notitia*, entirely complete and uncorrupted, had been published in 1648 by a learned Catholic, namely Jacques Goar of the Order of Saint Dominic, in the appendix to Codinus Curopalates. Codinus is one of the authors published at Paris in the royal press in the celebrated collection of Byzantine historians. But there is no time to dwell longer on these matters.

In what follows we shall cite this *Notitia* under the name “Leo’s *Notitia*.” To distinguish its various editions, we shall call one the edition of Jacques Goar, and the other that of Beveregius, or, as learned men commonly call it, the “Bodleian *Notitia*.” Some have also called it the *Notitia of Basil the Armenian*, because in Beveregius’s edition a certain Matthew the Armenian proceeds to say that he copied it.

### 4. CASTELLANUS

Among the Donatists who assembled for the Carthaginian Conference, Severinus, bishop of Castellum, is mentioned in chapter 180. It is uncertain, however, whether he was from Numidia, since cities called Castellum occur frequently in other African provinces. See below among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania, no. 75, and among the Sitifensians, no. 12.

Sallust describes Castellum as a strongly fortified place where the wealth of Jugurtha, king of the Numidians, was kept; it was finally captured by the consul Gaius Marius. Unless I am mistaken, this is the same town that Hirtius, in *The African War*, calls Castellum, situated in a fortified mountain position, into which Juba had gathered grain and other necessities for conducting the war.

In the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo published by Goar, Castellum is listed among the cities of Numidia. The Greek text, however, has Κασταβάγε; in Beveregius’s edition it has Κασταμάγαι, Latin *Castamagae*.

### 5. BURCENSIS

The Halleri codex reads *Bursensis*. The Oxford editor of the new edition of the works of Saint Cyprian judges that the Burca mentioned by Ptolemy is none other than Buruch, whose bishop Quietus delivered his judgment at no. 27 in the council of the rebaptizers under Saint Cyprian. Quietus is likewise called this by Augustine in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 34, where the holy doctor refutes his arguments. *Burucensis* could indeed have been derived from *Buruc*.

Nevertheless, in chapter 201 of the Carthaginian Conference, Lucianus, bishop *Burugiatensis* (of Burugiata), is mentioned among the Donatists.

### 6. CENTURIONENSIS

Both manuscript codices have *Centurianensis*. We have retained the reading of the printed editions, which is more consistent with the ancient records. For in chapter 202 of the Carthaginian Conference, Januarius, bishop of Centurium, was listed among the Donatists.

Optatus, book I, mentions Felix of Rotarium and Nabor of Centurion. A manuscript codex of the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Reims has *Felix a Ratorio* and *Nabor a Centurionis*. The same words occur in another manuscript of our monastery of Saint Theoderic near Reims. But *Ratorio* should be corrected to *Rotario*, as the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés reads.

From these words of Optatus, the passage in the acts of the Council of Cirta must be corrected. Augustine cites it in book III of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27, where Secundus, the primate, says, “To Felix of Rotaria, of Centurion,” etc. This reading was corrupted in the same way in the old editions of Optatus.
