That these words designate two cities, both in Optatus and in Augustine, is confirmed by the Carthaginian Conference. Besides the bishop of Centurion mentioned, as we have said, in chapter 202, Victor, bishop of Rotarium, appears among the Donatists in chapter 187.

Moreover, on the occasion of this bishop of Centurion, I may explain a passage from the *Passion of Saints James and Marianus*, which I published for approximately the year 259 among the *Sincere and Selected Acts of the Martyrs*. There, in no. 5, the magistrates of Centurion and Cirta are said to have been summoned to the aid of the *stationarius* (police officer) who was torturing the holy martyrs. In that passage Henschenius had replaced *Centurionum* with *centuriarum*, as though otherwise the sense were impossible.

I retained the reading of the ancient codices. It had not occurred to me, however, that the word *Centurionum* might designate the name of a city; this should now be evident to everyone. Indeed, from the same passage in the acts we learn the location of the city of Centurion, since those acts testify, in nos. 2 and following, that it lay not far from Cirta, or Constantina, the famous city, and from Muguis, which was a suburban settlement neighboring the same colony of Cirta.

### 7. VADENSIS

This is how both manuscript codices read, as do the printed editions. That there were two cities of this name in Numidia can be inferred even from this *Notitia*: besides Rufinianus of Vada mentioned here, Proficius of Vada is listed below, no. 117 [Col. 0294A].

Norisius, in his observations against Garnerius, thinks that the names *Vadensis* and *Vagensis* designate the same place. His view may be confirmed by the *Notitia* of Leo Augustus, in which the Greek text lists among the episcopal cities of Numidia Βάγης. In Jacques Goar’s edition this is rendered in Latin as *Vada*, but in Beveregius’s as *Bages*.

In the same Beveregian edition, no. 6 lists Βάδης, Latin *Bades*, and in the following number, *Meleum*. In Goar’s edition, however, these two cities are combined into one, called in Greek Βάδος Μηλέως and in Latin *Vagarmelita*.

At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Dativus of Badis, no. 15, and Libosus of Vaga, no. 30, gave judgments in favor of rebaptizing heretics. They are likewise called this by Saint Augustine, who answers the objection of the former in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 22, and that of the latter in the same book, chapter 37, and in book III, chapter 6.

Crescens of Vaga—or, as the Vatican copy reads, the bishop of Baga—attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus. At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 180, Pancratius, bishop of Badis, appeared among the Donatists. Baluzius thinks that he was the adversary of Potentius, bishop of Bladis, listed among the Catholics in chapter 121; the learned man believes that the names *Badiensis* or *Bladiensis* here designate the city of Vada mentioned in this *Notitia*.

Yet in the same Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215, two Catholic bishops of Vaga are mentioned, Ampelius and Primulus. Garnerius had judged that one should be called of Vada and the other of Vaga, and Norisius criticized him, since Pliny, book V, chapter 4, makes it certain that there were two cities of this name in Africa.

Ptolemy agrees: he places the first in Caesarean Mauretania in book IV, chapter 2, and the second in Numidia, which he says was under Cirta, in the following chapter. The location of the former is learned from the *Peutinger Table*. The anonymous Ravennas has Bada in Gaditanian Mauretania in book III, no. 11.

But even if there were not two cities in Africa called Vaga, nothing would need to be corrected here in the Conference, since only one city of Vaga is designated in this passage. It had two Catholic bishops at the same time: Ampelius, who had been elected and ordained by the Catholics, and Primulus, who, having previously been the Donatist bishop in that city and then having converted to Catholic unity, had been allowed to retain episcopal honor and place. Ampelius himself testified to this in the same Conference, chapter 176, where he states that from that time Catholic unity had always remained whole and inviolate in the Church of Vaga.

Therefore Privatus, the bishop of Vaga mentioned among the Donatists in chapter 177 of the same Conference, must be said to have belonged to the other city. Indeed, in the preceding chapter he had been called the bishop of Ausaga. From this Norisius infers that there was one city in Africa called Vaga which bore the additional name Ausaga.

Moreover, since chapter 179 also says that there were two Ausagas—one over which Januarius presided and the other over which Privatus presided as Donatists—the learned man concludes that there were four Vagas in Africa.

The learned Baluzius, however, shrewdly observed in his notes on chapter 176 of the same Conference that *Ausaga* was accepted here for *Vaga* only through an error of pronunciation. When the Notary had read “Privatus, bishop of Ausaga”—or, as the ancient manuscripts have it, and as the Africans seem to have pronounced it, “Ausvaga”—Ampelius, who was bishop of Vaga, did not hear the first syllable and thought that his own city of Vaga was being listed. He immediately interrupted, saying that perfect unity existed in his city. When he later understood that his own city had not been mentioned, the dispute was immediately settled.

Norisius nevertheless has some support in the fact that afterward Privatus is repeatedly called simply the bishop of Vaga in the same Conference.

In the same work, chapter 135, Valentinus, a Catholic bishop, is mentioned as bishop of Vaia; and in chapter 186, Quintasius, belonging to the Donatist sect, is said to be from the same place. In both passages Baluzius restored *Vaianensis*. See his notes on chapter 55 and the other notes cited there.

I say nothing further about Bagaia, which was made so famous both by the notorious pseudo-synod of the Donatists at Bagaia and by Donatus of Bagaia, whom those same Donatists honored so fervently as a martyr. Optatus discusses him at length in book III.

This city became still more famous because of the monstrous tortures inflicted by the Donatists upon its Catholic bishop Maximianus. Saint Augustine explains these at length in letter 85, nos. 26 and following, and frequently praises the same holy confessor. His memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 October; for that date, see the notes of Baronius. There the most distinguished cardinal collected much material about this excellent confessor.

Donatianus, bishop of Bagaia and a Donatist, also attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 176, as did Felix of Bagaia at the council of the rebaptizers under Saint Cyprian, no. 12.

From all that we have presented, anyone can easily understand how difficult it is, amid so many complications, to establish anything certain concerning the names of these cities [Col. 0295B].

We learn the location of the city of Vaga in the province of Numidia from the acts of Saint Mammarius and his fellow martyrs, which Dom Jean Mabillon recovered from the famous library of the principal Benedictine monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland and published in volume IV of the *Ancient Analecta*. There Mammarius is said to have been arrested at the city of Vaga in Numidia, not far from Lambese, another well-known city of the same province. From the same acts it may also be inferred that Tamugadi, Tigisis, and Boseth, surnamed Anforaria, were not far away.

I had almost forgotten to mention that in the ancient Carthaginian calendar, the martyrs of Vaga are commemorated on 4 Kalends of November [29 October]. Mabillon admits that they are unknown to him. Someone might perhaps suspect that they were Mammarius and his companions, whose acts we have just cited.

Although they were brought to completion in the city of Boseth, Mammarius, who was in a sense the father and chief of them all, was first arrested at Vaga and from there was led with the others through various cities. All were interrogated at Vaga and imprisoned by the count; finally they were sent to Anulinus, who was in the city of Boseth. From that time they could have been called “the martyrs of Vaga,” and that name was transmitted to posterity.

Whatever the case, we have discovered that the memory of Mammarius and his companions—whom the same learned man had thought universally unknown—is celebrated in Lorraine. Andreas Saussayus, bishop of Toul in that province, bears witness to this in the supplement to his *Gallican Martyrology*, p. 1131:

> 10 June (the fourth Ides of June). In Lorraine, the commemoration of Saint Mammarius and his companions, martyrs, whom a savage persecutor slaughtered because they persevered in one confession of the supreme Godhead.

This agrees very well with Mabillon’s acts, in which the same martyrs are also said to have suffered at the sixth hour on 4 Ides of June [10 June]. Notkerus, moreover, lists Mammarius among other African martyrs on 14 March; but neither the names of his companions nor his feast day can be reconciled with the acts. On these matters, see the Bollandists under the same date, 14 March [Col. 0295D].

### 8. NIBENSIS

The distinguished Baluzius suspects that Justus, bishop of Nicibis, who attended the Carthaginian Conference among the Donatists in chapter 201, presided over this same see. In the same Conference, chapter 197, Quodvultdeus of Nebbitum is mentioned; he is discussed below among the Byzaceni, no. 14, under Laetus of Neptitum.

Ortelius, however, thinks that *Nobensis* should be read instead of *Nibensis* in the *Geographical Thesaurus*. Yet not only the printed editions and the Laudunensis codex, but Halleri’s own codex, read *Nibensis*, as Ortelius himself testifies. See below among the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania, no. 91. The *Peutinger Table* has Nobas of Fuscianus in Numidia.

### 9. GIRENSIS

According to Baluzius, Lucianus, bishop of the Church of Guira, in chapter 125 of the Carthaginian Conference, belonged to this same place. Charles of Saint Paul suspects that this city is Gurra, mentioned in the *Peutinger Table*. Certainly there was more than one city in Africa called Giru: below, no. 52, Giru of Marcellus; no. 121, Giru of Tarasius; and among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania, no. 9, Girumontum.

### 10. CUICULITANUS

Cresconius, a Catholic bishop of the Church of Cuicul, is mentioned in chapter 121 of the Carthaginian Conference. He testified that his adversary had died. Elpidophorus, bishop of Cuicul in the province of Numidia, is mentioned in the Council of Carthage under Boniface, on the basis of another synod held under Gratus. Hence both editions of that synod in volume II of Labbe’s *Councils* must be corrected: in column 717, chapter 11, they read *Elpidophorus Cuizitanus*, or *Chuzitanus*, or *Cuicialitanus*; in column 1825, on the basis of the Vatican codex, he is called *Cuiccalitanus*.

Crescus, or Cresconius, bishop of Cuicul, subscribed the Fifth Ecumenical Council. Yet older than all these is Pudentianus of Cuicul, who pronounced a judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 71. Augustine answers his objection from the replies he had already made to the arguments of others, in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 35. This city is mentioned in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*.

### 11. AMPORENSIS

In chapter 198 of the Carthaginian Conference, Servatus, bishop of Amphora, is listed among the Donatists. Norisius thinks that this is the same man who, in chapter 121, is called the adversary of Donatus, bishop of the Church of Anbura.

Besides Norisius, the learned Jean Garnerius, in his notes on Marius Mercator, and Stephen Baluzius, in his notes on the Carthaginian Conference, also assert that Anbura and Ampora, or Amphora, were one and the same city. In the passage cited, Baluzius reads *Amburensis* for *Anburensis* and notes that in manuscript codices the letters *p* and *b*, or *o* and *u*, are frequently interchanged.

For this reason Lucas Holstenius should not be followed when he thinks that *Abbirensis* should be read for *Anburensis*.

### 12. FESSEITANUS

This is how both manuscript codices read, as do the printed editions. At first, anyone reading this passage will think of Fezza, a city celebrated in our own times in present-day Barbary, together with the kingdom bearing the same name. Some think it to be the city of Volubilis mentioned by Ptolemy, Antoninus, and other ancient writers.

But Volubilis, and the entire kingdom of Fezzan, belong to that part of Africa once called Tingitanian Mauretania; Fezza itself lies on the coast facing Spain and is therefore far distant from Numidia, to which the city of Fesseitana mentioned here belonged.

### 13. BOCCONIENSIS

In chapter 198 of the Carthaginian Conference, Donatus, bishop of Bucconium, appears among the Donatists. He must doubtless be assigned here.

### 14. DAMATCORENSIS

As the learned Baluzius advises, this should be read *Bamaccorensis* or *Vamaccorensis*. Cassianus, bishop of that place, attended the Carthaginian Conference in chapter 128 with Donatus, his adversary.

Baluzius is surprised that Donatus, in chapter 187 of the same Conference, should have said that he had no adversary among his people except Absalon, since, as the learned man says in his notes on that passage, Cassianus is named a Catholic bishop of Bamaccorum in chapter 128 and is acknowledged by Donatus.

But I am mistaken if Donatus, by the name Absalon, intended anyone other than Cassianus himself. He calls him Absalon—that is, “a rebellious son”—because, although Cassianus had previously been his Donatist presbyter, he had converted to Catholic unity and had been placed in charge of him and of the Church itself by the Catholics.

Thus in chapter 128 Donatus says: “I recognize that Cassianus; he was my presbyter.” In chapter 187, after the same Donatus had said, “I have no adversary except Absalon,” Aurelius, the Catholic bishop of Macomades, added: “This is the bishop Cassianus who is present.”

On the occasion of this bishop, Baluzius also corrects a corrupt passage from the Council of Carthage held under Saint Cyprian, a correction which the Oxford editor had already suspected. The man who, in the common editions, pronounced judgment as Felix of Amaccura or Amachorra, number thirty-eight, should be called Felix of Bamaccura.

The name of this city must likewise be corrected in Augustine, book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 40, where the holy doctor answers the objection of the same Felix [Col. 0297A]. Finally, Pliny, book V, chapter 4, mentions the city of Vamacures, which Baluzius thinks to be the very city under discussion here.

Jean Hardouin, however, seems to have a different view. Consult those authors if you wish. It is not fitting for me to set myself up as judge between such distinguished men.

### 15. AUSUCCURENSIS

This is how both manuscript codices and the printed editions read. It cannot be concealed that Felix of Amacurra, mentioned in the preceding number from Cyprian and Augustine, is called Felix of Accura or Acura in most of Augustine’s manuscript and printed copies. From this, some might perhaps think that *Auccurensis*, or *Ausucurrensis*, could have been derived.

### 16. IDICRENSIS

In the common editions of the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128, Marcianus is listed as a bishop called *Idierensis*; in the Masson edition, *Idurensis*. He is opposed by Martialis the Donatist. But this is a scribal error. For in chapter 187 the same Martialis is called *Idicrensis* in all the printed editions. Moreover, in Baluzius’s edition, which is the most carefully corrected of all, he is called *Idicrensis* in both places.

Likewise, in book II of Optatus, Felix the Donatist is called *Edierensis* in the Remigius manuscript and shortly afterward *Idicrensis*. Optatus gives a fuller account in the same book of the wicked deeds of this Felix. Antoninus mentions Idicra in his *Itinerary*.

### 17. PUTIENSIS

Chiffletius has *Puriensis*, but incorrectly. Sirmondus, from whom he copied this *Notitia*, clearly has *Putiensis*, as does the manuscript of the Church of Laon. Ortelius, on the basis of Halleri’s codex, has *Putiensis* and *Putientis*. Below, among the cities of the province of Byzacena, *Putiensis* occurs again, no. 18.

In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 204, Felix, bishop of Putiensis, appeared among the Donatists. Baluzius thinks that he is the same Felix who, in chapter 133 of the same Conference, is called the adversary of Ambibius, the Catholic bishop of the people of Pisita.

In chapter 149, Florianus, also of the Donatist sect, is mentioned as bishop of the people of Putizium; or, as Baluzius adds in his notes on this passage of the Conference, “of Putiensis in the province of Byzacena,” as is clear from the *Notitia*.

But even if it were granted that the names *Putiensis* and *Pisitensis*, or *Putiziensis*, were used interchangeably in the Conference for the city of Putea, I cannot agree that the Felix mentioned in chapter 204 was the same Felix who in chapter 133 had been called the adversary of Ambibius of Pisita.

For Felix of Putiensis was present at the Conference: he attended, appeared, issued a mandate, and subscribed. But Felix, the adversary of Ambibius, was absent from the Conference, as the Donatist deacon Valentinian testified in chapter 133; he sent a letter of excuse on account of his old age.

The learned Henri Norisius thinks that Ambibius of Pisita, of whom we are speaking, belonged to the proconsular province, and that he presided over the city of Pisita mentioned in book I, chapter 13, of the *Miracles of Saint Stephen*, under the name of Evodius of Uzalum.

From that city, therefore, there was another Pisita, or Pisida, which the learned Baluzius proves from the *Peutinger Table* to have been situated on the border of the provinces of Tripolitana and Byzacena: Pisida is placed there between Putea, a city of Byzacena, and Sabrata in Tripolitana.

Since neither Norisius’s Pisida—for he says that it lay in the proconsular province—nor Baluzius’s Pisita or Pisida—which he places on the borders of Byzacena and Tripolitana—can be assigned to the city of Putiensis mentioned here in the *Notitia*, and since the same learned man has assigned Florianus of Putizium to Byzacena, it remains that only Felix mentioned among the Donatists in chapter 204 of the Conference can be said to have presided over the Numidian city of Putiensis discussed here.

### 18. SUGGITANUS

In chapter 209 of the Carthaginian Conference, Cresconius, a bishop of Siguitum belonging to the Donatist sect, is mentioned and may perhaps be assigned here.

At the same Conference, chapter 187, Paschasius, a Donatist bishop *Tuggensis* (of Tugga), was present. The learned Baluzius thinks that he presided over the municipium of Togium, whose bishop Victor subscribed the synodical letter of the Fathers of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, cited in Session 2.

There was also a city in Numidia called Sugus, which may perhaps be designated here in the *Notitia*. Antoninus mentions it more than once in his *Itinerary*; it was twenty-five miles from Cirta, the colony and metropolitan city of the province. It is called Sigus in the *Peutinger Table*.

### 19. LAMVIRITANUS

The Laudunensis codex reads *Lamviritanus*. Ortelius, from Halleri’s codex, has *Jamviritanus*. But in some manuscript codices the letters *L* and *J* can scarcely be distinguished except by the sense. The printed editions have *Lambiritanus*.

In chapter 206 of the Carthaginian Conference, Crescentilianus, a Donatist bishop of Latambiris, openly professed that there were no traditors among his people; this was the name by which those schismatics called the Catholics.

The anonymous Ravennas, book III, no. 6, lists Lambrese and Lambridin among the cities of Numidia. Lambridi also appears in the *Peutinger Table*. There was in the same province a city called Lambese, frequently mentioned by the ancients.

Moreover, two bishops called after Lambese appear among the rebaptizers at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian in the Oxford edition, but incorrectly. See below, no. 112. I omit Felix, bishop of Lambia and a Donatist, about whom the Conference says more in chapter 201.

### 20. TAGURENSIS, OR PERHAPS TAGORENSIS

There were two Tagoras. For in chapter 133 of the Carthaginian Conference, Posthumianus, bishop of the people of Tagora, is mentioned; he professes that he possesses unity. In chapter 143, Restitutus, likewise a Catholic bishop of Tagora, is listed; he was keeper of the records.

That one of these cities was in Numidia is evident from this passage of the *Notitia*. The same conclusion follows from Antoninus’s *Itinerary* and from letter 59 of Saint Augustine, where Xantippus, bishop of Tagora, is said to have contended with Victorinus over the primacy of Numidia.

In the new edition of Augustine’s works, however, this Xantippus is called bishop of Tagosum, a see which Norisius suspects was different from Tagora, in book II of his *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 8. Indeed, as our scholars observed in their notes on the letter just mentioned, almost all the manuscripts call this bishop Tagosensis; one has *Tagonensis*.

The Louvain editors substituted *Tagastensis* for *Tagosensis*, but incorrectly, as learned men have repeatedly pointed out. Justellus made an even worse error when he thought that *Constantiensis* should be restored in canon 86 of the African Collection.

Norisius places one of the two Tagoras in the proconsular province in his observations against Garnerius, on the basis of the *Peutinger Table*, where Tagora, or Tachora, appears. This must nevertheless be distinguished from Tagarata, whose bishop, both among the Catholics and on Donatus’s side, is mentioned in the Conference, as is clear from what we said in note 43 (Col. 189) on the proconsular bishops.

In the acts of Saint Crispina, which I published from two manuscript codices of Saint Theoderic near Reims among the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, this most famous martyr is called Thagarensis in no. 2. She was harassed by the proconsul Anulinus and suffered death in the colony of Theveste, which certainly belonged to Numidia.

### 21. FOSSALENSIS

The manuscripts read this way, but the printed editions have *Fussalensis*. The case of Antonius, bishop of Fussala, is famous in African history; Augustine explains it at length to Pope Celestine in letter 209. There he writes that this city was only forty miles from Hippo and testifies that it had for some time belonged to the parish of the Church of Hippo.

The same holy doctor narrates, in book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, miracles performed there through the merits of Saint Stephen.

Source/review notes: The sentence on Felicianus in no. 71 is a source-derived sentence fragment in the draft; it requires adding “was” rather than a replacement that leaves the text unchanged.

22. **TUBUSICENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices; the printed editions, however, have *Tubursicensis*. Antoninus indeed mentions *Tubursicum* in the *Itinerary*. Pliny calls it the town of *Tuburnicum* in Book V, chapter 4. Augustine, in Letter 44, mentions Fortunius, bishop of Tubursicum, from the Donatist sect. In chapter 100 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, the city of Thubursicum in Numidia is mentioned; Maurentius the bishop is discussed there, and from the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 143, we learn that he presided over that Church. There Maurentius is said to have appeared as bishop of the Church of Tubursicum, together with Januarius, his opponent from the Donatist party. Januarius is likewise recorded in chapter 201, where he is called bishop “of Tubursicum of Numidia,” so that this city may be distinguished from Tubursicum Burae, whose bishop Servus Dei, bishop of the people of Tubursicum Burae, is recorded in the same Conference, chapter 121. He is the very man whom Augustine, in Book III against Cresconius, chapter 43, calls Servus, the Catholic bishop “from Tubursicubure.” This Church, however, is proved to have belonged to the proconsular province by the Council of Carthage under Boniface, where, among the other bishops of that province, Reparatus, bishop of Tubursicubura, subscribed. From the Conference it is clear that *Bura* was merely an additional designation of Tubursicum; for Donatus, in chapter 121, is called the opponent of Servus Dei “of Tubursicum Burae,” while in chapter 207 he is simply called bishop of Thubursicum. Norisius has already made this observation against Garnerius. It was customary among Africans to pronounce two words joined together in this way; thus below we find “the bishop of Leptiminum,” and so forth. [Col. 0299A–B]

23. **LAMSORTENSIS.** Ortelius’s Halleri codex has *Jamsortensis*; nevertheless, the common reading should be retained. For Antonianus, the Donatist bishop of Lamsortum, attended the Carthaginian Conference in chapter 149; he is again recorded under the name Antonius in chapter 163, where he openly professed that he had no Catholic opponent. Norisius says more about Antonianus of Lamsortum in his work against Garnerius. The learned man is mistaken, however, when he says that this Antonianus was nowhere called Antonius; but he rightly criticizes Garnerius, who had introduced this worst of Donatists as a Catholic bishop. Further, Florentius, the Catholic bishop of Lamsortum, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525. Among the bishops of Mauretania Sitifensis, below, no. 21, there is Vindemius of Lemfoctum.

24. **TIDIDITANUS.** Halleri’s codex has *Tiditanus*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, Lampadius, bishop of the people of Tiseditum, was listed among the Catholics, together with Donatus, his opponent; Baluzius restored this reading from chapter 198, where Donatus appeared among the Donatists as bishop of Tiseditum. Garnerius now argues, on the basis of the *Notitia*, that the text of the Conference should be emended; Norisius, on the contrary, maintains that the *Notitia* should be emended from the Conference, and therefore that *Tisiditanus* should be restored here. Baluzius leaves the matter undecided; in any event, it is sufficient that both agree that the two names designate one and the same city. Sallustius favors Norisius, since he describes *Tisidium* in his *War with Jugurtha*, chapter 62. The *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, mentioned above, appears to support Garnerius: in the Latin edition of Goar, *Tididita* is listed among the cities of Numidia, and is called in Greek Τίτισιν (*Titisin*). But Beveregius’s Greek and Latin edition has Τιτήσεον (*Titēseon*). [Col. 0299C]

25. **MONTENSIS.** Donatianus, bishop of Montenum, apparently presided over the same city; he is mentioned among the Catholic bishops in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121. [Col. 0299D] *Monte* occurs in the Peutinger Tables.

26. **NOBABARBARENSIS**, or *Nova Barbarensis*, as Halleri’s codex has it.

27. **IDASSENSIS.** Halleri’s codex has *Idacensis*. Rogatianus, the Donatist bishop of Idassum, appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 182; from this passage we infer that the city was not far from Macomadia. For when Rogatianus had professed that he had no Catholic bishop opposed to him, Aurelius, bishop of Macomadia, interjected that he had there a presbyter named Florentinus, until a bishop should be ordained for that see.

28. **NOBAGERMANIENSIS.** Halleri’s codex has *Nobagermonensis*, that is, *Nova Germania*, so called in order to distinguish it from the city of Germania, which is mentioned below, no. 97. The elders of Nova Germania are mentioned once and again in chapter 100 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. If we are to believe the Oxford editor of the works of this holy man, the confessor Jambus, mentioned as “from Germaniciana” in the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, presided over that city. But he should rather be referred to Germania, mentioned below at no. 97, as we shall say there. [Col. 0300A]

29. **VILLATICUS DE CASIS MEDIANENSIS.** He was one of the bishops who presented a statement of faith to King Huneric, as is clear from Book III of Victor of Vita, above, p. 33 (Col. 234). In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, Honorius, bishop, subscribed on behalf of Januarius, bishop of the people of Casæ Medianæ. Januarius nevertheless appeared and declared that he had an opponent from the party of Donatus named Aemilianus. This Aemilianus is listed among the Donatists in chapter 198, where he is called bishop of the people of Casæ Medianæ. Among the Byzacene bishops, below, no. 27, there is Antacius of Medianum.

30. **SUSICAZIENSIS.** Ortelius cites from Halleri’s manuscript codex a place called *Susicazium*.

31. **DE NOBA CAESARIS.** The Oxford editor of Saint Cyprian’s works thinks that this city was the same as *Vicus Caesaris*, in his notes on the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 23; there Januarius gave his opinion “from Vicus Caesaris.” Pamelius, however, writes that in that passage the name *Vicus Caesaris* designates Iol, or Julia Caesarea, in Mauretania.

32. **VAZARITANUS.** Calipodius, bishop of Vazaritum, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 188, among the Donatists; in chapter 129 he had been called the opponent of Adeodatus, bishop of the people of Bazaritum. A learned man otherwise of the highest distinction carelessly confused this city with the Byzacene city of Vararitana, discussed below, no. 70. A place called Vazaritum is mentioned in chapter 54 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. That place, however, seems to have belonged to the proconsular province. For Epigonius, bishop of Bullensium Regiorum, complains against Julianus that, although he had baptized a cleric and appointed him lector in the Church of Mappalia, Julianus nevertheless ordained him a deacon on the pretext that he was a citizen of Vazaritum; and, in support of his own case, he invoked the authority of Victor of Puppiana’s ordination. Epigonius and Victor of Puppiana, however, were from the proconsular province. Yet since it is not said there to which province Julianus belonged, and since the diocese of Bullensium bordered Numidia, nothing prevents Julianus from being called a Numidian, against whom Epigonius brought complaints before the council in the presence of the primate of all Africa. The Peutinger Tables contain *Vatari* and *Bararus*. [Col. 0300B–C]

33. **TIGILLABENSIS.** Donatus, bishop of Tigillabum from the party of Donatus, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215. Earlier, in chapter 133, he had been called the opponent of Reginus, bishop of Tigillavum.

34. **RESSANENSIS.** Octavianus, bishop of the people of Ressanum, belonged to the same place. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, he professed that he possessed Catholic unity. Verissimus, the Donatist bishop of Tacaratum, nevertheless complained in chapter 121 that four bishops had been ordained by the Catholics in his community; among them he listed Octavianus. Baluzius thinks that this was the same man who is called Ressanensis in chapter 126.

35. **AUGURENSIS.** Without doubt Montanus presided over this city; he is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, where he is called “bishop of the Catholic Church of Auguritana,” that is, of the Catholic Church of Auguritana. The common editions, joining the last two words into one, had called him “bishop of the Cathauguritan Church,” as Baluzius notes in his remarks on this passage of the Conference. Augustine mentions the estate of Audurus in Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. [Col. 0300D]

36. **OCTABENSIS.** Among the fathers of the province of Byzacena, no. 38, there is Albinus of Octavum, and at no. 24 Sabinicuus of Octabium. Ortelius, however, does not find either of these in Halleri’s codex, although he mentions the city of Octavum from other authorities. In the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 78, Victor “from Octavum” gave his opinion. Optatus, Book III, mentions a place called *Octavum*, where very many Circumcellions were killed.

37. **MADENSIS.** Thus both the manuscripts and the printed editions. The *Book of the Lists* mentions the frontier district of Madum, section 55.

38. **MATHARENSIS.** Honoratus, the Catholic bishop of Matharum, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 120; he had no Donatist bishop opposed to him. [Col. 0301A]

39. **CENTENARIENSIS.** Cresconius, bishop of Centenarium, was listed among the Catholic fathers in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, although bodily illness prevented him from being present. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna lists *Centenaria* in Book III, no. 6. The Peutinger Tables have *Ad Centenarium* in segments 1 and 2.

40. **GILBENSIS.** There is also, below at no. 90, Donatus of Gilbum. From this it may be inferred that there were two cities of this name in Numidia. In the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Lucius “from Castrum Galba” gave the seventh opinion among those who rebaptized. On this passage the Oxford editor observes that Galba and Gilba designate the same place, and that there were two cities of this name, one distinguished by the addition *Castrum*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, Victor, bishop of Gibbum, was listed among the Donatists. Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 7, mentions Urbanus of Girba, who perhaps should be assigned to one or the other of these cities. For he was not from Tripolitana, where there is also a bishop of Girba. Victor distinguishes Urbanus—that is, the bishop of Girba—from the Tripolitans. Indeed, in the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525, besides Vincentius of Girba from Tripolitana, there occurs Donatus, bishop of the people of Gervitum. [Col. 0301B]

41. **MIDILENSIS. Confessor and Martyr.** Jader of Midila attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, concerning the rebaptism of heretics; Augustine answers his objection in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 9. Baluzius had judged that Serenianus presided over the same city; in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 142, he is called bishop of Miditum. But Baluzius corrected this error in his note on chapter 194 and at the end of volume I of the *New Collection of Councils*, col. 1591. We nevertheless have a bishop of Midilum in the same Conference, namely Julianus, the Donatist bishop of Midila; since he was absent because of illness, the presbyter Rufinus appeared and subscribed in his place, chapter 142.

42. **TABUDENSIS.** Victorinus, bishop of the people of Tabudum, presided over this city, as Baluzius restored the text in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133. There the reading had previously been *Tabudesenen­sis*. Shortly afterward Victorinus himself says that he is bishop of Tabudum, and in chapter 202 Argutus, his opponent from the Donatist sect, is called bishop of Tabudum. The Peutinger Tables have *Thabudeos*. Paulus, bishop of Tabucum, subscribed among the bishops of the proconsular province to the synodical letter read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. [Col. 0301C]

43. **CASENSI–CALANENSIS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Fortunatus is called bishop of the place Casæ Calanæ. Furthermore, the city of Casa Calanea is mentioned in the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, edited by Goar; in Beveregius’s edition, however, it is called *Cascala*. In both places the Greek text has Κασκάλα (*Kaskala*), evidently through the omission of the final syllables of each of the two words.

44. **PUNENTIANENSIS.** Thus both manuscripts, together with the printed editions. It must nevertheless unquestionably be read *Pudentianensis*. For in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, Cresconius, bishop of Pudentianum, is mentioned as belonging to the party of Donatus. Gregory the Great, Letter 33, Book II, indiction 10, likewise mentions Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Pudentiana, situated in Numidia; after being corrupted by money, he had allowed a Donatist bishop to be ordained in his own city.

45. **NOBASPABSENSIS.** Halleri’s codex has *Nobaspartensis*. Ortelius, however, shortly before this mentions *Nova Sparsa*; and Antoninus mentions *Novae Sparsae* in the *Itinerary*, from which it is clear that this city was situated not far from Sitifis.

46. **METENSIS.** Gratianus, bishop of the people of Metum, presided over the same city in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126. Baluzius corrected the reading from an ancient manuscript codex, since it had previously been *Metenensis*. This emendation is confirmed by the fact that Fortunatianus, who in chapter 126 is called Gratianus’s opponent, is also called bishop of Metum in chapter 187 in the other editions. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book V, no. 6, has *Mata*. [Col. 0302A]

47. **CAESARIENSIS.** It can be inferred from the Acts of Saint Maximilian, which we published above among the genuine acts of the martyrs, that there was a city of Caesarea in Numidia. There Praepositus of Caesarea is mentioned as having appeared before the proconsul Dion in the forum at Theveste. As everyone knows, Thebeste belonged to Numidia. In the Carthaginian Conference, besides Deuterius, bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania, who is mentioned in chapter 143 with Emeritus from the party of Donatus, there occurs in chapter 188 Cresconius, the Donatist bishop of Caesarea; he nevertheless appears to have been from Mauretania Sitifensis. For in chapter 189 Novatus, the Catholic bishop of Sitifis, testifies that a Catholic presbyter was present in that city, and explains at greater length how many evils the Donatists had committed there.

48. **NOBASINENSIS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, Restitutus, bishop of the people of Novasinnum, is listed among the Catholics together with Felix, his opponent from the party of Donatus; Felix is again mentioned among the Donatists in chapters 187 and 208. [Col. 0302B]

49. **CAELIANENSIS.** Thus both manuscripts, together with the printed editions.

50. **JANUARIUS JACTERENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices. The printed editions, however, have *Zactarensis*, a reading that seems preferable to the other, not only because Zactara is a very well-known city of Numidia, but also because one of the four bishops who presented a statement of faith to King Huneric was Januarius of Zattara in Numidia, as Victor of Vita testifies in Book III, p. 33 (for us, col. 234). See note 139 (Col. 234, note e), where some manuscript codices have *Zatterensis* for *Zattarensis*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128, Licentius, bishop of the people of Zattara, was listed among the Catholic fathers. Felix, bishop of Zactara, a legate of Numidia, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525, and another council in the same city under Archbishop Reparatus in the year 534. We also have Cresconius, bishop of Zattara in the province of Numidia, who attended the Fifth General Council, as may be seen in Baluzius, volume I of the *New Collection of Councils*, col. 1498.

If, however, someone wishes to distinguish the bishop of Jacterum, who is mentioned here in the *Notitia* according to the manuscript codices, from Januarius of Zattara, who presented a statement of faith to Huneric, he may support his own view by the example of Boniface of Gratianum. Although Victor listed him among those who presented that same statement to the king, he nowhere appears in the *Notitia*. Moreover, Januarius of Zactara, who presented the statement of faith, was earlier than Villaticus of Casae Medianae, whom Victor places before him in the passage cited; yet here in the *Notitia* Januarius is listed at no. 50, although Villaticus’s name had already been recorded at no. 29. [Col. 0302C]

51. **DE CASTELLO TITULI.** Halleri’s codex has *Castello Titulitano*. Joannes Garnerius judged that Cresconius, bishop of the people of Titulus, mentioned among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, had at some time presided over this see. Norisius, however, criticized him on this point. For Victor, who is said there to have been Cresconius’s opponent, is called bishop of Titulitanum in chapter 202. The bishop of Titulitanum, however, was from the proconsular province, as we saw above among the bishops of that province, no. 51. [Col. 0302D]

52. **DE GIRU MARCELLI.** From Halleri’s codex Ortelius has *Giga Marcellae*. The place is equally unknown to me under either name. Lucidus, bishop of Marcelliana, perhaps presided over it; he appeared among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133. Julianus “from Marcelliana” also attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. In Augustine, Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 30, some printed editions and most manuscripts call him *a Marcellina*.

53. **THARASENSIS.** Among the Byzacene fathers below, no. 32, there occurs Domninus of Tarasum. Ortelius cites from Halleri’s codex the city of Tarazum, mentioned by Victor of Utica; but he does not indicate the province. Zozimus of Tharassa attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian; Augustine answers his objection in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 20. [Col. 0303A]

54. **SILLITANUS.** Faustinus, bishop of the people of Sillitum, presided over the same city; he appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128, together with Possidonius, his opponent. Baluzius does not distinguish this Possidonius from Possidius of Sililitum, or, as he himself reads it, of Silitum, who is listed among the Donatists in chapter 197. Furthermore, the same learned man also assigns to Numidia Squillacius, bishop of the Church of Scillitum, mentioned with Donatus, his opponent, in chapter 143 of the same Conference, on the basis, he says, of the *Notitia*. Yet in the *Notitia* there is no bishop of *Scillitum*, whereas *Sillitanus* occurs only once.

Indeed, it is clear that the city of Scillitum belonged to the proconsular province from the synodical letter of the bishops of that province to Paulus of Constantinople, which was read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. Among others, as we have already observed in the notes on Victor, Pariator, bishop of the holy Church of Scillitum, subscribed. Add to this Speratus and the other martyrs, famous under the name of the Scillitans, who were brought before the proconsul at Carthage and condemned by him, completing their martyrdom, as is clear from their acts, which we published among the genuine acts of the martyrs, p. 77.

It must nevertheless be admitted that in the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, among the cities of Numidia, there is Σκήλη (*Skēlē*), which in Goar’s version is called *Scilita*. But that the provincial divisions had by then been altered is clear from the fact that Carthage is there assigned to Byzacena. [Col. 0303B]

55. **HIZIRZADENSIS.** Thus both codices and the printed editions. Baluzius judges that Felix, bishop of Izirianum, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, belonged to the same place. But it is uncertain whether the *Notitia* should be emended from the Conference, or the Conference from the *Notitia*.

56. **MUNICIPENSIS.** I do not know how it escaped the learned Joannes Garnerius that he confused this city with the municipium of Mopta in the province of Mauretania Sitifensis. For Mopta, or rather *Mopti*, is called a municipium for no other reason than that it was not a colony—that is, a city granted the Latin right—but a city that lived under municipal law, as the learned Norisius observes. Hence Felix the Donatist, who in chapter 143 of the Carthaginian Conference is called the opponent of Leo, bishop of the municipium of Mopta, is later called simply the bishop of Mopta in chapter 180 among the Donatists. [Col. 0303C]

57. **ARSICARITANUS.** Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts.

58. **CASENNIGRENSIS.** Halleri’s codex has *Cassenigrensis*. Everyone knows the famous Donatus “from Casæ Nigræ,” the principal leader of the nascent Donatists, from whom, as most learned men think, they took their name. Among all the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 149, Januarinus, bishop of Casæ Nigræ, is listed first. [Col. 0303D]

59. **VASELITANUS.** Halleri’s codex has *Vesolitanus*. It should unquestionably be written *Vegeselitanus*. There were two cities of this name in Africa. For in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, Reginus, bishop of the Church of Vegesilum, is mentioned together with Gavinus the Donatist, his opponent; earlier, in chapter 133, Privatianus, bishop of the people of Vegesilum, had already been listed among the Catholics.

One of these cities certainly belonged to Numidia, both from this passage of the *Notitia* and from the Council of Carthage under Boniface, where Januarius, bishop of Vegesilum in the province of Numidia, subscribed on his own behalf and on behalf of Januarius of Masculum. This is undoubtedly the city of Megesela, which Antoninus places near Masculum in the *Itinerary*. Privatus, bishop of Vegesela (*Vegesilitanus*), attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus; and Augustine, in Letter 64, praises the Vigisilitan people (*Vigisilitanam plebem*) because they steadfastly refused to receive a bishop who had been deposed in a plenary council of Africa.

There is likewise mention of the estate of Vegesela in Numidia, where the famous Donatist Marculus and others of the same sect were, as they claimed, mistreated by the Macarians, in the *Passion of Marculus* edited by our Mabillonius in volume IV of the *Analecta*. There it is written *Vaegesselae*, but in the Corbie manuscript, against which we collated this passion, it reads *Vegesele*.

The learned Baluzius proves that the other Vegesela belonged to Byzacena from the *Itinerary* of Antoninus, in which Vegesela, or Vegersalla, is placed among the cities of Byzacena between Amudarsa, Autentum, Sufetula, and Meneges, or Menefes. He confirms the same from the Conference, where the Privatianus mentioned above admits that he had a Donatist bishop of Cillitum as his opponent. Donatus of Cillitum, appearing there, acknowledged Privatianus and testified that Vegesela had belonged to his diocese.

“But the city of Cillitum belonged to Byzacena,” says Baluzius, “as is certain from the *Notitia* itself,” since among the fathers of that province below, no. 64, Fortunatianus, bishop of Cil(l)itum, is mentioned. Yet we shall show there that two cities called Cillitum may be admitted; consequently, one could have belonged to Byzacena and the other to another province, namely Numidia, if it can otherwise be proved that both Vegeselae belonged to Numidia.

Indeed, if Januarius of Velesilum, listed below at no. 20, presided over the other Vegesela, two cities of this name in Africa must be admitted. The passage of Antoninus cited above is no obstacle; from it, as Norisius observes, nothing more can be inferred than that Vegesela lay on the border of Byzacena and Numidia. [Col. 0304A–B]

60. **MADAURENSIS.** A city famous because Apuleius was born there, but much more fortunate because Augustine learned literature there, as he himself testifies in Book II of the *Confessions*, chapter 3. See also his Letter 232. The same holy teacher defends the martyrs of Madaura against the grammarian Maximus in Letter 17. Ptolemy places Madura under the Third Legion Augusta in Book IV, chapter 3. Antigonus, bishop of Madaura, attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, Placentinus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Madaura, appeared together with Donatus, his opponent from the Donatist sect. In his notes on this passage of the Conference, the learned Baluzius points out and proves that some have wrongly confused the city of Madaura with Quidia. [Col. 0304C]

61. **RUSTICIANENSIS.** Leontius, the Donatist bishop of Rusticianum, appeared in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198, and professed that he had no opponent. The Peutinger Tables have *Rustici*. Macomadia Rusticiana is mentioned below at no. 84.

62. **VILLADEGIENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices. It should be read *Villaregensis*. Felix, bishop of this place, attended the Carthaginian Conference, together with Victor the Donatist, his opponent, in Baluzius’s edition, chapter 128. Victor is again mentioned among the Donatists in chapter 207. In chapters 48 and 77 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, Cresconius, bishop of Villaregum in Numidia, is censured because, having abandoned his own see, he had invaded the Church of Tubia. Augustine, in Book II against the Donatist Cresconius, chapter 10, praises Candidus, bishop of Villaregum, for whom episcopal honor was preserved after he had become Catholic from being a Donatist.

63. **BUFFADENSIS.** The most distinguished Stephanus Baluzius suspects that the bishop of this place was Hilarus, who in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 120, is called bishop of the Church of Bofetum, or, as other editions have it, *Bofet*. But perhaps *Boset* would be a better reading there. Nor is it an obstacle that below, in chapter 126, Palatinus is listed as bishop of Bosetum together with Felix, his opponent, who in chapter 202 is called *Vosetanus*. Palatinus belonged to the proconsular province, as Baluzius infers from the letter of the proconsular bishops reported at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. Among the signatories was Cresciturus, bishop of the Church of Busitum, or, as the Beauvais manuscript has it, of Bositum.

We have, however, another city called Boseth in Numidia, from the Acts of Saints Mammarius and his companions, published by our Joannes Mabillonius in volume IV of the *Analecta*. That city is mentioned three times in the acts: first it is called the city of Boseth Amphoriaria, secondly simply the city of Boseth, and finally the city of Boseth Amphoriaria. We infer that this city belonged to Numidia because the aforesaid martyrs were driven through various cities of Numidia—namely Vaga, Lambaesis, Thamugadi, and Tigisis—and were finally brought by Numidian soldiers themselves to Boseth, where they completed their martyrdom. [Col. 0304D–0305A]

64. **SISTRONIANENSIS.** Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts. [p. 131]

65. **TIPASENSIS.** Below, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 99, there is Reparatus of Tipasa. The Peutinger Tables, Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, and the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, Book III, no. 6, mention Tipasa in Numidia. Firmus, bishop of the Church of Tipasa and legate of the province of Numidia, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525. The same Firmus—or a successor of the same name and see—attended the Fifth General Council as bishop of Tipason in the province of Africa.

66. **TIBILITANUS.** Ortelius’s copy of Halleri’s codex has *Tiblitanus*. Joannes Garnerius argues that Donatus, the bishop of Tisilita, who is listed among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, presided over this city. Against him, however, stand the learned Henricus Norisius and Stephanus Baluzius, who decisively prove that the city of Tibilitum must be distinguished from Tisilita, on the basis of this very passage of the Conference, which Garnerius had cited to establish his own view.

For there Donatus of Tisilita openly professed that he had no Donatist bishop opposed to him, and no one objected. Yet in chapter 197 Sallustius, bishop of Tibilitum, appeared among the Donatists; he too asserted that he had no Catholic bishop opposed to him. Moreover, Florentius, bishop of Tisilia, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525.

A more serious difficulty is whether the city of Tibilitum mentioned here should be distinguished from Aquae Tibilitanae. Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae, a Donatist, occurs in Optatus, Book I; he is the very man who attended the Council of Cirta among the Donatist traditors, as Augustine relates from the acts of that council in Book III against the Donatist Cresconius, chapter 27. The same Augustine, in Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, reports a miracle that occurred at Aquae Tibilitanae in memory of Saint Stephen, under Proculus, bishop of that place.

The anonymous geographer of Ravenna has *Tibili*, but does not mention Aquae Tibilitanae. Since the Peutinger Tables nevertheless have both *Thibilis* and Aquae Tibilitanae, I would readily believe that there were two distinct cities. [Col. 0305B–C]

67. **SINITENSIS.** Possidius testifies in the *Index* that blessed Augustine delivered a sermon against the Donatists at Sinitum. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 202, Cresconius, bishop of Sinitum from the party of Donatus, appeared. Near the city of Hippo there was a Castle of Sinitum, according to Augustine, Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. See also his Letter 105, no. 4, where Marcellinus, bishop of that place, is discussed; Baluzius suspects that his name has fallen out of the acts of the Carthaginian Conference. The Peutinger Tables have the colony of *Sunitum*.

68. **CETHAQUENSUSCA.** The learned Baluzius observes that this monstrous name arose as follows. In an old exemplar the word had been written *Cethaquensis*. A reader, noticing that the first syllable of the name had to be changed to *ca*, wrote these two letters in the margin. Later scribes, joining them with the earlier reading, produced *Cethaquensusca*. From this he infers that Pascentius, mentioned here in the *Notitia*, presided over the same city as Bonifacius, who in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 143, is called bishop of the Church of Cataquum. There Speratus, the Donatist opponent of Bonifacius, is also recorded, as he is again below in chapter 202. Finally, Saint Augustine discusses the bishops Paulus and Bonifacius of Cathaquum in Letter 96 and the following letters of the Benedictine edition. [Col. 0305D]

69. **TEGLATENSIS**, or *Tegulatensis*. Donatus, the Donatist bishop of this place, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198. It is surprising that Carolus a Sancto Paulo counts this Donatus among the bishops of Sardinia, in which island he places Tegula between Sulci and Nora in his *Sacred Geography*. *Teglata* occurs in segment 3 of the Peutinger Tables.

70. **ZABENSIS.** Halleri’s codex also mentions this place. There was also a city of Zabum in Mauretania Sitifensis, whose bishop is listed among the bishops of that province at no. 40. Lucius, a bishop of Zabum from the party of Donatus, who attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198, belonged to one or the other of these cities. In the already cited *Notitia* edited by Goar, under the province of Byzacena—which incorporates several cities from the proconsular province, Numidia, and Byzacena—there occurs *Zabi*. In Beveregius’s edition it is called *Subiba*, and in both editions the Greek reads Σούβιβα (*Soubiba*). Holstenius thinks that this is the royal city of Zama. [Col. 0306A]

71. **MUSTITANUS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, Victorianus, bishop of the people of Mustitum, is mentioned. He complains there that he has two Donatist opponents, namely Felicianus of Mustitum and Donatus of Turris. Augustine discusses them in the brief summary of the first day’s conference, chapter 12.

Henricus Norisius nevertheless argues in his observations against Garnerius that these bishops belonged to the proconsular province, where he finds the cities of Mustum and Turris. He proves the former from the synodical letter of the fathers of the proconsular province, cited at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2; among the signatories was Januarius, “by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Mustitum.” In the Conference, chapter 122, Felicianus was asked whether he was in communion with Primianus, who was the bishop of Carthage from the sect of Donatus and therefore from the proconsular province. To be entirely candid, however, the issue there was not the province, but the schism that had arisen among the Donatists themselves, some adhering to Primianus and others to Maximianus.

That Felicianus was one of those who attended the Council of Cabarsussum in the year 393 and was condemned the following year in the Council of Bagaium. Augustine frequently mentions the Mustitans together with the Assuritans in his books against the Donatists. The Assuritans belonged to the proconsular province, as we saw above (Col. 282).

According to Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, Musti lay on the border of the two provinces, the proconsular province and Numidia. I believe that it is the same place called *Mubsi* in the Peutinger Tables. Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 3, mentions the village of *Muste* between the two Syrtes. Furthermore, *Thurris Sicilibae*, which appears near it in the Peutinger Tables, seems to have been assigned to the same proconsular province. We shall discuss this city again below, among the Byzacene bishops, no. 28.

Although Norisius admits a city of Mustitum in the proconsular province, he nevertheless does not deny that another city of the same name existed in Numidia. Its bishop, a Donatist named Cresconius, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 206, where he is called bishop of Musti. If this view is admitted, Baluzius’s emendation must be rejected, since he substituted *Musertitanus* for *Musti*. But, as the learned man himself observes, this was conjectural; for he admits that the old exemplar, together with all the printed editions, reads *Musti*. See below, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 76. [Col. 0306B–C]

72. **TUBUNIENSIS.** Norisius observes in his *Remarks against Garnerius* that the name of this city must be written *Tubuniensis*, although in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, the reading is Cresconius, bishop of the Church of Tubinium. Take care, however, not to confuse this city with Tubium in Mauretania Caesariensis. That they were different can be demonstrated by the fact that, besides Cresconius mentioned above and Protasius, his opponent, Felix, bishop of Tubium, appeared in the same Conference, chapter 133; he too was a Catholic.

That a city of Tubuna nevertheless existed in Mauretania Caesariensis is certain. Indeed, later in this same *Notitia*, Tubuna is listed among the sees of that province that had no bishops. Nemesianus of Thubuna, the fifth among those who gave their opinions in favor of rebaptizing, spoke at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian; Augustine refutes his objections at greater length in Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 12.

Augustine had held a conversation at Tubuna with the comes Boniface, who at that time wished to abandon everything and embrace the monastic life. After Boniface had fallen into worse things, Augustine recalled this conversation to him in Letter 220. Ortelius, however, citing Victor, as he says, the manuscript of Victor of Utica, mentions *Tubania* as a place in Numidia. But *Tubania* has entered here through a scribal slip for *Tubunia*. [Col. 0306D–0307A]

73. **AQUAENOBENSIS.** Felicianus, bishop of Aquanovum, appeared among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198.

74. **BABRENSIS.** So too Halleri’s codex in Ortelius.

75. **TEBESTINUS.** The colony of Thebeste was very famous; blessed Crispina, whose glorious martyrdom made it illustrious, suffered there. We published her acts from two manuscript codices of our monastery of Saint-Thierry near Reims among the genuine acts of the martyrs under the year 304, p. 494. Lucius of Thebeste gave his opinion at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian in favor of rebaptizing heretics, no. 31; Augustine answers him in Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 38. Romulus Thebestensis was present at the Council of Carthage under Gratus. At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, Urbicus, Catholic bishop [Col. 0307B] of the people of Thebestis, attended with Perseverantius, his adversary, who is again listed among the Donatists in chapter 180; there he is called the bishop of Tevestis, under which name he had previously subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussa. Optatus also mentions a Donatist synod of Thevestis in Book II.

Ptolemy calls it Theveste in Book IV, chapter 3, as does the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and the Peutinger Tables. It would be superfluous to collect more about this city from ancient writers. Procopius asserts in Book II of *The Vandalic War* that it was six days’ journey from Carthage. There, as the same author reports, the Romans fought the Moors, in which battle Solomon, whom the emperor Justinian had appointed over Africa, was killed. Finally, in the Bodleian *Notitia* Tebete is listed among the cities of Numidia. But Goar’s Latin edition has *Telepte*, while the Greek has Τελέστη (*Teleste*).

76. **MOXORITANUS.** Thus the Laudun manuscript, together with the printed editions; the Halleri manuscript, however, as cited by Ortelius, has *Maxoritanus*.

[Col. 0307C] 77. **TAMOGAZIENSIS.** Thamugadi, or, as others write it, Tamugada, was famous among the other cities of Numidia. On it the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius collected much material in his notes to the *Acts of Caecilianus’s Purification*, volume II of the *Miscellanies*, p. 480. Novatus of Tamugadi, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 4, judged that heretics ought to be rebaptized; Saint Augustine refutes his objection in Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 11.

There were two celebrated bishops of this same city from the Donatist sect: namely Optatus, frequently mentioned by blessed Augustine, whose birthday the Donatists celebrated; and Gaudentius, whom those same schismatics, together with six other bishops of their sect, chose to defend their common case against the Catholics at the Conference. At that conference he appeared together with Faustinus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Thamugadi, chapter 128. Saint Augustine wrote two books against this same Gaudentius; they are included in volume IX of the Benedictine edition.

The Peutinger Tables have *Tamogadi*, and the *Itinerary of Antoninus* *Tamugadi*; it is likewise called [Col. 0307D] this in the acts of Saint Mammarius, already cited by us, from which we learn that this city was not far from Vaga, Lambese, and Tigisi. It was destroyed by the Moors, as Procopius testifies in Book II of *The Vandalic War*; but from the same author it may be inferred that it was restored shortly afterward, since he writes a little later that it possessed a very abundant supply of grain.

78. **LEGIENSIS.** Januarius Legensis is mentioned below, no. 85. From the Carthaginian Conference we infer that there were two cities called Legensis in Africa. For in chapter 121 Dacianus, Catholic bishop of the people of Legensis, declared that he had no Donatist opponent. But in chapter 187 Cresconius, bishop of Legensis on Donatus’s side, professed that he neither had nor had ever had an opponent. Perhaps in one of the two passages of the Conference *Legiensis* should be read for *Legensis*; or certainly *Legensis* should be written in both places in the *Notitia*. Baluzius further believes, in his notes to chapter 121 of the Conference, that the diocese of Legensis, over which Dacianus presided, had been separated from Tacaratensis.

79. **RESPECTENSIS.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions.

80. **VALESITANUS.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. See what we observed above concerning Veselitanus, no. 59. The Peutinger Tables have *Velesi*, in segment 3.

81. **MAZACENSIS.** At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215, Apronianus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Mazacensis, gave his assent to the mandate to which he had not subscribed because of his absence.

82. **LUGURENSIS.** Thus the Laudun manuscript together with the printed editions. The manuscript codex cited by Ortelius, however, has *Jugurensis*.

83. **CIRCENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices. The printed editions, however, have *Cirtensis*. Indeed, nowhere else in this *Notitia* is a bishop of Cirta, or Constantina, mentioned, although it was the metropolis of the province, as it is called in the code of the canons of the African Church, chapter 86. In the old Lyon edition of the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, *Circa* is found almost everywhere in place of *Cirta*.

Pamelius notes, in his observations on the Council of the Rebaptizers under Saint Cyprian, that Augustine’s Letter 130 was addressed *Circensibus* rather than *Cirtensibus*. He reports several examples showing that *Circa* was often written for *Cirta* in ancient monuments; yet no one will deny that this arose solely from scribal error. In the letter just mentioned, now numbered 144, the reading has been corrected to *Cirtensibus*.

Nevertheless, it was not permissible here to alter the manuscript reading, since many other cities occur elsewhere in this same *Notitia* that are otherwise unknown, while some otherwise very famous cities are omitted—perhaps because at that time they lay destroyed, such as Hadrumetum, Hippo Regius, and others. Certainly the *Notitia* lists only fifty-four episcopal cities in the proconsular province, whereas Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 9, asserts that at the time when the Vandals crossed into Africa there were 164 bishops in the proconsular province.

Moreover, among the bishops who attended the Council of Chalcedon, Abramius, bishop of Circensis, is mentioned [Col. 0308C]. But he does not seem to have been from Africa. More relevant is Rufinus Principalis of Circensis, mentioned by Augustine in Letter 139, otherwise 158. Although our editors substituted *Cirtensis*, they nevertheless noted that three manuscript codices and an equal number of printed editions have *Circensis*.

84. **PARDALIUS MACOMADIENSIS.** This appears to be that same Pardalius who, as bishop, attended the Roman council in 487 with three other African bishops. Henry Noris distinguishes three cities of this name in Africa; their locations can easily be determined from Antoninus.

He places the first in Numidia, 53 Roman miles from Cirta. The second, called Macomades Minores in the Peutinger Tables, he places between Thabalta and Thenas, cities of the province of Byzacena, and shortly afterward between Thenas and Vicus Villas, then Tacapas. From this we learn that it lay on the border of Byzacena and Tripolitania. The same is clear from Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, where, listing the cities of Byzacena, he writes [Col. 0308D]: “Rhuspina, Thapsus; then Thenae, Macomades, Tacape, Sabrata.” The cities listed before Macomades belonged to Byzacena; those that follow belonged to Tripolitania. Hence the Macomadian frontier is placed under the command of the duke of Tripolitania in the *Notitia of the Western Empire*.

Finally, the third city, Macomades of the Syrtis, occurs on the route from Leptis Magna to Alexandria; it is therefore entirely different from those mentioned above.

At the Carthaginian Conference, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Macomades, frequently spoke, and appeared among the Catholic Fathers in chapter 116 with his adversary on Donatus’s side, Sallustius. That he was from Numidia is clear from chapter 182, where he testified that he had a presbyter in the city of Idassa while a bishop was being ordained there. Idassa certainly belonged to Numidia, as is clear from this very *Notitia*.

The other Macomades mentioned in the same Conference must therefore be assigned to Byzacena. For Garnerius alone devised two Macomades in Numidia, without the testimony of any author, ancient or modern. We learn from chapter 197 of the Conference that this city was called Rusticiana. There Porficentius, a Donatist bishop of Macomaziensis, appeared and professed that he had no opponent. Fortunatianus, the Catholic bishop, asked from which Macomades he came; when Porficentius replied, “from Rusticiana,” Fortunatianus said nothing further.

Cassius of Macomades took the side of the rebaptizers at the Council of Carthage, no. 22; Augustine answers his objection in Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 29. The same Augustine praises Donatus, bishop of Macomades, who had abandoned the Donatist schism and passed over to the unity of the Catholic Church, in Book II of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 10. Ptolemy has *Macodama* in Book IV, chapter 3, for *Macomada*.

85. **LEGENSIS.** See above, *Legiensis*, no. 78. It is absent from the Halleri codex.

86. **AD TURRES CONCORDI.** In Ortelius, from the Halleri codex, it is called *Turris Concordiae*.

87. **LAMFUENSIS.** Ortelius, from the Halleri codex, has *Jamfuensis*. In the Laudun codex that we examined, the first letter is formed in such a way that it can equally be read *Jamfuensis* or *Lamfuensis*. The reading of the printed editions is supported by the Carthaginian Conference, where, in chapter 133, Safargius, bishop of the people of Lampuensis, is listed among the Catholic Fathers. Pontius, bishop of the people of Lamfuensis, also subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius doubts whether the town of Lemfoctum, praised by Ammianus Marcellinus in Book XXIX, was the same as this city of Lamfuensis. We shall remove this doubt in our notes on the bishops of Sitifis, no. 21, where we restore the city of Lemfoctum from the manuscript codices.

88. **VAGRAUTENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices together with the printed editions.

89. **TIGISITANUS.** We learn the location of this city from the acts of Saint Mammarius, already cited more than once. From them it may be inferred that Vaga, Lambese, the place called Ad Centum Arbores, Tamugadi, Tigisi, and Boseth were not far from one another. Procopius mentions Tigisim as a city of Numidia in Book II of *The Vandalic War*.

Secundus Tigisitanus, primate of Numidia during the persecution, who presided over the Council of Cirta, is famous in the history of the Donatists. Optatus discusses him in Book I *Against Parmenianus*; Augustine in Letter 43 to Glorius [136] and others, formerly numbered 162; and frequently in his books against the Donatists. More about him was contained in the third hearing of the Carthaginian Conference, chapters 137 and following, as is clear from the index published by the learned Baluzius in volume I of the *New Collection of Councils*. But the actual proceedings have perished; they can nevertheless be supplemented to some extent from Saint Augustine’s *Brief Summary* of the same Conference, in which much concerning Secundus Tigisitanus is found in chapter 13 and following of the third day of the Conference.

There were two cities in Africa called Tigisis. For below, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 27, Passitanus Tigisitanus is mentioned. *Tigisi* and *Thigisi*, besides *Thiges*, occur in the Peutinger Tables.

Indeed, at the Carthaginian Conference, in addition to Sollemnius, the Catholic bishop of the people of Tigisis, and Paschasius, his Donatist opponent, mentioned in chapter 135, Gaudentius, bishop of the Tigisitani place and a member of the Donatist sect, is listed in chapter 209. Since he had remained behind on the journey because of illness, Cresconius, bishop of Siguitanum, subscribed in his place.

Which of these should be assigned to Numidia is uncertain. Baluzius infers that Sollemnius was a Numidian because Restitutus—who, he says, can be no one other than the Novasinnensis bishop in Numidia—subscribed in his place. But Cresconius of Siguitanum subscribed for Gaudentius. Sugus was in Numidia, 25 Roman miles from Cirta, as is certain from the *Itinerary of Antoninus*; and in segment 2 of the Peutinger Tables, Tigisi is placed midway between Sigus and Cirta, while in segment 3 *Siguese* is mentioned. Above, no. 18, Victor Suggitanus is also listed [Col. 0310A].

There was nevertheless a colony called Siga in Mauretania Caesariensis, mentioned by Ptolemy in Book V, chapter 2, which Antoninus calls the municipium of Siga. Some may therefore suppose that Cresconius was called Siguitanus from this place.

90. **GILBENSIS.** Felix Gilbensis was already listed above, no. 40; there we said more about this city.

91. **REGIANENSIS.** Ortelius also mentions this one from Victor. Sirmondus gives only the name; but in the Laudun manuscript the abbreviation *prbt.* [“presbyter”] is added, as with most of the other names.

Gregory the Great, Book X, Letter 32, writes to Columbus, bishop of Numidia, concerning a certain Paulinus, bishop of Regensis, who had been accused before the most holy pontiff. I would rather believe that this man presided over the Church of Regianensis than over Regiensis, listed below in Mauretania Caesariensis, because Gregory seems there to be speaking of a bishop from the province of Numidia. See Sitifis, no. 37.

92. **SILENSIS.** Baluzius suspects that Saturnus, the Donatist bishop of Sitensis mentioned in chapter 197 of the Conference, may be assigned here. But the bishop of Sitensis belonged to Mauretania Caesariensis; he is listed below among the bishops of that province, no. 112.

93. **GAUDIABENSIS.** Thus the printed editions and manuscripts. In chapter 201 of the Conference, Saturninus, bishop of Gazabianensis, is listed among the Donatists. Antoninus’s *Itinerary* has *Glaudi* in Numidia.

94. **MARCULITANUS.** I think *Masculitanus* should be read. Nevertheless, it was not permissible to alter the reading of either manuscript codex. In the geographical index prefixed to the Oxford edition of the works of Saint Cyprian, besides *Mascula* there is also *Marculi* in Numidia, but perhaps this derives from this passage of the *Notitia*.

Mascula, however, was a city of Numidia known to everyone. At the time of the Carthaginian Conference, Malchus, bishop of the people of Masculitana, presided there; he is listed in chapters 128 and 201 with Vitalis, his opponent. Long before this, Clarus of Mascula, a confessor, had attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. Januarius, bishop of Masculitanus, likewise subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. Donatus Masculitanus, a Donatist, is mentioned more than once by Optatus in Book I and by Augustine in Book III *Against Cresconius*, from the acts of the Council of Cirta, which he attended with other traditors of the same sect. Victor of Vita praises Archinimus Masculanus in Book I, no. 15. On him see note 52 (Col. 199, n. d).

95. **CENTURIENSIS.** In chapter 87 of the code of the canons of the African Church, Quotvultdeus, bishop of Centuriensis, is mentioned. I believe he is the same man who is listed among the Catholics at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, with Cresconius, his opponent on Donatus’s side. Procopius testifies in Book II of *The Vandalic War* that a fortress called Centuriae existed in Numidia.

96. **SUABENSIS.** Thus the printed editions, from the Laudun codex. The Halleri codex has *Suavensis*, which is the same reading. Litorius, Catholic bishop of the people of Suavensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133. Garnerius incorrectly called the place *Suanensis* [Col. 0310D] in order to make him a bishop of Sugunensis; Noris rightly criticized him for this.

97. **GERMANIENSIS.** The anonymous Ravenna geographer, Book III, no. 6, mentions the city of Germani, and the Peutinger Tables have *Ad Germani*. Above, no. 28, Florentius Noba Germaniensis was listed. The author of the Oxford edition of Saint Cyprian’s works believes that Innocentius, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Germaniensis mentioned at the Carthaginian Conference, presided there. The same author assigns to that place the confessor Jambus of Germaniciana, one of the rebaptizers who attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. It is more plausible, however, that he should be assigned to this city of Germania, with which we are here concerned.

The same learned man is also mistaken in assigning Germaniciana, as he says, to the new province of Byzacena, since it is certain from this very *Notitia* that both Germania Nova and the other city simply called Germania belonged to Numidia. Antoninus, however, seems to admit a Germaniciana in Byzacena in his *Itinerary*. Augustine, who himself was a Numidian, testifies in Letter 251 that the Germaniciani belonged to his care.

Moreover, at the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419, Candidus, bishop of Germania, subscribed in chapter 133 of the code of the canons of the African Church. But this bishop belonged to Abbir Germaniciana. For in another codex, as Justellus notes, he is called “bishop of the Church of Abitinensis, of the Church of the Germaniciani”; and in the preface to the same council he is called Candidus Abbiritanus. In Labbe’s edition, volume II of the *Councils*, column 1603, he is called Abbiritanus or Abderitanus, and in column 1605 Abbiritanus, otherwise “of the Germaniciani.” In both places, however, he is listed among the bishops of the proconsular province.

Successus of Abbir Germaniciana, mentioned in the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 16, presided over this city. See the note on Victor of Vita above, p. 75 (Col. 209, n. c).

98. **VADESITANUS.** Thus both manuscript codices together with the printed editions. [Col. 0311B] According to the distinguished Baluzius, Cresconius, the Donatist bishop of Baiesitanus mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, presided over this city. He believes him to be the same Cresconius who is called, in chapter 126, the opponent of Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Undesitana; for this reason that learned man corrected the reading there to *Vadesitanae*.

99. **GAURIANENSIS.** Thus it is written in both manuscript codices and in the printed editions. Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 2, mentions *Garra*; and below, in Byzacena, no. 22, Secundinus Garianensis is mentioned.

100. **NARATCATENSIS.** The Halleri codex has *Narateatensis*. Our reading is confirmed by the Council of Carthage under Boniface, to which Columbus, bishop of the people of Naraccatensis, subscribed.

101. **LAMIGGIGENSIS.** Thus the Laudun manuscript codex. The printed editions have *Lamiggizensis*. Our reading is better, although a bishop Lamiggigensis is again found below. It is clear from the Carthaginian Conference that there were two cities of this name. In chapter 133 Innocentius Lamiggigensis is listed with Junianus, his Donatist opponent, who also appeared again in chapter 298. In chapter 187 Recargentius, the Donatist bishop of Lamiggigensis, is mentioned; he professes that he has no opponent.

This restored reading removes the difficulty noted by the learned Baluzius, who, in his notes to chapter 187 of the Conference, suspects that *Lamiggizensis* should be read there for *Lamiggigensis*. Likewise, in the more recent catalogues, where *Lamiggiza* has been introduced, it should be restored to *Lamiggiga*. In the Halleri codex, as Ortelius reports, one of these cities is called *Lamigginensis*, the other *Jamigginensis*. See Gregory the Great, Book I, Letter 82, where Argentius is called *Lamigensis*.

102. **GARBENSIS.** Felix Garbensis, a prominent Donatist, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 209.
