In the common editions of Optatus, bishop of Milevis, Book I, he is called *Garbiensis* or *Gabriensis*; in two manuscript codices—one of Saint Remigius of Reims and the other of Saint-Thierry near that city—he is called *Gardensis*; in a third, belonging to Saint-Germain-des-Prés, he is called *Gabrensis*.

Victor, sent by those same Donatists to Rome so that he might hold the episcopate of their sect there, is called *Garbiensis* in Book II of the same editions of Optatus, but *Garbensis* in the manuscripts cited above. Victor of Garbe is mentioned in the acts of the Council of Cirta preserved by Augustine, Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27.

103. **VAGARMELITANUS.** The Halleri codex has *Vagormelitanus*. It should be written *Magarmelitanus*, as Baluzius rightly observes in his notes to chapter 126 of the Carthaginian Conference, where Secundus, bishop of the people of Magarmelitana, is listed with Felix, his opponent, who was also present among the Donatists in chapter 298.

This Secundus mentioned in the Conference is, I believe, the same man who subscribed to Leporius’s *Book of Correction*, published by Sirmondus, in these words: “Secundus, bishop of the Church of Aquae (Aquensis), or of Megarmitana.” In the letter written on that occasion to the Gallican bishops, he is called Secundinus.

[Col. 0312A] In the *Notitia* composed under Leo the Wise, the city of Vagarmelita is listed among those of Numidia in Goar’s edition. The Greek text, however, has Βάδης Μηλέων (*Bades Meleon*); Beveregius’s edition divides this into two cities, Βάδης and Μηλέων, Latin *Bades* and *Meleum*, which are listed as numbers 6 and 7.

104. **FORMENSIS.** Below, no. 108, a bishop Formensis is again mentioned. One of the two was Justus, the Donatist bishop of Formensis, for whom, when he was ill, Martialis Idicrensis subscribed at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 209. The same must be said of Urbanus, the Donatist bishop of Formensis, whom Optatus discusses in Book II.

105. **DE TURRES AMMENIARUM.** Others, as Carolus a Sancto Paulo notes in his *Sacred Geography*, have *de Turres Armeniarum*. The Halleri codex has *Turris Sammeriarum*.

106. **BALESASENSIS.** The Halleri codex has *Balesasensis*. Baluzius suspects that this is the same city whose bishop, Adeodatus Belalitensis, was listed among the Catholic Fathers at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126.

107. **FATENSIS.** Ortelius, citing Victor of Vita, mentions a place called Facensis in Mauretania Sitifensis that possessed an episcopal see. But no bishop of this name is listed below among the bishops of that province.

108. **FORMENSIS.** Ponticanus Formensis was already listed above, no. 104.

109. **MULIENSIS.** The Halleri codex, cited by Ortelius, also mentions this one. At the Council of Carthage under Boniface, Marianus, bishop of the municipium of Tulliensis from Numidia, subscribed as a legate. We observed above that Latinus, the bishop of Mugia and a member of the Donatist sect, subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussa. *Milia* occurs in the Peutinger Tables.

110. **OSPITENSIS**, or, as it would seem, **HOSPITENSIS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, Benenatus, Catholic bishop of the people of Hospitensis, occurs. When, in chapter 133, he had asserted that there was no other bishop in his place, Lucullus, the Donatist bishop, said: “Persecution has always driven me away.” In chapter 198 the same Lucullus, bishop of Hospitia, professed that he had two Catholics opposed to him, one of whom had only recently been ordained. This evidently means that, when Lucullus had been driven from Hospitia and had withdrawn to some town of the same diocese, the Catholics there ordained a bishop to oppose him.

Carolus a Sancto Paulo, however, thinks that *Ospitensis* should be read *Ospinensis* in this *Notitia*, and he praises Leo, bishop of Ospinensis, mentioned at the seventh Council of Carthage. But the same author, when discussing Mauretania Caesariensis, places Oppinum in that province, a place mentioned by Ptolemy in Book IV, chapter 1; he says that Leo, bishop of Oppinum, presided there and subscribed to the seventh Council of Carthage. The sole Leo of Oppinum subscribed to this synod, and indeed from Tingitana, as we shall say below when discussing Byzacena, no. 82, and Sitifensis, no. 33, under the heading **MOZOTENSIS**.

111. **VAGADENSIS.** The Halleri codex has *Vagradensis*. Donatus, bishop of Vageatensis, mentioned among the Donatists at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 180, perhaps belonged to this same place.

Bagrada is otherwise a famous river of Africa, which had a city bearing the same name. Livy writes that Roman envoys were seized there by the Carthaginians in violation of the law of nations. The anonymous Ravenna geographer, Book III, no. 6, mentions the city Bagradas and the river Bagrada.

I favor the opinion of those who believe that the city called Vagadensis here is the town of Bagai, so famous in the history of the Donatists. On it see more above, no. 7 (Col. 293).

112. **LAMASUENSIS.** This city is called *Lamasbua* in the Peutinger Tables and *Lamasba* by Antoninus in his *Itinerary*. The Carthaginian Conference permits both readings: in chapter 128 Avitus, bishop of the people of Lamasuensis, is mentioned with Januarius, his opponent, who in chapter 187 is called *Lamasbensis*.

Pusillus, bishop of this same city, attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian in favor of rebaptizing heretics; Augustine answers his objection in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 39. In the Oxford edition he is called Pusillus of Lambesa, but this is, I think, a scribal error. The earlier editions, together with Augustine, have “of Lamasba”; and, indeed, in the same synod, no. 6, Januarius of Lambese had already been mentioned.

113. **TACARATENSIS.** I do not know how Holstenius and Harduinus came to write in their notes on Pliny, Book V, chapter 3, that this bishop was so called from the city of Tacatua. There was a city called Tacarata in Numidia, whose diocese was so extensive that Verissimus, its bishop on Donatus’s side, complained at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, that the Catholics had established four bishops in his diocese.

Among these, Aspidius, bishop of the people of Tacaratensis, is listed in the same place. Learned men think that the others were Datianus Legensis, Octavianus Ressianensis, and Fortunatus Casensis Calanensis, who attended the Conference. Verissimus, in the passage cited, listed four Catholics opposed to him, but did not give the names of the towns in which they had been established.

We do not, however, deny that there was a city called Tacatua in Numidia, and indeed a famous one, praised by Ptolemy in Book IV, chapter 3, by Antoninus in his *Itinerary*, by Pliny in Book V, chapter 3, by the anonymous Ravenna geographer, and by the Peutinger Tables. From Antoninus’s *Itinerary* we infer that it was situated between Rusucada and Hippo Regius.

We also have a Tagarata distinct from these; concerning it, see Tagura among the proconsular cities, no. 43, in Numidia, no. 20, and Tagariata in Byzacena, no. 37.

114. **MILEVITANUS.** Optatus, bishop of Milevis, made this see illustrious; everyone knows his books to Parmenianus on the Donatist schism, which have often been printed. His name is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 4 June among the holy confessors.

Several synods were held in this same city, among them the famous one held in 416 concerning the Pelagians. Its synodal letter to Pope Innocent survives among Augustine’s letters as no. 176, and that pontiff confirmed it in Letters 182 and 183 of the Benedictine edition.

Adeodatus, bishop of Milevis and a member of the Donatist sect, was chosen with six other bishops to conduct his sect’s case against the Catholics at the Carthaginian Conference, where he frequently spoke. Severus, the Catholic bishop of the same city, had died shortly before, as is stated in chapter 215.

Antoninus’s *Itinerary* has *Mileum*; the Peutinger Tables have the colony *Mileu*. At the Council of Cirta, Secundus, the primate, rebuked Purpurius of Limata for killing two sons of his sister at Mileum. Carolus a Sancto Paulo distinguished this city from Milevis, but other learned men disagree.

115. **ULLITANUS.** The Halleri codex, cited by Ortelius, has *Villitanus*, perhaps for *Vallitanus*, as Holstenius thinks in his annotations to Carolus a Sancto Paulo. Indeed, Boniface, bishop of the people of Vallitanus, is listed among the Catholic Fathers at the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135.

According to Optatus, Book II, Boniface Ballitanus succeeded Victor Garbensis, the Roman bishop of the Donatists, as they themselves claimed. Antoninus and the Peutinger Tables place *Vallim* in the proconsular province. Certainly Restitutus, bishop of the people of Vallitana, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface. But at the same synod Restitutus Viltensis and Porpirius Vullensis are mentioned; perhaps one of the two should be assigned here, if he belonged to Numidia.

116. **SELEUCIANENSIS.** Ortelius, from the Halleri codex, has *Seleuciamensis*. At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, Terentius, Catholic bishop of Seleucianensis, appeared with Messianus, his Donatist opponent, who is mentioned again in chapter 206. In the edition of Papirius Massonus, however, chapter 121 has *Solencianensis*, while chapter 206 has *Seleuciamensis*. Perhaps Ortelius copied the name of this city from the latter passage, since he cites the Carthaginian Conference together with a manuscript of Victor.

117. **VADENSIS.** We have said more about this city above, no. 7.

[Col. 0314A] 118. **TAGASTENSIS.** The Halleri codex, cited by Ortelius, has *Tagartensis*. This was a famous and prosperous city, which gave birth to the great Augustine and had as its bishop Alypius, Augustine’s friend. He attended various councils of the African Church and frequently spoke at the Carthaginian Conference, where he was one of the seven bishops chosen to defend the cause of the Catholic Church against the schismatics.

The same Augustine praises the steadfastness of Firmus, bishop of Tagaste, in his book *On Lying*, chapter 13: Firmus was unwilling to lie and could never be compelled, even by the most atrocious tortures, to betray a man whom he had concealed. His memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 31 July.

It would be superfluous to say more about Tagaste. In Antoninus’s *Itinerary* it is placed midway between Hippo Regius and Naraggara.

119. **MAXIMIANENSIS.** The Halleri codex has *Maximinensis*. At the Council of Carthage in 525 under Boniface, Peter the abbot, defending the liberty of his monastery, cited the example of the monastery of Baccis. Although it was near the Church of Maximianensis, it nevertheless resorted for consolation to the primate of the province of Byzacena.

Liberatus, primate of Byzacena, mentions the Maximianenses in his letter to Boniface of Carthage concerning the Council of Junca. From the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 29, it may be inferred that this city was not far from Ruspe. There that holy bishop is praised for suppressing quarrels among neighboring communities, especially for calming the anger of the people of Maximianensis, who refused to accept the bishop ordained for them.

In the synodal letter of the Fathers of the province of Byzacena, read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin in session 2, Boniface, bishop of the holy Church of Justini and Maximiensis, subscribed among the others.

120. **ZARADTANSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices; the printed editions have *Zaradtensis*. Baluzius cites the Council of Carthage of the year 525, but there a bishop Zactarensis subscribed. At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128, Cresconius, bishop of the people of Zaraitensis, was listed with Rogatus, his opponent, who also appeared among the Donatists in chapter 203.

Ptolemy mentions Zaratha, which he lists among the cities of Mauretania. More suitable here is the city of Zarat in Numidia, which Antoninus places near Lamasba in his *Itinerary*.

121. **DE GIRU TARAZI.** It was not possible to find this city in Ortelius from the Halleri codex.

122. **LAMIGGIGENSIS.** This see was discussed above, no. 101.

123. **VICOPACENSIS.** The name of this town is, I believe, *Vicus Pacis*. The Halleri codex has *Vicuspacensis*. Asterius, bishop of the people of Vicensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 143, with Urbanus, a Donatist bishop, who in chapter 206 is called bishop of Vicensis; yet neither of them knew the other.

Baluzius suspects that these passages designate a bishop of Vicipacensis, although, as he himself continues, there were other cities in Africa called Vici. Florentianus Vicopacatensis, a legate from Numidia at the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525, is better assigned here; there he is also called Vicopacensis.

[Col. 0314D] *124. THERE ARE 125 IN NUMBER.* Yet only 123 are listed; perhaps some were omitted through the negligence of copyists.

## TO THE PROVINCE OF BYZACENA

* **VASSINASSENSIS AND AQUIS.** In the printed editions these words are placed after several dots, as though what had previously stood in the codex could not be read. We have reproduced them exactly as they appear in the Laudun manuscript, in which nothing at all appears erased or damaged, leaving everyone free to judge the matter as he wishes.

Nevertheless, there can scarcely be any doubt that these words once designated two sees. Ortelius cites an episcopal place in Africa called Vassitanus, from Victor of Vita; it occurs nowhere else in the *Notitia*. At the Council of Chalcedon, session 15, Valerianus Bassianensis from Africa subscribed.

[Col. 0315A] 1. **AMUDARSENSIS.** Sirmondus has: “Liberatus of Amudarsa, *per.*” But in the same Laudun manuscript it reads: “Liberatus, *prb.* [‘presbyter’], of Amudarsa.” In the Masson edition of the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, we read: “Maius, bishop Plenius Auvidarsensis”; other editions have *Amudarsensis*. Baluzius corrected the passage as follows: “Majus, bishop of the people of Amudarsensis,” that is, of the same city mentioned here in the *Notitia*.

Indeed, the ancient writers mention Amudarsa, which, as the same learned man observes, Ptolemy and the older editions of Antoninus’s *Itinerary* call *Amurdasa*. Bertius’s edition of Antoninus has *Amudarsa*.

2. **MANSUETUS AFUFENIENSIS.** Thus both manuscript codices together with the printed editions. This appears to be the same Mansuetus whom Victor of Vita praises in Book II, no. 16. On him see the note above, 93 (Col. 215, n. b).

3. **SEPTIMUNICIENSIS.** Thus the printed editions and manuscripts. Antoninus mentions Septimunicia in his *Itinerary*. Ferrandus also reports several canons of the Council of Septimunicia in his *Brief Summary*.

[Col. 0315B] 4. **BENEFENSIS.** We learn the location of this city from chapter 14 of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, where a monastery near the shore is praised—Vicensis, or, as other codices have it, Juncensis—lying for the most part contiguous to Benefensis. Fulgentius withdrew there because the ancient discipline of a rigorous way of life was preserved there.

Guntasius, bishop of Benefensis, subscribed to the Donatist Council of Cabarsussa. At the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Aemilianus, Catholic bishop of the Church of Benefensis, was present on the very day when his opponent Maximianus died, as the Donatists stated both there and in chapter 198.

5. ANCUSENSIS. The bishop of this same place was Donatus, a bishop of the Donatist sect, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208. Baluzius thinks that he was the same Donatus who, in the commonly printed editions, is called the adversary of Gududi, bishop of Aniusensis or Avinsensis, in chapter 126. Hence he himself substituted Ancusensis for Aniusensis.

[Col. 0315C] 6. MIDIDITANUS. This is perhaps the bishop called Meditlitanus in Haller’s manuscript. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208, Liberalis, bishop of Milidiensis, is listed among the Donatists; Baluzius suspects that Mididiensis should be read instead. Likewise, in the Life of Saint Fulgentius, chapter 12, where the printed editions mention the city of Ididi, the same learned man notes that Mididi is found in the old Colbert manuscript. Moreover, in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 142, Serenianus, bishop of Miditensis, is mentioned, whom some may perhaps think should be assigned here. For he belonged to the province of Byzacena. When he had professed that he possessed Catholic unity, Peregrinus, the Donatist bishop of Sufes, replied: “I have Victor there as presbyter; the diocese is mine.” No one can deny that Sufes belonged to Byzacena, since it is mentioned below, no. 21.

7. TUBULBACENSIS. Haller’s manuscript has Tubolbacensis. Our reading is preferable. For in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, Januarius, a Catholic bishop of the people of Tubulbacensis, is mentioned.

[Col. 0315D] 8. VADENTINIANENSIS, or Valentinianensis. For in the synodal letter of the Council of Byzacena to the Emperor Constantine, which was read in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in session or secretary’s record 2, the last among others to subscribe was Rodibaldus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Valentinianensis. In Haller’s manuscript a bishop of Vadaciniensis in Africa is mentioned.

9. MASCLIANENSIS. If Ortelius has read Haller’s manuscript correctly, it has Masdianensis. Antoninus mentions Masclianas in the Itinerary. Plutianus, a Donatist bishop of Masclianensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208. In this connection the learned Baluzius observes that, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Julianus a Masclianis was present among those who rebaptized. But I have not been able to find him in the printed editions, nor does Augustine mention him in his books On Baptism against the Donatists, in which he refutes one by one the objections of the prelates who attended that council. Indeed, I would be mistaken if this Julianus mentioned by Baluzius were not the same as Julianus a Marcelliana, who is mentioned by Cyprian and Augustine, as we said above in note 52 under Numidians. Nor should one say that Marcelliana and Mascliana were the same city. For in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Lucidus, bishop of the people of Marceltianensis and Basitensis, says that Catholic unity was present among his people; yet, as we said shortly before, Plutianus, the Donatist bishop of Masclianensis, appeared in chapter 208. Likewise, through the error of copyists, Numidius, who is mentioned at the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, was called Masclianitanus in volume II of the Council editions of Labbe, column 1160. For that bishop was Massylitanus, as is clear from the appendix to the same volume, where that council is corrected from the Vatican manuscript, and from chapter 8 of the code of the canons of the African Church.

10. SEBERIANENSIS. Thus both the printed editions and the manuscripts.

11. NARENSIS. Antoninus mentions Nara in the Itinerary. Januarius, a bishop of Narensis from the Donatist sect, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 206.

[Col. 0316B] 12. DECORIANENSIS. The name of this city is written with a single different letter in the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers to the Emperor Constantine against the Monothelites. This letter was read and approved in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in session or secretary’s record 2; among others, Paschasius, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Detorianensis, subscribed to it.

13. TAMBEITANUS. Victor of Vita, book V, no. 5, mentions the city of Tambaia. The martyr Secundianus from Thambeis attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 80; Augustine resolves his objection in book VII of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 44. Gemelius, bishop from Tambeis, subscribed, with the other bishops of the Donatist sect, to the Council of Cabarsussis. Finally, in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198, Faustinus, likewise a Donatist and bishop of Tambeiensis, appeared. He is doubtless the same man who, in chapter 128, is called the adversary of Sopatrus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Tambalensis. Hence the learned Baluzius restored Tambaiensis there.

[Col. 0316C] 14. LAETUS NEPTITANUS. This is the celebrated martyr whom Victor of Vita praises in book II, no. 18; we have said more about him in note 98 above (col. 217, no. c). Nepte is mentioned by the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, book III, no. 5. Baluzius suspects that Quodvultdeus, bishop of Nebbitanus, belonged to this same city; he was listed among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 197.

15. CUSTRENSIS. Haller’s manuscript has Custensis. The printed editions have Castrensis. I have thought it best to retain the reading of the Laon manuscript until a reason for changing it presents itself. Castra appears in the Peutinger Table, but outside Byzacena.

16. FLABIANUS BULELIANENSIS. The printed editions have Flavianus Bubelianensis. Apparently the index prefixed to the works of Saint Cyprian, following them, mentions Bubelia; Ortelius likewise has this form from Haller’s manuscript. The same author mentions Bulula, an inland African town captured by Cornelius Balbus, citing Pliny as his witness. But Pliny, book V, chapter 5, among the towns whose images Cornelius Balbus brought in triumph, lists Buluba and the nation of the Bubeii.

17. THEUZITANUS, or Theuditanus. For, as we have already observed, among Africans the interchange of the letters z and d was common. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, mentions Theudensis among the free towns. Haller’s manuscript, however, has Zteusitanus.

18. SERBANDUS PUTIENSIS. The printed editions have Servandus. For more about the city of Putiensis, see above, page 122 (col. 297, no. 17), where Gaudentius Putiensis is discussed under the Numidians, no. 17. Add to this that the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, book III, no. 5, lists Putea and Ad Putea among the African cities. Ptolemy lists Putea among the cities situated under Hadrumetum; it should therefore be assigned here.

19. THAGAMUTENSIS. Milicus, bishop of the people of Tagamulensis, belonged to this place; he is mentioned among the Catholic prelates in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126. Baluzius said that this city was the same as Tadamatensis, listed below among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania, no. 105.

[Col. 0317A] 20. PRAESIDIUS SUFETULENSIS. This prelate is praised by Victor of Vita, book II, no. 16, and in note o on this passage (col. 215, no. b). Privatianus from Sufetula sat at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian among those who rebaptized, no. 19. Jocundus, bishop of the people of Subfetulensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 127, together with Titianus, his adversary. Titianus likewise appeared among the Donatists in chapter 208. Moreover, the same Jocundus was a legate of the province of Byzacena to the Council of Carthage in 419, as we learn from that same synod and from chapter 127 of the code of the canons of the African Church. Ferrandus praises the Council of Sufetula in chapter 2. Finally, Antoninus mentions Sufetula in the Itinerary.

21. EUSTRATIUS SUFETANUS. The manuscript has Eustrasius. We have nevertheless retained the common reading, since Victor of Vita himself confirms it in book I, no. 7, page 7, where Eustratius is praised. He is called Eustachius by Ado, however, as also in the Roman Martyrology, on 28 November. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 20, Privatus from Sufes delivered his judgment; Augustine responds to him and to Privatianus Sufetulensis, mentioned in the preceding entry, in book VI of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapters 26 and 27. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 142, when Serenianus, bishop of Miditensis, had been named, Peregrinus, the Donatist bishop of Sufetanus—also so called in chapter 187—immediately replied, asserting that this place belonged to his diocese, where he had a presbyter named Victor. In chapter 215, Maximinus Sufetanus—or, as other editions have it, Sufetus, bishop—appears among the Catholics who had not yet subscribed. Sufes, moreover, is mentioned in Antoninus’s Itinerary. At the synod of Sufetana, blessed Fulgentius humbly begged the Fathers to grant Quodvultdeus, the bishop, a place above himself, as is related in his Life, chapter 29. Augustine, in letter 50, mentions sixty martyrs from Sufes, whom the inhabitants of this town slaughtered because they had broken an image of Hercules. The Roman Martyrology commemorates them on 30 August.

[Col. 0317C] 22. GARRIANENSIS. Ortelius, from Haller’s manuscript, has Garrensis. This reading supports the opinion of the Oxford editor of Saint Cyprian’s works, who thinks that Victor from Gor, mentioned in the Council of the Rebaptizers, no. 40, may be assigned to this city of Garrianensis. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, has Garrha, but among the cities of Mauretania. The distinguished Baluzius, however, thinks that Gattianensis should be read here, because Victor, a Donatist bishop of Gatianensis, is listed in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198; and because among the four bishops who offered a profession of faith to King Huneric in Victor of Vita, near the end of book III, there was Bonifacius Gattianensis. This opinion has the disadvantage that the Gattianensis bishop who presented the statement of faith to Huneric is called Bonifacius by Victor, whereas the bishop of Garrianensis mentioned here in the List is called Secundinus. Nor can one easily persuade oneself that Secundinus had then been appointed Bonifacius’s successor, when this List was written. For, as even its title shows, it lists the bishops who had assembled for the Carthaginian meeting by order of King Huneric; moreover, Secundinus was among the earlier bishops, since he was at least twenty-second out of one hundred and seven. If, nevertheless, anyone prefers the opinion of the distinguished Baluzius, then Januarus too must be said to have presided over the same see: he was, by the grace of God, bishop of the holy Church of Gatianensis and subscribed to the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. See the notes on Victor, page 81.

23. ABARADIRENSIS. Ortelius, from Haller’s manuscript, gives Abaradira as an African bishopric.

24. SABINICUUS OCTABIENSIS. The printed editions have Sabinianus. See Numidians, no. 36, where Pascencius Octabensis is discussed.

[Col. 0318A] 25. MACTARITANUS. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Marcus from Mactari delivered his judgment among those who rebaptized, no. 38; Augustine refutes his objection at greater length in book VII of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 2. In the Carthaginian Conference, however, Comparator, bishop of Mactaritanus, was listed among the Donatists. Finally, Pliny, book V, chapter 4, counts Matterense among the free towns. The learned Joannes Harduinus judged this to be the same as Mactaritanus. But perhaps Matterense—which, as Harduinus admits, all manuscripts prefer—fits better with the town of Mattaritanus, listed below at no. 50, than with Mactaritanus.

26. AQUIABENSIS. The Laon manuscript has only Aquiaben. Among the Donatists who subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussis was Januarius, bishop of Aquenensis.

27. ANTACIUS MEDIANENSIS. The printed editions have Autacius. Donatus, bishop from the Medianes of the Zabunii, was listed among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 202. But he seems to have belonged to Sitifian Mauretania. For there Novatus, bishop of the Catholic Church at Sitifis, professed that he had ordained a presbyter in that city over the body of the deceased Catholic bishop, to govern this Church until a bishop could be consecrated there as soon as possible. Below, however, among the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania, no. 86, appears Valentinus, bishop of Castellum Medianum. Hadrianus Valesius thinks that this place is mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus; we shall discuss it there.

[Col. 0318B] 28. TURRENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, Maximianus, a Catholic bishop of the people of Turensis, is mentioned; he declared that he had no Donatist adversary. Nevertheless, in chapter 197 Pascasius, bishop of Turensis, appeared among the Donatists; through a lapse of memory Baluzius assigned him, from the List, to Numidia. For in the List this is the only Turrensis among the Byzacenes, while none is listed in Numidia. We do not, however, dare to deny that there was one bishop of Turensis in Numidia. For Donatus Turensis and Felicianus Mustitanus are called the adversaries of Victorianus, the Catholic bishop of the people of Mustitana, in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121. Mustitana belonged to Numidia, or at least to the proconsular province, as we explained above in the notes on the Numidians, no. 71. Thus this Donatus presided over a third Turensis, distinct from the two mentioned above.

We therefore have, from the Conference, three bishops of Turrensis in Africa, and indeed from different provinces. That one of them belonged to Byzacena is certain from the List we are explaining. Baluzius assigns the second to Sitifian Mauretania on the basis of the Bodleian List, in which Turris—or, as Goar’s edition has it, Tures—is listed among the cities of the second Mauretania. But, unless I am mistaken, this Turris mentioned in the Bodleian List was outside Africa and therefore cannot be assigned to Sitifian Mauretania. It is the city listed below, no. 6, among the cities of the island of Sardinia; this can be demonstrated from the Bodleian List itself, where Turris, the metropolis of Calaris, and Sulci—both certainly belonging to Sardinia—are listed together.

Nor should “second Mauretania” in that List be understood as Sitifian Mauretania, since Sitifis itself is listed outside that province, namely in Numidia. Likewise, the “first Mauretania” mentioned here was not Caesarean Mauretania, since only the city of Rhiconorura—or rather, as Goar’s edition and both Greek texts have it, Rhinocorurum—is listed. Finally, there was another city of Turensis, which had been torn away by the Donatists from the diocese of Mustitana; it must be assigned either to the proconsular province or to Numidia, as we have said. Samfacius, bishop of the people of Turrensis, seems to have presided over it; Augustine discusses him in letters 34 and 83.

Finally, I would have the reader note that a bishop of Turrensis or Turensis is written indifferently in the authors, a fact that could be established by many arguments. One example will suffice: Donatus is called bishop of Turensis in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, but in Augustine’s Brief Summary of the same Conference, day 1, chapter 12, he is called Turrensis.

29. AGGARITANUS. The city of Aggaritana occurs again below, no. 108. Aemilianus, bishop of Aggeritensis, presided over one or the other of these cities; he appeared among the Catholic prelates in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, together with his adversary Candorius from the Donatist sect. Candorius is also mentioned in chapters 149 and 163. Hirtius, in his book On the African War, mentions the town of Agar in Byzacena. Aggar appears in the Peutinger Table, not far from which Aggar Selnepte, and then Agarsel, can be seen; near the former Aggar lies Aggerfel, which, however, seems to have been situated in the proconsular province.

Moreover, Pliny, book V, chapter 4, lists Acharitanum among the free towns—or, as other manuscripts have it, Accharitanum or Accaritanum. The distinguished Joannes Harduinus thinks that this name designates the city of Aggaritana, mentioned in the List, over which Donatus presided. It is the same city listed below at no. 108. I readily admit that Pliny’s passage may be assigned to either of the two; but it is impossible to determine which of them Pliny intended.

30. EGNATIENSIS. Thus both manuscripts together with the printed editions. I have nowhere been able to find this city.

31. GERMANUS PERADAMIENSIS. This is the same man who is praised by Victor of Vita, book II, no. 16. See note 93 on that passage (col. 215, no. b). Unless I am mistaken, this is the same city that Hirtius calls Parada in his book On the African War, where he describes its pitiable fate. Lucas Holstenius suspects that this city was Ferradum Minus, over which Felicianus, bishop of the people of Feraditana Minor, presided; he is mentioned among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133.

32. ERMIANENSIS. Facundus Hermianensis made this a celebrated Church; he wrote twelve books to the Emperor Justinian in defense of the Three Chapters. Benadus, bishop of Hermianensis, subscribed to the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. This city is more often written with an aspirate, as is clear from the examples cited and from the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, where Secundinus, bishop of the people of Hermianensis, appears with his adversary Maximianus. In the old editions, however, this same Maximianus is called Ermianensis in chapter 187. Procopius, book I of The Vandalic War, mentions Hermion, a place in Byzacena.

33. TENITANUS. Haller’s manuscript has Tevitanus. Pliny, book V, chapter 4; Antoninus in the Itinerary; and the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, book III, write Thenas with an aspirate; the latter has Thaenas in book V. Thus also Gruter, page 363, where Mercurialis Thaenit. is mentioned. Ptolemy writes Theaenae. Ferrandus praises the Council of Thenita in his Brief Summary of the Canons. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 29, Euchratius from Thenas delivered his judgment among those who rebaptized. At the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, the synodal letter of the bishops of the province of Byzacena was read; among others, Felix, bishop of the city of Thenisiis, subscribed to it.

In the Carthaginian Conference, however, chapter 133, Latonius is written as bishop of the Church of Tenitana; his adversary in chapter 201 is called Securus, bishop of the city of Tenitana. Finally, Pontianus, bishop of Thenitanus, is mentioned in the Life of Saint Fulgentius, chapter 29.

34. TARAZENSIS. Secundus, bishop of the holy Church of Tagasensis, who subscribed to the frequently mentioned synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, perhaps presided over this same city. That see, however, may better correspond to the town of Tagestensis—or, as other manuscripts have it, Tagesensis—which Pliny lists among the free towns of Africa, book V, chapter 4. Theodorus, bishop of the Church of Tamazeni, also subscribed to that synodal letter; and Lucas Holstenius cites Stephanus Taracensis from the same letter, who is called Taraquensis in the printed editions. Above, among the Numidians, no. 53, Cresconius Tharasensis was listed.

35. TROFINIANENSIS. Probantius, bishop of the people of Trofimianensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, among the Catholic prelates; Lucas Holstenius prefers this reading to the other.

[Col. 0320A] 36. LEPTIMINENSIS. Haller’s manuscript has Leptimiensis, that is, Leptis Minor; Ptolemy has Λέπτις Μικρά, “Leptis Minor”; Antoninus has Leptis Minor; and the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, following the Peutinger Table, has Lepte Minus. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Demetrius from Leptiminus delivered his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics, no. 36. Romanus, bishop of the people of Leptiminensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, with Victorinus, his adversary; the latter also appeared among the Donatists in chapter 187, where, in editions preceding Baluzius’s, he is wrongly called the bishop of Eptiminensis.

Some have called this city simply Leptis, without an additional epithet, such as Pomponius Mela, who in book I of On the World’s Geography, chapter 7, lists Leptis in Lesser Africa and shortly afterward another Leptis. Pliny does exactly the same, although after the word “another” he adds, “which is called Magna.” Sallustius says that Hippo, Hadrumetum, Leptis, and other cities on the coast were founded by the Phoenicians, in his book On the Jugurthine War. Hirtius calls Leptis a free city in On the African War; Polybius has Λέπτην, “Lepten,” near the end of book I of his Histories; and Titus Livy mentions the city of Leptis in book XXXIV, situated on the coast of the Lesser Syrtis. He says that it was so powerful that it paid the Carthaginians a daily tax of one talent. This was more probably Leptis Magna.

The contrary opinion is nevertheless supported by the fact that Massanissa, king of Numidia, claimed that this city belonged to his kingdom. Finally, in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, Criscentinus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of the city of Leptis, subscribed to the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers. We shall discuss Leptis Magna when treating of the Tripolitan cities, no. 1.

37. TAGARIATANUS. This is the reading of the Laon manuscript. The printed editions have Tegariatenus. Tagarata was in the proconsular province, as we saw in note 44 on the bishops of that province. In Africa there were two places called Tagora or Tagura; see note 20 on the Numidians. There was also Tacarata in the same province, discussed below at no. 113. Nothing occurs to be said about Tagariata or Tegarieta, except that in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, Felix, bishop of Tagaraiensis, was present among the Donatists. Was he from the same place? Ortelius, from Haller’s manuscript, mentions the town of Tagaritanum, which perhaps belongs here. Ptolemy also lists Targarum among the cities situated under Hadrumetum, and therefore in Byzacena.

148 38. OCTABENSIS. See among the Numidians, no. 36.

39. FERADIMAIENSIS. Vincentianus, bishop of the people of Feraditana Major, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, belonged to this same city. There was another Feraditana, called Minor, according to chapter 133 of the same Conference, where Felicianus, bishop of the people of Feraditana Minor, appears; in both cities Catholic unity was present. See above, no. 31.

40. CREPEDULENSIS. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Barbarianus, bishop of Crepenulensis, is mentioned among the Catholic prelates. The reading in the List is confirmed by the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2; Spes, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Secrepedulensis, subscribed to it. Apparently it had been written: “bishop of S. E. Crepedulensis,” that is, “of the holy Church,” etc. The copyist joined the abbreviation to the place-name, and perhaps another later copyist added the words “holy Church” again, since they occur in all the other subscriptions.

41. CYPRIANUS UNUZIBIRENSIS. This is the same man who is praised by Victor, book II, no. 11; see note 83 on that passage (col. 211, no. b). Donatus, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Uniziverensis, subscribed to the synodal letter of the Byzacene Fathers, so often mentioned, at the Lateran Council. Baluzius thinks, in his notes on the relevant passage, that Maximinus, bishop of Uzabirensis, listed in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, also presided over this same city on the Donatist side. There he also notes that Ptolemy called this city Οὐλιζέβιρρα—“Ulizebirra.” It also occurs in Pliny, book V, chapter 4, among the free towns of Africa, as Ulusubritanum.

[Col. 0321A] 42. MUZUCENSIS. Norisius criticizes Joannes Garnerius for confusing the African cities of Maxa, Muzu, and Muzucum. The same author, however, did not sufficiently distinguish Muzulensis from Muzucensis, as Baluzius notes together with Norisius in chapter 133 of the Carthaginian Conference. Compare what we observed above in note 49 on the bishops of the proconsular province.

In the Conference itself, chapter 133, Restitutus, bishop of the people of Muzucensis, is mentioned with Idaxius, his adversary, who appeared again in chapter 206. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 34, Januarius Muzulensis delivered his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics. In the Corbie manuscript, as Rigaltius observes, it reads a Muzucha; Holstenius, from a very old manuscript, insists that Muzuca should be read, as Baluzius reports; Baluzius himself also asserts that the Colbert manuscript reads Modulensis. Augustine has Muzulensis in book VI of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 41, where he resolves Januarius’s objection. The Peutinger Table, as the Oxford editor observes, displays Muzula. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, mentions the Misulani—or, as other manuscripts have it, the Musulani—among the larger communities that could be called nations. Tacitus, book II of the Annals, calls the Muzulani a powerful people near the deserts of Africa. Florus, however, book III, chapter 1, has the city of Mulucha.

43. MASSIMANENSIS. That is, Maximianensis, as the distinguished Lucas Holstenius notes. Hence he thinks that Bonifacius, bishop of the Church of Justini and Maximiensis, should be assigned here; he subscribed, with the other Byzacene Fathers, to the synodal letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. Certainly the letter x is often changed into ss, which is why a bishop Maxulitanus from the proconsular province is frequently called Massylitanus. A bishop Maximianensis is listed among the Numidians, no. 119.

44. VICTOR VITENSIS. The author of the books On the African Persecution; we discussed more about him and his see in our preface, and it would be superfluous to repeat it here.

45. SCEBATIANENSIS. Thus both manuscript codices. The printed editions [Col. 0321C] have Sebastianensis.

149 46. PEDERODIANENSIS. Thus the manuscript codices and the printed editions.

47. CIRCINITANUS. Haller’s manuscript has Circitanus. Chiffletius thinks that this name designates the island of Circina, to which Saint Fulgentius withdrew shortly before his death, as is related in his Life, chapter 29. Hirtius mentions the island of Cercinna and its inhabitants, the Cercinnates, more than once. Ptolemy also lists the island and city of Cercina among the islands adjoining Africa, and Polybius mentions the African island of Cercina in book III. According to Antoninus’s Maritime Itinerary, it is situated between Sicily and Africa, 622 stadia from Tacapes. From Titus Livy, book XXXIII, it can be inferred that it was not far from Acylla and Thapsus.

48. FLORENTINUS TUZIRITANUS. The printed editions have Florentius. From Ptolemy’s book IV, chapter 3, we have three cities situated under Hadrumetum and therefore in the province of Byzacena which, although somewhat similar in name, must nevertheless be distinguished from one another before we say anything about the Tuziritan see mentioned here. They are Turzo, Tisurus, and Thysdrus. Thurusa in the proconsular province must also be distinguished from them, and perhaps Tuzurus in Arzugitania.

All these cities must be treated individually, since some have at times conflated two, or even three, of them into one. The distinguished Joannes Harduinus, in his notes on Pliny, thinks that Tusdritanum, which Pliny lists among the free towns in book V, chapter 4, is the same as the city of Tuziritana mentioned here in the List. He then goes further and assigns Aptus, who is called the bishop of Tuzuritanus in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 187, to the same town of Tusdritanum.

But although some might perhaps think that Florentius Tuziritanus could equally be assigned to Thusdrus or to Tisurus, since the letters d and z were habitually used interchangeably among Africans, no one can deny that there was another city of Tuzuritanus, over which Aptus presided, distinct from Tuziritana, which Harduinus believes to have been Tusdritana. This can be demonstrated by two arguments drawn from the Carthaginian Conference, in which the bishop of Tusdritanus is clearly distinguished from the bishop of Tuzuritanus.

Aptus Tuzuritanus, mentioned by Harduinus, is the same man who appeared among the Donatists in chapter 187 and had already been called, in chapter 120, the adversary of Asselicus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Tuzuritana. Consequently, another bishop appears in the same Conference, chapter 206, among the Donatists: Tusdritanus, named Honoratus. Moreover, the exceptionally perceptive Baluzius discovered the Catholic bishop of this same city. For in chapter 122 of the same Conference, Navigius, bishop of Dydritanus, is listed among the orthodox Fathers; the learned man noted that Tusdritanus should be restored in its place, so that Honoratus, who is there called the adversary of Navigius from the Donatist sect, may be the same person whom we have said was called Tusdritanus in chapter 207.

Baluzius supplies a second argument: namely, that the city of Tuziritana or Tusdritana mentioned here did not belong to the same province as the Tuzuritana over which Aptus presided. Certainly Thusdrus, as no one denies, belonged to Byzacena; from Antoninus’s Itinerary we know that it was situated not far from Hadrumetum, Leptis Minor, and Usulis. But Aptus belonged to the province of Arzugitania, as Asselicus himself declares in chapter 208 of the Conference in these words: “Under the testimony of Almighty God . . . I say that we set out from Arzuges on the third day before the Kalends of May.” Arzugitania was a part of the province of Tripolitania, or at least adjacent to it, as is clear from chapter 49 of the code of the canons of the African Church, where “in Tripoli and perhaps in Arzuge” barbarian peoples seem to lie between them.

Although it bordered Byzacena, Thusdrus lay in another part of Byzacena, toward the proconsular province, as we saw from Antoninus. Indeed, no one has ever placed Thusdrus outside Byzacena. Hirtius mentions the town of Tisdre in his book On the African War, and Benerius, bishop of the Church of Turditana, subscribed, with the other bishops of the province of Byzacena, to the synodal letter. Herodian has Θύστρος—“Thystros”—in book VII.

In addition to all these, we also have a bishop of the people of Turuzitana, named Serotinus, mentioned among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133. Garnerius had written that he presided over the city of Thurza or Turzo in Byzacena, which we cited above from Ptolemy; Norisius criticized him because Thurusitanus is not correctly declined from Thurza, and thinks that this prelate should more properly be assigned to the proconsular province.

For when Serotinus himself said that he had no Donatist adversary, Habetdeus, Primianus’s deacon at Carthage, replied: “There is a presbyter there, Cattus.” Yet it is certain, as Norisius himself admits, that Habetdeus sometimes replied even when other provinces were under discussion. The Peutinger Table, moreover, displays Thusuros on the borders of the proconsular province and Byzacena, and Helpidius, the Donatist bishop of Tusdritanus, subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussis in 393.

49. MARAZIANENSIS. Antoninus calls it Marazania in the Itinerary. I think that Felix from Marrazana, who attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian among those who rebaptized, no. 46, belonged to this same place. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Eunomius, bishop of the people of Marazanensis, was listed; his adversary Habetdeus from the Donatist sect complains at length there that neither he nor his predecessor had ever been admitted into the city, although they had been ordained for it. Ferrandus praises the Council of Marazanensis in his Brief Summary of the Canons. Lucas Holstenius also thinks that Saturinus, bishop of the Church of Miricianensis, presided over this city; he subscribed, with the other Fathers of the province of Byzacena, to the synodal letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2.

50. MATTARITANUS. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, Cultasius, bishop of the people of Mataritana, is mentioned; he professed that he possessed unity. See above, MACTARITANUS, no. 25. Marcus from Mactari, mentioned from the Carthaginian Council by Augustine in book VII of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 2, is called a Mattari in most of Augustine’s manuscript codices, as we said above at no. 25.

Pliny, book V, chapter 4, has the town Matterense, for which Hermolaus improperly inserted Madaurense, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts, as Harduinus complains in note 17; others have carelessly adopted that reading. Holstenius thinks that Victor Martyritanus, an African bishop who is said by Cassiodorus, in book On Divine Institutions, chapter 29, to have purged Cassianus’s Conferences, presided over this same city. Certainly the manuscript codices, as our Joannes Garetius observed in the new edition of this author’s works, have Martaritanus. The Paris edition of 1529 indeed has Martyritanus in the text, but in the margin it cites a manuscript that had Mattaritanus.

51. PRAECAUSENSIS. Thus the manuscripts and the printed editions. Holstenius suspects that the monastery of Praecisu, mentioned at the Council of Carthage under Boniface in connection with the immunity that Peter, its abbot, was attempting to assert for his monastery, may be assigned here. From the same abbot’s humble petition, however, it can be inferred that the monastery of Praecisu lay within the boundaries of the diocese of Leptis Minor. See below, no. 92.

52. AQUISALBENSIUM. Among the Donatists, Januarius, bishop of Aquae Albae, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 197. But it is uncertain whether he presided over this city or over another of the same name, listed below in Mauretania Sitifensis, no. 5.

151 53. IRPINIANENSIS. It is written somewhat differently in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 133, where Barbarus, bishop of the people of Hierpinianensis—or Hierpiniacensis in the Labbean edition—is listed among the orthodox Fathers.

### 54. USULENSIS

Cassianus, bishop of Usula, attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus; and Theodorus of Usula, a notorious Donatist, about whom Augustine frequently writes in his books against Cresconius, signed the proceedings of the Council of Cabarsussa in 393 and was condemned the following year at the Council of Bagai. In the manuscript of the Colbert Library, however, he is called Uculensis, as Baluzius observes, although it seems certain that the city of Usula was different from Ucula. For in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, Privatus, a Catholic bishop of the plebs of Usilensis, appeared among the Catholics, while in chapter 128 Cericius, also a Catholic bishop of the plebs of Uculensis, is mentioned; he professed that Catholic unity existed in his community. We learn that the latter belonged to the province of Proconsular Africa from the synodical letter of the Fathers of that province, which was read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, where Crisconius is said to have subscribed as bishop of the Church of Ucula.

Laurentius, bishop of the city of Usilabis, subscribed the synodical letter of the Byzacene bishops that was likewise commended at the same Lateran Council; he may perhaps be assigned here. At the Council of Carthage under the confessor Saint Cyprian, Irenaeus *ab Ululis* sat among the bishops. The Oxford editor of Saint Cyprian’s works considers him to have been bishop of Usula; indeed, earlier the Louvain editors, in Augustine’s sixth book *On Baptism against the Donatists*, where the holy Doctor refutes Irenaeus’s arguments in favor of rebaptizing heretics, had printed *Usulis* instead of *Ululis*. Our editors, however, restored the passage according to the manuscripts.

Ptolemy mentions Οὐτίλλα (*Ōtilla*); Antoninus places the city of Usula between Thysdrus and Thenae. It is called *Usyla* by the anonymous geographer of Ravenna, book III, no. 5, and again book V, no. 5. Finally, on the Peutinger Map the municipality of Usilla is placed midway between Ruspe and Thaprarura.

Beware, however, of confusing the city of Zella with Usilla. That they were different can also be established from the fact that, in the Carthaginian Conference, in addition to the bishops of Usula and Ucula mentioned above, chapter 134 has Donatianus, a Catholic bishop of the plebs of Zella, together with Natalicus, his opponent, who is again mentioned among the Donatists in chapter 163.

### 55. HABETDEUS TAMALLUMENSIS

There were at least two cities in Africa called Tamalluma. For below Rufinus of Tamalluma is listed first among the bishops of Mauretania Sitifensis. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 127, Gregory, bishop of Tamamallensis, is mentioned; for this name the distinguished Baluzius printed *Tamallensis*, correctly indeed, since Lucius the Donatist, who is there called Gregory’s opponent, is named bishop of Tamallensis in chapter 208.

Besides this bishop, chapter 126 mentions Sabratius, bishop of the plebs of Turre Tamalluma, together with Jurata, his opponent, who appears again among the Donatists in chapter 208. Baluzius believes that Gregory, mentioned in chapter 127, was bishop of Tamalluma in the province of Sitifensis, and that the Tamalluma mentioned here in the *Notitia* was none other than Turre Tamalluma, over which Sabratius presided; he also thinks that Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, had been exiled there.

Certainly no one can deny that Turre Tamalluma existed in Byzacena. Among the other bishops of the province of Byzacena who subscribed at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in the second session, to the synodical letter sent to the emperor Constantine, there is Pentasius, bishop of the holy Church of *Turrium Tamulus*, or *Turrium Tamal*, as Baluzius corrected the text from the manuscript of the Church of Beauvais.

Vincentius of Girba had invaded the church of Tamalluma, on the advice of the Council of Junca. Hence it is conjectured that this city lay at the extreme edge of Byzacena, toward Tripolitania, to which Girba belonged. Indeed, Antoninus shows in his *Itinerary* that Turre Tamalleni lay on the Tripolitanian frontier, where this heading occurs:

> The route which runs along the Tripolitanian frontier through Turre Tamalleni from Tacapae to Lepcis Magna.

Then, listing the settlements, he writes:

> From Tacapae to the Waters, Agarlaba, Turre Tamalleni, Ad Templum, etc.

Moreover, the name *Tamalleni*, used here by Antoninus, confirms Baluzius’s view that Eugenius was exiled at Turre Tamalluma. For in the *Notitia* Eugenius is said to have been exiled at Tamallenum.

If, however, Turre Tamalluma is not to be distinguished from the Byzacene city of Tamalluma, then the Habetdeus mentioned here in the *Notitia* must be considered different from the Habetdeus whom Victor praises in book V, no. 12; for in that case he would have been exiled to his own city, which no one would readily accept. Yet no other Habetdeus occurs in the *Notitia* besides this one.

Nor should one say that Victor, in the passage cited, is speaking of Habetdeus of Theudalis, whom he had already praised in book I, no. 7. For unless Victor has completely disturbed the chronological order, that man was already dead, since Victor of Theudalis—or, as Baluzius himself thinks it should be read, of Eudalis—is listed in the *Notitia* among the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa.

Perhaps Turre Tamalluma, or Tamalleni, must be distinguished from the Byzacene city of Tamalluma. Victor seems to suggest this when he says that Antonius was in a city near the desert and immediately adds that Eugenius had been exiled in the very regions of the desert. Yet in the following entry he writes that Habetdeus likewise had been exiled in the city of Tamalluma itself. For this reason, in note 188 to my commentary on Victor’s *History* (col. 250, note d), I interpreted the Byzacene Tamalluma as the Tamalluma of Mauretania Sitifensis listed below; nevertheless, this interpretation seems contrary to Victor’s meaning.

For he is speaking of Tamalluma, which was near the province of Tripolitania; but between Tripolitania and Mauretania Sitifensis lay Byzacena and Numidia. I leave these difficulties to be resolved by more perceptive scholars.

### 56. CULULITANUS

Restitutianus, bishop of the plebs of Sululitana, listed among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, may perhaps be assigned here. See below, no. 93.

The Oxford editor thinks this was the same city as Chullabi, whose bishop Aurelius attended the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. Procopius, in book VI of *The Buildings of Justinian*, lists Cululim among the inland cities of Byzacena fortified by that emperor against the Moors.

In the *Notitia* of Bodleian manuscript, edited by the distinguished William Beveridge, the cities of the province of Byzacena include, at no. 12, *Colules*, in Greek Κολούλης. It is clear that this name designates the city of Cululitana from the edition of the same *Notitia* prepared by Goar, where the Latin form is *Cululi*, although the Greek text has Κουκούλης.

### 57. MENEFESSITANUS

In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, Mensurius, bishop of the plebs of Medefessitana, is mentioned; this reflects the common change of the letter *n* into *d*. Our reading is confirmed by Procopius, book II of *The Vandalic War*, chapter 23, where he mentions the city of Menefesen in Byzacena. Antoninus, in his *Itinerary*, has *Menegesem*, situated between Vergersalla and Theveste.

### 58. CASULIS CARIANENSIS

According to the distinguished Baluzius, Silvanus, bishop of Carianensis, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, presided over this city. Holstenius, however, there read *Cartanensis* in order to identify the city of Cartenna, but incorrectly.

Antoninus mentions Casula, situated in the province of Proconsular Africa. In one or the other of these cities, a certain scholar collated a manuscript of Saint Hilary’s works at the beginning of the sixth century, as appears from an old inscription copied from that manuscript and reported by Dom Joannes Mabillon in book V of *On Diplomatics*, p. 355:

> I collated this in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, while established at Kasulis, in the fourteenth year of King Thrasamund.

Moreover, Mabillon and D. Michael Germanus, in the *Italian Journey*, p. 143, testify that they saw this precious monument of sacred antiquity at Rome. It had been written nearly twelve hundred years earlier—approximately in the middle of the century before it was collated—and is preserved in the library belonging to the Vatican Church.

### 59. ACOLITANUS

The name is sometimes written with an aspiration, *Achola*, as in Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 3. Strabo, book XVII, lists Achola among the free cities; the Peutinger Map places it between Thapsus and Ruspe.

Quintus, bishop of Acolitana, subscribed the synodical letter of the Byzacene bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2. The anonymous geographer of Ravenna lists *Acola* in book V, no. 5.

Holstenius, in his notes on Charles of Saint-Paul, and Hardouin, in his notes on Pliny, book V, chapter 4, think that this was the Acilla mentioned by Hirtius; there the town of Acolitanus is listed among the free communities. Ortelius, however, expresses some doubt about this in his *Geographical Thesaurus*.

Titus Livius seems to favor Holstenius and Hardouin, for in book XXXIII he writes that Acylla was not far from Thapsus and the island of Cercina. Thapsus was in Byzacena, and Cercina likewise belonged to that province, as is clear from this very *Notitia*, above, no. 47. Hence Sigonius and Glareanus, in their notes on this passage of Livy, asserted that Achola and Acylla were the same city.

Holstenius likewise thinks that the inhabitants of this city were the Aquilitani mentioned by Gruter, inscription DXII, together with the Leptitani and Usallitani.

### 60. VINDEMIALIS CAPSENSIS

More will be said about this most holy bishop in the historical commentary, chapter 8, beyond what is found in the *Passion of the Holy Monks* who lived in the territory of Capsa, above, p. 55 (for us, col. 263).

In this entry the manuscript has *Cabsensis* instead of *Capsensis*, but the meaning is the same. Capsa was a famous city, which Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 3, lists among the cities subject to Hadrumetum. That it was fortified is evident from the fact that, according to Strabo, book XVII, the treasures of King Jugurtha were kept there.

Sallustius writes of the same city in his book *The Jugurthine War*:

> Among immense deserts there was a large and powerful town called Capsa.

He later describes its destruction, as does Florus, book III, chapter 1. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, mentions the Capsitani among those peoples who may properly be called not merely cities but, for the most part, nations. The Peutinger Map marks Capsa as a colony.

Saint Cyprian mentions the city of Capsa in letter 56, addressed to Fortunatus and other bishops. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Donatulus of Capsa sat among those who favored rebaptism, no. 69. Fortunatianus of Capsa attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus. At the Council of Cabarsussa in 393, Quintasius of Capsa subscribed among the Donatists.

In the Carthaginian Conference, Fortunatus, bishop of the plebs of Capsa, appears in chapter 126 together with Celere the Donatist, his opponent, who is also mentioned in chapter 206. I do not know how it happened that, in chapter 208, Donatianus, likewise a Donatist bishop of Capsa, is listed in the same Conference; yet no one raised an objection on this matter.

Finally, *Capses* appears in the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, both in William Beveridge’s edition and in that of Jacob Goar.

### 61. DURENSIS

In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 197, Antonianus, bishop of Drua, is mentioned among the Donatists; in the following chapter, Bebianus, bishop of Dusa; and in chapter 197 Paschasius, bishop of Dusita—all on the Donatist side. Whether any of these was bishop of Dura, others may conjecture.

### 62. CUFRUTENSIS

The Halleri manuscript has *Cufratensis*. Our reading is preferable to that one. For Felicianus, bishop of the plebs of Cufrutus, attended the Council of Carthage in 403 and is also listed among the Catholic bishops in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128.

### 63. TASBALTENSIS, OR TASVALTENSIS

The scribes who copied the acts of the Conference changed *v* into *f*, since the two letters had the same sound, and thus wrote: Julianus, bishop of the plebs of Tasfaltensis. He is listed among the Catholics in chapter 128.

Our reading is confirmed by the Oxford edition of the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, in which, at no. 35, Adelfius of Thasbalta gave his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics. Augustine replied to him in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 42; some manuscripts there have *a Thasvalte*, as do the editions of Cyprian prepared by Pamelius and Rigault.

The Halleri manuscript, cited by Ortelius, also adds the aspiration, giving *Thasbaltensis*. Antoninus, in his *Itinerary*, mentions Tabalta among the cities of Byzacena. Innocentius of Thebalta likewise subscribed the Council of Cabarsussa in 393 among the other bishops of the Donatist sect.

### 64. CILLITANUS

Tertiolus, bishop of the plebs of Cillitana, listed in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128, seems to have belonged to this same place, together with Donatus, his opponent, who is again mentioned among the Donatists in chapter 187.

But Privatianus, the Catholic bishop of Vegesela, says in chapter 133 that he had as his opponent Donatus, bishop of Cillitana. Donatus there says that Vegesela belonged to his diocese and that he had presbyters there. From this the distinguished Baluzius concludes that Vegesela must be admitted as a city in Byzacena.

It could nevertheless have happened that Donatus of Cillitana, Tertiolus’s opponent, was different from Donatus of Cillitana whom Privatianus of Vegesela called his opponent; in that case, two cities called Cillitana would have to be admitted.

Among the Byzacene Fathers who subscribed the synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, there is also Fortunius, bishop of Cellensis, perhaps for *Cillensis*. Antoninus places Cellas Picentinae on the boundary of Byzacena and Tripolitania; shortly afterward he mentions a village called Cellas. Both were thirty miles from Tacapae. Perhaps the same place bore two names. The same author also mentions Cilio in Byzacena.

### 65. TIZIENSIS

The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius thinks that Aptus, bishop of the plebs of Tigiensis, presided over this city; he attended the Carthaginian Conference among the Catholics in chapter 120.

In his notes on chapter 126, where Pascasius, bishop of the plebs of Tijucensis, likewise appears among the Catholics, he observes that the *Notitia* has Honoratus, bishop of Tiziensis. He then cites Augustine, who, in his book *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 22, mentions the city of Tizica and seems to place it in Proconsular Africa.

He leaves it to others to judge whether Tizica was the same city as Tujuca. Certainly, in such uncertainties it is better to bring forward what is found in the ancient authors while suspending judgment in the meantime. See Maurit. Caesar, no. 27.

### 66. BONIFACIUS FORATIANENSIS

The Laudun manuscript has *Fortianensis*, while Halleri’s has *Forianensis*. We have nevertheless retained the received reading, which agrees with Victor of Vita. In all his printed and manuscript copies, Bonifacius—one of the four bishops who presented a profession of faith to King Huneric—is called *Foratianensis*.

This makes one wonder why *Foratiana* is counted among the seats of an uncertain province in the index prefixed to Saint Cyprian’s works.

### 67. SERVIUS ARSURITANUS

This is the reading of the Laudun manuscript. The printed editions, however, have *Servus*.

The distinguished Joannes Hardouin, in his notes on Pliny, book V, chapter 4, thinks that *Apsiritanus* should be written here in the *Notitia*, so as to identify Abzirita, whose bishop Fructuosus attended the Carthaginian Conference in chapter 128.

But the city of Abzirita belonged to Proconsular Africa, since it is the same as the city otherwise called Abdera. Abdera was unquestionably in Proconsular Africa; Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 3, places it under Carthage.

That Abderitana and Abzirita were the same city is proved not only by the fact that the letters *d* and *z* were commonly used interchangeably to indicate the same sound, as Hardouin himself demonstrates elsewhere, but also by the Council of Carthage under Genethlius. There Victor is called *Abziritana* in the printed editions and in some manuscripts, but *Abderitana* in others, as the learned Norisius and Baluzius observed; the same variation is noted in the margin of Labbe’s edition of the Councils.

Beware, however, of confusing the city of Abdera or Abzirita with Abbiritana, for Norisius proves against Garnerius that they were entirely different.

Besides these, Pliny also mentions the town of Azurita. Hardouin observes that this name designates Assuras. We have said more about that city where we discussed the bishops of Proconsular Africa, no. 19.

In the index prefixed to Saint Cyprian’s works, Arzuri is placed in Byzacena, perhaps on the basis of this passage of the *Notitia*. Nor should the conjecture of Charles of Saint-Paul be dismissed: in his *Sacred Geography* he thinks that Bonifacius was bishop of this city of Arsura, and that he subscribed the synodical letter of the Byzacene Fathers commended at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, in the following form:

> Bonifacius, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Sasura.

The Peutinger Map has the village of Sassura.

### 68. FORONTONIANENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript, cited by Ortelius, has *Ferontonianensis*. Below, no. 71, we find Bonifacius of Frontoniana.

### 69. FERIANENSIS

There can be no doubt that Sallustius, bishop of the holy Church of Rebianensis, presided over this same see. He subscribed the synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, together with the other Byzacene Fathers. Holstenius thinks that the synodical letter should be corrected on the basis of this passage of the *Notitia*.

### 70. VARARITANUS

This see must be distinguished from the Numidian city of Vazarita, which we discussed in the notes on the bishops of that province, no. 32.

The Peutinger Map has the municipality of Bararus in Byzacena. Among the cities that Ptolemy says were subject to Hadrumetum, there is also Cararus.

### 71. FRONTONIANENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Frotonianensis*. Above, no. 68, we find *Forontonianensis*.

### 72. MIMIANENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Miminensis*. Saturinus, bishop of the holy Church of Miricianensis, listed among the Byzacene bishops who subscribed the synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, may perhaps be assigned here rather than to Marazana.

Certainly, the many corrupt city-names in the subscriptions to this letter make me bolder in conjecturing than would otherwise be appropriate.

### 73. BOANENSIS

According to the learned Baluzius, Januarius, bishop of the Church of Bana, may have belonged to this same place. He subscribed the synodical letter to the emperor Constantine Augustus among the other Byzacene Fathers at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2.

Victor, bishop of the plebs of Bahanna, also attended the Carthaginian Conference among the Catholics in chapter 126. This appears to have been the same city as Boana.

The learned Lucas Holstenius also assigns here Beianus the Baianensian, a Donatist of the Maximianists who was deposed at the Council of Bagai.

### 74. MARAGUIENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Maraguinensis*. Stephanus, bishop of the holy Church of Taraquensis, may perhaps have belonged to the same place; he subscribed the synodical letter among the Byzacene Fathers at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2.

It is uncertain which reading should be preferred, although the subscriptions to the synodical letter are more corrupt than the *Notitia*. In the synodical letter, Holstenius reads *Taracensis* instead of *Taraquensis*, as we said above, no. 34.

### 75. NATIONENSIS

Faustinus, bishop of Nationensis, is mentioned among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208.

### 76. FAUSTUS PRAESIDIENSIS

This Faustus seems to be the same man who, while living in exile not far from his own see, presided over the monastery to which Saint Fulgentius withdrew, as is related in his *Life*, chapter 4. More about him may be found below in the historical commentary, chapter 11.

Leontius, bishop of Praesidium, is listed among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208.

Praesidium occurs more than once on the Peutinger Map, usually as an adjunct, like *municipium*, *colonia*, and so forth. In segment 1 it is *Praesidium*, and in segment 4 *Praesidio*.

### 77. TETCITANUS

This is the reading of two manuscripts and of the printed editions. In the *Notitia Dignitatum*, under the authority of the duke of Tripolitania, there is a *Praepositus limitis Teuchitani*, commander of the Teuchitan frontier.

### 78. GURGAITENSIS

Both manuscripts, as well as the printed editions, have this reading; perhaps it should be *Gurgitensis*. For at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 74, Felix of Gurgites gave his judgment in favor of rebaptizing heretics. He is called by the same name by Saint Augustine, book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 38, where the holy Doctor answers this bishop’s objection.

### 79. FILACENSIS

I have been unable to find this city in Ortelius, perhaps because it was lacking in Halleri’s manuscript.

### 80. MACRIANENSIS

Baluzius thinks that Ferox, bishop of the plebs of Greater Macrianensis, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 125, belonged to this same place; yet through a lapse of memory he assigns the city to Numidia on the basis of the *Notitia*.

In the *Notitia* there are only two bishops of Macrianensis: one in Byzacena, whom we are discussing, and the other in Mauretania Sitifensis, no. 23.

From the Conference we infer that there were three cities of this name in Africa, since it mentions three Catholic bishops of Macrianensis. For besides Ferox, mentioned above, and Pomponius, his opponent on the Donatist side, who is mentioned in the Council of Cabarsussa, Silvanus appears in chapter 133. He states that he had no Donatist opponent. In chapter 215, among the Catholic bishops who had not previously appeared but later subscribed, there is Felix, bishop of Macrianensis.

The learned Baluzius rightly observes, however, that one cannot immediately infer from the number of bishops of the same communion said to have presided over a place that there were as many cities of that name as there are bishops. Sometimes two Catholic bishops occupied one and the same city, especially when a Donatist had joined the unity of the Catholic Church. His name and episcopal seat were then left to him, as is clear from Ampelius and Primulus, bishops of Vaga, mentioned in chapter 176 of the Carthaginian Conference. We discussed them above in the notes on the bishop of Vaga among the Numidians, no. 7.

The Silvanus mentioned above as bishop of the plebs of Macrianensis subscribed the Council of Carthage in 403. Ferrandus cites the Council of Macrianensis in his *Summary of the Canons*.

### 81. TELEPTENSIS

Saint Fulgentius was born in this city. Julianus of Telepte gave his judgment at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian.

Donatianus, bishop of the Church of Telepte, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 121, together with Bellicius, his Donatist opponent. Bellicius is mentioned again in chapter 198.

Yet in chapter 208 Datianus, bishop of Telepte, again appears among the Donatists. Baluzius thinks this should be attributed to the shamelessness of the heretics, who intruded false bishops, unless some error has entered the passage. Perhaps the reading should be *Taleptulensis* or *Talaptensis*. A bishop of this name occurs below, no. 103.

Donatianus, bishop of Telepte, the primatial see of Byzacena, is frequently mentioned in the councils. For Telepte and Talapta, mentioned in the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, see below, no. 103.

According to Procopius, book VI of *The Buildings*, Justinian Augustus fortified Telepte, an inland city of Byzacena.

### 82. OPPENNENSIS

The printed editions have *Openuensis*, and Halleri’s manuscript, cited by Ortelius, has *Opemiensis*. The geographical index prefixed to Saint Cyprian’s works, agreeing with our reading from the Laudun manuscript, mentions *Oppenna*.

Leo of Ospinensis, or Opinensis, subscribed the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419, as recorded by Labbe, volume II of the *Councils*, columns 1603 and 1605. But this bishop belonged to Mauretania Tingitana, as we shall say below, no. 33, in the section on the bishops of Sitifensis.

Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 1, lists Oppinum—or, as the Palatine manuscript has it, Opinum—among the towns of Mauretania Tingitana.

### 83. TAGARBALENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Targabolensis*. In Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, between Tacapae and Turre Tamalleni on the Tripolitanian frontier, Agarlabas occurs.

### 84. CARCABIANENSIS

At the Council of Cabarsussa in 393, Victorianus, bishop of Carcabiana, subscribed among the other Donatists. The following year, while a serious schism was raging among the Donatists, he was deposed from his see at the Council of Bagai.

Augustine discusses him in letter 108 and frequently in his books against the Donatist Cresconius, as well as in sermon 2 on Psalm 36. Donatianus, Victorianus’s successor and a member of the same sect, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201.

### 85. RUFINIANENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Ruffianensis*. Marianus, bishop of the plebs of Rufinianensis, belonged to this same place, as Stephanus Baluzius restored the text in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128.

For, as the same learned man observes, when the manuscript read *Marianus episcopus plebis Rufinianus*, or perhaps *Rufinian.*, Pithaeus thought that *Rufinianus* designated some bishop and that something had been omitted by the copyist. He therefore printed:

> bishop of the plebs . . . . . . Rufinianus.  
> The same man said, etc.

In Papirius Masson’s edition there is in fact only one point after the word *plebis*, from which it may be inferred that nothing had been worn away in the manuscripts.

### 86. AQUARUM REGIARUM

In chapter 126 of the Carthaginian Conference, Maximianus, bishop of Aquae Regiae, was listed among the Catholic bishops. He professed that no other bishop existed in his homeland.

This same man, as legate of the province of Byzacena, attended the seventh Council of Carthage under Aurelius. In Labbe’s edition he is called bishop of Aquae Regiensis; in the manuscript of the canons of the African Church, chapters 127 and 133, he is simply called Maximianus of Aquae, although in other manuscripts, as Justellus observes, he is called *Aquensis Regiorum*, legate of the province of Byzacena.

In both places, however, the Greek text has Ἀκυρεγενσιώτης (“of Aquae Regiae”).

The Peutinger Map and Antoninus in his *Itinerary* call the city Aquae Regiae. Victor of Vita also praises the same city in book V, no. 5.

### 87. QUAESTIORIANENSIS

Halleri’s manuscript, cited by Ortelius, has *Quaestorianensis*, without the diphthong.

Among the Fathers of the province of Byzacena who sent a synodical letter to Constantine Augustus at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, there is:

> Beatus Stephanus, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Questorianensis.

### 88. RUFINIANUS VICTORIANENSIS

Unless I am mistaken, this is the very man whom Saint Fulgentius, as an African exile living a monastic life on an island near Sicily, consulted, as is related in the *Life* of that holy man, chapter 13; see that work.

Saturninus of Victoriana gave his judgment at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 51, in favor of rebaptizing heretics; Augustine answers his argument in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 15.

Getulicus, bishop of Victoriana, subscribed the Council of Cabarsussa among the Donatists. Saturninus, bishop of Victoriana, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, belonged to the same sect.

Augustine praises Restitutus of Victoriana in letter 105. He had been converted from the schism of Donatus to Catholic unity, and the schismatics harassed him with various punishments.

There was another Victoriana, a village mentioned by the same Augustine in book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. Different from both was Victoria, listed by Ptolemy among the cities of Mauretania Caesariensis, book IV, chapter 2.

### 89. GUMMITANUS

In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215, Joannes, bishop of Gummitana, is mentioned among the Catholic bishops who had not subscribed but later appeared.

In the eleventh century, when only five bishops remained in Africa because of the flood of barbarian invasions, one of them was the bishop of Gummitana.
