Perhaps because he was older than the others, he sought the name and honor of primate of Africa against the privileges of the Church of Carthage. Saint Leo IX restrained his attempt in letters 3 and 4.

There can be no doubt that Stephanus, bishop of the Church of the city of Gummasis, belonged to the same city. He sent a synodical letter to Constantine Augustus with the other bishops of the province of Byzacena; the letter is preserved in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2.

The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius also assigns here Sabnianus, bishop of the plebs of Gummenarta, who attended and subscribed the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

### 90. MATERIANENSIS

This is also the form found in Halleri’s manuscript, according to Ortelius.

### 91. MOZOTCORITANUS

Both manuscripts have this form, whereas the printed editions read *Moroteoritanus*. In the index prefixed to Saint Cyprian’s works, *Moroteri* occurs in Byzacena.

### 92. VICOATERIENSIS

Ebasius, bishop of the holy Church of Vico Ateriensis, subscribed the synodical letter of the Byzacene Fathers at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, with this same form.

At the Council of Carthage in 525 under Boniface, Peter the abbot, defending the immunity of his monastery against Liberatus, primate of the province of Byzacena, cited the example of the monastery of Praecisu. Although it lay within the territory of the Church of Leptiminus, it had the consolation of the bishop of Vico Ateriensis, who was located at a distance, while the neighboring bishop had been passed over.

Rogatianus the Donatist, in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198, is called bishop “of Vico Ateri.”

### 93. SUBLECTINUS

The anonymous geographer of Ravenna likewise writes *Sublecte*, namely in book III, no. 5, and book V, no. 5. Among ancient authors, however, the name more often occurs with a double *l*.

The Peutinger Map has *Sullecti*. Martianus of Sullectum, a Donatist, was condemned by other Donatists at the Council of Bagai in 394, as reported in Baluzius’s collection of the Councils, column 98. Saint Augustine likewise attests this frequently in books III and IV against Cresconius.

Holstenius assigns here Restitutianus, bishop of the plebs of Sulullitana, mentioned among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 135, as well as Hilarius of Sullita, a Donatist who appeared in chapter 201. But this cannot be said of either one indiscriminately, since Restitutianus professed that he possessed Catholic unity.

Baluzius thinks it more likely that Restitutianus belonged to Mauretania; we have conjectured that he may be assigned to the city of Cululitana, listed above, no. 56.

From Procopius, book I of *The Vandalic War*, we learn that Sullectum was a coastal town where Belisarius first landed when he came to restore Africa from the Vandals, after he had won over the bishop of the place and the leading citizens.

We also learn the town’s location from this passage: the Romans then proceeded through Lepcis and Hadrumetum to Grassa, and afterward to Decimum, a place nearly seventy stades from Carthage.

### 94. IRENSIS

The learned Franciscus Chiffletius, in his notes on Ferrandus, thinks that *Idirensis* should be read here, saying that the bishop of that place attended the Carthaginian Conference.

In the Conference, chapter 128, there is indeed Marcianus, bishop of Idicrensis. In the old editions he is called *Idierensis*, and in the edition published by Papirius Masson, *Idurensis*. But this bishop belonged to Numidia; we discussed him in the notes on the bishops of that province, no. 16.

It is more likely that the city of Irensis was the same as Irinensis, as Charles of Saint-Paul, bishop of Avranches, thinks on the basis of Fuliensis [reading uncertain]. The bishop of the latter city is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215, among the Catholic bishops who had not subscribed at the beginning of the Conference; he is called Tertullianus, bishop of Hirenensis.

Certainly he belonged to Byzacena, for at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, Theodorus, humble bishop of the holy Church of Hirinensis, subscribed the synodical letter with the other Byzacene Fathers.

### 95. TICUALTENSIS

According to Baluzius, following Holstenius, Asmunius belonged to this same place—or *Somnius*, as the old editions have it—bishop of Tigualensis, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126.

He complained that two bishops, Gaianus and Privatus, had been ordained by the Donatists in his diocese. Gaianus appeared in the same chapter and again below, chapter 186; he had previously attended the Council of Cabarsussa in 393.

Alypius, however, the Catholic bishop of Tagaste in Numidia, spoke on Asmunius’s behalf. This does not establish that they belonged to the same province.

### 96. AUZEGERENSIS

Donatus, a Donatist bishop of Auzegerensis, is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208.

### 97. TEMONIARENSIS

The reading must undoubtedly be *Temonianensis*. In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 126, Cresconius, bishop of the plebs of Temonianensis, is listed among the Catholics. Baluzius thinks that this is the same Cresconius who is mentioned in chapter 127 of the manuscript of the canons of the African Church.

Victorinus, bishop of the Church of Temunianensis, subscribed the synodical letter of the Byzacene bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2.

### 98. TURREBLANDINUS

A Donatist bishop of the same city is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 208, where Maximinus is called bishop of Turreblandensis, or, as the old editions have it, *Turreblansis*.

The synodical letter of the Byzacene Fathers at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin gives a slightly different form: Datianus, bishop of the holy Church of *Turreblandis*, in Greek Τουῤῥεβανδής (“of Tourreblandis”).

From Victor’s manuscript in Halleri’s codex, Ortelius has *Turris Blandini* and *Turris Blansis*.

### 99. RESTITUTUS SEGERMITANUS

The Laudun manuscript has *Restutus*.

Another Restitutus, bishop of Segermitana and a Donatist, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 198. He had already appeared in chapter 126, when Felix, bishop of the plebs of Segermitis, was listed among the Catholics.

Nicomedes of Segermis gave his judgment among those favoring rebaptism, no. 9, at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. Augustine replied to him in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 16.

### 100. GAUVARITANUS

Halleri’s manuscript has *Gaunaritanus*. Rogatus, bishop of Gaguaritana, attended the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 128; he had passed from the Donatists to Catholic unity.

### 101. ELIENSIS

This is also written thus in the Carthaginian Collation, where, in chapter 126, Fuscinullus, bishop of the people of Eliensis, is mentioned. In the anonymous Ravennate, book III, section 5, it appears as *Elie*, as also in several manuscript copies of the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, although the printed editions have *Elices*, as our Placidus Porcheron observes in his notes on this passage of the anonymous author. There he cites the Peutinger Table, which has *Aeliae*. Among the Byzacene Fathers who subscribed the synodical letter commended in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, there occurs Constantinus, bishop of the holy Church of Heliensis.

### 102. RUSFENSIS

Thus the Laon manuscript. Ortelius, however, from Haller’s manuscript, has *Rufensis*. The printed editions have *Ruspensis*. We have retained the reading of the Laon manuscript, although the reading of the editors seems preferable. This variation, however, concerns only spelling. Formerly the letters *ph* together, or the single letter *p*, were used indifferently, as in *Trophaea* for *Tropaea*, *Typhus* for *Typus*, and similar cases. But *ph* and *f*, according to our manner of pronunciation, sound alike; hence *Ruspensis* was written *Rusphensis*, and afterward was both pronounced and written *Rusfensis*.

No one at all familiar with ecclesiastical history can be unaware of the city of Ruspe, celebrated above all on account of the great Fulgentius, illustrious for holiness of life, the glory of his confession, and his writings. We shall say more about him in the historical Commentary, especially chapters 11 and 12. Julianus, bishop of the holy Church of Ruspensis, subscribed the synodical letter of the Fathers of the province of Byzacena, which was read in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2.

John Hardouin does not distinguish Ruspina from Ruspe in note 13 on book V of Pliny, since, as he says, the authority of a single Ptolemy is not great enough in this matter: Ptolemy makes them different in book IV, chapter 3, whereas other authors commend only one or the other. Yet, with all respect to the learned man, the Peutinger Table represents both, as does the anonymous Ravennate in book V. Secundus, bishop of the Church of Ruspitensis, belonged to one or the other of these cities; he is listed among the Catholics in chapter 121 of the Carthaginian Collation. Garnerius carelessly assigned him to Numidia, but Henricus Norisius has demonstrated the error of that attribution. Ruspina is famous in the historians of Roman history who described the war waged by Caesar in Africa—Hirtius, Dio Cassius, and others.

### 103. TALAPTULENSIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Taleptulensis*. Stephanus, bishop of the holy Church of Talaptulensis, subscribed, with the other Byzacene Fathers, the synodical letter addressed to Constantine Augustus, which was read in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2. Whether this Stephanus should rather be assigned to this see than to Telepte, others may judge. The same must be said of Datianus of Telepte, mentioned in the Carthaginian Collation; see above, no. 81.

Likewise, in the *Notitia* of Emperor Leo as published by Beveregius, *Taleptes* is mentioned, whereas in Goar’s edition it is called *Talapta*. In both places the Greek text has Ταλέπτης (*Talēptēs*). A little farther below, among the cities of Numidia, Goar has *Telepte*; but this seems rather to be Thebeste, as we stated above concerning the Numidians, no. 75.

### 104. AUTENTESIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Auteniensis*, for *Autentensis*. Antoninus places Autentum in Byzacena. Optatus, bishop of the holy Church of Autentensis, subscribed, with the other bishops of the same province, the aforementioned synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2.

### 105. JUNCENSIS

At the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 187, Valentinianus, bishop of Juncensis, was present among the Donatists, as the distinguished V. C. Baluzius restored the reading from an old manuscript, whereas previously it had read *Inucensis*. Henricus Norisius nevertheless believes that the latter reading should be retained in his criticism of Garnerius, distinguishing the cities of Juncensis and Inucensis. He places the former in Byzacena, but the latter—whose bishop was Valentinianus—in the proconsular province.

Inuca appears in the Peutinger Table not far from Major Tuburbo, which Antoninus places near the city of Carthage in his *Itinerary*, where it is called *Unuca*, midway between Vallis and Carthage itself. The anonymous Ravennate agrees in book III, section 5. *Junces* is mentioned among the cities of Byzacena in the Bodleian *Notitia*; in Goar’s edition it is called *Juca*. The Greek text has Γούγκη (*Goungē*).

A celebrated Council of Junca was held under Liberatus, primate of the province of Byzacena, at the beginning of the year 524, that is, in the first year of King Hilderic. From it legates were sent to the Council of Carthage, which was to be held under Boniface the following year. Ferrandus the deacon reports a canon of this council in his *Abridgment of the Canons*, no. 26.

At this same council—although some printed editions have *Vincensi*, but incorrectly, as learned men point out, while our manuscript of eight hundred years has *Juncensi*—Saint Fulgentius was preferred to Quodvultdeus as bishop. A little later, however, he yielded his place to him at the Council of Sufes, as the author of the Life of that saint relates in chapter 29.

Perhaps Numidius presided over this city. He is said to have subscribed, with the other bishops of the province of Byzacena, the synodical letter addressed to Constantine Augustus and read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2, in these words: “Numidius, humble bishop of the holy Church of Sosiana Juncis.” Holstenius conjectures that the Greek was written Σουγίκνης Γούγκης (*Sougiknēs Goungēs*), and that the church at this place was dedicated to Divine Wisdom. But this is conjecture.

I had almost omitted the monastery mentioned in the Life of blessed Fulgentius, chapter 14, situated near the shore of Junca, as the manuscript of Saint-Germain already cited explicitly states, and adjoining Benefe. Moreover, among the Fathers of Caesarean Mauretania, Glorinus of Junca is listed first, below.

### 106. JUBALTIANENSIS

Geta, bishop of the people of Jubaltianensis, was present at the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 128. He is the same Geta, as the distinguished V. C. Baluzius believes, who was a legate from the province of Byzacena to the Council of Carthage in 403, as reported in chapter 90 of the book of canons of the African Church.

I readily agree with this learned man and with Holstenius that the bishop of the same place was Restutus or Restitutus, who is called bishop of the holy Church of Jubeclidiensis—or, as the manuscript of the Church of Beauvais has it, *Jubalidiensis*—in the subscriptions of the synodical letter of the Byzacene bishops at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2.

### 107. SERVITIUS UNURICOPOLITANUS

The printed editions have *Servilius*. Haller’s manuscript has *Unorecopolitanus*.

### 108. AGGARITANUS

Above, no. 29, appears Filtiosus of Aggaritanus; there we made several observations about the city of Aggaritana. The index prefixed to the works of Saint Cyprian indeed presents two cities called Aggar, one in Byzacena and the other in the proconsular province. But both Aggaritan bishops in this *Notitia* belonged to Byzacena.

### 109. VIGILIUS TAPSENSIS

He was a celebrated writer whose works were published and elucidated by the learned priest Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius of the Society of Jesus. Chiffletius recorded many details worthy of knowledge about this bishop and his works, since his memory had previously been somewhat obscure, as is evident from Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 495, and from Labbe’s historical dissertation on the same subject.

Casimirus Oudinus cannot be excused: after Chiffletius’s edition of Vigilius, he wrote in Bellarmine’s supplement that Vigilius flourished in the year 560.

The name of this city is often written with aspiration by ancient authors. Ptolemy, Titus Livius in books XXIX and XXXIII, and Lucius Florus in book IV of Roman History, chapter 4, have *Thapsus*. Hirtius, in his book *On the African War*, and Pliny in book V, chapter 4, call it the coastal town of Thapsus. The Peutinger Table, the epitome of the lost book CXIV of Livy, and the anonymous Ravennate, however, have *Capsum*. This town was famous for the flight of King Juba and the other enemies of Julius Caesar; on that occasion Dio Cassius gives an excellent description of its location in book XLIII of his *Roman History*.

### THE NUMBER IS 107

Thus the Laon manuscript and Sirmond’s edition. Chiffletius, however, gave 111, because in addition to the 109 bishops listed here, there seem to be two whose names had fallen out at the beginning.

### 110. MADASSUMA

Haller’s manuscript has *Madyssumma*. In Antoninus’s *Itinerary* it is called *Mardarsuma*. Primulianus, bishop of Mandasumitanus, presided over this city on behalf of the Donatists; he is mentioned in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 187. He also seems to have attended the Council of Cabarsussa, for among those who subscribed appears Primulianus, bishop, although his see is not specified.

The *Notitia* of Emperor Leo, published by Goar, lists Madassumma among the cities of Byzacena. The Greek text there, however, as also in Beveregius’s Latin and Greek edition, has Μαδασούβα (*Madasouba*).

### 111. DIONYSIANA

Haller’s manuscript has *Donisiana*. Pomponius, a confessor from Dionysiana, gave his opinion in favor of rebaptizing heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 48; Augustine answers his objection in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 12.

Fortunatus, bishop of Dionysianensis, likewise subscribed, with other Donatists, the Council of Cabarsussa in 393. Victor, also of the same sect and bishop of Dionysianensis, was listed in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 198; but he did not appear because he was ill, as Primianus, the Donatist bishop of Carthage, testified.

### 112. SULIANIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Sulianae*. Urbanus, bishop of Sulitanus, who appeared among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 201, may perhaps be assigned here. Holstenius, however, believes that this passage refers to the place called *Silvani* in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*.

### 113. ORREA CAELIA

In the manuscript this city is read on the same line as the preceding one, with a small space between them, although elsewhere each city occupies its own line. Moreover, at the end it says, as though there were not two cities, “There are five in number.”

The name of this city is often written with aspiration by the ancients, as in Sirmond’s edition. Antoninus calls it *Horrea Coelia*, a village of Byzacena. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 67, Tenax of *Horreiscaelia* was present among those advocating rebaptism. The name is written in the same way by Augustine in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 31, where the holy doctor answers Tenax’s objection.

In earlier editions of the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 201, Januarius, bishop of *Haran . . . . . . . celtensis*, is listed among the Donatists. But, as the learned Baluzius restored it, it should read *Horreae [lacuna] celtensis*, that is, *Horreae Caeliensis*. Finally, Hilarinus, bishop of Orreocaelensis, attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419 as a legate of the province of Byzacena. In the book of canons of the African Church, after chapter 127, he is called Hilarianus, bishop of *Horreocellorum*; another manuscript has *Horreicaeliensis*, as Justellus observes. In Greek, however, the name is Ὁῤῥεοκελίων (*Orreokeliōn*), while in the subscriptions it is *Horreoccellensis*, in Greek Ὀῤῥεοκέλης (*Orreokelēs*).

### 114. CUNCULIANA

Without doubt Januarius, bishop of the people of Cenculianensis, presided over this city. He is mentioned among the Catholic Fathers in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 128; Baluzius mistakenly assigned him to Numidia.

In the *Notitia* published by Goar, Cenculiana is mentioned under the province of Byzacena. The Greek text has Καηβακίλεως (*Kaēbakileōs*). Beveregius’s Bodleian *Notitia* divides this word into two and records two cities in Latin, *Campsa* and *Cileos*, and in Greek Χαμφία (*Champhia*) and Χίλεως (*Chileōs*).

### 115. TICIBUS

The same name occurs in the synodical letter of the Byzacene Fathers at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2. Among the subscribers is Romulus, bishop of the holy Church of the city of Ticibus.

The anonymous Ravennate mentions *Tices* in Getulia, book III, section 9. Ptolemy has the city *Ticena*. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 121, Gallus, bishop of Ticensis, appeared among the Catholics.

If Candidus, bishop of Dicensis by birth, who subscribed the aforementioned synodical letter of the Byzacenes, presided over the city of Ticensis, then the city of Ticensis must be distinguished from Ticibus. Otherwise two bishops of the same city would have subscribed the synodical letter, a conclusion no one would readily accept.

## FOR THE PROVINCE OF CAESAREAN MAURETANIA

### 1. JUNCENSIS

See what we said above about the bishop of Junca among the Byzacenes, no. 105.

### 2. TEBERIANUS QUIDIENSIS

The printed editions have *Tiberianus*. Ortelius cites this city from a manuscript of Victor of Utica, but places it in Numidia; I believe this happened through a lapse of memory.

No one can deny that some people call this same city *Quizia* or *Quiza* under different names, since the letters *d* and *z* were used indifferently by Africans, as we have already noted more than once. This can be demonstrated particularly from the city’s appearance in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 143. There Priscus, bishop of the Church of Quidiensis, had testified that the Donatist bishop who opposed him, together with his own parents, had converted to Catholic unity, and that no schismatic of that sect remained in his city.

Honoratus the Donatist then interjected and said: “Our bishop of Quizicensis succumbed during the persecution,” as the learned Baluzius corrected the text. Previously it read: “Our bishop who succumbed to the people of Zica during the persecution.”

Pliny, book V, chapter 2, calls this city *Quiza Xenitana*, “the town of foreigners”; by these words the same city is designated in three languages. Hardouin says that it was called *Quiza* by the Moors, and *Xenitana* by the foreigners who founded it. For Greek ξένος (*xenos*) means “foreigner,” which Pliny explained in Latin in the words that follow.

Different authors assign the city different ranks, as the learned man also observes. Pomponius Mela, book I, chapter 6, calls it a fortress; Antoninus, in his *Itinerary*, a municipium; and Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, a colony, where he has *Buiza*, while the Palatine manuscript calls it *Cuiza*.

The distinguished man who produced the new Oxford edition of the works of Saint Cyprian conjectures that Secundinus “of Cedias,” who spoke eleventh among those advocating the rebaptism of heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, presided over the city of Quidia, so that *Cedias* was written for *Quidias*.

But if this conjecture is accepted, two cities called Quidia must now be admitted. Besides Priscus already mentioned, who in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 143, as we said, affirmed that he then had no opponent—a statement also acknowledged by the Donatists—there appears in chapter 163 Fortis, bishop of Cediensis on Donatus’s side, who protested that he had no Catholic opponent.

Secundinus of the Cyprianic council is also called “of Cedias” by Augustine in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, where the holy doctor answers his objection. For this name, however, two manuscripts, as our editors observed in the new edition, have *a Cezas*, and several others have *a Chezas*. Pamelius’s reading in his notes on Cyprian is nearly the same. But this variation of readings does not resolve the difficulty.

### 3. SUFARITANUS

Below, no. 87, a bishop of Sufaritanus is mentioned again. In Haller’s manuscript, however, the name occurs once as *Sufaritanus*, while the other time it is *Susaritanus*. If our reading is accepted, we must either say that there were two cities of this name in the province, or certainly that there were two Catholic bishops in one city, one of whom perhaps had converted from the schism to unity while retaining the place and dignity of bishop.

According to the learned Baluzius, Reparatus, bishop of the people of Sufasaritanus, presided over this same Church at the time of the Carthaginian Collation. He appeared among the Catholic bishops in chapter 135. Moreover, in chapter 188, where the text formerly read “Reparatus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Sifaitensis,” Baluzius restored *Sufasaritanus*.

In Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, *Sufasar* is mentioned once and again among the cities of Mauretania; the anonymous Ravennate calls the city *Sufasa*. In the *Notitia* of Emperor Leo published by Goar, *Suffara* occurs among the cities of Mauretania Secunda, but in Beveregius’s edition it is called *Senaphas*. See below, in the province of Sardinia, *Sonaster*, no. 3.

### 4. CORNICULANENSIS

Thus both the printed editions and the manuscripts. The anonymous Ravennate mentions *Corniclano* in book III, section 4, but in the Mauretania called Cyrenensis. It occurs again in book V, section 6; its location can be learned more accurately from the Peutinger Table.

### 5. ITENSIS

Nothing is found concerning this city. Tertullus, bishop of Abitensis, sat among the Donatists at the Council of Cabarsussa; but he should rather be assigned to the proconsular province, where Antoninus places Abitta. Ptolemy lists this city among those that belonged to the Third Augustan Legion.

### 6. TIMICITANUS

Victor, bishop of the people of Timicitanus, attended the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 135. He had Optatus as his Donatist opponent, mentioned there and again below in chapter 197.

Pliny, book V, chapter 2, lists *Timici* among the cities. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, lists *Timice* with the other cities of Caesarean Mauretania; in the following chapter *Timica* likewise appears among the places belonging to the Third Augustan Legion.

### 7. NOBICENSIS

This is also called *Nobicensis* in Haller’s manuscript, for *Novicensis*, as Ortelius believes.

### 8. MILIANENSIS

Without doubt Victor, bishop of the people of Malianensis, presided over this city. He is listed in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 135, together with Nestorius the Donatist, his opponent, who also appeared again among the bishops of his sect in chapter 208.

Antoninus places *Malliana* in his *Itinerary* between Sufasar and Tigavas Castra, cities of Caesarean Mauretania. Bertius’s edition has *Tivaga*, but this is a copyist’s error.

Augustine wrote a letter, no. 236 in the new edition and formerly no. 74, to Deuterius the bishop, on the occasion of a certain Victorinus, a subdeacon of Malliana from the Manichaean sect.

### 9. GIRUMONTENSIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Girumentensis*.

### 10. ALTABENSIS

Thus the manuscripts and the printed editions. Antoninus places *Altabam* in Numidia. In the *Notitia* of Leo the Wise, among the cities of the same province, Goar’s Latin edition has *Altaba*, while the Greek has Αλκάδους (*Alkadous*). In the Bodleian edition, however, the place is called *Leradus* in both Greek and Latin.

The Carthaginian Collation mentions a bishop of Assabensis; see below, among the Sitifensians, no. 24.

### 11. PANATORIENSIS

The learned Baluzius conjectures that Pelagius, bishop of Vanarionensis, belonged to this place. He is listed among the Donatists in chapter 187 of the Carthaginian Collation, where he declares that he has no opponent.

Certainly *Banatoriensis* may originally have been written for *Panatoriensis*, since the letters *b* and *v* were used indifferently for one another by the ancients.

### 12. COLUMPNATENSIS

The *Book of the Notitiae of the Empire*, section 54, mentions the commander of the Columnatensian frontier. The copyist added the letter *p*, just as some wrote *Dompnus* for *Domnus*.

### 13. SUCARDENSIS

In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 135, the name of Pompeianus, the Catholic bishop of Sucardensis, was read out. Because he was ill, Alypius answered on his behalf. His opponent, Donatus of Sucardensis, was also ill, as Marinianus the Donatist testified in chapter 210.

### 14. IDENSIS

Ortelius, citing Victor—as he calls him—of Utica, mentions a bishop of Idensis in Caesarean Mauretania. He does not say, however, whether this city was listed once or twice in Haller’s manuscript. See below, no. 16.

Holstenius conjectures that this was the town of Ididi mentioned in the Life of Saint Fulgentius. But two manuscripts, one Colbertine and the other that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written eight hundred years ago, have *Mididi*. This city was in Byzacena, above, col. 000.

### 15. TITILTENSIS

Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts. Holstenius conjectures that Donatus, bishop of Tisilitanus, should be assigned here. He was listed among the Catholic Fathers in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 121. Concerning him, see above, col. 000.

### 16. IDENSIS

Already above, no. 14, Subitanus of Idensis was listed, and in no. 5 Lucius of Itensis.

### 17. FIDOLOMENSIS

Thus it appears in the manuscripts and the printed editions.

### 18. TABORENTENSIS

In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 115, Marinus, or Martinus, of the Catholic Church of Taborensis, is said to have appeared with Victor, his opponent, who was again listed in chapter 201 among the bishops of his sect.

The distinguished V. C. Baluzius proves by two arguments that this man belonged to the proconsular province. First, among the bishops of that province who subscribed the synodical letter to Paul of Constantinople, reported at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2, there occurs Constantius, “by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Talborensis.”

Second, when, in chapter 126 of the same Collation, Felix, bishop of the people of Visitensis, said that he had no opponent, Victor, bishop of the city of Taborensis—that is, the Donatist mentioned above—said: “He departed recently.” Baluzius interprets this to mean: “He died a few days ago; I am caring for his people.”

But the Church of Visitensis belonged to the proconsular province, for Valentinianus, bishop of the people of Visicensis, subscribed the aforementioned synodical letter of the proconsular bishops. The learned man does not distinguish Visitensis from the Church of Visicensis. Therefore, if his opinion is correct, another Church of Taborensis must be sought in Mauretania, over which our Victor, praised here in the *Notitia*, presided.

### 19. VERECUNDUS NOBENSIS

Haller’s manuscript likewise has *Verecundus Nobensis*, according to Ortelius. See below, no. 93, where Mingin is also called Nobensis.

Felix, the Catholic bishop of Novensis, belonged to one or the other of these cities; he is mentioned in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 215. At the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, Rogatianus “of Nova” gave his opinion in favor of repeating the baptism of heretics, no. 60. Augustine answers his objection in book VII *Against the Donatists*, chapter 24.

There are several cities in Africa with this name, but with an additional designation, such as Nova Sparsa, Nova Caesaris, and so forth; these will be discussed in their proper places. Antoninus’s *Itinerary* has *Ad Novas*, not far from Oppidum Novum, mentioned below in this same province, no. 64.

### 20. ZUCABIARITANUS

In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 135, Maximianus, bishop of the people of Zugabbaritanus, is listed among the Catholic Fathers. In the editions preceding Baluzius’s, he was incorrectly called *Suboabburitensis*. The learned Baluzius corrected this because Germanus, who is described here as Maximianus’s Donatist opponent, is explicitly called bishop of Zuggabaritanus in chapter 182.

Older editions of Pliny, book V, chapter 2, mentioned *Succubar*. John Hardouin corrected the passage from all the manuscripts, as he says, and has *Succabar*, a city there called a colony of Augustus. It is likewise called this in Golzius’s *Thesaurus*, page 238.

Ammianus, book XXIX, mentions the municipium of Sugabaritanus, situated on the Transcellensian mountain. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, has *Zuchabari* in the Palatine manuscript as printed by Bertius; earlier editions had *Buchambari*.

Pamelius, in his notes on Saint Cyprian, believes that Fortunatus “of Tucchabori,” who was present among those advocating the rebaptism of heretics at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, no. 17, presided over this city. But this is incorrect. Stephanus, bishop of Tuccaboriensis, is listed among the proconsular bishops who subscribed the synodical letter at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, act 2.

### 21. CAESARIENSIS

This is the most distinguished city of the entire province, from which Caesarean Mauretania received its name. Pliny gives its eulogy in a few words in book V, chapter 2:

“There is the most celebrated town of Caesarea, formerly called Jol, the royal city of Juba, granted colonial status by the deified Claudius, who settled veterans there by his order.”

Ptolemy, book II, chapter 4, calls it *Jol Caesarea*; Antoninus calls it *Caesarea Colonia*; Pomponius Mela, book I, chapter 6, calls it “Jol, once an obscure town by the sea, now illustrious because it was Juba’s royal city and is called Caesarea.” Solinus likewise maintains that it had been the royal city of Bocchus:

“First the royal city of Bocchus; afterward, it was given to Juba by the favor of the Roman people as a gift,”

as he says in chapter 28.

Procopius calls it μεγάλη καὶ πολυάνθρωπος ἐκ παλαιοῦ οὖσα (*great and populous from ancient times*). I omit the other profane authors who collected further information about this city. What remains today, as many think, is under the name of Algiers, the celebrated capital of the kingdom bearing the same name; Samson and other learned geographers, however, reject this opinion.

Formerly it was the civil metropolis of the whole province. Saint Augustine transferred this title also to its bishop: as we have observed elsewhere, at the beginning of his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus, the Donatist Bishop of Caesarea*, he calls Deuterius the metropolitan bishop of Caesarea.

This Emeritus was one of the seven bishops whom the Donatists had chosen to conduct the defense of their cause at the Carthaginian Collation, and he is frequently recorded as speaking there. He was also present with all the bishops of the province and the entire people when Augustine preached at Caesarea. Augustine himself relates in book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 51, that Emeritus, finding nothing to answer, listened like a mute.

Deuterius, however, the Catholic bishop of the same city, was one of the custodians of the records at the Collation. They appeared together and recognized one another in chapter 143.

From this passage of the *Notitia* the opinion of those who believed that the African primates—even in provinces other than the proconsular—were appointed according to the dignity of their sees rather than according to the time of their ordination is shown to be false. That opinion has now been rejected by everyone.

### 22. RUSUBIRITANUS

*Rusubus* is mentioned by Ortelius from a manuscript of Victor of Utica. Ptolemy has *Rusicibar* in book IV, chapter 3; see below, 167, no. 77. The Peutinger Table shows *Rusippisim* as a municipium.

### 23. SUBBARITANUS

Haller’s manuscript has *Subarritanus*. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 1, mentions *Subur* among the cities of Tingitana. Carolus a Sancto Paulo writes that Maximianus, bishop in the Carthaginian Collation, was called *Suburitanus* from this place.

But there is no Maximianus Suburitanus in the Carthaginian Collation. Maximianus, who in the editions preceding Baluzius’s is called *Subo-abburitensis* in chapter 135, should be called neither Suburitanus nor Subbaritanus, but Zuggabaritanus, as Baluzius corrected. See above, no. 20.

The martyrs of Suburba are mentioned in sermon 32 of Saint Augustine, published by Sirmond; it is no. 345 in the new edition. See our admonition on the Passion of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas, no. 3, in the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, page 82.

### 24. AQUENSIS

There were several cities in Africa of this name, even apart from those distinguished by an additional designation. Secundus, who subscribed Leporius’s libellus, called himself bishop of the Church of Aquensis, or Megarmitanus; but he belonged to the Numidians, as we said in the notes on the bishops of that province, no. 103.

Victorinianus, a bishop of Aquensis from the Donatist sect, attended the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 208. It can be inferred from that same passage that he belonged to the province of Arzugitana. There Asselicus, the Catholic bishop of the municipium of Tusuritanus, interjects that he had departed from the Arzuges on the third day before the Kalends of May, and that Victorinianus had been ordained on the road by the Donatist faction.

Cresconius, also a Donatist bishop of Aquensis, is listed in chapter 198. It can easily be inferred from the same passage that he belonged to the Numidians. When Cresconius said that he had no traditor, Aurelius, the Catholic bishop of Macomadia, interjected and said: “We have a presbyter here; he was also a bishop there, but he has now died, and no one has yet been ordained in his place.”

We proved above, in the notes on the bishops of that province, no. 84, that Aurelius was the Numidian bishop of Macomadia.

Besides all these, we have another bishop of Aquensis from the Collation who seems to have been bishop of this city of Aquensis in Mauretania. He is Helpidius, bishop of the people of Aquensis, who is listed in chapter 135 together with Reparatus, his opponent. Reparatus again appeared among the Donatists in chapter 197.

Antoninus’s *Itinerary* places *Aquae* between Sufasar and Caesarea itself. The bishop of Aquensis mentioned here seems to have presided over that place.

The distinguished V. C. Stephanus Baluzius believes that the Aquensis city mentioned here is the very city of Aquitana whose metropolitan, Crescens, is mentioned in book I of Victor of Vita’s *History*, no. 7. We discussed this matter more fully in the notes on that passage of Victor, no. 22.

Certainly the Aquitani were named from Aquae in Gaul, as John Hardouin observes in book IV of Pliny, chapter 19. Hence, according to Baluzius, they were indifferently called *Aquenses* and *Aquitani*. Baluzius is also supported by the statement that Crescens presided over 120 bishops: exactly that number of bishops of Caesarean Mauretania appears in the *Notitia*, besides six other sees that at that time had no bishops.

### 25. MURUSTAGENSIS

Thus the manuscripts and the printed editions.

### 26. VAGALITANUS

On behalf of Donatus, Miggin, bishop of Vagalitanus, presided over the same city. He is listed in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 208. Antoninus’s *Itinerary* mentions Vagal among the towns of Mauretania.

### 27. TIGISITANUS

We have already seen, among the bishops of Numidia, no. 89, a bishop of Tisigitanus. There we reported what could be gathered concerning the two cities of that name; consult that passage.

Ortelius mentions *Tigisitanus* and *Tigistanus* from Victor, as he calls him, of Utica. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, lists *Tigis* among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania. The anonymous Ravennate has *Tigisim* in book III, section 8.

Lucas Holstenius believes that the Catholic bishop Aptus of the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 120, should be assigned here. Baluzius, however, says that he presided over the city of Tiziensis in Byzacena, as we stated above among the Byzacenes, no. 65.

### 28. FALLABENSIS

Ortelius does not mention this city, perhaps because it was not present in Haller’s fragment.

### 29. USINADENSIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Usidanensis*.

### 30. FLUMENZERITANUS

Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts.

### 31. CASTELLOMINORITANUS

Ortelius does not have this name from Haller’s fragment.

### 32. RESTITUTUS FLORIANENSIS

Thus the printed editions; the Laon manuscript has *Restutus*. This variation occurs frequently in this *Notitia*. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, mentions *Phloryia* among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania. The Greek text has Φλωρύϊα (*Phloryia*), from which, without doubt, the name *Phloryanensis* or *Florianensis* is derived.

### 33. ALAMILIARENSIS

Ortelius writes the name of this place from Victor as though it were composed of two words, namely *Ala-Miliarensis*. In the *Notitia of the Empire*, *Ala Miliaria*, or *Ala Miliarensis*, indeed occurs more than once. Perhaps this city received its name from that designation, just as Germania received its name from the Germans.

### 34. TIGAMIBENENSIS

Haller’s manuscript has *Tigamibemensis*.

### 35. AMAURENSIS

Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts. The anonymous Ravennate, among the cities belonging to another part of Sitifensian Mauretania, mentions *Amabu Mune*, that is, a municipium. From this the name *Amauvensis*, and then *Amaurensis*, may perhaps have been derived.

### 36. SESTENSIS

Thus both the manuscripts and the printed editions. Below, no. 117, we find *Sertensis*. Ortelius conjectures that *Septensis* should be read here, although he supplies no information about the city of Septensis, which is nevertheless very well known.

Procopius reports in book I of *The Vandalic War* that *Septum* was so called because seven hills rose beside that city. He writes that one of the Pillars of Hercules stood not far away; he repeats substantially the same account in book II.

The same Procopius testifies in book VI of *Buildings*, chapter 7, that after the Vandals had been expelled from Africa, this fortress was restored by Emperor Justinian, who ordered a church to be built there in honor of the Virgin Mother of God.

The Bodleian *Notitia* mentions *Septum* twice among the cities of Mauretania Secunda. There the first three cities of the province are presented as follows: first, simply *Septum*; the second time, *Septum ad partem Thenissi*; and third, *Spanias*, to which the Greek text reported there corresponds.

In Goar’s edition, however, all these are contained in a single entry, in Greek: Πεπτὸν εἰς τὸ μέρος Ἱσπανίας (*Pepton in the region of Spain*). The Latin version reads: “Benepota in the part of Spain.”

### 37. TERNAMUNENSIS

Sarmentius, a bishop on the Donatist side, belonged to this place. He is mentioned in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 180, in Baluzius’s edition. Other editions, in chapter 179, have *Cernamusensis*, while Masson’s has *Cerramusensis*.

Without doubt this is the city called *Taranamusa Castra* by Antoninus. Hence Baluzius concludes that *Ternamusensis* should be read here in the *Notitia* for *Ternamunensis*. In his notes on the cited passage of the Collation, he discusses at greater length—and, as is his custom, learnedly—the various changes of letters that commonly occur in ancient documents, especially African ones.

### 38. CAPUTCILLENSIS

Antoninus mentions this place in his *Itinerary*, where it is called *Caput Cila*. In section 54 of the *Notitia of the Empire*, the commander of the *limes Caput Cillensis* is recorded under the authority of the duke of Caesarean Mauretania.

### 39. NASBINCENSIS

Haller’s manuscript, as reported by Ortelius, has *Narbincensis*.

### 40. BACANARIENSIS

This is the reading of both manuscripts and the printed editions.

### 41. BALLENS VILLENOBENSIS

Thus the Laon manuscript. The printed editions have *Valens*. Haller’s manuscript has *Baleus*. Ortelius says that Victor mentions *Baleus Villenobensis*.

### 42. MASUCCABENSIS

Thus the Laon manuscript and the printed editions; Haller’s manuscript, as cited by Ortelius, differs by a single letter.

Mazuccaban.

43. **PAMARIENSIS.** Ortelius also cites it on the authority of Victor. Antoninus places the island of Palmaria in the Maritime Itinerary between Africa and Sardinia.

44. **BENEPOTENS.** Thus in both manuscripts and the printed editions. Above, no. 36, we saw that in the *Notitia* of the Emperor Leo Benepota is listed among the cities of Mauretania Secunda. [Col. 0340A]

45. **VARDIMISSENSIS.** Victor, bishop of the congregation of Bartimisia, must be assigned here; he was listed among the Catholic bishops in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135.

46. **AMBIENSIS.** Maximus the martyr is said in several manuscript codices to have suffered in the Ambian province, as we observed in the note to the acts of that same saint, no. 2, in the *Acta Martyrum sincera*, p. 143.

47. **MEDIENSIS.** Ortelius does not mention this bishopric from Haller’s codex. The Peutinger Tables have *Ad Medias* in segment three, but, unless I am mistaken, outside Mauretania.

48. **CATULENSIS.** Thus in the manuscripts and the printed editions. Antoninus, as we have already observed, mentions Casula in the Itinerary. But since that place lay not far from Carthage, it cannot be assigned here. Cerealis, an African bishop who is said by Gennadius, ch. 96, to have published a book against the Arians, is called bishop of Castula [Col. 0340B] by the ancient anonymous author of the twelve ecclesiastical writers preserved by Miraeus. See below, no. 119.

49. **MINNENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Minuensis*. At the Council of Carthage under Boniface, Secundinus, bishop of the congregation of Minna in the province of Mauretania—and indeed in Caesariensis—subscribed, as is clear from Boniface’s letter reproduced there, where he is called Secundus. Antoninus has *Mina* once in the Itinerary, and elsewhere *Minna*. Another is Minna, the Villa of Mars, which the same author locates near Leptis Magna.

50. **CARTENNITANUS.** This see was distinguished by Victor, bishop of the city of Cartenna in Mauretania, as Gennadius says in his book on ecclesiastical writers. He wrote one lengthy book against the Arians, which he offered to King Geiseric to be heard through his agents, and so forth. The manuscripts, moreover, vary in recording the author’s name: he is called *Victor Carthenae* in the manuscript codex of the monastery of Fécamp; but in our very ancient codex he is called *Maurus Cartennae*. That he joined piety and knowledge of the Scriptures with fervor of faith is attested by Gennadius, who in the same place commends other works of his. Among these is a *Little Book of Consolation to a certain Basil concerning the death of a son*, which learned men believe to be the very work that appears under the title *On Consolation in Adversity* among the works of Saint Basil the Great in certain printed editions.

He also wrote a book *On the Publican’s Repentance*, or rather *On Public Repentance*, as our already-mentioned copy of Gennadius has it; that copy was written approximately eleven hundred years ago. In the Fécamp codex, about six hundred years old, it is called *On Repentance*, without any addition; this may perhaps be the genuine title. For a book *On Repentance* has been published in the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose, whose author himself calls himself Victor; learned men consider him to be the Victor whom Gennadius mentions in the passage cited. In the Sorbonne codex, however, this work appears under the name of Saint Ambrose, but incorrectly.

Most learned men, however, believe that it should be attributed to Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, because in one codex of the cathedral church of Reims and in another of the monastery of Hérival it bears the following title: “Here begins the book of Saint Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, the historian, *On Those Who Have Fallen*.” The Reims codex is of the highest quality and was written at least eight hundred years ago; Archbishop Hincmar gave it to that church, as is indicated more than once in the codex itself. The title quoted above was written by the first hand.

Moreover, Saint Augustine mentions Rusticus, a Catholic bishop of Cartenna, at the beginning of his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, the Donatist bishop of Caesarea. Rogatus, bishop of Cartenna, is famous; in the Donatist schism he gave his name to the Rogatist faction. Vincent succeeded him; Augustine refutes his letter in Letter 93, which could rightly occupy a place among the books.

Ptolemy mentions Cartenna in book III, ch. 2, and Antoninus in the Itinerary. Pomponius Mela has *Cartennam*, or, as Isaac Vossius observed from manuscript codices, *Cartinnam*. Pliny reports in book V, ch. 2, that this same city was granted the title of a colony of Augustus.

The very ancient Carthaginian Calendar commemorates the holy Carthennenses on the fourth day before the Nones of February. Augustine preached a sermon on their feast, entitled *On the Nativity of the Carthennenses*, as Possidius testifies in ch. 9 of his *Index*. Our Mabillon suspects, in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 421, that these martyrs may be assigned to Cartenna, a city of Mauretania. The conjecture of learned men is supported by the passage in the Fécamp codex mentioned above.

We have already noted, in the remarks on the Byzacenes, no. 58, that one learned man conflated Carianensis and Cartennensis—two episcopal cities in Africa—into one; Holstenius had done the same earlier.

51. **RIGIENSIS.** Victor of Vita, book I, no. 13, mentions a certain place called Regia, where the Arians violently violated a church and, among others, pierced with an arrow a lector who was singing in the pulpit. In the index prefixed to Cyprian’s works there are two cities called Regium, one of which is assigned to Mauretania. This may perhaps be the place called *Ad Regias* in Antoninus’s Itinerary. See the Numidians, no. 91, where there is a bishop **REGIANENSIS**.

52. **VANNIDENSIS.** Thus in both manuscript codices. The printed editions, however, have *Vaunidensis*.

53. **CAPRENSIS.** Victor of Vita himself mentions a desert called Caprapicta. Did the bishop of Capra receive his name from this place, or at least from some town bearing a similar name? Certainly a new church is recorded as having been established in this region by the author cited, book I, no. 11.

54. **METCUN RUSUCCURITANUS.** The printed editions have *Metcur*. Fortunatus, a Catholic bishop of the congregation of Rusuccurris, presided over the same city; he is listed in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135, together with Optatus, his adversary, who is mentioned again among the Donatists in ch. 176.

Nicellus of Rusurri, or Rusurriana, should also be assigned here. He was a legate of Caesarean Mauretania to the Council of Carthage in 419 under Aurelius, as recorded in the codex of the African Church. The reading in Labbe is more favorable to us: it has *Nivellus Ruscuriensis*, with *Rusuccurrensis* or *Rusocorensis* in the margin, volume II, columns 1603 and 1605.

Pliny, book V, ch. 2, says that Rusucurium was honored with civic status by Claudius. Antoninus in the Itinerary and the Peutinger Tables call it a colony. Other authors also mention it; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, calls it *Rusuccore*.

55. **SFASFERIENSIS.** Thus in both manuscripts and in the printed editions.

56. **OBBITANUS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 195, Felicissimus, bishop of Obba, appeared among the Donatists. Valerian, bishop of Obba in the African province, also attended the Fifth Ecumenical Council, as recorded in Baluze’s new collection of councils. In Labbe’s edition he is said to be of the proconsular province, with “African” in the margin.

Older than all these, however, is Paul the confessor from Obba, who at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian spoke in favor of repeating baptism for heretics, no. 47. Several manuscripts and printed editions have *a Bobba*, which is also the reading in Augustine, book VII *Against the Donatists*, ch. 11. The Oxford editor of Saint Cyprian’s works says that this reading can be confirmed from Pliny, who, as he reports in his notes, places Bobba, a colony of Augustus, in Mauretania, forty Roman miles inland from Lixa.

57. **TIMIDANENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Timidianensis*.

58. **FRONTENSIS.** Thus it is written in both codices and in the printed editions.

59. **ICOSITANUS.** The Laudunensis manuscript expressly has this reading. The printed editions have the erroneous *Leositanus*. Everyone knows Icosium, a celebrated city among both sacred and secular writers, which enjoyed the name and privileges of a colony. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, writes that Vespasian granted it Latin rights. Ptolemy, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus, Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, the anonymous Ravennate, [Col. 0342A] and many others mention it.

Solinus, in the *Polyhistor*, ch. 28, says that twenty companions of Hercules gave the city both its name and its origin. When Hercules was passing through the region, according to that author, twenty men deserted his company, chose a place, and built walls; and, so that no one might claim private glory from the name he had imposed, the city was named from the number of its founders. For Greek *eikoti* (Εἵκοτι) means “twenty” (*viginti* in Latin).

Laurentius Icositanus was bishop of this same city. He was a legate of Caesarean Mauretania to the Council of Carthage held under Aurelius in 419, as recorded in the codex of the African Church. Crescens, also Icositanus, but from the Donatist sect, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 197.

It is therefore clear that *Leosita* must be expunged from the catalogue of African cities; some had introduced it from the corrupt reading of this *Notitia*.

60. **TABLENSIS.** Perhaps Urbanus, a Talensian bishop mentioned among the Donatists in the Conference, ch. 198, presided over this same city. Holstenius assigns to this place the Tablacian frontier mentioned in the *Notitia Imperii*.

[Col. 0342B] 61. **RESTUTUS LAPIDIENSIS.** Here too the printed editions have *Restitutus*. Ptolemy mentions Laudias in book IV, ch. 2, where he discusses the cities of Mauretania. The name, however, would fit better the city of Lapdis—or, as it is read in certain codices, Labdis—whose bishop is listed above among the proconsular bishops, no. 18, were it not for the distance between the provinces.

62. **VONCARIENSIS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 208, Felix, a bishop of Boncara from the Donatist sect, is mentioned. There is no doubt that this name designates the Voncariensis city recorded here.

63. **RUSGUNIENSIS.** It is remarkable how variously the name of this city is written by different authors, and even by the same authors in different codices, as the learned Baluze discusses at length in his notes to ch. 180 of the Carthaginian Conference, on the occasion of the word *Ternamusensis*.

Numerianus, bishop of Rusgunia, one of the legates of Caesarean Mauretania, attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419. The same city is mentioned in Antoninus’s Itinerary under the title of a colony, where, as also in the anonymous Ravennate, books III and V, it is called *Rusguniae*. Harduinus believes it to be the Augustan colony *Rusconias* mentioned by Pliny, book V, ch. 2. Ptolemy calls it *Rustonium*; and in the index prefixed to Cyprian’s works, *Rustonium* and *Rusgonia* are said to designate the same place.

64. **BENANTIUS OPPIDONEBENSIS.** Thus in the Laudunensis manuscript. The printed editions, however, have *Venantius*. Ortelius, from Haller’s codex, has *Benantius opidonobensis*. This name designates Oppidum Novum, mentioned by Pliny in book V, ch. 2; by Antoninus in the Itinerary; by the anonymous Ravennate; and by others, to whom Ptolemy should be added in book IV, ch. 2. There he has Ὀππινδονεο, Latin *Oppidoneum*, which is marked there with the title of a colony, as also in Antoninus.

65. **CASTELLI JABARITANUS.** This is perhaps *Castellum Aboritanum*, which Ortelius cites from Victor of Utica in the *Thesaurus Geographicus*. Elsewhere, from the same author, he mentions an Auboritanus bishop in Caesarean Mauretania. [Col. 0342D] See below, no. 72.

66. **AQUISIRENSIS.** It is likely that Honoratus, the bishop of Adquesira mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 188, presided over this place on behalf of the Donatists.

67. **CALTADRIENSIS.** Thus in the manuscripts and the printed editions.

68. **TIGABITANUS.** Among the Catholic bishops whom Augustine lists at the beginning of his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* occurs Palladius, bishop of Tigaba. Honoratus presided over the same see shortly afterward; to him Saint Augustine wrote an excellent letter, no. 228 of the new edition. In it he discusses at greater length whether pastors may abandon their own congregations while persecution is raging. Possidius reproduces almost the entire letter in his *Life of Saint Augustine*.

In ch. 97 of the code of the canons of the African Church, mention is made of the city of Thigaba in Mauretania, over which Primosus seems to have presided. The manuscript codex, as Holstenius notes, has *Tigavensis*; the Greek text in the printed editions reads τῆς Θιγαβενοσίας πόλεως, “of the city of Thigabenia.” Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, calls it *Tigava*; the Palatine codex has *Pigava*. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, mentions the city of Tigava. Ammianus Marcellinus praises Tigavia, book XXIX, ch. 5.

It is clear from Antoninus’s Itinerary that there were two places with this name in Mauretania: *Tigavas*, a municipium, and *Tigava*, a camp; *Oppidum Novum*, a colony, occurs between them. Bertius’s edition, however, has *Tivagas castra*.

69. **RUSADITANUS.** Harduinus believes that it should be read *Rusadiranus*, or rather *Rusadiritanus*, because Pliny, book V, ch. 2, mentions the town and harbor of Rusadir in Tingitanian Mauretania. Antoninus in the Itinerary calls it a colony, *Rusadder*; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 1, has Ῥυτσάδιρον. Pomponius Mela also lists Rusadir and Siga as small cities in Tingitanian Mauretania, adding that otherwise there was nothing in that province worth mentioning.

Yet, unless I am mistaken, the bishop called Rusaditanus in this *Notitia* received that name from Rusazus. Rusazus was a colony of Augustus, which Pliny himself lists somewhat farther below in Caesarean Mauretania. Antoninus calls it the municipium of Rusazus; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, also places it in the same province. Besides the location of the place, the familiar writing practice of the Africans supports us: as Harduinus and other learned men have repeatedly observed, they used the letters *d* and *z* indifferently, so that *Ruzasus* and *Rusadus* are the same name.

70. **REPERITANUS.** Ortelius, from Victor, gives the town of Reperitanum. The anonymous Ravennate, book III, no. 8, mentions the city of Repetiniana in Caesarean Mauretania; our Placidus Porcheron suspects that *Reperitana* should be read there.

71. **UBABENSIS.** Ortelius, from Victor of Utica, mentions Ubada in Caesarean Mauretania. Ptolemy also has Ubata in Africa Propria, which he says was below Hadrumetum in book IV, ch. 3; it should therefore be assigned to Byzacena. The Peutinger Tables have the fortress of Ubasa, but, as it seems to me, in Numidia. Holstenius believes that Ubaba is the same city as Baba, mentioned by Ptolemy and Stephanus.

72. **OBORITANUS.** Among the sees of this province that are said below not to have had bishops at the time when the bishops of Africa were ordered by the king’s command to assemble at Carthage, Oboritana is listed at no. 6. Of the several cities that Ortelius mentions from Victor of Utica, one is the city over which an Auboritanus bishop presided in Caesarean Mauretania; Ortelius thinks that this bishop was so called from a city named Aubureum.

I, however, believe that this name designates no one other than Peter Oboritanus, mentioned here in the *Notitia*. It is no objection that Ortelius himself, from the same Victor, mentions the city of Oboritana, since, as we were saying, a second see of the same name occurs below.

73. **CASTRASEBERIANENSIS.** Ortelius mentions, from Victor, the place called *Castrorum Seberianensis*.

74. **CASTRANOBENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Castronobensis*. This is the city that Antoninus calls *Castra Nova* in the Itinerary. The anonymous Ravennate mentions a city of the same name in Tingitana, book III, no. 9.

75. **CASTELLANUS.** Voconius, bishop of Castellum, a town of Mauretania, made this see better known than most of the other cities of the province. Gennadius counts him among the ecclesiastical writers in his *Catalogue*, ch. 78, and praises him because, besides what he wrote against the Jews, Arians, and other enemies of the Church, he also published an excellent volume on the Sacraments.

This bishop, as Miraeus observes, is called *Buconius* by Honorius and Trithemius; this reading is also found in an old copy of Gennadius from the Fécamp library. In our very ancient codex, however, he is called *Vuconius*.

For Cerellus Castellanus, who also earned a place among the ecclesiastical writers, see below, no. 119. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 180, Severinus, a Castellanus bishop of the Donatist sect, is listed. Baluze says in his note to this passage that he does not know whether Severinus was from Numidia or from Caesarean Mauretania. Nevertheless, above, in ch. 135 of the same Conference, where Severinus, a Donatist bishop, gives testimony in a matter concerning the Caesarienses, Baluze acknowledged that he was a bishop of Castellum in Mauretania.

The anonymous Ravennate mentions Castellum among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania, book III, no. 8.

76. **MUTECITANUS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 133, Leontius, bishop of the congregation of Musertium, is mentioned. The distinguished Baluze suspects that the reading should be *Mutecitanae*. Ortelius, in the *Thesaurus Geographicus*, praises the city of Mutecita from the Carthaginian Conference, although I have nowhere been able to find it.

A little farther below, when the same author praises the Mutecitian frontier in Caesarean Mauretania from the book of the *Notitia*, where it appears in section 54, he notes that the parchment codex has *Mauticitani* in place of *Muticitani*.

When Leontius, mentioned above from the Conference, had asserted that he had no Donatist adversary there, the deacon Habetdeus replied that Cresconius had just been ordained for that city. From this Baluze infers that the Donatist Cresconius who is called bishop of Mustita below, in ch. 206, is the very Cresconius whom Habetdeus had mentioned; consequently, *Musertitanus* should be restored there in place of *Mustitanus*, which he did.

But, as we said above in the notes on the bishops of Numidia, no. 71, and on the Byzacenes, no. 28, Henricus Norisius maintains that this Cresconius was truly a bishop of Mustita in Numidia. He writes that there were two African cities of this name, one belonging to the proconsular province and the other to Numidia.

Finally, in the Carthaginian calendar, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, Saint Quintasius is commemorated. Dom Joannes Mabillon suspects that this is the same Quintasius who is called a Mutecitanus bishop here in the *Notitia*. In the widely circulated Hieronymian Martyrology, however, as the same learned man observes, Quintasus is commemorated among other Africans on that day. In this martyrology, fewer of the more recent saints appear to have been written by the first hand.

77. **RUBICARIENSIS.** This is also the reading of Haller’s codex. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 197, Constantius, bishop of Rusubiccara, appeared among the Donatists. Baluze says that from the *Notitia* it can be inferred that he belonged to Caesarean Mauretania.

In the *Notitia*, however, no bishop of Rusubiccara appears, unless that learned man intended by this name the city of Rubicaria, which we are discussing here, or at least Rusubirita, listed above at no. 22. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 5, mentions the fortress of Subicara situated in Mauretania. It is very likely that this was no different from the town of Rusubiccara or Rubicaria.

Certainly the distinguished Hadrianus Valesius, with whom Baluze declares that he readily agrees, suspects that *Rusubbicarense* ought to be read in Ammianus at that place. If, however, the reading of the *Notitia*, which has *Rubicariensis*, is better, the common reading of Ammianus should rather be retained, since *Rubicariensis* is closer to *Subicarensis* than to *Rusubiccariensis*. [Col. 0344D]

Antoninus has *Rusubricari* in the Itinerary; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, has *Rusubeser*, and in the following chapter *Rusiciber*. The Peutinger Tables have *Rusibricari*.

78. **MAMMILLENSIS.** Victor, bishop of Mammilla, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135, together with his adversary Serenianus, likewise mentioned in ch. 208. Whether the region of Mammae, where the princes of the Moors are said by Procopius, book II *On the Vandalic War*, to have had their camp, could be assigned here, others may judge.

It nevertheless seems to have belonged to Byzacena. The same author, in book VI *On Buildings*, ch. 6, has Mammam as an inland city of Byzacena. The *Notitia* of the Emperor Leo, preserved by Goar, lists Mamilla among the cities of Byzacena; but the Greek text has Μαμηδα, while the Bodleian edition gives Μαμιδα in both Greek and Latin.

79. **ALBULENSIS.** Thus in both manuscript codices and in the printed editions. In Antoninus’s Itinerary this city is called *Ad Albulas*. The anonymous Ravennate mentions Albulas in Sitifian Mauretania, book III, no. 8.

80. **SICCESITANUS.** Thus in the printed editions and in both manuscript codices. Ortelius thinks that this name derives from Sicca Veneria, a famous city. But he is mistaken. In the Carthaginian Conference, besides Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of Sicca, who is frequently mentioned, and Paul, his adversary on the Donatist side, as we said in the notes on the bishops of the proconsular province, no. 41, Martinus, bishop of Siccesita, appeared among the Donatists, ch. 197.

Moreover, no one has ever assigned Sicca to Mauretania. It might perhaps more appropriately be called *Sicelitanus*, from Sicelia, a city of Mauretania which, according to Dio Xiphilinus, was the native city of the emperor Macrinus; hence *Siccesitanus*.

81. **GRATINOPOLITANUS.** Publicius, bishop of the congregation of Gratianopolis, sat in this city. He is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, together with Deuterius, his Donatist adversary, ch. 135. There was another city of the same name over which Philadelphus, bishop of Gratianopolis, presided at the time of the Council of Ephesus. He is found among the other Fathers of that synod who subscribed its acts.

82. **MANACCENSERITANUS.** Haller’s codex also has this reading.

83. **BITENSIS.** Tertullus, bishop of Abita, subscribed the Council of Cabarsussum, as we already said above, no. 5.

84. **FLENUCLETENSIS.** This name does not occur in Ortelius from Haller’s codex.

[p. 175] 85. **BIDENSIS.** Baluze believes that this city should not be distinguished from Vindensis. In his notes to ch. 208 of the Carthaginian Conference, Reparatus, bishop of Vinda, appears among the Donatists.

But the bishop of Bida mentioned here is so called from Bida, a city and colony that Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, lists among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania. In section 54 of the *Notitia Imperii*, the frontier of Bida is listed under the command of the duke of Caesarean Mauretania. The anonymous Ravennate places the municipium of Bidda in Caesarean Mauretania, book III, no. 8.

Bina must be distinguished from these places. Its bishop, Faustinus Binensis, a Donatist, subscribed the Council of Cabarsussum; among the Catholics, Victor, bishop of the congregation of Vina, is listed in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128.

It is clear that this city belonged to the proconsular province from the synodical letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, session 2, to which Fructuosus, bishop of Vina, subscribed; and from the Council of Carthage in 525, where Boniface’s letter to certain bishops of the proconsular province is reported, among whom Cresconius Binensis is mentioned.

We also learn its location from Antoninus’s Itinerary, where it is placed midway between Carthage and Putput.

86. **VALENTINUS CASTELLI MENDIANI.** Our Mabillon believes this to be the very man commemorated in the Carthaginian calendar on the Ides of November. Above, among the bishops of Byzacena, no. 27, Antacius Medianensis is listed.

In Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 5, there is mention of a fortification called Mediana, which Valesius believes may be assigned to Caesarean Mauretania. Indeed, Marcellinus’s narrative does not permit us to interpret this place as the Median city of Byzacena.

87. **SUFARITANUS.** Above, no. 3, a Sufaritanus bishop was listed, where we made several observations about this city. As we noted there, one of the two bishops in Haller’s codex is called *Susaritanus*. But Ortelius, who preserved the readings of this manuscript for us, does not state which of these two was called *Susaritanus* or *Sufaritanus*.

88. **MAURIANENSIS.** Ortelius likewise writes this from Haller’s manuscript. Holstenius believes that the city of Malliana can be assigned here; we discussed it more fully above, no. 8.

89. **BULTURIENSIS.** Thus in both manuscripts and in the printed editions.

90. **MATURBENSIS.** Ortelius mentions Maturbum from Victor.

91. **BALIANENSIS.** Sirmond added the little word *per*; [Col. 0346A] the manuscript codex, however, has nothing of the sort. At the Council of Cabarsussum held in 393, Pancratius, bishop of Balia, subscribed among the other Donatists. The learned Baluze infers that this city must be distinguished from Baiana, because in the following year, at the famous synod of Bagai, Beianus of Baiana was expelled from his see along with several others.

Certainly, at the aforementioned Council of Cabarsussum, Donatus, bishop of Beliana, was also present. It is certain that these names designate different cities, unless someone wishes to assert that several bishops of the same Donatist sect simultaneously occupied one and the same city—something that no one will easily persuade himself to believe.

92. **SEREDDELITANUS.** Ortelius also cites it on the authority of Victor.

93. **NOBENSIS.** Above, no. 19, Verecundus Nobensis is listed. In Haller’s codex, indeed, two cities called Nobensis are mentioned, whose bishops were Verecundus and Paulus, as Ortelius testifies. Verecundus, as we have already said, is listed above; the other, both in the printed editions and in the Laudunensis codex, is called *Mingin*.

That name was not unusual among the Africans, as it would not be difficult to prove by numerous examples. Hence I fear that Ortelius confused the city of Nobus with Nibis. For among the bishops of Numidia, above, no. 8, Paul of Nibis is listed.

The same Ortelius praises Nibis from Haller’s manuscript, but immediately adds that perhaps *Nobensis* should be read. From this I infer that Ortelius later wrote affirmatively what he had earlier stated only with hesitation.

94. **CASTELLI TATROPORTENSIS.** I was unable to find this name in Ortelius from Haller’s codex.

95. **ARSINNARITANUS.** Thus in both manuscript codices, although the printed editions have *Arsinuaritanus*, which is erroneous. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, mentions Arsennaria, a town of Latin rights; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, calls it the colony of Arsenaria; Antoninus and the anonymous Ravennate call it Arsenaria.

Pomponius Mela, book I *On the Situation of the World*, ch. 6, calls the same city Arsinna. Isaac Vossius observes in his note on this passage of Mela that it is commonly called Arsenaria.

In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 133, mention is made of Adsinnar. But this passage must be assigned to the city of Sinnarita, as we said above in the notes on the bishops of the proconsular province, no. 3.

96. **VASSINUS ELFANTARIENSIS.** The printed editions have *Vassinus*. At the Council of Cabarsussum in 393, Miggin of Elefantaria, a Donatist bishop, subscribed; the following year he was deposed at the Council of Bagai. Augustine discusses him frequently in books III and IV *Against Cresconius*.

Elefantaria occurs in the Peutinger Tables, but apparently in the proconsular province, not far from Utica. The anonymous Ravennate indicates that there were two African cities of this name: he lists Elefantaria among the cities of Numidia or the proconsular province, book III, no. 6; and later, in no. 8, while listing the towns of Caesarean Mauretania, he mentions Helepantaria.

97. **CATABITANUS.** Thus in the manuscripts and the printed editions.

[Col. 0346D] 98. **VINCEMALUS BAPARENSIS.** The Laudunensis codex has *Vincemalos*. Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, mentions Vabar among the cities of Caesarean Mauretania. From this the city may have been called *Vabarensis*, and from that perhaps *Baparensis*.

99. **TIPASITANUS.** Rusticus of Tipasa was already listed above among the bishops of Numidia, no. 65. At Tipasa, a city of Caesarean Mauretania, according to Optatus, book II, Urbanus Formensis and Felix Idicrensis—two torches inflamed with hatred—and other Donatists dared every kind of outrage against the Catholics.

Men were mutilated, matrons dragged away, infants killed, and pregnancies forcibly aborted. Moreover, as Optatus narrates somewhat farther below, those same bishops, in a deed of horror, ordered the Eucharist to be poured out for dogs. But the dogs, immediately inflamed with rage, tore their own masters apart with avenging teeth, as though they were robbers guilty of profaning the holy body.

The flask of holy chrism which they had thrown out through a window was carried up by an angelic hand and came to rest unharmed among the rocks. [Col. 0347A] Victor of Vita, book V, no. 6, praises the outstanding faith of the inhabitants of this same city.

Ptolemy also mentions the city, book IV, ch. 2. It occurs in Antoninus’s Itinerary, adorned with the title of a colony. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, says that it was granted Latin rights. In Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 5, *Tiposa* is read in error, unless I am mistaken, for *Tipasa*, through the mistake of copyists.

100. **TAMADENSIS.** This is the reading of Haller’s codex. The printed editions, together with the Laudunensis codex, have *Tamadempsis*. Pomponius Mela, book I, ch. 5, mentions the river Tamunda. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, praises the same river together with a city bearing its name. Following Ortelius, Charles of Saint-Paul believes that this city should be called *Tanuda*; its bishop, Donatus Tanudatensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference among the Donatists, ch. 197.

But this place seems different from our Tamada. The printed editions indeed have *Donatus Tanudaiensis*.

101. **VONCARIANENSIS.** Voncariensis was already listed above, no. 62, and both names are also found in Haller’s codex.

[Col. 0347B] [p. 177] 102. **MURCONENSIS.** Thus in both manuscript codices and in the printed editions. Nevertheless, in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135, Auxilius, bishop of the congregation of Nurcon, appeared among the Catholic bishops and stated that he was from Caesarean Mauretania.

103. **TABADCARENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Tababcarensis*. It is written somewhat differently in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135, where Victor, bishop of the congregation of Tabaicara, and Marcianus, his adversary on the Donatist side, are listed.

104. **SUMMULENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Sumulensis*. Silvanus, bishop of Summa or Zumma, is well known, but he was from Numidia, whose primate he was; Augustine frequently calls him “the Elder Silvanus.” See Letter 141.

Holstenius believes that the place called Subbula, mentioned by Optatus of Milevis, book III, may be assigned here. But this rests on conjecture; our manuscript of Optatus, like the printed editions, has *Subbulensi*.

105. **TADAMATENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Tadamensis*. This reading does not support the opinion of the distinguished Baluze, who believes that Milicus, bishop of the congregation of Tagamuta, mentioned among the Catholics in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 126, presided over the town of Tadamata. See above, Byzacenes, no. 19.

106. **CATRENSIS.** Thus in both manuscript codices and in the printed editions. Charles of Saint-Paul nevertheless prefers to read *Castrensis*, because Antoninus mentions a place called Castra, which is also found in the Peutinger Tables. It was not permissible, however, on the basis of conjecture alone, to alter the reading of both the manuscripts and the printed editions.

107. **CISSITANUS.** Ptolemy has *Cissus* (Κισσος). The Peutinger Tables have the municipium of Cissi; Antoninus, in the Itinerary, differs by one letter and has the municipium of Cisi. Without doubt Flavosus, the Cissitanus bishop listed among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 207, must be assigned here. For him and Quodvultdeus, who is also sometimes called a Cissitanus bishop, see above, proconsular province, no. 27.

[Col. 0347D] 108. **TASACCUBENSIS.** Thus in both codices. Antoninus’s Itinerary lists Tasagora among the major cities of Mauretania. We believe that it is not different from this Tasaccurra.

109. **TABUNIENSIS.** Ortelius also gives this name from Victor. Hirtius mentions the Thabenenses as situated in the coastal region at the farthest limits of Juba’s kingdom; but Henricus Norisius proves at length and learnedly that they belonged to Sitifian Mauretania.

110. **TUSCAMIENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Tuscamensis*.

111. **GUNUGITANUS.** The printed editions have *Gunagitanus*. Haller’s codex, however, has *Gunaitanus*. Our reading, which is that of the Laudunensis codex, is nevertheless better. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, mentions the colony of Augustus called Gunugi. It also occurs in Antoninus’s Itinerary and in the anonymous Ravennate, books III and V, where it is *Gunugus*.

112. **SITENSIS.** Saturnus, a Donatist bishop of Situm, belonged to this place; he is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 198. This should lessen the suspicion suggested by Baluze, who in his notes on this passage of the Conference hints that this Saturnus presided over the city of Silis in Numidia.

113. **VISSALSENSIS.** Haller’s codex has *Vissalensis*. Visalta occurs in the Peutinger Tables, but in Numidia.

114. **MAXITENSIS.** This is also the reading of Haller’s codex in Ortelius, who praises, from Trogus, Hiarbas as king of the Maxitani. Ammianus Marcellinus frequently mentions the Mazices in book XXIX.

115. **ADSINNADENSIS.** The printed editions have *Adsinuadensis*. The Cyprianic Index has *Adsinuada*. Whether the Donatist Cyprian mentioned in ch. 133 of the Conference should be assigned here is uncertain, because the passage is so corrupt in the printed editions and manuscripts that it can bear no intelligible meaning. It reads as follows: “Cyprian is said to be the bishop who there asserts [a claim to] Adsinuar,” or, as the manuscripts have, “Adsinnar.” See Baluze’s note on this passage.

116. **SATAFENSIS.** Below, among the Sitifenses, no. 6, Festus Satafensis is recorded. Adeodatus, bishop of the people of Satafensis, belonged to one or the other of these places; he appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, together with Urbanus, his opponent, and again among the Donatists in ch. 187. Pliny, book V, ch. 4, mentions the town of Salaphitanum, which Hardouin admits is unknown to him. He therefore proposes various conjectures, one of which is that the reading may be *Sataphitanum*, so that the passage could be understood of the city of Satafensis mentioned in this *Notitia*. Saint Pope Leo the Great praises Donatus of Salicinum, a bishop in Caesarean Mauritania who had converted from the sect of Novatus to Catholic unity, in letter 1, alternatively numbered 87. Lucas Holstenius maintains that he was Satafensis, since in the very old Vatican manuscript no. 1342 he is also called bishop of Satafensis.

117. **SERTENSIS.** So both manuscripts read, as do the printed editions. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 135, Proculus, bishop of the people of the place Serrensis, is mentioned. V. C. Baluzius judges that this place was the same as Sertensis, which is recorded here in the *Notitia*.
