Besides him, two other bishops called Zertenses occur in the Conference: namely, Gaudentius, bishop of Zertensis on Donatus’s side, recorded in ch. 187, who had no opponent from the Catholics except a presbyter; and, in ch. 201, Salustius, bishop of Zertensis, again appeared among the Donatists. Perhaps one of the two came from the proconsular province, for among the bishops of that province who signed the synodical letter sent to Paul of Constantinople, Florentius, “by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Zentensis,” subscribed. Whether the other came from Mauritania is uncertain. Certainly neither of them was Proculus’s opponent, since Proculus himself, in the passage cited, professed that he possessed unity. Indeed, if the reading of St. Augustine’s letter 141 is sound, there was also a city Zerta in Numidia, which gave its name to the council held against the Donatists at Zertensis in Numidia.

118. **NUMIDENSIS.** Januarius, bishop of Numidensis in the Donatist party, belonged to the same city and took part in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 188; there he declared that he was from Caesarean Mauritania. In the same place Reparatus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Sifaitensis—or, as Baluzius emends it, Sufasaritana—complained that this same see had been cut off from his diocese. Ortelius, moreover, on the basis of Haller’s manuscript, praises a bishop of Nuooidensis from a manuscript of Victor; by that name, I think, Numidensis should be understood.

119. **CEREALIS CASTELLO RIPENSIS.** Ortelius, from Haller’s manuscript, mentions Castellum Ripense. Lucas Holstenius, in his annotations on Charles of Saint-Paul, thinks that the Cereal mentioned here is the same Cereal, an African bishop whom Gennadius praises in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 96, for a short work he composed against Maximinus, an Arian bishop. We possess this little work in the *Library of the Fathers*, where the author calls himself Cereal, bishop of Castellum. He should therefore be trusted rather than the anonymous writer on the twelve ecclesiastical writers, or other authors of later times, who write that he was bishop of Castulum or Castalum. Gennadius did not report the name of the see itself. He wrote at the time when the Vandals ruled in Africa after capturing Carthage.

120. **TAMAZUCENSIS.** Haller’s manuscript reads *Tamazensis*. Nevertheless, Charles of Saint-Paul assigns to Byzacena the bishop of Tamazensis whom Ortelius cites from Victor of Utica, because Theodorus, bishop of Tamasenus, signed the synodical letter of the bishops of that same province at the Lateran council mentioned under St. Martin. Yet among the Byzaceni there is no bishop of Tamazensis in this *Notitia*. Perhaps Dacianus, bishop of Tamicensis, presided over this place; he is mentioned among the Donatists in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 163. For he was not bishop of Timicensis, the city discussed above under no. 6.

121. **MAJUCENSIS.** Ortelius likewise reads this from Victor, as he says, Victor of Utica.

122. **NABALENSIS.** This is the second see among those that at that time had no bishops. Ortelius nevertheless says that Haller’s manuscript mentions a bishop of Nabalensis, but this appears to be a lapse of memory. Pliny mentions the Nabades, a people of Caesarean Mauritania.

123. **TUBUNENSIS.** See what we said about this city in the notes on the bishops of Numidia, no. 72. Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, lists Thubuna among the cities of Caesarean Mauritania. The Anonymous of Ravenna, book III, no. 8, has *Tubonis*.

124. **MAURENSIS.** So read the printed editions and the manuscripts. Perhaps Crescentianus Marrensis—or, as others have it, Murensis—belonged to this place; he was from the Donatist sect and subscribed to the council of Cabarsussis. The Anonymous of Ravenna, book III, no. 11, lists Maurum among the cities of Mauritania, which he calls Gaditanian Mauritania.

125. **TINGARIENSIS.** Ortelius likewise reads this from Victor.

126. **OBORITANUS.** A bishop of Oboritanus has already been recorded above, no. 72. Consult that passage.

**NO. 3.** This entry is absent from the printed editions. It nevertheless shows that the copyist intended numbers of this kind to designate verses or lines, not the number of cities. Although it is therefore clear that six cities are listed here, since two occur on each line, the notation “no. 3” was added.

## TO THE PROVINCE OF SITIFENSIAN MAURITANIA

1. **TAMALLUMENSIS.** Ortelius, in his *Geographical Treasury*, mentions Tamulluma from Victor, as he calls him, of Utica; there he says that in Caesarean Mauritania the Peutinger Tables have *Tamannuna* or *Tamaununa*. Indeed, they read *Tamannuna*, a municipium and a castellum. Moreover, among the cities of Byzacena listed above under no. 55, a bishop of Tamallumensis is also recorded; there we discussed these cities more fully.

2. **SITIFENSIS.** This city is well known, if only because it gave its name to the entire province. Novatus, bishop of Sitifensis, is praised by Augustine in letter 229, written near the end of Augustine’s life. He attended the council of Carthage in 419 as legate of his province and spoke more than once at the Carthaginian Conference, where he appeared with Marcianus, his opponent, in ch. 143. Optatus of Sitifensis is likewise praised in the letter of Boniface of Carthage in volume IV of the councils, col. 1633. The bishop Optatus mentioned in St. Augustine’s letter 185 either was not bishop of Sitifensis or sat between two bishops named Novatus. Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2, calls Sitifa a colony. *Sitiphi* occurs frequently in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*. I omit the other authors. Moreover, under the province of Numidia, *Sitiphi* occurs in the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo edited by Goar, although the Greek text there, and the Greek and Latin texts together in Beveregius’s edition, have **Σίτιφνος** (*Sitiphnos*).

3. **COVIENSIS.** Ortelius says nothing about this city. I would readily believe it to be the *Coba* municipium mentioned by Antoninus. Antoninus himself indicates that this town belonged to the province of Sitifensis in the *Itinerary*, where Coba is placed among the cities of the province of Sitifensis between Saldae and Igilgili. The Peutinger Tables likewise have *Choba municipium*, and the Anonymous of Ravenna agrees with them: in book III, no. 6, he lists *Choba mune*, that is, “the municipium,” among the other places of Mauritania.

4. **ICILGITANUS.** Haller’s manuscript reads *Igillitanus*. Without doubt it should be written *Igilgilitanus*. The colony of Igilgili is famous; it is praised by Ptolemy, Pliny, book V, ch. 2, and the Anonymous of Ravenna. It also occurs in the Peutinger Tables, the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, and elsewhere. Nevertheless, Ammianus Marcellinus favors the reading of the *Notitia*, book XXIX, ch. 5, where he mentions the coast of Sitifensian Mauritania, which the inhabitants call *Igilgitanum*. The manuscripts cited by Valesius, however, had *Gilgitanum*; and in the province of Sitifensis there was a city *Gegitana*, whose bishop is listed below under no. 13. Finally, in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 121, Urbicosus, bishop of the people of *Eguilguilitana*, was recorded among the orthodox Fathers. There learned men believe that *Igilgilatinae* should be read.

5. **AQUAEALBENSIS.** Ortelius, from Victor of Utica, cites the episcopal place of Aquae Albensium in Sitifensian Mauritania. Above, among the Fathers of the province of Byzacena, no. 52, a bishop of Aquae Albensium was recorded; there we mentioned Januarius, bishop of Aquae Albensis and a Donatist, who is recorded in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 197.

6. **SATAFENSIS.** Cresces Satafensis was already mentioned above among the Fathers of Caesarean Mauritania, no. 116. It is clear from its location that this later Satafensis is the one mentioned in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, for that author places Satafi between the cities of Sitifensis and Ficum.

7. **HORRENSIS.** Baluzius believes that the same see is mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 198, where Cresconius, bishop “from Horrea Aninicensis,” appeared among the Donatists, although Horrea, surnamed Coelia, belonged to Byzacena. There was also a city Horrea in the proconsular province, for among the bishops of that province who signed the synodical letter to Paul of Constantinople at the Lateran council under St. Martin, session 2, appears Donatus, bishop of Orreensis, as Baluzius restored it from the Beauvais manuscript; the printed editions have *Ortensis*. Certainly the Anonymous of Ravenna, book III, no. 7, and book V, no. 4, mentions *Horea* in Sitifensis, and another city of the same name in book III, no. 4, midway among the cities of the proconsular province and Byzacena. These seem to be indicated in the Peutinger Tables, where the first is called *Ad Horrea Orbita*, and the second *Musiubio Horreta*. Finally, Avus, bishop of the people of Horreensis, subscribed to the council of Carthage under Boniface. We plainly find Sitifensian Horrea designated in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, where it is said to lie between Sitifis and Tubusuptum, eighteen miles from the former.

8. **THUGUSUBDITANUS.** So read the printed editions and both manuscripts. Hardouin, however, in his notes on Pliny, book V, ch. 2, observes that *Tubusubditanus* should be read. Valesius cites Maximus Tubusubditanus from this very *Notitia* in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus. Indeed, in the section of the *Notitia* concerning the provinces, section 20, there is a commander of the frontier of Tubusubditanum. The ancients, however, wrote *Tubusuptum*. So do Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 2; Pliny in the passage cited; Antoninus in the *Itinerary*; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 5; and others. The Anonymous of Ravenna, book III, has *Tubusubros*. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 187, Florentinus, a Donatist bishop “from Tubusuptum,” is mentioned. Baluzius believes that in this passage the same city is called *Subuttuta* in the Peutinger Tables, where it is indicated not far from Leptis Magna. We learn the location of Tubusuptum from the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, where it is mentioned once and again near Saldae, eighteen miles from that city. Certainly in the passage cited from Ammianus, the town of Tubasuptum is said to adjoin Mount Ferratus. Mount Ferratus, however, as is clear from the Peutinger Tables, extended from the colony of Rusuccurrum as far as Saldae.

9. **JERAFITANUS.** Haller’s manuscript reads *Gerafitanus*.

10. **LESUITANUS.** Romanus, bishop of Lesuitanus, attended the Carthaginian Conference among the Donatists, ch. 198. Lesbi is located approximately midway between Saldae and Sitifis in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, twenty-five miles from Tubusuptum.

11. **EQUIZOTENSIS.** Haller’s manuscript reads *Equotensis*. The Peutinger Tables have *Equeheto*. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 201, Victor, bishop of Equizetensis, is mentioned as a Donatist. The earlier editions of Baluzius have *Eguizetensis*; no one will deny that these words designate the same city.

12. **CASTELLANUS.** The name *Castellum* was common among the Africans. Nothing particular concerning this place occurs to be said. See above, under Numidia, no. 4, and under Caesarean Mauritania, no. 75. Yet one cannot agree with Holstenius, who thinks that this Castellum was the same as the city Castellum of Caesarean Mauritania, listed above among the cities of that province under no. 75.

13. **GEGITANUS.** In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, Quadratus, bishop of the people of Gegitana, is recorded among the Catholics. But it is uncertain whether he came from Sitifensis. See note 29 on Victor of Vita (above, col. 193, note a) and note 41 on the proconsular province (above, col. 288).

14. **EMINENTIANENSIS.** The opinion of those who regard this passage in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 208, as corrupt is not implausible: “Marcianus the bishop, Eminentius the bishop, remained on the road; Felix Novasinnensis subscribed in his place.” They think it can be corrected as follows: “Marcianus, bishop of Eminentianensis, remained on the road,” and so forth. The Marcianus and Felix mentioned here belonged to the Donatist sect.

15. **SOCIENSIS.** Ortelius assigns this place to Caesarean Mauritania on the basis of a manuscript of Victor, but, unless I am mistaken, through a lapse of memory.

16. **LEMELEFENSIS.** So both manuscripts read, as do the printed editions. Ortelius doubts whether this was the city called by Optatus, book II, the castellum of Lemellum. Its location suggests this, for Januarius of Flumenpiscensis and Felix of Diabensis, Donatist bishops who are said to have hastened there, came from the province of Sitifensis. Optatus also mentions a Catholic bishop of the same place, named Primosus, and reports that the church of that city had been violated by the Donatists. On that occasion many deacons were wounded while defending the altar, and two of them—Primus and Donatus—were killed. Their memory is commemorated on 9 February in the Roman Martyrology.

17. **CELLENSIS.** See above, among the proconsular bishops, no. 45, where Cyprianus Cellensis is recorded. Antoninus mentions Cellas in Sitifensis in the *Itinerary*, where this city appears midway between Perdix and Macri.

18. **MACRENSIS.** Maximus, bishop of Macrensis, a Donatist, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 206. As we just said, Macri is located near Cellas in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*. The Peutinger Tables have *Magri*.

19. **NOBALICIANENSIS.** This is also the form used in Haller’s manuscript. The name of the city appears to have been *Nova-Liciana*.

20. **ZALLATENSIS.** So read the manuscripts and the printed editions. Ptolemy mentions Zalapa, but among the cities that belonged to Hadrumetum and therefore to Byzacena.

21. **ZEMFOCTENSIS.** So both manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have *Lemfactensis*, from which perhaps the index prefixed to Cyprian’s works derives *Lemfacta*. Our reading is confirmed by Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 5, where the town of *Lamfoctum* is mentioned as situated among the peoples of the Tyndenses and Massinissenses. If this restoration had been known to Valesius, he would readily have affirmed that Ammianus’s Lamfoctensian town was the very place recorded here in the *Notitia*; instead, he ventured to propose it only hesitantly. Baluzius likewise would not have suspected that Ammianus’s Lamfoctensian town was the same as the Byzacensian city of Lamfuensis, discussed above, col. 135 (col. 309, no. 87).

22. **FICENSIS.** Felix, a Catholic bishop of Ficensis, appeared at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 215. The Peutinger Tables mention *Ad Ficum*; the *Itinerary of Antoninus* says that this place lay between Satafa and Igilgili.

23. **RESTUTUS MACRIANENSIS.** The printed editions have *Restitutus*. There was also a city Macrianensis in Byzacena, whose bishop was recorded above, no. 80, among the bishops of that province, p. 156 (our col. 328); consult that passage. Haller’s manuscript, as Ortelius testifies, recognizes a bishop of Macrianensis in Sitifensian Mauritania, and says nothing of a Byzacensian bishop. Augustine, letter 93, mentions Deuterius, bishop of Macrianensis from the Donatist sect, and suggests that he was from Mauritania.

24. **ASSAFENSIS.** So both manuscripts read, as do the printed editions. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, Sextilius, bishop of the people of Assabensis, is mentioned together with Martianus the Donatist, who is likewise called this in ch. 198. *Asava* or *Ad Sava* is found as a municipium in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and in the Peutinger Tables. Perhaps Lucius of Ausafa, who under St. Cyprian judged that heretics ought to be rebaptized at the council of Carthage, no. 73, presided over this same city. Augustine responds to his objection in book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 37. Salvius, bishop of Ausafensis and a Donatist, subscribed to the synod of Cabarsussis in 393 and was deposed the following year at the council of Bagai. Augustine frequently discusses him in his books against Cresconius the Donatist. See *Ausanensis* among the proconsular bishops, no. 47.

25. **FLUMENPISCENSIS.** Victor, bishop of Flumenpiscensis, appeared among the Donatists at the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 205. From this, learned men have judged that in Optatus, book II, where Januarius Flamenpistensis is mentioned, *Flumenpiscensis* should be read. The certainty of this is established for us by three manuscript codices: one from the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims, another from the monastery of Saint-Thierry near the same city, and finally one from our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

26. **INVENTINUS MARONANENSIS.** The printed editions have *Juventinus Marovanensis*. Haller’s manuscript, according to Ortelius, has *Maronensis*. Which of these readings should be preferred cannot be determined.

27. **MOLICUNZENSIS.** So reads the Laon manuscript. Ortelius, however, reads *Molicuntensis* from Haller’s manuscript. The printed editions have *Melicbuzensis*, and from them, unless I am mistaken, the Cyprianic index records *Melicbuza*.

28. **SERTEITANUS.** So both manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have *Sertcitanus*. Our reading is confirmed by the Carthaginian Conference, where in ch. 80 Maximianus, bishop of Serteitanus, is mentioned as a Donatist; in ch. 215, Felix, the Catholic bishop of Serteitanus, is said to have suffered pain in his foot, although in earlier editions he is called *Sertertensis* or *Sertirtensis*.

29. **CEDAMUSENSIS.** So both manuscripts read; the printed editions have *Cadamusensis*. The Cyprianic index mentions *Cidamum*. Procopius, book VI of *Buildings*, mentions the city of Cidamum, inhabited by the Moors, but on the Tripolitan frontier. Pliny, book V, ch. 5, has *Cydamum*, opposite Sabrata and therefore in Tripolitana. Our reading, however, is supported by the learned Baluzius, who suspects that *Ceramusensis* should be read; Severianus, Catholic bishop of Ceramunensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 133. Consult Baluzius’s extensive discussion of this matter in his notes on the cited passage of the Conference.

30. **THAMAGRISTENSIS.** In Haller’s manuscript it is written without aspiration, *Tamagristensis*. The same form occurs in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 128, where Primulus, Catholic bishop of the people of Tamagristensis, is mentioned together with Saturninus the Donatist, his opponent, who is again recorded in ch. 197.

31. **PRIVATENSIS.** Ortelius, citing Victor, mentions Privatum as an episcopal place. Antoninus has Villa Magna and Villa Privata, but in Tripolitana. Cyprian, bishop of Villa Magna, subscribed to the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops at the Lateran council under St. Martin.

32. **PARTENIENSIS.** Ortelius likewise writes this form on the basis of Victor.

33. **MOZOTENSIS.** So read the manuscripts and the printed editions. This is undoubtedly the city otherwise called *Moctensis* or *Moptensis*. The Peutinger Tables have *Mopti municipium*. This gave Garnerius occasion to confuse the city with the municipium in Numidia, for which reason he incurred the censure of Norisius. In the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 143, Leo, bishop of Moptensis, is recorded among the Catholic Fathers; he had Felix, on Donatus’s side, as his opponent. The same Felix appeared among the Donatists in ch. 180. This Leo is the same person who attended the council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419 as legate of the province of Sitifensis, although in the printed editions he is repeatedly confused with Leo, bishop of Oppinum, who had been sent as legate from Tingitanian Mauritania to the same synod.

Indeed, the Latin text of the codex of the African Church expressly has *Leo of Moctensis*, both in the preface to the council and in the subscriptions. In the Greek subscriptions it reads **Λεως αἰτο Μοκτη** (sic; perhaps “Leo of Moctus”); but in the preface he is called **Λέων Οπτενσιακός**, “Leo of Optensis.” In the Labbe edition, volume II of the councils, col. 1603, two Leos likewise occur: each is called legate of Tingitanian or Sitifensian Mauritania. There the see of the latter is not indicated, while the former is called bishop of Ospinensis; in the margin appears the note “Alternatively, Moctensis,” as though the two names indicated a single city.

But since we are certain that Opinum and Moctum were two distinct cities, and that the legate of Tingitanian Mauritania and the legate of Sitifensian Mauritania were not one and the same bishop, we have no doubt that of these two Leos one was Opinensis, a legate from Tingitanian Mauritania, the legate of Mauretania Major, about whom see above among the Byzaceni, no. 82, while the other was Moctensis from the province of Sitifensis. These matters may perhaps become clearer if a more accurate manuscript should ever appear.

34. **TAMASCANIENSIS.** Donatus, bishop of Tamascaniensis and a member of the Donatist sect, mentioned in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 197, undoubtedly belonged to this place. The Peutinger Tables show the municipium of Tamascani.

35. **ACUFIDENSIS.** Ortelius cites Acufida from Haller’s manuscript.

36. **ASVOREMIXTENSIS.** So both manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have *Asuoremitensis*. Hence the Cyprianic index has *Asvoremita*. Charles of Saint-Paul cites a manuscript in which *Asaoremixtensis* is read. This, however, is perhaps a scribal error. Nor do I think that Charles of Saint-Paul saw any manuscript other than Haller’s, which Ortelius cites.

37. **THUCCENSIS.** It is often written without aspiration, *Tucca*. Norisius proves in his *Censure against Garnerius* that there were four cities of this name in Africa. The Sitifensian city under discussion is accurately located by Pliny, book V, ch. 2, in these words: “The town of Tucca is situated upon the sea and the river Ampsaga.” Ampsaga separated Numidia from Sitifensian Mauritania. Hence the Peutinger Tables have “Tucca, the boundary of Mauritania and Africa”; and the Anonymous of Ravenna, book III, no. 6, has: “The city of Tuca, which beside the Great Sea divides Numidia and Sitifensian Mauritania.”

There was another Tucca, surnamed Terebinthina, which the *Itinerary of Antoninus* indicates was situated at the farthest boundaries of the proconsular province and Byzacena. At the council of Carthage under St. Cyprian two bishops of Tucca were present: Saturninus, the confessor, “from Tucca,” no. 52, and Honoratus “from Tucca,” no. 77, besides Fortunatus “from Tuccabor,” mentioned under no. 17. The Oxford editor thinks that this name designates Tucca Terebinthina. The bishop of Tuccabor, as we said in note 20 on Caesarean Mauritania, came from the proconsular province.

There was a more recent bishopric of Tuccensis, or Tuncensis, in Numidia, over which at the time of the Carthaginian Conference presided Sabinus, a Catholic bishop. For there, in chs. 65 and 130, Adeodatus, the Donatist bishop of Milevis, complained that this town had been torn away from his diocese. Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 3, mentions Tucca in New Numidia and another under the Third Augustan Legion. Holstenius refers to this place Paulinus Tuggensis, bishop in Numidia, whom Gregory the Great discusses in book X, letter 32. But he is nowhere called Tuccensis, and perhaps not even Tuggensis. In the edition of Gessanvillaeus this Paulinus is called bishop of the city of Tegessis, on the basis of most manuscripts, as the author himself observes; other codices, together with the printed editions, have *Tegesis*. In Labbe, volume V of the councils, he is called *Regensis*, as we said in the notes on Numidia, no. 91.

The same Holstenius cites Metus Tuccanensis from the council of Carthage under Gratus; but in the common editions he is called *Taccanensis* or *Cannensis*. See the proconsular province, no. 54. We also have Tucca Castellum, built in the proconsular province by the emperor Justinian, as Procopius reports in book VI of *Buildings*. Finally, the *Notitia* of the emperor Leo, edited by Goar, lists Tucca among the cities of the second Mauritania. The Greek text, however, has **Χάστρον Τοῦζα**, to which Beveregius’s edition conforms, where in Greek and Latin it is called *Castrum Tutar*.

38. **SURISTENSIS.** So read both the printed editions and the manuscripts.

39. **PERDICENSIS.** Antoninus mentions Perdix in the *Itinerary* between Zarat and Sitifis itself, twenty-five miles from the latter. Silvanus, bishop of the people of Perdicensis, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 124, with Rogatus the Donatist, his opponent, who appeared again in ch. 187. Silvanus, legate of the province of Sitifensian Mauritania, is mentioned at the council of Carthage in 303. Holstenius judges that this was the same man who is called bishop of Perdicensis in the Conference.

40. **ZABENSIS.** A city of this name has already been recorded in Numidia, no. 70. Antoninus’s *Itinerary* mentions Sabi between the towns of Macri and Aras, the former of which is listed above under no. 18. The bishop of this city was Felix Diabensis, mentioned by Optatus, book II, together with Januarius of Flumenpiscensis. Although the printed editions—and even the Remi and Saint-Thierry manuscript codices—call him Diabensis, our codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés expressly has *Zabensis*. Certainly, not everyone holds that the letters *di* and *z* were used indifferently among the Africans.

Whether Fidentius, the Donatist bishop of Dianensis who attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 198, should also be referred to this see or to the Numidian city of Zabensis is uncertain to me. It is certain from the *Itinerary of Antoninus* that there was a Diana in Numidia; Baluzius mentions this city in his notes on the same passage of the Conference. Procopius, book II of *The Vandalic War*, mentions the region of Zeben, whose capital is Sitifis, and which perhaps took its name from this city of Zabensis.

41. **SALDITANUS.** Ortelius does not find this see in Haller’s manuscript, although he cites the colony of Saldae from Ptolemy, where, in book IV, ch. 2, it is listed among the cities of Caesarean Mauritania. It is likewise given the title of colony in the Peutinger Tables and in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*. Pliny, book V, ch. 2, calls it the colony of Augustus, *Salde*. Holstenius suspects that Donatus, the bishop of Saiensis mentioned in ch. 126 of the Carthaginian Conference, may be referred to this place. In Baluzius’s edition he is called Donatus of Saiensis, perhaps instead of *Suensis*, as Baluzius thinks, since Maximus, bishop of Suensis, subscribed among the proconsular bishops to the synodical letter at the Lateran council under St. Martin.

42. **VAMALLENSIS.** So read the manuscripts and the printed editions. The town of Gemellum could be referred here, if everyone did not assign it to Numidia. Since the letters V and G were very often used among the ancients to represent the same sound, *Vemellensis* could have been written for *Gemellensis*. Certainly it can be inferred from the *Itinerary of Antoninus* that the city of Gemella lay on the borders of Sitifensian Mauritania and Numidia. It is placed midway between Nova Sparsa, which belonged to Numidia, and Sitifis itself, twenty-five miles from the latter; the same is repeated in the following entry, where it is situated between Nova Petra and that same Sitifis. Whether this is a different place from the one listed somewhat later in the same *Itinerary* between Theveste, a city of Numidia, and Capsa of Byzacena, I leave to others to judge. Littaeus of Gemella was one of those who advocated rebaptism at the council of Carthage under St. Cyprian, no. 82, and in St. Augustine’s book VII, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

**No. 44.** Yet only forty-three are listed; perhaps several names have dropped out.

## TO THE PROVINCE OF TRIPOLITANA

1. **LEPTIMAGNENSIS.** Leptis Magna is a city of great fame among the ancients and was the civil metropolis of the province of Tripolitana. It was called Magna because another city, Leptis—namely, Leptis Minor—was located in Africa; we discussed it above among the Byzaceni, no. 36.

The Oxford editor of St. Cyprian’s works, in his notes on the council of the rebaptizers, says that Leptis Magna was a city of Tripolitana formed from three cities, Taphra, Abrotonum, and Leptis Magna. He derived this from Julius Solinus’s *Polyhistor*, where ch. 30 reads: “The Greeks, in their language, designate Tripolis by the number of its three cities: Taphra, Abrotonum, and Leptis Magna.” But what Solinus said about the province or region, the Oxford editor interpreted as though it had been said about the city itself.

Hardouin, in his notes on Pliny, book V, ch. 4, reports Solinus’s words differently: “The Greeks, in their language, designate Tripolis by the number of its three cities: Oea, Sabrata, and Leptis Magna.” Yet Pliny, describing the coast between the two Syrtes in the passage cited, says: “There are the city of Oea, the river Cynips, and the region. The towns are Neapolis, Gaphara, Abrotonum, and the other Leptis, which is surnamed Magna.”

Hardouin admits in his fuller notes, no. 14, that all the books have *Taphra* rather than *Gaphara*. He nevertheless inserted *Gaphara* from Ptolemy, on the ground that, he says, no town called Taphra exists anywhere in Africa. But he did not follow Ptolemy either, for Ptolemy has the harbor *Garapha* in book IV, ch. 3. Scylax, as Hardouin himself attests, has a somewhat different form, namely **Τράφαρα πόλις**, “Traphara, a city.” Thus Hardouin removed the city Taphra, which Solinus and Pliny explicitly had, in order to introduce Gaphara, despite the testimony of Scylax and Ptolemy, whom he himself had enlisted in support.

Moreover, in the passage cited, besides the harbor Garapha mentioned above, Ptolemy lists Neapolis, Tripolis, and, according to the Palatine manuscript, Leptis Magna—the three names of a single city. The Tripolitan city is still famous, together with the kingdom bearing the same name in Africa, commonly called Tripoli di Barbaria.

Antoninus frequently mentions Leptis Magna in the *Itinerary*. Its bishop Dioga is mentioned at the council of Carthage under St. Cyprian, and Victorinus, a Donatist bishop of Leptis Magna, subscribed to the council of Cabarsussis in 393. Salvianus, also a bishop of that city from the Donatist sect, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 208, where he is simply called the bishop of Leptis. We infer that he presided over Leptis Magna from the fact that Victorinus the Donatist is called bishop of Leptiminensis in the same Conference, as we said above, no. 36, among the Byzaceni. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, ch. 6, likewise calls the same city simply Leptis, without an additional designation. Procopius, book II of *The Vandalic War*, mentions Leptis Magna, Tripolis, and Pentapolis. Aurelius Victor testifies that Leptis was the birthplace of the emperor Severus; from book VI of Procopius’s *Buildings* we learn that this must be understood of Leptis Magna.

2. **SABRATENSIS.** Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 3; Antoninus in the *Itinerary*; the Peutinger Tables; Pliny, book V, ch. 4; and others praise Sabrata. Procopius, book VI of *Buildings*, calls it Sabatra. Nados, a Catholic bishop of Sabrata, attended the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 133, where he said: “I had one on the opposing side, but now I do not have one.” He had evidently had Donatus as his opponent; Donatus had subscribed, together with other Donatists, to the council of Cabarsussis in 393 and had been deposed the following year at the synod of Bagai. Augustine frequently discusses him in his books against Cresconius. Pomposius was bishop of Sabrata in the time of St. Cyprian, as we shall say below under no. 4. Finally, Vices Sabratenus is found in Victor, book I, no. 7; we discussed him more fully in note 23 on the same author (above, col. 190, note c).

3. **GIRBITANUS.** At the council of Carthage under St. Cyprian, Monnulus of Girba attempted to prove that heretics ought to be rebaptized, no. 10; Augustine refutes his objection in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 17. Proculus Girbitanus, a Donatist bishop, subscribed to the council of Cabarsussis. From the same sect, Evasius, bishop of Girbitanus, is recorded in the Carthaginian Conference, ch. 199. Baluzius judges that this was the same Evasius who in ch. 126 is called the opponent of Quodvultdeus, bishop of Givirtensis—or, as Baluzius himself reads it, Girbitanus.

In the following century, specifically in 525, Vincentius, bishop of the people of Gervitana or Girbitana and legate of the province of Tripolitana, attended the council of Carthage under Boniface. The preceding year he had been accused at the council of Junca of having invaded the congregations of the Tamallumensian Church, as is clear from the title of that synod in Labbe, volume IV of the councils, col. 1627, and from the letter of Boniface, bishop of Carthage, in the same volume, col. 1644. See Numidia, no. 40.

Girba is said to have been the episcopal see of the island of the Lotophagi; Ptolemy, book IV, ch. 3, calls its city Gerra. Antoninus’s maritime *Itinerary* mentions the island of Girba. The Peutinger Tables depict Girba, Tipasa, and other places on the island. Finally, in section 42 of the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a procurator of the Girbitan dye-house is mentioned in the province of Tripolitana. Gallus and Volusianus are said to have been proclaimed emperors on the island of Menynge, which is now Girba, according to the *Epitome* of Sextus Aurelius Victor.

## 4. CRESCONIUS OENSIS

Our Victor of Vita writes that this man himself was banished into exile by Geiseric, in Book I, no. 7. Yet it is remarkable how varied the authors are in writing the name of this city; I would prefer, however, to attribute this to the copyists of the manuscripts, as is clear from what we observed in note 23 to the cited passage of Victor (above, col. 901, n. c). Antoninus has *Oceam* in the *Itinerary*; Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 3, has *Heoam*. Pliny calls it the city of Oea. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIX, chapter 6, mentions the Oean territory in the province of Tripolitania.

Apuleius is said to have had a statue among the *Coenses* in letter 138, otherwise 5, of Augustine to Marcellinus [Col. 0356C]; but one must read *Oeenses*, as is proved not only by the two manuscripts that have this reading but also by Augustine’s own context. For after this word comes the statement “from which city he had his wife”: Pudentilla, however, the wife of Apuleius, was Oean, as Apuleius himself testifies in the *Apology*, as Hadrian Valesius observed in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus.

Augustine frequently mentions Oea, or Ea, although the name is written variously in different manuscript copies, as our writers have observed. Moreover, Natalis of Oea spoke both for himself and for his fellow provincials Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Lepcis Magna at the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian. Augustine refutes the arguments he brought forward in favor of rebaptizing heretics in Book VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 47. Marinianus, bishop of Oea and a partisan of Donatus, took part in the Carthaginian Conference, no. 201.

## 5. TACAPITANUS

Ptolemy mentions Tacape in Book IV, chapter 3, on the basis of the Palatine manuscript; other copies have *Cape*. The Peutinger Tables call it *Colonia Tacape*, and Antoninus in the *Itinerary* calls Tacapas a colony; Pliny, however, in Book V, chapter 4, simply has *Tacape*. Procopius also discusses it in Book VI of *Buildings*.

Dulcitius, a Catholic bishop of the people of Tacape, took part in the Carthaginian Conference, no. 133. He had Felix as his opponent, from the Donatist sect; but Felix, hindered by illness, was unable to appear. From this passage of the Conference, as Baluzius notes, the see of Bishop Dulcitius becomes known; he is said to have been a legate of the province of Tripolitania at the Council of Carthage in 303.

Gaius, bishop of the same city and legate of his province, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. In the acts of the council, however, he is called Gallus.

## 6. NO. 5

There were no more bishops in this province in the time of Aurelius. For when, at the Council of Carthage, the bishops Honoratus and Urbanus had requested that the synod decree that episcopal ordinations should be performed only by twelve bishops, Aurenus replied [Col. 0357A] that the ancient practice ought to be maintained, so that no fewer than three should suffice. Otherwise the matter would become extremely difficult for those living in Tripolitania, since, as is asserted, there were only five bishops in that province.

# 188. TO THE PROVINCE OF SARDINIA

## Names of the bishops of the island of Sardinia

The neighboring islands must also be added, whose bishops are here assigned to Sardinia because they regarded Caralis, the principal city of that island, as their metropolitan see. Justinian, moreover, assigned seven provinces to the prefect of the praetorium of Africa; the last of these is called Sardinia, *Code*, title 27, constitution 1.

## 1. LUCIFER CALARITANUS

Another Lucifer of Caralis, a bishop famous for both good and bad repute, endured innumerable labors and the harshest exiles, prisons, and other severe hardships for defending Christ’s divinity and for the cause of the Church under the Arian emperor Constantius; at last he gave occasion for, or at least his name to, a schism [Col. 0357B]. Whether this stain was of such a kind that his name ought consequently to be removed from the catalogue of holy confessors is a serious controversy, especially among more recent writers.

Ambrosius Machinus, archbishop of the same city, attempts to defend Lucifer’s sanctity on the basis of the tradition of the Church of Caralis and of the ancient sacred buildings found throughout Sardinia under his name. His view was adopted by the learned Daniel Papebrochius in the *Bollandists* on 20 May, the day on which the name of Lucifer of Caralis is written in the sacred calendars.

Natalis Alexander, however, suspects that the Lucifer whom the Sardinians venerate as a saint is the same person whom he discusses in the fourth century, article 13, and whom this *African Notitia* records as having been persecuted by King Huneric during the Vandal persecution. Since this opinion can be supported by no foundation beyond conjecture, Papebrochius rejects it as groundless, asserting that the arguments for affirming the sanctity of the former Lucifer are much more numerous and weightier [Col. 0357C] than those for admitting the public cult of the latter, otherwise scarcely known.

There is no opportunity here to gather more information from ancient monuments concerning the city of Caralis or its bishops. Even in the ninth century Sardinia belonged to Africa, as is clear from the *Notitia* of Leo the Wise, in which Caralis is counted among the cities of Mauretania Secunda, placed under the most glorious prefect of Africa. The Greek text has Χάραλος; hence Beveregius’s edition translates it as *Caralus*. Most of the ancients write *Caralis*: Antoninus, Hirtius, the Peutinger Tables, and others.

## 2. FROM FORUM TROJANI

The printed editions have *de Foro Trajani*, “of Forum Trajani.” We have nevertheless retained the reading of the manuscript. Although this city is better known under the name *Forum Trajani*, several manuscripts, as Ortelius observes, regularly have *Forum Trojani*. Justinian Augustus surrounded this city with walls, as Procopius reports in Book VI of *Buildings*.

## 3. FROM SANAFER

We believe that this place is mentioned in the *Notitia* of the Emperor Leo, in Beveregius’s edition [Col. 0357D], where, among the other cities of Mauretania Secunda—which includes Sardinia and the neighboring islands—*Sanaphas* is listed at no. 10 and is likewise written in Greek. Goar’s edition, however, has *Suffara*, in Greek Σουμάρφα (*Soumarpha*).

## 4. FROM MINORICA

Minorica is one of the Balearic Islands, 600 stades distant from Majorica, according to the maritime *Itinerary* of Antoninus. We possess a letter of Severus, bishop of this island, concerning the miracles of Saint Stephen; it was published in the appendix to volume VII of the Benedictine edition of the works of Saint Augustine.

From this letter we learn that the island had two towns, but only one bishop. Among the episcopal sees assigned to the province of Mauretania Secunda in the *Notitia* of the Emperor Leo, edited by Goar [Col. 0358A], Minorica is mentioned; in Greek it is called Μήνυκα νῆσος, “the island of Mēnyca.” It is written in the same way in the Greek text of Beveregius’s edition; there, however, it is translated into Latin as *Menyca insula* rather than *Minorica*.

## 5. SULCITANUS

Pliny mentions the Sulcitani in Book III, chapter 7. Pomponius Mela, in Book II of *The Situation of the World*, chapter 7, says: “The most ancient of the cities are Caralis and Sulchi,” and so forth. Sulchi is also mentioned in the *Notitia* of Leo cited above, and in exactly the same form in both editions, in Latin and in Greek. Antoninus has *Sulcei* in the *Itinerary*. The Peutinger Tables have *Sulci*. The place is frequently celebrated by various authors.

The see of Sulci was first transferred to the Church of Villa, or Valli; after that see was later entirely extinguished, the diocese of Sulci was joined to the Church of Caralis.

## 6. FROM TURRIRUS

Antoninus mentions *Ad Turrem* among the towns of Sardinia in the *Itinerary*. Pliny, Book III, chapter 7, has *Turrim Libysonis*; in Ptolemy, Book III, chapter 3, this is *Turris Byssonis*. The Anonymous of Ravenna lists the islands near Sicily as follows: *Turribus, Sibrorum, Cuniculari, Ficaria*, and so forth. The Peutinger Tables have *Turribus* [Col. 0358B] between Caralis and Nuba.

The commonly circulated martyrologies frequently commemorate several martyrs who suffered for Christ there. The *Notitia* of the Emperor Leo also counts this city among the cities of Mauretania Secunda, in both editions. It was later raised to archiepiscopal rank, which dignity was eventually transferred to Sassari.

## 7. FROM MAJORICA

The island is so called because it is the larger of the two Balearic Islands. It was still subject to the prefect of Africa in the time of Leo the Wise, as is clear from the *Notitia* often cited above, where, among the cities then assigned to Mauretania Secunda, the island of Majorica is listed in Goar’s edition; in Greek it is Μαιούρηκα νῆσος, “the island of Maiourēca.”

The Greek text of Beveregius’s edition, however, changes the first letter and has Ναιούρηκα νῆσος, which is there translated as *Najurica insula*, “the island of Najurica.”

The Balearic Islands were later occupied by the Moors while they were ravaging Spain. They established a kingdom there from these two islands and Ebusus, which continued until the middle of the thirteenth century [Col. 0358C]. From this arose the name of the kingdom of Majorica. In 1252, however, James, king of Aragon, expelled the Moors and added the islands to his kingdom. At that time an episcopal see was restored at Majorica together with the Christian religion. Its bishop was at first subject to the metropolitan of Tarragona; later, when Valencia was raised to archiepiscopal rank, the see was counted among the suffragans of the metropolitan of Valencia.

## 8. FROM EVUSO

Ebusus is an island in the Mediterranean Sea, one of the two Pityusae, situated near Majorica; the Spaniards call it Ivica in their vernacular. Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, writes that Ebusus appears in the inner sea as though in its vestibule, a good seven days’ voyage from the entrance of the Ocean; he says that Majorica and Minorica lay near it. In Book II he reports that these same three islands were not very far from the mouth of the Ocean.

Antoninus mentions Ebusus in the maritime *Itinerary*. Our Victor speaks of the same island in Book I, no. 5. The island has, as all historians proclaim with one voice, the remarkable distinction that no poisonous animal [191] can either be produced there or survive there if brought from elsewhere.

## 9. AND SO THE TOTAL BECOMES 466

Nevertheless, no more than 461 are mentioned, unless the two Numidians discussed above are added—see above, p. 141 (col. 314, no. 124)—together with several Byzaceni, whose names may perhaps have dropped out. See pp. 141 and 57 (for us, cols. 314 and 271).

As for the remaining numbers, anyone can readily correct the errors that have slipped in either through the carelessness of copyists or for some other reason. As we have already noted, we have accurately transcribed the readings of the Laon manuscript; those readings which Sirmond corrected we have reported within brackets.

[Col. 0359]

# APPENDIX THREE, OR THE HISTORICAL COMMENTARY OF TH. RUINART ON THE VANDAL PERSECUTION

[Col. 0359A]

[193]

Although the principal events of the Vandal persecution must be drawn from the *History of Victor of Vita*, which we have just presented, we have judged that we would be doing no one a disservice if we gathered here into one place whatever is found on the same subject in reliable and ancient authors. By this assistance, not only may those matters that Victor perhaps narrated somewhat too briefly be set out more fully, but those also that the same author omitted may, insofar as the great distance of time and events permits, be supplied by us in some manner.

Since the task of describing the Arian persecution in Africa by the Vandals has fallen to us, we were not permitted to omit anything that seemed useful for illuminating so distinguished a portion of ecclesiastical history. But in order that the narrative might proceed without confusion, it seemed worthwhile to divide it into several chapters.

# CHAPTER ONE. The Incursion of the Vandals into Gaul

[Col. 0359B]

## 1

The authors do not hold a single opinion concerning the origin of the Vandals. According to Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, they were a branch of the Gothic nation, devoted to the teachings of Arius, like the other barbarian nations; they once had their settlements near Lake Maeotis. After abandoning those places because of a shortage of necessities and taking the nation of the Alans with them, they first invaded the regions situated around the Rhine, then possessed by the Franks. Shortly afterward, together with other savage and barbarian nations, they entered various provinces of the Roman Empire and utterly devastated them.

Hadrian Valesius, however, at the beginning of Book III of *Frankish Affairs*, says that it seems astonishing to him that this opinion concerning the origin of the Vandals could have been accepted by anyone. He maintains [194] that it is entirely opposed to the testimony of all the ancients: Pliny the Elder counts the Vandals—called by some *Vindili*, by others *Vandili*, and by others *Vandalii*—among the five Germanic peoples; Tacitus numbers them among the ancient peoples of Germany [Col. 0359C]. Dio Cassius in Book LXXII, Julius Capitolinus, Eutropius, the Theodosian Map, and Jerome place them near the Danube and the source of the Elbe, neighboring the Marcomanni and Quadi, the Germanic peoples.

The same author later suggests, however, that Procopius’s opinion can be confirmed by the authority of Salvian, Sidonius, and other writers. Since these men flourished in the period when the Vandals were still ravaging various provinces of the Roman Empire, no one can deny that this opinion concerning the origin of at least the later Vandals was then the generally accepted one.

## 2

Ancient and modern historians alike assert that all these barbarians were summoned by Stilicho, whose services he intended to use in securing the imperial power for his son Eucherius. “Thus,” says Paul Orosius near the end of Book VII, “that treacherous man, so that he might clothe one boy in purple, gave the blood of the whole human race.”

The Franks were the first to resist the efforts of the Vandals. After killing nearly twenty thousand of them by the sword and slaying their king Godigisel, they would have destroyed them completely had not the Alans come to the Vandals’ aid; the Franks were subsequently put to flight. The Vandals, therefore, joined with the Alans, replaced Godigisel with his son Gunderic, crossed the Rhine, and invaded Gaul, which Stilicho [Col. 0360A] had left without garrisons.

Some ancient historians—Prosper, Cassiodorus, and others—say that this occurred during the consulships of Arcadius for the sixth time and Probus, toward the end of the year 406 and the beginning of the following year. Others, together with Paul Orosius and Marcellinus Comes, hold that the disaster occurred two years later, during the consulships of Bassus and Philippus, that is, two years before Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths.

All agree, however, that at that time Gaul was first ravaged, then Spain, and finally the African provinces. These disasters were the more atrocious because those who inflicted them were themselves the more savage in spirit. For, apart from the cruelty introduced by heretical deceit, the character of the Vandals, as compared with that of the Romans, was formed without any natural gentleness or any trace of civilized refinement.

## 3

The savagery and fury with which they first invaded Gaul is described by an unimpeachable witness, Saint Jerome, in his letter to Ageruchia. He writes:

> I shall pass briefly over the miseries of the present time. Innumerable and exceedingly savage nations have occupied all Gaul. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, has been laid waste by Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Alans, Gepids, Heruli, Saxons, Burgundians, Alemanni, and—O sorrowful commonwealth!—the enemies of Pannonia. For Assyria has come with them.

Then, listing the more distinguished cities of Gaul that on this occasion were destroyed or plundered, he continues:

> Mainz, once a noble city, has been captured and overthrown, and many thousands of people have been slaughtered in the church. The Vangiones have been destroyed by a long siege; Rheims, a powerful city; Amiens; Arras; and the Morini, the furthest of peoples; Tournai; the Nemetes. Strasbourg has been transferred into Germany. The provinces of Aquitaine, the Nine Peoples, Lugdunensis, and Narbonensis have been devastated everywhere except for a few cities, and even these are ravaged from without by the sword and from within by hunger. I cannot mention Toulouse without tears; the merits of its holy bishop Exsuperius have prevented it from collapsing up to [195] this day.

The same Saint Jerome inveighs elsewhere against Stilicho [Col. 0360C], whom he calls a half-barbarian traitor, because, having sprung from the Vandal nation and risen to the highest offices of the Empire, “he armed our enemies,” he says, “with our resources against us.”

In a letter to Heliodorus, speaking of such barbarian incursions, he mentions noble matrons and virgins of God treated as objects of mockery, bishops captured, priests and various ranks of clergy killed, churches overturned, horses stabled at altars, the relics of martyrs dug up, and other similar atrocities by which the Roman world had already been overwhelmed before the destruction of Rome itself.

## 4

Salvian, a presbyter of Massilia, also laments these same calamities of Gaul; he himself had been present during the events. Thus, among other things, he speaks in Book VI of *The Government of God* about those who had escaped the destruction of the cities:

> Every city was a tomb, with evils increasing even after the destruction. For those whom the enemy had not killed in the destruction were overwhelmed by calamity after the destruction; what had escaped death in the destruction did not survive calamity after the destruction. Some were killed by wounds driven deep through prolonged deaths; others, scorched by the flames of the enemy, were tortured by punishment even after the flames. Some perished from hunger, others from nakedness; some wasting away, others stiffening; and so, through different forms of dying, they collapsed together into one end, death. And why say more? The destruction of one city afflicted other cities as well. For everywhere there lay, as I myself saw and endured, the naked and mangled corpses of both sexes, defiling the eyes of the city, torn apart by birds and dogs. The stench of the dead was a plague to the living; death breathed forth from death. Thus even those who had not been present at the destruction of the aforesaid city suffered the evils of another’s destruction.

It should not be supposed that Salvian said these things merely in the manner of an orator, with exaggeration, in order to summon peoples to repentance, since all the surviving monuments of that period bear precisely the same witness.

We cite as a most substantial witness to this matter the author of the book *On Divine Providence*, published under the name of Saint Prosper. In the prologue to that work he asserts that the Gauls endured the utmost extremities in these disasters, lamenting the calamities of his homeland, which he had before his eyes. He says that no city, no town, no fortress or stronghold, indeed not even the fields themselves, escaped destruction, and in a single statement:

[Col. 0361B]

> If the whole Ocean had poured itself across the fields of Gaul,  
> more water would still have remained in its vast expanse.

The same author writes that the barbarians raged no less against human beings than against cities: sparing neither sex nor age, they slaughtered everyone they encountered.

> Nor shall I complain that the common people were extinguished without distinction:  
> let death itself also cease to envy the foremost.  
> What of innocent boys? What had the girls done,  
> to whom their brief life had given no crimes?  
> Why was it permitted that the temples of God be ravaged by fire?  
> Why were the vessels of sacred service violated?  
> Neither the dignity of vowed virginity  
> protected the unmarried women,  
> nor the love of religion the widows.  
> Even those who had been accustomed to live  
> in deserted caves,  
> praising God night and day,  
> suffered no different death from that of any pagan:  
> the same storm swept away the good and the wicked.  
> No reverence for the priests’ venerable name  
> distinguished them from the punishments of the wretched people.  
> Thus they were beaten with cruel whips; thus burned with fire;  
> thus hands confined in chains groaned.

[196]

## 5

The author just cited testifies that Gaul was afflicted by these calamities for a full decade. This must, however, be understood principally of the Goths. Paul Orosius, in Book VII, chapter 40, reports that the Vandals and their other barbarian allies remained for some time in Gaul because they were prevented by the ridges of the Pyrenees from reaching Spain quickly:

> The nations summoned by Stilicho—the Alans, Suevi, Vandals, and many other peoples with them—overthrow the Franks, cross the Rhine, invade Gaul, and advance directly as far as the Pyrenees. Repulsed for a time by that barrier, they pour back through the surrounding provinces.

The same author especially praises Didymus and Verinianus, two noble and wealthy brothers who, with their slaves and other men whom they had hastily gathered as peasant soldiers, remained loyal to the emperor Honorius and protected Spain, as long as they lived, not only from the tyrant Constantine but also from the incursions of the barbarians [Col. 0361D]. Meanwhile, however, the barbarians spread through Gaul and ravaged everything with sword and flame.

## 6

Since these barbarian nations were infected with the Arian corruption or still devoted to various pagan superstitions, they threatened the salvation of souls no less than that of bodies. There is no doubt that in those times many of our countrymen in Gaul endured severe punishments in order to preserve the integrity of their faith.

Although no one published a separate account of these matters—at least none that has come down to us—some traces nevertheless survive both in histories and in the ecclesiastical calendars. From them it can easily be inferred that at that time the martyrdoms of many saints were both frequent and illustrious. Certainly the passages quoted above from the prologue of *On Divine Providence*, no. 4, may be referred to this subject.

The Church of Rheims celebrates on 14 December the feast of its most blessed bishop Nicasius. Together with the virgin Eutropia, his sister, Florentius the deacon, and Jocundus the lector, he suffered glorious martyrdom at the very threshold of the church [Col. 0362A]; on that occasion many others of every sex, age, and condition also fell by the hands of the barbarians.

Although some attempt to assign their deaths to the time of Attila, king of the Huns—when, it is said, about forty-three years later, the city of Rheims was again conquered by that king—the venerable tradition of this distinguished Church remains unshaken. It consistently asserts that Nicasius and his companions were killed by the Vandals. That this tradition was already regarded as ancient in the ninth and tenth centuries can be inferred from Hincmar and Flodoard.

Moreover, since almost innumerable barbarian nations flooded Gaul in those times, it is not surprising that some attributed such disasters to the Vandals, others to the Huns or the Alans. The barbarians, meanwhile, ranging through the various territories of Rheims, killed those whom they happened to encounter. Some of these, later renowned for miracles, were honored with the title of martyrs.

Among them was Aderius, who suffered at the village of Chaniac [Col. 0362B]. His relics were discovered by miracles under Bishop Gervasius in the eleventh century and were afterward held in great veneration by the surrounding peoples.

More celebrated was Oriculus, who was killed together with his two sisters, Oricula and Basilica, near Sindunum, a village of the district of Dulcomus. Their sacred bodies were brought into the city because of the turmoil of war and are most devoutly preserved in the renowned archmonastery of Saint Remigius.

At Arras, Diogenes is venerated. He is said to have been sent by the Roman pontiff, consecrated as the first bishop of these peoples [197] by blessed Nicasius, and killed in the general calamity of Gaul Belgica. **Note:** There are no ancient testimonies for this, as the Bollandists observed in volume I, February 6, in the preliminary material to the life of Saint Vedastus.

Some have also handed down that Augusta of the Veromandui was caught up in the same disaster. But the ancient author of the *Life of Saint Salaberga* testifies that Laudunum—or, as the ancients write, *Lugdunum Clavatum*—was attacked by the barbarians but not at all conquered [Col. 0362C].

## 7

The other metropolis of Belgica, Augusta Treverorum, experienced the same fate as the city of Rheims. Although Jerome did not list it in the passage cited among the principal cities of Gaul that were then plundered by the barbarians, it nevertheless seems beyond doubt that it suffered this common disaster, since, according to Salvian at the beginning of Book VI of *The Government of God*, it was plundered and overthrown as many as four times during these barbarian incursions.

An ancient author who described the deeds of the first bishops of that city expressly asserts this in the life of Saint Maternus. Andreas Saussayus, in the *Gallican Martyrology* on 16 July, reports that during this very Vandalic invasion, which we are now discussing, Valentinus, bishop of Trier, fell by the sword of the barbarians. The memory of Valentinus, bishop of Trier, is likewise celebrated on that day in the Roman Martyrology, but without any mention of the time or circumstances of his death [Col. 0362D].

Browerus, who composed the *Annals of Trier*, does not mention Valentinus, although he says much about the Vandals.

## 8

After the devastation of the regions of Belgica, the entire body of Gaul also, as Salvian puts it in Book VII, burned in the fire of the Vandals. After spreading through its various provinces, they raged throughout the other regions with the same fury with which they had ravaged Belgica.

The people of Besançon, the chief people of the province of Maxima Sequanorum, celebrate Antidius, bishop and martyr, who was killed by the Vandals, on 17 June.

At Pseudunum, a fortress among the Aedui in Lugdunensis Prima—as our Mabillon proves in Part II of the fourth century of the Benedictine *Annals*, p. 494—Florentinus and Hilarius suffered martyrdom. They are celebrated in the common martyrologies on 27 September. Some, deceived by the similarity of the name, have thought that they completed their martyrdom at Sedunum, which is now the capital of Upper Valais. But the old manuscript copies of Usuard’s martyrology, and the autograph itself that we possess, expressly have *Pseudunum* [Col. 0363A].

Indeed, in a very old manuscript of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims, written about eight hundred years ago, there is a complete passion of these same martyrs, in which they are said to have won the crown of martyrdom at the fortress of Pseudunum, in the territory of the Aedui.

The people of Coutances, in Lugdunensis Secunda, also refer Heterius, a martyr, to this same persecution on 16 July; Saussayus, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, says that he was killed on the island of Gersuo.

The same author also commemorates, on 26 December, another 366 martyrs whom the same persecution carried off in the celebrated district of Vastinum in Lugdunensis Quarta.

Furthermore, Fraternus, bishop of Auxerre, was crowned with martyrdom on the very day of his consecration by the barbarians who were devastating his city. “From the most ancient annals of Auxerre,” says Papirius Massonus in his *History of the Calamities of Gaul*, he draws this account; in that passage he judges that the barbarians mentioned there were none other than the Vandals.

To these must also be added [Col. 0363B] DESIDERIUS [198], bishop of the Lingones, who, together with an innumerable multitude of his clergy and people, is said to have been killed by the Vandals. His feast is celebrated in the calendars of the Church on 23 May.

Valerius, archdeacon of Desiderius, and the martyr Prudentius are also said to have suffered in those same times. The *Gallican Martyrology* records the feast of the former on 22 October and that of the latter on the sixth of the same month.

There is also a celebrated memory among the Ligurian people of Genoa of Desiderius, a bishop likewise killed by the Vandals, according to Ferrarius in the *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* on 23 May. But he is the same person celebrated by the people of Langres, as may be seen in the Bollandists on 23 May.

I also suspect that he is the very same person whom Saussayus, on the nineteenth of the same month, and other authors with him, commemorate as having suffered among the people of Chartres.

Ausonius, a martyr of Angoulême, perhaps ought also to be referred to this period. Although he is commonly said to have died as a martyr under King Chroco in the time of Valerian, the things related about him seem to fit these times better.

At Arcey, a town in the diocese of Troyes, the feast of Saint BALSEMIUS is celebrated on 16 August; he too is said to have been crowned with martyrdom under the Vandals. But if this tradition is true, he must be considered a different person from Balsemius, the nephew of Saint Basolus, since it is established that Basolus came to Rheims long after this persecution, in the time of Archbishop Aegidius.

## 9

Finally, other martyrs are venerated in other places and are commonly said to have been crowned with martyrdom under the Vandals, but there is no opportunity to discuss them at greater length. Some of them are said to have suffered under King Chroco, whom some hold to have invaded Gaul in the time of the emperor Valerian, although there are also those who confuse the time of Chroco with the Vandal persecutions under discussion.

The records of these periods are so mixed with doubtful and uncertain matters, indeed sometimes with things certainly false, that scarcely any secure reliance can be placed on them, especially concerning chronology [Col. 0363D].

Nevertheless, I believe that no one can deny that those saints whom both secular and sacred ancient history unanimously report as having fallen by the swords of the Vandals should, for the most part, be assigned to the persecution we are discussing.

Nor is it an obstacle that most of them are said to have suffered while the Vandals were still devoted to pagan superstitions. It is certain that these barbarian nations retained various pagan superstitions for a long time even after they had professed the Christian religion. Indeed, there is no doubt that many of them at that time were still held fast by the errors of paganism.

But we must pass on to other matters. We have already dealt with these subjects somewhat more fully than was necessary, although it was not permissible to omit what could contribute something to illuminating the martyrs of our own people.

# CHAPTER TWO. Spain Occupied and Oppressed by the Vandals

[Col. 0364A]

## 1

After Gaul had been plundered, the Vandals entered Spain and likewise devastated it with sword and flame. For, as Orosius says in Book VII, chapter 28, after carrying out great and bloody raids, they inflicted grievous devastation upon property and people.

The same author writes that this occurred after the deaths of the brothers Didymus and Verinianus, when the Honoriaci—this was the name given to certain barbarians whom the Romans had recruited into military service and to whom [199] Constans, the son of the tyrant Constantine, had entrusted the guardianship of the Pyrenees—opened the way and admitted into the provinces of Spain all the peoples who were wandering through Gaul, so that they themselves might thereby have greater freedom to plunder.

Prosper in his *Chronicle*, together with Cassiodorus and others, testifies that Spain was occupied by the Vandals during the consulships of Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius for the third time, that is, in the Christian year 409.

Idatius agrees in the consular fasti. In his *Chronicle*, however, he gives not only the consuls or the era from which the year can be determined but also the very day on which this calamity befell his homeland. He records it in these words:

> The Alans, Vandals, and Suevi entered Spain in the era 447. Some record the fourth day before the Kalends, others the third day before the Ides of October; on the fourth day, a Tuesday, during the consulships of Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius, son of Arcadius, for the third time.

## 2

The Vandals attacked Spain with the same fury with which they had raged in Gaul. Salvian, the most eloquent writer of those times, explains this in a single statement when, in Book VII of *The Government of God*, he reports that the Spaniards also burned in the same flames in which the Gauls had burned.

Idatius of Lemica, a bishop in Gallaecia who was present for the most part at the events, sets out these calamities somewhat more fully. Among other things, he writes:

> While the barbarians raged throughout Spain, and the evil of pestilence raged no less, a tyrannical tax-collector plundered wealth and the property stored in the cities, and the soldier drained it away. A dreadful famine spread, so that human flesh was devoured by human beings under the force of hunger; mothers too, after their children had been killed or cooked, fed upon the bodies of their own offspring. Beasts, accustomed to the corpses of those killed by the sword, hunger, and pestilence, slew the strongest of the people wherever they found them, and, feeding upon their flesh, ranged everywhere to the destruction of the human race.

When Saint Augustine was asked by Honoratus, bishop of Thigava, what the pastors of churches ought to do during a barbarian invasion, he proposed the example of the Spanish bishops in words from which it can be inferred that great disasters occurred in Spain at that time. For he mentions cities utterly overthrown, peoples led into captivity, and other calamities of this kind.

Thus, says the holy doctor in his letter to the Honoratus just mentioned, new edition 228, otherwise 180:

> Thus certain holy bishops fled from Spain, after their congregations had partly escaped by flight, partly been killed, partly consumed by siege, and partly scattered into captivity; but many more remained there because of those for whose sake they remained, remaining amid the density of the same dangers.

### 3.

No one doubts that the Vandals remained longer in Spain. For after defeating the Roman forces under their leader Godigisel—as Procopius relates in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, though it should be written “Gunderic”—they settled in Spain. We learn from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, supported by Cassiodorus and Hydatius, that the Romans were defeated by the barbarians in Spain under Castinus, master of the soldiers, during the consulship of Honorius XIII and Theodosius X—that is, in the year 422 of the Christian era—after he had rejected Count Boniface from participation in the war. Salvian, in Book VII of *The Government of God*, also recalls this victory of the barbarians over the Romans. There he observes more than once that the Spaniards had been defeated and utterly subdued by the Vandals—that is, by what he calls the weakest and most cowardly of enemies—with God so disposing matters that, by recognizing the blow of the heavenly hand even in this, they might repent of their former sins.

“After the provinces of Spain had been overturned,” says Hydatius in his *Chronicle* [Col. 0365A], “by the aforesaid ravaging of calamities, the barbarians, through the Lord’s mercy, were turned toward making peace.” He writes that this occurred in the second year after their entry into Spain. The conditions under which, after so many disasters, the Romans who remained in Spain were subjected to Vandal servitude are set out more fully by Paul Orosius in Book VII, chapter 28.

The barbarians, however, divided the provinces of Spain among themselves by lot. As Hydatius writes, the Vandals and Suebi occupied Gallaecia; the Alans, Lusitania and the province of Carthaginensis; the Vandals called Silingi, Baetica; while the Spaniards who had escaped the general disaster in forts and cities were entirely subjected to the rule of the barbarians who dominated the various provinces.

Indeed, Hugo Grotius, in the prolegomena to his *Histories of the Vandals, Goths, etc.*, asserts that traces of Vandal rule still survive in Spain in the very name of Andalusia, a province of Spain. He maintains that this region was formerly called *Vandalu(s)ia*, or, in the Vandal language, *Wandaloth*, by those barbarians [Col. 0365B].

Paul Orosius, in the passage cited, praises the barbarians because, after the treaty had been concluded, they became so gentle that they regretted having inflicted such disasters upon Spain; and because some Romans were found who preferred to possess a poor freedom under Vandal rule rather than endure the burdensome anxiety of taxation among the Romans.

But how brief was that peace—if it ought ever to be called peace at all! For what peace could the barbarians have maintained with others, from whom they were so alien in nature, customs, and religion, when they were never able to maintain it even among themselves?

### 4.

It does not belong to our purpose to describe the various disturbances of war by which Spain was then shaken. Yet we cannot pass over without notice the extremely severe persecution which, according to Gregory of Tours, bishop and author of Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 2, was stirred up in Spain against the orthodox. He is mistaken, however, in calling the king under whom he says it was provoked “Thrasamund.” From the sequence of his narrative, and especially from the following chapter, where he names Huneric as Thrasamund’s successor, it can easily be inferred that by this name he always meant Gaiseric. There is little point in investigating at length how this came about. It is clear that the persecution was exceedingly bitter, since, according to the same Gregory, the tyrant drove the orthodox throughout Spain, by tortures and various forms of death, to consent to the Arian impiety.

### 5.

In the passage just cited, the same author recounts the martyrdom of a certain noble girl. It seemed appropriate to reproduce his own words here:

> It happened, he says, that a certain religious girl, exceedingly rich in possessions and, according to the dignity of the world, distinguished by senatorial nobility—and, nobler than all these qualities, adorned with the Catholic faith and serving almighty God irreproachably—was brought to this examination. When she had been brought before the king, he first began to entice her with flattering words to be rebaptized. But when she repelled his poisonous dart with the shield of faith, the king ordered her possessions to be taken away, since in her mind she already possessed the kingdom of paradise; then, after subjecting her to punishments, he tortured her without hope of preserving her present life.
>
> What more need be said? After many examinations and after the treasures of her earthly riches had been taken away, when she could not be broken so as to divide the blessed Trinity, she was unwillingly led to be rebaptized. When she was being forcibly plunged into that muddy bath, she cried out: “I believe the Father with the Son and the Spirit 201 to be of one substance and essence.” She polluted all the waters with a worthy ointment—that is, she sprinkled them with a discharge of the bowels. From there she was led to the lawful examination; after the rack, the flames, and the claws, she was consecrated to Christ the Lord by the cutting off of her head.

These are Gregory’s words, which he had undoubtedly excerpted from older records. This may be inferred from the expression “lawful examination,” which the ancient Spanish author of the *Passion of Saint Vincent* and other early writers who described the contests of martyrs used to designate an examination more savage than the others [Col. 0366A].

What we especially regret is that Gregory concealed the name of this holy Virgin. The commonly circulated Spanish authors, cited by Tamayo Salazar in the *Spanish Martyrology* under 15 March, call her Vincentia—but their authority is Dexter, that is, a spurious author entirely without credibility. They say that she completed her martyrdom at Cauria in the year 424. Higuera, however, commemorates her feast on 16 May.

Cauria is a fairly notable city of Lusitania and the seat of a bishopric, formerly subject to the metropolitan see of Mérida and now to that of Compostela. But although the other details which those authors report about Vincentia might, in some fashion, be tolerated, the year assigned by them cannot in any way be reconciled with the successor of Gunderic, whom Gregory identifies as the author of this persecution.

Hydatius assigns the death of Gunderic to the fourth year of the emperor Valentinian. He writes that it occurred one year before Gaiseric, his successor, crossed over into Africa. But no one would say that the Vandals entered Africa before the year 428, or at least 427. Therefore this virgin cannot be said to have suffered before the year 427, or 426 [Col. 0366B].

### 6.

We might likewise refer to this same persecution of the Vandals in Spain the martyrdom of a certain widow named Victoria, whom the same Tamayo records as having been crowned at Ilorci in Spain under the Vandals on 17 November—if we had any guarantor of this matter besides the same spurious chronicle of the rogue Dexter and those who defended it, not to mention those who embellished it. But since Tamayo produces no witness other than this false one, religious scruple forbids us to place any confidence in him.

Such, then, was the condition of Spain when the Vandals, after devastating the Balearic Islands, as Hydatius puts it in his *Chronicle*, and after overthrowing Carthage Spartaria and then Hispalis, most distinguished cities, were summoned into Africa by Count Boniface, after Spain had, in a word, been thoroughly plundered. The occasion will be explained in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER III. The Vandals’ Entry into Africa.

[Col. 0366C]

### 1.

The reason for the Vandals’ arrival in Africa should be set forth in Procopius’ words. In Book I of his *Vandalic History* he relates the matter as follows:

> The calamity of Africa occurred in this way. There were two Roman commanders, Aetius and Boniface, both powerful and, in military knowledge, second to no one of their age. They were rivals in the administration of civil affairs. Yet such was their greatness of spirit and such their other virtues that, if anyone called either of them the last of the Romans, he would not depart from the truth. Thus all Roman glory had flowed together into those two men.
>
> Placidia appointed one of them, Boniface, over all Africa. Placidia was the mother of the emperor Valentinian III, the widow of Constantius, the daughter of the great Theodosius, 202 and the sister of Honorius; she administered the empire in her son’s name. Aetius was grieved by this, but he showed that the appointment did not greatly displease him. Their hatred had not yet burst into the open; it was concealed beneath the appearance of friendship.
>
> After Boniface had already departed for Africa, Aetius began to accuse him before Placidia as one who aspired to the throne and would wrest Africa from both her and the emperor. The matter, he said, was not difficult to establish. If she summoned Boniface to Rome, he would not come.
>
> When the woman heard this, she followed Aetius’ praised advice. But Aetius had secretly begun to write to Boniface that the emperor’s mother was laying traps for his destruction. As proof of this, he foretold that Boniface would suddenly be recalled without cause. These were the contents of his letter.
>
> Boniface did not disregard the letter. When those who had come to summon him to the emperor were present, he declared that he would obey neither the emperor nor his mother, while keeping Aetius’ warning to himself. When Placidia learned this, she regarded Aetius as wholly faithful to the emperor and Boniface as suspect.
>
> Boniface, however, neither regarding himself as a match for the emperor’s power nor hoping for safety if he went to Rome, began to consider how he might attach the Vandals to himself. They held Spain, which lay near Africa.
>
> After Godigisel’s death, his two sons had succeeded him: Gontharis, born in lawful marriage, and Gizeric, born otherwise. The former was sluggish in age and character; the latter was highly practiced in war and outstanding in resourcefulness.
>
> Boniface therefore sent to Spain some of his most important friends. Through them he entered into an equitable treaty with both sons of Godigisel: a third of Africa would be ceded to each of them, and, if either were attacked in war, the danger would be shared.
>
> These terms having been agreed upon, the Vandals crossed the strait at Gades and came into Africa.

### 2.
