From this account of Procopius it can be inferred that Boniface made his treaty with the Vandals while Gunderic was still alive, although they crossed into Africa only after his death.

Hydatius also seems not to have been far from this opinion. In his *Chronicle*, under the first year of the emperor Valentinian, he reports that the Vandals, after plundering Spain, invaded Mauretania. Then, under Valentinian’s fourth year, he records Gunderic’s death; finally, in the following year, he observes that the Vandals, under King Gaiseric, abandoned Spain and crossed into Africa.

Hydatius further relates that Gunderic’s death in Spain was disastrous. He appears to be an authority beyond all exception on this point, and Saint Isidore derived his account from him in his brief history of the Vandals. Those authors say that Gunderic, after capturing the city of Hispalis and believing that everything was permitted to him, irreverently laid hands upon the city’s basilica, which Isidore, Grotius, and Roderick affirm was dedicated to Saint Vincent. They write that, punished by the divine hand for this crime, he was immediately seized by a demon at the very doors of the church, miserably tormented, and breathed out his soul.

Others, however—as Procopius testifies that he learned from the Vandals themselves—reported that Gunthar, the name by which he ordinarily calls Gunderic, was killed through the treachery of his brother Gaiseric.

But whatever the truth may be in this matter, everyone agrees that the Vandals occupied Africa under the leadership of Gaiseric; and, I think, no one can deny it [Col. 0367B].

### 3.

It is surprising that Hydatius, who mentions the Vandals’ invasion of Africa more than once, says nothing on this occasion about Boniface [Col. 0367C]. Prosper, however, who recounts Boniface’s defection, attributes the entry of barbarian nations into Africa to the fact that both he and the Romans were waging war against them:

> “From that time,” he says, “the sea was made passable for peoples who did not know how to use ships, 203 when they were summoned to give assistance by the parties contending against one another . . . The nation of the Vandals crossed from Spain into Africa.”

The author of the *Miscellaneous History*, commonly circulated under the name of Paul the Deacon, says the same. A little farther on, however, he places all the blame upon Boniface alone:

> “Boniface,” he says in Book XIV, “realizing that he could not safely hold Africa and seeing that danger threatened, inflamed toward the ruin of the state, summoned the nation of the Vandals and Alans, together with their king Gaiseric, from Spain and admitted them into Africa. They devastated almost the whole of Africa with sword, fire, and plunder, most cruelly overthrowing it; and, in addition, they subverted the Catholic faith by Arian impiety.”

To this may be added Jordanes, *On the Gothic Deeds*, chapter 33. He reports that Gizeric, king of the Vandals, was invited by Boniface to come into Africa, since, after incurring the displeasure of Augustus Valentinian, Boniface could otherwise vindicate himself only to the detriment of the state.

Cassiodorus writes in his *Chronicle* that the Vandals, driven from Spain by the Goths, crossed into Africa during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur [Col. 0367D].

### 4.

Although those authors make no mention at all of the crime by which Aetius deceived both the empress and Boniface, we do not think it follows that this history was either fabricated by Procopius or derived from a false rumor.

Indeed, if we examine somewhat more carefully what Hydatius and Prosper report on this occasion, traces of the matter may perhaps be found in their words, enabling us to discover the truth. Prosper says that war was brought against Boniface in the public interest, not only because his power and prestige within Africa were increasing, but also because he had refused to come to Italy.

That Boniface defected unwillingly from the emperor’s service is evident from the fact that, at the very beginning of the war, he returned to the Roman side as soon as the opportunity presented itself. Indeed, as Hydatius relates, when he was summoned to Italy by Placidia to oppose Aetius over Africa, he returned to the palace; immediately afterward Aetius was removed and Boniface was made master of the soldiers.

Matters ultimately reached the point at which Boniface and Aetius fought one another in open battle—and, if we are to believe Marcellinus Comes, they did so at the instigation of the empress Placidia. All this strongly confirms Procopius’ account. For, as we shall say below from Procopius, when Placidia finally learned of Aetius’ treachery, she thereafter consistently showed herself well disposed toward Boniface [Col. 0368A].

### 5.

Although I do not intend to excuse the wicked intentions of Boniface’s enemies, it must nevertheless be admitted that Boniface himself provided an opportunity for such accusations against him. After the death of his first wife, he had married another woman from the Vandal nation, thereby giving his rivals an occasion to slander him and the emperors grounds for suspecting him of evil intentions.

Perhaps he was also blamed for having dismissed Castinus, master of the soldiers, several years earlier, when Castinus was preparing to move against the Vandals, because of certain private disagreements; as a result, the Roman cause had met with an unhappy outcome [Col. 0368B].

How badly Boniface was regarded even among his friends on account of the marriage which, as we have said, he contracted with a Vandal wife, we learn from Saint Augustine, who had otherwise commended his virtues so highly. The most holy bishop severely reproved him for this act in Letter 220 of the new edition. There he complains that, although Boniface had taken this wife only after she had renounced the Arian sect and made a profession of the Catholic faith, the Arians nevertheless afterward gained such influence in his household that they obtained permission for a daughter born to him by her, as it seems, to be baptized according to the Arian rite. 204

“Moreover,” Augustine says, “unless the report was false, certain women dedicated to God were rebaptized by those same heretics.”

These are Augustine’s words. Remembering the friendship which he had once had with Boniface, he was attempting to lead him back to a better course before Boniface introduced the Vandals into Africa.

The holy man was also deeply distressed that barbarian peoples from the remotest parts of Africa—peoples who had never been subdued by Roman arms—had found a favorable opportunity, poured into the Roman provinces, and utterly devastated them. From these events almost innumerable disadvantages followed both for the Church and for the state.

Yet all these things were only a kind of prelude to the extremely grave calamities which occurred shortly afterward [Col. 0368C].

### 6.

Boniface, therefore, having been declared a public enemy of the Roman Empire because of Aetius’ treachery, was unable to withstand the war declared against him by his own forces. He made a treaty with the Vandals and summoned them into Africa, to the destruction of himself and the state.

Victor of Vita writes in Book I, number 1, that at that time they numbered eighty thousand persons of every age and condition. They had come intending to establish settlements in that province after killing or reducing its inhabitants entirely to slavery, and they devastated everything, sparing neither age nor sex.

Hydatius observes that all the Vandals, together with their families, crossed into Mauretania and Africa, abandoning Spain. He says that this happened in May, in the 302nd Olympiad, in the fifth year of Valentinian III.

The consular dating preserved in Prosper’s *Chronicle*, however, appears more reliable. There it is said that Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, crossed from Spain into Africa during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur—that is, in the common era 427 [Col. 0368D].

### 7.

While Africa was being shaken by so many and such great disturbances—all of which were attributed to Boniface’s rebellion—his relatives and old friends who were in Rome, and who had once known the man’s integrity of character and strength of spirit, could not persuade themselves that so great a man had defected from the Roman Empire because he was carried away by a desire to rule.

Therefore, by common agreement with the empress Placidia, some of them, as Procopius relates in the work cited, set out for Carthage in order to investigate the matter more closely [Col. 0369A]. After speaking with Boniface there, seeing Aetius’ fraudulent letters, and discovering the whole matter exactly as it was, they returned with all speed to Italy, intending to report to the empress and to all Boniface’s other friends the entire sequence of events and the device by which this treachery had been contrived.

Placidia then first understood that everything had occurred through Aetius’ treachery. Yet because she feared his power and needed his ability to support the failing strength of the empire, she concealed what had happened.

After revealing the whole affair to Boniface’s friends, she urged them to attempt by every means to recall Boniface to the emperor’s allegiance and service, binding herself by a solemn oath never to harm him for his defection.

I believe that the arrival in Africa of Count Darius should be understood in this connection. Saint Augustine congratulates him in Letter 229 for having been sent to Africa to establish peace without fighting or bloodshed:

> “Those who fight,” the holy bishop says to him, “if they are good men, seek peace—but through blood. 205 You, however, were sent so that no one’s blood would be sought.”

Darius’ hope was not disappointed. For, as Procopius continues, and as the sequence of events sufficiently proves, Boniface willingly complied with the requests of the empress and his friends. Immediately regretting the alliance he had made with the barbarians, he appealed to them by prayers and promises to return to Spain.

When they stubbornly refused to do so, open war was waged. But after Count Boniface, together with Aspar, commander of the eastern forces, had been defeated and routed by the barbarians, almost all Africa passed into the power of the Vandals [Col. 0369B].

### 8.

Procopius relates that an entirely remarkable event occurred on this occasion involving Marcian, who later became emperor. I gladly reproduce his account.

Marcian was then one of Aspar’s household officers and had been captured in battle by the Vandals along with many other Romans. One day, while he was sleeping during the daytime among the other captives, Gaiseric saw an eagle flying above him with its wings spread out, so that Marcian would suffer no harm from the burning heat.

After carefully considering the matter, the barbarian conjectured that Marcian would one day attain the imperial power. He therefore allowed him to depart free, after binding him by oath never to take up arms against the Vandal nation.

“Accordingly,” the same author says, “after the death of Theodosius, when Marcian was raised to the imperial office, he proved himself in all other respects an excellent ruler; but he left the affairs of Africa as he had found them.”

Evagrius Scholasticus has the same story in Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1, though he took it from Procopius.

Theodorus Lector, in Book I, nevertheless asserts that Marcian, as became an emperor, prepared to make war against the Vandals when he learned what Gaiseric had done against the empresses in the destruction of the city of Rome. He died, however, before accomplishing anything [Col. 0369C].

### 9.

After routing Boniface, Gaiseric, abusing his victory in the manner of barbarians, devastated everything at once in the African provinces, both sacred and profane. He did so with such cruelty that the barbarians themselves admitted that some hidden force was driving them to treat the Africans more savagely than their inborn ferocity ordinarily required.

Salvian testifies to this in Book VII of *The Government of God*:

> “That heavenly hand,” he says, “which had drawn them there—namely, the Vandals—to punish the crimes of the Spaniards, also compelled them to cross over to devastate Africa. In the end they themselves admitted that what they were doing was not their own work: they were being driven and compelled by divine command.”

From this one can understand how great our evils are, since the barbarians are compelled, against their will, to go forth to devastate and torment us.

Jordanes likewise suggests this in chapter 33 of *The Gothic Deeds*, writing that Gizeric, having received power in Africa, as is reported, ruled there for a long time.

The same author gives an excellent portrayal of Gaiseric’s bodily appearance, habits, character, and disposition in the passage cited above. It will be useful to reproduce his words, for I do not think anyone would dislike seeing the image of so remarkable a man depicted in true and natural colors:

> “Gizeric was well known for the Roman disaster in the City. He was of medium stature and limped because of a fall from a horse; deep in spirit, sparing in speech, contemptuous of luxury, turbulent in anger, greedy for possessions, extremely provident in stirring up nations, ready to sow the seeds of conflict and mix hatreds.”

Hydatius and Isidore, in the passages cited above, also observe that he apostatized from the Catholic faith and passed over into Arian impiety, according to the report of some. Whether this is true cannot be determined.

Certainly, as we have already said from Procopius, the Vandals were exceedingly devoted to the Arian heresy, which they had received from their fellow peoples, the Goths. Salvian and other 206 authors agree with him on this point [Col. 0370A].

### 10.

The condition of Africa at that time must be learned from Possidius. In chapter 28 of his *Life of Saint Augustine*, he mourns the calamities of his native land in these words:

> “By the divine will and power it came about that a huge force, armed with various weapons and practiced in war, belonging to the monstrous nations of the Vandals and Alans, together with the Gothic nation and persons of many other peoples, flowed in and burst into Africa from the transmarine regions of Spain.
>
> “Raging with every kind of cruelty and savagery throughout the regions of both Mauretanias, and passing from there into our other provinces and territories, it laid waste everything it could by plunder, slaughter, various tortures, fires, and other countless and unspeakable evils. It spared no sex, no age—not even the priests or ministers of God, nor the ornaments, vessels, or buildings of the churches.
>
> “A little farther on, that man of God, Saint Augustine, saw cities ruined by destruction, and the inhabitants of the rural settlements likewise destroyed together with their buildings: some killed by the enemy, others driven into flight and scattered; churches deprived of their priests and ministers; holy Virgins and all those living continent lives dispersed everywhere.
>
> “Among these, some had perished under torture, others had been killed by the sword, and others, having lost the integrity of mind and body and of faith in captivity, were serving their enemies in an evil and harsh manner. The hymns and praises of God had disappeared from the churches; the buildings of the churches had been burned with fire in very many places; the solemn sacrifices owed to God had ceased in their proper places; the divine sacraments were either not sought, or it was not easy for those seeking them to find someone to administer them.
>
> “Some who fled into the forests of the mountains, into rocky caves, and into caverns, or to whatever fortifications they could find, had been overcome and killed. Others had been stripped and deprived of the necessities by which they were sustained, so that they wasted away from hunger.
>
> “The superiors and clergy of the churches who, by God’s favor, had either not encountered them or had escaped after encountering them, were stripped and denuded of all their possessions and, in the utmost poverty, forced to beg; nor could all the assistance they required be supplied to them.
>
> “Scarcely three churches remained out of innumerable others—namely, the Carthaginian, Hipponian, and Cirtensian churches—which, by God’s favor, had not been destroyed, and whose cities continued to exist, supported by divine and human protection. Yet after his death, the city of Hippo, abandoned by its inhabitants, was burned by the enemies.”

These are Possidius’ words concerning the Vandal invasion. As he relates a little farther on, the Vandals kept Hippo under siege for fourteen months. Augustine died in the third month of that siege, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III—that is, in the year 430 of the Christian era, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September—having lived seventy-five years, nine months, and fifteen days [Col. 0370D].

### 11.

That Possidius described the calamity of the African region accurately and sincerely can also be confirmed from the apologetic letter of Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, to the Fathers of the general Council of Ephesus. In it he asserts that neither he nor any of the African bishops had been able to attend that council because of the wretched condition of all Africa, since they had not even been permitted to assemble within Africa’s borders to discuss the matter.

> “Every road and means of access,” he says, “has been blocked in this time. For the multitude of enemies poured out everywhere, and the immense devastation of the provinces, which presents to the eyes in every direction and over a great distance the complete appearance of desolation—with the inhabitants partly destroyed and partly driven into flight—has removed that ready opportunity for assembling.”

Cyril, together with all the Fathers, praised Capreolus’ concern for preserving the integrity of the faith. Vincent 207 of Lérins says in his second *Commonitory* that Capreolus’ letter breathed nothing other than the desire that, after novelty had been purged away, antiquity should be defended. Cyril of Alexandria, president of the council, ordered it to be inserted into the official acts of the council, in Action I. For this reason Bessula, Capreolus’ deacon, attended the council among the Fathers [Col. 0371A].

The first to publish in full another letter by the same Capreolus, directed against the Nestorians to Vitalis and Constantius—or rather Tonantius—Spaniards, extracted from a manuscript of the monastery of Hérivaux, was Jacques Sirmond. The letter was later reprinted several times.

Finally, Capreolus’ memory, with the title “saint,” which Vincent himself also gives him in the passage cited, is commemorated in the old calendar of the church of Carthage on [lacuna] before the Kalends of August. I thought this worth noting here, since not all the other bishops designated in that calendar are honored with this mark of sanctity [Col. 0371B].

## CHAPTER IV. The Beginnings of the Persecution by Gaiseric, King of the Vandals.

### 1.

As the fortunes of the empire declined and Valentinian was unequal to restraining the Vandals’ efforts, peace with them was established through the envoy Trigetius on the following terms: one portion of Africa would be left to the barbarians, while the other would remain under Roman authority.

Procopius, in Book I of his *Vandalic History*, mentions a second condition of this peace: Gaiseric was to pay an annual tribute to the emperor Valentinian and give him his son Huneric as a hostage. The same author asserts, however, that after friendship had been firmly established between them, Valentinian sent him back to his father.

Isidore writes in his *Brief History of the Vandals*, under the year 467, that all these arrangements were confirmed by oath. Prosper, however, gives the place and time at which the treaty was concluded. In his *Chronicle* he writes that this peace was made at Hippo on the third day before the Ides of February, during the consulship of Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV—that is, in the common era 435. This is also confirmed by Cassiodorus’ *Chronicle* [Col. 0371C].

### 2.

Although, through the benefit of this peace, the orthodox who remained under Roman rule were to some extent safe from barbarian attacks, a more serious storm consequently arose against those who had been subjected to the Vandals. Gaiseric attempted by open force to drag them into the Arian heresy.

Prosper dates this persecution to the second year after the treaty, during the consulship of Aetius II and Sigisvultus—that is, the year 437. He writes:

> “Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, wishing to subvert the Catholic faith by Arian impiety within the boundaries of his own habitation, persecuted certain of our bishops to such a degree that, after depriving them of the right to their basilicas, he expelled them even from their cities, since their steadfastness yielded to none of the terrors of the most arrogant king.”

Three of these bishops are listed in the edition of Prosper’s *Chronicle* by Labbe, volume I of the *New Library*, page 51, although their names are absent from the other copies. They are Possidius, Novatus, and Severianus, who are there said to have been more distinguished than the others [Col. 0371D].

Who those bishops were cannot be determined. At that time Possidius, bishop of Calama in Numidia, was famous and known to everyone because of the life of Saint Augustine which he published. 208 So too was Novatus, bishop of Sitifis in Mauretania by surname, who attended the Carthaginian Conference in the case of the Donatists and signed the Carthaginian council against the Pelagians under Bishop Aurelius.

It is certain that Novatus of Sitifis was still alive at the end of Augustine’s life, as is clear from the same holy man’s Letter 229 to Count Darius, cited above.

### 3.

This persecution was evidently stirred up not only against bishops, from what the same Prosper adds concerning Arcadius and his companions. He testifies that, after being tormented by various punishments, they finally ended their lives in glorious martyrdom [Col. 0372A].

This is the same Arcadius to whom there survives a letter from Antoninus, bishop of Constantina, while Arcadius was in exile for the orthodox faith. In it Antoninus exhorts him to endure martyrdom bravely in defense of the Catholic faith.

Baronius, under the year of Christ 447, suspected that this letter was different from the one attributed by Gennadius to Honoratus, bishop of Constantina, because in the published copies it circulated under the name of Antoninus.

The same title led Aubertus Miraeus, in chapter 114 of his *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*, to list an Antoninus, bishop of Constantina, who wrote a consolatory letter to Arcadius, sent into exile by Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, as though he were someone different from the Honoratus whom Gennadius mentions in his *Catalogue*.

Learned men now agree that the two were one and the same person, who was called Antoninus Honoratus. An ancient manuscript of our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés removes every ground for doubt. It was written about eleven hundred years ago in Merovingian or Frankish-Gallic script, and Gennadius’ *Catalogue* is appended to Jerome’s work. In it the author of the letter under discussion is, without any suspicion of falsification, called Honoratus Antoninus.

Thus it reads under number 225, corresponding to chapter 96 of Miraeus’ edition:

> “Honoratus Antoninus, bishop of the city of Constantina, wrote to Arcadius, who had been sent into exile in the regions of Africa by King Gaiseric for confessing the Catholic faith: a letter exhorting him to bear labors for Christ, strengthened both by contemporary examples and by testimonies from Scripture; and teaching that perseverance in confessing the faith not only cleanses sins but also obtains the merit of martyrdom.”

Here, however, “Constantinae” should be read for “Constantiae.” This city received the name Constantina from Constantine the Great, whereas it had previously been called Cirta.

Gisbert Cuperus, a man who rendered excellent service to literary studies, writes that the city is still famous under the same name of Constantina, in his notes on Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, at chapter 43, where he presents an engraving of its image and illustrates it with learned observations [Col. 0372B].

### 4.

Antoninus appears to have succeeded Fortunatus as bishop of the same city of Constantina. Fortunatus attended the Carthaginian Conference held between Catholics and Donatists in 411 and the Council of Milevis in 416. But in what year he ascended the throne of the church of Cirta is entirely unknown to me.

Both Gennadius and Honorius of Autun mention only his letter to Arcadius. Although it is brief, it is nevertheless a work that rightly earned its author a place among ecclesiastical writers; no one who has read it will deny this. Indeed, it is scarcely possible to find another writing from that century that breathes more strongly the spirit of earlier times and apostolic vigor. For this reason it seemed worthwhile to present it here in full, especially since it plainly belongs to the history of the martyrs of the Vandal persecution.

## EXHORTATORY LETTER OF HONORATUS ANTONINUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINA, TO ARCADIUS IN EXILE FOR THE FAITH

*(We published this letter in Patrologia, volume L, column 567.)*

[Col. 0372D]

5. Aroused by this letter of Honoratus, Arcadius brought to a glorious conclusion, with a precious end, the noble struggle which he had already begun in exile for the orthodox faith. For, scorning the immense wealth that surrounded him, rejecting the king’s friendship—which was being offered to him and through which he had previously enjoyed such influence—and even treating his wife’s affection as nothing, he bravely endured the various kinds of torture by which his constancy was tested and finally completed, through a glorious death for Christ, an illustrious martyrdom together with three other fellow countrymen of his, as Prosper reports in his *Chronicle* in these words:

> In the consulship of Aetius II and Sigisvultus—that is, according to our method of reckoning, in the year 437—at about the same time four Spanish men, Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychianus, had long been held in high esteem and honor by Genseric because of their wisdom and faithful service. To make them more closely attached to himself, the king ordered them to pass over to the Arian impiety. But when they resolutely rejected this crime, they provoked the barbarian to the most furious anger. First proscribed, then driven into exile, afterward tortured with the most atrocious punishments, and finally killed by different deaths, they wonderfully met their end in an illustrious martyrdom.

The same author then adds the struggle of the Catholic boy Paulillus, who preferred to become a wretched slave for Christ’s name, though he had been a very wealthy courtier, rather than renounce his profession of the Catholic faith:

> The boy Paulillus by name, the brother of Eutychianus and Paschasius, highly favored by the king because of the elegance of his appearance and intelligence, could not be driven away from the profession and love of the Catholic faith by any threats. He was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to the lowest form of servitude. He was therefore, as it appears, not killed, lest that age should also glory in the conquered cruelty of the impious king.

6. Writers of both ancient and more recent martyrologies celebrate the memory of these saints. Among them, Ado inserted Prosper’s entire passage into his martyrology under 13 November, and this was afterward also done in the Roman Martyrology. Usuard, however, reported only what concerned the first four, saying nothing about Paulillus; nor did Florus, in whose martyrology the same saints are likewise listed, though on the preceding day. There, as also in the Canisian edition of Prosper’s *Chronicle*, the fourth among them is listed under the name Eutychianus but is called Eutychius.

Spanish writers celebrate the feast of these martyrs of Christ as fellow citizens of their own country. And rightly so. That they were Spaniards is clear even from the passage of Prosper that we transcribed above. Tamayus Salazar has more about them than anyone else in his *Spanish Martyrology*, where he compiled their acts for 13 November from various authors. Indeed, there he also praises, as he reports it, the epitaph inscribed on their tomb, in which Arcadius is said to have been born at Toledo, while the others were born at Salamanca; they are called the first fruits—the earliest martyrs—of the Vandal persecution in Africa.

No one can deny that this final title is rightly theirs, on the basis of the letter of Honoratus Antoninus which we cited above [213]. There Honoratus addresses Arcadius in this way, no. 5: “You are Christ’s standard-bearer; you march first in the battle line. If you fall, you will not be exempt from the death of the others,” and so forth. But what that same author additionally relates about these martyrs from more recent sources will not easily be accepted by anyone without some guarantor of more reliable testimony.

7. Moreover, the authors whom we have cited indicate that many more martyrs and confessors fought in Africa at this time in defense of Christ’s divinity, although, for the sake of brevity, they have recorded only the names of a few. Nor were there lacking very holy bishops who opposed Genseric’s efforts like bronze walls in defense of the house of the Lord. Among their number Gennadius praises several in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers—men who, taking up the pen, vigorously defended the truth of the Catholic faith in their writings against the Arians.

Among others, Victor of Cartenna, a bishop in Mauretania, was famous. He arranged for a book which he had published against the Arians to be presented to Genseric himself, as Gennadius testifies in chapter 77, on the basis of the prologue to that book. See above, p. 169 (for us, col. 340, no. 50).

To the same period must undoubtedly also be assigned the *Summary of the Faith* written against those same Arians, which Jacobus Sirmond published in 1630 together with four other short works by ancient authors. We have already observed above, in note 20 on Victor of Vita (above, col. 188, n. e), that Sebastianus, a count whom Genseric tried to persuade to renounce his ancestral religion, drew from this *Summary* the reply by which he frustrated the tyrant’s efforts.

At the same time there appeared a *Book, or Declaration, concerning Various Passages on the Trinity against Varimadus, a Deacon of the Arian Sect*. This work was published in the *Library of the Fathers*, where its author states in the preface placed before the work that he wrote it while staying near Naples, a city of Campania, at the time when the Arians were boasting arrogantly of the power of unbelieving kings. He presents the book to Catholics as a most fully equipped arsenal against the Arians, so that from it they may draw what they should answer to the quibbles of heretics when attacked by them.

Indeed, the Arian deacon Varimadus, against whom this book was written, seems to be none other than Marivadus, as Sirmondus suspects in the preface to the five dogmatic opuscula mentioned above. According to Victor of Vita himself, book I, no. 16, Huneric honored this Marivadus in a singular manner while Genseric was still alive.

Peter Francis Chiffletius, moreover, identifies the author of the same work as Vigilius of Tapsus, in the second short work *On the Vindication of the Writings of This African Bishop*, which he also published under this title in three books. But the manuscript codices disagree: according to Chiffletius himself, they attribute the same work to Bishop Idatius. V. C. Joseph Antelmius attacks Chiffletius’s opinion in a dissertation which he recently published on the author of the Athanasian Creed, section 2.

Yet although we are convinced that the author of this work was Bishop Idatius, he was by no means Idatius Clarus, the Spanish bishop who became famous in the time of Theodosius the Great because he accused Priscillian as a heretic, as many recent writers have supposed, deceived by the similarity of the names. Nevertheless, we cannot deny that it may be attributed to another Idatius, namely the bishop of Lemica in Gallaecia, who is known to have flourished in the time of Genseric, when the Vandals, having abandoned Spain, crossed over into Africa. Indeed, in his own *Chronicle*, which he brought down to the third year of the emperor Anthemius, he repeatedly testifies that he was generally present at the events which he relates.

8. Shortly after this period, that is, after Genseric had already invaded Carthage, Cerealis, bishop of Castellum, composed a book against Maximinus, a bishop of the Arian sect. It is extant in the *Library of the Fathers* and is praised by Gennadius in chapter 66. The same Cerealis is listed in the *African Register* among the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania who, by order of King Huneric, assembled at Carthage to give an account of their faith; we spoke of him above, p. 179.

Voconius Castellanus flourished in the same province, or, as our old copy reads, “bishop of the city of Castallana in Mauretania.” Gennadius lists various short works of his in chapter 78. See above, col. 173 (for us, col. 343, no. 75).

Finally, Asclepius the African is described by the same author, chapter 73, as a man of great reputation for extemporaneous teaching. He is also said to have written much against the Arians, as well as against the Donatists. But various manuscripts write the name of his see in different ways, so that none of them appears free from corruption.

The printed editions read: “Asclepius the African, bishop in the territory of Bagai, of a not-large village.” Our oldest copy of Gennadius, however, reads: “in the territory of Gaba, bishop of Vicinaegrans,” and so forth; another hand, though not so ancient, has “of the city of Vicina.” The former reading is confirmed by the Fiscamnian codex, as our Dom Guillelmus Fillastre informed me, where he is called “bishop of Vicinigrandis in the territory of Navigus.”

Honorius, chapter 72, simply calls him “bishop in the territory of Bai.” Perhaps the name of some village is indicated here. For no one is unaware that there were bishops in African villages, estates, and rural districts; this could easily be proved from the Carthaginian Conference, chapters 181 and 182, and from other ancient records. But there is no time to dwell on these matters longer.

I pass over the other authors who flourished in subsequent periods, among whom blessed Fulgentius was especially distinguished. We shall say more about him in his proper place.

# CHAPTER V. Genseric, after capturing Carthage, rages against its citizens

1. The emperor seemed secure regarding Genseric’s good faith, confirmed, as we have said, by an oath because of the peace. But Genseric, seeing that the Romans were occupied elsewhere, expected to invade without much difficulty those cities which did not obey him. He therefore suddenly hastened to Carthage and subjected it to his rule, judging that, once he had captured the chief city of all Africa and held the senate and the noblemen in his power, no one would thereafter be strong enough to resist him.

But he erupted with such savagery against the citizens of that most wretched city that, unless we had almost all the writers of that age as witnesses to what Genseric perpetrated on this occasion, the whole account would seem to exceed all credibility. It is useful to set forth the matter in the words of others, lest anyone perhaps think that I have exaggerated the disasters of so famous a city. Thus Prosper speaks of this destruction in his *Chronicle*:

> In the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus—that is, in the year of the common era 439—while Aetius was occupied with settling affairs in Gaul, Genseric, whose friendship was not feared, invaded Carthage on 19 October under the pretext of peace. After torturing the citizens with various kinds of torment, he converted all its wealth to his own possession. Nor did he refrain from plundering the churches: after stripping them of their sacred vessels and depriving them of the ministry of their priests, he ordered them to be not places of divine worship but dwellings for his own people. He raged against the entire captive population, but was especially hostile to the nobility and to religion, so that it could not be discerned whether he had waged war more against human beings or against God.

Carthage suffered this captivity 585 years after it had begun to belong to the Romans. Isidore has the same account in his *History of the Vandals*, under the year 467 of the era: “Having violated the sanctity of his oath, he invaded Carthage under the pretext of peace,” and so forth, as in Prosper. He adds: “He introduced the Arian pest throughout Africa, expelled the priests of the Church, made very many martyrs, and, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel, having altered the sacred mysteries, he handed the churches of Christ over to their enemies.” He borrowed these final words from the *Chronicle* of Idatius.

Marcellinus Comes dates the event to 23 October, asserting that Carthage was occupied by Genseric on that day. But the authority of Prosper and Idatius is preferable.

2. Salvianus, a priest of Marseille, has much to say about the destruction of the African provinces and of Carthage itself in his books *On the Government of God*. The sixth and the two following books are almost entirely devoted to this subject. He says that these disasters should not be attributed to divine severity but to the wickedness of the Africans, who had drawn the Vandals toward them by a grave and prolonged iniquity before the Vandals set out for Africa.

He exaggerates the vices and depraved morals of those Africans to such an extent that he does not hesitate to assert that there was no good among them, but everything was evil—namely, that, after the original integrity of nature had been excluded, their vices had in some fashion created another nature in them. He attacks their immorality especially in book VII. In the following book he inveighs against them chiefly because they showed no reverence toward the servants of God, especially monks, whom he calls God’s saints. Instead, they mocked, cursed, detested, and persecuted them, doing to them almost everything that the impiety of the Jews had previously done to our Savior before it proceeded to the actual shedding of divine blood.

A little later he adds:

> Among the cities of Africa, and especially within the walls of Carthage, that wretched yet faithless people could scarcely bear to see, without insult and execration, a man wrapped in a cloak, pale, and shorn to the skin, with the flowing locks of his hair cut off. And whenever a servant of God from the monasteries of Egypt, or from elsewhere, came to that city for the work of divine service, as soon as he appeared before the people he was met with insults, sacrilege, and curses. Nor was this all: he was beaten as though with whips by the most shameless laughter of depraved men and the hissing of those who laughed in detestation—so that, if someone ignorant of the circumstances had witnessed it, he would have thought that not a human being was being mocked, but that some new and unheard-of monster was being driven away and exterminated.

Salvianus was carried away by his customary desire to summon peoples to repentance, and for this reason he relates these and many other things. But concerning the calamity of Carthage, one should consult especially Victor of Vita, book I. From him we learn that Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage, arrived safely at Naples in Campania with a very large part of his clergy, after they had been placed on an old ship so that they might be swallowed up by the waves. We shall discuss him below, chapter 9.

3. The nobler the citizens of Carthage were, the more pitiable was their fate. For Genseric feared that, if they retained even a small portion of their former authority, they would eventually become more hostile to him. He therefore compelled all who possessed any dignity, or who seemed in any way superior to the rest by nobility of birth, to sail across the sea after being stripped of all their possessions, unless they preferred to be reduced to the condition of the lowest slaves.

We learn from the life of blessed Fulgentius, chapter 1, that the grandfather of that saint suffered the former fate. Gordian—for that was his name—is said to have willingly undertaken the exile imposed upon him from the number of the Carthaginian senators, wishing at least, after losing his possessions, not to lose his freedom.

4. The letters of Theodoret teach us about the fortune of certain others who, driven from their homeland, traversed various provinces of the East and reached as far as Syria. Among them was a certain Coelestiacus—or, as other editions read, Coelestianus—whom Theodoret commends to Apellion in letter 29. In that letter, lamenting the fate of the Carthaginians, he splendidly describes the city’s calamity:

> What the Carthaginians have suffered would require the tragedy of Aeschylus and Sophocles, and the magnitude of their misfortunes might perhaps surpass even their language. Carthage, once scarcely captured by the Romans themselves—indeed, a city which had often contended with mighty Rome for supremacy and had brought her into the greatest danger—has now become merely a mockery of barbarians. And those who once adorned her most celebrated senate-house now wander throughout the world, supporting their lives from the hands of hospitable people. They move those who see them to tears and display the instability and fickleness of human affairs. I have seen many others who came from there, and I was afraid; for I do not know, as Scripture says [Prov. 27:1], what the coming day may bring forth.

Then he commends Coelestiacus to Apellion with particular affection, because he was making great spiritual progress amid the calamities that afflicted him:

> I especially venerate the most distinguished and magnificent Coelestiacus, who bears his calamity with an even spirit, turns the change of fortune into an occasion for philosophy, praises the Ruler of all, and considers it beneficial that He either ordered this to happen or did not prevent it from happening. For the reasoning of divine Providence is ineffable. May your magnificence receive him, together with his wife and children, with Abrahamic kindness. Trusting in the greatness of your soul, I introduce these guests and display your generous right hand.

5. The same Theodoret contains various letters addressed to certain bishops and other noblemen on this subject, in which he praises Coelestiacus’s extraordinary patience in enduring these calamities. “He bears poverty,” he says in letter 34 to Count Patricius, “as easily as few bear wealth.”

The most devout bishop also uses this occasion to place the fragility of human affairs before the eyes of those to whom he writes. Thus he says to Count and Primate Stasimus in letter 33:

> I inform your magnificence that his homeland [Coelestiacus’s] was once the Libya celebrated by everyone; that his city was the most distinguished Carthage; that his tribe and family belonged to that most illustrious senate; and that he possessed great wealth, flowing beyond what was necessary. But now all these things are a tale, and a narrative stripped of reality . . . Such, indeed, is human happiness, and so forth.

He repeats much the same in letter 30 to the sophist Arius and in letter 32 to Theotistus, bishop of Beroea. But what he writes about this same Coelestiacus to Domnus, bishop of Antioch, in letter 31 deserves attention:

> The homeland of the most distinguished and magnificent Coelestiacus is the famous Carthage, and his lineage was as illustrious as that city. But now, expelled from it, he travels through foreign lands and looks around for the hand of those who love God. He also bears a necessary burden which increases his cares: a wife, children, and servants, on whose account he requires greater expenses. I have admired his spirit. For, as though he were carried by favorable winds, he praises the pilot and considers the violent storm nothing. He has wrestled piety from his calamity, and misfortune has brought him this most blessed fruit. While he enjoyed prosperity, he did not admit such discourses; but once stripped of it, he cast away impiety at the same time and now possesses the riches of piety, for whose sake he despises this adversity.

I have thought it worthwhile to report these matters at somewhat greater length, so that it may be evident from them that the calamities and miseries of this life are generally quite necessary for those who wish to care for their salvation, since otherwise, when wealth and honors abound, it does not even occur to them to think about it.

6. The same Theodoret also took care to commend other African citizens who had been driven into exile from their homeland through his letters. Among these is letter 52, addressed to Ibas, bishop of Edessa, as well as the following letter to Sophronius, bishop of Constantina. In them he entrusts to their piety a certain bishop from Africa, named Cyprianus, who had fled because of the barbarians’ cruelty.

Here we must not omit what the same Theodoret writes on the occasion of that African persecution in letter 70, addressed to Eustathius, bishop of Aegae, on behalf of Maria, a noble girl who, sold into slavery amid the common disaster of her homeland, had reached as far as Syria. The matter should be presented in his own words, which require no interpretation:

> What is told about the most noble Maria is worthy of tragedy. For, as she herself relates and certain others have testified, she is the daughter of the most magnificent Eudaemon. But in the calamity which invaded Africa she lost her ancestral freedom and was sold into slavery. Merchants bought her from the barbarians and sold her to some of our countrymen. She was sold together with a girl who had formerly been her domestic servant. Thus mistress and maid alike bore the bitter yoke of slavery.
>
> The maid, however, did not wish to ignore the distinction between them, nor did she forget her former mistress. She preserved her kindness amid calamity and, after serving their common masters, also served the woman who was thought to be her fellow slave, washing her feet, making her bed, and performing the other services in the same way.
>
> The matter became known to the buyers, and the girl’s freedom and the maid’s goodness were reported throughout the city. When the most faithful soldiers who live among us learned of this—for I was absent at the time—they paid the purchase price back to the buyers and rescued her from slavery.
>
> After my return, when I had been informed both of the calamity that had befallen her and of the soldiers’ praiseworthy zeal, I wished them success. I entrusted the most noble girl to one of the most religious deacons [another edition: “to a most devout deaconess”] and ordered that sufficient food be provided for her.
>
> Ten months had now passed when, hearing that her father was still alive and holding office in the West, she rightly desired to return to him. When some people assured her that several merchants from the West would come to the market currently being held among you, she requested permission to depart with a letter from me. For this reason I have written to you, entreating your piety to care for a girl of noble birth and to order some religious person to deal with the sailors, captains, and merchants and entrust her to trustworthy men who could restore her to her father. Those who bring a daughter back to her father beyond all human expectation will certainly receive an immense reward.

This is what Theodoret wrote to the bishop of Aegae. That city was formerly an episcopal see under the metropolitan of Anazarbus, in the farthest part of Cilicia, where merchants from various parts of the world were accustomed to assemble.

7. Baronius appends to this history another account, that of a certain virgin named Julia. She was not only, like Maria, taken to Syria and sold after the Vandals captured Carthage, but also endured slavery and other calamities before finally completing them in a glorious martyrdom.

This is the famous virgin Julia, whose struggle Baronius reports under the year 440 from Ado’s martyrology—or rather, as he himself observes in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, from the appendix to Ado. We, having obtained the complete account of her passion from a manuscript which we compared with the Bollandist edition, have thought it worthwhile to present it here.

Although these things were not written by those who were present at the events, faith should not therefore be entirely denied to those who endeavored to hand them down to posterity as they had received them from their fathers, without additions of invention. Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that Julia is said in this account to have suffered at the hands of pagans who were attending to sacrifices to the gods. For the pagans had not yet been so completely eradicated that, at least in remote places, they had entirely abandoned their customary sacrifices.

Indeed, in the following century, as Gregory the Great testifies in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 8, Saint Benedict brought to the faith the pagans living near Mount Cassino and completely overthrew and destroyed their shrine dedicated to Apollo and the grove devoted to their superstition, which still remained.

Moreover, Cyrus, a pagan, held the highest offices of the Roman Empire at the very time when the Vandals invaded Carthage, and he was appointed consul in the year after that city was captured. Not long afterward, Marcellianus, also a pagan, was appointed commander of the Roman army against Genseric together with Heraclianus under the emperor Leo.

But why seek examples from abroad, when Saint Gregory makes it clear that in his own time there were still many pagans on the island of Corsica, where Julia herself is said to have suffered? In book VII, indiction 1, letter 2, he congratulates Peter, bishop of Corsica, because he was diligently occupied in promoting the conversion of the pagans, and he testifies that through Peter’s efforts many had already been recalled from the worship of idols.

The memory of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, is famous in both ancient and more recent martyrologies, which commemorate her feast on 22 May. On the same day she is also recorded by Ferrarius in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, where he says that Julia was killed near Bonifacio, a town of Corsica.

Her sacred body remained on the island of Gorgona until the year 763, when it was transferred by Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to Brescia. There it was placed in a Benedictine monastery which he had magnificently built, at the urging of his wife Ansa, for their daughter Angelberga. It is still honored there with the greatest devotion by the people.

# THE PASSION OF SAINT JULIA, VIRGIN AND MARTYR

*(From the manuscript codex of the arch-monastery of Saint Remigius of Rheims, compared with the printed edition.)*

## 219. THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

### I

It is written, dearest brothers: “They will tell these things to their children, so that they may place their hope in God and not forget all that God has done among his saints” (Ps. 77:6ff.).

In those days, when we asked the elders what the life of Saint Julia the martyr had been like, or what trophy the palm of martyrdom had obtained through her suffering [Bollandus: *palmam*, rather than *palma*], they faithfully related to us that they had received the following account from their parents. We believe that we ought to transmit the same account to posterity in some little written page—not so much with elegance of speech as with the most faithful simplicity—lest, perhaps, as faith grows old, the passion of so great a martyr be neglected in obscurity.

[Note: The Remigius Codex reads: “lest the hidden [or obscure] passion of so great a martyr be expended.” Perhaps: “lest no worship be given to so great a martyr,” and so forth.]

She consecrated the whole province through the shedding of her blood at the Cape of Corsica in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Cape of Corsica: a promontory at the limits of the island of Corsica, toward Italy. The whole island is now under the rule of the Genoese.]

## THE PASSION BEGINS

### II

At the time when the city of Carthage had been captured, blessed Julia was taken captive from it and, by lot, came into the service of a certain man named Eusebius. But the venerable martyr observed the apostolic command. She served her earthly master, not serving merely to please human eyes, but serving as one subject to God’s every high command (Eph. 6:6; Col. 3:22). [Note: Bollandus reads: “subject to authority, she served openly.”]

Although her master was a pagan, he admired the extraordinary virtue of her service and therefore also revered, to some extent, the steadfastness of her religion. [Note: Papebrochius thinks that “Arian” or “Saracen” should be restored; but the whole sequence of the Passion requires the reading “pagan.”] Whenever she was given rest after completing her service, she either devoted herself to reading or persisted in prayer.

Thus, when, through mortification of food, she devoted herself to the love of God [Bollandus: *affligeret*, “afflicted herself”], her master could not induce her to relax her abstinence by flatteries or admonitions, even for a single day, as is said—except on the Sunday of the Resurrection.

[Note: By these words understand any Sunday, as in many authors of the later period. See letter 11 of Saint Leo in the Quesnel edition, addressed to Dioscorus of Alexandria.]

Her face grew pale through fasting, but her faith remained firm; her limbs withered through affliction, but her mind, intent upon heaven, was daily nourished by the words of God. She grew pale with the violets of abstinence [perhaps: “grew white”] and burned with the lilies of chastity.

### III

Accordingly, her earthly master Eusebius, a citizen of Syria in Palestine, was hastening to Gaul with the most valuable merchandise. Without our expecting it, he left behind at the Cape of Corsica what he possessed that was precious.

When they had brought their ship to rest there at anchor with vigorous rowing, they saw from a distance the rites of sacrifices being performed there by pagans. At once Eusebius and all his companions hurried down to sacrifice. On that very day they were offering a bull to their demons.

Meanwhile, while they were reveling in drunken feasts, holy Julia drew deep sighs from the bottom of her heart because of their error. His attendants reported to Felix that there was a girl on the ship who mocked the worship of the gods.

[Note: The Bodec Codex, as cited by Bollandus, adds: “who was the chief among the crowds of sacrificers.” In Ado’s appendix he is called “the prince,” which perhaps means that he was the principal man of that place. Below he is called “Felix Saxo,” perhaps “Sago,” from Sagona, a now-ruined city of Corsica, as Papebrochius suspects. Ferrarius, in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, calls him “Felix the Tribune.”]

The son of the serpent addressed Eusebius, saying:

> Why did not all those who are with you come down to worship our gods? Moreover, I hear that there is a girl there who mocks the names of our gods.

Eusebius replied:

> The girl of whom you speak I have been completely unable to turn away from the worship or superstition of the Christians, nor have I been able to bring her over to our religion even by threats. And unless I needed her for her most faithful service, I would already be punishing her.

Then Felix Saxo said to him:

> Either compel her to pay her vows to our gods, or certainly I will give you whichever four of my maidservants please you best [Roman Codex: *ancillis*]; or set whatever price has been fixed and give her to me for that sum.

Eusebius replied:

> Even if you wished to give me your entire fortune, it could not equal the value of her service.

### IV

Then, after taking counsel, the most poisonous serpent prepared a feast. Eusebius became drunk from his cups and was overcome by deep sleep. Immediately the furious crowd of pagans boarded the ship and then brought holy Julia ashore.

Felix Saxo said to her:

> Sacrifice to the gods, girl. I will pay your master whatever he demands for you and release you from the bond of your condition.

But holy Julia replied:

> My freedom is the service of Christ, whom I serve daily with a pure mind. As for this error of yours, I not only do not venerate it; I also detest it.

Then Felix Saxo ordered her to be struck on the face. Holy Julia said:

> If my Lord Jesus Christ received spittle and blows upon his face for me, why should I not be struck on the face for my own sake [perhaps: “for him”], and why should my cheeks not grow stiff with my tears in place of spittle?

Again the most savage dragon ordered her to be tortured by her hair. The venerable martyr of God was tortured and scourged. But in her confession she cried out:

> I confess him who was scourged for me. For if my Lord was crowned with thorns for me and received the trophy of the cross, why should I, through the softness of my hair and through his banner of faith, not endure the struggles of this passion, so that I may deserve to attain the palm of martyrdom?

### V

Therefore the dragon hurried, lest he suffer the defeat of his savagery, and immediately ordered the holy servant of Christ to be placed upon the cross. When Eusebius awoke, she, the victor, there finally mastered the greatest struggles of the flesh.

[Note: We have retained the reading of the Bodecensis Codex. The Florentine and Remigius codices read: “And when they had opened the doors of the tomb, subject to her merits, a dove flew swiftly from her mouth toward the stars.” There also, and so forth.]

When he had loosened the restraints of sleep, that holy soul, released from the flesh and crowned with the roseate palm of martyrdom, joyfully sought flight to the stars of heaven with the angels. There, in the bridal chamber of the cross, she recited her dowry before the angels with a full confession of faith and signed it with the shedding of her blood.

Through the angels, by divine dispensation, this was announced to the congregation of holy monks on the island of Margarita.

[Note: The Remigius Codex adds: “which is now commonly called Gorgona.” It lies between the island of Corsica and the coast of Tuscany; formerly it belonged to the Pisans, but now, like Pisa itself, it is subject to the grand duke of Etruria. Gregory the Great speaks of the monks of the island of Gorgona in book I, letter 50.]

They immediately boarded a ship and, raising their sails, reached the Cape of Corsica in haste, with the wind providing them assistance. When they sought the place, they found everything just as it had been revealed to them by the angels. With every reverence they took the body of Christ’s holy martyr down from the cross, placed her in the ship, raised the sails, and sailed back with all speed, the wind again providing assistance.

[Note: The Bod Codex reads: “With a favorable wind they reached their monastery,” and so forth.]

### VI

Then monks from the island called Capraria met them in a ship, with the wind granting them great assistance. They were astonished that, contrary to the strength of the wind, the full sails were carrying them on their course like birds.

[Note: The island of Capraria lies midway between Corsica and Gorgona. Augustine praises the monks of this island for their holy way of life in letter 48, addressed to their abbot Eudoxius. Mascezel, preparing to fight in Africa against his brother Gildo, who had rebelled, spent nights in prayer with the monks of the island of Capraria. He even took some of them with him to Africa, so that he might fight with weapons while they fought with prayers. After spending the night in vigil with hymns and prayers, strengthened by the mysteries of the heavenly sacraments, he entered battle and, with a small band of soldiers, put a huge army of rebels to flight, as Paul Orosius, an author of that period, relates in book VII, chapter 25. Jerome writes in the epitaph of Fabiola that Fabiola visited the monks of the islands of the Etruscan Sea. See Baronius and the authors whom he cites under the year 398. The Bodec Codex, however, says nothing about this meeting with the monks of Capraria.]

The monks approached and carefully inquired what divine power was present in the ship. The others explained everything to them in order, just as it had happened, and asked them for a blessing from the relics. Having obtained it, they returned to their own place.

The others reached the island of Gorgona. They took her body from the ship, embalmed it with spices, and placed it in a tomb with great joy.

These things took place on 22 May. In that place the prayers of the saints flourish to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# CHAPTER VI. Genseric Invades Rome and Ravages Various Provinces of the Empire

[Col. 0381A]

1. When Genseric, after capturing Carthage, knew that he had nothing to fear for himself in Africa, he attacked Sicily in the same year in which he had invaded Carthage, as the author of the Paschal Chronicle writes. Learned men, however, following Idatius, Prosper, and Cassiodorus, judge that this incursion should rather be assigned to the following year, during the consulship of Valentinian Augustus V and Anatolius—that is, the year 440 of the common era.

This was undoubtedly the calamity of his native land which Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, bishop in Sicily, deplores in his letter to Pope Leo the Great. In it he complains that, because of the bitterest captivity, he had suffered nakedness and other hardships. Indeed, from other authors who wrote about this matter it can also be gathered that this calamity of Sicily was severe. Isidore testifies in his brief History of the Vandals that, in the year 467 of the era, Genseric, after plundering all Sicily, also laid siege to Panormus, the chief city of the entire island. He drew this account from the Chronicle of Bishop Idatius, who writes that on this occasion a severe persecution against the Catholics in that province was stirred up by the barbarian king, at the instigation, namely, of Maximinus, a supporter of the Arian sect, because he had shortly before been condemned by orthodox bishops.

These are the words of Idatius:

> Gaiseric, having plundered Sicily, besieged Panormus for a long time. At the urging of Maximinus—condemned by the Catholic bishops and leader of the Arians in Sicily [the transmitted wording is corrupt]—Gaiseric rushed against the Catholics, so as to compel them by every means into Arian impiety. Some withdrew; others, persevering in the Catholic faith, completed their martyrdom.

Theodoric, king of the Goths, testifies in Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, letter 4, that Genseric was never able to invade that province, any more than Bruttium, because Cassiodorus the Elder had bravely protected both.

2. Genseric was therefore wholly occupied with this expedition. “He was severely afflicting Sicily,” says Prosper in his Chronicle, and Cassiodorus after him, “when, upon hearing of the arrival in Africa of Count Sebastian, he interrupted the undertaking.” For he feared that so great a man, while he himself was absent, might cause him some trouble, and immediately returned to Carthage.

Sebastian, however, was seeking by flight nothing other than his own safety. He had succeeded Boniface, whose daughter he had married, but shortly afterward had been compelled to yield his place to Aetius. Idatius writes that he was immediately expelled from the palace by Aetius. Then, after several years had passed in exile and flight, he sailed to the palace of the East, as the same Idatius testifies. Driven from there by a similar fortune, he fled to Theodoric—thus Idatius calls Theodoric—the king of the Goths. Finally, crossing into Africa to the Vandals, he was killed near Carthage after some time had passed, on Genseric’s orders, through fabricated accusations against him.

Idatius records all these events in various places; Count Marcellinus summarizes them in a single entry under the year 435. Prosper, however, assigns his arrival from Spain in Africa to the year 440.

Above all, what deserves praise in Sebastian is his supreme steadfastness in preserving the purity of the orthodox faith. Victor of Vita discusses this in Book I, no. 6. For this reason some people undertook to enter his name in the ecclesiastical calendars, as we said in note 20 on Victor (above, col. 188, n. e).

3. While these events were taking place in Africa and Sicily, Theodosius Augustus prepared a huge fleet and made war against the Vandals, but with an unsuccessful outcome, as Prosper reports under the year 441, when Cyrus was consul. Ariobindus and the other commanders whom the emperor had placed in charge of the fleet, by delaying the undertaking through prolonged hesitation, were more a burden to Sicily than a defense of Africa.

Moreover, when in the following year, during the consulship of Dioscorus and Eudoxius, the Huns under King Attila entered Thrace and Illyricum and devastated those provinces, Theodosius was compelled to recall the army which he had directed against the Vandals. Whether Attila undertook this invasion of the eastern provinces on his own initiative, or was induced by money to do so by Genseric, a man of great cunning, as some maintain, is uncertain.

[Col. 0382A]

4. Valentinian, having been disappointed in every hope of recovering Carthage for the empire, renewed peace with Genseric three years after it had been captured by the Vandals, during the consulship of Dioscorus and Eudoxius—that is, in the year 442. The emperor, as Prosper, Cassiodorus, and others report, divided Africa between them according to fixed boundaries and surrendered to the barbarians Byzacena, Tripolitania, and the province called Proconsular, while retaining both Mauritanias—Caesariensis and Sitifensis—Numidia, and that region which had once been part of ancient Mauritania and was later known by the name Tingitana, but which belonged to the diocese of the Spains.

Victor of Vita adds part of Numidia in Book I, no. 4, where he writes that Genseric reserved for himself Byzacena, Abaritana, Getulia, and part of Numidia, while the Proconsular or Zeugitana was assigned to the army. “The remaining provinces,” he says, “although devastated, were still being defended by Valentinian.”

Here it is useful to recall the supreme solicitude for the Church of God entrusted to him shown by Leo, the Roman pontiff, Great more by his deeds than by his name. Fearing that, amid the great turmoil of the wars by which Africa was shaken, the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline might suffer some loss, he judged that the peace which, as we said above, had been confirmed between the emperor and Genseric provided a suitable opportunity for sending a legate to those regions, who would act in his place and attend to all their affairs.

We learn from his letter to the bishops established throughout Mauritania Caesariensis—numbered 87 in earlier editions, but the very first in the Quesnel edition—that Potentius was chosen by the blessed pontiff for this task and sent to Africa. In that letter the most vigilant pontiff rebukes the bishops of Mauritania because, whether made too lenient by the disturbances of the times, the presumptuous ambitions of aspiring men, or popular uprisings, they had elevated certain unworthy persons to the pastoral dignity. He ordered them to be removed from office, while nevertheless preserving the moderation demanded by the necessity of that most difficult time.

In the same place he prescribes what should be done with the servants of God who had lost the integrity of their chastity amid barbarian oppression.

Some African bishops were present at the Council of Chalcedon, held against Eutyches during this period of tranquillity in the year 451. Among them were Valerianus of Bassiana and another Bassianus, an African; they subscribed the sixteenth session. Aurelius, bishop of Hadrumetum, and Rusticianus, an African bishop, had already been mentioned in the sixth session.

5. Thus, in the other part of Africa, those who worshipped the true faith and had remained under Valentinian’s rule were able to breathe somewhat more freely. Those who were subject to Genseric’s power, however, suffered every extreme, so that they could scarcely breathe safely at all, as Victor of Vita recounts more fully in Book I, no. 7.

The tyrant was no less savage toward his own people when he learned that certain nobles among them had plotted against his life. Indeed, to forestall the attempts of others, whom he suspected would be inclined to venture the same thing when an opportunity arose, he ordered many to be tortured with various punishments and killed. “The king’s suspicion,” says Prosper under the year 442, when Dioscorus and Eudoxius were consuls, “brought such ruin upon so many that through this concern for himself he lost more strength than if he had been defeated in war.”

6. Nevertheless, the name of Valentinian Augustus had some influence with the barbarian king. At Valentinian’s supplication, as Victor of Vita says in Book I, no. 8, the tyrant permitted a bishop to be ordained for the Church of Carthage after a long period of desolation and silence—about thirteen years, namely, after Quodvultdeus had been driven into exile, placed on an old ship.

Deogratias, a most holy man, was raised to this dignity. Victor, in the work cited, no. 8, praises his outstanding virtues, especially his supreme charity toward those who had been carried captive from the city of Rome into Africa. The author of a chronicle, which Canisius published from an Augsburg manuscript under the name of the younger Prosper in Volume I of *Antiquae Lectiones*, recorded the day and year of his inauguration, and even the place itself. It reads:

> During the consulship of Aetius and Studius—that is, according to our customary method of reckoning, in the year 454—Deogratias was ordained bishop at Carthage, in the basilica of Faustus, on Sunday, the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 0383A]

Victor, whose testimony has been cited, writes that Deogratias presided over the Church of Carthage for three years, and from this we infer that his death occurred around the year 457. As we said in note 27 on Victor (above, col. 191, n. b), the Roman Martyrology celebrates his feast on 22 March. In the Carthaginian calendar, however, which was written shortly after his death, the deposition of this blessed bishop is recorded on the Nones of January.

7. Such was the state of affairs in Africa when, during the consulship of Aetius and Studius—that is, in the year 454—Valentinian, driven by the secret schemes of Maximus, whose wife he himself had violated, killed Aetius under the pretext of suppressing a revolutionary movement.

Prosper wrote in his Chronicle, on the basis of common report, that Augustus committed this crime at the instigation of the eunuch Heraclius. But Maximus made use of Heraclius’ services, as can be gathered from Count Marcellinus. After Aetius had been removed, Maximus, believing that no one would oppose him, killed Valentinian himself in the following year. He immediately seized not only the imperial power but also, after his own wife had died, as Procopius reports, compelled Eudoxia, Valentinian’s widow, to marry him against her will.

From this arose the ruin of the Roman state and the disaster of the city itself. For when Maximus had once recounted to Eudoxia the whole sequence of events and confessed that Valentinian had been killed through his agency, because, as he said, he desired to marry her, she was inflamed with anger—although she tried to conceal it—and resolved to avenge her husband’s death, which some suspected had been arranged by her herself, by whatever means she could.

Then, unable to tolerate delay, she immediately sent a message to Genseric at Carthage, begging the barbarian not to permit the treacherous murderer of Valentinian, the best of emperors, whom he had had as a friend while alive, to enjoy the murder with impunity. Under Maximus’s tyranny she too was groaning together with the entire empire. She promised to reveal everything to Genseric if he was willing to help her in this desperate situation.

8. Genseric readily lent an ear to Eudoxia’s plans. He was a man avaricious beyond measure, as was the fault of both himself and his entire nation. Seizing with both hands, as they say, the opportunity to plunder Italy and the city itself, he assembled the forces which he was accustomed to maintain for piracy and sudden expeditions. Having quickly prepared a huge fleet, he crossed into Italy.

He immediately set out for Rome and, finding no one there to resist him, took possession of both the city and the palace. Maximus, who had taken flight upon hearing the report of the barbarians’ arrival, had already been killed by the populace and the imperial officials, and torn to pieces.

[Col. 0383D]

No one can express in words how shameful the condition of the Senate and Roman people then was, although Prosper writes that Genseric, moved by the prayers of Pope Leo, refrained from fires and massacres. He lamented this immense disaster in the following words, under the year 455 of the common era, which he dated by the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius:

> When this parricide—that is, the murder of Valentinian Augustus—had been committed, Maximus, a man of two consulships and patrician rank, seized power . . . . He forbade the Augusta to mourn the loss of her husband and compelled her, within a very few days, to enter into his marriage. But he did not long enjoy this incontinence. For after two months, when the arrival of King Genseric from Africa had been announced and many nobles and common people were fleeing from the city, he too, when he had granted everyone permission to depart, wished to leave in panic, but was torn apart by the royal servants [the Canisius edition adds: “perhaps the queen’s”], thrown limb by limb into the Tiber, and deprived even of burial.

After Maximus’s death, the Roman captivity, worthy of many tears, followed immediately. Genseric took possession of the city, empty of every defense. Outside the gates, holy Bishop Leo met him; and his supplication, through God’s agency, so softened Genseric that, although everything was in his power and the city had been handed over to him, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and punishments.

For fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its wealth through unrestricted and secure searching. Many thousands of captives, selected according to whatever age or skill each possessed, were carried off to Carthage together with the empress and her daughters.

This is Prosper’s account. Since the other authors who wrote about the same Roman disaster agree with him, it would be superfluous to reproduce their words. Sidonius Apollinaris, in Book II, Letter 13, mourns the unhappy fate of Petronius Maximus, who could not endure being master when previously he had not endured being under a master.

9. Evagrius, however, writes in Book II, chapter 7 of his *History* that Rome was set on fire by Genseric. Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, asserts that Genseric loaded gold, silver, and the other imperial treasures onto ships and carried them back to Carthage. According to common report, one ship laden with statues was lost in a shipwreck.

Finally, the same author asserts that nothing of any value in the imperial palace remained untouched by the barbarian: “He had left behind not even bronze,” he says, “or anything else from which a price could be obtained.” He also plundered the Capitol, the temple of Jupiter, and removed half of the roof tiles. These, made of the purest bronze and lavishly covered with gold, presented a magnificent and truly wondrous appearance.

Among these spoils, we learn from the same author in Book II, were the objects that Titus Vespasian had once brought to Rome after capturing Jerusalem. In the following century, the emperor Justinian, after recovering Carthage, restored them to Jerusalem. Justinian himself, in his constitution concerning the office of the praetorian prefect of Africa, also lists among the things captured by Genseric at Rome and carried into Africa the imperial ornaments, which likewise, after the capture of Gelimer, were brought to Constantinople.

10. A tradition accepted by popular authors, especially those of a later age, holds that Genseric spared Rome’s three principal basilicas; they attribute this clemency to the prayers and admonitions of Pope Leo. The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* even adds that the vessels consecrated by the emperor Constantine in various sacred places of Rome, and transferred to the three basilicas just mentioned, escaped the common disaster. With them, the most holy pontiff restored the other churches that had been plundered and damaged by the hands of the barbarians.

Certainly, the holy Leo himself, in Sermon 81, entitled “On the Octave of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul,” testifies that a public festival had been established at Rome because the city had been freed from the barbarians. In that sermon the holy pontiff complains that this celebration—at which previously, as he says, the entire body of the faithful used to gather to give thanks to God for “the day of our chastisement and liberation”—had been so neglected in the year in which he delivered the sermon that scarcely anyone had assembled for it.

[Col. 0384D]

Against Baronius, who believes that in this passage Leo the Great was speaking about Attila’s invasion, Quesnel proves from the context of the entire sermon that it must altogether be understood of the sack of Rome under Genseric.

Leo attributes this liberation of the city not only to the ineffable mercy of almighty God, who deigned to calm the hearts of the raging barbarians, but also to the care of the saints, which restored the city to safety, rescued it from captivity, and defended it from slaughter. These words correspond less appropriately to Attila’s invasion but very well to Genseric’s attack.

The chronological circumstance designated by Saint Leo also supports this interpretation. Since he complained on the eighth day of the apostles’ festival about the neglect of the commemoration of the liberated city, it is clear that this commemoration was customarily celebrated at Rome around that time. It can be inferred that the city had been freed from Genseric’s tyranny at precisely this time because Maximus was killed on the day before the Ides of June, and Genseric invaded Rome on the third day thereafter. After plundering and stripping it for fourteen days, as we have said from Prosper, he finally departed to cross into Africa.
