Nor is it an obstacle that in this sermon the most holy pontiff says the Romans were more devoted to circus games—which were certainly not held in June—than to the worship of the saints. His words do not entail that games of this kind were being celebrated at the very time when he was speaking.

11. After returning to Carthage, Genseric gave the younger Eudoxia in marriage to his son Huneric. He sent Placidia, her sister, who had been betrothed to Olybrius, together with their mother, the Augusta Eudoxia, to Constantinople, to the emperor Leo, as Procopius, so often cited, relates.

Evagrius, however, writes in Book II, chapter 7, that Genseric returned them to Marcian, in order to appease him, since he was inflamed with anger both because of the burning of the city and because the Augustas had suffered such an insult. The author of the Alexandrian or Paschal Chronicle agrees with Procopius; under the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VIII and Anthemius, he reports that these imperial women were ransomed from Genseric’s captivity by the emperor Leo.

But Marcian was still alive at that time. Idatius writes in his Chronicle that Eudoxia was sent back to Constantinople in the sixth year of the emperor Leo, after she had been detained in Africa by Genseric for several years.

This variety of opinions can nevertheless be reconciled as follows: Marcian, enraged by the great injury inflicted upon the imperial family, may have promised to release the Augustas, although he did not carry out the promise until several years later, after Marcian’s death. Certainly, above, in chapter 4, no. 8, we observed from Theodorus the Reader that Marcian prepared an army against the Vandals, although his efforts were frustrated by his intervening death.

Meanwhile, as the same Procopius testifies, Genseric, in order to secure Africa against attacks by the Romans, stripped all its fortified cities and towns, except Carthage, entirely of their walls. His purpose was not only to deprive Africans who might wish to attempt some new enterprise of a place of refuge, but also to ensure that those who might perhaps be sent by the emperors would have no hope of attempting anything against the Vandals.

12. His persecution of human beings, however, was more severe than his treatment of city walls. For, as the same author continues, those whom he knew to be distinguished by reputation or wealth he handed over, together with their estates and all their money, like slaves, to his sons Honoric and Genso . . . [lacuna] . . . He deprived other Africans of very many excellent estates . . . [lacuna] . . . Their former owners, free men indeed but oppressed by poverty, were permitted to depart wherever they wished . . . [lacuna] . . . He left inferior lands to their former owners, but under so heavy a tax that nothing came back to them from their own property.

“Hence,” he says, “it happened that many fled, and many were also killed on various charges, the most common being that they were said to be concealing money. Thus all Africa was caught up in the gravest calamities.”

Victor of Vita describes this persecution more fully in Book I, from no. 9 to the end of the book. There he also relates the sufferings of certain martyrs who achieved glory by completing their martyrdom in various provinces. But these matters must be taken from Victor himself; see above, p. 8 (col. 193) and following.

13. Genseric was no less savage outside Africa, as the same author testifies. In the work cited, no. 17, he lists thirteen provinces in which that most cruel tyrant unleashed a bitter persecution.

“What he did,” he says, “in Spain, Italy, Dalmatia, Campania, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, Sardinia, the Bruttians, Venetia, Lucania, Old Epirus, or Greece, those who suffered there will better recount in lamentation and misery.”

The savagery of the barbarian king did not confine itself within the borders of Africa. Every year, engaging in piracy, he ravaged Sicily, Italy, and the other provinces of the Romans which he knew to be deprived of defense because the empire had grown weak.

Sidonius Apollinaris complains of this in Poem 2, his panegyric for the emperor Anthemius, in these verses:

> From here the Vandal enemy  
> Presses on, and every year, with a numerous fleet,  
> Wages war for our destruction; and, with the order of fate reversed,  
> Burning Byrsa brings upon me Caucasian furies.

14. We have a particularly clear witness to the same matter in Procopius. In Book I of *The Vandalic War* he reports that such incursions became more frequent after Valentinian’s death, when the Moors, in addition to the Alans, joined the Vandals in these expeditions.

“Made stronger by the aid of the Moors,” says Procopius, “after Valentinian had died, whenever spring returned Genseric ravaged and afflicted now Sicily, now Italy. Some towns he reduced to servitude; others he demolished; others he completely emptied through plunder. At last, driven away from there by the devastation of the places and the scarcity of resources, he turned toward the lands subject to the emperor of the East, and invaded all Illyricum and the Peloponnese, the islands adjoining them, and other territories bearing the Greek name. From there, returning again to Italy and Sicily, he plundered whatever had recently been left behind.”

The previously cited Sidonius Apollinaris certainly records that the Moors, mixed together with the Vandals, invaded Italy. In Poem 5, he congratulates the emperor Majorian on the victory won over these barbarian peoples:

> . . . [lacuna] . . . with the south winds blowing across Campania,  
> Entering Campanian land, he attacks the farmer,  
> Secure with a Moorish soldier. The fat Vandal sat across the benches,  
> Awaiting the prey which he had ordered to be dragged there  
> By a captive captor; but suddenly your troops  
> Had thrown themselves into the open ground between the two enemies.

On this occasion, the same author describes a great defeat inflicted upon the Vandals: their barbarian army was completely scattered and routed, and its commander had been the husband of Genseric’s sister.

Idatius also records in his Chronicle a great victory won against the Vandals under Avitus. He asserts that a large number of them were surrounded and killed by Ricimer, after they had set out with sixty ships toward Gaul or Italy. [Col. 0386C] He testifies in the following entry that this occurred on the island of Corsica.

15. “Majorian,” says Procopius, “surpassing in courage all who had previously ruled the Romans, could never endure the loss of Africa lightly, and was prepared to dare everything in order to restore this part of the world to Roman rule.”

With this purpose, it is said, he crossed into Africa in disguise, intending to investigate Genseric’s strength and other circumstances personally before undertaking the war. According to the Chronicle of Idatius, he also arranged for several ships to be prepared in Spain for the crossing and was already hastening to send them immediately to Africa. But the Vandals, having been warned by traitors, seized them. Thus the emperor returned to Italy without accomplishing his purpose.

Cassiodorus reports that this occurred during the consulship of the two Augusti, Leo and Majorian—that is, in the year 458 of Christ.

Although Majorian had been struck by so great a loss to his fleet, he was not at all deterred from the undertaking. He never abandoned his plan of recovering Africa, while the Romans hoped for this very thing from the emperor’s courage. Genseric, on the contrary, did everything possible to obtain peace from him. Idatius observes that shortly after the ships mentioned above had been seized, Genseric requested peace from the emperor through ambassadors.

But while Majorian was wholly occupied with this expedition, he was suddenly consumed by a disease of the bowels, says Procopius, “a man moderate toward his subjects and terrifying to his enemies.” Latin authors, however, report that he was killed by Ricimer. Their authority ought to carry greater weight in this matter, as Papirius Massonus says in his *History of the Calamities of Gaul*.

Indeed, in addition to the proximity of the places, the circumstances of the times support them. Idatius, who expressly records the event, as well as Ennodius of Ticinum and Cassiodorus, were living at the same time as Majorian. Count Marcellinus and Marius of Aventicum, or Lausanne, indicate the place in their Chronicles, as does Jordanes in Book 45 of *On the Getic Affairs*, where they testify that Majorian’s death occurred at Dertona, on the river Ira.

The fact that this death was brought about by Genseric’s schemes seems to me highly probable from the very wickedness of the man, who dared far more through fraudulent machinations than through military valor or greatness of spirit.

After Majorian’s death—which occurred during the consulship of Dagalaiphus and Severinus, that is, in the year 461 of the common era—the state gradually moving toward destruction, his successors undertook nothing against the Vandals. Procopius admits that these successors were scarcely known even by name to the Vandals: “For,” he says, “their rule was neither long-lasting nor distinguished by notable deeds.”

16. Since Genseric therefore no longer had anyone who resisted him, he ravaged the provinces of the Roman Empire with impunity. Sidonius calls him a pirate and robber; in the passages cited above he has much to say about the Vandals’ depredations.

The terror of Genseric and the Vandal name was so great that no province of the empire believed itself safe from his attacks. The author of the *Life of Saint Daniel the Stylite*, chapter 33, printed by Surius under 11 December, relates that at that time a report had spread throughout all the provinces of the empire that Genseric would shortly come with a huge fleet against the Romans, and that the prize of this war would be the city of Alexandria itself.

Procopius records of him an extraordinary statement: when that savage ruler had once put out from the harbor of Carthage, a sailor asked him where he wished to carry the war. He replied, “Against those with whom God is angry.” “Thus,” the same author adds, “he attacked anyone at all in a hostile manner, without any reason.”

For this reason King Theodoric, in Cassiodorus, Book I of the *Variae*, letter 4, calls the Vandals a sudden and savage enemy: without cause or any declaration of war, they attacked whatever provinces they pleased in order to ravage them.

17. Some authors attempt to refer to one of these annual barbarian excursions the famous act of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, which Gregory the Great relates in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 1.

There the most holy pontiff says that he had learned from the elders that blessed Paulinus, after completely exhausting all his possessions in ransoming captives and assisting the poor, was approached by a poor widow. She asked what price would be required to ransom her son, who had been captured by the Vandals while they were ravaging Campania and carried away into Africa. Since he had nothing left to give, Paulinus offered to exchange himself into slavery in place of the widow’s son.

But since all these deeds of Saint Paulinus, and the other matters related there, cannot at all be reconciled with the period we are discussing, another way of preserving the account must be sought.

Saint Augustine writes in Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 10, that Paulinus was afflicted by barbarians ravaging Campania. When they came to Nola, over which blessed Paulinus presided as bishop, they seized him and subjected him to various tortures in order to extract from him the place where he had hidden his wealth.

But since he had kept nothing at all for himself from the immense riches he had once possessed, he prayed to God, in the words Augustine reports in the passage cited:

> Lord, let me not be tortured for gold and silver; you know where all my possessions are.

Everyone agrees, however, that this occurred when the Goths, after capturing Rome under Alaric, had spread through the various provinces of Italy and devastated everything.

I would regard this history as having furnished the basis for the account related by Saint Gregory as an ancient tradition of the elders, were it not that many things reported there by the most holy pontiff concerning the Vandals dissuade me from that opinion.

Baronius indeed maintains that Paulinus was actually carried away into Africa under Guntharis, Genseric’s brother, in the year 431. But, as we said above, this same king was killed in Spain before the Vandals crossed into Africa.

Chiffletius discusses Paulinus’s captivity at length in his book entitled *Paulinus Illustratus*; Peraldus does so in the preface to his French poem about the same Saint Paulinus; and the author who prepared a new edition of the works of this holy man in Paris in 1685 treats it as well. If you have the opportunity, consult these and the other writers who have discussed this controversy more fully.

18. In his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under 25 May, Ferrarius praises Sentius—or Sensius, or, as others write, Senzia—whom he reports to have been carried into Africa with the priest Mammilianus and three monks, Covuldeus, Istochius, and Infans, when Genseric was ravaging Campania in Italy.

But nothing certain is known about these saints, as can be seen from what Godefridus Henschenius observed under 25 May. There he publishes the acts of the same Saint Sentius, but they possess no authority.

This alone is certain: Sentius is venerated at Blera, commonly called Bieda, in Etruria, as the principal patron of the place. His sacred relics, however, are honored at Spoleto in the church of nuns of the Order of Servants, with a great concourse of people.

19. For some time it seemed plausible to me that the martyrdom of Majorian, who was the slave of a certain nobleman of Tibur, had occurred during the same period as Genseric. Yet Peter Equilinus, bishop, says in the *Catalogue*, Book IX, chapter 104, and Ferrarius in the *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under 24 October, that he was seized in the Vandal persecution under King Huneric.

Huneric, however, never possessed any authority at Tibur. Those authors report various tortures which the barbarians inflicted upon him. First, they say, he was long beaten with clubs; then he was repeatedly raised high by pulleys and swiftly lowered again, so that he fell upon sharp stones. Next, his wounds were rubbed with stones until his entrails were exposed and spilled out.

In these tortures he yielded nothing of his steadfastness. Indeed, when he appeared even more constant in confessing the Catholic faith, he was finally struck with a sword and completed his noble martyrdom on the ninth day before the Kalends of November. His body, buried there—that is, at Tibur—still remains.

So those authors relate. But while I was copying these words, it occurred to me that in those writers no one else is indicated here than Servus of Tuburbius Major in Africa, a martyr whom Victor of Vita explicitly praises as having suffered under Huneric at the beginning of Book V. If anyone compares their words with Victor’s text, he will easily understand that in reality they are referring to the same martyr. Because of the similarity between the names Tuburbius and Tibur, Ferrarius, carelessly following Peter, inserted him into his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*.

Cardinal Baronius acted more cautiously. Without making any mention anywhere of a martyr Majorian of Tibur, he celebrated this Servus, mentioned by Victor, on 7 December in the Roman Martyrology.

From this and similar cases, however, we can understand how such authors sometimes, on the basis of a slight conjecture, assign martyrs to places or times that do not belong to them, mixing truth with falsehood in order to make their conjectures appear more probable. Hence history becomes confused, and the deeds of martyrs—which otherwise would have been more authentic—lose their authority.

[Col. 0388D] **20.** It is also worthwhile to offer another example of this matter. For it belongs to our purpose to strive, insofar as we are able, to elucidate the deeds of the martyrs said to have suffered under the persecutions of the Vandals. The same Peter Equilinus, in book XI, chapter 59, of his *Catalogus sanctorum*, reports a summary of the life of Saint Habetdeus the martyr, whom he asserts to have been bishop of Luna. Hence Ughelli, in volume I of *Italia Sacra*, column 892, lists Habetdeus first among the bishops of that same Church. The Church of Sarzana, to which the episcopal see of Luna was transferred, celebrates his feast under that name every year on 17 February. On the same day Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, and the Bollandists likewise commemorate this saint, reporting the following about him, on Peter’s authority:

> Habetdeus, bishop of Luna and martyr, suffered martyrdom in Italy during the time of the Vandal persecution. While he resisted the Arian confession, he was first banished into exile. Then the Vandals recalled him and, having stopped his mouth, rebaptized him with water according to the custom of the Arians, thinking by this means to violate his conscience. But while he still resisted them more firmly, he was beheaded by them.

Ferrarius and the Bollandists labor in vain to identify this Habetdeus, whom they conjecture to have been one of those bishops who, during the Vandal persecution, fled or were driven from Africa and took refuge in Italy, and whom they suppose to have been killed by the Arians in Italy for defending the Catholic faith. For this man, as indeed seems certain to me, is none other than the bishop Habetdeus who, according to Victor of Vita, book V, no. 12, was banished to the city of Tamallum, rebaptized there by Antonius, and subjected to the same treatment that Peter Equilinus recounts concerning his martyr of Luna. Hence, without a doubt, Habetdeus of Luna found no place in the Roman Martyrology. [231]

From the same workshop of Peter came Victor, bishop of Carthage, whom that author, in book IV, chapter 70, of his *Catalogus sanctorum*, says flourished during the reign of the emperor Anastasius, [Col. 0389B] and to whom he attributes all the works that Gennadius records as having been written by Victor, bishop of Cartenna in Mauretania. Although nothing could be more disgraceful than this error, several later writers nevertheless inserted Victor of Carthage into their martyrologies on this basis. See the admonition concerning Victor of Vita, no. 7.

Finally, those are mistaken who think that the island of Lérins, together with the famous monastery of Saint Honoratus, was plundered by Genseric in those same Vandal incursions. Those who assert that the abbot Porcarius and countless monks of that island suffered martyrdom on that occasion are peddling fables. Anyone who wants arguments for refuting them should consult Baronius under the year 453, or at least Mabillon, volume III of the *Acts of the Saints of Our Benedictine Order*, pages 525–526. Let us now return our discourse to the point from which it digressed.

**21.** Emperor Leo, wearied by so many disasters that he received reports of Genseric’s daily infliction upon various provinces, [Col. 0389C] and wishing at last to apply a remedy to these calamities of the Empire, prepared immense forces against the Vandals, whom he decided to attack simultaneously by land and sea. Marcellianus, already patrician in the West, had completely driven them from the island of Sardinia; and Heraclius, the other commander, whom the emperor had sent from the imperial city to Tripoli in Africa, had already defeated the Vandals stationed there in battle and was leading his men directly toward Carthage, intending shortly to seize it. But through the negligence—or, as others prefer, the treachery—of Basiliscus, who commanded the emperor’s fleet of 1,100 ships, these splendid beginnings had the most disgraceful ending.

Greek authors report that the matter happened as follows. Basiliscus, brother of the empress Verina, notorious for his impiety and for the Eutychian heresy that he supported, secretly entered into an agreement with the generals Aspar and Ardaburius, men wholly devoted to the Arian sect, on these terms: Aspar and Ardaburius, who stood above the other commanders, would secure the imperial power for Basiliscus; once he had obtained it, he would repay them by allowing the Arians to propagate their own sect safely. Some add that the imperial power was promised to Basiliscus on the condition that he betray the imperial fleet to Genseric, whom Aspar and Ardaburius secretly favored as the most determined defender of the Arian sect. The more common opinion, however, was that Basiliscus did this after being corrupted by Genseric’s money, as Theodore the Lector plainly declares in book I of his *Excerpts from History*.

Whatever the truth may be concerning these various reports, everyone agrees on this one point: through Basiliscus’ fault the Roman fleet, already almost at the walls of Carthage, was lost. He had hesitated indecisively for too long, whether corrupted by Genseric’s money or deceived by his trickery. Otherwise, if he had proceeded directly to Carthage, he would undoubtedly have occupied it easily, since it was then entirely without Vandal defenses. Once the fleet had been scattered, Genseric—who shortly before had seemed utterly dispirited—attacked the soldiers of the Roman land army, who had been completely deprived of their hope of taking Carthage: some he killed by trickery, [Col. 0390A] while others he expelled from Africa by force, as Procopius recounts at greater length in book I of *The Vandalic War*. Thus Leo’s expedition came to nothing.

**22.** No more successful were the efforts of Anthemius, whom, as the same Procopius testifies, Leo had encouraged to assume the imperial power in the West so that he might employ him against the Vandals. Idatius, in his *Chronicle*, testifies that Anthemius’ first attempt against them, immediately after he had been elevated to the imperial office, was rendered useless by a change of plans and the untimeliness of the voyage. We learn from the same Idatius, however, that around this time the Vandals were routed and put to flight in Sicily under the command of Marcellinus. But this victory was later stained by the murder of Marcellinus, whom Count Marcellinus reports to have been killed by the Romans themselves while he was attempting to bring aid to those hastening toward Carthage. Cassiodorus writes that this happened in Sicily during the consulship of Anthemius II—that is, in the year 468.

Later, Anthemius himself was removed by Ricimer during the consulships of Festus and Marcianus—that is, in the year 472. Nor thereafter did the emperors of the West undertake anything further against the Vandals.

**23.** Genseric, elated by this, plundered Roman possessions even more than before, says Procopius. The same author writes that he took it badly that Anthemius, after Olybrius had been rejected, had been appointed by Leo to the imperial power in the West. Genseric had strongly and repeatedly recommended Olybrius because of the relationship he had with him through Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III and sister of Eudoxia, the wife of Huneric, who had married Olybrius, as we have already observed above.

Having suffered this rejection, Genseric began to rage more savagely against the provinces of the Empire, being otherwise always ready for plunder. The same author recounts a horrifying incident near the end of his first book. When this same tyrant, at some point desiring the Peloponnese, had landed at Taenarum and had been driven out after many of his men were killed, he shortly afterward came to Zacynthus. After killing many of those whom he found there and carrying five hundred of the leading citizens away into slavery, he set out from the shore. But when he was already in mid-Ionian Sea, he ordered the bodies of all these people to be cut into pieces and thrown into the sea. Procopius relates this as an example of Genseric’s cruelty.

Since Zeno, who at that time administered the Empire, could not prevent the continual incursions of so savage an enemy, he finally, says Procopius, came to terms with Genseric and established a perpetual treaty, so that the Vandals would never undertake anything hostile against the Romans, nor suffer anything of the kind from the Romans. This treaty, as the same author adds, continued until the time of Justinian. For Justinian, undertaking war against the Vandals, freed Africa from their domination.

Moreover, Cassiodorus praises Theodoric, king of the Goths in Italy, in his *Chronicle*, because, among his other splendid deeds for the benefit of the commonwealth, he freed Sicily from the Vandals’ continual depredations. We have another most trustworthy witness to this in Ennodius of Ticinum, bishop, in the panegyric that he delivered to the same King Theodoric, where he addresses him as follows:

> How shall I speak of the restrained depredations of the Vandals, who obey the winds, for whom your friendship is sufficient in place of an annual payment? They do not know how to wander beyond what is possible; under the guidance of wisdom they have deserved to be your neighbors, because they do not refuse to obey.

But this occurred long after Genseric’s death, namely in the year 491, during the consulship of Olybrius. Moreover, in consideration of the treaty that had been made, Genseric, when Zeno was petitioned through the patrician Severus, restored some measure of peace to the Church, as Victor writes in book I, no. 17. The church of Carthage was reopened, as the same author testifies—the church that Genseric had previously ordered to be closed after its presbyters and ministers had been scattered and dispersed among various places of exile. Thus they all returned from exile.

**233 — CHAPTER VII. Genseric Is Succeeded by Huneric; Under Him Many Martyrs and Confessors Flourished, Especially Those Who Spoke with Their Tongues Cut Out**

[Col. 0391A]

**1.** Shortly after making peace with the emperor Zeno, Genseric, after the devastation of many provinces and the plundering and slaughter of the Christian population in Africa, departed this life, says Victor of Tunnuna in his *Chronicle*. According to Procopius, this occurred in the thirty-seventh year after the capture of Carthage, namely in the fortieth year of his reign, during the consulship of Olybrius and Rusticus—that is, in the year 464 of the common era, as Victor of Tunnuna writes in the passage cited. But no one doubts that both authors departed from the truth, although Isidore followed the same error in his brief *History of the Vandals*, where he copied Victor’s words. He was also mistaken in thinking that the destruction of Rome and the captivity of the empresses occurred after the death of the emperor Majorian.

The truth of the matter should instead be drawn from the *History* of Victor of Vita, who at the end of book I testifies that Genseric remained in power for thirty-seven years and three months, after the capture of Carthage, as we have already observed from Procopius. Otherwise he would have died before Zeno was emperor, which no one has ever asserted. Since, by universal agreement, the destruction of Carthage occurred in October of the year 439, it is correctly inferred that Genseric died at the beginning of the year 477.

Furthermore, since in an old fragment appended to Prosper’s *Chronicle* in the Augustan manuscript published by Canisius in volume I of *Ancient Readings*, six days are added to the number stated above, and since it is certain from another source, as we said in chapter 5, no. 1, that Carthage was captured on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, the death of Genseric was rightly assigned by the most learned Henry Noris, in book II, chapter 21, of his *History of Pelagianism*, to 25 January 477.

**2.** Huneric, the eldest of Genseric’s sons, succeeded him. He was notorious for his cruelty toward the orthodox, especially toward the bishops of the Churches. This alone is the name by which he is known to the authors, since neither glorious deeds in war nor any expedition of great importance, as had happened with his father, made him distinguished. Procopius thus concludes his life in a brief summary in book I of *The Vandalic War*:

> This Huneric, he says, was the most savage and unjust of all who ever lived toward the Christians dwelling in Africa. For wishing to force them by violence into the doctrines of the Arians, he killed those whom he found resisting him by fire and other tortures. He also cut the tongues from the throats of many, who even in my time walked about in Byzantium, speaking perfectly and feeling none of their former punishment. Two of them, however, after they had mixed with women of prostituted modesty, ceased to speak. When he had completed eight years of rule, he was removed from human affairs by disease.

**3.** Other authors, including some older than Procopius, also celebrated those African confessors who spoke correctly after their tongues had been cut out. Among them were Victor, bishop of Vita, and Aeneas of Gaza, who flourished under the emperor Zeno. Victor’s words should be taken from book V, no. 6, of his history, [Col. 0391D] where he testifies that, at the very time when he was writing, one of those confessors, named Reparatus, a subdeacon, was still alive. Because of this miracle, the empress held him in the highest veneration while he lived at Zeno’s palace. For the other things this author says about the matter, see above, page 43 (for us, column 249).

The testimony of Aeneas is no less authoritative. Victor reports what had happened in Africa; Aeneas, however, committed to writing what he knew well from Constantinople, in his book *On the Immortality of the Soul and the Resurrection of Bodies*, specifically in the dialogue entitled *Theophrastus*. After prefacing certain remarks about Greater Libya—for that is what the Greeks called Africa—which he says was suffering under a harsh tyranny, he adds the following:

> The tyrant considers the piety of those subject to his rule a crime, and orders the priests to deny that doctrine so glorious and good. To those who do not obey, alas for the crime, he cuts out the tongue dear to God . . . But they implore the Creator of nature himself, who on the third day afterward grants them a newer nature—not by giving them another tongue, but by granting them the power to speak articulately, with a faculty of expression greater than they had ever possessed before.

This author says that he did not learn of so great a miracle through ordinary rumor or through the report of some other person. Rather, he testifies that he had investigated the matter himself with the greatest care, so that no room for doubt—or even suspicion—might remain:

> I myself saw those men, and heard them speaking, and marveled that a voice could be so articulate. I examined the instrument of the voice, and, not trusting my ears, entrusted judgment to my eyes. With their mouths open, I saw that their entire tongues had been torn out by the roots; and, astonished, I wondered—not, to be sure, how they formed their voices, but how they had survived. Medical science declares, and nature also bears witness, that cutting the tongue is the killing of the person from whom it is cut.

Eusebius gives the same testimony in connection with Saint Romanus, as we observed in our *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, page 381. Perhaps Aeneas learned from this passage of Eusebius the medical opinion that he cites.

Moreover, Aeneas, a follower of Platonic philosophy, drew from the miracle of these confessors an argument to prove the future resurrection of bodies. He also testified that from this event he had learned that God is so completely Lord of all nature that we should regard nothing among visible things as firm or fixed if God should wish to move it from its place.

**4.** Marcellinus Comes relates in his *Chronicle* a still more astonishing event: a Catholic boy who had previously been mute spoke correctly after his tongue had been cut out. It will be useful to reproduce the author’s entire passage, since he touches briefly upon this African persecution and records events that he himself witnessed:

> Indiction VII, during the consulship of Theodoric and Venantius—that is, in the year 484 of the Christian era—the cruel persecution of Huneric, king of the Vandals, was brought upon our Catholics throughout Africa. For, after more than 334 orthodox bishops had been driven into exile and scattered, and their churches had been closed, the faithful people, subjected to various torments, completed their blessed contest. At that time the same King Huneric ordered the tongue of a single Catholic youth, who from birth had lived without any speech, to be cut out. Yet the same mute youth, having learned by faith to believe in Christ without human hearing, immediately spoke after his tongue had been cut out and gave glory to God at the very beginning of his speech. Finally, from this company of the faithful I myself saw several most devout men at Byzantium, with their tongues cut out and their hands amputated, speaking in an unimpaired voice.

> This cruelty of the Arians toward the devout worshipers of Christ began to be inflicted during the consulship mentioned above, in the month of February. For the council of Carthage had been summoned for the Kalends of February, and from this the tyrant took the opportunity to afflict the orthodox bishops more severely.

**5.** Finally, Gregory the Great must be added to the witnesses of so great a miracle. [235] Although he relates only what he had learned from others, his authority should not be rejected. In book III, chapter 32, of his *Dialogues*, he reports that, while staying at Constantinople, he became acquainted with an elderly bishop who testified that he had once seen several of those African bishops who spoke without tongues. One of them, having fallen into carnal sin, was immediately deprived of this gift.

Gregory writes, however, that these bishops suffered this punishment during the African persecution raised by the king of the Vandals in the time of the emperor Justinian. Some think that this was said by Saint Gregory through a lapse of memory. Indeed, Procopius writes that some of the earlier sufferers, whom it is certain had suffered in the time of Huneric, survived into his own age—that is, the reign of Justinian—as we said above.

The emperor Justinian himself, in the constitution *On the Office of the Prefect of Africa*, book I of the *Code of Justinian*, title 27, testifies that he saw these venerable men, who, with their tongues cut out by the roots, miserably spoke of their sufferings. Evagrius praises this constitution of the emperor Justinian in book IV, chapter 14, where he inserted into his own *History* the very things that we reported above from Procopius concerning these holy men.

**6.** Victor of Tunnuna writes in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of the emperor Zeno, that these same confessors were buried at Constantinople. He says that “the royal city bears witness that they spoke perfectly to the very end with their tongues cut out, and that their bodies lie there.” Near the end of his *Chronicle*, the same author also testifies that Theodore of Cabarsus, an African bishop who had been sent into exile with him on account of the Three Chapters and who was then living in the imperial city, was buried after his death beside the confessors whose tongues Huneric, king of the Vandals, had cut out.

The Greeks celebrate the memory of those confessors—said to have numbered sixty—both in the *Menologion* and in the great *Menaia*, as they call them, where they are called **λογώβατοι** (“tongue-cut”).

In the *Menologion* that Canisius included, from Cardinal Sirlet’s translation, in volume II of *Ancient Readings*, several are commemorated together: some were killed near Carthage, while others, their tongues cut out, were sent into exile under King Huneric. The event is narrated there as follows:

> On the same day, namely 7 December, three hundred holy martyrs in Africa were brought to completion by the sword, under the emperor Zeno and Huneric, the Arian king. They were beheaded near the city of Carthage because of their confession of the orthodox faith, since they refused to agree with the Arians. Devising still greater punishments for the priests, they burned two of them, while they cut out the tongues of sixty who were more eloquent. Scattered throughout the entire Roman world, these men proclaimed, even without tongues, the supreme power of God in working miracles. They uttered distinct and clear articulated words, so that those who saw and heard these things were astonished. One of their number, after the grace of confessing Christ, fell into carnal sin and caused divine grace to depart from him.

**7.** Although ancient authors particularly praise, among the confessors who spoke fluently after their tongues had been cut out, the bishops who endured this monstrous punishment—so much so that scarcely any mention is made of the others—we think this happened either because these men were more conspicuous on account of their dignity, or because, after being dispersed through various provinces of the Roman Empire, they became better known than the rest, especially in the imperial city, where most of them lived. Nevertheless, it seems beyond doubt that many others, of both sexes, also suffered this punishment.

We have an unimpeachable witness to this in Victor of Vita, who, in book V, no. 6, reports that most of the citizens of the city of Tipasa fled to Spain when they learned that an Arian bishop had been appointed to their city. As for the rest who remained, because they had celebrated the divine mysteries according to Catholic practice, both their tongues and their right hands were cut off.

> When this had been done, he says, those most holy confessors, through the power of the Holy Spirit, spoke and speak in such a way as they had spoken before.

**8.** There were also many other confessors who either completed their martyrdom in Africa or were made exiles from their homeland, whether voluntarily or through the violence of their persecutors, and were compelled to wander through various regions of the world without fixed homes. It is certain, moreover, that many others, enslaved in harsh captivity in Africa itself, entered upon a glorious contest in defense of the divinity of Christ, as may be gathered from various passages of Victor’s *History*.

In chapter 4 of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, the bishop Faustus is praised. Because of his confession of the Catholic faith, he had been banished not far from his own see and had built a monastery at the very place of his exile. On this occasion the same author of Fulgentius’ *Life* observes that many other bishops of Africa had at that time been punished by a similar exile. The Arian persecutors believed that in this way they could more easily harass those holy bishops with various hardships and induce them to deny God; otherwise, it would have been extremely difficult if they migrated beyond the borders of Africa and lived among Catholics.

> For the cunning wickedness of Huneric, that tyrannical persecutor, had arranged this concerning many priests: that, while suffering the hardship of exile near their own homeland, they might easily be bent to deny God.

That these holy men were by no means secure from the harassment of the heretics during their exiles is shown by the same author. Later, in chapter 8, he adds that, when the persecution grew fierce again, Faustus moved from place to place and hid in various retreats so that he would not be exposed to the attacks of the barbarians. It is therefore not surprising if many preferred to lead a quiet and impoverished life among foreigners rather than endure so many calamities in their homeland.

Among these men was undoubtedly Rufinianus, bishop of the province of Byzacena. Saint Fulgentius visited him, after he had escaped from the African persecution by flight, while he was living the monastic life on an island near Sicily, as we learn from the *Life of Fulgentius*, chapter 13.

**9.** The evidence already presented sufficiently proves that the persecution stirred up by Huneric was exceedingly bitter; the same is clear from other authors who wrote on this subject. Isidore of Seville speaks of it as follows in his brief *History of the Vandals*:

> Huneric, stirred up by Arian fury, persecutes the Catholics throughout Africa more savagely than his father. He abolishes the churches, sends the priests and all clergy of the sacred order into exile, and banishes about four thousand monks and laypeople to harsher exiles. He makes martyrs and cuts out the tongues of confessors, who, with their tongues cut out, spoke perfectly to the very end.

Victor of Tunnuna, older than Isidore, mentions the same persecution in two places in his *Chronicle*. But he confuses the order of events, recalling it the first time to the third consulship of Leo Augustus—that is, to the year 467 of the common era, more than a decade before Huneric succeeded his father. There, nevertheless, after writing that Huneric, stirred up by Arian fury, persecuted the Catholics more severely than his father, he adds:

> He abolishes the churches of the Christians and sends the priests into exile.

Several years later, he recounts that the same persecution, now fully raging, attacked the other orthodox as well. We have thought it worthwhile to reproduce his words, since they list places to which the holy confessors were banished—places otherwise unknown to us. He writes as follows:

> During the consulship of Zeno Augustus, that is, in the year of Christ 479—for here Victor is dealing with the third consulship of Zeno Augustus—Huneric, king of the Vandals, pressing the persecution throughout Africa with excessive violence, banishes to harsher exiles the Catholics of Tibunnis, Macri, and [otherwise, Nippii] Nippis, and of other regions of the desert. He banishes not only the priests and clergy of every order, but also monks and laypeople, about four thousand in number, and makes confessors and martyrs. He also cuts out the tongues of the confessors, and so forth.

> At that time Laetus, bishop of the Church of Nepta, was crowned with glorious martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and Eugenius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, after dreadful exiles in the desert, was renowned for very many afflictions and punishments.

He concludes all these events with the infamous end of Huneric the persecutor. Amid the countless massacres arising from his impieties, which he inflicted upon the Catholics, Huneric, in the eighth year of his reign, ended his life, as Isidore, cited above, says, with all his internal organs pouring out—just as his father Arius had miserably ended his life. Isidore copied these words from this passage of Victor.

Moreover, the fragment appended to the *Chronicle of Tyro*, which we have already cited more than once from Canisius’ edition, assigns Huneric’s persecution to the seventh year of his reign in the following words:

> At the end of the seventh year of his reign he persecuted the Catholic Church, closed all the churches, and sent all the priests of the Lord, together with Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, into exile. He ended his life, swarming with worms by God’s judgment.

**10.** The entire course of the persecution stirred up by Huneric must, however, be reconstructed from the *History* of Victor of Vita. He carefully observed and accurately described both its beginning and its successive developments.

It began shortly after the ordination of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, which took place in the year 481, as we shall say in the following chapter. For, as the cited author narrates in book II, no. 3, when Eugenius’ fame was celebrated everywhere, the Arian bishops suggested to the tyrant that he should not allow the blessed bishop to address the people and should demand other things from him that were contrary to our religion.

> From this, he says, Huneric’s persecution took its beginning of grief and travail.

Later he decreed that no one might serve in the palace or perform public functions unless he had made himself an Arian. Then he banished to Sicily and Sardinia those who had abandoned military service on that account, as stated in no. 7. In the same passage Victor describes the insults inflicted upon consecrated virgins and other acts by which the tyrant sought to find a path through which he could make the persecution public.

In the following section, through no. 13, he admirably describes the journey of almost innumerable confessors who were deported into exile at the tyrant’s command. But these were only the preludes to a greater persecution. For, says Victor in no. 13:

> Huneric was contemplating harsher measures against the Church of God, so that, having cut off some of its limbs, he might destroy the whole body by tearing it apart.

For this reason he summoned all the bishops of Africa to Carthage for a conference concerning the Catholic and Arian faiths to be held the following year. The edict was issued in May of the seventh year of Huneric, which corresponds to the year 483 of the common era.

**11.** In the year 484, therefore, Eugenius, together with the other defenders of the orthodox faith, came on the appointed day to confer with the Arians. But the tyrant, who in his edict had promised the Catholics complete security, immediately violated his pledge by laying hands upon those who had come in good faith. He then raged especially against the most learned, killing some of them. Among these was the famous Laetus, who on this occasion completed his martyrdom in a blessed contest, as stated in no. 18.

Victor also lists others, in no. 16, whom Huneric had previously ordered to be beaten with clubs and thrust into exile. Yet the Catholic bishops were not broken in spirit by these injuries. Those who remained alive assembled at the appointed place, prepared to hold a conference concerning matters of faith.

When the Arians could not endure this, they provoked a disturbance and subjected the Catholics to various accusations. Then, says Victor:

> All the sons of the Catholic Church who were present were ordered to be beaten with hundreds of clubs.

The orthodox therefore realized that they would accomplish nothing by words and produced the statement of faith that they had written earlier. Thus the conference ended. For the Arians, ashamed that they had been defeated and who in turn should have produced their own confession of faith, shouted that the **ὁμοούσιοι** (“Homoousians,” as they called the Catholics) were seditious and insolent. They so persuaded Huneric of this that from then onward he was always most hostile toward the orthodox.

The tyrant therefore ordered the Catholic churches to be closed throughout Africa and commanded that their property and that of their bishops be assigned to his own people. He issued an edict against the orthodox containing whatever statutes Catholic emperors of various periods had enacted against heretics. Victor reproduces the entire edict in book IV.

Not content with this, Huneric ordered all the bishops who had assembled at Carthage to be driven into exile. They were immediately stripped of their possessions in the lodgings where they were staying and expelled beyond the walls, since the most severe penalties had forbidden anyone to receive them into his house or provide food to any of them, as the same Victor relates in book IV, no. 3.

**12.** The cited author explicitly writes in book V that a general persecution had been stirred up by Huneric in Africa even before the bishops were expelled. In no. 1 he reports that, throughout all the provinces of the African land, the most savage torturers had been dispatched at one time . . . so that no age and no sex would be spared except those who submitted to their will.

He recalls that some were beaten with clubs, others suspended, and still others tortured by fire. He then describes the various contests of the holy martyrs in different provinces, which should be sought from no. 2 through no. 15. He also testifies that, during the same period, many who fled the violence of the heretics were killed in deserts and caves by hunger or cold.

But shortly afterward the tyrant died in his sin, when the sun had recoiled from such cruelty, to use the words of Gregory of Tours. Concerning this eclipse that the sun suffered at that time, one should consult the most learned Henry Noris, book II, chapter 21, of his *History of Pelagianism*, especially for the corrections found at the end of the work.

**13.** We learn from Evagrius that Pope Felix sympathized with the enormous calamities of the African Church. In book III, chapter 20, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Evagrius praises a letter of Pope Felix to the emperor Zeno in which he reminded him of the persecution that Huneric had stirred up in Africa.

Those papal letters have been lost. We may nevertheless infer that the emperor complied with them from the fact that Uranius, Zeno’s ambassador to Huneric, boasts before Victor, book V, no. 7, that he had come to Carthage in defense of the Catholic churches.

But how much this embassy accomplished with Huneric must be learned from the same Victor. For, he says:

> To show him that the tyrant feared no one, he stationed several torturers, and the most savage ones, in those streets and alleys through which ambassadors customarily pass as they ascend to and descend from the palace, plainly as an insult to the commonwealth itself, [Col. 0396B] and so forth.

**CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Saint Eugenius, Bishop of Carthage, and Several Other Confessors and Martyrs Who Were Harassed under Huneric’s Persecution.**
1. Although much material concerning the blessed Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, is found in Victor of Vita’s *History*, it nevertheless seemed worthwhile to treat him separately, because many things—some of no slight importance—occur here and there in other authors concerning his deeds, and these cannot be omitted. So great, indeed, was the reputation of this most holy confessor among everyone that one finds few authors of that age who did not celebrate him in their writings.

Among others, Gregory of Tours, the bishop, deserves praise on this account. At the beginning of Book II of his *History of the Franks*, he observes that already in his own time accounts of the sufferings of the African martyrs or confessors who had distinguished themselves in the Vandal persecution had been written. He testifies that he had read several of them, and from these he extracted certain things for incorporation into his own *History* [Col. 0396C]. Yet in this matter he would have served posterity better if, not content with excerpts, he had entrusted such precious records to writing in their entirety. For it can be established from this alone that he had seen something besides Victor of Vita’s *History*: among the few things that he records as having drawn from those passions, several occur that are lacking in Victor’s books.

Even if these passages once existed in Victor’s *History*, as some suspect who maintain that Victor’s work has not come down to us complete, they would still be no less useful to us for filling at least these gaps in Victor’s *History*. But whatever the truth may be concerning these matters, we are convinced of this one thing: namely, that what Gregory relates about those holy men may be regarded as certain and beyond doubt, since no one can deny that it was written by authors contemporary with Eugenius. For Eugenius and Gregory both passed from this life in the same century—Eugenius, that is, at its beginning, and Gregory as the sixth century was drawing to a close [Col. 0396D]. It is therefore impossible that the passions of the martyrs, which Gregory found already written before composing his *History*, had not been published at least at the beginning of his century.

Indeed, if conjecture may be permitted, it is likely that such precious records were brought into Gaul by Eugenius and his companions. In this, as also in their endurance of persecutions, Eugenius and his companions imitated the example of their fathers, who in the third century had been driven into exile for the faith and always kept before them the notable acts of Saint Cyprian’s confession, so that by reading them they might be trained for martyrdom, as we have already observed in *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 193.

We also judge that we possess Eugenius’ letter to his people, written when he was being carried into exile, from no other source. Hence it is clear that nothing can be concluded against the truth of these acts from Gregory’s having erred in listing the names of the Vandal kings. For these names he supplied from his own resources [Col. 0397A], whereas the rest of what he reports about Eugenius and the other African confessors he drew from older and reliable records.

In any case, everything that he relates about this persecution, both in the *History of the Franks* and in the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, we shall present below in its proper place, after first setting out what other authors have recorded concerning those most holy confessors.

2. Victor of Tunnuna, bishop, speaks as follows in his *Chronicle* concerning Eugenius’ ordination:

> “When Vivianus, V. C., and Basilius were consuls, Eugenius was ordained bishop of the Church of Carthage after Capreolus and Quodvultdeus.”

The year designated by these consuls corresponds, according to Victor, to the Christian year 463, in which Eugenius’ ordination certainly cannot be placed. For it is certain from the other Victor, namely Victor of Vita’s *History*, that Eugenius was placed over this Church under King Huneric, when that barbarian, at the appeals of the emperor Zeno and of Placidia, the widow of Olybrius, had permitted the Catholics of Carthage to elect a bishop, as that author relates more fully at the beginning of Book II [Col. 0397B].

But in the year 462, Genseric, Huneric’s father and predecessor, was still alive, and Zeno had not yet ascended the imperial throne, as is certain and could also be established from Victor of Tunnuna’s *Chronicle* itself. It is clear from several other passages of this Victor’s *Chronicle* that, when listing bishops of different sees, he sometimes gathered several into a single year even though no one would deny that they had been ordained at different and widely separated times. Thus, a little farther on, he places the Roman pontiffs Hilary, Simplicius, and Felix together, as he also does the Constantinopolitan bishops Gennadius, Anatolius, and Acacius and, to say nothing of the others, the Antiochene bishops Alexander, Martyrius, and Julian.

Moreover, at that point Victor makes no mention whatever of Bishop Deogratias, who is nevertheless known to have governed the Church of Carthage between Quodvultdeus, driven into exile for the faith, and Eugenius.

The time of Eugenius’ ordination can be inferred from much more certain evidence, namely, from what we observed above in chapter 6, no. 6, concerning the blessed Deogratias, his predecessor. Since it is clear from that discussion that Deogratias died about the year 457, and since it is established elsewhere from Victor of Vita, Book II, no. 1, that the Church of Carthage remained without a bishop for twenty-four years after his death, it follows also that the ordination of Eugenius—who, as we learn from the same author, succeeded the blessed Deogratias—should be dated approximately to the year 481 [Col. 0397C]. In that year, moreover, the grave persecution with which Huneric later so greatly disturbed the African Church had not yet begun, as we explained above in the preceding chapter, nos. 10 and following.

3. Victor of Tunnuna, in the passage just cited, further observes that after dreadful exiles in the wilderness Eugenius became renowned among all for his many afflictions and punishments. This can also be confirmed by the testimonies of other distinguished writers of the same age.

Concerning what he endured from Antonius, the Arian bishop of Tamallum, who was placed with him in exile [Col. 0397D], we need no other witness than Victor of Vita, whom one may consult in Book V, no. 11.

Pope Gelasius greatly commends Eugenius’ courage in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania. He places before their eyes the example of Eugenius and his companions, in order to show that it is the duty of priests to resist the efforts of rulers when they attempt, by royal authority, to establish things contrary to the laws of justice. “Behold,” he says, “recently a great and excellent priest, Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, and many Catholic priests with him, firmly resisted Huneric, king of the Vandal nation, in his fury; enduring every extremity, they still do not cease resisting their persecutors.”

Gennadius of Massilia also honors this most holy bishop with the title of public confessor in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, which he composed while Eugenius was still alive. There, in chapter 97, he asserts that Eugenius still lived for the strengthening of the Church [Col. 0398A]. It will not be out of place to quote the whole passage, from which we learn about the labors of so great a man by which he enlightened the Catholic Church.

It reads as follows in the oldest manuscript codex of our library at Saint-Germain, written in Franco-Gallic or Merovingian letters about eleven hundred years ago, as we have already said:

> Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, a city of Africa, and public confessor, having been asked by Huneric, king of the Vandals, composed an exposition of the Catholic faith and especially an explanation of the word *homoousios*, with the assent of all the bishops and confessors of Africa, Mauretania, Sardinia, and Corsica who remained in the Catholic faith: a book on the faith, fortified not only by testimonies from the Holy Scriptures but also by those of the Fathers. He submitted it through his fellow confessors for conveyance.  
>   
> [The printed editions read *perrexit*, “he proceeded”; but now the reading is *asportandus*, “about to be carried away.”] When he was about to be carried into exile as the recompense for his faithful speech, he left for his flock, in his own stead, like an attentive shepherd, documents of instruction concerning the faith and the one sacred baptism that must be preserved. He also wrote down the disputations which he had conducted against the Arian bishops through intermediaries, and sent them to Huneric through the chief officer of the household to be read. Likewise, he offered the same ruler prayers for the peace of Christians, as though they were defenses. He is said still to live for the strengthening of the Church.

Of the small works of Eugenius listed by Gennadius, apart from the book of the Confession of Faith—which has been incorporated in its entirety into Victor’s *History*—and the petition presented to King Huneric, only one letter of his remains with that author: the letter he wrote to his fellow citizens of Carthage when he was about to be dragged into exile, in order to strengthen them in the Catholic faith.

There is no doubt that this same work is designated by the term *commonitoria*, or, as the printed editions have it, *epistolas*. We shall present it below from Gregory of Tours, who preserved it for us, collated with several manuscript codices.

4. Cardinal Baronius, under the year 495, maintains that Eugenius, variously harassed by Guntabundus, Huneric’s successor, was eventually expelled from Africa, arrived in Gaul, and died there at the city of Albi in Aquitaine in that same year, which he also declares to have been Guntabundus’ final year.

But Henricus Norisius, V. C., in Book II of his *Pelagian History*, chapter 21, believes that Eugenius died no more than a decade later. And rightly so. For Victor of Tunnuna, the bishop, who—as we have already said—had previously declared that Eugenius, after various exiles in the wilderness, became renowned for his many afflictions and punishments, explicitly asserts that the same holy man died during the consulship of Theodorus, that is, in the year 505 of the common era.

Here are his words:

> “When Theodorus, V. C., was consul, Eugenius, bishop of Carthage and confessor, dies.”

Nor can Victor be accused here of conflating several events into one, as we said above concerning him. In this passage he speaks only of Eugenius’ death, whereas earlier he had gathered into a single kind of bundle many events that occurred at different times.

Norisius also joins to Victor’s testimony the authority of another ancient writer, namely, a very old fragment appended to the *Chronicle of Tyro*, printed by Canisius in volume I of *Ancient Readings*. There Eugenius is said to have been so favorably regarded by Guntabundus that not only was he himself recalled from exile by that king, but, at Eugenius’ prayers, complete liberty was restored to the other orthodox bishops as well [Col. 0398D].

The author says:

> “In the third year of his reign, Guntamundus ordered the cemetery of the holy martyr Agileus at Carthage to be given to the Catholics, Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, having already been recalled from exile.”

He then adds:

> “In the tenth year of his reign he opened the churches of the Catholics and, at the request of the bishop of Carthage, recalled all the priests of God from exile.”

Later writers also testify to the same thing. Among them, Hermannus Contractus seems to have copied the words of the cited fragment in his *Chronicle*, stating that in the tenth year of his reign Guntabundus, persuaded by Bishop Eugenius, recalled all the Catholic bishops from exile and opened the churches, which had long been closed and had been restored [Col. 0399A].

Nor should one say that after this period of clemency Guntabundus eventually turned back to cruelty. For the author of the fragment, who writes that Guntabundus died in the second year after this general relaxation of exile, makes no mention of any persecution. From this it may be inferred that none was in fact initiated by that king, and that Eugenius’ second exile should rather be assigned to the time of Trasamundus, a king who, as everyone knows, stirred up a most severe persecution against the orthodox.

Certainly Pope Gelasius, who wrote the letter to the bishops of Dardania mentioned above while Victor—or rather Viator, V. C.—was consul, that is, in the year 495, testifies that at the time he was writing Eugenius was still resisting the persecutors together with the other African bishops. He would certainly not have said this of Eugenius if Eugenius had been living in Gaul.

5. The memory of the blessed Eugenius is celebrated in both recent and ancient martyrologies. In them his feast is observed on 13 July, together with the other confessors of the Carthaginian clergy whom Victor of Vita records as having suffered in Huneric’s persecution.

Florus expresses the matter more briefly:

> “In Africa, the birthday of the holy confessors Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, glorious in faith, virtues, and miracles, and of the entire clergy of that same Church.”

Ado adds the following:

> “They were worn down by slaughter and hunger, nearly five hundred or even more; among them were very many readers, and little children rejoicing in the Lord. They were driven far away into cruel exile.”

He then praises Salutarus and Muritta, who are well known from Victor’s *History*. All these things are reported in exactly the same words by Usuard and Notker, as also in the present Roman Martyrology.

Notker, however, after the word “confessors,” has “indeed, victorious martyrs.” He also joins the little children to the readers with the conjunction *and*, so that no one might think that the readers and the little children mentioned here were the same persons.

I have thought this worth noting because Baronius advised, in the notes to the Roman Martyrology for this day, that the passage should be read this way in Usuard. We have found that the illustrious cardinal’s conjecture is supported by Notker’s authority, although in Usuard’s autograph the words are clearly written *lectores infantuli*, “readers, little children.” These words are taken from Victor of Vita, Book V, no. 9 [Col. 0399C].

It would be superfluous to quote individually the wording of the more recent martyrologies. Galesinius has Eusebius, bishop of Carthage, instead of Eugenius.

6. Although such a great multitude of authors agrees on this point—that the feast of Eugenius should be celebrated on 13 July—it cannot nevertheless be inferred that this was the day of the holy man’s deposition. For in the oldest African calendar, certainly written not long after his death, the deposition of the holy bishops Deogratias and Eugenius is celebrated on the Nones of January, that is, 5 January.

Andreas Saussayus commemorates his arrival in Gaul on 1 January in the supplement to his *Gallican Martyrology*, in these words:

> “At Albi in Aquitaine, the arrival of Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage and martyr.”

He seems to have taken this from an old tradition of the Church of Albi. But what he adds afterward—namely, that Eugenius, condemned to a second exile by Guntabundus, king of the Vandals, arrived in Gaul set upon a frail raft, along with several similar statements—he drew from Baronius and other recent writers, or even supplied from his own resources [Col. 0399D].

7. The true day of Eugenius’ death could perhaps be recovered more reliably from the tradition of that same Church of Albi than from any other document. Since that most holy bishop died there and his sacred relics were always held in veneration there, it is probable that his feast day was established as the very day that had once been the day of his death.

That day is 6 September. On it the feast of the blessed Eugenius is still celebrated in the Church of Albi with a double rite, according to an ancient tradition of many centuries. This is evident from an old manuscript codex of the Colbert Library, in which the *Passion of Saint Eugenius*, taken from Gregory of Tours and to be presented below, is preceded by this title:

> “Here begins the Life of Saint Eugenius, bishop, who died in the village of Viance on the eighth day before the Ides of September.”

The Breviary of Albi has the following concerning his death:

> “Eugenius, driven into Gaul, settled in the territory of Albi, beside the River Vère, near the tomb of the martyr Amaranthus. There, after building a monastery and enduring many labors and hardships, he died, and his tomb became glorious.”

The rest has been excerpted from Victor of Vita and Gregory of Tours.

8. Viance is a village not far from the city of Albi. In the declining years of the tenth century, Pontius, count of Toulouse, gave it to Amelius, bishop of Albi, and to the canons of Saint Cecilia. This is clear from Pontius’ charter in Catellus, Book I of the *History of the Counts of Toulouse*. In it Pontius decrees that the village of Viance shall remain secure in the future in honor of the holy confessor of Christ, Eugenius; the holy martyr Amerandus; and the other saints who rest there [Col. 0400B].

The charter was issued after the death of King Lothair, in the second year in which his son Louis began to reign. In it Adelard, abbot of Viance; Aymerius, provost; Amelius, precentor; and the other canons are praised.

Raymund, count of Toulouse and son of Count Ildefonsus, confirmed this donation of his grandfather, in the same Catellus, at the passage cited; this too was done in honor of Saint Eugenius and the other saints who rest at Viance.

In the twelfth century a dispute arose between the monks of Aurillac and the bishop and canons of the Church of Albi concerning the church of Viance, which both parties claimed for themselves. Pope Alexander entrusted the matter to the bishops of Rodez and Cahors, as is clear from a letter of that pontiff published from a Colbert manuscript by Stephanus Baluzius, a man of consular rank, in Book IV of his *Miscellanies*, p. 466.

We infer that the monks of Aurillac lost the case from the records of a visitation conducted by Simon de Bello Loco, archbishop of Bourges, published by the same Baluzius in the cited book. There it is said that in April 1286, while visiting the diocese of Albi, Archbishop Simon came to Viance, a priory of the Church of Albi, where he was received and provided for by the provost of that place. In 1291 the same prelate again visited the diocese of Albi and was received, as before, at Viance, the provostry belonging to the Church of Albi [Col. 0400C].

Finally, Louis de Ambesia, bishop of Albi, arranged for the bodies of the saints Eugenius, Vindemialis, Longinus, and Amaranthus the martyrs, together with that of Charissima the virgin, which had been placed in the church of Viance in the territory of Albi from the time of their deaths, to be transferred in 1404, on 29 September, to the cathedral church dedicated to Saint Cecilia. They are still preserved there with the greatest reverence, although the memory of this translation is celebrated chiefly on 2 October, as we learn from the Breviary of Albi.

9. At this point one may ask by what right Trasamundus exiled Eugenius to the city of Albi, situated in the Gothic kingdom and therefore not subject to Trasamundus, since it was separated from Africa by a great distance of land and sea [Col. 0400D].

Why did he not instead order him deported to Sardinia, which lies opposite the shores of Africa? Why not to the remotest deserts of Africa? For it is not likely that Eugenius was given a choice of exile. If that choice had been granted to him, I do not think he would have preferred the lands of the Goths, whom he knew to be enemies of the Catholic faith.

No more probable reason for this action occurs to us than the ancient affinity between the Vandals and the Goths, and their common sect and religion. This consideration led Eugenius’ persecutors to send him, separated from his fellow confessors, among the Goths—most stubborn defenders, evidently, of the Arian doctrine, ruled at that time by Alaric—so that he might drag out a more miserable life because it was a longer one.

10. Some also raise another question, namely, whether Eugenius ought to be given the title of martyr. But it is of little importance to dwell on this. Since Eugenius, after overcoming various labors for Christ’s name and enduring immense hardships, was driven once and again from his homeland and finally ended his life in exile, those who raise the question may decide whether only those who expire amid torments and punishments can be called martyrs.

Certainly, if Eugenius is granted only the title of confessor, no one will deny that he nevertheless received the merit and reward of martyrdom. In the ancient writings cited above he is called a confessor. In the present Breviary of the Church of Albi, however, he is called a martyr, though in a somewhat broader sense, since the responsory assigned to him is one that is customarily recited for those who did not shed their blood.

11. Besides Eugenius, Gregory of Tours mentions three other confessors: the bishops Longinus and Vindemialis, and the archdeacon Octavian. Because ancient records are lacking, only a few things can be said here about them.

In the *African List*, which we presented after Victor’s *History* [above, col. 269], among the bishops of various provinces who came to the Carthaginian assembly at Huneric’s command, Longinus, bishop of Pamaria in Caesarian Mauritania, is listed as number 43, and Vindemialis, bishop of Capsa in the province of Byzacena, as number 60 [Col. 0401B].

The same Vindemialis is given the title “saint” in the *Passion of the Holy Monks*, no. 3 [above, col. 263], and is called an outstanding priest and faithful bishop of Christ.

Although we do not dare to assert absolutely that these are the very men praised by Gregory, it nevertheless seems probable to us. For no other bishops bearing these names appear in the ancient records who could have fought with Eugenius of Carthage against Huneric and Cyrila for the faith of Christ.

The people of Albi believe that these same men came into Gaul with Eugenius and say that they were buried at Viance. In the Breviary of Albi, under 2 October, we read that the bodies of the holy martyrs Vindemialis and Longinus were transferred, together with the sacred relics of Saint Eugenius, from the village of Viance to the cathedral church of Albi [Col. 0401C].

Indeed, in the charters of the counts of Toulouse that we cited above from Catellus, not only are Eugenius and Amaranthus said to rest in the church of Viance, but other saints as well, whose names are not given.

Italian writers also celebrate the bishops Vindemialis and Eugenius. Since some have thought them to be the same men as Eugenius of Carthage and Vindemialis mentioned by Gregory of Tours, they must be discussed here with greater care.

12. Tarvisium is a famous city in Italy, which gives its name to the entire March of Treviso. Its inhabitants honor the holy bishops Florentius and Vindemialis as the principal protectors and patrons of their homeland. They say that the latter was African by origin and the companion of Eugenius, likewise an African bishop.

Petrus de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio in the same march, praises them in Book IV, chapter 116, of his *Catalogue of the Saints*. He writes that their bodies were brought from the island of Corsica to Treviso by Titianus, bishop of that city, when Corsica was being devastated by the Saracens [Col. 0401D].

Ughellus also mentions this translation in volume V of *Sacred Italy*, in his catalogue of the bishops of Treviso. There he says that Titianus governed this Church around the year 400.

How far he departed from the truth in assigning the period of this bishop’s life can be established from the fact that Vindemialis, whose life Titianus is said to have written, is reported to have attended the Carthaginian assembly held with the Arians at Huneric’s command.

Although Ughellus does not expressly mention this conference under Huneric, he appears to have identified it sufficiently when he writes that Eugenius and Vindemialis were present at the Carthaginian council against the Arians and that the same men, driven from Africa by the Arians, went down into Italy.

13. It is of no importance to discuss this author’s meaning at greater length, since in volume I of the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*, under 2 May, we have the life of these bishops, recovered by Godefridus Henschenius from a manuscript codex belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden. Since it is said to have been written by Titianus himself, something may perhaps be learned from it both about the time when Titianus governed the Church of Treviso and about Eugenius and Vindemialis, whom the Italians celebrate.

It begins as follows:

> When the universal synod was being convened at Carthage by King Huneric, six hundred and seventy bishops from all the kingdoms and islands that at that time lay under his rule gathered together on the first day of February, to contend for the faith of the holy and indivisible Trinity. But he himself, deceived by the perfidy of the Arians, ordered all of them to be condemned to exile. Among them the bishop of Carthage, Eugenius, and Vindemialis, men of the highest learning and holiness, stood out, and with an unwavering voice they taught inviolably the faith of the holy and indivisible Trinity. For this reason they were expelled from their own sees and, for the sake of pilgrimage, hastened across the sea, and so forth.

Thus far the *Life*. In the short work by the same author concerning the translation of Vindemialis and Florentius, we read the following:

> Although their birth, life, and passing had flourished among those people, the Lord nevertheless revealed their venerable bodies to us at the time when he willed, and so forth.

He says nothing about Florentius’ life, but resumes as follows concerning Vindemialis and Eugenius:

> Therefore the most blessed Vindemialis was born and raised on African soil. He was instructed, however, by the blessed Appianus, bishop and confessor of Christ, and imbued with heavenly conduct, faith, and religion. Having attained the dignity of priest, in which he worthily served God, he advanced even to the burden of the episcopate. There, in the regions of Africa, together with Eugenius, the almighty Lord deigned to perform through them many magnificent and innumerable signs.  
>   
> Then, both for the sake of pilgrimage and for preaching out of love for Christ, they reached the island of Corsica, where, while they were preaching the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth. . . .  
>   
> Saint Vindemialis, returning from the regions just mentioned and traveling around the maritime shores, proceeded farther amid stormy waves and reached the fortress of Sauve, together with the most holy Eugenius, with whom he had also performed many miracles in the regions of Africa and at Carthage. From there they came to the fortress of Vande, and in those regions they won a very great multitude of people for our Lord Jesus Christ by their preaching.

Then Saint Eugenius is said to have died on an island near the fortress of Vande, two miles distant from it. “At his tomb,” says Titianus, “the almighty Lord deigned to perform many and innumerable miracles.”

Saint Vindemialis, however, departed from the aforementioned fortress and hastened to Corsica, where he surrendered his spirit undefiled in his holy purpose.

The author then continues his account of the translation he carried out:

> After learning from the report of many people that Corsica had been captured by the Saracens and that many churches of God had been destroyed from their foundations, I, Titianus, bishop of the holy Church of Treviso, came to that island by divine will. There, from sailors and from the inhabitants of the place, we learned where the bodies of the most blessed confessors of Christ had been placed in sarcophagi—namely, those of the bishops Vindemialis and Florentius. . . .  
>   
> We then lifted their bodies and reached the territory of Treviso. . . . We placed them in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

14. We have reported these matters at somewhat greater length because they are necessary for clarifying the history of these saints. Several conclusions can be drawn from Titianus’ account.

First, Titianus himself did not live at the beginning of the fifth century, as Ughellus thought. For he reports that Vindemialis and Eugenius took part in the Carthaginian assembly convened under King Huneric in the year 484.

The same point is also supported by another argument. Titianus says that he transferred the bodies of the saints Florentius and Vindemialis to his own city at the time when the churches had been destroyed after the island of Corsica was captured by the Saracens. This circumstance is much more compatible with the seventh or eighth century, when the Saracens were ravaging that island and the neighboring regions, than with the fourth or fifth century, since at that earlier time Corsica was subject to Roman or at least Vandal rule [Col. 0403A].
