Second, from Titianus’ account we infer that Titianus himself wrote many things about Eugenius, Vindemialis, and others that were not sufficiently known to him and were even contrary to the truth. For, to say nothing of Vindemialis, he thinks that the Eugenius whom he praises was the famous bishop of Carthage who attended the Carthaginian assembly.

Yet this conflicts with certain and indisputable historical records. Let anyone read what Victor of Vita, a completely trustworthy witness, wrote in Book V, no. 11, about the exile of Eugenius of Carthage and the hardships he endured from Antonius at Tamalluma; everyone will notice that those accounts cannot in any way be reconciled with what Titianus relates about his Eugenius.

Furthermore, according to Gregory of Tours, an almost contemporary author who is by reason of geographical proximity altogether unsuspect, Eugenius of Carthage died at Albi in Aquitaine [Col. 0403B]. His tomb was already famous at that time because of its frequent miracles, as can also be confirmed by the continuous tradition of that Church and by ancient documents.

Titianus, however, writes that his Eugenius died on an island near Italy.

15. Since it is therefore clear to us that the Eugenius and Vindemialis mentioned by Titianus are different from those most holy bishops celebrated under the same names by Victor and Gregory of Tours, there is nothing further to say about them except that they may perhaps have belonged to the number of those confessors who, driven from Africa by the Vandal persecution, came to Corsica. There they died confessing the divinity of Christ and became famous.

Many centuries later Titianus, bishop of Treviso, found their relics. He pieced together their life from what had been spread abroad by the public reputation of that region and also from what he had learned elsewhere about the distinguished deeds of Eugenius of Carthage, mixing the true with the false—as commonly happens—without due care [Col. 0403C].

From this there arose among authors who later flourished in those regions the opinion that the Eugenius and Vindemialis whom they venerated were the same as Eugenius of Carthage and Vindemialis, bishop of Capsa, whom the ancient historians had celebrated so greatly.

16. Vindemialis experienced almost the same fate in the Roman Martyrology under 2 May. Since Vindemialis of Corsica was mentioned on that day in the ancient calendars without any addition, those who later prepared the Roman Martyrology, thinking that this Vindemialis was the same as the other whom Gregory of Tours praises, added Gregory’s eulogy to the earlier commemoration. Thus, by making one person out of two, they proposed neither of them for proper remembrance.

For the passage there reads:

> “Saint Vindemialis, bishop.”

These words had been said of the Corsican Vindemialis. The following was added from what Gregory wrote about the other Vindemialis:

> “And martyr, who, together with the holy bishops Eugenius and Longinus, contending against the Arians by teaching and miracles, was ordered by King Huneric to be beheaded.”

Ferrarius, moreover, as though there were no mention here of Vindemialis of Corsica, listed him together with Eugenius among the saints not included in the Roman Martyrology, in his *Catalogue* under the same day, 2 May.

### 17

Finally, in the same way that Eugenius and Vindemialis became famous in Corsica and were incautiously taken to be Eugenius of Carthage and Vindemialis, bishops of Capsa, so Florentius was listed among the African prelates by Maurolycus, Galesinius, Ferrarius, and other writers of the more recent period, because his body was transferred from Corsica to Treviso together with the relics of the African Vindemialis. Yet Titianus, who, as we saw above, arranged this translation and committed its history to writing, nowhere said anything from which even the slightest suspicion of this opinion could arise.

Indeed, Petrus Equilinus suggests precisely the contrary in Book IV of his *Catalogus*, chapter 116, under 2 May, where, after setting forth the varied fortunes of the African bishops Eugenius and Vindemialis—apparently from Titianus’s account—he testifies that Vindemialis returned to Corsica, died there, and was buried where Saint Florentius had formerly rested. Neither Titianus nor Petrus says anything further about the deeds of this Florentius. Hence, if it is permissible to indulge conjecture in so obscure a matter, we may suspect that Florentius was an ancient bishop of the island of Corsica, and that the confessor Vindemialis was perhaps buried beside his tomb as a mark of honor, just as Eugenius of Carthage, according to Gregory of Tours, merited burial in Gaul near the tomb of blessed Amaranthus.

The memory of this same Saint Florentius is still famous on the island of Corsica because of the city of Saint-Florent, so called from his church; to that city the ancient episcopal see of Nebbio, situated half a mile from Saint-Florent, was later transferred. From this one might conjecture that Saint Florentius was bishop of Nebbio. Yet I would have what we have said understood in such a way that we do not deny that the Florentius mentioned here may perhaps have been one of the number of those confessors who, under King Huneric, were exiled from Africa to Corsica.

This may seem more plausible to some because, in the African *Notitia*—that is, in the catalogue of those bishops who were persecuted under Huneric for the sake of the faith—Florentinus of Utica and Florentius of Seminensis are listed among the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa as having been exiled to Corsica, in addition to several other most holy bishops of the same name who are listed there from other provinces.

Moreover, in the martyrology of Florus, as also in the ancient Roman martyrology published by Florentinius, the Passion of the holy Vindemialis and Eugenius is commemorated on 1 February. But who these men were, neither of those works indicates, and we are not permitted to guess. Certainly, as we have already observed more than once, the martyrologies of Florentinius contain few or no martyrs from the persecutions of the later period.

But enough of this; something must now be said about Octavianus.

### 18

Gregory of Tours was the first to mention Octavianus the archdeacon; from him later writers entered his name in the martyrologies. Following them, Baronius inserted his elogium in the Roman Martyrology under 22 March, in these words:

> At Carthage, Saint Octavianus, archdeacon, and many thousands of martyrs who were slain by the Vandals because of the Catholic faith.

Victor of Vita, Book V, no. 9, mentions another Carthaginian archdeacon named Salutaris. Octavianus either succeeded him, or Salutaris himself certainly succeeded Octavianus. At that time there was only one archdeacon in each church; the man who followed him was second in the order of ministers, as Victor says concerning Muritta in the passage cited.

But let us now hear Gregory of Tours speaking about the persecution of the Vandals in Africa. We have compared his fragment with three manuscript codices: one from the Royal Library, another from the Colbert Library, and a third which we possess ourselves. In the latter two it is copied under the title *Passion of Saint Eugenius*, which title we have retained. It is found in the same Gregory of Tours, Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 2 and following.

**PASSION OF SAINT EUGENIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, AND OF THE OTHER CONFESSORS**

(See below, column 769.)

**LETTER OF SAINT EUGENIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO HIS FELLOW CITIZENS, CONCERNING THE PRESERVATION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH**

(See this letter below, column 769.)

## CHAPTER IX  
### On the holy confessors who, during the persecutions of the Vandals, under the reigns of Genseric or Huneric, were expelled or fled from Africa and flourished in Italy

### 1

Victor of Vita frequently praises numerous defenders of the Catholic faith who, driven by the persecutions of the Vandals, brought distinction to Africa. Since there is nothing to say about them beyond what Victor himself records, or what we have noted in the annotations to the text of Victor’s *History*, or certainly in the preceding chapter concerning Saint Eugenius and his companions, our principal concern here must be with those who, expelled from Africa or voluntarily going into exile, were brought to Italy and became distinguished there.

Although little remains to be said about them from the ancient authorities, it was not permissible for us to omit them, lest anyone rightly complain that such distinguished men—famous for their confession of the faith, the holiness of their lives, and also their frequent miracles—had been disregarded by us.

### 2

Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 4, relates that after capturing Carthage and dividing Africa among his Vandals, Genseric ordered that bishops and noble laymen alike be driven naked from their own places and churches. If they refused to obey, he ordered them reduced to slavery. The same may be inferred from chapter 1 of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*.

But he ordered far harsher measures to be taken against Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage, perhaps so that the others might be deterred from the true religion by such an example. As the same author relates in the cited book, no. 5, he ordered Quodvultdeus, together with a very large crowd of clergy, to be placed on broken-down ships, stripped naked, and expelled. In God’s merciful goodness, however, he deigned to bring them by a prosperous voyage to Naples, a city of Campania.

This is Victor’s account. He says nothing further about that most holy prelate, doubtless because he intended to describe only what happened within Africa, as he explicitly declares elsewhere. That Quodvultdeus’s memory had not perished among the Carthaginians is evident from the very ancient Carthaginian calendar, where, under 8 January, the deposition of Quodvultdeus the bishop is commemorated.

It is said in the Roman Martyrology, under 26 October, that he died as a confessor in exile at Naples; Ferrarius likewise commemorates him on that day in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*. His sacred relics are reverently preserved in a church of that city dedicated under the name of Saint Gaudiosus.

### 3

The ancient records of the Neapolitan church list Gaudiosus among the other companions of Quodvultdeus in exile. His memory was more celebrated than that of the others in that city because of the monastery which is said to have been built by him and in which Agnellus, a most holy abbot, later flourished.

This is testified by the ancient author of Agnellus’s *Life*, a fragment of which Baronius inserted into his *Ecclesiastical Annals*. The following is said there about our Gaudiosus:

> Agnellus the abbot was elected in the monastery which blessed Gaudiosus, surnamed Septimus Coelius, bishop of the holy Bithynian Church in Africa, endeavored to found in this city of Parthenope, at the time when he came from the regions of Africa with Saint Quodvultdeus and the other bishops, fleeing the persecution of the Vandals.

It is not surprising that Gaudiosus, an exile in a foreign land, founded a monastery. Those most holy confessors were so devoted to the monastic life that, as soon as they arrived at the place of exile, they established monasteries there. This could be confirmed by numerous examples.

To pass over Faustus, who built a monastery not far from his own see after being banished from it, Eugenius, as we said in the preceding chapter, built a monastery near the city of Albi in Gaul, at the village of Viancium. Fulgentius and other holy bishops who were expelled to Sardinia under Thrasamund did the same. The same Fulgentius visited the African bishop Rufinianus, who was living the monastic life on an island near Sicily, when Fulgentius was making a journey to the holy places.

Gaudiosus is therefore rightly praised by Ferrarius in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* for having lived a monastic life, together with Quodvultdeus and other bishops expelled from Africa, in the monastery he built near Naples. The Roman Martyrology agrees under 28 October, where it says that Gaudiosus rested in a holy death in a monastery near that same city.

### 4

Even today Naples possesses a very celebrated convent of sacred virgins, with an adjoining church dedicated to God under the name of blessed Gaudiosus. Caracciolus, however, in his *History of Naples*, insists that this monastery is entirely different from the one founded by Gaudiosus. He believes that the monastery of Gaudiosus is now known under the name of Saint Agnellus.

Our Mabillon observes in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, under the year 596, where he discusses Saint Agnellus, that the monastery of blessed Gaudiosus once stood on the site where the Dominicans later erected a half-ruined church in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, commonly called “of Sanità.” He says that he learned this from Paolo Regio’s Italian *Life of Saint Agnellus*. Ughellus writes that the same place was formerly called Caput-Trii.

We can identify the site of the ancient church of blessed Gaudiosus from John the Deacon. Writing in Ughellus about Saint Nostrianus, bishop of Naples, who lived shortly after Saint Gaudiosus’s arrival, he reports that Nostrianus was buried in the church of blessed Gaudiosus, confessor of Christ, situated outside the city, on the road leading to Saint Januarius the martyr, in a portico. On this church of Saint Januarius, see Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 114.

### 5

Ughellus calls Gaudiosus bishop of a city of Bithynia in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, where he writes that Gaudiosus arrived in Italy during the time of Timasius, bishop of Naples. Certainly, the anonymous Ravennate mentions Bithyna among the other cities of Africa; by that name I readily believe that the well-known city of Abitina is meant.

It is indeed probable that Gaudiosus presided over a city near Carthage. Abitina was a city of the province of Proconsular Africa, and a sufficiently distinguished one, as is clear from the synodal letter of the bishops of that province to Paul, patriarch of Constantinople. This letter was read at the Lateran Council under Saint Martin, in session 2. Among others, Augustalis, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Abitina, subscribed it.

We published the acts of the martyrs of Abitina—formerly, and incorrectly, called the martyrs of Alutina—among the genuine acts under the year 304, p. 409. From them it is also clear that this city belonged to Proconsular Africa. That it was an ancient episcopal see can be inferred from the Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian, at which Saturninus of Avitina took part among the rebaptizers.

Augustine mentions the same city in Book III *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, and elsewhere more than once. Finally, Victor, a Catholic bishop of that Church, one of those who had initially been absent, eventually subscribed to the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 215, when Felix, his opponent, had already appeared among the Donatists in chapter 201.

### 6

Ughellus, following Capaccius, states that Gaudiosus died in the year 453—but on what basis? Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 28 October, the day on which his feast is recorded, says that he flourished around the year 411.

Certainly, in October 439 Genseric invaded Carthage, and shortly afterward expelled Quodvultdeus, whose companion in exile Gaudiosus is said to have been. The body of this holy man is preserved with the greatest reverence at Naples in the convent church mentioned above.

He must therefore be distinguished, as Cardinal Baronius advises, from another holy prelate of the same name whose relics are preserved at Salerno in the lower crypt of the cathedral church, although some authors have mixed together the acts of the two.

The feast of Gaudiosus of Salerno is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology under 26 October. Nevertheless, we do not think it can rightly be inferred that saints of the same name were different merely because their relics are said to be preserved in different places. It often happens that parts of a saint’s body are kept in different churches, yet in both places are designated by the name of the body.

That this manner of speaking is extremely ancient in the Church is evident from Theodoret. In Letter 130, addressed to Bishop Timothy, he writes as follows about the matter, treating it as a thoroughly established usage:

> Even to this day, when we enter the shrines of the triumphant martyrs, we customarily ask who is called the one enclosed in the reliquary. Those who know answer, “Perhaps the martyr Julian, or Romanus, or Timothy.” And although the bodies are not even intact there, but only very small relics, we nevertheless call them also “the body” by the common designation.

The Greek text reads:

> Καίτοι πολλάκις οὐδὲ τελείων τῶν σωμάτων κειμένων, ἀλλὰ σμικροτάτων λειψάνων, ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως τῷ κοινῷ ὀνόματι καὶ τὸ σῶμα προσαγορεύομεν.

> “Although often the bodies are not lying there complete, but only the smallest relics, nevertheless by the common designation we also call them ‘the body.’”

Furthermore, Baronius testifies in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 26 October that, in the very ancient cemetery of the Neapolitan suburb, he saw among other notable monuments of sacred antiquity an inscription formerly placed on the tomb of Saint Gaudiosus. Because of its age, although it was already almost obliterated, he copied it; we reproduce it here as well:

> **HERE RESTS SAINT GAUDIOSUS, WHO LIVED [—] YEARS [—], ON THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER [—], INDICT[ION] VI.**

Capaccius and Ughellus also discuss this funerary inscription. But it is impossible to determine whether it was placed on his tomb immediately after Gaudiosus’s death. Apart from the fact that Gaudiosus is called a saint there, although the title “confessor” would have suited him better, some may perhaps find it strange that no mention is made there of his episcopal dignity.

### 7

On the occasion of this same holy man, Italian authors mention an ancient tradition of the Neapolitan Church, which we could not omit here. They say that Gaudiosus, driven into exile from Africa, brought to Naples among other relics of the saints a glass ampulla filled with the congealed blood of blessed Stephen, the proto-martyr. It is preserved to this day in the church of that saint.

Baronius says in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 3 August:

> The miracle continues to this day: when the ampulla is placed upon the altar during the solemn celebration of Mass, it may sometimes be seen to liquefy like freshly shed blood.

Baronius likewise testifies that, in the year when the Roman calendar was corrected by the authority of Pope Gregory XIII, this miracle occurred on the very day on which the feast of blessed Gaudiosus was celebrated, whereas previously it was accustomed to be seen only on the tenth day after the feast of this saint. He cites as witness Francesco Maria Tarasio, cardinal, who was then living at Naples and celebrating Mass in the chapel of that same saint; the blood appeared to him to liquefy.

Certainly, Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Stephen*, published under the name of Evodius among the works of Saint Augustine, mentions in chapter 1 an ampulla of this kind which was preserved in Uzal, a city of the province of Proconsular Africa.

### 8

Antonius Caracciolus, in *Sacred Naples*, chapter 26, thinks that Priscus and eleven other confessors belonged to the same fellowship of the exiled Saint Quodvultdeus. He does not believe that they were bishops, but rather clerics of various orders—namely, those clergy of the Church of Carthage whom Victor of Vita records as having arrived at Naples after being placed, together with their bishop, on an old ship.

This opinion, however, has not pleased others. Indeed, if some credence may be given to the surviving monuments concerning these matters, Caracciolus’s view cannot stand, since it can be supported neither by the testimony of more recent writers nor by the authority of the ancients.

The distinguished Godefridus Henschenius published in volume II of the Bollandists’ *February*, under the 11th of that month, the *Life of Saint Castrensis the Bishop*, one of the number of these confessors. From it some light may perhaps shine upon the clarification of their deeds.

Although the work is not free from blemishes and was written by an author entirely ignorant of events that had occurred before his own time—or at least was corrupted by a later interpolator who confused the persecution of the Arian emperor Valens with that of the Vandals—its credibility must not be entirely rejected.

For in chapter 3, no. 16, the author testifies that he received certain details from the report of some priests who had been present when Castrensis was near death. I believe these words belonged to the ancient author of the *Life*, while what follows came from an interpolator:

> “These things,” he says, “which enduring piety has transmitted to our senses through the sayings of the holy Fathers, we have therefore taken care to record, so that whenever one of the faithful celebrates the solemnity of some saint—one of the companions of Castrensis, that is—he may at the same time rejoice in the triumph of them all.”

There he explains why, in the *Life of Castrensis*, he inserted the deeds of others as well: they had been expelled from Africa together with him, scattered through various cities and regions of Italy, and were celebrated after dying there.

### 9

The same author lists the names of these confessors in chapter 2, no. 8, in the order in which they entered the ship. The first is said to be Rosius; then Secundinus, who is called “the offspring of fruitful progeny”; next Heraclius, who boldly scattered the laws of Christ among the peoples.

After him came Benignus, Priscus, Elpidius, Marcus, Augustinus, Canion, and Vindonius. In the eleventh place was Signifer, the teacher of Castrensis, to whom the ship’s citadel was entrusted to hold, he who by his disposition had ruled adverse winds. Finally came Tammarus, to whom the steering of the ship’s prow was entrusted.

The same men are found in the Roman Martyrology under 1 September and in Ughellus, volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, where he discusses the archbishops of Capua, except that in both authors Adjutor appears instead of Benignus, and Augustus instead of Augustinus.

That most of them were distinguished by episcopal dignity is suggested, besides the traditions of various Italian churches, also by the author of the *Life* cited above. In chapter 2, no. 6, Castrensis addresses his fellow brothers and fellow bishops as follows:

> “My brothers and lords,” and so forth.

Moreover, in chapter 1, no. 3, he had already said that the tyrant had ordered the holy men in chains to be brought from every province:

> When an immense multitude had been assembled, there were also holy men [...] endowed with the honor of the highest priesthood, who walked joyfully with the flocks entrusted to them, believing that through the triumph of martyrdom they would attain eternal life. Among these Rossius, Priscus, and Tammarius shone especially—or, as another codex has it, Zamorus and Castrensis.

### 10

Thus the storm engulfed not only the shepherds but also the flocks themselves, as the same author of the *Life* relates at length. In chapter 1 he writes that boys and old men, women and men alike, hastened to the contest.

This occurred at the beginning of the persecution. When it later became more intense, the holy men of God were brought in chains in crowds from every province, and were tortured with various punishments before being committed to the sea, as is said in no. 3.

At first they were thrust separately into prison, one apart from another. Then they were gathered together in one place: some were beaten with rods, others with slaps, and others with stones. When they had been tested in various ways, and their steadfastness could not be broken by threats or beatings, they were finally placed, at the advice—I know not whose—of Aristodemus, on a very old ship, so that, drowned in the sea, no remnant of them might remain.

But by God’s will they arrived safely in Campania, Italy, and illuminated that province by their miracles and holiness of life.

The Roman Martyrology agrees under 1 September, where it says that those twelve holy men, who were, as it were, the leaders and teachers of the others, were afflicted in various ways during the Vandal persecution because of the Catholic faith and, having been placed on an old ship, reached the shores of Campania from Africa. There, scattered through the region and placed over various churches, they wonderfully propagated the Christian religion.

The often-cited author of the *Life of Saint Castrensis* assigns their arrival in Italy to the fourth year of the Vandal persecution. But since elsewhere he thoroughly confuses the chronology, no secure reliance can be placed on his reckoning.

If, however, we wish to indulge conjecture, there is scarcely any year under Vandal rule to which this persecution could not be attributed. Nevertheless, we do not think that they belonged to the fellowship of Quodvultdeus, because Castrensis is called the standard-bearer and teacher of that company. This title would have suited Quodvultdeus better, especially because of the precedence of his see, yet no mention of him is made here at all.

Their stories must be treated individually.

### 11

Rossius—or, as others write, Rosius—is listed first among the other confessors in the *Life of Saint Castrensis*, chapter 1, no. 3. There it is recorded that he excelled not only in the dignity of the highest priesthood but also in merits, character, and the beauty of his understanding.

The reason why he held the first place is given in chapter 2, no. 8:

> “Let Rossius enter first,” said the guards, “endowed with reverend gray hair and holiness.”

Although these words were spoken by the persecutors, they nevertheless indicate that the orthodox regarded Rossius as such a man.

We know nothing of his deeds in Italy. But several martyrologies among the Bollandists celebrate his feast on 16 May. He is especially venerated at Benevento because his sacred body was transferred to the church of Saint Sophia, which Arechis, one of the Lombard dukes, built with great magnificence in that city.

The memory of Rossius is also celebrated in the diocese of Sessa. We infer that a church was formerly dedicated to him in that city from a charter of Athenulf, bishop of Capua, in Ughellus, volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, column 675, where he discusses the bishops of Sessa.

### 12

We know nothing reliable about Secundinus except what we have drawn from the *Life of Saint Castrensis*. The body of Saint Secundinus the bishop is preserved in the principal church at Troia, a wealthy city of Apulia, where his feast is celebrated on 11 February. Some consider this man to be the same as the one praised here, but the matter is uncertain.

More about the discovery of Secundinus of Troia is found among the Bollandists under the date just mentioned. Michael the monk testifies in the *Capuan Sanctuary* that Secundinus’s feast is celebrated at Mantua on 8 December. There he praises a very ancient calendar in which the feast of Saint Secundinus is recorded under 27 May.

The same author infers that this saint’s memory was once celebrated among the people of Mantua from the many churches dedicated under his name that are found throughout the diocese of Mantua. A church of Saint Secundinus is also mentioned in the diocese of Sessa in the charter of Athenulf which we cited in the preceding section.

Finally, Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, commemorates the bishops Secundinus and Castus at Sinuessa on 1 July. He nevertheless admits that they are famous at Sessa, either because the name Sinuessa has intruded in place of Sessa, or because, after Sinuessa was destroyed, their sacred relics were transferred to Sessa, where, according to Ferrarius, they still rest.

He insists that this Secundinus is different from the one from Troia whom he had praised elsewhere under 11 February.

Peter the Deacon, in his *Book on the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, chapter 29, praises the *Life of Saint Secundinus* written by Benedict, also called Guaiferius, a monk of Cassino. Our Mabillon, who went to Italy several years ago, copied this *Life* from a manuscript at Cassino.

But it is nothing other than the history of the discovery of Secundinus, which Bollandus published from Cardinal Baronius’s manuscript under 11 February, together with another account which the learned man considers older.

From these accounts we learn that, when the city of Troia in Apulia was being built over the ruins of the ancient city called Ecana, a marble tomb was found in the cemetery of Saint Mark bearing the following inscription. The lower portions of the stone had been worn away, but the inscription could nevertheless be read easily:

> **Here rests Saint and venerable Secundinus, bishop, who restored the buildings of the saints, taken into rest on the third day before the Ides of February.**

When the fame of the discovery of the sacred body had spread throughout the city, nearly all the inhabitants immediately hurried there. Thinking, as Guaiferius says, that “what is pious must be lawful,” they began to kiss the relics, and so forth.

But the bishop of the place could not be persuaded to permit them to be venerated until he had first been punished by divine intervention. The relics were therefore thrown into the fire, according to the custom of those times, but could not be harmed in any way. The fire was fanned from every side; the relics became reddish in color. Finally, they sprang out of the fire, and no mark of burning was found upon them, as those who were present reported.

Peter the Deacon also praises several short works published by Guaiferius in honor of Saint Secundinus. He testifies that Guaiferius lived in the times of the emperors Alexius and Henry and of Abbot Desiderius.

Guaiferius himself, however, reveals his own period in the prologue to the *Life* just mentioned, where he says that he wrote it at the command of Abbot Desiderius. Desiderius succeeded Pope Gregory VII after his death in 1086, under the name Victor III; he had been made a cardinal by Nicholas II in 1059.

Bollandus has more about Guaiferius in the passage cited. Arnold Vion and Hugh Menard commemorate the blessed Guaiferius, a Cassinese monk, among the saints whose birthdays are unknown, in the appendix to the Benedictine martyrology.

### 13

There is nothing to say about Heraclius except that a church dedicated to him is mentioned in the charter of Athenulf cited above.

The people of Foligno in Umbria venerate the martyrs Heraclius, Maurus, and Justus. Their bodies are preserved in the cathedral church there. But who these men were, or in what place or at what time they were crowned with martyrdom, they entirely ignore.

### 14

The name of Benignus, an exile from Africa, occurs only in the *Life of Saint Castrensis*. The man called Benignus there is called Adjutor or Adjutorius by others, as we have already observed.

The memory of Adjutor is celebrated at Benevento and Cava, where his sacred relics are kept. There is also a substantial town near Benevento that is very well known under the name of Saint Adjutor.

Philip Ferrarius records the feast of this holy man on 19 November in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, where he discusses this most holy confessor. Tamayus Salazar, however, has much more about him on that same day in the *Spanish Martyrology*. He writes that this same holy man crossed from Spain into Africa with Genseric, in whose army he served.

But when Adjutor saw the orthodox being afflicted by the king with various punishments, he abandoned military service and withdrew to the city of Abba. He later became bishop of that city. Finally, under King Thrasamund, he was placed with other confessors on an old ship and arrived in Campania, where he served as a bishop at Cava in that province and eventually died.

This is Salazar’s account, drawn from various authors whom he cites, as is his custom, dragging all manner of saints into Spain by fair means or foul. But we await an ancient author as a witness to these events.

Certainly, Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 12, praises Valerianus of Abbenza, or Abba, as we observed in note 41, for his illustrious confession. Yet in the *Notitia of Africa* neither he—for he was already dead—nor any other bishop of that see is mentioned.

Nor will anyone easily persuade himself that Adjutor, whom they claim first served as a soldier in Spain and then crossed into Africa with the Vandals in 427, was later, under Thrasamund—who assumed rule over the Vandals in 496—expelled as a bishop into Italy, where he also administered a bishopric.

Finally, Abba, or Aba, was a city belonging to Proconsular Africa, as is certain from Polybius, Book X, who mentions that it stood not far from Carthage. But from Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 9, it is clear that in his own time no bishops at all remained from the provinces of Proconsular Africa and Zeugitana except the three whom he lists there.

He was writing in the year 487, as he himself testifies—that is, eleven years before Thrasamund gained the throne.

### 15

Priscus was especially celebrated. According to the account in the *Life of Castrensis*, chapter 1, no. 3, the barbarians separated him and Castrensis from the others in order to test their steadfastness, thinking that once these two had been overcome, the others would easily yield.

The feast of Priscus is chiefly commemorated in the Roman Martyrology and by Ferrarius in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under 1 September. It seems that the names of his other companions are listed only because of him.

Michael the monk testifies in the *Capuan Sanctuary* that Priscus’s memory was celebrated at Capua by ancient tradition. He writes that Priscus had been bishop of Mantua. Following this author, Ughellus assigned the same Priscus the twelfth place among the bishops of Mantua in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, where he says more about him, but things that are entirely uncertain.

### 16

Little can be found about Elpidius, and nothing is certain. Michael the monk, in the often-cited *Capuan Sanctuary*, writes that the feast of this holy man is celebrated in the church of Casapulla on 26 May.

Others, however, think that a different Elpidius is celebrated there, distinct from our African, and that he presided over the Church of Atella in the fifth century. His feast is celebrated both in the Beneventan Church and in the town called Saint Elpidius, near Aversa, on the 24th of the same month.

These difficulties cannot be resolved without more reliable evidence. Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, asserts that the relics of Elpidius of Atella are preserved in the Church of Salerno; he too distinguishes him from the African Elpidius.

The Bollandists have more on this subject in volume V, under 24 May.

### 17

We know Marcus by name only. Marcus, bishop of Bovino in Apulia, is celebrated in that city and at Benevento, where his feast is commemorated on 14 June.

There is also another bishop of the same name at Ecana, whose feast is celebrated on 13 October, as Ughellus observes in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, where he discusses the bishops of Capua.

But who these men were is uncertain.

### 18

The man called Augustinus in the *Life of Saint Castrensis* is called Augustus in the Roman Martyrology, with Ughellus in *Sacred Italy*, Ferrarius in the *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, and other published authors agreeing.

Apart from this, Augustinus or Augustus is entirely unknown, except that Michael the monk mentions a church dedicated under his name in the *Capuan Sanctuary*.

Fortunatus, in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, praises Augustinus of Concordia in Italy as a distinguished man, but we think that he was someone quite different from ours. Ughellus likewise calls him bishop of Concordia.

Yet it is surprising that neither in Ferrarius’s two catalogues nor in the works of the other collectors of the saints of Italy whom we have been able to consult does his memory appear, although he was already very well known in the time of Fortunatus. The latter author lists him among the more illustrious patrons of the cities of Italy in these verses:

> If you seek that road which Concordia surrounds,  
> There stands precious Augustinus, and Basil.

There is also another Augustinus, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished shortly after Rome was destroyed by the Goths, at the very time when the other Augustinus was bringing distinction to the African Church. Norisius observes this from Henry Palladius in his *Censure of Garnerius*, which he dedicated to the distinguished Antonio Magliabechi, librarian of the Grand Duke of Tuscany.

### 19

Canion is famous among the people of Acherontia, who venerate him with great devotion and religiously preserve his body in the metropolitan church.

But if any credence may be given to the fabulous acts which they display, this Canion is entirely different from the man about whom we are speaking here. That Canion completed his martyrdom under Diocletian and Maximian, whereas ours acquired the title of confessor only under the Vandal persecution.

Nevertheless, since the people of Acherontia say in those acts that their Canion was first a bishop in Africa and was then transferred to Italy, where he was buried by Elpidius, bishop of Atella, the Bollandists and other authorities, following Michael the monk and Ughellus, rightly infer that the two should not be distinguished from one another.

You will find more about this, if you have the time, among the Bollandists, volume VI of May, under 25 May, on which day the feast of blessed Canion is chiefly celebrated at Acherontia.

### 20

I was unable to find any memory whatsoever of Vindonius. Ughellus inferred from an old charter of the nuns of Saint John that a church of Mindonius once existed outside the city of Capua. He suspects that the name Mindonius had slipped into the charter in place of Vindonius.

21. Castrensis is the more celebrated among the twelve confessors; indeed, nearly all the others are known only from his Acts, as is evident from what we have said throughout almost this entire chapter. The author of his Life plainly declares that he was a bishop before he was transferred to Italy; but he maintains complete silence everywhere about which Church he governed. I myself have more than once suspected that the name *Castrensis* designates not the name of a man but that of an episcopal city, which, after his own name had been lost, was transferred to the bishop himself. The form of the word seems to suggest this: at first sight, everyone would judge that it indicates a place rather than a person. Moreover, the name *castrum* is frequently found attributed to cities in ancient African records; indeed, among the Fathers of the province of Byzacena there appears, in Sirmond’s edition of the *Notitia Africana*, Felix, bishop of Castrum.

[Col. 0412B] Yet since every author, both recent and ancient, has consistently called him Saint Castrensis, we could not depart from them without any authority beyond conjecture. Furthermore, when Castrensis arrived in Campania, he made for the city of Suessa, where, leading an angelic life in a certain little hut in the suburbs, he became renowned for miracles—as the author of his Life relates in chapter 3—and departed this life on 11 February, the day on which his feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology. He was buried at Castrum Vulturni, which at that time belonged to the bishops of Capua; and there his sacred body was still preserved in the ninth century, as is clear from the ancient epitaph of Radalpertus, bishop of Capua. Henschenius quoted it from Michael the Monk in the preliminary material to the Life of the same Saint Castrensis, paragraph 2, number 6.

[Col. 0412C] Later, in the twelfth century, apart from the head, it was transferred by William II, surnamed “the Good,” king of Sicily, to the metropolitan church of Monreale. This pious prince had built that church after summoning Benedictine monks of the Cluniac family from the monastery of Cava. In any event, the fact that the memory of blessed Castrensis was celebrated throughout the whole region of Campania is proved not only by the numerous churches which, as Michael the Monk, Ughellus, and other authors everywhere testify, were dedicated to God under his name, but also by the various ancient martyrologies which commemorate him. Some of these, moreover, adorned Castrensis with the title of martyr, since he endured much for the confession of Christ’s divinity.

Certainly, his cult can be shown to be very ancient from a calendar written, as Godefridus Henschenius says, before the year 741, in which the memory of blessed Castrensis is celebrated. His name is also read in the old Roman Martyrology circulated under the name of Saint Jerome, although it must be considered more recent, or at least augmented by the names of many saints. I shall not list the rest of the evidence, which may be seen in the Bollandists under 11 February.

[Col. 0412D] Peter the Deacon, in his *Book of Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, chapter 6, praises a certain Laurence, a monk of Monte Cassino who became a bishop of uncertain see, and who around the tenth century composed the passion of Bishop Castrensis in verse. Finally, the cult of this same saint spread from Italy to Sicily when his sacred relics, as we said above, were transferred to the church of Monreale, where they are still reverently preserved by our Benedictine monks who remain in that metropolitan church.

22. The last in the group of twelve confessors is Tammarus, or, as another manuscript has it, Zammarus; Ferrarius, in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under 11 February, calls him Tomasus. Ughellus, following Viperanus, lists him among the bishops of Benevento in volume VIII of *Italia sacra*. Others, however—including Ferrarius, who seems to incline toward this view in the *Catalogue* cited under 15 October—believe that Thammarus of Benevento was different from our saint.

[Col. 0413A] The feast of the former is celebrated at Benevento on 15 October; his sacred relics rest beneath the high altar in the metropolitan church of that city. Michael the Monk writes in the *Capuan Sanctuary* that the memory of the African Tammarus is celebrated in the diocese of Capua on 16 January. He observes that this same confessor ended his life in the village of Pontano, formerly called Saint Tammarus and now belonging to the diocese of Aversa, and that he was buried there, in the very place where his tomb is still visited.

23. These, then, are the observations that seemed worth making concerning those holy confessors driven from Africa into Italy. Although their deeds are mixed with uncertain, doubtful, and sometimes even false material, it was nevertheless impossible to pass over them untouched, since their memory is celebrated in most of the cities of Italy.

[Col. 0413B] Indeed, even if we lacked the authority of Victor, I think no one would wish to deny that, after Africa had been devastated by the Vandals, almost countless people of every sex and social condition were dispersed from that region into various provinces, especially into Italy, which was somewhat more peaceful than the other provinces of Europe because of the presence of the emperors. We infer that many of them were bishops from the fact that, even before Augustine’s death, as Possidius affirms, only three Churches remained in Africa that still had their own bishops.

Moreover, the barbarians persecuted bishops more fiercely than others because they knew that bishops were more devoted than anyone else to the orthodox faith. Victor himself testifies that all of them were repeatedly driven from their sees under the rule of Geiseric and Huneric. Therefore, although we have listed only very few here, it must not be inferred that there were no others whom we have omitted, either because they were not sufficiently known to us or because we lacked even reasonably credible sources with which to illuminate their deeds.

[p. 264] [Col. 0413C] 24. Theonestus may serve as an example. Driven from Africa by Huneric, he is nevertheless said to have been placed by Damasus, Roman pontiff, in charge of the Church of Altinum. It is remarkable how greatly the various authors differ in describing the fate of him and his companions. They so disturb and confuse the times, places, persons, and every circumstance that absolutely nothing certain can be gathered from their writings.

Some say that there were two Theonesti who were combined into one; others maintain that there was only one. Among Theonestus’s companions, Albanus is famous. He is said to have been killed near Mainz, a city of Upper Germany, while disputing against the Arians; they also wish Ursus to have suffered the same fate at Augusta in Rhaetia. Some even report that Theonestus himself experienced the violent hands of the Arians. They say that, near Treviso in Italy, he was killed by those raging heretics together with two other companions, namely Tabra and Tabrata.

[Col. 0413D] Some, however, think that Albanus, Ursus, and Theonestus himself—the last of whom is especially venerated at Vercelli—were soldiers of the Theban Legion, and that later writers carelessly transferred them to the period of the Arians. Thus Ferrarius, in his *Life of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli*, distinguishes two Theonesti: one of Vercelli, who completed his martyrdom under the emperor Maximian together with his companions Ursus and Albanus, from the Theban Legion; and another, the bishop of Altinum, who had Tabra and Tabrata as companions.

Ferrarius follows the same opinion in his *General Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, where he commemorates Theonestus of Vercelli on 20 November and Theonestus, bishop of Altinum, on 22 November. The people of Mainz, however, claim that their Albanus was a disciple of Bishop Theonestus, whose companions likewise were Tabra and Tabrata. They call these men Tabraamus and Tabrothaamus, names which Serarius thinks are Punic.

But it is not possible to linger longer over resolving—or rather, merely presenting—these difficulties. Anyone who wants more should consult the aforementioned book by Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli and a most learned man, *The Life of Saint Eusebius*, pp. 121 ff., and Nicholas Serarius, S.J., priest, book II of *Moguntine Affairs*, especially chapters 27 and 28. There he discusses Saint Albanus and his companions at length and with learning; under their name there formerly existed near that same city a noble monastery of our Benedictine order.

[Col. 0414A] I should nevertheless point out that the name Honorius has intruded into the history of Albanus’s life, as it has into most of the Lives of the saints of that age, in place of Huneric. I think this happened through the ignorance of copyists who knew the name of the emperor Honorius better than his character and substituted him for Huneric—or, as the older manuscripts generally have it, Honoricus—who was no less a raging Arian than an impious tyrant.

Hence there arose in many of these narratives such formulas as “while the persecution of the emperor Honorius raged,” and “when Honorius was a most savage persecutor,” along with similar expressions. These led others to alter even the names of popes and other details which they saw did not sufficiently accord with the period of Honorius in the earlier accounts. Thus everything was thrown into confusion, and those narratives lost all their authority.

[Col. 0414B] 25. No more certain are the accounts given by the citizens of Mirandola, a town in Lombardy, concerning Possidius, bishop of Calama, the friend of Saint Augustine and author of his Life. These citizens boast that they possess the body of this holy man.

Nothing else has been established concerning the matter except that the relics of a certain Saint Posidonius, a priest or bishop, were transferred to this place from Apulia in the ninth century, as [p. 265] Daniel Papebrochius observed under 17 May in the Bollandists, where he discusses the matter at length.

Yet somehow he came to claim there that Possidius and Posidonius were different names. To prove this, he observed that the bishop of Calama is called Possidius in the Conference of Carthage, whereas Posidonius, who is listed in chapter 127, conference 1, of that same gathering, was a bishop of the “upper place”—as though those words indicated some city so named.

It is astonishing, I say, that this learned man did not notice that Posidonius mentioned there, together with Vitalis, Donatus, and the others whom he observes are called bishops of the “upper place” or “upper city,” were Donatists. They were bishops of their own sect in the upper place or city—that is, in the same see as the Catholic bishop who had been named immediately before.

[Col. 0414C] Thus Faustinus, the Catholic bishop of the plebs of Sillium, was listed by the notary as saying: “I am present.” Immediately afterward Posidonius of the upper place—that is, of Sillium—appeared on Donatus’s side and said: “I acknowledge him.” In other words, the Donatist bishop of Sillium admitted that he acknowledged the Catholic bishop of Sillium.

26. Finally, there are other confessors who are said to have arrived from Africa in Italy during the time of the Vandal persecution. But since most authors assert that they lived down to the time of Totila, king of the Goths, it seemed preferable to refer their exile to the persecution of Trasamund.

# CHAPTER X  
## The Persecution of the Vandals in Africa under King Guntabund

[Col. 0414D] 1. After Huneric’s death, Guntabund—or, as others write, Guntamund—obtained the rule of the Vandals in Africa toward the end of the year 484. Huneric, who had succeeded his father in the beginning of the year 477, had reigned almost eight full years.

The author of the fragment already cited explains the matter accurately. It was added to Prosper’s *Chronicle* in Canisius’s first volume of *Ancient Readings*, where Huneric is said to have held the Vandal kingdom in Africa for seven years, ten months, and twenty-two days. From this it is clear that he died on the Ides of December, since, as we inferred above from the same fragment in chapter 7, section 1, he had succeeded his deceased father on 25 January.

Procopius writes in book I of *The Vandalic War* that Guntabund was the son of Genzon, Geiseric’s son. Some think that he was the Godagis mentioned by Victor of Vita in book II, section 5. He obtained the kingdom in preference to Huneric’s son Hilderic because he was the eldest of Geiseric’s children.

[Col. 0415A] Geiseric, the founder of the Vandal kingdom in Africa, had indeed ordered in his will, as we have already observed, that the kingdom should always pass to the eldest among all those of his agnatic line.

2. There is disagreement among the authors as to whether this Guntabund should be counted among the persecutors of the orthodox, since writers—including ancient writers—do not hold a single opinion on the matter. Procopius, in book I of *The Vandalic War*, explicitly states that the Catholics were harassed during his reign.

“This Gundemund,” he says, “after fighting many battles against the Moors and treating the Christians most harshly, died of illness.” From these words Baronius inferred that Guntabund was removed by God from the life of men because he had renewed a persecution after it had been interrupted for some time. During that persecution, he thinks, Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, was expelled from his see for the second time and [p. 266] sent to Gaul, where he ended his life.

[Col. 0415B] The same opinion seems to be supported by a letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops of Dardania, issued at the beginning of the year 495, as we have already observed, and therefore while Guntabund was still reigning. In it the blessed pontiff praises Saint Eugenius because, together with other colleagues of his rank, he had steadfastly resisted the fury of the Vandals in defense of the Catholic faith, and because, at the very time when Gelasius was writing, he continued to resist.

By these words Gelasius clearly wished to indicate both what Eugenius had done with the other African bishops at the Conference of Carthage and what he was suffering under Guntabund’s rule.

Saint Isidore of Seville, however, embraced an entirely opposite view. In his brief *History of the Vandals*, he concludes Guntabund’s entire reign in the year 514 of the era with these words:

“Huneric was succeeded by Guntamund, who reigned for twelve years. He immediately restored peace to the Church and recalled the Catholics from exile.”

[Col. 0415C] Victor of Tunnuna, himself a bishop in Africa and older than Isidore, speaks in much the same way. In his *Chronicle* he writes:

“Huneric was succeeded by Guntamund. He reigned for twelve years and immediately recalled our people from exile.”

3. The letter of Pope Felix may also be brought into the discussion. Baronius himself cites it as addressed to the African bishops during the consulship of Dynamius and Sufidius—that is, in the Christian year 488.

In this letter, after lamenting the disaster of the African Church, in which not only the common people and clergy of the lower orders but also some deacons, priests, and bishops themselves had fallen, the pontiff prescribes the manner and conditions under which those who had been polluted by a second baptism at the hands of the Arians were to be received into penance.

This same letter had already been read at the Roman council of the preceding year. Since such remedies are not usually required while persecution is raging, it is probable that at that time the African Church enjoyed some measure of peace, either granted or at least tolerated by Guntabund.

[Col. 0415D] Four African bishops attended this Roman council. Perhaps they had been sent as envoys by their colleagues to Rome so that, as Magnus Cyprian had once done, they might seek the judgment of the apostolic see concerning the restoration of those who had fallen. They should not be thought to have come there by chance, since that synod dealt almost exclusively with the needs of the African Church.

These four African prelates are called in the subscriptions Pardalius, Rusticus, Donatus, and Victor. But the Churches over which they presided, or the African province from which they came, are not indicated. If conjecture may be permitted, and if it is likely that they had attended the Conference of Carthage under Huneric, their sees can be extracted from the *Notitia Africana*.

In that work only one Pardalius is listed: the bishop of the Church of Macomades in Numidia. Two Rustici occur: the first, bishop of Tipasa in Numidia; the second, bishop of Tetcita in Byzacena. But since nineteen Donati and twenty-two Victors are listed there, it is possible to guess only recklessly which of these attended the Roman council.

[Col. 0416A] 4. The various opinions of the authors which we have just presented concerning Guntabund’s persecution may seem so far apart that it is difficult to reconcile them. Nevertheless, I think they can be tolerated to some extent if we attend to what [p. 267] is reported about King Guntabund in the *Chronicle of Prosper of Tyre*, or rather—as Henry Norisius calls it in book I, chapter 21 of his *History of Pelagianism*—in the noble fragment of the appendix to Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Henry Canisius published it from an Augsburg manuscript in volume I of *Ancient Readings*, as we have already said.

It is worthwhile to set out the author’s entire passage, since it is especially well suited to reconciling the statements about Guntabund’s reign that appear contradictory in the ancient authors. It reads as follows:

“After him”—that is, after Huneric—“Guntamund, the son of Gentunis, the brother of that King Huneric, reigned for eleven years, nine months, and eleven days. In the third year of his reign he ordered the cemetery of the holy martyr Agileus at Carthage to be given to the Catholics, after Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, had already been recalled from exile by him.

[Col. 0416B] “In the tenth year of his reign he opened the churches of the Catholics and, at the request of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, recalled all the priests of God from exile. These churches had been closed for eleven years [read ‘ten,’ as follows], six months, and five days—that is, from the eighth year of Huneric, from 7 February, until the tenth year of King Guntamund, 10 August, on which the aforesaid ten years, six months, and five days were completed. The aforementioned King Guntamund afterward lived two years and one month.”

No one can deny that this was written by an accurate and diligent man who evidently witnessed the events, since he was able to specify the months and days so carefully.

From this fragment we infer that Guntabund favored the Catholics at least in the third year of his reign. Otherwise he would not have permitted them to possess a church in the royal city itself. Indeed, it is also clear that Eugenius himself was especially acceptable to him, since he recalled him from exile long before the other orthodox bishops and afterward, at Eugenius’s request, permitted the other bishops as well to return to their sees after restoring their churches to them.

[Col. 0416C] It does not follow, however, that persecution ceased in Africa during the earlier years of Guntabund’s reign. It is much more probable that he at least permitted the persecution, and this was sufficient for the raging Arians to dare many things. Indeed, since it was not completely revoked before the tenth year of his reign, as we infer from the cited fragment, no one who remembers reading in Victor of Vita that the Arians were even more savage than the savage king Huneric can deny that throughout this entire interval the Catholics were treated most harshly by the Arians and endured many grievous afflictions.

“More cruelly,” he says in book V, section 11, “the bishops, priests, and clerics of the Arians raged than the king and the Vandals.”

5. It is certainly clear from the *Life of Fulgentius* that the persecutions of the Arians flared up again more than once during this period. When Fulgentius had withdrawn, in chapter 4, to the monastery built by blessed Bishop Faustus—not far from his own cathedral and at the very place of his exile—he was forced to leave it because, as the author of the Life says in chapter 8, “a persecution of the faith of such a kind arose again that it compelled Bishop Faustus, of holy memory, to move about through various hiding places and did not allow him to rest continually even in the monastery itself.”

[Col. 0416D] It is nevertheless clear that this persecution was directed chiefly against the bishops, since Fulgentius is said shortly afterward to have withdrawn to a neighboring monastery governed by Felix, an abbot who was his friend, where he was entirely safe from the attacks of the Arians.

We therefore readily agree with Cardinal Baronius, who asserts that this storm was raised especially against the priests because many [p. 268] Catholics who, under the pressure of Huneric’s most savage persecution, had been polluted by the Arians through repeated baptism were received into penance in accordance with the decree of the Roman council and the letter of Pope Felix.

[Col. 0417A] For this reason Felix the Arian priest persecuted Abbot Felix and Fulgentius more fiercely, because, as the author of the Life observes in chapter 10, he suspected that they had come to his homeland in order secretly to reconcile those whom he himself had perverted.

6. We cannot, however, agree with Baronius when he attributes the deaths of several martyrs to the persecution under Guntabund. In his notes on the Roman Martyrology he repeatedly writes that they suffered martyrdom around the year 490, following Peter Galesinius imprudently in this matter.

Galesinius, without legitimate foundation, transferred to the period of the Vandals various martyrs who much more probably suffered in Africa during the ancient persecutions of pagan rulers. He deceived the most learned cardinal by praising an ancient manuscript in which the memory of these saints was said to have been recorded in an old martyrology. I would not deny that he actually saw such a manuscript; but, if my conjecture does not deceive me, it contained nothing except the bare names of the martyrs.

[Col. 0417B] From these names that author assigned to the Vandal persecution, according to his own arbitrary judgment and indulging his conjectures beyond measure, several who were said to have suffered in Africa. John Bollandus and his successors, devoted lovers of sincere sacred learning, have already made this observation more than once concerning some of them.

It seemed worthwhile to bring forward a few examples here, so that no one, placing too much confidence in the testimony of such authors, might fall carelessly into error.

7. Under 27 January Galesinius writes:

“In Africa, the holy martyrs Datius, Reatrius, Aemilianus, Archiminus, Armatus, Caius, Avitus, and Adiutus, who, when the Vandals were attacking the Church of God, undertook a vigorous struggle for the faith of Christ and received the crown of martyrdom.”

To confirm this, he cites an old manuscript martyrology. I readily grant that he truly saw it, but in that work the names of the martyrs were recorded without any mention of the Vandal persecution.

[Col. 0417C] Indeed, in the old martyrology circulated under the name of Saint Jerome—which the distinguished man Franciscus Maria Florentinius, a nobleman of Lucca, edited from several published and manuscript copies—the same martyrs appear under 26, 27, or 28 January, although some of their names are slightly altered. Some of them are even commemorated there as having suffered outside Africa.

If desired, consult that author and Bollandus under 27 January. The same must be said of Saints Verulus, Secundinus, Servulus, and their twenty companions, whom Galesinius likewise writes were gloriously crowned at Hadrumetum in Africa under the persecution of the Vandals on 21 February.

Of those twenty martyrs, Baronius names Siricius, Felix, Saturninus, and Fortunatus. They are indeed listed in various ancient martyrologies cited by Florentinius and the Bollandists on the same day, but without any indication of time from which it could be inferred that they died under the Vandals rather than under the persecutions of other rulers.

[Col. 0417D] 8. The same Galesinius went further under 23 May. From a manuscript, as he himself says, and from Victor, he cites Quintius, Lucius, and Julian, who “in the Vandal persecution, having undertaken vigorous struggles for Catholic piety, were crowned as the bravest soldiers of God with crowns of victory.”

Baronius adopted these martyrs, except that in place of Quintius—or Quintus—he [p. 269] substituted Quintianus, so that he might find in Victor of Vita, book II, a bishop of that name. But this was done without any even probable foundation, as is clear from the observations made about these martyrs by Florentinius and the Bollandists under the same date.

Moreover, since Galesinius cited Victor in support of his assertion that these martyrs belonged to the Vandal persecution, although it is certain that Victor says absolutely nothing about them, why should we not also deny him credence when he cites a manuscript martyrology that differed so greatly from all the others?

[Col. 0418A] I do not wish to believe that he acted in bad faith; but he cannot be excused for indulging his conjectures beyond measure, since on such a slight foundation he transferred martyrs to the Vandal persecution solely because they were said to have suffered in Africa.

9. The same criticism applies when, under 14 March, he praises Peter and Aphrodisius as martyrs in Africa under the Vandals, saying that they are mentioned by Victor of Vita. Yet that author maintains complete silence about them.

On the basis of this passage of Galesinius, Baronius writes that the same martyrs completed their martyrdom around the year 490 and cites Usuard for the matter. But neither Usuard nor the other writers of martyrologies cited by Florentinius or the Bollandists, who mention these martyrs, say anything about the Vandal persecution. Indeed, nowhere do they join Aphrodisius—or Euphrosius—to Peter.

That all these martyrs whom we have listed from Galesinius and similar authors did not belong to the Vandal persecution can also be demonstrated by the fact that their memory is frequently found in the most ancient martyrologies cited by Florentinius. In those records not one of the more illustrious holy men whom we certainly know to have flourished in Africa under the Vandals appears.

[Col. 0418B] Who could persuade himself that Deogratias, Eugenius, Laetus, Maxima, the seven holy monks, the two Frumentii, and other famous confessors and martyrs of the same kind would be absent from those very Calendars in which several otherwise unknown persons, whom some think suffered under the same persecution, had been admitted?

No more certain are the accounts given by Andreas Saussayus in his Gallican martyrology under 23 May and 27 October concerning Florentius, who suffered near the fortress of Tyle during the Vandal persecution. He writes that this martyr was beheaded with a ploughshare while standing upon a huge rock in a river, and testifies that his sacred head was miraculously carried to Barbarian Island near Lyons, where it is honorably preserved.

[Col. 0418C] 10. The illustrious cardinal therefore proceeded more cautiously under 18 February. There he says, on the basis of Galesinius’s manuscript so often cited, that Lucius, Silvanus, Rutulus, Crassicus, Secundinus, Fructulus, and Maximus were assigned to Africa, but he admits that they suffered at an uncertain time and in an uncertain place.

Galesinius himself, however, confidently asserts that the same men—apart from *Classicus* (a form distinct from the preceding *Crassicus*), Secundinus, and Fructulus, about whom he says nothing—were cruelly tortured under the Vandal persecution and bravely endured torment and death for the Catholic faith. He also adds their ranks: he says that the first three were clerics and that Maximus was a monk.

Ghinius went further, attributing all of them without exception to the same Vandal persecution, although nothing more can be gathered from the ancient martyrologies cited by the Bollandists and Florentinius than that these martyrs were famous in Africa. If there is time, consult the authors mentioned under 17 and 18 February.

Another example should also be presented, [p. 270] from which it will be clear that Baronius himself did not adhere closely to Galesinius’s much-praised martyrology. In the published martyrologies, under 14 January, Saint Euphrasius, bishop, is commemorated. Concerning him Galesinius confidently wrote, as elsewhere:

“In Africa, the holy martyrs Euphrasius the bishop, Cyriacus the deacon, and their companions, who, tortured by the Vandals with the most dreadful punishments in defense of the Catholic faith, were crowned with a noble martyrdom.”

[Col. 0418D] In his notes, however, he warns that *Eustrathius* should be read instead of *Eupharasius*, so that he might confuse this man with Eustratius—or, as others write, Eustachius—bishop of Suffetula, who is recorded by Victor of Vita as having suffered under Geiseric.

Baronius, however, paying no attention either to Galesinius’s text or to his notes, suspects that the Euphrasius mentioned here was Euchratius, to whom Saint Cyprian wrote Letter 61 and who gave his opinion at the council of the Rebaptizers under the name of the bishop of Thenita.

[Col. 0419A] 11. It must nevertheless be admitted that authors existed before Galesinius who, without legitimate foundation, attributed certain African martyrs to the Vandal persecution. Among them Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, had committed this error long before in his *Catalogue of the Saints*.

We have an example in Saint Aquilinus and his companions, about whom he writes in book II, chapter 44:

“Aquilinus, Geminus, Eugenius, Martianus, Quintus, Theodotus, and Tryphon, martyrs in Africa, were crowned with a most glorious martyrdom under the Vandal persecution on 4 January, as Ado says.”

Galesinius, Maurolycus, and Canisius received these words, as they say, with both hands. In his notes, Baronius cites Ado through Peter as his authority for the matter. But, so far as we know, Ado never wrote this.

In Florentinius’s martyrology and in others cited by Bollandus, their commemoration is said to take place in Africa, but neither the time nor the place of their passion is indicated.

Apart from those whom we have mentioned, other martyrs may perhaps be found whom later writers imprudently attempted to transfer to the Vandal persecution. But we think it unnecessary to write more about them, since what we have presented is sufficient to warn readers against the empty conjectures of these authors.

[Col. 0419B] We have dealt with them somewhat more fully here because Baronius repeatedly assigned their martyrdom to around the year 490. Even if it were certain that they had suffered under the Vandals, he should not have assigned them to the time of Guntabund. For Guntabund never raged against the orthodox to such a degree that it could be affirmed that so savage a persecution arose during his reign. On the contrary, we know for certain that he moderated the persecution.

Indeed, before the year 490 he had already recalled Eugenius from exile and ordered the cemetery of Saint Agileus to be restored to him.

12. Whatever the indulgence of King Guntabund toward the Catholics may have been, they were nevertheless not so secure from the attacks of the Arians that they did not sometimes experience their fury.

This is clear from the example of Saint Fulgentius. When he and Abbot Felix had been forced to change their residence because the province had suddenly been disturbed by an incursion of barbarian forces, they arrived at the district of Sicca. There they were subjected to insults and beatings by a certain Arian priest and obtained the crown of a glorious confession, as the author of Fulgentius’s Life relates.

[Col. 0419C] It is easily gathered from the same author that this occurred when no persecution—at least no open persecution—had been raised against the Catholics. In chapter 11 he testifies that the bishop of the Arian sect at Carthage was prepared to avenge Fulgentius for the injuries he had received, if [p. 271] Fulgentius himself had wished to bring complaints against the Arian priest.

An Arian bishop would certainly not have dared to do this while persecution was raging. It will nevertheless be worthwhile to set out the entire account of this confession from the author of the Life, so often cited, who was a disciple of Fulgentius himself, after we have said a few words about Abbot Felix.

[Col. 0419D] 13. Felix was abbot of the monastery to which Fulgentius, as we said above, had withdrawn after spending some time in the monastery of Bishop Faustus. The humility of this most modest abbot was so great that, as soon as Fulgentius entered the monastery, he wished him to preside over the others in his own place. He did not abandon what he had begun until he had made Fulgentius at least a partner in his dignity and responsibilities, so that both were abbots of the monastery, as the author of the Life, so often cited, relates.

“Therefore,” he says in chapter 8, “Abbot Felix received Fulgentius with joy. Knowing himself unequal to his virtues, he handed over to him both the name and authority of abbot. Fulgentius, filled with zeal for humility, refused the privilege of authority. After many struggles of piety, and with the consent of the entire congregation, he endured the violence of charity and scarcely consented to become the colleague of his good partner.

“Thus the two most holy men [lacuna] undertook the good yoke of governing the congregation [lacuna] One of them, namely blessed Fulgentius, devoted himself especially to teaching the brothers; the other labored more diligently in the daily ministry [lacuna] neither doing anything without the consent of the other, and so forth.”

But now the struggle of both men for the faith must be related.

# CONFESSION OF ABBOT FELIX AND OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, LATER BISHOP OF RUSPE

[Col. 0420A] [p. 274]

# CHAPTER XI  
## The Persecution of Trasamund, King of the Vandals, in Africa

1. After the death of his brother Guntabund, Trasamund obtained the Vandal kingdom in Africa in the year 496, according to the argument of the learned Norisius in book II, chapter 21 of his *History of Pelagianism*. From the fragment cited repeatedly above, whose words we quoted in the preceding chapter, he proves that Guntabund died on 24 September in the year 496, although Baronius, Petavius, and other learned men assign Guntabund’s death to the preceding year.

2. No one has ever called into question that a persecution was stirred up by King Thrasamund against the orthodox [Col. 0420B]. But what precisely it was, how far it advanced, or which confessors or martyrs suffered in it, is not so certain, since the authors of that period did not describe it with sufficient accuracy. Certainly Procopius, in Book I of *The Vandalic War*, relates that Thrasamund—whom elsewhere he adorns with many commendations—proceeded against the Catholics more by cunning than by open force. He writes:

> His brother Thrasamund succeeded him—that is, Guntabund—and was outstanding in appearance, intelligence, and greatness of spirit. Desiring to bring the Christians over to the ancestral doctrine, however, he did not attack their bodies by force, as his predecessors had done; instead, he displayed honors and offices, was generous with money, and pretended not to know who was disobedient. Indeed, if any who had become entangled in serious crimes either by design or by chance changed their sect, he granted them immunity from their offenses.

Baronius uses these words of Procopius under the year 495 to prove that Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, had been driven into exile under Guntabund. For, as he himself says, it is not plausible [Col. 0420C] that a ruler whom Catholic writers praise as endowed with so many outstanding qualities—and whom Fulgentius himself, who certainly knew Thrasamund well, calls a king better than his father—was responsible for banishing so holy a man to such distant regions.

Yet, as it seems to us, we demonstrated above, in chapter 8, on more certain grounds that Eugenius was in fact punished with exile by Thrasamund. Nor are the arguments there advanced weakened by Procopius’ words, nor is the authority of blessed Fulgentius opposed to them. Procopius was not unaware that many confessors had been driven into exile by Thrasamund; and even if he had been unaware of it, six hundred other authors would bear witness to the fact, as Baronius himself does not deny. At the very time when Fulgentius honored Thrasamund with the praise just mentioned, Fulgentius himself, together with the other bishops of the province of Byzacena, was banished from his homeland and see.

3. It is certain, moreover, that Thrasamund began a persecution against the Catholics long before the year 508, in which we have argued that Fulgentius’ ordination took place. He had issued an edict forbidding new bishops to be appointed to the sees of deceased Catholics. The Fathers of Byzacena were ordered by the king to go into exile only after they had transgressed this law. 275 We learn from Fulgentius’ own disciple, the author of his *Life*, that Fulgentius was not ordained immediately after the edict of prohibition had been promulgated. Concerning that edict, the author writes in chapter 16:

> At that time the royal authority had forbidden bishops to be ordained, and it was not permitted to provide shepherds for peoples deprived of their pastors. Nor did the Catholic bishops immediately oppose it. Indeed, as the same author observes, Fulgentius—whom the neighboring churches ardently desired to have as their bishop—spent the period of this prohibition securely in the monastery. The orthodox did not attempt to conduct ordinations while many churches had been deprived of pastors.

Afterward, the same author says [Col. 0421A]:

> When the sacred company of the bishops who remained, having conferred together, determined to celebrate the ordination of bishops in every place contrary to the king’s command . . . a common undertaking suddenly began: they hurried eagerly to seize, bless, and consecrate priests, deacons, and any others whom the election might discover, in each place.

Meanwhile Fulgentius remained hidden, and did not return to the monastery, while he considered that bishops had been appointed to the sees nearest at hand. Since ordinations had therefore ceased long before the year 508—and since it is not plausible that, within the space of one or two years, so many bishops had died that the present danger could be met by new ordinations—we infer that this edict of prohibition was issued by Thrasamund at the beginning of his reign.

Moreover, according to the opinion of Baronius, who assigns the beginning of Saint Fulgentius’ episcopate to the year 504, Eugenius can only be said to have been driven into exile after the persecution had been openly declared. Nor should it seem strange that Eugenius, whom the Arians detested above all others, was punished with exile by Thrasamund’s [Col. 0421B] command. Guntabund had been responsible for recalling the Catholic bishops from exile, and Eugenius himself openly professed the Catholic religion at Carthage.

4. The often-mentioned author of Fulgentius’ *Life*, in chapter 16, indicates that this transgression of the royal command furnished the occasion and opportunity for open persecution. The bishops of the province of Byzacena undertook this action because they were considering either that the king’s anger, if it existed, might perhaps be appeased, so that those who had been ordained could more easily live in their own places and among their own peoples; or that, if the violence of persecution arose, those whom they found worthy of promotion might also be crowned through confession of the faith, and that they would more easily fulfill their ministry and provide consolation to their own peoples amid the tribulations themselves.

But the opposite happened entirely. For, as the same author says, when greater sorrow followed, the joy of the ordination that had been undertaken was turned into public mourning. Thrasamund grew furious because the law he himself had enacted had been violated, and immediately [Col. 0421C] decreed that all the bishops should be punished with exile.

5. The first assault of the king’s anger was borne by Victor, primate of the province of Byzacena. He was the first of all to be seized by the king’s departing servants and brought to Carthage. But, as the author of Fulgentius’ *Life* says in chapter 17:
