> So that a most faithful preacher of the Catholic faith against the Arians should not be lacking, God did not wish to conceal the chosen vessel during the time of tribulation—namely, Saint Fulgentius. The people of Ruspe, therefore, asked Victor, the primate, who had been stationed along the road, to permit them to have Fulgentius ordained as their bishop by neighboring bishops; with Victor’s consent, this was immediately done.

This took place in the year 508, as Henry Noris infers from the author of the *Life*, Book II of his *Pelagian History*, at the final chapter. He holds that the saint died in the year 533, on the Kalends of January themselves 276, after having held the see of Ruspe for twenty-six years.

6. The often-mentioned author of the *Life* [Col. 0421D], in chapter 18, sets out at length the virtues of this most blessed man in his episcopate. It will not be irrelevant to recall them briefly here, since by these practices the blessed bishop prepared himself for the crown of glorious confession. The author of the *Life* says:

> He accepted the episcopate without any ambition . . . and, having become a bishop, he did not cease to be a monk; but after receiving the dignity of a bishop, he preserved the integrity of his former profession. The integrity of his profession, moreover, gave greater adornment to the dignity of a bishop. He never sought costly clothing, never omitted his daily fasts, never ate delicately prepared foods, even among guests, and never wished, by reclining at table, even to rest or relax his rigorous resolve. Instead, he patiently wore one very cheap tunic, both in summer and in winter. He never used a stole, as all bishops do; he wore a leather belt like a monk. Thus he avoided ostentation in clothing: he did not even accept the footwear of the clergy, nor use either the outer shoes in winter or the light shoes in summer. Within the monastery [Col. 0422A] he sometimes wore sandals; he frequently walked barefoot. He neither possessed a costly chasuble or one of proud color, nor permitted his monks to possess one . . . . Trusting, with God as his witness, in his continence, he slept in the tunic in which he celebrated the sacrifice; and he used to say that at the time of the sacrifice hearts, rather than clothing, ought to be changed.

> No one ever forced this most blessed priest to eat meat of any kind. He ate only simple vegetables, gruels, and eggs—without oil as long as he was young; but after he grew old, he ate them with oil poured over them. He was persuaded to accept oil so that the growing dimness of his eyes would not impede the task of reading. When in good health, he always abstained from wine . . . . Before the brothers announced the hour of vigils, he was always awake in mind and body, either praying, reading, dictating, or devoting himself alone to some spiritual meditation . . . . Sometimes he came down to keep vigils with the servants of God, but the private vigils he held by himself, with the studies I have mentioned, were much more praiseworthy.

These were Fulgentius’ delights. Therefore, as the same author continues in chapter 19, he was never seen living anywhere without monks [Col. 0422B]. When he had been placed in charge of the Church of Ruspe, he obtained this first favor from his fellow citizens: that a monastery should be built for him. It was founded not far from the church, with the people of Ruspe eagerly contributing the expenses for its construction. Among them, Posthumianus, a most Christian and highly distinguished man among his people, is especially praised because he voluntarily offered the blessed bishop a field ideally suited to the work.

7. While the most holy bishop was wholly devoted to feeding his flock and was at the same time being trained for martyrdom through the disciplines of monastic life, suddenly, as the author of the *Life* says in chapter 20:

> Ministers of royal fury were dispatched, so that he too, once detained, might be thrust into exile in Sardinia together with the others, a noble confessor of Christ. He was swiftly led away . . . but overcame sorrow with greater joy, because he was beginning to share in so glorious a confession. Accompanied by monks and clergy alike, the outstanding master of both professions departed; while all the laypeople wept, he hurried from the chair of honor to the place of combat.

When he had been brought to Carthage [Col. 0422C], he ordered that the gifts offered to him by the faithful be sent for the benefit of his monastery, which he had begun to build at Ruspe. He himself boarded the ship with his heart crucified and his body stripped. Once established in exile, he relaxed nothing of his customary severity of life. As far as circumstances permitted, he endeavored to practice, with the few monks who had accompanied him, the same life that he had led in the monastery 277. Indeed, when two bishops, Illustrius and Januarius, had also been brought to live with him, he wisely fashioned something resembling a great monastery by uniting monks and clergy.

After describing at some length the strict discipline of life observed by Fulgentius and his companions, the author concludes:

> Who could worthily explain the praises of that dwelling? That house was then an oracle of the city of Cagliari. The afflicted came there to receive the remedy of consolation; there, among those in disagreement, faithful pacts of peace and concord were established; to those wishing to hear the divine reading more diligently, the Lord there supplied the edification of a most complete exposition. [Col. 0422D] Noble men delighted, if it were possible, to see blessed Fulgentius disputing every day, etc.

It seemed worthwhile to excerpt these passages somewhat more fully from the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, since scarcely anything else concerning this persecution of Thrasamund is found in the other ancient authors. Nor could we omit the outstanding virtues of so great a man, whose reputation alone, according to the testimony of the author of his *Life*, refreshed the people of the Church of Carthage during the persecution and stirred them to greater joys: namely, that the Catholic faith, in so great a bishop—who was both the intellect and the tongue of the others—was gloriously triumphing over heresy and its supporters.

8. This would be the place to inquire how numerous were the confessors who, in that period, were harassed by the tyrant for the truth of the faith. The often-mentioned author of the *Life* reports that more than sixty bishops were then bound in the chains of exile, besides many monks and clergy who, as may be inferred from the same author, followed their bishops into exile.

[Col. 0423A] Felicianus, afterward Fulgentius’ successor in the see of Ruspe, had lived as a priest in exile in Sardinia with the blessed bishop, as is clear from the prologue to the *Life*. The author of the *Life* himself—whom Chifflet and other learned men believe to have been Ferrandus, the celebrated deacon of the Church of Carthage—also indicates more than once that he belonged to the same company of confessors.

Other writers, even very ancient ones, report that far more bishops than this author mentions were driven from Africa into Sardinia at that time. The author speaks only of the bishops of the province of Byzacena; the others also list those expelled from other provinces. Victor of Tunnuna, certainly, a bishop in Africa who flourished under Justinian, expressly states in his *Chronicle* that one hundred and twenty bishops from all Africa were thrust into exile by Thrasamund. These are his words:

> Thrasamund, full of Arian madness, persecutes the Catholics, closes the churches of the Catholics, and sends one hundred and twenty bishops from the whole African Church into exile in Sardinia.

Isidore says the same in his brief *History of the Vandals*, under the era 526 [Col. 0423B]. The author of the *Miscellaneous History*, commonly attributed to Paul the Deacon, lists the same number. Sigebert and Marianus Scotus add five. Hermannus Contractus, however, records that two hundred and thirty bishops were afflicted by Thrasamund in Sardinia and various islands. Other writers of that period say nearly the same; it is of no use to list them individually. But the example of Eugenius of Carthage alone clearly shows that bishops from provinces other than Byzacena were also driven from their sees by Thrasamund.

9. What chiefly moves us is that, for 278 almost all of these great men, not only their deeds but even their names are completely unknown to us. What we have been able to gather concerning them from the ancient monuments of the African Church is as follows.

First, it is certain from chapter 16 of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* that Victor, primate of the entire province of Byzacena, was the first of all to be thrust into exile. The author cited above says:

> When the king’s [Col. 0423C] savagery had been aroused, he had already decreed that all should be consigned to exile. The sentence first proceeded against the very ordainer—that is, the primate—Victor by name, who had already been seized by the departing servants of the king and was being led to Carthage, etc.

Chifflet believes that this Victor was the same person who, under the name Victor of Vita, is famous for having written the history of the African persecution. We explained the basis of this conjecture in the preliminary notice to that same history, no. 6. There we also observed that Victor the primate mentioned here—whoever he ultimately was—died in exile.

Fulgentius himself was added shortly afterward to Victor and the other bishops of Byzacena who were being thrust into exile. For this reason, as the author of the *Life* relates in chapter 20, he was detained by the ministers of royal fury and brought to Carthage.

The same author, in the chapter just cited, also mentions two bishops from among those holy confessors, namely Illustrius and Januarius, who, as we observed above, lived with Fulgentius at Cagliari.

[Col. 0423D] Without doubt Quodvultdeus, the bishop who attempted to take precedence over Fulgentius at the council of Junca—for the old manuscript codices establish that it should be written *Juncensis*, and the city of Junca, not Vinca, is found in Byzacena—must also be counted among them. The holy man later voluntarily yielded precedence to him at the council of Sufes.

Finally, in the last chapter of the same *Life*, two other bishops are listed, apparently from the number of the confessors: Dacianus, primate of Byzacena, and Ponticanus—or, as others have it, Pontianus—bishop of Thenita. When he was hastening to Ruspe to choose Fulgentius’ successor, the same holy man appeared visibly to him and declared that he had already ordained his successor.

There seems to be no difficulty concerning Dacianus. Since in Africa the dignity of primate was ordinarily conferred upon the senior bishop of the province by order of ordination, Dacianus must have been senior in ordination to Fulgentius, who was never a primate, and therefore must have been deported to Sardinia with the others [Col. 0424A]. Indeed, this is the same Diacianus—or so I believe—who, in the letters of the Scythian monks that we shall presently cite, is listed first of all among the Fathers of Byzacena.

There is greater difficulty concerning Ponticanus, unless the titles “blessed” and “holy,” which the author of Fulgentius’ *Life*—contrary to his usual practice—assigns to this bishop, seem to prove that he belonged to the number of the confessors, and indeed to those who excelled in greater holiness, as may be inferred from the text of the *Life*. The author says to Felicianus, Fulgentius’ successor:

> Recall the most faithful vision of blessed Ponticanus, bishop of Thenita, etc., to whom the most blessed Fulgentius appeared during a time of quiet, and, greeting him affectionately with the friendly appearance he usually had, said: “Where is your holiness now hastening?” To which, etc.

10. We also have Pontianus as a bishop from the province of Byzacena; he took part in the council of Junca immediately after his return from Sardinia. But whether he is the same man whom we praised in the preceding section is not sufficiently clear to us. He is certainly sometimes called Ponticanus [Col. 0424B], as is evident from the letter of Boniface, bishop of Carthage, to Liberatus the primate and the other bishops of the province of Byzacena.

Under the year 546, Baronius 279 cites a letter of Pontianus, an African bishop, to the emperor Justinian concerning the celebrated controversy over the Three Chapters. From this letter, because it was written by Pontianus in the name of several bishops, Chifflet infers that its author was primate of the province, and perhaps the very Pontianus whom we have praised from the *Life of Fulgentius* and from the council of Junca.

Even if this is not entirely certain, it is certain that Pontianus, or Ponticanus, who took part in the council of Junca, belonged to the number of the confessors, as did his colleague Restitutus. Both of them were sent from the aforementioned synod as representatives of all the bishops of the province of Byzacena to the council of Carthage, which Boniface convened immediately after his ordination.

Finally, Liberatus, primate of the same province of Byzacena, must with complete certainty be counted among these confessors. Immediately after his return from exile, he presided under that name over the often-mentioned council of Junca. On these matters, see Volume IV of the Labbe edition of the Councils, column 1627 and following.

11. Several more of these holy confessors became known to us through the Scythian monks. They had been sent to Rome because of certain questions raised in the East and wrote to Fulgentius and his other colleagues exiled with him in Sardinia, seeking their judgment concerning the questions under discussion.

Among the works of Saint Fulgentius there is a letter, or book, written on that occasion by the deacon Peter and his other brethren. Its inscription lists seven of these confessors. It reads:

> To the most holy lords, worthy to be named with all veneration, Datianus—some published editions have *Diaconus*—Fortunatus, Albanus, Orontius, Boethus, Fulgentius, Januarius, and the other bishops adorned by their confession of Christ: the insignificant deacon Peter, John, Leontius, another John, and the other brothers sent to Rome in the cause of the faith.

The African Fathers [Col. 0424D] replied, fifteen in number—that is, nine besides those mentioned in the preceding letter. Albanus, who was listed in the earlier letter, does not appear in this reply, perhaps because he had already died. They are listed in the following order:

> Datianus, Fortunatus, Boethus, Victor, Scholasticus, Orontius, Vindicianus, Victor, Januarius, Victorianus, Photinus, Quodvultdeus, Fulgentius, Felix, and Januarius.

All of these, except Fulgentius, Felix, and Januarius, wrote another letter to John the archimandrite and the deacon Venerius concerning the grace of God and human free choice. It is surprising that Fulgentius’ name is absent from the inscription of this letter, since it is thought to be his work and has been published among his other works.

Such, then, are the names of the bishops exiled from the province of Byzacena that we have been able to gather from the more certain monuments of the Church.

12. During the same period there was also the celebrated African bishop Possessor, though his province is uncertain. At Constantinople [Col. 0425A] he fought brilliantly against the emperor Anastasius, Timothy, the bishop of that city, and other supporters of the Eutychian heresy.

A letter of Pope Hormisdas of Rome to this same Possessor survives on this matter. In it Hormisdas praises his faith and steadfastness splendidly and urges him to persevere in what he had begun. He writes:

> Hearing of the excellent earnestness of your charity, and recognizing the path of right living which you defend without tumult, we continually give thanks to our God, so that you may persist in that disposition 280 and offer the others an example to follow. These are heavenly gifts; these are signs of divine recompense; these are the judgments of God, which have not permitted you to be separated from the fellowship of Catholic priests. Therefore, dearest brother, by this present address we exhort you to persevere in the steadfastness with which you began, and to add growth to beginnings worthy of approval. For a good work, especially one that concerns the teaching of the faith, seems to diminish unless it continually grows. And if worldly tribulation should occur, setting the rewards to come before your eyes, we counsel you with apostolic admonition: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us,” etc. (Romans 8).

We have thought it worthwhile to report this somewhat more fully, since there can scarcely be any doubt that Possessor was driven from Africa by the Arians because of his defense of the Catholic faith. Cardinal Baronius does not hesitate to affirm this under the year 517. He also says much about the same Possessor under the year 520, where he publishes the letters written by Possessor to Hormisdas and by Hormisdas to Possessor on the occasion of John Maxentius and the Scythian monks.

The Fathers of Byzacena, in the fifteenth of the letters attributed to Fulgentius, addressed to John and Venerius, mention the letter of Hormisdas written to Possessor; there they call the same bishop “our holy brother and fellow priest Possessor.”

Baronius also counts among the confessors, under the year 504, the blessed bishop Primasianus, an African bishop whose exposition of the Apocalypse Cassiodorus praises in chapter 9 of the *Divine Institutions* [Col. 0425C].

Boniface mentions Optatus of Sitifis, detained by royal command, at the Council of Carthage in the year 525. But he does not state why, when the others had been restored, this man was forbidden to return to his church.

Maracinus, a bishop who subscribed to the Second Council of Toledo in the year 531, may perhaps also be included here. His subscription reads:

> Maracinus, bishop in the name of Christ, assigned to exile in the city of Toledo on account of the Catholic faith . . . I attended, reread, and subscribed.

Finally, during the same period Pomerius flourished in Gaul. According to Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, he was a Moor by nationality.

13. If we follow the traditions of certain Italian churches, we must further admit that several confessors driven from Africa arrived in Italy under Thrasamund. Since they are said to have flourished in those regions under Totila, king of the Goths, their exile cannot be referred to the earlier persecutions that arose before Thrasamund’s time. Otherwise those holy men would have come to Italy before the year 496, when Guntabund [Col. 0425D]—Thrasamund’s predecessor—died; yet more than forty years later, after Totila had assumed the Gothic kingdom in Italy—not before the year 541—they would still be said to have been placed over various churches. I think no one would easily persuade himself of this.

The most prominent of them was Regulus. According to the Roman Martyrology under September 1, he came from Africa to Italy and completed his martyrdom at Populonia in Umbria under King Totila.

Cerbonius is said to have been his disciple. Ughelli lists him first among all the bishops of Populonia in Volume III of *Sacred Italy*.

In Volume I, the same author lists Justus the African as second among the bishops of Volterra. Fleeing the persecution of the Vandals, Justus came to Italy, where the people of Volterra elected him bishop. He was assisted in his pastoral ministry by his brother Clement and by his colleague Octavianus.

Ferrarius also includes Bishop Felix in his 281 [Col. 0426A] general *Catalogue* under September 1, the same day on which, as we have said, the feast of Regulus is celebrated. He also includes him under September 3, which he says is sacred under the name of Octavianus; he likewise celebrates Justus and Clement, but on June 5.

14. Several others might be added whom the Sardinians, and especially the people of Cagliari, claim were buried among them. We do not wish to deny that, among the great multitude of confessors who endured exile on the island of Sardinia, many died before returning to their homeland. Yet we have not so far been able to find suitable monuments from which their names could be listed here.

Certainly, from the single inscription that Papebrochius presents under May 20 in Volume V of the Bollandists, we can easily infer that such documents are altogether uncertain and without authority. It reads:

> + Saint Januarius, bishop and martyr; Saint Ludovicus, bishop and martyr; and Saint Egidianus, bishop and martyr [Col. 0426B] are Africans.

There is no opportunity here to discuss the defects of this inscription individually. The single name Ludovicus—at that time used neither among the Africans nor among the Romans, and not even written in this form among the barbarians—is more than sufficient to prove that these monuments are wholly suspect, being corrupted, if not entirely fabricated.

The various inscriptions found in the ruins of the Church of Turris in the preceding century by Gavinus, archbishop of that place, or of Sassari, are of better quality. But they contribute absolutely nothing to elucidating the history of the African persecution. See them in Jacobus Pintus, Book III, *On the Crucified Christ*, title 4, section 12.

1. But, to return to the subject from which the discussion has digressed somewhat, Symmachus, who presided over the Apostolic See while the persecution of Thrasamund was raging in Africa, received news of so savage a storm against the Catholic Church. Believing it his duty to strengthen his brothers, who were placed amid tribulations and hardships [Col. 0426C], he composed an outstanding letter to them, exhorting them both to endure the labors of exile with equanimity and to maintain steadfastness in defending the cause of the Church. We have this letter in Ennodius, Book II, Letter 14, and it seemed worthwhile to reproduce it here from that source.

**LETTER OF POPE SYMMACHUS TO THE BISHOPS DEPORTED TO SARDINIA**

*(We shall publish this letter together with the works of Symmachus.)*

282 16. From this concern for gathering relics, with which we infer that these confessors were ardently occupied from the aforementioned letter of Symmachus, support may be given to the tradition of several Italian churches. They claim to preserve the bodies of holy martyrs brought from Africa by these confessors.

Cardinal Baronius thinks that among these were the relics of the holy martyrs Marcellus, Castus, Aemilius, and Saturninus, in his notes to the Roman Martyrology under October 6 [Col. 0426D], on which their feast is celebrated 283 at Capua. Ferrarius also mentions Castus and Cassius, celebrated bishops there, in his general *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under November 7.

Other relics are said to be found in other churches, but it is not worth the effort to list them individually.

At Naples, indeed, on the occasion of the translation to that city of Saint Severinus, apostle of Noricum, Baronius congratulates the city under the year 496 because it had always been remarkably devoted to the relics of holy martyrs and confessors. It was not satisfied merely to receive Saint Januarius from nearby—he was bishop of Beneventum—or to be enriched from distant Africa with such treasures, but also obtained from the holy pontiff Gelasius the sacred remains of Saint Severinus, brought to Italy from the banks of the Danube.

17. Among the other treasures that the African bishops brought with them to Sardinia, one of the most precious [Col. 0427A] was certainly the body of blessed Augustine.

Although no writer of that period mentions its translation, we know with complete certainty from subsequent events that it took place then. It is established that at the beginning of the eighth century the body of the most holy Doctor was transferred from Sardinia to the suburban monastery of Pavia, already called Coelum-Aureum, by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, when Sardinia was being devastated by the Saracens. Ferrarius says in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under May 7 that this was done at the urging of Peter, bishop of Pavia.

At that time it was universally believed that the relics of the same holy Doctor had been brought to the island by the holy confessors whom the Arian Vandals had driven from Africa into exile. We have as a witness to this Peter Oldradus, bishop of Milan, who, by order of Charlemagne, committed the history of this translation to writing.

Baronius publishes Oldradus’ letter to the same emperor on this subject under the year 725. It contains the following:

> The body of Saint Augustine was transferred to Sardinia [Col. 0427B] by faithful and Catholic bishops who, on account of their faith in Christ, had been banished to that same island by the wicked King Thrasamund, together with Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, and countless faithful of Christ, at the time when the Vandals were ravaging Africa by force of arms. So that so great a jewel and treasure should not be defiled by unclean spirits, they carried it with them, together with some other relics of the saints. There it became famous through many miracles.

Paul the Deacon also mentions both translations in Book VI, chapter 48, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*. He writes:

> Liutprand, hearing that the Saracens, after devastating Sardinia, were also defiling those places where the bones of Augustine had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the devastation of the barbarians, sent there; and, after paying a great price, he received them and transferred them to the city of Ticinum, etc.

Bede also agrees. In his genuine *Martyrology*, under August 28, he writes:

> In Africa, Saint Augustine, bishop, who was first transferred from his own city to Sardinia because of the barbarians, and recently brought back to Ticinum by Liutprand, king of the Lombards [Col. 0427C], and honorably buried there.

The memory of this translation was celebrated in many churches and is still commemorated in various martyrologies on February 28. It took place, as our Mabillon proves in his *Italian Journey*, page 221, in the year 712. He therefore corrected what he had written in the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, where he had dated this translation to the year 722.

The monastery of Coelum-Aureum, which for a long time remained under the order of our Holy Father Benedict, passed in the thirteenth century to the canons regular, who were later joined by the Augustinian hermits. On these matters, see Baronius and Mabillon in the places cited.

284 18. But Pope Symmachus, whose consolatory letter we quoted above, aided the confessors of Christ not merely by voice or pen, but also in reality and by his deeds. Following the example of his predecessors, he shared in the sufferings of the holy confessors of Christ by supplying what was necessary for food and clothing.

Anastasius writes:

> Every year, throughout Africa or Sardinia [Col. 0427D], he supplied money and clothing to the bishops who were confined in exile.

We have another witness to this, namely the author of the *Life of Saint Avitus, Bishop of Vienne*, which the learned Philip Labbe extracted from an ancient manuscript codex and published in Volume I of the *New Library*, page 693. There we read:

> In the time of this blessed Avitus, a most grievous persecution of the Vandals and of the other peoples in Africa broke out, and Pope Symmachus supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the five hundred and fifty bishops who were in exile.

The author of the *Miscellaneous History*, under the name of Paul the Deacon, writes in Book XVII that blessed Symmachus did not cease to provide them with daily assistance. I omit Ado in his *Chronicle*, Hermannus Contractus, and other later writers who merely copied the ancients.

19. After expelling the shepherds, Trasamundus thought that he would invade the flocks without difficulty. He left nothing unattempted in order to bring the orthodox partly by force, partly by promises, and even by arguments—for he possessed eloquence and great facility of speech—to his own position, as the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* relates; he is almost the only writer we possess who composed a fuller account of that persecution.

“Meanwhile,” he says in chapter 21, “Trasamundus the king’s implacable mind and terrible anger against the Catholic religion, amid harsh persecutions and treacherous plots, by which he now compelled Catholics through terror and now enticed them by promises to deny that Christ was equal to God the Father, began to pretend that he was simply seeking an explanation of the Catholic religion, supposing that no one could be found whose assertion might convict him of his errors. Finally, he proposed many [or: to many] snares of foolish questions; and if anyone wished to answer him, he neither despised nor rejected him, but, as though listening patiently, declared that he could not be satisfied.”

To this should be referred what we observed above from Procopius: that Trasamundus persecuted the Catholics more by cunning than by tortures. Yet everyone can see that this persecution was much more dangerous than the others. Nevertheless, God did not permit the faithful orthodox to be deprived of the help they needed in these difficulties. For, as the same author says, many religious men, through the steadfastness of their bold faith, took advantage of opportunities prepared by the Lord to convict the zealous king of his blasphemies.

20. There were also some who lacked the ability to respond to the king’s objections or to those of others. They therefore wrote letters to the exiled bishops, so that from them they might learn by what method the quibbles of the heretics could be refuted. Several treatises on this subject are extant among Fulgentius’s works, by which he strengthened the absent in the faith.

Thus, in his book *On Orthodox Faith*, he instructed Donatus, whom the Arians were attempting to recall from the true faith by proposing various questions against Christ’s equality with the Father. He also wrote to Felix the Notary, so that he might more easily avoid the snares of the heretics with whom he had to associate.

In the second book addressed to Monimus, which Monimus himself, reporting to Fulgentius, called “outstanding,” he refutes the Arians’ question concerning the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood—a question that many thought was offered to the Father alone:

“Why,” he says in chapter 6, “should the Son himself be unable to sanctify the sacrifice of his body which we offer, when he himself sanctified his body, which he offered in order to redeem us?”

So great, moreover, was Fulgentius’s authority, even when he was absent, that, as the author of his *Life* says in chapter 20, whenever anyone in any community of the exiled priests attempted in agitation to cause trouble or to despise the commands of his own bishop, he was rebuked in his absence at the dictation of blessed Fulgentius in such a way that, seeking the remedy of satisfaction, he would immediately become present after crossing the sea.

21. Trasamundus, seized by a desire to see and hear so great a man, ordered him to be brought from Sardinia to Carthage. After he had quickly sent him certain writings to read, filled with the poison of treachery, the holy bishop answered them so plainly that, although the king praised his wisdom and extolled his humility, he nevertheless did not deserve, because of his obstinate mind, to understand the truth.

Meanwhile, when the people of Carthage, interpreters of a spiritual triumph, openly acknowledged with joyful murmuring that the king’s propositions had been refuted, and gloried in the Catholic faith as always victorious, they also celebrated the praises of blessed Fulgentius.

A little later the unbelieving king attempted to enter a second battle. He sent Fulgentius new questions, by which he supposed that nearly every opportunity for reflection or writing had been taken away from him, and that he would never be able to give an adequate answer. But how far that cunning ruler was cast down from his expectation is shown by Fulgentius’s three books addressed to Trasamundus, which the blessed bishop composed on that occasion.

With the same ease he refuted Pinta, an Arian bishop who had attempted to avenge the defeated king, in a separate book published against him.

It is astonishing how greatly Fulgentius then benefited the Catholic religion. As the frequently mentioned author of his *Life* testifies in chapter 21, he taught some who had already been rebaptized to lament their error and reconciled them; he warned others not to destroy their souls for the sake of earthly advantages; and those whom he sensed to be already near perdition he soothed with such gentle words that, because of his benevolence, they were ashamed to carry out the wickedness they had conceived and quickly returned to repentance.

Others, strengthened by his words and seasoned with the salt of his teaching, rebuked the Arian heretics with complete confidence. Thus, by a marvelous grace, it came about that through the ministry of persecution the Catholic faith received increase rather than decline.

Indeed, in chapter 24 the Arians complain that Fulgentius’s teaching had prevailed so greatly that “he reconciles some of your priests”—they address the king—“to the Church. Therefore, unless you come to our aid quickly, our religion will fail, and everyone baptized by us, once publicly reconciled, will again preach *homoousion*. Nor, even if you wish to stir up persecution, will royal savagery be capable of inspiring fear. For the presence of Fulgentius greatly strengthens and makes steadfast all the bishops.”

22. The Arians therefore left nothing unattempted to drive Fulgentius from Carthage. But Trasamundus could not agree with them. Whether because he revered the blessed bishop’s teaching and virtues and did not wish to decide anything against him, or because by doing so he would seem openly to confess that he had been defeated by him, he wanted to retain him longer within Carthage.

Only under great pressure, then, and when his own supporters insistently represented to him that otherwise they would labor in vain against the Catholics, and that their diligence could accomplish nothing for their sect so long as Fulgentius remained in Africa, did he reluctantly and almost unwillingly agree that he should again be carried into exile—yet on the condition that this should be done at night and secretly from the people.

But God willed that the triumph of his servant should be public. For, because contrary winds were blowing, Fulgentius spent many days on the shore, so that almost the entire city gathered there for many days and, bidding him farewell, received Communion from his hand.

Afterward, when the weather became calm, he was carried back to Sardinia. This restored joy to the hearts of the fellow bishops in exile, while Christians from every direction hastened with gladness to see the strongest athlete of Christ, who in single combat had broken the violent assault of the raging king and had returned to the divine camp adorned with distinguished laurels.

When Fulgentius had returned to exile, he built a monastery, with the permission of Brumatius—or, as others write, Primasius or Viliatcus—the bishop of Caralis, near the basilica of the holy martyr Saturninus outside the city walls. There, having gathered more than forty brothers, he preserved the order of coenobitic discipline unimpaired. By the example of his stricter life and by his writings, with which he enlightened the Church, he increased the glory of his confession and remained there until Trasamundus’s death.

23. What Trasamundus decreed against the orthodox after Fulgentius’s departure from Africa, the authors do not report. It is nevertheless plausible that, once so invincible a defender of the faith had been removed, the Arians aggravated the king’s hostility against the others.

The frequently mentioned author of Fulgentius’s *Life* records that at that time Fulgentius sent the people of Carthage a letter distinguished by lofty exhortation, in which he set out, with the gravest lamentation, almost all the deceits and seductive flatteries by which wretched souls were being led astray to death.

Fulgentius himself—or whoever else wrote the book included among his works against Pinta, then an Arian bishop—indicates that open violence was inflicted upon the orthodox. In section 4 it is shown that the faith then grew through the exiles of the innocent, the proscriptions of the wretched, and the tortures and oppression of captives.

The same may be inferred from a letter of Boniface, bishop of Carthage, to Missor, primate of Numidia, written in the second year of Hildericus, where he says:

“After the almost continual burden of the gravest tribulation which the Church throughout the entire province of Africa endured in common.”

Felix Zactarensis, bishop and legate of Numidia to the Council of Carthage under the same Boniface, speaks in nearly the same way:

“After the deadly dangers by which episcopal dignity was narrowly confined and oppressed.”

Indeed, no one can deny that Trasamundus burned fiercely against the Catholics, since it is clear that he persecuted them not only while alive but, as far as he was able, even after death. For, when he was close to death, as Victor of Tunnuna and other authors also assert, he bound Hildericus, who was to succeed him, by an oath never either to return the churches to the Catholics or to restore their privileges.

How hostile the Vandals then were to the Catholics may be inferred from a single example which Procopius, although excessively favorable to Trasamundus in other respects, inserted in book I of his *History of the Vandals*. He says that the Vandals were preparing to wage war against the Moors who lived around Tripoli. On the very first day, as soon as they had pitched their camp, they brought horses and other animals into the Christian churches, indulged their lust without refraining from any insult, and forced the priests whom they encountered—after striking them in the face and beating their backs repeatedly—to perform the tasks usually imposed upon the vilest slaves. Nor did the Vandals cease committing the same offenses each day along the way.

But by provoking God’s vengeance against themselves through these and similar crimes, they were put to flight and utterly defeated by the barbarians. A short time later Trasamundus, worn down by grief, departed this life in the year 523, on 28 May, as Norisius proves in book II, chapter 21 of his *Pelagian History*.

## CHAPTER XII. Peace Restored to the African Church

1. With Trasamundus’s death, the condition of the African Church was completely changed. “The remarkable goodness,” says the author of Fulgentius’s *Life* in chapter 28, “of Hildericus at the beginning of his reign restored liberty to the Catholic Church established throughout Africa, gave the people of Carthage their own bishop, and with the most merciful authority ordered episcopal ordinations to be carried out everywhere.”

An old author of a fragment appended to the chronicle of Tiro, preserved by Canisius, testifies that at the beginning of his reign Hildericus ordered Boniface’s ordination to take place in the church of Saint Agileus at Carthage, after liberty had been restored to all Catholics.

Victor of Tunnuna, however, maintains in his *Chronicle* that Hildericus did this before he assumed the kingdom. As we stated above, he had been bound by an oath to Trasamundus not to restore liberty to the Catholics once he had obtained the kingdom.

“Hildericus,” he says, “who was born from the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, captured by Gaiseric and joined to Huneric, reigned seven years and three months. Though bound by an oath from his predecessor Trasamundus not to open churches or restore privileges to the Catholics in his kingdom, before he became king—and without overstepping the terms of his oath—he ordered the Catholic priests to return from exile and the churches to be opened; and, at the request of the entire city of Carthage, he consecrated Boniface, sufficiently vigorous in divine doctrines, as bishop of the Church.”

Isidore gives the same testimony in his brief *Chronicle of the Vandals*, under the year 553 of the Spanish era.

Hildericus’s great benevolence toward the Catholics persuaded some that he had professed the Catholic faith, which he had received from his mother Eudoxia. Others, however, think that this should rather be attributed to his innate gentleness, since, according to Procopius, he had never been burdensome to anyone, whether Catholic or otherwise.

2. The author of the same saint Fulgentius’s *Life*, chapter 29, describes the devotion of the people of Carthage, who joyfully welcomed the holy confessors, especially Fulgentius, as they returned from exile:

“Divine praise,” he says, “resounded from every tongue. For the people, following and preceding them, celebrated the noble triumph of the blessed confessors as they proceeded to the basilica of Saint Agileus. But the affection of all for blessed Fulgentius was extraordinary.

“When Fulgentius’s face appeared, an immense cry arose, as everyone disputed who should first greet and recognize him, who should place his head beneath the bishop’s blessing hand, who might deserve to touch the one walking by his extremities or at least his fingers, and who might see him even while standing at a distance.

“When an immense rain suddenly came upon them, the people’s gathering was not hindered. Rather, the faith of the nobles grew so great that, gladly spreading their cloaks over blessed Fulgentius, they drove back the rain and ingeniously constructed a new kind of tabernacle through their loving devotion.”

Here it is worth observing the great piety of the blessed confessors. Returning from a long journey, as soon as they reached the shore they disembarked and immediately hurried to the church of Saint Agileus, intending to offer public thanksgiving to God. Indeed, as the praised author of the *Life* says a little later, when Boniface, a bishop of holy memory, had scarcely approached, they all appeared before him, blessed him, and together praised God.

3. After several days Fulgentius set out for Ruspa. Throughout all the roads of his long journey he encountered still greater rejoicing, as peoples from every direction hastened to meet him with lamps, torches, and branches of trees, giving thanks to the ineffable God. Throughout all the churches he was received as their own bishop.

Restored to his see, he lived together with his monks, yet in such a way that he did nothing concerning the affairs belonging to the monastery without the knowledge of Abbot Felix. He often took monks into ecclesiastical service, regulating everything so carefully that no dispute ever arose between the monks and the clergy.

The same author of the *Life* provides much more concerning Fulgentius’s diligence in governing the people and the various books he published in defense of the Catholic faith. But to discuss these matters more fully does not belong to our present purpose.

It is nevertheless impossible to omit the outstanding example of supreme humility reported by the author of his *Life* in chapter 29. When, after his return from exile, the Byzacene fathers had assembled at the Council of Juncus to restore ecclesiastical discipline, Fulgentius was preferred by the judgment of all to Bishop Quodvultdeus, who considered himself senior to him. At the time the blessed bishop silently accepted this, lest he seem to diminish the authority of the council by making excuses.

But shortly afterward, at the Synod of Sufes, he poured forth humble prayers before all the Fathers, asking that Quodvultdeus should be placed before him according to his own wish, because he feared that his honor might cause scandal to his brother. He judged it better to become lesser through charity than greater without charity.

While he devoted himself entirely to repairing the ruins of his Church—and while Boniface, bishop of Carthage, was also arranging for this throughout Africa by convening a general council of the whole of Africa, held in the year 525—Fulgentius, longing for a more perfect life, withdrew with a few brothers to the island of Circina. There, shortly afterward, he remained in sound mind until his final hour. As the author of his *Life* says, he departed this life on the Kalends of January, after celebrating Vespers, in the twenty-fifth year after he had been placed over the Church of Ruspa and in the sixty-fifth year of his age. Henry Norisius proves in book II, at the final chapter of his *Pelagian History*, that these words indicate the year 533 of the common era.

The more recent as well as the ancient martyrologies commemorate Fulgentius on 1 January. The Catholic Church rightly venerates him as a most holy teacher, a most vigilant bishop, and an invincible confessor of Christ.

4. The peace granted by Hildericus was, however, only a kind of prelude to that profound tranquility which the African Church attained a few years later. For Gelimer, born of Gelilaris, the son of Genseric, to whom the kingdom of the Vandals belonged after Trasamundus’s death, impatient of delay, expelled Hildericus and seized the kingdom in the year 531.

Hildericus’s character favored his rebellion. He was so timid that he could not even endure the sight of a sword. Moreover, Hildericus had alienated the Goths because of the death of Amalafrida, the daughter of the great Theodoric.

She had married Trasamundus. But after her husband’s death, as Victor of Tunnuna relates, she fled to the barbarians and was intercepted in battle near Capsa, close to the desert; shortly afterward she was put to death in custody [the printed text is uncertain]. Athalaricus, the son of Amalasuntha and grandson of Theodoric, who ruled the Ostrogoths in Italy, took this badly and complained about it to Cassiodorus in book IX of the *Variae*, letter 1, addressed to Hildericus. There he says that Amalafrida’s death had been violent and threatens that he would soon avenge with arms the murder of the queen born from the blood of the Amali, unless satisfaction were given to her and to the entire Gothic people.

Procopius writes in book I of his *Vandalic History* that Amalafrida was held in chains and that all the Goths were killed by the Vandals, having been accused of plotting revolution to the ruin of the king and kingdom.

We do not, however, read that the Goths attempted anything against Hildericus at that time; perhaps Hildericus was shortly afterward thrown from the throne by Gelimer without much difficulty. The tyrant, who was aspiring to the kingdom, had doubtless appeased their feelings.

The praised Procopius testifies that Theodoric did not avenge these injuries because he judged himself insufficiently strong in naval power to seek Africa.

Hildericus was nevertheless supported by Justinus Augustus and by Justinian, who shortly afterward obtained the imperial power, because Hildericus, born from Eudoxia his mother, was related to the Roman emperors.

Indeed, after Justinian became emperor and Gelimer had overthrown Hildericus, he broke the treaty once made between Zeno and King Genseric. Having assembled a huge army, he recovered all Africa through the general Belisarius, who defeated and captured Gelimer and shortly afterward brought him to Constantinople in triumph. Procopius gives a full account of this in his books *On the Vandalic War*.

The same author vividly depicts Belisarius’s triumph. On that occasion Gelimer provided, both in deed and in word, a striking example of the fragility of human affairs. He was led to the circus together with the royal princes and other Vandal nobles, who were distinguished either by birth or even by the height of their bodies. As soon as he saw the emperor seated on a lofty throne and considered the depths of misfortune to which he himself had fallen, he did not give way to tears or lamentations, but broke into these words taken from the sacred books:

“Vanity of vanities, vanity.”

Procopius lists the more valuable spoils brought back from the Vandals and carried in the triumph. “They included,” says the praised author, “the things customarily used in serving the Vandal king: golden thrones and carriages that had carried the royal matron; in addition, an astonishing splendor of gems; golden cups and whatever other adornments of the royal table there were. There were also several hundred thousand pounds of silver and other objects of immense value, which Gaiseric had taken after once plundering the Roman palace. Among them were the things that Titus Vespasian had brought to Rome after the capture of Jerusalem.”

Justinian the emperor testifies in the *Code*, book I, title 27, that all the imperial ornaments which Genseric had transferred to Africa after capturing Rome were restored to him.

In the following year, which was 535 of the common era, Belisarius became consul and triumphed in the manner of the ancient consuls. According to Procopius, he was carried on the shoulders of captives and placed upon a chariot; from there he scattered among the people objects taken from the Vandal spoils—silver vessels, golden belts, and various instruments of royal luxury—which the crowd received with loud applause.

5. The greatest fruit of this victory, however, was peace for the African Church. Everyone admits that the persecution—which some maintain had grown fierce again under Gelimer’s tyranny—was at that time completely extinguished.

Certainly no one will persuade himself that Gelimer favored the Catholics. Everyone agrees that he was exceedingly savage even toward his own people—not to mention Hildericus, an excellent prince, whom he cruelly ordered to be killed together with his other kinsmen, as Victor of Tunnuna testifies in his *Chronicle*, under the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus. This author repeatedly observes that many African nobles were killed by the same king, whose property he afterward plundered by lawful and unlawful means.

We infer from Procopius that Gelimer was most devoted to the Arian sect. In book II of *The Vandalic War*, Procopius relates that Gelimer was indeed given by Justinian beautiful estates in Galaria, where he lived with his relatives, but that he did not obtain the dignity of patrician because he refused to depart from the teachings of Arius.

6. Africa was therefore recovered by the Romans in the twelfth indiction, during the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus and the consulship of Paulinus—that is, in the year 534 of the common era—after one hundred and seven years had passed since it had been occupied by the Vandals.

At the same time the city of Carthage was restored to the empire, in the ninety-fifth year after it had been captured by Genseric.

Justinian Augustus offered public thanksgiving to Almighty God on this account in the constitution concerning the office of the praetorian prefect of Africa, found in Justinian’s *Code*, book I, title 27. There he congratulates himself on the great benefit granted to him by God:

“We cannot comprehend in our mind or express with our tongue what thanks or what praises we ought to offer to the Lord our God Jesus Christ. We have indeed previously received many gifts from God and acknowledge his innumerable benefits toward us, for which we recognize that we have done nothing worthy. Above all, however, this deed, which Almighty God has now deigned to display through us for his praise and for his name, surpasses all the wondrous works that have occurred in the world: that Africa should through us recover its liberty in so short a time, after having been held captive by the Vandals for ninety-five years, those who had been enemies alike of souls and bodies.

“For they transferred souls to their treachery by rebaptizing them, since they could not endure various tortures and punishments; but they subjected bodies distinguished by free birth to the barbarian yoke with the greatest severity. They also defiled God’s most sacred churches with their treachery, and made some of them stables.

“We saw venerable men who, after their tongues had been torn out by the roots, spoke of their sufferings miserably—or, as I would rather read, miraculously. Others, after enduring various tortures and being scattered through various provinces, spent their lives in exile.

“With what speech, then, or by what deeds can we offer God worthy thanks?” etc.

In this constitution the emperor wishes Africa to be restored to its former condition and to enjoy the same privileges that it had previously possessed. In addition to the praetorian prefect, whom he ordered to reside at Carthage, he appointed other officials who were to have their own seats in the larger cities throughout the various regions of Africa, and he assigned stipends individually to all of them.

He divided the African diocese into seven provinces: namely, Tingitana; Carthage, formerly called Proconsularis; Byzacium; Tripolitania; Numidia; Mauretania; and Sardinia. He wished the first four to be administered by consular governors and the last three by presidents.

In the following constitution he discusses military offices and judges, assigning the places in which the military commanders appointed throughout the various African provinces were to maintain their seats.

7. Nor was the emperor content with this. In order to restore Africa to its former splendor, he built new cities, fortified others with walls, and adorned and protected the entire region with magnificent buildings and necessary defenses against the barbarians, as Procopius relates at greater length in book VI of *The Buildings*, from chapter 3 to the end.

Among these he lists Caput Vada in Byzacium and Tucca in Proconsularis as cities newly constructed. At Leptis Magna, the metropolis of Tripolitania, which had almost collapsed, he built walls and restored the ancient palace, once constructed by the emperor Severus, who had been born there, but which had almost entirely fallen into ruin.

He wished Carthage to be called Justinianeia. He also gave this name to Hadrumetum, the metropolis of Byzacium, formerly called, as Pliny observes, “Black Sissa.” This city had been so neglected by the barbarians that it scarcely retained a shadow of its ancient splendor.

At Basa in Proconsularis, previously scarcely known, he truly made a city, as Procopius says. Its citizens, so as not to seem ungrateful, called it Theodorias in honor of Theodora, Justinian’s wife. From the name of the same empress, the baths of Theodoriana, worthy of inspection, were so called, says the same author.

For other public buildings constructed by the same emperor in various places in Africa, see the praised author.

8. Justinian was no less magnificent in constructing sacred than secular buildings. Procopius relates in the work cited that he built five churches in Leptis Magna alone. One of them, dedicated in honor of the Virgin Mother of God, surpassed the others.

He built another under the name of the same most blessed Virgin at Septa, situated on the coast of Africa near the other Pillar of Hercules:

“By dedicating and consecrating this coast of the empire to Mary the Mother of God,” says Procopius, “he made this fortress impregnable to the entire human race.”

The same author also records that Justinian built a distinguished church at Sabratha, a city of Tripolitania. At Carthage he ordered two churches to be built: the first in the palace, dedicated to the Mother of God; the second outside the palace, dedicated to Saint Prima, who, says Procopius, was one of the holy indigenous women.

For this reason he founded a monastery within the walls of the same city, near the harbor called Mandracium.

Moreover, the same emperor took care that the property of the churches which the barbarians had seized should be restored to their respective places. He also enacted many other measures in favor of the churches and sacred ministers, which are found in the *Novels* and other imperial constitutions.

The joy was increased by the conversion to the faith of Christ of several peoples, namely the barbarians who lived around the Tripolitan frontier. Among these Procopius mentions the Moors surnamed Pacati, who inhabited the city of Cidama, in book VI of *The Buildings*, chapter 3; and, in the following chapter, the Moors of Gadabos, whom he says lived not far from the city of Leptis Magna.

9. After Boniface, bishop of Carthage, died during these events, Reparatus was appointed in his place under the consulship of Belisarius, vir clarissimus—that is, in the year 535, if we trust Victor of Tunnuna.

Those who nevertheless maintain that the Council of Carthage was held under Reparatus in the year 534 must necessarily assign his ordination to at least that same year. Certainly, the letters of Agapetus written to Reparatus are dated in September after the consulship of Paulinus, by which the same year 535 is indicated.

Immediately after his ordination, Reparatus recovered the episcopal see of Carthage at the basilica of Faustus, richly endowed with relics of holy martyrs, which the Arians had forcibly occupied under Huneric. There he celebrated a general council of all Africa, to which 217 bishops are said to have assembled.

The canons of the ancient councils were read there, and many decrees were issued for restoring ecclesiastical discipline, which the harshness of earlier times had weakened in those regions.

Two embassies were also sent from that synod: one to the Roman pontiff and the other to Justinian Augustus. By the latter embassy they petitioned the emperor that Catholic bishops and other sacred ministers might recover the property of the churches which the barbarians had plundered. We have already observed that this was granted by the emperor, and it is clear from *Novels* 36 and 37.

Through the other embassy, the African Fathers informed the Roman pontiff that peace had been restored to the churches. They also asked his opinion concerning the reception into the Church of Arian presbyters who returned after renouncing their heresy, as well as concerning several other matters of ecclesiastical discipline.

The envoys were Gaius and Peter, bishops, together with Liberatus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, who became famous for his written *Breviarium*.

When John II had died, Agapetus, appointed in his place, received these envoys when they arrived at Rome. The acts of the Council of Carthage have perished. We do, however, possess the synodical letter to the pope, as well as the reply of Agapetus, which the pontiff addressed to Reparatus, Florentius, Dacianus, and the other bishops. From this we have inferred that they were the primates of the provinces: Reparatus of Carthage, Florentius of Numidia, and Pontianus of Byzacium.

Agapetus also sent a separate letter to Reparatus of Carthage, who shortly after the embassy had been sent wrote to him after receiving his ordination in place of John. In it the pontiff congratulates him on the liberty restored to the African Church and prays that, after thanks have been rendered to Almighty God, it may become useful and fruitful.

Such was the fortunate condition of the African Church. After so many calamities, it had at last been freed from the oppression of the barbarians and quickly recovered its former splendor.

# In the Year of Our Lord 482. Sidonius Apollinaris, Bishop of the Arverni.

## Prolegomena

### Dedicatory Letter

**James Sirmond to the Lord of La Rochefoucauld-Randan, Cardinal Bishop of Senlis of the Holy Roman Church**

My most illustrious cardinal, it has come about, as I desired, that I should at last bring our Sidonius to the press after several years, almost on the very days when cheering Gaul was welcoming you home from Italy with public and private congratulations.

Since I felt that, through the bond of our former patronage, I owed you some gift upon your arrival, I certainly wished to find something capable not only of bearing witness to our wishes but also of winning and deserving your favor.

Now something has been offered of its own accord which, if you love yourself, you must necessarily love and approve. For what else do I offer you when I offer Sidonius than another you to yourself—that is, a bishop of the highest rank by birth, learning, and virtue, endowed with the same praises and ornaments as you?

He was born to a father who was prefect of Gaul and was the son of the master of the Gallic army; he was prefect of the city of Rome, occupying a position in the Roman Church scarcely lower than that of a cardinal; and finally he was bishop of the Arverni, just as you were bishop of the same Arverni see.

Although you withdrew from your Arverni long ago, and preferred that they should miss your presence rather than possess you forever as the good in which they had delighted, the most grateful memory of your episcopate remains and flourishes in everyone’s hearts.

Nor will any age ever fail to celebrate those five lustrums during which, seated at the helm of the Church of Clermont, you fulfilled for it every duty of the wisest and most vigilant shepherd. You instructed the people entrusted to you in heavenly disciplines, not only by words and speech but also through written volumes as a teacher of true piety. You also so shaped your own life and the whole pattern of your conduct that, in accordance with those whom you succeeded and whose chair you occupied, you seemed continually to meditate upon and strive to imitate, worthy of emulation:

At one time the holiness of Austremonius and Illidius; the piety of Venerandus and Eparchius; the constancy of Quintianus; and the modesty and kindness of Gallus.

At another, you seemed to strive so that, through contempt for human affairs, you might renew Bonitus; through devotion to sacred places, Genesius; through recalling the erring to the true faith, Avitus; through relieving the distress of the poor, Sidonius; and, finally, the entire senate of the once distinguished bishops, in their own Arvernia, through the light and examples of your virtues.

But why do I say these things, when I did not set out to write your praises and, even if I wished to do so, had no need to reopen the past, since the praises that Rome recently honored in you, that the court now admires, or that perhaps your delighted people of Meaux proclaim, are readily available and surpass every commendation?

Nevertheless, from this you can see, my most illustrious cardinal, with what confidence I present to you a native and almost domestic gift, trusting that, although you customarily embrace with kindness every effort made by those devoted to your name, our Sidonius nevertheless deserves special favor from you, since he is bound and consecrated to you by so many ties.

I therefore fear that even this delay in fulfilling my duty—so slow after so many years—may not be counted against me. Rather, I seem likely, if I am not mistaken, to receive from your judgment an easy pardon, or even praise, when you understand that by this very acknowledgment of an old debt I am declaring my ancient and constant perseverance in veneration and service to you.

**To Your Most Illustrious Eminence, most devotedly, JAC. SIRMONDUS, priest of the Society of Jesus**

## Notice Concerning Sidonius Apollinaris

*(From Galland)*
[Col. 0437A] I. The city now called *Clarus Mons*, Clermont in French, the leading city of Aquitania I, was formerly called Augustonemetum and was subsequently called Arverni, as is clear from Pliny [Note: [Col. 0437C] Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIV, chapter 7]; and it was designated almost everywhere by this name alone among the ancients and in the councils [Note: [Col. 0437C] Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, p. 222]. Sidonius therefore held the bishopric of this city. He was born at Lyons [Note: [Col. 0437C] Sidonius, books I, letters 5 and 8; and Sirmond on poem 17], on 5 November [Note: [Col. 0437C] The same, poem 20], around the year 430. His full name was Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius; he was, as Gregory of Tours says [Note: [Col. 0437C] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 21], a man “most noble according to the dignity of the age,” and one of the foremost senators of Gaul.

Pagius attempts to establish from various of his letters that Sidonius ascended the see of Arvernia in the year 473 [Note: [Col. 0437D] Pagius, *Prolegomena to the Dissertation on the Hypate*, §§31–32, and on the year 472, §5], contrary to the course taken by the eminent Baronius, who assigns the beginning of his episcopate to the preceding year, 472 [Note: [Col. 0437D] Baronius on the year 472, §14]. Learned men are known to adhere to Baronius’s opinion, especially Sirmondus [Note: [Col. 0437D] Sirmondus on Sidonius, letter 1, book VI, and letter 12, book IX], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0437D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 749, note 6 on Saint Sidonius], and Sammarthanus [Note: [Col. 0437D] Sammarthanus, cited work, p. 232]. Nor should Labbeus be heeded, for he asserts that it is proved by the frequent letters Sidonius sent to various persons during that period that Sidonius was ordained several years before 472 [Note: [Col. 0437D] Labbeus, *Historical Chronology*, part I, p. 344, Paris edition, [Col. 0438C] 1670].

II. Although he was therefore unwillingly raised to the episcopate—having previously nearly exhausted himself in cultivating the liberal disciplines—he thereafter turned his mind and all his studies to the treatment of the divine Scriptures. Such, moreover, was the esteem in which his prudence was held that, when a heated dispute had arisen over the election of the metropolitan bishop of Bourges, the bishops of the province wished that the decision in this election should depend upon him [Note: [Col. 0438C] Sidonius, book VII, letters 5, 8, and 9]. We learn chiefly from his own letters addressed to several bishops that our prelate was endowed with great humility of spirit; he was consequently worthy to be raised by God to the summit of holiness [Note: [Col. 0438C] Baronius on the year 472, §16]. Finally, after spending nearly eighteen years in the bishopric of Arvernia, a man distinguished no less by learning than by outstanding moral integrity, he departed this life for heaven, and his name was entered in the ecclesiastical calendars under 23 August.

III. But learned men do not agree about the year of Saint Sidonius’s death or about his final day. If Pagius is followed [Note: [Col. 0438C] Pagius on the year 484, §28], we are entirely ignorant of the matter. Tillemont assigns the year 490 and the day 21 August [Note: [Col. 0438C] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, pp. 274 and 755, note 16 on Saint Sidonius]. The authors of the *Literary History of Gaul* come very close to Tillemont’s view [Note: [Col. 0438D] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 557]. Sammarthanus, finally, omitting others, records the death of the holy prelate on 21 August in the year 482 [Note: [Col. 0438D] Sammarthanus, cited work, p. 233].

Since the learned men just mentioned were unaware of what Scaliger wrote on this matter, it may perhaps not be amiss to report it here. He writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0438D] Scaliger, *On the Correction of the Times*, book VI, p. 613 ff.]:

“Gregory of Tours, when discussing Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Augustonemetum of the Arverni, guided us toward investigating the year in which that eminent man died by what he records about the time of his death. He says [Note: [Col. 0438D] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 23, p. 75, Ruinart edition] that the day immediately following his death was a Sunday. Now it is established from the church of Augustonemetum (called Clermont) that he died on 23 August. Therefore the 24th was a Sunday, with Sunday letter E. An old Cluniac manuscript containing his epitaph additionally stated that he died while Zeno was emperor. Without doubt, therefore, this occurred in the year of Christ 480, solar cycle 13 [Note: [Col. 0438D] Compare Labbeus, *Technical Chronology*, part I, p. 114, under the year 480]. For it does not seem to have been in the year 486, solar cycle 19; the interval is too long.

“In that manuscript, therefore, the epitaph was written as follows; our P. Pithoeus, a man of the highest integrity and learning, communicated it to us [Note: [Col. 0438D] The complete epitaph appears below, appended to the *Life of Sidonius* composed by Sirmondus]:

> C. Sollius Apollinaris Modestus Sidonius,  
> Close to the saints and the sacred father,  
> Apollinaris lives here by his merits . . . . . . . . . .  
> There Sidonius is invoked for you.  
> 21 August, Emperor Zeno.

“He gives 21 August, whereas the church of the Arverni has retained from the earliest antiquity 23 August. Otherwise, if he died on 21 August, this would have been in the year of Christ 482, but in the seventh year of Zeno’s reign. Sidonius therefore died in the fifth year of Zeno Augustus, after the consulship of Zeno himself (III) and of Flavius Basilius the Younger, vir clarissimus, in the second year of Clovis, in the third indiction, on 23 August, a Saturday.” Thus far Scaliger.

[Col. 0439A] V. But, to speak with Baunius [Note: [Col. 0439D] Baunius, preface to vol. I of Sirmondus’s works, §11 toward the end], “there is no compelling reason to depart from the opinion of Cardinal Baronius [Note: [Col. 0439D] Baronius on the year 484, §§136, 139], which Sirmondus appears to have approved and considered more probable [Note: [Col. 0439D] Sirmondus on letter 12, book IX]: namely, that Sidonius lived until the year 484, and that this is understood from his letter to Oresius, in which he writes that from the beginning of his religious profession he had renounced poetry and that three Olympiads—twelve years—had already passed in that silence [Note: [Col. 0439D] Sidonius, letter 12, book IX]. For both Baronius and Sirmondus rightly understand the words ‘from the beginning of his religious profession’ to refer to the beginning of his episcopate, since Gregory of Tours testifies that, when Eparchius departed, Sidonius was substituted for him from the office of urban prefect [Note: [Col. 0439D] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 21]; Baronius and others refer Eparchius’s departure to the year 472.” So he writes. But enough of this.

[Col. 0439B] V. Sidonius was especially distinguished in poetry and rhetoric, and in this respect second to none of his age; consequently, he was held in great esteem and honored with the highest praises by the leading men of that time. Among these were the holy bishops Lupus of Troyes, Euphronius of Autun, Principius of Soissons, Remigius of Reims, and Ruricius of Limoges, to omit others.

Claudianus Mamertus, who dedicated his books *On the Status of the Soul* to our author when he was still prefect, calls him in the dedicatory letter [Note: [Col. 0439D] Claudianus, p. 417] “a most learned and excellent man, foremost among the eloquent, most learned among men, and renewer of ancient eloquence.” Elsewhere, writing to him when he was already bishop, he says [Note: [Col. 0439D] The same, letter 1, p. 455]:

> “When you search out the mysteries of the heavenly Scriptures, the more diligently you imbibe them, the more abundantly you pour learning into others.”

Gennadius writes the following about the same Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0440D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 92]:

> “Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, wrote various pleasing little works, of sound doctrine. A man thoroughly imbued with both divine and human learning and sharp in intellect . . . is regarded as a Catholic father and distinguished teacher.”

Saint Avitus of Vienne, speaking of Apollinaris Sidonius’s son, extols “the delights of his father’s eloquence” (that is, Sidonian eloquence) “and the rivers of his father’s fountains” [Note: [Col. 0440D] Avitus of Vienne, letter 38]. Writing again to Apollinaris himself, he says [Note: [Col. 0440D] The same, letter 45]:

> “Here and now I call God to witness before your sincerity that I speak neither falsely nor flatteringly: I was so delighted by your judgment that, as though I had confessed to having heard what your lordly father Sidonius had composed, I felt that I had placed myself, in every moment of praise, under a censor.”

Finally, Gregory of Tours says [Note: [Col. 0440D] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 22]:

> “Saint Sidonius possessed such eloquence that, often improvising, he could compose with the greatest brilliance whatever he wished, with no delay obstructing him.”

The writers of later ages—Flodoard, Sigebert of Gembloux, Honorius of Autun, Hugh of Fleury, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, and others—judged no differently of our bishop. It is neither necessary nor desirable to reproduce their praises.

VI. It will be useful, however, to hear Sirmondus on how highly Sidonius should be esteemed, for Sirmondus knew the qualities of his writings well. In the eulogy of Sidonius that he appended to his works [Note: [Col. 0440D] Sirmondus, *Life of Saint Sidonius*, following column], he writes:

> “Although he wrote many other memorials of his genius, he wished only those that remain to be made public. In these, whether bound in meter or free and unbound, whether he narrates or advises, praises or censures, and whatever subject he treats, there is equal success and abundance in all things, together with such variety both of words and of thoughts [Col. 0440B] that an extraordinary force of genius and a certain abundance of learning immediately shine forth in him . . . . Nor did he reveal his greatness only in what he considered and worked out with greater care, but also in extemporaneous and sudden compositions. His facility in these was so ready that he not only poured forth on the spot a considerable number of unpremeditated verses . . . . but sometimes completed substantial works in both kinds of discourse with equal speed . . . .

> “Yet although Sidonius was in every respect such a great man, and although his writings were wonderfully approved by everyone, he alone seemed to think modestly of himself and never to be fully satisfied with himself. Thus he suppressed many things, and, having undertaken certain works—such as the war of Attila—he abandoned them, weary of the task. When Leo, adviser to King Euric, urged him to write a history of his own times, he also declined, saying that the undertaking of writing history was hardly suitable for clerics.”

Thus far Sirmondus.

VII. Finally, following Baunius [Note: [Col. 0440D] Baunius, preface to Sirmondus’s works, vol. I, §11, beginning], we have committed to the press that edition of Sidonius’s works which Sirmondus himself, having revised and illustrated it with the greatest care, published. Yet we have omitted none of the material: neither what Labbeus added in a later edition from Sirmondus’s manuscripts, nor what the editor of Sirmondus’s works extracted from numerous manuscripts of both the Royal and Colbert libraries in order to correct the text of Sidonius. We have also added the observations that the editor just mentioned, for the same purpose, transcribed in the preface to volume I of the Sirmondian collection from the various works of learned men. Finally, here and there we have appended a few notes drawn from other sources.

[Col. 0441]

# LIFE OF SAINT SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS, PREPARED BY SIRMONDUS

[Col. 0441A] It is established that Sidonius was born of the noblest family among the Gauls, and that both his father and grandfather were prefects of the Praetorian Prefecture of Gaul. Although others hold different opinions about his birthplace, he himself indicates more than once, and in unmistakable words, that he was from Lyons. The frequent mention of the Arverni in his books, among whom he first married the daughter of the emperor Avitus and later obtained the episcopal see, gave some people reason to suspect that he was an Arvernian.

Born therefore at Lyons, and educated by the best teachers of the liberal arts with whom Gaul was still richly supplied at that time—among them he mentions Ennius in poetry and Eusebius in philosophy—he attained in every field such distinction through nature and study that he was regarded as the most learned and eloquent man of his age, as the praises of Claudianus Mamertus show. Especially famous for poetry [Col. 0441B], he was valued not only by his contemporaries and friends but also by the princes themselves. The former is shown by the epigrams and poems of every kind that he wrote at his friends’ request on various subjects with the greatest devotion; the latter by the three panegyrics in which he publicly praised the emperors Avitus, Majorian, and Anthemius, receiving from each the fruits of their goodwill.

At Rome, under Avitus, he earned a statue among the poets in the library of Trajan’s Forum. When Majorian gave the games at Arles, Sidonius was admitted among the honored guests at the emperor’s ceremonial banquet and was vindicated, in a unique example, from the hostility of Satyra, of which he was accused. Finally, under Anthemius, after he had already been adorned with the office of *comes* and other dignities, he was created prefect of the city and patrician, and thus made patrician the family that he had inherited from his ancestors as a prefectural family.

Not long afterward, when Eparchius, bishop of the Arverni, died, Sidonius was substituted in his place, although he resisted and was not yet a cleric. He undertook this office with the greatest modesty and administered it with equal holiness and vigilance amid the most turbulent circumstances and the greatest private and public difficulties. First, when the Arverni were besieged by the Goths, he endured the hardships of a long and fierce assault. Then, when the town had been handed over to the power of the enemy through the treaty made by the emperor’s nephew, he was exiled for some time by them under the pretext of an embassy.

At last restored to his people, he devoted himself to the care of his office, omitting no duty of an excellent shepherd among the barbarians. Although he showed singular kindness toward everyone and extraordinary generosity toward the needy, and injured no one himself, he nevertheless aroused against himself the hatred of rivals, as is customary: specifically, two presbyters who, after stripping him with the greatest insult of all authority over his Church, cast him into the greatest distress in every respect. But divine vengeance did not permit that calamity to last long. Restored, therefore, to his former position, though he did not long survive afterward, and with Aprunculus designated as his successor—not without divine foreknowledge—he departed to the rewards of heaven on 21 August. That day has since been dedicated among the Arverni to the annual commemoration of him and was inscribed on his tomb together with an epitaph.

By his wife Papianilla, whom he married before the episcopate, he left children: a son, Apollinaris, and daughters, Roscia and Severiana.
