Although he wrote many other memorials of his genius, he wished only those that remain to be made public. In these, whether bound in meter or free and unbound, whether he narrates or advises, praises or censures, and whatever subject he treats, there is equal success and abundance in all things, together with such variety both of words and thoughts that an extraordinary force of genius and a certain abundance of learning immediately shine forth in him.

[Col. 0442B] This, I think, is why even learned men of his own age, such as Ruricius of Limoges, judged him obscure and thought that he required an interpreter. Nor did he reveal his greatness only in the works he considered and elaborated with greater care, but also in extemporaneous and sudden compositions. His facility in these was so ready that he not only poured forth on the spot a considerable number of unpremeditated verses—for example, the distich by which he pleaded with Majorian against Satyra’s slander, and the reciprocal verse with which he played upon a torrent, or the quatrain he composed for Philematius—but sometimes completed short works in both kinds of discourse with equal speed.

Of this sort were the sermon at Bourges, which he dictated in a few hours, and the Anacreontic poem that he suddenly produced at Bordeaux in response to the book of Peter, master of the correspondence, when he competed with the eminent poets of that age, Domnulus, Severianus, and Lampridius. Yet he never displayed more brilliantly what he could do in this genre than when, as Gregory of Tours relates, the little book from which he habitually recited was taken away from him during the sacred rites, and nevertheless he set forth the entire sequence of what had to be said appropriately and brilliantly.

Although Sidonius was in every respect such a great man, and although his writings were wonderfully approved by everyone, he alone seemed to think modestly of himself and never to be fully satisfied with himself. Thus, as has been said, he suppressed many things, and, having undertaken certain works—such as the war of Attila—he abandoned them, weary of the task. When Leo, adviser to King Euric, urged him to write a history of his own times, he declined, saying that the undertaking of writing history was hardly suitable for a cleric.

All this, and much more besides, may be learned about Sidonius from Sidonian works themselves. Among the Arverni, as we have already noted, the memory of this illustrious bishop is honored on an appointed day and according to the rite of the saints, and his sacred bones are reverently preserved in the basilica of Saint Genesius. They record that his remains were long ago transferred there from the old chapel of Saint Saturninus, where he had first been buried.

[Col. 0444A] His epitaph, mentioned above and taken from an old Cluniac manuscript, reads as follows:

[Col. 0443]

# EPITAPH OF SIDONIUS (C)

[Col. 0443A]

Close to the saints and the sacred father,  
Thus Apollinaris lives by his merits,  
Illustrious in titles, powerful in honor,  
Commander of the army and judge of the forum.  

Calm amid the swollen waves of the world,  
Now and again guiding the disturbances of lawsuits,  
He gave laws to barbarian fury,  
When kingdoms were at war with one another;  
By his ample counsel he restored peace.  

Yet amid all this, and while philosophizing,  
He wrote things destined to be cherished through endless ages.  

And after such gifts of gratitude,  
Sitting in the chair of the supreme pontiff,  
He returns worldly pursuits to his offspring.  

Whoever you are, while you pray to God here with tears,  
Pour forth favorable prayers over the tomb.  

Unknown to no one, but to be read by the whole world,  
There may Sidonius be invoked for you.  

21 August, Emperor Zeno.

[Col. 0443]

# TESTIMONIES ABOUT SIDONIUS APOLLINARIS

## MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, PRESBYTER OF VIENNE

[Col. 0443B] There survive three books of Mamertus Claudianus, *On the Status of the Soul*, written to Sidonius. In them, among other praises, he calls him “foremost among the eloquent, most learned among men, and renewer of ancient eloquence.” The title of the letter prefixed to the work is:

> To the prefectural and patrician, most learned and excellent man, Gaius Sollius Sidonius, Claudianus sends greetings.

## GENNADIUS, PRESBYTER OF MARSEILLES, *ON ILLUSTRIOUS MEN*, CHAPTER XCII

Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, wrote various pleasing volumes of sound doctrine. A man thoroughly imbued with both divine and human learning and sharp in intellect, he wrote for various people a distinguished volume composed in different meters or in prose, in which he displayed what he could accomplish in literature. Strong, moreover, in Christian vigor even amid the hardness of barbarian ferocity, which at that time oppressed the Gauls, he is regarded as a Catholic father and distinguished teacher. He flourished at the time when Leo and Zeno ruled the Romans.

[Col. 0443]

[Note: [Col. 0443C] We have moved the first five pages of notes, as well as the final three, to the end of Sidonius’s works, where they are printed under the title *Coronis*, from the middle of our pp. 747–748 to the end of pp. 751–752. We have not printed these eight pages in larger type, since the reader is not referred to them in the index. Editor.]

6. Some manuscripts also add the name Modestus, in the following form: “Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Modestus Sidonius.” It was not unusual in that age for one person to have five names. But this praenomen is nowhere mentioned by Sidonius, unless he perhaps alludes to it when, writing to Oresius, he indicates that he would rather be considered modest than witty. The name Sidonius is placed last because it is the true and proper name. Therefore those who, following Angelo Poliziano and certain others who first called him this nearly a hundred years ago, call him Sidonius Apollinaris in the reverse order are acting contrary to the custom of the Sidonian age. The same error is made by those who write “Prosperus Tiro,” whereas he should be called “Tiro Prosper,” as he is designated in ancient copies.

# LETTERS OF GAIUS SOLLIUS APOLLINARIS SIDONIUS

## BOOK ONE

[Note.]

N.B. In the Sirmondian edition the notes were published separately after the text. To serve the reader’s convenience, we have brought them beneath the text. We have printed their pagination, as it appears in Sirmondus, in larger type, so that the analytical index may subsequently be reprinted with benefit in connection with the notes. Editor.

## LETTER ONE

Sidonius sends greetings to his Constantius [Note: [Col. 0444C] A presbyter of Lyons, whose two books on the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre* survive. Sidonius often honors this same man with many praises, both in the other letters he writes to him or to others and especially in the final letter of all, addressed to Firminus. In Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men* he is called a bishop, but wrongly, I think.]

[Col. 0443C]

1. You have long urged me, my greater lord, with the greatest authority of persuasion—as you are exceedingly wise in matters requiring deliberation—that, if any somewhat polished letters have flowed forth on various occasions, as circumstance, person, and time elicited them, I should gather them all, after revising and examining the copies, into a single volume, intending to follow in the footsteps of Quintus Symmachus’s roundness and Gaius Pliny’s discipline and maturity [Note: [Col. 0444C] Some manuscripts read “presumptuous”]. For I think it better to remain silent, in the epistolary style, about Marcus Tullius [Note: [Col. 0444C] Not because he disapproves of Cicero’s style in general, as Petrarch and Poliziano judged, but because he considers it presumptuous to promise himself an imitation of Cicero, whom not even Titianus could adequately reproduce], whom Julius Titianus [Note: [Col. 0444D] Senior, father of the younger Titianus, who was tutor to the son of Maximinus Augustus. Capitolinus says: “He used Titianus the son of Titianus the elder as an orator; he wrote beautiful books on the provinces and was called the ape of his age because he imitated everything.” Ausonius likewise calls him Julius Titianus by both names in his letter to Probus, letter 16; Cassiodorus calls Julius an orator in book I of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 25. He wrote various works mentioned by ancient authors: books on the provinces, or *Cosmography*, according to Capitolinus, Servius, and Cassiodorus; Aesopic fables according to Ausonius; books on agriculture according to Diomedes; rules of rhetorical art according to Isidore; and Virgilian themes according to Servius. In this passage Sidonius also indicates that Titianus published letters—not genuine letters, but fictional letters under the names of illustrious women, like Ovid’s letters called the *Heroides*] expressed entirely under the names of illustrious women with worthy resemblance.

For this reason, all the other [Note: [Col. 0445C] Followers of Cornelius Fronto, who was the foremost orator of his age, “held first place,” as it appears in the epitome of Dio, “among the Romans of that time in legal cases.” Different schools and families existed among philosophers, poets, and orators in each age. Thus, just as some poets were called Virgilian and others Ovidian, and some jurists Cassian and others Proculian, so orators of that age were called Frontoans when they professed to imitate Fronto, and perhaps Festians when they followed Postumius Festus. An old inscription reads: “To Postumius Titianus, orator, great-grandson and follower of Marcus Postumius Festus, the orator”] of the Frontoans, imitating him as a fellow member of the same school, called him “the ape of orators” because he imitated the diction of former ages.

As for all these men, it is astonishing to say how much I have always yielded to my own judgment and how much I have declared that each should retain the precedence due to his time and accomplishments. Yet I obeyed you, and entrusted these works to your examination—not merely for review, which would be too little, but, as they say, to be purged and polished—knowing that you are an immoderate patron not only of studies but also of students.

Therefore you now thrust us, extremely hesitant, into this sea of reputation. In fact, concerning such a little work we had remained more safely silent, content with the opinion that our verses had been published more successfully than skillfully [Note: [Col. 0445D] From this it is evident that Sidonius’s poems were published considerably earlier than his letters], and that, after sailing into the harbor of public judgment and dropping anchor in sufficient glory once the Scyllas of envious barking had been passed, I had long been satisfied. But if envy does not promptly fix its true molar tooth in these ravings as well, volumes of greater extent, overflowing with very abundant conversation, will soon be multiplied for you by us. Farewell.

## LETTER TWO

Sidonius sends greetings to his Agricola [Note: [Col. 0445D] His brother-in-law, the brother of his wife Papianilla, as letter 12 of book II will explain].

You have often requested that, since popular report praises the civility of Theodoric, king of the Goths, his stature and appearance should be described to you in writing, as well as the quality of his life [Note: [Col. 0445D] The younger Theodoric. There were two Gothic kings of this name in Gaul: the first was the successor of Wallia and fell in the battle of the Catalaunian Plains; the second was his son, who, after the killing of his brother Thorismund, obtained the kingdom in the third year after the battle. Sidonius therefore gives a vivid description of the appearance, character, and conduct of this still-living king]. I gladly comply, insofar as an epistolary page permits, praising in you the sincerity of so refined a concern.

He is a man worthy to be known even by those who regard him less familiarly: God, judgment, and nature—joined with the gift of perfected excellence—have endowed his person to the full. His character, moreover, is such that envy of it deprives even kingship itself of nothing from its praises [Note: [Col. 0446C] He adds this because it is rare for princes not to be disliked by their subjects. Seneca, *Thyestes*: “At the same time the creator of the world, God, established hatred and kingship.” Cicero, *For Flaccus*: “What difficulty is there in stirring up the dregs of the cities, especially against one who recently possessed the highest authority, yet could not be greatly loved because of the authority itself?”].

If his appearance is sought: his body is well proportioned, shorter than the very tall, but taller and more imposing than men of ordinary stature. The crown of his head is rounded; on it, slightly withdrawn from the flatness of his forehead toward the crown, his curly hair bends backward. His neck is not slack in its sinews. A bristling arch of eyebrows crowns his twin eyes. If his eyelids are lowered, the edge of the lashes nearly reaches the middle of his cheeks.

[Note: [Col. 0446C] *Ligulae* are known as small table utensils resembling spoons (*cochlearia*). A *cochlear* is one thing and a *ligula* another; but today we call *cochlearia* what are more properly *ligulae*. From their likeness Sidonius called the ears *legulae*, because they are curved and hollow; Apuleius likewise calls the tentacles of squids *ligulae* for the same reason. Conversely, elsewhere Sidonius and Alcimus Avitus call the spleen’s broad, straight form a *regula*. No less elegantly Severianus of Gabala attributes a cymbal to the ears, in Homily 5 on the *Hexaemeron*: “Hearing has its function; it has its appearance. For the cymbal placed around it adorns the creature.” Glossaries also recognize *legula* for *ligula*, which they translate as μυστρόν, “ladle.”] The little ear-flaps, as is the custom of the nation [Col. 0446B], are covered by locks of hair lying above them [Note: [Col. 0446D] It was the custom of the Gothic people to part the hair and let braided locks fall over the ears and down the back. Isidore, *Etymologies* XXIX: “Certain peoples claim for themselves distinctive marks, as it were insignia, not only in their clothing but also on their bodies, as we see the curls of the Germans and the *grani* and cinnabar of the Goths.” By *curls* I understand hair gathered into a knot, which Tacitus makes the characteristic emblem of the Suebi, who occupied most of Germany. By *grani* I understand these same locks of hair, about which the Council of Braga also speaks when it forbids lectors to let their *grani* hang down according to pagan custom. Garsias Loaysa correctly advised that this should be read in that way, but incorrectly explained it as a secular and elongated garment, since Isidore’s own words clearly show that *grani* have nothing to do with clothing. Agathias, book V, and Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 24, and elsewhere, show that locks of hair were also customary among the Franks, especially those born of the royal line].

His nose is most gracefully curved. His lips are delicate and not enlarged by the widening of the corners of his mouth. If, by chance, his orderly row of teeth should be exposed, it immediately displays a snowy color. The hairs growing beneath the cavities of his nostrils are cut daily. His beard is shaggy at the hollow temples; as it rises from the lower part of his face, a persistent barber tears it out by the roots with pincers as far as the cheeks.

The skin of his chin, throat, and neck—neither obese but full—is milky, though, when viewed more closely, it is suffused with youthful redness. This color often comes to him not from anger but from modesty. His shoulders are rounded, his upper arms strong, his forearms hard, his hands broad; his chest advances as his belly recedes. A lower ridge of the spine divides the surface of his back between the projecting ribs. Each side is knotted with prominent muscles.

4. Strength rules in his tightly girded loins. His thigh is hornlike, and the joints of his knees thoroughly masculine. His greatest distinction lies in knees scarcely marked by wrinkles. His legs swell, supported by bulging calves, while the foot that supports his large limbs is moderate in size.

If you inquire into his long-established public routine, he seeks at dawn the assemblies of his priests with a minimal retinue and reveres them with great devotion, although, if the conversation is private, you may observe that he preserves this reverence more from custom than from reason [Note: [Col. 0447B] The later edition reads “religion.” The Savaronian edition and some manuscripts agree]. He assigns the rest of the morning to the administration of the kingdom. His armed count stands around his chair; a crowd of fur-clad guards is admitted lest it be absent, but expelled lest it make a disturbance. Thus, outside the doors, it murmurs [Note: [Col. 0447B] Corippus likewise, in book III, describing the audience chamber of Justin II, places the protectors outside the curtain, in these verses:

> Nobility inhabits the midst of the imperial house,  
> Surrounded by four distinguished columns.

And afterward:

> Curtains cover the doorposts; guards keep watch over the lofty  
> Thresholds and obstruct those wishing to enter unworthily,  
> Dense in number, formidable in pride and gesture.

The doors of the royal audience chamber were screened by curtains; the station nearest them was enclosed and closed by railings. Within the curtain—that is, in the audience chamber itself—the counts and members of the council were admitted; the guards stood between the railings and the curtains. Cassiodorus, *Variae* XI.7, and ancient glosses speak of the railings that likewise surrounded the offices of judges and all administrative chambers: “A pen, railings before the judge. Outside the pen, outside toward the courtyards.” The Greeks call them *kiklídes* (κιγκλίδες), that is, “lattice doors of offices or courts,” according to Suidas] shut out by curtains and shut in by railings.

During this time, when embassies of different nations are admitted, he hears many things and answers few. If something is to be discussed, he postpones it; if something is to be settled, he hastens it. Is it the second hour? He rises from his throne, intending either to inspect the treasuries or to visit the stables.

If a hunting expedition has been announced, he considers it beneath royal dignity to fasten a bow to his side. Yet if you show him a wild bird or animal at close range, whether while hunting or by chance while traveling, a boy places the bow in his hand, which he has bent behind his back, with the string or thong hanging loose. Just as he considers it childish to carry the bow in its case, so he regards it as womanly to receive it already strung.

Then, once he has received it, he sometimes draws it taut with the ends facing one another; sometimes, with the knot turned toward the ankle, he follows with a wandering finger the slack loop of the cord as it hangs down. Soon he takes arrows, fits them, and shoots them; before you can say what you wish to be struck, he anticipates you. You choose what he should do, and he strikes what you have chosen. If one of the two must err, the archer’s blow misses less often than the intending spectator’s gaze.

If they go to a banquet—which on ordinary days is indeed like a private meal—a gloomy servant does not place upon tables yielding beneath their weight an uncouth heap of tarnished silver. At that point the greatest weight lies in the words, since either nothing is narrated there or only serious matters.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] In book II, letter to Serranus, “a silk-covered chased vessel”; and in book IX, in the Anacreontic poem, “a red-gold chased vessel in fine linen.” In all these passages he uses *toreumata* for bed coverings and misuses the word, following Prudentius’s example in the *Psychomachia*:

> where the wet  
> couches and chased vessels are drenched with much wine  
> and ancient dew.

And also Salvianus, book IV, *To the Church*. Properly speaking, *toreumata* are engraved Thericlean vessels, having nothing in common with purple and fine linen. *Toralia*, by contrast, are the covering fabrics of couches and dining beds; they were commonly made of skins, but according to wealth and luxury they became purple and silken. Cicero, *Philippics* 2: “You would see couches laid out in the servants’ rooms with Gnaeus Pompey’s purple hangings.” Martial, book III:

> He jostles the guests with his elbows, and then …]

Resplendent in purple and silken cushions. ] Sometimes the furnishings are brought out in the manner of embossed vessels and hangings, in shell-purple; sometimes in byssus. The dishes please by the skill of their preparation, not by their cost: [Note: [Col. 0448B] Most read *pondere* (“weight”); others, as does the Pithoean manuscript, *splendore* (“brilliance”), which is no less appealing. For Pliny likewise joined these ideas when discussing the murrhine vessels of Carmania, Book XXXVII, chapter 2: “Their brilliance is without strength, and their sheen is more truly sheen than brilliance.”] the courses by their brilliance, [Col. 0448B] not their weight. With the rare offerings of cups and saucers, it is easier for thirst to accuse one than for drunkenness to refuse one. Why say more? There you may see Greek refinement, [Note: [Col. 0448C] Sulpicius Severus repeatedly mocks this in his dialogues; and Luitprand of Ticinum attests that it was familiar to the Franks, Book I, chapter 6: “The bishop of Metz,” he says, “served him much food according to Frankish custom.”] Gallic abundance, Italian speed, public magnificence, private attentiveness, and royal discipline.

As for [Note: [Col. 0448C] Festive days, on which there was greater luxury at public and private banquets—so much so that Antisthenes the Cynic called a festival “an opportunity for gluttony” (*ἑορτὴν γαστριμαργίας ἀφορμήν*). There can be no doubt that festive days are meant. For he contrasts them with working days, whose banquets he said were without luxury. He was speaking, of course, in the manner of Sacred Scripture, which calls all festivals, whenever they fall, Sabbaths: “They call every festival a Sabbath,” says Isidore of Pelusium, Book III, chapter 10. It is indeed established that Eastern Christians formerly kept holidays in the church on Sabbaths as well as Sundays and held sacred assemblies on them. For this reason Asterius, bishop of Amasea in Pontus, in his homily on divorce asks, “Is not the pair of the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day beautiful?” (*καλὴν τὴν συνωρίδα τοῦ σαββάτου καὶ τῆς κυριακῆς*); and Gregory of Nyssa in one of his speeches calls those days brothers and reproves the luxury and delights of the Sabbath. Western Christians, by contrast, content with Sunday, neglected the Sabbath holidays as proper to the Jews. Hence Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*: “We are placed second among those who devote the Sabbath day to idleness and luxury”; that is, “we keep holiday on Sunday, as they do on the Sabbath.” Thus it is possible that the Goths, as pupils of Greek discipline, also kept holiday on the Sabbath according to the Greek rite; nevertheless, it is more fitting that by “Sabbath” here we understand all festive days.] that Sabbath-like luxury, I shall refrain from relating it, since even hidden persons cannot remain hidden in it. Let us return to what we began.

After the meal, the midday sleep is often absent, always brief. During those hours the man enjoys the gaming board: he gathers the dice swiftly, examines them carefully, turns them skillfully, throws them eagerly, [Note: [Col. 0448D] In some manuscripts, “playfully.”] addresses his opponent jokingly, and waits patiently. When the throws are good, he is silent; when bad, he laughs; when neither good nor bad, he grows angry; in both cases he philosophizes. He disdains either to fear or to make favorable throws; he rejects opportunities when offered and passes over those opposed to him. He comes through without agitation and escapes without collusion. You might think that even among the counters he is handling weapons. His sole concern is victory.

### 6

When it is time to play, he temporarily sets aside the severity of a king and encourages play, freedom, and fellowship. I shall say what I think: he is afraid of being feared. Finally, he takes pleasure in the agitation of the defeated; and only then does he believe that his companion has not yielded to him, when the other’s anger has confirmed his victory. And what you may wonder at, that joy, arising from the smallest occasions, often brings good fortune to great affairs. Then, for petitions long since tossed about amid the wreckage of advocacy, the harbor of sudden acquittal opens. Then I too, when I am about to make some plea, am happily defeated, whenever the gaming board asks this of me so that my case may be saved.

Toward the ninth hour that great burden of ruling grows fierce again. Those who knock return; those who drive others away return; everywhere the contentious murmur of the throng seeking access is heard. Drawn out until evening, it grows thinner when the royal dinner intervenes, and afterward is dispersed among the courtiers according to the differing needs of the patrons, to keep watch until the time of night’s repose.

To be sure, during dinner, though rarely, comic witticisms are admitted, so that no guest is struck by the gall of a biting tongue. Yet it is arranged that there neither do the hydraulic organs sound nor, under the direction of a vocal trainer (*phonasco*), does a rehearsed musical performance of voices thunder at the same time. No lyrist, choral flute-player, [Note: [Col. 0449C] This concerns the pantomime dancers called *cordacistae*, who danced the *cordax*, “an indecent and unseemly dance” (*αἰσχρὰν καὶ ἀπρεπῆ ὄρχησιν*). The person who gave signals with castanets or the clapping of his hands was called the *mesochorus*, because he stood in the middle of the chorus, as an old scholiast on Juvenal’s eleventh satire has taught us. Referring to this, Pliny the Younger, in Book II of his letters to Maximus, not inappropriately called the person who, among the ring of listeners, gave the signal for applause to the others hired to praise the orator, a *mesochorus*.] *mesochorus*, female tambourine-player, or female lyre-player sings. The king is soothed only by those strings with which virtue no less charms the mind than song charms the ear.

When he rises, he begins the night watches of the palace treasury. Armed men stand at the entrances of the royal residence, and the hours of the first sleep are guarded by them. But what does this have to do with my purpose, since I promised to tell you not much about the kingdom but a little about the king? At the same time, it is fitting that the pen be brought to an end: you wished to know no more of the man than his interests and character, and I have undertaken to produce not a history but a letter. Farewell.

## LETTER III

Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0449C] To the advocate of Lyon, concerning whom see Book V, Letter 17, addressed to Eriphius, his son-in-law.] sends greetings to his Philimatius.

Go now and ask me, when I am questioned under the laws concerning electoral corruption [Note: [Col. 0449C] The Calpurnian law had once ordained that those condemned for electoral canvassing should “neither govern nor sit in council” (*μήτε ἄρχειν, μήτε βουλεύειν*), and so be permanently barred from access to the curia and public offices. The Julian law mitigated the penalty and reduced it to five years; Dio is the authority, Books XXXVI and LVI. But, as Modestinus teaches, the Julian law ceased to operate at Rome once magistrates began to be appointed by the emperor; other penalties were subsequently decreed against those who canvassed before the emperor, as in Book I of the Theodosian Code, On the Julian Law concerning Canvassing. Therefore, when Sidonius says that the Senate altered the laws concerning canvassing, he refers not to his own age but to the practice of earlier times.], why I devote sleepless cares to attaining a hereditary dignity in which my father, father-in-law, grandfather, and great-grandfather shone through urban and praetorian prefectures, [Note: [Col. 0449D] The masterships of offices: these were the offices of the palace command, described by the rhetor Eumenius in his speech on behalf of the schools of the Aedui. The master of offices governed the entire administration of the palace and all the ranks and duties of the schools. Hence his name, either from the offices or from the court and palace itself. Rutilius Namatianus writes:

> “When as master I governed the royal halls through the offices,  
> and the guards of the pious emperor.”

The Greeks likewise call him at one time “the leader of the imperial residences” (*ἡγούμενον τῶν βασιλείων*), as Theodoret does in Book V; at another, “the commander of the ranks in the court” (*ἡγεμόνα τῶν ἐν αὐλῇ τάξεων*), as Zosimus does in Book II. Our glossaries say: “*Magister officiorum* is a name signifying no less than the leader of the palace registers” (*μάγιστρος ὀφφικίων ὄνομα οὐδὲν ἧττον τοῦ ἡγουμένου τῶν αὐλικῶν καταλόγων διασημαῖνον*).] and through palace and military masterships.

And behold, my Gaudentius, until now merely a tribunician, has risen above the sleepy indolence of our fellow citizens [Note: [Col. 0450C] The vicariate prefecture: hence the title *vicarianus* and the dignity of the vicariate, or simply “vicariate,” as we explained concerning the mastership. Vicars were those who, in place of the praetorian prefects, administered the dioceses of several provinces entrusted to them. Thus there were three vicars of the praetorian prefect of Italy: of the City of Rome, of Italy, and of Africa; likewise three vicars of the praetorian prefect of Gaul: one of the Spains, another of Britain, and a third of the seven provinces throughout Gaul, which I believe is meant here. We should not listen to those who place three vicars in one Gaul, since the *Notitia* correctly states that there were only six vicars in the West—namely, those whom we have listed. Since they stood immediately below the prefects in rank, Ausonius in the *Mosella* calls the vicariate “the second prefecture,” and designates the vicars of Italy and Britain in these words:

> “Whether they held the peoples of Italy  
> or the northerly Britons  
> under the title of the prefecture’s second rank.”] by the summit of the vicariate.

The trampled nobility of our young men mutters, to be sure; but he who passes by his detractors is moved only by the pleasure he takes in it. Thus they now honor the man whom until then they despised, and, astonished at the sudden gifts of fortune, look up to him from their seats whom they had looked down upon when he sat among them. As he passes, he strikes the ears of his snoring slanderers with the hoarse voice of a herald. Although hostile goads spur them against him, they are nevertheless assigned to friendly benches. [Note: [Col. 0450D] He advises him to accept the seat in the prefecture’s council offered to him and, by the privilege of this office, repair the loss of an honor now obsolete—perhaps the loss of another seat he had held under the vicar. Assessors, the counselors of prefects, were adorned with many privileges after completing their service and were finally placed on an equality even with the vicars themselves, as stated in the Theodosian Code, under “Counts who have served as assessors.” Those who had served only under vicars or other lesser judges lacked this prerogative. Hence he says that Philematius should fear that, if he comes into the council outside the prerogative of a prefect’s assessor, he may in fact discover that he has gained no benefit from having served under vicars.]

Therefore, since you are enjoying the privilege of the prefecture, it will be fitting for you also to repair swiftly the loss of your obsolete honor in the office [Note: [Col. 0450D] In a later edition, “which you seek to share.” So it appears in other printed books.] to which you have been summoned for participation, [Col. 0451A] lest, if you enter the council without the prerogative of an assessor, you appear to have performed only the functions of vicars. Farewell.

## 8. LETTER IV

Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0451C] To the vicar of the seven provinces, who had then obtained the highest rank and letters patent of that office.] sends greetings to his Gaudentius.

Congratulations, most eminent man, on the fasces you have won through the endowment of your merits. To obtain their titles and distinction, you did not count upon your mother’s revenues, your ancestral largesse, your wife’s jewels, or your father’s money. For, on the contrary, at the emperor’s court, your integrity, observed; your diligence, tested; and your admitted companionship were counted to your praise. [Note: [Col. 0451C] The vicars under Emperor Anthemius were appointed by the emperor himself, not by the prefects. Senator Cassiodorus says in the formula for the vicar of the City: “The jurisdiction granted by the emperor is properly his.” Accordingly, that fierce prefect of the praetorium, Maximinus, whom Marcellinus mentions in Book XXVIII, when he desired the vicariate assigned to Doryphorianus, did not assign it himself but obtained it from the emperor. Provincial governors were different: they were sent and removed by the prefects themselves without special imperial authority, as is clear from Book III, “On the Office of the Prefect of the East and Illyricum,” and Book IX, “On Advocates of Various Judges.” For that reason they were said to judge only in the prefect’s place; vicars, however, judged “in the sacred place,” as those who possessed jurisdiction from the emperor. The same Senator says: “You pronounce judgment in the sacred place.” And in Book I, “On the Office of the Vicar”: “The dignity of the vicariate possesses the power of sacred jurisdiction and is accustomed to represent the reverence of our judgment.”]

O thrice and four times blessed are you, from whose elevation joy is given to friends, punishment to the envious, [Col. 0451B] glory to posterity; and, besides, an example to the vigorous and energetic, an incentive to the idle and sluggish. Yet if there are people who henceforth emulate you in whatever spirit, they may perhaps owe themselves to you if they catch up with you; but they will certainly owe you the fact that they follow you.

I seem to see—with the good people’s leave—that indolence swelling with pride among the envious, and that familiar disdain of those inactive in military service, when, despairing of advancement, they philosophize over their cups and praise the holidays of the dishonored—not from a desire for perfection but through the fault of laziness. The pursuit of this way of life was rejected by their elders’ judgment, lest it should still be of use to boys. Thus, when they compared the little speeches of young men to woven pieces of cloth, they understood that youthful utterances are produced more laboriously in brief form than extended utterances are cut short.

But enough of this. I ask you to remember what follows: I wish to repay you in kind for this devotion, provided God, favoring my just undertakings, keeps me safe and brings me back. Farewell.

## LETTER V

Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0451D] Sent from Rome to Lyon, like the two preceding letters and all the remaining letters of this book except the last. This letter contains an especially elegant description of the whole Roman journey.] sends greetings to his Heronius.

While staying in Rome I received your letter, in which you anxiously ask whether the beginning of my journey is proceeding according to our common plan. You also ask how and by what sort of road I have traveled: what rivers I have seen famous in the poets’ songs; what cities renowned for the arrangement of their walls; what mountains made celebrated by the reputation of their names; and what plains conspicuous through the repetition of their battles. For you consider it pleasurable to learn from the faithful recollection of those who have seen them what you have discovered through reading.

Accordingly, I am glad that you wish to know what I am doing; for interest of this kind [Note: [Col. 0451D] In other books, “from.”] springs from inward affection. At once, and even if things have gone otherwise, yet with God’s help, I shall begin with favorable matters, [Col. 0452B] just as our ancestors used to begin their accounts even of their misfortunes by unfolding their earlier successes.

When I had left [Note: [Col. 0451D] Lyon, the common homeland of both of us. Just as Sidonius sometimes calls it Rhodanusian, so others sometimes call it Ararian, because it lies at the confluence of the two rivers. Elsewhere in his Anacreontic poem he called other cities situated on the Rhône “Rhodanusians.” Irenaeus, however, called the region and tract around the Rhône itself *Rhodanusia*, “Rhodanusian.”] the walls of our Rhodanusian city, the public transport service was available to me, [Note: [Col. 0452C] Otherwise it would not have been lawful to use public horses privately, since the law of Honorius prohibits this except in the following case: “Let no private person henceforth usurp the public transport service for himself, unless he is summoned by us or departs from the presence of our Clemency.” It was customary, however, for emperors to grant transport to those whom they summoned, as is shown by the letter of Constantius Augustus summoning Athanasius, preserved by Theodoret in Book II, and by Julian’s words to Eustochium: “Come to receive the consulship. The public route will carry you in a single vehicle, with a spare horse” (*ἧκε μεθέξων ὑπατείας. Ἄξει δέ σε δημόσιος δρόμος ὀχήματι χρώμενον ἑνί, καὶ παρίππῳ*).] since I had been summoned by sacred letters, and indeed traveled through the homes of friends and relatives. There my journey was delayed not by any shortage of public horses but by the multitude of friends, who, bound to me in a close embrace, vied in prayers for a prosperous journey out and back.

Thus we approached the ridges of the Alps. My ascent was swift and easy, and between the two terrifying sides of the precipitous mountains, paths had been softened for travel by cutting through the snow. As for rivers, whenever they were not navigable, there were convenient fords, or at least passable bridges, which antiquity vaulted with hidden arches from their foundations up to the roadway paved with walkable stone. [Col. 0452C] [Note: [Col. 0452C] This passage shows that the public transport service consisted not only of horses and vehicles but also of boats and river craft distributed, as circumstances required, along rivers, lakes, and inlets. This is certainly true. It is sufficiently apparent from the itinerary map, which, marking the route from Verona to Ravenna through Hostilia, notes that from Hostilia to Ravenna the journey was to be made along the Po; and from Senator Cassiodorus, who records King Theoderic’s letter to the boatmen of Hostilia in Book II of the *Variae*: “And therefore our authority has commanded the count of the sacred largesses that you are to be stationed at Hostilia, so that, refreshed by fiscal generosity, you may make your journeys along the bed of the Po with the public horsemen in the customary manner; so that the horses of the public service may assist when the labor is divided, since your route is not worn down when it is conveyed along liquid roads.” The *dromonarii* were rowers of *dromones*; the *dromones* (*δρόμωνες*) were swift, light vessels assigned to this purpose.]

At Ticinum I boarded a courier vessel—for that is the name given to such a boat. Carried by it soon to the Eridanus, I laughed at the often-sung Phaethontian sisters and their fictitious tears of arboreal metal, served up to us as after-dinner amusement. I inspected, even in their own waters, the Ulvosus Lambro, the blue Adda, the swift Athesis, and the sluggish Mincius, which arose among the Ligurian and Euganean mountains. Their banks and channels were everywhere clothed with oak and maple groves. Here the sweet chorus of birds resounded. Their piles of nests swayed, now placed in hollow reeds, now among the sharp rushes, now in the knotless bulrushes. All these shrubs had grown luxuriantly in clusters along the riverbanks, nourished by the moisture of the water-absorbing soil.

Passing on, I reached Cremona, whose proximity Tityrus, the Mantuan, once sighed for. Then, while the Venetian rower gave way to an Aemilian sailor [Note: [Col. 0453A] Just as on military roads there were fixed stations for changing the vehicles and horses that served the public transport, so on the rivers there were stations for changing the *dromones*. We have seen this concerning Ticinum and Hostilia; now we learn it concerning Brixillum. For he indicates that at Brixillum, a town on the right bank of the Po in the province of Aemilia, there was a change of rowers, and that Aemilians succeeded Venetians. Thus, above Brixillum the boatmen were Venetians; below it, Aemilians.] we entered the town of Brixillum, only so far as to leave it, and soon afterward, making our way by a more right-hand course, reached Ravenna. [Col. 0453B] There one might wonder whether the old city and the new harbor, [Note: [Col. 0453C] The harbor itself also had the appearance of a third town. For Ravenna is tripartite in Jordanes’ *Getica*: the first Ravenna, the last Classis, and the middle Caesarea. Thus the old city is Sidonius’s Ravenna, “the ancient city” (*πόλις ἀρχαία*) in Zosimus. The new harbor is Classis, which acquired that name from the fleet Augustus stationed there. The Caesarean road is Caesarea itself, lying between the city and the sea. The following “double town” does not refer to these three divisions but only to old Ravenna, which the branch of the Po flowing into it made double.] were joined or separated by the middle road of Caesar.

Moreover, one branch of the Po flows through the double town, while another washes against it. The river, torn away from its principal channel by the obstruction of public embankments and drained through them by diverted channels, divides its waters in such a way that, flowing around the walls, they provide defense, while flowing into them, they provide commerce. Everything useful to the market was brought here, especially whatever was suitable for eating—except that, since the salty sea drove itself against the gates on one side, while on the other the movement of barges stirred up the ditches with sewer-like mud, and the sluggish, weakened flow of the water was itself fouled by the adhesive sediment of the perforated riverbed, we thirsted amid the waters. For nowhere was there either the pure liquid of aqueducts, a cistern that could be cleansed, a flowing spring, or a mud-free well.

From there we proceeded to the Rubicon, which takes its name from the red color of its gravel. It was once the boundary for the Cisalpine Gauls and the ancient Italians, [Note: [Col. 0453D] Formerly the Rubicon was the boundary of Italy. Cicero, in the sixth *Philippic* against Antony, says: “that he should lead the army across the Rubicon, which is the boundary of Gaul.” For it divided Italy from Cisalpine Gaul. After Augustus added Cisalpine Gaul to Italy, the boundary of Italy was the Alps, not the Rubicon. Strabo, Book V: “After the foothills of the Alps comes the beginning of present-day Italy” (*Μετὰ δὲ τὴν ὑπώρειαν τῶν Ἀλπέων, ἀρχὴ τῆς νῦν Ἰταλίας*).] when it separated the towns of the peoples on either shore of the Adriatic.

From there I reached Ariminum and Fanum: the former memorable for Julian’s rebellion, the latter stained by Hasdrubal’s death. For there the Metaurus lies, whose good fortune, gained in a single day, extends so far into the distance that it seems even now to carry bloodstained corpses into the Dalmatian sea and discolor its waters.

From there, as soon as I entered the remaining towns of Flaminia, I immediately left them, passing the Picentes on my left and the Umbrians on my right. There either the Calabrian Atabulus or the pestilential Tuscan region infected my overheated body with air made poisonous by noxious blasts, alternating now heat and now cold. Meanwhile fever and thirst ravaged the deepest recesses of my heart and marrow. To their avidity we promised not only the pleasant waters of springs or the hidden waters of wells—although these too—but all the streams that were either nearby or in our path: the glass-clear Fucinus, the icy Clitumnus, the blue Anio, the sulfurous Nar, the pure Fabaris, and the turbid Tiber, though fear deceived desire.

Amid these places Rome also came into view. Of it I seemed likely to drink not only from the aqueducts [Note: [Col. 0453D] Aqueducts. Cassiodorus says in the *Account of the Aqueducts of the City*: “In the aqueducts of Rome, two things are especially important: that the construction be marvelous and the water’s healthfulness extraordinary.” According to Vitruvius, there are three kinds of water conduits: channels built of masonry, leaden pipes, or earthen tubes. The masonry channels are properly called *formae*. The name evidently comes from the fact that they were constructed with forms beneath them. In the same way, the Africans’ and Spaniards’ *formacei* walls were so called because they were packed with earth between two boards enclosed in a mold, as Pliny teaches in Book XXXV, chapter 14.] but even from its naval battle basins. There [Note: [Col. 0454C] The basilica of Saint Peter was outside the *pomerium*. It was not enclosed until the time of Pope Leo IV, who surrounded the new city bearing his name with walls so that it might protect the basilica against the Saracens.] before I had touched even the city boundaries, I prostrated myself at the apostles’ triumphal thresholds and at once felt every illness driven from my weakened limbs. After these proofs of heavenly protection, I was received in part of a rented lodging and, still lying here as I write these lines, devote a little time to rest. I have not yet stood before the tumultuous doors of the emperor and his courtiers.

For I arrived during the wedding of the patrician Ricimer, [Note: [Col. 0454D] This wedding is also mentioned in Letter 9 and in the *Panegyric for Anthemius*: “Thus the Augustus-in-law was blessed by the son-in-law Ricimer.” It was an ill-fated marriage, which Anthemius reproaches his ungrateful son-in-law for, in Ennodius’s *Life of Epiphanius*: “Who among the former emperors,” he asks, “ever did this, that, among the gifts which had to be given to the fur-clad Goth for the sake of the common peace, a daughter should be offered? We do not know how to spare our own blood while preserving another’s.” We have noted in the annotations to Ennodius that the emperor Anthemius’ daughter was not named Ascyla, as some have thought, and at the same time indicated the source of the error in the words of Gregory of Tours. It might indeed have been noticed that the barbarian name Ascyla did not suit a Greek girl, since it was customary among the Greeks to use names derived from their fathers and bearing clear meanings.] to whom the daughter of the eternal Augustus was being joined in hope of public security.

Therefore, amid this joy not only of persons but also of ranks, factions, and parties, it seemed more expedient for me to remain on your Transalpine side, especially since, at the very time when these words were being written for me, a Fescennine song was being performed throughout nearly all the theaters, mansions, praetoria, fora, temples, and gymnasia, [Note: [Col. 0455C] So the best manuscripts read. Others have *thalassia*, which has nothing to do with the matter. The word and song *talassio* are well known in weddings.] “Talassio!”

And even now, by contrast, let intellectual pursuits be silent, business rest, judgments be hushed, embassies be postponed, electoral canvassing be idle, and, amid the buffoonery of actors, the entire order of serious affairs wander abroad. The bride has already been handed over; the bridegroom has already been crowned [Note: [Col. 0455C–D] Early Christians did not use crowns at weddings. Since every crown depicted on coins belonged to the protection of some deity, they abstained lest they seem participants in a profane religion. Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, says: “Marriage too crowns bridegrooms; and therefore we do not marry pagans, lest they lead us as far as idolatry, from which marriage begins among them.” Once this danger ceased, they adopted the former custom, which Isaiah attests to have been most ancient among the Hebrews when he describes the bridegroom adorned with a crown, chapter 61. Basil of Seleucia, in his work on Thecla: “For I shall dance at your wedding; and I too shall place upon you—I shall place upon your bridegroom—the much-prayed-for crown” (*Χορεύσω γὰρ ἐπὶ τῷ σῷ γάμῳ . Κᾀγὼ δὲ περιθήσω μέν σοι, περιθήσω δὲ τῷ νυμφιῳ τῷ σῷ τὸν πολυευκτον Στέφανον*). The author of the *Chronicle* of Theophanes, on Copronymus: “He joined Irene to his son Leo, crowning them in the church of Saint Stephen with the crown alike of empire and marriage” (*Ἔζευξεν Εἰρήνην Λέοντι τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ, στέψας αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ ἁγίου Στεφάνου τῷ τῆς βασιλείας καὶ τοῦ γάμου*).], the consul is already honored in the palm-embroidered robe; the *pronuba* in the *cyclas*; the senator in the toga; the undistinguished man already lays aside his cloak. Yet the entire pomp of the bridal chamber has not fallen silent, since the new bride has not yet migrated to her husband’s home. [Note: [Col. 0455D] Severianus, in Homily 5 on the *Hexaemeron*, proves that the first example of leading a bride to her husband and the law came from God, who led Eve to Adam: “Examine the law: every ancient word of God was a rule of nature. God led the woman to Adam, and that law remains to this day: the woman is led to the man, not the man to the woman” (*Καὶ ὅρα τὸν νόμον· πᾶσα γὰρ Θεοῦ φωνὴ ἀρχαία κανὼν ἦν τῆς φύσεως. Ἤγαγεν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸν Ἀδάμ καὶ ἔμεινεν τοῦτο νόμος ἕως σήμερον τὴν γυναῖκα ἄγεσθαι τῷ ἀνδρὶ, οὐ τὸν ἄνδρα πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα*).] When this festivity has run its course, the rest of my labors will be disclosed to you, provided that the completed ceremony ever brings this city’s intensely occupied holiday to an end. [Col. 0455B] Farewell.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0456C] To a nobleman, still a private citizen at that time, later praetorian prefect of Gaul; see Book III, Letter 6.] sends greetings to his Eutropius.

For some time I had desired to write to you, but now I am especially impelled to do so, that is, as I travel toward Rome, God willing. My reason for writing is either the only one or the greatest one: namely, that I should summon you, drawn out from the depths of domestic quiet, to undertake the duties of palace service. [Note: [Col. 0456C] Not genuine military service, but in the sense in which all who are active in the court were said to “serve in the palace,” even if they did not handle weapons—such as notaries, record-keepers, financial officials, and others, concerning whom there is a title on the privileges of those who serve in the sacred palace. Indeed, the laws contrast palace service with genuine armed service. They distinguish three kinds of service altogether: armed or military service, which began to be called this after the name of military service was transferred to other functions; palace service, belonging to those who served within the palace; and the service of all the rest, who appeared before various judges and authorities, such as the service called proconsular or prefectural. The emperor Honorius says, under “Various Offices and Attendants”: “The attendants of every judge, among whom we also place the prefectural attendants, if they have transferred to any other service, whether palace or military, are to be recalled; we grant this power to those whom they abandoned.”]

To this is added the fact that, by God’s gift, your vigor of age, body, and mind is intact and suited to you; then that, equipped with horses, arms, clothing, expense money, and servants, you fear only—unless I am mistaken—to make a beginning. Though lively at home, you become sluggishly fearful when undertaking a journey abroad.

Yet can a man of senatorial stock, who is daily confronted by the portrait-images of his ancestors in their consular robes, rightly say that he has traveled abroad if, once and only in youth, he has seen the dwelling of the laws, the gymnasium of letters, the council-house of dignities, the summit of the world, the homeland of liberty, in whose single citizenship of the whole world only barbarians and [Note: [Col. 0456D] In some books, “of the world.”] slaves travel as foreigners? [Note: [Col. 0456D] That is, of the Roman world. After Antoninus Pius, who completed what Maecenas—if trust may be placed in Dio—had urged Augustus to do, Roman citizenship became common to all subjects. See Justinian’s Novel 78. Thus Rome became the one homeland and citizenship of all, in which, as Sidonius says, only foreigners were counted as those to whom that law could not apply: slaves and barbarians who did not obey the empire.] 

### 14

And now—what shame!—you may be left among rustic farmhands and snorting swineherds. For if you plow the field with a trembling plowshare, or, bent over, cut down the flowering wealth of the meadow with a curved sickle, or, stooped like a digger, turn over a vineyard heavy with branches using a rake, then you regard this as the highest fulfillment of your hopes.

Rather, wake up, and let your spirit, made sluggish and enervated by fat idleness, lift itself toward greater things. For a man of your birth, cultivating his own person is no less important than cultivating his estate. Finally, what you call an exercise of youth is the leisure of veterans, in whose withered hands rusty swords are belatedly exchanged for a hoe.

Granted: multiplied vineyards may make your must foam; barns bursting with gathered grain may provide countless heaps; a fat shepherd may enclose dense flocks with swollen udders in the milking pail, among the reeking folds. What does it matter that you have advanced your patrimony by such a sediment-laden profit—and not only hidden among these things, but, more shamefully, hidden because of them?

At the time of a council, after the young men have taken their seats and cast their votes, the judgment of an honored poor man will not unfairly crush you—a disgraced rustic standing, an old man hiding, a nobleman concealed—when you see with grief that you have gone ahead of those whom it would have been disgraceful for them to follow in our footsteps.

But why say more? If you tolerate me as a companion and helper in encouraging your efforts, I shall be your forerunner and partner in them. But if, entangled in the seductive snares of pleasure, you prefer, as they say, to join yourself to the teachings of Epicurus, who, after admitting the destruction of virtue, defines the highest good solely by bodily pleasure, behold, I call our ancestors and our descendants to witness: I am not party to this offense.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Vincentius.

I am distressed by the misfortune of Arvandus [Note: [Col. 0456D] The ancient chroniclers frequently remember this Arvandus, praetorian prefect of Gaul, and the trial by which he was condemned at Rome for treason by Anthemius, but with his name corrupted. Cassiodorus, followed by Marianus and Hermannus, calls him Aravundus. Paul the Deacon calls him Servandus, as do Sigebertus, Otto, Conrad the Abbot, and others. The true name, together with the complete history, is owed to Sidonius.] and do not conceal that I am distressed. For this too adds to the emperor’s praises: that those condemned to death may openly be loved.

I was his friend, beyond what the ease and changeability of his character allowed. The envy recently stirred up against me on his account bears witness to this; its flame scorched me because I had been somewhat incautious. But I owed it to myself to stand firm in friendship.

As for his nature, he did not possess the diligence required for perseverance. I complain freely, not insultingly, because, despising the counsels of loyal men, he was in every respect Fortune’s plaything. In the end, I am more astonished that he stood so long than that he ever fell. How often he himself boasted that he had endured adversity! Yet we, moved by deeper affection, pitied the recklessness that would one day bring about his ruin, judging that a man is not fortunate if he was repeatedly thought to be fortunate rather than always so.

But you ask for the sequence of his administration. With due regard for the loyalty owed even to an afflicted friend, I shall set out the matter briefly. He governed his first prefecture with great popularity, and the next with the greatest devastation. Equally oppressed by the burden of debt and the fear of creditors, he regarded the leading men who were to succeed him as rivals. He laughed at everyone’s conversations, probed their counsels, despised their services, and allowed himself to suspect their infrequent visits and grow weary of their constant ones.

At last, surrounded by the mass of public hatred, and placed under guard before he was stripped of office, he was captured and sent to Rome. Immediately he swelled with pride because he had sailed across the stormy Tuscan coast with a favorable passage, as though the elements themselves, in a sense, were serving a man conscious of his own merit.

He was held on the Capitoline by his host, [Note: [Col. 0457C] Identified in an ancient inscription as Flavius Eugenius Asellus. At this time he was count of the sacred largesses; later he was prefect of the City. In that office he restored the dome of the high altar in the basilica of Saint Paul, together with the square circuit of exedrae around the altar. We ourselves saw the marble bases beneath the porphyry columns while the work was still incomplete—for it has now been destroyed—and on them, two at each entrance, the following words were inscribed:

> FLAVIUS EUGENIUS ASELLUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS,  
> PREFECT OF THE CITY, V. S. I., RESTORED [THIS].

] Flavius Asellus, count of the sacred largesses, who still revered the dignity of the prefecture recently extorted from him, though it was already half extinguished.

Meanwhile the envoys of the province of Gaul, Tonantius [Note: [Col. 0457C] He had been praetorian prefect of Gaul. In the poem *Propempticon*:

> “Here you will find the father of learned Tonantius,  
> the ruler and pillar of Gaul,”

*[The supplied source ends here, mid-note.]*
[Col. 0457D] Priscus Ferreolus, the peer of Syagrius. But concerning Ferreolus, Sidonius’s relative by marriage, more will be said in Letter 12 of Book VII. For now it is enough to warn that those who distinguish Tonantius from Ferreolus at this point are mistaken, as though they were two men, when in fact there is only one Ferreolus, whose first name was Tonantius; just as Afranius Syagrius is the designation not of two men but of one. Otherwise there would have been four legates from a single province, although the laws forbid more than three from being sent.]

Ferreolus, former prefect, [Note: [Col. 0457D] All the fasti mention the consulship of Syagrius, which he held with Antonius during Gratian’s reign; only Sidonius gives Afranius as his first name. As for Onuphrius’s calling him Postumus Syagrius in his commentaries, he does so in his customary fashion. That most diligent scholar habitually joins together names that he once remembers as associated, applying them to everyone whom he sees connected with any one of them. Thus, after several years, he calls Atticus, who was Caesarius’s colleague, Pontius, because he had read of a highly distinguished man named Pontius Atticus during that period; yet from the funerary inscription seen at Rome it is certain that this consul Atticus’s cognomen was Nonius, not Pontius. In the same way, by combining the names of Mariniani, Asclepiodorus’s colleague, he fabricated Rufius Praetextatus Marinianus in place of Flavius Avitus Marinianus, as he is called on another marble; and, in place of Sidonius’s Petronius Maximus, Anicius Maximus. He proceeds in the same manner in several other cases, which it is not my purpose to pursue here. Syagrius will be discussed in the note to Book V.] grandson through the daughter of the consul Afranius Syagrius, [Note: [Col. 0458C] Apollinaris writes to his brother Thaumastus in Book V, Letter 6; to Petronius of Arles, as I believe a legal expert, in Books II, V, and VIII.] and also Thaumastus and Petronius—men endowed with the greatest knowledge of affairs and language, and worthy to be counted among the chief distinctions of our homeland—followed with the official records, intending publicly, in the name of the province, to accuse Arvandus. [Note: [Col. 0458C] These records contained the provincial decree concerning the accusation of Arvandus; what is called below the “provincial mandate” is called, in the decree’s own terminology, the page of the decree in the assembly at Bourges. Legates were not heard without the decree tablets of the city or province by which they had been sent. Book II of the Theodosian Code, under “Legates.”]

Among the other matters that the provincials had instructed them to pursue, they brought intercepted letters, which Arvandus’s secretary, after being arrested, admitted that his master had dictated. The letter appeared to have been sent to the king of the Goths, [Note: [Col. 0458C] To Euric, who had succeeded Theodoric, the brother mentioned in Letter 2, two years earlier. The Greek emperor with whom Arvandus did not want peace was not Leo, who ruled in the East far from the Goths, but Anthemius, who had come to Rome from Greece and whom Arvandus therefore mockingly calls “the Greek emperor”; Ennodius likewise calls Ricimer “the Galatian” and “the little Greek” in his *Epiphanius.] advising against peace with the Greek emperor, demonstrating that the Britons settled along the Loire ought to be attacked, [Note: [Col. 0458D] “Armoricans.” So that no one would think of the island of Britain, he added a designation identifying the Gallic Britons. Their king, as Sidonius writes, was Riothamus—the same man whom Euric, according to Jordanes in the *Getica*, defeated near Bourges while he was bringing aid to the emperor Anthemius.] affirming that Gaul ought to be divided with the Burgundians according to the law of nations, and containing many other such mad proposals, which would bring wrath upon a fierce king and shame upon a peaceful one.

The legal experts eagerly interpreted this letter as a charge of treason. Auxanius and I—[Note: [Col. 0458D] That Arvandus was born of a prefectorial father will soon be shown by his own words. Besides this Arvandus, the same period produced two other notable men named Auxanius in Gaul: one was a bishop who, together with Faustus of Riez, attended the synod as Hilary’s legate in the case of Hermes of Narbonne, as Hilary’s letters attest; the other was an abbot, the successor among the Arverni of Sidonius’s Abraham, concerning whom see Book VII, Letter 17, to Volusianus.] considering it treacherous, barbarous, and cowardly to avoid Arvandus’s friendship, however compromised, in his adversity—did not allow this proceeding to escape the notice of that outstanding man. We therefore reported to him, who suspected nothing of the kind, the entire counter-strategy which those vigorous and fiery men had devised with the greatest skill to conceal until the trial: namely, to entangle their unwary opponent, who had rejected the counsel of his companions and rashly trusted in himself alone, through an unexpectedly precipitate declaration. [Note: [Col. 0459C] The entire order and preparation of the accusation undertaken. Since the legates were permitted to attack Arvandus on two charges—treason, on account of the letter sent to Euric, and extortion, on account of the depredations marked in his later prefecture—they presented only the latter, deliberately concealing their zeal concerning treason, so that they might overwhelm him at trial unprepared and off guard.]

We therefore explained what we thought safe for ourselves and for our more intimate friends. We advised him to admit nothing as trivial, if his enemies demanded it even as something of the smallest importance; that very dissimulation, we said, would prove exceedingly troublesome, since it would more easily lull him into a false confidence. On learning this, he sprang up and burst into sudden abuse:

“Begone, degenerates,” he said, “unworthy sons of prefects, with this outlandish panic! Since you understand nothing, leave this part of the business to me. Arvandus has enough in his own conscience; I shall scarcely deign to allow advocates to defend me in an action for extortion.”

We withdrew sadly, bewildered no less by the insult than by grief. For what physician would rightly be disturbed whenever madness seized a hopeless case?

Meanwhile our defendant traversed the Capitoline area dressed in white: at one moment feeding on the deceptive greetings of flatterers; at another, listening willingly, as though recognizing them, to the crackling bubbles of adulation; at another, inspecting the silk, jewels, and every costly parcel of the money-changers, as though he intended to purchase them—handling, appraising, turning them over—and, while doing so, complaining at length about the laws, the times, the senate, and the emperor, because they had not avenged themselves upon him before subjecting him to examination.

A few days passed. The senate, in full attendance, went to the hearing chamber; this I learned afterward, for I had departed during these events. Our man proceeded to the senate-house shortly after having his hair cut and his skin polished with pumice, while the accusers, dressed in half-mourning and unkempt, were kept waiting for the messengers from the decemvirs, [Note: [Col. 0459D] Some conjecture that the reading should be “from the five men,” since five senators chosen by lot judged cases involving the life of a senator together with the urban prefect, according to the final law of the Theodosian Code, Book XVII, “On Jurisdiction,” and Book XIII, “On Accusations.” That this practice continued even after Sidonius’s time is shown by the judgment of Basil and Praetextatus in Cassiodorus, *Variae* 4. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts agree on “the ten men” at this point.] and through deliberate squalor had forestalled the accused’s due sympathy by casting suspicion upon his shabby accusers.

The parties, once summoned, were admitted; as was customary, they took their places facing one another. Before the opening of the proceedings, the former prefects were offered the right to sit. Arvandus, already displaying the unhappy shamelessness of his character, thrust himself forward at a hurried pace almost into the midst of the judges’ benches. Ferreolus, with his colleagues standing around him, sat modestly and quietly at the end of the lower benches, so that he might remember himself to be a legate no less than a senator. For this conduct he was afterward praised and honored all the more.

While these proceedings were taking place, and the leading men who had been absent were arriving, the parties rose and the legates presented their case. After the provincial mandate mentioned above, the letter was produced; and when it was read aloud slowly, Arvandus, before being questioned, declared that he had dictated it. The legates replied, although it was quite clear that he himself had dictated what was so wicked.

But when, in his frenzy and unaware of how far he was falling, he pierced himself by repeating his confession twice in succession, the accusers shouted out and the judges cried aloud that they had caught the defendant confessing treason. In addition, he was being strangled by thousands of legal formulas that established the same point.

Only then, it is said, did the laborious man grow pale with belated remorse for his loquacity, realizing too late that even a man who had not aspired to wear the purple could be pronounced guilty of treason. At once he was stripped of the privileges of his two prefectures, which he had governed for five years with repeated fasces, and was assigned to the public prison, returned to a plebeian family not as an addition but as a restoration.

The most pitiable circumstance, as those who witnessed it related, was that because he had entered the court adorned and polished beneath his black-clad accusers, he was shortly afterward led away in disgrace, but did not appear pitiable. For who would be deeply moved by the condition of a man whom he saw carefully prepared and dripping with luxury as he was carried off to the stone quarry or the prison workshop?

After the trial had been postponed for scarcely a fortnight, he was sentenced to death and cast onto the island of the Epidaurian serpent, Aesculapius. [Note: [Col. 0459D] Arvandus therefore experienced three forms of custody during this trial. First he was handed over to the free custody of his host Asellus, a concession to the dignity of a man whose trial had not yet been constituted, according to Book I of the title “On the Custody of Defendants.” Defendants distinguished by rank, such as senators, were not committed to prison before conviction. Alluding to this, Jerome writes against Vigilantius: “It is characteristic of senatorial dignity,” he says, “that they are confined not in the most dreadful prison among murderers, but in free and honorable custody, on the Fortunate Isles and in the Elysian Fields.” After this, once the public crime had been established, he was committed to the public prison. Venuleius, same code, Book 5: “If the defendant has confessed, he must be thrown into public chains until judgment is pronounced.” Finally, once condemned by the judges’ sentence, he was thrown onto the Tiberine island until the matter should be referred to the emperor.]

There, stripped of every grace even to the grief of his enemies, and as though spat out from human affairs by the nausea and vomit of fortune, he now—[Note: [Col. 0460D] This was done by order of the emperor Tiberius, so that the punishment of those condemned by the senate would always be delayed until the tenth day, as Tacitus, *Annals* III, and Dio, Book LVII, relate. In Arvandus’s case, however, the punishment was delayed not for ten but for thirty days. Accordingly, Justus Lipsius considered Sidonius to have suffered a lapse of memory, attributing to the senatorial decree of Tiberius what properly belonged to the Theodosian law *Si vindicari*, under the title “On Punishments,” which ordered a thirty-day suspension of punishment. But the facts themselves prevent us from agreeing with that most polished scholar. The Theodosian law, as its wording makes clear, restricted only the emperor’s judgments, whereas the senatorial decree concerned only judgments of the senate, as Dio notes. Arvandus’s trial, however, was senatorial and therefore had to be regulated by the senatorial decree, not by the law. The fact that he assigns thirty days to the senatorial decree therefore indicates that, after the old ten-day decree—at an uncertain time—another twenty days were added and nevertheless attributed to the same decree. Legal interpreters have observed that this was the practice with the Julian laws and others: provisions later added to them were commonly attributed to the original laws.] under the ancient senatorial decree of Tiberius—draws out a life of thirty days after his sentence, shuddering hour by hour at the hook, the Gemonian Steps, and the noose of the turbulent executioner.

For our part, according to our strength, we offer prayers both in his absence and in his presence, doubling our petitions and supplications, that, with the blow suspended and the drawn sword already poised, August clemency might grant even exile to him, half-dead though his property had been confiscated. [Note: [Col. 0461C] Anthemius seems to have granted this in response to Sidonius’s prayers. For Cassiodorus, Paul the Deacon, and others write that Arvandus was punished by order of Anthemius not with death but with exile.]

Yet whether he awaits the final end or endures it, nothing could be more wretched for him—if, after so many marks of disgrace and insults branded upon him, he now fears something beyond merely living.

Farewell.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Candidianus.

[Note: [Col. 0461C] He was a native of Caesena but lived at Ravenna, having moved there. Another Candidianus, bearing the same name and old enough to have been his grandfather, performed many courageous deeds near Ravenna against the tyrant John; Olympiodorus mentions him, among others, in Photius’s excerpts.]

You congratulate me on lingering at Rome, though you do so with a kind of wit seasoned with the salt of my fatigues. You say that you rejoice because at last your indispensable friend is seeing the sun, which the occasional drinker Ataricus must have viewed only rarely. You reproach me with the mists of my fellow citizens of Lyons and complain that our day, obstructed by morning darkness, scarcely opens under the heat of noon.

And you, are you chattering this nonsense to me as a home-born slave of Caesena’s furnace rather than of its town? What you yourself felt about that soil of your birth, whether for pleasure or advantage, you showed when you moved away. Yet you live more happily in exile at Ravenna, with your ears pierced by the mosquitoes of the Po and surrounded by the talkative crowd of the municipal frogs.

In that marsh, where everything proceeds according to a perpetual reversal of nature’s laws, walls fall, waters stand, towers flow, ships sit, the sick walk about, physicians lie down, baths grow cold, homes burn, the living thirst, the buried swim, thieves keep watch, authorities sleep, [Note: [Col. 0461C] Clerics were far removed from the business of lending at interest. The canons order those who lend at interest in any manner to be removed from the clergy: *καθαιρεῖσθαι τοῦ κλήρου*, “to be deposed from the clergy.” Among the Syrians, however, lending at interest was a characteristic occupation. Thus, by “Syrians,” he includes the entire class of moneylenders, as Salvian writes in Book IV *On Providence*: “Let us consider only all the crowds of merchants and Syrians, who occupy almost the greater part of all cities.”] clerics lend at interest, Syrians chant psalms, [Note: [Col. 0461D] Merchants were forbidden not only armed service but every kind of military service. The Code says: “Merchants must not serve in the army.” Soldiers, in turn, were forbidden not only commerce but also other businesses undertaken for private use. Ambrose, Book I *On Duties*: “For if a man who serves the emperor is prohibited by human laws from undertaking litigation, conducting forensic business, and selling merchandise, how much more ought one who serves in the army of faith to abstain from every commercial activity.”] merchants serve as soldiers, soldiers engage in commerce, [Col. 0462A] old men study ball games, young men dice, [Note: [Col. 0461D] That eunuchs could not lawfully serve in the army is indicated by Law 4 under “Military Affairs”; Claudian likewise writes in *Against Eutropius*: “Leave arms to men.” The *foederati*, whom he again mentions in Book II, Letter 13, were a class of soldiers drawn from barbarian peoples who served Roman emperors. Among them were readily included the Gothic princes, first hired by Constantine and thereafter receiving the name *foederati*. The Greek epitome of Novel 11 has *Γότθοι φοιδεράτοι*, “Gothic federates.” Olympiodorus in Photius’s excerpts, and Theodosius’s Novel 31, which mentions Saracen federates, show that the term *foederati* was also applied to men from other peoples. Procopius likewise uses it in Book I of the Persian War.] eunuchs bear arms, federates study letters.

Consider what sort of city it is where your household shrine is situated, a city that could more easily possess a territory than land. [Note: [Col. 0462C] Because of the surrounding marshes, which occupy part of the soil and deny its use. Properly speaking, “land” is what is plowed and cultivated; “territory” is the area over which a city’s boundaries and jurisdiction extend.] Therefore remember to spare the harmless Transalpine peoples. Content with the gift of their own climate, they gain little glory if they become illustrious only by comparison with worse places.

Farewell.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius sends greetings to his Heronius.

[Note: [Col. 0462C] To him he wrote Letter 5, of which this is in some sense a sequel, continuing the remainder of the Roman narrative after he had already obtained the urban prefecture.]

After the marriage of the patrician Ricimer—that is, after the resources of both empires had been scattered and exhausted—we at last returned to the regular business of public affairs, which opened a door and a field for action. Meanwhile, [Note: [Col. 0462C–D] Nothing is known of this host of Sidonius, Paul, whom he praises so highly.] received into the venerable household of Paul, a former prefect, honored for both learning and holiness, we were treated with the courteous offices of gracious hospitality. Indeed, no one in every branch of the arts is more outstanding than this man. Good heavens, what riddles he constructs in his propositions, what figures in his maxims, what cola in his verses, what mechanical devices with his fingers!

Yet one thing surpasses in him the summit of all his studies: his conscience stands higher than this eminent learning. Through him, therefore, I first investigated whether anyone could in any way gain access to the court’s favor; with him I considered which of the leading men might most effectively assist our hopes.

There was little need for hesitation, since there were few about whose patronage one could be uncertain. Most senators were indeed distinguished by wealth, exalted by birth, venerable in age, useful in counsel, elevated by rank, and accessible in their condescension. But, with due respect to the rest, two men of the highest eminence, both former consuls, [Note: [Col. 0462D] Colleague of the emperor Valentinian in his seventh consulship, in the year 450. An old inscription at Rome, in the basilica of Saint Paul, reads:

*Flavius Celerin(us), illustrious man, chief registrar of the distinguished patrician seat, discharged from office on the Ides of November, in the consulship of our lord Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and of Avienus, illustrious man.*

Two years after his consulship, he also undertook, together with Leo the Great, an honorable embassy to King Attila, as I learned from Prosper’s *Chronicle*. I therefore append his words here because they contain knowledge of a memorable and previously unheard-of event, although it is absent from the common editions of Prosper. The ancient copy reads as follows:

*In the consulship of Herculanus and Sporatius.*

After Attila had restored the strength he had lost in Gaul, he planned to enter Italy through Pannonia, with our commander Aetius making no provision according to the conduct of the previous war, so that he did not even use the Alpine barriers by which the enemy could have been kept out.
