He thought that the only hope remaining to his people was to withdraw from all Italy together with the emperor. But when this seemed full of disgrace and danger, shame restrained fear, and his ferocity and hostile desire were believed to have been satisfied by the broad devastation of so many noble provinces. Of all the counsels of the emperor, the senate, and the Roman people, none seemed more salutary than to seek peace through ambassadors from the most savage king. The blessed Pope Leo, relying upon God’s help—for he knew that God had never been absent from the labors of the pious—undertook this task together with Avienus, a former consul, and Trigetius, a former prefect. The outcome was no different from what faith had anticipated. For after receiving the entire embassy with respect, the king rejoiced so greatly at the presence of the supreme priest that he ordered the war to be abandoned and departed beyond the Danube, with peace promised.]

Gennadius Avienus and [Note: [Col. 0462D] Five years before this he had been consul with Vivianus. He had also been prefect of the praetorium of Italy for several years, and a patrician, as the Novels of Majorian and Severus attest. After him, two other consuls of this name followed: one in the final year of Odoacer, whom Cassiodorus, to distinguish him from our Basil, calls Basil the Younger; he too was prefect of the praetorium of Italy and a patrician. The other was consul in Justinian’s fifteenth year, the last of the ordinary consuls. This note belongs to page 19. EDITOR.] Caecina Basilius were conspicuous above the others. In the most exalted order, setting aside the privilege of the military branch, [Note: [Col. 0463D] The armed branch is distinguished from the civil branch. In Majorian’s panegyric, concerning Peter, his master of letters:

“He who governs the reins of the civil branch  
Supports the burdens of the armed.”

Vegetius Renatus likewise writes in Book I: “More men followed the armed military service, for the civil branch had not yet drawn away the more vigorous youth.” Those who handle weapons are counted among the former; those who practice law and the other peaceful studies among the latter. Thus, just as Sidonius distinguishes two senates here, Paulinus distinguishes two courts of the emperor Maximus in Book III of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

“Additional couches hold the leading men, whom the nearby splendor  
Of the royal heights joins to the neighboring honor;  
Distinguished by the trabea, they hold the authority  
Of laws and arms, the rights of the forum or the trumpets of war.”]

they were easily the foremost men after the emperor in purple.

Yet even among these men, although both were remarkable, their characters were different, resembling one another in temperament rather than in intellect. I shall speak briefly about them. Avienus had reached the consulship through good fortune; Basil through merit. Accordingly, Avienus was praised for the agreeable speed of his advancement, Basil for the belated abundance of his dignities.

Whenever either man went out from his household, a multitude of clients pressed before, behind, and around him. Yet the hopes and energies of their associates were very different despite their equal rank. Avienus worked to advance his sons, relatives, and brothers; and because he was always worn down by the petitions of his household candidates, he was less effectively able to deal with the needs of those seeking favors from outside. In this respect the Decian family was preferred to the family of the Corvini: whatever Avienus, while girded with office, obtained for his own people, Basil, though ungirded, conferred upon strangers.

Avienus’s spirit opened to everyone, and quickly, but with less practical benefit; Basil’s opened to only a few, and slowly, but more usefully. Neither was difficult to approach, and neither was expensive. But if one cultivated both, one obtained familiarity more easily from Avienus and a benefaction from Basil.

After weighing these matters on both sides for a long time, mutual deliberation settled upon this arrangement: while preserving the reverence due to the senior consul, we would attach ourselves rather to Basil’s household, which we visited neither too rarely nor too often.

At once, while through this most eminent man we were working on something connected with the requests of the Arverni embassy, behold, the Kalends of January arrived. On them they were awaiting the name of the emperor who was about to become consul, [Note: [Col. 0464B] Anthemius, who had previously been consul in the East as a private citizen and was now about to assume the office again after taking up the imperial power, as was customary for new emperors. New emperors ordinarily assumed the consulship on the nearest Kalends of January after the beginning of their reign, as all the fasti show; Sidonius writes of Avitus in Poem 8:

“His year, once that of the emperor, now shines as consul’s,  
And his deserved diadems grow through the trabea.”

Pliny the Younger likewise praises Trajan’s moderation because he preferred to entrust to private consuls the year that by custom was due to his fasces, whereas other emperors sought it with such eagerness that many transferred it to themselves after it had been assigned to designated consuls. Hence, after Justinian’s time, when the ordinary consuls had been abolished and imperial and consular dates were joined in public records, the consular era was one year behind, as in the formula: “Given on the Kalends of May at Constantinople, while Flavius Heraclius Augustus was emperor, in his ninth year, and after his eighth consulship,” because Heraclius had assumed the empire in March and the consulship in the following January. At the Sixth Synod, session 1, however, the emperor Constantine’s twenty-seventh year is compared with the twelfth year after his consulship, a great interval between the two numbers, because in the years of the imperial reign all the years are counted in which he had ruled with his father still alive before his own consulship.] August, soon to be consul.

Then my patron said: “Come, my Sollius, although you are weighed down by the burden of the office you have undertaken, I want you to bring forth your old Muse in service to the new consul, composing some votive offering, even if on improvised strings. I shall provide you access when you seek admission, encouragement when you recite, and support while you recite. If you trust one who has experience, many serious advantages will come to you through this amusement.”

I obeyed his instructions. He did not withdraw his favor from the task he had imposed; and, an unconquerable supporter of the devotion laid upon me, he dealt with my consul so that he would make me prefect of his senate. [Note: [Col. 0464D] Some manuscripts read “I, therefore.”]

But you, if I am not mistaken, detest the length of a letter and will now linger more pleasurably over rereading the verses of the little work itself, I know. For this reason the letter carries the loquacious poem in what follows, so that, in my absence while I am on my way, it may converse with you for a few days in my place. If it receives as well the marks of your critical judgment, that will be as pleasing to me as if, while I was speaking in the assembly or among the rostra, the applause of not only the broad purple stripe but also the tribunes were rousing my “bravo.”

I warn you plainly and expressly: do not measure these trifles of mine against your hexameters. When my verses are compared with yours, they will rightly be judged not by the trappings of heroic poetry but by the dirges of epitaphs.

Nevertheless, rejoice that this very panegyric, even if it has not received approval, has certainly received the reward of a successful outcome. Therefore, if gloomy matters must still be made pleasant with jokes, I wish to conclude the page with a glorious—or, rather, Thrasonian—ending, imitating Plautus’s *Miles Gloriosus*.

Accordingly, since I have reached the prefecture through the opportunity afforded by my pen, may you at once order me, as one invested with authority, [Note: [Col. 0465C] My prefectorial authority, naturally. Prefects and all other magistrates who possessed the right to carry swords were girded; their distinctive insignia was the belt, *οἱ ἀρχὴν ἄρχουσι μετὰ ξίφους καὶ τελαμῶνος*, “those who exercise authority with sword and baldric,” as Gregory of Nazianzus says in his letter to Africanus. The honor of the belt is frequently mentioned in legal sources. Hence the earlier expressions “Avienus girded, Basil ungirded,” and, in Book V, Letter 7, “rights for the girded, privileges for the ungirded.”] to carry me to the stars amid acclamations gathered from every direction for all my praises—eloquence, if I please you; good fortune, if I displease you.

I seem to see you laughing, because you perceive my boasting to resemble that of Plautus’s most ferocious comic soldier.

Farewell.

## LETTER X

Sidonius sends greetings to his Campanianus.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] This is how the ancient books read, not “Campanius.” The same form occurs in the inscription of Julius Ferox Campanianus, an illustrious man and urban prefect in the time of Diocletian, and in Cassiodorus, Book IX, *Variae*, where Campanianus is called a most eloquent man.]

I received [Note: [Col. 0465D–0466C] He was under the authority of the urban prefect. Sidonius therefore soon sends him to the port of Ostia to ensure that the grain brought by ships from Brundisium is conveyed to the City by river barges. Although increasing the City’s supplies was properly the responsibility of the prefect of the grain supply, it also concerned the urban prefect as the superior authority, Code, “On the Office of the Urban Prefect,” law 1. Thus both Sidonius here and Symmachus, Book X, Letter 48, while holding the urban prefecture, share responsibility for provisions with the prefect of the grain supply.] your letter through the prefect of the grain supply, in which you introduce him to me, a new judge, as your old companion. I give him great thanks, and you the greatest, because you have determined concerning my friendship either to presume upon its security or to regard it as unharmed. For my part, I embrace the acquaintance and friendship of this man not merely willingly but eagerly, since I know that by this service my own favor toward you will also be more closely joined.

But commend me—by which I mean the condition and reputation of my office—to his vigilance. I fear that the hunger of the Roman people may resound through the uproar of the theater, and that the public famine may be attributed to my misfortune. [Note: [Col. 0466C] Complaints about bread, by which the populace would riot when famine threatened, often hung over the head of the urban prefect, as the example of Tertullus shows in Marcellinus, Book XIX. Such complaints were heard especially in theaters and circuses, where the crowd was large and greater license prevailed. Tacitus, *Annals* V, in the consulship of Domitius and Scribonius: “In the same consulship, because of the severity of the grain supply, matters came close to sedition; and many demands, and demands for many days, were made with greater license in the theater.” Eunapius describes another circus riot at Constantinople in his account of Sopatrus; Zosimus, Book V, describes a Roman one, when the ports were held by Heraclian, count of Africa, and that fatal cry was heard in the circus: “Set a price on human flesh.”]

I am therefore preparing to send this very man immediately to the port, because I have learned that five ships which sailed from Brundisium, carrying shipments of wheat and honey, have reached the mouths of the Tiber. If he acts energetically, he will quickly arrange for their cargoes to be offered to the expectations of the populace, commending himself to me, me to the people, and both of us to you.

Farewell.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius sends greetings to his Montius.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] To a Sequanian, as the opening words immediately show. The letter was written in the time of Anthemius, but it recounts events that occurred during Majorian’s reign, in the year indicated by the consulship of Severinus, 461.]

You ask, most eloquent man, that a certain satire, if it has been written out by me, be sent to you as you set out for your Sequani. I am astonished that you should have asked this. It is not right that you should so quickly form a mistaken opinion about the character of a friend.

I was naturally about to devote myself to this theme, now having the leisure for it and possessing the years that would have made it presumptuous for me to dictate such a work when I was a young soldier, but dangerous to publish it. For which grammarian, even when greeting someone, has not heard that Calabrian poet say:

“If anyone has composed evil verses against another,  
There is a law and a judgment—”

But lest you should form any further similar opinion of your companion, I shall explain at somewhat greater length, but from the beginning, what it was that breathed upon me the rumor and smoke of an unfavorable suspicion.

During the reign of the Emperor Majorian, a document circulated at court, but without a title, filled with biting satirical verses—verses which, having made sufficiently abusive use of the naked disclosure of names, attacked vices most severely, and people even more severely. Meanwhile the people of Arles, where the affair was taking place, began to murmur and ask which poet deservedly bore the burden of the public fury, especially those against whom the unknown author had directed his attack by means of unmistakable indications. It happened by chance that Catullinus, then an illustrious man,

[Note: In the heading of the poem he is called no more than “most illustrious.” He must therefore subsequently have been adorned with some honor or privilege by which he became illustrious.]

[Col. 0466C]

came there from the Arverni, at a time when he was always friendly to me, but especially so because of our recent military service together. For travel often makes fellow citizens more intimate friends. Thus Paeonius and Bigerus laid this trap for the unsuspecting man: in the presence of many people they asked him, as though casually and jokingly, whether he recognized this new poem. He replied, “If you tell me that it is.” When they fruitlessly poured out various insinuations as if in jest, Catullinus burst into laughter and, with an untimely expression of approval, began to exclaim that the poem was worthy of being preserved forever in letters of gold and rightly to receive a rostral tablet, or even a Capitoline one.

[Note: “A satire worthy,” he says, “of being engraved in bronze and set up before the Rostra or in the Capitol among the tables recording laws and public monuments.”]

[Col. 0467A]

Paeonius flared up, for that satirical poem had bitten him too eagerly with a burning tooth. Turning to the bystanders and busybodies, he said: “I have now found the culprit in a common injury. Do you see how Catullinus is dying of laughter? It is clear that he recognizes what is being mentioned. For what compelled him to rush into such a hasty judgment, unless he already knows the whole matter—he who judges so confidently from a part of it? Therefore Sidonius is now in Arverni territory; from this it follows that the affair was woven by that author and heard by this man.”

They rushed into madness and insults against one who was absent, unaware, and innocent; no room was left for an inquiry into his good faith. Thus the popular figure, by whatever method he wished, acquired the easy support of the fickle crowd. Paeonius himself was wholly a man of the people, frequently stirring up the sea of seditions with tribunician blasts. But if you had asked what his lineage was and where his family came from,

[Col. 0467B]

you would have found that he was no more distinguished than one born in a municipal fashion:

[Note: His ancestors, evidently, had attained no public distinction, but had grown old within the honors and rights of their own municipalities. Suetonius likewise relates, in chapter 2, that Augustus’ grandfather had been content with municipal offices. Cicero, in *Pro Sulla*, says: “For he himself is municipal on his mother’s side.” In the same sense, because everything in municipalities is humbler and less conspicuous, Ausonius called a school “municipal” in his poem to Gratian, and Sidonius called municipal orators in Book IV, Letter 3, and municipal poets in his poem to Felix, meaning obscure and undistinguished.]

[Col. 0467C]

yet whom, from the very beginning, the brilliance of his stepfather rather than that of his father had caused to be recognized. Nevertheless, he continually sought to rise by fair means and foul: sparing money through avarice, lavish through ambition. For, so that he might at least through a daughter, though a most honorable one, be joined to a superior family, our Chremes had, as they say, promised a splendid dowry to his own Pamphilus, contrary to the strictness of civic custom.

When the Marcellian conspiracy was being prepared to seize the diadem,

[Note: That of the patrician Marcellianus, formerly a companion of Aetius. Procopius records in Book I of *The Vandalic War* that, after Aetius was killed, Marcellianus had pursued revolutionary designs in Dalmatia and acquired a power formidable to both empires. Excerpts from the rhetor Priscus confirm this as well. The interregnum, however, which Paeonius used as an opportunity to seize the prefecture of Gaul, did not occur after the murder of Maximus, whom Avitus soon succeeded, but before Majorian’s accession, after Avitus had been deprived of imperial power. The interval lasted more than ten months, and the state was thrown into confusion by Ricimer’s factions.]

[Col. 0467D]

he had made himself standard-bearer to the faction of the noble youth. A man still new in old age, he remained so until, at length, by experiments in successful audacity, he gave the obscurity of his birth some brilliance through the opening created by the interregnum. For while the court was vacant and the state in disorder, he alone was found who dared to gird himself for the administration of Gaul with the fasces before receiving his credentials, and who, after many months, mounted the tribunal as a prefect conspicuous among men of illustrious power. After a year had passed, he was scarcely honored, in the manner of the *numerarii*, at the end of his military career,

[Note: The office of the *numerarii* is not itself a dignity but an official position attached to a dignity. Nevertheless, the emperors decreed precedence of honor to *numerarii* who, after serving in the office of the prefect of the praetorium, laid down their military service. In Sidonius’ time they became praetorian tribunes; later the Emperor Anastasius honored them with the dignity of the *comitiva*, as is stated in the final law of the Code, *De Numerariis*. The same judgment applies to the advocates of both prefectures, who, after completing their office, were dismissed with the *comitiva consistoriana*, according to Law 8, *De Advocatis diversorum judicum*. Paeonius is compared with these men because he received the credentials of the prefecture he had usurped only toward the end of his administration.]

[Col. 0468A]

or rather in the manner of advocates, whose dignities begin only when their cases have ended.

Thus this man, a prefect in this fashion, a senator in this fashion—whose conduct I do not render in full measure with the praises appropriate to it because I owe that omission to the character of his family—aroused the hatred of many, rather than of good men, while I still knew nothing of it and was still his friend, as though I alone were capable of singing in verse about my age.

I came to Arles, still suspecting nothing—for why would I have suspected anything?—although my enemies had thought that I would not come. After seeing the emperor the following day, I went down to the forum as usual; but as soon as he appeared there, the crowd immediately grew frightened, as the poet says, “the sedition sat down, attempting nothing boldly.” Some, nevertheless, threw themselves at my knees more than was proper; others, so that they would not have to greet me,

[Note: The forum at Arles was evidently crowded with such people, as were the forums of almost all cities. John Maxentius, in his *Apology*, says: “They came out into public, even shouting around the statues of kings.” Basil alludes to this practice of hiding behind columns when speaking about moneylenders, whose debtors avoid meeting them: “No boxer avoids the blows of his opponent so completely as the borrower avoids meeting his creditor, shading his head behind columns and walls.” Ambrose, imitating Basil, writes in *On Tobit*, chapter 7: “The informer counts each step of the man he denounces and watches for him when he turns aside; the other immediately shades his head behind columns.”]

[Col. 0468C]

fled behind statues or hid behind columns; others, gloomy and sullen-faced, walked with their sides pressed against mine. I wondered what this behavior meant—excessive arrogance in some, the appearance of humility in others—yet I did not volunteer to ask the reasons, when one man, planted there by the factional crowd, presented himself to greet me.

As our conversation proceeded, he said, “Do you see this?”

“I see it,” I replied, “and I am certainly astonished at their behavior, though I am not amazed.”

Then our interpreter said: “They either curse or fear you as a satirist.”

“Why? When? Who has acknowledged the charge? Who has reported it? Who has proved it?” I replied.

Then, smiling slightly, I said: “Go on, my friend, if it is no trouble, and kindly consult those swelling with my name, asking whether the informer or accuser who invented the claim that I had written a satire might also have invented the claim that I had written it out in full. Perhaps it will be safer for them to withdraw, so that they may cease to be arrogant.”

When the messenger reported this, all of them immediately—neither modestly nor one by one, but hastily and in a crowd—

[Col. 0468C]

gave me kisses and their right hands. Only my Curio, who had attacked the treachery of deserters, was carried off and borne home by chair-bearers, as evening came on, more hideous than gravediggers.

The next day the Emperor ordered us to attend his banquet at the circus games.

[Note: It is worth observing where each person lay, so that this example may teach us what the ancient order of reclining was in a *sigma*, that is, on a semicircular couch or *stibadium*. Majorian’s banquet took place on a *sigma*. The *sigma* had two ends, like horns. Since Majorian was placed on the right horn of the *stibadium* and the consul Severinus on the left, there is no doubt that the first place was the one occupied by the emperor, and the next by the consul. Nor, I think, is there anything surprising in this. Among us too these are the first and most distinguished places at table. Juvencus writes in Book III:

“If anyone invites you to dinner, arranging a banquet,

Whoever is wise avoids placing his guests

Upon the highest horns.”

What may seem novel, and more remote from our practice, is that the third, fourth, and remaining guests followed in order the person who was first on the left horn. After the consul Severinus came Magnus, formerly consul; then Camillus, Paeonius, Athenius, Gratianensis; and finally Sidonius, moving toward the right horn where Majorian lay. Thus, on the full semicircular couch, the last person was nearest to the first, while directly opposite the first he was farthest away, the second person occupying that position. The same order was observed at the banquet of Maximus, which Saint Martin attended, according to Sulpicius Severus and others. On the right horn lay the Emperor Maximus; on the left, the consul Evodius; then came the companions of Maximus—his brother and paternal uncle—and the remaining nobles in order. Among these lay the presbyter Martin, in the middle; outside the *stibadium*, Martin sat on a chair to the right of Maximus. Paulinus, in Book III of his *Life of Martin*, after mentioning the nobles, writes:

“Among them, in the middle, where the *sigma* bends in its arc,

The presbyter reclined; on his right and left the order

Of powerful leaders, their limbs resting upon golden couches,

Pressed the purple beneath them, spread over costly fleece.

The venerable old man, holy in countenance,

Sat to the right of the king.”

He could not, of course, have sat to the right of Maximus unless Maximus had been reclining on the right horn. Thus the most honored place on the *stibadium* was the right horn, and next came the left, as we have said. Hence, in Gregory of Tours, *Miracles*, Book I, chapter 80, the Arian who occupies the horn on the right side and places his Catholic guest on the left treats him with mockery in this respect as in all others.

But mention of the *stibadium* and of the order of those reclining prompts us to investigate also the Lord Christ’s Last Supper, which is known to have been celebrated likewise on a spread *stibadium*—

[Note: There are also two letters on the same subject from Sirmond to Joseph Maria Suaresius. They appear among Sirmond’s works, vol. IV, pp. 665 ff., where representations of the Lord’s Supper and of the banquet at the house of Simon the Pharisee are also included; the learned Baunius found them in Sirmond’s papers.]

[Col. 0469D]

“upon a *stibadium*,” as Chrysostom says in Homily 27 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians; or “on a little couch,” as Tertullian writes in *On the Crown*: “I must recognize Christ also as reclining on a little couch.”

Christ did not recline in the middle, with the apostles crowding his sides on either hand, as our painters commonly represent him, but on the right horn,

[Col. 0469A]

in the position in which we saw Maximus and Majorian lying. This is shown both by other ancient monuments in books and on panels and by the mosaic work at Capua, dedicated by the abbot of Casino, who later became Victor II. If these representations were made according to an authentic image—and certainly no reason is apparent why they should not be regarded as such—it would not be difficult to understand why John, who perhaps was the youngest, reclined close to Christ upon his breast, or why Peter, who was farther away, is said to have signaled to John to ask Christ about the betrayer.

The ordinary consul Severinus, a man whose favor remained constant amid the immense upheavals of rulers and the unstable condition of the state, occupied the first place on the left horn. Beside him lay Magnus, formerly a prefect and recently a consul, a man equal to his doubled honors; behind him reclined Camillus, his brother’s son, who, after completing two dignities himself, had likewise adorned his father’s proconsulate and his uncle’s consulship with his own. Paeonius lay next, and Athenius on the other side, a man seasoned by the changing circumstances of lawsuits and times. Gratianensis followed him, a man who must be separated from every infamy, who, just as he came after Severinus in honor, had preceded him in favor. I lay last, where the left side of the purple-robed emperor extended along the right edge.

When much of the meal had been completed, Caesar directed his conversation toward the consul, and the consul replied briefly. From there the conversation passed to the former consul, and, because it was repeatedly brought back to literature, it eventually shifted by way of an opening to the illustrious Camillus. The emperor said: “You truly have an uncle, brother Camillus, for whose sake I am glad to have conferred one consulship upon your family.”

Then Paeonius, who wished for something similar, found his opportunity and said: “Not one, Lord Augustus, but the first.”

The remark was received with tremendous applause, so loud that even reverence for the emperor could not restrain it. Then the emperor asked Athenius something, and, whether by chance or deliberately I do not know, his imperial address passed over Paeonius, who was lying above him. Paeonius took this omission badly, and, still more disgracefully, replied to the man who had been addressed while remaining silent himself. The emperor smiled, preserving his authority, and, having joined in the conversation, was full of jokes; through his laughter Athenius received no less vengeance than he would have received injury.

The very experienced old man then gathered himself together,

[Note: “Most experienced.” Above, of the same man: “a man seasoned by the changing circumstances of lawsuits and times.” The word is of Greek origin, from *tribax*. In this sense Demosthenes called Aeschines *peritrimma tēs agoras*, “the worn-out man of the marketplace,” because he had spent time in the forum and been worn smooth by experience. Martial uses the word in the same sense in Book VII, speaking of Pompeius Avitus:

“Wet with legal business, polished by varied experience in the toga.”

Nor is the meaning of *trebaciter* different in Book IX, Letter 11: “I preferred to confess the deed simply rather than deny it craftily”—that is, cunningly and astutely. Thus, just as *legula* appears above for *ligula*, so here *trebacissimus* is used for *tribacissimus*; these letters are easily interchanged.]

[Col. 0470D]

and, as he was always inwardly consumed by the heat of shame, said: “I am not surprised, Augustus, if he tries to deprive me of my place to stand, since he is not ashamed to seize from you the right to speak.”

The illustrious Gratianensis said: “A broad field for satirical attacks is opened by this quarrel.”

At this point the emperor turned his neck toward me and said:

[Note: “With his neck turned.” Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, chapter 16, writes: “Does it not seem to you that Christ fell upon John’s neck, when John was reclining with his neck turned upon Jesus’ breast?”]

“Sidonius, I hear that you write satire.”

“And I hear that too, Lord Emperor,” I replied.

Then he said, smiling—

[Note: The manuscript reads “smiling.”]

—“Spare us, at least.”

“But because I refrain from unlawful acts, I spare myself,” I replied.

“What shall we do, then,” he said, “with those who provoke you?”

“Whoever he is, Lord Emperor, let him accuse me publicly. If I am refuted, let me, once convicted, suffer the punishment I deserve. But if I successfully disprove the charges brought against me with reasonable plausibility, I ask that, by your merciful indulgence and without injury to the law, I may write against my accuser whatever I wish.”

At this, the emperor looked toward Paeonius and began by a gesture to consult the man, who was himself nodding, whether the proposed condition pleased him. But when Paeonius remained confused and silent, and the emperor pressed the embarrassed man for an answer, he said: “I grant your request, if you ask for this very thing immediately in verse.”

“Let it be so,” I said. I turned around as though I were asking for water with my hands, delayed only as long as the servants moving rapidly around the *stibadium* required, and returned my elbow to the couch.

The emperor said: “You promised that you would ask in improvised verse for permission to write satire.”

And I replied:

“The man who blames me for writing satire, most noble prince,

I ask that you decree this: let him prove it, or fear.”

There followed a thunderous applause—unless I am boasting in saying so—equal to Camillus’ remark. It was not so much the dignity of the poem as the speed with which it was produced that earned it.

The emperor said: “I swear by God and by the condition of the state that henceforth I shall never prevent you from writing whatever you wish, since the charge brought against you cannot in any way be proved. It is also profoundly unjust to attribute to the judgment of a purple-robed official such private hostilities that the innocent and secure nobility should be endangered because of known hatreds and an uncertain accusation.”

When I modestly gave thanks for this judgment with bowed head, the faces of my haranguers began to grow pale. A little earlier anger had been followed by sorrow; now they nearly froze, as though they had been ordered to expose their necks to a drawn sword. Shortly afterward we rose.

We had gone only a short distance from the emperor’s sight and were still putting on our cloaks when the consul fell upon my breast, the former prefects fell at my hands, and that very friend of mine humbled himself repeatedly and abjectly, while everyone pitied him. I began to fear that by his entreaties he might arouse against me the resentment which he had not aroused by his accusations.

At last, pressed by the entreaties of the nobles gathered around him, I said that he should understand that nothing would be composed in verse against his attacks, provided that in future he spared my actions; for it ought to be enough that the accusation of satire had won me fame and him infamy.

In short, my lord Majorian, I endured not so much the advocate of the slander as the spreader of the rumor. But since I was satisfied in this way—since, in compensation for his guilt, so many summits and rights of powers and dignities had been brought under submission to my breast—I confess that the beginning of such an insult was so great that its end became glory.

Farewell.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0471]

## LETTER ONE

Sidonius sends greetings to his brother-in-law Ecdicius.

[Note: To his brother-in-law: for that is how he calls him in poem 20, namely Papianilla’s brother, the son of the Emperor Avitus. He was first a *comes* and military commander in Gaul under Anthemius, and was later made a patrician by Nepos. His actual name was Ecdicius, as in the manuscript and in Julian’s letters: “to Ecdicius, prefect of Egypt.” So too Alcimus Ecdicius was bishop of Vienne. Ecdicius is correctly called and written by this name in Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 24; in Jordanes the name has been shortened to “Decius.”]

[Col. 0471B]

Your Arverni now suffer two evils at once.

“What are they?” you ask.

The presence of Seronatus and your absence.

Seronatus—I shall first speak of him even by name—seems to me as though Fortune, foreseeing the future, were playing with words, just as, by contrast, our ancestors called battles “wars,” although nothing is uglier than battles; and, with a similar contradiction, they called the Fates “Parcae,” although the Fates do not spare anyone.

He, the Catiline of our age, has returned recently from the Aturres,

[Note: John Savaro, a man of distinction, rightly established this reading from the manuscripts; the correction had escaped us. The Aturres were, as he also showed, a people in Novempopulania on the river Aturrus, later called the Adour; accordingly, *Aduris* is also read in the words of Anianus prefixed to the Theodosian Code after the authority of Alaric. The name Aturres, or Adures, originally belonged to the people, not to the town. The town of the Aturres was called Vicus Julius, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in Book IX, chapters 7 and 20, and in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 52. Thus Rusticus of Vicus Julius, who signed the Second Council of Mâcon, was bishop of Adur. The same judgment applies in the *Life of Saint Philibert*, where he is said to have been sought by the citizens of Vicus Julius. But just as, in the same Novempopulania—formerly the territory of Cossio Vassatum—the Vasates later took their name from the people, so Vicus Julius became known as Aturres. At this time the Aturres, along with all old Aquitaine, were under the power and rule of the Goths. Thus Seronatus was returning from Gothic territory.]

[Col. 0472C]

so that he might wholly mingle here the blood and fortunes of the wretched people, which there he had made them taste only in part. You should know that, day by day, the spirit of a long-concealed madness is opening itself in him: he envies openly, pretends abjectly, behaves arrogantly like a slave; he imposes levies like a master, exacts them like a tyrant, assigns them like a judge, brings accusations like a barbarian; armed all day with fear, hungry for avarice, terrible through greed, cruel through vanity. He never ceases either to punish thefts or to commit them. Publicly, with summoned witnesses laughing, he belches out battles among citizens and letters among barbarians. Though insufficiently initiated even into the first letters, he dictates his correspondence publicly out of boastfulness and revises it out of shamelessness. He treats everything he desires as though he were purchasing it, neither paying prices because he despises them nor accepting documents because he distrusts them. In council he is silent; in the assembly he commands; in church he jokes; at dinner he preaches; in the bedroom he condemns; during investigations he falls asleep. Every day he fills the forests with fugitives, the villas with guests, the altars with defendants, and the prisons with clergy; exulting over Goths, insulting Romans, mocking prefects, and conspiring with *numerarii*.

He tramples upon Theodosian laws and produces Theodoric laws, seeking new taxes for old offenses.

[Note: The Theodosian laws are Roman laws collected in the Theodosian Code, which was then in force; the Theodoric laws are Gothic laws issued by the Gothic kings named Theodoric. Although, when Sidonius wrote this, Euric, successor of Theodoric’s brother, ruled the Goths in Gaul, Sidonius preferred to say “Theodoric laws” because of the punning resemblance to “Theodosian.” From this it may further be inferred that, when Isidore’s *Chronicle* says that Euric was the first to give the Goths a body of laws, this should not be understood as though the Goths had had no laws before Euric, but rather that Euric was the first to collect them into a corpus and code. Isidore’s own words concerning Leovigild make this perfectly clear.]

[Col. 0473A]

Therefore, quickly explain your delays, and cut short whatever it is that holds you back. The last remnant of liberty among your trembling citizens is waiting for you. Whatever is to be hoped for, whatever is to be feared, let it be accomplished through your intervention and under your leadership. If the republic has no strength, no protection, if the resources of the Emperor Anthemius are not as great as rumor claims, the nobility has decided, under your leadership, either to abandon their homeland or to cut their hair.

[Note: Either to undergo voluntary exile or to enter the clergy. The Arvernian nobility evidently preferred this to serving on the Gothic side if their territory should come under Gothic control. Clergy were exempt from military service. Those who became clerics were tonsured, as is well known; sometimes, however, they said that they were not cutting their hair but letting it down and growing it long, as Gregory of Tours repeatedly relates. If Sidonius is speaking according to this usage, he also means Gothic surrender, since the Goths wore long hair.]

## LETTER TWO

Sidonius sends greetings to Domitius, the grammarian and teacher.

[Note: Concerning his learning and censorial strictness, see the *Propempticon*:

“And first you will enter the home of the stern master,

While the Muses tremble.”]

You complain that I am in the country, when I ought rather to complain that you are now being detained in the city. Spring is already giving way to summer, and the sun, rising high along its extreme paths,

[Note: As it inclines toward the tropical solstice of summer, to which Plutarch’s words to an unlearned ruler also refer: “When the sun reaches its greatest height, rising among the northern regions.”]

[Col. 0473B]

extends its wandering ray toward the Scythian axis. What should I say about the climate of our region? Its expanse has been stretched out by the divine craftsman in such a way that we are more exposed to the vapors of the western world. What more? The world burns; Alpine ice is destroyed; the earth is marked throughout by the winding cracks of parched fissures; gravel lies barren in the shallows, mud along the banks, dust in the fields; and the water itself, wherever it flows continuously, grows sluggish through its delayed course. The stream is now not merely hot but boiling. And while one man sweats in linen and another in silk, you, wrapped externally in a traveling cloak and bound internally with bandages, moreover compressed into the hollow seat of the Camerinian municipality,

[Note: The word *Camerini* is absent from some manuscripts and deleted in others, so that it may appear to have been added as a gloss explaining the municipality. Some copies read *Amerini*, making it possible to suspect that a glossator wrote *municipii Arverni*, “of the Arvernian municipality.” The town of Arverni seems to be meant.]

[Col. 0473C]

begin yawningly to expound to pupils who grow pale no less from fear than from heat: “The Samian mother was mine.”

Why do you not rather, if you care for anything wholesome, quickly withdraw from the breathless narrowness of the city and, gladly inserted into our company, escape the cruelty of the dog-star season in this most merciful retreat?

If you wish, I shall tell you the situation of the estate to which you are being invited.

[Note: Almost all the ancient books write it this way. The name is derived from Avitus, the father of Papianilla, the owner of the estate, just as Ausonius has *Pauliacus* and *Lucaniacus*, from Paulus and Lucanus. From the ancient copies we likewise restored the reading in poem 18:

“If you should deem it worthy to visit our Avitacum.”

The remains of this estate, which Sidonius describes with exceptional elegance and fullness, were once thought to survive near Lake Serlieva, a short distance from the municipality of the Arverni. A few years ago, however, the lake was completely drained by diverting the waters that had stagnated there, revealing the groundlessness of that opinion. Some identify Papianilla’s lake with the lake at Cambon; this is somewhat more plausible. Yet, in my judgment, Sidonius’ description does not fit that lake sufficiently either.]

[Col. 0474C]

We are at Avitacum; that is the name of this estate, and because it came to me through my wife it is dearer than my paternal property. Here, with my household, under God’s protection, we live in harmony—unless you fear some evil spell.

A mountain on the western side, although composed of earth, is nevertheless steep; like a double support, it pours out lower hills from itself, separated from it by a width of about four *jugera*. But until the open ground of the forecourt suitable for the residence appears, the sides of the slopes follow the middle valley in straight lines as far as the edge of the villa, which stretches with its façades turned toward north and south.

The bathhouse clings on the southwest to the roots of a wooded cliff. If the coppiced forest along the ridge is cut down, its fallen timber strikes the mouth of the furnace in a seemingly spontaneous cascade of collapsing beams. From there rises the chamber of heated waters, which corresponds in equal dimensions to the adjoining anointing room, except for the semicircle of the spacious bathing basin. There the force of the boiling water, carried through a perforated wall in winding channels of flexible lead, gurgles and spurts.

Within the heated chamber there is solid daylight, and such an abundance of enclosed light that it makes even the most modest people feel that they are wearing more than nakedness. From there the cold room opens out, one that could not improperly rival pools constructed for public use.

The roof, first, is raised to a peak in the form of a cone; its four sloping ridges, converging from the corners, are covered with the tiles between them. The structure itself is squared with the greatest precision and ample dimensions, so that, without the attendants’ service interfering with one another, it can accommodate as many chairs

[Note: This must unquestionably be read in this way, not *quot solet*, as has appeared in printed editions until now. Cyprian, Letter 76 to Magnus, says: “Both a bathing basin and a pool are needed, in which the little body may be washed and cleansed.” The reference is not to a *sigma* or *stibadium*, but to the basin of the heated room, which Sidonius shortly before called the semicircle of the basin; here he calls the basin’s *sigma*, using the same sense, from its semicircular shape. For this reason reclining couches, or *stibadia*, are also called *sigmata*, just as Julian’s Constantinopolitan portico, in Zosimus Book III, was called a *sigma* because of its semicircular form. In the baths, those who washed passed from the heated chamber and its basin to the cold room, where they sat on chairs. Thus there needed to be as many chairs in the cold room as there were places in the heated room.]

[Col. 0474C]

as the semicircular basin can accommodate people. The builder placed two windows opposite one another at the junction with the suspended ceiling, so that they opened to the gaze of those looking upward a crafted coffered ceiling.

The inner surface of the walls is content with the whiteness of smooth cement alone. Here no shameful scene is displayed through the naked beauty of painted bodies—a scene which, just as it adorns art, disgraces the artist. There are no ridiculous actors in costume and painted faces, imitating the multicolored furnishings of Philistion,

[Note: The poets of mime, the makers of laughter—ridiculous men, dead in the very act of laughter—as Suidas reports. Eusebius, in his *Chronicle* under Tiberius, says that Philistion, a mime-poet of Magnesian nationality, was famous at Rome. Cassiodorus, at the end of Book XIV of the *Variae*, makes him the inventor of mimes. Epiphanius, speaking of the Manichaeans, says: “As for the rest, who could fail to laugh at their account? For what Philistion wrote may perhaps seem more necessary than the myths this man has fabricated.” Who could mention the rest without laughter, when what Philistion composed seems in a certain way more plausible than the fictions invented by this man?]

[Col. 0475A]

and no slippery, twisted wrestlers, contorted by boxing and grappling holds. Their living struggles, if they became indecently entangled, would immediately be separated by the chaste rod of the gymnasium officials.

[Note: “Baton, gymnasium director,” on the Ancona marble. Concerning the rod, Servius writes in his commentary on Book I of the *Aeneid*: “Even today contests between athletes and gladiators are brought to an end by a rod.” But the rod of the trainers, by which they imposed discipline on gladiators, was properly called a *rudis*. The old glosses read: “*Rudis*: a rod, the staff of the supervisors of the gladiators.”]

What more is there to say? Nothing will be found impressed upon those walls that it would not be more holy to have never seen.

[Note: A tetrastich, namely, placed above the doors of this pool, which appears among Sidonius’ poems, under title 19:

“Enter, chilled, the waves after the burning baths,” and so forth.]

A few little verses, nevertheless, will delay the visiting reader, in a moderation I do not at all disapprove, since one feels no desire to read them again, nor any irritation at reading them through.

Now, if you ask about the marbles, neither Parian, Carystian, Proconnesian,

[Note: The sense requires *Proconnesos*. Proconnesus was an island in the Aegean Sea, famous for its quarries of white marble, as Strabo records in Book XIII.]

[Col. 0475C]

Phrygian, Numidian, or Spartan stones have set slabs of variegated rock there. Nor, among Ethiopian crags and purple cliffs colored with genuine shell-dye, do scattered stones deceive me by imitating bran.

But although we are not enriched by the hardness of foreign rocks, our little huts, or *mapalia*, nevertheless possess a civic coolness. Rather, listen to what we have than to what we do not have.

Attached externally to this basilica, toward the east, is a pool—or, if you prefer to use Greek, a baptistery—which holds approximately twenty thousand *modii*. For those who come here washed clean from the heat, a triple entrance is opened through arched intervals in the middle wall. The supports in the middle are not piers but columns, which more skilled architects have called the purples of buildings,

[Note: Ornaments. Just as purple provides brightness to a garment, as I may put it in Fabius’ words, so columns provide brightness to buildings. Writers extend the word “purple” to everything signifying ornament and beauty. Sidonius below, in Letter 10, writes: “All the purples of noble speech.” Cicero, in *The Orator*, writes: “With what rhythms they should be mixed, as with purple.” Lucian, in *Hippias*, speaking of the parts of a bath, says: “The inner chamber is most beautiful, full of much light, and flowered like purple.” Finally, on an onyx gem, which we owe to the beneficence of the excellent Cardinal Baronius, these words are carved by the hand of the artist: “ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ, ΜΑΚΕΔΟΝ, Η ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑ ΤΩΝ ΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ”—“Be fortunate, Macedon; purple, that is, the honor and jewel of the brothers.”]

[Col. 0475D]

and into this pool six projecting pipes pour water drawn from the brow of the mountain, carried around in channels and bent along the outer sides of the bathing pool. The pipes pour through artificial lion heads, which to those entering carelessly will seem to display real grates of teeth, fierce eyes, and unmistakable manes around their necks.

If a household or visiting crowd surrounds the master here, the reciprocal exchange of voices is less intelligible because of the noise of the falling stream. The people therefore converse in one another’s ears: pressed down by the alien sound, public speech absurdly seeks secrecy.

From here, as one emerges, the front of the women’s dining room presents itself. Next to it, with the loom room nearby, is a storeroom, separated from it only by a wall built in the manner of a military enclosure. From the east, a portico looks out upon the lake, more

[Note: I do not understand what *collyria* means here. I believe Sidonius wrote *coluria*. He means piers constructed from several stones cut into a circular shape. He contrasts them with columns, just above saying, “The supports in the middle are not piers but columns,” because columns are made from a single stone, whereas piers are made from many. Stones cut into a circle could not more appropriately be called rounded *coluria*. Things truncated at their outer end are called *colura*; Suidas explains *kolouraios petra* from Callimachus as “a hollow, bent, or rounded stone,” and Hesychius defines *kolouria* as “a cut-off piece.” A similar contrast between piers and columns occurs in Natalis, poem 10, concerning Paulinus:

“For the piers had stood in a massive, shapeless row;

Now, made more beautiful, the same supports stand as columns.”]

And they gained an increase of both space and light. Supported by rounded *collyria* [Note: [Col. 0476B] “*Coluriis*.”], rather than by conspicuous monumental columns [Note: “Monolithic”: such columns as are commonly used on monuments. Cyprian the deacon, near the end of Book I of the *Life of Saint Caesarius*: “And to provide the holy virgins whom she had gathered with the necessary care for burial, she had movable coffins newly cut from enormous stones for the bodies to be buried.”]. From the side of the vestibule, the length [Note: Some books read “within.”] extends beneath a roof on the inside, uninterrupted by intervening walls. Since it itself looks out upon nothing, and is [Note: The correction is certain and supported by all the manuscripts; the printed editions erroneously give *hippodromum*, that is, “circus.” He does not mean a circus—for what would a circus be doing in the vestibule of a house, or what connection would it have with a cryptoporticus? Rather, he means a covered length, an enclosed walkway closed on every side, such as are found in the vestibules of the great, or such as Tertullian calls “shaded racecourses” in his *To the Martyrs*, chapter 28. *Hypodromus* is so called because one walks beneath it, just as *peridromis* in a roofless *xystus* denotes a walk around, and *diadromis* a passage through; it is also a part of the bathhouse in Lucian’s *Hippias*. The word was not unknown to Angelo Decembrio, who in Book V distinguishes *hypodromus* from *hippodromus*, nor to Aldhelm, the most learned man of his age, who in his book *On Virginity* says that the martyr Babylas is led to the palace apartments and to the *hypodromus* of the imperial vestibule. In these words one sees an image of Sidonius’ portico, if Sidonius, because it looked out upon nothing, preferred to call his a cryptoporticus. Pliny the Younger, from whom Sidonius certainly borrowed the word, calls the natural portico of his Tuscan villa a *hypodromus* in Book V, Letter 6: it was woven from the interlacing and bending branches of trees and shrubs, such as are produced in gardens by nature or art, and such as Sidonius depicts in his own Voroangus estate in the *Propempticon*. Cyprian likewise describes a vine-covered portico in his letter to Donatus: “The neighboring retreats offer seclusion; there, while the wandering tendrils of vines creep through the supporting reeds with hanging bonds, they make a leafy-roofed vine portico.” Pliny’s words require no interpretation, but I shall quote them so that it may immediately be clear that Sidonius properly restored to him the word he had drawn from his treasury. For in Pliny too *hippodromus* is wrongly read for *hypodromus*. Thus Pliny’s text runs: “Far and wide before this arrangement and pleasantness of the buildings extends the *hypodromus*. Its middle is open and at once presents itself in its entirety to the eyes of those entering. It is surrounded by plane trees; they are clothed with ivy, their upper parts green with their own leaves, their lower parts with those of another. Ivy wanders over the trunk and branches and joins the neighboring plane trees by its passage. Boxwood lies between them; laurel surrounds the outer boxwood, and contributes its shade to that of the plane trees. This is the straight boundary of the *hypodromus*. At the far end it is broken by a semicircle and changes its appearance; cypresses surround and cover it, making it darker and more deeply shaded under a denser shadow.” Plato seems to call a portico of this kind a *κατάστεγος δρόμος* in the *Euthydemus*: “When we had entered,” he says, “we walked in a covered walk.” Moreover, just as *hippodromus* is found in these passages for *hypodromus*, so in another passage of Pliny, Book V, chapter 32, one finds *Hippius* mountain, and in Ptolemy’s description of Bithynia *Ἵππιος ποταμός*, “Hippius River,” incorrectly written for *Hypius*. The subject is the city of Prusa, which was double in Bithynia: one beneath Mount Olympus, the other on the Hypius River. The inscription on ancient coins of Lucius Verus and Diadumenian teaches that the name must be written thus: *ΠΡΟΥΣΙΕΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΥΠΙΩ*, “of the Prusians by the Hypius”; and an old stone at Rome likewise distinguishes *ΠΡΟΥΣΑΕΙΣ ΑΠΟ ΟΛΥΜΠΟΥ* and *ΠΡΟΥΣΑΕΙΣ ΑΠΟ ΥΠΙΟΥ*, “Prusians from Olympus” and “Prusians from Hypius.”] if not a *hypodromus*, then at least, in my rightful usage, it will be called a cryptoporticus [Col. 0477A].

Yet this structure, taking away something from the space at the outer end of the walkway, creates a very cool room. There, when a public couch has been set up, the most talkative chorus of clients or nurses sings its retreat while I and my companions have gone to our sleeping chamber.

From the cryptoporticus one enters the winter dining room, whose arched fireplace has often been animated by fire and stained with dark soot. But why tell you this, when I am certainly not inviting you to the hearth now? Let me speak instead of matters that concern you and the present moment.

From this dining room there is a passage into the apartment, or little dining room [38], which is almost entirely open to the lake and wholly faces it. In it are a couch and a polished sideboard; to their floor, or platform, one gradually ascends from the portico below, not by shortened or narrowed steps. Reclining there, if you have any leisure during the meal, you may occupy yourself with the pleasures of looking out.

If some decoction is brought to you from that celebrated fountain of ours, you will see, in cups suddenly suffused with cold, flecks and fragments of snowy cloud; and the slippery brightness of the cups dulled by a kind of richness, as though by the sudden cold. Then you will see drinks answering the cups—drinks whose freezing vessels would frighten any thirsty person, not to say one wholly unaccustomed to wine.

From there you will watch the fisherman propel his alder boat into the open water; stretch stationary nets upon cork bark; or, by markers placed at fixed intervals, balance the lengths of the ropes bearing hooks—so that during nocturnal excursions across the lake the most voracious salares may be driven into traps made for their kind [Note: Ausonius mentions this fish in his *Mosella*:

> And the salar, distinguished by purple spots along its back.

From the indication of purple markings, and because he teaches that trout (*truttae*) become *fariones*, and *fariones* become salmon, many infer that salares are trout, hence called salmon-trout and believed to change into salmon. Alan of Lille, *The Complaint of Nature*: “There a little trout, entering the sea and baptized in the open water, was reckoned by the name of salmon.”]. For what could I say more appropriately here, when fish is deceived by fish?

When the food is finished, a guest room will receive you—because it is not at all sultry, and is especially suited for summer. For since it opens only toward the north, it has daylight but no sun. Between it and the dining room is a very narrow passage, where the chamber servants have a place for dozing rather than sleeping.

How pleasant it is here for cicadas to resound in the ears, chattering at midday; frogs to croak as twilight approaches [Col. 0478A]; swans and geese to cry out in the middle of the night; roosters and hens to sing together in the deepest darkness; and prophetic crows to greet with triple cries the crimson torch of the rising dawn; at daybreak, before the nightingale whistles among the shrubs, the procne (swallow) murmurs beneath the rafters [Note: Sidonius says that swallows *minuriunt*, and Spartianus that doves do so in the *Life of Geta*. Both expressions are elegant, for *minurition* denotes both the song of small birds generally and a plaintive sound such as the cooing of doves. Thus the Greek grammarians explain *μινυρίζειν* as “to sing softly and delicately, or to lament.” Cicero, *On the Orator* I: “If we wished to do this, those whose cases we had undertaken would be condemned before we had cited the paean or the *minurition* as often as prescribed”—he joins two kinds of song, the paean, which has a more vigorous voice, and *minurition*, which is softer. Plutarch, *On the Difference between the Flatterer and the Friend*: “Most men, in the presence of kings, would be Apollos if they murmured softly, Dionysuses if they became drunk, and Heracleses if they wrestled.”], and the crane murmurs among the beams?

To this concert you may add the pastoral muse of the seven-piped flute, which our sleepless mountain Tityri often exercise in nocturnal contests of song, echoing among the tinkling flocks across the grazed pastures. Yet these varied contests of voices and songs [Note: Some books read “melodies.”] will, by lulling your sleep more deeply, serve as its seduction.

When you leave the porticoes, if you seek the harbor of the shore, there is a common, though not distant, grove in a green meadow. Two enormous linden trees, their foliage joined and their trunks separated, produce a single shade from separate roots. In its darkness, while my Ecdicius enlightens me, we devote ourselves to ball games—but only until the image of the trees, becoming more compact, is confined within the space of the branches and thrown back upon itself; then it makes a gaming place for the weary, once the ball court has been exhausted.

But since, just as I have described the building, I owe you a description of the lake, learn what remains. The lake flows toward the southeast, and its waters, stirred by the winds, moisten by their alluvial deposits the foundations of the dwelling impressed upon its sands. Near its source it is indeed a marshy abyss, impassable to the foot of an observer; thus the fatness of the absorbent mud thickens, while cold springs and mossy shores surround it.

Nevertheless, if the breezes have ceased, the moving surface of the lake is cut broadly by little boats able to travel everywhere. If a southern storm has grown foul, it swells monstrously, so that the roar of the spray thrown over the trees standing along the margin drenches their crowns [40].

According to the nautical measurements they use, it extends for seventeen stadia. A river enters it, broken by rocky obstacles and whitened by its foaming impact; soon, freed from the steep rocks, it is swallowed by the lake. Whether chance causes it to enter, whether it runs into the lake, or whether it creates it, it certainly passes away, forced to be filtered through underground channels [Col. 0479A]—not so that it might be diminished by waves, but by fish. Driven back into a slower whirlpool, they stretch red flesh over white bellies. Since they can neither return nor are permitted to escape, their corpulence makes for them a kind of living, mobile prison.

The lake itself is, on the right, cut into, winding, and wooded; on the left, open, grassy, and level. Its surface is green from the southwest along the shore, because foliage extended over the water pours shade into the water just as the water covers the gravel. A matching crown of woods continues this color from the east. Along the northern side it has the character and appearance of a sea; toward the west there is common, disorderly brush, frequently bent beneath the weight of little boats gliding over it.

Around this, slippery tendrils of reeds twist themselves, while rich sheets of waterweed float together, and the bitterness of gray willows, ever nourished by fresh waters, grows [Col. 0479B]. In the middle of the deep water is a small island, where, above naturally piled millstones, a turning-post projects, worn smooth by the blows of oars that strike it in the circuits of naval games. There the merry wrecks of the players collide with it.

For it was the custom of our elders to imitate there the Drepani­tan contest of Trojan superstition [41], by which Aeneas honored his father at Drepanum in Sicily [Note: A mock naval battle, by which Aeneas honored his father at Drepanum in Sicily; see *Aeneid* V.].

The estate itself—though this is beyond what I owe you—is spread through woods, painted in meadows, rich in flocks upon its pastures, and wealthy in shepherds. But I shall delay no longer, lest, if the end of my writing is too long postponed, autumn find you already turning away. Therefore grant me the speed of coming, for you yourself will provide the delay of returning. You will forgive me because this letter, somewhat more meticulous than its required brevity, has exceeded its limits [Col. 0479C] while carefully examining the entire arrangement of the countryside; yet, in its desire to remove boredom, it has not even touched upon everything.

Accordingly, a fair judge and skilled reader will pronounce not the page that describes the spaces, but the spacious villa that is described, to be large. Farewell.

## LETTER III

Sidonius sends greetings to his Felix [Note: To Magnus Felix, son of Magnus the former consul. Propempticus explicitly says that these men descended from the patrician Philagrius, as does the panegyric to Avitus Augustus. More is said about Felix in poem 9, which is devoted entirely to him. The very high dignity for which Sidonius congratulates Felix is not the consulship, which Felix never attained, but the patriciate; Gennadius also bears witness to this in his account of Faustus.].

I rejoice that you, my superior, have obtained the insignia of the highest dignity. But I rejoice no less that this has been announced to me by a messenger sent for that purpose alone. For although you are now the most important magistrate, and the patrician rank has returned after so many ages to the household of Philagrius through your good fortune alone, you nevertheless, most faithful preserver of friendships, discover how the summit of your honors is raised by their sharing, and how, by a rare kind of example, you exalt your height through humility.

Thus once public favor preferred Quintus Fabius, master of the cavalry, to the severity of dictatorship and the arrogance of Papirius. Thus popular affection, never wearied of him, raised Gnaeus Pompey above his rivals. Thus Germanicus overcame Tiberian jealousy through the love of the whole people.

Therefore I do not wish the emperor’s benefits to flatter themselves excessively over your successes. They could have conferred nothing further upon you than that, if we had refused this, we should have passed over unwillingly [Note: Sidonius himself later became a patrician, as is clear from Book V, Letter 16, to Papianilla, and from Mamertus Claudianus’ dedication to Sidonius.].

That is distinctively yours; that is a singular mark of favor: you have not so much those who rival you as you fail to find those who can follow you. Farewell.

## LETTER IV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Syagrius.

The very distinguished Projectus, noble by birth, notable through a distinguished father and uncle, and made illustrious by a most excellent grandfather who was a priest, eagerly places himself within the bosom of your friendships, if you do not reject him. Since the splendor of his family, uprightness of character, wealth of patrimony, and youthful vigor are equally balanced toward every honor, he will nevertheless think himself carried to the summit of the highest happiness only if he obtains the fellowship of your favor [Col. 0480B].

Although he has sought and obtained from the mother of the orphan girl the daughter of the recently deceased, most distinguished Optantius, for marriage—may the matter prosper by God’s favor—he nevertheless considers the accomplishment of his wishes insufficiently advanced unless he secures your approval in all these matters, either through his own diligence or through the entreaty of my intercession.

For, so far as the girl’s upbringing is concerned, you have succeeded to the place of her dead father by sharing his responsibilities: you offer the maiden a parent’s affection, a patron’s authority, and a guardian’s duty. Therefore, since you are worthy that the most celebrated discipline of your house should be sought even by those placed far away, reward, as befits a man of good character, the modesty of the suppliant suitor with a kindly reply. Since he ought to seek the promised maiden whom he so earnestly seeks, confidently allow her to be promised;” for the balance of merit has placed you over this arrangement in such a way that even the surviving Optantius ought not to have greater authority over his children. Farewell.

## LETTER V

Sidonius sends greetings to his Petronius.

My friend John has fallen into an inextricable labyrinth of complicated business. Until either the merits of his documents, or your knowledge—or whatever knowledge belongs to you, if indeed you possess any—has examined the matter, he does not know what he should reject or what he should desire.

Thus the form of a divided lawsuit confounds him in such a way that he does not know which side his argument will defend or which it will attack. For this reason I earnestly beg you, after examining his papers, to instruct him in whatever the law grants him, showing what ought to be alleged and in what manner, and what ought to be refuted.

We shall not fear that the course of this case, if it flows from the fountain of your counsel, will be held back by any diversion made by those who oppose it. Farewell.

## LETTER VI [44]

Sidonius sends greetings to his Pegasius.

It is proverbially famous that delay is often better, just as we have now discovered. Your friend Menstruanus, observed here for a long time, has deserved to be counted among those dear and bound to us as well: timely, refined, modest, sober, frugal, devout, and endowed with such virtues of character that whenever he is admitted to the friendship of any good person, he obtains no more benefit himself than he bestows.

I have written this to you not because you were ignorant of it, but to satisfy my own judgment. Thus there are three reasons for rejoicing: first, for you, to whom it has fallen either to form or to choose friends of this kind; second, for the Arvernians, whose pleasure in him I affirm, since I do not doubt that you approved him; third, for the man whom all good people have judged to possess every good quality. Farewell.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Explicius.

Since your justice has rightly become venerable to the whole community through many proofs of uprightness, I gladly and eagerly send into your examination each individual who demands precisely this, hastening as soon as possible to relieve myself of the burden of investigation and them of the burden of litigation.

This will finally happen if, as a modest censor, you do not exclude the complaints of the parties without solid grounds [45]. Indeed, even the fact that you grant disputants access to you with difficulty is evidence that you will judge well. For who would not seek to have you as arbiter, either to have something forgiven for a price or to obtain favor?

Therefore forgive those who hurry rapidly and impetuously toward the privilege of so sacred a conscience. For neither does the defeated man, like a fool, accuse your judgment, nor does the victor, like a clever man, mock it. Those subject to you pay reverence out of regard for truth, while those whom you have freed pay gratitude.

I therefore earnestly beg you, as soon as the matters under dispute between Alethius and Paulus have been set out on both sides, to cut through them. For, unless I am mistaken, beyond the decisions of the decemvirs and pontiffs, the sole temperance of your character, with its customary healthy judgment, will cure the sickness of this nearly endless quarrel. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Desideratus.

I bring you this news in the deepest sorrow. Three days ago, not without a public cessation of business [Note: In place of *Philematia*. The ancient and correct name was *Philematium*, as it is written by Lucian in the dialogue *Charidemus and Tryphaena*, which ends with the words: “Let Philematium receive many greetings.” The name *Philematium* was formed diminutively from “kiss”; Lucretius suggests this in Book IV:

> Pretend that Silenus and a satyr are there, a lip-bearing *philema*.

It has the same form as Chelidonium, Eustochium, Glycerium, Musarium, Cymbalium, and other real or invented women’s names. A later age inflected these differently, so that they were called Philematia, Chelidonia, and so forth. Then *Filimatia* began to be written for *Philematia*, and *Filimatius* for *Philematium*, preserving the sound of the Greek word but not its spelling or quantity. Thus in the Theodosian Code Filimatius appears as *comes sacrarum largitionum* under Gratian; likewise in Sidonius, Book I, Letter 3, and Book V, Letter 17, where mention is made of the father of this Filimatia, as I believe. Among the ancients, not only *Philematium* but also *Philematio* was used of a woman. Just as Venuleia is called Philematium, so Aelia Philematio appears in ancient inscriptions, and Titia Philematio in this inscription from Ucecia:

> TITIA PHILEMATIO VIVA SIBI  
> ET SUIS FECIT.  
>   
> Titia Philematio, while alive, made this for herself and her family.

There is also an example of both forms on another very ancient stone, dug up in our own memory in the city near the Salarian Gate. Two married freedpersons are carved upon it, and beneath each image a separate epitaph is cut in rough workmanship. The woman’s begins:

> AURELIA L. L. PHILEMATIO.  
>   
> I am Aurelia, Philematium,  
> Born free, unmarked by reproach,  
> Chaste, modest, ignorant of vulgarity,  
> Faithful to my husband.]

the matron Filimatia has died: a compliant wife, a merciful mistress, a useful mother, a dutiful daughter, to whom a younger person owed obedience at home and abroad, an older person service, and an equal affection.

Long bereft of her mother, she had easily, through diverse kinds of endearment, ensured that her still-young father would not miss offspring of the other sex. But now, by the sudden final failure of her strength, she has pierced her father with bereavement.

Added to this is the fact that, by an untimely death, she left the father of five children to an unhappy fecundity. If those little ones had lost their already feeble father while their mother was alive, they would be considered less orphaned.

Nevertheless, if honor is not vainly bestowed upon corpses, she was not buried by the ominous services of undertakers and coffin-bearers. Rather, while all—even strangers—wept over her, clasped her, delayed her departure, and kissed her, she was received into the hands of priests and relatives and carried to her eternal resting place more like one asleep.

Afterward, at the entreaty of the bereaved father, I composed a funeral lament, not in elegiacs but in hendecasyllables, carved into marble with grief still almost warm. If you do not disapprove of it, a bookseller who deals in such things will undertake to attach it to the other volumes of my epigrams. If you think otherwise, it is enough that a poem of stone be contained in a stone.

This is the epitaph:

> Snatched away by a swift and cruel death,  
> From five children, her father, and her husband,  
> Here the hands of her grieving country  
> Laid the matron Philimatia in the tomb.  
>   
> O splendor of your family, glory of your husband,  
> Prudent, chaste, decorous, strict, and sweet,  
> And worthy even of the oldest to follow:  
> What things are usually thought discordant  
> You joined through the charm of your character.  
>   
> For the companions of your good life were  
> Dignified freedom and playful modesty.  
> Therefore we mourn that scarcely the thirtieth year  
> Of your life had been completed,  
> And that, in the season of vigorous life,  
> Your due was unjustly rendered to you [Note: This is a common lament for those carried away by premature death. Hence the expressions found on ancient monuments: “while the Fates judged wrongly,” and “she was taken from our eyes at the unjust command of fate.” On this young royal Abgar, whose epitaph Sirmondus presents here, see the conjectures of the learned Francis Wise in his letter to John Masson, *On a Coin of King Abgar*, published at Oxford in 1736, p. 21. An elegant example of this kind is the epitaph of the young royal Abgar, which Sirmondus says was unearthed a few years ago at the basilica of Saint Paul in Rome and which seems worthy of being woven into this passage. It is as follows:

> Having completed his twentieth year, Abgar  
> Came here, where fate spun out the thread.  
>   
> Envy, unjust as it was, extinguished  
> His dawning light, grieving his family  
> And his beloved companions.  
>   
> Antoninus placed this tomb for his brother,  
> Whose father had once been King Abgar.
>
> “Abgar had completed twice ten years;  
> Here he lies under the harsh command of the Fates.  
>   
> Unjust envy extinguished his first light,  
> Bringing grief to his family and companions.  
>   
> Antoninus gave this tomb to his brother,  
> Whose father had once been King Abgar.”]

Whether you like the poem or not, hurry and visit the city as quickly as possible. You owe the duty of consolation to the houses of two afflicted citizens. May God grant that, in fulfilling it, you never have to receive the same consolation yourself.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius sends greetings to his Donidius [Note: A distinguished man and citizen of Arvernia, as may be inferred from Book III, Letter 5. This letter was written in the territory of Nemausus, at the estates of Apollinaris and Ferreolus, which he describes.].

You ask why, since I set out for Nemausus some time ago, I prolong your longing by delaying my return. I shall give the reasons for my longer delay, and I shall not hesitate to disclose them, since what is sweet to me will also be sweet to you.

Among very pleasant estates, in the company of the most cultivated masters, Ferreolus and Apollinaris, I have spent an exceedingly delightful period. Their estates have adjoining rights and neighboring dwellings. Between them lies a carriage-road that tires the pedestrian and is insufficient for anyone traveling on horseback [Note: Here the word means a place and space in which one may be carried about, as in a Roman inscription: “In this orchard the carriage-way, by circling around, makes five thousand paces.” Elsewhere *gestatio* means the exercise itself, in which one is carried or rides, whether on horseback, in a litter, or in any kind of vehicle. Sidonius also transfers the word to walking, whereas others distinguish the uses. Seneca, Letter 55: “I am just returning from a carriage ride, no less tired than if I had walked as far as I sat; for being carried for a long time is itself labor.” Pliny, Book XXVII: “Walking, carriage riding, and these activities in several forms are especially beneficial.”].

The hills rising above the houses are cultivated by the vinedresser and the olive grower. You would think them the ridges of Aracynthus and Nysa, celebrated in the poets’ songs. One house looks out over level and open ground, the other over woods; nevertheless, the different settings delight in similar ways.

But why say more about the position of the estates, when the order of their hospitality remains to be revealed? First, each house, having assigned the most active scouts to this task, who would lie in wait for the route of our return, occupied not only the public roads and paths winding through shortcuts but also the shepherds’ lanes, lest by any chance we escape the ambushes of their arranged services.

We encountered them, I confess, but by no means unwillingly. We were immediately compelled to swear that we would not think of continuing our journey before seven days had passed. Thus every morning began with a friendly contest between the two hosts over which kitchen should smoke first with food for our guest. It was impossible to place the burden equally between them, although one was related to me and the other to my companions, because Ferreolus, a former prefect, possessed, in addition to the relationship due to him, the precedence of being the first inviter.

At once we were carried from one delight to another. Scarcely had we entered some vestibule when pairs of ballplayers were doubling through the revolving turns of their spinning movements in one place, while in another the frequent clatter of rattling dice-boxes and dice could be heard amid the competition of gamblers’ voices.

Books were abundantly available there.
