You might have thought you were looking at either grammar-school reading stands or the wedge-shaped benches of an Athenaeum [Note: Book IX, Letter 14: “the wedge-shaped benches of the Athenaeum.” The Athenaeum was the city’s public school of letters, which the emperor Hadrian established in Greek fashion, as Aurelius Victor reports. He does not say in which part of the city it stood; perhaps in Region 8 of the Roman Forum. For P. Victor places literary schools in that area, and in the same district, at the foot of the Aventine, the name “school of the Greeks” survives in the church of Saint Mary. It is also said that Saint Augustine taught there, and it is well known that he taught rhetoric in the Roman Athenaeum. Dio, through Xiphilinus, mentions the Athenaeum among other writers in his account of Didius Julianus: “He summoned us into the Athenaeum, so called from the training of those educated there.”]. Or you might have seen bookcases built by booksellers.

Yet, among the books placed in the women’s chairs, the style was found to be religious; those among the benches of householders were ennobled by the high style of Latin eloquence. Some volumes, however, preserved an equality of expression among authors of different subjects. For men of similar learning read here Augustine and there Varro; here Horace and there Prudentius.

Among them Adamantius Origen, translated by Tyrannius Rufinus, was diligently examined by readers of our faith. Likewise, according as different people expressed their judgments and spoke about whatever pleased them, some asked why certain men condemned Origen as a savage and dangerous interpreter of the primary mysteries. Yet he had been translated so literally in both sense and wording that neither Apuleius rendered Plato’s *Phaedo*, nor Cicero rendered Demosthenes’ *Ctesiphon*, so faithfully for the use and standard of Roman speech [Note: Rufinus translated a great deal of Origen. It is surprising that Sidonius praises his work so highly, since Jerome testifies concerning the books *On First Principles* that Rufinus interpolated, removed, and added much, and calls the translation infamous in his epitaph for Marcella. But I cease to wonder when I remember that nearly all our Gauls and westerners were favorably disposed toward Rufinus.].

While each of us was occupied with these studies according to his inclination, the chief cook suddenly approached and announced that the time had come to care for our bodies. This announcement, marking the progress of the hours by the intervals of the water-clock [Note: Two traces of ancient custom appear here: the water-clock and unequal hours. The Romans’ water-clock, that is, the clepsydra, was first made by the censor Nasica, as Censorinus records. Sidonius mentions it again in Letter 13 to Serranus. Cassiodorus, in a letter written for King Theoderic to Gundobad, says: “Another clock, by which the course of the sun is known without the sun, and the spaces of the hours are marked by dripping water.” He calls it a water-clock in the *Divine Institutions*. The Greeks call such devices *ὑδρία ὡροσκοπεῖα*, as Hero of Alexandria says in the *Pneumatics*: [lacuna] “thinking it to correspond to the mechanism of the water-clock, which is set out for us in four books.”], properly showed that his arrival was timely as the fifth hour was ending [Note: This is our eleventh hour. The ancients used unequal hours, twelve being counted each day from sunrise to sunset and the same number each night. Thus, according to the length of the day or night, the hours were unequal, sometimes shorter and sometimes longer. Augustine, considering this, says in *On True Religion*: “Compared with a summer hour, a winter hour is shorter.” Since their sixth hour ended at noon, the fifth was therefore always close to the eleventh. Persius refers to this same hour in Satire 3: “when the fifth line is touched by the shadow,” namely on a sundial, a heliotropic or shadow-clock on which such hours were marked. The fifth hour was also the hour of the midday meal. Martial, Book VIII:

> The boy has not yet announced the fifth hour to you,  
> Yet you already come to me as a guest, Caecilianus.

Ausonius, in the *Ephemeris*:

> Sosia, it is time to dine: the sun has already burned  
> Through the whole fourth hour and bends the shadow  
> Toward the mark of the fifth.]

We lunched briefly but abundantly, in senatorial fashion, according to the established custom by which many dishes are served on few platters, though the banquet varied in its foods, now roasted, now served in broth.

During the drinking, little stories were told, whose knowledge would amuse and instruct us, since they were woven in two ways and accompanied by both cheerfulness and learning. What more can I say? We were received with holiness, beauty, and abundance.

Then, rising, if we were at Voroangus—this was the name of one estate—we returned on foot to our baggage and lodging. If we were at Prusianus—the other estate was so called—we drove Tonantius and his brothers, the most distinguished leaders among their peers, from their beds, since the equipment of our sleeping quarters could not easily be carried back and forth so often [50].

After shaking off the torpor of midday, we rode for a little while, so that our chests, made sluggish by food, might more easily be sharpened for the hunger of the evening meal [Note: Above, Book I, Letter 2, concerning Theoderic: “After being filled with food, his midday sleep was always brief, often nonexistent. They call it *meridiatio*.” This is the sense of Julian’s passage to Libanius: “Yesterday I read the speech almost in its entirety before dinner. After dinner, before resting, I finished what remained.”].

Each host had a bathhouse under construction, but neither had one in use. Yet whenever my companions and servants stopped drinking even a little, a pit was quickly dug near a spring or river. A heap of heated stones was lowered into it, and the burning pit was covered with a cave woven in the shape of a hemisphere from flexible hazel rods. Over it were spread Cilician cloths; the open spaces between the rods were darkened by excluding the light, to repel the rising steam produced when the spray of boiling water strikes the heated flints.

We spent hours there, not without witty and playful conversation. Amid the mist of the hissing vapor that filled and enveloped us, health-giving sweat was drawn forth. When it had been released as much as one wished, we plunged into the heated water; relieved by its warmth, which dispelled our indigestion, we were then restored either by the cold of a spring and the chill of a well or by the plentiful water of the river.

For the river Vuardo runs between the houses, except when swollen by melting snow and clouded, red with yellow gravel. Otherwise it is clear, quiet, and pebbly throughout its channel, and no less rich in delicate fish.

I would also speak of our dinners—and very sumptuous dinners—if the paper had imposed a limit upon our talkativeness, which modesty has not imposed [Col. 0486A]. Their repetition would also make a pleasant story, if we were not ashamed to soil the back of the letter with wet ink.

But since we ourselves are already preparing to leave, and since we hope, with Christ’s help, to visit you very soon, the dinners of our friends will be more efficiently recalled to you at my dinner and yours—provided that the completion of the appointed week soon restores us to our desired hunger. For nothing repairs a stomach torn apart by gluttony better than moderation. Farewell.

## LETTER X

Sidonius sends greetings to his Hesperius [Note: He seems to be the man whom Sidonius calls “a magnificent man, a jewel of friends and letters” in Book IV, Letter 22. To him, therefore, he sends the hendecasyllables he composed about the basilica built at Lyon.].

I love in you the fact that you love literature, and I strive in every way to cultivate with the fullest praises the nobility of such devotion, by which you commend to us not only your beginnings but also our own studies. For when we see the minds of the young growing into this kind of discipline, for the sake of which we too submitted our hand to the rod, we obtain the richest fruit of our labor.

Add this as well: the multitude of the idle has grown so great that, unless at least a very few of you rescue the pure propriety of the Latin language from the rust of commonplace barbarisms, we shall soon have to mourn it abolished and dead. Thus, through the carelessness of the crowd, all the purple of noble speech will be discolored. But more of this another time.

Meanwhile, receive what you ask. You ask that, if any little verses have flowed from me after we parted from one another, I should count them out to you as a kind of payment for the delay. I obey your command. For although you are young, you possess such maturity of mind that we desire to obey even those older than yourself.

[Note: It is uncertain which church this was. The fact that it does not seem to have been the basilica of Saint Irenaeus is suggested by its being far from the Arar and by the location of the church not fitting Sidonius’s description. Papirius Masson interprets it as the church of Saint Stephen, which was once the metropolitan see. Since that church stood between the Arar and the public embankment, it readily accommodates Sidonius’s description, if it is established that it was built by Patientius; and the final letter of Book VI testifies that he founded or restored many churches in many places.]

A church has recently been built at Lyon, and through the zeal of Pope Patientius the work undertaken has reached its culmination—Patientius, a holy, energetic, strict, and merciful man, who through his abundant generosity toward the poor and his kindness toward humanity raises no lesser heights of good conscience. At the outer end of this building, at the request of the bishop mentioned above, I inscribed a makeshift poem in triple trochees, verses already thoroughly familiar both to me and now to you.

For the sides of the basilica near the altar shine with the hexameters of the distinguished poets Constantius and Secundinus.

[Note: Constantius is known from Letter 1 and elsewhere. Sidonius mentions Secundinus as a poet again in Book V, Letter 8.]

Our extreme modesty forbids those verses from being admitted to this page: comparison with better poems oppresses us as we hesitantly publish our own leisure-work. For just as nothing suits a new bride less than a more beautiful bridesmaid, and just as a dark man becomes darker when dressed in white, so our straw, however slight it may be, becomes cheap when surrounded by more powerful trumpets; and to declare it inferior in place and lowest in merit, and therefore more contemptible, is the result not merely of incompetence but also of arrogance.

Therefore their epigrams shine more justly than these verses, which we fashion only imaginatively and, in a manner, shadowily. But why say this? Let the poor reed of the song that was demanded rather murmur.

### 53

Whoever here praises the labor  
Of our father Bishop Patientius,  
With prayer that fulfills his vow  
Will find his request granted.

The lofty building shines; it is drawn neither  
To the left nor to the right, but, with the front  
Of its summit, it looks toward the rising  
Of the equinoctial sun.

[Note: Christian sacred buildings were customarily turned toward the East from the beginning. Clement, Book II of the Constitutions: “Let the house be long, turned toward the rising of the sun.” Paulinus, Letter 12 to Severus: “The front of the basilica does not face the East, as is the more usual custom.” If something obstructed this, at least they directed the altar that way; many examples of this arrangement are seen at Rome. For this reason the Antiochenes were once described as “peculiar in their customs,” because they departed from the customary rite. Socrates, Book V, chapter 21: “At Antioch in Syria the church has its position reversed; for the altar does not look toward the East but toward the West.”

The temple of the Jews, however, looked toward the region of the sky where the sun sets; the divine writings teach this, and Theodoret among others observes it. Nor do Aristeas and Josephus contradict this when they write that the temple was turned “toward the dawn and toward the East,” since they are speaking of the prospect from the vestibule, not from the front.]

Inside, light sparkles, and the sun is so drawn  
Toward the gilded ceiling that it wanders,  
Matching the yellow metal in its brilliance.

Marble, marked with varied splendor,  
Runs through the vault, the floor, the windows;  
And beneath its many-colored designs,  
A green, grass-like crust in springtime  
Bends sapphire-colored stones through emerald glass.

A triple portico is attached to it,  
Proud in its Aquitanian supports.

[Note: Its columns were cut from Aquitanian marble in the ridges of the Pyrenees. They are also mentioned in the Life of Pope Hilary, where Aquitanian, Tripolitan, and porphyry columns are named. The marble called “Aquitanian” by Greek writers is something else, as in Theophanes and Cedrenus concerning the funeral of the emperor Anastasius, who was brought from Acytos in the Sporades.]

In view of this, more distant  
Courtyards close the second porticoes,  
And a stone-clad forest of columns  
Clothes the central field from afar.

From here the embankment resounds; from here the Arar echoes.  
From here foot travelers and horsemen turn back,  
And the driver of the shrieking wagons;  
From here the curved chorus of haulers,

[Note: “While the sailors,” he says, “sing alleluia, the same sound echoes on the bank.” Thus he has expressed the theme of the song and used its proper term. For *celeuma* is properly a sailors’ song; hence sailors who sing such songs are called *keleuontes* (“those who give the rowing-call”) by Longus in Book III of the *Pastorals*, where he describes the *celeusma* with great elegance and has it answering, like Sidonius’s song on the riverbank, in a neighboring valley. The subject of Sidonius’s *celeusma*, however, was “Alleluia” and the praises of God. In this manner the ancient Christians often turned their melodies and songs to the honor of Christ and the saints.

And, not to depart from the sailors, Paulinus writes of Nicetas’s return:

“Joyful sailors will sing the customary rowing-call,  
Joining it in varied melodies to hymns,  
And with pious voices will lead their companions  
Across the waters and through the air.”

Likewise Asterius, bishop of Amasea, in his sermon on the martyr Phocas: “Sailors and rowers everywhere transfer the customary rowing-calls, by which they lighten the weariness of the voyage, into the common praise of the martyr; and Phocas is sung by the mouths of them all.” Augustine, on the New Song: “May the grace of Christ be our protection; let us sweetly sing our rowing-call, Alleluia, so that joyful and secure we may enter our eternal and most blessed homeland.”]

With the banks answering “Alleluia,”  
He raises a river-song to Christ.

Thus, thus sing praise, sailor or traveler:  
For this is a place that everyone should seek,  
Everyone whom the road leads toward salvation.

### 54

I have obeyed your commands as a younger man. Only remember that you must repay me with multiplied interest; and, for that to happen more easily and more pleasantly, you must read diligently without concealment and continue reading without end. Nor must you allow the wife whom you will soon happily bring home to turn you aside from this purpose. Remember especially how once Martia held candles and candelabra for Hortensius, Terentia for Cicero, Calpurnia for Pliny, Pudentilla for Apuleius, and Rusticiana for Symmachus while they read and studied.

Certainly, if you complain that, apart from oratorical work, the companionship of women dulls your poetic talent and blunts the polish of your speech, honed on the whetstones of constant study, remember the verses that Corinna often completed with her Naso, Lesbia with Catullus, Caesennia with Gaetulicus, Argentaria with Lucan, Cynthia with Propertius, and Delia with Tibullus.

Thus it is plainly clear that marriage offers students an opportunity for learning and gives the idle an excuse. Therefore apply yourself, and do not let a crowd of ignorant people cheapen literary diligence in your eyes; for nature has arranged that in every art the display of knowledge is more precious when it is rarer. Farewell.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius to his Rusticus: greetings.

[Note: To Rusticus of Bordeaux. Book VIII, Letter 11. Other distinguished men of that name also lived in Gaul shortly before Sidonius, such as Decimius Rusticus, concerning whom see Book V, Letter 9, and Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, to whom Pope Leo writes. I do not know whether the letter to Eucherius, which in the Corbie manuscript is placed after his *Questions on Scripture*, before Salvian’s and Hilary’s letters to the same Eucherius, should be attributed to either of these men or rather to someone else named Rusticus. Nevertheless, so that it may no longer remain hidden, I thought it would not displease the reader if I inserted this additional piece here.]

### Letter of Rusticus to Eucherius

To the truly holy lord Pope Eucherius, Rusticus sends greetings.

I have copied with joy and haste the two volumes that you sent me, asking that they be transcribed, and I immediately dispatched both to Your Blessedness. I could not have made clearer how greatly I admired that unique and incomparable learning which, by completely unfolding the questions of great mysteries from both Testaments, removes the veil from the eyes of the heart and pours in the true light of spiritual understanding, than by confessing that I am unable adequately to praise it.

But why should I say that I alone am unequal to exalting what you have published? With due respect to all who have been most excellently trained in what are called the liberal studies, I do not think that even they could sufficiently and worthily adorn the remarkable praises of your books. For although I judge it easier to pass judgment than to speak, I am nevertheless so convinced that this is not easy that I rightly declare that no one could be a more fitting herald of so splendid a work than its inventor and knower: since no one could discover it in the way that you did, no one could praise it in the same way.

As I silently turn these thoughts over in my mind, I recall something I once read in the library, when I was a boy studying secular literature, as the curiosity of that age leads one to do. The designer and master of the building mentioned above had placed, among figures rendered in colored stone or wax and depicting orators and poets, distinctive epigrams beneath the likeness of each. When he came to the poet of preeminent eloquence, he began in this manner:

“Virgil the poet is better praised by his own songs:

‘While rivers run into the sea, while shadows  
Move across the curved sides of the mountains,  
While the heavens nourish the stars,  
Your honor, your name, and your praises will endure forever.’”

And truly, provided that no fault attaches to my placing examples from worldly literature amid sacred writings and commemorations of the saints, when I recall the lord Eucherius in my mind, this work comes back to me as a fitting remembrance. For as long as the things written above endure, you will be celebrated by the mouth and love of all Christians, and you will be praised by future generations while you teach them. Pray for me, truly holy man and friend of God, Pope whom I must receive with every mark of reverence in Christ.

### LETTER XI

Sidonius to his Rusticus: greetings.

### 55

If our homes were near one another in position and distance, and the vast length of the journey did not separate us from one another’s presence, I would allow nothing to hinder the duties of the intimacy we have begun. Nor would I cease building, through different kinds of honor, the foundations of our friendship, already laid by the letters sent more than once.

But habitation spread over separated territories stands in the way of the union of our minds, though it will scarcely harm hearts once bound together. Yet from this very separation of our neighboring communities arises the fact that, although we are the closest of friends, we wish to turn into a common fault the rarity of conversation caused by the long interruption of distance, when the difficulty of natural circumstances ought to leave neither blame nor pardon resting upon us.

Illustrious lord, I received at a suitable time the bearers of your letters, trained in your discipline and displaying the modesty proper to their master; I listened to them patiently and explained matters appropriately. Farewell.

## LETTER XII

Sidonius to his Agricola: greetings.

You certainly sent me a light but sturdy boat, large enough for a bed and already supplied with fish. You also sent a highly experienced helmsman and strong, nimble rowers, who pass over the back of the opposing current with precisely the speed at which it flows downstream.

But you will pardon me for pretending that I will not come as your companion when you invite me fishing. For stronger nets of grief than those with which our people are lying ill hold me fast; they are matters that friends and strangers alike must lament. Therefore, if you are rightly moved by brotherly affection, I think that, when you take up this page, you will be thinking instead about returning.

### 56

Our common anxiety for Severiana, at first disturbed by the onset of a sluggish cough, is now also worn down by fevers that grow worse through the nights. For this reason she wishes to go out to the suburbs. Indeed, when we received your letter, we were already preparing to leave for the little estate.

Whether you come or delay, therefore, support our prayers with your prayers, so that the invigorating air of the countryside may bring a healthy change to one who longs for it. Certainly, I—or your sister—suspended between hope and fear, believed that we would increase her weariness if we obstructed the pleasure of the sick woman.

Accordingly, with Christ leading the way, we are withdrawing ourselves and the whole household alike from the city’s heat and torpor; and at the same time we avoid the mediocre advice of those who sit around her and disagree among themselves. These people, insufficiently learned but excessively assiduous, very dutifully kill many sick persons.

By right of friendship Justus will be called in. If I were inclined to joke amid sorrow, I could easily prove him trained more in Chiron’s art than in Machaon’s.

[Note: The mention of this Justus, a physician, recalls the very ancient and elegant epitaph of Lucius Primigenius, a physician called *periodautēs*, that is, a traveling doctor, which was unearthed at Iguvium among the Umbrians two years ago. Its text, sent to us from Rome by Petrus Marionus, a young man of outstanding talent and learning, is as follows:

“Lucius Sabinus, Lucius’s freedman, Primigenius, born at Iguvium:  
Having practised medicine in many towns,  
I am said to have been renowned for skill and still more renowned for integrity.  
As I rose in vigorous youth, Fortune abandoned me  
And laid me upon a swift pyre.  
The flames yielded my ashes to a Clusine tomb;  
My patron buried my bones in my native soil.”]

The two men are both distinguished; Chiron indeed was such an outstanding physician that Junius Philargyrius notes that he is said to have taught Aesculapius himself. Thus Sidonius does not detract from Chiron’s medical skill; rather, in order to point out the incompetence of the physician Justus, he makes a joke based on another meaning of the word *cheiron*, which signifies “worse,” and he often made many similar witticisms.

Thus Diogenes the Cynic, according to Laertius, once saw two centaurs very badly painted and said: “Which of these two is Chiron?”—that is, “Which is worse and more inept?” He was not referring to the centaur’s name but to the defect of the painting.

There is a similar joke, and one closer to Sidonius, in the speech of the rhetorician Aristides against the Asclepiads, whom he says were taught medicine by their father Aesculapius. There was no need to entrust them to Chiron’s instruction, since they had a teacher at home, beside whom Chiron, in accordance with his name, was far inferior. Let us hear Aristides himself:

“When they were born, their father raised them in the gardens of health. And when they reached the proper age, he did not have them taught the medical art, but taught them himself; for there was no longer any need for them to go to Chiron, since they had a master at home: the second of them was, by his very name, not much worse than Chiron.”]

Christ must therefore be asked and entreated with all the greater diligence to heal by heavenly power the illness whose cure our own care has not discovered. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII

Sidonius to his Serranus: greetings.

### 57

Your letter was brought to us by Marcellinus Togatus, a skilled man and a friend of friends. Its opening words offered a greeting; throughout the remainder of its considerable length it contained the praises of your patron, the emperor Petronius Maximus.

[Note: Maximus seized the imperial throne after Placidius Valentinian was killed in A.D. 455. This is known from all the historians. But a fact untouched by the writers hitherto published is that Maximus also had a son, Palladius by name, whom he made Caesar. We owe this solely to our complete copy of Idatius; for the work printed under Idatius’s title as the *Chronicle* is only an epitome of Idatius’s *Chronicle*. In our manuscript, after the murder of the emperor Valentinian, these words occur: “Soon afterward Maximus, one of the consuls, was proclaimed Augustus at Rome. Having become emperor, he married Valentinian’s widow; and he gave Valentinian’s daughter in marriage to his son Palladius, whom he had made Caesar by his former wife. Distracted by fear of the great disturbances that he anticipated, and because he had directed toward schemes for the throne the crimes committed by Valentinian against men whom he had killed, and those committed against Valentinian himself in bringing about his death, he wished to abandon the empire and Rome; but, after scarcely four months of his reign had elapsed, he was killed in the city itself amid a popular tumult and military mutiny.”]

[Note: *Togatus* means a legal advocate, as in Book IV, Letter 3, concerning the advocates of Arles: “He went on to consult the expertise of the toga-wearing advocates there.” In an ancient inscription cited in our discussion of Ennodius, Petilius Processius is called “illustrious, toga-wearing, prefect of the praetorium”; and *togati* appear frequently in the codes for officials of the praetorian and urban prefectures. Thus the toga itself came to signify advocacy and legal practice. Constantius, in the *Life of Germanus*: “He adorned the tribunals of the prefecture by his profession of advocacy. The state immediately advanced him to the insignia of honor, distinguished above all by the praises of his toga.” Marcellinus’s native city was Narbo Martius. Hence Sidonius praises him among the distinguished men of Narbonne in Poem 23.]

Yet you call him “most fortunate” with greater persistence and affection than correctness or truth would allow, on the ground that he had risen through the highest titles of office all the way to the imperial power. I never agree with such a judgment as to think fortunate those who stand upon the steep and slippery heights of public office. No one can say how much misery the life of these supposedly fortunate men brings them hour by hour, if indeed those deserve to be called fortunate who take this name for themselves, as Sulla did.

[Note: For he ordered himself to be called “Felix.” Plutarch says: “He ordered that he himself be called fortunate. For this is what Felix especially wished to signify.” Many people taunted Sulla with this name. In a passage close to Sidonius’s thought, Velleius Paterculus, Book II, writes: “He assumed the name Felix, which he would indeed have adopted most justly if he had had the same end in conquering as in living.” For no one is fortunate who is not always fortunate. Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I:

“Why, friends, have you so often called me fortunate?  
He who has fallen did not stand upon a firm foundation.”]

They imagine that supreme happiness consists in supreme power, having surpassed the common bounds of right and wrong. They are all the more miserable because they understand so little that they are subject to the most restless servitude. For just as kings rule men, so the desire to rule dominates kings.

### 58

If we set aside the falls of the emperors who preceded him or followed him, this one Maximus of yours alone can serve as the greatest illustration of the point. Although he had fearlessly climbed to the citadel of the prefecture, the patriciate, and the consulship, and had repeated the offices he held as though running around an endless track, nevertheless, when he arrived with all his strength at the precipice of imperial power, he suffered beneath the imperial crown a kind of vertigo produced by immense authority. He could not endure being master who had not endured being under a master.

[Note: His urban prefecture, which he held for a year and six months while Honorius was emperor, when he was scarcely more than a young man, is attested not only by the inscription on the statue of Petronius but also by this shorter inscription, which stands in the basilica of Saint Mary Major at Rome, although few have noticed it:

“Petronius Maximus, illustrious man, prefect of the city, took care of this.”

He repeated the praetorian prefecture under the emperor Valentinian; and his patriciate is indicated by Valentinian’s Novel 31, entitled “To Maximus, second prefect of the praetorium and patrician.” The records of his consulships are found in the *Fasti* for the years A.D. 433 and 443. Thus in the Pithoean manuscript of Tiro Prosper’s *Chronicle*, Maximus is called “a man of two consulships and patrician rank.”

In addition to all this, we have seen a new and unusual kind of honor bestowed upon Petronius Maximus by Valentinian on a large bronze coin. One side displays Valentinian’s face with the customary inscription, “Our Lord Placidius Valentinian, Pious and Fortunate Augustus”; the other shows Maximus seated in senatorial dress, holding a scroll in his right hand and a scepter with an eagle in his left, with his name written on either side: “Petronius Maximus, illustrious man, consul.”]

[Note: His reign lasted nearly three months. The anonymous chronicle of Cuspinian states: “After the death of the emperor Valentinian, Maximus was raised to the imperial dignity on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April; he was killed on the day before the Ides of June.” Thus it was nearly three months; and Marcellinus the Count rightly writes that he was torn limb from limb in the third month of his tyranny, whereas Cassiodorus wrongly says within two months, and Idatius after the completion of four.]

Consider the grace, power, and duration of his former life, and, by contrast, the beginning, whirlwind, and end of his principate, which lasted somewhat more than two months. You will certainly find that the man was happier before he was called most happy.

For the man whose banquets, manners, wealth, pomp, literature, fasces, estates, and patronage had previously flourished—whose very span of life had been so carefully guarded that it was measured out by the hours of arranged water-clocks—was now proclaimed Augustus and, under that appearance, confined within the palace doors. Before dawn he groaned because he had reached the object of his prayers.

Since the weight of his cares prevented him from preserving the measured portion of his former tranquillity, he immediately renounced the rules of his old way of life and recognized that the emperor’s business and the senator’s leisure could not proceed together. Nor did the future deceive the man who mourned it. After he had passed through all the other honors of the court in complete tranquillity, he governed the court itself with the greatest turbulence, amid the disturbances of soldiers, citizens, and allies. His new, swift, and bitter end revealed this—and the treacherous conclusion of Fortune, which had long courted him and, like a scorpion, struck him with the final part of her body, stained it with blood.

A learned man named Fulgentius, who on account of his intellectual merits had been quaestor and was certainly a great supporter of the better party,

[Note: He had been quaestor of the sacred palace. Since the quaestorship required literary ability, Senator calls the office “the dignity of letters,” *Variarum* I, 12.]

used to say that he had often heard Maximus himself remark, when he hated the burden of imperial power and longed for his former security: “You are fortunate, Damocles, who did not endure the necessity of kingship for longer than a single lunch.”

For, as we read, Damocles was a Sicilian by region and a Syracusan by city, a companion of the tyrant Dionysius. Since he praised his patron’s advantages with excessive enthusiasm, evidently because he had never experienced them, Dionysius said: “Do you wish, at least today, at this table, to share equally in my advantages and disadvantages?” “Gladly,” he replied.

Then Dionysius immediately stripped his happy client—though also terrified—of his common clothing, dressed him richly in a purple garment of Tyrian or Tarentine shell-dye, and, glittering with gems and pearls, placed him on a golden couch beneath a silken canopy. As bread made from the grain of Leontini was served to him, in the manner of a Sardanapalian about to dine, and as elaborate dishes were placed before him on even more elaborate vessels, and gems large enough for Falernian wine foamed with wine, and perfumes warmed in ice-cold crystal vessels, and as the dining room spread foreign fragrances from cinnamon and incense, and garlands thrown over his hair wet with nard dried them with flowers, suddenly a drawn sword began to swing above the back of the reclining man from the ceiling. It seemed about to fall at any moment upon the throat of the man now dressed in purple.

For it was fastened by a horsehair thread, and its weight made it so threatening that, in the fearful example of Tantalus, its point held his throat in check, lest food entering through his mouth should come out again in vomit.

Therefore, after prayers mixed with tears and many sighs, he was scarcely released; he leapt up and fled, rejecting riches and royal pleasures with the same speed with which people ordinarily pursue them. He was brought back to the desires of ordinary life by fear of supreme power, taking great care thereafter not to call or consider anyone blessed who, surrounded by arms and guards and therefore resting upon wealth seized by force, pressed down on gold while being pressed down by iron.

Therefore, my brother and lord, I do not know whether it is agreed that the blessed aspire to such a condition. It is certainly clear that the wretched arrive there. Farewell.

## 60. LETTER XIV

Sidonius to his Maurusius: greetings.

I hear that the vintage is answering your industry and our common hopes with a richer yield than the barren year had threatened. Therefore I suspect that you will remain for a longer time in the district of Vialoscum, which in an earlier age was called Martialis because of the winter quarters of Julius Caesar’s legions.

[Note: This is how all the books we have seen read it. The modern name of this village, however, is still uncertain. Since the passage indicates that its ancient name was Vialoscum and that it was later called Martialis because of Julius Caesar’s winter quarters, Savaron’s conjecture should not be dismissed: he thinks it was Martiacum, a village in the territory of Ricomagus, near Volvic.]

There you have not only a fertile vineyard but also an estate whose greatness is no less impressive to its master, since its varied abundance of crops and dwellings keeps you and your people there. If, once your granaries, storehouses, and pantry are full, you intend to spend the months of snowy January and February in smoky leisure—or in the quiet of a tunic—until the swallows or storks return, then our causes for delay in the town will immediately be cut short, so that while you enjoy the countryside, we may enjoy you. As you recognize, the land with its abundant revenues is no more dear or pleasurable to us than a neighboring equal with good character. Farewell.

# BOOK THREE

## 61. LETTER I

Sidonius to his Avitus: greetings.

[Note: Apparently his cousin. Sidonius thanks him for the suburban estate at Cuticiacum, which Avitus had donated from his inheritance through his sister to the Church of the Arverni, of which Sidonius was already bishop.]

From early boyhood until we reached youth, many bonds of affection had joined us in mutual devotion. First, because our mothers were connected by the closest ties of blood. Then because we ourselves were born at the same time, had the same teachers, were trained in the same arts, spent our leisure in the same games, advanced under the same emperors, and completed the same periods of service. And, what is stronger and more effective for enlarging friendships, in every individual we competed in equal judgment concerning the traits that should equally be sought or avoided.

For all these reasons, apart from the inward consciousness that is far superior and more exalted in you, the similarity of our outward actions had greatly joined our wills. But, as must be admitted, after the structures of our mutual affection had long been raised, you yourself placed the precious summit upon them by making a most timely gift to the church of the little municipality of the Arverni, over which I seem, though unworthy, to preside.

[Note: The city of the Arverni is called *urbs Arverna* in Letter 12, *oppidum Arvernum* in the final letter of Book VI and in Book VII, Letter 5. Gregory of Tours likewise calls it *urbs Arverna*. Jordanes calls it *urbs Arvernata* and *civitas Arverna*, all with an added qualifier. No one among the ancients, I think, used *Arverna* alone, like Rome, although some have recently begun to do so. They used the complete name of the people, Arverni, as with Parisii, Petrocorii, and Remi, after the practice became established that the chief town of each people and state should be honored by the common name. Thus Pliny, Marcellinus, Orosius, Paulinus, the *Notitia of the West*, and others call the city that we call Clermont “the city of the Arverni”; they never call it *Arverna*.]

You enriched that church’s possessions greatly through the suburban estate of Cuticiacum, honoring the brotherhood of our vocation no less by the nearness of the place than by its income. And although you and your sister appear to be the two co-heirs of your sister’s inheritance, your example of faith moved your surviving sister to imitate your good work.

Thus the merit of your action and the encouragement of another’s action are rightly returned to you from heaven. You are therefore found worthy of being exalted by the divine power through an unusual succession of inheritances. Yet that power did not even delay long before enriching your religious devotion with gifts multiplied a hundredfold; and, as we trust, it will be no less generous with heavenly gifts now that you have already distributed earthly ones.

For, if you do not know, the inheritance of Nicetiana was the heavenly price of Cuticiacum. What remains is this: we ask that, just as you care for our church, so also you share an equal concern for the city. It has long belonged—and from this time above all will belong—to your protection, or on account of your patrimony.

Whatever its value may be, especially if it is frequently visited by your presence, or entrusted even to the Goths,

[Note: The disturbances of the Visigoths in Gaul that Sidonius mentions at various points in the following books belong for the most part to the reign of Julius Nepos, that is, to the year A.D. 474, when the Arverni were besieged by King Euric. As Jordanes relates, when Euric had seen frequent changes among the Roman emperors within a few years, he gained hope of successfully advancing his affairs and immediately invaded their territories.

Nepos sent the bishop Epiphanius of Ticinum as an envoy. After successfully concluding what appeared to be an agreement with Euric, Epiphanius returned to Nepos. Ennodius recounts the events of the embassy in his *Life of Epiphanius*. Euric soon broke the treaty. Having decided to extend his empire to the Rhone and the Loire, he attacked the intervening peoples by force and, out of hatred for the Catholic party, punished their bishops—some by exile, others by the sword.

He besieged the Arverni, who alone remained loyal to the Romans, while they were bravely defended by Count Ecdicius, master of the soldiers and Sidonius’s brother-in-law. Once the siege had been lifted, the enemy withdrew into winter quarters. Licinianus, a quaestor sent from Rome to the Goths, then ordered the Arverni to surrender according to the agreement. Sidonius protested in vain and was forced into exile, remaining away from his people for some time. Ecdicius withdrew to the kings of the Burgundians. Euric placed Count Victorius over the Arverni. Sidonius discusses these events in Letters 1, 3, 4, and 7 of this book, and in Book VII, Letters 1, 6, 7, and 17; Book VIII, Letter 9; and Book IX, Letter 2.]

who very often even disdain or abandon their own Septimania,

[Note: The boundaries of their empire. The Goths’ first settlements in Gaul were in Septimania. This name was initially applied to the district and territory of Béziers. Just as Arles was called the city of the Sixth Legion and Fréjus that of the Eighth Legion, from the military colonies of the sixth and eighth legions, so Béziers—or Baeterrae—was called the city of the Septimani, according to Pliny, and the territory subject to the city was called Septimania.

In this sense the ancient martyrologies call Aphrodisius the first bishop of the people of Béziers in Septimania, and the *Life of Louis the Pious* places Vadala monastery in Septimania. Nor are there lacking writers who say that the Goths first settled in this part of the province of Narbonne; the account of them by Olympiodorus of Thebes, preserved by Photius, supports this.

Thus this was initially Gothic Septimania; later the name spread to the whole of First Narbonensis, which even today some say is called Languedoc from the Goths, as though it were “Land of the Goths.” In the testament of Charlemagne: “Pepin shall receive part of Burgundy with the province, and Septimania, or Gothia, as far as Spain.” Gregory of Tours, Jonas of Orléans, Nithard, John VIII in Letter 111, and others likewise consistently use Septimania for First Narbonensis.]

provided that, with God as your guide, you stand between them and the state, you may form calmer hopes. For although they, having broken through the boundaries of the ancient frontiers, extend the limits of their disturbed possession toward the Rhone and the Loire by force or weight of every kind, your authority, in keeping with the dignity of your judgment, will so regulate both sides that our people will learn what they ought to refuse when asked, and the opposing party will cease demanding what is refused.

Farewell.

## LETTER II

Sidonius to his Constantius: greetings.

[Note: To Constantius of Lyon, as noted in Book I, Letter 1. Written after the siege of the city of the Arverni, when Constantius had come from Lyon. The difficult journey he describes is therefore the road between Lyon and the Arverni. It is represented on the Peutinger Map, though with a longer winding route, as is customary with military roads, in the following manner: from Lyon to Feurs of the Segusiani, sixteen miles; to Mediolanum, fifteen; to Raidomna, twenty-one; to Ariolica, twelve; to Vorogium, fourteen; to the Hot Springs, eight; to Augustonemetum, twenty-two.]

The people of Arvernia greet you, whose small cottages you filled as a great guest—not by the retinue of one who seeks display, but by affection that sought you out. Good heavens! What joy there was among the laboring people when you set your holy foot within the half-ruined walls! How closely you were surrounded by every class, sex, and age! What a finely balanced measure of speech you gave to each individual! How the children judged you affectionate, the young affable, the old dignified! What tears, like a parent of all, you poured over houses collapsed in fire and dwellings half-burned! How deeply you grieved over fields buried beneath unburied bones! What encouragement you then offered, what vigor in urging their restoration!

To this is added the fact that, when you found the city emptied no less by civic discord than by barbarian assault, by urging peace upon all and mutual affection, you restored them to one another and to their homeland. As they returned at your urging no less to a common plan than to a common town, the walls owe you their restored people, and the restored people owe you concord. Therefore they consider you sufficiently their own, and themselves sufficiently yours; and—which is your greatest glory—they are not at all mistaken.

For day after day the following thought presents itself to each of their minds: that you, a person venerable through age, fragile through weakness, exalted through nobility, and revered through religion, for the sake of affection alone broke through so many barriers and so many obstacles placed in the way of your coming: namely, the length of the journeys, the shortness of the days, the abundance of snow, the scarcity of fodder, the broad expanses of wilderness, the narrowness of lodgings, and the chasms of the roads—either made rotten by rainwater or thorny through the dryness of frost; besides, embankments rough with stones, rivers slippery with ice, hills rugged to climb, and valleys worn away by the continual sliding of their slopes. Through all these hardships, because you were seeking no private advantage, you brought back a public love.

For the rest, we pray God that, as the limits of your life advance according to your wishes, you may tirelessly seek out, obtain, and bring back the friendship of good men; and may the affection that you leave behind follow you. Wherever grace has been initiated through you, may both its foundations and its summits be returned to you for a long time. Farewell.

## Letter III

**Sidonius to his Ecdicius, greetings.**

[Note: To the Arvernian Ecdicius, son of the emperor Avitus, as stated in Book II, Letter 1. At this time he, as comes and master of the soldiers, had defended the city of Arvernia, besieged by the Goths, and had performed many brave deeds against the Goths, which Sidonius praises here.]

If ever, then certainly now, you are most greatly missed by my Arvernians, whom an immense love for you governs—and for many reasons. First, because the land that gave you birth rightly claims the highest place in your affection. Then because, in your own age, you are almost the only mortal who has made his homeland give birth to no less longing than it had felt joy at your birth. The period of your mother’s former labor supports this claim: as the conception progressed, it was reckoned in harmony with the prayers of your fellow citizens.

I pass over those matters common to all, though they are no slight incentives to affection: your having crawled over the clods of this soil. I omit that you first broke in these parts the grasses by walking, the rivers by swimming, and the woods by hunting. I omit that here the ball, the *pyrgus*—the gaming tower—the hawk, the dog, the horse, and the bow first served you in play. I pass over the fact that, for the sake of your childhood, literary pursuits flowed here from every people, and that nobility, once destined to shed the scales of Celtic speech, was then steeped, sometimes in oratorical style and sometimes even in poetic measures, out of regard for your person.

What chiefly kindled the affection of the whole community for you was that you forbade those whom you had once compelled to become Romans to be barbarians thereafter. Civic hearts can never forget how, and in what manner, only recently every age, order, and sex watched you from the half-ruined embankments of the walls, when, having crossed the intervening plains and advanced against the enemy, you passed through several thousand Goths in broad daylight no less openly than across the middle of a field—a feat which posterity will scarcely believe—accompanied by a company of scarcely eighteen horsemen.

[Note: In Gregory of Tours only ten are counted. Thus, in Book II, chapter 24, he writes of this very flight of the Goths: “Many report that Ecdicius possessed remarkable swiftness. For on one occasion he is said to have put to flight a multitude of Goths with ten men.”]

At the sound of your name and the sight of your person, a highly trained army was overwhelmed by astonishment, so that, in their admiration, the enemy commanders did not know how many accompanied themselves or how few accompanied you. The entire battle line was immediately withdrawn to the brow of a precipitous hill; although it had previously been drawn up for the assault, at the sight of you it was not deployed for battle.

Meanwhile, after you had cut down all the best men—the men whom audacity rather than cowardice had placed at the rear of the column—you alone occupied the broadest possible plain, none of your men having been lost in the combat, though the battle had not given you as many companions as a table usually gives guests.

Then, when you were being brought back leisurely into the city, what offices, applause, tears, and joys came forth to meet you—this prayer can attempt to imagine better than words can disclose. Indeed, one could see, in the atria of the capacious house filled to overflowing, that very happiest ovation of your crowded return: some snatched up your dust with kisses; others received the horse-bits fat with blood and foam; others reclined upon the sweat-soaked saddle-cloths; others loosened the fastenings of the flexible plates as you emerged from the hollow of your helmet; others busied themselves undoing the bonds of your greaves; others counted the notched sides of your swords blunted by slaughter; others measured with livid fingers the rings of your cuirasses, pierced by cuts and thrusts.

Here, although many danced and clung to you in the embraces of your people, the greatest surge of popular joy nevertheless gathered around you. At last you had entered an unarmed crowd, indeed, but one from which even an armed man could not have escaped unscathed; and you carried with elegant good humor the foolish extravagances of those who congratulated you. While you were being seized in the tumultuous embrace of those rushing upon you, you had reached such a condition, as the most devoted interpreter of public affection, that it was necessary for you to return fuller gratitude to the man who had done you the more unrestrained injury.

I say nothing further about how you gathered from private forces the appearance of a public army, helped from outside by the modest resources of more important men, and restrained the lower populations of the enemy by first chastising their raids. I say nothing about how, in several surprise attacks, you slaughtered wedge-shaped squadrons, scarcely two or three of your own men being missed after the battle; or how much calamity your unexpected engagements inflicted on the opposing side, so that they considered, by an even more disgraceful stratagem, how to conceal the number of their dead.

Indeed, those whom the hastening night had prevented from burying lay exposed with their heads severed, as though it were a lesser indication to let a hairy corpse be recognized by its locks than to leave it headless. After daylight returned, when they realized that the theft of their disaster had been exposed in cruel disgrace, only then did they publicly busy themselves with funeral rites, concealing their defeat by fraud no more than their fraud by haste. Yet even so, they did not bury the bones beneath a mound of hastily heaped earth; they provided neither washed garments for the unwashed nor graves for the clothed, paying such funeral rites to the dead as they justly deserved.

Bodies lay everywhere, brought in dripping wagons; and since you were continually pressing upon the stricken enemy, they were hastily cremated amid fragments of funeral pyres, enclosed within houses whose roofs were collapsing.

But why do I chatter about these matters at greater length than justice permits? I have not presumed to weave the full history of your labors, but only to preserve a part of their memory, so that you might more readily believe the prayers of your people, whose anxious expectation no remedies will heal more soundly or swiftly than your arrival.

Therefore, if you yield in any degree to the prayers of your countrymen, hasten at once to sound the trumpet of your return to your homeland, and quickly withdraw your constant presence from the dangerous intimacy of kings.

[Note: Of the Burgundians, with whom Ecdicius was on familiar terms. He afterward withdrew to Burgundy, when the city had been surrendered to the Goths, and lived there, as the passage from Gregory cited above shows.] The most eminent men rightly compare association with them to the nature of flames: just as flames illuminate what is at a little distance from them, so they burn what comes sufficiently close.

Farewell.

## Letter IV

**Sidonius to his Felix, greetings.**

[Note: Through this same Felix he writes in Book IV, Letter 5. He was therefore of Narbonian origin, like Magnus Felix.]

Gozolas, a Jew by nation and a client of your high office, brings my letter—one which I have written in great anxiety. I too would have held his person dear, if his sect were not held in contempt. Our town, as though it were a kind of obstacle placed against the boundary of its own territory, is terrified by the arms of the peoples surrounding us. Situated amid peoples hostile to one another, we are a pitiable prize: suspect to the Burgundians, close to the Goths, and lacking neither the anger of attackers nor the resentment of defenders. But that is for another time.

Meanwhile, if matters are proceeding properly among you, all is well. For we are not so constituted that, even if we ourselves are punished by open penalties because of hidden crimes, we should wish things not to prosper wherever we may be. It is certain that the man who has not preserved good hopes even amid evil times is as much a captive of vices as of enemies.

Farewell.

[Note: Likewise the Burgundians, who had remained faithful to the Romans after the peace granted by the general Aetius. Accordingly, they had been present with Aetius in the battle of the Catalaunian Plains; and recently, under Anthemius, they had received Riothamus, a king allied with the Roman state, after he had been defeated and put to flight in battle by the Goths. It is therefore unsurprising that they also assisted the Arvernians in this war. For this reason, after becoming master of the peoples as far as the Rhône, Euric soon attacked the Burgundians as well, as Jordanes testifies.]

## Letter V

**Sidonius to his Hypatius, greetings.**

If the distinguished Donidius, who examines and admires your character, had considered only his household advantage, your loyalty would have been more than sufficient for his interests, even if no intermediary had intervened. But he was led by his affection for me to make me ask for what he had obtained on his own. Thus your honor now receives this additional increase: two of us become debtors, although only one of us receives the benefit.

[Note: Ebrolium is today a small town of the Arvernians on the river Sicaula, known for its ancient Benedictine monastery. Donidius came from there; at that time he was a cleric and an inhabitant of the city of Arvernia. For this reason Sidonius calls him, by place, a fellow citizen; by profession, a son.]

He wishes, with your support, to have added to his own right half of the estate at Eborolacum, which had been devastated even before the barbarians and which now falls under the rights of a patrician household. He is moved to this request not by the spur of greed, but by regard for ancestral memory. For the integrity of the estate itself had witnessed the ownership of his family until the recent death of his stepfather, who passed away only recently.

Now, a man who does not covet what belongs to another and is sparing with what is his own is distressed by the alienation of the ancient property not so much because of the loss as because of the shame. He is compelled to try to redeem it not by the vice of avarice but by the necessity of modesty. Deign to grant his wishes, my requests, and your own character, so that with your patronage he may reach full possession of this estate. Since the property belonged to his parents and was known to him—not merely known, but crawled over by him in the earliest beginnings of infancy—it seems scarcely profitable merely to have recovered it, and exceedingly feeble not to have purchased it.

For my part, I shall be bound by your grant as though whatever my brother in age, son in profession, fellow citizen in place, and friend in loyalty receives were of particular benefit to my own property.

Farewell.

## Letter VI

**Sidonius to his Eutropius, greetings.**

[Note: To a noble man devoted to the study of philosophy, now prefect of the Gauls. For he congratulates him on this dignity. Since he had previously encouraged the same man to undertake military service and offices, in Book I, Letter 6, he recalls that letter here and calls the treatise an exhortation.]

If your loyalty now remembers the old comradeship and the favor renewed day by day thereafter, you surely understand that you have risen to the summit of dignities just as we have risen to the summit of our hopes. We all rejoice so greatly in your office that we judge the household raised by it to be no less our friendship than your own.

That treatise is witness, in which the incentives of my exhortation had no small force: by them you could scarcely be brought to join a prefecture to philosophy, when the school of the Platonists had carried you, as one devoted to the doctrines of Plotinus, into the depths of untimely retirement. I then argued that the profession of that discipline would be free once it owed nothing to a household. Moreover, that contempt for military service was thought close to idleness; and spiteful men declare that men of good principles cannot rise to it, rather than that they are unwilling to do so.

Therefore, as is fitting in the first place, we offer abundant thanks to Christ, who has hitherto adorned your lofty position with the nobility of your parents and now raises it still higher through the equality of your titles. At the same time, with our hopes lifted, it is right thereafter to expect better things.

Certainly, the frequent talk of the provincials is that a good year should be judged from great administrations, not so much by crops as by governors. In this matter, my lord and superior, it is your responsibility to reward our expectation with suitable arrangements. The entire community has persuaded itself, remembering your noble origin, that as long as the family of Sabinus governs us, the family of Sabinianus need not be feared.

Farewell.

## Letter VII

**Sidonius to his Felix, greetings.**

You have kept away from letters for a long time. Thus each of us follows his accustomed practice: I chatter, and you remain silent. Hence, since you are distinguished in all the other duties of loyalty, I suppose it is a kind of virtue that you cannot be wearied by so much leisure.

What is this? Will you never be moved by regard for our old intimacy, so as at last to withdraw your foot from the resolve of uninterrupted silence? Or do you not know that failing to answer a chatterbox is an insult? You are silent, whether amid libraries or amid the world of the toga, and you expect from me the service of impoverished speech, although, if you see clearly, I possess more ease than ability in writing.

Certainly, let our fear at least provide material for your pen. Remember to burden the hands of travelers with letters, so that the care of friends may be lightened; and hasten to tell us whether, God going before him, the quaestor Licinianus has opened a door of security for our mutual anxiety.

[Note: We have mentioned above that he was sent as ambassador by the emperor’s grandson to King Euric. From this letter it is clear that he came at the time when the Goths had withdrawn from the siege of the Arvernians into winter quarters. Sidonius will write again about Licinianus in Book V, Letter 16, to Papianilla.]

For, as they report, he is a person of great expectation, greater upon arrival, exalted by report, still more exalted by inspection, and remarkable for every gift of fortune and nature. The highest strictness joined with equal courtesy, and a prudence and good faith suited to both the envoy and the sender. Nothing affected or feigned; in the weight of his words there is genuine seriousness rather than an imitation of seriousness. He is not like the many who, when they report what has been entrusted to them with hesitation, wish to appear to have acted more cautiously.

Nor, as they say, is he one of those who, trading upon the secrets of the princes who sent them, seek to have the barbarians treat the envoy well rather than the embassy. A favorable report has brought us this account of the man’s character.

Send word swiftly if the facts correspond to what has been said, so that those who keep watch without sleep may for a time draw breath—those whom neither a snowy day nor a moonless and stormy night persuades to sound the retreat from their watch on the walls. For even if the barbarian withdraws into winter quarters, they defer rather than abandon the fear once rooted in their hearts.

Touch us with good news, because our situation is not so far removed from yours as our homeland is.

Farewell.

## Letter VIII

**Sidonius to his Eucherius, greetings.**

[Note: He calls him an illustrious man in the assembly at Bourges; Gregory of Tours calls him a senator. I infer that he was Eucherius the senator, whom, according to Book II, chapter 20, the general Victorius oppressed and killed through fabricated accusations.]

I honor the men of old, but not in such a way as to place the virtues or achievements of my contemporaries below them. Nor, because the Roman state has sunk into this extremity of misery, so that it never rewards those devoted to it, do my times therefore fail to produce Bruti and Torquati of equal worth.

“What is the point of this?” you ask. My speech concerns you and is addressed to you, most effective of men, to whom the state owes what history praises as having been paid to the men mentioned above. Therefore, let the ignorant suspend their rash judgments and not persist in either looking up to the men of the past or looking down on those of the present. For it is readily apparent that the state delays its benefits, while you deserve them.

Yet it should not be greatly wondered at if, while a nation of moneylenders not only administers Roman strength uncivilly but also tears it out by the roots, the deeds have not been lacking so much as the rewards of noble and military men, and of those whose warlike achievements have surpassed both the hope of our side and the expectation of the opposing side.

[Note: In several manuscripts, *moderari*—“to regulate.”]

Farewell.

## Letter IX

**Sidonius to his Riothamus, greetings.**

[Note: To the king of the Britons, as I think. Euric defeated him in battle in the district of Bourges when he was bringing assistance to Anthemius with twelve thousand men, as Jordanes reports in his *Getica*. It is not surprising that he is not called Riothamus—or, as Jordanes writes, Riothimus—since neither Pope Hilary calls Gunduicius king nor Sidonius calls Chilperic king, although each was king of the Burgundians.]

Our customary manner of speech is preserved: we mix complaint with greeting. We do not deliberately strive for our style to be courteous in its headings and harsh in its pages; rather, such things always occur that a man of my place or rank must become disliked if he speaks, and commits a fault if he remains silent.

But we also behold the burden of your shame, whose constant modesty has been to blush for the faults of others. The bearer of the letter, humble, obscure, and contemptible even to the point of suffering from the harm caused by innocent cowardice, laments that his slaves have been carried off after the Britons secretly solicited them.

I do not know whether his complaint is well founded; but if, with the parties face to face, you impartially examine the charges brought, I think he can prove what he alleges—provided that, among clever, armed, tumultuous men, defiant in courage, numbers, and companionship, a solitary, unarmed, abject, rustic, foreign, poor man can be heard with equity and justice.

Farewell.

## Letter X

**Sidonius to his Tetradius, greetings.**

[Col. 0502B]

Our young men gain great praise in character whenever, uncertain about the merits of a case, they resort to the advice of experts. So now the distinguished Theodorus—noble at home, but still more noble in the reputation of his most modest conduct—through my letters proceeds with laudable eagerness to your letters, that is, to the purest fountain of knowledge. There he will not only find something to learn himself, but perhaps also bring back something to teach.

Against powerful and factious men, if your expertise did not abundantly assist him, prudent counsel would suffice for him. We beg you to reply—unless the united prayers of both of us will be considered a burden or annoyance to you—to his own judgment and my testimony; and support the substance and cause of the petitioner, which are wavering, with the healing and salutary benefit of your reply.

Farewell.

## Letter XI

**Sidonius to his Simplicius, greetings.**

[Note: Perhaps the same man who, a few years later, was appointed bishop of Bourges at Sidonius’ designation. The conjecture is supported by what he says about the sons of this Simplicius: “Your sons have surpassed you”; and, in an assembly concerning the sons of Bishop Simplicius: “Compared with whom the father begins to be happier precisely because he is surpassed.”]

Although our longing is accompanied by such great adversity that even now you are begrudged to our eyes, you are not, best of men, one whose lofty qualities are hidden from us. Thus all our countrymen, and the most eminent men among them, with a unanimous proclamation commend you as a most excellent head of household, possessing the finest and most exacting qualities.

The judgment of good men supports this opinion of you, whether in the son-in-law chosen in this way or in the daughter brought up in this way. Their union has produced such a happy contest for your wishes that you are uncertain whether you have surpassed them more by judgment or by upbringing.

Yet here above all let both parents, who are worthy of reverence, rest assured: you surpass the others because your children have surpassed you. Therefore forgive this first letter. Just as laziness had not yet prevented me from sending it, so I fear that loquacity may have made it unwise to send it.

Our service of speech will certainly be free of the blemish of talkativeness if, following the example of a returning conversation, you absolve the boldness of this page.

Farewell.

## Letter XII

**Sidonius to his Secundus, greetings.**

[Note: To his brother’s son. He sends him the epitaph of his grandfather Apollinaris, which he had composed the previous night, and instructs him to have it carved in marble and placed on his tomb. He also urges him to arrange this while he himself is absent—that is, before his return. Since he writes this while traveling toward the city of Arvernia, it follows that the tomb of his grandfather Apollinaris was not near the city of Arvernia but near Lyon; for at the very beginning of his journey he encountered the violators of the tomb. That the tomb was not far from Lyon is clear from the fact that, after reporting the punished criminals to the bishop, he received the reply immediately on the journey itself. He therefore calls his bishop Patient, the bishop of Lyon, and in the epitaph calls Lyon the homeland of Apollinaris.]

Yesterday, alas, profane hands had almost violated the tomb of my grandfather, your great-grandfather; but God was present so that such an outrage was not perpetrated. The field itself, long filled with both pyre ashes and corpses, had for a long time received no further trench. Yet the earth laid over the buried bodies had returned, when the heaps settled under the weight of snow or the prolonged flow of rain, to its original level and spread-out surface. This gave the bearers of corpses the opportunity to defile the place, as though it were empty, with funeral rakes.

What more? The black turf had already replaced the green; fresh clods already lay above the ancient tomb. As I happened to be traveling toward the city of Arvernia, I saw the public crime from the brow of a neighboring hill. Spurring my horse across both level ground and precipices, impatient even of a brief delay, I restrained the audacious deed with a warning cry before I arrived. While those caught in the crime hesitated whether to flee or remain, I came upon them.

I confess my error: I could not postpone the punishment of the captured men. Yet above the very covering of our old man I tortured the thieves in a manner sufficient to satisfy the concern of the living and the security of the dead. For the rest, I reserved nothing for our bishop. Knowing my own case and his person, I acted with the common good in mind, so that neither this matter would be avenged too leniently nor the other too severely.

When I had sent him the entire sequence of events from the journey, as an explanation, the holy and just man granted glory to my anger. I had asked no further pardon, and he declared that, according to the custom of our ancestors, those guilty of such great recklessness could rightly be considered to have been put to death.

[Note: *Lapidicidae*, stonecutters. The Code, *On the Excuses of Craftsmen*, Book I: “The *quadrātāriī*, whom they call by the Greek term λιθοθῆκται (*lithothēktai*),” and “stone-cutters,” in Cassiodorus’ commentary on the Psalms. The stone-cutting craft is mentioned in the *Acts of the Holy Coronati* and in a fragment of an ancient stone at Rome in the church of Saint Agnes.]

But so that such accidents, which we ought to avoid by example, may have no power in the future, I ask you to see to it promptly, even in my absence and at my expense, that the scattered heap be raised again into a mound and covered by a smoothed slab. I have left the price of the stone and the payment for the work with the venerable Gaudentius.

This poem, which follows, I composed the previous night. It is not polished, I think, because I was considerably occupied with the journey. I ask that, whatever its size, it be quickly put upon the tablet. But see that the stonecutter does not introduce an error into the marble, whether deliberately or through negligence, for a hostile reader may attribute it more to me than to the stonecutter.

For my part, if you kindly carry out what I ask in pious devotion, I shall give thanks as though nothing of praise or glory accrued to you as well—although, in the absence of your uncle, that is, of me, the solid diligence of your present service would remain appropriate to the rank of your lineage.

Farewell.

Late, after my uncles and my father, I, a grandson

not unworthy of my grandfather, dedicated this poem:

Lest at some future time, traveler,

ignorant of the reverence due to the buried dead,

you trample the unmounded earth.

Here lies the prefect Apollinaris,

after directing the praetorian offices of the Gauls,

received into the bosom of his grieving homeland.

Most learned and most useful,

cultivator of the countryside, military service, and the forum,

and, by his example, a perilous model to others,

free beneath ruling tyrants.

But this is proved to be his greatest distinction:

that, cleansing his brow with the cross and his limbs in the font,

he was the first among his fathers

to renounce sacred sacrileges.

[Note: In baptism, which he was the first of his family to receive. Hence the error of Beatus Rhenanus is evident: he attributes to our Sidonius what was owed to his grandfather. An ancient inscription of the city also supports this. It may be added to the other inscriptions published from the Palatine Library, from a manuscript of Saint Mary of Verdun:

At the church of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, also called *in Prasino*. At the Fountain.

This renowned saving font contains its waters,

and is accustomed to cleanse human pollution.

Do you wish to know what gifts the sacred liquid possesses?

The holy streams bestow the ruling faith.

Wash away the contagions of your former life

in the sacred fountain;

O exceedingly happy one, live reborn through water!

Whoever seeks this fountain abandons earthly things

and subjects blind services beneath his feet.]

This is the first honor, this the proud virtue:

to precede in hope those whom you join in honor,

and those parents who here are your equals in titles

to surpass there in merits.

I know that the quality of this epitaph does not correspond to the doctrine of our distinguished author; but a discerning soul does not reject musical offerings to the dead. It is not fitting for you either to consider it tardy that we, the third and fourth heirs, discharge our obligation, since, after the passage of so many years, we have learned that Alexander the Great performed funeral rites for the shades of Achilles, and that Julius Caesar paid Hector funeral rites as though to his own ancestor.

Farewell.

## Letter XIII

**Sidonius to his Apollinaris, greetings.**

[Note: Some manuscripts assign this letter to the son. For it is a father’s exhortation to his son, and that Apollinaris was Sidonius’ son is shown both by Book V, Letter 9, and by Book IX, Letter 1, as well as by Ruricius, Book II, Letter 25. This Apollinaris seems to be the man whom Gregory of Tours says was released from custody at Milan through the help of Saint Victor, *Miracles* I.45. He later took part with the Arvernians in the battle of Vouillé, Book II of the History, chapter 37, though he did not perish there, despite what some add concerning their own account. For the same Gregory, as I believe, elsewhere bears witness that he later died as bishop in the see of Arvernia.

Furthermore, Apollinaris’ son by his wife Placida was Arcadius; the same author writes about him in Book III, chapters 9, 12, and 18. Arcadius’ daughter was Placida, once the wife of Leontius the Younger, bishop of Bordeaux. From these facts Fortunatus will receive clarification when he traces this Placida’s ancestry back to the emperor Avitus, Book I, poem 14:

I am compelled by affection to say a few words about Placida,

who was then your wife and is now your dear sister.

A light shines forth from Arcadius, her father,

through whom, Avitus, your Augustan lineage endures.

You who ruled the splendor of empire throughout the whole world,

whose senate still possesses powerful laws.

If you seek the highest summits of the human race,

nothing can surpass the imperial name of Caesar.

Quite truly. For she was the great-granddaughter of Avitus through his daughter Papianilla and Sidonius. Accordingly, the passage in Gregory, *Miracles* I.65, is corrupt and should be restored as follows: “Alcima, sister, and Placida, wife of Bishop Apollinaris.” This is clear from Book III, chapters 2 and 12.]

I approve wholeheartedly, rejoice, and admire the fact that, out of a concern for chastity, you shun the company of the shameless—especially those who have no regard for anything, nothing sacred, when seeking and prattling about obscenities; and who, because they pollute the dignity of public ears with immodest words, think themselves consummate wits. Understand that the greatest standard-bearer of this vileness is the parasite of our country. He is a whirlpool of tale-spinners, fabricators of accusations, and disseminators of malicious opinions; himself loquacious but not witty, ridiculous but not cheerful, arrogant but not steadfast, inquisitive but not perceptive, and, with his indecently affected charm, more rustic than refined. He cultivates the present, criticizes the past, and despises the future.

When seeking a favor, he is importunate in asking, a detractor when refused, a rival of the recipient, clever at altering what he has received, querulous when he has demanded something, and garrulous when it is restored. But when someone must ask him for something, he pretends to be ready, conceals what has been requested, sells what he has provided, publishes what was secret, maligns what has been delayed, and denies what has been paid. He hates fasting and pursues feasts, expressing approval not of a man who lives well but of one who feeds well.

Yet amid all this he himself is utterly greedy, and is nourished less by good bread than by someone else’s bread. He eats nothing at home except whatever he has sent ahead from his plundered dishes amid storms of slaps. Nor is it right entirely to pass over the frugality of this otherwise praiseworthy man: he fasts whenever he is not invited. Even then, however, with parasitic fickleness, he excuses himself if invited, investigates if avoided, reproaches if excluded, exults if admitted, and waits to be beaten. Once he has reclined at table, he is said to turn immediately to robbery if he eats slowly; to tears if he is quickly satisfied; to complaints if he is thirsty; to vomiting if he becomes drunk; to insults if he tires others; and to rages if he himself is tired. He is altogether the equal of a fetid sewer, which becomes more foul the more it is stirred.

Thus he lives as a pleasure to few, loved by none, and a laughing-stock to everyone: a breaker of bladders and destroyer of cudgels; greedy for drinking, greedier still for slander; breathing filth through his rabid mouth, foaming wine, and speaking poison. It is difficult to decide whether he should be considered more shameless, more drunken, or more criminal.

“But,” you say, “he colors over the disgrace of his mind with his face, and the quality of his body pleads pardon for the foolishness of his mind.” A handsome man, evidently, and exceedingly comely, whose appearance is striking to those who see him! In truth, that appearance is dirtier and more deformed than a royal corpse which, half-burned when the torches have been applied and then rolled down as the pile of logs collapses, the already disgusted embalmer recoils from returning to the pyre.

Besides these features, he has eyes that are without light; like a Stygian marsh, they roll tears through darkness.
