He also has ears hideous in their vastness; an ulcerated skin surrounds their two-branched canal, with stony knots and porous, moisture-swollen warts protruding along the curved edge. He carries a nose which, though broad at the nostrils and narrow along the bridge, opens so widely to horror that it is constricted for smelling. He displays a mouth with leaden lips, an animal-like gape, pus-filled gums, and boxwood-colored teeth. The mephitic odor exhaled from the hollow of his rotting molars frequently fouls it; over this is heaped the belch of food from yesterday’s meals and the overflowing cesspool of his dinners.

He also displays a forehead which, by a most disgusting movement, wrinkles the skin and stretches the eyebrows. He grows a beard which, though whitening with age, is nevertheless black with a Sullan disease.

**81** Finally, his entire face is so pale that it seems to have been saddened for hours by ghostly shadows. I say nothing of the rest of his bulk, bound by gout and loosened by fat. I say nothing of his brain, deeply furrowed by repeated scars, which is scarcely more covered by hair than by cicatrices. I say nothing of the shortness of his neck, by which the nape, thrown backward, seems attached to the boundary of his shoulders. I say nothing of the honor that has fallen from his shoulders, the grace from his arms, or the strength from his forearms.

I say nothing of his gouty hands, wrapped in greasy cloths smeared with poultices as though they were boxing gloves. I say nothing of the fact that, enclosed by the reeking and souring caves of his armpits, he pollutes the nostrils of those around him with the stench of a double Ampsanctus. I say nothing of his breasts, lying broken beneath the weight of fat, which it would be disgraceful even for a male chest to have protruding, but which here have fallen like a mother’s breasts.

I say nothing of the hanging nets of his bent belly, covering his genitals, since these private parts—weak as they are—are provided with a still more disgraceful covering of ugly wrinkles. Why should I now mention his back and spine? Although the curvature of his ribs, bursting from the supports of its internal joints, covers the surface of his chest, this entire branching framework of bones nevertheless lies hidden beneath a single sea, as it were, of his overflowing abdomen.

I say nothing of the bulk of his loins and his buttocks, beside whose thickness his belly is judged slender. I say nothing of his withered and splayed thigh, his massive knees, delicate hamstrings, hornlike shins, glassy ankles, small toes, and large feet. Though he is so dreadful in the distortions of his features, through which his bloodless, half-alive body displays a manifold pestilence, he neither feels himself carried nor walks when supported, yet in words he is more execrable than in limbs.

For although he suffers from an itch for indecent speech, he is especially to be feared with regard to his patrons’ secrets. In prosperity he praises them; in uncertainty he betrays them. But if circumstances urge him to disclose the hidden matters of his friends, then through this Spartacus whatever is closed is broken open, and whatever is sealed is unlocked. Thus, whatever he cannot attack openly with the engines of declared hostility, he assaults through the tunnels of clandestine treachery.

By this contrivance our Daedalus builds the summit of friendships. Just as he joins his companions, like Theseus, amid favorable circumstances, so afterward, amid adversity, he slips away from them like Proteus.

Therefore you will fulfill my wish if you do not join the company of such men, not even at your first meeting—especially those whose prostituted, theatrical speech is restrained by no reins and preceded by no barrier of modesty. For those whose unbridled tongues are polluted by the dregs of wantonness while they boastfully chatter without the luster of decency possess also the most sordid consciences. In short, it is easier for someone who speaks seriously to live obscenely than for anyone to be shown who is at once wicked in speech and upright in conduct.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIV

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Placidius.

Although your own Gratianopolis keeps you, **[Note:]** This name was bestowed by Gratian. Its old and proper name was Cularo; hence the Cularonian walls are still mentioned in an ancient inscription on the city gate. It is also named in the Peutinger Table and in the *Notitia Imperii*, which teaches that the tribune of the First Flavian Cohort had his station at Cularo. In Plancus’s letter to Cicero, the twenty-third of Book X of the *Letters to Friends*, we long ago judged that the final words should be read: “at Cularo, in the territory of the Allobroges,” not “at Civarone,” as is commonly printed. Gratianopolis marks the territory of the Allobroges because it lies on the Isère, which bounds the Allobroges and separates them from the Vocontii.

I have nevertheless learned, on the trustworthy report of old acquaintances, **83** that you consider my trifles—whether composed in prose or made songlike in the poets’ style—worthy of more volumes of reading. I rejoice at this very thing: that I have discovered your leisure occupied with my little pages. But I understand perfectly that, in accordance with your character, this pleasure has been produced not by the accomplishment of the work but by affection for its author. I therefore owe you the more, because the point of glory that you would deny to my diction you grant to friendship.

As for the other detractors of our studies, I have not yet decided what I should say about them in full. For the man who considers himself especially learned turns over sound and unsound diction with nearly equal appetite, desiring no more eagerly what is elevated, which he may praise, than what is contemptible, which he may mock. In this way, learning, display, and the propriety of the Latin language are held in the greatest contempt by the judgments of idle men. Negligence accompanies their buffoonery; wishing to read only what they can criticize, they do not use letters but abuse them.

Farewell.

# BOOK FOUR

## 84 LETTER I

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Probus.

**[Note:]** To the brother of Magnus Felix, a man of outstanding learning and judgment. For he addresses Felix in poem 9:

> Yet remember first to summon  
> Probus, the pillar of learning, as your own brother.

Probus’s wife was Eulalia, at the end of poem 24. Therefore Eulalia was Sidonius’s sister here, but his paternal cousin. For just as *brother* is sometimes used not only for a full brother but also for a paternal cousin, so *sister* may mean either a full sister or a paternal cousin, or even a first cousin.

The woman who is a sister to me is a wife to you: hence there is between us a supreme and primary bond, and one that is indeed a relationship of paternal cousins, not of full siblings—a relationship that usually loves itself more purely, more strongly, and more genuinely. For once the dispute over property between full brothers has been quieted, those born from brothers contend over nothing among themselves. Hence affection among cousins is often greater, because rivalry arising from division ceases, while affection arising from shared blood does not.

A second bond between our minds has been added through the equality of our studies, since in literature we feel, criticize, and praise the same things, and every expression pleases or displeases us equally. Yet I claim too much for myself when I compare my judgment with yours. For who among young or old does not know that you were my particular teacher, even when we seemed to have a common one? And if the heroic poet established anything lofty, the comic poet anything graceful, the lyric poet anything songlike, the orator anything mature, the historian anything truthful, the satirist anything figurative, the grammarian anything regular, the panegyrist anything applause-worthy, the sophist anything serious, the epigrammatist anything wanton, the commentator anything clear, and the jurisconsult anything obscure—did you not convey all these things to each of them in every manner, unless someone lacked talent, or lacked it for himself?

Good heavens! How our fathers gloried in this, when they saw that, with Christ’s help, you could teach and I could learn; and not merely that you did what you could, but that you wished to do what you did—and therefore that you were judged good no less than learned.

Indeed, within the household of Eusebius you had received, as it were, a certain coinage of such disciplines, having been formed on its philosophical anvil. At one moment, with the approval even of the one who had taught you, you displayed various methods of treating subjects and language; at another, like Plato—a disciple already nearly superior beneath Socrates—you, now under our Eusebius, practiced Attic refinement as a dialectical craftsman among Aristotelian categories, while he was still tempering our young age—mobile, tender, and raw—sometimes with corrective severity, sometimes seasoning it with the wholesome flavor of commands.

But of what kind, good heavens, and how precious! If anyone were to carry such teachings abroad to philosophize, whether to the marsh-dwelling Sicambri, the Caucasus-born Alans, or the horse-milking Geloni—to nations with bestial, rigid hearts of horn and icy sinews—they would without doubt soften and thaw those hearts. Nor would we laugh at, despise, or fear their savage stupidity, which, behaving like beasts, grows dull, becomes brutal, and is inflamed.

Therefore, since kinship has joined us just as our studies have, I ask you, wherever you are, to preserve the rights of our friendship unshaken; and, though we may be absent in place, to remain present to me in affection. As far as depends on us, the undefiled parts of this friendship will endure forever, for as long as any life remains.

Farewell.

## 87 LETTER II

**[Note:]** Mamertus Claudianus, a presbyter of the church of Vienne and brother of Bishop Mamertus. The two full brothers must be distinguished: Mamertus the bishop and Mamertus Claudianus the presbyter, to whom this letter belongs. They share the name Mamertus, but for the bishop it was his proper name, whereas for the presbyter it was a surname; his proper and true name was Claudianus.

Claudianus sends greetings to Pope Sidonius.

**[Col. 0509A]**

We published this letter in *Patrologia*, volume 53, column 779; see it there.

## 88 LETTER III

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Claudianus.

This letter also may be found in *Patrologia*, volume 53, column 781.

## 92 LETTER IV

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Simplicius and Apollinaris.

**[Note:]** He joins them again in Letter 12, though elsewhere he writes to each separately. They seem to have been brothers, since they were bound to Sidonius by a relationship of affection. This is clear concerning Apollinaris from Letter 9 of Book II.

Here, at last, is my promise, your expectation: Faustinus, a father of a household, noble in his own household and now to be counted among the greatest ornaments of the country that he and I share. He is my brother by equality of birth and my friend by similarity of character. With him I often mixed serious matters and jokes; and when we were young, not long ago, we were always united in ball games, dice, jumping, running, hunting, and swimming, because affection remained even amid competition.

He was older than I, though by no more than was necessary for me to honor him rather than merely take pleasure in imitating him. He too was more gratified by this, because he understood that he was loved rather than, as it were, worshiped. But as he advanced in age and passed from military service into the clergy, he became, having previously been lovable, now worthy of reverence.

Through him I declare that I eagerly desire, with Christ’s help, to see you as soon as possible, if public circumstances permit. Therefore, unless my desire seems burdensome, when the aforementioned man returns I shall become informed about your places and circumstances. I am determined to struggle through the difficulties of private engagements and to assign whatever length of service may be required to embrace your hearts—provided that, as we still fear, superior force does not disrupt these arrangements.

You too may deliberate on this matter with your brother Faustinus, sharing your discussion as circumstances advise; I have sent him because I love him as one who loves me. If he responds to my judgment, I give thanks. Besides, although everyone considers a good man to be good, a man is not worse simply because he is not the best.

Farewell.

## LETTER V

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Felix.

A repeated greeting repeats the bearer. Your Gozolas—may God grant that he become ours—has become the bearer of my letters for the second time. Therefore remove the common embarrassment from both of us. For if you still plan to remain silent, everyone will judge both me, to whom you ought to write, and him, through whom you ought to write, unworthy.

I shall say nothing now, as before, about the state of affairs, lest it burden your character if you report adversity when prosperity does not follow. Since it is not fitting for you to send false reports, and since there is likewise nothing favorable to report, I avoid learning whatever evil there may be through indications of good.

Farewell.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Apollinaris.

**[Note:]** To the same man. Simplicius and Apollinaris, invited to the solemn feast of a martyr among the Arverni, had abandoned their planned journey because of fear of the enemy. Sidonius praises what they did and rejoices that their household—that is, their family—had not, up to that time, been disturbed by any adversity or exposed to enemy incursions.

Therefore do not repeat this to the learned man at the fortress of Poliniac, nor persuade yourself that the fortress once belonged to Apollinarius or that its name was derived from Apollo. Gabriel Simeonius, an Etruscan, seemed in an ingenious conjecture to have divined this. The old name of the fortress was Podomniacus, as may be read everywhere both in other ancient monuments and in the letters of Pope Urban V to King Charles on behalf of Armando, Viscount and lord of the place.

Through the bishop Faustinus, bound to me no less by the fellowship of our old life together than by the communion of our new profession, I had sent you a word of warning. I rejoice that you obeyed what was said. For it is implanted deep in the hearts of prudent people to avoid chance dangers. It is equally absurd, if events oppose bold undertakings, to rise up in complaint and to turn the blameworthy outcomes of ill-considered plans into a means of interpreting the uncertainties of accidents.

“What is the point of all this?” you ask. I admit that I was excessively afraid that, at a time of public danger, you would not be afraid; that the secure peace of your solid household, unshaken up to this time, would tremble before the stormy attacks of the enemy because of an ill-timed devotion; and that the desired solemnity would begin to lose its value in the tender minds of women. Yet innate holiness had so marked out for itself a special dwelling in their hearts that, if anything contrary had happened to travelers, they would have rejoiced to have endured a kind of martyrdom in place of the martyr.

But I, whose greater distrust arises from lesser innocence, more readily cling to the safer opinion in this uncertainty, and I am not reluctant to side even with those who fear what is safe. Therefore you did well to postpone the perilous journey for your own safety, and the condition of so great a household was not placed within the throw of so great a hazard.

Even though the journey you began might have turned out favorably, I shall not give my white stone to advice of this sort, whose rashness can be acquitted only by the favor of good fortune. Divine providence may indeed cause such vows to advance through worthy successes, and it may still be possible to remember these terrors beneath the pleasant shelter of peace. But present circumstances make people cautious who, in the future, will see themselves secure.

Meanwhile, at this moment, the bearer of these pages sighs over certain losses inflicted upon him by your Genesius. If you see that his complaint is not contrary to the truth, please grant the man who has been convicted reparation and the stranger speed. But if envious malice inflames a punishable accusation, the man who has been attacked has already received his revenge in this: the insolent petitioner, exhausted by expense and travel, is sweating out the hardships of a lawsuit rashly brought forward. And this at the height of winter—literally, “at the peak of summer and winter”—amid the greatest heaps of snow and crusts of ice.

As far as litigants are concerned, this season is often short for the hearing but always long for the injury.

Farewell.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Simplicius.

One usually says that a man who is already running is advised when he is asked to do what he would have done even without being asked. Perhaps you will inquire what this introduction is meant to convey. The bearer of these pages earnestly requests that he may carry a letter from me to you. Once we learned of his journey from us, he would certainly have had to be asked to do precisely this if he had kept silent; for it was your affection, rather than regard for the bearer, that elicited this service.

Besides, this very man counts it as a favor that he has earned by performing it, although he has received exactly what he requested again and again; but he does not at all understand the rights of friendship that we observe. Hence, although he is absent, I can easily imagine what sudden amazement will strike him when, graciously admitted into our presence, he realizes that he had been more idle in requesting my page than in delivering it.

I seem to see how everything will be new to a man not excessively clever to the point of envy when the stranger is invited into a home, the timid man into conversation, the rustic into merriment, and the poor man to the table. While here the common crowd lives on raw onions and food-induced drunkenness, there he will be treated with such courtesy as though until now he had been belching among Apician banqueters and Byzantine dancers.

Nevertheless, whatever sort of man he is and however insignificant, he has made me abundantly the recipient of the service I desired. Although people of this sort are often almost contemptible, nevertheless, in cultivating companions through letters, affection suffers considerable loss if it is deterred from the practice of frequent address by the lowliness of the bearers.

Farewell.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Evodius.

**[Note:]** Some books read *Ennodius*, others *Euhodius*, according to the ancient custom. To this man he sends an epigram that he had written at his request to be engraved on a silver shell, which he intended to present to Ragnahild, queen of the Goths and wife of Euric.

When your letter was delivered to me by the messenger who said that, at the king’s command, you would soon be setting out for Toulouse, we too were heading from the town toward a distant country estate. I had been delayed from early morning, and your page barely shook me loose from the persistent crowd of those seeing me off, so that I might fulfill your command, whether as a traveler or as a horseman.

My household had already gone ahead at dawn and was preparing a tent eighteen miles away, a place offering many conveniences for relaxing one’s baggage: a cold spring beneath a wooded hill, a low-lying field abundant in grass, and, before one’s eyes, a river rich in birds and fish. Besides these, an old friend possessed a new house adjoining the bank; one could set no limit to his immense hospitality, whether one accepted it or declined it.

Therefore, when we had stopped here because of you, so that the boy might be sent back more quickly even from the head of the village, the second hour had already well advanced. The grown sun had already absorbed the moisture of the dewy night with its strengthening ray; heat and thirst were increasing; and, in the deep calm, the only cloud that sheltered us from the heat was one of dust.

**[Note:]** Four hours after sunrise. He called another hour the “second hour” at Narbo: “When morning had newly emerged, and the sun, growing warm, gave the second hour.” This corresponds to our hour somewhat later than the ninth hour in summer.

The length of the road, exposed to the eyes across the green surface of the open field, was lamented, especially because of this very reason by those who would dine late. For although the travelers had not yet been worn down by exertion, expectation already frightened them.

All these preliminaries, dear brother, are intended to prove to you that when I complied with your request I was not free of concern in mind, body, or time. Let us now return directly to the substance of your letter. After the words that first conveyed greetings, you asked me to send an epigram completed in twelve verses, suitable for a capacious shell whose two sides, from the side of the handles to the far end of the circle, were hollowed out with six parallel grooves.

**[Note:]** The shell had to be made striated so that it would resemble a natural one. Certain sea shells are striated, according to Pliny and Apuleius. What the grooves and striations on columns and vessels are is known from Vitruvius. Here the bellies are the projecting grooves—channels, as it were, like a furrow in a plowed field—while the curved heads are the striations, the raised parts resembling ridges between furrows.

You intended, I think, to inscribe one verse on each of the projecting bellies, or, better advised, if that seemed more appropriate, on the curved heads; and, having polished it in this style, you intended to offer it to Queen Ragnahild, thereby preparing invincible protection for your wishes and actions alike.

**[Note:]** To the wife of Euric. The chronological circumstances in which these letters were written, together with the author’s concealment of the epigram—as though he feared that its discovery would diminish the gratitude owed for the gift—make me think that she, rather than Theodoric, was the recipient. Sidonius would not have said this while Theodoric was alive, since Theodoric was his patron and friend. We therefore owe the queen’s name to Sidonius alone. Gregory of Tours mentions another woman of the same name, the wife of our countryman Sigivald, in the *Life of Aemilianus*.

I serve your instructions as best I can, though not as I wished. But first forgive your own fault: you gave the silversmith more time than the poet, although you surely knew that, within the workshop of literary men, whatever the metrical anvil produces from a poem is polished no less by a strong and rough file.

But why these or similar remarks? Here is the finished piece:

> The shell that bears Cytherea through the sea-bearing Triton—  
> let it not hesitate to yield when this one is set beside it.  
> We ask you, bend your sovereign head a little,  
> and, great patroness, accept a small gift.  
> Do not disdain Evodius, your willing client;  
> by making him great, you too will be greater.  
> Thus, for you whose father, father-in-law, and husband are kings,  
> may your son also be king with his father and after his father.  
> Happy are the waters enclosed by the gleam of metal,  
> yet they bathe their mistress’s countenance, brighter still.  
> For when the queen deigns to bathe her face here,  
> brightness passes from her face into the silver.

**[Col. 0512D]**

If you are so devoted to our friendship that you are not ashamed to write these trifles, meet their author, secure as regards your own part. For in such a forum, whether it be the Forum or the Athenaeum, your paper will receive more praise than our writing.

**[Note:]** He alludes to places in Rome where poems and speeches were customarily recited. Lampridius testifies concerning the Athenaeum in his *Life of Alexander*: “He frequently went to the Athenaeum to hear Greek and Latin rhetors and poets.” Capitolinus likewise mentions it in his lives of Pertinax and Gordian; and Sidonius himself, in Book IX, Letter 14, writes to Burgundio: “He was wholly worthy for Rome to cherish him in her applauding arms, and, when he recited, for the wedge-shaped benches of the resounding Athenaeum to shake.” Symmachus also mentions it in Book IX, 84.

Concerning Trajan’s Forum, Fortunatus writes to Bertheramnus, bishop of Le Mans:

> Scarcely now does venerable Rome in Trajan’s  
> brilliant forum hear poems with such polished splendor.

Concerning the Forum of Mars, an old marginal note in an Apuleian manuscript of the Vatican Library says:

> I, Sallustius, read and corrected this successfully at Rome, when Olibrius and Probinus were consuls, declaiming a controversy in the Forum of Mars before the orator Endelechius. I revised it again at Constantinople when Caesarius and Atticus were consuls.

From this passage we also learn when Endelechius the rhetorician held his chair at Rome—that is, as I interpret it, Severus, the holy Endelechius, a Christian orator and poet, whose brief poem on the death of cattle survives. Yet there was another argument from the same period in Paulinus, who mentions Endelechius as his friend in Letter 9 to Severus.

**[Note:]** A silver shell on which Sidonius’s verses were to be engraved.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Industrius.

Recently I visited Vectius, a distinguished man, and examined his daily conduct most closely, as though at leisure. Since I found it worthy of knowing, I judged it not unworthy of reporting.

First, and what by right we shall place before all other praises, he preserves for the master of the house an equal purity of conduct: useful slaves, obedient country slaves, agreeable town slaves, and friends obedient to and content with their patron. His table feeds the guest no less than the client; his hospitality is great, and his sobriety greater.

These are lesser matters: the man of whom I speak is second to none in training, displaying, and transporting horses, dogs, and hawks. There is supreme elegance in his clothing, refinement in every detail, splendor in his harness; his bearing is magnificent and his mind serious. One quality asserts public trust, another private dignity; his relaxation does not corrupt, his correction does not bleed, and his severity is of a temperament that is not grim but austere.

Amid all this, he frequently reads the sacred books, through which, even while eating, he often takes nourishment for his soul. He reads the psalms frequently and sings them still more frequently. In a new manner of life, he fulfills the role of a monk—not beneath a little cloak but beneath a military mantle. He abstains from the flesh of wild animals and is content with running; thus, though religious in secret and delicately so, he uses hunting without really using it.

**[Note:]** The cloak was a distinguishing mark of monks, as of philosophers. The Greek Fathers also called the monastic life and ascetic practice “philosophy.” Hence the bands of cloaked monks at the funeral of Saint Martin in Sulpicius Severus. And just as the Greeks rightly mocked philosophers who philosophized only as far as their cloak and beard, so our people mocked monks who imposed upon the world by their dress, as Sidonius says—men for whom “philosophy was the coarse cloak.” Isidore of Pelusium writes in Letter 22: “Brothers, the display of a coarse cloak and beard is not the fulfillment of ascetic practice.”

He raises an only daughter, a little girl left to him after his wife’s death, with ancestral tenderness, maternal diligence, and paternal kindness, finding in celibacy a consolation. Toward his household he is neither threatening in his speech, nor disdainful in admitting advice, nor relentless in investigating guilt. He governs the condition and circumstances of his subordinates not by domination but by judgment. One would think that he does not own his household but rather administers it.

Having observed the man’s diligence and temperance, I judged that it would be useful for the conduct of others if such a life were made known, even in the briefest outline. All men of our profession would be most usefully encouraged to follow it, apart from the dress by which he meanwhile imposes upon the present age. For—to speak with the indulgence of my order—if only individual virtues are found in individual men, I admire the priestly man more than the priest.

Farewell.

## LETTER X

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Felix.

I break into a greeting, though a late one, my lord, having myself gone many years without greeting you. I did not dare preserve the frequency of our former service after the hardships of exile had driven me from the borders of my native land and broken me. Therefore it is fitting that you too forgive those who are ashamed; for it is appropriate that the humbled pursue humble things and not maintain the same constancy of intimacy with those to whom it might perhaps be improper to offer more love than reverence.

For this reason I have been silent for a long time, and when my son Heliodorus came here, I accepted your silence more patiently than willingly. Yet you used to say, even when it wearied you, that you feared my eloquence.

That excuse, even if it had once been true, had passed away, because, after completing the little book that is scarcely more polished, I am again composing the remaining letters in my customary language, although a more polished style is no better suited to me.

**[Note:]** Below, Letter 22: “When you have brought the care of letters to an end, let us turn it from their books to the style of history.” Both passages show that the first edition of Sidonius’s letters was not the one dedicated to Constantius, but that some small collections of them had been published before the Constantian collection.

**[Note:]** In Latin, certainly, but in the rough and unpolished form then commonly used in Gaul. In earlier times the Gauls had a language peculiar to themselves and different from Latin. Hence Varro, according to Jerome, called the people of Massilia trilingual because they knew Greek, Latin, and Gaulish. Later, continual intercourse with the Romans led them to use Latin, but, as commonly happens with foreign peoples, they used it in a rough and uncultivated form, which therefore required refinement through the study and diligence of teachers. For this reason Sidonius praises Ecdicius in Book III, Letter 3, because, following his example, the Gallic nobility, having shed the scales of Celtic speech, carefully learned Latin in the schools. The same point is intended in Book VIII, Letter 2, to John.

For it is not so important to polish formulas that will never be published. But if you restore your affection to the former course of conversation, we too shall return to the tracks of our old loquacity.

Besides this, with Christ going before us, wherever you may be, we shall eagerly hasten to you, provided that our patron, once returned, grants permission. In this way friendship, which had grown sluggish through infrequent speech, may be strengthened by deeds.

Farewell.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius sends greetings to his dear Petreius.

**[Note:]** To the son of the sister of Mamertus and Claudianus. To him he sends the epitaph of Claudianus, his maternal uncle, who had recently died.

The loss suffered by my age troubles me deeply: your uncle Claudianus has recently been snatched from our eyes, and I doubt whether they will ever afterward see anyone equal to him. He was a provident, prudent, learned, eloquent, energetic man, and the most ingenious of the men of his age, place, and people. He philosophized unceasingly without compromising religion; and although he did not cultivate his hair and beard—

**[Note:]** He likewise joins the club with the cloak among the insignia of philosophers in Book IX, Letter 9, and in poem 15:

> In poem 15, Prudentius commends the grim cloak of the knotty club:

> In the *Hamartigenia*: “Hence poor Wisdom carries the Herculean club,”

And displays his Gymnosophists by neighborhoods.

**[Col. 0515D] 46** From the Greeks, Lucian says in *The Parasite*: “They carry sticks even when going to the bath, and when going to dinner …” Libanius, in Letter 136 to Andronicus: “But let those who do not philosophize say farewell to beard, cloak, and staff.” “The philosophers,” he says, “bid farewell to beard, cloak, and staff.” And, more closely resembling a club, Chrysostom, *On the Statues*, XVII: “Where now are those who have wrapped themselves in cloaks, displaying a thick beard and carrying clubs in their right hands—the philosophers from outside?” [That is:] “Where now are those who wear cloaks, show off a long beard, and carry clubs in their right hands—the foreign philosophers?”

Though he sometimes mocked and even reviled the cloak and club, he was nevertheless separated from the company of the Platonists only by his outward appearance and religious adherence. Good heavens! What was it like whenever we gathered at his house solely for consultation? How readily and without reluctance he immediately opened everything to everyone! He considered it an exquisite pleasure if, perhaps, the labyrinthine insolubility of some question brought the treasures of his learning into the open.

When we had gathered in large numbers, he assigned the duty of listening to everyone, but the right to speak to only one whom we might have selected. He would distribute the resources of his learning individually and in turn, not amid tumult, and not without some carefully contrived, theatrical gesture. Then, whatever he had said, we immediately challenged with the opposing arguments of conflicting syllogisms. But he repelled the rash objections of us all. Thus nothing was accepted unless it had been carefully weighed and tested.

For this reason also he enjoyed the greatest reverence among us: he did not bear too harshly with sluggish compliance in certain matters. This fault was pardonable in his eyes; hence his patience toward us was praiseworthy even without our imitation of it. For who would consult unwillingly about hidden matters a man from whose fellowship in discussion not even the questioning of ordinary, ignorant people was rejected?

So much for his studies. But who could praise the rest of his virtues with an adequate encomium? Always mindful of the human condition, he comforted clerics by his work, ordinary people by his speech, the sorrowful by exhortation, those deprived of support by consolation, captives by paying their ransom, the fasting by food, and the naked by clothing. I consider it superfluous to recount more about these matters. For he preferred, in hope of future recompense, to conceal his merits, by which, having impoverished himself in wealth, he enriched his rich conscience.

He showed the bishop, his elder brother, the most affectionate respect: he loved him as a son while venerating him as a father. And the bishop held him in very high regard, having in him an adviser in judgments, a deputy in the churches, an administrator in business, a steward on the estates, a record-keeper in matters of taxation, a companion in readings, an interpreter in explanations, and a fellow traveler on journeys. Thus each rendered to the other the duties of brotherly loyalty with a mature fidelity, to the point of making their example almost envied.

But why, instead of moderating our grief, do we furnish it with fuel from the very causes of grief? Therefore, as we began to say, for this man we have composed, in the words of that line of Maro, “for ungrateful ashes”—that is, for one who would not return our gratitude—a sad and mournful dirge, with almost painful effort, because disuse had made composition difficult. Yet my naturally most sluggish mind was kindled by grief, heavy with tears. This is the poem about him:

**The glory and grief of his brother Mamertus,**

**The unique spectacle of all admiring bishops,**

**Claudianus gives these limbs beneath this mound.**

**Under whose teaching the threefold library—**

**Roman, Attic, Christian—shone:**

**All of it, as a monk in his flourishing years,**

**He drank in through secret instruction.**

**Orator, dialectician, poet,**

[Col. 0516C] [Note: Earlier he said: “an interpreter in explanations,” which may be referred to the same matter. For *tractatores* were called interpreters and teachers of sacred Scripture. For this reason Sidonius contrasts them with the *authentici* in Book VII, Letter 9; and Claudianus himself, *On the State of the Soul*, Book I, writes: “But I see that the prophets, evangelists, and apostles—the authoritative writers—were followed by many interpreters, who gave the names of their own works to their volumes.” He writes similarly in Book II, where he especially praises Jerome among the interpreters; and Severus, in *Dialogue* 1, calls Origen a most skilled interpreter of sacred Scripture. The word is very common among writers of that age; Vincent of Lérins seems to indicate its origin in the *Commonitory*: “The teachers,” he says, “who are now called interpreters—whom this same Apostle sometimes calls prophets, because through them the mysteries of the prophets are disclosed to the peoples.”]

**Interpreter, geometer, and musician.**

**Skilled at loosening the bonds of questions,**

**And at cutting sects apart with the sword of words,**

**If any assail the Catholic faith.**

**Here a tuner and trainer of the psalms,**

**Before the altars, while his brother rejoiced,**

**He taught the ordered choirs to sound.**

**Here he prepared the annual solemn rites,**

**So that what was read might accord with each season.**

[Col. 0516D] [Note: A bishop in the order and rank of presbyter. He says that Mamertus, his brother the bishop, supported him in so many matters that, although he was only a presbyter, he seemed in a certain sense to be a bishop himself. The first order among the clergy is that of bishops, the second that of presbyters, and the third that of deacons, and so on. Optatus of Milevis, Book I: “Why should I mention the laypeople, who at that time held no position of dignity in the Church? Why mention the many ministers? Why the deacons in the third order? Why the presbyters established in the second priesthood? The bishops themselves, the highest and chief of all,” and so forth. Thus for Sidonius the second order is the order of presbyters. Odo of Canterbury, concerning Saint Wilfrid, when he was made a presbyter:

“At last, bowing his neck beneath the sought yoke,

He is appointed, a celibate, to the honor of the second order.”

[Col. 0517C] Innumerable testimonies of this kind could be produced; but a law of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian will suffice for all. In a very ancient codex it is read in these words:

“THEODOSIUS AND VALENTINIAN, AUGUSTI, TO VERUS, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM.

“We indeed venture to speak, seized by more than our customary fear, concerning the holy and venerable priests, and the second priests, or even the Levites, and to name them with every reverence, before whom the whole earth bows its head.” And later: “As for persons under accusation, if any should walk with a bishop, or with a presbyter, or even with a deacon, whether in the street, in the countryside, or in any place whatsoever, we order that they not be detained or brought in any way, since the Church consists in its priests.” Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III.

From this, I think, everyone can see that presbyters were sometimes called “second priests,” or priests of the second order. By this designation they were distinguished from bishops, who were priests of the first order and were called chief priests.

As for what the very learned Savaron happened to think—that presbyters were formerly also called bishops, and that Sidonius therefore calls Claudianus a bishop here—that notion is utterly foreign, to put it briefly, both to Sidonius’s intention and to ancient usage. Nor can I sufficiently wonder that the empty tale of bishops of the first and second order has gained such credibility in certain minds that they have nothing more frequently in their speech and writings than the claim that, once upon a time, there were supposedly two bishops in each see.

It is a mere fable, as I have said; and to support it they produce nothing that does not collapse of its own accord. Indeed, others have already pointed out that the passage in Gennadius where he seems to call Claudianus a bishop is corrupt. For why would he contradict himself by calling him a bishop here, when he later calls him a presbyter?

As for Justus, who is identified on the sarcophagus seen in the basilica of Saint Illidius as bishop of the city of Clermont, he is not that Justus who was archdeacon of Saint Illidius, the bishop; rather, he is another Justus, who was in fact bishop of Clermont after Avolus and before Caesarius. His name should not be sought in Gregory of Tours’ list of bishops, because he lived after Gregory.

Finally, concerning John, archdeacon of Chalon, there is a similar error, as Letter 25 will reveal.]

**A bishop in the second order,**

[Col. 0517A] **104 lifting his brother’s episcopal burden.**

**For from the dignity of the supreme pontiff**

**He took the insignia; this one, the labor.**

**But whoever you are, grieving reader,**

**Who thinks that almost nothing remains of so great a man,**

**Spare your wet cheeks from watering the marble;**

**Mind and glory cannot be buried.**

Behold the poem that, when I first arrived, I wrote over the bones of my beloved brother. For I had been absent when he was buried; yet because of this I did not entirely lose the most desired opportunity for weeping. While I happened to be meditating, I loosened the reins as my soul gave birth to tears, and composed for the epitaph what others had composed for the tomb.

We have therefore written this to you, lest you suppose that we cultivate only fellowship with the living, and lest we seem, in your judgment, to be unworthy unless we always remember friends who have died just as we remember those who are safe and well. For from the fact that even among the living an image of loyalty is scarcely preserved, you will not unreasonably conclude that very few people love the dead. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XII

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Simplicius and Apollinaris.

Good heavens! How closely the movement of human emotions resembles a storm-tossed sea, especially when it is thrown into confusion by the adverse whirlwinds of news as though by a storm of its own. Recently my son and I were savoring the wit of Terence’s *Hecyra*. I sat beside him as he studied, remembering nature and forgetting my profession. And, so that he might follow the comic rhythms with more complete and eager receptiveness, I myself also had in my hands Menander’s *Epitrepontes*, a play with a similar subject.

[Col. 0518C] [Note: Stobaeus, in Discourse 87, cites Menander’s *Epitrepontes* and produces these lines from it:

Ἐλευθέρῳ τὸ καταγελᾶσθαι πολὺ  
Αἴσχιον ἐστι, τὸ δ᾽ ὀδυνᾶσθ᾽ ἀνθρώπινον.

“For a free man, being mocked is greatly more shameful; but suffering is human.”

In other passages he likewise uses the forms *epitrepontas* and *epitropoi*. Alciphron also counts *Epitrepontes* among Menander’s plays in his final letter, as does Athenaeus in Book XIV. Quintilian mentions it without naming the author, teaching that the *Epitrepontes* contains a complete conception of rhetorical judgment, Book X, chapter 1.]

We read together, praised it, and joked; and, as commonly happens, the reading captivated him, while he captivated me. Suddenly a household servant appeared with a troubled expression. We asked him what was wrong, and he said: “I saw the reader Constans returning from the homes of Lords Simplicius and Apollinaris at the door. He gave me letters that he had received, but he lost the letters he had been given.”

When I learned this, the serenity of my joy was immediately darkened by a cloud of grief, and the contradiction in this message stirred such bile in me that for many days I inexorably forbade that utter blockhead from appearing before my eyes. I would have been very angry if he did not return to me every scrap of writing, whoever had written it and whoever had sent it. I say nothing of your letters, which, while my mind remains sound, I shall judge all the more desirable because they are so infrequent.

But after the anger that had gradually raged within me had subsided with the passage of time, I asked whether he had brought anything else verbally. Although he was fearful and trembling, stammering from guilt and looking about him with bewilderment, he replied that everything by which I could be informed and delighted had been committed to the pages that had been lost.

Therefore return to your writing tablets, take up your parchments again, and rewrite what you wrote. For I shall patiently accept an outcome adverse to my desire only until our message reaches you, while your message has not reached us. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Vectius.

[Col. 0518D] [Note: To an illustrious man mentioned above in Letter 9. He calls it the church of Cantilla, from an ancient fortress of the Clermont region, mentioned in the Peutinger Map. The *Annals of Pippin’s Deeds*, under the year 762, say: “Having entered Aquitaine, he took certain towns and fortresses by force; among the chief were Bourbon, Cantilla, and Clermont.”]

Recently, at the request of the distinguished Germanicus, I inspected the church of Cantilla. He himself is easily first among those settled in that place; and although, having left twelve lustres behind him—

[Col. 0519D] [Note: Sixty years, as in Juvenal, whom he imitates in Satire 8:

“He marvels at this, who has already left

Sixty years behind him, born under the consul Fonteius.”]

—he does not merely fail to grow younger each day in his conspicuous dress and grooming, but in a certain sense grows young again.

Indeed, his garment is tightly fitted, his boot taut, his hair cut in the shape of a wheel, his beard trimmed close to the skin with scissors and buried amid the hiding places of his wrinkles. In addition, by heaven’s gift, his limbs are firmly joined, his sight is unimpaired, his stride broad and vigorous in rapid movement, and his teeth form an unbroken, milk-white structure within healthy gums.

[Col. 0519D] [Note: Both were among the refinements of ancient grooming; Leviticus XIX provides: “You shall not cut the hair of your head into a circle, nor mar the appearance of your beard.” This is, as Jerome explains: “Do not round-cut your hair, nor shave your beard,” as Hesychius says in Book VI on Leviticus, those accustomed to cultivate luxuriant hair and beard do.]

His stomach is not troubled by nausea, his veins are not inflamed, his heart is not shaken, his lungs do not sigh, his loins are not stiff, his liver is not swollen, his hands do not grow weak, and his spine does not bend. Endowed with youthful health, he claims for himself only the reverence due to old age.

Because of these special gifts of God, and because the claims of friendship between us are strong—for we are neighbors—I beg and urge you that he not place too much confidence in uncertain things in reliance on your counsel, to which he grants the very highest authority with a great conscience, nor trust excessively in excessive good health. Rather, once he has embraced the profession of religion, let him grow strong in the powers of a restored innocence, and make himself, though old in years, new in merits.

And since scarcely anyone is without hidden offenses deserving punishment, let him be released from those matters that he remembers having secretly committed by openly poured-out satisfaction. For the father of a priest, and the son of a bishop, unless he is holy, becomes like a thornbush: though born from roses, producing roses, and standing amid flowers born and giving birth, he is enclosed by the roughness of brambles that must be compared with his piercing sins. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XIV

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Polemius.

[Col. 0519D] [Note: Prefect of the Gauls, for whom he had also composed the wedding song for his bride Araneola in Poem 15. In that poem and in the dedicatory letter he says much about Polemius’s learning and devotion to philosophy.]

C. Tacitus, one of your ancestors, a consul during the time of the Ulpiani, reported in his history, under the words of a certain Germanic commander, saying:

[Col. 0519D] [Note: These are the words of Claudius Civilis, leader of the Batavians, in Tacitus, Book V of the *Histories*, though Tacitus phrases them somewhat differently: “Toward Vespasian,” he says, “I have an old respect, and when he was a private citizen we were called friends.”]

“I have an old friendship with Vespasian, and while he was a private citizen we were called friends.”

“To what,” you say, “does this preface refer?” Clearly, so that you may remember that, at the time when you bear a public office, you must always remember private favor.

Nearly two years have passed during which we have enjoyed your being prefect of the Gauls—not because of any new favor of yours, but because of our still-standing former affection. If the adversity of Roman affairs allowed it, we would find it hard to endure unless individual persons—I do not say provinces—were enlarged by various benefits through you.

And now, when what your ability does not possess is not sought from your modesty, I should like you to say how you will be humane in deeds when you remain miserly in words. Compared with your knowledge, you can surpass not only the orators of the Cornelian family but also the Ausonian poets.

If a new glory has suddenly seized you, now that you have been philosophizing until this point, because of your jurisdiction—

[Col. 0520D] [Note: For he had been prefect of the city; and that dignity, together with the office of master of the soldiers, possessed a prerogative comparable to that of the praetorian prefecture, Book I of the Theodosian Code, concerning the prefects of the praetorium or the city and the masters of the soldiers.]

—then we too have borne some name and distinction.

But if the humility of our profession is to be despised because, so that Christ may heal human affairs and lives, we open with the knife the foul ulcer of corrupt consciences—and although in men of our order something may still stink of negligence, nothing now swells with pride—then I want you to know that matters are not the same before the judge of the world as before the presiding judge of the court.

For just as the person who has not concealed his own crimes from you is condemned, so among us the person who has confessed those same crimes to God is absolved. Hence it is perfectly clear that it is improper for you to pronounce too great a guilt from your side when the case belongs more properly to another tribunal.

Therefore you will no longer be able to pour out the complaint that threatens from our grief; for when prosperity follows, whether you forget or neglect your old friendship, the result is equally bitter.

Accordingly, if you value the future highly, write to a cleric; if the present, write to a colleague. Cultivate this virtue in yourself: if it is natural, develop it; if not, graft it onto yourself—that you may never grow weary of old companions because of the novelty of what follows.

Moreover, you will appear to use friends like flowers, finding them pleasing only so long as they are fresh. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XV

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Elaphius.

Prepare a lavish feast and couches of the greatest capacity; people are coming to you by many roads and in numerous crowds. Thus the company of good men has settled the matter, since the date of the future dedication has become known to everyone.

For you write that the baptistery which you formerly built can now be consecrated. These festivities summon you because of your vow, us because of our ministry, many because of their duty, and all because of their faith. It is indeed a great example that, at a time when scarcely anyone else would dare repair old churches, you are raising new roofs for churches.

For the rest, we hope that, just as you fulfill your vows to our God for many fruitful years, so you may vow to fulfill them again. And may this be done not only through hidden religion but also through open conversion. With the condition of the times made more favorable, may Christ indulge my desire as well as that of the people of Rodez, so that you may offer sacrifices for those for whom you are now offering altars.

Besides, although late autumn is already shortening the day, and the anxious ears of travelers are surrounded by the crackling sound of leaves falling throughout the forest, and although the fortress to which you invite us—encircled, as it is, by Alpine crags—is more difficult to climb with winter approaching, nevertheless, with God going before us, we shall come along the rugged sides of your mountains without fearing either the cliffs below or the snows above.

Although the deep descent of the ridges, broken by a winding path, often has to be retraced, you are nevertheless sufficiently worthy, even if there were no solemn occasion, that, as in Tully’s phrase, Thespiae be visited on your account.

[Col. 0521D] [Note: In *Against Verres*, Book IV: “Praxiteles made the Cupid—the one who is at Thespiae—for whose sake Thespiae are visited. There is no other reason for seeing it.” Strabo likewise relates in Book IX: “Thespiae were formerly known because of the Eros of Praxiteles, which he sculpted there and which the courtesan dedicated to the Thespians. Formerly, therefore, some people climbed up to see the Eros, since otherwise the place was not worth seeing.”]

Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XVI

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Ruricius.

[Col. 0521D] [Note: He also composed the wedding song of Ruricius’s wife Iberia in Poem 11. Ruricius later became bishop of Limoges. He is the man whose two books of letters were published a few years ago from the library of Saint Gall; some were written while he was bishop, others before his episcopate. Among them are several addressed to Sidonius, including the eighth, to which Sidonius replies here. He also writes to him elsewhere in Books V and VIII, before Ruricius became bishop.]

I received your page through Paterninus, and it is uncertain whether it contains more honey or salt. In any case, it displays such abundance of eloquence and exhales such flowers that it is clear you are progressing not only through open reading but also through stolen reading.

Although this theft, which you apologize for, of a copied booklet deserves not so much forgiveness as praise. For what can you do without virtue, when you commit even your sins without forfeiting praise?

As for whatever fraud has been imposed on me, absent as I am, I willingly hear of it and embrace it as a principal gift, since I have in a certain manner suffered a loss without loss. For what has been added to your use has not been subtracted from my property, nor have you advanced in knowledge through damage to another’s possessions.

Indeed, from now on you will rightly not lack a more abundant commendation, since with your fiery intelligence you have fittingly imitated the nature of fire: if one wishes to take something away from fire, the whole of it remains in what is transferred.

Therefore cease trembling, and be rather less ready to believe ill of a friend’s character. For in this action the fault soils us more if the blow strikes with envy. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XVII

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Arbogastes.

[Col. 0521D] [Note: From Sidonius’s words we learn that Arbogastes practiced writing amid arms, was a Belgian by birth, and lived by the Moselle, not far from Auspicius, bishop of Toul among the Leuci. A letter of Auspicius to Arbogastes was recently published and confirms all this. It teaches that Arbogastes was the son of Arigius, count of Trier, descended from the other Arbogastes, a Frank who was count under the younger Valentinian. I therefore interpret the barbarians among whom he lived as Franks, who already at that time dominated Belgica Prima; the bishop of the city as the bishop of Trier; and Lupus as the bishop of Troyes, to whom Sidonius writes more than once.]

Your friend Eminentius, my lord and superior, brought me a learned letter that you yourself composed, filled with the adornment of a threefold, smiling grace. Of these virtues, affection is certainly first: it compelled you to show esteem toward us, though strangers or already wishing to remain hidden. Next comes modesty, through whose impulse you are praised even while trembling without cause. Third is urbanity, by which you most wittily claim to be foolish; filled with the eloquence of the Quirinal spring, you, a drinker of the Moselle, belch forth the Tiber.

Thus, familiar with barbarians yet ignorant of barbarisms, you are the equal of the ancient commanders in tongue and hand—of those whose right hands were accustomed to wield the stylus no less than the sword.

Accordingly, whatever grandeur of Roman speech still exists anywhere, though it has been extinguished in the Belgian or Rhineland lands, has taken refuge in you. While you remain unharmed or plead your case, even if Latin law has fallen at the very frontier, words do not falter.

Returning your greeting in turn, I rejoice greatly that at least in your noble breast some traces remain of writings that are fading away. If you continue them through frequent reading, you will experience day by day that, to the extent that human beings surpass beasts, the educated surpass the uncultivated.

As for the pages that you wish me, an incompetent interpreter, to babble about in spiritual matters, such questions would more properly be asked of priests nearby in place, advanced in age, renowned in faith, widely known for their deeds, ready in speech, tenacious in memory, and in every respect superior through every excellence of elevated merit.

To leave aside the bishop of your city, a consummate man, blessed alike in the consciousness and reputation of all virtues, it would be far more appropriate for you to consult the illustrious fathers and chief initiates of the Gauls concerning any questions: Lupus, who is not so far away, and Auspicius, who is not so near. Your consultation is not enough to exhaust the abundance of their learning.

Therefore, because I did not comply with this part of your request, kindly—but also justly—forgive me. For if it is fitting that you avoid ignorance, it is also fitting that I avoid boasting. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XVIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Lucontius.

You forget what you are asked, but conversely, if you impose something, you remember to repeat it in full. It would take too long to recount what you and your people promised me and mine about your speedy return, none of which has been fulfilled, even in the smallest degree.

Indeed, when you were plotting your flight from us, so that we thought you would return to us for the holy Easter, no heavy baggage was transported from the town to the estate, no wagon and no cart were brought up for carrying loads.

And, not to complain about the deception of the women’s party, whom you took with their luggage already prepared, you and your brother, our common friend Volusianus—

[Col. 0522D] [Note: Sidonius’s brother, to whom he writes in Book VIII, Letter 17.]

—were surrounded by scarcely more than the retinues of individual clients and boys. Through this you deceived the concern of those who accompanied you by the vain hope of your soon returning.

Certainly your brother Volusianus, who perhaps was traveling to the estates at Bayeux and intended to traverse the entire province of Lugdunensis Secunda—

[Col. 0522D] [Note: In Sidonius’s age there were four provinces of Lugdunensis, and all four are likewise described in the *Notitia Dignitatum*, retaining their ancient metropolitan cities to our own time. The capital of the first was Lyon, discussed in Book V, Letter 7. That of the second was Rouen, and the city of the Baiocasses belonged to it here. The third had Tours as its capital, which is named in the letter of Leo of Bourges and of other bishops, “That Clerics Should Not Seek Secular Judgments,” addressed to the bishops of the Third Province. Thus it should be read there in accordance with the ancient copies, not “Thrace,” as it is commonly read among the letters of Pope Leo, into which it was inserted rather carelessly, since it is not his. The metropolis of the fourth was Sens, from which it is called Senonia in Book VII, Letter 5, and in the *Notitia* concerning the Armorican district. Originally, when the provinces of Lugdunensis began to be divided, there were only two; later, I infer, they became four under Theodosius. Rufius Festus counts only two, as does Ammianus Marcellinus, who places Tours in Lugdunensis Secunda and Sens in Prima. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the Third was formed from the Second and the Fourth from the First.]

—eluded our expectation by the appearance of a shorter journey.

And now you yourself, idling for so many days contrary to your promise, say that if I later compose any metrical trifles, they ought to be sent to you. I agree to what you command, because you are worthy to read such things. For the poem that is now slipping from my hands is so rustic and unpolished that you will think I am sending it not to the country but rather from the country.

[Col. 0523D] [Note: Gregory of Tours discusses this basilica of Saint Martin, which Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, built after removing the former small one erected by Briccius, in Book II, chapter 14, and in Book X in his list of bishops. At Perpetuus’s request, various epigrams by different poets were inscribed on its walls. Once collected, they are still found appended to the end of the *Life of Saint Martin* in many manuscripts of Sulpicius Severus. Among them is this epigram of Sidonius, which they record as engraved in the most distinguished part of the basilica, namely its apse, into which Saint Martin’s body had been transferred; then another by Paulinus of Périgueux, above the basilica door on the side of the Loire, consisting of twenty-five verses, beginning:

“Whoever, bending to the ground, has plunged his face in the dust,”

and those that follow. They were published at the end of the six books on the *Life of Martin*, but without a title; Paulinus himself also writes of them in his letter to Perpetuus. There are besides in the same place little verses by Martin of Dumium, namely those which, as Gregory relates in Book V, chapter 37, were later added above the door on the southern side.]

The basilica of the holy bishop and confessor Martin, Perpetuus the bishop—most worthy successor to so great a predecessor—has been rebuilt much larger than the former structure, which had stood until then. It is, they say, a great work, worthy of mention; and because it was made in honor of such a man, it was fitting that such a man should have made it.

The priest mentioned above compels me to inscribe this epigram on its walls; you will read it, since in all matters he is most imperiously demanding whatever the privilege of affection permits. And would that the offering of this service did not in some way disfigure the splendor of that massive building or its gifts! I fear very much that it will do so.

Unless, perhaps, amid all its beauty, the ugliness of this epigram will please like a black blemish on a shining body—a blemish that is accustomed to provoke laughter rather than receive approval. But what more need be said? Lay aside your pastoral pipes, and extend your hand to my elegy, since it limps in its meter.

**114**

**The body of Martin, venerable throughout all the lands,**

**In whom honor lives on after the end of life,**

**This structure once covered with common and humble workmanship,**

**Which was not worthy of the confessor it served.**

**Nor did the great glory of the man cease**

**To burden the citizens with shame because of the site’s smallness.**

**But the bishop who is reckoned**

[Col. 0524C] [Note: Perpetuus is called the sixth after Martin because, I suppose, he counts Justinianus and Armentius, who held Martin’s see after Briccius was expelled; Gregory omits them from his list of bishops and therefore makes Perpetuus the fourth after Martin there. But in Book II he follows another reckoning and makes him the fifth.]

**as the sixth after Martin himself,**

**Perpetuus removed the long-standing reproach:**

**Removing the inner recess of the modest shrine,**

**And raising spacious roofs in the outer building.**

**Together they grew—through the bounty of a powerful patron—**

**The building in dimensions, the founder in merits:**

[Col. 0524C] [Note: Those who replace ancient buildings with new ones often assign this reason, as can be seen in Christian monuments erected over ancient inscriptions. At Nola, in the suburban church of Saint Felix founded by Bishop Paulinus, verses still remain that most people judge to be by Paulinus himself, composed when he rebuilt the basilica, as in *Natale* X:

“Previously the place was small, too narrow for sacred rites,

And unable to open its hands to those who prayed.

Now it offers spacious altars for the sacred rites of the people,

In the embrace of the martyr at its center.

Everything renewed for God is pleasing; Christ always renews all things,

And enlarges them, adding to the accumulation of light.

Thus, honoring the throne of beloved Felix,

He increased it alike in splendor and in space.”]

**What can contend with Solomon’s temple,**

**The seventh wondrous structure in the world?**

**For if that one shone with gems, gold, and silver,**

**This one surpasses all metals through faith.**

**Away, biting envy, and let earlier generations be acquitted;**

**Let chattering posterity neither change nor add anything.**

**And until Christ comes to rouse all peoples,**

**May the roofs of Perpetuus endure perpetually.**

As you see, we have offered what came most readily to hand from a recent song. But if you delay, we shall shake the stars no less, employing satirical verses as well if circumstances demand—verses that you will falsely think can be matched in gentleness with this poem. For human nature censures something more effectively, quickly, and ardently than it praises it. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XIX

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Florentinus.

You accuse both our delays and our silence. Both can be cleared: for we have come and we are writing. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XX

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Domitius.

You, who often take pleasure in looking at arms, armed men, and armed forces—what pleasure do you suppose you would have conceived in your mind if you had seen the royal young man Sigismer, adorned according to the dress and customs of his people, as a bridegroom or suitor, approaching the praetorium of his father-in-law?

[Col. 0524D] [Note: It has not been sufficiently determined whether he was a Goth, Frank, or Burgundian. It is certain that this Sigismer, contrary to the opinion of a learned man, is different from Sigismer, the count of King Athalaric of Italy, mentioned by Senator in Book VIII, Letter 2. The places and times differ, and there is nothing to suggest that the latter count was of royal blood.]

Horses equipped with trappings, indeed horses loaded with shining gems, went before him and also followed him. Yet what appeared more dignified there was that he himself, in the middle, walked on foot alongside his forerunners or attendants: flaming with scarlet, gleaming with gold, white as milk in silk, and matching in hair, complexion, and skin the richness of his attire.

The appearance of the princes and their companions was formidable even in peacetime. Their foremost men had their feet bound up to the ankles in shaggy boots, while their knees, legs, and shins were uncovered. In addition, they wore high, tight-fitting, multicolored garments that scarcely reached their exposed knees; their sleeves covered only the beginnings of their arms. Their green cloaks were edged with purple borders.

Their sides, enclosed in studded fur-cloaks, were girded with swords hanging from the shoulder, their belts crossing over them. They were armed with the same adornment with which they were arrayed: their right hands were filled with hooked spears and throwing axes, while shields shaded their left sides. The light on their rims was snowy, the light on their bosses tawny, and these features displayed their wealth as much as their taste.

Everything was precisely such that in a marriage ceremony the pomp of Mars did not appear inferior to that of Venus. But why say more? Your presence alone was missing from such a spectacle. For as I watched what is beautiful to you without seeing you there, I longed for the very impatience of your desire at that moment. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XXI

Sidonius sends greetings to his own Aper.

There is certainly a primacy in displaying one’s lineage that belongs to the prerogative of the father’s side. Nevertheless, we owe much to our mothers as well. For it is not right for us to honor something less highly because we are the weight of their bodies than because we are the seed of those men.

But let the natural philosophers determine the matter and method by which our origin is to be defined. We shall pursue the subject from which we began these remarks.

[Col. 0525C] [Note: The Aedui and Arverni were connected both by the proximity of their territories and by many private and public treaties. An ancient marble altar bears witness to this; it was once set up by Suavis the Aeduan to the Genius of the Arverni and remains in the suburban Mausiacene monastery of our Ricomagus, with these words:]

**TO THE GENIUS OF THE ARVERNI,**

**SEXTUS ORCIUS SUAVIS, AN AEDUAN.**
] Your father is a Haeduan, your mother an Arvernian. You owe your first allegiance to the Haeduans; therefore you are not owed to them alone—or, because of that example from our Maro, in which Pallas is so described as an Arcadian, an example that could likewise have moved the Samnite against Mezentius, had he not, as a foreigner, derived a portion of his homeland also from his Sabine mother. [Col. 0525C] Behold a great proof from the greatest authority: the maternal homeland and region must also be counted as part of one’s fatherland—unless you think that poets, even when they do not depart from history, are lying.

Thus, if the Arverni in turn claim some portion of you by right, at least patiently receive the complaint of those who long for you. Through the service of my single voice, they have poured forth the secret of no single heart. Imagine them saying openly and face-to-face:

“What such harm, ungrateful man, have we committed against you, that for so many years you flee what was once your nurturing soil as though it were enemy territory? Here we sheltered your cradle; [Col. 0526A] here we formed the nursing limbs of your crying infancy; here you were carried in the arms of your fellow citizens. Here your grandfather Fronto was gentle toward you and stern toward himself—a man who could have served as an example to those whom we have as examples among us. Here was your grandmother Auspicia, who, after your mother’s death, alone undertook the care of two.

“Here also was your maternal aunt; and from here too came Frontina, holier than the holy virgins, whom her mother revered and her father venerated—a girl of the strictest abstinence, the greatest rigor, and immense fidelity. She feared God so greatly that she was feared by human beings.

“Here grammarians and rhetoricians, whose flourishing studies competed in instruction, cherished you as you were imbued with the liberal disciplines. From this education you did not emerge so poorly trained that you may permit yourself not to love the Arverni, even on account of literature.

“[Note: [Col. 0525D] Here one may see the same thing, although I would not readily assert it, in the case of Fronto the count, who served as envoy to the Suebi in Spain on two occasions, first under Valentinian and then under Avitus. Our Idatius mentions both of them: the former under the eleventh year of Marcian, the latter three years afterward, in these words: ‘Through the emperor Avitus, Count Fronto is sent as envoy to the Suebi, and likewise by Theuderic, king of the Goths, because he was loyal to the Roman Empire; so that, since they were joined by one treaty of peace, they might observe the promised terms of the treaty.’]

“I say nothing of the distinctive charm of the territory. [Note: [Col. 0525D] The fertility of our Lower Arvernia, which is called Lemane by its particular name, is adorned by him in many [Col. 0526C] verses of his panegyric to Avitus. The pleasantness of the Lemanean countryside vies with its fertility. The fame of its pleasantness is attested by the words of King Childebert, which [Col. 0526D] Gregory recounts, and by Gregory himself, the Arvernian, in Book III, chapter 9: ‘The king,’ he says, ‘was accustomed to say, “Would that I might one day behold the Arvernian Lemane, which is said to shine with such great delightfulness.”’]

[Col. 0526B] “I say nothing of that level expanse of fields, in which profitable waves roll harmlessly through the crops: the more diligently a person frequents it, the less he is shipwrecked. It is gentle for travelers, fruitful for farmers, delightful for hunters. Mountain ridges surround it with pastures, slopes with vineyards, lowlands with estates, rocky ground with castles, shaded places with groves, open places with cultivated fields, hollows with springs, and precipices with rivers. In short, it is of such a kind that, once seen by a newcomer, it often persuades him to forget his homeland.

“I say nothing of the city itself, always so devoted to you that you ought to prefer nothing to the company of its nobles. You were happily seized and incorporated into it when it laid hands upon you; and thus everyone enjoyed your presence, though no one was ever sated by it.

“What, then, should I say about your property here [Col. 0526C]? Its condition is such that it will more easily bear your expenses because they occur more frequently. For when the farmer-owner tends his household here, he spends in such a way that he also increases his income.”

I alone, or at least in the desire, request, and place of all good citizens, chatter this to you. Since they seek you with such honor and long for you with such love, it is clear that, when you grant what they ask, you will obtain more joy than they will.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Leo.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Leo was counselor to Euric, king of the Goths, and, as it were, his quaestor; this is what Sidonius’s references to him in Book VIII, Letter 3, signify. Sidonius repeatedly praises his eloquence, poetic studies, and exceptional knowledge of civil law. Ennodius likewise mentions him in the *Life of Epiphanius*, speaking of his embassy to Euric: ‘At that time,’ he says, ‘there was a man named Leo, both counselor and director of the prince’s deliberations, and arbiter; through the merit of his eloquence he had already won more than one prize in declamation. He announced the bishop’s arrival to the public with the greatest joy.’ Leo also survived Euric and held the same office at the court of his son Alaric; Gregory calls him Alaric’s counselor as well in Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 92.]

The distinguished Hesperius, a jewel among friends and men of letters, recently returned to the city from Toulouse and told me to direct the care of my letters—now that their books have been completed [Col. 0527A]—toward the style of history. I embrace such a judgment with the utmost reverence and affection: you declare a man suited to greater works when you think he ought to abandon lesser ones. Yet, to confess the truth, I more readily dare to admire such an opinion than to undertake its counsel.

The project is indeed worthy of your command, but no less worthy of your execution. In ancient times, when Gaius Cornelius had urged Gaius Secundus to undertake something comparable, he himself afterward took up what he had imposed. You now approach the task more advantageously by his example: I rise as a pupil before Pliny, while you surpass Cornelius by the ancient right of narrative. If he were to return to life in our age and see how learned and eminent you are in letters, he would be a truer Tacitus.

[Col. 0527B] Thus you rightly undertake the burden of the subject proposed to you, since, beyond your singular eloquence, you have an excellent opportunity for immense knowledge. Each day, through the counsels of the most powerful king, who is concerned with the whole world, you learn alike his affairs and laws, treaties and wars, places, distances, and merits. Who, then, could more justly prepare himself for this task than one known to have learned the movements of peoples, the variety of embassies, the deeds of commanders, the agreements of rulers, and, finally, all the secrets of public affairs? And, placed at such an eminent height, he has no need either to suppress the truth or to embellish falsehood.

Our condition, however, is far different. For us, a new journey brings grief, and old reading brings no practical benefit. Moreover, our profession is regarded as religious, our ambition as humility, and our modesty as obscurity; nor is as much placed in present [Col. 0527C] reality as in future hope.

Finally, weakness is an impediment, and by now, even if late, indolence has become our heart’s companion because of that very weakness. Certainly, concerning our studies, no praise is now owed to our care—not even posthumous praise. We have firmly resolved to seek little glory from history, because among men of clerical office our own affairs are rashly discussed, those of others boastfully, the past fruitlessly, the present incompletely, falsehood shamefully, and truth dangerously.

This is the nature of the subject—or of the work—in which mention of good men earns little gratitude, while mention of notable men earns the greatest offense. At once the color and odor of satire become mixed into the diction. Historical writing therefore seems wholly alien to our way of life: its beginning is envy, its continuation labor, and its end hatred.

But [Col. 0527D] such things arise when anything is composed by clerics, who are fixed in the serpent-like molars of their detractors. If we publish anything simply, we are called mad; if precisely, presumptuous. But if you yourself—who have been granted the power to trample or outrun the necks of those who disparage you—willingly take up this province of writing, no one will write more loftily than you, no one more anciently, even if you choose to speak of recent matters.
