Since you were already filled with an abundance of words and now [Col. 0528A] with an abundance of words and now with an abundance of affairs, you have left no reason for anyone to cut you with a poisonous bite.

For this reason, in the future, usefulness will consult you, pleasure will listen to you, and authority will read you.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Proculus.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] This letter has the same subject as Pliny’s Letter 22 in Book III, except that Pliny pleads with Sabinianus on behalf of a freedman, whereas Sidonius pleads with a father on behalf of his son.]

Your son—indeed, our common son—ran to me. Having left you, he grieves that he has committed an offense, overwhelmed by the shame of his flight and repentance. After hearing the extent of his fault, I rebuked him, as he hid away, with bitter words and a threatening expression, speaking in my own voice but acting in your place. I declared him deserving of disinheritance, the cross, the sack, and the other punishments appropriate to a parricide.

At this he was confounded and blushed. He did not plead his error with shameless excuses; but when I refuted him on every point, he joined tears [Col. 0528B] to his modesty. They flowed so freely and abundantly that they gave credibility to the correction that would follow.

I therefore ask you to be merciful toward one who is severe toward himself. Following the Lord’s example, do not, as his judge, condemn one who confesses himself guilty and deserving punishment. If, without pity, you order him to undergo unheard-of punishments, he cannot be tormented by you more than he is already tortured by shame.

Free his despair from fear; free my confidence; and, by the necessity of paternal affection—if I interpret the matter correctly—free yourself as well. You are being consumed inwardly by what your son is consumed by in public grief. It is certain that I have done him a great injury, unless you do at least a little. Yet I hope you will not do so, unless you are harder than rocks or more rigid than uncut diamonds.

Therefore, if I rightly presume better things about your character and friendships, [Col. 0528C] graciously pardon the accused. I confidently promise that, once reconciled, he will remain faithful thereafter. When you swiftly release him from his fault, I shall be bound to you by your kindness. I earnestly ask not merely that you forgive him, but that you admit him at once—when he returns—not only into your house but also into your heart.

Great God! How joyful a day will arise for you, a joyful message for me, and a joyful spirit for him, when, falling at his father’s feet and expecting a reproach from that wounded and terrifying mouth, he receives a kiss.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Turnus.

That line of the Mantuan poet fits your name and your situation well:

> Turnus, what no one would dare promise  
> [Col. 0528D] The god who grants wishes, rolling time has brought freely.

Your father Turpio, a man of tribunician rank, formerly requested and obtained a loan from Maximus Palatinus, if you remember. He set aside and pledged neither silver as security nor estates as collateral. But, as the written acknowledgment shows, the lender was protected by interest at the *centesima*—one percent per month, or twelve percent annually. Over a period of two lustrums, this brought the principal to twice its amount.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] I think he belonged to the class of men who served in sacred or private largesses and were accustomed to be sent into the provinces by the counts; see Book I of the Theodosian Code, *On the Palatines of the Sacred Largesses and of Private Affairs*.]

[Note: [Col. 0528D] The *centesima* produces twelve coins each year on every hundred. Thus, if one hundred gold pieces were given to Turpio by Maximus under this arrangement, interest accumulated for ten years, together with the principal, would amount to two hundred and twenty: a sum that not only equals twice the principal but exceeds it. Sidonius, however, as learned men have observed, did [Col. 0529C] not reckon the amount exceeding twice the principal, because he knew that ordinary interest above twice the principal could neither be owed nor exacted; see Digest 12.6.26, *On What Was Paid Without Being Owed*, and Digest 22.2.4, *On Maritime Loans*. Plutarch mentions this law, though as a private law imposed on the Asians by Lucullus: ‘He cut off,’ he says, ‘the longer-lasting interest beyond the ancient rate’ (*Τοὺς μακροτέρους, inquit, τοῦ ἀρχαίου τόκους ἀπέκοψεν*). Diodorus also mentions a law formerly issued to the Egyptians by Bocchoris: ‘He forbade those who lent under a written contract to make more than twice the principal through interest’ (*Τοῦ μετὰ ξυγγραφῆς δανείσαντας ἐκώλυε διὰ τοῦ τόκου πλεῖον ποιεῖν ἢ διπλάσιον*).]

[Col. 0529A] Your father, however, fell ill with a disease that brought him near death. For this reason the public authority pressed the unwell head of the household more violently to settle the debt, and the violence of the executors could no longer be endured. As I was setting out for Toulouse, your father—already despairing—ordered me by letter to ask your creditor to grant at least a brief postponement.

I promptly complied with the petitioner’s request, since I possessed with Maximus not merely the old rights of acquaintance but also those of hospitality. I therefore went willingly to my friend while still on the journey, although his estate lay many miles from the public road.

[Col. 0529B] When I arrived, he himself came to meet me. I had previously known him as upright in body, quick in step, free in speech, and generous in appearance; now he was greatly changed from his former bearing. His dress, gait, modesty, complexion, and speech were religious. His hair was short, his beard long; three-legged stools stood about, curtains of sackcloth hung at the doors, the bed had no feathers and the table no purple. His very hospitality was so kind because it was frugal; he was not so rich in meat as in vegetables. If there was anything especially rich in the food, he indulged not himself but his guests.

When we rose, I secretly asked those standing by which of the three modes of life he had adopted: whether he was living as a monk, a cleric, or a penitent. They said that he had recently entered upon the priesthood, to which civic affection had forcibly bound him against his will.

[Note: [Col. 0529C] In these words one may observe the ancient custom of the Gallican clergy and of the whole Western Church: those who had girded themselves for sacred service [Col. 0529D] immediately cut their flowing hair short. Prudentius says of Saint Cyprian:

> The flowing hair is restrained into short locks.

Traces of this custom remain in the sacred rite by which clerics are made. The bishop, when admitting men, clips their locks here and there; this is called the first tonsure, and those clerics were formerly tonsured at that stage. In earlier times they were genuinely shorn, and afterward it was not permitted them to grow their hair long. The Synod of Agde, canon 15, says: ‘Clerics who grow their hair shall be shorn by the archdeacon, even against their will.’ Hence canon 44 of the Fourth Council of Carthage: ‘Let a cleric neither grow his hair nor shave his beard,’ or, as other ancient books read, ‘nor cut it.’ They therefore grew their beards, as the Greeks do today and as many Latins also do. I therefore cannot understand what Gregory VII writes to the judge of Cagliari in Book IX, Letter 10: ‘[Col. 0530C] From the very beginnings of the Church of Christ, the clergy of the whole Western Church have maintained the custom of shaving the beard.’ Later, most Latins did shave their beards. The difference between Greek and Latin clergy is accurately discussed by the Synod of Limoges, which says that it does not injure our religion. In its record for the second day, the canons of the Synod of Bourges are recited; the seventh orders all clerics to have the ecclesiastical tonsure—that is, a shaved beard and a crown on the head. So various have the changes of time been in this respect as well.]

When daylight had returned and the boys and retainers were occupied in catching animals, I asked for an opportunity for a private conversation. He granted it. I embraced him while he suspected nothing, and began by congratulating him on the dignity of his state; then I mingled my requests with my congratulations.

[Col. 0529C] I presented the petitions of our Turpio, pleaded his necessities, and lamented his extremity. These things seemed all the harder to grieving friends because a man bound by usury was being released from his body. He should therefore remember his new profession and his ancient fellowship, and moderate for a time the barbarous [Col. 0530A] insistence of the collectors barking around him. If the sick man should die, he should grant the heirs a year free from payment. If, as I hoped, Turpio recovered his former health, he should allow him, after his resources had been exhausted, the leisure to regain his strength.

[Note: [Col. 0530C] Sidonius’s uncertainty enables us to understand that short hair and a long beard were common to monks and penitents [Col. 0530D] as well as to clerics. Concerning monks, Hilary of Arles says in the *Life of Honoratus*: ‘The luxuriant hair is reduced to short locks; the splendor of garments is transferred to the brightness of the mind; the beauty of the milk-white neck is covered by stiff cloaks’—words by which he describes a monk. Salvian likewise says in Book VIII: ‘The people could scarcely bear to see within the walls of Carthage a man wrapped in a cloak, pale, and shorn to the skin of his flowing locks and mane’—that is, a monk. As for penitents, it is clear that they too habitually cut their hair, from canon 15 of the Synod of Agde, canon 12 of the Third Synod of Toledo, and Book V of the capitularies. Gregory of Tours says in Book VI, chapter 57: ‘He shaved his head and, receiving penance, gave up his spirit.’ Hence we read in the *Onirocritica*: ‘If someone sees that he has cut his own head as in the form of a monk, he will repent, or will cast off affliction’ (*Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ ὅτι ἐκούρευσε τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ μοναχοῦ, μετανοήσει οὗτος, ἢ ἀποβαλεῖ θλίψιν*).]

I was still pleading when suddenly the man, full of every kind of charity, began to weep heavily—not over the delay of the debt, but over the debtor’s danger. Restraining his sobs, he said:

“Far be it from me to demand from a sick cleric what I would scarcely have asked from a healthy soldier. I love his children so much that, even if something adverse should happen to my friend, I would not seek from them anything beyond what the measure of my duty permits.

“Therefore write to those who are anxious. Let them believe your letter, and add mine as well, whatever the outcome of the illness—which we nevertheless hope will be favorable to our brother. I will [Col. 0530B] extend the period for repayment by a year, and I will forgive the half that has accrued under the name of interest, being content with the restoration of the principal alone.”

At this I gave the greatest thanks to God and great thanks to my host. He loved his reputation as much as his conscience. I assured him that a friend sends ahead to himself what he will relinquish to you, and that he purchases the heavenly kingdoms by refusing to sell earthly favors.

What remains, then, is for you to strive, under your direction, to have the borrowed sum repaid immediately, while nevertheless giving immense thanks in the name of those joined to you by kinship who, perhaps because of their age, cannot yet understand what gift they are receiving.

Do not begin to say, “I have coheirs; the division has not yet been completed. I have been treated more harshly than my coheirs. My brother and sister [Col. 0530C] are still under guardianship; a husband has not yet been found for my sister, nor a guardian for my brother, nor a guarantor for the guardian.” All this may be said well to creditors, but badly to benefactors.

[Col. 0531A] When such a person enters into an agreement with someone willing to remit half, although he could demand the whole, and the debtor delays what he had granted out of compassion, he rightly demands it back because of the injury he has suffered.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Domnulus.

[Note: [Col. 0531C] To Afro, a learned man and, on account of his literary attainments, a former quaestor: the first point is established by Letters 13 and 15 of Book IX, the second by the letter to Polemius preceding Sidonius’s epithalamium. The author of the *Life of Hilary of Arles* also counts Domnulus among those who distinguished themselves by their writings. The name is a diminutive (*ὑποκοριστική*) from *domnus* or *dominus*. Salvian writes in a letter to Hypatius: ‘That Palladia of yours, that little crow of yours, that little lady of yours, with whom you once played through all these names in the most indulgent affection.’]

I cannot delay sharing with you, in haste, the immense joy we share. You surely wish to know what our father in Christ, and likewise Bishop Patiens, did after setting out for Chalon in accordance with his religious character and customary steadfastness.

[Note: [Col. 0531C] It was an ancient custom of the Church, when bishops were appointed, that the metropolitan should proclaim as bishop the man whom the clergy of the church and the people of both orders had chosen and whom he and the assembled provincial bishops had approved. Leo writes to the bishops of Gaul concerning the election of Ravennius: ‘Therefore, in the city of Arles, after the death of Hilary of blessed memory, you consecrated Ravennius, a man also approved by us, according to the wishes of the clergy, the honored men, and the people acting unanimously; by our judgment we confirm the good work of your brotherhood.’ He says likewise to the bishops of the province of Vienne: ‘[Col. 0531D] Let those who are to preside be sought in peace and quiet. Let the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the honored men, the consent of the order, and that of the people be secured; let the man who is to preside over all be chosen by all.’ Patiens, metropolitan of Lyon, Euphronius, bishop of Autun, and other provincials had therefore assembled to act properly according to custom. Since they found the citizens divided in their preferences, they themselves chose the bishop whom the people would receive once he had been proclaimed.]

When he came to the aforementioned town, partly preceded and partly accompanied by a college of provincial priests—namely, so that a distinguished bishop might be appointed for the municipality, whose church had been left unsettled after the younger bishop Paul had departed and died—the town’s conflicting [Col. 0531B] desires received the episcopal council, together with those private interests that always overturn the public good. A triumvirate of competitors had inflamed these interests: one, deprived of every other virtue of character, belched forth the ancient privilege of his birth; another was thrust forward amid parasitic uproar, purchased with the support of the kitchens and the applause of Apician banquets; a third had promised, by a silent agreement, that if he obtained the coveted office, the estates of the Church would become booty for his applauders.

When the holy Patiens and the holy Euphronius saw this—the men who, beyond hatred and favor, first upheld the firmness and strength of the sounder judgment—they secretly consulted with their fellow bishops before [Col. 0532A] declaring their decision publicly. Ignoring the uproar of the furious crowd, they suddenly laid hands upon and lifted up the holy John, who had expected and desired nothing less than what was being done.

John was a man distinguished by integrity and gentleness. First he had been a reader, then a minister of the altar, from childhood; later, with the passage of time and labor, an archdeacon. He had long been retained in that rank and ministry because of his diligence, but his rank could not for a long time be increased, lest he be released from his office. Nevertheless, he was already a priest of the second order.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] That is, a presbyter, which is the rank of the second order and immediately follows the bishop, as was said in the note on [Col. 0532C] Letter 11, concerning Claudianus. ‘John,’ it says, ‘after having long been retained in the rank of archdeacon because of his diligence, was already a presbyter, with his dignity increased, when he was elected bishop.’ The order and rank of archdeacons was formerly no different from that of deacons. Therefore, when they became presbyters, they ceased to be archdeacons, as is clear from all the ancient histories. Hence the canons that assign sacred orders to archdeacons prescribe no order other than the diaconate. The Synod of Urban II at Clermont, canon 3, says: ‘Let no one become dean in a church unless he is a presbyter, nor archdeacon unless he is a levite.’ Discipline was subsequently relaxed, and custom prevailed so that the archdeaconate was also conferred on presbyters.]

Amid the discordant voices of the factions—who postponed praising a man who did not seek praise, but did not dare condemn one worthy of praise—the schemers stood amazed, the wicked were ashamed, the good applauded, and no one objected. They consecrated him as their colleague.

[Col. 0532B] Now, then, since the monasteries of the Jura are sending you back—monasteries to which you have been accustomed gladly to ascend—and since you are already rehearsing the heavenly and supernal dwellings, it is fitting that you rejoice in the agreement of our common fathers or patrons, whether they reached this conclusion through consensus or this consensus through their conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 0532C] These are the Jura monasteries, frequently mentioned in the Jura Mountains. Gregory of Tours, in the *Life of Lupicinus and Romanus*, says: ‘Those secluded places of the Jura desert, which lie between Burgundy and Alamannia and are adjacent to the city of Aventicum.’ The chief of these was readily the monastery of Saint Eugendus, later called Saint-Claude. Just as these places are called Jurensian, so the kings of the Jura are [Col. 0532D] called Jurenses by Flodoard in his *Chronicle*: Rudolf and Conrad, who ruled in that region of Burgundy.]

Rejoice also in the name of the man whom Euphronius created by testimony and Patiens by the laying on of hands, both acting by judgment. Euphronius did what befitted not only the length of his old age but also the longevity of his dignity. Patiens too, a man equal to the greatest praises, did what was fully appropriate for one who is the head of our city through his priesthood and the head of your province through that city.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] Lyon, whose head is Patiens because he is its bishop; and, through the city, because Lyon is the metropolis of the province, he is likewise the head of the whole First Lyonnaise. Lyon is also Sidonius’s city and homeland. When he wrote this, its bishop was Patiens, whom he therefore calls at the beginning of the letter his father in Christ.]

Farewell.

# BOOK FIVE

## BOOK V

[Col. 0531]

## LETTER I

Sidonius sends greetings to his Petronius.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Petronius was a citizen of the toga-bearing court at Arles; we saw him go to Rome with others as [Col. 0532D] an envoy in the case of Arvandus, Book I, Letter 7. [Col. 0533D] Sidonius therefore commends Vindicius, a deacon of his church, to Petronius as a jurist; he mentions Vindicius again in Book VII, Letter 4.]

[Col. 0531D] I hear that you devote a pleasurable [Col. 0532D] patience to reading my letters. This is a great quality and most suitable to a man of letters: although you yourself excel in the greatest studies, you embrace even the smallest things in others. From [Col. 0533A] this very fact, however, the most complete glory is returned to you, for the man who supports another’s talent is sufficiently distinguished by the merits of his own.

I commend to you my close friend Vindicius, a religious man and highly suited to the Levitical dignity which he has recently acquired. Since he had no leisure, while passing through your province, to transcribe from my notebooks what you had ordered, he has brought you this small gift of little poems. Yet your holiness always regards even my letters as great rewards.

Meanwhile, I explain the necessity of the bearer, whom the twofold condition of the matter that has arisen has drawn into this undertaking. He has proceeded on the following understanding: either he must enter into litigation or approach the inheritance. His paternal cousin has died unmarried and intestate, and he is prepared to succeed by the privilege of agnation, unless factional [Col. 0533B] force obstructs his plans.

Against all these difficulties, however, after Christ’s help, you alone are sufficient for your suppliant. I am confident that, if the man obtains your favor, his case will obtain victory.

Farewell.

## LETTER II

Sidonius sends greetings to his Nymphidius.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] Concerning Claudianus and his author, see much in Letters 2 and 3 of Book IV.]

Mamertus Claudianus, the most learned Christian philosopher and foremost of all scholars who cultivated every limb, art, and division of philosophy, took care to adorn and refine the three-volume work entitled *On the State of the Soul*. He revealed that the nine disciplines called the Muses are not women but fields of study. For in his pages the attentive reader will find the truer names of the Camenae, which generate their own designation from themselves.

There [Col. 0533C] grammar divides, rhetoric declaims, arithmetic counts, geometry measures, music weighs, dialectic argues, astrology foreknows, architecture constructs, and metrics modulates.

Delighted by the novelty of this reading and stimulated by its maturity, you asked that I have it quickly reviewed and transcribed, as you had seen it; and, as you asked, you obtained it, promising its prompt return. Neither should I deceive you nor should you deceive me. The time has come for the borrowed book to be returned. For if the book pleased you, it ought by now to have provided satisfaction; if it displeased you, it ought by now to have aroused disgust.

Whatever it may be, quickly discharge your obligation, lest, if you prepare to return the requested little book too late, you seem to love the parchment more than the literature.

Farewell.

## LETTER III

[Col. 0533D]

Sidonius sends greetings to his Apollinaris.

It would have been fair for our loquacity to be restrained by an equal retaliation for your silence. But since perfect affection ought not so much to remember what services it has rendered as to remember what it owes, even now, loosening the reins of [Col. 0534A] modesty, we repeat the service of an impudent address.

Your shamelessness is especially evident in this: you remain silent. Brother, did I not deserve to know what you were doing during the time of hostility? Have you concealed from a friend anxious for you either your security or your fear? What else does it mean, if you suppress your activities from one who asks about them, than that he who is concerned for you must be suspected either of not rejoicing when he learns good news or of not grieving if events turn out otherwise?

Let this impious suspicion depart from good manners, and let true affection, in its candor, remove the blemish of so miserable an opinion. For, as your Crispus says, “To wish and not to wish the same things: that, at last, is firm friendship.”

Meanwhile, if you are well, that is good. I, however, weighed down by the [Col. 0534B] burden of an unhappy conscience, recently came near the end of my life through the violence of fevers. I am a man upon whom, wholly unworthy, the burden of so great a profession has been imposed—one compelled to teach before learning and to presume to preach the good before practicing it. Like a barren tree, since I have no works for fruit, I scatter words for leaves.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] Ambrose says something similar concerning the assumption of the episcopate, in Book I of *On the Duties of Ministers*: ‘Since we can no longer escape the duty of teaching, which the necessity of the priesthood imposed upon us when we were reluctant.’ And afterward: ‘For I was snatched from the tribunals and the insignia of administration into the priesthood, and I began to teach you what [Col. 0534D] I myself had not learned. Thus it happened that I began to teach before learning.’]

What remains is for you to pray that our return from almost the seat of hell may prove worthwhile, lest, if we remain in our former crimes, the fact that we live begin to pertain more to the death of the soul.

Behold, we have made known what we are doing; behold, we still inquire what you are doing. On our part, what is pious has been done. For the future, do what seems right to you. But believe this engraved in bronze, like the laws of Athens: with Christ’s help we shall never admit an end to the [Col. 0534C] love whose beginning we have striven to establish.

Farewell.

## LETTER IV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Simplicius.

That I have not received the writings I sent, I attribute to friendship, but I assign the greater share to modesty. For, unless I am mistaken beyond what is reasonable, the failure to acknowledge the greeting owed to me was not insolence but embarrassment.

But if you close the door against my further chattering on the page and put the bolt across it, I willingly grant your quiet, though I warn you that I shall find my culprits not far from you. It is not unjust for me to turn the entire unpopularity of your silence against the pride of your sons. Since they feel that they are loved, they suffer a certain annoyance at my attentiveness. You ought to admonish them, by the authority of your fatherhood, not to cease sweetening the bitterness of the [Col. 0534D] offense they have caused me with polished expressions.

Farewell.

## LETTER V

Sidonius sends greetings to his Syagrius.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] Syagrius was the great-grandson of Afranius Syagrius, formerly consul; Tonantius, mentioned in Book I, Letter 7, was also descended from him, though through the maternal line, as the son of his daughter. Sidonius writes to this Syagrius again in Book VIII, Letter 8. The Syagrii were people of Lyon. The tomb of the consul Syagrius was at Lyon, as appears from Letter 12 of this book; and a Syagria of the same family, whom Ennodius calls the treasure of the Church in his *Life of Epiphanius*, flourished at Lyon under Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, among whom this Syagrius too was held in honor. Thus, when Symmachus [Col. 0535C] says in Book I of his letters that the consul Syagrius lived beyond the Alps, Lyon is to be understood.]

Since you are the great-grandson of a consul, and that through the male [Col. 0535A] line—although this has little bearing on the case to be presented; since, then, you are descended from a poet whom letters would undoubtedly have given statues, had the trabea not given them—whose author’s cultivated words still testify to this, and whose descendants have not degenerated at all, especially in this respect—it is astonishing to say how amazed I am that you have seized, with such ease, a knowledge of the German language.

I remember that your boyhood was suitably imbued with liberal studies, and I know well that you often declaimed sharply and eloquently before an orator. Since this is so, I should like you to tell me where your heart suddenly drew the euphony of a foreign people, so that now, after the schoolroom rods of Maronian reading [Col. 0535B] and after sweating over the wealth and eloquence of the man from Arpinum, you seem to burst forth as a new falcon from an old Hilary.

[Note: [Col. 0535C] Peter Colvius, from the Claromontane manuscript: ‘as though a new Frank were bursting forth from an old Syagrius?’]

[Note: [Col. 0535C] Most books read this way; others vary between *harilao* and *harilio*, so that it is difficult to determine what Sidonius wrote. The sense is: ‘so that you seem to me to have changed from your ancestral homeland into a foreign one, from Gallic into Germanic.’ Ruricius uses a similarly elegant expression in Book I, Letter 3, writing to Hesperius that someone had suddenly been changed from Arion into Orpheus, meaning that a learned man had suddenly emerged from a rustic: ‘Indeed,’ he says, ‘as forgetful of my customary manner as I am [Col. 0535D] oblivious as I am oblivious to my rusticity, suddenly changed as though from Arion into Orpheus, I should like to appear to your most eloquent ears, with my chattering mouth, not so much dutiful as offensive.’]

It cannot be estimated how much amusement you provide me and others whenever I hear that, in your presence, a barbarian fears to commit a barbarism in his own language. Stooped German old men marvel at you as you interpret letters and choose you as arbiter and judge in their mutual affairs. You are a new Solon of the Burgundians in explaining laws, a new Amphion on the lyre—though on lyres with three strings. You are loved, frequented, sought out, delighted in, chosen, summoned, and heard; you decide.

Although they are rigid and immovable in body and understanding alike, they embrace in you both their native speech and a Latin heart, and they learn from you at the same time.

Only this remains, most witty of men: when you have leisure, devote no less effort to reading and preserve, as befits your exquisite taste, this [Col. 0535C] balance—that the one language may be held by you lest you be laughed at, while the other is exercised so that you may laugh.

Farewell.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius sends greetings to his Apollinaris.

[Note: [Col. 0535D] To his brother Thaumastus, Sidonius’s kinsman.]

[Col. 0536A]

When summer first gave way to autumn, and the fear of the Arverni could for a little while be moderated by the season, I came to Vienne, where I found your brother Thaumastus—whom, by right both of blood and age, I embrace with reverent affection—in the deepest distress. Although he was greatly shaken by his recent bereavement, he was scarcely less anxious on your account. For he feared and apprehended that some barbarian tumult or military misconduct might fabricate an accusation against you.

For he reports [Note: Of Chilperic, king of the Burgundians and, I think, father of our Clotild. At this time four kings ruled the Burgundians: Gundobald, Gundegisclus, Chilperic, and Gundomar, sons of Gundeuch, as Gregory teaches in Book II, chapter 28—the man who, after Gundicarius had been slain by Aetius, held the kingdom with his brother, the other Chilperic. Jordanes mentions them in his history of the Goths. Thus it might be uncertain which Chilperic Sidonius means, unless in the following letter he called him tetrarch, identifying the four brothers who reigned together. Now, in calling this Chilperic not king but master of soldiers, he follows the usage by which Alcimus Avitus calls Sigismund, son of Gundobald, a patrician, and Pope Hilary calls Gunduic or Gundeuch—or Gundiac, as Jordanes has it—the father of these four, likewise master of soldiers, in a letter to Leontius, bishop of Arles.] that the town of Vaison [Note: Vaison, called *Vasio* by the Vocontii in Pomponius Mela and Pliny, and Οὐασίων by Ptolemy. A later age said *Vasense* instead of *Vasionense*. But formerly the territory of the Vocontii extended very widely within the province of Vienne. Pliny writes, *Natural History* III.4: “The confederate state of the Vocontii has two chief towns, Vaison and Lucus Augusti; besides these there are nineteen insignificant towns.” But Lucus is now obscure, and Tacitus reports that it was already disfigured by fire from the army of Fabius Valens, *Histories* I. The city of Dea is more famous; on an inscription at Arles it is called *Colonia Dea Augusta Vocontiorum*. Mons Seleucus was also among the towns of the Vocontii, made famous by the disaster of Magnentius; but its name has been corrupted by almost everyone. For Socrates reads Μιλτοσέλευκος, Sozomen Μοντιοσέλευκος, and elsewhere Μοῦρος Σέλευκος. The true designation, preserved by the *Tripartite History*, is Mons Seleuci, situated between Lucus and the borders of the Vocontii and Vapincum, as may be seen from the itineraries of Aethicus and Bordeaux. It is a journey of somewhat more than three days from Lugdunum. Therefore what Socrates, II.27, attributes here to Mursa should be referred to Mons Seleucus.]

had been attached to the cause of the new ruler [Note: There is no doubt that he calls him a new prince who had begun to rule at Rome; but, amid the great number and variety of changes among rulers that occurred within those few years, it is not clear whom he means.]—especially through your contrivance.

If this arouses any suspicion in you and your people, quickly inform me by the return of the household correspondence, lest the opportunity for your relief or for my presence be lost to you. I shall take particular care, if you think anything nevertheless needs to be guarded against, to have him make you either secure through obtained favor or more cautious after his anger has been tested. Farewell.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius to his Thaumastus, greetings.

At last we have tracked down those who, before our tetrarch [Note: Chilperic, who held power at Lugdunum, since at that time the Burgundian realm was divided into four kingdoms.], denounced the friendship of your brother and, on the other side, of the party of the new prince—if, that is, the clues left by the secret informers have not eluded the loyal shrewdness of our associates. These, indeed, are the men whom, as you heard when you were present, Gaul has long lamented having to endure even among the more merciful barbarians.

These are the men feared even by those who are feared. These are the men whom this particular province is doomed to suffer: to bring accusations, inform against persons, issue threats, and carry off property. These are the men whose occupations you hear praised in leisure, whose plunder is praised in peace, whose flights are praised amid arms, and whose victories are praised amid wine.

These are the men who, when appointed to hear cases, delay them; when passed over, obstruct them; when admonished, take offense; and, when enriched, forget. These are the men who purchase lawsuits, sell interventions, appoint arbitrators, dictate what must be judged, tear apart what they have dictated, draw litigants forward, drag out those waiting to be heard, haul away the condemned, and pull back those who are settling.

These are the men who, even when you seek a favor with no one opposing, are reluctant to promise, ashamed to refuse, and regret having granted it. Compared with these men, Narcissus, Asiaticus, Massa, Marcellus, Carus, Parthenius, Licinus, and Pallas would raise a finger [Note: All were imperial freedmen of bad character and notorious for informing: Narcissus, Pallas, and Licinius under Claudius Augustus; Massa, Marcellus, and Carus under Nero; Asiaticus under Vitellius; Parthenius under Domitian. Seneca, Persius, Juvenal, Martial, Tacitus, both Plinys, Suetonius, and Dio write about them.]

These are the men who begrudge the civilians their leisure, the soldiers their pay, the couriers their travel allowances, merchants their fairs, envoys their gifts, tax-farmers their commissions, provincials their estates, municipal officials their priestly offices [Note: *Flaminia*, the priesthoods of flamines. The ancient glosses recognize *flamonii* as a form of *flaminio*, as does an inscription from Alba Julia:

“L. FL. VALENS, IN HONOR OF THE FLAMONIUM, B. P. D.”

This office is called *flaminicum* in another ancient inscription. It is established that flamines existed in municipalities and were specially assigned to municipalities, just as provincial priests were assigned to provinces. Drepanius Pacatus, in his panegyric, speaks of “flamines revered in municipal purple, priests distinguished by their headgear.” The fifteenth Novel of Marcian says: “That a municipal flamen, a priest of the province, might be permitted to have a wife who was a slave.”], officials their weights, appointed inspectors their measures, record-keepers their salaries, accountants their assignments, praetorians their allowances, cities their truces, tax-collectors their revenues, clerics their reverence, nobles their ancestry, leading men their seats, equals their intercourse, men in office their rights, private persons their privileges, pupils their schools, teachers their fees, and the educated their learning.

These are the men who, drunk with newly acquired wealth—to let you recognize even the smallest details—display through their intemperance in using possessions their ignorance of possessing them. For they gladly walk armed to banquets, dressed in white to funerals, wrapped in furs to churches, dressed in black to weddings, and clad in beaver-fur to litanies [Note: They are wearing beaver or castor fur. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIX, says: “*Fibrinum* is the wool of beavers, and a *fibrina* garment is a beaver garment, having a weft made from beaver wool.” Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*: “We seek beaver-fur and silk garments; and he considers himself higher among bishops who has put on the more splendid garment.” The beaver skins mentioned by Einhard in *Charlemagne* belong to the same category.]

No class of people, rank, or season is dear to them. In the marketplace they are Scythians, in the bedchamber vipers, at banquets buffoons, in exactions Harpies, in conversation statues, in investigations beasts, in negotiations snails, and in contracts money-changers. For understanding they are stones; for judging, wood; for taking offense, fire; for forgiving, iron; in friendships, leopards; in jokes, bears; in deception, foxes; in arrogance, bulls; and in consumption, Minotaurs.

They place firm hopes in upheavals of circumstances, prefer uncertain times because they are more secure for them, and, trembling equally through cowardice and conscience, are lions in the courts, hares in the camps. They fear treaties lest they be scrutinized, and wars lest they have to fight.

If anywhere the breeze of a rusty purse has blown upon their nostrils, you will immediately see there employed the eyes of Argus, the hands of Briareus, the claws of the Sphinxes, the perjuries of Laomedon, the cleverness of Ulysses, the deceptions of Sinon, the loyalty of Polymestor, and the piety of Pygmalion.

By these practices they overwhelm a man distinguished no less by goodness than by power. But what can one man do when surrounded on every side by a poisonously interpreting adviser? What, I ask, can he do whose nature is allied to the good but whose life is entangled with the wicked?

Under their counsels Phalaris would become more bloodthirsty, Midas more greedy, Ancus more boastful, Tarquin more arrogant, Tiberius more cunning, Gaius more dangerous, Claudius more sluggish, Nero more impure, Galba more avaricious, Otho more reckless, Vitellius more extravagant, and Domitian more savage.

What surely provides the chief remedy for the afflicted is that our Lucumo is moderated by his own Tanaquil [Note: The wife of Lucumo—that is, Tarquinius Priscus—was Tanaquil. Sidonius figuratively transfers these names to Chilperic and his wife; a little later he similarly designates them by the names Germanicus and Agrippina, since Agrippina was the wife of Germanicus, father of Caligula.], who, by the opportunity of her witty speech, scrapes away the poisonous dregs of the whisperers with which her husband’s ears have been filled.

You ought to know that, through her efforts, no harm has meanwhile been done, nor—God being favorable—will be done, to the peace of the common younger brothers in the mind of our common patron [Note: Their character recalls those brothers Tlepolemus and Hiero from Cybira in Cilicia, whose services Verres used in plundering Sicily. Cicero writes about them in the sixth *Verrine Oration*. Those who write or pronounce the city’s name otherwise corrupt it. The ancient coin of the Cybiratae themselves has ΚΙΒΥΡΑΤΩΝ, “of the Cybiratae,” written on it, and Tacitus correctly has *Cybiratica civitas*, *Annals* IV.]—provided that, for as long as the present power governs Lugdunensis Germany [Note: He calls the region of Lugdunum “Germany” because Burgundians of Germanic origin ruled there. Nothing is more familiar to Sidonius than to play upon the name “Germans” when he is speaking of the Burgundians, who had come from Germany, as I have said. Above, Letter 5: “the curved old age of the Germans.” In Poem 12: “and sustaining German words.” It was permissible to call that part of Gaul occupied by the Burgundians, later named Burgundy in its own right, “Germany,” just as we know that the island of Britain was sometimes called “overseas Saxony” by certain writers, and by the English who had crossed there from Saxony.]—our present Agrippina may govern our own Germanicus.

Farewell.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius to his Secundinus of Lugdunum, greetings [Note: Secundinus of Lugdunum, who has already been mentioned as a poet in Book II, Letter 10.].

For a long time we have read with amazement and praise the works in which you served the hexameter with such familiarity. The subject matter was pleasing, whether you were describing the wedding torches of a bridal chamber or wild beasts pierced by royal blows.

But recently, when you joined triple trochees into hendecasyllabic meter, you made nothing which, even in your own judgment, resembled it. Good heavens! Did I not plainly see what gall, what playfulness, and what peppered eloquence were present there [Note: Some manuscripts read *mellis*, “of honey,” instead of *fellis*, “of gall.”]? Except that the thunderbolt of your fervent genius and the salty freedom of your eloquence were perhaps impeded more by the persons than by the subjects, so that it seems to me that the consul Ablavius no more figuratively pierced Constantine’s house and life in a pair of verses than he bit them in the following distich, secretly hung upon the palace doors:

> Who would seek Saturn’s golden ages?  
> These are jeweled—yet Neronian.

For that Augustus, at nearly the same time, had extinguished his wife Fausta in the heat of a bath and his son Crispus in the cold of poison [Note: The order is reversed: he first killed Crispus, then Fausta. Sidonius alone says that poison was given to Crispus; Gregory of Tours is the only later author who follows him. The rest is discussed at length by Zosimus, Book II, who usually writes out of hatred for Constantine. The story resembles the legends of Hippolytus and Phaedra. Since many authors relate different versions, I do not know how certain it can be considered that, in an ancient collection of spectacles of Constantinople, found in many libraries, I remember reading that Constantine, after killing his son Crispus and being struck by remorse for his error and crime, erected a silver statue overlaid with gold, with a golden head, bearing this inscription: ΗΔΙΚΗΜΕΝΟΣ ΥΙΟΣ ΜΟΥ, “My son, wrongfully injured.” Those who defend this account praise Herodotus and the chroniclers Hippolytus.] Nevertheless, apply yourself no less boldly, at least to the colors of playful satire.

For your writings will profit from the faults of our tyrannopolites [Note: The Burgundians. Secundinus—so runs our conjecture—had directed his satirical tooth against those four tetrarch brothers mentioned earlier. The tragic funerals of the royal house are known to everyone: Gundobald stained his hands with the blood of two brothers, Chilperic and Gundemar, from whose control of part of the kingdom he himself had previously been expelled by force of arms. He also drowned the wife of Chilperic, whom Sidonius praised above. This, therefore, is the subject he compares with the story of Constantine. We learn from Ennodius’s *Epiphanius* that after these crimes Gundobald held the royal throne at Lugdunum and his brother Gundegisclus at Geneva.]. For those whom our judgments, ages, and places consider fortunate do not swell so moderately that posterity will not eventually labor to recall their names.

For the disgraces of wicked men, like the praises of the good, remain immortal.

Farewell.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius to his Aquilinus, greetings.

I count it among my obligations, most capable of all virtues, if you too consider it worthy, that we should have as many personal friendships as we have reasons for friendship. What I seek is ancestral. At present I shall call as witnesses to this matter the grandfathers of Apollinaris and Rusticus [Note: This concerns the prefecture of the Gauls held by Sidonius’s grandfather Apollinaris, as his epitaph teaches us in Book III, Letter 12. Aquilinus’s grandfather was Decimius Rusticus, whom Renatus Frigeridus wrote had likewise been made prefect by the same tyrants after serving as master of offices. Thus the dignity of both was equal. Concerning his death, the same Frigeridus writes in Gregory of Tours, II.9: “In those same days Decimius Rusticus, prefect of the tyrants, Agraecius, formerly chief of the notaries under Jovinus, and many other nobles were captured among the Arverni by the generals of Honorius and cruelly put to death after the tyranny of Constantine had been defeated. This Rusticus also seems to be the man whom Olympiodorus, as quoted by Photius, says sang an epithalamium with Attalus and Phaebadius at the wedding of Placidia and Ataulf.”], whom the similarity of letters, dignities, dangers, and convictions had joined in honorable intimacy.

This occurred when Constantine [Note: He transferred his tyranny from Britain to Gaul and established his seat at Arles. From there he sent his son Constans to seize Spain, with Gerontius as master of soldiers and Apollinaris, Sidonius’s grandfather, as prefect of the praetorium. Zosimus, Book VI, writes: “After this Constans crossed into Iberia, having Terentius as general and Apollinaris as prefect of the court.” Zosimus also reports that Apollinaris was afterward stripped of his prefecture by Constantine; this may be the inconsistency Sidonius notes. The consulship of this Constantine is indicated by an inscription at Trier, whose Greek text Joseph Scaliger produced in Book V of *On the Correction of the Chronology*, as follows:

ΕΝΘΑΔΕ ΚΕΙΤΑΙ ΕΥϹΕΒΙΑ ΕΝ ΕΙΡΗΝΗ ΟΥϹΑ ΙΕΡΟΚΩΜΗΤΙϹ ΑΠΟ ΚΩΜΗϹ ΑΔΔΑΝΩΝ ΖΗϹΑϹΑ ΜΙΚΡΟΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΕΤΩΝ ΙΕ. ΥΠΑΤΕΙΑ ΟΝΩΡΙΟΥ ΤΟ Η. ΚΑΙ ΚΩΝϹΤΑΝΤΙΝΟΥ ΤΟ Α. ΜΗΝΙ ΠΑΝΕΜΟΥ ΙΒ. ΗΜΕΡΑ ΚΙ. Β. ΕΝ ΕΙΡΗΝΗ

“Here lies Eusebia, resting in peace, a sacred village-woman from the village of Addana, who lived a short life of nineteen years, in the consulship of Honorius for the eighth time and Constantine for the first time, on the twelfth day of the month Panemus, day twenty-two. In peace.”

Scaliger asks—and admits that he does not know—who this Constantine, colleague of Honorius in his eighth consulship, was. I have no doubt that he was the tyrant Constantine, who had come to Gaul two years earlier and, after bringing these regions under his power, proclaimed himself consul in the year 409, enrolling himself as consul with Honorius Augustus, with whom, as Olympiodorus of Thebes writes, he sought harmony and a partnership in rule.], showed inconsistency; Jovinus [Note: He too assumed the purple when Constantine was being held under siege at Arles by the generals of Honorius. They, together with his brother Sebastianus, whom he had made partner in his tyranny, defeated them in battle, and eventually killed them at Narbonne, as our Idatius relates.] showed pliancy; Gerontius [Note: Against Constantine and Constans. When Constans entrusted Spain to Gerontius, Gerontius suddenly changed his mind, stirred up the barbarians, and left his client Maximus in Spain adorned with the royal insignia. After crossing into Gaul with his army, he captured and killed Constans at Vienne. Orosius, Book VII; Sozomen, Book IX, chapter 13.] treachery; each vice in each man, and all of them [Note: Claudius Postumus Dardanus, prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. It was chiefly through his efforts that the tyrant Jovinus was defeated after King Ataulf had turned away from his alliance with him, as Prosper Tiro records in his *Chronicle*; Olympiodorus also confirms this. Dardanus’s prefecture is attested by the law of Honorius, Book 11 of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions*, and by an old inscription visible not far from Sistaricum in the province of Narbonensis II, carved by human workmanship into a cliff commonly called the Split Rock:

“Claudius Postumus Dardanus, most illustrious man and of patrician rank, former consul of the province of Vienne, former master of the archives, former quaestor, former prefect of the praetorium of Gaul; and Nevia Galla, illustrious and noble woman, his wife and mother of the household, at the place called Theopolis, provided access for travelers by cutting away both sides of the mountain, and supplied walls and gates, wishing what had been established on their own estate to be held in common for the protection of all. With the assistance also of the most illustrious count and brother of the aforesaid man, Claudius Lepidus, former consul of First Germany, former master of memory, former count of private affairs, they caused an inscription of their zeal and public devotion toward the safety of all to be displayed.”

An excellent monument of distinguished workmanship. From it we have learned not only the names of Dardanus and his wife Nevia Galla, but also the various dignities of Dardanus himself and of his brother Claudius Lepidus. Jerome and Augustine also write about Dardanus; Augustine does not mention his offices, while Jerome records his two prefectures.] were condemned together in Dardanus.

In middle age, our fathers, living under one roof, advanced from barely childhood through their entire adolescence, serving the emperor Honorius as tribunes and notaries [Note: Secretaries of the emperor, a gateway to honors for noble youth. Cassiodorus Senator, *Variae* I: “Under the emperor Valentinian, the father of the candidate honorably held the dignity of tribune and notary—the honor then bestowed upon the outstanding, since it is clear that men were selected for the imperial secretariat in whom no fault of reproach could be found.”], with such affection between them that the least of their reasons for concord was that they were remembered as the sons of friends.

During the reign of the emperor Valentinian, one governed part of Gaul and the other governed its whole extent [Note: Aquilinus’s father must have been consul or governor in some province of Gaul. For Sidonius’s father governed all Gaul as prefect of the praetorium, Book VIII, Letter 6.]. Yet, in a kind of fraternal balancing of their titles, they weighed one another so evenly that the one who was later in dignity was earlier in the period of holding the fasces [Note: Some books read *tenore*, “in duration” or “continuance.”].

The matter has come down to us—that is, it has come down to the grandchildren. Nothing should they guard more carefully than lest, through us, the affection of our parents and ancestors should seem somehow to have grown old.

Besides our inherited prerogative, many circumstances compel us toward a similar intimacy: our ages are no less joined than our homeland. One game trained us, one teacher instructed us; one joy unrestrained us, severity restrained us, discipline formed us. Henceforth, if God permits, as we already strike against the beginnings of old age, let us be—unless you refuse—two souls and one spirit. Let us train our children in mutual affection, so that they may will and reject, avoid and pursue the same things.

And this would be beyond our fathers’ hopes, if through Rusticus and Apollinaris the hearts, as well as the names, of our praiseworthy great-grandfathers should be restored.

Farewell.

## LETTER X

Sidonius to his Sapaudus, greetings.

If the illustrious Pragmatius does anything particularly well among his other virtues, it is this: he loves you with an exceptional love of learning, because in you alone, or at least especially, he notices the traces of ancient knowledge and diligence to have remained.

Nor is he your supporter without reason, for he owes a very abundant honor to letters. When he once pleaded a case and broke the rhetorical benches with an applauded speech, his eloquent father-in-law voluntarily admitted him into the patrician family, although, apart from his lineage and wealth, his age, grace, modesty, and protectors also supported him.

But, as I learned, even then this grave man blushed at having pleased through the gift of his appearance; for he was rightly satisfied with being loved on account of his talent. Indeed, every truly excellent person pleases more through outstanding character than through beauty. Moreover, the bodily adornments that pass swiftly with advancing time fade through its progress and decline.

Priscus Valerianus, who was later prefect of the Gauls [Note: A former prefect. He had been prefect of the praetorium of Gaul and had employed his son-in-law Pragmatius as his assessor in that office. He was already a former prefect under the emperor Avitus, as the heading of Poem 8 shows.], also associated him with his councils and tribunals, steadfastly preserving his ancient judgment, so that, having joined his descendant to him under the pretext of knowledge, he might join him to his dignity as well.

Your diction, however, is so brilliant and conspicuous that the division [Note: Of all these men, nothing survives today except the declamations of Quintilian. Eusebius mentions Palaemon, a rhetorician of Hadrian’s time, in his *Chronicle*; Seneca mentions Gallio, his brother, in the preface to the *Natural Questions*; Ausonius praises Atticus Tiro Delphidius in Poem 5 of the *Professors*, and also Censorius Atticus Agroecius in Poem 15; Jerome mentions Atticus in his *Chronicle*. The memory of Adelphius is more obscure. The reputation of the great Roman orator Magnus is clearer from Jerome’s Letter 84 and his first *Apology against Rufinus*. Victorius may have been a rhetorician of Massilia whose poems survive. Palladius seems to be the man about whom Symmachus wrote in Book I, Letter 9: “The new guest of the Athenaeum moves the Latin assembly by the art of division, abundance of inventions, gravity of thought, and brilliance of words.”] of Palaemon, the gravity of Gallio, the abundance of Delphidius, the discipline of Agroecius, the strength of Alcimus, the tenderness of Adelphius, the rigor of Magnus, and the sweetness of Victorius could be written not merely as inferior to yours, but scarcely equal to it.

Indeed, lest you think that under this apparently hyperbolical catalogue of rhetoricians I have flattered you and offered you some favor, I do not hesitate—in fact, I am quite content—to compare your sharpness only with that of Quintilian and your splendor only with that of Palladius.

Therefore, if anyone after you favors Latin learning, he gives thanks for this friendship and for your fellowship, and, if he possesses anything human, wishes to be admitted as a third member of your society. Yet, what is more serious, this ambition should not be enough to awaken disgust in you, since few now honor learning. At the same time, it is naturally fixed and rooted in human hearts that those who do not understand the arts do not admire their artists.

Farewell.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius to his Potentinus, greetings.

We love you greatly, and indeed this affection is neither mistaken nor accidental. For I judged that I should become more closely bound to you as a companion. It is my custom to choose first and love afterward.

“What did you find pleasing and worthy of approval in me?” you ask. I shall say so gladly and briefly: one reason is supplied by favor, the other by the written page. In your actions I venerate the fact that you do many things worthy of imitation by every good man. You cultivate the land like one most skillful; you build like one most orderly; you hunt like one most effective; you feed others like one most exact; you joke like one most witty; you judge like one most equitable; you advise like one most sincere; you are moved like one most slow to anger; you are appeased like one most swiftly; and you return love like one most faithful.

If my Apollinaris follows all these examples of living from his boyhood onward, I rejoice; certainly I urge him to follow them. In teaching and training him, if what has been arranged succeeds with Christ’s help, I shall be exceedingly glad to borrow from your character the greatest part of my model for life.

Farewell.

## LETTER XII

Sidonius to his Calminius, greetings.

The fact that our page travels to you less frequently is caused not by our arrogance but by another’s inability. Nor should you seek any clearer explanation of this matter, since an equal fear on your side interprets the necessity of this silence.

I grieve openly only over this: separated by the storm of opposing factions, we enjoy one another’s sight not at all. Nor are you ever presented to the anxious eyes of your homeland, except perhaps when, at the command of another’s terror, armor protects you and fortifications protect us.

There you are brought captive for this sole purpose: to empty quivers of arrows and fill your eyes with tears; and we, too, do not refuse this, although your wishes are planning something quite different from missiles.

But because sometimes, even if not through the reality of treaties, at least through the appearance of truces, a window onto the freedom of our hope shines open, I earnestly beg you to favor us, whenever you most can, with the voice of a frequent letter. Know that among the hearts of your besieged fellow citizens there remains for you that gratitude which forgets the resentment of the besieger.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIII

Sidonius to his Pannychius of Bourges, an illustrious man [Note: So he is described in the address in Book VII.], greetings.

You know Seronatus returning from Toulouse. If you do not yet know this—and I believe you do not—learn it through the following account. Evanthius is now making his way toward Clausentia, and he is compelling the contracted laborers to dig out the earth, in case a heap has somehow become dirty through the fall of decaying leaves.

Certainly, if there is anything hollow or chasm-like, he anxiously levels it by filling the pits with earth brought from elsewhere, since he is about to precede his own beast, in ducal fashion, from the valley of the Tarmis; his muscles, like those of a whale, guiding his bulk through rocky or shallow places.

But although he is swift through anger, he is slow through bulk—like a dragon barely emerged from its cave—he is already being brought upon the bloodless Gabalitani nearby through fear. He drains them one by one, scattered and without fortified towns, by unheard-of kinds of levies; now he entangles them in the winding fraud of accusations. Nor does he allow them, even after they have paid the annual tax, to return home from their labor.

This too is a sure sign of his impending arrival: wherever he turns, prisoners are dragged along in crowds, dragging their chains. He rejoices in their pain and feeds upon their hunger. Above all, he considers it beautiful to disgrace those condemned before punishing them: he lets men’s hair grow, but cuts women’s hair. Yet if rare forgiveness ever looks upon some of them, venality releases these, vanity releases those, and mercy releases none.

To explain such a beast, neither Marcus of Arpinum, chief of orators, nor Publius of Mantua, chief of poets, would suffice. Therefore, since this very plague is said to be approaching—may God oppose his treacheries—anticipate the disease with the healthfulness of foresight. Settle lawsuits against quarrelsome men, if any arise, by agreements; settle taxes by receipts [Note: “Receipts” are *apochae*, documents recording payments. Symmachus, Book X, Letter 43, calls them *syngraphai*, evidently the documents that those paying taxes receive from the collectors as security. Cassiodorus, concerning the registrar of Venetia, writes: “They found against you valid receipts, and their misfortune gave them inviolable securities; it violently took away what you were seeking.” Hence the office of chief secretary of receipts in the household of the count of private affairs.], so that the wicked man may find nothing in the property of the good either to harm or to benefit him.

In short, do you wish to know what I think of Seronatus? Others fear suffering harm through the damage described above; I suspect even the robber’s benefits.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIV

Sidonius to his Aper, greetings.

At present you are enjoying the Calensian Baiae, its water, violently belched out through rough cavernous pumice stones, and its sulfurous pool, medicinal for those languishing with liver disease and consumption [Note: Some books of Caius read *Caienses*, while others read *Calenses*. Baiae is famous for its hot springs. There are also such springs today among the Arverni, and they have given their name to a village; for in the language of the homeland they call hot springs *calidas aquas*. They are also named *Aquae Calidae* on the Peutinger Table, along the road from Augustonemetum to Lugdunum.].

Or perhaps you are living in a mountain retreat amid fortified settlements, and, in selecting a place of refuge, are suffering some difficulty from the abundance of fortifications. Whatever the case may be, although you are free from business, you will nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, be recalled to the city by the contemplation of the Rogation ceremonies [Note: Concerning the Rogations instituted by Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, there is a homily by Alcimus Avitus, bishop of that same Church, and all ancient writers agree with it. Therefore those labor in vain who, because they read that litanies and supplications existed in the Church before Mamertus, want him to be called not the first author but merely the restorer of the Rogations. In vain, I say. The question is not whether he was the first to introduce the use of litanies into the Church, for it is clear that this custom was much older, but whether he instituted those celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension and now specifically called Rogations. On this point, as I have said, everyone agrees, and the words of Sidonius—“found, instituted, introduced”—leave no room for doubt. Mamertus was therefore the first author of the Rogations. He not only instituted fixed and solemn supplications for those days but also prescribed a form of supplication holier and more august than the customary one.].

Our father and pontiff Mamertus first found, instituted, and introduced their solemn observance, with a most reverent example and a most useful experiment. Previously—let it be said without offense to the faith—they had been wandering, lukewarm, infrequent, and, so to speak, sleepy supplications. They were often dulled by the obstruction of intervening lunches, especially when they sought either rain or fair weather. At such observances, not to say more, neither potter nor gardener was obliged to attend.

But in those which the aforementioned high priest both brought forth and organized, people fast, pray, sing psalms, and weep. For this reason I ask you to seek the festivals of bowed necks and the sighing fellowship of citizens lying prostrate. And if I rightly judge your spiritual disposition, you will come all the sooner because you are summoned not to banquets but to tears.

Farewell.

## LETTER XV

Sidonius to his Ruricius, greetings.

In the prefatory language of duty, I introduce your bookseller—not graciously but judicially examined—whose faithfulness in his heart, and whose speed in his work, concerning the lord whom you and I share, I have proved sufficiently and abundantly.

He now carries the book of the Heptateuch [Note: Just as the ancients called the five books of Moses the *Pentateuch*, so they called the three books that follow immediately—the books of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth—the *Triteuch*. Athanasius writes similarly to Marcellinus, calling all eight books joined together the *Octateuch*. So too Cassiodorus, Chapter 1 of the *Divine Institutions*, and all the Greeks whose writings are read, εἰς τὴν Ὀκτάτευχον, “on the Octateuch.” Since the Hebrews, as Epiphanius and Jerome observe, combine the story of Ruth with Judges into a single book, many consequently called it the *Heptateuch* instead of the *Octateuch*, as do Jerome in Letters 7 and 28 and Sidonius here.], written with the utmost speed and the utmost polish, although it has also been reread and revised by us.

He is also delivering a volume of the prophets, which, though completed in my absence, has nevertheless been cleared by his care and hand of superfluous passages. Nor did the man who had promised his assistance always read *contra* for him [Note: An old annotation in a manuscript of Martianus Capella, which I reproduced in full in connection with Ennodius, Book I, Letter 19, reads: “I, Felix the rhetorician, was correcting while Deuterius, my scholarly pupil, read against me.” Whoever corrects books by collating better manuscripts employs a companion who reads while he himself examines one manuscript. The companion was said to read *contra*. In another manuscript of Macrobius Theodosius, the corrector had written: “I, Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, was correcting at Ravenna with Macrobius Plotinus Eudoxius”; by these words he indicates that Eudoxius read *contra*.], I believe because illness prevented him from fulfilling what he had promised.

It remains for your encouragement, or your promise, to reward this servant suitably—whether as a student eager to please or according to his merit—with fitting gratitude. If this is paid for such labor, it will certainly begin to reflect credit upon your reward as well.

But since I ask this of you solely as a favor, you should consider what he deserves, for it is clear that he seeks the affection of his master more eagerly than a reward.

Farewell.

## LETTER XVI
Sidonius [Note: Avitus Augustus’s daughter, Sidonius’s wife before his priesthood and now his sister, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons and the longstanding custom of the early Church. In that Church, those who were admitted to the priesthood from marriage were separated from their wives’ beds and thereafter treated them no otherwise than as sisters. Jerome, Letter 1 to Pammachius: “Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are either chosen as virgins, or as widowers, or certainly remain perpetually chaste after the priesthood.” Faustus of Riez, in an unpublished letter: “He who still wishes to exercise the office of a husband forfeits the grace of consecration.” To omit the canons, which are encountered everywhere, there is an excellent letter of Lupus of Troyes and Euphronius of Autun, bishops, which attests this custom; but there will be another place for publishing it. With God’s help [This letter was published above, col. 66.] For now, let the example of Paulinus of Nola suffice, to whom Terasia, formerly his wife and now his sister, as Idatius says in his Chronicle: “From wife she was changed into a sister”; and that of Germanus of Auxerre, of whom the presbyter Constantius writes in his Life: “A wife is changed from wife into sister”; and of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, of whose Placidina Fortunatus likewise writes; and finally that of Urbicius, bishop of Clermont, whom Gregory relates in Book I, chapter 44, to have washed away with many tears the fact that he had once rashly violated ecclesiastical custom. Since, then, Sidonius remembered what had been sanctioned by law and custom and attested by the conduct of his predecessor, how could anyone either be ignorant of it or despise it with impunity? Yet there are those who think that this passage can be glossed over because of the mention of Papianilla; and because in Book IV, Letter 12, when Sidonius the bishop reads Terence and Menander with his son Apollinaris, they argue that the son—already a youth, already initiated into the authors of Greek and Latin literature—was received by his father after the latter had become bishop. The facts themselves show that all the letters of the Constantinian collection—that is, of the first seven books—which the bishop dictated were composed almost at the very beginning of his episcopate. But what can one do with people who, while saying nothing true, nevertheless want to be believed with their eyes closed?] sends greetings to his Papianilla.

[Col. 0545C] The quaestor Licinianus, coming from Ravenna [Note: Of his second arrival in Gaul he has already written above, Book III, Letter 7. Here he speaks of the letters patent of the patriciate, which he brought to Count Ecdicius from Augustus Nepos.], as soon as he had crossed the Alps and set foot on Gallic soil, sent letters announcing his arrival. In them he states that he is the bearer of the letters patent by whose arrival your brother Ecdicius, whose patrician honor you rejoice in no less than in my own titles, receives the dignity of patrician: very quickly, if you consider his age; very late, if you consider his merits.

For long ago he paid the price for entering upon this dignity not in the balance but in the field of battle; and, while still a private citizen, he enriched the public treasury not with money but with spoils. Yet the most scrupulously honorable Julius Nepos, supreme alike in arms and character as Augustus, has discharged—more swiftly, and therefore more commendably—the debt of his predecessor Anthemius, which had been incurred by your brother’s exertions, since he fulfilled what the other had so often promised.

The result is that henceforth every excellent man may and ought, for the commonwealth, to devote whatever strength he possesses—securely, and therefore eagerly—when the emperor, even after his death, always restores to the devotion of those who labor whatever the prince has promised. [147]

Meanwhile, if I rightly understand your feelings, now that you have learned these things you take great consolation amid the greatest adversities; nor does the fear of a neighboring siege cause your spirit to stray from the path of shared joys. For I know very well that you have not rejoiced even in my honor—which you share with me by law—in such a way: for although you are a good wife, you are also an excellent sister.

Therefore, with Christ our God propitious, I hastened to inscribe the enlarged titles of your family in a letter of congratulation, at once relieving your anxiety and your brother’s modesty. If you did not already know that he would reveal nothing concerning his own dignity because he was modest, you would be wrong to judge him impious on that account.

For my part, I rejoice not so much in your insignia—which until now you awaited the more impatiently the more freely you awaited them, although I rejoice greatly in them also—as in your harmony. I pray that it may remain equal toward our children and toward your own in the future. In common prayer I ask that, just as we have received both our families into the prefecture and by divine favor have made them patrician as well, so may they themselves make consular the family which they receive as patrician. [Note: The correct order of dignities. The honor of the patriciate lies between the prefecture and the consulship, as Cassiodorus teaches in his Formula of the Patriciate. But the consulship is the summit of all dignities, “the crown and the head,” to use Chrysostom’s words from his homily On the Title of the Acts. “In worldly affairs,” he says, “there are many offices; but they are not all of equal worth. Some are greater, others lesser. For example, to begin the enumeration from the lowest, there is the advocate of the city; above him is the ruler of the nation; after him there is another, a greater magistrate; then there is the general; there is the prefect; and above these is the office of the consuls.” And later: “The office of the consuls, like a crown and head, is set above them all.”]

Roscia sends you greetings, our common concern. She is being raised in the most indulgent bosom of her grandmother and aunts—something rarely granted to other people’s grandchildren—and is nourished with discipline as well. Yet this does not weaken her tender age; it forms her character. Farewell.

## 148 EPISTOLA XVII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Eriphius. [Note: To Eriphius of Lyons, son-in-law of Philematius. He sends him the four-line poem which he had written in honor of his father-in-law when they had met together at the Basilica of Saint Justus. The annual solemnity of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons, fell on the fourth day before the Nones of September, that is, at the beginning of autumn, as Sidonius hints.]

You are, my Eriphius, exactly as you have always been; and never do hunting, city, or country so call you away that you are not incidentally held by the pleasure of literature. This enthusiasm makes you disdain neither our writings, for, as you write, we smell of the Muses to you. Yet that judgment is generously proved false: it clearly arises either from jest, if you are cheerful, or from affection, if you are more serious.

In any case, it is far from just when you attribute to me qualities which could scarcely be suitably assigned to Maro, and scarcely even to Homer. Let us leave these matters aside and speak of the reason for which you wrote.

You order the verses to be sent to you which, at the request of your highly distinguished father-in-law, I willingly composed. He lives in the company of his peers, equally prepared by character both to command and to obey. But since you wish to know both the place and the occasion, so that you may more easily understand this unusual matter, blame yourself rather than me if the preface to the work proves more talkative than the work itself.

We had assembled at the tomb of Saint Justus, but illness prevented you from being present then. There had been a procession before dawn, an annual solemnity, and a huge crowd of both sexes, which the very spacious basilica could not contain, although it was surrounded by porticoes and crypts spreading widely around it.

After the vigil had been completed—a vigil which monks and clerics, taking turns in sweet harmony, had celebrated with psalmody—we each withdrew in different directions, though not far away, since we were to be ready at the third hour, when the sacred service was to be performed with the priests.

We were exhausted by the confinement of the place and the crowd and by the numerous lights that had been brought in. At the same time, the summer, with night still near, had scorched us, enclosed in a silent vapor; yet the dawn of autumn was already beginning to thaw with its first coolness.

So, while bodies of people from the various ranks were scattered here and there, it seemed good for the principal citizens to gather together at the burial-place of the consul Syagrius, which was no farther apart than the length of a cast arrow. [Note: “Tomb” and “monument.” Petronius: “She even followed the dead man to the burial chamber.” Suetonius, Augustus 18: “He honored the burial chamber and body of Alexander the Great after placing upon it a golden crown and sprinkling it with flowers.” And in the epitaph of Charlemagne: “Under this burial monument lies the body of Charlemagne, the orthodox emperor.” In ancient inscriptions, requietorium is also used.]

Here some of us sat beneath the shade of a mature vine, whose foliage, spread over raised and latticed supports, formed a covering; others sat on the green turf, fragrant with flowers.

Our conversation was sweet, playful, and restorative. Moreover—and this was most blessed—there was no mention of offices or taxes; no conversation directed toward advantage, no person seeking advantage. Anyone could have related a story worthy of being told and worthy of distinguished reflections, and it was listened to with the greatest eagerness. Nor, for that reason, was the narration lacking in structure, because cheerfulness was mingled with it.

After we had long languished in idleness, it seemed desirable to do something. Soon, according to our ages, we were divided into two groups, and amid shouted encouragements a ball was brought to some and a board game to others.

I was the first standard-bearer of the ball, which, as you know, is no less my companion than a book. On the other side, my brother Domnicius, a man of the greatest charm and wit, had taken the dice and was shaking them; like a trumpet-call, he summoned the gamblers to the gaming-board.

We played abundantly with a crowd of students, exercising through healthy running limbs which had been dulled by the torpor of sedentary work.

Here the illustrious Philematius, as the Mantuan poet says:

> He too dared to test with his hand the labor of young men,

steadfastly joined the companies of ball-players. He had done this beautifully enough, but when he was still younger.

Since he was frequently pushed from his standing position by the force of the runner charging through the middle, and, now that he had been admitted into the playing area, neither avoided the ball flying before him nor watched for the one thrown overhead, so that he might not interrupt its course; and since he often fell headlong in a somersault and with difficulty recovered himself from his disastrous turning, he was the first to withdraw from the game at the prompting of a sigh, his entrails growing hot.

For frequent pains pricked him as well, with the fibers of his little liver swelling. I immediately stopped too, intending to show affection by sharing his withdrawal, lest brotherly fatigue suffer embarrassment.

When we had therefore sat down again, sweat soon reminded him to ask for water for his face, and it was brought to him. A towel, loaded with nap, was also supplied. It had been polished by yesterday’s scraping and, by chance, hung swaying from a pulley-rope raised by the doorkeeper beneath the two-leaved doors of the little shrine. While he leisurely dried his cheeks with it, he said:

“I wish you would order some four-line poem of the same sort of service to be written for the cloth.”

“Let it be done,” I replied.

“But,” he said, “let it also preserve my name in its meter.”

I answered that whatever he requested could be done.

“Then speak,” he said.

Smiling, I replied: “You will know at once that the Muses are being stirred if I attend to their choir without witnesses.”

He replied forcefully and very wittily—as is natural for a fiery man and an inexhaustible fountain of eloquence:

“Take care, master Sollius, lest Apollo be more greatly stirred because you are summoning his foster-daughters alone to secret places.”

You can now imagine what applause greeted a remark so sudden and so amusing. Without further delay, I summoned his secretary, who was holding a writing tablet nearby, and composed the following epigram for him:

> At the new morning, whether the hot baths call,  
>   
> or when his brow, heated by the hunt, drips,  
>   
> let handsome Philematius warm this wet face,  
>   
> so that the liquid may pass from his face into the thirsty fleece.
