Our Epiphanius had scarcely finished writing out the lines above when word was brought that, at the appointed hour, the bishop was proceeding from the reception room. We rose.

Forgive the little song you requested. But the other work—the greater one—which you recently ordered me to compose about a certain man who was perversely enduring good days, in a parable or figurative form, and which will be sent tomorrow when it is finished—review it secretly together. If you approve, encourage it by publishing it; if you disapprove, forgive me by destroying it. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XVIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Attalus. [Note: To the count of Autun; this, I think, is what he means when he says that Attalus had begun to preside over the city of the Aedui. Gregory of Langres governed the county of the Aedui for forty years before occupying the episcopal chair, as Gregory of Tours relates in his Life. Attalus was his nephew; the same author speaks of him in Book II, chapter 15. Before these men, however, there was another Attalus.]

I gladly and joyfully learned that you had begun to preside over the city of the Aedui. There are four reasons for my joy: first, that you are my friend; second, that you are just; third, that you are strict; fourth, that you are near.

Hence you are abundantly willing, obligated, and able to assist the dealings of our people and of our friends. I therefore embrace, within the old intimacy of our friendship, the new right of the power you have acquired, and I have long been seeking an opportunity for your kindnesses.

Know that I trust in them so greatly that, even if I do not find what I might ask, you seem to me likely yourself to seek what you might grant. Farewell.

## 152 EPISTOLA XIX

Sidonius sends greetings to his Pudens.

[Col. 0549C] Your son has abducted the daughter of my nurse: an outrageous act, one that would have made you and me enemies, had I not immediately known that you did not know it was going to happen. But after offering the purgation of your conscience, you deign to ask that pardon be granted for the still-burning offense.

I grant it on condition that you, now his patron rather than his master, release the ravisher from his original tenancy. [Note: That twofold distinction among agricultural laborers—between registered or tributary tenants, who are slaves, and free coloni, who are also called inquilini—is neither perpetual nor consistent, not even among the jurists themselves. Accordingly, Sidonius can be tolerated here when he makes the same man at once a slave agricultural laborer, an original tenant, and a colonus, and wishes him to be manumitted so that from master he may become patron and from slave client. Thus, in Book II of the Code, “In What Cases Coloni May Accuse Their Masters,” the masters and patrons of agricultural laborers are also distinguished.]

That woman is now free. She will then be seen not to have been assigned to dishonor but to have been taken in marriage, if our defendant, for whom you plead, soon becomes a client instead of a tributary and begins to occupy a plebeian rather than a tenant’s status.

For this alone, whether it be called settlement or satisfaction, makes good, to no small degree, the insult done to me: I accept this in deference to your wishes and friendship, provided that freedom releases the husband and punishment does not bind the abductor. Farewell.

## EPISTOLA XX

Sidonius sends greetings to his Pastor.

[Col. 0550A] The better part of the community accepted as deliberate your absence yesterday from the city’s council meeting. It supposed that you had avoided it lest the burden of a future embassy be placed upon your shoulders.

I congratulate you on living by such principles that you must fear being chosen for office. I praise your effectiveness, suspect your prudence, and pursue your good fortune with praise. Finally, I wish you blessings equal to those of the men whom I love equally.

Many people, driven by detestable popularity-seeking, frequently seize the hands of the city’s leading men, lead them away from the public assembly, press kisses upon them when they have been set apart, and promise their services without being asked. To make themselves appear envoys in the assertion of the common cause, they refund the cost of transportation, voluntarily decline the expenses themselves, and secretly ask each individual to request publicly that they be chosen by all.

Thus, although their unpaid exertion might readily be accepted, the modest are nevertheless chosen more willingly and more agreeably, and this even at their own expense. Such weight does the impudence of those who thrust themselves forward carry, even when no travel allowance is imposed upon the tributary in their name. [Note: Thus it should be read, not “of the fasces to the tributary.” “Even,” he says, “when they take the expense of the journey upon themselves and nothing is added to the burden of the taxes because of them.” Travel allowances are ordinarily granted to envoys. Arcadius, Book on Civic Duties, Digest, “On Duties and Honors”: “Envoys who are sent to the emperor’s shrine also sometimes receive a travel allowance, which is called the legative.”]

Therefore, although you have not failed to perceive what good men were planning, nevertheless yield to the wishes of those awaiting you, and prove the affection of those who seek you, since you have already proved your modesty. Your first absence is attributed to restraint; the second delay points toward laziness.

Moreover, as you travel to Arles, you will have on the journey a venerable mother, brothers who love you, and the soil of your native land, which loves and is loved in return and to which one comes joyfully even apart from any opportunity. Then there is your own house, whose founder, vineyard, harvest, olive grove, and even roof it is pleasant to inspect as you pass by.

Therefore, sent by us, you will also arrive for yourself. For, if I am not mistaken, the circumstances and opportunity of your journey and of our cause will be such that you may at any time be regarded as charging the city with a benefit because you have seen your own people. Farewell.

## 154 EPISTOLA XXI

Sidonius sends greetings to his Sacerdos and Justinus.

[Note: It may be asked, since the dates do not conflict, whether this is the Victor of Aquitaine who composed the Paschal Cycle of Hilary the archdeacon, later bishop of Rome, at his request, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus, as is clear from Victor’s letter to Hilary. Sidonius again mentions Victor’s nephews Justinus and his brother without giving the brother’s name in the Propempticon.]

Your uncle Victorius, as distinguished as he was learned in every respect, was powerful in all else and most powerful in composing verse. I too have always cared for the Muses from childhood.

Now you come as heirs to your kinsman, both by right and by merit. Therefore I, by profession, become close to the poet, while you are close by descent. It is entirely just, then, that when each of us has completed his day, each should succeed in the manner in which he is joined to him.

Therefore keep the estates and produce the poems. Farewell.

# BOOK SIX

## 155 EPISTOLA I

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord Pope Lupus. [Note: Bishop of Troyes. The letters in this and the following book are collected as letters written to bishops. Among the Gallican bishops of Sidonius’s age, Lupus was easily foremost, distinguished both by his other achievements and by his embassy to Britain and by the glory of having brought peace to his citizens in the face of Attila.]

[Col. 0551A]

Blessed be the Holy Spirit and the Father of almighty God, because you, father of fathers, bishop of bishops, and another James of your age, from a watchtower of charity—and from no lower Jerusalem—look down upon all the members of the Church of our God. You are worthy to comfort all the weak and rightly to be consulted by all.

And what worthy response can I, this guilty, rotten, and fetid earth, now make to such condescension? Suffering both from the need and from the fear of your saving conversation, I am led by the memory of a life deserving punishment to cry out to you what that colleague of yours said to the Lord: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5:8).

But if this fear is not tempered by affection, I fear that I may be abandoned to the example of the Gerasenes, and that you may depart from my territory. Rather, I will bind you by a condition that is more beneficial to me, as my fellow leper, and say to you: “If you will, you can make me clean” (Matthew 8:2). By that sentence the leper revealed no more of what he was asking from Christ than he proclaimed of what he believed.

Therefore, although you are unquestionably foremost throughout the whole world, so far as the world extends, among bishops; although the entire company of your colleagues submits to your precedence and trembles at your judgment; although, in comparison with your gravity, even the hearts of the aged become childlike; although, after the vigils of the Lérins campaign [Note: Faustus of Riez calls the service of the angelic congregation on the island a military campaign in Letter 5 to Ruricius, using similar language of Lérins, which at that time was a common gymnasium for those renouncing the world. That Lupus had spent time there is shown not only by this passage and Book VIII, Letter 14, but also by Eucherius’s letter to Hilary, On the Praise of the Desert: “It possessed,” he says, “Lupus of revered name, who brought back to us that Lupus from the tribe of Benjamin; it possessed his brother Vincent, a gem shining with inward brilliance.” He calls Vincent, Lupus’s brother, a presbyter and a writer of most distinguished name. He seems especially to have recalled these men to Hilary of Arles because Lupus had once been married to Hilary’s sister Pimeniola.] and after nine full five-year periods have elapsed in the apostolic see [Note: Forty-five years. From these words Cardinal Baronius calculates the date and concludes that Sidonius, who wrote this letter not long after obtaining the episcopate, began to occupy the episcopal chair in the year of Christ 472. For at that time Lupus had been a bishop for forty-five years.], both orders of saints in the spiritual camp may acclaim you as a most famous chief centurion, yet you, for a little while removed from the company of standard-bearers and front-line soldiers, do not despise your last camp-followers and servants.

You carry the banners of the cross to the very last of the baggage-bearers, who through their ignorance still sit among the burdens of the flesh, and you extend the hand of your tongue to those wounded in conscience. You know, it seems, how to gather the wounded from the opposing line, veteran commander; and, as a most skillful trumpeter, to sound the retreat to Christ from sins. [157] Following the example of the evangelical shepherd, you do not rejoice more if the healthy remain than if the despairing are not abandoned.

You, then, pattern of morals, you, pillar of virtues, you, if the guilty may flatter you, true sweetness because holy, have not been reluctant to touch with the fingers of exhortation the sores of a most despised worm. You have not considered it beneath you to feed with admonitions a soul weakened by the frailty of greed, and from the storehouse of your deepest love to pour out for us a measure of humility that must be pursued.

But pray that I may at some time come to my senses, and recognize how heavily the mass of the burden placed upon me weighs down my shoulders. In the continuation of my crimes, miserable man that I am, I have reached such a necessity that I am now compelled to pray for the sin of the people, for whom even a people of innocent persons could scarcely obtain pardon by supplication.

For who can properly administer a remedy while sick? Who, feverish, can distinguish a healthy pulse by touch? [Note: In some manuscripts: “by the touch of one who is arrogant and sick.”] Who would rightly praise military knowledge as a deserter? Who, while eating his fill, can competently rebuke a person practicing abstinence? I, the most unworthy of mortals, must say what I shrink from doing; and, condemned by my own words, I am daily compelled to pronounce against myself the sentence I impose upon others.

But if you stand as an intercessor between me and him with whom you are crucified, Jesus Christ our Lord, on behalf of the people of my crimes—like a younger, rather than lesser, Moses—we shall no longer descend alive into hell; and, inflamed by the kindling of carnal vices, we shall no longer kindle a strange fire upon the Lord’s altar.

For although, as guilty men, we do not share in the balance of glory, [158] we shall nevertheless rejoice sufficiently and more than sufficiently if by your prayer we are able to relieve our inner man and to present a breast, if not whole for reward, at least scarred for forgiveness. Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA II

Sidonius sends greetings to Pope Pragmatius. [Note: It is not clear whose see he held. Those who conjecture that he was bishop of Autun and the successor of Euphronius, who took part in the Synod of Epaon, are refuted by the decisive fact that Euphronius was bishop of the Aedui at this time. Since his name is read together with that of Pragmatius in Faustus’s letter to Lucidus, it follows that this Pragmatius is different from the bishop of the Aedui.]

The venerable matron Eutropia, a woman of singular example in what concerns us [Note: A widow from Clermont whose son had married the daughter of Agrippinus. Some, on slight conjecture, also think her to be Saint Eutropia, whose name has been entered in the martyrology on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October. Yet one may compare her with another woman of singular example, whose virtues, outstanding and especially becoming to her sex, are praised by an epitaph once visible in the ancient Basilica of Saint Peter at Rome. It reads as follows:

> GABINIA GAUDENTIA, daughter of H., in whom there was incomparable chastity, most honorable modesty, incomparable innocence, rests forever in peace. She lived eighteen years, eleven months, and twenty-one days. Varius Victor, to his well-deserving wife, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

], vying in frugality and kindness, feeding the poor no less with fasts than with food, and so watchful in the worship of Christ that she alone compels sins to sleep within herself—has had the necessity of a lawsuit added to the griefs imposed by bereavement. She hastens to seek the perfection of your consolation as a remedy for this double evil, and will gratefully regard it whether you count this as a brief journey or a long-standing duty.

The aforesaid venerable brother of mine, Agrippinus, now a presbyter, harasses her—if it would be offensive to call it wickedness, it is certainly sophistry—and takes advantage of the woman’s weakness and does not cease to trouble the serenity of her spiritual soul with the blasts of worldly trickery. The two recent wounds caused by the loss of her son and, not long afterward, her grandson are added to the wound of prolonged widowhood.

We attempted to reconcile the two parties, especially since our profession gave us a new right over them and our friendships an old one. We issued some judgments, offered some advice, and made many entreaties. What may surprise you is that the female party withdrew more readily from every position favorable to reconciliation.

Although the father boasted that his paternal privilege would benefit his daughter more profoundly, the daughter-in-law nevertheless preferred the offer of her mother-in-law’s generosity.

The half-suppressed quarrel is now brought to your bosom. Reconcile the contestants; by the authority of your episcopal judgment impose grace upon the parties who fear one another, and speak the truth.

For holy Eutropia, if you believe anything on the strength of my testimony, counts it a victory if, even after her losses, she does not litigate. Hence I suspect that you will have to pronounce one household discordant, although you find both households at odds. Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA III

Sidonius sends greetings to Leontius, my lord pope. [Note: Bishop of Arles. There are many features in Sidonius’s words that designate Arles, such as his reference to the privilege of the place and to the men in the toga pleading there. The bishop of Arles at this time was certainly Leontius. This is shown by the letters of Pope Hilary, from which we also learn that Leontius entered the see in 462, approximately ten years before Sidonius. There was also the Synod of Arles mentioned by Faustus, which the same Leontius presided over; and the fifteenth letter of Ruricius to Aeonius, in which he indicates that Aeonius succeeded Leontius after his death. Leontius of Fréjus, whom a learned man suspects, was earlier than Sidonius; the Leontius of Bordeaux was later.]

Although no exhortations have inspired the beginnings of our profession, and although the thirst of our secular ignorance has so far been watered by no rain of heavenly teaching, I am not so forgetful of myself that I presume our sides can be weighed against one another with an equal balance of duties.

For since my mediocrity is easily surpassed by your excellence in age of life, duration of office, privilege of place, renown for learning, and gift of conscience, we deserve no equal exchange of correspondence, if we expect one.

Therefore, not censuring your silence but rather trying to excuse my talkativeness, I commend to you the bearer of this letter. If you favor his journey with ready goodwill, a broad harbor of security is opened for his affairs.

He has a testamentary matter. The merits of his own documents are hidden from him. He has gone to consult the expertise of the men in the toga who plead there, intending to count it as a victory if he understands that he has been defeated lawfully—provided only that he is not blamed for having wrongly failed to protect himself and his own through negligence.

I venture to commend him to you to this extent: if the considered advice of an advocate disdains graciously to instruct him, may the authority of your clerical crown nevertheless strive to extract a prompt reply from those who are evasive. [Note: Ennodius, Book IV, Letter 22 to Pope Symmachus: “May the mercy of your crown, when entreated, raise up the little ones.” That is, “your authority,” “your mercy.” Just as we sometimes use “purple” for the emperor, so we use “crown” for the cleric, because the latter is the cleric’s distinguishing mark as the former is the emperor’s. Augustine, Letter 147 to Proculianus: “Your people adjure us by our crown; ours adjure you by your crown.” The clerical tonsure was formerly made in such a way that only a circle of hair remained, resembling a crown. Gregory of Tours describes it in this way when speaking of Nicetius, bishop of Trier: “Saint Nicetius was designated a cleric from his birth; for when he had been brought forth, his entire head, as is customary with children, was seen to be bare of hair, but around the middle of the hair a row appeared, so that you might think that a cleric’s crown had been marked out by it.” In our own day, only monks and boy choristers for the most part retain the ancient form of the crown. For the short circle on the crown of the head worn by much of the clergy was formerly unusual and unknown in the Church, as the fortieth canon of the Fourth Council of Toledo teaches.] Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA IV

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord Pope Lupus.

In addition to the duty that is endlessly owed to your incomparably exalted apostolic office, even if it is discharged without interruption, I commend to you, because of a new necessity, an old relationship in the persons of these petitioners. They have traveled a long journey to the region of Auvergne—for in these times it is indeed a long one—and have arrived after fruitless labor.

They had learned from reliable, though not recent, evidence that a woman connected with their family [Note: A woman related by affection. Paulinus, author of the Eucharisticus:

> When my house was full of dear affections.

And later:

> Already long deprived of every affection,  
> first by the loss of my mother-in-law and mother,  
> then by the loss of my wife.

] had been carried off by an incursion of the Vargi—for this is the name by which they call the native brigands [Note: Sidonius himself interprets the term as “native little robbers.” Properly, however, Vargi were exiles and people expelled from their homeland, as in the Ripuarian Law 87 and Salic Law 57: “If anyone digs up and strips a body that has already been buried, let him be a wargus,” that is, expelled from that district. Naturally, native robbers arise from fugitive exiles. In a similar sense they were sometimes also called Bagaudae. Aurelius Victor, On Diocletian: “He raised up a force of peasants and robbers whom the inhabitants call Bagaudae.” Likewise the Scamari, in title 1 of the Lombard laws and in Jordanes’ Getica. Eugippius, Life of Saint Severinus: “As he passed along the waters of the Danube, he hurried after the robbers whom the common people called Scamari.”]—had been brought there several years earlier and sold there.

Before they arrived, this same unfortunate woman had openly been sold in the house and under the authority of our merchant, when a certain Prudentius—such is the name of the man whom rumor reports now to be living at Troyes—praised the transaction of men unknown to us. His subscription appears within the formula of the market sale, as that of a qualified guarantor.

The authority of your person and the advantage of your presence will have power among the parties brought before you, if you deign to investigate the whole sequence of the violence. What is more serious, according to what the bearers report, is that the crime was aggravated by the fact that one of the travelers is known to have been killed during that very act of robbery.

But since they seek the remedy of your judgment, and since those who are producing a criminal case are seeking civil treatment, it belongs equally, if I judge correctly, to your office and your character to help the grief of the one party and the danger of the other by some settlement injurious to neither; and, through a healthy moderation in your judgment, to make one side less afflicted, the other less guilty, and both more secure.

Thus may the state of the quarrel, in accordance with the civility of the time and place, not depart at the end in the condition in which its beginning found it. Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA V

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord Pope Theoplastus. [Note: His name appears among the bishops who subscribed to the Synod of Arles mentioned by Faustus.]

The man who carries my letter to you is acting without knowing my cause. While he becomes a suitable bearer of a service desired by me, he grants a benefit which he thinks he is receiving.

So it is now with the venerable Donidius, worthy to be numbered among the most distinguished men. I commend to you his client and his children, who have set out either to seek the need of their patron or that of their master.

Protect the labor of these travelers with whatever help, kindness, and intercession you can provide. And if their friend himself, through inexperience and unfamiliarity with public affairs, should appear in any respect less effective, consider instead what the absent man’s cause deserves, not what the present man’s person deserves. Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA VI

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord Pope Eutropius. [Note: A letter of Pope Hilary to him, among others of the bishops of Gaul, survives from the year 464. He also took part in the Synod of Arles mentioned above. Some think him to have been bishop of Orange, whose commemoration is mentioned in the martyrologies on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.]

After I learned that the treaty-breaking people had returned to their own settlements and were preparing no ambushes for travelers, I thought it wrong to delay any longer the expression of my duties, lest your affection should attribute to my fault the rust of a sword left unpolished through infrequent care.

Therefore, sending a bearer of letters for this one purpose, I anxiously inquire how sound the condition of your body is and whether matters are proceeding according to your wishes. I hope that the love you once granted me will not be weakened either by the length of the intervening journey or by the long duration of our common absence, because the goodness of the Creator closes the dwelling of human beings within final limits, but not affection.

It remains for your blessedness, through the healthy sting of your conversation, to feed the hungry longing of our ignorance. It is very useful to you that, through your exhortations, the emaciation of our inner man is repeatedly filled out by mystical fat and spiritual richness.

Remember us, my lord pope.

## EPISTOLA VII

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord Pope Fonteius. [Note: Bishop of Vaison. This is taught by Book VII, Letter 4, addressed to the same man. Fonteius therefore also seems to be the man to whom letters of Leo the Great and Pope Hilary were addressed, together with those to his fellow bishops. It is clear from the profession of the presbyter Lucidus that Fonteius was present with the others at the Synod of Arles.]

[Col. 0556B]

If the preceding relationship of our elders contributes anything toward beginning a favor with their descendants, I too approach your apostolic dignity with the advantage of familial familiarity. For I remember you always to have been my family’s strongest patron in Christ, so that I regard your friendship not so much as something to be sought as something to be renewed. To this is added the fact that the priestly office, imposed upon one so utterly unworthy as I am, compels me to flee to the protection of your prayers, so that the wounds of my still ulcerated conscience, too gaping, may at least be scarred over by your intercession. Therefore, commending myself and my family, and excusing the lateness of this letter, I earnestly beg you, by your accustomed intercession, in whose powers you possess immense strength, to protect in us the creeping beginnings of clerical apprenticeship; so that, if the unchanging mercy of God deigns to alter anything in the perversity of our character, we may owe the whole of it to the advocacy of your prayers. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter VIII

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Graecus.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] To the bishop of Massilia, as Letter 2 of Book VII will show, as well as the other letters which he later writes to him on behalf of the same Amantius—for this is the name of the lector whom he commends. He signed the Synod of Arles. And since he was a new bishop when Sidonius wrote this, it would not be an idle conjecture to believe that he was the Greek deacon to whom Faustus of Riez addressed a letter against Nestorius.]

The bearer of letters supports his poor life solely by the business of trading. He has no craft for profit, no military service for advantage, no cultivation for gain; even what he is known to obtain through hired errands and rented labor increases his reputation, but his resources increase through another’s means. Nevertheless, because he enjoys great trust, even if his substance is small, whenever he visits the markets of some newly arrived ships with money aboard, he offers his creditors, who readily trust him, only the proof of his character as security.

[Note: [Col. 0556D] Ships that had put in at the harbor of Massilia. Strictly speaking, those things which are imported are said to καταπλεῖν, “to sail into port.” Hence in the old glosses, cataplus means the arrival of ships. Sidonius uses the word again in Book VII, Letter 7. Thus Cicero uses cataplus Puteolanus in *Pro Rabirio Postumo*, Martial uses Niliacus, and in another sense Lalagaea cataplus appears in Marcellus—or, as others prefer, in Vindicianus’ poem *On Medicine*. 66 Conversely, when a ship leaves the harbor, it is called an ἀνάπλους, “a sailing out”; this was also the name of a harbor at Constantinople.]

These matters were suggested to me while I was dictating, and for that reason I do not hesitate to assert confidently what I have heard, since those who are close to me are not a few, and he himself is very close to them. I therefore commend his tender youth and his difficult beginnings; and, since his name has recently been entered on the roll of lectors, you will recognize that, for one about to depart, I owed a letter to a citizen and a *formata* to a cleric. [Note: [Col. 0557A] He means this letter which he was dictating: private correspondence, by which he was going to commend Amantius as a citizen, even if he had not been a cleric. A *formata* means a canonical letter. A bishop was obliged to give such a letter to a lector, because clerics were not permitted to travel without one, as all the councils repeatedly show. But, to discuss *formatae* somewhat more freely, there were two kinds. Clerics either transferred to another diocese in order to remain there, and letters of dismissal were given to them, which the Synod in Trullo, canon 18, properly calls ἀπολυτικάς, “letters of release”; without these they were not enrolled among the clerics of another church: μηδένα τῶν ἁπάντων κληρικῶν ἐκτὸς τῆς τοῦ οἰκείου ἐπισκόπου ἐγγράφου ἀπολυτικῆς ἐν ἑτέρᾳ κατάπτεσθαι (sic) Ἐκκλησίᾳ, “that no cleric whatever should be attached to another Church without the written letter of release of his own bishop.” All the *formatae* read in Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian belong to this type. Or they did not migrate completely, but went away temporarily for private or public business, as Amantius did, and those who went to the imperial court; to these only letters of commendation were given. The Greeks indiscriminately call these now συστατικάς, “letters of introduction,” and now εἰρηνικάς, that is, “peaceful letters.” Although canon 40 of the Synod of Chalcedon shows that “peaceful letters” were sometimes distinguished from letters of commendation, it is nevertheless clear that others neglected this distinction. Accordingly, when the Greeks themselves transmit the formulas of these letters, they usually ask only about the two kinds: πῶς γράφουσιν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς συστατικὸν, καὶ πῶς ἀπολυτικὸν γράμμα, “how bishops write a letter of introduction, and how a letter of release.” The Latins, however, included both kinds under the name *formatae*, so that *formatae litterae* universally correspond to κανονικαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς, “canonical letters”—which is also how they are called at the Synod of Meaux, canon 50, and by Hincmar in his *formata* to Aeneas, bishop of Paris—and were divided into letters of dismissal and letters of commendation, just as the Greek letters were divided εἰς ἀπολυτικὰς καὶ συστατικάς. Since letters of dismissal were not issued without some commendation and token of peace, they were sometimes also called letters of commendation and peaceful letters; but the reverse was not true, since letters that were merely commendatory were not called letters of dismissal. From this it is clear that the Greek translator of the Synod of Carthage acted more correctly when, following the force of the word *formata* in canon 23, he translated it as τετυπωμένην rather than explaining it as ἀπολυτικήν, because the passage was not speaking of letters of dismissal but of purely commendatory letters. Councils, then, are full of references to *formatae*, as I have said; and the system of numbers to be added to *formatae* is well known. Atticus of Constantinople published it from the prescription of the Council of Nicaea; Gratian derived it from Atticus, as did the other collectors of canons, who also append examples of *formatae*. Anyone who is not wholly ignorant of Greek letters and the numbers represented by each can readily perceive the entire system, especially by comparing the examples. But because the examples they publish are generally corrupt and mutilated through the fault of copyists, they must first of all be corrected and restored. Let us therefore take as our example the one produced by Gratian in a later place under distinction 73. It is a *formata*, not “A,” as the printed books have it, but the letter of Wolfeo, bishop of Constance, to Bernalt of Argentaria—both cities once among the greatest of the province of the Sequani—written not on behalf of Hermann but on behalf of Anno. Thus it reads in an old manuscript:

Π. Υ. Α. Π.

“To the most holy brother in Christ, Bernalt, bishop of the city of Argentaria, to be embraced with the highest sweetness of charity: Wolfeo, bishop of the Church of Constance, wishes perpetual blessedness and salvation in Christ.”

Υ. Ε. Ν. Σ.

“Furthermore, let your holy fraternity know that this cleric, named Anno, instructed and tonsured in our parish, asked our humility to write him a letter of commendation.”

Then, after other material:

“May the Holy Trinity grant your blessedness perpetual well-being in the governance of its holy Church.”

θʹ, indiction 10.

This *formata* contains the total number 1,325. The number is correctly written as MCCCXXV. For it is formed from all the Greek letters and marks, both common and proper, collected together according to Atticus’ formula. I call those letters common which occur in every *formata*; those which vary in each individual letter I call proper, as follows:

**Common letters**

Π, the first letter of *Father*: 80.  
Υ, the first letter of *Son*: 400.  
Α, the first letter of *Holy Spirit*: 1.  
Π, the first letter of *Father*: 80.  
θʹ, the numerical sign: 99, corresponding to Α Μ Η Ν, that is, 1,000, 40, 8, 50.

Total: 660.

**Proper letters**

Υ, the first letter of Wolfeo, who writes: 400.  
Ε, the second letter of Bernalt, to whom he writes: 5.  
Ν, the third letter of Anno, who receives the letter: 50.  
Σ, the fourth letter of Constance, from which it is written: 200.  
Χ, the sign of the indiction: 10, which was current at the time when the *formata* was written.

Total: 665.

Total of both: 1,325.

In this way you will immediately calculate the total of any *formata*, if you add to 660—which, as you see, is common to all—the other number produced from the proper letters of each individual letter and from the indiction. There are, moreover, those who think that the name *formatae* was derived from these numbers and from the fact that the letters were woven together according to a definite formula. It is more correct, as we have observed elsewhere, that *formata* was named from the form of the seal by which it was secured. Thus the old Vatican glosses interpret *formata epistola* as “a sealed letter”; and this was undoubtedly what the person intended who translated *formata* into Greek at the Council of Carthage as τετυπωμένην. For τυποῦν ἐπιστολήν means “to seal a letter”; 68 and it is certain that a seal was customarily attached to *formatae*. The Second Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, canon 50, says: “Letters in which the names of the bishop and the city are impressed in lead.” Ratbod, bishop of Trier, says in his *formata* preserved by Ivo: “We have decided to secure this letter here and there with Greek letters, and have judged it proper to seal it with the ring of our church.” He uses *bullare*, “to seal,” in the terminology of his age, corresponding to βουλλεύειν and βοῦλλας ἐπιβάλλειν. Nicetas Choniates speaks of a *bulla*, that is, a seal, and of impressing a τύπον, or form. Bernard, Letter 230: “There are letters complete and sealed.” Finally, just as in later centuries imperial constitutions were called not only τυπικά, “formal,” but also θεῖοι τύποι, “sacred forms,” in both languages, and later the diplomas of emperors and popes were commonly called *bullae* from their seals, so they seem to have called a letter *formata* from its form, just as a letter is called *bullata* from its bulla.]

I believe that before long he will rightly become a prosperous merchant, if, hurrying to your service, he often prefers the merchant’s fountain to the coolness of civic fountains.

[Note: [Col. 0558D] Some read *mediatoris*, others *medicatoris*.]

Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter IX

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Lupus.

[Col. 0558A]

This now respectable Gaul, because he did not delay when ordered to return to his wife, brings back, through the service of my letter, compliance with my wishes and the effect of yours. When the page you had sent was opened for him, he immediately groaned in remorse and judged that the letter, although addressed to me, contained a sentence against himself. Therefore he at once promised, prepared, and undertook the journey to his homeland. Because of this very speed of his repentance, we took care to address him not in reproach but rather in consolation, since a correction made quickly was approaching innocence. For no one, even one conscious of his own rectitude, can presume to do more, provided that he has not abandoned the path of your correction; since the very words we read—words of merciful judgment—are powerful incentives to the greatest amendment. For what could be more precious than the tenor of this chastisement, in which a sick spirit, perhaps ill through sin, finds an inward remedy when it cannot find a rebuke from without? Finally, we beg you, by your frequent prayer, through which you exercise immense mastery over every vice, to cause us also—as it is clear that the Gospel magi returned—now to return by another way of life to the homeland of the blessed. I had almost omitted something that should by no means have been passed over. Give thanks to Innocentius, a man of rank, who, as you had ordered, diligently complied with what was enjoined. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter X

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Censorius.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] To the bishop of Auxerre, concerning whom there is a letter of Ruricius, Book II, Letter 1, and another by Constantius the presbyter at the beginning of the books on the Life of Saint Germanus. Both, however, call him Censurius.]

A courier of the levitical order is dignified by his office. While he was fleeing with his household from the storm of Gothic plunder, he was carried into your territory, driven, so to speak, by the very force of his flight. There, on the estate of the Church over which your holiness presides, this newcomer, hungry and almost exhausted, planted a small seed in a half-ruined plot; he begs to be allowed to gather its full produce. If you support him with the domestic hospitality owed to faith—that is, if the customary rent of the soil is not demanded—he will count it a sufficient gain that, although a stranger, his income and his spirit may be as modest as if he were farming in his native land.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] Nearly all the books read *non petatis*, “do not demand,” as in Poem 23, *Usuram petimurque, reddimusque*, “We both demand and repay interest.” Properly, he called the *canon* the rent owed from an emphyteutic estate, the ἐμφυτευτῶν munus, or burden: τὴν γῆν γεωργεῖν, καὶ τέλος παρέχειν, “to cultivate the land and furnish the payment.” Hence *canonicarii* are those who collect the public *canon*.]

If you grant him, as is customary, the lawful disposal of his very small crop, he will return with thanks, as though richly supplied with provisions for the journey. Through him, if you grant me a share in your customary favor by your writing, your letter will be regarded by me and by the brotherhood settled there as though it had been delayed a little. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter XI

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Eleutherius.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] To a bishop of uncertain see. For some have thought of Eleutherius of Tournai, but Sidonius seems to have been somewhat earlier than he was.]

This present letter commends a Jew—not because I approve the error in which they are entangled and through which they perish, but because, while a person is alive, it is not fitting for us to declare any one of them wholly condemnable. For he remains in hope of absolution, since he still possesses the ability to convert. He himself will more properly explain in person the course of his affair. For it is quite contrary to prudence to extend, by a rambling account, the concision due to an epistolary form. Certainly, since according to earthly knowledge or judgment such people are accustomed to have honorable causes, you too can defend the person of this troubled man, even while opposing his unbelief. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter XII

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Patiens.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] To the bishop of Lyon, concerning whom see Book XI, Letter 10, and the last letter of Book IV. He is the man to whom Constantius wrote the Life of Saint Germanus, whose name appears among other bishops in the letters of Faustus and Lucidus and in the martyrology. For the people of Lyon celebrate him annually on the third day before the Ides of September. Gregory of Tours mentions this Sidonius’ letter and the generosity of Bishop Patiens in Book XI, chapter 24. When he writes there of the famine that ravaged Burgundy, he confirms that the king understood by Sidonius to be the king of the Burgundians—namely Gundobad, who, as we noted earlier, had his seat at Lyon.]

I judge that a person especially lives for his own good when he lives for another’s, and that, moved by pity for the disasters and poverty of the faithful, he performs heavenly works on earth. “Why this?” you ask. This statement applies above all to you, most blessed pope, who are not content merely to help those needs of which you have been informed, but, extending the net of your charity to the farthest boundaries of Gaul, habitually consider the causes of the needy before you inspect their persons. No one’s poverty or weakness is harmed if he cannot seek you, for you reach out your hands in advance to the one who cannot come to you on foot. Your vigilance passes into foreign provinces, and the breadth of your care is spread out for this purpose: to console the distress of those who live far away. Hence, since you are moved no less by the modesty of those absent than by the complaint of those present, you have often wiped the tears of people whose eyes you had not seen.

I omit those matters which you daily endure, through sleepless watches, prayers, and expenditures, because of the distress of impoverished citizens. I omit the fact that you always conduct yourself with such moderation, and are always judged so humane and so abstinent, that it is clear that the present king continually praises your banquets and the queen your fasts. I omit the way in which you adorn the Church entrusted to you with such care that an observer might hesitate whether new works are rising or old ones being repaired. I omit the fact that through you the foundations of basilicas are rising in many places and their ornaments are being doubled. And while many things in the condition of the faith are increased by your arrangements, the number of heretics alone is diminished: by a kind of apostolic hunt you entangle the minds of the Photinians in the nets of spiritual preaching, and, whenever they are refuted by your words, you do not allow these barbarians, already your followers, to depart a single step until you, that most fortunate fisher of souls, have drawn them from the deep whirlpool of error.

[Note: [Col. 0560D] The Arians. The Burgundians were Arians, and Patiens was working to bring them to the orthodox faith. The Paulianists, Photinians, and Bonosians, although differing in certain respects, followed errors related to Arianism, denying Christ’s eternal generation.]

Some of these matters, however, may perhaps be shared with your fellow bishops. But this is owed to you under what the jurists call the title of a special legacy, and your modesty cannot deny it: after the Gothic devastation and after the crops had been consumed by fire, you sent grain at your own expense, free of charge, to the common poverty throughout the desolated regions of Gaul. You would have given the peoples wasting from hunger an abundance too great if this provision had been a commodity rather than a gift. We saw the roads narrowed by your grain; we saw, along the banks of the Saône and Rhône, not merely one granary filled by one man.

Let the fictions of the gentile myths yield, and let Triptolemus—the man supposedly carried up to heaven for discovering the novelty of grain—yield as well. Greece, illustrious for its masons, painters, and sculptors, consecrated temples to him, formed him in statues, and represented him in images. His doubtful fame claims that, among the still-rude peoples of Dodona, he wandered in two ships, carrying unknown seed; the poets later assigned to those ships the form of dragons.

[Col. 0561B]

But you, to say nothing of your generosity in the interior, when you were going to distribute food to the cities of the Tyrrhenian Sea, filled your granaries with two rivers rather than two ships. Yet if a religiously minded person is offended by Achaean examples from the superstition of Eleusis, as though they were less suitable, let us set aside the reverence due to mystical interpretation and compare the historical diligence of the venerable patriarch Joseph, who easily provided the remedy he had foreseen against the sterility that was to follow seven fertile years. Nevertheless, according to the moral meaning, in my judgment he is no less great who, when a similar necessity suddenly arrives, does not foresee it but still comes to the aid of those in need.

Therefore, although I cannot fully estimate how great are the thanks which the people of Arles, Riez, Avignon, Orange, Alba, Valence, and the city of the Tricastini owe you, may you, their possessor, receive them; for it is difficult fully to measure the prayers of those whom one knows to have received nourishment without payment.

[Note: [Col. 0561B] Some read *Regenses*, “the people of Riez”; this is also the form used by Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, 83. Others call them *Regii*, as in Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Faustus. This is the well-known city of the Second Province of Narbonensis, whose episcopal see was made famous by Maximus and Faustus. Its true and ancient name was the one used by Sidonius in the *Eucharisticus*, where he calls the inhabitants *Reii*. An ancient inscription from the same province confirms this, and at the same time shows that the Reii were surnamed Apollinares; the Peutinger Map also teaches this. There should therefore be no doubt that the corrupt passage of Pliny, Book III, chapter 4, concerning Gallia Narbonensis, must be corrected in the same way. Pliny says: “Latin towns: Aix, of the Salluvians; Avignon, of the Cavares; Apt, of the Vulgientes; Alebece, of the Reii Apollinares; Alba, of the Helvii; Augusta, of the Tricastini.” The common editions wrongly read *Alebeciorum Apollinarium*. But the Vatican manuscript has the correct reading, which I have presented. The inscription reads:

*M. SEVERIUS M. F. FABULATOR FLAM[EN] ROM[ANUS] ET AUG[USTALIS] III VIR PONT[IFEX] COL[ONIAE] REIOR[UM] APOLLINAR[IUM] SIBI ET CAREIAE CAREI FIL[IAE] PATERCLAE OPTIM[AE] UXORI*

“Marcus Severius Fabulatus, son of Marcus, flamen of Rome and Augustus, triumvir and pontiff of the colony of the Reii Apollinares, [made this] for himself and for Careia Patercla, daughter of Careius, his excellent wife.”

There is another inscription at Nîmes containing the epitaph of Pompeius Maternus, a citizen of Riez, and this too should be referred to the matter.]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] The people of Viviers. In the *List of the Cities of Gaul* it is called *Civitas Albensium*, now Viviers. Those whom our contemporaries call Vivarienses were formerly called the Helvii, and their principal city, according to Pliny, was Alba Helviorum; hence they too were called Albenses. In a letter of Pope Paschal II to Guido, archbishop of Vienne, it is called “Alba, which is also called Vivarium.” The error has now been rejected by those who, following Marlianus, confused the Helvii with the people of Albi. The Helvii, according to Pliny and all geographers, were in Gallia Narbonensis, separated from the Arverni or Vellauni—who at that time were assigned to the Arverni—only by Mount Cévenne, as Caesar reports. The Rhône also flowed by them, as Strabo notes. All these facts fit the people of Viviers, not those of Albi, who were situated in Aquitania, far from the Rhône and the Arverni. Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 24: “The city of Viviers and the city of Avignon were grievously devastated by the bubonic plague.” Sidonius would have said “the city of Alba.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562C] Concerning Valence, a very well-known city and, as Tiro Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*, the noblest city of Gaul, it should be noted that those who make it a city of the Cavares are led into a slight error if they think they have Pliny as their authority, since Pliny seems to place Valence in the territory of the Cavares in Book III, chapter 4. Pliny’s words should instead be punctuated according to the corrected manuscripts, so that it is not Valence but Orange that is understood to lie in the territory of the Cavares; and this is correct. For Orange, like Avignon, belonged to the Cavares. Valence, however, was not a city of the Cavares but of the Segalauni, as Ptolemy teaches, placing the Segalauni—whom Pliny above calls the Cavares—between the Allobroges and the Cavares.]

[Note: [Col. 0562C] The Tricastini are closest to the Segalauni on the east, and are known from Livy and Ammianus Marcellinus, who, in describing Hannibal’s route from the Allobroges to the Cottian Alps, lead it through the Tricastini, Vocontii, and Tricorii. They are also known from the *List of the Cities* and from the councils in which the city of the Tricastini and the bishops of the Tricastini are named in their proper places.]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] The following is the opinion of Hadrian Valesius in *Notitia Galliae*, p. 60: Augusta and Neomagus, which not only Sirmond but also Joseph Scaliger and Holstenius considered two different cities, are one and the same city, which Pliny designated by its Latin name and Ptolemy by its Gallic name. Pliny assigns no other city to the Tricastini besides Augusta; likewise Ptolemy, who habitually assigns each people its principal city and capital, gives those same Tricastini one city, Neomagus. Therefore neither recognized any other capital of the people. “For it is unlikely,” says Valesius, “that the small and insignificant people of the Tricastini had two capitals.” —Baunius, editor of Sirmond, preface to volume I, § 11.]

Pliny records the city of Augusta, Ptolemy Neomagus; a small town in that region preserves traces of the name and is called Niomus. Today, however, the capital of the Tricastini bears the name of Saint Paul, where the bishops have their see, together with the designation of the Tricastini.

[Col. 0562C]

I myself, in the name of the town of the Arverni, offer the fullest thanks. When you planned to come to its aid, you were moved neither by the community of the province, nor by the nearness of the city, nor by the convenience of the river, nor by the prospect of payment. Therefore, through me, they give immense thanks, since through the abundance of your bread they have attained their own sufficiency.

Thus, if I seem to have adequately fulfilled the duties of my commissioned office, I shall be a messenger as an envoy. I want you to know immediately that your glory is proclaimed throughout Aquitania: you are loved, praised, desired, and honored in every heart and in every prayer. Amid these evils of the times, you are a good priest, a good father, and a good year. It was worth their undergoing hunger at their peril, if your generosity could not otherwise have been proved by experience. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

# Book Seven

## Letter I

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Mamertus.

[Note: [Col. 0563C] To the bishop of Vienne, mentioned above. He is also called Mamertus by Pope Hilary and Lucidus, by Avitus, Gregory of Tours, and others. Those who write *Mamertum* depart from the ancient books and from the origin of the name. For *Mamertus* is derived from *Mamers*, and *Mamertinus* from *Mamertus*, not *Mamercinus*. This letter should be compared with Alcimus Avitus’ homily on the Rogations, mentioned in connection with Book V, Letter 14. They are very similar not only in subject but throughout the entire sequence of the narrative.]

It is reported that the Goths have moved their camps onto Roman soil. In every such invasion we wretched Arverni are the gateway. For we provide our enemies with particular incentives for hatred, since, because they have not yet fixed their boundaries from the Ocean to the Rhône along the bed of the Loire, they endure their only delay, under Christ’s protection, from our obstruction alone. The whole extent and tract of the surrounding regions has long been consumed by the unwelcome advance of a threatening kingdom.

Yet in the rash and dangerous boldness of our resistance we do not trust that either the burned face of our walls, the rotten lattice of the stakes, or the ramparts worn down by the breasts of their guards will help us. We are comforted only by the assistance of the Rogations brought in by you: through their initiation and establishment the Arvernian people have begun to be instructed, unequal in result perhaps, but certainly not unequal in devotion, and for this reason they have not yet turned their backs on the terrors surrounding them.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] The Rogations of Mamertus, which precede the Lord’s Ascension, were imitated not only by the neighboring peoples of Gaul, as this passage and the Fifth Council of Orléans show, but also by other nations and eventually by Rome itself, through the authority of Leo III, as the authors of the liturgical books teach. They were therefore called the Gallican litany, because their institution came from Gaul, and the lesser litany, to distinguish it from the greater litany celebrated on 25 April.]

For we are not unaware of what our inquiry has revealed: when these supplications were first instituted, the city divinely entrusted to you was being emptied by terrors of what kind of prodigies. At one time the outward façade of the public walls was shaken by repeated earthquakes;

[Note: [Col. 0563D] “Outward façade”: derived from the stage of a theater. Tertullian called it the “stage of the body” in *On the Soul*, and Eumenius the “stage of triumph” in his *Panegyric on the Schools*: “Some are terrified by the sound of trumpets and the clash of arms, others by a certain stage of triumph.” The expression has, however, been carelessly omitted from the printed editions.]

at another time fires, often blazing, buried the crumbling ridges of the roofs beneath a mountain of ashes; at another, the terrifying gentleness of bold stags placed their astonishing couches in the forum. While the withdrawal of your leading citizens and common people had emptied the city’s public life, you hastened to follow the new examples of the ancient Ninevites, lest your own despair also insult the divine warning.

And truly, after the evidence of your virtues, you could no longer distrust God without sin. For once, when the city had begun to burn, your faith grew hotter amid that fire; and when, before the eyes of the frightened crowd, the fire was driven backward merely by the opposition of your body and curved away in retreating coils, there occurred a terrible, new, and unprecedented miracle: the flame yielded out of reverence to one whom by nature it had been unable to feel.

First, then, you announce fasts to the few men of our order, prohibit wickedness, proclaim punishments, and promise remedies. You explain to everyone that neither punishment nor pardon is far away; you teach that the threats of the announced desolation must be removed by the frequency of prayers; you warn that the persistent violence of the raging fire can be quenched by the water of the eyes rather than by the water of rivers; you warn that the threatening convulsion of earthquakes must be strengthened by the stability of faith.

The humble crowd immediately followed this counsel and became an encouragement even to its leaders. Those who had not been ashamed to flee were not ashamed to return. God, the examiner of hearts, appeased by this devotion, made your supplication a means of salvation for you, an example for others, and a protection for both. From then on, there were neither losses to afflict them nor omens to terrify them.

Knowing that all this had happened previously to your people of Vienne and had not happened afterward, this people embraces the instruction of so sacred an example, earnestly asking that the blessedness of your conscience send the support of its prayers, by which you transmitted these examples.

And since, in the western regions, after the time of our forebears, it has been granted to you alone—after the confessor Ambrose, discoverer of two martyrs—to undertake the intact translation of the martyr Ferreolus,

[Note: [Col. 0564C] Ambrose himself speaks of the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, discovered by him at Milan, in Letter 15 and Sermon 91; Augustine speaks of them in Book IX of the *Confessions* and Book XXII of *The City of God*; Gregory of Tours speaks of them in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapter 47.]

and to transfer intact the body of the martyr Ferreolus,

[Note: [Col. 0564D] The Viennese had first placed the intact body of Ferreolus, together with the head of Julian, which had been brought from the Arverni to Vienne by the bloody hand of an executioner for a once-turbulent persecutor, in a humble basilica on the bank of the Rhône. Mamertus transferred them to a larger church which he had built there, with this inscription:

*Heroas Christi geminos haec continet aula*  
*Julianum capite, corpore Ferreolum.*

“This hall contains two heroes of Christ: Julian in his head, Ferreolus in his body.”

Gregory of Tours quotes this passage of Sidonius in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book II, chapter 2. After the Saracen plunder, Wilicarius, likewise bishop of Vienne, placed the same relics of the martyrs in a church of his own within the city, as Ado reports in his *Chronicle*.]

with the head of our Julian added—the head which the bloodstained hand of an executioner once brought back from there to a turbulent persecutor—it is not unreasonable for us to ask in return that a portion of patronage come to us from there, since a portion of a patron has returned from here to you. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter II

Sidonius sends greetings to the lord pope Graecus.

[Col. 0565A]

You burden my modesty, most accomplished of bishops, by heaping it with praise of many kinds, if I have ploughed out anything with my rustic pen; and would that what I have connected at this first encounter of letters—though within a narrow compass—things nevertheless discordant with and different from truth, be free from fault. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Amantius. For he is so called in Letters 7 and 11 of this book; and we have indicated this above at Book VI, 8. Moreover, Gregory of Tours, Book IV, 46, has a not dissimilar story, but with the opposite outcome, about Andarchius of Marseille, who by cunning fraud sought to marry the daughter of Ursus, a citizen of Auvergne.]

A clever traveler imposed upon my ignorance. For while he pretended merely to be acting as a merchant, he extracted my letters in place of a *formata*—representing himself as a reader—though they ought to have contained some expression of thanks. For, as I later discovered, he had benefited more from the kindness of the Massilians than his position, whether judged by his property or by his household, allowed. [Col. 0565B]

Yet if someone worthy of recounting them were to unfold these events as they happened, they would become delightful to remember. But since you yourself command that a page from me should bring you something cheerful and copious, forgive me if, while respecting the severity of your ears, I touch upon this very hospitality of our letter-carrier as something comparable to comic wit, lest I appear to be learning only now what was already insinuated to me a second time. At the same time, if it is the custom of the rules that openings for speech be drawn from every subject, why should anything be sought or awaited here from farther afield than whatever subject I am going to discuss, unless our speech itself is to serve as the cause, for which our speech will be the burden?

His homeland was Auvergne; his parents were of birth not proud but respectable, and, just as they boasted of nothing distinguished, so they feared nothing servile. [Col. 0565C] They were content with a modest fortune, though one sufficient—or at least free from obligations. Their military service had been spent in a clerical rather than a palatine retinue. His father was exceedingly thrifty and ungenerous to his children; through excessive parsimony, he preferred to be more useful than pleasing to his young son.

Abandoning him, the young man then set out for you with very little baggage; and that was the greatest impediment to his first endeavors, for nothing is heavier than light traveling provisions. Nevertheless, his first entrance within your walls was quite favorable.

[Note: The Massilian see had been governed successively by the bishops Venerius, Eustathius, and Graecus. Eustathius therefore succeeded Graecus—or, as others write, Eustasius. For this is how it is read in Pope Hilary’s letter of the year 464. Eustathius is mentioned by Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the *Museum*.]

Holy Eustachius, who had succeeded among you, at once proved a double blessing in word and deed: lodging sought in haste and easily found through Eustachius’ care; rapid admission; and courteous accommodation. He began at once to cultivate his neighbors by frequent visits, and repeatedly to receive their greetings without disdain. He dealt with each according as age permitted: he bound the elderly to himself by attentions and his contemporaries by services. Above all, he pursued chastity and sobriety—virtues as praiseworthy in youth as they are rare.

Thereafter he became known and familiar to the leading men, and at that time to the count of the city, as no less useful than he was constant in his watchfulness; thus, day by day, his diligence was advanced through the companionship of his superiors. Every good man eagerly encouraged him: all by their good wishes, many by advice, private persons by gifts, and everyone by kindness. Through these means his hopes and resources were rapidly and progressively increased. [176]

It happened by chance that near the lodging which he had taken over there lived a woman suitable no less in property than in character. Her daughter had already passed beyond the years of infancy, though she had not yet approached marriageable age. To her this man, being gracious toward her—since she was still of an age at which such behavior was proper—would give now some trifle, now some object suited to a maiden’s play. By these gifts, insignificant as they were, the girl’s affection for him became very great.

The years passed, suitable for marriage. Why delay over details? A young man alone, poor, a foreigner, a dependent son, departing from his homeland not only without his father’s consent but even without his knowledge, sought and obtained as his wife a girl not inferior in birth and superior in wealth, with the bishop’s support because he was a reader, the count’s assistance because he was his client, a mother-in-law who did not inspect his property, and a bride who did not disdain his person. He married her.

The marriage documents were drawn up; and whatever provincial rusticity our little town possessed was inserted there into the matrimonial documents and recited with theatrical extravagance. [Col. 0566C] Once the lawful formality and customary deception had been completed, the beloved poor man carried off his wealthy wife. Having carefully investigated and packed away whatever belonged to his father-in-law, and having also extracted a not inconsiderable supplement by exploiting the ease and credulity of his mother-in-law’s generosity, the undefeated trickster sounded the retreat to his homeland.

When the girl’s mother consequently began to bring an action for the recovery of the *hyperbolic* documents—

[Note: Some read *perhyperbolicis*. Jacques Cujas, a man of great and exact judgment, believes that *hypobolici* should be read. I would strongly approve this if it were supported by the authority of some ancient book. For these documents are what is being discussed. Yet whichever way one reads it, the meaning is the same. For either he calls them *hypobolica*, that is, betrothal instruments, such as he immediately calls them, namely the gift *propter nuptias*, which legal interpreters teach was called *hypobolum* by the Greeks; or he calls those same instruments *hyperbolica*, in which Amantius had extravagantly bestowed many estates—not his own but other people’s—in the name of the *hypobolum*, and which he was now, naturally in vain, attempting to reclaim. Moreover, the mention of the betrothal gift advises us to restore this word to our Ennodius in the *Life of Epiphanius*, whose speech is recorded in Letter 72 to King Gundobad: “Let the liberation of captives,” he says, “be your son’s betrothal generosity; let him offer his promised bride a gift which Christ too may accept.”]

—and then began to lament the smallness of the slaves included in the betrothal gift, only when she was already rejoicing in the large number of grandchildren, our Hippolytus had gone to appease her, after first presenting my letters. [177]

There you have the history of an outstanding young man—a tale comparable to a Milesian or Attic story.

[Note: I have never doubted that Sidonius wrote it this way, not *militia*, whose meaning is unsuitable here. The tales of the Milesians were amorous and *ἀκόλαστοι*—“unrestrained” or “indecent.” Thus all stories of that kind and subject are called Milesian, in the genre in which Aristides excelled. Plutarch, in *Crassus*, says of Surena celebrating his triumph at Seleucia: “After gathering the senate of the Seleucians, he brought in indecent books of Aristides’ Milesian tales” (*Τὴν δὲ γερουσίαν τῶν Σελευκέων ἀθροίσας εἰσήνεγκεν ἀκόλαστα βιβλία τῶν Ἀριστείδου Μιλησιακῶν*). Lucian also mentions them in the dialogue entitled *Ἔρωτες* (“Loves”). Hence Apuleius’ *Milesian Tales* were called “Punica Milesia” by the emperor Severus in a letter, because they were written by a Carthaginian author in the spirit of the Milesians. Jerome likewise refers to them in *Apology 1 against Rufinus*: “As though the crowd of curled-haired Milesians did not chant fictions in the school.”]

At the same time, forgive me for extending beyond the proper epistolary formula. I prolonged it with a lingering style so that you would not receive as an unknown man one whom you have made a citizen by your kindness. It is likewise established by nature that to those on whom we bestow attention we offer affection.

You will show that Bishop Eustachius died a truly worthy heir in every respect if, just as you pay inheritances to relatives according to a will, so you pay the legacies of patronage to your clients. Behold, I have obeyed, and I have filled the duty of obedience with chatter. Even though an unlearned man who assigns a lengthy task should not be displeased if he has received letters not so eloquent as talkative.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER III

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Megethius.

[Note: To the bishop of Bellac. He is numbered among the bishops who attended the Council of Arles.]

[Col. 0567B]

For a long time and at length I deliberated, although affection of heart and eagerness to obey kept pressing me, whether I should send, as you command, the little attestations which I myself composed. In the end the judgment that determined that I must obey you prevailed; therefore I sent what you requested.

And what shall we say now? Is this great obedience? I think it is great—but my shamelessness is greater. With such a face we could send water to rivers and timber to forests; with such audacity we could present Apelles with a paintbrush, Phidias with a chisel, and Polyclitus with a hammer. You will therefore pardon the presumption, holy, eloquent, venerable pope, which with its natural garrulousness babbles before your most learned judgment.

Our custom treats it as a rule that, even when it produces little, it writes much—just as dogs are born so that, even when they do not bark, they nevertheless growl.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER IV

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Fonteius.

I am already afraid to commend anyone, because when we commend people we offer words, while you offer gifts—as though it were not itself to be counted a principal benefit that, when I depart from you, a sinner, a portion of holy communion is opened to me.

Our Vindicius is witness to this. He returned home more slowly under the burden of your generosity, consistently affirming wherever he is that, although you are great in reputation and very high in rank, you are nevertheless more deserving of praise for your graciousness than for your dignity. He praises the holy, honeyed, and flower-laden pleasantries that proceed from your tempered fellowship; yet, for all this, nothing is lost from your episcopal dignity. You do not diminish the height of the priesthood by courtesy, but bend it toward others.

When I recognize these qualities, I grow so ardent that I shall judge myself most fortunate whenever, with divine assistance, I am permitted to embrace, while standing before you, a heart so secure in its God—even if my boldness is excessive—with close embraces. [179]

Accept my confession: I regard you as excessively severe, and, conscious of my weakness, I bear harshness toward me with equanimity. But, as must be admitted, such character makes us submit more readily through humility than join ourselves through familiarity. In short, let him see with what quality of conscience he swells who makes himself rigid toward those who court him. For my part, I would rather imitate the character of one who seeks to kindle affection for himself even in those who are far away.

This too is deeply dear to me among the greatest matters: I have learned that you abundantly extend the patronage of your apostolate, through unceasing intercession, to the truest lords of my soul, Simplicius and Apollinaris. If this is true, I ask that your charity not come to an end; if it is false, I ask that it not delay having a beginning.

Furthermore, I commend to you the bearer of this letter, for whom something arising from necessity in that place—that is, in the town of Vaison—can be remedied by the weight of the reverence owed to your authority.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER V

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Agraecius.

[Note: To the metropolitan of Senonia, that is, of the fourth province of Lugdunensis. The people of Sens celebrate his feast day among those of their holy bishops on the Ides of June. Take care not to confuse him with the other Agroecius, whose name is read in the Council of Agde and to whom a letter of the Council of Carpentras is extant. For the latter was much later and was bishop of another see, namely Antipolis in the province of the Maritime Alps. Sidonius will later discuss the election of the bishop of Bourges, for which he had come to Bourges, in Letter 9. From this letter and from the eighth, addressed to Euphronius and placed immediately after this one in some copies, it may be observed that it was formerly customary, when bishops were being appointed, that if the lawful number of provincial bishops was lacking, others should be summoned from neighboring provinces. Even when the number was not otherwise lacking, the decrees of the Council of Nicaea teach that such neighboring bishops could be added at the discretion of the provincial bishops. This is shown by the letter of the Council of Constantinople quoted by Theodoret, Book V, chapter 8: “Concerning the separate churches, an ancient custom, as you know, has prevailed, as has the ordinance of the holy fathers at Nicaea: in each province the ordinations are to be carried out by the bishops of that province and, if they should wish, together with the neighboring bishops, for the sake of what is beneficial” (*Περὶ δὲ τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις παλαιός τε, ὡς ἴστε, θεσμὸς κεκράτηκε, καὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῇ Νικαίᾳ πατέρων ὅρος, καθ’ ἑκάστην ἐπαρχίαν τοὺς τῆς ἐπαρχίας, καὶ εἴπερ ἐκεῖνοι βούλοιντο, σὺν αὐτοῖς τοὺς ὁμόρους, πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον ποιεῖσθαι τὰς χειροτονίας*).]

I came to Bourges at the request of its citizens, issued by decree. The reason for the summons was the tottering condition of the Church, which, recently deprived of its supreme bishop, sounded a kind of trumpet-call to seek the priesthood from both orders of society. [Col. 0568C] The people seethe, divided by factions: a few propose others, while many not only put themselves forward but force themselves forward.

If you consult, according to your manly share of responsibility, in accordance with God and truth, everything comes rushing in light, shifting, and painted over—and what shall I say? Only shamelessness is simple there. Unless you should judge my complaint unjust, I would dare to say that most of them are so headlong and dangerous in spirit that they do not shrink from seeking the sacred see and its dignity by offering a price; and the matter could long ago have been put up for sale and auction, if a buyer ready to purchase it could be found as readily as a seller desperate enough to sell it.

Therefore I ask you to adorn the novelty, modesty, and necessity of my office by the companionship of your distinguished arrival, and to protect it by your assistance. Nor, although you are the head of Senonia, should you withdraw from these uncertainties your attention to the healing of the Aquitanians, since it matters very little that the province in our dwelling is divided, when the matter is joined in religion.

[Note: The fourth province of Lugdunensis, as observed at Letter 18 of Book IV.]

Moreover, of the cities of Aquitania Prima, only the town of Auvergne remained to the Romans; wars brought the rest into other hands. [Col. 0569A]

[Note: As in Book IV, Letter 18, concerning Lugdunensis Secunda. Provinces, when they were originally undivided, were later often divided into several at the command of the emperors. Hence the names arose by which some were called First, others Second, Third, and so forth according to the number of provinces. There were therefore two Aquitanias: the First, whose capital was Bourges, and the Second, whose capital was Bordeaux. Whenever provinces were divided, the part containing the metropolis—which had been the capital of the entire province before the division—always retained the name First: thus Narbonensis Prima was the province containing Narbo, Lugdunensis Prima the one containing Lugdunum, and Aquitania Prima the one containing Bourges. Hence the metropolitans of the First Provinces were primates over the other provinces bearing the same name. Just as the bishop of Lugdunum, as is clear from Gregory’s Letters 35 and 36 of Book VI, is Primate of the four Lugdunensian provinces, so the bishop of Bourges was Primate of both Aquitanias. Much the same custom prevailed in other provinces when one became several: the primate was the bishop of the province that was first and oldest among the metropolitan sees.]

Accordingly, in appointing the bishop of the aforesaid city, we lack the required number of provincial colleagues unless we are reinforced by the assent of the metropolitans.

For the rest, as far as concerns the prerogative of your honor, no one has hitherto been named by me, no one invited, no one elected. Everything is preserved for your judgment, untouched and entire. I take upon myself only this: to invite your persons, await your wishes, and praise your decisions; and when each man is appointed to the place and rank of bishop, then, according to your command, obedience will proceed from me.

But if—which I nevertheless think will hardly happen—an ill-advising interpreter should oppose my requests before you, you will be able to excuse your absence rather than your fault. Conversely, if you come, you will show that a limit could indeed be placed upon your region, but not upon your charity.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Basilius.

[Note: Probably to the bishop of Aquae Sextiae. The reason for this conjecture is that near the end of the letter he says that Basilius was situated midway between Leontius of Arles, Faustus of Riez, and Graecus, bishop of Massilia; and the metropolitan city of Aquae lies almost midway between those cities. The prudent counsel and action of this Basilius, then still a presbyter, at the funeral of Hilary, bishop of Arles, are narrated by the author of Hilary’s life.]

By God’s gift, the ancient rights of friendship are ours, an example new to our times; and it has long been the case that we love one another equally. Moreover, as concerns our common conscience, you are my patron—although I speak of this itself presumptuously and arrogantly. For my iniquity is so great that even the effectiveness of your supplication can scarcely heal the continual recurrence of my falls.

Since, therefore, you are twice my lord, alike through patronage and affection, and since I remember well how powerful you are in the fire of feeling and the fountain of speech: I have seen the Gothic citizen Modaharius brandishing the darts of the Arian heresy and have seen with what sword of spiritual testimony you pierced him, while preserving both the reverence due to the other bishops and peace. It is not unjustly, then, that I lament to you how the wolf of this age, who fattens himself on the sins of dying souls, gnaws in secret at the ecclesiastical folds with a bite whose tooth has not yet been recognized.

For the ancient enemy, in order that he may attack more easily the bleating of sheep left without protection, first begins to threaten the necks of shepherds who are asleep. Nor am I so mindful of myself that I fail to remember that I am such a shepherd—one whose conscience still weighs upon him and must be washed by long weeping; yet whose filth, under Christ’s protection, will one day be dug out by the mystical rakes of your prayers.

But since public welfare rises above the shame of private guilt, I shall not fear, even if a hostile interpreter attacks my zeal on me, to disclose the cause of truth under the suspicion of vanity.

Evarix, king of the Goths, whether he protects or extends the frontier of his kingdom by the right of arms, after breaking and dissolving the ancient treaty, is not something that we sinners are permitted here to accuse, nor something that you saints are permitted here to investigate.
