[Note: Euricus, also called Eoricus, in Book VIII, Letter 9. Thus Deudorix in Strabo, and Theuderis and Theodoricus, are one name. Gregory of Tours mentions this persecution of the Catholics by Euricus, as well as Sidonius’ letter, in Book II, chapter 25: “In the time of Sidonius, Evarix, king of the Goths, crossing beyond the Spanish frontier, inflicted a severe persecution upon the Christians in Gaul. He cut down everywhere those who did not consent to his perversity, forced the clergy into prison, and sent some priests into exile and butchered others with the sword. For he also ordered the entrances of the sacred temples themselves to be closed with thorns, evidently so that the rarity of entry might cause forgetfulness of the faith. At that time the cities of Novempopulana and of the two Aquitanias were especially devastated by this calamity.” Sidonius’ distinguished letter to Bishop Basilius on this subject is still extant. So much for Gregory, following Sidonius’ footsteps. The cities of Novempopulana are Elusa, Vasates, Convenae, and Ausci; the rest belong to the two Aquitanias. But Gregory’s text is corruptly printed: “the two Germanias.”]

Rather, if you ask, it is a matter of order that here the rich should be clothed in purple and linen, while here Lazarus should be afflicted with sores and poverty. It is a matter of order that, while we move about in this allegorical Egypt, Pharaoh should proceed with his diadem and the Israelite with his basket. It is a matter of order that, while we are being baked in the furnace of this figurative Babylon, we should mourn spiritual Jerusalem with Jeremiah in sighing wails, while Assur, thundering with royal arrogance, tramples the holy things of the saints.

Observing these exchanges between present and future blessedness, I endure our common hardships more patiently. First, because, when I look within and consider what I deserve, whatever adversity should come will seem lighter to me; and next, because I know for certain that the greatest remedy for the inner person is for the outer person to be threshed in this threshing-floor of the world by the various scourges of suffering.

But I must admit that, although the aforesaid king of the Goths is terrifying because of the merits of his strength, I fear that he is lying in wait not so much for Roman walls as for Christian laws. So much, they say, does the mention of the Catholic name taste bitter to his mouth and his heart that you might wonder whether he holds primacy more in his own nation or in his own sect. Moreover, powerful in arms, fierce in spirit, vigorous in years, he suffers from this one error: he thinks that success in negotiations and counsels is granted to him on behalf of the lawful religion, when in fact he achieves it through earthly prosperity.

Therefore, Catholics, learn quickly the hidden illness of your condition, so that you may hasten to apply an open remedy.

Bordeaux, Périgueux, Rodez, Limoges, Gévaudan, Elusa, Vasates,

[Note: There is no injustice in placing the Elusans before the other peoples of Novempopulana. There was a time when Elusa was the metropolis of the whole province, with the city of the Auscians under it along with the others; the city of the Auscians is now the metropolis. This is attested not only by the ancient lists of provinces, in which the cities of Novempopulana are described as follows—“the metropolitan city of the Elusans, the city of the Aquenses, and last, after the others, the city of the Auscians”—but also by the subscriptions of ancient councils. At the Council of Agde, Clarus, metropolitan of Elusa, and Nicetius, bishop of the Auscians, subscribed; at the First Council of Orléans, Leontius, not of Toulouse, as it was incorrectly printed, but of the metropolitan city of Elusa, and the same Nicetius, bishop of the Auscians, subscribed. Finally, at the Council of Reims, according to Flodoard, Book II, chapter 5, Senocus of Elusa and Audericus of Auch likewise subscribed; and the same example is found elsewhere for as long as Elusa remained a metropolis. Now, what changes fortune brings! It has been reduced almost to a village, without a bishop. Scaliger rightly taught, in his commentary on Ausonius, that the inhabitants call it Eusa or Eosa. They are mistaken, however, and attribute an error to Ammianus Marcellinus when, in his words in Book XV—“In Narbonensis Narbo and Toulouse are enclosed”—they wish *clausa* to be read as *Elusam*. For Elusa is in Novempopulana, not in Narbonensis. No less mistaken are those who identify Eluson in Paulinus’ Letter 6, or Elusion, as it appears in the Bordeaux Itinerary, with Elusa, since Elusio was situated between Toulouse and Narbo in Narbonensis, while Elusa lay between Auch and Bordeaux in Novempopulana, as stated above. To it also belongs the old inscription from Nîmes containing the epitaph of L. Taurinus Aurelius, a citizen of Elusa.]

Convenae, and the Auscians—and a much larger number of cities, after their chief priests had been cut down by death,

[Note: Victor of Utica likewise laments this in the Vandal persecution, speaking of the bishops driven into exile by Huneric: “When, while they were in exile, death came upon them, they were not permitted to ordain others in their cities. Therefore, when the bishops had been removed by death and others were not substituted in their place, through whom presbyters, deacons, and clergy of the lower orders might be appointed, it was inevitable that the greatest desolation should follow in all the churches.”]

and no bishops subsequently being substituted in the offices of those who had died—through whom, of course, the ministries of the lower orders would have been supplied—has drawn out a broad limit of spiritual ruin.

It is generally agreed that this deficiency of the fathers who die advances day by day so far that it could bend not merely any heretics of the present but even the heresiarchs of former times. Thus the sad despair of interrupted faith weighs upon peoples deprived of their bishops.

There is no care for the deserted dioceses and parishes. You may see in the churches either the rotten collapse of roofs or, with the doors torn from their hinges, the entrances of the basilicas blocked by thickets of bristling brambles. You may see, alas, cattle lying not only in vestibules that stand half open, but even grazing the grassy sides of green altars.

But now solitude is found not only throughout rural parishes; the gatherings of the urban churches themselves are also growing sparse. For what comfort remains to the faithful when not only clerical discipline but even its memory perishes? Indeed, whenever a cleric dies, if he does not receive an heir to his dignity through a succession of blessing, the priesthood dies in that church, not the priest.

And so what hope, you may ask, can remain where the end of a man brings the end of religion? Look more deeply into the losses of the spiritual members; you will surely understand that, as many bishops are taken away, so the faith of just as many peoples is placed in danger.

I say nothing of your colleagues Crocus and Simplicius,

[Note: A letter of Lucidus the presbyter is addressed, among others, to Bishop Crocus. From this it is clear that he attended the Council of Arles. He was bishop of Nîmes; concerning Simplicius, there is no certainty.]

whom, expelled from the sees entrusted to them, a similar punishment of exile torments in dissimilar ways. One of them grieves that he does not see where he may return; the other grieves that he sees where he cannot return.

You are situated midway, in city, order, and affection, among the most sacred bishops Leontius, Faustus, and Graecus. Through you the business of treaties passes; through you the agreements and terms of both kingdoms are conveyed.

Work to ensure that this friendship becomes princely concord: with episcopal ordination permitted, let us hold in the faith the peoples of Gaul whom the boundary of the Gothic allotment has enclosed, even if we do not hold them by treaty.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Graecus.

[Note: To the bishop of Massilia, mentioned above. It was written at the time when, under the peace treaty concluded by Nepos with Euricus, the Auvergnats—whom the Goths had been unable to capture by force—were ordered to be handed over, as stated in Letter 1 of Book III. For this reason Sidonius rightly complains that the condition of the Auvergnats had been better during war than under peace.]

Behold, once again our trifling Amantius is returning to his Massilia, to carry home, as is his custom, something from the city’s spoils—if only the merchant voyage smiles upon him. Through him I would chatter at greater length in jest, if the same spirit were equally capable of practicing cheerfulness and enduring grief.

For this is now the condition of our unhappy corner of the world; and, as report confirms, its condition was better under war than under peace. Our slavery has become the price of another’s security. Alas, the slavery of the Auvergnats! If ancient matters were recalled, these were once bold enough to call themselves brothers of Latium and to reckon their peoples by Trojan blood. If recent events are remembered, they are the men who with their own strength held back the weapons of public enemies; the Goth was often no object of fear to this people when enclosed within walls, while in turn the same people became a terror to attackers stationed within their camps. They are the men who, against the battle-line of their neighbors, served alike as commanders and soldiers.

Yet concerning the outcome of their battles: if anything prosperous occurred, you were comforted by the favorable results; if anything adverse, the disasters broke them. They, through their love of the commonwealth,

[Note: Concerning this, see Book II, Letter 1, and Book V, Letter 23.]

did not fear to hand Seronatus over to the laws, though he was pouring the provinces out to the barbarians; and once he was convicted, the commonwealth scarcely dared to execute him.

Did poverty, fire, sword, pestilence, swords made fat by slaughter, and warriors made lean by fasting deserve this? [186] Yet in expectation of this celebrated peace we drew grasses torn from the cracks in the walls for food. We were often infected through ignorance by poisonous plants, which, green with indistinguishable leaves and juices, were repeatedly gathered by hands whose color matched that of hunger.

For such and so many proofs of devotion, our people have suffered a loss, as I hear. We beg you to be ashamed of this treaty, neither useful nor honorable. Embassies pass through you. To you first, although the prince is absent, not only are negotiations already conducted disclosed, but those still to be conducted are entrusted.

We ask that the harshness of truth be pardonable in your ears; grief removes the odium of this reproach. You consult too little for the common good; and when you assemble in council, you are concerned less with healing public dangers than with pursuing private fortunes. Since you have done this often and for a long time, you have now begun not to be first among your fellow provincial bishops but last.

[Note: The bishops of the province of Arles. Massilia had once belonged to the province of Vienna, but in Sidonius’ time it was assigned to Arles. By then, through the decree of Leo the Great, the province of Vienna had already been divided into two, so that one part belonged to the metropolitan see of Vienna and the other to Arles. Among the cities of the province of Arles, Massilia had formerly been first, followed by Avignon, Orange, Carpentras, Vaison, and others. Thus the Massilian bishops were originally first among their fellow provincials. But now, says Sidonius, since nearly all the other cities had been reduced under Gothic or Burgundian power, they had begun to be not first in that province but last.]

But how long can these tricks continue? For our superiors will not long boast of this title, since they are beginning to have no subordinates.

Therefore, by whatever counsel you can offer, cut short this disgraceful condition of the treaty. If it is still necessary to be besieged, still to fight, still to hunger, we are willing. But if we are being handed over—though we could not be taken by force—you have certainly discovered, cowardly men, what barbarous counsel to give.

But why do we loosen the reins to excessive grief? Rather, forgive the afflicted, and do not charge it against those who mourn. [Col. 0574A] For another region, once surrendered, hopes for servitude; Auvergne expects punishment.

If you cannot heal our final wounds, at least accomplish this through diligent prayer: let the blood of those whose liberty is destined to die continue to live. Prepare land for exiles, ransom for captives, and travel provisions for those who will wander. If our wall is opened to enemies, let your hospitality not be closed to guests.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Euphronius.

[Note: To the bishop of Autun, to whom Letter 2 of Book IV is addressed and whom the final letter of Book IX concerns. He is venerated among the saints on the third day before the Nones of August. He subscribed to the letter of Faustus and to the Council of Arles. Before his episcopate he built the basilica of Saint Symphorian in his own city, as Gregory of Tours records in Book II, chapter 15. We possess a letter from him and Lupus of Troyes concerning bigamous clerics and those who married wives; we lack another letter which, according to Hydatius, he wrote to Count Agrippinus concerning prodigies seen in Gaul around the arrival of Attila.]

Since the bonds of clerical office bind me, I would pronounce the condition of my modest station most fortunate if our walls were as near to one another as our territories.

[Note: The Auvergnats border the Aedui. Thus nothing intervenes between the dioceses and territories of the two peoples; but considerable distances of several days lie between the cities themselves.]

In matters of the least importance, then, I would consult your crown, and in matters of the greatest importance as well. The course of my actions would be like the calmest and most unobstructed flow of some river if it flowed from your counsel as from a most health-giving spring. Without doubt it would then be neither frothy through boastfulness, nor muddy through pride, nor foul through conscience, nor headlong through youth. Rather, if anything dirty and rotten clung to it, the stream of your counsel, mingled with it, would dissolve the whole.

But because long stretches lie between us and obstruct wishes of this kind, I earnestly ask you to release one consulting you from the difficulty of an uncertainty into which he has fallen. Since the people of Bourges are demanding that the distinguished man Simplicius be ordained bishop, decide what I ought to do in so weighty a matter.

For you possess such graciousness toward me and such authority among the rest that, if you wish anything to be done—and you will wish whatever is most equitable—you ought not so much to advise as to command.

Concerning Simplicius, however, know that many good things are reported, and by many good men. At first glance these testimonies did not seem pleasing to me, because they seemed too favorable. But after I saw that his rivals did nothing more than remain silent, especially those who support the faith of the Arians, and that no unlawful objection was raised against him, although he does not yet belong to our profession, I realized that a man may be judged most exacting concerning whom a bad citizen could not speak and a good one could not remain silent.

But why have I foolishly added these things, as though I were giving advice after having asked for it? Rather, everything will be arranged according to your nod, judgment, and letters, and will be made known to priests and people. For we are not so entirely foolish that we would not first decide to summon you, if it is possible for you to come, and, if not, at least to consult you—since in every matter we shall obey.

Remember to be mindful of me, my lord pope.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius sends greetings to Bishop Perpetuus.

[Note: To the bishop of Tours, metropolitan of Lugdunensis Tertia, over whose province he presided at two councils, the Council of Vannes and the Council of Tours. Sidonius therefore sends him the sermon which he delivered to the people of Bourges during the election of Bishop Simplicius. Concerning Perpetuus and the basilica of Saint Martin which he built, see what was already said in Book IV, Letter 18. Paulinus mentions him with praise in several places in Book VI of the *Life of Saint Martin*, and in his verses concerning Nepotulus.]

Desiderius to Sidonius: Since you are thoroughly familiar with the library of the Catholic faith through both authoritative writers and disputants, you wish to know even those things that are especially unworthy, as you yourself suppose, of occupying your ears’ attention. For you instruct me to send you the address which I seem to have delivered to the people of Bourges in the church—an address to which neither rhetorical division, nor oratorical threats, nor grammatical figures supplied appropriate elegance and order. For there, as is customary with those who plead their case precisely, I did not care to fit in either historical weights, poetic patterns, or sparks of controversial clausulae. When factional quarrels, partisanships, and divisions were dragging me in different directions, injury supplied me with material for dictation, while lack of time carried it away.

Indeed, the crowd of candidates was so great that the very numerous aspirants to a single episcopal chair could not have been accommodated even by two benches. Everyone pleased himself; everyone displeased everyone else. Nor could we have reached any common decision unless the people, making a sacrifice of their own judgment, had been appeased and submitted themselves instead to sacerdotal judgment: while a few of the presbyters chattered in corners [Note: Like sparrows’ manner of chattering. For it is characteristic of sparrows to chirp or twitter. Hence Sidonius, Book IX, Letter 2: “He properly called them the whispering chirps of sparrows”; and *fringillus* is a kind of sparrow. The Glosses: σπίνος ὁ στρουθός, “the finch, the sparrow,” *fringillus*.]; while, in public, most did not even mutter, because the majority feared their own order no less than the others.

Thus, while each individual publicly avoided all the others, it came about that everyone listened without disdain to what they would thereafter eagerly seek. Therefore take the page appended to the volumes below: dictated, with Christ as my witness, during two watches of a single summer night. I greatly fear that you will believe the reading itself—which demonstrates what it is—more than you believe me. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## ADDRESS

190 Secular history reports, beloved, that one of the philosophers first taught his arriving disciples the patience of keeping silent rather than the practice of speaking; and that he kept each beginner mute for five years among the chairs of disputing fellow-students, so that even the quicker talents of some might not be praised before they deserved to be recognized. Thus it happened that, after a long silence, when they began to speak, everyone began to listen to them and did not remain silent; for until nature has absorbed knowledge, it is no greater glory to have said what you know than to have kept silent about what you do not know.

But now a very different condition awaits my mediocrity: as I move through sighing chasms and the mire of sins, the burden of this profession has been laid upon me. Before I can render the obedience of a learner to any of the good, I am compelled to owe the duty of a teacher to others. This impossibility is increased by the burden of embarrassment: you have entrusted me with the authority to choose a bishop through a decretal document [Note: What we noted concerning the votes of the people in the election of bishops in the final letter of Book IV applied equally to the assemblies for creating a metropolitan. Presiding over these assemblies was the man who preceded his provincial colleagues by right of precedence. Leo the Great, Letter 82 to Anastasius, says: “When the metropolitan has died, the provincial bishops must assemble in the metropolitan city, so that, after the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best presbyter, or even deacon, of that Church may be chosen.” Thus the people of Bourges would have acted according to the old custom. But once the provincials had been removed by Euric, bishops from neighboring provinces had to be summoned; and since the people, uncertain whom they should seek from the large number of candidates, were unable to decide, by common decree they placed their votes in the judgment and will of Sidonius, bishop of Clermont. Sidonius chose Simplicius, a distinguished man [Note: This means not the surname *Benedictus*, but an epithet with which many people adorned Christian men. Paulinus, Letter 9 to Severus: “Another little book is among those which I seem to have written to Endelechius, my blessed—that is, Christian—friend.” Endelechius’s names were indeed Sanctus Severus Endelechius, as has been observed elsewhere. Thus *blessed Paschasius* in the same Paulinus’s letter to Victricius; *blessed Eleutherus* in Tertullian’s *On the Prescription of Heretics*; *blessed Pope Cyprian* in the letter of the Roman clergy to the Carthaginian clergy; *blessed Paulinus* in Faustus of Riez; and *blessed Tetradius* and *blessed Agricola* in Gregory of Tours, *Glory of the Confessors* 86 and *History* Book III, 16.].]

—in the presence of a most holy and most eminent pontiff [Note: Agroecius of Sens, whom he had invited in Letter 5. Before this metropolitan, therefore, he was to speak about the election of the metropolitan of Bourges, while himself only a provincial bishop—although among the bishops of First Aquitaine he held the leading place as bishop of Clermont.]. Since he is the head of his province and is superior to me in training, eloquence, privilege, length of service, and age, I, both a provincial and younger man, must endure equally the embarrassment of inexperience and the ill will of the insolent, while speaking before a metropolitan. But since your error has so pleased you that I, lacking wisdom, should seek for you, with Christ’s help, a wise bishop in whom many good qualities converge, know that by such an assent I receive much honor, but more responsibility.

First of all, consider the great burden of public opinion: you have imposed perfected judgments upon a beginner and demand from me the straight path of the council in a matter where you still remember that you recently went astray. Therefore, since this is what you desired, I ask that, as you trust us by faith to be, so you may make us through intercession; and deign rather to raise our humility to heaven through your prayers [Note: He rejects the empty applause that the crowd of hearers used frequently to raise, even in sacred sermons. Chrysostom likewise says in *On the Statues* XI: “What benefit do I gain from these clappings? What from these praises and uproars? My praise is that all of you demonstrate by your deeds what has been said.” Some homilies of Bernard show that this custom continued even in his time.] than through applause.

Yet first you ought to know into what Scyllas of abuse and what whirlpool of the barking of certain human tongues, attempting to defame you, I have been cast. Such is the force of evil customs that the crimes of a few disfigure the innocence of the multitude [Col. 0577A], whereas, conversely, the rarity of the good cannot excuse the offenses of the many through shared virtues.

If I name some monk, even though the distinction of a practiced anchorite accompanies him and he may be compared with Pauls, Antonys, Hilarions, and Macariuses, immediately my ears, surrounded by an uncouth uproar, are struck by the muttering of base dwarfs who complain: “This man who is being named fulfills the office not of a bishop but rather of an abbot; he can intercede more for souls before the heavenly judge than for bodies before an earthly one.”

But who would not grow angry on seeing the purity of virtues dirtied by the accusation of vices? If we choose a humble man, he is called contemptible; if we put forward an upright man, he is judged proud. If he is less educated, he is thought worthy of ridicule because of his ignorance; if he is somewhat learned, he is called inflated because of his knowledge. If he is strict, he is feared as cruel; if indulgent, he is blamed for laxity. If simple, he is despised as stupid; if sharp, he is avoided as cunning. If diligent, he is declared superstitious; if relaxed, he is judged negligent. If skillful, greedy; if quiet, he is pronounced lazy. If we put forward an abstainer, he is taken for a miser; if one who nourishes himself by dining, he is attacked for gluttony; if one who fasts while feeding others, he is accused of vanity.

They condemn freedom as wickedness; they disdain modesty as rusticity; they do not love the strict because of his austerity; among them the charming become cheap through their fellowship. And however one may live among them, the conduct of the good will always be snagged by the tongues of slanderers, as though by the two-headed hooks of barbs.

Meanwhile, the stiff-neckedness of the people and the license of the clergy submit only with difficulty to monastic discipline. If I mention a cleric, those who come after imitate him, while those who came before disparage him. For a few of them—said with the peace of the rest—reckon that only length of clerical service should be counted as merit, so that when we consecrate a bishop they wish us to choose not usefulness but age, as though one ought to have lived a long time rather than well in order to attain the highest priesthood, in place of the privilege, adornment, and embellishment of every grace.

And so men who are sluggish in service but swift in slander, idle in deliberations but occupied in seditions, weak in charity but strong in faction, steadfast in preserving rivalries but wavering in asserting opinions, strive to rule the Church, although old age already requires them to be ruled.

But I do not wish, on account of the ambitions of a few, to mark out the persons of the many any longer. I assert only this: although I now name no one, he confesses his rejection who declares his offense. I say more freely that among the surrounding multitude there are many who possess episcopal qualities, but that they cannot all be bishops; and although individuals possess the distinctive features of different gifts, everyone is sufficient for himself, while no one is sufficient for all.

If I happen to name a military man, immediately this is said: “Sidonius was transferred to the clergy from a secular profession; therefore he pretends not to be able to obtain a metropolitan from a religious congregation. He swells with noble birth, is made arrogant by the insignia of rank, and despises Christ’s poor.” Therefore for the present I shall fulfill the trust that I owe not so much to the charity of the good as to the suspicion of slanderers.

The Holy Spirit, our almighty God, lives; he condemned through Peter’s voice Simon Magus, who thought that the grace of blessing could be bought for a price. I swear that, in the man whom I judged suitable for you, I have favored neither money nor personal influence; after weighing the circumstances sufficiently and more than sufficiently—of the person, the time, the province, and the city—I have believed him to be the most suitable man, whose life will be briefly recounted in what follows.

Blessed Simplicius, hitherto belonging to you and henceforth, if God grants it through you, to be regarded as a companion of our order, answers both parties in conduct and profession, so that the state may find in him something to admire and the Church something to love.

If reverence is owed to birth—and the evangelist shows that birth must not be disregarded, for when Luke undertook to praise John, he counted it most excellent that John came from a priestly line, and, intending to praise the nobility of his life, first exalted the dignity of his family—then his parents presided either over episcopal chairs or over tribunals. His illustrious ancestry in both modes of life flourished either through bishops or through prefects; thus his forebears always dared to dictate either human or divine law.

But if we weigh his own person with more careful consideration, we find that he holds here a place among the distinguished leaders [Note: Municipal leading men, *principales*. The Glossary: “Leader,” πρωτοπολίτης, “chief townsman” or “leading citizen.” Above, in Letter 8, he called Simplicius “a distinguished man.” To Eucherius and Pannichius he wrote in Books III and V.]. But you say that the illustrious men Eucherius and Pannichius are regarded as superior. Let them have been considered so until now; but for the present case they are not required by canon, since both have entered into second marriages [Note: According to the canons, bigamists cannot be bishops; indeed, not even clerics of any rank, according to the first canon of the Synod of Valence and various other authorities, although the rules concerning orders of the lower ranks varied according to local custom.].

If we count his years, he possesses the effectiveness of youth and the counsel of old age. If we compare his learning or talent, nature contends with education. If humaneness is required, it is offered to citizen, cleric, stranger, the least and the greatest, even beyond what is sufficient; and more than once the man who was not going to return it acknowledged his own bread from him.

If the need to undertake an embassy has arisen, he has more than once stood on behalf of this city before kings clad in skins and before purple-robed princes. If there is doubt under what teacher he was imbued with the rudiments of faith, to speak proverbially, he had at home someone from whom he could learn.

Finally, this is the man, beloved, for whom, when he was held in the darkness of prison, the doors of a barbarian jail, secured by many locks, were divinely opened. You will cry out that this man ought to be led to the priesthood, leaving behind both his father-in-law and his father [Note: From this it is clear that Palladius and Eulodius, who had been the immediately preceding bishops of Bourges, were respectively Simplicius’s father-in-law and father. Palladius’s daughter was therefore Simplicius’s wife. Below: “His wife descended from the stock of the Palladii.”]. At that time he brought especially great praise to his household, when he preferred to be honored by the dignity of his parents rather than by his own.

I had almost passed over what ought not to have been passed over. In the days of Moses, as the psalmist says, in ancient times, when the form of the tabernacle of the covenant was being raised, all Israel in the wilderness heaped up before the feet of Bezalel the symbolic offering of contributed expenditure. Later Solomon, in order to build the temple in Jerusalem, shook the solid resources of the people into the work, although the captured wealth of the Philistines and the tribute payments of the surrounding kings, together with the treasure of the southern queen of Sheba, increased the hoard.

This man built you a church while young, a soldier, poor, alone, still a son in his father’s household and already a father. Neither the thrift of the old nor the sight of the young held him back from his intended devotion; and yet he possessed a character formed to remain silent [Note: He was so composed in character that, avoiding praise, he suppressed in silence the church he had founded. Ruricius uses the same expression in Letter 14: “I have sent the horse you ordered: gentle in temper, strong in limb, firm in strength, excellent in appearance, well-formed in build, and restrained in spirit.”].

For he is, unless I am mistaken, a man wholly removed from popular seeking: he does not court the favor of everyone, but of the good; he is not cheapened by indiscriminate familiarity, but made precious by tested fellowship. In good manliness he wishes to benefit his rivals more than to please them, resembling strict fathers who consider not so much the wishes of their young sons as their welfare.

Steadfast in adversity, faithful in uncertainty, modest in prosperity, simple in dress, genial in speech, equal in companionship, outstanding in counsel. He eagerly seeks tested friendships, steadfastly retains them, and preserves them forever. He practices declared enmities honorably, is slow to believe, and quick to lay them aside. He is all the more worthy to be sought because he is least ambitious; he does not strive to obtain the priesthood, but to deserve it.

Someone will say to me: “How have you learned so much about him so quickly?” I reply: I knew the people of Bourges before I knew Bourges itself. We come to know many people on the road, many in military service, many in business, many in deliberation, many in their own country, and many in our exile. Much knowledge also comes through reputation, and reputation provides shortcuts, because nature has not set such narrow boundaries for fame as it has for one’s homeland.

Therefore, if the condition of cities is to be assessed not so much by the circuit of their walls as by the renown of their citizens, I recognized not only what you were but also where you were.

His wife descended from the stock of the Palladii, who held, with honor to their order, either chairs of learning or seats at the altars. Since the dignity of a matron requires that she be mentioned modestly and briefly, I shall assert confidently that this woman answers to the priesthoods of both families, both where she was raised and where, after being chosen, she went.

They both train their sons well and wisely. Compared with them, the father begins to be happier precisely because he is surpassed by them.

And since you have sworn that the judgment of my smallness will prevail in this election—for it is no stronger to speak oaths than to write them—in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I declare that Simplicius ought to become metropolitan of our province and high priest of your city.

But you, if you follow my new judgment concerning the man of whom we speak, agree with it in accordance with your former one.

## LETTER X

Sidonius to Auspicius, bishop of Toul among the Leuci [Note: Written at the time when the Goths were waging war against the Romans and the Burgundians were, as stated above, assisting the people of Clermont against the Goths.], sends greetings.

If the circumstances of times and regions permitted it, I would take care to cultivate friendships once begun not merely through the duties of words. But since the storm of warring kingdoms strongly interrupts the hope of fraternal peace, at least among those who are separated and far apart, the custom of correspondence will rightly be maintained; long ago introduced under the pretext of affection, it now receives approval from ancient examples.

It remains for you to pardon the failure of your anxious admirer to pay his due visit. The reason he cannot constantly enjoy the sacred contemplation of your presence is that he now fears danger from neighbors, now jealousy from patrons. But there is much more that could be said about these matters.

Meanwhile I commend to you Peter, a man of tribune rank, bearer of our message. He earnestly requests this very favor and can briefly make known what business he brings. I pray that, out of whatever help lies within you, consideration of the present page may assist him, while regard for fairness nevertheless remains—the fairness against which I have never been accustomed to recommend even the causes of my closest friends. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius to Pope Graecus, greetings.

I envy the good fortune of your customary messenger, through whom it has happened that you have often been seen. But why should I speak of Amantius, when I envy even my own letters, which will be opened by your sacred fingers and examined by your eyes? I, meanwhile, enclosed here amid the half-burned narrow spaces of a fragile wall, with the terror of war close at hand, am in no way permitted to satisfy my longing for you.

Would that this were the condition or cause of the territory of Clermont, so that our excuses might be less open to blame. But what is harsher is that, through the merits of our injustice, it comes about that we are not without a just excuse.

Therefore, after offering the greeting required by duty, I earnestly ask you meanwhile to remit the debt of a visit to one who pays it in words. For if peace restores freedom of travel, I shall fear all the more that the constant presence of my company may instead become wearisome. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## LETTER XII

Sidonius [Note: That Tonantius Ferreolus, grandson through a daughter of the consul Syagrius, was praetorian prefect of Gaul may be inferred from Letter 7 of Book I. This letter further teaches that he held that office after A.D. 450, perhaps after Sidonius’s father. For it contains events from Attila’s time, against whom Aetius—whom he calls the liberator of the people of Orléans on the Loire because he freed them from siege—and the Goth Thorismodus fought for the Romans.] sends greetings to Ferreolus.

If I were considering the time, rank, and status of our friendship and kinship rather than your person, then rightly, in this work, however small it may be, the first rubric of titles and the first duties of speech would be dedicated to you. My pen would have proceeded through your ancestral curule offices, while also recounting your patrician insignia; it would not have been silent about your three prefectures, nor would it have denied your Syagrius praise for the proclamations changed so many times [Note: Ambrose mentions the prefecture of Afranius Syagrius at the Council of Aquileia. The following words of his concerning the Eastern bishops must be understood of Syagrius: “Finally, even the prefect of Italy sent a letter, so that, if they wished to assemble, they had the power to do so.” Ammianus Marcellinus also mentions him in Book XXVIII. Sidonius calls it threefold because he continued in that office for three years: namely, in 380, as the laws of the Theodosian Code addressed to Syagrius, prefect of Italy, show—Book VII, 18, and Book XI, 30; then in 381, Book VIII, 5 and 7; and again in 382, the year in which he was also consul, Book XI, 16, and Book XII, 1. Before his prefecture he had been master of offices in 372. Several letters of Symmachus, Book I, are addressed to the same Syagrius. The epigram of Ausonius prefixed at the beginning of the work also celebrates the profound goodwill and intimacy of both men.].

It would then have passed over your father and uncles, who must by no means be omitted; and although it might have grown weary amid the triumphal laurels of your family, it would not thereby have been emptied of strength in explaining the genealogies of your ancestors, so that it became duller in recounting your glory. Even if it had been blunted while writing about the virtues of your forebears, it would again have been sharpened by your own merits.

But as it prepared to send you the greeting owed to you, it considered not what you had been but what you are now. It passed over the Gauls that you administered when they were at their most flourishing. It passed over the fact that you endured Attila, the enemy of the Rhine; Thorismodus, the guest of the Rhône; and Aetius, the liberator of the Loire [Col. 0582A], through the salutary arrangement of your policies alone; and that, because of such great prudence and foresight, the provincials voluntarily placed their necks beneath your chariot with the greatest accompaniment of applause, since you governed the reins of Gaul in such a way that the exhausted landowner was relieved of the yoke of tribute.

It passed over the fiercest king of the Goths, bent by your honeyed, weighty, penetrating, and extraordinary speech [Note: Thorismodus, after obtaining the kingdom, began to be more hostile to the Romans; for that reason he was killed by his brothers, who desired peace. Prosper, with fuller detail, in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Opilio, vir clarissimus: “Among the Goths settled within Gaul, disagreement arose among the sons of King Theodoric, of whom Thorismodus, the eldest, had succeeded his father. When the king began to undertake actions hostile both to Roman peace and to Gothic tranquility, he was killed by his brothers because he persisted irrevocably in harmful policies.” Others also recount Thorismodus’s death, but this is the only account that reveals its cause.]; and he passed over the fact that you removed him from the gates of Arles by a meal, although Aetius could not have removed him in battle [Note: Before the Goths gained possession of Arles, they attempted more than once, unsuccessfully, to take it. I think there were three sieges. The first was by the great King Theodoric, who was repelled by the valor of Aetius, as Prosper records in his *Chronicle*, during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus II and Valentinian Caesar—that is, in A.D. 425, long before Ferreolus’s prefecture; consequently that siege does not belong to this passage. The second was Thorismodus’s, which Sidonius mentions here, attributing to Ferreolus the credit for averting the danger. He says that Ferreolus could have softened the enemy more effectively by a meal than Aetius would have done by arms, had Aetius been present; for thus he alludes to the earlier siege. The third is mentioned by Paulinus in Book VI of *The Life of Saint Martin*, where he tells how Count Aegidius, surrounded by an enemy army, made a sortie and put the enemy to flight, not without the heavenly assistance of Saint Martin. Although he does not name Arles, he clearly indicates it in these words:

> Not otherwise, and in the very same order of events, came  
> The message that that city had been freed from so great a siege,  
> The city that subdued the headlong Rhône with a gentle bridge  
> And joined its twin banks by a connected passage.

I think this should be referred to the time of the younger Theodoric, after the death of Avitus and before he renewed his treaty with Majorian. For Aegidius was then master of the soldiers and did not survive into the time of Euric, by whom Arles was eventually captured together with Marseilles, as Isidore and Jordanes report.].

It passed over all these things, believing that your greeting would more appropriately be joined to the names of bishops than to those of senators [Note: This does not mean that Ferreolus had already become a bishop, but that Sidonius was associating him with bishops by inserting the letter addressed to him among those written to bishops throughout this book. Ferreolus certainly could not have been bishop of Arles, as a learned man has thought, since Leontius, who held that chair at this time, was succeeded there by Aeonius, and Aeonius by Caesarius.]; and it judged that it would be more fitting for you to be counted among Christ’s perfected men than among the prefects of Valentinian.

Nor should a malicious interpreter reproach you for being associated with priests. For gross ignorance of ranks causes some to find fault with this arrangement: when a public festival provides one banquet after another, the guest who is first at the first table comes after the guest who was first at the second. Thus, without conflict, in the judgment of good men one who is more eminent in rank but less religious is reckoned below one most highly honored for religion.

Farewell. Pray for us.

## LETTER XIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Sulpicius.

Himerius, your son, a bishop known to me hitherto little by face but sufficiently by reputation—which was extending in a good direction—recently came from Troyes to Lyon [Note: The printed note calls Sulpicius, to whom the letter was written, *filius Himerii nepos* (“son; Himerius’s grandson”), a syntactically uncertain phrase. It is established that he was trained and promoted by Saint Lupus; but it is uncertain what place he presided over. Some identify him with Camelianus, the successor of Saint Lupus, but this cannot be demonstrated and is refuted in many ways. I suspect rather that he was an abbot than a bishop. Sidonius also calls abbots “bishops,” as he does Abraham in Letter 17.]. There, when I caught a hurried and brief glimpse of him, he restored to us through imitation of his character the holy bishop Lupus—easily the foremost of the Gallic pontiffs—the teacher of his profession and the source of his dignity.

Good heavens! What discernment joined with grace the man possesses, whenever he happens to deliberate or advise! He abounds in wit when consulted and in sweetness when he gives counsel. He is profoundly concerned with learning, especially religious learning, in which he is occupied more with the marrow of meaning than with the foam of words.

Christ is the whole aim, speed, and delay of all his actions. And, what you might wonder at or praise, he does nothing idly, since he does nothing that is not tranquil. He delights in fasts and rests content with food: he clings to the former because of the habit of the cross, and bends toward the latter because of the grace of charity. He exercises the greatest moderation in both, for whenever he decides to dine, he restrains his appetite; whenever he decides to abstain, he restrains his ostentation.

He multiplies his own duties and avoids those of others. Although it would also be fitting for others to meet him in turn, he prefers that mutual honor be owed to him rather than repaid. At a banquet, on a journey, and in an assembly, he yields to those beneath him; with the result that the throng of his superiors more gladly yields place to him.

He regulates his conversation with his interlocutor with the greatest restraint. In it he permits no outsider to suffer embarrassment, no intimate to suffer injury, no trusting person to incur hatred, no curious person to meet rejection, and no suspicious person to encounter wickedness; nor does he allow the knowledgeable to be slandered or the ignorant to be disgraced.

He preserves the dove’s simplicity in church and the serpent’s cleverness in the marketplace; he is judged prudent toward the good, cautious toward the wicked, and cunning toward neither.

What more can I say? He has already returned you to us in your entirety. He has copied, in a delightful likeness, all your moderation, religion, freedom, modesty, and that most chaste tenderness of a refined mind.

Therefore, as much as you wish henceforth to enjoy privacy and indulge in retirement, you may indulge in it; for in my brother Himerius we already possess a grandfather in name, a father in appearance, and both in wisdom.

Farewell.

## LETTER XIV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Philagrius.

Recently, among the most eminent men (and the gathering was numerous), mention was made of you. All agreed in judging everything about you good, although each individually spoke of different kinds of virtue. Indeed, when someone vaunted himself beyond what was reasonable on the basis of your presence, as though he knew you better than the rest, I became angry. For when I could not calmly accept the claim that a man versed in every branch of learning was better known to neighboring rustics than to people more remotely situated but educated, the dispute advanced further. And when some stubbornly argued over this error—for it is characteristic of fools both to be easily refuted and difficult to restrain—I maintained firmly that, if recognition from eloquent friends never comes to learned men, that is harsh, though in any event tolerable: for their talents prevail, talents before which civic ignorance wanders abroad and, with the pen as its aid, extends itself toward the desires of distant provinces. Through the pen, the affection gathered for absent learned persons is often as great as that produced even by personal attentiveness.

[Col. 0583D] Therefore, if this is so, let those who praise faces rather than character cease to reproach the necessity of our common absence. Indeed, if human substance is to be judged more correctly by bulk than by mind, I do not understand what there is to admire greatly in a human being, however far extended in space, since nothing has been produced by the condition of our birth that is equally wretched and helpless. For nature provides, as though in opposition to us, the ox with hair, the boar with bristles, and the bird with feathers; and, in addition, horn, tooth, and claw are their native weapons, whether for attack or defense. But you would judge our limbs to have been thrown into this world rather than brought forth, since nature, like a mother with an open lap, meets the birth of other animals with manifold protection, while she has poured forth only human bodies, against whose weakness she has acted, as it were, like a stepmother.

For, as I judge, I who consider your mind superior to your limbs, there is no equality between us and the beasts. The reasoning of the intellectual soul has raised our condition above cattle through its knowledge of truth and falsehood. If those who mock their friends and observe them not judicially but merely with their eyes should for a while remove this dignity, let them say, I ask, what they think sufficiently excellent or remarkable in the human form.

Is it height? As though this were not often more suitably fitted to beams. Or strength, which reigns more powerfully in the muscular folds of a lion’s neck? Or the beauty of bodily features, which clay more often impresses better upon statues, and wax upon paintings? Or speed, which is more appropriately attributed to dogs? Or vigilance, in which even the owl competes? Or voice, in whose clarity the ass would not yield? Or diligence, with which even the ant does not fear to be compared according to its own measure?

But perhaps they prefer the power of sight, as though the sight of eagles were not superior. They prefer the effectiveness of hearing, as though the bristly boar did not surpass us in hearing. They prefer the subtlety of smell, as though the vulture did not lead us in scent. They prefer the discrimination of taste, as though in this respect we did not yield greatly even to the ape. What should I say about touch, the fifth bodily sense of ours, which philosopher and little worm alike exercise indiscriminately? I say nothing here about seductive appetites, which human pleasure, inclined toward the bestial movement of the flesh in sexual intercourse, shares with the beasts.

Behold the wretchedness which those men prefer and cultivate when, because you are known to them merely by sight, they insult me in their arrogance. But I have always seen that Philagrius whom, if I saw only his silent face, I would not see as Philagrius. Hence the familiar comparison, which someone made in a different case but with the same judgment: “The Roman people did not recognize Marcus Cicero’s son when he was speaking.”

For the dignity and virtue of learning have been proclaimed by universal judgment; by its privilege one ascends through degrees of merit to the highest summit. First, even a bestial body, if it has already been formed, surpasses unformed matter in dignity. Next, an animate body is placed above a formed one. Third, the human mind surpasses the soul of a beast; for just as flesh is inferior to life, so life is inferior to reason. The craftsman God made our substance capable of attaining reason, but the beast incapable of it.

Yet the condition of the human mind possesses a twofold character. For just as, among souls that reason in human fashion, the duller and slower are trampled underfoot by the intelligence of the prudent and keen, so, if there are any who flourish through natural wisdom alone, they readily concede that they are surpassed by the merits of the learned.

Observing these distinctions of rank, I always contemplate that Philagrius with the eye of my heart; my mind makes him known to me through the likeness of our character. Although you please all good men, no one has been able to look inwardly upon you more deeply than the man who strives outwardly to imitate you.

[Col. 0585B] How I shall become a follower of your pursuits will be disclosed in the next part of the page. As I have learned, you love quiet people; I love even the lazy. You avoid barbarians because they are thought to be bad; I avoid them even when they are good. You apply diligence to reading; I too allow myself little harm from laziness in that activity. You fulfill the role of a religious man; I fulfill even the appearance of one. You do not desire what belongs to others; I even turn it to profit, provided I do not lose what is mine. You delight in the companionship of the learned; I call any large crowd ignorant of literary art the greatest solitude. You are said to be extremely cheerful; I too decree that all tears should perish except those shed when someone supplicates God. You are reported to be most humane; no guest has recoiled from our little table as from Polyphemus’ cave. You are said to show the greatest clemency toward servants; nor am I tormented if, whenever mine have sinned, they are not tormented every time. You think one should fast on alternate days? I do not hesitate to follow you. Should one dine? I am not ashamed to go ahead.

For the rest, if it is granted me, through Christ’s gift, to see you, may I rejoice as one from whom nothing lesser than what I have learned about you has been taken away. Moreover, I now know well what is greater in you. Because of this, it may more easily happen that, if I should ever inspect your face when you are present before me, some fresh joy concerning you will come to me rather than any new judgment.

Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER XV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Salonius.

[Col. 0585C] **Note:** To a man of Vienne, though not a bishop; some have inferred that he was one from the mention of a brother. From this they conjectured that he was one of Salonius and Veranus, brothers and sons of Eucherius, born before their episcopate. Yet from Salvian’s words in his letter to Eucherius it is clear that Eucherius’ sons, while their father was still alive—that is, when Sidonius was scarcely a boy—had already begun to serve as bishops, teachers of churches. Sidonius does not indicate that these brothers were bishops. They therefore seem to have been other men. The letter of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus, bishops, written to Pope Leo and preserved among Leo’s letters, should rather be referred to the sons of Eucherius. Later there was also another Salonius, bishop of Geneva, who subscribed to the Council of Lyon in the time of King Guntram, about a hundred years after Sidonius.]

Whenever I come to Vienne, I would gladly pay the highest price for you and our mutual brother, a resident of the city, to spend more time there—where you share with me not only affection but also a common profession. Yet he evades my reproach under the pretext of his frequenting the suburbs, through which it comes about that he is neither present nor accountable to us; and you have an excuse in the meantime, because a newly recovered possession scarcely yet holds you for long.

Whatever the matter may be, come now. From this point onward you will obtain leave to depart on the condition that you either return in turn or do so later. For however vigorously you may fulfill the duties of farmers while settled in the country, you will truly make your own land fertile if you cultivate the church as much as possible—indeed, if you cultivate it more.

Farewell.

## LETTER XVI

Sidonius sends greetings to Abbot Chariobaud.

You do something equally characteristic of your affection and your character, O unique patron in Christ, when you relieve the cares of an exiled friend with consoling letters. Would that you always remembered me in such a way that, as an exhorter, you lessen the anxieties themselves, linked together by uninterrupted distress, and, as an intercessor, cut them apart.

For the rest, I think that your freedmen, having completed the cases you had entrusted to them, have returned. They are known to have carried out their task so energetically that they needed no assistance. Through them I have sent the nocturnal hood in which, with your limbs exhausted by fasting, you may graciously cover yourself while praying and sleeping. It is true that a shaggy garment is not sent at a very opportune time, now that winter has ended and the season of summer is approaching.

Farewell.

## LETTER XVII

Sidonius sends greetings to his brother Volusianus.

[Col. 0585D] **Note:** Nearly all books add the word “brother”; Sidonius calls Volusianus his brother not only in this letter but also in Book IV, Letter 18. To him Sidonius sends the epitaph of Saint Abraham, a Persian by birth who had been abbot of Saint Cyricus in a monastery outside Clermont, as Gregory of Tours records in his *Life* and in Book II, chapter 21 of his *History*.

You command me, my lord brother, in accordance with the law of friendship, which it is impious to violate, to place my long-idle fingers once more upon the anvils of the old workshop and inscribe a funeral dirge for blessed Abraham, who has died, in mournful verse. I shall swiftly comply with what has been imposed upon me, drawn both by your authority and, above all, by the devotion of the most illustrious man—

[Col. 0585D] **Note:** Sidonius calls him a *comes*, while Gregory of Tours calls him a *dux*: Victor, whom King Euric appointed to govern the Auvergne. Sidonius therefore had in view the administration of a single Auvergne city, whereas Gregory considered the many cities over which Victor presided. Gregory writes in Book II, chapter 20:

“Euric, king of the Goths, placed the duke Victor over seven cities. As soon as he arrived among the Auvergnats, he wished to add the city [of Clermont].”

For in Gregory’s age, and in the period before it, this was the established distinction between counts and dukes: a count governed one city, while a duke governed many cities, each of which had its own count. The same author writes in Book VIII, chapter 18:

“Nicetius, removed from the countship of Auvergne, sought the dukedom from King Childebert; and thus he was appointed duke in the cities of Auvergne, Rodez, and Uzès.”

And in Book IX, chapter 7:

“When Ennodius was administering the dukedom of the cities of Tours and Poitiers, he also received authority over the cities of Vieux-Juliers and Béarn; but when the counts of the city of Tours and of the city of Poitiers went to King Childebert, they obtained his removal from office.”

There was therefore a progression from the countship to the dukedom. Fortunatus wrote to Count Sigoald:

“May King Childebert, as he grows, make you grow also;  
he who now gives you the rights of a count, may give you those of a duke.”

Hence in Visigothic laws the duke of a province is called the count of a city; and hence ecclesiastical writers compare bishops with counts and archbishops with dukes, because bishops governed individual cities, while archbishops governed an entire province.]

—the Count Victor, whom I honor as a client under secular law and love as a son under ecclesiastical law.

[Col. 0587C] **Note:** Gregory writes much about Victor in various places, and his accounts show that Victor was not always consistent with himself. Having fled from the Auvergne because of his lust, he eventually ended his life at Rome, where he was stoned to death for the same crimes. Gregory tells this story in the passage cited above. But in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 33, Gregory says that when Victor refused to offer prayers at Ricomagus before the relics of Saint Amabilis, he was compelled by a divine miracle to obey.]

He showed sufficiently what kind of ardent concern he bore for Christ’s servants when, bent over the bed of the dying bishop no less for his dignity than for his limbs, and made like him in grief before a face paling with approaching death, he showed by tears what he wished done for the man. Since he himself had seized the principal parts of the burial rites, contributing all the equipment and expense appropriate to the funeral of a priest, we at least offer words for the remaining service. We shall inscribe with the scratching impression of our pen nothing else but a testimony to mutual affection. Otherwise, the man’s character, deeds, and virtues would be weighed most inadequately by my words.

[Col. 0587B]

Abraham, rightly to be joined to the holy patrons,  
whom I would not hesitate to call your fellow-companions:  
for they so go before that you yourself soon follow;  
a share in martyrdom grants a portion of the kingdom.

Born beside the Euphrates, you suffered imprisonment for Christ,  
and loosened five-year chains through hunger.  
Escaping the savage king on the coast of Susis,  
you alone hastened all the way to the western land.

But signs of virtue follow the confessor:  
as a fugitive, you drive evil spirits into flight.  
Wherever you come, the crowd of ghosts proclaims itself defeated;  
you command demons to go forth, an exile into exile.

All seek you, and no territory contains you:  
the honor conferred upon you is more burdensome than any other.  
You shun Romulean and Byzantine clamors,  
and the walls shattered by the arrow-bearing Titus.

Alexander’s wall does not hold you, nor Antioch;  
you disdain the Byrsan roofs of the house of Elissa.  
You reject the crowded fields of marshy Ravenna,  
and the places that take their name from wool-bearing swine.

This corner and its poverty-stricken retreat please you,  
and the hut whose roof is pressed down by straw.

[Col. 0587C]

Here you yourself build a venerable temple for God,  
you who had first become God’s temple in your body.  
Here the course of life and of your journey is finished;  
for your labor, a double crown remains.

Now thousands of sacred Paradise surround you;  
now Abraham has you as his fellow-pilgrim.

[Col. 0588A]

Now you enter the homeland from which Adam fell;  
now you can go to the source of your river.

[Col. 0587D] **Note:** “Of the Euphrates.” Abraham was a Persian, born beside the Euphrates. By the dwelling-place of the blessed he means Paradise, alluding to Eden, from which Scripture says that the Euphrates flows. I shall append to this epitaph of Abraham another epitaph, not yet published, I believe, by the presbyter Augustus, which an old manuscript of Saint Mary of Verdun preserves, formerly inscribed in the Basilica of Saint Agnes at Rome.

**EPITAPH OF AUGUSTUS THE PRESBYTER**

Augustus, this tomb indeed covers your limbs,  
but a small earth never encloses your merit.  
The earth holds your body; the heavenly kingdoms, your soul.  
Thus each properly occupies its appointed dwelling.

Devoted to the Lord, you lived with faithful heart,  
fulfilling the office of presbyter in piety.  
Generous to the poor, rich for yourself, dear to your friends,  
you honored the commands of the divine law.

And happy, crowned with so great an honor of praise,  
now may you rightly enjoy perpetual blessings.

Behold, as you had commanded, we have paid the remaining rites due to the buried man. But if, in turn, it is fitting for brothers, friends, and fellow soldiers to obey the commands of charity, then I ask that you also undertake to console his disciples, distinguished by the principles you embody. And quickly form the wavering rule of the abandoned brothers according to the statutes of the fathers of Lérins or of the monks of Grigny.

[Col. 0588C] **Note:** Most of the older manuscripts read this way; it is more correct than the reading of the manuscripts from Grigny. Alcimus Avitus, Letter 65 to Bishop Maximus, writes:

“For some time, occupied with the monasteries of Grigny, I had been absent from my city dwelling.”

The monks of Grigny were in the diocese of Vienne; they are mentioned in the *Life of Saint Clarus, Abbot of Vienne*. Although common copies mistakenly call them “Grimanenses,” the correct form is “Griniacenses.” In those early centuries, before the Rule of Saint Benedict had been adopted, nearly every monastery had its own laws and statutes.]

The holy Auxanius seems indeed to be set over them. As you know, he is somewhat more infirm in body than is fitting and modest in temperament, and therefore readier to obey than to command. He asks that you be entreated to admit him, the master of the monastery, under your own instruction; and, if any of the younger brethren despise him as inexperienced or faint-hearted, that through you alone he may feel that neither quality is scorned with impunity. If any of them are rebellious, punish them yourself; if any are obedient, praise them yourself. What more need be said? If you wish to know briefly what I want, I ask that Brother Auxanius be abbot over the congregation, while you are above the abbot.

[Col. 0588D] **Note:** This does not mean that he himself should be the principal abbot, but that he should ensure that all obey Abbot Auxanius. For the learned man who again makes two grades of abbots here, as though some were principal and others secondary, is no less absurd than his earlier distinction—which we refuted—between bishops of the first and second order. There was indeed, in monasteries, a provost of an inferior rank under the abbot; but Sidonius intends Auxanius to be understood as the abbot appointed over the monks, not as provost.]

Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Constantius.

[Col. 0588D] **Note:** The first letter with which he dedicated the work was addressed to Constantius; this one is likewise addressed to him. This, then, is the end of the Constantian edition, which contained only seven books; the remaining two, which follow, were each added separately afterward.]

With you it begins; with you it will end. I have sent you the requested work, having hastily reread the copies. Only a few came into my hands because, since I had not been planning to compose this little book, the copies could not until now be found, having been left unguarded. I quickly completed these few pieces, which are themselves slight, although once my mind had been stirred it had not yet ceased wanting to write. I carefully maintained this form of moderation: that the text of the letters should not be extended if their number were kept short.

I also judged that the book you, a very refined reader, desired would be sufficiently manageable and not difficult to excuse if, since the lightness of its thoughts and structures might offend you, you were at least burdened less by bundles of pages. I therefore commend the various movements of my heart to your judgment, quite aware that the mind lies open in a book as the face appears in a mirror.

[Col. 0589A] **Note:** There is a parallel in Democritus: “In mirrors the character of the eye is seen, but in conversations the character of the soul is seen.” Cassiodorus Senator says in *Variarum* Book VI, Letter 9: “The words of men are the mirror of the heart.”

I dictated some passages in exhortation, many in praise, some in counsel, a few in mourning, and several in jest. And if you have sometimes found me more impassioned against certain people, know, I wish, that with Christ’s right hand assisting me, I shall never tolerate slavery of spirit. I hold it thoroughly established that judgment concerning human character is divided in two ways. For just as the timid call me rash, so the steadfast call me free.

Among these matters I judge that the role of the man whose opinion must remain hidden is sufficiently prostrate. But I return to my subject. Meanwhile, if you take a breath from your continued reading of Sacred Scripture, you may use these little dirges to distract yourself. Their subject will not cause boredom through its vastness, because, since each topic is nearly concluded in a single letter, once you have quickly learned what you have turned your eyes toward, you will stop reading before you cease wanting to read.

Farewell.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0589]

## LETTER I

Sidonius sends greetings to his Petronius.

[Col. 0589C] **Note:** To an illustrious man, a togatus of Arles, as stated in the note to Book V, Letter 1. At his request this book was published after the preceding ones.]

You are certainly acting beautifully; this is your custom. Persevere, most worthy of the praise of all good men wherever they live, in flattering the glory of your friends wherever there is an opportunity. This is why you also ask that the Arvernian chests be aired out—that is, that the writings stored in them be brought forth. We thought it would be enough if we published anything from what had appeared in the earlier edition.

Therefore we shall comply with your requests, though we shall prolong the labor of our pen only so far that the series of letters, begun, to be sure, from the beginning of the volume, may extend at its outer end to the total of a small number, crowning the completed work, as it were, with a border along its margin.

But we must take greater care lest, because of the late increase of an already published volume, we fall into the hands of certain critics. Even Demosthenes and Cicero, craftsmen of judgment and smiths of eloquence, could not escape tongues naturally sharpened on the whetstone of envy. The earlier orator endured Demades as a detractor, the later Antony his detractor; although those men were renowned for malice but obscure in expression, they reached posterity through their hatred of virtue.

But since you urge me, let us loosen our sails after repeated storms, and let us who have crossed seas as it were navigate this little pond. I have firmly resolved that, just as diligence must be applied in writing, so steadfastness must be maintained in publication. In the end, there is no middle course: either the least of these dangers must be feared, or one must remain entirely silent about everything.

Farewell.

## LETTER II

Sidonius sends greetings to his John.

[Col. 0589C] **Note:** Apparently a grammarian and teacher in some city of Gaul, like Eusebius, a professor of philosophy, in Book III, Letter 1, and Lampridius, a rhetorician of Bordeaux, in Book IX, Letter 13.]

Most learned man, I believed that I would commit an offense against learning if I delayed praising the letters whose extinction you have deferred: letters whose restorer, supporter, and defender you are celebrated as being, so that you alone, as a teacher throughout Gaul in this time of war, have kept the Latin tongue in harbor while weapons have suffered shipwreck.

Therefore our contemporaries and our descendants alike should, with universally fervent prayers, consecrate you as a second Demosthenes and a second Cicero, now in statues, if that is permitted, now in images. Formed and instructed by your teaching, they will retain, in the midst of this unconquered yet foreign people, the likenesses of such ancient men.

For once the successive ranks of dignity have been removed, by which every highest person used to be distinguished from every lowest, the sole mark of nobility hereafter will be knowledge of letters. We, moreover, and the rest of us, are bound by the benefits of your teaching: since we have grown accustomed to writing something and laboring over what future generations may read, at least from your school or teaching there will arise a suitable crowd of readers.

Farewell.

## LETTER III

Sidonius sends greetings to his Leo.

[Col. 0589D] **Note:** A counselor of King Euric; concerning him, see Book IV, Letter 22. You had asked Sidonius to copy for you Philostratus’ *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*. Sidonius sends it and at the same time indicates from what source it was copied: namely, from a manuscript which Victorianus had corrected. He adds further that Victorianus had copied it from the exemplar and correction of Nicomachus, and Nicomachus from Philostratus’ own autograph. Nicomachus and Victorianus, therefore, are names not of the authors who wrote the *Life of Apollonius*, nor of ancient scribes, but of eminent men who corrected texts badly written by copyists for the sake of precision and intellectual pleasure.

Testimonies to this kind of work are common in ancient manuscripts of old authors. In support of our conjecture, and apparently relevant to Sidonius’ passage, many copies of Livy exist in which it is noted that Nicomachus and Victorianus performed the same work on Livy, in these words:

“Nicomachus Dexter, *vir clarissimus*, corrected this according to the copy of my father Clementianus, *From the Foundation of the City*. Victorianus, *vir clarissimus*, was correcting it for the lords Symmachi.”

And elsewhere:

“I, Nicomachus Flavianus, *vir clarissimus*, prefect of the city, corrected this at Henna, *From the Foundation of the City*. Victorianus, *vir clarissimus*, was correcting it for the lords Symmachi.”

Since there were two Nicomachi, Sidonius perhaps added the designation “the elder” so that there could be no ambiguity. Victorianus had corrected Livy for the Symmachi, just as Sidonius here corrected Philostratus for Leo, and in Book V, Letter 15, corrected the *Heptateuch* for Ruricius, while Quintus Symmachus corrected the same Livy for Valerianus in Book IX, Letter 13. “The gift,” he says, “of the entire work of Livy which I promised is still delayed by the diligence of correction.” Learned men did not consider their duty complete when they arranged for a book to be copied for a friend from their manuscripts unless they also made it as accurate as possible through their own work.]

I have sent you the life of Apollonius the Pythagorean, not as the elder Nicomachus copied it from Philostratus, but as Tascius Victorianus copied it from Nicomachus’ notebook, because you had ordered it. As I hurried to comply, it was rapidly run off into a rough copy: a confused, hasty, and obscure transcription.

[Col. 0591C] **Note:** “Copying.” So also in Book IX, Letter 16, concerning copies of his letters: “I copied [them] hastily and under compulsion”; and in Book IX, Letter 11, “the opportunity for copying.” Ruricius likewise writes to our Sidonius in Letter 8: “For I admit that I transferred the manuscript which you had ordered me to receive from my brother Leontius”—that is, as he says afterward, “I copied it.” This passage, as well as another in Book IV, Letter 12, concerning Menander’s *Epitrepontes*, which Sidonius was reading, proves that Sidonius was skilled in the Greek language and refutes those who think otherwise.]

Do not, therefore, fault me for not having worked on the task longer. For while the delay of the walls of Liviana kept me confined—

[Col. 0591D] **Note:** Liviana, a fortress on the borders of the province of Narbonensis, not far from Carcassonne, as may be inferred from Aimoinus, Book II of the *Translation of Saint Vincent*, chapter 4. The Peutinger Map likewise places it between Carcassonne and Narbonne, but calls it Liviana, twelve miles from Carcassonne. After the surrender of the Auvergne, Sidonius was confined by the Goths in this fortress; he professes that he was liberated chiefly through Leo’s efforts.]

—whose hardship, after Christ’s assistance, I owe to you—my troubled mind could not run even in leaps through the material that had to be delivered, sometimes distracted by nightly sighs, sometimes by the duties of the day. Moreover, when the hour of twilight returning from the watch had brought me, exhausted, back to my lodging, scarcely any brief rest was granted to my bent eyes. For immediately there arose the clamor made by two Gothic old women living beside the impluvium of my room; nothing could ever be more quarrelsome, more drunken, or more given to vomiting than they.

When at last some leisure was restored to me, I offered you this unpolished, half-raw book, or, as they say, “new wine,” remembering your desire more than my own duty.

[Col. 0592C] **Note:** “Fresh and uncooked,” like must. Pliny the Younger, for example, called a book *musteum* in Book VIII, Letter 21; Velius Longus used *mustaceum*. Likewise Pliny the Elder uses *musteum caseum* (“fresh cheese”) in Book II of his *History*, chapter 42, and *musteae pyrae* (“fresh pears”) and *musteum succinum* (“fresh amber”) elsewhere.]

Therefore, for a little while set aside your Pythian laurels and your Hippocrene, and those modes of poetry most intimately familiar to you alone, though such things, among learned men such as yourself, spring not so much from the fountain as from the brow. Suspend also that most celebrated torrent of rhetorical declamation which is not only native but domestic to you, and which is poured into your breast through successive generations from your great-grandfather Fronto.

Set aside for a little while the much-proclaimed speeches which you compose in the place of the royal mouth.

[Col. 0592D] **Note:** Leo was Euric’s quaestor, for a quaestor is the mouth of the ruler. “Transmarine peoples” here means the Vandals, who in Africa were separated from the Goths of Septimania only by the sea. “The barbarians at the Vachalis” are our Franks, as in Poem 12:

“Let the shorn Sicamber drink the Vachalis.”

“The boundary of an advanced lot” must refer to the borders of the Roman Empire, to which Euric had extended his power, as stated above from Ennodius.]

With these speeches he himself, the illustrious king, now terrifies the hearts of the transmarine peoples; now, from his higher position, victoriously binds a treaty with the barbarians trembling beside the Vachalis; now, along the boundary of his extended fortune, he restrains peoples under arms and arms under laws.

Free yourself, as far as possible, from your unbroken cares, and steal your leisure away from courtly burdens and movements. You will review the history requested at a suitable and fitting time if, wholly devoted to reading, you travel with our Tyanaean, now to the Caucasus and India, now to the gymnosophists of Ethiopia and the Brahmans of India.

Read this man—after first declaring peace for the Catholic faith—who in many respects resembles you: sought by the wealthy, yet not seeking wealth; eager for knowledge, restrained toward money; abstemious amid banquets; wearing linen amid men clad in purple; censorious amid alabaster vessels; matted, bristling, and shaggy, venerably precious in his squalor amid nations anointed with perfumes and among the myrrh-scented, pumice-smoothed, and malobathrum-perfumed satraps of tiara-wearing kings.

Although he supplied nothing from an animal for his own food or clothing, the kingdoms through which he traveled regarded him as an object not merely of suspicion but of distrust. Fortune obeyed him in every respect, yet he asked only for benefits which he was more accustomed to grant when asked than to receive when offered.
