Why say more? If we measure and assess things truthfully, it may perhaps be that the writer of the philosopher’s life has approached the times of the ancients; certainly, through you as reader, he has come to be the equal of my own age.

Farewell.

## LETTER IV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Consentius.

[Col. 0592D] **Note:** To a man of Narbonne, distinguished by birth and learning, probably the son of the elder Consentius. There were two men of that name, as stated in Book IX, Letter 15 to Gelasius. More concerning the same man is found in the material on Narbonne.]

Will that field of yours, Octavianus, ever see us together by God’s will, my lord and elder—your field, yet belonging not only to you but also to your friends? Situated near the city, the river, and the sea, it feeds guests with banquets and you with guests. Besides this, it is beautiful in the position visible to those who look upon it: first, because the dwelling rises with walls skillfully placed in architectural harmony; then because it shines broadly with a chapel, colonnades, and conspicuous baths; and further because it is delightful in its fields, waters, vineyards, olive groves, vestibule, plain, and hill.

Moreover, beyond its abundant provisions and furnishings, it is richly stocked with the treasures of a library. There, while you devote yourself no less to the pen than to the plow, it is difficult to discern whether the cultivated estate or the cultivated intellect belongs more to its master.

Here, as I recall, you composed swift iambics, polished elegies, rounded hendecasyllables, and other poems fragrant with the flowers and thyme of music—now to be sung by the people of Narbonne, now by those of Béziers—so that it would be difficult to decide whether they shine more swiftly or more beautifully. Certainly, whenever your verses were brought to me from the anvil of meditation, as though still hot, I seemed to be a man who, although I do not write well, judge well.

But what must be admitted is that an earlier age was rightly free for such studies—or, more truly, occupied by them. Now is the time for serious things to be read, serious things to be written, and for thought to be given to eternal life rather than memory; and for us to remember too deeply that after death it is not our little works but our deeds that will be weighed.

I do not say this as though you did not accomplish both kinds of things worthy of praise, or as though, if joy still endures in speech, judgment were not guarded in action. Rather, since by Christ’s favor you are secretly holy, now publicly, as one to be revered for piety, submit both neck and heart to the salutary yoke. Let your tongue devote itself to heavenly praises, your soul to sound judgments, and your right hand to gifts—above all, to gifts—for whatever you scatter among the churches, you gather for yourself.

The thought that, while placed amid whatever wealth there may be—which fools falsely call good—whatever we do is ours, but whatever we possess belongs to another, will above all be able to stir you to the practice of this virtue.

Farewell.

## LETTER V

Sidonius sends greetings to his Fortunalis.

You too will enter the pages of my work, Fortunalis, pillar of friendship and illustrious ornament of the Iberian regions. Your familiarity with letters is not so slight that it would be unfitting for something about you to survive through these very pages after you are gone.

The glory of your name will live—yes, it will live in the future. For if our little sheets possess any grace, reverence, or loyalty, however slight, I want a later age to know that nothing was firmer than your loyalty, more beautiful than your appearance, more just than your judgment, more enduring than your patience, or more delightful than your conversation.

It will also recognize above all else that the praises of your virtues have arisen from the contradiction of circumstances. For it is nearly judged the greater distinction that adversity proved you steadfast than if prosperity had concealed you as fortunate.

Farewell.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius sends greetings to his Nammatius.

[Col. 0593C] **Note:** It is unclear whether this is Nammatius, Ruricius’ relative by marriage, to whom, and to his wife Ceraunia, several letters of Ruricius himself are extant.

C. Caesar the dictator, whom they say no one administered military affairs more masterfully, was claimed in turn by the pursuits of dictating and reading. And although, in the person of one and the same prince, at his own time, the care of military and oratorical knowledge nearly competed for equal glory, he nevertheless never considered himself adequately established at the summit of both arts until, by the testimony of your fellow countryman of Arpinum, he was preferred to all other mortals.

The same thing has happened to me also, if I may compare small things with great, each according to my own measure, though in a very different degree. You above all ought promptly to recognize this, since my glory and my embarrassment alike concern you greatly.

[Col. 0593C] Flavius Nicetius, a man clarissimus by birth, spectabilis by privilege, illustris by merit, and, in the prudence and expertise of the people of our homeland, equally outstanding among men, extols the volumes of this present little work with praise, as I have learned, immense in scale. Moreover, he declares that I, still vigorous in age, have surpassed many young men and not a few old men in various kinds of dictating and military service.

[Note: [Col. 0593C] Lugdunensis, formerly advocate of the praetorian see and assessor, a man of rank. He distinguished three grades of honor in one class: the clarissimate, the rank of spectabilis, and the rank of illustris. Cassiodorus discusses these in *Variae*, books VI and VII. They are likewise designated in King Huneric’s edict, preserved by Victor of Vita, book III, as illustres, spectabiles, and senators—that is, clarissimi. Of the three grades of judges, moreover, provincial governors were clarissimi, vicars of the larger dioceses spectabiles, and the prefects of the praetorium illustres. Thus Nicetius had become clarissimus through his senatorial birth; spectabilis through the privilege of his long praetorian advocacy, under Valentinian’s Novel on pleading, which grants advocates after fifteen years the right to vicariate rank; and finally his merits made him illustris.]

[Col. 0594B] For my part, insofar as it can be done without boasting, I rejoice in the authority of so distinguished a man, if he is correct; in his affection, if he is mistaken. Yet who, when challenged to deeds, will not be the least sluggish of his ancestors, and who, when challenged to words, will not be the least inarticulate?

For the ruler of the ages has bestowed the virtues of these arts more upon the ancient centuries than upon the centuries of our own time. Through the age of the world, now growing old, their seeds have, as it were, been exhausted; and in whatever persons they appear today, they display only a little, and that little is found remarkable and memorable in few.

Yet I fear that his judgment—although he is the head of all studies and letters, and although I have always cultivated the person himself—has been expressed with an affection heavier than truth warrants. Nor would I deny that I have often attended his brilliant performances. It is proper that I recall them, even if only in part and cursorily, though I may seem to be repaying a mutual debt.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] Sidonius nowhere discloses his father’s name. That his father was prefect of the praetorium of Gaul in the year 448 is shown by the consulship of Asterius, which gave its name to the year 449. Accordingly, because he was born to a praetorian prefect, Sidonius was called by Arvandus, in book I, letter 7, “the son of a prefect,” and his father is said to have presided over the security of Gaul in book V, letter 9, to Aquilinus. From this, moreover, Sidonius’s age may be dated, since he indicates that at that time he had entered adolescence.]

I heard him when I was a young man, and indeed only recently out of boyhood, while my father presided over the tribunals of the Gallic praetorium. Under that magistracy, as it happened,

[Col. 0594C] the consul Asterius, invested with the ceremonial robe of office, had opened the doors of his consulship for the year with a public celebration.

[Note: [Col. 0594C] Turcius Rufius Asterius was consul with Protogenes in the year 449, as I have already said. We have made some observations about him in the notes on Ennodius. It should now be added that, according to Hydatius, Asterius had been master of both branches of the military before his consulship. For he writes of him under the year 440: “Asterius, commander of both branches of the army, sent to Spain, slaughtered a multitude of Bacaudae in the territory of Tarragona.”]

I clung to the curule chair—not hidden there by rank, and certainly not seated there by age, but mingled with the troop of official attendants wearing the *paenula*.

[Note: [Col. 0594D] For the *censuales* were ordered to use *paenulae*, like the other officials. *Codex Theodosianus*, “On the dress that ought to be used within the city.”]

I was among the attendants nearest the consul.

[Note: [Col. 0594D] In Labbe’s edition: “I was next to the consul’s nearest attendants.”]

And so, as soon as the brief ceremony had been completed and the not-small ceremonial gift had been distributed,

[Note: [Col. 0594D] Ceremonial gifts, which were customarily scattered or sent on the inauguration of the consulship and of other magistracies. Trebellius Pollio, on Gallienus’s ceremonial gift: “He invited the matrons to his consulship and gave each of them, as they kissed his hand, four gold pieces bearing his name.” Symmachus, book IX, final letter: “I owe the ceremonial gift of my consulship both to our friendship and to your honor. I have sent it in solid coin, asking you to receive the small offering of my official duty with a kindly spirit.” On the consulship of the emperor Justin, Corippus writes in book IV:

“They prepared the gifts of the Kalends, for which the officials take care,  
and fill the palace with fortunate troops.  
They carry gleaming gold in capacious baskets.”

The name derives from these baskets. Our glossary has: “*Sportula*: gifts given in a basket” (*τὰ ἐν σπυρίδι διδόμενα ξένια*).]

[Col. 0595A] the ceremonial tablets were given,

[Note: [Col. 0595B] I think these were ivory tablets engraved with the consul’s name, which Claudian indicates were customarily given at the inauguration of the consulship, in book III of *On the Praise of Stilicho*:

“Then he gathers green panthers and the other marvels of the South,  
and Latona’s tusks, exempt from labor—  
those cut by iron into tablets and gleaming with gold,  
inscribed with the radiant consul’s name in chased work—  
to go among nobles and common people.”

They were sent to nobles and friends and scattered among the populace. Just as the consular registers are joined here with the ceremonial gift, so in book I of the *Codex Theodosianus*, “On the expenses of games,” the diptychs are joined with ceremonial gifts. Likewise, in Symmachus, ivory writing tablets or an ivory diptych are mentioned with *apophoreta* or little silver baskets—that is, ceremonial gifts—in book II, letter 81, book IX, letter 109, and elsewhere. I therefore believe that the passage refers to the same thing, and that the names of consuls or other magistrates who gave the customary gifts were engraved on those diptychs. An excellent ivory diptych of this kind may be seen in the monastery of Compiègne, with an inscription showing that it was once offered to the senate by Philoxenus, the eastern consul in the year 520. It reads:

“Flavius Theodorus Philoxenus Sotericus Philoxenus, vir illustris, domestic count, former master of the army in Thrace, and ordinary consul.”

“This gift to the wise senate  
I, Philoxenus, consul and magistrate, offer.”

“Made consul, I Philoxenus offer this gift to the learned and wise senate.”

[Col. 0595D] From the same class were the ivory counters on which, as Prosper—or whoever wrote the books *On the Promises and Predictions of God*—reports, the names of the proconsuls of Africa were written. In the conclusion of that work occur these words:

“On ivory counters,” he says, “the names of the proconsuls were written, and in Carthage, in the forum, before the people, they were called out by the presiding judge under specified titles. It was a solemn day of public reckoning. Those who, overcoming greed, had administered the commonwealth faithfully, without scandals or crimes, were honored even in their absence. But those whom rapacity had overcome the people marked with insults and hisses.”

This was a memorable custom, and one that appears relevant to law 102 of the *Codex*, “On the office of the provincial governor.]

and the consular registers had been presented, the entire assembly of Gaul applauded. The leading advocates asked that the hours before dawn, which had been anticipated by the festivities and were silently awaiting the late-coming day, should be honored with praise appropriate to the merits of the official fasces.

[Note: [Col. 0596B] Panegyrics for consuls, delivered publicly on the Kalends of January, when they entered office, attest to this custom of publicly praising consuls. They were delivered in both languages, sometimes in verse and sometimes in prose, by Mamertinus, Libanius, Themistius, Claudian, and Sidonius. Augustine too delivered one for the consulship of Bauto, as he himself relates in book III, chapter 25, *Against Petilian*: “When I came to Milan before Bauto’s consulship, I recited praise of him on the Kalends of January, in the assembly and before the eyes of the people, in accordance with my rhetorical profession at that time.”]

Nicetius, who had been seen by all, immediately found himself surrounded by those who had been seen. He was not approached quietly and individually, but tumultuously and all together. With a kind of preliminary gesture of modesty, he lowered his face decorously and blushed. Thus the greatest “bravo” was given him first for modesty rather than eloquence.

He spoke in an orderly, weighty, and impassioned manner, with great force, greater eloquence, and the greatest discipline. He made the palm-decorated spectacle—drunk with Tyrian dyes amid the crackling of embroidered panels—more graceful by a speech more richly painted and more golden.

At almost the same time, to speak in the manner of the decemvirs,

[Note: [Col. 0596B] This is Valentinian’s Novel concerning the thirty-year limitation, to be pleaded against all actions; it bears the date of the present year. In it he says that he was preceded by a law of his father Theodosius. The learned Cujacius interprets this as Theodosius the Elder, in book XVIII, chapter 26, of his *Observations*; I believe it means Theodosius the Younger. Cujacius’s opinion that Valentinian could not call Theodosius the Younger his father is certainly frivolous: Valentinian unquestionably calls him that in Novel 12, “On Episcopal Judgment,” and in another, “On the Restoration of the Right of Arms,” which was wrongly—and not only there—published among the Theodosian laws, since Theodosius was both his father-in-law and the author of his imperial authority. Theodosius in turn calls Valentinian his son in Novels 1 and 2. Again, he calls Theodosius “lord,” not “divine,” as he calls the divine Honorius, because Theodosius the Younger had not yet died. But in Novel 12, where he says that the age of minority was exempted from that law of Theodosius, he calls Theodosius “of divine memory,” since he had already been dead for two years. That law of Theodosius the Younger is recorded in both codes: the single law in the *Codex Theodosianus*, “On actions limited by a fixed period,” and law 3 in the *Codex*, “On the thirty-year limitation.” In the latter, the same exception for minority appears, and the limitation is set against absolutely all actions. Every detail agrees with Valentinian’s Novel, although the word “all” is absent. If one considers only the words of the Novel, that word, I think, need not be supplied; yet it could have stood in full in the Theodosian law, of which only a small portion survives. No law of the great Theodosius concerning a thirty-year limitation is mentioned; and the very constitution of Theodosius the Younger sufficiently proves that none existed, since he openly declares himself to be the first author of this limitation—a remarkable point to have escaped so great a scholar.]

[Col. 0596A] the law concerning the thirty-year limitation had been publicly proclaimed.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Promulgated. Mamertus Claudianus writes to Sidonius: “That little work, published without an author and proclaimed everywhere.” The word derives from the *Quirites*.]

Its entire litigation, extinguished by the decisive provisions of the statute of limitations, was being extended into its sixth five-year period. This orator, whom we are discussing, was the first to introduce the law into pleadings, publish it in the courts, make it known to the parties, and add it to the headings throughout Gaul, where it had previously been unknown: in crowded assemblies, with the judge rarely seated, in few rulings, but with abundant praise.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] For Theodosius and Valentinian did not enact this law together. Theodosius enacted it at Constantinople, while there was an interregnum in the West because of the tyranny of John, in the consulship of Victor. Twenty-five years elapsed from that year to that of Asterius, in whose year Valentinian gave the law to the Gauls. Thus it is not without reason that he says it had previously been unknown within Gaul.]

At other times I also observed his learning—according to the practice by which a man is more quickly learned—without being noticed, when the prefecture that governs the provinces through the fasces was being administered under Nicetian counsel. Why say more? I heard nothing that I would not wish to be mine, nothing that I did not admire.

For all these virtues situated in the man, I rejoice that he has been celebrated by the unanimous voice of all as a censor. His judgment carries great weight concerning either opinion he may hold of me. If we find it true,

[Note: [Col. 0596D] In some editions: “if we find it genuine.”]

[Col. 0597A] it favors my confidence as much as the opposite judgment would nourish my fear. For the rest, I have firmly resolved that, once I know the matter completely, I shall either loosen the reins of silence or tighten the bridle on my chatter. If I am confirmed by the assent of the man mentioned above, I shall be more talkative than Athens; if not, I shall be more silent than Amyclae itself.

But enough about my companion and myself. What are you doing amid all this? It is no less important to me to know in turn what occupies you. Are you hunting? Building? Farming? Are you doing one of these things, each in turn, or all together?

But whether you follow Vitruvius, Columella, or both, you are acting most becomingly. You can be both, in the best manner—that is, a cultivator and one of the foremost architects.

For the rest, I especially urge you not to flatter yourself too much concerning the duties of the hunter. You call boars uselessly to the hunting spears, since you have become accustomed, with the most compassionate dogs, of which you have an abundance, and quite alone, to move them rather than set them in motion.

Let it be worthy of indulgence that your whelps are afraid to approach creatures terrible in appearance and bulk. But I do not know how you can excuse this: they pursue roe-deer, the horned herd, and likewise fallow deer, which are naturally inclined to flee, with spirits cast down, breasts held high, slow steps, and incessant barking.

Therefore, for the rest, you more profitably surround the rugged rocks with nets and snares, driving the stationary enclosure through woods suitable for shading the lairs; and, if you have any sense of shame, you refrain from shaking the open fields with your running and lying in wait for the little hares of Oleron—creatures which, since you pursue them only rarely, are not worth troubling in the open with dogs led on coupled leashes.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] What appears here in Olarius is Uliarus in Pliny: an island in the Bay of Aquitania, opposite the Santones, among whom Nammatius lived.]

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Scaliger understood this passage of Sidonius differently from Sirmondus; Papebrochius follows Scaliger, as Wesseling has observed in his notes on the *Ancient Roman Itineraries*, p. 453.]

[Note: [Col. 0597D] It must certainly be read this way, not as in the common editions, “by overcoming the cliffs.” He means the couples of hunting dogs. In the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne, the word is already corrupted: “That bishops, abbots, and abbesses may not keep couples of dogs, nor falcons, nor hawks.” A *copula* is *ἀλισίδιον*, that is, in Suidas’ explanation, “a kind of braid around the neck,” or “a neck-band.” Ovid writes: “The coupling is removed from the dogs.” Hence the dogs joined by collars.]

Unless, perhaps, our Apollinaris comes to join you and your father, in which case they will be exercised more properly.

Jokes aside, at last let me know what you are doing, and what is happening around your household. But look: just as I was wishing to close this letter, which has been chattering for a long time, a messenger suddenly arrived from the Santones. While, for your sake, we drew out a few hours of conversation with him, he firmly asserted that recently you had sounded the trumpet on shipboard and that, now performing the duties of sailors and now of soldiers, you were roaming along the curved shores of Ocean against the broad *myoparones* of the Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Hegesippus, book V, on these same Saxons: “A powerful race of men, superior to the others, relying only on pirate *myoparones*, not on bodily strength.” The Saxons once harassed the peoples neighboring the Rhine and the sea with continual raids, after the time of Diocletian. From them the name “Saxon Shore” arose in Belgica II. They also sailed beyond it and, with the same license, plundered the Nervian and Armorican regions. Besides this letter, the matter is indicated by another to Lampridius and by the panegyric of Avitus. Since they now threatened Aquitania II, they were in conflict with the Goths, whom he calls the victorious people.]

The number of rowers you see is, in your judgment, the number of arch-pirates: so alike do they all command, obey, teach, learn, and practice robbery.

This gives me the greatest reason to warn you, so that you may now be especially cautious. The enemy is more savage than any enemy. He attacks without warning; when foreseen, he slips away. He despises those who oppose him and lays low the unwary. If he pursues, he intercepts; if he flees, he escapes.

Shipwrecks train them; they do not frighten them. They possess with the dangers of the sea not merely familiarity but actual intimacy. For since a storm itself makes those to be attacked secure on the one hand, and on the other prevents those who intend to attack from keeping watch, they risk themselves amid waves and shattered reefs, buoyed by the hope of a joyful surprise.

Moreover, before they loosen their sails from the mainland for their homeland and pull their biting anchors from the hostile seabed, it is their custom to kill every tenth captive, through equal and cruciform punishments—made all the more grievous by the fact that they do so according to a superstitious rite—and to distribute the injustice of death equally by lot among the assembled crowd of those doomed to die.

[Col. 0598B] By such vows they choose their victims and discharge their obligations through sacrifices of this kind. By these practices they are not so much cleansed by sacrifice as polluted by sacrilege, and they think that the perpetrators of an ill-omened slaughter should exact religious satisfaction from the captive’s head through torture rather than through payment.

For this reason I fear many things and suspect various outcomes, although enormous considerations urge me in the opposite direction. First, because you accompany the standards of a victorious people; next, because I am less willing to grant that chance may prevail against men whom you rightly count among the wise; and third, because, in the case of companions joined to us by loyalty but separated by distance, remote and doubtful actions frequently cause every unfavorable possibility to strike us with grief. Fear more readily augurs evil concerning matters that are distant and uncertain.

But you may say that the things I dread should perhaps not be taken so seriously. That is true, but this is also true: we fear most those whom we love most.

[Col. 0598C] Therefore, all the same, I beg you to remove as soon as possible from our senses the anguish that has arisen because of you by sending us a favorable report. For I can never entirely bend myself to this position: concerning friends traveling abroad—especially those whom the military and martial token wear down—not to fear adversity until I learn of their prosperity.

As you had requested, I have sent Varro’s *Logistoricus* and Eusebius the chronicler. If they reach you after passing through your editorial file, and if, amid your vigils—as befits life in camp—you obtain even a little time by lot, then, after wiping the dust from your arms, you will be able to scrape the rust of silence from your mouth as well.

Farewell.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius to his Audax, greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0598D] Prefect of the City under Nepos, as is shown by a Roman inscription on a marble weight of urban standard, marked on both sides in the following manner:

“Under the protection of our lord Julius Nepos, perpetual Augustus, Audax, vir clarissimus, prefect of the City, made this.”

This, then, is the prefecture for which Sidonius congratulates him. Another inscription is also a testimony to the same man; it discloses the rest of Audax’s names and indicates that he completed some work at Rome after the barbarian incursion, in these words:

“Castalius Innocentius Audax, vir clarissimus, prefect of the City, judging with sacred authority, restored what had been destroyed by the barbarian incursion.”

We took this from the new collections of John de la Marc. He notes that it once stood at Rome, though it no longer exists, beside the church of Saint Mary the New.]

Where, I should like you to say, are those men now hiding who often flattered themselves over the great masses of accumulated wealth and the heaps of silver already blackening with age? Where also is the privilege of those who, contrary to the nature of younger men, grew swollen merely through the opportunity afforded by greater age?

Where are those whose relationship is recognized by no clearer sign than rivalry? Surely, when the time came for good deeds and, at last, not the scale of money but of character was placed on the principal judge’s balance, there remained only those who had most arrogantly supposed that they should be valued solely by their census; those who, lying upon vices as upon riches, wish their person to appear to have risen independently of vanity, while they do not want their substance to be marked as having grown through greed.

Yet in this arena of detraction, trained as though in oil, they are softened by the poisons poured in by rivalry.

But you—well done!—who, enlarged by the titles of the prefecture, though until now you were counted illustrious by your lineage, have worked with no less personal effort so that your descendants might be numbered more gloriously because of you.

For nothing is nobler, in the judgment of every good and generous person, than for anyone—whether in intellect, body, or wealth—to devote a steady effort to this: that he may be placed before his ancestors.

For the rest, I ask God that your sons may equal you—or, which is more fitting to wish, surpass you. And may anyone who cannot bear to love you as a man advanced in honor continually exact from himself, from the marrow of his being, the penalties of his own seething envy; and although he has never had grounds for pity toward you, may he have grounds for envy.

For rightly does he lie low beneath a just prince who is least in himself and great only through his possessions, living small in spirit and immense in estate.

Farewell.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius to his Syagrius, greetings.

Tell me, flower of Gallic youth, how long will you, busy with rural labors, despise urban pursuits? How long will your hands, worn down by the former throws of dice, claim for themselves, against right and law, the instruments of agriculture?

How long will your Taionnac estate wear you out as a farmer descended from a patrician line?

[Note: [Col. 0600D] See whether Taionnus may be placed here. The itinerary table locates him among the Aedui, not far from Augustodunum.]

 How long do you hide the remnants of the luxuriant meadow in winter fallow, not as a horseman but as a plowman? How long do you set down the weight of a blunt mattock without driving it through the unpierced soil?

As a rival of the Serrani and Camilli, when you guide the plow, why do you pretend not to desire the palm of victory? Only refrain from farming in a way that provokes envy against your nobility.

If you cultivate your field moderately, you possess it; if excessively, you will be possessed by it.

Give yourself back to your father, back to your country, and back also to your faithful friends, who rightly belong among the objects of affection.

Or, if the life of the dictator Cincinnatus delights you so greatly,

[Note: [Col. 0600D] I have restored this by following the traces of the old manuscript, where it read “lead Racilia.” Racilia was the name of Lucius Cincinnatus’s wife in Livy, book III.]

lead Racilia before you, so that she may yoke the oxen.

I do not mean that a wise man should not attend to domestic affairs, but he should do so with such moderation that he considers not only what he ought to have, but what he ought to be.

For if, having rejected all the other pursuits of noble men, the single nettle of enlarging your household estate troubles you, then, although you recall your name derived from the ceremonial robes, your ivory curule chairs, your gold-covered litters, and your purple-stained consular registers, you will plainly be found to be the sort of man whom the censor ought to regard as industrious for hiding his true nature, but whom the census should burden.

Farewell.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius to his Lampridius, greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] A rhetorician of Bordeaux and an outstanding poet, as he is described in the letter to Lupus, book IX, letter 11, and in the letter to Tonantius, book IX, letter 13. He was among Sidonius’s closest friends, as is especially clear from what Sidonius writes to Lupus about his death. At this time he was away from Bordeaux. When Sidonius had come there to petition King Euric for an end to his exile, he composed the following poem, exceedingly elegant and especially suitable for contemplating the grandeur of the Gothic court.]

[Col. 0600B]

When first I came to Bordeaux, your messenger brought me a letter full of nectar, flowers, and pearls. In it you blame my silence and ask for some of my verses in exchange for verses of yours, which customarily pour forth for you through the musical hollow of your mouth, ringing in varied tones as though from many-piped flutes.

But you now do this, already secure after receiving the king’s gifts, taking sufficient advantage of his generosity; perhaps you do not remember that satirical saying about the satirist:

“Horace is satisfied when he says ‘Evoe.’”

Why say more? You rightly order me to sing from leisure, because you already take pleasure in dancing.

Whatever the matter may be, I obey. I do so not merely under compulsion, but even willingly. Only moderate, as best you can, the Cato-like judgment of your stern-browed face.

[Col. 0600C] You know the condition of poets, which is almost happiness. Their talents are caught by griefs as little fish are caught in nets; and if anything harsh or sad occurs, poetic tenderness does not immediately extricate itself from the bond of the suffering it has encountered.

I have not yet obtained anything from my father-in-law’s inheritance, even for use under the terms of a third share. Meanwhile, you will see what title for an epigram you may find pleasing. My anxiety does not permit me now to have one thing in my actions and another in my poem.

You would certainly act unjustly if, for the moment, you were to compare our writings as though they were equal. I am engaged in hardship; you are yourself fortunate. I am still an exile; you are already a citizen. For that reason I sing unequal things, because I ask for things alike and do not obtain things equal.

If by some chance you receive these trifles, which I composed amid the punishments of my spirit, with a more indulgent nod, you will persuade me that they were like the songs of swans, whose cry is more melodious in suffering; like the strings of a lyre stretched more violently, which are more musical the more tightly they are wound.

But if verses devoid of leisure or merriment cannot win approval, you too will find nothing pleasing in the page I have appended below. Add to this that a subject whose recipient is not a listener but rather a reader gains nothing from the delivery of an absent author. For once the work has been sent away, what can even the most sonorous poet do, when distance prevents him from doing what the choruses of pantomimes customarily do—commend poorly written words by means of beautiful singing?

[Note: [Col. 0601C] Pantomimes had their own chorus, whose song they expounded through appropriate and coordinated bodily gestures. Manilius, book V of the *Astronomica*:

“He will reproduce every face of Fortune through his limbs,  
and will make the songs equal to the chorus.”

Cassiodorus Senator, book IV of the *Variae*, final letter: “When the pantomime first comes onto the stage, harmonious choruses, trained in various instruments, attend him.” Aristaenetus, letter 26, addressed “To the dancer”:

“And like a Pharian Proteus, you seem at one time to change into one thing, at another into another, in harmony with the melodious song of the dances.”

Augustine likewise, book II, chapter 2, *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, and an old poet in book IV of the Pithoean collection of epigrams, on a pantomime:

“Entering the stage, the dancer greets the people;  
with skillful hand he hangs upon the task of expressing words.  
For when the sweet chorus pours forth pleasing songs,  
he himself confirms through movement what the singer makes resound.”]

What are you now trying to stir into song, Lampridius, glory of my Thalia—the springs of Cyrrha, or the Hyantian Muses, the learned liquors of the Heliconids, carved by the blow of the neighing winged horse?

And you compel me to write in this fashion, as though I had brought Delphic instruments to your Delian Apollo: as though I were a new Apollo, carrying the tripod, the tripod-bowl, the lyre, the quivers, the bow, and the griffins; and from one side shaking berries of the double foliage, from the other, ivy clusters.

### 229

Now you, O Tityrus, after recovering your fields, wandering through myrtles and plane trees, strike the lyre; your mouth and plectrum resound together in concordant melodies. You are a singer astonishing in string, voice, and meter.

But us, placed here and seen only once, the moon has now seen twice in its monthly course. Nor does the master himself have much leisure, while the subdued world seeks his answers.

Here we see the blue-eyed Saxon, formerly accustomed to fear only the sea, now fearing the land. Along the outer edges of his crown, the blade, not content to keep its own bites, raises the margin of his hair; and when the hair is cut close to the skin, the head diminishes and the face is increased.

Here, with his back of the head shorn, the old Sicamber, after being defeated, draws his neck backward and elicits new hair toward the old locks.

Here the Herulian wanders with gray-blue cheeks, inhabiting the deepest recesses of Ocean, almost the same color as the seaweed-covered deep.

Here the seven-foot Burgundian frequently begs for rest on a bent knee.

Here the Ostrogoth thrives through these patrons, while repeatedly pressing his neighboring Huns; he takes pride in what is subjected to him and in those whom he has overcome.

[Col. 0602A] From here, Roman, you seek safety against the hordes of the Scythian region, if the bear of Parrhasia brings any tumult,

[Note: [Col. 0601D] This is how all the books I have seen read, except one or two, whose reading is corrupt. There can be no doubt that the subject is King Euric, not Theodoric. Sidonius was an exile under Euric. It is false, in my opinion, that anyone could correctly call Euric by the name Theodoric as well. The emendation is therefore certain.]

Eroic, your hands are sought,

so that powerful Garumna may defend Mars, through the Inquilian [district?], and the slender Tiber.

The Parthian Arsaces himself prays that he may hold the summit of the palace at Susa under a tributary treaty.

[Note: [Col. 0602C] The king of the Persians—not because this was his proper name, for Perozes was reigning at this time, but because all the Arsacids were called by this name after the first. Strabo, book XV: “All are called Arsacids, but individually one is Orodes, another Phraates, and another has another name.”]

For when he senses that Bosphoran forces are rising from here in great array, he scarcely believes that sorrowing Persia can defend the Euphrates bank from the din of battle.

Although he imagines the stars related to him and swells with proximity to Phoebus, he nevertheless fills this mortal man with supplication.

Meanwhile, we wear away empty delays. But you, O Tityrus, refrain from provoking me. For I do not envy you; rather, I marvel that, although I deserve nothing and spend my prayers in vain, I have begun to be Meliboeus.

Here is the poem, which you may review at your leisure, looking upon our sweat and dust like a charioteer already crowned from the podium. For the rest, do not suppose that I shall repeat a similar service, even if you enjoy the present one, unless I first cease prophesying losses rather than songs.

Farewell.

## LETTER X

Sidonius to his Ruricius, greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0602D] Later bishop of the Lemovices, as stated in the note on book IV, letter 16. Among Ruricius’s letters to Sidonius is book I, letter 9, in which he praises him wonderfully; it may be regarded as the letter to which Sidonius is replying here.]

I rejoice greatly that letters are at once useful and dear to you. I would assert more freely how much either the flame of ideas or the flood of words accompanies your style, were it not that, while you strive so earnestly to praise me, you forbid yourself to be praised in return.

Although affection preserves sweetness in your letter, nature preserves eloquence, and expertise preserves discipline, you went wrong only in your choice of subject—though even this may be praised in the intention, since you appear to have erred in judgment.

You apply immense titles of praise to my character. But if you had taken any account of my modesty, you ought to have remembered that saying of Symmachus:

[Note: [Col. 0602D] It does not survive among Symmachus’s works, though it was in the mouths of many. It is cited by Caesarius of Arles in homily 25 and by Pope Pelagius in a letter to Sapaudus: “Although the eloquence of your speech has set forth those things in praise of us, and although it is clear that your voice has done what was fitting, we recognize nothing of our own in all that has been said and instead incur the greater embarrassment, recalling to mind the saying of that most learned man: ‘As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.’” The saying of Theophylact Simocatta in his *Ecumenical History* is similar: “Fabricated praise is more dishonorable than blame” (*ἐπίπλαστος ἔπαινος ἀτιμότερος ψόγου*).]

“As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.”

Yet here too, if I properly assess your mind, you have acted skillfully in addition to the great affection you display. It is customary for eloquent men to test the power of their intellect by the difficulty of their tasks, and to drive their practiced style—like a plowshare from a fertile breast—into the place where a barren subject, like the dry clod of a poor field, lies sterile.

The world teems with similar examples. A physician is recognized in desperation, a helmsman in a storm. The fame of all such men is enhanced by the dangers that precede them; and that fame certainly remains hidden unless it finds an occasion on which to be tested.

So too a great orator, if he undertakes a narrow case, then displays his expansive talent more convincingly.

M. Tullius surpassed all others in his other speeches, but in the case of Aulus Cluentius he surpassed himself.

[Note: [Col. 0603B] Cicero’s finest speech is said to be his greatest, as Pliny the Younger says of the speech for Cluentius. Elsewhere, too, Pliny writes that his speech for Variola was regarded as outstanding above all others. But this speech, like the speech of Cornelius Fronto for Pelops, has perished, along with the other works of his that are praised by Charisius, Fulgentius, and the panegyrist of Constantius, with this encomium: “Fronto was not second to Roman eloquence, but its second glory.”]

M. Fronto stood out among his other speeches, but in the case of Pelops he placed himself above himself.

C. Pliny brought home greater glory from the centumviral tribunal in defense of Attia Variola than when he delivered a panegyric comparable to the incomparable prince Marcus Ulpius.

So have you acted too: while wishing to exercise your expertise, you did not fear that even my own conscience might impede you.

Rather, by supplication, heal my weaknesses. Do not crush the still-sick fragility of my soul under the weight of false glory through the snare of a flattering eloquence.

Indeed, since your life is made more beautiful by your beautiful speech, you indulge me more if you prefer to plead for my sake than to deliver a formal oration.

Farewell.

## LETTER XI

Sidonius to his Lupus, greetings.

What are the Nitiobriges doing?

[Note: [Col. 0603C] We formerly corrected this passage by conjecture, when we read *quidve Sonnici*, aided partly by one manuscript and partly by the proximity of the two peoples. For the Vesunnici are near the Nitiobriges. Ptolemy writes: “Below the Cadurci are the Petrocorii and the city of Vesunna; beside the Petrocorii are the Nitiobriges and the city of Aginnum” (*Ὑπὸ τοὺς Καδούρκους Πετροχόριοι, καὶ πόλις Οὔεσουνα, ὑπὸ Πετροχορίους παρήκουσι Νιτιόβριγες, καὶ πόλις Ἄγιννον*).

When we reported this emendation, as was our custom, to the most learned Pierre Pithou, he approved it so highly that he rewarded us with an ancient inscription not yet published at that time, which is preserved at Vesunna to this day. It reads:

“Tutela Augusta of Vesunna; Secundus Soter, at his own expense and by his own decree.”]

89 Thus, just as we restored the name Vesunna, which had previously been wrongly transmitted, so the inscription on the coin of the Emperor Postumus ought to be restored. On it, Hercules is called *Hercules Deusoniensis*, after Deusona, the ancient city of the Franks beyond the Rhine, near which, according to Jerome in his *Chronicle*, the Saxons were slaughtered by the Franks during the reign of Valentinian. Hubertus Goltzius incorrectly disseminated and entered the reading *DEUS ONIENSIS* in the *Thesaurus*, dividing the word wrongly. We have also seen other bronze and silver coins on which the same inscription appears, though with a bare image of Hercules, without a temple.

What are your Vesunnians doing, those among whom there is always a holy rivalry over claiming you for themselves? One people possesses you by inheritance, the other also by marriage; and while one has you by birth, the other by wedlock, what is better is that both possess you by judgment. Yet, by God’s gift, you are fortunate amid all this: it is worthwhile that the eager affection of these peoples should contend for the longer occupation and possession of you.

You, however, apportion your presence prudently between the two, taking turns: now you restore Drepan[ius] to the one, now Anthedius to the other. And if these people demand rhetorical instruction from you, they do not require Paulinus, while the others do not require Alcimus.[^c0065-1] I am all the more astonished at you, then: the poverty of a many-volume library, constantly tossed about, daily wearies you, yet you demand from me some old little songs.

I obey, although recalling jokes may seem untimely in a time of grief. Only now have I first learned that the orator Lampridius is dead;[^c0065-2] his death would have consumed my affection in the deepest anguish, even if violent force had not snatched him away from human affairs. Once, in friendly jest, he called me Phoebus, while he himself had received from us the name of the Odrysian poet.[^c0065-3] This agrees with what was related earlier, lest the figurative names obscure the poem that follows.

When I was visiting Bordeaux on one occasion, I sent him a preliminary letter, as though it were an advance lodging-place and reception—*καὶ καταγωγήν*—for that is the function of *metatores*, advance agents.[^c0065-4] I think this may be offered to you more freely than if, composing something mournful over the death of one whom I did not please by my eloquence, I were to displease by the subject matter.

[^c0065-1]: The Latin *Drepanius Pacatus* has left a panegyric delivered at Rome to Theodosius, in which he openly declares himself Transalpine and Aquitanian. Ausonius praises the same excellent poet in *Idyll* 7. Sidonius also counts Anthedius among the poets in poem 9 to Felix and in the letter to Leontius that precedes *Burgus* (poem 22). Alcimus appears to be the rhetorician whom Jerome says taught with Delphidius in Aquitania with great distinction. See *Fortitude of Alcimus*, book V, letter 10. It is less certain which Paulinus he means. Besides Paulinus of Nola, several others known from their writings lived in the Sidonian age: Paulinus, bishop of Béziers, whose letter Hydatius mentions around A.D. 420; Paulinus, author of the *Eucharistic Poem*, whom I seem to have recognized from his verses as Ausonius’ grandson through his son Hesperius; and finally Paulinus, author of six books on the *Life of Saint Martin*, also written in verse. Since the old Vatican and Corbie manuscripts call him Paulinus of Périgueux, perhaps *Petrocorium*, that is, a Vesunnian, may be suspected. But Sidonius praises Paulinus for rhetorical, not poetic, skill.

[^c0065-2]: This distich should be separated from the rest of the poem as its title or heading, an *ἐπιγραφή*, as I already noted concerning Ennodius, book II, letter 1. The same kind of thing occurs in the first three verses of poem 9 to Felix, and again at the beginning of several letters of Ausonius. It also occurs in Ruricius, in the hendecasyllables addressed to Sedatus, bishop of Nîmes:

> Ruricius, a dependent to his holy patron,  
>   
> Seda, obedient to paternal admonitions,  
>   
> Sings his thanks and sends his greetings.

Our glossary interprets *commonitorium* as *ἐπιστολὴ προστακτική*, “a letter in which something is commanded,” such as the heading of the Theodosian Code: “A memorandum to Timothy, the most illustrious count.” In the Sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 3: “A memorandum to our brother Faustinus and to the presbyters Philip and Asellus,” from Zosimus, bishop. The passage should therefore be read as follows.

> To Thalia, greatly beloved and special friend,  
>   
> Phoebus sends this memorandum.  
>   
> Lay aside your plectra for a little while, fosterling;  
>   
> Bind up your scattered hair with a green fillet,  
>   
> And let more unencumbered ivy  
>   
> Gird the folds of your ample robe.  
>   
> Beware of carrying perfumes, nor, as usual,  
>   
> Let your foot be loose and high in the cothurnus.  
>   
> Instead, take care to fasten sandals such as  
>   
> Harpalice tied, or that woman  
>   
> Who struck down her defeated suitors with the sword.  
>   
> You will proceed better in such attire with flying leaps  
>   
> If your bare, bandaged feet  
>   
> Guide your steps at their upper part with bare toes,  
>   
> Firm in rapid movements; and if the links  
>   
> Of the chains run together, let the chain  
>   
> Turn back and rise to the shin through its arch.

234 In this nimble attire, remember to visit my Orpheus,

[^c0065-3]: Lampridius. In these verses, as he announced beforehand, Phoebus and Sidonius are represented figuratively, while the poet Orpheus, or the Odrysian, represents Lampridius.

> Who softens the daily rocks and oaks  
>   
> And the hornlike fibers with his melodious art.  
>   
> Whom now the Arpinate enriches with thunderous speech,  
>   
> Now the Maronian pen,  
>   
> Or that by which you, Horace, ennoble Latium—  
>   
> A lyrist superior even to Alcaeus.[^c0065-4]  
>   
> Now he swells the epic of tragedies;  
>   
> Now he tempers it with playful comedy;  
>   
> Now the satires blaze, and the declamation  
>   
> Of tyrannical controversies.  
>   
> Say, “Phoebus has arrived,” and after the post-horses  
>   
> He beats the sail-bearing Garonne with oars.  
>   
> Tell Leontius to come out to meet him,  
>   
> But first prepare to receive him as a guest,  
>   
> Leontius, whom Livia gives us from the ancient senate.[^c0065-5]  
>   
> Say, “He will be here at once”—a sufficiently witty phrase;  
>   
> And, by his name alone, see Rusticus.[^c0065-6]  
>   
> But if the houses refuse you entry, saying they are occupied,  
>   
> Go at once to the bishops’ thresholds,  
>   
> Kiss the hand of holy Gallicinus,  
>   
> And ask for a brief place of refuge.  
>   
> Otherwise, if I am deprived of the house that has been refused me,  
>   
> I shall mourn as I go to the dripping taverns;  
>   
> And, repeatedly closing both nostrils,  
>   
> I shall lament beside the smoke-filled kitchens,  
>   
> Where, through chains bearing sprigs of savory,  
>   
> A red little sausage smells,  
>   
> When the smoke of pots is mingled  
>   
> With the vapor of crackling pans.  
>   
> Here, when a festal day begins to summon harsh songs  
>   
> And the voluptuous clamour of buffoons to crackle,  
>   
> Then—then, stirred by the Muse of a wine-soaked host—  
>   
> I, a barbarian, shall murmur songs more worthy for you than theirs.

[^c0065-4]: He shortens the final syllable in accordance with the usage of that period. Martianus Capella discusses this in book III: “In Greek names it is short, as in *Anchises*.” In the same way, in poem 6 he pronounces the final syllable of *Alciden* short.

[^c0065-5]: Pontius Leontius, son of Livia of Bordeaux, to whom poem 22 and its accompanying letter are addressed; he is also discussed in letter 12. Rusticus likewise received letter 11 of book II. We owe the preservation of the memory of Gallicinus, bishop of Bordeaux, to this single passage.

[^c0065-6]: The manuscript tradition mostly has *Eschoicos*, or something similar. Since nothing more suitable has appeared, I have removed a letter and printed *Echoicos*. He seems to call those elegies “echoic” which have the same half-line at beginning and end; Hermogenes would call them *ἐνιαυτούς καὶ κύκλους*, “years and circles.” Pentadius’ complete epigram on the coming of spring is of this kind, including this distich about Echo herself:

> Echo sounds through hollow rocks with the lowing of cattle,  
>   
> And the rebounding voice sounds through hollow rocks and hills.

Servius, in his *Centimeter*, defines an echoic verse as one whose final syllable corresponds to the penultimate syllable, as in:

> Rare grace exercises fraternal minds.

But that kind does not suit Sidonius, who is discussing the artistic devices visible in elegies. It should not seem strange that Pentadius’ elegies and others of the same sort are called echoic, since the rhetorician Caestius used to call similar repetitions in prose “echoes.” Seneca the Elder, book VII, *Controversy* 7, says that one auditor of Caestius began in this manner: “To begin with the words of your leader—your leader, judges, of course—‘Beware of treachery,’” and ended his declamation by saying, “In that place where the commander ends his life, ‘Beware of treachery.’” Caestius called this kind of sentence *ἠχώ*, “echo,” and immediately shouted to a student who was speaking, *μὴ τὴν ἠχώ*, “not the echo.” In the suasoria in which Alexander deliberates whether he should sail across the ocean, when the words “How long, unconquered one?” had been heard, someone began his declamation from those words and ended with them. As the speaker ended, Caestius said to him: *ἐν σοὶ μὲν λήξω, σέο δ’ ἄρξομαι*, “In you I shall end, but from you I shall begin.”

> And elegies now echoing, now  
>   
> Recurrent,[^c0065-7] now joined by anadiplosis  
>   
> At their endings and beginnings.[^c0065-8]

[^c0065-7]: Not those that return letter by letter, discussed in book IX, letter 14, but those that return word by word, which grammarians call *reciprocal*. According to Victorinus, reciprocal verses either return by individual verses—which does not suit this passage—or throughout the entire elegy. Sidonius is concerned here only with the latter kind. Such is this distich by Sidonius himself, in which he played upon a torrent in the same letter of book IX, and this one by Optatianus Porphyrius:

> Thus the stars grant the fatherland and the father’s empire  
>   
> To distribute gifts through everlasting ages.

If it is read backward, it reads:

> The stars grant the empire of father and fatherland, *saecus* [uncertain as printed],  
>   
> Gifts to distribute—thus well, perpetually.

[^c0065-8]: These are formed by anadiplosis, as Diomedes and others explain, when the final word of the preceding verse is repeated at the beginning of the next, for example:

> The fairest Astur follows,  
>   
> Astur, trusting in his horse.

The entire first poem of Ausonius’ *Technopaegnion* consists of this kind, except that all its verses are hexameters. If the same device were used in elegies, it would be a specimen of Lampridius’ work. An old epitaph of the charioteer Eutyches reads:

> Cruel fate begrudged my years,  
>   
> Fate against which you could not raise your hands.

The examples cited above in place of echoic verses could also be referred to anadiplosis.

Here, when he had undertaken the work as it had been suggested to him,[^c0065-9] he varied his ethical diction according to the character of the person, the time, and the place—*ἠθικὸν λόγον*, the rhetoricians’ term for speech “that follows each individual character.” Sidonius means speech suited to the person, place, and time. Latin writers call such speech “characterized,” because it expresses manners. In this genre, Terence excelled among comic poets, in Varro’s judgment. He writes of him in Nonius: “In plots Caecilius claims the palm, in characterization Terence, in dialogue Plautus.” Among painters, Pliny says of Aristides of Thebes, in book XXXV, chapter 10: “Aristides, the contemporary of Apelles, was the first of all to paint the soul and all the emotions which the Greeks call *ethe*, as well as disturbances.” This might be called ethical painting. Seneca the Elder also speaks of “ethical controversies” in book II, *Controversy* 2.

[^c0065-9]: The addition “and here” was wrongly printed earlier. I already indicated the correction in the notes to Ennodius. Rhetoricians call ethical diction *ἠθικὸν λόγον*, “the speech appropriate to character.” Latin writers call such discourse *morata*, because it expresses moral character. Varro’s judgment was that Terence excelled in this respect. The passage on Aristides concerns the painting of character and emotion.

In controversial material he was strong and muscular; in satire, watchful and biting; in tragedy, fierce and tearful. In comedy he was urbane and many-sided; in the *fescennine* mode, flowering in his words and burning with his desires; in bucolic poetry, vigilant, frugal, and richly songful; in georgic poetry, so rustic in manner that he was not rustic at all.

As for epigrams, he pleased not by abundance but by sharpness. They ended neither more briefly than in a distich nor more extensively than in a tetrastich. Although you would find many of them peppered with pungency and many sweetened with honey, you would see that all were seasoned with salt.

In lyric poetry, following Horace, he was now swift in iambics, now weighty in choriambics, now flowing in alcaics, now inflated in sapphics. What more can I say? He was subtle, apt, well equipped; in whatever direction his mind carried his pen, he was altogether eloquent. You would rightly judge that, after the swans of Horace and Pindar, he would fly on the wings of glory.

He was not equally devoted to dice and ball games. When dice occupied him for work, he played ball only for pleasure; he willingly tired himself, and—what is even more pleasing—was more willing to be tired. He wrote constantly, although he more often had a craving to write than actually wrote. He also read authors without interruption, revering the ancients and envying no moderns. And what is most difficult among human beings, he yielded the praise of genius to no one grudgingly.[^c0065-10]

[^c0065-10]: On this passage, see Cotelerius’ note to the *Recognitions of Clement*, book X, chapter 11, note 3.

There was, however, one thing in this man that was not merely blameworthy but fatal: at one time he consulted mathematicians about the end of his life. They were citizens of African cities—people whose spirit, like their climate, is fiery. After examining the constellation of the questioner, they announced the year, month, and day alike, saying that these would be his climacteric periods,[^c0065-11] since, when his horoscope had been laid before them, the configuration of a bloody nativity had appeared. For, they said, in the year of his birth a fortunate sphere of the planetary stars had raised a favorable rising in the Zodiac; at its setting, however, they had inflamed it with bloody fires—whether Mercury, above the opposition, was unaspected, or Saturn, above the square, retrograde, or Mars, above the center, in its return, had made it savage.[^c0065-12]

[^c0065-12]: Astrologers speak of the aspects of the stars according to their intervals, or *diastemata*, from one another. They call the opposition *διάμετρον*, “diameter,” occurring in the sign seventh from the first; the trine *τρίγωνον*, “triangular,” in the fifth; the square *τετράγωνον*, “quadrangular,” in the fourth; and the sextile *ἑξάγωνον*, “six-sided,” in the third. Configurations joined by no such rays are called by the Greeks *ἄβλεπτα καὶ ἀσύνδετα*, “unseen and unconnected.” Conversely, the pivots of heaven are four: *ὡροσκόπος*, the ascendant; *μεσουράνημα*, the meridian; *δύσις*, the setting; and *ὑπόγειον*, the lower heaven. Sidonius touches on all these, though he specifically names the center, *τὸ μεσουράνιον*, because it is the head and chief of the pivots.

But whatever these things are, and however they are supposed to operate, although they are utterly false and therefore deceptive, nevertheless, if anything more fully and clearly fits the facts—and although you yourself study arithmetic and, with your usual diligence, carefully read Julianus Vertacus, Thrasybulus, and Saturninus, since you are always meditating on nothing but what is secret and lofty—nothing conjectural or ambiguous occurred in the present case. For time and the circumstances of the predicted death ensnared this rash inquirer into the future, who had long been making futile evasions.

[^c0065-13]: Astrology, as a vain and meddlesome occupation, was forbidden by divine and human laws. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, writes: “You know nothing, astrologer, if you did not know that you would become a Christian. If you did know it, you ought also to have known that you would have nothing to do with that profession. It would itself instruct you concerning its danger, since it has guarded against the climacteric periods of others. You have no part or share in that calculation; one whose finger or rod abuses heaven cannot hope for the kingdom of heaven.”

[^c0065-14]: Sidonius names Julianus Vertacus among the mathematicians in his letter to Polemius, poem 22; he also mentions Fullonius Saturninus. Lampridius tells us about the age of Thrasybulus in his life of Alexander: “Thrasybulus,” he says, “was his very close friend, a mathematician, who told him that he was destined to die by a barbarian sword. At first Alexander rejoiced, believing that a military and imperial death awaited him,” and so forth.

For, at home, he was crushed and strangled by the hands of slaves: his breath blocked and his throat constricted. I will not say that he died like Lentulus, Jugurtha, or Sejanus, but certainly with the death of Scipio of Numantia.[^c0065-15] This made the slaughter less grievous, because the crime itself, together with the perpetrator of the parricidal deed, was discovered at dawn. For who, so far removed from ordinary human perception—or so blind in both eyes—that, after looking upon the lifeless corpse, would not immediately gather the signs of a life violently extinguished? The evidence was at once supplied by the livid skin, the protruding eyes, and, in the disfigured face, traces of anger no less than of pain.

The earth was indeed found wet with fallen gore, because after the crime the robbers had turned the dead man’s face downward toward the pavement, as though an overflowing stream of blood had emptied him. But the man who had been the spark, instigator, and ringleader of the faction was immediately seized, and the other accomplices were arrested and separately interrogated. The truth of the crime was drawn from their unwilling hearts by the terror of torture.

Would that he had not deserved to meet this end while imprudently consulting vain superstition. For whoever presumes to investigate things forbidden, secret, and prohibited, I fear that he will depart from the rules of the Catholic faith and become worthy of entering a condition in which evils answer those who seek unlawful things.

Vengeance did indeed follow the dead man’s extinction, but such examples benefit the living more. Whenever a murderer is punished, vengeance is not a remedy but a consolation.

My affection has driven me rather far, because I could not exhale its anguish in silence. Meanwhile, if there is anything there worth knowing, quickly let me know—at least write for this reason, so that reading may lighten my spirit, weighed down by sadness. For my heart was confused with grief, and justly so, when I committed these matters to the pages alone. At this time I have no sufficient desire to write, speak, or deliberate about anything else by hand, by speech, or by counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER XII

Sidonius sends greetings to his lord Trigetius.[^c0065-16]

[^c0065-16]: I believe this is the same man whom the fragment of Prosper that we cited in book I, letter 9, calls a prefect and testifies was sent as an ambassador to Attila with Saint Leo and Avienus. He had therefore been prefect. He also held a military command, as may be inferred from Sidonius’ words. Prosper likewise records, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian, that peace was made with the Vandals through Trigetius; the history of Paul the Deacon confirms this.

Can the city of Vasates, built not on turf but on dust, hold you back so completely? Can the Syrtic land, the wandering soil, and the sands blown about by contending winds possess you so entirely that neither high demands supported by earnest entreaties, nor separation across a short distance, nor the expectation of many days can draw you to Bordeaux—not authority, friendship, nor oysters fattened in rich fishponds?

Or do winter seasons suspend you through uncertainty about the roads? And because the Bigerrian whirlwind is accustomed to confuse the marks of shifting embankments, do you fear some kind of terrestrial shipwreck on foot during the journey? Where, I ask, has Calpe, recently subdued beneath your footsteps, so quickly vanished from your mind? Where are the tents fixed at the western boundary of the Gaditanians? Where is that endpoint of travel which once marked the limit for my Trigetius, as for Hercules?

Have you become so unlike yourself that you have wholly surrendered to the rights of idleness? Once, while you traversed the hidden places of legendary regions, the activity of labor failed before the impulse toward fatigue. And after this, do you tread so sluggishly on the harbor of Alingon,[^c0065-17] as though you were now required to proceed to the Danubian frontier against the invading Massagetae,[^c0065-18] or as though your ships were even now crossing the waters of the Nile, feared by the native crocodiles?

[^c0065-17]: The name of the town remains on the Garonne in the diocese of Vasates. Today it is called Langon, from which the journey to Bordeaux downstream is short. Paulinus mentions the place in letter 2 to Delphidius and again in letter 2 to Amandus. Above Alingon, in Novempopulania, lies Cossio of the Vasates; farther away, near the Pyrenean pass, are the Bigerri, now the Bigorrenses, from whom the wind blows that mixes the sands of Vasates like the sands of the Syrtis.

[^c0065-18]: Strabo, book XVII, on Berenice: “From this city, in thirty days on foot, Marcus Cato traversed the Syrtis, leading an army of more than ten thousand men.” From that city Cato crossed the Syrtis within thirty days, leading an army of more than ten thousand men. Many celebrated this event as something resembling a prodigy. Cato’s own epitaph reads:

> Through an uncertain path he traversed the trackless Syrtis.

And since not even the obstacle of twelve miles delays you in this way, what should we think you would have done with the army of Marcus Cato in the Lepitane Syrtis?

Yet although you tremble at the mere names of the winter months, the face of the sky is so mild, so warm, so clear, and has breezes rather than winds, that the season cannot hold you back more forcefully than the temperate weather invites you.

But if you disdain the imperial summons,[^c0065-19] I believe you will not resist verses either—gentle persuaders and, as I suspect, energetic executors of my longing. Their camp will move against you in two days.

[^c0065-19]: The letters of the emperors to which he alludes were called *evocatoriae*. By them absent persons were summoned to the imperial court, or those who desired an imperial audience were given confidence to come. Without such a summons no one was permitted to come to court, according to book III of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions and Silentiaries*. Senator, book VII of the *Variae*, gives formulas of both kinds. An example of the former occurs in Jordanes, in the summons by which Zeno ordered Theodoric to come to Constantinople.

Look: my Leontius, easily the foremost of the Aquitanians, and Paulinus, only slightly inferior to his father,[^c0065-20] will soon meet you at the place I mentioned above, traveling along the returning waters of the Garonne—not merely with a fleet, but with the river itself.

[^c0065-20]: From letter 11 we learned that Livia was the mother of Pontius Leontius and that her son was Paulinus; from poem 22, that Pontius Paulinus was the leading member of his family.

There you will sing your praises to a measured rowing-song, while the rowers sing among the thwarts and the helmsmen among the stern ornaments. There a bed constructed of cushions awaits you; there a board spread with two-colored counters; there a busy die will resound along the ivory steps of the gaming towers. There, so that the swinging bilge-water may not wet your dangling foot, the hollow bellies of the ships will be furnished with platforms woven from fir beams. There, beneath the bent latticework of awnings,[^c0065-21] you will avoid the uncertain winter weather.

[^c0065-21]: *Paradae* are coverings for ships, intended to ward off the sun, cold, and other hardships of the weather. Ausonius writes to Theoni, letter 6:

> Hurry swiftly to the stern, and spread the curving sails;  
>   
> The breeze of the Medullian Notus will carry you.  
>   
> I lie beneath the awnings, exposed,  
>   
> On my couch, so that the burden of so great a body is not disturbed.

What more could be expended for your delicate idleness than for you to discover that you have arrived when you scarcely feel yourself traveling?

Why do you mutter? Why do you delay? I think crawling snails, with their native houses, will overtake your arrival before you do.

Besides, you have an abundant supply of provisions, lavishly filled with heaped-up delicacies—provided that your spirit is as large as the expense of airing them out. What more need be said? Come, so that you may feast or provide a feast—or rather, what is more agreeable, both.

Come equipped with inland provisions to defeat and subdue these banqueters of Medulian furniture. Here let the fish of the Aturri challenge the mullets of the Garonne; here, against the abundance of locusts from Lapurdum,[^c0065-22] let the common crowd of worthless crabs yield.

[^c0065-22]: “Of the people of Bayonne.” The city that is now Bayonne, in Novempopulania, was formerly the fort of Lapurdum, where a tribune of a cohort of Novempopulania had his station, as recorded in the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the West. The bishops of Bayonne are likewise called bishops of Lapurdum in ancient lists. Finally, the region itself retains the complete name *Lapurdi* in the native language. Sidonius therefore calls the locusts *Lapurdenses*, because they were caught at Bayonne, at the mouth of the Aturri.

Although you will be contending with the others in this kind of battle, if you accept my judgment—for it is not unjust to trust one who has experience—make our senator and my host exempt from this contest. If you take your place at his table and under his roof, you will think the dishes Cleopatra’s and the accommodations luxurious.[^c0065-23]

[^c0065-23]: I believe Sidonius wrote *loca lautia* rather than *loca Latia*, and this is exactly how the oldest and most trustworthy manuscript reads; a later hand, however, altered *lautia* to *Latia*. *Loca lautia* means the luxurious quarters customarily decreed for ambassadors: a roof, of course, and more sumptuous food. The expression was later extended to other contexts, as in Apuleius, book III: “He will provide me with lodging and luxurious quarters”; and Symmachus, book IV, letter 56: “You have given the Muses luxurious quarters in the palace.”

For although he and his homeland compete in this pursuit, the verdict was long ago delivered: he surpasses all the other citizens, just as his homeland surpasses all the other cities. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his lord Nonnechius.[^c0065-24]

[^c0065-24]: The name is more accurately written *Nunechius*, *Νουνέχιος*, in the Council of Venice, which he signed. Later there was another bishop of the same name, Nonnechius, bishop of Nantes, during the reign of King Guntram. He was the cousin and successor of Bishop Felix, whom Gregory of Tours discusses in books VI and VIII.

We rejoice that many kinds of virtue have been heaped upon you, most blessed bishop, by heavenly favor. You are said to act nobly without arrogance, powerfully without envy, religiously without superstition, learnedly without boastfulness, gravely without ineptitude, humorously without frivolity, steadfastly without harshness, and familiarly without vulgarity.

Moreover, fame adds this most outstanding feature to these many good qualities: it asserts that you surpass all these graces from the lofty citadel of the highest charity. I say “fame”—the fame that, while singing many things about your praises, conceals still more. For to those who are far away it can indicate the purpose of your actions, but not their number.

Inflamed by reports of these things, I hasten first of my own accord to discharge my obligations, as befits one far inferior to you. Nor do I fear being accused of loquacity, since I could have been blamed until now for silence.

I commend to you Promotus, bearer of this letter, previously known to us but recently made our fellow citizen through your prayers. Though Jewish by race, he has chosen to be considered an Israelite by faith rather than by blood. Desiring citizenship in that heavenly city, and despising the letter that kills in favor of the life-giving Spirit, he contemplates on one side the rewards appointed for the righteous and on the other foresees that, unless he defected from circumcision to Christ, he would suffer equally enduring punishments throughout the eternal ages. He preferred that Jerusalem rather than *Hierosolyma* should be reckoned his homeland.

Once these things are recognized, may the spiritual Sarah, with maternal arms, receive this arriving son of Abraham as the truer son. For he ceased to belong to the slave-woman Hagar when he exchanged servitude to legal observance for the freedom of grace.

As for the reason that brought him here, he himself will be able to explain it fully in a way useful to the present moment. He is dear to us for the reasons stated above. I mention this because the person who most effectively commends someone is the one who lays open the genuine grounds for a just recommendation.

Deign to remember us, my lord bishop.

## LETTER XIV

Sidonius sends greetings to his lord Principius.[^c0065-25]

[^c0065-25]: Bishop of Soissons and brother of Remigius, bishop of Reims; Sidonius also praises him and their father Aemilius without naming them. Flodoard discusses all of them in book I, chapter 10. As for Antiolius, whom Sidonius indicates once inhabited the monastic desert of Lérins with Lupus of Troyes and Maximus of Riez, it is uncertain of which see he was bishop.

For a long time now, venerable bishop, although we have not yet seen your face, we have inspected your conduct. The widely diffused praise of holy merits is not confined by spatial limits. Hence, because a good conscience has no measure, a good reputation has no boundary either.

Consider what I say false unless a suitable witness comes forward in support of my testimony: the venerable Antiolius, once a conspicuous leader in that Lérins monastery, a fellow-cellmate of Lupus and Maximus, striving through the paths of austerity to rival the Egyptian and Palestinian archimandrites.

This Antiolius, by his account, made me eagerly wish to learn who your father was, what sort of brothers you were, and with what distinction of character you both exercised the highest priesthood; and I remember rejoicing that I had learned it.

To that father, who once possessed you as sons, the house of the ancient priest Aaron could scarcely have been compared in merit. Although that first priest, standing amid the people of the hermitage, was drenched with the oil of sanctification by the right hand of his lawgiving brother and summoned his sons to similar offices, yet Nadab and Abihu, struck by lightning, dimmed his happiness despite Ithamar and Eleazar.[^c0065-26] We may believe that the souls of those who were killed were absolved, but we know that their persons were punished.

[^c0065-26]: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu were consumed by divine fire for offering unauthorized fire.

But when you approach the altar page, you offer, as I hear, no foreign fire. Accompanied by sacrifices of charity and chastity, you burn the most fragrant incense in the censers of your hearts.

Whenever you bind the yoke of the law around the necks of the proud through the bonds of preaching, you spiritually sacrifice bulls to God.

Whenever you drive those polluted by the filth of a luxuriant conscience toward the fragrance of chastity with the goads of correction, Christ counts it as though you had offered him the stench of goats.

Whenever, at your exhortation, a soul pricked by guilt recalls its faults with penitential sighs, who could doubt that you have offered a mystical sacrifice corresponding to pairs of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which represent by both number and lamentation the double substance of our twofold human nature?

Whenever, at your instruction, someone burns away an obese body and the fatty swelling of a distended belly in the fire of frequent fasting, no one doubts that you are then consecrating fine flour fried in a certain pan of self-restraint.

Whenever you persuade someone who has been constructing the fabrications of a faithless mind to answer with sound doctrine, to believe the faith, to keep the way, and to hope for life, who could doubt that, in the reform of this convert—now freed from heresy, freed from hypocrisy, freed from schism—you dedicate the purest bread of confession together with the unleavened loaves of sincerity and truth?

Finally, who does not know that whatever was figuratively sacrificed in bodily forms during the days of the law, all of that you openly offer in conduct in the age of grace?

Therefore I give abundant thanks to God, because, judging from the quality of your page, I readily recognize that the bishop mentioned above, when he said great things about you, kept still greater things silent. Hence no one will doubt that, since you are good when reported, better when read, you are best of all when seen.

Megethius the cleric, bearer of your eloquence, has carried the gifts of your writings to me and, since he has accomplished his commission successfully, brings back my services in return. At least I have helped him with my good wishes, since perhaps I cannot do so in reality. Through him I earnestly beg you both, as brothers, to refresh our thirst frequently with learned letters—you more often than he.

But if the difficulty of the intervening journey opposes your wishes, then at least occasionally pray for us who are suppliants. It is a greater favor if you deign to grant us salvation through rare intercessions than dignity through frequent words.

Deign to remember us, my lord bishop.

## LETTER XV
# Sidonius to Pope Prosper: Greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0613C] 94 To Prosper, Bishop of Orléans, whose mention, apart from this passage and Bede’s Martyrology on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, is scarcely found among the ancients. Prosper the bishop who took part in the councils of Carpentras and Vaison was a different man, and later; for at the time of those synods the bishop of Orléans was not Prosper but Eusebius or Leontius. Closer to this man in date, and plainly his contemporary, was Prosper of Aquitaine, whom some make bishop of Riez in Gaul, others bishop of Reggio in Italy. In my judgment, however, he was never a bishop. He could not have presided over the church in Province II at Riez—as many distinguished men, I see, have thought—for it is certain, whether on Sidonius’s authority or otherwise, that Faustus succeeded Maximus in that see.
