Maximus was already bishop in the days of Hilary of Arles, as is clear from the councils of Riez and Orange and from Hilary’s own Life; hence he was still alive when Prosper, who continued his Chronicle beyond Hilary’s lifetime, indeed down to the capture of the city by the Vandals, was still living. Faustus, Maximus’s successor, as Sidonius’s letters show, outlived Prosper, whom everyone agrees did not survive to the time of the emperor Anthemius. It follows that Prosper of Aquitaine could have governed the see of Riez neither before Maximus nor after Faustus. But the reason I think he was not a bishop at all is the authority of all the ancients: Victorinus, in his work on the Paschal cycle addressed to Hilary; Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 84; Pope Gelasius, *On Apocryphal Books*; Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, book I, chapter 30; Marcellinus Comes in his genuine and uncorrupted Chronicle; and others. Although they relate everything else about Prosper, they make no mention whatsoever of episcopal rank. I therefore believe that Prosper, who is numbered among the bishops of Reggio Lepido, was a different man from the Aquitanian, and that those who, with Trithemius and Flaminius, confuse the two are mistaken.] Greetings to Prosper.

Since you wished the holy Anianus, that greatest and most consummate pontiff, equal to Lupus and not inferior to Germanus, to be celebrated with the highest praises, and since you desired that the character, merits, and virtues of so great and good a man be impressed upon the hearts of the faithful—who is also justly granted this further glory, that he died leaving you as his successor—you had exacted from me a promise that I would disclose in writing to posterity the war against Attila, containing, in particular, the siege, assault, and entry into the city of Orléans, though not its plundering, together with that famous prophecy of the priest heard from heaven. I had begun to write, but when I saw the burden of the work I had undertaken, I grew weary of having begun it; and for that reason I entrusted to no ears what I had first condemned as a critic. I hope that your petition and the merits of the supreme bishop will obtain this for us, so that we may serve his praise on some occasion—indeed on the earliest possible occasion. Meanwhile, as a just creditor, you will laudably forgive the rash imprudence of your debtor, so that what seems insoluble to me may seem to you also impossible to demand. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER XVI

Sidonius to his Constantius: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0614C] To whom this book was specially dedicated: see Letter I. “So that,” he says, “the series of letters may be extended by the sum of a still small number.”]

I had promised Petronius, an illustrious man, that I would dispatch this little work in a few letters; I did not spare his ears while I spare yours. For I preferred that he should see the labor of correction, while you received the honor of publication, and that this volume should come into your hands at the risk of another but through my service. The promise has been fulfilled. For if your expertise examines the marks of titles collected on the parchment, you are already, if I am not mistaken, pressing upon a substantial copy; already we are coming to the edges of the bosses; already it is time, as the satirist says, that our Orestes should be finished even upon its back.

I have not here summoned some counterfeit Terpsichore in the manner of my former studies; nor have I drawn my pen beside the spring of the Aganippian fountain, along dewy banks and moss-covered rocks. And would that nothing soft, nothing fluid, nothing borrowed from crossroads and street-corners were found here. For a mature reader, such as you are, prefers not merely language stripped of its bones, tender, weak in the loins, but language somewhat old-fashioned, sinewy, and almost manly. Yet let these things be reserved for better writers. It is enough for me if you quickly forgive us for being slow.

Moreover, if the illustrious man had demanded that something still longer be written, we should have fallen into great delays. For our little cupboards and private studies did not retain anything worthy of being brought forth.

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “Through the chests and little studies.” Pliny the Younger, in his description of his Laurentine villa, book II, Letter 17: “Against the middle wall a little study withdraws most elegantly; covered with window-panes and curtains, drawn back or closed, it is now added to the bedroom, now taken away; it holds a bed and two chairs.” Likewise book V, Letter 6, in the description of his Tuscan villa: “Next, a little study retreats as though into the same room and yet another; here is a small couch and windows on every side.” There is no doubt that Sidonius borrowed this word from Pliny. Yet the current copies of Pliny, through the fault of correctors—because throughout the entire text of both letters there is frequent mention of *diaetae* or *zaetae*—here too display *diaetam* and *diaetulam* in two places; but the reading of the ancient manuscripts, which I have reproduced, is certain. From Pliny’s words it is not difficult to understand that *zothecae*, properly so called, were more private rooms and little dwellings attached to the bedrooms of a house, in which the owners withdrew and devoted themselves to private studies—what we commonly call studies or cabinets. Sidonius uses the same word again in book IX, Letter 11; it also occurs in an inscription at Tivoli published by Savaro, and in this previously unpublished inscription from Reate.

[Col. 0615B]

“To Tiberius Claudius Felix Scapulanus, freedman of Augustus, D. III, Q. III, quinquennial, exempt, *triplicarius*, well-deserving: by resolution of the entire council they publicly gave a *zotheca* as an honor. Atimetus, freedman, furnished it at his own expense.”

]

Understand, then, that although we have not yet begun to keep silent, we have certainly already decided to wish to keep silent, for two reasons: so that, if we please, the little we write may kindle pleasure in those who read it; and, if we are rejected, the abundance may not arouse disgust. For this is a style in which there is no urban elegance, but rustic simplicity.

Whence should we have that harsh and extremely ancient manner of speech? Whence those Saliarian or Sibylline words, or those summoned from the Sabines all the way from Cures—words that some herald, priest, or antiquated interpreter of legal riddles might reveal more readily, while teachers generally remain silent?

[Note: [Col. 0616B] Symmachus, book III, to Siburius: “If you have so great a love of antiquity, let us return with equal zeal to ancient words, in which the Salii sing, the augurs consult the birds, and the Decemvirs composed the tables.”]

[Col. 0616A] We have published these little works in dry and meager speech, for the most part certainly commonplace. Its distinction lies here in its rarity, because its use is frequent; and its favor is difficult because its invention is easy. I openly confess that, just as there is nothing sharp or eloquent here, so nothing has been inserted that was not taken from an example.

But why say more? My language—which is enough for me—pleases my friends. Among these I embrace both possibilities: either they are not deceived in their judgment, or they are deceived by affection. For what remains, I ask God that those who come after us may either be similarly deceived or form the same judgment. Farewell.

# BOOK NINE

## LETTER I

Sidonius to his Firminus: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] To Firminus of Arles, a man distinguished by birth and piety. I infer that he is the man whom Cyprian praises in the *Life of Saint Caesarius*, and from whom, he testifies, Caesarius received hospitality and assistance. Ennodius also has two letters to this same man.]

[Col. 0615B]

My lord son, you demand that, breaking through the boundary of my earlier letters, my style run farther forward and not be content to be enclosed within the privilege of the number already stated. You add the reasons why this ninth book should increase the eight preceding volumes: namely, that Gaius Secundus, whose tracks you declare that we are following in this work, brings his epistolary composition to an end under an equal number of titles.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] We have ten books of Pliny’s letters; but he does not count the tenth—entirely addressed to Trajan and written from the province—with the others. In the same way, Symmachus’s letters properly comprise nine books, those addressed to private individuals; the tenth contains reports sent to emperors during his prefecture of the City. Others after Sidonius also adopted this very number of books, such as Avitus of Vienne, as Gregory of Tours records, book II, chapter 33. In book VI, chapter 7, the same Gregory states that Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès, also composed several books of letters, apparently in imitation of Sidonius; but he does not specify the number of books.]

What you order is not unreasonable, although the very task you piously impose is difficult and not suited to a reputation, however slight, that has already been acquired. First, because the late joining of this addition to a work previously published is awkward; and second, because, before any judges, unless we are mistaken, it is exceedingly improper for a single, simple beginning of one subject to have three conclusions.

Likewise, I do not know how it can become pardonable that our loquacity refuses to be restrained even after a limit has been announced—unless perhaps the measure that cannot be imposed upon pages cannot be imposed upon friendships either. Therefore you ought to stand, as it were, as a lookout defending my reputation, and reveal to the curious the reason for this action; and you should disclose to me, by as frequent a reply as possible, what the very best men think about it.

Moreover, if you compel me to chatter while you persist in silence, it is not altogether unjust that you too should be punished in turn by retaliation for our silence. So, first and foremost, forgive the business and the service that you impose. We, for our part, if any copy should come into our hands, shall quickly add it to the margins of the eighth book.

And if your Apollinaris—

[Note: [Col. 0616D] Other manuscripts read this with a different sense: “whose mind is negligent in all other matters, and in this one certainly most negligent.” For he is held by very little reading, whether under compulsion or by choice. Yet, as it seems to me, I would not refuse to join him to those fathers whose zeal, hope, and fear make it possible—though difficult—to persuade a son to do something praiseworthy, and more difficult still to satisfy him.]

—if your Apollinaris, whose zeal in other matters is certainly most negligent in this one, since he gives himself to very little reading, whether under compulsion or voluntarily; yet, so far as I can see, I would not refuse to join myself to those fathers by whose zeal, hope, and fear something praiseworthy is instilled in their sons, though with difficulty, and satisfies them with greater difficulty still. Farewell.

## LETTER II

Sidonius to Euphronius, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0616D] Bishop of Autun; see Letter 8 of Book VII. When Sidonius was asked by him to expound some part of Sacred Scripture, he most modestly declined.]

Bishop Albiso and the Levite Proculus, who deserve to be called teachers of character because they deserve to be your pupils, brought me a letter in which you granted me the gift of your sacred speech. Yet that letter imposes upon me a great deal of honor, and still more of a burden. Hence I rejoice in its blessing in such a way that I am confounded by its command; for I am altogether disturbed and in part disobedient.

You order something at once so difficult and so slight, and you decree that a work be unfolded which is completed by my feeble powers with as much difficulty as it is begun with presumption. But if I rightly measure the abundance of the piety I have experienced in you, you have labored more to make the affection of your heart known than the product of our work.

For when Jerome the interpreter, Augustine the dialectician, and Origen the allegorist are bringing forth for you, from the fruitful harvest of salutary doctrine, ears heavy with spiritual meanings, will not the dry straw of my fasting tongue crackle in its place? In this way you would rightly associate, with the songs of swans, hoarse geese, and with the measured complaints of nightingales, the chirping murmurs of worthless sparrows.

And what would be more arrogant and improper than for me to undertake the burden of the task commanded—a new cleric, an old sinner, slight in knowledge and heavy in conscience? Thus, if I were to send you any written work, my person would not then be absent from the laughter of the judges, even though it had been absent from their sight.

Therefore, my lord pope, do not press too hard upon my modesty, however it may be hiding, so that I am disfigured by the presumption of this undertaking. For the spite of detractors is so great that the material you send will receive disgrace in its unfinished state more quickly than, once completed, it will obtain approval. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER III

Sidonius to Faustus, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] Bishop of Riez in Province II, formerly abbot of Lérins; he held both offices after Maximus, and is therefore called twice the successor of Maximus in the Eucharistic poem near its end. How highly Hilary of Arles esteemed him while he was still an abbot is shown by the author of Hilary’s Life in these words: “At that same place and time he honored Saint Faustus, then both presbyter and abbot, with such foreknowledge of the future that he made him sit between himself and the holy priests Theodore and Maximus.” More about Faustus elsewhere. For now it is enough to note that, besides this elder Faustus, another Faustus also occupied the same episcopal see of Riez about eighty years later. The complete subscriptions of the Fifth Council of Orléans have taught us this, lest it remain wholly unknown: among those who subscribed on behalf of absent bishops, Claudianus is read as “deacon sent by Faustus, bishop of the Church of Riez.” He was plainly the later bishop of that same see, and he attended the Council of Paris at which the case of Promotus, bishop of Die, was considered, as the acts of that council which we possess testify.]

Your eloquence and piety preserve their accustomed character. Therefore we receive with great pleasure your eloquence, because you write so expressively, and your affection, because you write so gladly.

For the present, however, after first asking and obtaining your pardon, I think it most cautious and salutary to send more frequent written messages through these cities which are widely separated by their situation, while the roads are made dangerous by the movements of peoples; and meanwhile, postponing for a time the diligence of our mutual conversation, to undertake rather the duty of keeping silent.

Although this is extremely harsh and bitter between persons bound together by affection, it is not brought about by just any causes, but by many, certain, and necessary ones, arising from different sources. The first of these will be counted as follows: a courier does not pass through the guards of the public ramparts without being questioned. Although he is free from guilt and therefore from danger, he usually suffers a great deal of difficulty, while an ever-watchful investigator searches out every secret of the messengers.

If by chance his answer to the questions should hesitate even slightly, anything not found written down is believed to have been entrusted to him. Thus the person sent usually suffers injury, while the sender suffers suspicion—especially at a time when the treaties once established among rival kingdoms are again being made uncertain by discordant conditions.

Besides this, our own mind lies wounded on every side by domestic losses. For, under the appearance—or, more truthfully, the necessity—of office, I have been driven from my native land and sent into exile, assailed by various disturbances everywhere; here I suffer the hardships of a foreigner, there the losses of a proscribed man.

Accordingly, I am either asked to compose somewhat polished letters at an unsuitable time, or I undertake them shamelessly. To exchange letters that are witty in jest or elegant in style belongs to happier men.

Moreover, there is a barbarism of character, pleasant speech, and a distressed mind.

[Note: [Col. 0618C] The best authors often transfer the word *solecism* with equal elegance to other matters. Cicero, *To Atticus*, book II, Letter 11: “I do not like watching the games at Antium; for it is a solecism, since I wish to avoid every suspicion of luxury.” Jerome, *Against Helvidius*: “Among Christians it is a great solecism and a fault, a shameful thing either to say or to do.” Likewise Lucian, *On the Dance*, says that for Heracles to deliver a monody on stage would seem a *solecism*, although it could be acceptable in *Andromache* and *Hecuba*. The sophist Polemo, speaking of an actor who said “O Zeus” while pointing toward the ground, and “O Earth” while extending his hand toward heaven, says: “This man has committed a solecism with his hand”—as Philostratus relates in his *Life* of him.]

Rather, as one whose soul is ill-conscious and trembles hour by hour at the recollection of the obligations of a punishable life, reward me with those frequent and powerful gifts of your prayers. You are skilled in the prayers of the islands, which you transferred from the training-ground of the eremitic community and the senate of the monastic cells of Lérins into the city whose sacred supervision you now exercise, unchanged from abbot into priest.

[Note: [Col. 0618D] Some think that this passage allows one to infer that Faustus had only recently been promoted to the episcopate when Sidonius wrote this letter. But he calls the dignity “new,” not because it had then been acquired, but because it had succeeded the earlier dignity of the abbacy. That Faustus had been a veteran bishop—bishop for more than twelve years—when Sidonius wrote this is shown by the letters of Pope Hilary, which mention that Faustus, already a bishop, carried out a mission to Rome with Auxanius in the year 462.]

For under the pretext of your new dignity you have not relaxed the strictness of your former discipline. Obtain, then, by those most effective prayers, as I said above, that the Lord may be our portion; and that, enrolled among the bands of our fellow Levites in sorrow, we may not remain earthly, since the earth does not remain ours; and that, just as we have begun to be strangers to the profits of the world, so also we may begin to be strangers to its sins.

The third, and perhaps greatest, reason why I have delayed writing to you is this: I greatly fear to attempt in your presence that tropological and figurative mode of composition, conspicuous for its words polished in many ways, which your letter, the one we received, displays.

For although I have heard your sermons—sometimes improvised, sometimes prepared when reason demanded it—with a hoarse clapping of hands, especially when, at the request of your holy colleagues, you were entreated to preach at the weekly festivals dedicated in the church of Lyons, there we surrounded you with minds raised and ears bent down as you delivered something midway between spiritual and forensic discourse, being highly learned in both disciplines. In that setting you satisfied our judgment, though you left our desire only partly fulfilled.

For these reasons I have restrained my pen and shall restrain it still: I have spoken briefly in order to obey, and I shall be silent at length in order to learn. The rest is your task, my lord pope: to devote yourself sufficiently to salutary and singular teaching through works destined to live. Whoever listens to you teaching and disputing learns not so much to speak as to do what deserves praise.

For the present, then, pardon this rustic page that serves you; it has, in comparison with your letters, a style that is infantile even when I am its author. But why do I foolishly make these excuses? To apologize excessively for follies is itself the greatest folly. In these matters you are the sole judge: if you strip away the covering and examine the matter completely, you will laugh at many things and blame more.

I also welcome this possibility: if, in accordance with the affection in which you are strong, you are not altogether strict in judging; that is, if your judgment should mark something in these lines as antiquated. For then I shall rejoice more certainly that you approved the rest, if I learn that you erased something. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER IV

Sidonius to Graecus, my lord pope: greetings.

Our traveler and courier wears down the accustomed paths, often retracing the distance of road and region that separates our towns. Therefore it is fitting that we too follow the duties of diligence once undertaken. Since Amantius in particular is traveling among the other messengers, we ought to redouble them with a certain concentration of mind, lest he seem to demand letters from custom more than we compose them from affection.

Therefore, my lord pope, remember more fully those of us whom we presume to count among your people; just as we are lifted by your prosperity, so we are depressed by your adversity. For it has reached us, in a mournful report to mourners, that recently you endured many anxieties because of the need of certain brethren.

But you, flower of priests, jewel of pontiffs, strong in knowledge and stronger in conscience, despise the threats and waves of worldly storms. For you have often taught that one reaches the promised banquets of the patriarchs, or the nectar of heavenly cups, through cups of earthly bitterness.

Whether willingly or unwillingly, everyone who attains the kingdom of the despised mediator follows his example. However many cups of anxiety the affliction of the present life may offer us, we endure little if we remember what he drank at the place of execution who invites us to heaven. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER V

Sidonius to Julian, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] To a bishop—not the bishop of Carpentras, who attended the Council of Epaon somewhat later and, at nearly the same time, the previously unpublished Council of Lyons concerning Stephen and Palladia, under Sigismund, king of the Burgundians; not this Julian, I say, who is known to have survived even to the time of the Second Council of Orange, but Julian, bishop of another unknown see, who also subscribes to a letter of Faustus and is numbered by Lucidus among those who assembled for the Council of Arles. A different Julian, apparently earlier than both, is the one to whom Leo the Great wrote with other bishops of Gaul in the year 452.]

Although we live in a place perhaps more widely separated than our common affection desired, our diligence would not be hindered by the obstruction of the intervening journey, so far as fulfilling our duty is concerned, unless, divided among kingdoms, we were recalled from more frequent conversation by the law of different fortunes.

Now at least, after the pact of peace has been made, our letters will begin to travel more frequently, since they have ceased to be suspect, because the kingdoms are being joined together in faithful hearts.

Therefore, my lord pope, join your prayers with those of your holy brethren, so that Christ may deign to prosper what we undertake; and, restraining the disputes of our dominion and curbing arms, may reward them with innocence, us with peace, and all of us with security. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER VI

Sidonius to Ambrosius, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] To the bishop to whom Ruricius wrote in book II, Letter 43.]

Your holiness prevailed with Christ on behalf of our dearest friend—what need have I to mention his name or person? You will recognize everything—through the effectiveness of your intercession. Concerning his youthful accessibility you often complained, now openly before summoned witnesses, now sighing in silence.

Recently, then, by breaking off his association with a most shameful maidservant, to whom he had wholly bound and enslaved himself through an infamous relationship, he provided for his property, his descendants, and his reputation by a sudden reform of himself. For, emptied by the losses of his estate, as soon as he began to understand and reconsider how much of his ancestral and paternal goods the extravagance of his household Charybdis had swallowed, he at last, though late in recovering his senses, as it were bit the reins, shook his neck free, and, fixing Ulysses’ wax—so they say—in his ears, fled deaf to vices and to the allurements of the prostitute’s shipwreck. He took the girl into marriage untouched, as was fitting, and deserves praise for doing so; she was as distinguished in character and birth as in wealth.

It would indeed be glory if he had abandoned pleasures in such a way that he did not even marry. But although it may happen that someone moves from error to good conduct, it belongs to few to begin with the greatest things; and those who have long indulged themselves in everything do not immediately and all at once renounce everything.

Therefore it is your task to obtain as quickly as possible, by joined and diligent prayer, the hope of children for this couple. After one or two sons have been received—and I have said too much—he who presumed upon unlawful things will thereafter abstain from what is lawful.

For the spouses themselves, although recently married, conduct themselves with such character and modesty that, if you see them even once, you will truly recognize how greatly that most honorable conjugal love differs from the inventions and enticements of concubinage. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER VII

Sidonius to Remigius, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] To the bishop of Reims, metropolis of Belgica II, apostle of King Clovis and of the Franks. Flodoard inserted this letter, together with Sidonius’s praise, into his *History*, book I, chapter 12. None of Remigius’s declamations, whose eloquence Sidonius so highly commends, has survived to us. Nor is this a recent loss, since Hincmar himself and Flodoard appear to have been entirely unaware of them.]

A certain man traveling from the Auvergne to Belgica—his identity is known to me, his purpose unknown, and it does not matter—after reaching Reims, apparently won over your secretary or bookseller either by payment or by service, extracted from him, willingly or unwillingly, a most abundant bundle of your declamations.

When he returned to us, very proud, naturally enough, after receiving so many volumes, he thrust upon us as a gift whatever he had brought, although he had been ready to buy it—which, nevertheless, was not unjust to either party.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] In Labbe’s edition the reading is *utilius* (“more advantageously”); some manuscripts have *(quod tamen cujus nec erat, injustum)*: “which, however, since it was not his, was unjust.”]

It immediately became my concern, and that of those who are devoted to study, to retain as much as possible, since we deservedly longed to read it, and to transcribe everything. By common agreement it was declared that few things could now be composed like it.

For rare, or perhaps nonexistent, is the person who, when preparing to write, can have an equal arrangement of material by subjects, placement by letters, and composition by syllables. In addition, there is appropriateness in the examples, reliability in the testimonies, precision in the epithets, urbanity in the figures, strength in the arguments, weight in the thoughts, a river in the words, and lightning in the clauses.

The structure is strong and firm, and the interwoven conjunctions are exceedingly elegant, joined by unbreakable caesuras. Yet it is no less smooth and light, rounded in every respect, and so well formed that it releases the reader’s tongue without hindrance or impropriety, lest, after encountering rough joints and being rolled about in the chamber of the palate, it should stammer.

Finally, the whole is perfectly fluid and pliable, as when a finger without a striking fingernail glides over crystalline crusts or onyx surfaces; nothing tenacious, caught by cracked obstacles, delays it with a splintered break.

What more can I say? At present there is no speech of any living person that your skill could not, though not without labor, overtake and surpass. Hence I almost suspect, my lord pope, that because of your overflowing and unspeakable eloquence—pardon the expression—you are proud.

Yet although you shine in goodness of conscience as well as in the most orderly expression, you must not flee from us, who praise what is well written even though we do not write what deserves praise. Therefore do not in future avoid our judgments, which contain nothing biting and threaten no reproach.

Otherwise, if you delay enriching our barrenness with eloquent conversation, we shall lie in wait for the markets of flying thieves; and, while we connive and supply accomplices, clever hands will plunder your chests. Then, robbed by theft, you will begin in vain to stir yourself, if now, when asked, you are not moved by duty. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER VIII

Sidonius to Principius, my lord pope: greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] To the bishop of Soissons, as stated in Book VIII, Letter 14. In that letter he also names the cleric Megethius, through whom he had received and returned letters; for that reason he now calls him an old courier.]

Although your letters were delivered by an old courier without our expecting them, though we desired them, he proved a suitable person to whom the repeated duty could rightly be entrusted, since he had carried out the first so well.

Therefore, after receiving a second greeting—or rather a blessing—I too return another “hail,” joining service to service, equal in number, though not in merit.

And because, my lord pope, we now live with regions joined to some and separated from others, and because the separation of our dwelling places prevents us from enjoying mutual sight, pray that, when the holy day of judgment shines forth, we may, having happily and religiously departed this life and discharged its anxieties and burdens, be joined to your ranks to serve with them at the resurrection—or perhaps under the pretext of Gibeonite servitude.

For according to the heavenly promises, which pledged that the sons of faith would be gathered from the nations, if forgiveness assuages us who are guilty, while glory awaits you who are blessed, then, although we shall be separated by the difference of our deeds, we shall not be separated by distance of place. Deign to remember us, my lord pope.

## LETTER IX

Sidonius to Faustus, my lord pope: greetings.

You have complained that I have kept silent too long about our common concerns. I recognize the diligence of your side in this matter; I do not recognize guilt on ours. For some time ago I was ordered to chatter, and I did not remain silent in these letters sent ahead.

When these letters reached Riez, even as they were being read—

[Note: [Col. 0621D] The correction of this passage was not difficult, in place of the reading “because you were then suitably present.” Those who handle ancient manuscripts know that copyists who neglect diphthongs rarely distinguish these forms. The meaning, therefore, is that Faustus was then at Apt, a nearby city, when Sidonius’s letter was carried to Riez. Sidonius says most aptly and appropriately that Faustus was absent from Riez, so that the letter would not so quickly come under his judgment. Apt Julia Vulgentium—for this is how Pliny calls it in book III, chapter 4—lies approximately midway between Riez and Avignon, as can also be seen from the Itinerary of Aethicus and the Peutinger Table. The following inscription from Arles shows that Apt was a colony:

“Julius Caius Tertullinus, flamen of the colony of Apt; Lucius Vallius Atilianus, descendant, [erected this].”]

—because you were then at Apt, you were most suitably absent. This was greatly welcome and very much desired by me: that the assigned letter should neither be refused as written in friendship nor subjected, once read, to judgment.

Let us set these matters aside. Again you order that an ample page be sent. My wishes are ready to obey one who hurries me, but my reasons are absent. For unless a greeting carries with it some active matter of business, it is concise; and whoever extends it with unnecessary words departs and wanders from the path of Sallust, who criticizes Catiline for possessing eloquence enough but too little wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] From this it is clear that the ancients were accustomed to write “Ave” and “Salve” at the beginning of a letter, just as they wrote “Vale” at the end. Ausonius to Paulinus:

“Why should anything forbid the ready brevity of ‘Hail’ and ‘Farewell’?”]

To write “Greetings” and “Farewell” and send such brief messages in little books? Traces of this practice remain in certain imperial rescripts: “Have, dearest Felix”; “Greetings, Cynegius, most noble and distinguished man.” This was derived from ordinary daily usage, for they used the same formulas when meeting and departing. Among the Greeks: “Χαῖρε καὶ Ὑγίαινε” (“Greetings and good health”), as appears in Dio’s *Hadrian*. Plutarch, in *On Talkativeness*, relates of Augustus that when Fulvius had rashly blurted out something or other and came to him the next day saying, “Hail, Caesar,” he replied, “Farewell, Fulvius”:

> “When he came at dawn, as Fulvius was accustomed to come to him, and said, ‘Greetings, Caesar; good health,’ he said, ‘Fulvius.’”

After saying “Greetings,” we shortly afterward say “Farewell”; pray for us.

But all is well—yes, all is well—for just as I was about to fold up the sheet, an important matter suddenly came to me. If my joy or anger restrains itself any longer from reproaching you for it, I shall judge myself worthy of having received the insult. You have come into my hands, master, and I do not merely rejoice but exult—yes, you have come; and indeed such a man as our long-standing desires had been awaiting.

I am genuinely uncertain whether you came unwillingly, but certainly you resemble one who came unwillingly: for either through your foresight—or, if you deny this too strongly, through your acquiescence—I have remained unacknowledged by your books, and, what is far more injurious, while they passed through the territory of Auvergne, they scraped not only my walls but even my sides.

Were you afraid that we would begrudge your writings? But by God’s favor we are addicted to no fault less than to envy; and if I were subject to envy on my part in the same way as to all other faults, despair of attaining the thing would likewise remove from me the rivalry of competing for it. Or did you fear my raised eyebrow, as though I were a difficult and severe applauder? What neck of expertise is so stiff, or what dropsy so swollen, that it would not pursue even your lukewarm productions with the most ardent praise?

Or did you therefore take care that I should be despised and neglected because you held the younger man in contempt? I scarcely believe it. Or because I am unlearned? That I tolerate more readily, though in such a way that, while I do not know how to speak, I do know how to listen; for those who attend the Circus do not pronounce an opinion on the chariots.

Or were we at odds for some reason, so that you thought we would disparage the little books you had published? Yet, with God presiding, not even an enemy can pretend that our friendship is superficial.

“Why all this?” you ask. I shall now reveal it, whether I am glad that I have discovered something or angry that you concealed it from me.

I read your volumes, which Riochatus, bishop and monk, and twice a pilgrim from this world, is carrying back to your Britons on your behalf. He has become, for the present, a second Faustus who does not grow old and who, after burial, will not be absent from the living, but will become a survivor of himself through the very works he wrote.

This venerable man, then, while staying near our town until the storm of the roused nations had died down—for a whirlwind of that kind had then bristled on either side—uncovered the rest of your gifts in such a way that, with great urbanity, he concealed what he was carrying that was more valuable, pretending not to illuminate my thorns with your flowers.

But after two months or more, when someone had informed us that he had departed from us and that travelers were secretly carrying treasures of mystical wealth in closed wrappings, I pursued him as he left on swift horses, which could easily overtake the distances of the previous day. I sprang upon the throat of the captured robber in a human joke but with a wild beast’s gesture, like a tiger deprived of her cubs that leaps upon the neck of a kidnapper with the light-footed strength of a Parthian, as though about to tear apart whichever of the cubs she might find.

What more need be said? I clasp the knees of my captured guest, halt the animals, tie the reins, undo the packs, find the volume I had sought, bring it out, read it, and excerpt from it the principal sections of a great work. The eager obedience of the scribes also supplied a kind of shorthand, with skipping strokes: they grasped by signs what they could not retain in letters.

How many tears we shed, drenched in turn by one another’s mutual weeping when we were separated after repeated embraces, would take too long to tell and is irrelevant. It is enough to say that I returned home like a conqueror, laden with the spoils of charity and in possession of spiritual booty.

You now ask what judgment I form of my plunder. I would not yet reveal it, so that you might hang longer in suspense; for I should avenge myself more fully if I kept silent about what I felt. But you yourself are not vain without reason, since you understand that you possess the power to plead your case in such a way that the force of pleasure excludes the need for praise, whether your reader is reluctant or willing.

Therefore receive what we judge concerning your writings and the injury we have suffered.

[Note: Cardinal Baronius thought that there were two books, *On the Grace of God and the Free Will of the Human Mind*. Cardinal Baronius argues at length in Volume VI of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* that Sidonius is speaking of these here. But since Sidonius asserts that this work of Faustus was divided in two according to the form of a dialogue and in four according to the subject matter of the questions—and this description fits neither these two books nor any other of the surviving books of Faustus—it remains, in my judgment, that the work in question either perished or is still hidden somewhere.

Sirmondus’ note appears thus in the later edition of Sidonius, supervised by Labbeus. In the earlier edition of Sidonius, however, where the words read, “We read a work … divided in two according to the form of a dialogue,” Sirmondus had interpreted them in his notes, p. 162, following Cardinal Baronius, as referring to two books, *On the Grace of God and the Free Will of the Human Mind*:

“Baronius says that Sidonius is speaking here of these books, and supports this at length in Volume VI of the *Annals*; nor do we see among the remaining works of Faustus any other to which these words could more aptly apply. What reason, then, is there for their being adorned by Sidonius with so many praises, when it is certain that Gelasius, Fulgentius, Avitus, Caesarius, Facundus, and others either condemned them or refuted them in works opposed to them? Yet it is not difficult to remove Sidonius from the hazard of this judgment: he praises Faustus’ talent, art, and eloquence in this work, but does not touch upon the principles and judgments of his doctrine. Faustus, and those who at that time in Gaul—something that cannot be concealed—shared his views, seem to be excused to some extent by the fact that they lived before the Council of Orange, whose decrees the Church afterward used as the norm of doctrine against the errors of the Semi-Pelagians.”

—Baunius, in the cited place; consult him there.]

“We read a most laborious, manifold, vigorous, sublime work, arranged under headings and heaped up with examples, divided in two according to the form of a dialogue and in four according to the subject matter of the questions.”

You had written many things ardently, more things pompously; these simply, those neither subtly nor craftily; serious things with maturity, profound things with care, doubtful things with constancy, argumentative things in a disputatious manner; some severely, some gently; all morally, elegantly, powerfully, most eloquently.

And so, having followed you through so many kinds of narration across the whole vast field of your dictation, I easily perceived nothing in the eloquence of others or in their intellects that was equally polished.

You sufficiently approve that I truly feel these things, since even when not offended I judge in the same way. Finally, an absent man’s speech, as we suppose, cannot grow any further unless perhaps the voice, hand, movement, and modesty of the author speaking in person add something to it—the artist himself.

Endowed, therefore, with these gifts of mind and writing, you have wedded to yourself a beautiful woman—though one who, with Deuteronomy approving, is a bride—and this, lord pope, you did when still young. You saw her amid hostile troops, loved her there in the battle-line of the opposing side, and, with the arm of desire overcoming all the intervening fighters, carried her away, repulsed by nothing.

I mean Philosophy, violently removed from the number of sacrilegious arts, with the superfluities of false religion shorn from her cropped head, the arrogance of secular learning removed from her brow, and the wrinkles of very ancient garments cut off—that is, the convolutions of gloomy dialectic concealing false and illicit morals. Now purified through a mystical embrace, she joined her limbs with yours.

For many years she has been your attendant from earliest youth; she has been an inseparable companion at your side, whether you were exercising yourself in the urban gymnasia or wearing yourself out in hidden solitudes. She is the companion of the lecture hall, the companion of the monastery; with you she rejects worldly disciplines, with you she proclaims heavenly ones.

Whoever attacks you, joined in marriage to this woman, will discover that the Academy of Plato serves the Church of Christ and that you philosophize more nobly. First, you assert the ineffable wisdom of God the Father together with the eternity of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, you do not nourish a luxuriant head of hair, nor boast or aspire to boast in cloak or club as though these were sophists’ insignia; you do not cultivate pride in the distinctiveness of your clothing, display in its brilliance, or ostentation in its squalor.

Nor is it enough for you to imitate the figures painted throughout the gymnasia: the Areopagus or Prytaneum; Zeusippus with bent neck; Aratus with open mouth; Zeno with contracted brow; Epicurus with stretched skin; Diogenes with flowing beard; Socrates with falling hair; Aristotle with arm extended; Xenocrates with leg drawn up; Heraclitus with eyes closed in weeping; Democritus with lips opened in laughter; Chrysippus with fingers clenched to indicate numbers; Euclid with them extended to mark measurements; Cleanthes with them worn down on account of both.

Rather, whoever engages with you will experience Stoics, Cynics, Peripatetics, and heresiarchs shaken by their own weapons and by the devices of their own construction. For if their followers resist Christian doctrine and understanding, once bound by you as their teacher they will be thrown headlong into their own nets, caught in the bonds of their native speech. The hooked syllogisms of your proposition will denounce their slippery, evasive tongue, while you will tie up slippery questions with categorical coils, after the manner of skilled physicians who, when reason compels them, prepare a remedy against poisons from the serpent itself.

But this belongs to the present age only, whether under the contemplation of your conscience or through the power of your teaching. Who could follow your footsteps with an equal stride? You alone have been granted to speak better than you have learned and to live better than you speak.

Therefore all good men will rightly celebrate you as most blessed, and above all others in your generation. Your life and deeds have so brightly illuminated your words that, whenever you have already counted your years with your right hand—

[Note: Juvenal, *Satire* 10, concerning Nestor:

> “And now he counts his years on his right hand.”

This saying comes from the practice of the ancients, who indicated numbers by various bends of the fingers; Tertullian calls these counting gestures of the fingers *supputatorii digitorum gesticuli*. A little book among the works of Bede encompasses the entire art and is entitled *On the Speech of the Fingers*.

They counted with the fingers of the left hand up to one hundred; at one hundred they transferred to the right. Jerome, *Against Jovinianus* 1: “The hundredth number is transferred from the left hand to the right.” He therefore implies that Faustus was very old—not that he had actually reached his hundredth year, for this is hyperbole, though much more modest than that of the poet Nicarchus concerning the old woman Cotyttaris, whom he says began to count her years a second time on her left hand. This occurred when they had reached ten thousand. Thus he sings:

> “She who has seen more dawns than a stag,
> who has begun a second time
> to count old age on her left hand.”

She who has seen more suns than a stag now counts her years again on the joints of her left hand.]

—and, praised by your age but desired by another, you depart admirable in both kinds of conduct, leaving yourself to outsiders and your possessions to those near you. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter X

Sidonius sends greetings to his lord, Pope Aprunculus.

[Note: To Andemantus, bishop of the Lingones, to whom Sidonius, after leaving the Arvernian church out of his former hatred of the Burgundians, later transferred his own see when he was dying.]

He has delivered my letter to you, although it would have been fitting for him to bring yours to me; for our brother Coelestius, lately returned to you from Baeterræ, extracted from me a bond of cession concerning the status of our offender. I wrote this, no less overcome by your modesty than moved by your wish. For it was proper that we should voluntarily hasten to meet your modest reluctance, as it were, with the feet of obedience.

[Note: The name is also written thus in Book VIII, Letter 4. In Greek it is Βαίτεραι (“Baeterræ”), which more closely approaches an ancient Narbonensian inscription, where the Septimanii of Baeterræ are recorded as follows:

> M. JULIO PHILIPPO NOBILISSIMO CAES. PRINCIPI JUVENTUTIS SEP. BAETERR.
>
> “To Marcus Julius Philip, most noble Caesar, prince of the youth; the Septimanii of Baeterræ.”]

Therefore, with my consent, take possession of this concession also—but generously; for, as I suspect, you yourself did not seek any greater consolation of this kind. Through this letter, which is no less a letter of restoration than of recommendation, I now introduce him to you, already appeased; but in such a way that he should attend you, obey you, and follow you. If he remains with you, let him be judged the servant of neither of us; if he should depart, let both of us seek the fugitive. Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter XI

Sidonius sends greetings to his lord, Pope Lupus.

[Note: To the bishop of Troyes. Sidonius had sent him the volume of the preceding books on the condition that it should afterward be conveyed to another bishop; when Lupus complained on this account, Sidonius excuses the fault in this letter.]

Because you thought that the little book had been sent not so much to you as through you, I received your letter as written not so much to me as against me. I answer your reproaches according to the justice of the case, not according to equality of eloquence. Yet who am I now, or how great, that I should presume to act as though innocent when you charge me?

Therefore I immediately beg forgiveness for this offense, however small it may be, confessing an error of distrust, not of arrogance. For although the severity of your judgment in your letters is as fearful to me as it is in your conduct, I nevertheless confess that, in the opening and disclosure of the volume and work itself, it was more burdensome to me than the affection you claim would suggest.

I do not make this inference without just cause, since a natural force exists in the minds of mortals: if something is done wrongly, friends are less forgiving and more severe. I had written a book, as you declare, full and laden with a varied accumulation of causes, times, and persons. I seemed likely to do something utterly shameless if everything pleased me so much that I trusted nothing in it could displease you.

Furthermore, whatever the outcome of the judgment might be, I saw that my own conduct would in no way rest on a solid foundation of piety unless the volume had first been brought to you, and unless it appeared to have been offered to you. The arrangement was this: if I happened to please you, I would not be judged to have passed you over through arrogance; if the reverse, I would not be judged to have sought you through presumption.

Nor did I think that I would have to plead with much effort for the causes of embarrassment that I had avoided. I also knew that you understood this: authors, when publishing their works, are suited more by modesty than by confidence; and that the censor’s harsh points are brought forth more slowly by the reader’s boldness than by his hesitation.

Otherwise, if there is anyone who publishes a work on a previously unheard-of subject—

[Note: In certain books it is widely circulated.]

—with the advantage of confidence, he begins to return more to public expectation than he has paid out, however much he may have discharged.

Moreover, whatever judgment you may form concerning the tenor of this reply, I preferred simply to confess what I had done rather than to deny it in a stammering fashion.

Someone else might have said: “I preferred no one to you; I gave no special letters to anyone. The man whom you suspected I had plundered departed content with the form of a single letter—and that letter, indeed, conveyed nothing concerning the present matter.”

But you, who complain that you were omitted, after being wearied by three most talkative pages, are instead driven to nausea, while you linger repeatedly over the empty words of a silly reading.

Add also that, even in what you perhaps did not notice, consideration was shown for your reverence and merits: just as your title in the book comes before the titles of the other bishops, so his name sounds scarcely once, and then only on the page assigned to him; whereas, besides the pages assigned to you, the others are frequently illuminated by your name.

Add this too: if anything there happens to please you, so that you read through my advice, he will owe it at some point to your favor. He, crushed by envy of my little gift in vain, has not yet, as I suspect, reached the ability to read, while you yourself have long since reached the power to translate.

I say this as though he would not consider the pages holographs if he had received even a copy of what you read first.

[Note: The copy sent to you was in my own hand. Things written by the author’s own hand are called *holographa*, *idiographa*, or *archetypa*: for example, a holograph testament, which the testator himself wrote out; and Jerome’s holograph letter to Rufinus, written in the author’s own hand.

To write holographically is to write with one’s own hand. In the old code of the Nicene canons: “Atticus, bishop of the church of Constantinople, issued the canons of the holy Fathers, subscribed by me in my own holograph hand.”

Accordingly, what is often added at the end of imperial rescripts and private letters—“in the divine hand” or “in another hand”—means essentially “in holograph hand,” because in such letters only these clauses were written by the author’s hand, while the rest was written by notaries. A holograph letter, however, is entirely by the author. Examples are common.

Thus, in Valentinian’s Novel concerning the ordination of bishops: “And in the divine hand: May the Divinity preserve you for many years, dearest parent.” Augustine, Letter 45, to Armentarius and Riparius: “And in another hand: Let us rejoice in you in the abundant grace of Christ, excellent lords, and deservedly honorable and desirable sons.” This is how it appears in the best manuscripts. But in the printed copies the notation of another hand, here and elsewhere in Augustine and other authors, has been omitted through the recklessness of copyists.]

Nor will any scarcity or abundance of punctuation be blamed in the things you have handled. Indeed, in the end it is plainly clear that the work’s property has also been transmitted to you: you have received the right of use without any fixed limitation of time, and you may use the aforesaid little book for so long that memory will contain it no less than your book-chest.

These and more perhaps someone might say. I, however, pass over everything and prefer to ask pardon rather than, if this is thought to be the case, plead against a charge.

I do not now excuse the negligence of this present letter either: first, because, although I wish to write more elegantly, I am scarcely able to do so; then because, once the labor of the little book was complete, my mind at last preparing to rest refuses to polish what it hesitates to reveal.

Yet since in everything I yield to you sufficiently, and deservedly—what comparison could there be?—since for ten five-year periods now you have been preferred and placed ahead not only of priests of your own age but also of the ancients, I wish you to know this: although you shake the heavens with your complaints and summon the ashes and embers of your ancestors as witnesses to injured affection, I shall not withdraw my foot from your contest if we must compete in mutual love. For in other matters as well as in this, it is especially disgraceful to be surpassed in affection.

This firm declaration, whether you wish it or not, is fairly weighed against those insults of yours, which certainly surpass all the honey of flattery.

Behold, you have a letter almost as garrulous as you requested, although all letters are talkative—if there are any talkative ones at all. For who would you not compel to dare conversation, when you draw forth the talents of all learned men—not counting me—even though their eyes are reluctant, just as the sunbeam is accustomed to extract water hidden in the earth’s innermost parts through its absorbent atoms?

The point of that light penetrates not only fine sand or yielding soil; even if the vein of hidden springs is concealed beneath the weight of a rocky mountain, the more violent nature of the heavenly elements opens the secret of the flowing substance.

So, holy man, if you perceive any scholars who are quiet, modest, or hiding in the obscure recesses of buried reputation, the brilliance of your eloquence, addressing them with artful conversation, brings them into public view.

But why this? What delay is there? Let us return to the matter, concerning whose excessive chatter I obey you. I beg that, once I have confessed my errors, you may be appeased and grant me forgiveness through your merciful indulgence. Although your holy joy and fellowship would be more abundantly delighted if a written defense of my fault, rather than a satisfaction, were brought to you.

Deign to remember us, lord pope.

## Letter XII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Oresius.

[Note: To a Spaniard, as in Book VIII, Letter 2, to Fortunalis. He wrote this after he had completed three Olympiads—twelve years—in the episcopal office. Thus, according to Baronius’ calculation, it was the year of Christ 484.]

A page sent by you has come into our hands, and it bears much resemblance to Spanish salt cut on the Tarraconensian mountains. For when examined, it is bright and salty, yet on that very account no less honeyed; its speech is sweet and its propositions sharp. Thus it delights through eloquence while disturbing through command, since, scarcely measuring what sort of business I conduct, you now demand that I compose poems for you.

From the beginning of my religious profession I principally renounced this exercise. For verse might be accommodated to ease if the levity of poetry had occupied me, while the gravity of my actions had begun to claim my attention.

Moreover, it is evident that every activity is difficult to resume if it has rested for a long interval. Who does not know that the greatest distinction comes to all crafts and craftsmen through practice? When customary pursuits are not maintained, arms grow sluggish in bodies and talents in the arts.

Hence also the saying that, when belatedly or rarely taken up, the bow rebels against the hand, the ox against the yoke, and the horse against the bridle. In addition, the shame accompanying our laziness inclines my judgment to this conclusion: after I have passed three Olympiads in silence, I am as ashamed to compose a new poem as I am reluctant.

It would also be wrong to deny you things difficult to accomplish, since the desire of one who fears no refusal so steadfastly should be deceived all the less.

We shall therefore keep to something midway. Just as I shall now dictate no new epigrams, so, if any letters lie filled with verse—written, naturally, before the necessity of my present office—I shall send them to you. I ask only that you not be so much a transgressor against justice as to think that I shall never again abstain from such composition.

Nor would your vote increase me less if you should perhaps judge me now modest rather than witty. Farewell.

## Letter XIII

Sidonius sends greetings to his Tonantius.

[Note: To the son of Tonantius Ferreolus, mentioned in Book II, Letter 9. He is called the learned Tonantius in the *Propempticon*, where his mother Papianilla is also praised.]

I confess that your opinion of my verses was once so flattering and favorable that you thought me comparable to the most distinguished poets, and certainly superior to many. I would believe you if, just as you are very wise, you also loved me very much. Hence your affection can lie about my praises, but it cannot deceive.

Besides this, you ask me to send you some Asclepiads shaped on the Horatian anvil, so that you may practice reciting them while drinking. I comply with your command, although I am now more occupied and constrained than ever by the prose manner of speaking.

In the end you will discover that, in our case, enthusiasm for meters has for the most part grown cold. For it is not easy for one and the same person to do something well and to do it rarely.

For a long time now we have played with polished hendecasyllables,

> rubbing the thumb upon the pens,
>
> which you could sing more freely than as choriambics
>
> with your nimble foot released.

But you want our orbit henceforth to run along the embankment of the Calabrian road,

> where Flaccus bent his lyric horses
>
> to Pindaric music with reins powerful through the plectrum,
>
> while the cord is shaken in Glyconic meter,
>
> and also in Alcaic or Pherecratean,
>
> joined with Lesbian or anapaestic,
>
> blossoming through eclogues of varied song,
>
> with many-colored violets of words.

To fashion this—grant pardon—is difficult for ancient poets, and difficult for me:

> to make an epigrammatic mouth, sounding variously,
>
> stumble over none of the frequent letters,
>
> which luxuriant singing and lavish rhythms
>
> forbid masculine diction to make wanton.

This scarcely could Leo, king of the Castalian choir, accomplish; scarcely could Lampridius, who follows him,

> declaiming beneath the weight of a double style
>
> before his pupils at Bordeaux.

This is fitting for me and for you; spare me, I ask, your jokes. I beg that concern for the promised work of the orator preserve modesty to the very end,

> since nothing is worse if it is rigid at the beginning
>
> but soft at the end.

Indeed, whenever you are made cheerful by a more lavish dinner, devote yourself to religious narratives, which I approve more highly. Let frequent conversation serve to present them, and attentive listening to repeat them.

Certainly, if you are still inclined too sluggishly toward wholesome diversions, as a young man, borrow at least the formulas of convivial questions from the Platonic man of Madaura—

[Note: Apuleius, who wrote *Convivial Questions*, as Macrobius testifies in Book VII, chapter 3: “Either propose convivial questions yourself or solve them.” The ancients did not regard this kind of subject as too slippery, since Aristotle, Plutarch, and your Apuleius of Madaura all wrote something on it. John of Salisbury adds Fronto, repeating Macrobius’ words in *Polycraticus* VIII, 10.]

—and, so that you may become better equipped, solve the questions proposed and propose others to be solved; exercise yourself in these studies while you have leisure.

But since mention of banquets has occurred once, and since you diligently demand this poem from me, although it was composed for another occasion and another person, so that you cannot allow me to hesitate any longer about publishing it, receive gladly what, in the time of the emperor Majorian Augustus, when we had gathered for dinner at the request of a certain companion, I suddenly poured forth after the book of Peter, master of the imperial correspondence, had been suddenly produced—

[Note: Of the emperor Majorian Augustus: according to the *Panegyric* of Majorian near its end, through this man’s agency and interpretation Majorian expelled the military garrison placed in the city of Lyon. Sidonius also presented Majorian himself with that panegyric, Poem 3.]

—while the king of the banquet delayed over arranging the fish sauce, for my fellow guests Domnulus, Severianus, and Lampridius were composing equal pieces—

[Note: This concerns Domnulus, mentioned in Book IV, the final letter. Severianus is praised again in Letter 15 and in Poem 15, where he is called “excellent in the trumpet,” that is, grandiloquent. I think this was Julius Severianus, whose concise rhetorical rules are read. This passage shows that the rhetorician Lampridius, whose death Sidonius mourned in Book VIII, Letter 40, held the chair at Bordeaux.]

—indeed, I say this boastfully, or rather, they composed better ones—whom the emperor had summoned from cities everywhere into one city and chance had brought together, as guests, at one dinner.

The delay lasted only while we divided the kinds of meter by lot. It seemed fitting, because of our collegial affection, that although all had the same subject for writing, the epigrams of the individual writers should not be presented in the same meter, lest one of us, who had spoken more weakly than the others, should first be bitten by shame and then by envy.

For it is more quickly recognized in any reciter whether, if the others sing in one meter, he too writes with the same skill. You, however, will praise what follows more appropriately when you have given yourself wholly to your companion. For it is not just that you should begin as a censor to examine strictly what a friend could not compose with seriousness.

>

[Note: Statius Papinius, in the *Lament for Hetruscus*:

> “... heap Cilician and Arabian harvests upon the pyres.”

Tibullus likewise, Book IV, in praise of Sulpicius:

> “The wealthy Arab, cultivator of a fragrant harvest.”

The Arabian “harvest” and “crop” mean every kind of fragrant plant growing in Arabia. Hence comes the ready emendation of a line of Orientius which exercised learned men: read *Arabum* (“of the Arabs”), not *arvum* (“field”). For he writes of bodies preserved with spices:

> “Not only those which stones well laid away preserve in tombs,
> or which Arabian dust and scent, preserving, hold.”

“Arabian dust and scent” is a familiar figure for Arabia’s fragrant dust.]

> it snatches the palm from here and there.
>
> It is carried through learned mouths.
>
> Far from here let us drive
>
> Hippocrene,
>
> the Aganippian springs,
>
> and tuneful Apollo
>
> accompanied by the Camenae;
>
> and remove Minerva,
>
> as though she were the leader of song,
>
> from foolish fabricated speech:
>
> one God brings these things about.
>
> The power of the diadem,
>
> the toga, the soldier,
>
> the equestrian order,
>
> and the Roman people
>
> stood amazed at the man speaking.
>
> Even now the forums,
>
> temples, countryside, and camps
>
> roll the word “wise.”
>
> Above these, the Po,
>
> his fosterer, gives him resonance,
>
> and so does the love of the Ligurian cities.
>
> A similar favor echoes
>
> through the cities of the Rhône;
>
> and the fierceness of the Iberians
>
> will imitate the Gauls.
>
> Nor will he remain on this axis:
>
> quickly he will proceed to the fields
>
> of the East Wind,
>
> and will be carried onward
>
> by the North, South,
>
> and West Winds.

Behold: while I ask what you are singing, I myself have sung. I now bring to light such trifles, perforated by mice at the bottom of a chest, after approximately twenty years, such as Ulysses, absent for an equal period, might have found when he returned home.

Therefore I ask you gladly to forgive these present amusements. But I enjoin this neither modestly nor immodestly: what I myself pronounced about the complete book of my friend, you should, as though prompted by the necessity of the example, judge about mine. Farewell.

## Letter XIV

Sidonius

[Note: To a young scholar. In a letter he asks what are called “recurrent verses” and presents two kinds of them. For either they recur through the individual letters, as in a quasi-distich of Leo the Wise, in Book VI of the Greek *Anthology* of epigrams, as follows:]

Σόφος ἔγωγε ἤδη ὢν ἄνω, χαρᾷ τῶν ἄνω, γελῶ τὰ

Κάτω, λέγων, ἂν ᾦ ταραχῶν ἄνω, ἤδη ἔγωγε σοφός.

“I, being already above, rejoice in the things above; I laugh at the things below, saying: if one is above disturbances, then indeed I am already wise.” For when this is read backward, from the end to the beginning, without moving the letters from their places, it returns unchanged.

Or they may recur only by individual words: this type Diomedes and Victorinus, who do not mention the former kind, call reciprocal. But there are again two species of these. For reciprocal verses either return by individual lines, and then are of the same kind, as this pentameter of Porphyrius:

> Ausoniae decus, et lux pia Romulidum,

into the second pentameter:

> Romulidum pia lux, et decus Ausoniae.

Or they are different, as this hexameter of the same Porphyrius:

> Omne genus metri tibi pangens, optime Basse,

into a Sotadic verse:

> Basse optime pangens tibi metri genus omne.

Or they recur through the entire elegiac couplet: such is Sidonius’s couplet about a torrent, and this poem of Nicodemus of Heraclea in the same sixth book of the *Greek Anthology*:

> Πηνελόπη, τόδε σοι φᾶρος καὶ χλαῖναν Ὀδυσσεὺς  
> Ἤνεγκεν, δολιχὴν ἐξανύσας ἀτραπόν.

“Penelope, Odysseus has brought you this cloak and mantle, after completing the long road.”

It recurs thus:

> Ἀτραπὸν ἐξανύσας δολιχὴν, ἤνεγκεν Ὀδυσσεὺς  
> Χλαῖναν καὶ φᾶρος σοὶ τόδε, Πηνελόπη.

“After completing the long road, Odysseus brought you this mantle and cloak, Penelope.”

Sidonius sends greetings to his Burgundian.

I am tormented in two ways because both of us are confined to our beds. Nothing is harder than when present friends are separated by a shared illness. For if it happens that they do not even lie sick in the same room, there are no words, no consolations, and finally no reciprocal exchange of prayer. Thus each suffers great grief, and each suffers it more on the other’s account: for although you are yourself weak, you can scarcely help fearing for yourself when the one you love is in danger.

But God has removed from me, as I trembled for you, the strongest cause of anxiety, because you are beginning to recover your former strength. They say that you now wish to rise—and, what I desire more, that you are already able to do so. You certainly consult me in this way: with an almost premature concern, you exercise me with little questions in letters, now seeming vigorous in every respect, eager to hear me, although I am still ill, disputing about morals with Socrates rather than about bodies with Hippocrates.

You are altogether worthy of having Rome embrace you in her applauding arms, and of having the wedge-shaped benches of the resounding Athenaeum shake when you recited. This you would unquestionably have achieved if the condition of peace and place had permitted you to be educated there, mingling with the company of the senatorial youth. From the quality of your speech I infer that you are capable of both that glory and that fame: when recently you delivered with the greatest propriety what you had written extemporaneously, your well-wishers admired, the proud were astonished, and the learned lingered.

But lest we improperly weigh upon your modesty with excessive praise, let us more justly proclaim your merits about you than to you. Let us rather introduce the matter that occasioned this letter. You therefore ask, through the bearer of your little letter, which verses I call recurrent, so that I may explain quickly, but by example.

Those are called recurrent which, while the meter remains fixed and the letters are not moved from their places, are read from beginning to end and then from the end back to the beginning. Thus runs the ancient example:

> Roma tibi subito motibus ibit amor.

“Rome, your love will suddenly go through changes.”

And this:

> Sole medere pede, ede perede melos.

“Heal, Sun, with your foot; produce, consume, and reproduce the melody.”

Those also are regarded as recurrent which preserve the law of their feet and are repeated not letter by letter but word by word. Such is a distich of mine—I think I have indeed read many of this kind by many authors—which I composed in play about a stream. Fed by the sudden descent of storms, it had overflowed the public embankment in a ruinous flood and inundated the cultivated land beside the road, although it was soon to lay aside its mad excess: swollen by successive rains, it was not reinforced by any substantial volume from an everlasting spring.

Thus, while I was there—for I had arrived as a traveler—looking more for the bank than for a ford, I joked in the following epigram and crossed, at least with these feet, the back of the turbulent torrent:

> Praecipiti modo quod decurrit tramite flumen,  
> Tempore consumptum jam cito deficiet.

“The river that now runs along its headlong course will soon fail, its force consumed by time.”

If this is read backward, it is as follows:

> Deficiet cito jam consumptum tempore flumen,  
> Tramite decurrit quod modo praecipiti.

“It will soon fail, the river already consumed by time, which now runs along a headlong course.”

There you have verses whose syllabic structure you may admire. As for the magnificence they do not possess, they will not teach it. I think I have sufficiently indicated what you thought should be sought.

You yourself do something similar if, when you restore what has been proposed in an equally different form, you explain what you repeat. For you are distinguished by the votive restoration of a very celebrated theme—namely, the eulogy that must be completed, which Julius Caesar had published. This subject is so grand that, whoever among students may be most eloquent, he ought to take no greater precaution than not to say too little.

For if we set aside what is written in the Patavian volumes under the titles of the undefeated dictator [Note: That part of Livy’s work had not yet perished. Symmachus also refers to it in *Letters* IV.17: “You ask that the ancient memories of the Gauls be brought into your hands; turn over the final books of the Patavian author, in which the deeds of Gaius Caesar are unfolded.”], who could match in speech the works of Suetonius, who the history of Juventius Martialis [Note: Some read *Viventii*. Perhaps this is the same person as Gargilius Martialis, whom Vopiscus in *Probus* and Lampridius in *Alexander* count among the authors who committed the lives of the Caesars to writing; he lived in the time of the latter. Gargilius is also called Martialis by Aemilianus, Servius, and Cassiodorus, who likewise mention his books on the care of gardens.], or, finally, the *Ephemeris* of Balbus? [Note: Plutarch and Servius, in their commentaries on Book XI of the *Aeneid*, cite Julius Caesar’s *Ephemeris* concerning his own affairs. There is also Hirtius’s Book VIII of Balbus, which he added to Caesar’s remaining seven books of *Commentaries*. We find no mention elsewhere among ancient authors of Balbus’s *Ephemeris* explaining the achievements of Gaius Caesar.]

But we reserve these matters for your wax tablets. It is more properly our duty to arrange benches for the audience and prepare ears for the thunderclaps that will soon resound; while you speak of the virtues of another, we shall undertake to speak of yours.

Nor should you fear that I shall summon certain Catonian judges, who conceal now their envy, now their ignorance beneath a cloak of affected severity—although the unlearned deserve indulgence. But whoever is so bad that he understands what is well written and nevertheless does not praise it, good men understand him and nevertheless do not praise him.

Therefore I release you from this anxiety. Everyone will listen favorably, everyone will encourage you, and we shall all share in the joy you will create when you recite. Many will praise your eloquence, very many your talent, and everyone your modesty. For it will be no less a matter of praise that a young man—or, what is more beautiful, one still almost a boy—should carry away from the public contest of the schools the votes of character as well as of literature. Farewell.

## LETTER XV

Sidonius sends greetings to his Gelasius.

You prove—and I do not deny—that I have done wrong: I have indeed done wrong, since I have not yet attached any letter bearing your name to my work. Yet you write that my error will be pardonable if I send you something that I myself also sing, following an example; for I previously sent my Tonantius, on a similar occasion, letters in two meters.

Besides this, you complain that, if my page is turned into a game, it is filled only with hendecasyllables. For this reason, with my trochaic chatter suspended, you ask for some little senarii. I comply with your command; only receive them calmly, whether you prefer to call this very piece a *veoda* [term uncertain] or an eclogue. For a meter long neglected is woven with greater difficulty.

> You order, my friend, that through our volumes  
> The fierce iambus resound with more energetic rhythms,  
> And that the trochee, until now,  
> Add its sluggish teams and fourfold measures;  
> Let the spondee introduce delay,  
> So that the swift-footed trimeter may have  
> Little of its innate speed.  
>   
> Let that mixed foot resound, the swiftest of all,  
> Once properly named by the art of Pyrrhichus,  
> To be placed anywhere in the final position:  
> The spondee will give the verse weight,  
> Sometimes at the beginning, now at the end;  
> The anapest too, although it is more complete  
> When pronounced with the following third foot,  
> When a long syllable is joined to the second  
> Of two short syllables.  
>   
> These things the ordinary poet scarcely knows how to regulate,  
> As you yourself see Sollius to be.  
> He goes astray on the lyre, and his wandering tongue  
> Does not properly unfold its turn through the hollow mouths.  
>   
> But Leo would have fashioned this poem more aptly,  
> Following the tracks of Leo and Consentus,  
> Singing in Latin what was first Attic,  
> The survivor of the father of the Consentii,  
> Said to have sung, in faith, voice, and meters,  
> A song of every form beside the streams of Pegasus;  
> And whenever he put Greek words into verse,  
> He held the lofty stars together with Pindar,  
> And, victorious, crossed the mountain with its double peak,  
> Second to none beneath the Delphic stars.  
>   
> Yet if either poet should fit a Latin song  
> To the lyre of poetry without Doric character,  
> You, Venusine Horace, would ineptly extend your plectra,  
> A swan of Apulian Aufidus in spring,  
> And, overcome, groan as the Atax thunders  
> With its own swans.  
>   
> Nor are these the only learned breasts,  
> Although these are more learned than the learned:  
> The rhetorician Severianus would have said these things  
> With greater elevation;  
> The clever and polished Domnulus, an African,  
> More elegantly;  
> And the scholar Peter, with more rounded  
> Muses, more sharply.  
>   
> An epistolary style in every respect  
> Would not prevent the man, had he been able,  
> From always composing such astonishing things  
> More effectively—  
> Proculus, sprung from Ligurian soil and race,  
> Whose poetic verses resound with melodious strokes,  
> Who refines every witty poem  
> So that he challenges Mantua, the Venetian, in favor;  
> Himself equal to Homeric glory,  
> Pursuing Maro’s chariot with comparable art.  
>   
> I, rightly despicable in heart and mouth,  
> What am I to babble among these men, at your request,  
> Proving the shamelessness of my loquacity,  
> My wishes, bereft of literary skill? [Note: The text is defective up to this point, as though the wishes were separated from the letters. A certain and necessary emendation was required, although the manuscripts offered no help. The meaning is clear: wishes are said to be abandoned by letters when someone desires to write but cannot through lack of skill.]  
>   
> But what shall I refuse, and not be terrified by shame?  
> Love does not know how to fear; therefore I obeyed.  
> Forgive me for repeating what has long been neglected,  
> And for expecting nothing more, after fulfilling what you ordered,  
> Than indulgence for my rarity.  
>   
> If afterward you command similar things of me,  
> So that I may become more obedient,  
> You will arrange, in place of a song,  
> Either dictate what I am to sing,  
> Or dance what I am to laugh at. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI

Sidonius sends greetings to his Firminus.
