If you remember, my lord and son, you had ordered me to attach this ninth little book, dictated especially for you, to the other eight that I wrote to Constantius—a man of singular intelligence and salutary judgment, certainly surpassing other eloquent men in public deliberations, and excelling them in the gifts of eloquence whether he decides different or identical matters.

My pledge has been fulfilled, not indeed exactly, but at least with urgency. For when I had perhaps traversed the dioceses and returned home, I hastily and laboriously copied out whatever draft was lying carelessly among decayed and timeworn papers, acting as a hurried translator, without being delayed by the winter season from completing your commands at once—even though the antiquarian page was held back by unthawing frost, and the drop on the pen was harder than you might have supposed, so that under the pressure of the fingers it did not flow but broke.

Even so, I made it my first concern to discharge my duty before our twelfth month—which you call the month of Numa—was wedded by Favonius’s warm breeze and the rains of its birth. It remains for you, as judge, not to demand from us things wholly incompatible: maturity and speed. For whenever a book is ordered to be written quickly, its author looks not so much to the honor arising from merit as to that arising from obedience.

Furthermore, since you say that the iambics recently sent to Gelasius, a most kindly man, pleased you, I shall also present you with these little blossoms of the Mytilenaean town.

> My little boat has now driven its bold course  
> Across the alternating sea of speech;  
> Nor has it feared, amid the divided stream,  
> To turn the helm.  
>   
> It has loosed the antennae and gathered the high sails;  
> Its hand lowers the little oar, and, with the benches  
> Joined to the shore, it seeks the sand  
> That must be kissed.  
>   
> Although the muttering chorus of the envious  
> Reveals its futile canine rage,  
> It says nothing openly and fears  
> The public judgment.  
>   
> They strike the stern and shake the keel;  
> They fan the rounded sponsons of the sides;  
> Around the mast the left-hand tongues  
> Whirl their hisses.  
>   
> Yet, with skill as our companion, we keep the prow straight,  
> Not puffed up and fearing no storms,  
> And bring it into harbor, having gained  
> A double crown of foliage:  
>   
> One which the people of Quirinus granted me,  
> Or which the Senate, bearing the leaf-bringing title, bestowed;  
> And one which the allied order of those skilled  
> In judgments gave.  
>   
> So that Nerva Trajan might see,  
> Set up with my works, an enduring statue  
> Bearing inscriptions, fixed among the authors  
> Of both libraries.  
>   
> And, when I had appeared again after an interval of nearly ten years,  
> I received the office—an honour in itself—  
> Which once alone governed jointly the rights  
> Of Senate and people.  
>   
> Besides heroic poems, I wove many jokes  
> From many pieces; I frequently rolled out elegiacs  
> Set beneath six feet  
> In a couplet of two cola. [Note: Otherwise the pentameter is faulty unless it consists of two cola, each of which, as Terentianus says, has its own proper ending. He also criticizes this line: “Among our people a foreign horse wanders,” because it lacks divided cola; and Hephaestion criticizes the following line of Callimachus: “Now sacred is the child of Dioscurides.”]  
>   
> Now accustomed to riding through eleven  
> Syllables, I played swiftly; and often  
> I sang in Sapphic meter, while rarely  
> Using the hurried iambus.  
>   
> Nor can I remember how much I wrote  
> As a young man in my first ardor.  
> Would that most of it might be silenced  
> And hidden away.  
>   
> For when the boundary of old age is nearer,  
> Whatever we associate with our final years  
> Causes greater shame when we now remember  
> That our age once played with something trivial.  
>   
> Dreading this, I transferred every kind of care  
> To the cultivated style of letters,  
> So that I might not be guilty of more wanton song  
> And guilty of conduct.  
>   
> And lest I be thought to dissolve into charming words  
> If I join figures and decorations to my pages,  
> So that the reputation of a poet might stain  
> The strictness of a cleric,  
>   
> Hereafter I shall not rush eagerly  
> Toward every epigram, nor shall I quickly be forced  
> To produce a poem in delicate  
> Or weighty meter.  
>   
> Unless perhaps I speak of persecutors,  
> Of their tortures, and of the martyrs who deserved heaven and purchased  
> The rewards of life at the price of death.  
>   
> Of these, may the first hymn sing for me  
> Of the one who held the see of Toulouse,  
> Hurled down from the highest step  
> Of the Capitol,  
>   
> Saturninus, denier of Jupiter and Minerva  
> And confessor of the blessings of Christ’s cross,  
> Whom the frenzied populace bound to the flank  
> Of a yoked bull,  
>   
> So that, when the bull was driven over a precipice,  
> Scattered the mangled corpse,  
> With the hot pulp of the brain  
> Loosed and spattered over the stained rocks. [Note: The first bishop of Toulouse, Saturninus. The metrical pattern rejected the name *Saturninus*, but the poet disregarded the rule of the poem lest he pass over the memory of the holy man. Poets commonly offer the same excuse with names of this kind: Prudentius does so with another Saturninus in *Against the Martyrs of Zaragoza*; Martial with Earinus in Book IX.12; and Terentianus in a pariambe. An old epitaph at Rome displays a double license:

> Θ Κ  
> Φιλήτῳ τόδε σῆμα κατοιχομένῳ συνομεύνῳ  
> Ἀβασκαντὶς γαμετή μνημοσύης ἕνεκεν.

“That is:

> To Phileto, her husband dead and gone,  
> Abascantis set this tomb in grateful memory.”

The author uses contraction in *Phileto* and pleonasm in *Abascantide*. Namatianus is more scrupulous in his *Itinerary*. Since he could not include the true name of Venerius Rufius Volusianus—namely, the final element—within a verse while preserving the laws of meter, he was content to record his wish:

> Here we learn that the prefecture of the sacred city  
> Was conferred, dear friend, upon your merits.  
>   
> I should wish to include your true name in song,  
> But the harsh rule of the feet avoids some names.  
>   
> In verse, Venerius Rufius, most dear to Venus,  
> Our page has long sung you by that name.

He addresses, as I have said, Volusianus, son of Albinus, whose proper name was Volusianus and whose cognomina were Venerius Rufius. A little earlier he likewise writes:

> Rufius, great glory of Albinus his father,  
> Who derives the name of Volusus from an ancient line.

The prefecture of the city conferred on Volusianus, which Namatianus congratulates him on receiving, is attested by Volusianus’s own edict against the heretic Coelestius. Therefore, in our judgment, the title of Namatianus’s *Itinerary* should be restored as: “To Rufius Venerius Volusianus.”]

After Saturninus, I want the plectra to sing of those other patrons whom I have found hard and anxious helpers for me through my labors.

The words cannot contain them individually,  
As pious naming would now require in verse;  
Yet what the strings cannot sound,  
The hearts will sound.

Let us return at the end to the oratorical style, intending to bring the present subject to its conclusion in the orderly arrangement once adopted. Otherwise, if we close a prose work with musical epilogues, it may seem, according to Horace’s rules, that when an amphora began to be formed, a jug rather than an amphora emerged. Farewell.

## C. S. APOLLINARIS SIDONII, POEMS

### POEM I. PREFACE

**To the Panegyric delivered to the Emperor Anthemius, Consul for the Second Time**

[Note: The order of Sidonius’s panegyrics is reversed. The correct sequence was that the panegyric of Avitus should appear first, then that of Majorian, and finally that of Anthemius, who succeeded Majorian after Severus—“a most Christian man and one who governed the empire piously,” as Theophanes writes in his *Chronicle*. From this you may refute the vanity of Damascius, who in the life of Isidore of Alexandria invented Anthemius as impious and “Greek-minded,” and as secretly turning over plans for restoring the worship of idols.

The occasion and reason for Sidonius’s panegyric to Anthemius are explained in Letter I.9. From it it is clear that the speech was delivered at Rome on the Kalends of January, when the Emperor Augustus Anthemius, having recently assumed the empire, was ceremonially inaugurating his second consulship in the traditional manner of the emperors; for he had held his first consulship while still a private citizen at Constantinople, in the year of Christ 468.]

> When nature placed young Jupiter above the stars  
> And a new god took up the ancient kingdoms,  
> The divine powers competed to honor their own divinity,  
> And in different ways all sang the same praise.  
>   
> Mars proclaimed his father’s praises  
> With the blare of the trumpet,  
> And praised his thunderbolts  
> With thunderous sound.  
>   
> The Arcadian and the bow-bearing god  
> Resounded on ringing strings,  
> One more skilled in the strokes of the cithara,  
> The other on the lyre.  
>   
> The chorus of the Castalian maidens applauded  
> With varied melody—  
> In songs, reeds, fingers, voice, and foot.  
>   
> But afterward, it is said, the god sustained  
> Even the modest songs of demigods  
> After those of the heavenly beings.  
>   
> Then fauns, Dryads, and Mimallones  
> Suited to the Satyrs poured forth  
> A rustic melody, a crowd of stones.  
>   
> The Panes who play the hemlock-pipe  
> Left high Maenalus,  
> And after the lyre, the hoarse pipe  
> Pleased Jupiter.  
>   
> Among them Chiron, dancing to ringing plectra,  
> Bent the awkward limbs of his comic horse-body.  
> Half-man, he deserved to be heard  
> And deserved to please,  
> Although, while singing, he produced a neigh.  
>   
> Thus rich and poor alike made offering  
> With their sacred tongues,  
> And then the song was the supreme sacrifice of prayer.  
>   
> So we, Caesar, greatest hope of our age,  
> Offer tiny grains of incense after the great nobles,  
> Singing boldly in the presence of learned Victor,  
> Who is accustomed to speak either with Phoebus’s voice  
> Or with yours.  
>   
> Although he is your perpetual quaestor  
> In the eternal court,  
> He will be our perpetual teacher.  
>   
> Therefore let tongues of every kind honor you, prince:  
> For you make new temples of our hearts.

## POEM II. PANEGYRIC WHICH SIDONIUS DELIVERED AT ROME TO ANTHEMIUS AUGUSTUS, CONSUL FOR THE SECOND TIME

> By auspice and by number, Augustus, raise  
> Your second fasces; shining beneath the weight  
> Of trabeal metal, unfold the new year,  
> An old consul, and without arrogance  
> Write “twice” in the Fasti.  
>   
> Although you go crowned with a diadem,  
> And a Sarian chlamys, painted with purple,  
> Enclose your shoulders in the manner of former men,  
> Let more purple than before contain you,  
> For it is always a rare thing through the ages  
> To be a frequent consul.  
>   
> And you, Janus, to whom the annual laurel  
> Is owed, bind your hair again with any foliage,  
> Once released from torpor,  
> And do not fear the sudden light  
> Of the emperor, nor suppose that the elements  
> Of the universe are being moved.  
>   
> Nature changes nothing: the sun too  
> Has come here from the east.  
>   
> This is the man, nobles, whom Roman valor sought,  
> Whom your affection sought;  
> To him the commonwealth, broken as though by storms  
> And lacking a pilot, presented itself—  
> So that it might be guided better by a worthy master,  
> And might fear neither storms nor you, pirate.  
>   
> The country folk sought you with prayer,  
> The army joined by treaty sought you with assent,  
> The camps sought you with trumpets,  
> The senate with applause;  
> Your threefold endorsement wrote you in its records,  
> And your colleague sent you to us,  
> And sent you the empire.  
>   
> There are as many votes as the world can gather.  
> I confess that we all trembled,  
> Lest your pious colleague wish to yield  
> The public wishes to your vote.  
> Posterity will believe, prince,  
> That everything may be permitted against us  
> In the same way.  
>   
> Not everything was permitted to you concerning Leo.  
> You surpass the deeds of former men, Augustus Leo,  
> For he who commands others to reign  
> Stands above kingdoms.  
> Your commonwealth will now be better as one,  
> Since it has thus been made the possession of two.  
>   
> Hail, summit of scepters, queen of the East,  
> Rome of your world, sent to me  
> With the emperor of affairs.  
>   
> You are no longer merely the venerable seat of empire  
> For the eastern Quirite; you are more precious  
> Because you stand forth as the mother  
> Of empire. [Note: This is the ancient and correct reading, and neither the sense nor the structure of the sentence allows another. If one reads *Quirini*, as a learned man preferred, the meaning is corrupted and the Greek expression *τὸ Eoo ἀσυνάρτητον* remains disconnected. He therefore calls the Constantinopolitan citizens “eastern Quirites.” It follows that if Constantinople is a new Rome, its inhabitants should be called Quirites.]

> Your land bears Rhodope and Haemus,  
> A Thracian soil, a shore fertile in heroes.  
>   
> Here ice receives newborn children,  
> And civic snow hardens the tender limbs  
> From the mother’s womb.  
>   
> Scarcely anyone is nourished at the breast;  
> Drawn away from the udder, he drinks more  
> Through the wound of the horse.  
> Thus, leaving milk behind,  
> The whole people drinks courage.  
>   
> They grow a little, then play at war with javelins.  
> The wound supplies their nurse’s games.  
> Boys suited to hunting empty the wild lairs of beasts.  
> Youth enriched by plunder observes the law of the sword.  
> Nor are they ashamed to end completed old age  
> By the sword.  
>   
> In such an order of life the citizens of Mars live.  
> But you, surrounded by the sea between Europe and Asia,  
> Gather from both sides their temperate climate.  
> For the nearby east wind moderates  
> The Bistonian gorges of the north  
> With the slowly calming trumpet of the Chalcidian east wind. [Note: The east wind blows toward Byzantium from nearby Chalcedon; hence the poet calls it *Chalcidian* for *Chalcedonian*, as Paulinus writes in *Natalia* XI:

> “And where Euphemia the martyr, on the Chalcidian shores,  
> Marks the consecrated coast with virginal blood.”

No one is unaware that Saint Euphemia suffered at Chalcedon. Some call Apollonius the Stoic philosopher, teacher of the Caesars Marcus and Lucius, “Chalcedonian,” as Capitolinus does in *Marcus*, and Eutropius in Book VIII; others call him “Chalcidian,” as do Jerome, the translators of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, and Cassiodorus in the *Fasti*. Capitolinus likewise says in *Antoninus Pius* that Apollonius was summoned from Chalcis, whereas others say from Chalcedon.

“Chalcidian” from Chalcis in Euboea is one thing; “Chalcidian” from Chalcis or Chalcedon in Bithynia is another. Today everyone writes the city’s name “Chalcedon,” and the Greeks write Χαλκηδώνα; Stephanus likewise judged that it should be written in this way under the entry Καρχηδών. But those who deal with ancient monuments observe a different spelling everywhere. Finally, the fourth ecumenical council is called not Chalcedonian but Calchedonian in the oldest copies. Most persuasive of all, ancient coins never use another spelling. We have seen many coins, both Caesarian and older, including one bearing on its obverse the head of Apollo, whose temple in that city is attested by Lucian in the *False Prophet*, and on its reverse a tripod with the inscription ΚΑΛΧΑΔΟΝΙΩΝ, the same inscription found on all the others. Many coins of the Chalcedonians are also seen: some bear Mercury, others a lyre, others dancers, and others various designs.]

[Note: This should be read in this way, not *Chalcidici*, as Sirmondus notes. But Heribert Rosweydus, in his notes to Saint Paulinus, page 860, says: “All ancient writers defend the received spelling, and Stephanus expressly does so under Καρχηδών. Ancient copies should not greatly influence us, since it is certain that many names containing the added letter *h* are written in different ways, and that *h* is often transposed. Thus even in the oldest copies one finds *Chartago* for *Carthago*, *Phyton* for *Python*, *Cherintus* for *Cerinthus*, and likewise *Cheruci* for *Ceruchi*. Nor can any certain argument be drawn from coins, since their spelling too varies. In Hubert Goltzius’s *Thesaurus of Antiquities*, one coin of Sabina Tranquillina has ΧΑΛΚΗΔΩΝΙΩΝ; another has ΧΑΛΚΕΔΩΝΩΝ; and a coin of Annia Faustina has ΚΑΛΚΗΔΩΝΩΝ. In Goltzius’s *Greece*, two coins have ΧΑΛΚΕΔΩΝΩΝ.” See Hardouin, *Ancient Coins*, p. 235.—Baunius, editor Sirmondus, preface to vol. I, §11.]

> Meanwhile Susa trembles before you,  
> And the Achaemenian Persian bends  
> His crescent-shaped tiara in suppliant worship.  
>   
> The Indian, his hair drenched in fragrant amomum,  
> Disarms the throats of his wild fosterlings  
> For your gain, so that the curved ivory may hang down;  
> Thus the elephant, stripped of its trunk,  
> Carries its dishonored face to the Bosporus  
> As tribute.  
>   
> You stretch out a vast city with spacious walls,  
> Yet the people make it seem narrow:  
> They go out upon the sea  
> On its massive structures,  
> And the new land draws the ancient waters together.  
>   
> For the sand of Dicaearchia, transported there,  
> Solidifies in the invading waters,  
> And the hardened mass supports fields  
> Brought into a foreign gulf.  
>   
> Thus, with you arranged and looking out upon harbors  
> On every side, enclosed by the sea,  
> The advantages of the earth surround you.  
>   
> Fortunate enough, Rome, to have shared the triumphs.  
>   
> And now we do not complain: may the division  
> Of the empire endure. Its parts agree on the scales,  
> Since you receive our weights and have made them equal. [Note: Anthemius was a native of Constantinople, as we learn also from the book *On the Buildings of Constantinople*, where we read that Anthemius, when he departed from Constantinople, consecrated his house there and founded in it a church, an old-age home, and a bathhouse. It reads: “The house of Anthemius: it was the house of Anthemius the magister in the time of the emperor Marcian, whom the city crowned and sent to Rome as emperor. This same Anthemius built his house into a church, raised an old-age home, and established a bath.”]

> From such a city you shine as a citizen, with Procopius as your father; his ancient stock descended through maternal forefathers from emperors—  
> A lineage that cannot be expressed  
> In worthy eloquence.

[Note: To the praises of his native city he adds those of his father and maternal grandfather. His father was Procopius, of royal blood, namely descended from the Cilician Procopius who contended with Valens for the purple and the empire; Marcellinus, Book XXVI, states that this Procopius was a kinsman of the Emperor Julian and a relative of Constantius. Our Idatius, however, calls Anthemius Procopius’s brother, not his son: “Anthemius, brother of Procopius, was sent from Constantinople by the Emperor Leo, with Marcellinus and other chosen companions, and with a great multitude of troops; by God’s ordering he advanced abundantly into Italy.”]  
>   
> Not even if he should now rise from Avernus,  
> The man who bent rocks with song  
> And compelled the listening forests  
> To run toward his melodious plectrum,  
> While the waters of the Hebrus stood still  
> And the astonished river, its course arrested,  
> Thirsted for the song more than for its own current.

[Note: Sidonius says that peace with the Persians was renewed by Procopius, who was soon afterwards made master of the soldiers in the East and patrician. The whole description of the peace is taken from Claudian’s first poem against Stilicho: the subject is the same. Stilicho concluded a treaty of peace with Persia as ambassador, and Procopius concluded one too. Peace was made twice with Persia in that period. The first treaty was made by Theodosius the Great with Artaxerxes—or another king, if it was another—when Richomer and Clearchus were consuls, in A.D. 384. Pacatus in his panegyric, Socrates in Book V, Marcellinus the Count under the consuls named above, and others mention the Persian embassy that sought peace from Theodosius. The appendix to Victor says: “He also made peace with the Persians when they sought it.” This is the peace arranged by Stilicho as ambassador and described elegantly and fully by Claudian. The second treaty was struck by Theodosius the Younger with King Vararanes, after a fierce and prolonged war, under the consulships of Honorius XIII and Theodosius X, in A.D. 420, as Socrates and Marcellinus record. There is no controversy that Sidonius speaks of this treaty, since Theophanes and Cedrenus confirm that it was made through Procopius.

> To this young man was once entrusted  
> The restoration of the Assyrian peace.  
> In his early years the Parthian was astonished  
> That he could not bear the counsel of an old man.  
> Every satrap sitting beneath the king  
> Remained terrified and motionless.  
> Thus the genius of the envoy had bound them all.  
> The Median countryside trembled,  
> And Babylon at last seemed too open to itself—  
> It had not closed its gates against the dragon-born enemy.  
>   
> But after he established a new formula for the treaty  
> Between the two sides, [Note: The received text had read *Procopio dictante Magis: magis juratur*, and made no sense. We have corrected the passage by punctuation and restored *Magis* as a name. Claudian writes of Stilicho’s peace:

> “With heaps of fragrant incense and a Sabaean harvest …”]

The altars reconcile peace, and the Magi, according to Chaldean ritual, slaughtered young bulls; the king himself inclines the gleaming bowl in his right hand and bears witness to the hidden rites of Bel and to Mithras, who rolls the wandering stars. For the Magi were the theologians and priests of the Persians, skilled in and ministers of divine matters. Porphyry shows that this is what the word itself signifies in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, Book III:

> “Among the Persians, those who are wise concerning the divine and servants of it are called Magi. For in the native dialect this is what the word *Magus* signifies.”

In the penultimate verse of Claudian I have restored *Beli* in place of *belli*. For he means Bel, whom the Chaldeans worshipped as a local god, as Minucius Felix observes in the *Octavius* and Sulpicius Severus in Book II of his *History*.

[Col. 0644C] As Procopius dictates, “by the Magi”; by them is sworn

[Note: [Col. 0644C] It is well established that the Persians regarded these beings as gods. Herodotus, in the *Thalia*: “The Persians consider fire to be a god.” In the same book he testifies likewise concerning water, as does Strabo in Book XV, and Diogenes Laertius in the preface to his work. But their principal worship was directed toward fire. Chrysostom, *On the Statues*, IV: “Among the Persians fire is considered a god, and the barbarians honor it with very elaborate service.” Hence their sacred fire-temples, *pyreia*; and in Socrates and Evagrius, in the camps of the kings Isdigerdes and Chosroes, “the revered fire.” For they carried fire perpetually around in sacred vessels. Pagan Persian writers attribute the origin of the religion to [Col. 0644D] the Persians; our writers attribute it to Nimrod, the grandson of Ham, as Marius Victorinus does in Book III of his commentary on Genesis.]

“Fire and water are gods; and also the agreements that are to remain firm;

Here he calls his divine ancestors to witness. The Chaldean old man, in accordance with the custom of the priesthood, performed the secret mutterings over the entrails; the king himself holding back the gem-studded bowl, bent low and poured the wine-cups upon the incense-burning altars.”

[Note: [Col. 0644D] After the Persian treaty, Procopius was made Master of Both Services and patrician by Theodosius. This is attested by Law 36 of Theodosius’ Code, *On the Distribution of Military Rations*, whose heading reads: “Given to Procopius, Master of Soldiers through the East, in the consulship of Victor”—that is, two years after the peace. In the Eastern Empire, Theodosius the Great had divided the Masters of Soldiers into three commands by dioceses: through the East, through Thrace, and through Illyricum. The chief city of the Diocese of the East was Antioch on the Orontes; its frontier, as Marcellinus says in Book XIV, extended from the ridge of Mount Taurus and the banks of the Euphrates as far as the Nile. Thus it reached even the borders of Ethiopia. [108] Therefore Sidonius could not have summarized the entire administration of the Master of Soldiers through the East either more briefly or more aptly.]

From this point he receives the returning man, bearing the double summit of honor:

“Patrician, and also Master of Infantry and Cavalry,

[Col. 0644B] He is placed in command of the camps, where he restrains the passes of Taurus,

And drives the wandering Ethiopians back by the terror of war,

So that, with the waters pacified, he may watch the servant Orontes.”

[Note: [Col. 0644D] Anthemius, prefect and consul under Arcadius, was the maternal grandfather of Augustus Anthemius.—surely the man who, after Arcadius’ death, bore the entire burden of the empire on his own shoulders on behalf of the still underage Theodosius. Synesius calls him “great Anthemius”; Socrates, “the wisest of the men of that time”; and Chrysostom adorns him with many exceptional praises in Letter 147. He held the consulship with Stilicho in 405. He continued in the prefecture for thirteen years.]

His father-in-law was Anthemius, prefect and consul as well;

[Col. 0645A] 292 He ruled the peoples and the year in his name.

Fortune always accompanies men of purple with imperial splendor;

Only this is changed among them:

The man who was consul now reigns. But let us pass over all the rest.

Now come to the lyre, you whose hair, worn down by the helmet,

Reached the diadem; for you the glowing imperial purple of Caesar

Is given when the cuirass is laid aside, and the hand emptied of the sword

Must be filled with the scepter. Your cradles shone with

The signs of empire, and the earth, foreseeing the future,

Promised golden ages from the offspring that had changed its form.

They say that, at your birth, rivers flowed forth with honey,

Their currents sweetened; streams of oil went running

While berries hung from the astonished presses.

The field brought forth a waving crop without seed,

And the vine begrudged its grapes, born without itself.

[Col. 0645B] Winter roses grew red, and, scorning the cold,

Lilies flaunted themselves amid mingled frost.

Whenever Lucina loosens such a birth,

The order of the elements yields, and the novelty of things

Becomes proof of the kingdom that is to come.

Thus nature declares that blessed gods have arrived;

Gentle flames caressed the tender hair of the hesitating Iulus.

Astyages, perhaps destined to be driven out by his grandson Cyrus,

Was terrified by the spreading vine-cluster of the womb.

The pregnant she-wolf offered her breasts to the fearless Quirinus.

Julius came into the light while the laurel was blazing,

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Concerning this prodigy at the birth of Julius Caesar, it would be difficult to find anyone who records it besides Sidonius. Nevertheless, I shall not on that account diminish its credibility. For how many things are there in Sidonius that today are not read elsewhere!]

And great Alexander, as well as Augustus, is held

To have been conceived by a serpent-god. They claimed Phoebus and Jupiter

As their respective fathers: one of them sought his father

Beneath the Cinyphian Syrtis:

[Note: [Col. 0645D] These words must be separated from what precedes so that they connect with what follows and refer to Augustus, not to Alexander. For concerning Olympias, Alexander’s mother, no one writes that a mark left by the serpent from which she had conceived remained upon her body. But Asclepiades of Mendes had written this about Attia, Augustus’ mother, from whom Tranquillus derives his account in chapter 95.]

On the mother’s body were marks.

[Col. 0645C] 293 The other rejoiced to be thought Phoebus-born,

Boasting of the Epidaurian sign of the Paeonian dragon.

Eagles have encircled many men, and throughout the world

A servant wing suddenly played at crowns that were to come.

But it was granted to know even then, excellent nobles,

That this man was being summoned to the scepter,

When, by chance, a vine, already cut away from its own stock,

Put forth shoots from his ancestral household.

That was the springtime of empire; beneath the image of foliage,

Everything blossomed at the right hand along the dry staff.

But after the child had passed his earliest years,

He crawled over his father’s weapons. Although the tight-fitting blade

Wore against his neck, he clasped it with both arms,

And, with his loosened crest, crept toward the livid kisses.

It was a game for the boy to handle quickly with eager hand

The arrows snatched from the enemy, and through captured bows

To force the resisting strings, bent toward the horns,

[Col. 0645D] And to push them into tension.

[Col. 0646A] Now to whirl the trembling javelin with his tender arm,

And, with the weight of a spear, to transfer by a leap

The chains of steel armor onto the back of a snorting horse;

To drive out beasts discovered in hiding beneath the leaves,

To search for those caught, now enclosing them in tight nets,

Now piercing them with a twisted hunting spear; then often

To be praised amid the shouting of his companions,

When, growling, the beast bore the iron

And the weapons came out through its pierced shoulders.

Hide your Pelethronian honors, bold boy and hunter,

Son of Aeacus: although, pressing down on the back of your master’s horse,

And therefore safely roaming the wilds,

You rather were carried by the horse;

The Paean, standing above Python, did not direct his arrows

More skillfully than our prince, when, with his quiver almost empty,

He struck the many coils of the serpent with innumerable shafts.

294 Nor did he hear these things less from the ancient sophists:

“Because Thales of Miletus censures legal securities;

Because Cleobulus of Lindus sings, “Let moderation be best”;”

Because Periander from Corinth meditates on the whole of life;

Because Solon of Attica wisely considers the end of existence;

Because, Priennean Bias, the crowd of the afflicted is dear to you;

Because, Pittacus, born on Lesbos, you urge men to recognize the right time;

Because Chilon from Lacedaemon wishes everyone to know himself.”

Moreover, he learned the various doctrines of the different schools:

Whatever Anacharsis praised in the Scythian fields;

Whatever Sparta achieved under the lawgiving Lycurgus;

Whatever the crowd of Cynics, [Note: [Col. 0646D] If one considers the origin of the two schools, Antisthenes, the father of the Cynics, was older than Epicurus; if one considers their doctrines, they were very dissimilar, especially concerning the end of goods. How, then, did the Cynics follow the Epicureans? Augustine explains in Book XIX of *The City of God* that there were people who, along with the Epicureans, proclaimed pleasure the highest good; yet they were accustomed to be called Cynics because they adopted the Cynics’ dress and habits. Sidonius seems to be speaking of these people, as does Origen in Book XV of his commentary on Exodus.]

Imitating your Epicurean companions,

Turns over in the gymnasia;

Whatever the double Academy declares,

Maintaining that nothing is true;

Whatever Cleanthes savors while gnawing his nail;

[Col. 0646C] Whatever Pythagoras, Democritus, and Heraclitus

Lamented, laughed at, or kept silent about;

Whatever Plato’s genius, stationed in the citadel,

Teaches in its threefold order;

Whatever Aristotle, dividing the parts of speech,

Gives to argumentative syllogisms as nets;

Whatever Anaximenes, Euclid, Archytas, Zeno,

Arcesilaus, Chrysippus, and Anaxagoras contributed;

And whatever the Socratic soul, alive after death in the *Phaedo*,

Despising the vast chains upon its emaciated leg,

While death itself trembled before the accused

And the executioner’s pale hand brought poison

To the fearless master.

Moreover, whatever ancient times strove to place

In Latin books, he was accustomed to travel through it all:

The battles that Mantua sang, and the dangers of the sea,

Imitating the trumpets of Smyrna;

295 Whatever help the consul from Arpinum provides in speech;

[Col. 0646D] Whatever, speaking without end, the man born of a smith

Sends forth—his polished tongue greater in eloquence

Than his despised father; or whatever volumes

The Euganean pages of Padua send into the ages;

[Col. 0647A] The brevity with which Crispus pleases, the weight of Varro,

The genius of Plautus, the thunder of Quintilian,

The grandeur of Tacitus, who must never be mentioned without praise.

Trained in these studies, born of such ancestry,

And imbued with such character, he was chosen as son-in-law by the prince

To whom the world, from East to West,

Was then yielding its scepters, and whose marriageable

Only daughter owed her father descendants clad in purple.—not so that, idle in luxury,

Content with his father-in-law’s fortune and pursuing leisure,

He would owe nothing to himself:

[Note: [Col. 0647B] Sidonius says that Anthemius was adorned with the insignia of a count when he was sent to defend the Danubian frontier. [Col. 0647C] This should not be understood as the Count of the East, which had nothing to do with the Danubian region. Rather, it was the rank of Count of Military Affairs, whose holders, when they were placed by the emperor in command of military forces of the first order, were customarily put in charge of provinces and equated with provincial commanders. Theodosius the Younger, in the Code, *On Counts of Military Affairs*, says: “Those whom, under the dignity of Count of the First Order, we specifically appoint, by the authority of our divine power, to defend any province or provinces with soldiers entrusted to them, we make equal to commanders.” This was a kind of step toward the Mastership of Soldiers, to which they were afterward promoted. Marcellinus, Book XXVI: “Equitius is placed over the Illyrian army, not yet a master, but a count”; and later: “Valentinian intended Equitius, having been increased to the dignity of master, to return to Illyricum.” We likewise read that Constantius, Boniface, and Aetius were first counts and afterward masters; and our Anthemius, immediately after this expedition, was made Master of Both Services.]

But in the duly conferred right of a count

He circles the banks of the Danube and the broad frontier region;

He urges, arranges, investigates, and arms.

[Col. 0647B] Thus, under his father, the Pious One governed his father’s camp with moderation;

Thus Marcus, while Pius lived, commanded innumerable legions,

Both destined afterward to give laws.

From this point every honor is given to the returning man, and he shines

As Master of Both Services and consul:

[Note: [Col. 0647B] *Omnis* is used archaically for *utriusque* (“of both”). The most ancient writers, Priscian testifies, also ended every genitive in *-ius* with the letter *i*. Caecilius the comic poet: “For the sake of no other thing than their friendship.” Afranius, in the *Suscepta*: “So that satisfaction might seize you for the whole family.” By ancient usage one could also say *utraque*, as Fortunatus did to Bodegisilus: “There is dispute over your goodness in each region.”]

The power of the patriciate joined,

He advanced rapidly from private rank,

And the boy himself mounted the curule chair of the elders;

As a young man, a veteran, he sat in the gold reserved for the experienced.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] This is found in the best copies, and there can be no doubt that Sidonius wrote it so. For the common edition has *paris divos*, which is ridiculous and means nothing. Marcianus is called a god after death, just as Julius and Augustus are called gods on coins, and Trajan is called a god in this fragment of an ancient inscription, unearthed a few years ago in the territory of Ricina:

> DIVOS TRAJANUS, AUGUSTUS  
> CONCESSA TUSCILI NOMINATI HEREDITATE REIPUB. RICINENSI BALNEUM ET PLATIAS . . . . . . . .

“Trajan Augustus, a god, having received the inheritance called Tuscilia, granted to the Ricinian commonwealth a bath and plazas …”

So also below concerning Marcianus himself:

> . . . . . may the divine star of the father rejoice in Euphemia,  
> [as she is] clothed in her father’s purple.

He says: “Now, after Marcianus had died without a male heir, the empire was owed to you because of his daughter, your wife. But you, having no desire at all to reign, allowed Leo to be preferred to you, so that afterward you yourself might be called to share the kingdom, not by the prerogative of birth but of virtue.” Thus everything up to this point occurred while Marcianus was alive. What follows belongs to the time of Leo, namely Anthemius’ two wars, the Gothic and the Hunnic.]

And now his father is a god; but you had no desire for empire:

[Col. 0648A] You endured the long rejection of diadems.

They chose a distinguished man whom afterward you could not

Despise; fortune alone conferred this distinction upon you,

Although your rank demanded it,

296 So that you might be chosen as prince rather than appear abandoned.

After your father-in-law became Augustus, you reign;

But the purple did not come to you through the marriage chamber,

Nor was your royal wife the cause of your glory, but rather its praise;

For the commonwealth chose not a son-in-law by the reins of law,

But a noble man.

Unless I am mistaken, the world proves this matter on its twofold axis.

The West surrounds you; the East appoints you ruler;

You fight toward the North, and you are feared toward the South.

Yet before your colleague made you his associate,

I wish to recall the triumphs Illyria’s shore witnessed,

When it groaned that it had been abandoned to Valamer’s arms, perhaps through the fault of our commander.

[Note: [Col. 0648C] The author of the Gothic war was Valamer, king of the Ostrogoths. He was the man who, together with his brothers Theodemir and Videmir, followed Attila in the Gallic war and, after Attila’s death, received settlements in Pannonia from Marcianus, along with annual gifts. When these gifts were afterward supplied more slowly by Leo, he devastated almost the whole of Illyricum by plundering it, as Jordanes relates in his *Getica*. Therefore Sidonius calls the Goths “plunderers,” and says that they were driven back by Anthemius’ forces. The emperor was nevertheless compelled to provide the customary gifts, with the son of Theodemir, Theoderic—later king of Italy—given by the Goths as a hostage for the peace. I infer the date to have been around [Col. 0648D] 462, from the age of Theoderic as Jordanes records it.]

[Col. 0648B] Just as once, when Caepio was defeated, the strength

Of Ausonia yielded under sudden disaster.

After Jugurtha’s neck had been broken, the terrified commonwealth,

About to choose an avenger from Arpinum for the Calpurnian treaties,

Set him against the frenzied Cimbrian.

When the province first saw your eagles,

It ceased at once to dread the hostile dragons.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] This does not mean that dragons were absent among the Roman standards, but that the eagle was their distinctive and principal standard. For, according to Vegetius Renatus, just as the eagle was the first standard of the entire legion, so dragons belonged to individual cohorts. And just as there was an eagle-bearer in the camp who carried the eagle, so there were dragon-bearers who carried the dragons. Themistius, in Oration VI: “Neither a golden eagle, nor dragons of delicate woven fabrics”; and Prudentius, concerning soldiers who were becoming Christians:

> They abandon Caesar’s standards and choose the sign of the cross;  
> And instead of the wind-filled cloaks of dragons that they carried,  
> They bring forth the distinguished wood that subdued the dragon.

Sidonius himself, in his panegyric of Majorian:

> . . . now the woven serpent  
> Runs through both battle lines, Roman and Vandal.]

At once subdued in war and stripped of booty,

[Col. 0649A] They themselves soon lie as your booty; but let us pass over them

As plunderers. I recall more important deeds of war.

That war was undertaken neither by a small band nor by Spartacus,

Breaking out of prison and preparing for the gladiatorial arena,

But by a wandering multitude from the Scythian region,

Full of savagery, terrible, rapacious, violent,

Barbarous even among the barbarian peoples themselves,

Whose leader and fellow citizen was Hormidac,

For whom such soil, walls, and birth were their inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0649C] This description of the Huns should be compared with what Marcellinus, Book XXX, Zosimus, Book IV, and, most accurately of all, Jordanes, drawing on the rhetor Priscus, the ambassador of Theodosius to Attila, write concerning the origin, appearance, and customs of that people. Much of it is extremely similar to Sidonius’ words.]

White Tanais, driven through the Hyperborean valleys,

Falls from the Rhipaean crag and lies beneath the axis of the Bear:

297 A race threatening in spirit and in body.

There is a native horror even in the faces of its infants;

A round mass rises into a narrow crown of head;

Beneath the forehead, sight appears through twin hollows,

With eyes that seem absent; a light scarcely reaches

The withdrawn orbits through the chamber of the brain,

[Col. 0649B] And yet they are not closed. For within a not spacious vault,

They see great expanses, and, in deep wells,

Transparent points compensate for the use of greater light.

Then, lest the double tube grow outward through the cheeks,

A band wrapped around crushes the tender nostrils,

So that they may yield to helmets. Thus maternal love deforms

Those born for battle, because, when the cheeks are stretched,

The area of the face becomes broader without the intervening nose.

The rest of their bodies is handsome: broad chests stand firm,

Their shoulders are notable, and their belly is girded for agility.

Their stature is of medium height on foot,

But they appear tall if you see them as horsemen;

Indeed, they often seem long when they are seated.

Hardly has the infant, deprived of its mother, begun to stand

When a horse immediately offers its back.

You would think their limbs joined to those of men,

So fixedly does the rider always cling to his horse.

[Col. 0649C] Another race is borne upon the backs of horses;

It lives upon them. Smooth bows and arrows are their passion;

Their hands are terrible and sure, and their fixed confidence

In carrying death by the javelin never fails in its stroke,

Their fury is taught not to miss.

This people, bursting forth suddenly and carried

Across the Danube, made solid for wheels,

Had come and cut furrows through the divided waters.

You, advancing directly against them, wandering through the Dacian fields,

Drew them together, attacked, overcame, and enclosed them;

And when Serdica saw you, having marked out the camp’s space,

298 You pressed them under siege. For a long time, stationed in the rampart,

It was astonished that no soldier went out into the fields,

Neither on lawful nor on secret raids.

Although Ceres was often absent for them, and Lyaeus always,

Discipline was not absent. Therefore, with the enemy nearby,

They feared their commander all the more. Thus at last it happened

That your ally at that time, soon afterward a traitor,

Fled them in vain at the moment of the battle:

[Col. 0650B] And while he was already fleeing, turning his foot and baring his horns,

You alone stood in the battle line;

The scattered band sought you when its leader fled;

The horseman came back seeking you, sweating in infantry combat;

The soldier, following your standards, did not feel abandoned in the struggle.

Go now and bring forth the praises of ancient Tullus:

The gray age of the fathers, by its beautiful exhortation,

Concealed the wavering treaty of the deserter Mettius.

Nothing similar occurred here, and you do not like to deceive your enemy.

Then the soldier won, while thinking that he had to be helped;

Here he won after discovering that he had been abandoned.

The commander fled: you pursued him. He renewed the battle: you conquered.

He was enclosed: you stormed him. He escaped: you overwhelmed him.

And you set his own deaths as the price of the Sarmatian peace.

The deserter was delivered up and underwent the death that had been ordered;

[Col. 0650C] Your victim fell beneath a foreign sword.

Look again, if you wish, to the conflict of ancient times:

That fierce Hannibal, when he was perhaps being sought for punishment,

If he did not possess the right to life,

At least at his final hour he possessed the right to death;

Him the blind prison, the hook,

And the executioner who watched to break his neck

Drank poison from him, more steadfast than his guest from Bebrycia.

299 But the man who fled you, killed by the death that had been commanded,

Perished not so much by the victor’s as by the judge’s sentence.

[Note: [Col. 0651C] This is the second part of the panegyric, which contains the auspices of the empire and which the poet treats with poetic genius. For he imagines that, after Severus’ death, Italy, being without an emperor, came to the sources of the Tiber and asked it to persuade Rome to go toward the dawn and request an emperor from the East. The Dawn, in turn, grants Anthemius to Rome in response to its prayers. Thus he describes all these persons and encounters in the manner of poetry.]

Now come, Paean, whose laurel-trained bridle-bits bind

The hooked griffins whenever you bend their winged shoulders

With ivy of two colors through leafy reins.

Turn your lyre here. This is not the time to tell

Of Python’s destruction, nor to sound the twice seven wounds

Of the daughters of Tantalus, whose deaths your song preserves,

And whose lives, though dead, live in everlasting song.

You also, Castalian Muses, reveal in a few words

By what divine will Anthemius came to us,

With the compact of a joint empire:

The peace of the world has sent one who can govern wars.

[Col. 0651B] Severus, by the law of nature, had increased the number of the deified emperors.

[Note: [Col. 0651C] Libius Severus—for this is how ancient coins call him—held the empire through the agency of Ricimer after the murder of Majorian, beginning on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December in A.D. 461. Then, four years later, he was killed, as was reported, by Ricimer’s treachery, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. Cassiodorus records: “In the consulship of Herminericus and Basiliscus, in these consulships, as is said, Severus was killed by poison at Rome in the palace through Ricimer’s treachery.” Others say that he died a natural death, as Paul the Deacon does in Book VI. Sidonius too seems to have intended this meaning when he says that he died according to nature’s law—either because he believed it, or in order to free Ricimer, Anthemius’ son-in-law, from that accusation. We have come across a brief list written in Justinian’s time, in which all the emperors from Augustus onward are described, with the number of years they reigned and the place and manner of their deaths. Concerning Severus it says: “Severus ruled at Rome for four years and died there, having lived religiously.”]

Soon afterward, when Italy saw this event from the bronze crags of the Apennines,

she proceeded to the glassy halls of the blue Tiber,

His cheeks enclosed neither by a helmet

Nor by a sewn circle that wove a cuirass

From interlocked hooks.

His head was bare; instead of hair, a vine

Spread over his forehead, clasping many strongholds,

And over his smooth shoulders and shining arms

Hung cloths fastened by gem-bearing bosses.

His divine spirit moves more slowly, and, retaining his venerable limbs

With a vine-haired staff, he bends upon an elm.

Yet abundance follows him: wherever he approaches,

His footsteps make the road fertile,

And the joyful vintage, accompanying his stride,

Sprinkles the prints he leaves behind.

[Col. 0652A] At once he enters the cavern of the Tiber’s whirlpool.

The river flowed in repose, and the tall reed-forest

Ran green with hair of the same color.

300 Water falling from his chin made a sound,

Although the rough beard beneath greatly softened the noise.

From his breast he belched liquid; with swift movement

The torrent furrowed its already wet belly.

The goddess is terrified at his approach, and from her relaxed hands

Oar and urn fall. As she prepares words of supplication,

She begins:

“I come, if it pleases you, to bend Rome,

Widowed of her ruler, through tears.

Let her seek the regions of the Dawn,

And, setting pride aside, let her obtain this one favor:

That she may now be deemed more worthy of love.

Tell me what powers she should seek,

And in what part of the world she should ask for a leader;

Whoever was created under my axis,

The fortune of empire at once broke his wheels there.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] There are two reasons why he wishes an emperor to be sought from the East. First, all the native rulers who had reigned in preceding years—Maximus, Avitus, Majorianus, and Severus—had enjoyed short and inauspicious reigns. Second, Ricimer, who after Severus’ death governed the commonwealth during the interregnum, could not resist Genseric alone. Therefore it was necessary to act quickly, so that an emperor might be proclaimed from there who would reign long and successfully and restrain the Vandals.]

From that quarter the Vandal enemy presses upon us

And every year wages war against our destruction with a numerous fleet;

And, with the order of fate reversed,

The burning Byrsa brings Caucasian frenzies upon me.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] After Genseric captured Carthage, and especially after Valentinian’s death, he did not cease ravaging the provinces of both empires with continual raids. He did so with such confidence in himself that, when a shipmaster once asked him where he should order the sails to be set, he is said to have replied, “Wherever God drives us.” This clearly explains why Sidonius calls him a wandering pirate, and why he is called a sudden enemy by Theodoric in Cassiodorus, *Variarum* I.4, and why his sudden assault and chance plundering, feared by every shore, are mentioned in Valentinian’s Novel 20 among the Theodosian laws. Since it is contrary to custom for Scythians—that is, Vandals and Alans, whom Sidonius elsewhere calls Caucasus-born—to rush in from Africa, he says:

> “And with the order of fate reversed,  
> The burning Byrsa brings Caucasian frenzies upon me.”

And in Poem 23, with the same antithesis, he called Genseric

> “the Tanaite rebel  
> Of African soil.”]

Moreover, the unconquered Ricimer, whom the public fortunes

Look upon favorably, scarcely repels him alone by his own strength—

The pirate wandering through the countryside, who, avoiding battle,

Acts the victor while a fugitive.

Who could endure an enemy who refuses both peace and war?

For he makes no treaty with Ricimer. Hear why he hates him so deeply.

He loudly claims an uncertain father, although he has a mother certainly a slave; now, to make himself a king’s son, he parades his mother’s adultery; then he begrudges Ricimer because two kingdoms call him to rule:

[Col. 0653A] His father was a Suevian, and on his mother’s side he was a Goth.

At the same time he remembers this:

That his grandfather Vallia, in the lands of Tartessus,

[Note: [Col. 0653C] Vallia’s victories over the Vandals and Alans at Tartessus and Calpe must be sought in Hydatius and Isidore. They relate that around A.D. 418 Vallia destroyed the Siling Vandals in Baetica and so crushed the Alans that they afterward united into a single kingdom with the Vandals who obeyed King Gunderic in Gallaecia. There is no doubt that Sidonius is speaking of these wars.]

Struck down the Vandal troops and the Alans,

Joined in the same warfare,

And covered the setting Calpe with corpses.

301 Why recount ancient flights and the losses of former times?

He recalls the disaster of the Agrigentine plain.

[Note: [Col. 0653C] This refers to the Sicilian defeat in which Genseric himself was routed by Ricimer on the Agrigentine coast and learned that he was facing the grandson of Vallia, once the conqueror of the Vandals—probably during Avitus’ reign. Priscus, in the excerpts of the embassies, states that Ricimer was sent by Avitus against the Vandals with an army. Hydatius also records, among the deeds of Avitus, that a multitude of Vandals who had sailed from Carthage with sixty ships was cut down through the stratagem of Ricimer, their commander.]

Therefore he rages, because this man has taught him sufficiently

That he is the grandson of the man whom, whenever you saw him,

You, Vandal, always fled.

For you do not return more illustrious from the Sicilian fields,

Marcellus, through whom our arms crushed the Syracusan

Household gods on land and sea;

Nor you, Metellus, to whom it fell to surpass Curtius’ chariot,

Exhibiting to us a crowded line of elephants,

When a black herd covered the white tusked beasts

With its bulk,

[Col. 0653B] And the triumphal procession concealed their master.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Some read *Curium curru*, “Curius with his chariot,” which has the same meaning. Curius Dentatus was the first commander to lead elephants in triumph after triumphing over Pyrrhus, in the year 427 from the founding of the City—but only a few, four in all, as Eutropius reports. But Lucius Metellus, in the triumph that he celebrated over the Carthaginians conquered in Sicily in the year 503 from the founding of the City, led one hundred and twenty elephants, according to Livy, as reported in the *Epitome* of Book 19, and Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 14. “Metellus,” he says, “when celebrating a triumph over the Carthaginians conquered in Sicily, led before his chariot, alone among all the Romans, one hundred and twenty captive elephants.” Metellus therefore surpassed the chariot of Curius—and not only Curius’, but those of all who triumphed afterward.]

This man is feared because he keeps the Ostrogoth

Contained in Noricum;

Because he restrains the war of Gaul along the Rhine,

He is a terror to them.

[Note: [Col. 0654C] Ricimer is the terror of the barbarians. The reason the Ostrogoths do not burst into Italy through Noricum, and the Franks and other Germanic peoples into Gaul across the Rhine, is that they are held back by fear of him.]

Because the Vandal enemy, my kinsman through the Alan,

Plundered me while he ravaged,

This man avenged me by his own weapons.

Yet he is only one man and cannot alone

Bear such dangers, though he can postpone them.

Now we need an armed prince,

One who, following the custom of ancient fathers,

Will not merely order wars but wage them himself;

One at whose movement the standards

Make land and sea tremble,

So that at last, by duly restored right,

The Roman trumpets may command fleets that have forgotten them.”

The father heard these words and nodded assent.

At once they set out for the City.

He himself sees the goddess and humbly worships her;

His chest and the exposed horns touched her breast.

From there he carries back the prayers entrusted to him.

The goddess follows them and prepares to set out:

[Col. 0653C] She binds up her loosened, fierce hair,

And the towers, enclosed in her helmet, lie hidden.

Her fillet was laurel; rough with enemy bosses,

A baldric fastened at her left side held the sword rising upward.

302 The victorious hand is inserted into the shield;

The she-wolf, the Tiber, Love, Mars, and Ilia fill its circle.

[Col. 0654A] A brooch with biting tooth catches the garments fleeing from her breast;

Her spear flashes threateningly, and the oak curved with trophies

Trembles, while the peaceful burden wearies the goddess.”

[Note: [Col. 0654D] “Solea.” He describes the kind of buskin visible in ancient statues: in it, to use Gellius’s words, only the heels of the feet are covered at the very bottom, while the rest is bare and bound with rounded straps. Thus he used *solum* for *solea*, as Plautus, Martial, and others did. By *fornix* he means the sloping part opposite the hollow of the foot, which in Book VIII, Letter 11, he called *camera*, describing footwear likewise bound with straps, in which, as the loops of the ties converge, a chain bent back toward the leg rises through the arch. Some manuscripts, however, read not *fornice* but *fomite*.]

The sole stands continuously upon the ground, but a band is fastened at the first toes; from the bound arch the big toe sends two fastenings in the opposite direction, to tighten the sandals and, as the loops of the straps converge, to weave broad chains up the legs.

Thus, after she had crossed the liquid air, she sought the warm rising-place of the newborn Sun. There is a region of ocean near the distant Indians, stretched beneath the eastern sky toward the Nabataean east. There spring is continuous; the earth, interrupted by no cold, does not grow pale, but fields painted with everlasting flowers know nothing of foreign frosts.

[Col. 0654B] The countryside breathes roses, and fragrance rises through the indescribable fields. The meadows produce violets, cytisus, thyme, privet, lilies, narcissi, cassia, colocasia, marigolds, costus, malobathrum, myrrh, opobalsam, and frankincense; and when old age comes knocking, the neighboring phoenix seeks his renewed cinnamon from here.

Here is Aurora’s house, crusted with gleaming metal, displaying smooth stones amid its berries. Different things snatch the eyes, and by the skill of their maker each surpasses whatever you see; yet all beauty is concealed beneath the presence of its mistress, and her excessive radiance makes the varied fires of the gems grow dim, because she possesses them herself.

Her combed hair poured forth saffron, and a golden comb, pressed down by her bent arm, arranged her temples.

303 Her eyes poured forth rays; their color was fiery, but there was no heat in them, although at night, shaken from the darkness, the dews are accustomed to imitate sweat.

Two belts encircle her breast, and the bosom itself makes the small breasts an object of envy; the outer edge of her robe carries purple folds down to her reddened legs.

[Col. 0654C] Thus the queen sits upon her throne. In place of a scepter, her right hand [Note: [Col. 0654D] 114 Aurora’s torch is assigned in place of a scepter, a usage derived from ancient custom. For she was represented with a torch, whence she was also called *λαμπαδηφόρος* (“torch-bearer”), and she is commonly seen in that guise on ancient monuments. Ovid, *Fasti* V:

“On the following day, when the stars of Hyperion have been driven away, she will raise the rosy lamp upon her morning horses.”

And Sidonius himself, in poem 9, called the Indians “scorched by Aurora’s civic torch.”] fills with the shaft of a lamp. Night stands close beside the goddess; already, turning back her retreating feet, she draws forth behind the tribunal the scarcely perceived crown of light.

From here, seeing Rome approaching along a clear path, she sprang up quickly and was the first to begin speaking with gentle words:

“What brings you back, O head of the world, to my kingdoms? What do you command?”

After a brief silence, mingling harshness with gentleness, she began:

“I am coming—stop your agitation, and do not tremble too much—not so that the Araxes, pressed beneath an imposed bridge, may flow; nor so that, in the ancient manner, the Indian Ganges may drink from the Ausonian helmet; nor so that a consul, armed with a quiver, may joyfully devastate Artaxata Caspia through the tiger-bearing fields of the Niphates.

[Note: [Col. 0655C] I have judged that it should be read *non Pori*, not *Pharii*, as in the printed editions. [Col. 0655D] The kingdom of Porus lay beyond the Hydaspes; on its bank, as Curtius relates in Book VIII, Alexander was victorious after Porus had attempted in vain to prevent his crossing. We read of Ionian, Boeotian, and Aetolian Erythrae, but nowhere of Hydaspian Erythrae—that is, Indian Erythrae. Martial speaks of Bacchus’s Erythraean triumphs, and Claudian of Erythraean gems and emeralds, as do others in similar expressions; they derive the name not from any city but from the Erythraean Sea, which washes India. Sidonius, however, thought it was the name of a city, and regularly calls them Hydaspian, arrow-bearing, warm Erythrae, to distinguish them from the others.]

I do not merely ask for the kingdoms of Porus, nor that a ram hurled against these arms should shatter the Hydaspian Erythrae.

[Col. 0655B] I am not rushing upon Bactra, nor do I seek the Arsacid houses that provoke battles, nor is the military signal given for Ctesiphon. We have ceded to you this entire region of the world, and yet do I not deserve that you should protect my old age?

Everything between the Euphrates and the Tigris you once held alone. This territory was purchased for me with the blood of Crassus:

304 I recorded the price at Carrhae, and I did not remain unavenged; or did the land purchased in this way perish? If I am mistaken, you proved it when Sapor, slain by Ventidius, paid the penalty. Nor is that enough:

“I gave you Armenia and Pontus, won by war—let Sulla tell you of them; perhaps one witness is not believed: consult Lucullus. I am silent now about all the Cyclades. Crete, acquired by my Metellus, serves you. I transferred the Cilicians, whom Magnus once defeated. I added the Isaurians of Syria, whom you now rule:

[Col. 0655C] Servilius also subdued these beneath our arms. I granted you the ancient Aetolians and the fields of Achelous; too credulously I transferred the Attalid inheritance. You retain Epirus—you know that Pyrrhus owed it to you. I look to you to send laws into Illyricum and the lands of Macedon; and you, Paulus, have descendants.

“I gave you the grain of Egypt; Agrippa had once conquered it for me in the Leucadian straits. Judaea is held under your rule, as though you had sent Titus there with his illustrious father. Cyprus is counted among your gains. I, a poor man, praise the warlike Catos; Doric land and Achaean laws tremble before you, and you extend your fortunate kingdoms into two-sea Corinth.

“Tell me: which Byzantine accomplished this service for you, Mummius?

[Note: [Col. 0656C] “In return for so many provinces of Roman law that I have transferred to the Constantinopolitan empire, grant me Anthemius as emperor. Let divine Marcian see Euphemia, his daughter, as Augusta and Anthemius’s wife; add also the marriage of Ricimer to Anthemius’s daughter. All these matters are known from other passages of Sidonius, except for the name Euphemia, which we owe to this one passage. Hubert Goltzius nevertheless produces an inscription from an ancient coin in which she is called Flavia Marciana Augusta; if that is correct, Flavia Euphemia must have been called Marciana. Besides the unnamed daughter who married Ricimer, Anthemius and Euphemia had three sons—Marcianus, Romulus, and Procopius—about whom Theodorus Lector says much in his *Collectanea*, Malchus the Sophist in his *Byzantine History*, and Candidus Isaurus in Book II of his *History*.]

“But if it should perhaps please you to put old quarrels to rest, grant me Anthemius. Let him be Augustus in these regions, and let Leo live long; let the man I have sought govern my rights. Let the star of his father rejoice that his daughter Euphemia is clothed in the imperial purple.

“Moreover, add a private bond to the public treaty. Let Augustus, as father-in-law, be blessed with Ricimer as son-in-law.

305 They shine in nobility: you have a royal maiden, and I have a royal man. If you agree harmoniously to this, you will soon allow me to hope for Libya. Look around at the ancient marriage-torches: no union equal to this is available to you.

“Let Greece produce here the marriage-beds won by ancient contests, if that is not shameful. Let Pisa, with its restored chariots, raise Oenomaus, whom the waxen barrier, collapsing when the axles were loosened by his daughter’s treachery, brought down.

“Let the Colchian maiden, first recognized by her husband for her crime rather than her sex, come forth before him. Let Atalanta, pale with fear for her suitors, look out from the circus prison, and let her no longer gather the apples for handsome Hippomenes merely for their golden color.

“Let Deianira, made strong by her Achelous exercise, adorn your marriage-torches, and, pressed by breathless Hercules, nurse her exhausted rival in competing streams.

“However often I recall the marriages of the ancient age, these surpass the heroes, and that one the heroines.

[Col. 0656C] “Virtue, Ricimer, demands these marriage-beds as your bridal attendant, and the laurels of Mars give you the myrtle of Dione.

“Come, then: take a man who is not nourished by sluggish leisure or weighed down by pleasures, but one whom the sailor’s heat now burns, together with the bay of Abydos and the Sestian coast, surrounded by the storms of the Hellespont;

[Note: [Col. 0656D] He means Anthemius, who, when he was summoned to the imperial office, had commanded the Hellespontine fleet, which the emperors used to keep in the harbors of that strait. There were also other fleets dispersed throughout that sea for various purposes, such as the Carpathian, Seleucian, and Alexandrian fleets, mentioned in the Augustan laws.]

“the straits of the sea which I would not believe even that man had held in such a way—he whose Athos was cut through, for whom Median rowers drove swollen sails across the wooded mountain.

[Col. 0657A] “Nor, if these waters had been surrounded by Lucullan ships, did the sluggish enemy sit idle beside distinguished Cyzicus: though forced by hunger to eat the corpses of his kindred, he lived by his own death. But why do I delay my wishes? Give him to me more quickly.”

306 Then his wife, the daughter of Tithonus, briefly replied:

“Lead on, holy mother, although I have the greatest need of a mighty and invincible leader, provided you remain gentler and we guide our united reins more wisely.

“For if it should please you to remember ancient labors, and the man of your Julian house who fought for his country—to say nothing more—I was the first to send Memnon away from here.”

They finished. Concord joined the two sides, since at last Rome obtained the ruler she had chosen.

[Col. 0657B] [Note: [Col. 0657C] By this expression he sets Anthemius against and above several ancient Roman leaders, because, unlike them, he had not been promoted to imperial power after first suffering some injury. Lucius Cincinnatus was mourning the exile of his son Caeso when he was summoned to the dictatorship and to conduct the war against the Aequi. Marcus Camillus was himself living in exile at Ardea when he was created dictator for the second time against Brennus. Marcus Livius Salinator—for he was the man who, in his second consulship, defeated and killed the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal at the Metaurus—had previously been condemned and fined in a public trial after his first consulship. Livy explains these individual cases in Book III, chapters 5 and 27.]

“Now, antiquity, boast that you have read of men with a like wish or affection—men whom envy never spared when they were eminent and had earned their honors. Bring Camillus forth from exile against Brennus’s arms; recall Cincinnatus to the axes after Caeso’s expulsion; summon the grieving father from the plow to the rostra; and, amid wretched turmoil, first drive out those whom you are to seek once defeated. If the Carthaginian crosses the Alps, return to those who were afflicted and condemned.

“Let the Metaurus, stained by the disgrace of Barcina, make the guilty consul blush; let the fined consul march for you—he who, after laying low thousands of Hasdrubal’s men and forging for himself a shining sword, carried the congealed head. Our judgment has another kind of favor: he knows that he is loved without having suffered injury.

“But now excessive winds are driving my sails. Halt, Muse, your delicate melodies, and let the anchor of my song settle on a calm seabed as I seek harbor.

[Col. 0657C] “Nevertheless, prince, whatever fleet and arms are now being prepared for you, however great the force you command, and however briefly the time may be—

[Col. 0657D] if God should advance my wishes in their proper order, I shall soon speak either of your son-in-law as twice consul or of you as consul for the third time.”

[Note: [Col. 0657D] He wishes Ricimer a second consulship, since he had already held the first in 459, and Anthemius a third, since he was then entering his second.]

“For now our festivals summon us and call you to the Ulpian forums,

307 where you will grant liberty to Romans, whose joyful cheeks await the blows [of ceremonial manumission]. Go on, happy father of your country, under a favorable omen: as a new captor, bind your captives; as an old one, release them.”

## Poem III. Edition of the Panegyric, Addressed to Peter

[Note: [Col. 0658C] This poem was wrongly attached to the panegyric of Anthemius, as though it belonged to that work; in fact it belongs to the panegyric of Majorian, whose edition Sidonius dedicates to Peter, his master of correspondence. It is therefore placed before that poem, just as the poem addressed to Priscus Valerianus is placed in the ancient books before the panegyric of Avitus, whose edition it introduces. The edition of the panegyric of Anthemius lacks an epigram of dedication, as do all the works of Claudian.]

What makes fields rejoice, what season is dear to harvests, flocks, vines, and bees, was once published under the name of Maecenas:

“From this, Maro, you dared afterward to speak of arms and the man.”

But for me Peter will be the Maecenas of this age, since I run across the sea of fame beneath his star.

[Col. 0658B] If he approves, he releases my poems; if he condemns them, he conceals them, and he does not brand us with the snorting rhinoceros.

Go, book: believe that he protects our modesty. Under such a judge, even to have displeased is pleasing.

## Poem IV. Preface to the Panegyric Delivered for the Emperor Majorian Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0658C] 116 Majorian succeeded Avitus Augustus after an interregnum of several months, in the year of Christ 457. In the following year he held the consulship in the customary manner; after crossing the Alps in a severe winter with a great army, he came to Lyons, which he had shortly before brought under his power. Sidonius welcomed his arrival with this panegyric, having already obtained pardon from him for his association with the enemy, as he says in the preface. This is the distinction between this panegyric and the others: the other two were delivered on the Kalends of January to celebrate the auspices of the consulship, whereas this was delivered on another occasion, toward the end of the year, while Majorian was nevertheless still consul. Thus Carolus Sigonius cannot be excused for assigning its delivery to the year 460, two years later. For Sidonius clearly says:

‘The emperor,’ he says, ‘now holds the consulship.”]

Tityrus, once, beneath the shelter of the spreading beech, was allowed to roll his murmurs through his swelling reeds. Caesar granted the afflicted man the right to life and land, and his anger did not stand higher than the humble defendant. While Tityrus praised the granted countryside in a generous prince, rustic song gave heaven in exchange for earth.

308 Nor was it an inferior gift to return Phoebus’s favors: one made a lord, the other made a god.

[Col. 0658C] And for you, Flaccus, who followed the ranks of Brutus and Cassius, he is the author both of song and of pardon.

Thus, when I recently fell beneath a different Mars, you ordered me to be victorious with a peaceful spirit. Let the tongue of a poet whom you saved therefore serve you, and let the praise of my life be the price you receive.

I shall not now attack Maro with biting tooth, nor criticize your fellow citizen, land of Sabine soil. The subject is smaller than my talent, but greater than Caesar: let them surpass us in eloquence, provided that we yield to our lord.

## Poem V. Panegyric Delivered for Julius Valerius Majorianus Augustus

Take into your mind, commonwealth, the triumphs of the past: the consul now holds the empire, one whom purple covers no more than cuirass; whose diadems cover his forehead not with luxury but with law; for whom, after the palm of victory, a palm-bearing robe comes as the reward of labors. All the honors of kingship accumulate the fasces, and the prince grows through the consul.

[Col. 0659B] [Note: [Col. 0659C] In the panegyric of Avitus:

‘Diadems increase through the marks of office.’

For although emperors considered all other dignities beneath themselves, they nevertheless believed that the insignia of the consulship not only suited their fortune but also added honor to the Augustan name, as Valentinian says in his Novel addressed to Sporatius. For that reason they alone among all offices assumed this one. Claudian, in *Against Eutropius* I:

‘This office alone

the palace accepts; to you fathers it returns,

this alternating honor.’

The rhetor Libanius, in his speech for Julian:

‘For this alone of honors was suited to the fortune even of a king.’

Julian himself, in his encomium of the Empress Eusebia:

‘Neither private citizen nor king has existed who did not consider it desirable to be named consul.’

Claudian likewise, in *Against Stilicho* II:

‘Do we consider a title slight and a decoration small

with which they confess that they adorn the Augusti?’]

Your name therefore resounds through heaven, countryside, cities, and seas. Europe rejoices and cries “Excellent!” because you are its ruler, you who had been its victor. I confess that the world had trembled while you refused to claim victory for yourself, grieving with excessive modesty that you had earned a kingdom and were undertaking, after a sad rebuff, an office you had thought should be defended rather than governed.

309 Warlike Rome sat with breast exposed, her tower-crowned, crested head; behind her capacious helmet, loosened hair streamed over her back. Stern dignity restrains her joy; her terror increases through modesty, and beauty, though unwilling, prevails through courage.

The fabric of her purple-colored robe was devoured by a clasp’s curved, biting tooth. Whatever her breast poured forth, the gem enclosed within its open recess.

[Col. 0659C] From here a gleaming boss supports her left side with its broad circle. Here you may see, cast in heavy metal, the caves of Rhea and the nursing she-wolf; with jaws exposed, even her gentleness was terrifying, although the pictured wolf does not fear to devour the sons of Mars.

[Col. 0660A] The nearest part represents the Tiber. Here, poured beneath rough tufa, he breathed his damp sleep through a greenish throat. A mantle covers her breast, woven by Ilia, the wife who, united in a flowing bed with the Tiber, desires to raise her murmurs with liquid waters and preserve the sleep of her wave-bearing husband.

These things gleam upon the shield. An ivory-shafted spear rises, drunken with the slaughter of men; beside it Bellona erects a trophy and bends an oak beneath the weight of captives.

The throne rises from stones cut from the red mountain of the Ethiopians, where native purple, beneath the nearby sun, has scorched the rocks with its breath. Here Sinnadian stone is joined; there Numidian stone is added, counterfeiting ancient ivory. Behind it, a radiant row of green Lacedaemonian marble shines.

[Col. 0660B] When she had thus placed herself at the center of the throne, the whole earth hastened together; then each province displayed its own products:

310 The Indian brings ivory, the Chaldaean amomum, the Assyrian gems, the Seres silk, the Sabaean frankincense; Attica honey, Phoenician palms, Lacedaemonian olives; [Note: [Col. 0660C] The printed editions read *Argos*, but the agreement of the ancient books persuades me that Sidonius wrote *Arcas*. Otherwise Argive horses would also be praised, just as Arcadian horses are. Strabo, Book VIII: “The Arcadian breed of horses is the strongest, as is also the Argolic.” Homer calls Argos “rich in horses”; Euripides calls it “horse-bearing Argos”; Horace, “Argos suited to horses.”] Arcadia horses, Epirus mares, Gaul cattle; Chalybes weapons, Libya grain, Campania Bacchus; Lydia gold, Arabia the drop, Panchaia myrrh; Pontus castoreum, Tyre purple dye, Corinth bronze.

Sardinia brings silver, Spain ships,

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The Ceraunian gem. Claudian, in praise of Serena:

“Beneath the caves of the Pyrenees

the Nymphs gather fiery ceraunian stones struck by lightning.”

Solinus, in chapter 36 of his *Polyhistor*, and Isidore, *Etymologies* XVI, say that they are found not on the Pyrenean peaks but in Lusitania. There are two kinds of ceraunian stones: one brought from Carmania, resembling crystal, but shining blue and, when placed in the open air, catching the brilliance of the stars; the other from the Lusitanian shores of Spain, whose color is close to red. Ruricius alludes to this in Book II, Letter 14, speaking of ceraunian stones: “So that, according to your name, you may shine like true ceraunian stones among that blessed company, and prove the source of your name.” The name derives from the fact that such stones are found nowhere except in places struck by *κεραυνός*, that is, lightning.]

and lightning’s stone. Lightning-throwing fire stains it, and the fertile anger of the gods mates with the kindled flint. Whenever the sky is stirred there, the earth is stronger there.

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The figure and speech of Africa, which also owes not a little to Claudian’s *Gildonics*. There Africa complains there that she was oppressed by Gildo; here, by Genseric, who, ruling the Vandals in Africa, held barbarian scepters, as Sidonius says, and was especially hostile to the noble and honored, as Prosper and Victor observe. Three years before this he had also captured Rome and stripped it of its wealth.]

Suddenly tearful Africa fell forward, her black cheeks torn, and bowed her forehead, having already broken upon her crown the ears that were scarcely fertile.

[Col. 0660C] Thus she began to speak:

“I come, the third part of the world, unhappy because of one happy man. Once born a servant here, this plunderer now holds barbarian scepters in my land, after destroying my masters long ago; and, driven mad by the expulsion of the nobility, the stranger loves nothing that is not himself.
