“O sleeping vigor of Latium, your wall laughs that it has yielded to his intrigues. Do you not shake your spear? Do you not grieve for me, even though I am captured? Surely your destiny is thought to rise through my misfortunes and your ruin to become higher.

“But the better course is the one by which terror departs: if you fight, it remains for you to conquer, as you have been accustomed to do after defeat.

[Note: [Col. 0661C] What once happened to Porsenna, Brennus, and Hannibal—that they were driven away by the Romans after the greatest disasters and terrors—she promises will now happen to Genseric if Majorian turns his arms against him. It is as though fate had ordained that he would come, as she says, to Libya’s destruction and would take from it a third name after the Scipios.]

“Porsenna, bringing proud Tarquin against us, once filled the Janiculum with Etruscan soldiers. But while he prepared to break through the gates by siege, you carried your whole burden upon the single shield of Cocles; many thousands pressed upon the man, while the roadway hung over the river. When the bridge collapsed, he did not fall with it.

311 “At last that same king, warned by the death of a secretary, learned that war could be made against him even when there was no war. Then, after peace had been sought, he returned to his kingdom—not so much driven out by the blow as by the man who blazed before him. For Scaevola had stood firm in his frozen heart and had condemned his right hand to the fire placed beneath it. He was more fortunate in his guilty hand: when the attendant grew pale before the steadfast accused and fled the tortures of the captive, he fled from the one who was to be his torturer.

“You trembled before Brennus, but afterward you were stronger. Whatever was yours, whatever you were called, was then alone Tarpeian; yet one man again drove back the entire army, while the noisy goose announced it and your destiny remained vigilant without soldiers.

“Forgive me also, since once we waged war: after Trebia and Cannae you subdued me. Hannibal saw Roman homes before my Scipio saw our own.

“What have I deserved? I am compelled by fate to make war upon you, whether I wish it or not. The trembling enemy terrifies you, but he is safe behind the enclosing strait, like a bristling boar lying near the high wilderness, shut in and raising its black snout, heavy with white tusks. A huge pack of dogs barks around it, if it should perhaps wish to run into the field.

“He swells and boasts through the intervening thorns, strong because of his slight strength and powerful because of his position, while the hunter nearby sounds from the hill. The familiar voice of the master restores the exhausted frenzy; then blind fury refuses to feel its wounds. Why do you delay the battle?

[Col. 0662A] “Why do you fear the sea, on whose behalf the sky itself often fights for triumphs? Why, when you now have an exceptional prince whom the prophetic ages proclaim destined to come for Libya’s destruction, one who will receive a third name from me?

312 “The fates owe this labor to you, Majorian. If you order me to tell in sequence why I should wish you to climb aboard the fleet, enter my harbors, and approach my city, I shall speak briefly.

“The city where Martian Acincus stands is said to possess Pannonia; your ancestor ruled Illyricum alone together with the regions of the Ister. When Theodosius took the name of Augustus at Sirmium, he had Majorian as master of both military commands, since he was about to come to the eastern parts of the empire.

[Note: [Col. 0661D] This is a city of Pannonia II, in which Sirmium was also the provincial capital. It is written *Acincus*, not *Acinthus*, likewise in Marcellinus, in the itineraries, and in the *Notitia*, where Acincian soldiers are also listed under the master of cavalry in Gaul. It is also certain that in the later centuries of the empire the name Illyricum was no longer restricted, as it once was, to the territory of a single province on the Adriatic coast, but extended to many surrounding provinces. This was the “greater Illyricum” of Ausonius’s epigram 1. In the time of Festus Rufus it embraced seventeen provinces; later, nineteen. After the division of the empire described in the *Notitia*—that is, after the time of Arcadius and Honorius—some of these were assigned to Western Illyricum, such as Noricum, the Pannonias, and Dalmatia; others to Eastern Illyricum, such as Upper Moesia, Dacia, Macedonia, Epirus, and others listed in the same *Notitia*. Sidonius therefore rightly places Pannonia in Illyricum. But Majorian’s power as master of the soldiers extended beyond the borders of Illyricum as well. The river Hypanis belongs to Scythia, and the island Peuce, adjoining the mouths of the Ister, belongs to the provinces of Lower Moesia, not to those of Illyricum. The authority of the masters of soldiers had not yet been divided by Theodosius; according to Zosimus, Book IV, he was the first to distinguish it in such a way that one master of soldiers was in Illyricum and another in Thrace, whereas previously one man had commanded all.]

“The deeds of the commander have been recorded in Roman annals: how often, when the trumpets of war were sounded against the Scythian settlers, the sutler mocked the freezing Hypanis and Peuce with its greeting of frost from the mountains.

[Col. 0662B] “His father-in-law is the father of this man, a distinguished husband, always content with a single summit of military office, so that in uncertain circumstances he might follow one friend joined to him. More than once Aetius’s court tried to take him away by offering him the fasces, but he remained with the more honorable man. Loyalty not captured by payment began to become more precious through payment.

“He was what he had once been as quaestor under the consuls: he administered the public treasury lawfully with his own resources and kept such restraint that rumor already said he spared his son’s possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] Aetius’s wife. The stories told of her hatred for the young Majorian are not invented without reason, as though she feared that he might attain the imperial power ahead of her son. In fact Aetius was preparing the empire for his son Gaudentius.]

“She had perceived this, but by chance the commander’s wife was already growing jealous. She saw the boy’s reputation increasing, and, steeped in bile, she cooked an inward poison through her barbarian heart.

[Col. 0662C] “At once she explores the sky, runs through the whole art of astrology in calculated figures, questions the shades, examines the lightning, and sees the entrails, rejoicing everywhere that she has snatched a secret from God. Thus the grim Colchian woman had stood at the prow of the Pelasgian ship while her husband trembled:

313 she was about to scatter Absyrtus before his father and commit a crime against her murdered brother greater than death, while fighting at the funeral and making weapons of her brother for herself; or when she, hotter than the flames themselves, overwhelmed the fire of the bulls and covered her trembling husband with a cold flame, whom, while the poison protected him, they say had grown cold among the blazing bulls.

[Note: [Col. 0661D] Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 1626, wants this written: “*Germani plus morte (nefas!)*”—“a crime against her brother greater than death,” since otherwise it would be strange to say *plus nefas facere* for “to commit a greater crime.” [Col. 0662D] —Baunius, Sirmond’s editor, preface to vol. I, § 11.]

“Thus, at last unable to contain herself, after hearing that imperial power had been established for him and for a long time, she tore her arms and entered the chamber where her husband lay stretched out, and broke forth against him in a raging voice:

“‘You lie secure, forgetful of your family, you lazy man, and prince of the world! Such are the demands of the ages: Majorian will be emperor. The stars proclaim it by their signs; men proclaim it by their prayers. Why, then, do I ask the stars about this man, for whom love has made another destiny? Nothing is stronger than he.

“‘The boy is never greedy for possessions, but sparing in acquiring them. Though still poor, he already scatters riches; he gives weighty counsel and follows it; everything he thinks is lofty. He presses forward toward what he hopes for.

“‘If I should perhaps reopen the contest, whatever you might suppose was accomplished by arrows, his single day accomplished. Three arrows made the serpent, the deer, and the boar tremble.’

[Note: [Col. 0663C] He mentions this again in poem 13, and an ancient distich on the same matter survives in Book IV of the epigrams, which Pithoeus conjectured to be by Sidonius himself:

“Deer, boar, and snake escaped your blows,

Majorian, not by running, tooth, or poison.”]

“Yet he did not launch his missiles against the enemy in the same way as Alcon,

[Col. 0663C] who, when a serpent’s body was wrapped around his son, was more afraid while coming to his aid. With those same shots he had to give death and life, keeping his hand steady in a trembling heart and bringing his whole skill to its completion as fear drew nearer to hope; he gave death to one among the two bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0663C] This is Alcon of Crete, about whom Manilius also speaks, together with his son Phalerus, in Book V of the *Astronomicon*, and Valerius Flaccus in Book I of the *Argonautica*. The Greek poet in Book VI, epigram 11, is no less elegant:

“Father Alcon, seeing his child bound by a deadly serpent,

         bent his bow in his fearful hand.

He did not miss the beast, for through its mouth the arrow

         passed just above the infant.

After ending the slaughter, beside this oak he hung

         his quiver, a memorial of success and good aim.”]

“Let him choose a contest with the boxing glove: Sicilian Eryx yielded, nor did Sparta display comparable skill when Amycus, stretched out upon the Bebrycian sands, beheld the fat-bodied boxer of Therapnae.

314 [Note: [Col. 0663D] The printed editions understand this in the opposite sense, reading “Amycus stretched out.” Amycus is the man who admired the strength of Pollux, the Therapnaean or Lacedaemonian boxer, after being struck down by him, although he used to defeat all the others.]

“What strength he has in his feet! In vain did Opheltes yield to him the Sicilian prize and his proud feet; not so swiftly did the Arcadian son of Atalanta raise himself through dry Nemea,

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Parthenopaeus, the son of Atalanta by Milanion. Statius also calls him an Arcadian and makes him victorious in the race at Nemea in Book VI of the *Thebaid*. Apollodorus, in Book III, listing the leaders in the Theban war, writes: “Parthenopaeus, son of Milanion, an Arcadian”; and again: “Atalanta bore Parthenopaeus from Milanion, and he joined the expedition against Thebes.”]

whose mother Hippomenes feared as she flew through the dust of the Aetolian [Note: [Col. 0664C] Atalanta. Earlier editions read *Martem* (“Mars”), which makes no sense. The emendation is therefore certain and necessary, although it depends only on one manuscript and another, neither of them among the best. He mentions the mother on the occasion of her son, just as Statius does in the same passage:

“Who does not know the renowned glory in the race

of Maenalian Atalanta, and her footprints

that no suitor could overtake?”] racecourse.

[Col. 0663C] He had been sent ahead in contempt, when the swift heroine sprang from the prison’s cavern before the trembling crowd, touching nothing in her entire stride. Pale, he looked back and saw the field shrinking behind him; pressed by the wind at his back, already he ran anxiously beneath the hostile shadow.

[Col. 0664A] At last, when he was nearly left behind at the turning-post, she broke her speed three times by scattering the apples.

Whoever sees this horseman despises the son of Leda, and your young man, Stheneboea, to whom antiquity grants the back of a winged horse and who is said to have overcome the Lycian Chimaera, though one wound bore away three lives. If fate had then given you life, fierce Majorian, you would have forbidden Castor to know bridles, Pollux to know boxing gloves, Alcon to know arrows, and you would have mocked the exploits of Bellerophon.

If he takes up a shield, he surpasses the son of Telamon, who among the Greek ships defended even Ulysses’ treacherous fleet against Hector’s fire.

If you ask with what weight he hurls a missile, Metabus, trembling for Camilla bound as a bundle to the spear, hurled his weapon less powerfully,

[Col. 0664B] nor did the whistling ash of the son of Peleus pass through Troilus with so great a whirl.

315 Nor did the Athenian son of Aegeus break with a Marathonian oak the funeral pyres that delayed Creon so forcefully; nor did the avenging thunderbolt for Phoebus’s violated daughter strike the Danaans so forcefully, when Greece kept the night of Troy and, fixed on the rocks of Caphareus amid the waters, Oileus belched forth flame like a torch.

“I speak of small things. What of the fact that whenever wars are waged for you, the pupil appears not as a soldier but as a teacher, and shapes his disciple while watching as a rival from the opposite side? He hates what you have conquered and loves those whom you conquer. In his presence the great Alexander is wholly asleep—the Alexander tormented by his father’s glory.

“What shall I do, unhappy mother? What kingdoms shall I prepare for my son if the commonwealth passes me by, excluded from the Gothic scepters, and if Gaudentius, small as he is in this matter,

[Col. 0664C] is crushed by fate? Gaul already praises him, and whatever there is throughout Europe. He bathes him in its rigid waters—”

Rhine, Arar, Rhône, Meuse, Marne, Seine, Ledus,

[Col. 0664D] In this catalogue of the rivers of Gaul which he says Majorian surveyed on his campaigns, few are not immediately recognizable. For Elaris is unquestionably our Elaver, well known from Caesar’s *Commentaries*, which flows across the plains of the Arverni, receives several tributaries on either side, and empties into the Loire somewhat below Nevers. Ledus, in Septimania, flows from the Cévennes through the territory of the Volcae Arecomici and past Montpellier into the Gallic sea. There is a single controversy concerning Clitis: most agree with Papirius Masson, who demonstrated that it is the Clain of the Pictones. The *Olitis* of Theodulf of Orléans, which others have preferred, cannot be admitted into this passage unless the verse has been corrupted.

[Col. 0665A] Clitis, Elaris, Atax, Vachalis, and the Loire, which, cut down by the axe, drinks in fragments; while, [Note: I suppose they feared the neighboring Armoricans, who had long aspired to freedom, as is clear from Zosimus, Book VI, and either themselves attacked the Romans with arms or were attacked by them: as when Litorius, with Aetius absent and the Huns assisting, waged war against them, as the panegyric of Avitus records, in about the year 438, as we shall show.] fearing war,

you defended the Turoni, though you were absent. A short time afterward

you fought together, where the Frank, [Note: One manuscript reads this; it certainly seems more suitable than what appears in others: “You fought together against the Franks, where Cloio.” Almost everyone refers this Frankish war, in which Aetius and Majorian fought against King Clodio, to the consulship of Felix and Taurus, in the year 427, since Prosper and Cassiodorus report that in that year the part of Gaul near the Rhine which the Franks had occupied was recovered by the arms of the general Aetius. But how could Majorian have been present then and fought so fiercely, when thirty years later, in his own consulship, he was still a young man? Moreover, the earlier expedition was to the Rhine, whereas this one was against the Atrebates and the village of Helena, whose remains still survive in the Atrebatian district beside the river Caucium, for they call it Old Hedin. It is therefore more certain that these events occurred after the year 445, when, as our annals relate with Gregory and Sigebert, Clodio, having come out of the territories of the Thuringi, after crushing the Romans who were on this side of the Rhine, entered the Carbonarian Forest and soon occupied the cities of Tournai and Cambrai, as well as everything else as far as the river Somme. Those cities are plainly close to the lands of the Atrebates. I therefore conjecture that, when the Franks later invaded these regions also, they were checked by Aetius and driven back by the victory praised here by Sidonius.] was spreading through the open lands of the Atrebates:

here, meeting them, you closed the narrow roads, and by the bow subdued

the village of Helena; at the same time, along the long embankment,

a causeway, strengthened with beams laid beneath it, carried the river across.

There, with you stationed upon it, Majorian the horseman fought

beneath the bridge itself. Perhaps upon the neighboring hill

the barbarian wedding song resounded, and, amid Scythian dances,

a new bride, like her yellow-haired husband, was being wed.

316 These men, then, as they say, he struck down. Helmets rang

beneath the blows, and breastplates with their opposing scales

warded off the smiting of spears, until the enemy, routed and turning,

gave his back. You might have seen the waters glittering with the wagons

of that barbarian bridal bed, the dishes flung everywhere,

the captured banquets, and cauldrons crowned with garlands,

fragrant with wet foliage.

At once Mars grows stronger, and Bellona, more ardent,

breaks the torches of the bridal chamber. The victor seizes the wagons

and the bride, not as the Semelean Evan once mingled

the Pholoetian monsters with the Pelethronian Lapiths,

while the women of Haemon set the revels ablaze,

rousing Venus and Mars, consuming the first bloody food

for war, and, as Bacchus’ cup revolved, imagining

that their cups were weapons—until, as the tumult grew savage,

Centaur blood stained Mount Othrys in Thessaly.

[Col. 0665C] Nor should the quarrels of the cloud-born brothers be celebrated more highly.

[Col. 0666A] Here too he subdues monsters, [Note: A vivid description of the ancient Franks: he follows not only their facial appearance and entire dress—tall bodies, reddish hair, gray-blue eyes, hair drawn forward over the forehead while the back of the head is shaved, thin beards on the shaven face, tight garments defining each limb, bare knees, and broad belts—but also their characteristic weapons, their manner of fighting, and their spirits unbroken by war. Agathias, Book II, attributes the same kinds of weapons to the Franks, namely axes and short spears, which they called *anconae*. The axes themselves were called *franciscae* from their use among that people, as Isidore notes, and as the Gallic annals show in their account of Clovis. Julian the emperor also asserts the military valor of the Franks, making the Franks and Saxons the most warlike of the Germans in his encomium of Constantius, where he speaks of Magnentius, in whose camp both peoples served: “They followed him as allies, eagerly joining him because of their kinship—the Franks and Saxons, the most warlike of the peoples beyond the Rhine and the western sea.”]

whose reddish hair, drawn from the crown of the head,

lies over the forehead, while the bared neck

shines through the loss of its bristles. Then their watery gray gaze gleams white,

their faces are everywhere shaven, and instead of a beard

thin ridges are combed out with a comb.

Their tightly sewn garments confine the tall limbs of the men;

with their tunics raised, their knees are exposed,

and a broad belt hangs over their narrow waists.

To hurl swift double-edged axes through the vast air,

to anticipate the place of the blow, to whirl their shields,

to outstrip their spinning spears with leaps,

and to reach the enemy first—this is their sport.

In childhood they are mature in their love of war; if by chance

they are pressed either by numbers or by the difficulty of the ground,

317 death overwhelms them, but not fear. Unconquered, they persist,

and even when almost beyond life they survive in spirit.

Such men, with you as witness and praising them, he put to flight.

Who could endure it? Everything accomplishes all things with you,

and accomplishes much without you. Many fight for the prince;

I fear that now this man fights for himself. If he holds the kingdoms,

you conquer for him whatever you subdue. Fate leaves no middle course here:

for if you refuse to be the executioner, you will be a slave.

Certainly, if the Chaldaean preserves the stars upon a straight course,

if the Colchian knows the herbs, if the Tuscan understands lightning,

if the Thessalian draws forth shadows, if the Lycian lots speak truth,

if our birds utter our fate in flight, if Ammon

groans out the sacred answer beneath the sand,

if Phoebus, Themis, and Dodona sing the truth,

then, after our time, this Julius will be Augustus.

Moreover, he is joined in affection to the great young man

[Col. 0666C] who is armed by [Note: Ricimer’s; Vallia’s, as was said in the poem to Anthemius, the grandson through his daughter of the Gothic king.] the spirit of his royal grandfather.

[Col. 0667A] Where will you turn? This man bears fate toward the heights of the world.

Both possess courage: rise up, and attack them while they are unaware.

You will not be able to kill either of them, even if you order both to die;

but weave deceitful flatteries around one, while the other must be attacked

with the sword.

Why do I speak in vain? There is nothing against which we take such great precautions:

he will reign; he will be victorious. Aetius, stirred to anger, [Note: Aetius, whose killing his wife was urging, was satisfied merely to deprive Majorian of his military command and send him home. Thus, after Aetius’ death, Valentinian summoned him to court. What had been prepared for his destruction therefore became the means of his safety.] replies briefly:

“Restrain the impious desires of your raging heart.

Shall I order the death of an innocent man, while saying nothing of our own?

Can anyone pray that it be considered a crime to have been well born, though guiltless?

Who would summon fate to punishment? Shall I attack your very being

with the sword, Majorian? If Phoebus shines by night,

if the moon shines by day, if the twin wagon of Parrhasis

318 is renewed upon the sea, if the Tanais sees Atlas,

if the Bagrada sees the Caucasus, if a boat woven from the trunks

of the Hercynian forest plows the Nabataean Hydaspes instead of the Rhine,

if the Spaniard drinks the Ganges, and the Indian water-bearer

comes from the warm Erythraean waters to the Tartessian Ebro;

if Castor bathes himself in the blood of Pollux;

if Theseus overthrew Pirithous, or Orestes felled Pylades,

or if the pious matricide seized the Tauric rites

with his frenzied hand—then perhaps I might do this.

But lest I seem to have despised your grief,

let him live, and for a little while be deprived of military service.

Alas! he could have owed us his fortune, unless you had thought it grievous.”

Thus he spoke, and ordered him to exchange his accustomed labors

in the countryside for other work, while the wheel of fate was turning,

so that he might learn in the fields what awaits a landowner,

what manner of conduct civil law requires, lest he bring to empire

only the art of the soldier.

At once the retired young man hung up his weapons,

fertilizing the sterile fasts of the earth with the plowshare.

Thus once, when you were consul with the curved fasces,

you turned the fields, if you had relaxed the trumpets for a little peace;

your strong left hand guided the plow after the standards,

while the palm-bearing hand of the victorious ox-driver,

joined to the humble hearth, drank in the smoke.

[Note: Aetius was killed by Valentinian in 454, and in the following year Valentinian himself was killed by men close to Aetius. Majorian, therefore, could already have reigned. But it was a benefit that his accession was delayed, lest Rome be captured by the Vandals during his reign. It was also to his glory that Majorian restored the empire before he assumed it. For most Caesars seize a throne left to them by others; he, in a sense, created a new one after many disasters, as Vespasian once had done.] Meanwhile Aetius had met his lamentable fate by the sword

of the prince. To join him more safely

to the great ranks of the Palatine troops,

he summons him by entreaties; but the punishment of shed blood

does not delay itself. He had gathered the number of the people,

[Col. 0668A] not their spirit. He paid the evil crimes of steel with steel,

319 and that man fell more heavily upon our ruin.

Already at that time the golden Fates were spinning

the good fortune of the present prince’s empire;

but public disasters avoided the man’s reproach. Whoever

was chosen for the name of Augustus held the throne

left behind by the Caesars. After you, captive, struggled,

this man made what he possesses.

Nerva called Trajan when he was already a victorious pledge;

he was Germanicus in title because he had been so in merit.

The course proceeds in order, and whoever begins in this way

courts this reputation. Once, after Tiberius’ Capri,

after the shameful divinities of Caius, the censorship of Claudius,

and Nero’s lyre and bridal chambers, after the monstrous spectacle

of the mirror in which that ugly man saw himself as beautiful,

after Otho, beautiful because Vitellius was ugly,

after Vitellius’ five thousand, condemned to the abyss

of his notorious belly—Vespasian too was chosen prince

with these titles and for a similar task.

[Note: Genseric: he denies that Genseric is any longer greatly to be feared, since, luxurious with his people, like Hannibal at Capua, already broken and enervated, he relies only upon the valor of the African soldiers. This is what Africa complains of: that her own vitals are being armed against her, and that she gives birth to those whom she must endure. Others have understood the passage differently, referring it to the treachery of Boniface and to Genseric’s sons, whose yoke Africa would one day have to bear. But the peoples of Libya enumerated below show whom he means.] But do not suppose perhaps that I am confined

by the strength of a brigand: his national power

has consumed itself in him—the corruption of life has destroyed it.

Scythian savagery is held not by strength but by desires.

Having gained immense spoils, he has already lost all the vigor

by which he prevailed when poor. He now arms his own vitals

against me, for his own sake. I have been torn apart for so many years,

captured by his right and by my own valor; fertile in punishments, I give birth to those

whom I suffer.

He accomplishes nothing with his own arms, but is feared by Gaetuli,

Numidians, Garamantes, Autololes, Arzuges, Marmaridae,

Psylli, and Nasamones.

[Note: Orosius says that the region of the Arzuges was the same as the province of Tripolitania, in which Leptis Magna lies: “Although,” he says, “the Arzuges are generally so called along the whole length of Africa.” I think this is more accurate, since I see that the Arzuges are always distinguished from the Tripolitanians, as in the African synod, canons 16 and 19, and by Augustine in Letter 48, who says that they lived farther inland toward the south—that is, on the very frontier of Africa. Publicola writes to Augustine in Letter 153: “Among the Arzuges, as I have heard, the barbarians customarily swear allegiance to the decurion who is in charge of the frontier, or to the tribune, swearing by their demons, who have agreed to lead the baggage trains.” In a letter of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, against Caelestius and Pelagius, the province is called Azuritana, evidently for Arzugitana.] He is sluggish and, amid great gold,

no longer knows the sword.

His own complexion is bloodless, troubled by drunkenness,

and pallid fatness holds him; pressed down by perpetual gluttony,

320 his stomach cannot release its souring breath.

His people’s life is the same. Not so did the wealthy Barcian

Hannibal perish at Capua, when the strong bodies

which had been formidable in war were softened by the delights of Baiae,

and the Massylian swimmer flung his dark arms

where Gaurus slopes toward the Lucrine waters.

Therefore, after so many ages, give me this master

as my avenger, I pray, so that Carthage may no longer fight

against Italy.” Thus she groaned, overcome by grief,

and strengthened her prayers with rising tears.

[Note: Rome answers Africa’s prayers by promising that Majorian will come to liberate her, but says that he must first visit Gaul, which, for sixty-six years after the death of the younger Valentinian, had seen no legitimate prince. Here he silently accuses Honorius and Placidia Valentinian of negligence: enclosed almost within the walls of Ravenna, they allowed the barbarians to tear the provinces apart, while one needed advisers because of his inactivity and the other because of his age.] Rome answered her thus: “Bind up your long lamentations,

[Col. 0669A] devoted one, for Majorian will be your avenger

in the name of the gods. But I shall briefly unfold a few matters.

[Note: As above, and Claudian frequently, for metrical reasons. An old inscription at Constantinople above the Golden Gate reads:

‘These places Theodosius adorns after the tyrant’s death.

He bears golden ages, who builds the gate in gold.’

Gratian was Theodosius’ *auctor*—his patron and source of imperial authority—since Theodosius had received the empire from him; Valentinian was that *auctor*’s brother. Arbogast, who cut Valentinian’s throat, later killed himself when he was defeated by Theodosius together with the tyrant Eugenius, about seven years after Valentinian, driven from the empire by Maximus, had been restored through Theodosius. Thus men are called *auctores* who have been as parents to others, either by descent or by wealth and honor. Spartianus calls Trajan Hadrian’s *auctor*; in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXI, the Senate calls Constantius Julian’s *auctor*, since they had been raised to imperial power through them. Sidonius himself calls his grandfather Apollinaris his *auctor* in the letter containing his epitaph. An earlier panegyrist does the same in Maximian’s *Genethliacum*: “And likewise, Maximian, your Hercules was your *auctor* when he was among men, having pacified all lands and monsters.” This is how the passage should be read. He makes Hercules Maximian’s *auctor*, just as shortly before he makes Jupiter Diocletian’s, because they wished to appear descended from them. Finally, when Symmachus in Book X, Letters 22 and 57, mentions Theodosius’ *auctor*, he means his father, Count Theodosius, whom he calls the African and British commander because of the military laurels he brought back from both peoples. But here Theodosius is the *auctor* by descent, Gratian that of his empire.] From the time when Theodosius, after defeating the tyrant,

restored the common laws to the *auctor*’s brother, whose throat

the hand that would later turn against itself cut,

my Gaul has still been unknown to its masters of affairs,

and, ignorant, serves. From that time much has perished,

because, when the prince was shut away, whatever there was

of the wretched world in its various regions was accustomed

to be ravaged. What kind of life could have pleased anyone

when a ruler had to be governed? For so many years

nobility lay despised; the commonwealth repaid

its strong man with hatred.

Our prince corrects all these things. Adding strength

from the nations, he comes to war through wars;

for the greatest labor is to march there, not to fight.

Why waste time in words? He arrives, and he conquers.”

When this council had ended in such speech,

and the bronze had served the goddess’s words,

the golden sisters drew their concordant threads.

These labors of Rome and Libya, which I have sung,

321 taught human prayers to speak. Now it is time

to turn my step to those matters which must be spoken,

or for which, with Apollo silent, your Mars will serve as my Muse.

He had climbed the Alps, and the savage Alamannian,

led along the ridge of the Rhaeti through long silences,

had emerged after ravaging Roman territory,

[Note: The Campi Canini lay in that part of Raetia bordering Liguria. Marcellinus, Book XV, also indicates their location: “The emperor went out for that expedition and came to Raetia and the Campi Canini.” To remove all doubt, there is Bilitio, an ancient fortress situated in these fields and still well known today. Gregory, *History* X.III: “The duke Olo, approaching the fortress of Bilitio, situated in the Campi Canini, too boldly, was wounded by a spear, fell, and died.”] and through the fields once called Cani from their name

had sent nine hundred of the enemy out for plunder.

You were already commander, and you sent Burco there

with a small accompanying force; but that was enough

when you ordered them to fight. Victory is assured for our men:

fortune carries out a triumph because you commanded the battle,

not because of the army’s numbers but because of your favor.

I do not object that you send only a few troops into the field;

this fortunate outcome of the war looks to you:

the battle was fought under the authority of the commander,

under the destiny of Augustus.

[Note: Majorian’s second victory was over the Vandals and Moors, whom, after they had been transported from Africa to Campania, Majorian, already emperor, not only stripped of the booty they had gathered but also crushed with a severe defeat and drove into flight. He describes the site of the battle in such a way that the plain of the Sinuessan district is clearly indicated: it extends from the mouths of the Liris to the Volturnus, bounded on one side by the sea and on the other by the ridge of Mount Massicus. He calls the Moors captives because they had been subdued by the Vandals, and cleverly says that the booty they were carrying was “captured by a captor”; shortly afterward he says that they themselves became booty, when, driven from the forces of Majorian and prevented from reaching their ships, they were captured by the Campanians whom they had captured.] Recently, after the enemy had opened

the sea, he wandered slowly across it; at the same time,

the whole ordered sequence had granted you the kingdom:

people, senate, soldiers, and your colleague alike.

Entering Campania with the south winds blowing,

the Vandal, secure in his Moorish troops,

attacks the farmer. The stout Vandal sat among the benches,

waiting for the booty which he had ordered to be brought there

by a captive carrying off captives. But suddenly your ranks

had placed themselves between the two enemies on the plains

which cut across sea and hill and, by the river’s retreating bend,

make a harbor. At first the terrified crowd sought the mountains,

[Col. 0670B] and, shut out from the ships left behind, became booty—the booty of the booty;

then, rushing forward with the whole force, the pirate gathered

for battle. Some, from hollowed boats, unload their already trained horses;

some put on iron armor of the same color;

others unroll their polished bows,

322 and arrows carrying poison infused into the metal,

which, shot once, strike twice. [Note: Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 1 *Against Julian*: “All manner of serpent-emblems, breathing through dreadful gaping mouths, suspended from the tips of spears and driven by the wind through their coils, flutter in woven folds patterned with scales—a sight at once most pleasing and terrifying to the eyes.”] Then a woven serpent

runs through both lines. Its throat swells with the winds forced into it;

through its open jaws the painted image imitates

an angry hunger, and the air gives it fury whenever

its flexible back grows dense with wind

and its belly can no longer contain the air within.

But the trumpet blared with a terrible, harsh roar;

the shout answered the clarions, and suddenly courage

raged even in the cowardly or the weak. Iron fell everywhere.

[Col. 0671A] [Note: On Majorian’s side. Weapons were thrown from both sides, he says, but those from this side sought the throats and inflicted deadly blows, whereas the weapons of the Vandals did not.]

From this side, however, they struck at the throats. A twisted fire-spear

flies past one man, scarcely failing to bring a second death;

the stroke of a spear makes one spin; another falls, pierced by an *aclis* through his horse;

a third by a javelin; this man lies beneath a winged missile,

having lost his right hand though it is far from him;

one lives, though his knee has been severed, to the resentment of death;

another carries away part of his brain with part of his helmet,

and with a strong arm splits his pitiful skull

with a two-edged sword.

As soon as the Vandal turns his back with his weapons reversed,

slaughter follows, with no distinction between battle and flight.

They are strewn across the fields, and in trembling flight

every coward performs brave deeds. Pale, the horseman enters

the sea and rides through the ships; then, swimming shamefully,

he returns from the open water to a boat.

So once was Pyrrhus’ third battle, when Dentatus

pressed him with thousands slain. The shattered remnants

of his fleet scarcely carried him back to Epirus,

after he had scattered Chaonians, Molossians,

and the forces of the Thracians and Macedonians

along our shores, and after pale Italy,

and Tarentum itself, which he had attacked,

had trembled in fear.

323 With the enemies driven out, there is leisure now to survey

the great field that stretches before us. Here, beneath that slaughter,

you may see the courage of both sides: every one of yours

has been struck in the chest; every one of theirs

has been pierced in the back. The wounds of the first

[Note: Sersaon, as Savaro conjectured from Victor of Vita, who calls him a kinsman of King Genseric.] brigand commander proclaim this—

he is said to have married the sister of the avaricious king.

Shut in by blinding dust and crushed beneath spears,

he still bears the disgraceful traces of his shameful flight.

Thus your troops retain the field with its spoils

and rejoice in Mars.

[Col. 0671C] [Note: On Majorian’s preparations for the fleet to Africa, which Sidonius extols so highly that he does not hesitate to compare it with the naval forces of Agamemnon, Xerxes, Antony, and Cleopatra, Procopius, Idatius, and Cassiodorus write. Procopius expressly testifies that the army was enormous. Yet so great an undertaking had an unsuccessful outcome, because the Vandals, warned by traitors, plundered the ships in the ports of Spain before they could put to sea. Thus Majorian’s hope of a Vandalic war was frustrated. It was not, however, frustrated in every respect, because, according to Idatius, Genseric later sought and obtained peace from him.] Meanwhile, while you build a fleet on the twin shores,

on the inland and the open sea, all the forest falls

into the water for you. The Apennine slopes,

cut down too long on both sides and rich in naval timber,

send into the sea no less of their forests

than you send water. Although Gaul is worn out

by continuous taxes, she wants to show that she has pleased

by this contribution and does not feel the burden,

because she proves that it is useful.

[Col. 0672A] Not with so many ships did the elder son of Atreus

cover the Carpathian Sea when the Dorian enemy,

about to carry off the wealth of the Troad,

closed the Rhoetean Pergamum with his fleet.

Nor was Xerxes’ fleet so large when he joined Sestos

to Abydos, laid the swollen waters flat,

placed the sea beneath a bridge, and invaded the pools

with arrogant and sacrilegious steps, while crowded troops

leaped across the depths of the Hellespont.

Nor did the Mareotic fleet at Leucas conceal the Actian waters

so completely when, from Egyptian Canopus,

the dowry-bearing crowd came to the husband’s war,

while fierce Cleopatra, surrounded by her ancestral sistrum,

loaded her gilded ships with dark-skinned soldiers

and pressed upon the spread waters of the Doric sea

the wealth of Ptolemy.

324 You do not fight with that splendor, but in the manner of your ancestors,

[Col. 0672B] richer in iron, to which the gold of the wealthy coward

must submit. Do not despise such rebels:

even if they do not adorn the battle line, they nevertheless adorn

the triumphs.

Nor shall I regret recalling the Lagid line

as an example of your enemy; for I foresee

[Note: Roman and African. Sidonius hoped that what had happened after the battle of Actium to Cleopatra and her kingdom would now happen in the same way to Genseric: that once he had been defeated and killed, Africa would come under Majorian’s power. The struggle, after all, is between the same kingdoms, Romans and Africans; Genseric’s luxury equals Cleopatra’s, and Majorian’s valor is no less than Augustus’.] a similar fortune for the same kingdoms,

since luxury is equal on that side,

and the Caesar on this side is no worse.

[Note: What he expressed obscurely above—“adding strength from the nations”—he now explains by enumerating the barbarian peoples under Majorian’s standards. The Bastarnae lived above Dacia, not far from the Roxolani, with whom they are associated in Aelian’s inscription at Tivoli and likewise in Capitolinus’ account of Marcus. Vopiscus and Zosimus, Book I, report that Probus transferred a colony of one hundred thousand of them to Thrace, onto Roman soil. Above them lived the Neuri, famous for the source of the Borysthenes and their legendary transformation into wolves. Licentius writes in a poem to Augustine: “In summer you will pursue the Neuri, in winter the Ister.” The Alites seem to be those whom Pliny calls the Alutae in Illyricum. Bellonoti are also counted among Attila’s forces in the panegyric of Avitus. Valerius Flaccus has Ballonoti in Book VI, where the Bisaltae, peoples of Scythia, are also placed above the Heniochi. Procustes was the name, or rather the surname, of an Attic robber, derived from his deed, as Diodorus relates in Book V of his *Ancient History*. Sidonius makes it the name of a people.] At once you undertake what no Augustus in our time

could have done: you seize for war the host of the sevenfold Ister.

Whatever the sluggish Bear beneath the Sithonian hinge

brings forth under the Parrhasian axis,

all of it fears your standards: Bastarna, Suevian,

Pannonian, Neurus, Hun, Geta, Dacian, Alan,

Bellonotus, Rugian, Burgundian, Vesus, Alite,

Bisalta, Ostrogoth, Procustes, Sarmatian, Moschian—

[Col. 0672C] all came behind your standards. All the Caucasus serves you,

and the drinker of Scythian waters, the Tanais.

What can fortune do to such a man? Whatever hands she threatens,

Rome has already trembled at them. Now, under you as prince,

let her not fear; she thinks almost insignificant, unless she serves him,

what she feared when another ruled.

You were already moving the camp, and thousands under various standards

were enclosing you.

[Note: The Huns, I think, whom he designates by three characteristics: that they came from the Ister, that they were returning to Italy, and that they lacked masters through war. All these things fit the Huns, who had come into Italy with Attila a few years earlier and, after Attila’s death, when all his sons wished to rule, lost the empire together in the quarrel among them. Driven from Pannonia by the Gepids, they settled near the shore of the Pontic Sea at the mouths of the Ister, as Jordanes relates in his *Getica*. He therefore says that the sedition of the rebels, suppressed by their slaughter, was unlike the mutiny that occurred in Caesar’s camp and is described by Lucan in Book V of the *Pharsalia*, because Caesar’s soldiers were Romans, whose destruction weakened his forces; this was a barbarian force, whose punishment was useful for intimidating the army because they refused obedience. Thus, although the Huns served in Majorian’s army, he does not call them soldiers, since properly speaking soldiers are Romans and are distinguished from barbarian auxiliaries and federates, as in Valentinian’s Novel on the restoration of military rights: “The general Sigisvultus must continue to arrange the protection of cities and coasts by both soldiers and federates”; and as Sidonius himself frequently does in his letters.] One people refuses obedience—the people that recently

brought back from the Ister a column more savage than usual,

which, lacking masters through war, offers its indomitable rage

to Tuldila for punishment in battle.

You, scarcely having laid down your arms, take up arms again.

As when the daughters of Biston and the followers of the Cicones

happen to fill the snows with Ogygian revels,

whether in the fields of the Strymon,

whether across Rhodope, or wherever rainy Ismarus

rolls the Hebrus into the sea from Hyperborean cliffs,

the wandering crowd gives itself to sleep; the revels,

worn out, rest together, nor does the double flute resound with its twofold breath.

Hardly any rest: already they bind the bridge;

the inspired Bassarid whirls the thyrsus,

horrible in the spotted skin of the Erythraean fawn,

and rouses the Odrysian mystics to their withered drums.

Yet you delay this punishment, though you were the author

of the greater bloodshed while sparing them. The more cautious hand

could endure this no longer for your sake and despised your shame

on your behalf. The first victim of the war falls:

everyone who was a rebel. You also divide the booty among those

whose loyalty had been devoted to you, who now serve in terror

and, instructed by the example, rejoice in the reward.

When Caesar was making for the Pharsalian fields,

he checked sudden anger with the sword.

But, cutting into his own limbs and compelled by the magnitude

of his cause, he wept for those whom he killed.

This mutiny benefits your arms: whatever you order,

unless a barbarian obeys, he falls, so that the soldier may fear.

[Note: From this it can be understood what we stated at the beginning: Majorian came to Gaul when his consulship was already nearing its end. His Novels make clear that he did not leave Ravenna before the Ides of November. The speech that follows, in which a Scythian soldier complains about the harsh frost near Mount Cinisii—for this is the subject—whether it is an actual event or invented for Majorian’s praise, is intended to display in him an outstanding natural capacity for imperial valor. He is therefore compared with Attila, whom he calls the northern king, and with other ancient Scythian leaders, hardened against cold and hardship. But Majorian, laughing at the delicately raised barbarian’s cowardice, predicts the summer heat of the Syrtes toward which he was heading after the winter frosts of the Alps—that is, extreme heat after extreme cold.] Already in winter you first climb

the marble Alps, the rocks that meet the joined heavens,

the cliffs of glass, threatening dry rain

through their crags. You secure your slippery steps

with a staff placed ahead of you.

You had reached the middle of the cliff, where the greatest mass

[Col. 0673C] was made rough with inward frost, which, enclosed

by the steep ridge and narrowing the roads, could not crawl

across the frozen ground as it rolled downward.

Perhaps one man from that column, whose wheel had worn smooth

the hoary Ister, cried out:

“I prefer swords, and the customary rest

326 that comes from death, to this cold. Torpor binds my limbs

with inert rigidity. My body, scorched by a kind of fire of frost,

is dying. We follow without end a young man

who presses on toward toil. Whoever he is, the strongest of men,

whether king or people, now shut within the camp,

lies in the sunshine or beneath a hide.

We are turning the use of the seasons upside down.

Whatever he orders will be law for circumstances;

he is never bent by what he has undertaken,

and considers it a loss if he fears the anger of the season

even through hardship. From what people do I say he was born,

since I, a Scythian, cannot endure him?

What infant drank the milk of a tigress beneath a Hyrcanian cliff?

What land, heavier than my own, raised this man?

Look! On the highest summit he compels freezing troops

and laughs at the cold, while he alone burns hotter in mind.

When I followed the trumpets of the northern king

and the arms of the Roman prince, I had heard

that the Caesarean household was sluggish in perpetual luxury.

It is useless for former masters to have gone before,

if this king too was strong. …”

He was preparing to say more, but you inflame him

with bitter words from the rock:

[Col. 0674B] “Whoever you are, you who fear the slippery slope before you,

break the skin of the hanging water, [Note: Savaro and Labbe read: “and, with the flowing water cut away by a chisel.”] and let the water,

made passable by your chisel, be a step for you.

Put away your shameful complaints. Idleness has cold in it.

Did nature give me the twofold limbs of Hylaeus?

Did Pegasus help me with wings in whatever I tread?

Do Calais and Zetes give me feathers for flight,

whom you see now treading the snowy backs of the ridge?

It is you whom the cold breaks, you whom the Alps break.

Now I shall strive to balance the frost:

I shall bring summer beneath the Syrtes.”

Thus you lift the army with your voice

and lighten it by your example; first you undertake

327 whatever labors you order, and then the rest of the crowd

obeys willingly, since the commander serves under his own laws.

[Note: To the praises of the prince he adds the praises of three companions: the master of the soldiers, the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, and Peter, master of the letters. He names only Peter; the identities of the others must be conjectured. As for the master of the soldiers, one may ask whether he means Ricimer, whom Majorian’s Novels show to have been master of the soldiers in Italy, or Nepotianus, who, according to our Idatius, is also said to have been master of the soldiers in Gaul in this same year.] What companions you had besides, and what a commander

of the army followed your ranks behind you,

[Col. 0674C] though not unwillingly—one before whom Sulla might yield in battle array,

Fabius in genius, Metellus in devotion,

Appius in eloquence, Fulvius in strength,

Camillus in skill.

[Note: Those who think that Basil is meant as the prefect of the praetorium fail to notice that Basil was prefect of Italy, whereas this passage concerns the prefect of Gaul. A more certain conjecture may perhaps be Magnius of Narbonne, whose completed prefecture Sidonius mentions in Book I, Letter 11, at Majorian’s banquet—that is, three years after this panegyric. The Gothic king who respected this prefect was the younger Theodoric, about whom there is a letter in Book II.] If you ask what man directs

the honor of the prefecture, he is a man whose authority

extends wherever Gaul spreads its open boundaries.

Scarcely anyone had similar qualities; with the senate as witness,

Ulpius had even entrusted to him the sword drawn against himself.

He who now dictates laws to the Goths, under your jurisdiction,

receives the fur-clad enemy’s sallow court-herald.

[Col. 0675A] Why should I speak here of the man [Note: Sidonius’ high opinion of Peter, Majorian’s master of the letters, is shown by the edition of the panegyric and by Book IX, Letter 13. The “sacred scrinia” are the prince’s archives; in our glossaries: *σκρινιάριοι, οἱ χαρτοφύλακες τῶν βασιλικῶν χαρτίων*, “the keepers of the imperial documents.” Symmachus calls them the “Augustan archives” in Book IX, Letter 53. There were other archives belonging to the praetorian office, as in Book 13 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Remission of Debts*, and others belonging to the seat of the patrician, as in an ancient inscription cited in the note to Letter 9.] who governs the sacred archives?

When, as a civilian, he manages the reins of the civil administration,

he also bears the cares of the armed forces; under his interpretation

the savage people are bent to your terms.

Why does Clio rashly attempt to praise Peter

with her small powers? Caesar deigns to speak throughout the world

from his mouth, although he also possesses eloquence

through a gifted quaestor. Nevertheless, most gentle prince, only recently …

After the hostage had been received, [Note: [Col. 0675B] From this passage it may be understood that the people of Lyons, when they refused obedience to Majorian’s authority, were subdued and captured by his arms; and that the military garrison imposed upon the captured city in order to keep it loyal was withdrawn, through Peter’s intervention, after hostages had been received. And because the people of Lyons had been worn down by many hardships in this war, they ask Sidonius for a relaxation of their taxes; he himself had shortly before obtained pardon for having shared in the rebellion. From this pardon, therefore, one should understand what he says a little below, “I remember, when you wished to spare, / This was the expression of your face,” and in the preface to the panegyric:

“Thus, when I had recently fallen beneath divergent warfare,  
You ordered me, victorious, to be of tranquil mind.”]

he drove the enemy, planted in the unhappy entrails of our city, away from our walls.

And because, when our affairs were utterly exhausted, you came as our sole hope, we ask you to aid our ruins: look upon your Lyons as you pass by, victorious. Broken by excessive labors, it asks leisure from you; to the ox to which you give peace, restore its spirit. The weary neck of a young bullock more gladly furrows the solid clod of earth after the plow has been laid aside; by ox, crop, and farmer, by citizens, its resources have been drained. What was the fortune of the standing city, while it was being captured—how great its misery! After joys, prince, it is pleasant to remember misfortune; though we fell through plunder and fire, on your arrival you restore everything with yourself. Since we were the cause of your triumph, the very ruin is pleasing.

When, victorious, you begin to mount your chariot, and the sacred hair is bound for you, according to ancient custom, by the mural, vallary, and civic laurels, and the golden Capitolia of kings look upon their chains—

[Note: [Col. 0675C] Thus several manuscripts; others read *vesties*, “you will clothe.” Either he disregarded the rule of meter, or he altered the conjugation, as Ennius does in Nonius, and as Fortunatus does in book IX with *fodent* for *fodient*. In the following verse he figuratively called Cinyphian Bocchus Genseric, who also held Mauritania, the kingdom of Bocchus.]

when you clothe Rome with spoils, when you paint, with rich wax, the captive huts of Cinyphian Bocchus, I shall myself go before the obstructing crowds amid hoarse tumult and shall say in a slender song, as now, that you have subdued the twin Alps, the Syrtes, the great sea, the straits, and equally the Libyan host.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Savaro: “Or that you have nevertheless conquered, since you turn your eyes toward me.”]

Yet first conquer for me. Because you turn your eyes toward me, and because you now look upon the wretched with a serene face, I delight in exulting: I remember, when you wished to spare, this was the expression of your face; gentle beauty gives the signs. Grant my prayer, so that Byrsa may breathe again beneath your trophies.

[Col. 0676B] [Note: [Col. 0675D] Others read *certum*, “certain.” But Sidonius seems rather to have written this: that is, with a straight and unturned step, *ἀνεπιστρόφως*, “without turning back,” so that those who are accustomed to feign flight and to hurl weapons while fleeing may truly flee. In the panegyric of Avitus:

“Or when the Persians, whom one must flee, flee still more in flight.”

But these prayers of Sidonius were futile, since events did not answer them. Majorian, after spending two years partly in Gaul and partly in Spain, and after his fleet had been dispersed by the Vandals, as has been stated, returned to Italy; there he was stripped of the imperial power by Ricimer and killed on the seventh day before the Ides of August in the year 461. That he was buried in a humble tomb is attested by the epitaph read among the works of Ennodius, as follows:

“When Fortune, growing harsher, sought a tomb,  
It bestowed its remains upon your ashes, Majorian.  
Now, Fortune, look upon the unworthy mass of pyramids;  
Leave mean graves to pious princes.”]

Thus may the Parthian flee straight, and the Moor go pale with fear; thus may Susa tremble, and Bactra, having laid aside its quivers and disarmed, stand around your tribunal.

## POEM VI. PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 0676B] 126. The panegyric of Avitus was delivered at Rome, as is immediately clear to the reader, at the inauguration of his consulship—that is, on the Kalends of January following the beginning of his reign, in the year of Christ 456. For he dedicated those days to his own fasces. The memory of Avitus as consul is preserved not only by the Idatian Fasti, which we have recently obtained conveniently, but also by two ancient stones at Rome. One of them, in the Basilica of the Lateran, bears these words:

“Timothea, deposited in peace, on the day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of our Lord Avitus.”

The other, in the church of Saint Agnes on the Nomentan Way, reads:

“Place of deposit of Gerontius, presbyter, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Eparchius Avitus.”

Although the latter inscription does not bear an imperial title, there should be no doubt that this is the emperor Avitus. For if this is denied, who is that other Eparchius Avitus? I pass over the fact that the style agrees with the period, and that the name Eparchius is shown to have been in use among the Gauls by Eparchius, bishop of the Arverni and predecessor of Sidonius, and by Eparchius, abbot of Angoulême, both of whom Gregory of Tours mentions.

What, then, shall we say is the reason why Avitus’ consulship is mentioned nowhere else, when in the Greek Fasti and by Marcellinus Comes, Cassiodorus, and all the other ancient writers, not Avitus but Vararanes and John are recorded as the consuls of this year? Savaro thinks that this happened because Vararanes was substituted for Avitus after Avitus had abdicated the empire. But, to say nothing else, this is refuted by the same stones, which record Avitus as consul after he had abandoned the purple, and by a constitution of the emperor Marcian in the Code, On Episcopal Hearing, in which Vararanes is called consul with John in the month of March—that is, before Avitus’ abdication.

It is therefore clear that throughout the whole year there were no consuls in the East other than Vararanes and John, whom Marcian had appointed, and none in the West other than Avitus. But the authors of the consular chronicles took no account of Avitus’ consulship because he was an emperor of uncertain status. Nor need any other explanation be sought for its omission, since they likewise omit the consulships of all other uncertain emperors. For all who had usurped the purple both assumed consulships for themselves and appointed as consuls others belonging to their party.

This can be seen in the little book on the prefects of the City, published by Cuspinianus, in which the consuls of Magnentius and likewise those of Maxentius are recorded; nevertheless, Cassiodorus and the others conceal both with equal silence. Again, in the Basilica of Saint Paul there is an epitaph of the sisters Dativa and Basilia, in which they are said to have been buried “in the consulship of John Augustus.” No one will deny that this was the John who invaded the empire at Ravenna after the death of Honorius in the year of Christ 425 and then, in the following year, assumed the consulship, as was customary for emperors. Yet no Fasti admit this John among the consuls.

Moreover, one can see that pairs of consuls were sometimes interpolated from the same source, and that one consul was joined with one colleague in one place and with another elsewhere. For example, on an inscription of Equitius at Rome there is the epitaph of a certain Eutychius, in which the consuls are given as “Theodosius Augustus III and Augustus, our lord.” By this I understand Eugenius, our prince—the very man who, after seizing the principate through the faction of Arbogast, ruled Italy in that year and, having published his consulship, called himself colleague of Theodosius Augustus, whereas in the East Theodosius had named Abundantius, whom all the Fasti recognize as consul and about Eugenius remain silent.

And in the Greek inscription at Trier which we discussed in connection with book V, letter 9, Constantine the usurper, who was then ruling in Gaul and held the consulship in that year, is assigned as colleague to Honorius VIII, not Theodosius III. Thus in public records and monuments in Gaul the consuls were written as Honorius VIII and Constantine; in the remaining provinces, however, which did not obey Constantine, it was not Constantine but Theodosius III who was paired with Honorius.]

## OF THE PANEGYRIC WHICH HE DELIVERED AT ROME FOR AVITUS AUGUSTUS, HIS FATHER-IN-LAW

While the lyre of the Thracian bard of Ismarus resounds with songs for the festival of war-resounding Pallas, while at Mopsopian Marathon the rivers that had stood still and the ground over which they had run are crowded, and while the sweet-toned murmur is stirred on the strings by the plectrum, they say that the goddess approved these praises with praise.

Goddess whom, in the time of the war with the Giants, an armed birth poured forth from a divided head; whom Latona did not bear beneath the Delian caves, she who was to fasten the wandering Cyclades with her offspring; nor she who, giving birth to Alcides on the Cadmean shores, prolonged her labour through three nights; nor she whose tower was drenched by a rain of metal when the charioteer-born son filled his mother.

But you, when you watched Phlegra tremble beneath the thunderer, were driven forth when the broken summit burst from his head. And while the gods possessed only their own strength for battle, their strength was greatly confused without you. Once your father’s wisdom-bearing head brought you forth, the gods prevailed all the more when they had you.

Because of you, the structure built by those dread hands yielded, now stretched almost to the gleaming heavens. Pindus, Othrys, and Pholoe fell beneath the Giants’ right hands; and Ossa, already massive, fell beneath Rhoetus’ hand. Aegaeon, Briareus, Ephialtes, and Mimas were struck down—those accustomed to lick the northern wheels with their feet.

Enceladus lay upon his father, and Typhoeus upon his brother: the one bears the Euboean rock, the other the Sicilian. Thereupon Orpheus turned himself wholly toward his mother and taught the strings to make Calliope speak. The Muses rose in praise of their sister, and the goddess was pleased more by filial devotion in song.

[Col. 0678A] But if it is a favour to sing a mother’s praises, and my faithfulness cannot equal that of old, Avitus is this public father, to whom I have vowed my song: the subject is greater, though my Muse is lesser.

## CARMEN VII. PANEGYRIC DELIVERED FOR AVITUS AUGUSTUS, HIS FATHER-IN-LAW

Phoebus, when you have at last traversed the world and seek one whom you can bear as your equal, give light to heaven: this man suffices for earth. Let the bearer of the signs no longer boast among the stars, whom Marmaric Atlas crushes with his head.

[Note: [Col. 0678C] Euripides, *Ion* 1:

“Atlas, with brazen shoulders,  
wearing down the sky,  
the ancient home of the gods.”]

His are stars such as shine when submerged; so Rome gleams amid adversity. From her beginning her fixed course was to grow through misfortunes; now she will rise with him as prince and consul.

[Note: [Col. 0678C] He means that Avitus was granted the consulship by the Senate together with imperial authority. For Avitus, as Sidonius himself will relate, after the death of Petronius Maximus, when the court was vacant, was first raised to the imperial office by the Gauls; then, as we learn from the chronicle of Hydatius, he was summoned and accepted by the Romans, and, with Marcian’s consent, joined him in a partnership of empire. Hydatius writes: “In Gaul, Avitus, a Gallic citizen, was first called Augustus at Toulouse by the Gallic army and the men of rank, then at Arles; he proceeded to Rome and was accepted.” A little later: “Through Avitus, who had been both summoned and accepted by the Romans as emperor, envoys were sent to Marcian for unity of rule.” And again: “Marcian and Avitus, united in their principate, exercised the Roman empire.”]

Indeed, Fathers, it delights you to see the fasces joined and to have the curule chair entrusted as partner to the scepters. Believe me, you will give greater things to the chariots: now bind the two-fronted locks of ambiguous Janus and gird yourself with a double laurel. This year shines first as the prince’s year, now as the consul’s, and crowns earned through office grow into diadems.

Now, Muse, you fear in vain that the South Wind has driven our ship’s sails, because we have begun to run across the sea of fame. Behold the star that will preserve us across the blue waters.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Much in Sidonius’ poems is fashioned after Claudian as a model, and he was led toward similarity of subject by imitation of him. Of this kind is the personification of the city of Rome in this passage. Both poets make Rome, neglected and disordered in bodily appearance, supplicate Jupiter. But the substance of the request in Claudian is that he restrain Gildo; in Sidonius, that he grant a prince.]

Perhaps the father of the gods looked down from heaven upon the earth. Behold, whatever he sees flourishes: to have looked upon the world was to have restored it; his single nod cherishes all things.

And now, as the gods assembled, the Tegeatic Arcadian flew now upon his feet, now upon his forehead; scarcely had he touched the fields. And from every quarter they descended: sea, earth, and air sent their native gods.

First you come, brother of the thunderer, accustomed to cleave the green Doris in your chariot, and quickly to scatter serenity over her astonished back. Phorcys accompanies the moist Nymphs; there you come, Glaucus, with Glauce. And you, Proteus, most unfailing of prophets, were true; afterward the gods come in a long procession: Liber crowned with vine leaves, savage Mars, shaggy Tirynthian Hercules, naked Venus, fruitful Ceres, quiver-bearing Diana, grave Juno, wise Pallas, turreted Cybele, Saturn in exile, wandering Cynthia, youthful Phoebus, frightened Pan, stern Fauns, and wanton Satyrs.

Those who hold the heavens by their power also assembled: Castor on horseback, Pollux with the boxing glove, Perseus with the harpe, Vulcan with the thunderbolt, Tiphys with his ship, Quirinus with his people.

Who could sing the palace of heaven, whose gleaming stars are themselves its pavement? Now the father seats himself calmly upon a golden throne; the elder gods sit down beside him. Even the old river gods were granted a place there: above all, Eridanus, broken into cups by its waves; swollen Rhine, amid blond Sicambri; Ister, riding through the wandering tribes of Scythia; and the Nile, better known than his unknown source.

When Rome, from a distant region of heaven, dragged forward her raised but sluggish steps, she carried her face bowed with curved neck. Her hair hung from her covered head, covered not by a helmet but by dust; her shield struck against her weary steps, and the spear was borne as a burden, not as a terror.

When she first fell upon the knees of the dutiful thunderer, she said:

“I call you to witness, holy father, and that divine power—whatever Rome I once was. I am sufficiently overwhelmed by the highest fate, and I envy the lowly. My narrow dwelling cannot sustain the weight of a loftier summit, nor does lightning threaten the valleys.

“What, I ask, did the Etruscan augur foretell for me by twice six vultures? Why, Romulus, poor man, when you laid my foundations on the ridges of the Etruscan hill, was I already exalted above all peoples?

“I was safer with the sword, when the Rutulian, Veientine, Auruncian, Aequian, Hernican, and Volscian pressed me with joined storm. I seemed great enough even to you, while the woman tore her violated body with the sword and, her modesty recovered, returned to the chaste wound.

“Then, when Tarquin, with his Etruscan ally, enclosed me behind fortifications: O the fires of Mutius! O the waters of Cocles! O grief! Where now is the torrent that brought the Samnite beneath my laws? Where is the Martian who struck the Volscian in the back, and the dictator and exile who scattered the Senones?

“I wish for the life of Fabricius, the deaths of the Decii: either the victor of that kind or the vanquished of that kind. Restore my beginnings to me. Alas, where now are the pageantry, the rich triumphs, and the poor consul?

“My spear terrified the Libyan sky, and I imposed a third yoke upon the treacherous Carthaginian. The Ganges of the Indians, the Phasis of the Colchians, the Araxes of Armenia,

[Note: [Col. 0679C] We once restored this reading, following the traces of a single manuscript and Claudian, *On Stilicho* I: “And Gir,” he says, “the river of the Ethiopians, most famous, which deceives the Nile with a similar whirlpool.” Others, following the common text, have *Tagus*, which has no connection with Ethiopia. Gir, Γὰρ in Ptolemy, is a river of inner Libya and of the Ethiopians. There is also Gira, a metropolis from which the Girraean or Giraean people are named, in Claudian’s idyll on the Nile:

‘This the unbridled Garamas drinks, and the Giraean,  
tamer of beasts, who inhabits vast caves beneath the rocks,  
who tears branches of ebony and teeth of ivory.’

The common reading *Cirtaeus* is wrong; nor is the substitution *Scopas*, *Candaeus*, any better, since both peoples are far removed from these regions.]

the Gir of the Ethiopians and the Tanais of the Getae trembled before my tribune. Once, defeated, you submitted to me together with the Teuton, Cimber, and I ordered hands previously burdened with swords to bear chains alone.

“Woe to me—what I was, when at my command Sulla, Asiagenes, Curius, Paulus, Pompey, ordered peace, kingdoms, flight, tribute, chains, and poison for Tigranes, Antiochus, Pyrrhus, the Persians, and Mithridates!

[Note: [Col. 0679D] This is the consistent reading of the ancient books. *Asiagenes*, Ἀσιαγενής, is indeed a Greek and valid word. But why did he prefer to call Lucius Scipio by this name, when the verse limps no less than if he had written *Asiaticus*? Antonius Augustinus, in his work on Roman families under the Cornelian family, inferred from the indications of the first edition of Sidonius, in which *Asia[e] gentes* was read, that the text should be *Asiagetes*. He thought that Lucius Scipio was first called this in Greece, and says that traces of this surname also survive on coins and in ancient Livian manuscripts.

I myself have hitherto found nothing in Livy’s books other than *Asiaticus*; as for the coins, the conjecture has always seemed to me extremely slight. Why should a Greek and unusual word occur on a Roman coin? Further, since, according to Fulvius Ursinus, the coins either bear *L. SCIP. ASIA. G.* or, without punctuation, *ASIAG.*, the former contributes nothing to the matter, while the latter provides no reason for reading *Asiagetes* rather than *Asiagenes*. Nevertheless, as the very learned man thought, Sidonius may have written *Asiagetes* here, or even *Asiagenetes*, since that form was used for *Asiagenes*, just as *Eugenetes* is used for *Eugene* in Ennodius and Senator, and Ἐρισθενέτης for Ἐρισθενής in Apollinarius.]

“I say nothing of the Sarmatian and the Moschian, the Getae accustomed to drink bloody milk and to stain their cups with veins, or of the Persians, whom, when they flee, one must flee all the more.

“Nor is it enough to have said that I subdued lands. Under your leadership I entered many seas in shining arms, and peoples far removed beneath the setting sun. Caesar, your victorious standards crossed over even to the Caledonian Britons.

“Although he may have routed the Scot and the Pict together with the Saxon,

[Note: [Col. 0679D] There is an obvious anticipation here. He speaks as though the Picts, Saxons, and Scots already inhabited Britain and had been routed by Caesar when he made war upon Britain. Yet it is certain that these peoples were then neighbors of the Britons but always hostile to them. Indicating this, the old panegyrist of Constantius says that before Caesar’s arrival the Britons were accustomed to enemies only in the Picts and Irish—that is, the Scots. For the Scots formerly inhabited Ireland, as the Picts inhabited Thule and the Saxons the Orkneys. Hence Claudian’s lines on the fourth consulship of Honorius:

‘The Orkneys were wet with Saxon blood,  
Thule grew hot with the blood of the Picts,  
icy Ireland mourned heaps of Scots.’

Only later, and not all at one time, did they transfer their homes to Britain: first the Picts, then the Saxons, and finally the Scots.]

“he sought enemies whom nature now forbade him to seek among further peoples. He saw you break Leucas, fierce Augustus, and Pharos, while the fleet at Actium shook the waters and greedy Antony, fleeing with his arms, emptied the incestuous Ptolemaic kingdom.

“And although earlier I used to complain that I was the boundary of the world at its narrowest, now I myself am the boundary. I am more powerful than I should be, O highest of the gods, because the Parthian voluntarily restored my standards in terror and, setting aside his tiara,

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Some, as I noted above, read Sapor, so that the name may stand for any Parthian king. It was Phraates who restored them. Cicero in *Pro Sextio*, and Plutarch in *Pompey* concerning Tigranes, likewise express the custom of a tiara being laid down in the submissive worship of tiara-wearing kings. Plutarch writes: “And finally, when he came before Pompey, he removed his tiara and rushed to place it before his feet.”]

mourned the deaths of the Crassi while making atonement for them. And now, alas, after the law of the people and Senate had been shaken off, I encountered what I feared: I am wholly in the prince, wholly the prince’s, and I become a kingdom torn apart from Caesar, though once I was a queen.

“I followed the Capreas of Tiberius, the boots of Gaius, the censorship of Claudius, and Nero, a man of mournful death. You strike down Galba, whom Piso had made feared, with Otho, who was thought handsome because of his mirror; while I was being captured, I was ugly. The gluttony of Vitellius brought me a filthy belly, and he, ruling for a short time, died too late. After me, Vespasian, renowned in arms, holds the exhausted empire; Titus follows him, and after Titus his brother.

“After him tranquil Nerva scarcely began to restore me to myself, having become greater than Caesar through adoption. Then came Ulpius, under whom Agrippina was feared by the Sicambri: brave, dutiful, upright, and vigorous. Captive, I pray for such a man.” I do not know whether anyone could equal Trajan, unless perhaps you, Gaul, should send another who could surpass him.”

Tears closed the suppliant’s voice, and all that remains of her lament makes her plea. From every side the nobles of heaven rise—Mars, Venus, Romulus, and the gods who founded you, Rome. Now Saturnia herself is softened, bends, and remits her former anger.

[Note: [Col. 0681D] The remainder of the poem is occupied by Jupiter’s speech, in which Jupiter himself unfolds the praises of the prince he has designated and describes his homeland, lineage, upbringing, achievements in peace and war, and finally the solemn transfer of imperial power to him by the Gauls.]

Jupiter speaks these words:

“Fate, by which all things are governed—and by which it was not permitted even for me to be broken—stands firm. Things set high always suffer, and Fortune has envied the powers raised by our gift, envying her own gifts. Yet take courage greatly, though broken.

“If Porsenna feared you more, trembling on the loosened bridge; if the walls captured by Brennus soon witnessed his flight; if finally we repelled dreadful Hannibal, amid the joined tumult of earth and sky, when his camps already stood near your walls, and lightning ran from the Colline Gate like a tower, and there nature again feared the trembling Jupiter who fought after Phlegra—lift your torpid eyes; let darkness leave your cleansed mind.

“It is strange that you should be conquered; when you begin to conquer, it will not be strange. And so that it may become clear to you how far you may finally rise, though now exhausted, I shall teach you after you have learned a few things.

“I have a land which claims the honour of being a foster-child of Latin blood, renowned for its men, to which nature, the maker of things, once gave no equal. Its field is fertile from the city; scarcely broken by the first plow, it thirsts for sluggish seeds, or, with its young bullock luxuriant, displays the secret richness of its pitch-black soil.

“It rose above the soil baked by the hot South Wind, the soil of the Nile and Libya; and the sickles of Mygdonia’s Gargara were always condemned when compared with it. Apulia and Calabria yielded; this is the one hope of the world.

“Cultivating this land, Arvernian, you yield to no one in foot-combat, and you defeat everyone on horseback. Let Caesar himself testify to me here, when Fortune was excessively afraid, as he was driven back from the hill of Gergovia and scarcely kept his army within its own camp.

“I intended these men to be so brave, but Avitus to surpass them, while I prepare him for you, Rome. Long ago the noblest shoot, embracing its ancestral stock, has shone; the palm-bearing dignity has run through his forefathers, and, Philagrius, as you attest, the patrician summit of his line gleams.

“But how much of praise is it to praise such ancestors? For it is established that he owes his curule offices and prefectures to his grandson. Others have descendants by whom their posterity may boast itself and count an ancient lineage among its titles. You alone, Avitus, ennoble your ancestors.

“I would like to recount the deeds of so great a man and run briefly through his early life.

“A noble mother had released the burden of a chaste womb in childbirth. Soon she gave clear signs of the future prince, and I filled the whole palace of his anxious father with favorable prophecy, although he himself blamed the great destinies of his newborn child and already saw kingdoms in the boy.

“But, seeing the trust of the world committed to him in so great a pledge, he assisted Fortune by his devotion, lest Rome should lose anything of you. First he exposed your infant limbs to snow, ordered ice to creep beneath your feet, and taught the little child to laugh at trampled frost.

“Your rising years were shaped by the Muses, and by the Cicero in whose voice you thunder.
