You also learned the deeds of your former commanders; you learned their battles and reread in books what you were to carry out in the field. Scarcely had you begun to be a child rather than an infant when by chance you struck down a raging she-wolf, preparing food with bloody jaws and a famished throat, more than for her cubs—for fragments lay nearby—

[Note: [Col. 0683C] Read *arreptam*, “having seized.” The sense is that the she-wolf, while seeking food for herself and her cubs, came upon Avitus, who, since no other weapon was available, struck her down with a stone that happened to lie among the fragments of a neighboring rock. Thus *propter* here takes the place of an adverb, as below: “king and commander had stood nearby.”]

having seized it from the rock. Her skull burst, and the stone remained embedded in the wound.

“Thus my Alcides, while wandering through the groves of Nemea, encountered the monster empty-handed, carrying neither club nor quiver. His trembling anger stood forth, and, with the enemy near, deceived valor relied upon its own arms alone.

“A small deed, certainly, but one that must be told: who was readier than he to submit the stretched necks of chained mastiffs? To learn, by the scent that interpreted them, beasts unseen as they lay in their lairs, and to seek their tracks in the air?

“Again, if by chance the shameless Umbrian frightened a boar with his barking, it was a game to break the white crescents beneath the black throat and, with struggling arm, drive huge hunting spears through the opposing prey.

“How beautiful he was when, returning home after the hunts, he shone with the horror of the boar, and his resisting valor revealed, through brave deeds, a modesty that had not sought them.

“Thus Hippolytus, in the fields of the chaste daughter of Triton, shone from his rosy face, sweating—

[Note: [Col. 0683C] Savaro and others read *sudum*, “clear.”]

but at the same time the Cretan woman, blazing with a twofold frenzy, surpassed mothers in affection and stepmothers in deceit.

“What of his zeal for birds which nature makes predatory against a people almost akin to them? Who was more skilled than he at arranging their varied contests beneath the clouds? He defeats birds with a winged creature, and with swift clapping through the air no fighter’s talon serves better than this one.

“Nor did he pursue these things less amid civil law.

[Col. 0684A] [Note: [Col. 0683C] This was Avitus’ first embassy, when he was sent by his fellow Arverni to Honorius Augustus to seek a reduction of tribute. In that emperor’s court was the count Constantius, who had married his sister Placidia. The year in which this embassy took place, or the calamities by which his homeland was then shattered, is unclear. But the embassy must have occurred before the year 421, since it was only in that year that Constantius was admitted by Honorius into partnership in the empire.]

“He was chosen first—young and alone—to bind up the misfortunes of his shattered homeland and ask that its excessive tribute be reduced. Constantius, then perhaps the foremost of the nobles there and afterwards himself emperor, granted everything, struck by so great a natural ability and astonished that in the young petitioner’s tender years there were the words of an old man.

“Now, Rome, I wish to unfold the battles of commanders and the treaties of kings. When Gaul had been buffeted by varied storms of war, it was ordered to give pledges of peace to the Getic king. Among them came you, noble hostage Theodore; out of duty to your kinsman, Avitus, safe under his pledged faith, sought you in the midst of the court of the fur-clad prince.”

[Note: [Col. 0683D] This refers to Theodoric the Elder, who became king of the Goths in Gaul after Wallia. Gregory of Tours calls him Theudo; Sidonius calls him Theuderic and Theodoric. This Gothic treaty, in which hostages were given by the Gauls—including Theodore, a relative of Avitus—must, if I am not mistaken, be understood as referring to the siege of Arles, when Theodoric, as Isidore writes in his Chronicle, not content with the kingdom of Aquitaine, besieged that city until it was liberated by the intervention of Aetius, in the year 425, as Prosper records. Sigonius deserves pardon: having found a defective manuscript in which the king’s name was distorted, he thought that this passage could be referred to King Wallia, who had already died.]

“Now Theuderic approves this lofty example of duty: it is a remarkable thing, worthy of report, that you were gracious and pleased the savage king.

“From that point he gradually tasted you with his deepest senses and wished you to be his own in spirit; but you rejected the idea of behaving as a friend more than as a Roman. He was amazed at the rebuff, and because of it you pleased him more. Thus, Pyrrhus, you saw the stern Fabricius: when the poor man fled from wealth thrust upon his mind, despising the king, while the king begged the pledge of friendship with gold in the form of a suppliant’s payment.

[Note: [Col. 0684C] Avitus accompanied the commander Aetius on two military expeditions. One was against the Juthungi, the other against the Burgundians. The campaign against the Juthungi took place around the year 430, to which the words of Prosper of Aquitaine refer: “Aetius intended to destroy the nation of the Juthungi.” He joins the Vindelici and Norici with them, who perhaps had revolted together at that time. Hydatius writes: “The Juthungi and the Norici are defeated by Aetius.” A little later, concerning the death of the patrician Felix: “The commander Aetius subdues the rebellious Norici.”]

“Meanwhile, because you had often been trained in Scythian warfare, you followed Aetius. Although he was lofty in arms, he accomplished nothing without you, while you accomplished very much without him.

[Note: [Col. 0684C] We have corrected this from the ancient books in place of *Vitbungos*. The panegyric of Constantius Caesar should apparently be corrected in the same way, for there is no mention of the Vitbungi anywhere else. The Juthungi, as Marcellinus shows, were a part of the Alamanni, neighboring Raetia, which they therefore frequently ravaged. Ambrose, concerning his embassy to Maximus, writes: “In the midst of the Roman empire the Juthungi were ravaging Raetia; and therefore a Hun was summoned against the Juthungus.” Earlier they had also been driven from there by Julian through the count Barbatio, as Marcellinus relates in book XVII. Now they were defeated in the same regions by Aetius. Yet Juthungi also existed among the federate peoples, under the duke of Syria and under the commander of the military forces in Egypt, as appears in the *Notitia*.]

“For after the Juthungian and Noric wars, when Vindelicus had been subdued, he freed the Belgian whom the savage Burgundian had oppressed, joined to you. There Herulus was conquered in flight, the Hun by javelins, the Frank by swimming, the Sarmatian by shield, the Salian on foot, and the Gelonian by the sickle.

[Note: [Col. 0684D] This was that memorable disaster in which nearly the entire nation of the Burgundians was destroyed by Aetius, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian, in the year 435, as Prosper and Cassiodorus record. Hydatius writes: “The Burgundians, who had rebelled against the Romans, were defeated under the command of Aetius.” The same author says that twenty thousand Burgundians and eight thousand Goths who were aiding them were killed in this battle. Sidonius, although he lists many peoples who were in their camp, deliberately passes over the Goths.]

“Or by a wound, if there is anyone who laments—for to weep is to perish—and who has plowed his cheeks through with iron, and buried the red traces of scars in his threatening face.

“Already then he was granted lofty distinction, his face still livid beneath gleaming helmet-plumes and scaly armour.”

[Col. 0685C] [Note: [Col. 0685C] The Gothic war followed the Burgundian one, again with the same Theodoric. It began with the siege of Narbonne in the year 436, was completed at Toulouse with the capture of Litorius, and was settled by peace in 439. Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes, and Salvian in book VII of *On Providence* testify that the Romans used Hun auxiliaries in this war.

“When Litorius was leading their bands from Armorica through the Arverni, and they were ravaging Arvernia with barbarous ferocity, Avitus’ attack upon them arose, together with his single combat against a Hun horseman, which Sidonius describes with such pomp. Sigonius reasonably assigns this to the year 437 in his books on the empire of the West; but he most wrongly attributes the ravaging of Arvernia, which should be assigned to the Huns, to the Goths, and twists these verses, which were written about Avitus, toward Theodoric.]

“Scarcely had he brought home weapons still soiled from the camp when the enemy again stirred up new wars and battle, destined to perish beneath the very walls of his homeland.”

“Litorius, having then perhaps subdued the Armorican, was leading Scythian horsemen into the Getic column through your lands, Arvernian. They destroyed everything near at hand in their march, with flames, iron, savagery, and plunder,

[Note: [Col. 0685D] We have already noted in the panegyric of Majorian that the Armoricans were frequently attacked by the Romans because of their rebellion. They had now therefore been subdued by Litorius; about ten years later they were subdued by Aetius through Eocharic, king of the Alans, whom he sent against them, as Constantius testifies in book II, chapter 5, of the *Life of Saint Germanus*. In that passage, however, *king of the Alamanni* is written corruptly for *king of the Alans*, as the verses of the monk Ericus show.]

“betraying the empty name of peace. Then one of these men, more savage than the others, soon to be struck by the servant of him whom he would attack, rushed forward and commended his grim fate

[Col. 0685B] to his absent master, and the share that was yet to come—”

Dying, he carries the hope of vengeance to the Stygian river.

And now rumor brings to the man guarding the towers and gates, through the gaze of the frightened populace, news of the deed accomplished. He is shaken, stands rigid, grows pale, reddens, freezes, and burns; and in one face his anger produces many changing expressions—or, as often happens to one in grief, he loves the dead more. At last he bursts forth, and with weapons—

339 Weapons he roars; his breastplate, still thick with blood, is borne upon him, the lance blunted by barbarian wounds, and the sword, toothed with repeated slaughter. He encloses his legs in greaves and places upon his head the gleaming helmet, whose yellow cone rises high and shoots angry light from its crest.

[Col. 0685C] And now he mounts his horse; tearing the gates from their hinges, he flashes forth. Courage, grief, and shame attend his companion. Eager, he attacks the armed ranks with his spear, seeking battle by fighting, and compensates by the slaughter of many for the one man who lies hidden.

Thus the son of Aeacus, demanding the Phrygian victor with an Aemathian spear, restrained his grief for his slain friend; through so many deaths, Troy, throughout your ranks, now content merely to have the worthless troops collapse and to draw his naked sword among the broad peoples. The earth swims buried in blood, and while the slaughtering crowd blunts the heavy weapon—

[Col. 0686A] Absent in every wound, Hector now falls for him.

When at last the man who was the cause of so great a disturbance was betrayed, Avitus says: “Come, you nurtured beneath the Scythian north, you who rage and trust only in a slain unarmed man; meet an armed opponent. My anger has already granted you much: I have allowed the battle and command you to resist. It is pleasing to have slain one who fights.”

So he speaks and leaps into the open space; and the savage enemy comes as well. As soon as they brought their chests and faces close together, the one trembles with anger, the other with fear. Now the rest of the crowd trembles with divergent hopes and hangs upon the outcome through the various blows. But after the first, second, and third circuits had been made, Avitus comes upon him and pierces the tall bloody man with his spear; afterward, the breastplate, split through twice in the chest, gives way, ruptured at the edges of the back.

340 And while the blood gurgles through the double opening, the divided wounds severed the twofold life.

After these deeds, O livid Styx, I call you to witness: when, as prefect, he administered inviolate laws for me, [Note: [Col. 0686D] Avitus, then prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, is credited with the praise of renewed peace with Theodoric. He says that Theodoric was chiefly moved to peace by Avitus’s letters after his victory—at the time, that is, when Count Litorius, who held command over the Hunnic auxiliaries second only to Aetius, rashly engaged the Goths in battle near Toulouse, was defeated and captured, and entered the same city of the enemy as a captive, as Salvian writes, which he had presumed to enter victor on that day, in the year 439, as we have already indicated. Avitus’s prefecture therefore fell within the same period.]

And Gaul, receiving this head, exhausted by its accustomed disasters, grew pale before the Gothic anger. Neither prayers, nor payment, nor soldiers could bend Aetius; once Litorius was captured, the loss of the lands became apparent. Theodoric had resolved to extend his boundaries to the Rhône, and there was no need to fight, but only to withdraw before the Goths. The victor, savage and enraged, aggravated his furious anger because he had experienced a Scythian enemy before the walls; he charges the frightened man with this, and nothing is heavier, if ever fortune grants victory, than fear.

After no defense remained anywhere, and nothing was left to your commanders, Rome, Avitus, renew the treaty. Your written word tames the savage king; it is enough that you command what the world requests. Will nations and peoples yet to come ever believe this? A Roman letter cancels what you conquer by barbarian force.

Therefore he governed the laws; for it was fitting that the defender of the laws should also become their author. The prince, head, commander, Caesar, and Augustus who was to be given to the peoples should not know only savage wars.

When at last he had completed the height of his prefecture—

[Col. 0687A] He had withdrawn to the countryside, yet never to leisure, never to the idleness of an unwarlike man: his devotion and care always remained with arms. Suddenly, when barbarism had poured all the North, in tumult, against you, Gaul—

341 With the warlike Rugian accompanied by Gelon, the savage Gepid follows and forces the Scirian along, while the Burgundian drives him onward. [Note: [Col. 0687C–D] Earlier printed editions read *Scotum*; manuscripts read *Scerum* or *Scoerum*, forms customarily written by copyists for *Scyrum*, just as *goerum* for *gyrum* in Ausonius. Jordanes teaches that the Scyri were a Scythian people, a division of the Alans, who settled in Moesia after Attila’s death and later followed Odoacer into Italy.] The Hun, Bellonotus, Neurus, Bastarna, Thuringian, Bructerian—whom either the wooded [Note: [Col. 0687D] Hadrianus Valesius, *Rerum Francicarum* book V, p. 221, wishes *Vicer* to be written. See below, the note on poem 23, verse 244.] Nicer washes with its waters—burst forth. The Frank cuts down the Hercynian forest with his double axe, quickly fells it into boats, and roofs the Rhine with alderwood.

And now Attila had spread himself with his terrifying troops over your fields, Belga; Aetius had scarcely left the Alps, leading a small and thin force without soldiers, foolishly trusting the Gothic auxiliary army and vainly presuming that it would be present in his own camp.

[Col. 0687B] But when the report struck the commander—that the Huns, now nearly despised in their own homes, were awaiting the Goths as their enemy—he turns everything over in his wandering mind and harasses his thoughts with waves of anxiety. At last, while hesitating, he settled upon the decision to entreat the lofty man; and, gathering all the leaders together, he addressed him humbly in these words:

“Avitus, salvation of the world—you for whom glory is no new thing—what Aetius requests, you have wished, and the enemy does no harm. Do you wish it? It benefits us. At your nod you hold so many thousands confined, and your favor alone is the boundary for the Gothic peoples. Though they are always hostile to us, they grant you peace.

“Go forth, bring out the victorious eagles; do this, excellent man: make the Huns, whose earlier flight once perhaps shook us, benefit me by becoming twice conquered.”

[Note: [Col. 0687D] “Formerly,” he says, “when you chose to urge victorious Theodoric to peace, he ceased to harm us; now, if you choose to entreat him again, he will help us with his auxiliaries.” Thus this passage must be read and punctuated; the received texts made no sense. Nor is the close of the speech less elegant: he wishes that the Huns—who, as auxiliaries in the Gothic war, had harmed Rome when defeated and by their flight had caused Litorius’s disaster—should now, as enemies, be defeated again and thus, twice defeated, prove useful.

Thus he spoke, and Avitus, having promised to fulfill his wish, created hope. Immediately he hastens forth and stirs his servile angers to battle. The troops clad in skins followed the Roman standards; when a Goth ran at the name [called by the trumpet], he feared to be called defeated—

[Col. 0688A] 342 Overthrown, ashamed of the reproach rather than fearing the loss.

Avitus, whether already a private citizen or still holding office, now drew these men to war, as hope for the world. So the Phoebean bird, bearing cinnamon to the pyre from the Erythraean hill, rouses the whole flock of birds: the obedient ranks hurry forward, and the narrow air cannot contain their wings.

[Note: [Col. 0687D] Varro, in Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 17, reports that he heard from the augur Vettius that, if matters were as historians related concerning Romulus’s auspices for founding the City, and if the Roman people had remained unharmed for 120 years because of the twelve vultures, it would live to 1,200 years. Remembering this prophecy, the Romans feared the destruction of the City when Alaric invaded Italy, as Claudian writes in *The Gothic War*, although the number of years had not yet been completed. Sidonius’s Jupiter announces that the fulfillment of the augury is impending upon the death of Aetius and Valentinian, at which time the city of Rome had exceeded 1,200 years by only a few years.]

Now almost the fate of your city was completing twice ten vulture-wings—“for you know your labors, Rome; you know them”—

[Note: [Col. 0688C] This marks the time and the reason why the command of the army was entrusted to Avitus by Petronius Maximus. After Valentinian was killed following the death of Aetius, and Maximus had assumed the purple, various disturbances immediately arose in Gaul among the Goths, Saxons, Franks, and Alamanni. To suppress them, Maximus judged nothing more expedient than to appoint Avitus commander of the infantry and cavalry throughout Gaul.]

Actium was slain by the mad eunuch Placidus, and scarcely had the diadem been placed upon your head, Petronius, when barbarism immediately arose; Rome seemed already captured for the Goths, and the land seemed about to yield to their fury. Just as by chance wolves, whose keen nostrils reveal the rich scent from the closed sheepfolds, are provoked and sharpen their hunger, and carry the appearance of plunder in their faces while concealing their starvation with open jaws, so the tender lamb is already, already, broken by hope, and the prey crackles in the greedy throat even before it is present.

Moreover, the Armorican coast expected the Saxon pirate, for whom it was sport to plow the British sea in a hide and to cleave the gray sea in a sewn boat.

The Frank was laying waste the German frontier first and the Belgic frontier second, while you, savage Alamann, were drinking the Rhine at the Roman banks and, proud in both lands—

[Note: [Col. 0688D] The Alamanni’s settlements were in Swabia beyond the Rhine. Now, after crossing the Rhine, they were also attacking the nearer bank belonging to the Romans. Thus on this side—that is, in Gaul—they were victors, while in the German land where they had long lived they were citizens. Not long afterward they also immigrated into Gaul and occupied the whole part of Maxima Sequanorum extending from the Rhine to Mount Jura; they gave it the name New Alamannia. Concerning this Cisrhenane, or Gallic, Alamannia, see various authors, including Gregory of Tours in the *Life of Saints Lupicinus and Romanus*: “Those secluded places of the Jura wilderness, situated between Burgundy and Alamannia, lie near the city of Aventicum.”]

You were either citizen or victor. But when he saw the lost expanses of the lands, Prince Maximus, now ruler, chose you, Avitus, as commander of the infantry and cavalry—the one office that remained. The report of the honor bestowed upon you found the farmer while he happened to be working the teeth of his bent hoe, or, leaning over his curved plow—

[Col. 0688C] 343 Turning the unbaked clod through the rich fields. Thus once, when the fortunes of the fatherland were broken, you, poor farmer Cincinnatus, came from the plow; when your wife clothed you in the old-fashioned robe before the oxen, the doors of willow received you as dictator, and the triumphal purple, bearing upon its shameful burden what had not been completed, carried the lowly seed to your own home.

As soon as he had taken upon himself the weight of the honor—you might read, Alamann, those seeking pardon for their madness—the Saxon’s attack ceased, and he restrained the Catthus with the marshy waters of the Elbe; scarcely does the moon see all this three times in a month. [Note: [Col. 0689C] That is, the Frank. The Chatti, a people of Germany near the Rhine, were counted among the Frankish peoples, or the peoples of the Frankish empire. Gregory, citing Sulpicius Alexander’s third book, had also written that they once served under the Frankish leader Marcomer against Arbogast.]

[Note: [Col. 0689C] Once the disturbances of the other peoples had been settled, the Goths remained; Avitus himself set out to make peace with them. [Col. 0689D] This was the later embassy I mentioned, to the younger Theodoric, son of the elder Theodoric. At his urging, while they were together at Toulouse, Avitus assumed imperial power after hearing of the death of Maximus Augustus.]

And now he extended his journey to the fierce peoples and countryside where the Ocean, driven back by the tide, scatters the returning Garonne through the cultivated lands, the sea running into the river. The bitter salt water crossed the gentle stream, and the salty stranger, striking through the riverbed, navigated its foreign depths.

[Col. 0689B] Here, after the duel had been arranged, rumor quickly suspended the anger of the leaders of the Vesians, [Note: [Col. 0689D] With a shortened form, he calls the Visigoths *Vesi*, or, as it is read in the old commentator on Horace, in Jordanes, and elsewhere, *Vesogothi*, as though they were a part of the Goths. In the panegyric to Majorian: “Goth, Vesus, Alites.”] reporting in a brief letter that Avitus had already entered the Gothic homes, laid aside for a time the burden of command, and assumed the authority of an envoy.

The leaders and the Scythian senate were equally astonished, and feared that he might perhaps deny them their peace.

So when the radiant axle of Phaethon was carrying the light charioteer, while day was already paling and the awakened world was blazing, the peace of the elements might rage, or the nearby dry vapor might seethe across the waters, and the mud might thirst upon the dusty bed of the sea; then alone the merciful flame of Phoebus extinguished the unaccustomed heat.

344 At that moment, some Goth, while reshaping a retempered sickle with blows and sharpening his sword upon a stone, already ready to have grown hot with trumpet calls and to bury the earth with repeated slaughter—not having buried an enemy—brightened at the first announcement of Avitus’s arrival and cried:

“War is finished; bring the plows back. If I recall the well-known leisure of the ancient peace, this man has more than once made me take up the sword. Shame! O gods! So great is the power of trust! Why do you threaten me, to my loss, with dilatory treaties on the faith I give? You command us to provide and to owe the advantages of peace—who would ever believe it? Behold, the Gothic kings, wishing to obey, think that they have ruled beneath another’s authority. Nor can I even say: ‘You love peace bravely.’ Avitus is already laying the parties low; moreover, Messianus, sent ahead, restrains the Gothic anger. You have only just commanded, and we lay down our arms.

“What remains that you might wish to be able to do? That we are not enemies I consider little, if you are known to me from your former conduct; I shall be your auxiliary, or at least I shall be permitted to fight.”

While the Vesus revolved these thoughts in his stern heart, Avitus had come into view. The king and the commander stood nearby: Avitus with erect countenance, the other blushing with joy and asking pardon through his blushes.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] Frideric. I think this is the man who, together with King Theodoric, protected Avitus standing between them, in his honor; he was close to Theodoric in age, according to Jordanes, who lists the sons of the elder Theodoric in this order: Thorismund, Theodoric, Frideric, Euric, Rotemeris, and Himmeric. Thorismund succeeded his father, who died in the battle of the Mauriacian Plains, and three years later was killed by his brothers Theodoric and Frideric. Thus Theodoric began his reign, to whom this embassy was sent. After Theodoric, Euric ruled, because Frideric, to whom the order of succession belonged, had fallen shortly before in Armorica, as Idatius reports. Pope Hilary mentions this same Frideric in a letter to Leontius of Arles.]

Then, with the king held on one side and the king’s brother on the other, they entered Toulouse, their hands joined, just as Romulus and Tatius, with their palms clasped at the sacred cushions, made a treaty concerning their parents—

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Some books read *icere*.]

—having inserted Hersilia among the Sabine women of the Palatine hill, with sword-bearing and furious husbands joined in kindred warfare.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] The name “parents” should be referred to the Sabine women, who, during the Sabine war, under the leadership of Romulus’s wife Hersilia, dared—as Livy says—to throw themselves among the flying weapons and, by pleading first for their fathers and then for their husbands, separate the hostile battle lines and move the leaders to make a treaty.]

345 Meanwhile the Vandal, using stealthy weapons, captured you unawares, and the Burgundian, under treacherous leadership, drew from you the terrified wrath that slew the prince. Alas, the crime! Once again the trumpets of perfidious Byrsa, Elissa’s city, grow savage for war and a fourth course of suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] All agree that Petronius Maximus, when Genseric’s arrival was announced, was killed amid the very panic of his flight; but writers differ remarkably concerning the author of the murder. Prosper says that he was torn to pieces by the servants of Queen Eudoxia; Cassiodorus, that he was killed by soldiers; Jordanes, that he was slain by Ursus, a Roman soldier; Theophanes, by his own followers: “Maximus took to flight; but those with him killed him.” Sidonius indicates that he was killed under the leadership of some Burgundian, perhaps from the corps of protectores.]

[Note: [Col. 0690D] The edition of Wouweren reads *nutristis* (“you have nourished”).]

“What evil, O Fates, have you nourished? The Massylian phalanx of Evander had climbed the citadel, and the Marmaric troops had pressed the hills of Quirinus; once again the forces which Barce had formerly given as captives brought back their pay.

“Exile for the fathers, suffering for the people, and the prince slain: the rumor carried the captive empire to Gothic ears.”

At the new light, according to the custom of the Goths, the ancient assembly gathers. Age stands there, old yet green, in its counsels. Their clothing is dirty, and the coarse linen grows greasy upon their thin backs; hides raised high cannot touch their shins, and with the knee bare a poor knot suspends the horseman’s boot.

[Col. 0691A] When honorable Poverty came into the council of the elders, and the king likewise asked for words of peace, the leader spoke:

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Avitus’s speech is represented as though Maximus were still alive, since he had not yet learned of his death.]

“I confess that, secure in my ancestral fields, I would always have cherished retired peace, from the time when, after three military duties, I had already held the proud summit of the prefecture for a fourth term.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Do not agree with those who infer from this passage that Avitus was three times commander of the army and four times prefect of the praetorium. He does not say that. Rather, after having served in three wars, not without an honorable title, he received the prefecture as his fourth distinction. In the same way he could now say of the military command that he had attained it as his fifth distinction; yet the meaning would not be that Avitus had been commander five times.]

“But when our prince, Maximus, recently ruler of the world, summoned me—ignorant, absent, and after a thousand refusals by the nobles—to the trumpets, after legal authority, and wished to exchange the herald for resounding bugles, I eagerly seized that office so that I might approach you as envoy.

“I pray for the ancient treaties which that old man, my former master, would now hold if I had perhaps commanded him—he under whose authority Avitus had always grown accustomed to serve. I used to manage Gothic affairs; you know that you often did not know what I advised unless it had been done. Yet Fortune snatched away the earlier opportunity; everything I deserved perished when, together with your father—you were still small—I had besieged Narbonne, worn down by famine, enclosing the trembling thousands [Note: [Col. 0691D] This was at the beginning of the Gothic war, as stated above, in the year 436. It is plainly the siege of which Prosper, Isidore, Paul the Deacon, and others write when they say that Count Litorius freed Narbonne from the danger of famine. Avitus recalls that Theodoric lifted the siege through his counsel.] and compelling them, now almost, to resort to infamous food. He already sadly believed that his own prey would escape if he should perhaps perish shut in, when he approved our counsels and released the walls from the war that was retreating.

“And you yourself—behold, these elders—were cherished at this breast. These hands held you weeping, if perhaps your nurse, when you did not wish it, took you away to be suckled. Behold, I come and reclaim the pledge of our former affection.

“If you have no trust, no reverence for a father, go, be harsh, and deny peace.”

A murmur bursts from the entire council; condemning both clamor and war, the seditious crowd stirs a united tumult.

Then the king speaks:

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Theodoric promises Avitus not only peace but also an alliance in war against the Vandals, provided that Avitus allows himself to be chosen emperor, since the imperial court was vacant after the killing of Maximus. In this way, the old destruction inflicted on Rome by Alaric would be expiated by vengeance against Genseric, who during those days had again plundered the City.]

“Long ago, illustrious leader, I blamed you for seeking our peace when you could compel our servitude and lead peoples eager for war. Please do not impose upon me hatred of a father’s name. What do I deserve, if you command nothing? To advise under that man what you could have done, now it is enough merely to wish; the only obstacle is that the Goths do not know what you desire. Long ago, through you, the Roman laws pleased me; my father even ordered me to learn a little at your words, so that the page written in Maro’s teachable song might soften my ancient Scythian character.

“Now you teach us to wish for peace; but understand its condition, and perhaps you will approve the terms of the treaty.”

347 “I call upon you, Rome, your venerable divine power, and the race descended from Mars that is allied with us—or whatever you possess from antiquity (the world has nothing better than you, nor does you yourself have anything better than the Senate)—as witness that I will preserve peace with you, or wish to erase what our grandfather did wrong, whose one stain is that he captured you, Rome.

“But if the gods favor our prayers, the vengeance of the present will be able to cleanse the guilt of the ancient destruction, provided that you, illustrious leader, alone assume the name of Augustus. Why do you turn your eyes away? It is better that you be unwilling; we do not compel you to this, but we bear witness.

“With you as leader, I am Rome’s friend; with you as prince, I am its soldier. You seize no one’s kingdom, and no Augustus possesses the Latin citadels. The court that lies vacant is yours. I bear witness: this is not enough merely to prevent me from harming you; would that it might be made so that, through your diadem, I might help you!

“It is my task to advise. For if Gaul compels you—since it has the legal power to do so—let the world obey you, lest it perish.”

He spoke, and together with his brother gave the requested oath of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 11, does not conceal that Avitus sought the purple; nor is what Isidore writes far from this view, namely, that Theodoric supplied Avitus with Gothic assistance for assuming the imperial dignity. Sidonius therefore attempts to remove this stain by asserting that the empire was imposed upon and thrust upon Avitus in sorrow and against his will. We have already stated, from Idatius, that Avitus was first proclaimed Augustus at Toulouse and afterward at Arles. This agrees with Sidonius. At Toulouse, evidently, the events that Sidonius has so far sung concerning Avitus’s meeting with Theodoric and the plans for assuming the empire took place; the assembly of Gallic nobles, at which he was received and inaugurated on his return, he will soon show to have gathered at the fortress of Arles.]

You depart, Avitus, sorrowful, knowing that it could not remain hidden from the Gauls how the Goths could serve with you as emperor. For as soon as it became clear to the frightened citizens that you brought treaties, they eagerly came out to meet you and prostrated themselves before your unsuspecting tribunal. And when the assembled nobility seemed sufficiently numerous—

[Note: [Col. 0692D] The Cottian Alps; but by this name he intended the other Alps as well, those that separate Gaul from Italy. The Cottian Alps lie between the Graian and Maritime Alps.]

—whose snow-covered rocks look down upon them, and whom the waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Rhine surround on various sides, or whom the long ridges of the Pyrenees lawfully hold apart from Spain—

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Others read *Pyrene*.]

—the joyful crowd approaches the man saddened by the great weight of his anxieties. Then the greatest among the nobles, worthy to assume the person of the fatherland, speaks:

[Col. 0692C] 348 “For a long time, under a youthful prince, Fortune has worn our country down through various harsh struggles amid its shattered fortunes. Perhaps it is a long complaint, great leader, when one who has been the chief among the grieving—while mourning the wounds of his country, you are harassed by overwhelming anxieties—speaks of these things.

“Amid these disasters and deaths of the world, living itself was scarcely anything but death. Yet while we honored idle laws through our ancestors’ words and thought it sacred to follow an ancient custom despite our losses, we carried only the shadow of empire. We were content to endure the faults of an ancient race and to see a people clothed in purple according to custom rather than law.

“Recently the opportunity shone forth by which Gaul might exert its own strength. While Maximus seized the trembling City, he could have seized even the world, if the whole realm had reformed itself under you as its master. Which of us is unaware of who stirred the Belgic fields, the Armorican coast, or the Gothic anger? In these great wars, illustrious leader, we yielded to you.

“Now the highest matters summon you. In a doubtful hour, an indolent man does not rule a kingdom. Every ambition is postponed when they seek the last and greatest men. After the losses of Ticinum and Trebia, when the republic trembled, it hastened to Fabius; after famous Cannae and the flight of Varro, Livy was chosen and broke the Carthaginian swelling with the funeral of the Scipios. The world, they say, lies captive in the City; the prince has perished; this man now possesses all authority. We ask you: ascend the tribunal—

[Col. 0693B] “Raise up the fallen. The times do not demand merely that someone else love Rome more; do not perhaps think yourself unequal to the kingdom. When Brennus’s standards pressed upon the Tarpeian rock, you know that our entire republic was Camillus, the avenger owed to his fatherland, who covered the smoking ashes with the slaughter of the enemy.

“You have not bought the people’s hundreds with gold, nor do tribes now come together for sale, redeemed by a numerous bronze coin. No one has purchased the votes of the world. You will be chosen poor, which alone is sufficient; you are rich in merit. Why do you delay the vows of your fatherland, which commands you to command? This is the judgment of all: if you become master, I shall be free.”

The crash fills the halls.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Variant copies. Some read *Thierni*, the name by which they now call an old fortress and town of the Arverni, known to Gregory of Tours and others as *Tigernum*. But the name *Thierni* agrees neither with the meter nor with the place. Other copies have *Vierni*, from which I made *Ugerni*. The same change is found when *Bagocasses* is written for *Baiocasses* in Ausonius. It was either *Ugernum*, or Οὔγερνον, a fortress of the people of Arles well known to Strabo, which Gregory likewise mentions in books VIII and IX, as does Cyprian, disciple of Caesarius, in his Life. Moreover, Idatius has already taught us that Avitus assumed the name of Augustus at Arles. Therefore no one will object that this emendation is certain.]

At Ugerni, perhaps, in that place, the devout crowd and the Senate had brought their force, vows, and prayers. The place, hour, and day are said to be favorable for imperial power; and immediately, with joyful skill, he orders the nobles to keep watch there.

[Col. 0693C] The third dawn had poured Hyperion out upon the retreating stars. The nobles gather, surrounded by soldiers, and on a constructed mound they establish a tribunal and crown the sorrowful man of the camp with a neck-ring, granting him the insignia of kingship.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] A mound of earth raised in the form of a tribunal, which Vopiscus in *Tacitus* calls a turf tribunal. We also read that others were crowned with a neck-ring in place of a diadem, including Julian at Paris and Firmus in Africa, whom Marcellinus mentions in books XX and XXIX, and others such as Hypatius at Constantinople, mentioned by Marcellinus under the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes. Concerning Julian, Socrates writes: “When a royal crown was not present, one of the spearbearers took his own twisted neck-ring, which he wore around his neck, and placed it upon Julian’s head.”]

He had already assumed only the cares of the prince. No differently once did the Tirynthian hero take upon himself the weight of heaven, as soon as the Giant withdrew beneath the Libyan rock and the structure sat more securely upon Hercules’s back.

I have given him to you, Rome, while Gaul resounds with applause in its open fields for Augustus, and the fortunate uproar carries the louder North Wind against the bloodless South Wind.

[Col. 0694A] He will restore Libya to you through its fourth chains. And since he alone, after many ages, brought back the lost Pannonias, it is now easy to believe what he will do in war. O what peoples he will often yoke to your wounded eagles! He, who as a private citizen fled the greatest omens of empire, when, by chance on a journey, he cast off the common cloak of the people.

But now, made happier by such a prince, ancient Rome, mother of the gods, lift your cheeks and lay aside your shameful torpor. Behold, this greater prince will make you young again, whom boys had made old. His father had scarcely ended his speech when the gods applauded and a roar ran through the assembly: the Sisters of Fate spun a happy age for your commands, Augustus, and for the year of your consulship they drew out the golden centuries on their revolving spindles.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] After being raised to imperial power and summoned to Rome, as we said from Idatius, Avitus, I think, diverted his journey through Trier, where the events occurred that Aimoinus relates concerning the wife of Lucius Senator, book I, chapter 3. From there he crossed into Germany and Noricum and, as Sidonius seems to imply, recovered Pannonia from the barbarians without arms. Received at Rome as emperor, he entered upon the consulship, under the auspices of which this panegyric was delivered. What Idatius adds concerning the envoys sent to Marcian and Marcian’s agreement with Avitus must be understood as occurring after Avitus entered upon the consulship, since we have shown that other men were consuls in the East.]

## Poem VIII. Edition of the Panegyric

[Note: [Col. 0694D] This poem is an edition of the preceding panegyric; for this reason it is placed before it in the ancient books, as I noted in the commentary on poem 3. Concerning Valerian and the bronze statue of Sidonius, see partly letter 10 of book V and partly the last letter of book IX.]

### To Priscus Valerianus, Prefect

Priscus, ever our glory, to whom lofty purple under Emperor Avitus joins a kindred lineage,

when my trifles run alongside yours for examination, I say: “Stop, wandering verses—where are you hurrying? He loves them.”

A censor always exacting, yet a loving friend, is at hand: with a stern brow he reads, though in gentle friendship.

It does no good to add to the poets’ praises that the Ulpian portico gleams with my bronze, or that, while the people and Senate still applaud together, hollow Rome echoes “bravo” for my work.

They reply: “We shall hurry, we shall go, and you will not hold us back; guilt pleases so great a judge.”

351 No examiner is better than this one; he weighs poems well, with slow contempt and swift judgment. And since I could not restrain my rash words, I ask you—do not hesitate—to dedicate these poems once you have read them; I ask this of you.

## Poem IX

[Note: [Col. 0694D] 136 This poem is the prologue, or a kind of preface, to the remaining poems that follow. Felix had asked Sidonius to gather into one book and publish the little poems he had written on various occasions. Although he knew how serious it would be to submit himself to another’s judgment, he could not fail his friend’s wish. He therefore excuses his edition by his eagerness to obey; hence the title of the poem in the ancient books: “An Apologia to the Illustrious Felix.” Felix is the man to whom we have seen several letters addressed, the son of Magnus, the consul known from Majorian’s banquet, from whom he also took his name, for he was called Magnus Felix. He was not consul, however, but only prefect of the praetorium and patrician. Before reaching the consulship, he left the world and embraced a religious life. At that time Faustus, bishop of Riez, wrote to him the notable surviving letter in which he gives a form of penance to the recently ἀποταξαμένῳ, “one who has renounced the world.” Gennadius writes of Faustus: “Afterward he wrote to Felix, prefect of the praetorium and a man of patrician rank, the already religious son of the consul Magnus, a letter exhorting him to the fear of the Lord, appropriate to persons who have resolved with full purpose to practice repentance.” He also mentions both men distinctly in the *Propemptic*.]

### An Apologia to the Illustrious Felix

Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius sends abundant greetings to Felix, his lord and pious brother.

Tell me, tell me what I ask, Magnus, please tell me—

Felix in name, mind, honor, reputation, children, [Note: [Col. 0695D] Attica by name. She seems to be the woman concerning whom there was once an old inscription at Rome in the church of Saint Lawrence in Damasus, where she had built some work at her own expense:

“Whoever seeks the mysteries of God with a mind filled by him,

come here: the sacred house stands open.

These are buildings always devoted to pious fear,

and here God lends an ear to prayers.

Therefore hasten to restrain your deadly passions;

hasten now, joyfully, to enter the holy doors,

so that you may lay down the sins of your past life

and whatever guilty error contains of crime.

Attica, most illustrious wife of Felix Magnus,

built this work at her own expense.”]

wife, brothers, father, the brothers of your father and mother, and your excellent cousin Camillus—

why do you order the rash trifles of a friend, scattered by the playfulness of tender youth, to be reduced to the form of a little book? Why suddenly gather a huge bundle of envy and destroy the page?

I obey your commands, but first I warn you of the rough places you will endure here as reader.

We do not run along an ancient embankment, nor will you find anything here where Thalia wears down the old tracks of earlier poets.

Here we shall not sing of the antipodes or the Red Sea,

[Col. 0695B] 352 nor of the Memnonian Indians, scorched by the civic torch of Dawn.

Not Artaxata, Susa, Bactra, or Carrhae; I shall not sound forth Babylon, baked by the sun, which, open to its nourishing river, drinks the Tigris enclosed between its banks on either side.

[Note: [Col. 0696C] Rather, the Euphrates, as all the historians and Propertius in book III report:

“And he who founded the citadels led the Euphrates through their midst.”

Therefore he has put the Tigris in place of the Euphrates.]

Here I shall not proclaim ancient Nineveh of the Assyrians, nor Arbaces, head of the Medes; nor how Sardanapalus, when fleeing the enemy, burned upon a pyre rich in its own ashes.

I shall not speak of Cyrus, grandson of Astyages, whom they say was nourished at a bitch’s breast, whose rapacity not even the Lydian wealth of Croesus could satisfy, whose savagery was not subdued even when two hundred thousand had been slain—

[Col. 0695C] forced into the narrow valley of Scythia, when he came to the water-skin of bereaved Tomyris.

I shall not sing of Cecropian laws or triumphs, nor of the battle in which Marathon reddens, nor of the time when Xerxes, swollen with the multitude of his numbers, stirred up a thousand thousands, and, after the rivers had been rapidly drained because they were deep enough, was still thirsty; nor of Thermopylae and the waters of the Hellespont, when, scorning the barriers of land and sea, he rode with mad squadrons and, having driven the swelling sea through Athos, went beside the summit of the leafy mountain through caverns carved for ships.

353 Not the offspring of the Garamantian thunderer, ruling over kings and princes—

[Col. 0696B] …

[Note: [Col. 0696C] He will speak of the rapidity with which Alexander subdued so many nations. Apelles painted Alexander as *κεραυνοφόρον* (“thunderbolt-bearing”), holding a thunderbolt. Although this could be referred to the fabulous ancestry from Jupiter his father, it is nevertheless clear that nothing ever suited him more aptly than the thunderbolt when, to use Papinius’ phrase, he “thundered” at his rising and setting—that is, overwhelmed men with equal swiftness and violence. Therefore our sacred interpreters teach that Daniel the prophet [Col. 0696D] compared Alexander of Macedon to a winged leopard, because that species of beast is exceedingly swift, and, as Jerome observes, nothing was swifter than Alexander’s victory.]

I shall speak of the lands of Asia, which the paternal thunderbolt traversed in flight,

and first struck down the tumultuous prefects and satraps of Darius; then he forced Darius himself, proud upon his fathers’ throne and boasting of gods akin to himself, to return to the condition of a man, after his wife, children, and parent had been captured.

Although he had stirred up the greatest wars, and had marshalled the whole of Persia’s gathered forces from every direction into a single field, he is said to have achieved only this: that he might sleep more comfortably for his enemy.

[Note: The Argonauts. Sidonius also observes a chronological sequence in mythical matters. For if you follow the narrative from the Argonauts, where he begins, to the Odyssey, with which he ends, he tells everything in the same order in which the events are imagined to have occurred. He therefore uses a chronological method (*χρονικὴ μέθοδος*). Lucian, however, content with a topographical method (*τοπικὴ*), in the dialogue *On Dancing*, after the matters concerning the gods—which he mentions first—divided the rest of mythology according to places and regions: Attic, Theban, Corinthian, Ethiopian, Laconian, Elean, Arcadian, Thessalian, and the others which he pursues along this thread. He assigns the Argonauts to Thessalian mythology: “the Argo, and its talkative keel” (*τὴν Ἀργὼ, τὴν λάλον αὐτῆς τρόπιν*).]

I shall not speak of the Minyans carried in the talking ship, nor of how they stood in the Phasian harbor,

when the heroine, stirred by the beauty of the Pelasgian leader, softened the savage bulls;

nor of how she was frightened even then, when her own farmer, after the dragon’s teeth had been sown,

trembling, watched an armed enemy spring forth into grain amid the hostile grasses,

and, with the ears of grain fighting on every side, saw brothers dripping with green blood above the warlike soil.

I shall not speak here of the earth-born band,

made more vigorous by the admixture of magic poison,

whose bodies, apart from their merely superficial appearance, lacked only this:

their serpents, with their massive coils,

extended high their scaly legs,

and ended in jaws in place of feet.

[354]

Thus the insolent youth of triple form, trampling the earth with ravenous feet,

ran with a gait terrifying for the number of their heads;

and when the trumpets of the divine powers sounded,

then, with a hiss answering the thunderclaps,

they dared to summon the gods with their feet.

Nor shall I enlarge upon the fields of Phlegra,

while mountains hurled through the stars fly forth—

Pindus, Pelion, Ossa, Olympus, Othrys—

with their woods, flocks, wild beasts, frosts,

rocks, springs, and towns lifted up,

brandished by a more spacious right hand.

[Note: He enumerates twenty-three labors of Hercules, and no fewer in poem 15. For the twelve that are celebrated were the principal and legitimate ones, imposed by Eurystheus; besides these there were very many works which the Greeks call *πάρεργα τῶν ἄθλων* (“subsidiary deeds to the labors”). Here, however, he mentions only eleven *athloi*, omitting the Augean stable, which Eurystheus himself is said not to have approved; but twelve *parerga*, among them the giant Alcyoneus, the host Busiris, the Libyan Antaeus, the paired peaks Calpe and Abyla, the maiden Hesione, and the wrestling river Achelous. The rest are better known.]

[Note: Their form is, if one considers the matter itself, twofold for giants; if their number, threefold: for they were human as far as the waist, but serpents in the rest; yet each had two serpents corresponding to the number of his feet. Hence Sidonius speaks of “triple form,” and Claudian of the triple soul of the giant Porphyrion slain by Mars: “And with one blow he kills three souls,” because two were in the feet and the third in the remaining body.]

I shall not cultivate here the labors of Hercules,

for whom the boar, hind, lion, giant, Amazon,

guest, bull, Eryx, birds, Lycus, and thief,

[Col. 0697C]

Nessus, Libs, the mountain passes, apples, maiden, serpent,

the Getan, Thracian horses, Iberian cattle,

the wrestling river, the three-formed dog,

and the pole he carried, gave a pole.

Nor shall I pursue in verse noble Elis with its chariots,

nor the river, no less famous for its love,

so that Alpheus might flow beneath the depths of the sea

and the overseas water fall into the waves of its marital beloved.

[Note: This is more correct than the reading in the common editions, *notam nimis*. He says that Elis is no less famous from the fabulous loves of Alpheus and Arethusa than from the Olympic games. Lucian also mentions both. But he assigns the story of the river Alpheus—“the love of Alpheus and his subterranean journey” (*Ἀλφειοῦ ἔρωτα, καὶ ὕφαλον ἀποδημίαν*)—not to Elean but to Arcadian mythology, since, although Alpheus flows past Elis, he takes his source and first course from Arcadia.]

Nor shall I reopen the house of Tantalus,

where, through their common ancestor Pelops,

the offspring became one another’s sister,

and the father, by a new monstrosity, produced an infamous grandson.

[355]

Nothing mournful is sung here; we do not compose laments over the edible feast of Thyestes,

who, in the crime against his brother, became a living tomb for the devoured pledges of kinship.

When, after these dishes, the setting Titan suddenly turned his chariot around toward the east,

he fled from the banqueter and drove the day into flight.

Nor shall you read here of the Phrygian shepherd,

who is said to have covered Dindymus with a fleet after its summit had been cut away,

when, under the protection of Venus,

he ravaged the lands of Oechalia and hospitable Amyclae,

seeking across the sea a following prey.

Nor shall I pursue Pergamum, nor the ten-year war,

nor the savage ranks of Agamemnon,

nor the perjuries of Sinon,

by which the citadel dedicated to the Palladium,

opened by the treacherous betrayer,

received the horse carrying infantry.

[Col. 0698B]

I shall not tell, in the style of the Maeonian Muse,

the courage and wisdom of the citizen of Dulichium and of Thessaly.

One of them is thought to have been trained in the cave of Pelion,

in hunting, music, wrestling, and herbs,

under an old man born of Saturn.

Now, as a boy, he traverses the lairs of wild beasts

and lies scattered across snowy Pholoe;

now, reclining in the beloved stalls,

he sleeps more softly upon his master’s mane.

[356]

Then, given to the parent of the Scyrian women,

he bore the name of false Pyrrha,

and moved hidden thyrsi among the choruses

of stern Minerva.

Finally, he was drawn away by the sound of the Phrygian theft,

by praises of Hector, who was destined to be dragged away.

But not even Smyrna’s volume adequately unfolds the story of him who was granted, in the fourth five-year period after leaving Ithaca, to return to his fatherland.

For who could continue recounting those labors

which land and sea imposed upon him?

The theft of the Palladium, the discovery of Achilles,

the capture of Dolon by swift feet,

and the dragging away of Rhesus’ snowy chariots

before they drank the waters of the Xanthus;

and the quiver also, which the protecting god

gave to you, Philoctetes, after it had been taken away?

Ajax son of Telamon, raging,

because, while he pleaded his case before the ships,

he eloquently carried off the prize of the contest?

Polyphemus avoided from that point, and Circe,

and the hunger of the Laestrygonian tyrant?

Then the orchards of wealthy Calypso,

the Sirens pleasing to those who were perishing,

the darkness avoided, and Nauplius’ beacon,

and the rapid groin of voracious Scylla,

or the Charybdis of Tauromenium,

which hollows out the rocks in the depths after belching forth the sea?

[Note: Minucius Felix calls “municipal gods” those consecrated with a distinctive cult in individual cities or provinces. Tertullian, *Apology* 24, Lactantius, book 1, and Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* 2, likewise compile catalogues of them. Sidonius, with his characteristic brevity, has enclosed two in each line; an old epigram assigns one to each, as follows:

“To you, Jupiter, Dodona is sacred;
to Juno, Samos; and Mycenae to Dis.
Taenarus belongs to the lord of the waters and sea.
Pallas guards the Cecropian citadels;
Pythian Apollo, Delphi, the navel of the world;
Delia, Crete and the Cynthian hills;
Faunus, Maenalus and the Arcadian woods.
Blessed Rhodes is the Sun’s protection;
Gades, Hercules’; and watery Tibur;
snowy Cyllene, the swift god’s.
Sultry Lemnos is more pleasing to the slow god.
The daughters-in-law of Aeneas frequent Ceres.
Oyster-rich Cyzicus worships the goddess who was carried off;
Cnidos and Paphos, beautiful Venus.”]

I do not sing of the special gods who favor

particular fields, cities, and islands:

[357]

Saturn for Latium, Jupiter for Crete,

Juno for Samos, and the Sun for Rhodes,

Persephone for Henna, Minerva for Hymettus,

Vulcan for Lipara, Dione for Paphos,

Perseus for Argos, Priapus for Lampsacus,

Evoe for Thebes, Vesta for Ilium,

Delian Apollo for Tymbra, the Arcadian for Lycaeus,

Mars for the Thracians, and Diana for the Scythians—

gods whom dedicated temples made divine,

through incense, salt, grain, sacrificial meal,

or the consecration of superfluous ceremonies.

[Note: The reference is to Ceres. Firmicus Maternus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 7: “He came to a place in Attica. There, received as a guest, she distributed to the inhabitants wheat previously unknown to them. The place received its name from the woman’s homeland and arrival. For it was called Eleusis because Ceres, having left Enna, had come there.” But Sidonius calls “venerable Eleusis” not the Attic city in which Ceres was worshiped, but Ceres herself, following Claudian, book 1 of *The Rape of Proserpine*: “And Eleusis raises the sacred torches; the serpents of Triptolemus hiss.”]

Nor do I sing of venerable Eleusis with Triptolemus,

who gave the first ears of grain to the peoples

fed through the Chaonian oak grove.

[Note: The proper god of the people of Memphis. Clement of Alexandria, in the *Protrepticus*, among the irrational animals (*ἄλογα τῶν ζώων*) consecrated by the Egyptians “village by village and city by city” (*κωμηδὸν καὶ κατὰ πόλεις*), assigns the ichneumon to the Heliopolitans, the sheep to the Saïtes and Thebans, the wolf to the Lycopolitans, the dog to the Cynopolitans, the goat to the Mendesians, and Apis to the Memphites—that is, in the language of the Egyptians, the bull. Tibullus, book 1, elegy 7, identifies him with Osiris:

“Barbarous youth sings of you, and marvels at his own Osiris,

taught to mourn the Memphite bull.”

Plutarch likewise reports, from priestly mysteries, that Apis is the soul of Osiris. From Osiris and Apis, moreover, King Sesostris made Serapis, as Clement likewise relates. Therefore Serapis, Osiris, and Apis are one and the same god of the Memphites.]

Nor shall I sound the Memphite Apis

as he is stirred by Mareotic sistrums.

[Col. 0700A]

Nor shall I say that the youth of Lacedaemon

dedicated their contests to the anointed Tyndarids,

whom the gymnasium of Therapnae, trained in their ancestral contests,

and the Bebrycian theater trembles to behold.

Nor shall I speak of the Lycian and Caerite lots,

[Note: Following Virgil’s example, “Lycian lots” means another kind of oracle, delivered through Apollo in Lycia. The Caerite lots, however, were properly lots, as were those of Praeneste, Antium, Falerii, and Aponus: namely wooden tablets inscribed with letters, consulted in place of an oracle. Plutarch calls them *γραμματεῖα* (“written slips”) when discussing the Falerian lots in his *Life of Fabius*. Those who employed this procedure were said to act “with the lots lifted.” An ancient Milanese inscription reads: *SACRO SUSCEPTO, SORTIBUS SUBLATIS*—“the sacred rite having been undertaken, the lots having been lifted.” Cicero, *On Divination* 2, says of the Praenestine lots: “From that olive tree an ark was made, and in it were deposited the lots which today are drawn at Fortune’s prompting.”]

nor of the earlier responses of Themis at Delphi.

[Note: Following Virgil’s example, he means another kind of oracle, one delivered through Apollo in Lycia. The lots of Caere, however, were properly lots, like those of Praeneste, Antium, Falerii, and Aponus: wooden tablets inscribed with letters, which they consulted in place of an oracle. Plutarch calls them *γραμματεῖα* when discussing the Falerian lots in his *Life of Fabius*. Those who used this method were said, after the lots had been lifted, to undertake an action. An ancient inscription at Milan reads: “After the sacred offering had been received, the lots having been lifted.” Cicero, *On Divination* 2, concerning the Praenestine lots: “An ark was made from that olive tree, and in it were placed the tablets which today are lifted at Fortune’s instruction.”]

Nor of the first one of all, who is imagined to have prophesied at Delphi

and to have taught Apollo himself. Orpheus says in a hymn:

“She first revealed to mortals the holy oracle,

giving judgments to the gods in the hidden place of Delphi,

in the Pythian sanctuary, where she first made Pytho queen;

she also first taught Phoebus the lord the pronouncements of divine law.”

Nor of what the Etruscan augur, after expiating the lightning,

sought from the gods enclosed within the bidental.

Nor of those whom the augur saw on the Antenorean hill,

while drinking the Euganean Timavus,

to stir up the Thessalian battle.

[Note: Cornelius was a priest who is said, while absent, to have suddenly seen with a disturbed mind an image of the battle at Pharsalus at the very hour when it was being fought, and to have announced it. See Lucan, book 7; Gellius, book 15, chapter 18; Julius Obsequens, chapter 64: “C. Cornelius, the Patavine augur, on that day, when the birds were being admitted, proclaimed that the battle was taking place and that Caesar was winning.”]

Nor of those gods whom Amphiaraus and Melampus

snatched from the very ashes,

while the flame flickered disastrously through the temple,

Metellus rejoicing in the light after its destruction.

[358]

Nor shall Ammon of Cinyphus be sung here,

raising his turbaned head above the sands,

scarcely accustomed to bring forth, after the hecatomb had been sacrificed,

his ritual offering from the abyss of the Syrtes.

[Note: This is the reading of a manuscript of excellent quality. It should have said *hecatomboeum*, which is *ἑκατόμβοιον*, as in Euboea, Stheneboea, and Boeotia. But since in the diphthong *oi* it is customary sometimes to remove the latter letter—as *ποίημα*, *poema*; *ποιητής*, *poeta*—so, conversely, it was not unusual in a later age to elide the first. Thus we read in Ausonius *solicismus*, and below, in poem 15, *miras*, and in the panegyric to the Aedui, *meticos*, where the Greek forms are *σολοικισμός*, *μοῖραι*, and *μέτοικοι*.]

Nor shall I describe Dindymus,

nor the Curetes sounding Berecynthian music with creaking boxwood,

nor Bacchus displaying the triennial rites,

nor the frenzied Bassarids moving in festive madness,

nor the veiled initiates whirling the sacred objects

around the altar fragrant with incense.

Nor shall you see here the rich Ascraean poems of Hesiod,

or the strings of Pindar.

Nor the jokes of sandal-wearing Menander,

nor the savage iambics of wounded Archilochus,

nor the weightier Muse of Stesichorus,

nor what the Lesbian girl composed.

Nor what stubborn Mantua added to Homer

in Latin speech,

at times enviously making Parthenope equal to its own

Maronian tomb.

Nor what Flaccus wished to make resound

through the satires of his epistles,

the wit of his conversations, his new epode,

his books of lyric poetry, and his poetic art,

written in praise of Phoebus and wandering Diana.

Nor what your Papinius, and mine,

sang amid the furies of the Labdacids,

or when, in a shorter rhythm of the feet,

he paints gem-like meadows of little groves.

[359]

[Note: Of the same men, Martial says in book 1, chapter 62, to Licinianus:

“Two Senecas and the one Lucan

are eloquently spoken by Corduba.”]

Nor should you think that Corduba, powerful in her foster-sons,

rouses here the eloquent man to be read.

One of them honors shaggy Plato,

and admonishes his Nero in vain.

The other shakes the orchestra of Euripides,

following Aeschylus, painted with filth,

or Thespis, accustomed to resound on wagons,

who, after the worn stage beneath the tragic buskin,

led out the male goats, stinking.

That third man spoke of the battle of Gallic Caesar,

how father-in-law and son-in-law drove Rome,

their kinship notwithstanding, into arms.

He gives such tears to his own Philippi

that he thinks the fall of Cremera light,

and judges the Allia worthy of even greater grief,

and considers Jupiter redeemed on the scales of Brennus.

He places Trebia and grievous Cannae afterward,

and does not mention the slaughter at Trasimene.

He is ashamed that the Scipio brothers should be passed over in silence,

whom the Tartessian world holds back.

Let him be silent about the Euphrates attacked without success,

and about Carrhae wet with the blood of the Crassi;

or about those whom you, Spartacus, used to drive away

from the consuls’ swords with your victorious dagger.

Let him not mourn even more deeply that very conflict

which, after the Cimbric trophies had been thrown into confusion,

and Jugurtha of the Nasamones had been bound,

Sulla of Arpinum wished to stir up

while seeking the Mithridatic triumph.

[Note: Greek epigrams by Lentulus Gaetulicus survive in the *Anthology*. Martial numbers him among the lascivious poets, while Pliny numbers him among serious men who wrote playful works, book 5, letter 3. Sidonius also mentions him in book 2, letter 10. The same Martial likewise numbers Domitius Marsus and Pedo among epigram writers. Of Marsus nothing remains today apart from a fragment of the *Cicuta*; several elegies of C. Pedo Albinovanus are read; and of Sulpicia, whom Martial also praises in book 10, there survives a single satire on the time of Domitian.]

Nor shall Gaetulicus be read here for you,

nor Marsus, Pedo, Silius, or Tibullus.

Nor what the Muse of Sulpicia composed as a jest,

writing sweetly flattering words to her Celenus.

Nor the severity of Persius, nor the charm of Propertius,

nor Terence’s measured verse.

Lucilius and Lucretius are not here.

Nor Turnus, Memor, Ennius, Catullus,

Stella, Septimius, and Petronius,

nor Martial, biting without end.

[Note: They were brothers and poets of the age of Vespasian: one tragic, the other satirical; see Martial, book 11, chapter 11. An old commentator on Juvenal gives a distich of Turnus from his satire; Fabius Fulgentius, *On Ancient Speech*, cites a tragedy of Hercules by Scaeva Memor. Papinius sang the praises and wedding poem of the poet Stella. Sidonius again mentions the lyric poet A. Septimius in his letter to Polemius, poem 14.]

Nor he who, in the time of the second Caesar,

dwelt forever in Tomi under perpetual exile,

nor he who, later, under a similar misfortune,

was exiled at the faint murmur of the common people

by the anger of an actor.

[Note: Juvenal. Thus he identifies Ovid by the place of exile; Juvenal by the author of his misfortune, the pantomime Paris; and Claudian by his Egyptian homeland and by the subject of his poem, the rape of Proserpine.]

Nor he born at Pelusian Canopus,

who sings of the couches of the iron-hued husband

and, with an upper Muse, of the underworld.

Nor those who, in the first period,

were once the greatest companions of our fathers.

[Note: The name of this poet of Cahors, who attached himself to Count Boniface and his son-in-law, is unknown. He calls Sebastian “headlong” because of his varied and sudden policies, which he often changed. First, according to Hydatius, after the death of Boniface, whom he had succeeded, he was driven from the court by Aetius and sailed to the court of the East. Then, after several years, when he began plotting a revolution, he was forced to flee and came to Gaul to Theodoric, king of the Goths, suddenly became his enemy, and attacked Barcelona. Expelled from there, he went to the Vandals and to Geiseric; by Geiseric he was eventually killed, not long afterward, with a happier end than his life had had, because of his hatred of the Catholic faith, as Victor writes.]

One of whom followed Boniface,

and also the headlong Sebastian,

the boy from Cahors detested his birth,

loving Pandionian Athens more.

If you read his varied poem,

you must not think that Phoebus, or the Hyantian maidens,

drunk and wet from Hippocrene,

then Amphion and Maia’s son,

then the Rhodopean poet,

were sounded in one and the same melody.

Nor shall you now read here you, nor your thunderbolt,

O Quintianus, most worthy of another Quintianus,

who, scorning the soil and household gods of Liguria,

loved Gaul after changing his home,

amid the standards, javelins, and squadrons,

praising Aetius and free for his book,

thrice crowned with ivy in the camp.

[Note: See whether this was Merobaudes. He was a poet, a Spaniard by birth, as they report, and son-in-law of Asterius, during whose consulship Sidonius’ father held the prefecture, and he was honored with statues. Hydatius, in his *Chronicle*: “Merobaudes, noble by birth and comparable with the ancients in eloquence, especially in the study of poetry, was sent as successor to Asterius, master of both military commands and his own son-in-law. He was advanced also by the testimony of statues.” A brief poem of his concerning Christ survives; it was published with other Christian poets.]

Nor shall that third man now be read,

who, once leaving his native Baetis,

went to Ravenna, thirsty amid its waters;

for whom the Romans, applauding his brilliance,

and the prince, beloved for his popularity,

[Col. 0703C]

placed a statue in the Forum of Trajan.

[Note: We learn from Sidonius himself, in his final letter and in poem 8, that statues were erected in this place; ancient published inscriptions show that others were erected elsewhere. To these may be added the following elegant inscription, not yet published, which we observed at Rome in the Montalto Gardens on the Esquiline:

“To Flavius Peregrinus Saturninus,

who from the first years of his youth labored for the state in peace and war; after constant military watches, military tribune; commander of the first rank; administrator of the distinguished imperial patrimony; second prefect of the city. Because of the evidence of his integrity of character and exceptional justice, the eternal emperors, by sacred judgment, conferred upon him the twin dignity of the distinguished urban prefecture, and, in consideration of his outstanding merits, ordered a shining statue, gilded, to be erected and set up in the Forum of the divine Trajan, to adorn the memory of posterity.”]

But do not compare with me such men,

whom I myself, though far inferior, love even more:

Paulinus, Ampelius, and Symmachus,

[Note: P. Pithoeus once informed us that some fragments of a longer work by L. Ampelius addressed to Marinus survive at Dijon in the library of St Benignus, and showed us its preface. Whether he was the same Ampelius as this one I shall not affirm.]

Messala, of sufficiently profound intellect,

[Note: I have no doubt that this is that charming poet whom Rutilius Namatianus praises, besides praising him for the splendor of his birth, honors, life, and letters, when discussing the Baths of Taurus in book 1 of the *Itinerary*:

“This land, celebrated in the poem of Messala,

also rivals the breathing places of the Pierian caves.

It receives the one entering and detains the one departing,

with a sweet poem fastened upon its sacred doors.

He is the one who traces his line from the first consul

to ancestors ennobled as far as the Publicolae.

He also governed the praetorian office at the prefect’s command,

but greater glory belongs to his mind and tongue.

He taught what dwelling eloquence requires:

whoever wishes to be good will be eloquent.”]

[Note continued: His praetorian prefecture, which he held during the consulship of Theodorus and the following year, is attested by various laws of the code; Symmachus likewise supports his other praises in book 7, letters 80 and following. An old Roman inscription calls him “Flavius Valerius Messala.”]

and no ordinary Martius Secundus,

[Note: He mentions Martius Myron at Narbo; but that man was a Gaul, whereas this one was Roman, and they must therefore be distinguished. The poet Villicus also requires investigation. The rest have already become known from other passages: Petrus, Majorian’s master of correspondence; Anthedius of Vesunna; Lampridius, rhetorician of Bordeaux; Leo, counsellor of Euric; and Julius Severianus, author of a handbook of rhetorical art.]

equal to the ancients in a new art of speech,

Petrus, astonishing whenever he speaks,

or the excellent Villicus,

whom the senate places above the municipal poets.

Nor shall I mention our own eloquent men,

whom their native land retains:

the sweet Anthedius and my teacher,

[Col. 0703B]

the highly esteemed Muses of Hoenius,

the keen Lampridius, the learned Leo,

and Severianus, outstanding on the trumpet,

and no less capable of writing

as Marcus Quintilianus was accustomed to do.

We, greatly lacking in the rhythms of the Muse,

believe these rare men unsuitable for a short page,

which properly ought to bear mackerel and pepper.

For what god will grant this to an outcast,

that, while receiving good fragrances,

he may preserve nard, and the rich alabaster jars

dyed with the juices of niceros,

Indian cinnamon taken from the pyre

on which the phoenix grows young by dying,

costus, malobathrum, roses, amomum,

myrrh, incense, and opobalsam?

Therefore protect my undertaking,

and, I beg you, defend the unguarded modesty

of your fellow student who obeys you,

but first remember to summon Germanus,

the pillar of learning,

[Note: The husband of Eulalia, to whom letter 1 of book 4 is addressed.]

who is able to apply himself well to close writing.

I know well, however, and do not deny the fault,

nor does an immodest poet please the learned.

Yet I shall not fear too much the swollen face

of a censorious reader,

if, as though you were a heavier and stricter

Cato Tetricus, rejecting the jest

of our Terpsichore,

you threaten a rhinoceros-like nose

with your wrinkled lip.

[Note: The older books read “the third.” Juvenal, satire 2: “The third Cato fell from heaven.” “The third Cato” is said in the proverbial manner in which Horace speaks of the “eighth of the wise men,” and Ausonius of “the ninth among lyric poets” and “the tenth of the Muses.”]

Do not let this excessively learned man frighten you:

but if you wish to test how great it is,

believe me, no one knows as much as he does not know.

[363]

POEM 10. PREFACE TO THE EPITHALAMIUM SPOKEN FOR RURICIUS AND IBERIA.

When, through the Pagasaean caves, the sea-dwelling bride of Peleus

unfolded festive celebrations beneath the Aemathian rock of Pelion,

the very ample equipment of the upper world narrowed the earth:

here the sky, there the sea, competed with their riches.

The father-in-law himself, nearly covered in a green garment,

led the dances, matching the azure cloak.

The bride too, coming naked from the whirlpool to the marriage chamber,

began to fear the limbs of her clothed husband.

Then every god who was present, putting fear aside,

played the part in which he was powerful.

Jupiter sent forth a warm thunderbolt without weight

and said, “Now Cytherea is warmer.”

Pollux then was praised for boxing, Castor for reins,

Pallas for her crests, Delia for her quivers.

Alcides played with his club, Mars with his spear,

the Arcadian with his staff, Bromius with his fawnskin.

The excellent Orpheus had also brought in the daughters of Pimpleia,

with strings, voice, hand, songs, and reeds.

Ambitious Hymen gathered all his arts there;

he pleased perhaps not by talent but by divine inspiration.

Yet the Fescennine verses were not admitted

until our Apollo thundered upon his customary lyre.

[364]

POEM 11.

[Note: I already explained in the note to letter 16 of book 4 that this Ruricius was the man who later became bishop of Limoges; this must be understood of the elder. There were two bishops of this see named Ruricius, one succeeding the other—that is, a grandson succeeding his grandfather. Fortunatus embraced both in a single epitaph, in which, among other things, he says:

“The twin flowers of Ruricius, through whom Rome,

joined to the ancestral summit of the Anicii,

rejoices:

linked in deed, mind, rank, hope, name, and blood,

grandfather and grandson exult together, one here, the other there.”

For this man, then, Sidonius sang this wedding poem when he took a wife among the Arverni. He married Iberia, daughter of Ommatius, a noble man; she later renounced worldly concerns, together with her husband Ruricius, in order to serve God more devoutly, as the letters of Faustus of Riez, 6 and 7, show.]

EPITHALAMIUM SPOKEN FOR RURICIUS AND IBERIA.

Between the Cyanean rocks, where the Ephyraean heights

raise Orithyia into the air above Ida,

the summit of the mountain eaten away by salt,

where, while fleeing the wandering Symplegad,

the frightened Tiphys fixed it,

and Malea, returning after belching it up, roared hoarsely,

a bay goes out from the rocky cliff toward the Isthmian sea,

its sides closed by the wings of rocks.

There, often, as though the whole light of heaven were gathering into one,

the collected day is narrowed,

and the hidden channel pursues the trembling waters;

the stream passes through, flooded with lofty brilliance,

and, in a wondrous exchange, the water drinks the sun,

while light, inserted into the thin current,

pierces the liquid with a dry ray.

Art has enlarged the space. For there the Lemnian god

played as though it were a temple for Venus,

and, abandoning the thunderbolt,

the iron Pyracmon often smoked there.

Here is a stone from five regions, displaying five colors:

[Note: He follows the Greek accent in *Aethiops*, not the quantity. The color of Ethiopian marble is purple. In the panegyric to Majorian: “Native purple breathed upon the scorched rocks,” and “stones dyed with their natural shell-purple,” book 2, letter 2. Phrygian, that is, Synnadic, marble is crimson and spotted. Statius, in *On the Bath of Etruscus*:

“Only the purple which, in the hollow cave of Phrygian Synnada,

Attis himself stained with shining spots.”

Parian marble is white. In the *Burgus of Leontius*: “I no longer desire glowing Parian marble.” Punic or Numidian marble is ivory-colored. In the same panegyric:

“Numidian stone is added to these,

imitating ancient ivory.”
