Laconian marble is green. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*:

“Which green Lacedaemon possesses, and spotted Synnada.”

Statius: “Here the hard stones of the Laconians are green.” Concerning all these, see also the *Burgus of Leontius*.]

Ethiopian, Phrygian, Parian, Punic, and Laconian stone—

purple, green, spotted, ivory-colored, and white (the verse lists both the marbles and their colors; the accompanying note supplies their individual identifications).

The golden brilliance of chrysolite flashes along the doorposts;

murrhine stone, sardonyx, amethyst, Iberian stone, jasper,

Indian, Chalcedonian, Scythian beryl, agate,

raise twin doors on silver hinges,

through which the shadow enclosed within pours out the light of emerald.

[365]

Thick onyx covers the thresholds, and nearby hyacinths

produce a harmonious blue color in the pools.

The outer surface is not a polished stone but rises high,

rough pumice worn by the continual beating of the waters.

Within, Mulciber imitated gold

on projecting crags spread broadly,

and, by the masterly art of his craft,

deceived uncultivated nature with immense ornament.

[Note: Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 1336, reads *ingenii cultu*, “by the cultivation of genius.”]

Engaged upon this work, which she had not yet learned—

the work for which she condemned him to Lemnian chains—

the scaly Triton carried Dione here through the waters,

between the boundaries where his twofold back comes together,

above the winding hollows of his twisted belly,

with its warm heart.

But Galatea, half-bestial, presses down his side

by the weight of the added radiant shell;

with a fixed finger she plucks it away

and, by a hidden touch, promises marriage.

Then, delighted, the lover smiles beneath the playful torment,

and already, sparing her, lashes his own sea-monster.

Behind him the troop of blazing Cupids advances.

One restrains a dolphin with roses;

another, carried upon a green bullock,

hangs from its horns, disregarding the reins;

others, standing, stagger with the movement,

slip upon their wet feet,

and steady the traces of their steps with fins.

She had lowered her soft face upon a bent arm;

the violets were fading,

and her neck, made heavier by sleep,

had begun to sink beneath the pressure of the flowers.

Only one of the brotherly band, the fairest of them,

was absent, Cupid, while he prepared a most celebrated festival for the Gauls,

[Note: Iberia’s father, to whom Sidonius’ poem 17 is addressed. His name was Ruricius, as was customary, and he later renewed it in his son. He gave his son the name Ommatius, as can be seen in his letter 18 of book 1 and 27 of book 2. From these passages it can also be inferred that Ommatius’ son was brought into the clergy while his father was still alive and was honored with the rank of priest.]

which Ommatius, the father-in-law,

greater than his great ancestors,

grandson of a patrician family,

was preparing under auspicious rites for his daughter and son-in-law.

[366]

Then, when that day perhaps shone,

he himself swiftly sought his mother in flight.

His torch, bow, and quiver hung there;

but he, head bowed and hanging at the edge of his left palm,

struck his balanced feet against the air with his wings,

thus plucking kisses from his mother

and, while she was sunk in sleep, lightly brushing her half-slumbering eyes

with his feather.

Then, more lively than before, he began:

“I bring new joy, mother, from a fortunate prize.

That proud Ruricius burns for our torches

and, touched by our sweet poison,

sighs in his heart with a pain that he wishes for.

If the present age still existed,

the Lemnian women would offer him sovereignty,

Crete the thread of its labyrinth,

Alcestis her life, Circe her herbs,

Calypso her apples,

Scylla her hair, Atalanta her feet,

Medea her madness,

Hippodamia her wax,

and the girl born from Jupiter in the form of a swan her crown.

Dido would go for him into the sword, Phyllis into the noose,

Evadne into the flames, and the girl of Sestus into the waves.”

To these words she replied:

“We rejoice, my son, that you overcome a rebellious man

and praise the man; but the girl has beauty.

Had the Stheneboean hero once seen her,

he would not, for contempt, have subdued the monsters of the Chimaera.

Nor would the man proud of his Thermodontian mother,

who rashly rejected the wishes of the Cnossian stepmother,

have died after seeing her—I admit it—but in a true accusation.

And if, perhaps, the fourth judgment had been mine,

the shepherd of Ida would have condemned me also,

the Rhœtean Paris.

[Note: Paris. He says that Paris would have preferred Iberia to Helen and, if given the choice, would have wanted her granted to him by me.]

“‘If you wish to conquer, give me this girl instead,’ he would have said.

I would have granted this beauty as the prize for beauty:

such dignity and divine grace are in her cheeks.

Compared with her blush, pale purple is hidden,

and her faces darken with the brilliance of jewels

fastened around her neck.”

[367]

Iberia would also have surrounded you with games of many kinds:

Pelops in the chariot, Hippomenes in the race,

Achelous in wrestling,

Aeneas in war, Perseus, displayed with the Gorgon.

Nor is the beauty of the woman less,

for whom Jupiter so often became

Delian Diana, bull, swan, satyr, serpent,

thunderbolt, and gold.

[Note: Diana, or, as in the epithalamium of Polemius, Dictynna:

“Now he changes Jupiter into the forms by which he was accustomed

to hold Mnemosyne, Europa, Semele, Leda, and Cynosura—

serpent, bull, thunderbolt, swan, and Dictynna.”

From this passage it is clear how each item here should be understood, except the satyr, which refers to Antiope. A Greek epigram reads:

“Zeus became a swan, a bull, a satyr, and gold through love

of Leda, Europa, Antiope, and Danae.”]

Come, then, let them be joined; for wealth, beauty, and birth

are in harmony: your fixed arrow has made nothing unequal here.

But why delay the vows? He spoke and called for his chariot,

whose yoke was furnished with crystals.

These, when the tender sphere of the earth was still in its first cold,

when ice enlarges Caucasus,

the Tanais crust had drawn together beneath Hyperborean frosts,

taking on the nature of a gem because it had lost that of water.

A shaft fashioned from yellow metal pierces it;

the river beneath whose current

the nymphs had warmed the Phrygian Midas,

who, poor in gold, enriched the streams of Pactolus

with wishes turned to reality,

had sent that metal.

The whole rim shines, encircled with transparent rays,

from the jaws of a Marmaric beast,

while the animal groans because its mouth,

its curved teeth torn out, has been stripped of its weapons.

The Indian sent this gift as well,

naked Erythras, warm and the color of an Ethiopian,

or the man who, rich in amomum,

agitates his flowing hair with fragrant hunts.

Yet she binds the swans accustomed to feed in Cyprus,

striped with myrtle,

and with their necks stretched out

their milk-white throats are curved by crimson coral.

Therefore they set out on their journey: the hanging wheel cuts through the empty air, and its orbit does not dissolve in the fluid expanse.

Here threefold grace accompanies them in a single bond. Here the abundance of Fortune breathes forth from her open horn; here Flora scatters everlasting flowers from her baskets; here Egyptian Osiris attends Sicilian Ceres; here Pomona carries her season-laden lap; here Pallas comes among the dripping winepresses and olive mills.

Here, marked by the dappled skin upon his side, Thyas, Indian Bromius, whirls the rites with Echion’s thyrsus. Here also that Corybas who revels in the caves of Mount Ida, already mutilated, grows hot again; from his hoarse throat the hollow pipes resound through their twin openings, proclaiming fire.

Thus they came to the bridal chambers: here are frankincense, nard, balsam, and myrrh; here the phoenix gives the cinnamon of a living pyre, even now breathing the warmth of the festival. Winter is already less cold, and things retaining the appearance of spring grant in this place what the seasons do not grant to the world.

Then the young man, embracing the right hand of the Paphian goddess and the right hand of the girl, sang the wedding rites in a few words, so that even the words themselves would cause no delay:

“Live out your years in harmony and happiness; may children be born to you, and grandchildren as well; and may a great-grandchild behold in his great-grandfather what he himself would wish.”

## POEM XII

### To the distinguished Catullinus, his close companion in military service, because he could not write a wedding song on account of the hostility of the barbarians

Catullinus, a distinguished man and familiar comrade of the author, is addressed in Letter 11 of Book I. Asked by him to write an epithalamium, he says that he cannot do so while among the Burgundians, in whose company he was living. He therefore calls them “long-haired,” as Lucan and Claudian do the other Germans. He also marks their harsh and unpleasant songs, such as Julian likewise attributes to the peoples beyond the Rhine in the *Misopogon*:

“I did indeed observe the barbarians beyond the Rhine, delighting in wild melodies fashioned from words, resembling the cries of harshly screaming birds, and rejoicing in songs.”

### A poem to Catullinus, because he could not write an epithalamium on account of the hostility of the barbarians

Why do you order me, even if I were able, to prepare a song for Dione, patroness of Fescennine verses, while I am stationed among long-haired troops and enduring Germanic speech, and am continually praising, with a gloomy expression, what the well-fed Burgundian sings, pouring sour butter over his hair?

Would you like me to tell you what breaks a poem? Since it has been driven away by barbarian plectrums, Thalia scorns the six-footed poetic measure, ever since she sees patrons seven feet tall.

[Note: Burgundio, Book IX, letter to Lampridius. Varro, in Book I of the *Hebdomads*, said that seven feet was the maximum height of the human body in its growth. Einhard, however, considered a proper height to be less than that. Thus he writes of Charlemagne: “He was of outstanding stature, though it did not exceed what was proper.” For it is agreed that his height was the measure of seven of his own feet.]

Happy are your eyes and ears, and happy, I should like to call, your nose, which at the first light of morning is not assailed by ten preparations of garlic and foul onions belched forth.

He is not besieged, like an old father’s aged parent or a nurse’s husband, before day has dawned, by so many and such huge Giants as even the kitchen of Alcinous could scarcely support.

But now the Muse is silent and holds the reins, having jested in a few hendecasyllabics, lest anyone call even these verses a satire.

[Note: As in the case of Paeonius, mentioned in Book I, Letter 11. The author is alluding to that poem. Thus he was writing this during the reign of Majorian.]

## POEM XIII

There is no doubt that this sharp and elegant poem in two meters was offered to Majorian when he came to Lyon after recovering that city. The matter is discussed in the *Panegyric*: “Indulgences are remedies for taxes.” Ennodius writes in the *Life of Epiphanius*: “He provided for the exhausted inhabitants of the city through the benefit of remedies.” The “heads” whose remedy he seeks are the taxes assessed upon individual persons. The ancient glosses define *tributum capitulare* as “a head-tax,” Greek *epikephalaíos phóros*, “a tax imposed by the head.” The panegyrist of the Aedui writes: “You remitted seven thousand heads, more than a fourth part of our revenues.” Sidonius asks that three taxes, which he owed in his own name or that of his people, be remitted to him.

### A poem in which he asked the emperor Majorian for relief from three head-taxes

Venerable antiquity declares that the son of Amphitryon earned the heavens while relieving the earth.

And although that grim hero broke, with his bare arm, the hoarse throat of the Cleonaean beast;

and although, with blazing sword, he scarcely struck down the Hydra, when death, doubled by the wound, produced two lives;

and although, carrying off the captive monster from the Erymanthian forest, he made the disarmed face of the savage boar laugh;

and although, tearing apart the smoky necks of the fire-bearing Fury, he at last ordered the straight-horned cattle to proceed;

let the bull, the hind, the giant, the guest, the wrestler, the Amazon, and the Cretan, together with the dog and the Hesperides, be memorials of the man.

Yet no combat was more famous than the one against Geryon, for whom alone he carried away a triple head after defeating him.

Such was Alcides once; but you, Tirynthian hero, are another—indeed, the foremost concern of the great God, the greatest among princes. The dragon, the stag, and the boar experienced you with equal arrows, when tooth, venom, and flight were powerless.

Suppose that we are Geryons, and that our tribute is a monster: take these three heads from me, so that I may live.

This suppliant servant has dedicated these prayers, awaiting a gracious and saving answer, that you may restore his homeland and, by relieving Lyon of its burdens, restore life to it amid its ruins.

Your own Sidonius makes this request of you.

So may purple, renewed with Sidonian dye, clothe you for many years.

So may, after the fifth year of your perpetual reign has been completed, the quinquennial celebrations be proclaimed with the lictors’ fasces.

[Note: From this it can be seen that quinquennial, decennial, and other celebrations of this kind were customarily held not at the beginning but after the final year of the period had been completed. This is also shown by a passage in Marcellinus, Book 15: “Constantius, wintering at Arles, after theatrical games and circus spectacles produced with lavish display on 10 October, which completed the thirtieth year of his reign.” For this designates the tricennalia. Majorian, however, reached only the beginning of his fifth year of imperial rule and did not complete it. Thus Sidonius’s hopes were in vain.]

So may the Sicambrian, his hair shorn, drink from the Vahalis after the swelling of both banks has been broken.

But if you will grant this to your poet, I shall consign it to the perpetual records to be read among all the triumphs you have won.

For now my talkative Muse is silent before the tribute, which, in place of Virgil and Terence, counts half-ounces and ounces of the treasury;

and she fears the hand and rope of Marsyas, who, from an ancient hatred of Phoebus, now threatens poets with hanging.

[Note: A statue of Marsyas stood in the Roman Forum, before which lawsuits were conducted. Horace refers to it in *Satires* I.6, “Marsyas must be visited,” and Martial in II.64:

“All the courts are seething with lawsuits;
Marsyas himself could become an advocate.”

Sidonius therefore cleverly says that Marsyas— that is, bail—must be feared by his poet if he delays the taxes, because Marsyas is hostile to poets on account of Apollo, who stripped the hide from the defeated Marsyas.]

Sidonius sends greetings to his Polemius.

While, after your departure, my dear Polemius, most loving brother, I was reflecting deeply with myself on how I might sing Fescennine verses in accordance with your wishes, a subject presented itself which, once completed, makes it easy to recognize that I have taken greater account of your learning than of your immediate purpose.

[Note: Savaro and Labbe read *valeret*.]

Accordingly, setting aside the tenderness of an epithalamium, I directed my style through the harshest and most rugged rules of philosophy. Their arrangement is such that the trifles themselves could not have been worked out without very many new words which— with the prior indulgence of many eloquent men—are especially familiar to you and to your fellow Platonists.

You may see whether certain ears, through ignorance, might rashly object to the mention of the center, proportion, intervals, climates, or the “wonders,” and think such matters unsuitable for a wedding poem.

[Note: See the note below on verse 66.]

But this I confidently affirm to a truly great consular man, and to the quaestorian Domnulus and the illustrious Leo: music and astrology, which are successive branches of philosophy below arithmetic, cannot possibly be designated without these terms.

If anyone despises them as Greek and foreign words, just as they are, let him understand that he must either refrain from discussing such an art altogether, or else recognize that he can say nothing about it in Latin—or at least nothing complete.

If anyone judges the matter to be otherwise than I assert, I gladly yield, though absent, to my detractors; but let those who disagree with my opinion know that they cannot condemn it without Marcus Varro, without Serenus—not Septimius but Sammonicus—and without Censorinus, who composed a distinguished volume on the birthday.

[Note: There are therefore two writers named Serenus. The first is Septimius Serenus, a lyric poet famous in the age of the Vespasians. He should not be separated from Serenus, as is commonly done when histories of ancient poets and their fragments are compiled, since Sidonius protests against this, as do Marius Victorinus in Book III of *On the Theory of Verse* and Terentianus himself, who calls him by both names and cites his little works on rural matters under Septimius, although others name their author Serenus.

The other is Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, who flourished in the time of Severus Augustus and, as Lampridius reports, was killed by his son Caracalla. He once had many books; now only one little book remains, written in verse, on medicine. Macrobius praises Sammonicus’s books of *Hidden Matters* in Book III of the *Saturnalia*, and it is likely that Sidonius means these here.

He left a son of the same name, Serenus Sammonicus, tutor to the younger Gordian, to whom, at his death, he bequeathed his father’s library, said to contain 62,000 books.

This has had to be explained at greater length because some people, through the opposite error from that made concerning Septimius Serenus, confuse this man with Sammonicus the father.]

You are also going to read here a new word, namely *essentia*, “essence”; but know that Cicero himself used this word.

[Note: Seneca also maintained that the word *essentia* belonged to Marcus Tullius, as Muretus correctly observed at the end of Book XV of the *Variae*. He immediately afterward judged that *indolentia*, “freedom from pain,” should be written not *indoloria*, because Cicero used the former more than once. Yet, although we have examined several ancient books of Sidonius, we found *indolentia* in only one; in all the others we found *indoloria*. This word is also said to occur in certain ancient manuscripts of Cicero, Book II of *On Ends*, where the common editions read *indolentia*.]

For Cicero called both *essentia* and *indoloria* by these names, adding: “It is permissible to impose new names upon new things.” And he spoke correctly. For just as from what is, for example, “to know” and “to understand,” we derive the nouns “knowledge” and “understanding,” so from what is “to be” we regularly do not refrain from saying “essence.”

Therefore, since the love I bear you has led me, a Gaul, to introduce material from the sophistic school, I ask you especially to be the advocate of my undertaking. Let those to whom such praise is suitable assign Venus, or the invented pigments of Love. Farewell.

## POEM XIV

### Preface to the epithalamium addressed to Polemius and Araneola

A fortunate day flashes for the marriage,

which kind Clotho marks with snow-white threads;

which the white pebble of the dark Indian,

which the tree of peace together with youth,

and the ever-green olive, may mark forever.

Come, Calliope, with shining palm,

grant me eloquence from the sacred stream,

the stream Pegasus struck with his flying hoof,

his mane wet with kindred venom.

Here there is no impiety, nor does the rivalry of suitors

give this girl over to death.

Here, in the bloody circus of Oenomaus,

Pelops does not hear the terms of his pact,

nor does pale Hippomenes, as the third apple falls,

delay Schoeneus’s daughter at the bottom of the turning-post.

Here astonished Calydon, from its Aetolian citadel,

does not behold the Herculean contests,

when Alcides was pressing down the horn

of the proud river, then repeatedly restoring

his weary breast from the watery enemy.

But a learned young man and a graceful maiden,

born of families holding the heights of Gaul,

are joined. Quickly, goddess, weave the cords;

and do not force our poverty into silence

because a greater song has thundered before us.

Yet Phoebus approved the torches of Thetis,

and Chiron too sang them on a lesser plectrum.

Nor did the pious crowd laugh at the rustic singer,

although the two-formed old man often broke the song there

with a neighing melody.

## POEM XV

### Epithalamium addressed to Polemius and Araneola

Pallas, returning from the stormy promontory of Caphareus after sufficiently avenging the outraged chastity of the Trojan Phoebad, was exchanging Trojan Xanthus for Erichthaean Hymettus.

Her head gleams with golden bronze, and she receives

a greater calm from terror; for, having set aside her thunderbolt,

she had not yet gladdened her fierce limbs

with the Cinyphian Triton’s trumpet.

The Gorgon occupies the middle of her breast, destined,

when seen, to create delay even in the viewer;

the treacherous image shines above the proud breast,

and its beauty lives although its life has perished.

A tall mass roughens her dark head with coils of horned serpents;

the biting hair twists its spotted coils,

and the angry locks hiss horribly.

Her scaly breast does not reach the middle of her belly;

beneath the breastplate, a cloak hangs down;

her outer robe covers her feet with its slanting folds and circuit.

[Note: The garment’s oblique fold and circular course. This is the reading of the best manuscripts, and it seems more suitable than *limi*, as some read. *Limus* is a kind of garment described by Servius as hanging from the navel to the feet; it does not fit Minerva well, unless one wishes to call *limus* that part of her robe which alone appeared below the breast like a *limus*. Elsewhere also he used *circites* for “circle,” as Marius Victorinus does in Book III of *On the Rainbow*:

“I shall pour forth rays, and at the summit a beautiful
circle will adorn me with the curved image of the Sun.”]

Her robe, with its circular folds, reaches her feet; when they move beneath the garment, the crisp wrinkles of the stiff train rattle.

A shield covers her left hand, full of the Phlegraean tumult.

Here Enceladus whirls Mount Pindus, having shaken it loose, and brandishes it toward the stars;

Ossa becomes a missile for swift Typhoeus.

Porphyrion carries off the Pangaean mountain, and Adamasthor lifts Rhodope together with the Strymonian spring; then, coming down from above, he extinguishes the hot thunderbolt with a twisted stream.

Here Pallas attacks Pallas, who, after seeing the Gorgon, finds that her sluggish spear has already encountered a solid corpse.

Here Mimas, in place of his brother, turns Lemnos against the aegis and shakes the island, hurled as a missile, against heaven.

Here the huge Briareus fights with his many-limbed body, carrying a kindred army; from a single head you can see hands branching like limbs from a tree.

Mulciber gave the monsters not merely their shapes but madness as well, and he himself feared the very rages he had fashioned.

In her right hand she holds the spear which Pallas herself, having laid it down in the valley of Aracynthus, drew out again.

[Note: A mountain of Boeotia, from which the goddess is called Aracynthian. Rhianus writes:

“Listen to my prayers, Aracynthian daughter of a noble father.”]

This had stood as a guardian spirit, so that the Marathonian olive might keep firm the goddess’s slipping footsteps at the olive-presses.

Here two temples gleam. Above one of them rises a place which, in its worth, corresponds to its occupants: it contains men who investigate with reason the heights of heaven, what mechanism governs the sky, what the earth is, what the sea’s hollow is, what the troubled air is, how night and daylight alternate, how the monthly moon grows—and why equal losses follow equal increases.

At once the seven sages of old sit here, the beginnings of countless philosophers.

Thales, born at Miletus, condemns legal sureties.

You, Cleobulus of Lindus, command that the best measure be moderation.

You, Periander, meditating upon everything, adorn Corinth.

Then the Attic Solon approves the single principle that nothing be excessive.

Bias of Priene, you say that most people are wicked.

You, Pittacus, born at Mytilene, recognize the proper time.

Chilon of Sparta, you taught people to know themselves.

Here the Samian Pythagoras, after learned silence, maintains that the solid universe is governed by music, that it returns harmony from the ordered stars, and that the signs which the zodiacal circle holds three times four around its highest axis do not move with their own motion, but are nevertheless placed at equal distances from one another.

He also says that the fixed stars are carried along together with the celestial sphere, and that the seven wandering stars give forth a special song from this fact, since each of the two numbers is perfect: according to this number, he says, everything revolves in this order.

He teaches that old, sickle-bearing Cronos—Saturn—travels through the highest reaches of the heavens; that Jupiter’s star proceeds next to it, with Mars in the middle; that afterward the sun bends along the fourth path; that the gentle Paphian goddess occupies the fifth interval; Mercury the sixth; and the moon, in the highest orbit, travels nearly thirty degrees through the tropical region.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *moeras*, from Greek *moíras*, as in Censorinus, chapter 8. Indeed the sense requires this, and the Greek diphthong supports it. But this type of spelling has already been discussed above, in Poem IX, under *hecatombion*. Greek astronomers use both *moîrai* and *moría* for what the Latins call parts of signs and degrees. Ambrose writes in *Hexaemeron* IV: “They divide each of those twelve portions into thirty small parts, which they call *merídes*.”]

Therefore, if the lyre, the harp, or the flute has produced melodies with the voice, it follows the model of this arrangement, adopting intervals according to the weights established by proportion and following the sevenfold spacing produced by the stars.

He also calls this “harmony,” because the four elements are so arranged according to these principles that the heavier element has the lower position. Since the center of the earth is also the true middle, it is clear that it is the lowest part of a sphere; hence the lighter waters rise above the earth. Above these is the purer air; heaven encloses everything through the supreme lightness of its nature, and all of it hangs together from the origin of the center.

Here too Thales investigates by numbers and stars, predicting in advance the eclipse of Phoebus and the moon’s decline; but he proposes an unproductive first principle when he believes that the universe rests upon water.

The opinion of his disciple is reversed: he says that each thing is always created from its own principles.

He determines that some things have particular springs, eternally irrigated and full of the seed of things.

Another follows him, believing that this air gives birth to everything, and likewise asserting that the gods were born from it.

Anaxagoras, the fourth, preserves the doctrines of Thales, but perceives a divine mind that made the universe.

A younger colleague sits beside him; he too believes that air is the material of all creatures, and concludes that God fashioned all things from it.

After these, Arcesilas conjectures that this mass was prepared by a divine mind and composed of those parts which he himself calls light atoms.

[Note: He lengthened the second syllable, as Prudentius does the third in the tenth hymn in the case of *Hippocrates*, because in *Socrates* and *Hippocrates* they lengthened those same syllables in accordance with the Greek accent, Σωκράτης, Ἱπποκράτης. So too Maximianus, Elegy I:

“Men relate that in this contest also of the virtues great
Socrates once earned the palm.”

And Paulinus, author of the *Eucharisticus*: “The doctrines of Socrates and the martial creations of Homer.” Elsewhere Sidonius has other instances of this kind: *Aethiops* and *Euripides* with a long penult; and *Aratus*, *Phaedonis*, *diastema*, *mathesis*, *Heraclitus*, and *sapphirus* with the same syllable short.]

After him shines the Socratic school, which, abandoning the weight of nature, transferred its practice to the refinement of human morals.

They say that Plato cultivated this school to the highest degree, but shaped it in a threefold manner, joining physics first and alone to logic, and logic to ethics.

He first discovered the difference between the primary essence and the supreme and sixth good. For rocks are merely what they are and are proved to be nothing except being.

Next come things for which being and living are possible; you can add nothing more to a tree or a plant.

The third class is that of animals, whose being and living are accompanied by movement and sensation.

Then the fourth concerns mortal creatures, to whom are granted being, movement, life, and sensation, and above all these the capacity by which they understand and can distinguish truth from falsehood.

The fifth reveals the higher creatures as substance. Some have called them gods, because they assume bodies to be contemplated by human beings and shortly afterward leave them again,

returning to their own form, if indeed that form is the most subtle.

Thus it becomes clear that the highest substance is the Creator:

yet the sixth is above it—indeed, nothing is above it, but everything is beneath it.

In this school of Polemius, wisdom cultivates life and herself cherishes Plato, joined to her.

Although the Academy opposes this doctrine with all its schools and denies truth, she honors him with truthful praises.

After these come the Stoics: Chrysippus and Zeno, in agreement with one another, teach that their precepts must be observed.

The Cynics have already been almost excluded, but remain at the threshold; virtue drives the Epicureans out everywhere.

But on the other side, in the first workshop of Minerva, shines the robe of Pallas, whose twice-boiled threads the Sidonian purple shell dyed in its bronze vessel.

Nor does the scarlet shell merely breathe intoxication: it contains a lightning flash inserted within it, and the heavy thread blazed from a pregnant fragment of thunderbolt.

Here green Glaucus hung in his ancestral cloak.

Here the folds billowed through art, and the storm, with its feigned swelling, submerged ships with curved prows in the woven cloth.

A third garment rose for the son of Amphitryon.

Here the little boy, girded with his stepmother’s twin serpents, smiles unknowingly at the monsters; thinking them a game, he loves the ambushes while unaware of them, and with the expression of one grieving he mourns the snakes he himself kills.

Besides these, the following figures are set among the scattered designs:

the boar, lion, hind, giant, bull, mountains, Cerberus, Hydra, the guest, Nessus, Eryx, birds, the Thracian, Cacus, and the Amazon;

the Cretan, river, southwest wind, apples, Lycus, maiden, heaven, and Oeta.

The hands of the maiden made this work, and whatever remains whose names are unknown.

But throughout the entire company Araneola shines among the Cecropian and Ephyran girls. Minerva herself strives to match her hands, but, defeated by the baskets, withdraws; while Araneola holds these threads, Minerva wishes to hold even more.

Thus, imitating the stiff ceremonial robes of her great-grandfather, she herself prepares for her father the palm-embroidered robe by which he, becoming consul, may attain Agricola as his grandfather; and may teach his descendants that it is permitted to join not only their great-grandfather’s but also their grandfather’s fasces.

[Note: The previous wording had been confused: “the father who was consul.” Araneola’s great-grandfather, who was also her grandfather on her father’s side, was the consul Agricola. While weaving the palm-embroidered robe for her father, she hoped that he too would become consul, so that her future children might be able to name not only their great-grandfather but also their grandfather as consul.

Agricola was consul with Eustathius in the year 421, during the reign of Honorius. In the preceding years he had also administered the prefecture of the Gauls, as is clear from his edict, and from the edict of Palladius, prefect of Italy, concerning the exile of Pelagius and Coelestius, which is inserted in the ecclesiastical annals.

It is also clear from the imperial constitution addressed to Agricola, prefect of the Gauls, concerning the holding each year at Arles of the assembly of the seven provinces. This constitution was first published by Nicholas of Cusa in Book III, chapter 35, of *Catholic Concordance*, and by Joseph Scaliger in Book I, chapter 24, of his *Ausonian Readings*, though both gave it a false heading.

It is not, as Cusanus thought, an enactment of Constantine the Great, nor, as Scaliger believed, of the tyrant Constantine, but of Honorius Augustus. This is confirmed by Hincmarus in Letter 6 and by an ancient Arles manuscript, from which I obtained, through the kindness of the distinguished Nicholas Fabricius Peirescius, senator of Aix, a complete copy of the constitution. It is here appended because it contains several passages better and fuller than those printed previously.

### Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Agricola, prefect of the Gauls

Having been clearly instructed by the most salutary recommendation of Your Magnificence, among the other interests of the state, we decree with an authority that shall endure forever what our provincials—namely, those throughout the seven provinces—ought plainly to have expected.

Since private and public necessities require either the inhabitants of individual cities, and not merely of individual provinces, to come or to send envoys for examination before Your Magnificence or before the honorable officials, whether the advantage of the landowners or the proper administration of public duties demands it, we judge it especially opportune and useful that, while the custom is preserved from this point onward each year, the seven provinces should begin to hold a council at the appointed time in the metropolitan city, that is, in Arles.

In this we provide equally for individuals and for all. First, so that, through the assembly of the best men in the distinguished presence of the prefecture—if the arrangement of public administration should permit it—salutary deliberations may be held about individual matters.

Then, whatever is discussed and established after the accounts have been examined will neither be hidden from the more important provinces, nor can an equal form of equity and justice fail to be maintained toward those absent.

We also believe that, beyond public necessities, considerable benefit will accrue to human intercourse itself from the fact that we order a council to be held every year in the city of Constantina. For the place is so conveniently situated, the supply of trade is so abundant, and the number of travelers there is so great that whatever is produced anywhere can be sold there more advantageously.

No province, however, rejoices so greatly in the special fertility of its own produce that it does not acknowledge this fertility as belonging particularly to the soil of Arles. Whatever the rich East, whatever fragrant Arabia, whatever luxurious Assyria, whatever fertile Africa, whatever beautiful Spain, and whatever strong Gaul can possess that is excellent flourishes there in such abundance that it seems as though everything considered magnificent everywhere were born there.

Moreover, the course of the Rhône and the return-flow of the Tyrrhenian sea necessarily make neighboring and almost adjoining whatever the one flows past or the other surrounds.

Since the earth gives this city whatever it possesses that is most valuable, and since whatever each place produces is brought to it by sail, oar, wagon, land, sea, and river, how could our Gauls fail to think that great service has been rendered them when we command that an assembly be held in the city where, by a kind of divine gift, such abundant convenience for trade and commerce is provided?

Indeed, the illustrious prefect Petronius has already ordered that this be observed, in accordance with a plainly reasonable and approved policy. What has been interrupted either by the negligence of the times or by the indolence of tyrants, we decree should be restored through the authority of our wisdom, dearest and most beloved Agricola.

Accordingly, Your Illustrious Magnificence, following both this command of ours and the earlier arrangement of its seat, shall cause this to be observed perpetually throughout the seven provinces: from the Ides of August, on any intervening day, until the Ides of September, the honorable officials and landowners, together with the judges of the individual provinces, are to know that an assembly must be held each year in the city of Arles.

As for Novempopulana and the second Aquitania, which provinces are situated farther away, if a definite obligation should detain their judges, they are to know that envoys must be sent according to custom.

Through this arrangement we understand that we confer considerable favor and advantage upon our provincials, and it is clear that we add not a little to the honor of the city of Arles, to whose loyalty we owe much, according to the testimony and support of our father and patrician.

Your Magnificence shall also know that a judge is to be fined five pounds of gold, and honorable officials or curials three pounds, if they delay coming to the appointed place within the prescribed time.

Given on 17 April; received at Arles on 23 May. In the consulship of our lords Honorius Augustus for the twelfth time and Theodosius Augustus for the eighth time.

That was the Dionysian year of Christ 418.

In another manuscript at Auxerre, the same constitution is called an enactment; Hincmarus calls it an edict. From its own wording alone, even without other arguments, it is easy to conclude that it cannot be attributed to the tyrant Constantine, since it notes the indolence of that and other tyrants; nor can it belong to Constantine the Great, although he first gave the city of Arles the name Constantina, since in the period after his reign there were not only the prefects Petronius and Agricola, but also the division into seven provinces of Gaul.]

She had also woven cloaks in which he, as master of the army, shone conspicuously through the cities of Tartessus, and in which, once the time of his prefecture had been imposed upon him, he became conspicuous and, as prefect, rendered the sacred laws effective.

Yet on the ceremonial robe she had played with a broad ornamental band, illustrious with ancient scenes.

First the Ithacan story and the heroes of Dulichium are fashioned; she depicts Penelope herself weaving and unweaving her lingering web.

Here the Thracian man, having twice lost his wife, strikes Taenarus uselessly with his lyre after violating the law of Avernus, and, thinking that this would help, does not look back at the shade a second time.

Here Alcestis vows to surrender her life in place of her husband; you can see her, in the very wool of the Fates, not yet fully spun out, her safety preserved by destiny.

Here the night of the daughters of Danaus shines in gold. Their impious father equips them with fifty swords and gives discord the command of harmonious madness.

Only Lynceus, saved by the kindness of Hypermnestra, escapes. You may see him trembling for her sake and see her grow pale only for the husband she has spared.

And now she changes Jove into the forms by which he used to hold Mnemosyne, Europa, Semele, Leda, and Cynosura:

a serpent, a bull, a thunderbolt, a swan, and Dictynna.

And now the work moved toward the tower of Danaë and the rain of metal; here too Jupiter dripped down in another form of gold.

When the maiden, looking upon this, saw Triton’s daughter turn her gaze and prefer to inspect the arts of the learned, she changed her purpose and, with a skillful thumb, began to paint Laïs victorious over the philosopher: with fragrant shears she had cut the perfumed beard from the chin and wrinkled neck of the wild Cynic.

[Note: Diogenes, whom Lucian reports in the *True Histories* to have taken Laïs as his wife:

“Diogenes of Sinope changed his way of life so greatly that he married Laïs the courtesan, danced while rising under the influence of drunkenness, and behaved outrageously.”]

[Note: Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume III, page 497, is surprised that Sirmond, in his note on this passage of Sidonius, stated that Laïs was married by the Cynic Diogenes according to Lucian’s Book II of the *True Histories*, as though this had actually happened, when Lucian wrote fictional narratives in those books.]

Pallas smiled and added these words with chaste lips:

“You will no longer laugh at our doctrines, maiden, once you are married to my philosopher. Rather, taking up the wedding torch, let this mother weave the work. Rise, illustrious glory of the sophists, Polemius, and now at last lay aside your Stoic frown. Imitating lovers among the Cynics, begin again to bear a little Plato for me.”

The teacher addressed the girl, who was hesitating, in these words:

“Proceed gladly, and do not perhaps condemn the marriage commanded by our old man, who was not reluctant to drink the god-condemned poison while Anytus turned pale.”

He had spoken. At once the man rose and, with modest expression, entrusted his severe cloak to the knotty club.

Then the goddess of both bound their hair with the green olive of peace, joined their right hands, and imposed the marriage covenant. Their grandfather Nymphidius witnessed it and approved the omen; the golden Sisters joined the concordant threads.

## POEM XVI

### A Eucharistic poem to Faustus, bishop of Riez

Concerning Faustus, bishop of Riez, written in Letter 3 of Book IX. Sidonius now gives him thanks for two reasons: first, because he faithfully guided the youth of his own brother—that is, an age friendly to vices—when it had been entrusted to his discipline; and second, because, when Sidonius once traveled to Riez, Faustus received him affectionately and accompanied him to greet his mother.

Scorn Phoebus, the nine Muses with Pallas as the tenth, Orpheus, the imitation of the fountain’s water,

and the Ogygian lyre, which, bending stones that followed its song, raised walls with ears through its music.

Rather, I pray that you now come, Spirit, to speak of your pontiff—you who entered the ancient breast of Miriam when dry Israel, seizing the timbrels, went through the hollow channels of the sea, surrounded by embankments of water, and the dusty crowd shouted your triumph through the midst of the waves.

You who assisted Judith’s hand when it struck Holofernes’s neck, and the headless trunk lay there with its throat cut, while the fragile sex was safely hidden in the powerful blow.

Or you who, by drawing the fleece dry and then saturating the ground from an untouched fleece, strengthened Gideon, spirit inserted into musical trumpets, while victory came through song alone.

You who also breathed upon the king, Jesse’s son, taken from the shepherding flock, when the enemy placed the ark of the covenant upon a cart, with no ox-driver to guide it, so that it might reveal the obscene disease in the swollen buttock.

[Note: This is a lapse of memory. David fell before the ark and danced with it when it was brought from the house of Abinadab to Obed-Edom, and from there into the city. See II Kings 6. The Philistines, however, before David—indeed, before the inauguration of King Saul—had been struck by that disgraceful wound and had placed the ark on a cart to be transported without a driver. When it stopped of its own accord in the field, it was brought into the house of Abinadab. See I Kings 6–7.]

You who once sounded in the throat of three boys, whom the dew-laden flame moistened in the furnace heated by the Chaldaean tyrants.

You who filled Jonah as he moved through the revolving passages of the belly, while the monster’s entrails resounded with food singing inwardly; or who filled the weight of the belly with the fasting prophet, though he was full and yet undefiled, while raw hunger belched forth from the groaning viscera, and the beast vomited him up in hunger with spasms of its entrails and a suspended bite.

You who once came doubly into the breast of Elisha, when the fiery chariot was carrying off the aged Tishbite and, leaving behind his torn cloak as a gift, the shaggy charioteer entered the burning reins.

You who are about to send Elijah a second time to the earth, mercifully bound the tongue of the righteous Zechariah, while the wrinkled woman was making him a late father, signifying that the prophet was commanded to remain silent, when grace shone forth so that he might know that the law was to be silent.

You who, being born from a virgin with no human seed, were God before all time and Christ in time, created yourself insofar as the body is concerned.

You, accustomed to restore sight to the blind and walking also to the lame,

hearing to the deaf, and to loosen the tongue of the mute—you came for this as well, so that dead limbs might rise from bed, bier, and tomb.

You also endured punishments in the flesh you had assumed,

[Col. 0719B] bearing blows, mockery, lashes, thorns,

the lot, bonds, the cross, nails, gall, the spear, vinegar,

and finally death—but you approached it in order to rise again,

rescuing whatever had passed under the ancient enemy’s jurisdiction

through our offense, when the first woman, breaking the commandment,

bound us in enduring guilt.

When he sought you in destruction, and found nothing in you

383 by which he could convict you as his own, he lost everything

that Eve had surrendered through her fall: that bond

by which mankind had been overwhelmed—this compensation broke it.

Free of sin, you became a great price for sinners;

as the new Adam, in place of the old, while dying you snatched us from death.

Thus death itself died;

thus it was deceived by the traps it had prepared.

For while it indiscriminately attacked the innocent and the guilty,

it brought about the possibility that those bound by crime might be acquitted.

You also commanded the righteous ashes to rise with you for a time,

when, after a long period beneath roofs, salvation hastened in,

and life, suddenly poured in, shook the solidified ashes from their tombs.

Grant your Faustus to praise you; grant him to offer thanks,

which it is a joy even now to owe. Great priest,

our little lyre sings here, though with an unequal plectrum.

[Col. 0720A] This, then, is the first reason, or first subject, of my praise:

that, while the slippery course of life is turning,

my brother’s honor is proved, through the Lord’s gifts, to have been preserved with you, his reputation and modesty not wavering.

This good—whatever its extent—looks to you;

its reward will be owed to him, and he to you.

Let there be praise if he did not wish to fall:

for whatever he was unable to do, in justice rebounds wholly upon you.

Moreover, because formerly, when I was coming to Relos,

when Procyon raged and the sun’s scorching fire

was writing thirsty fields with winding fissures,

[Note: [Col. 0719C] Book II, letter 2: “the earth is inscribed by the gaping curves of the cracks in the parched ground.” This kind of trope was extremely common among the ancients. Varro, *Marcipor*: “They are not astrologers who have written out the sky by painting it.” Virgil: “. . . dust is inscribed by the turned spear”; Lycophron: “With wings an eagle draws a line across the dry land.”]

you received our summer heat immediately as your guest:

peace, a house, shade, water, blessing, table, and bed.

Yet all these things are far surpassed by this one fact:

that you wished me to approach the holy threshold of the holy mother.

384 I stiffened, I confess, conscious of myself, and suddenly

[Col. 0720B] reverence stained the face of one who worshipped with awe.

Nor did I tremble otherwise than if Rebecca herself

were leading me to Israel, or the long-haired Samuel to Anna.

Therefore, whether we worship you with prayers without end,

we confess our great affection in small poems.

Whether the blazing Syrtes and inhospitable wastes hold you,

or a marsh green with mud,

or black rocks in a recess, more uncultivated,

where, with the sun withdrawn, hollow caves preserve ancient darkness;

whether you tremble on the Alps stretched out upon precipitous crags,

offering sleep wrapped in a girdle upon the icy turf—

[Note: [Col. 0719D] He may have written this through a case of *vocare*, “to call,” or *Anachoronta* should be read; traces of that reading remain in certain books. *Anachoronta*, however—ἀναχωροῦντα, “withdrawing”—could have been said in the form used by Juvenal and Sidonius himself, *Chironomonta*.]

—the hermit, who, although he bears the cold,

never subdues the warmth conceived from Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Although there were Egyptian monks who were called by these names, nevertheless, since he places these men above all others, there seems no doubt that he is referring to the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist. Hermits proclaim them the guides and leaders of their way of life, as Jerome testifies in the *Life of Paul*, and Socrates, Book I, chapter 12. Gregory of Nazianzus refers to this when, in the *Apology after His Return*, he says: “I was thinking of Elijah’s Carmel, and John’s desert, and the otherworldly life of those who practice philosophy in this way.”]

where now Elijah, now John commands you to go,

now the two Macarii, now the hero Paphnutius,

now Or, now Ammon, now Sarmata, now Hilarion,

now Antony, naked in that tunic, calls you—

the tunic which the kindly hand of his master made from palm leaves.

[Note: [Col. 0720C–D] Two islands in the Gallic Sea are well known, opposite the town of Antipolis in the province of Narbonensis II: Lero and Lerinus. Strabo calls the former Λήρων, Ptolemy Ληρώνη; Pliny calls the latter Lerina. Both are named by Aethicus in his *Itinerary* and by Ennodius in the *Life of Epiphanius*: “Returning from Toulouse, he visited each of the holy settlements—the Median Islands, the Stoechades, Lero itself, and Lirinus, the flat nurse of the highest mountains.” The former is now called Saint-Marguerite, the latter Saint-Honorat; in the latter, Honoratus first laid the foundations of the once-famous monastery renowned throughout Gaul. Its third abbot after Honoratus was Faustus, whom he therefore calls the ancient father of Lirinus, because at this time he was no longer abbot but bishop of Riez.]

Whether ancient Lirinus has embraced you as its father,

where, already broken, you often come for great repose,

to serve your disciples, scarcely capturing leisure for sleep,

scarcely cooked food; abstaining from wine, you pass your life

and paint your fasts with psalms inserted among them.

You tell the brothers

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Caesarius of Arles and Ennodius of Ticinum imitated this passage of Sidonius concerning the island of Lerinus. Caesarius says in Homily 25: “Blessed and happy is the island of Lirinus, which, although it appears small and flat, is nevertheless known to have sent innumerable mountains to heaven.” Ennodius says in the *Life of Blessed Epiphanius of Ticinum*: “He came to the Median Islands, the Stoechades, Lero, and Lerinus itself, the flat nurse of the highest mountains.”]

how many mountains that flat island

[Col. 0721A] has sent to heaven: the holy life of the old man Caprasius,

[Note: [Col. 0721B] Honoratus had him as a teacher of religious life. He was a man, as it is written in Hilary of Arles’ *Life*, who lived an angelic life in the islands; “venerable,” as Eucherius says in his little work *On the Praise of the Desert*, “equal in gravity to the ancient saints.”]

and the youth Lupus—

[Note: [Col. 0721B] Later bishop of Troyes. Eucherius says in the same work, concerning the island of Lirinus: “It possessed Lupus, a man of revered name, who brought back to us that Lupus from the tribe of Benjamin.”]

whose grace

[Note: [Col. 0721B] The founder of the monastery of Lirinus, as we have said. Eucherius says of the same island: “Worthy to have been founded by Honoratus, worthy to have received as father of so great an institution one who shone with the vigor of an apostolic spirit and the dignity of his countenance; worthy, when it received him, to send him forth—to the see of Arles, that is, to which he was raised from the governance of the island.”]

kept Honoratus as its father;

and Maximus, whoever he was,

[Note: [Col. 0721B–C] The successor of Honoratus in the governance of the monastery, and subsequently bishop of Riez. Eucherius says of Honoratus: “It now possesses his successor, Maximus by name, illustrious because he was worthy to be chosen after him.” Faustus says of Maximus: “Worthy was he to whom that first founder entrusted the helm of the ship of Lirinus to be guided after him.” He says this in the falsely attributed homily of Eusebius of Emesa on Saint Maximus. Among other things, this passage persuades me that the homily should be assigned to Faustus: “Rightly,” he says, “may that blessed island count you as its debt for this one and unique gift, although it blushes greatly on account of the other.” He means that the island of Lirinus gave Riez two bishops: Maximus, of whom it could rightly boast, and Faustus himself, of whom it could blush. No one but Faustus himself would have used these words of Faustus.]

under whose episcopate and abbacy you twice

ruled both the city and the monks as their bishop and abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Maximus succeeded Faustus, first in the office of abbot, when Maximus was summoned from the governance of Lirinus to the see of Riez; then again in the episcopate, when, after Maximus’ death, he was made bishop of Riez from being abbot. Thus, after Maximus, he governed both Maximus’ monks and his city.]

385 while celebrating in those praises

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Later bishop of Lyon. Eucherius himself testifies that Lirinus was his place of residence, in his little work *On the Praises of the Desert*: “Indeed, I owe reverence to all the places of the desert illuminated by the retirement of the devout; yet I embrace my Lirinus with particular honor, for it had received in its most pious arms those cast out by the shipwrecks of the stormy world as they came.”]

the journey of Eucherius as he came,

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Bishop of Arles. He indicates that Hilary lived on the island of Lirinus twice; this is true. First, overcome by the pleas of Honoratus, he withdrew there and lived for some time with Honoratus. When Honoratus was later transferred to the see of Arles, Hilary followed him at his request after leaving the island; but, finally seized by his former love of the desert, he returned to Lirinus. At that time Eucherius wrote for Hilary his elegant little work *On the Praise of the Desert*, which confirms all this, as does Hilary himself in his homily on Saint Honoratus.]

and the return of Hilary.

Whether the people entrusted to you hold you,

and a lesser man dares, in your presence, to despise the swollen ways of his superiors;

whether you anxiously care for the needs of one weakened by hunger,

or for what food a stranger lives on and what sustains him,

whose weakened legs a prison fetter makes thin;

whether you are more distracted in mind by funerals requiring burial,

if the livid bones of a poor dead man grow green

and you yourself carry an unoffending corpse to the grave;

whether you preach from the conspicuous steps

[Note: [Col. 0721D–0722B] In former times they customarily preached while seated on a tribunal, as the authors of ritual books also teach. Prudentius says of the church of Saint Hippolytus:

“Before the opposing façade, a lofty tribunal rises on steps,

from which the bishop preaches God.”

The Greeks too had this custom, as both their present practice shows and the report preserved by Socrates and others concerning Chrysostom, namely, that he mounted the ambo so that he could be heard by more people. They therefore preached before the steps of the altar, within the screen that separated the βῆμα or ἱερατεῖον—that is, the tribunal or sanctuary—from the *caphsum*, which they called the ναός, the nave. Gregory the Theologian refers to this place when, speaking of his sermons in Constantinople in his *Oration to the Bishops*, says that the screen had suffered violence from the crowd pressing forward to hear him, in these words: “Hail, lovers of my speeches, fellow-runners in your gathering, manifest and hidden tablets, and this screen, violently pressed by those who thrust forward for the sake of speech.”]

of the venerable altar,

[Col. 0722A] while you are about to preach,

[Note: [Col. 0722B–C] Nor should this be passed over: such was once the reverence for the divine word that people heard sacred sermons standing, not sitting, as is commonly done today. Augustine is the principal authority for this, in his sermon *On the Dignity of Clerics* and in Homily 26. It can also be inferred from Book IV of Optatus of Milevis, who denies that the people in church had permission to sit. Likewise Eusebius, in Book IV of the *Life of Constantine the Great*, testifies that Constantine, “standing upright” (ὄρθιον ἑστῶτα), lent his ears to one who was praying for him, saying that it was fitting that divine things should be heard while standing: “for it is holy to hear divine things standing” (ἑστῶτα γὰρ ὑπακούειν τῶν θείων ὅσιον). Nevertheless, one cannot deny that in some churches there were formerly seats for the hearers as well. Augustine teaches this and judges it more suitable for attention in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 13: “It is much more prudent in certain churches overseas that not only do the bishops speak to the people while seated, but seats are also provided for the people themselves, lest someone weaker, wearied by standing, be turned away from the most health-giving attention, or even be compelled to leave.”]

the attentive congregation surrounds you,

drinking the proclaimed law into their ears as medicine.

Whatever you do, wherever you are, always be Faustus to me,

always Honoratus, and always Maximus as well.

## POEM XVII. HE INVITES OMMATIUS, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, TO THE BIRTHDAY OF HIS HOUSEHOLD

[Note: [Col. 0722C–D] Poem 11 taught us that Ommatius, the father-in-law of Ruricius, was an Auvergnian; Gregory, Book X of his *History*, makes the same observation concerning the younger Ommatius, who was bishop of Tours. Here Sidonius, celebrating the birthday of one of his own family, invites him in a most beautiful epigram. Martin of Braga, formerly a bishop, liked it so much that he had it copied, with a few changes, in his dining room in the following form:

**By Blessed Martin, Bishop of Braga, in the Refectory**

“No meals here are adorned with gilded couches,

nor has Assyrian purple furnished you with a semicircular couch.

Nor will shining dishes be set out through the many compartments

of a gleaming sideboard, fashioned with the craftsman’s art.

No cup will be offered here whose twisted handle

might clasp its side crusted with glowing metal.

My wines are not Gazetic, Chian, or Falernian,

nor wines you might drink sent from the vineyard of Sarepta.

But whatever our slender supply cannot provide for the table,

we ask that your complete goodwill supply instead.”]

OMMATIUS, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, ON THE BIRTHDAY OF HIS HOUSEHOLD

Four days before the first light of the scorching August

brings forth its grain-bearing head from the horizon,

our sixteenth birthday will be celebrated—

a day made happy by your coming.

No meals will be set before you on gemmed tables;

Assyrian purple will not furnish you with a semicircular couch.

Nor through the many compartments of a gleaming sideboard

[Col. 0723A] will I bury weights of dark silver.

No cup will be offered here whose twisted handle

might clasp its side crusted with glowing metal.

Our dishes are modest, not so fashioned

386 that elaborate workmanship might make their great size supply the price.

No bread, accustomed to grow golden in the Libyan Syrtis,

will receive you on your Gallic rustic table.

[Note: [Col. 0723B–D] That is, a Celt of Lyon. Concerning Sidonius’ homeland, I am compelled to disagree with the learned Savaro, who makes him an Auvergnian. Since it would be impious to think otherwise than Sidonius himself indicates, and he repeatedly declares himself a man of Lyon—for example, in Book I, letters 5 and 8; Book IV, letter 25; and poems 5 and 13—I must do so. We have already shown from Book III, letter 12 that the tomb of Apollinaris, his grandfather, was not in Auvergne, as Savaro thought, but in the territory of Lyon. This passage now indicates that Sidonius was not Auvergnian by birth, since he calls himself a Gaul and thereby indicates for himself a different homeland from that of Ommatius the Auvergnian, that is, the Aquitanian. For that age distinguished the Aquitanians from the Gauls. Sulpicius Severus, *History* II: “But among our people—that is, among the Aquitanians, Gauls, and Britons—it seemed improper.” Ausonius, in his poem on Arles, writes:

“. . . other peoples and wealthy cities,

which Gaul enjoys, and broad-lapped Aquitania.”

This is also the point of the journey described in Aethicus’ *Itinerary*, from Aquitania into Gaul, from Bordeaux to Autun. In this sense Sidonius calls himself a Gaul because he is from Lyon; but Ommatius, because he was an Auvergnian, he wishes understood as an Aquitanian, but not a Gaul. The same distinction appears in Severus’ dialogues, where a man who was a Gaul in reality and in name says that he will speak as a Gallic man among Aquitanians: plainly because, in the sense just mentioned, Aquitanians were not Gauls.]

My wines are not Gazetic, Chian, or Falernian,

nor wines you might drink sent from the vineyard of Sarepta.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] The wine of Gaza is called Gazetic by Isidore, after the region from which it is brought, namely Gaza in Palestine; similarly Sareptan wine comes from Sarepta of the Sidonians. Alexander of Tralles calls it Σερεφθῖνον οἶνον, “Sareptan wine.” Both are praised by Corippus in Book III and Fortunatus in Book IV of his *Life of Martin*. Gazetic wine is also mentioned by Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors* 65, and by Cassiodorus, *Variarum* XII.12.]

The cups here do not bear the distinguished name of the district

that the Triumvir himself gave to our fields.

[Note: [Col. 0723D–0724C] He is not speaking of Auvergne’s wines. Otherwise, how could there be no wines in Auvergne that belonged to the Auvergnian country? He is speaking of the wines of his own homeland, Lyon. Which district of Lyon, celebrated for its vineyards, he means by the name “Triumvir” remains to be investigated. We know from Dio, Book 46, that the triumvirs who founded the colony of Lyon were Silanus, Lepidus, and Plancus, and that many names could have been derived from them.]

Yet we ask you to come: Christ will provide everything,

[Note: [Col. 0724C] He was born elsewhere, therefore, and later moved here. Thus Sidonius remains Lugdunensian by birth, Auvergnian by marriage and episcopal see. Let our Auvergnian people not be indignant that he is not granted to them wholly; they possessed the better part of him, since Sidonius’ dignity and splendor were not meant to illuminate only one homeland.]

here for me, who made this my homeland through your affection.

## POEM XVIII. ON THE BATHS OF HIS VILLA, SITUATED ABOVE A LAKE

[Note: [Col. 0724C] He described Avitacum, its baths, and its pool at length in Book II, letter 2.]

[Col. 0723B] If you deign to visit our Avitacum,

may it not displease you—if what you possess pleases you.

Its roofs rise in rivalry with the Baian cone,

and an equal peak shines from its boot-shaped summit.

The babbling wave murmurs more loudly than the waters of Gaurus,

having fallen over the brow of the neighboring hill.

Rich Campania would not want Lake Lucrinus

if it saw those waters of our lake.

That shore is adorned with crimson sea urchins;

in our fish you see both kinds, as a guest,

and, if you wish, you share the pleasures with a calm heart:

whoever you are, here in your mind you make your own Baiae.

387

## POEM XIX. A TETRASTICH OVER THE POOL

Enter, shivering, the waters after the hot baths,

so that the liquid’s cold may harden your warm skin.

And although in this one liquid you immerse your limbs,

your eyes swim across our pool.

## POEM XX. TO HIS BROTHER-IN-LAW ECDICIUS

[Note: [Col. 0724C] Papianilla, Sidonius’ wife, was the sister of Ecdicius. Therefore Ecdicius was Sidonius’ *sororius*, and Sidonius was Ecdicius’ *cognatus*. Properly speaking, *sororius* means a wife’s brother, and *cognatus* a sister’s husband. They are therefore set against each other, as on an ancient inscription at Brescia: “The dearest *cognatus* to his most loving *sororius*.”]

Our birthday reminds me that the Nones of November are approaching:

I do not ask you to come; I command you.

Let your wife be with you; now hurry here, the two of you.

But next year we hope that you will come as three.

## POEM XXI. ON FISH CAUGHT AT NIGHT

[Col. 0724B]

This night first threaded four fish upon the hooks.

Then I kept two; you also take two.

The ones I sent are the larger; it is the proper order:

for you were the greater portion of our soul.

388 Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius sends greetings to Pontius Leontius.

While I was lingering at Narbo, once called Martius but recently made so,

[Note: [Col. 0724C–D] An old inscription at Narbo, not yet published, in which the individual letters denote *Colonia Julia Paterna Narbo Martius*. Other monuments also adorn it with these names:

“Gaius Manlius, son of Gaius, of the Papirian tribe, Rufus Umber, discharged from the decuria of lictors and attendants, which belongs to the Colonia Julia Paterna Narbo Martius, made this for himself and his family.”

No one doubts that it was called Julia Paterna from the name of Julius Caesar, who, as Suetonius relates, refounded the colony there a second time. Those who think that the additional name Martius derives from Quintus Marcius, during whose consulship the colony was first founded, are refuted by manifest arguments, as others have shown; and they have Sidonius himself against them here, since he plainly refers the name to Mars. With this in mind, he says that Narbo had recently truly become Martius when it most courageously endured the fierce siege of the Goths, which he will again mention in the following poem.]

I began to consider composing a few hexameters in response to your affection.

When you read them, you would know that, although a household god dwells in places unequally distant from both of us—and somewhat more than is fair—

our minds are not therefore as far apart as our homelands.

Here, then, you have Dionysus languishing amid the delights of the Indian triumph;

and you have Phoebus, whom you rightly recognize as made your resident by his divine power—

that Phoebus, naturally, who is very close to my Anthedius,

whose prefecture of the poetic college enables him, by his art of discussion,

to surpass not only musicians of every kind but also geometers,

arithmetic experts, and astrologers.

For I would judge no one to have grasped more precisely

what the oblique stars of the zodiac,

what the wandering planets,

and what the scattered stars beyond the zodiac prevail to accomplish.

[Note: [Col. 0725D] Those placed outside the zodiac. Sidonius recognizes three classes of stars: planets, which wander in their own orbits; the stars of the zodiac, contained in its twelve signs; and the remaining stars outside the zodiac, which he therefore calls *exotica*, as though ἕξω τοῦ ζωδιακοῦ, “outside the zodiac.”]

Indeed, philosophy shines through these members, so to speak, in such a way

that he seems to have learned, without an interpreter and with genius alone as his guide,

the works of Julius Firmicus, Sammonicus, Julianus Vertacus, and Fullonius Saturninus,

writers supremely skilled in the mathematical sciences.

[Col. 0725B] Worshipping the traces of his learning,

we confess ourselves a hoarse goose before a melodious swan.

Why delay you further? I have made your Burgus my own,

as was fitting for a friend,

well aware that you would be pleased with the subject,

even if the finished poem should displease you.

389

## POEM XXII. BURGUS OF PONTIUS LEONTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0725D–0726D] The ancient name of the Burgus Pauliniana, which he describes in this idyll, still survives today: they call it the castle of Burgus. It stands on the bank of the Duranus, not far from the confluence of that river with the Garonne. Concerning Leontius, for whose benefit this was written, see Book VIII, letters 11 and 12. The origin of the word *burgus* is Greek. An old glossary says: Πύργος, “tower,” *burgus*. The Romans then called the towers or turreted fortifications placed along the frontiers *burgi*. From these, all similar fortified places also came to bear the name *burgi*. No other reason need be sought for Pontius Paulinus’ calling his estate Burgus, since his entire description reveals precisely this origin.]

The stable of the Bistonian king, the altars of Busiris,

the tables of Antiphates, the kingdom of Thoas,

and the Cyclops deprived of light by Ithacan cunning,

who, bearing across the open field of his forehead

a pair of dark lights through the hollow of his mountain,

go on, guest, if you have entered Burgus intending to keep silent:

although Phoebus does not everywhere relax the reins into song,

and here does not unfurl all the sails of speech,

whoever looks upon so great a household without praising it aloud

both sees and is seen; silent goodwill resounds without a voice,

for your own silence cries aloud that you are jealous of yourself.

Come, then, Erato, strike the Pierian strings for me.

Let the Satyrs answer, moving finger and foot;

let them play, but not break the songs with their trembling leaps.

Whatever a Dryad, or whatever a Hamadryad,

has ever clapped festively with the Napaeae joined together,

let them hang it here for you, Burgus;

or let the nourishing chorus of the Naiads and Nereids teach it here,

when you happen to come as the Garonne returns

and plows the sea within the river.

Reveal, then, Erato, the reasons,

and let the household gods be told who its genius is:

no height is without its guardian.

Perhaps, after plundering the arrow-bearing Erythraean peoples,

Evan was driving tigers harnessed with vine-reins to his chariot.

He entered where the pole penetrated the double grape-bearing arc.

390 He himself sits languid in the chariot;

his lofty neck drips with the dew of wine;

his head’s golden horns burst open

and hurl forth their native lightning fire.

He had first assumed this form at birth,

when long ago he passed from his mother into his father’s thigh.

Each season bears its own wealth,

and the vintage binds together the glowing flowers.

A cup and thyrsus are carried in his right and left hands;

his cloak does not conceal his exposed arms but merely touches them.

His eyes swim sweetly; if chance turns them against an enemy,

their very sight intoxicates the terrified Indians.

Whenever the axle jolts as it leaps over the rough places,

the wheel is everywhere drenched with falling must.

Silenus, now filled with the divinity of his pupil,

taught Bassarids, Satyrs, Pans, and Fauns to dance.

Yet he was careful about his head:

with his bare crown he tries to excuse his hair, lost with its wreaths.

[Col. 0726B] Then horned Ganges becomes the pageant of the new triumph.

With head bowed and wet mouth he stood, his face uncombed,

and with glassy tears he helped the dry waters.

Vine shoots bound his hands behind his back in chains;

then, slowly saturated with captive moisture,

the vine, of its own accord, grows leafy again along his dewy arms.

There too comes the wife of the stolen husband, bound,

with her saffron cheeks lowered

and her lamp forbidden to be hidden,

when dawn was glowing with the sun’s rays.

The phoenix was also present,

its cinnamon lost,

fearing that a second death might not remain for it.

A captive cohort follows,

carrying dishes laden with its treasures:

ivory here, ebony there, and gold,

and white berries torn from a pitch-black breast

391 are carried along.

Whatever sustains no fragrance is thrown into chains.

Here you may see punishments themselves pleasing,

and the green chains breathing the scent of violets.

Last of all the elephants advance, migrating as spoils.

Their herd has an uncouth appearance:

their backs are stiff with bristling skin,

scarcely able to endure iron.

For the savage creatures’ natural breastplate is so strong

that no weapons pierce it;

their drawn and stretched hides resound in turn,

and, accustomed to defend themselves,

they repel the missiles striking them with wrinkles thrown outward.

The victorious god was already making his way to Thebes

through the vast bronze,

and had raised his revels to the highest clouds,

when he saw Delion approaching from the Aonian citadel.

He too holds griffins.

Laurel leaves bind their curved faces

with toothed foliage;

green reins hang around them, entwined with ivy.

The fierce bird gradually flies through paths of air and earth,

lest, by the swift beating of its wings,

it break the wooden reins.

Phoebus himself shines eternally on his cheeks.

His temples have grown with clusters,

and his hair, of the same golden color,

sweeps the gilded axle.

In his left hand he holds a hoarse lyre,

made sweet by the great charm of its chased Python;

his right hand holds arrows

and strings sounding with another kind of murmur.

The Pimplean sisters went alongside,

and, surrounding the middle of the chariot with their ninefold train,

cast a shadow over it.

The Epidaurian serpent hangs among polished tripods,

its health-giving poison spread over sacred necks.

[Note: [Col. 0727D] Some read more correctly, “Here Pegasus too joined his maned wings,” as though the wings had been born from Pegasus’ own mane.]

Here too Pegasus joined his maned wings,

carrying Creon, eloquent in his learned foot.

When the choruses joined together,

each brother rose to embrace the other;

but Evan was somewhat slower,

392 because he was ashamed to reveal his unsteady feet if he stood.

Then Phoebus said: “Where are you going?

Are you perhaps seeking Thebes, Bacchus, the guilty city?

The offspring of Echion surely denies that you are a god.

Leave those walls, I beg you—leave them;

rather, turn your wheels with me.

Agave despised honoring you,

and Niobe despised us.

Since then she stands rigid and proud,

bearing as many wounds as she sees children in her womb.

She desired death, and mercy fixed her more cruelly.

It is often harmful to spare,

and to bring feeling into grief.

But after killing her own son,

will the mother Pentheus’ mother become still more frenzied?

Will she not be destined to become mad?”

“Therefore we too cannot inhabit the Aonian hills,

when an adulterer will possess the chamber of his murdered father—

the brother of his children, to be regarded as his mother’s husband,

and his own stepfather.

If it pleases you to join your steps to mine,

I will tell you on what land we may dwell together.”

[Note: [Col. 0727D–0728D] A description of the confluence of the Duranus and Garonne, where we have said that Burgus lies on the bank of the Duranus—or, as Gregory calls it in a name close to the modern pronunciation, in Book VIII, the Dordonia. Today it is called the Dordogne.]

“There is a place where the Garonne, turning through an irrigated cliff,

and you, Duranus, hastening with a similar fall into the open waters,

leaving your mossy, curving bed,

gradually mingle your sluggish streams.

Here the sea runs against the current

and, with many a returning surge,

both rejects and carries away the waters

which the rivers roll forward.

But when, driven back by the moon’s increase,

the Garonne itself gathers its tides upon its back,

it swiftly returns with rushing waves

and seems no longer to flow back toward its source

but to run downward from it.

Then it receives the water—though itself the lesser—

from its lesser, stagnant brother,

and it too swells toward the ocean

and makes the banks its own shores.

Between these rivers, closer to the one from which

393 a mountain breaks through the sky, splendid with a lofty summit,

there will be heroes of greater stature

and a springtime senate.

Pauline Pontius, once first among his people,

will surround the place with high walls

when Latin rule governs the homeland,

and lofty towers will send their air upward.

On their summits a common procession or aid will shine.

Neither siege engines, nor rams, nor a high mound,

nor the nearby embankment,

nor the catapult that hurls grinding stones with a shriek,

nor the tortoise, nor the vine, nor the moving wheel

will ever be able to shake those walls,

even after ladders have been set in place.

Already I seem to see what you will be, Burgus.

You will be called such:

for houses rise from the river,

and shining baths sit among the fortifications.

Here, when the heat is harried by pitch-black north winds,

the rocky pumice begins to bark

along its roughened bank;

but, leaping from the broken crags,

the torrent is thrown upward,

fills the roofs with spray,

lifts the boatmen,

and often plays in a comical shipwreck.

Then, when the storm is over,

the receding water leaves the fleets it had sent into the baths.

How large they are, and on what columns they are supported!

Let the costly purple of Synnada withdraw into its crimson cave,

and the hill of the Numidians,

which bears ivory-colored stones,

and the marble flowering with grassy veins.

I no longer desire white Paros;

I no longer desire Carystus.

The purple hanging from the red rock is cheaper.

And lest posterity doubt who the builder was,

a stone is fixed at the entrance:

it records the names of the authors.

But because of the water

and the tracks it carries away

and the mud it wipes clean with its spreading current,

394 [Col. 0728B] the wall, crusted with cut panels,

rises toward the golden roofs,

which must be hidden beneath an excess of yellow metal.

For the house’s wealthy fortune could not endure concealment:

when it hides its roofs in this way,

it reveals its riches.

After this, a portico rises behind

and overtops a double building;

it is itself double,
