not traversable by a single wagon.

One of its wings, drawn beneath the gentle curve of its roof,

looks back slightly through its opposing horns.

It sees the rising sun in its right-hand curve,

looks straight toward it at midday,

and will see it setting in its left-hand curve.

It loses nothing from the sky’s threefold hinge,

and preserves the whole sun through its crescent-shaped halls.

Here the father of Pharnaces immerses in the deep

the sacred herds of Jupiter who bears the trident.

You would think that the bodies of the horn-footed animals,

struck by the axe,

and the marked wounds,

were reddening with bloody dew;

the horror of the wound stands real,

and the painting lives through the slain chariots.

From this side the Pontic ruler encloses Cyzicus with numerous weapons;

from that side the consul Lucullus brings aid to his allies,

and, driven by hunger to undergo the utmost dangers,

the Mithridatic soldier envies the besieged enemy.

Here the ardor of the Roman soldier swims across the sea,

and transports dry paper on a soaked body.

Above, granaries grow beneath roofs extended lengthwise,

and narrow the buildings with their ample fruits.

Here will come as much as Africa harvests in its hot lands,

as much as the Calabrian,

as much as vigorous Apulia cultivates,

as much as the harvest swells in the heap of Leontine,

as much as Gargara entrusts to the Mygdonian furrow,

395 and as much as Attic Eleusis, honoring Ceres

[Col. 0728D] with silent dances, once stored,

when, after peoples abandoned acorns,

the golden ages had already perished,

replaced by golden grain.

From here the summer portico opens toward the cold Bears.

From here harmless warmth issues from the winter baths,

and softens the season for the place;

for that part is more suited to cold,

since what flees the lion’s mouth

poorly withstands the fury of the Lycaonian she-bear.

A higher stream comes a long way from the citadel to the baths,

falls upon the mountain,

and, carried through broad channels,

circulates the enclosed river through hollow divisions.

Toward the setting sun, beyond the granaries,

the shadowy winter house rises for its masters.

Here a good fire crackles,

having consumed the beams placed upon it.

The water, curved within the furnace,

dies in a globe of flame,

and, its lash broken,

sprinkles softened vapor throughout the roofs.

[Note: [Col. 0729D] Through little tubes inserted into the walls, as Seneca says in Letter 90. Pliny the Younger’s words in Book II, Letter 17, should likewise be read and understood in this way: “The sleeping chamber adjoins it, with a passage between; suspended and tubed, it distributes and supplies the vapor it has received in a healthy moderation here and there.”]

Then you may see, in succession,

what the builder dared to raise in rivalry with the weaving rooms of Pallas’ temples.

Here, once, the honored wife of Leontius,

than whom no Pontian daughter-in-law is more blessed

by the good fortune of an illustrious husband,

will be celebrated in a temple:

whether she emptied Syrian distaffs,

or twisted silken threads through light reeds,

or softened with the golden thread

the pregnant metal of the spindle.

Behind these joined walls shines a structure

[Col. 0729B] that bears the beginnings of the circumcised Jews.

The picture gleams perpetually,

and the long passage of time does not disfigure its figures

by diminishing their pigments.

Do you turn to the left?

A spacious portico receives you,

396 curved along straight paths.

At its upper edge it hangs,

and a stone forest of closely packed columns stands.

A lofty dining room opens here through revolving doors.

Nearby is a flowing channel;

water falls from above before the doors

in a suspended pool,

and fish, following the vein,

find watery dining rooms.

Close by rises either the first tower or the outermost.

Here, for the masters, winter dining on a semicircular couch will be death.

Sitting on its conspicuous summit,

I shall often look upon the beloved mountain of our Muses and goats;

I shall walk among these laurel branches,

and here I shall believe that trembling Daphne believes in me.

Now, if by chance you turn your steps twice toward the Bear,

so that you may come to the temple of the greatest god,

the storeroom and pantry, joined together, exhale luxury.

Here you will be a great brother to me.

Now divide the dwelling;

you shall yield to me my spring,

which, flowing from the mountain,

is shaded by a many-caverned arch in a spacious circuit.

It needs no adornment;

nature has given it beauty.

I take pleasure in nothing artificial;

no pomp produced by art,

no hammer echoing with a resounding blow,

no marble replacing exhausted tufa.

Here the spring suffices for us in place of Castalia’s water.

Keep the rest, rich as you are;

let the hills tremble beneath your authority.

Here release your captives,

and let the vineyards of Burgus become the joyous chains

of loosened bondage along its slopes.”

Silenus, already nearly sober,

confirms this speech,

and the choirs sing in approval together.

Farewell, Nysa, Bacchus;

farewell, double-peaked Parnassus, Phoebus.

Let Naxos not seek the one,

nor Cyrrha the other:

397 But Burgus, destined rather to please for ever—
be requested.

Behold, whenever you wish to enliven a feast with larger vessels, I have sent you something to read between your cups and your amystides. You will come to the aid of my modesty if these verses do not reach sober ears; nor do I ask this without justification or contrary to what is fair. For when my Bacchus is destined to undergo a decemviral judgment, a tribunal is erected earlier than is appropriate. But if anyone thinks that a poem is blameworthy because it has been carried to this length, exceeding the brevity of an epigram, it is plainly evident that he has read neither the baths of Etruscus, nor the Hercules of Surrentum, nor the hair of Flavius Earinus, nor Vopiscus’ Tibur, nor indeed any of the little silvae of our Papinius. That highly prejudiced man does not confine all these descriptions within the narrow limits of distichs or tetrastichs; rather, as lyric Flaccus prescribes in his volume on the art of poetry, he suitably extends subjects once begun, using many richly colored pieces of the common cloth. Let this suffice as an example for my defense, lest this very plea concerning length seem itself too long. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0729D] I have restored *the locks of Flavius Earinus* in place of *Cumae of Flavius Sabinus*, which was formerly read. The emendation is beyond doubt, since the subject of Book III of Papinius’ *Silvae* is the hair of Earinus; Martial likewise has an epigram on it in Book IX.]

## POEM XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0729D] Sidonius, once having gone to Narbo and been received and entertained there with kindness by Consentius, had resolved to repay his host’s favor in verses; but the latter had first challenged Sidonius with eclogues of several poems. Sidonius therefore sent him this poem, in which he commends Narbo with remarkable praises, but above all because it produced as citizens the most noble and learned Consentii: the man to whom he writes and his father. He mentions both in Book IX, Letter 15; Letter 4 of Book VIII, however, is addressed to the son.]

### Narbo to Consentius, *vir clarissimus*, a citizen of Narbo

[Col. 0730C]

When, in accordance with your merits, I was already preparing, Consentius, pillar and ornament of character, to devote a song of poor cicuta to the praises of your hospitality, you yourself, voluntarily locking the trumpet into your verses and reversing the order, challenged me with poems, as you are accustomed to provoke a companion more readily to play.

My Muse obeys you; but from now on she will move her shameless pen much more cautiously. For while you expressly ask for poems, you urge me to write and yet make me fall silent.

Recently, when you were travelling swiftly past Phocaea and the Sextian Baiae—cities illustrious in their renown and their battles, through two consular triumphs (for the former endured Julian Mars and, with Brutus as leader, the fury of naval war; while the latter endured the bloody battles with the Teutones, and Marius standing victorious over the fallen Cimbrian)—you sent me a varied poem, learned, noble, vigorous, and delicate.

[Note: [Col. 0730D] Massilia and Aquae Sextiae. It is agreed that the city of the Massiliots was founded by the Phocaeans, a people of Asia. But the Φωκαεῖς, Phocaeans, from the Asian city of Phocaea, differ from the Φωκεῖς, Phocians, from Phocis, a region in Greece. Yet many, even among the ancients, called them Phocians and their homeland Phocis, either confusing the names or the history. They called all hot springs Baiae, after those Campanian springs which, as Eunapius writes, were famous throughout the whole world. Hence Aquae Sextiae acquired that name because it possessed baths. Everyone agrees that it was called Sextiae after Sextius Calvinus, who was the first to enclose that city with a wall. Of that colony, the metropolis of Narbonensian Province II, this fine monument survives at Rome on an ancient statue-base:

L. Antonio Epitynchanus, lictor of the decury of Curiatia, which attends the public rites; quinquennalis of the guild of carpenters at Ostia; Augustal sevir in the colony of Aquae Sextiae in Narbonensian province.]

The proud hexameters went forward, and elegiacs, with their linked but shorter following feet, ran in five-foot measures. You also sent the metre of the threefold trochee, accompanied by spondee and dactyl, sweet hendecasyllables; and by gracious interest you bound Sollius, who is yours.

[Col. 0731B]

We both claim and repay the interest. For what I return in verse for your poem is one hundredth of your praises.

What shall I first honor and revere in your name? If I am not mistaken, your fatherland and your father alike.

Although he may rightly claim the highest place for himself, nevertheless he must yield to the fatherland that gives birth to fathers.

Hail, Narbo, powerful in healthfulness, worthy to be admired alike in city and countryside; in your walls, citizens, circuit, shops, gates, colonnades, forum, theater, shrines, Capitolia, mints, baths, arches, granaries, and markets;

[Col. 0731C]

in your meadows, fountains, islands, saltworks, ponds, river, merchandise, bridge, and sea.

You alone properly worship the gods: Lenaeus, Ceres, Pales, and Minerva, with ears of grain, vines, pastures, and olive presses.

Relying on your men alone, and not seeking nature’s assistance, you raise a summit higher than the mountains, left far behind; no open ditch, nor a rampart crowned with the projection of rough stakes, encircles you.

[Col. 0732A]

You do not set marble, bronze plate, or glass into your walls; nor the splendor of Indian tortoiseshell; nor, if the broken tusks of Marmaric elephants have supplied any beams of ivory, do you fasten them into your fortifications or adorn your golden gates with asarotic pebbles.

[Note: 156. Pebbles dyed in various colors, such as those in asarotic pavements. Statius writes of these in the passage on Vopiscus’ Tibur, and Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 20: “Sosus of Pergamum laid out what they call the asarotos oikos, because he had made the remnants of a meal on the pavement, which are usually swept away, appear as though they had been left there, using small pebbles dyed in various colors.”]

But, proudly displayed upon half-ruined citadels, showing the glory of an ancient war, you bear molars shattered by blows—more precious because of their admirable ruins.

Let other cities be threatening in their situation, cities whose low strength is built high, and which boast that their walls have never been cut down when placed upon precipitous ridges.

[Col. 0732B]

You please because you have been struck, and the vigorous loyalty that endured assault has proclaimed your worth.

[Note: The younger Theodoric, son of Theodoric the Great, concerning whom see Letter 2. The Goths, having entered Gaul under their leader Ataulf and occupied Narbo as well, were driven from it by the count Constantius in 416, as may be inferred from Orosius and Hydatius. After this, Theodoric the father, not content with Aquitaine, surrounded Narbo in that lengthy siege described here; but he was eventually repulsed by Litorius, as stated in the panegyric to Avitus. Finally, this younger Theodoric gained possession of Narbo after the city was betrayed to him by the count Agrippinus, in 462, as the same Hydatius makes clear. Therefore this poem must have been written by Sidonius after that year, but before 466, when Theodoric died.]

Hence that martial ruler, older in glory than his great father, Theodoric, loves you—the glory of the Goths, the pillar and salvation of the Roman people—and approves you as faithful to him through earlier times of upheaval.

But do not perhaps seem disgraced on this account, that frequent engines have pierced you. For in the bodies of brave men a scar is the greater glory.

To have received no wound while serving in the Marathonian camps is a great disgrace. Among the fierce-handed Publicolae, Mucius stands out with his maimed arm.

[Col. 0732C]

When the great Caesar’s rampart was crushing everything, among so many faces protected from the enemy, the one-eyed Scaeva was the more distinguished.

It is a difficult glory to endure hardship.

The idle virtue of the lazy, cowardly, and disreputable gnashes its teeth at much.

[Note: “This is represented differently elsewhere.” Horace writes: “Hidden virtue differs little from buried idleness.”]

And what of this: fertile in producing Caesars and blessed in a progeny of men, you gave us Carinus and Numerianus, born to rule together with their father?

[Note: Carinus and Numerianus, with their father Carus. Although Vopiscus shows that nothing certain was known about the birthplace of the emperor Carus—and, surprisingly, does not mention Narbo among the various opinions—Greek writers before Sidonius, Eusebius in his Chronicle, and Latin writers, Sextus Victor, Eutropius, and Orosius, stated that he was born at Narbo. Joseph Scaliger, because some had written that Carus was born in Illyricum, as Fabius Cerialianus did, reconciles the matter by claiming that he was born at a place called Narbo not in Gaul but in Illyricum, where he maintains that there was likewise a town of that name. But the Dalmatian town designated by Scaliger was called Narona, not Narbona, although it is mistakenly written as the latter in Ptolemy; it is called Narona in Vatinius’ letter in Cicero, as well as in Pliny, Aethicus, and the Peutinger Map.]

[Col. 0733A]

For who would pass over the Persian expedition, or the victorious camp of the emperor Carus, and the Niphates traversed by Roman legions—when the emperor, struck by lightning, completed a life equal to the lightning bolts?

With these citizens, city, and countryside flourishing, kindly Consentius, you beget a father for me: one in whom polished wit and Roman rigor were joined to Attic grace.

Milesian Thales himself could have marveled when he heard him; and so could Cleobulus, known throughout Lindus’ citadel; and you, Periander of Corinth; and you, Bias, whom Priene produced; and you, Pittacus, Lesbian sage;

[Col. 0733B]

and you, Solon, powerful in stern Athens, surpassing the Socratic schools; and you, Chilon, born at Therapnae of Tyndareus, earlier than Lycurgus the lawgiver.

If he had wished, while free from other concerns, to mark out the courses of the stars, Aratus would have run along different paths.

When he set his mind to geometrical arts, Euclid, who knew the measure of the heavens, could not have kept pace with him.

If he wished to turn rhythms, Chrysippus could not have delayed the man in his undertaking with a sorites.

When he devoted himself to Amphion’s art, with plectrum, thumb, voice, and pipe, the Thracian prophet, the Arcadian god, and Phoebus himself were all behind him; and you would have thought even the Muses not so very musical.

[Col. 0733C]

If, dressed in train and buskin, he had once entered the Attic theater, Sophocles and Euripides would have yielded.

And if, as a comic actor, he had wished to make the stage resound in the sock, Menander, raise your finger and award him the palm.

When he polished his six-foot style, learned in the manner of the Smyrnaean workshop, or when he devoted himself to serious history, rushing Herodotus and thunderous Homer could scarcely retain the first places.

[Col. 0733D]

There would once have been no one superior to that orator who moved the Pandionian theater by his art, tumultuously carrying away the audience whether he was attacking the one-eyed Philip or conducting the case of Ctesiphon; a man whose popularity always increased, who sat justly enthroned in the citadel of speech, and who, born to a craftsman father, preferred to polish the edge of his tongue.

[Col. 0734A]

What shall I say of you in the Latin eloquence, Arpinate, Patavine, Mantuan? And you, Terence, who teach comic drama? And you, Plautus, born in a stern age, who surpass Greek wit with your charm? And you, Varro, sufficiently formidable through the manifold abundance of your writings? And you, Crispus, powerful in brevity?

[Col. 0734B]

And you, Cornelius Tacitus, whose flowing genius is silent before no one’s eloquence? And you, Arbiter, planted amid the gardens of Massilia on the sacred stem, equal to the Hellespontine Priapus? And you, tender Naso, known through wanton poems and sent away to Tomi, once subjected under the fictitious name of Corinna to a girl too much of a Caesar?

[Note: Barthius, Adversaria, p. 489, reads from an old book: “What shall I say of the lofty Senecas?” For, in addition to Cornelius, there were others famous under the name Celsus. —Baunius, in Sirmond’s preface to volume I, §11.]

What shall I say of the lofty Senecas, or of that Martial whom lofty Bilbilis gives us, a native son of the Iberian lands? What of the poets produced by the twofold marriage torch of Argentaria Polla?

[Note: 157. Lucan and Statius. Lucan’s wife was Polla Argentaria, and after Lucan’s death she became Statius’ wife, as Statius himself explains in the Silvae. Some books read pallida instead.]

What of the many writers of varied style—witty, tender, weighty, and mocking—shall I enumerate? If Consentius was present, they remained hidden.

[Col. 0734C]

To this man of supreme genius, and likewise of supreme nobility and beauty, is joined a woman who, bringing the ancestral insignia of Jovinus into her husband’s house, filled the sophist’s home with consular robes.

[Note: The names trabea and fasti designate the consulship: that of Flavius Valens Jovinus, which he held with Lupicinus as colleague under the elder Valentinian, when he was master of cavalry in Gaul and routed the Alamanni with immense slaughter at Catalaunum, as Marcellinus records in Book XXVII. Flodoardus also writes of him in Book I, chapter 6 of his History, and quotes ancient verses composed by Jovinus for the basilica of Saint Agricola, which he had founded at Reims. Sidonius therefore says that this man’s daughter was married to the elder Consentius. What follows, however, must be understood of the younger Consentius, to whom he is writing.]

Thus, within your own household, Consentius, proud glory of your fatherland, your grandfather lives in the fasti and your father in books.

With such a lineage making you powerful enough, and yet more powerful in the summit of your character, I could not sound your merits in worthy praise—not even if, singing in the Odrysian cave, where the Hebrus resounds through the rocks of the Cicones amid trembling waters, that foremost of poets had trained me.

[Col. 0734D]

When the sweetly animated stones bore the strings through Rhodope as song drew them along, and in the reverse direction, with the springs bound fast, forced the panting earth to run;

[Col. 0735A]

nor if Ismarus had lain open to the sun, while the forest sought the listening lyre, and curved snows fell from Ossa, yielding to no heat; or if the Bistonians had seen the Strymon stand still while its swift water thirsted for song.

Nor if, given over to the two-bodied Centaur’s Pierian plectra, I had stood before the centauric strings, fearing the neighing of my double master.

Nor if that god had taught me to speak who, ordered to pasture his master’s flock, the herdsman-god, did so beside the river Amphrysus—he who with his bow struck down the rust-colored Cyclopes beneath the Liparian forges, releasing a heavier thunderbolt in his arrow.

[Col. 0735B]

From his first tender rising, nine sisters received him into their embrace, and you, crying from your mother’s womb, they covered in the glassy shallows of Hippocrene.

Then, immersed in this water of the eloquent stream, you drank letters rather than mere waves.

Then, already as a boy more capable than a teacher, you swallowed and devoured everything belonging to rhetorical instruction, to grammar, and to the wrestling school, as you had already imbibed it in early youth.

[Col. 0735C]

And the court received you, and the pious emperor immediately placed you among the distinguished tribunes whom the imperial consistorium possesses.

[Note: Pius Valentinian, by whom Consentius was made tribune and notary in the consistorium. Tribunes and notaries served in the emperor’s consistorium. See Theodosian Code, Book I, title 2, *On the Primicerius and Notaries*. The inscription of Petronius Maximus reads: “He served as tribune and notary, first in the sacred consistorium.”]

For the purple-clad ruler in the citadel of empire used to entrust you with offices, because your character deserved noble rank.

So lofty a rank and astonishing an honor are indicated by the distinctions recorded in the annals.

From there you followed an extensive military career, although, through legitimate recommendations, you might have increased your military fortune.

Nevertheless, abstaining from customary gain, you returned home richer in reputation, considering only what you had given to be yours.

Then, if perhaps the emperor wished anything to reach the ears of his Eastern father-in-law through a trustworthy and skilled interpreter—

[Note: Valentinian had married Eudoxia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius the Younger. Sidonius therefore says that Valentinian sent Consentius as an envoy to Theodosius in the East, and that he was suitable to be sent also to the Franks, Persians, Vandals, and other kings.]

—you were immediately chosen as one learned to discharge the commerce of two languages.

O, how often, when you spoke, did the Byzantine realms give you the title of “sage”?

And whether you sounded in Latin, as though born beneath the Roman Subura, or overflowed with the rounded form of the Greek tongue, as though created at Marathon, the Bosphorans applauded in amazement, admiring the Attic pupils less.

[Col. 0736A]

Hence, if the treaties of the world were broken, the fierce Chunnus, Sauromates, Getes, and Gelonian would give peace through you.

[Col. 0736B]

You would enter the Tuncrus, the Vachalis, Visurgis, and Albis, and the deepest marshes of the Franks, while the Sicambri revered you, safe among arms through your character alone.

[Note: Hadrianus Valesius, On Frankish Affairs, Book V, p. 221, reads not Tuncrus, a river unknown, as he says, to all geographers and historians, but Vicrus. “Vicer,” he says, “is a river of trans-Rhenane France, reaching a town of its own name, commonly called the Zuiderzee—that is, the Southern Sea marsh. I observe that it is placed by Claudius Ptolemy in Germany between the Rhine and the river Amisia, and that through scribal error Vidrus is written for Vicrus; today it is called Vectus.” —Baunius, in the same place.]

You would approach Lake Maeotis and the Caspian Gates; you would approach Bactra, ridden through by the Parthians’ swift horses, steadfast and fearless, so that the tyrant swelling with pride, who sits above the satraps and belches out claims of half-divine kinship, would lower his moon-shaped tiara before you.

If public destiny did not forbid you to seek Byrsa, or the rebellious Tanais of African soil, then, with the fury of Mars immediately laid aside, the merchant would set out full ships after the losses inflicted by piracy; and, with peace restored through you, wars would no longer sail toward me.

But if, as you were bringing serious business to an end, the spectacles of the theatre had perhaps caught you, the whole chorus of actors grew pale, as though the Archer-god and the nine Muses sat as judges beside the stage.

[Note: Names of famous pantomimes. One of them, Caramallus, is also praised by Aristaenetus in Letter 26 and by Leontius Scholasticus in Book IV of the Greek Anthology, 25. Pantomimes, or dancers, explained everything through gestures with silent mouths. Cassiodorus writes: “The most eloquent hands of the dancers, the talkative fingers, clamorous silence, silent exposition”; and an unknown author writes of the pantomime: “As many tongues as limbs grow there: marvelous is the art that makes the joints speak with a silent mouth.” The founders of the art at Rome in the age of Augustus were Pylades and Bathyllus. Since the ancients themselves used to sing and dance, these men arranged for a chorus and flute to play before them, as Lucian, On Dancing, Eusebius in the Chronicle, Zosimus in Book I, and others relate. Pantomimes had as many subjects as the poets’ stories, for there was no tale they did not represent. Sidonius therefore lists many here; Lucian lists far more in the dialogue mentioned above. Cyprian, On Spectacles: “For no one, twisting his limbs with obscene movements, danced out a story of Greek lust.”]

Before you, Caramallus or Phabaton, with throat closed and gesture speaking—by nod, leg, knee, hand, and every turn of his body—would not escape notice even once.

[Col. 0737A]

Whether Aeetes’ daughter and her Jason were introduced, and savage Phasis, before whom the scattered teeth thrown across the Colchian fields trembled when, amid the growing battle, the spear-bearing spikes swayed;

or whether someone represented Thyestes’ banquets, or the grim lamentations of Philomela, or the torn child, already made food for his now more innocent husband;

or the abduction of the Tyrian girl, and the bull that was Jupiter, more frightening in his brow than in his rejected thunderbolt;

or Danae’s tower, when it was drenched by a rain of wealth, providing more golden theft than metal;

[Col. 0737B]

or someone played Leda and the Phrygian youth, fitting him to the cup and making him sweeter to the thunderer than the juice of nectar;

or represented Mars, now sent into Lemnian chains, now assuming the form of a boar after his rejection, with a head and back roughened by bristles, bending smooth ivory into a curve with his shaggy jaws;

or depicted the beast’s rough back, its raised weapons continually bristling;

or acted the avenged maiden of Perseus, there represented with her husband’s harpe;

or the ten-year war, enclosed in poetry and fable, which brought battle to Pergamum—

What shall I say of cithara-players, choral flautists, mimes, rope-walkers, jesters, reeds, plectra, games, balls, and ropes, all displayed tremulously before you?

[Col. 0737C]

For since you yourself, amid the Circus games, had achieved such distinction as victor while Rome thundered, it was fitting that a joyous Muse should write about it.

Perhaps two-faced Janus was recalling his Kalends, while Phoebus circled the seasons of the year, which were to be assumed by the curule chariots.

This is the emperor’s custom: twice on a single day to arrange games, which they call private.

Then a gathering of young men, but courtiers, exercises the grim replicas of the Elean field with four-horse chariots moving across the course.

[Col. 0737D]

And now the urn selects you and the hissing acclamation of the hoarse crowd summons you.

[Note: Lots were drawn in the Circus for the selection both of positions and of chariots. Symmachus testifies to the selection of chariots in Book X, Letter 22: “I prefer to explain the roar of the Murcian valley, and that distribution of chariots in which the one who seemed fortunate to himself, when the urn immediately assigned him his choice, had an equal or better pair than the one whom the lot had made last. How often did the first envy the one who followed? Choice is uncertain when equals are judged.” Here he clearly says that the choice was assigned by lot, but all the chariots sent by Theodosius were so excellent that the lot seemed to contribute nothing, since they made the choice ambiguous. Yet selection of chariots was not always practiced; selection of positions never ceased. Thus, in Homer, Iliad 23, in Sophocles’ Electra, and in Statius’ Thebaid VI, because the ancient heroes drove their own chariots, only the positions were assigned by lot. Likewise Virgil, in the mock naval race of Aeneid V: “Then they select positions by lot.” These positions in the Circus were the gates themselves, the starting stalls of the horses: thus first or second position meant nothing other than the first or second gate. Consentius, therefore, whom the urn had called first, selected the axle—that is, the chariot—and entered the first gate; after him the others entered the remaining gates in order. Why lots were used in choosing positions, Donatus hints at but does not explain in his commentary on Virgil’s words just cited: “The labor is not the same in each position; therefore lots are used, as is customary in the Circus, so that there may be no dispute in the arrangement.” Why was the labor not the same? Obviously because the distance from each gate to the turning-post was not the same: from the first it was straight and shortest, from the last longest. Therefore the farther anyone was from the first, the longer the distance over which he traveled, and the more road and labor he had. This also makes clear why an ancient inscription praises the charioteer Diocles for winning “with the chief four-horse team, sent from the fourth gate.” Since four normally raced together, they used only the first four gates. Thus the one who left from the fourth raced with the last and chief chariot, whose victory was most difficult. In this same sense Ovidius writes in Amores III.2: “May this be granted me: when sent from the sacred starting stall, may I mount the horses and be carried with a brave spirit.” This is equivalent to saying: “With you favoring me, I would not hesitate to enter the contest even if sent from the sacred—that is, the last and sixth—gate, and to hope for the palm.”]

Then, where the gate of the Circus and the consuls’ seats are,

[Col. 0739A]

the wall runs round, vaulted with six crypts and starting-stalls on either side; having by chance chosen one of four chariots, you enter, pressing the curved reins.

Your colleague does the same, and the opposing faction likewise does its part:

[Note: The Circus factions were distinguished by the colors of their tunics. There was the white, red, green, and blue faction, as they are named in Diocles’ inscription: “those who use the white and fiery equipment, and that of the green and blue”; and in the Greek Anthology: “the blue, green, red, and white divisions and factions.” From these tunics of different colors, which Pliny the Younger calls vestes discolores, Dio stolai, and an old epigram peploi, Ovid calls the multicolored procession of charioteers. As is clear here, they used them not only in public games but also in private ones; examples are supplied by Commodus and Elagabalus, who are said to have driven at home in green. A few years ago, when we were in Rome, an old double inscription was excavated beside the Via Praenestina, at the third milestone from the city. It lists the palms won by the charioteers Polynices and Tatianus in the individual factions, with six Greek verses added; only the first two remain intact. It reads as follows:

“M. Aur. Polynices, born a slave, who lived 29 years, 9 months, and 5 days; who won 739 palms: in the red faction 655, in the green 55, in the blue 12, in the white 17; prizes 40, numbers 3, 30, 26; pure [victories] 11; with an eight-horse team 8; with a ten-horse team 9; with a six-horse team 3.

“Equal in the yoke with the preceding.

“M. Aur. Mollicius Tatianus, born a slave, who lived 20 years, 8 months, and 7 days; who won 125 palms: in the red faction 89, in the green 23, in the blue 5, in the white 7; prizes 30, number 2.”

“Rome, his fatherland, reared the renowned charioteer Polynices, and Tatianus, his brother, son of two blessed [parents?].” [The corrupt Greek is retained in translation with its uncertainty.]]

The colors glitter: white, blue, green, and red.

[The Greek labels cited above mean respectively “those using white and red equipment, and that of the greens and blues,” and “the blue, green, red, and white parties and peoples.”] Your attendants display your insignia; they hold the horses’ mouths and the reins in their hands, constrain the twisted manes with pliant knots, encourage them as they pass and aid them with generous applause, and by their bland cheering prescribe a pleasurable fury to the four-footed racers.

They rage at the barriers and at once lean against the gates; through the closed boards they breathe forth, and before the race the empty field is occupied by their breath.

They push, tremble, pull, resist; they burn, leap, fear, and are feared. They do not restrain their stride, but with restless feet lash the hardened beam.

[Col. 0740B]

At last, when the trumpet’s resounding blast gives the signal, the trumpeter calls the suspended chariots, and pours the swift cars out into the fields.

[Note: The magistrate gave the signal for releasing the chariots; when the signal was extended, all the stalls were immediately opened at once. At Rome it was customary for the signal to be given by throwing down a cloth. Sidonius omits the cloth, which perhaps had no place in private games, and mentions only the trumpet that followed the cloth—indeed, the only signal known to the ancients. Sophocles writes, “They sprang forth beneath the bronze trumpet”; Virgil, “Then, when the clear trumpet gave its sound”; Statius, “A roar sounded back against the Tyrrhenian.”]

[Col. 0740A]

Not so does the three-forked thunderbolt’s force, nor an arrow driven from a Scythian bow, nor the furrow of a falling star, nor a leaden storm of sling-bullets whirled by Balearic slings ever tear through the clear paths of heaven.

The earth yields to the wheels, and the air is darkened by the dust stirred up.

The drivers press on with their whips; already, bending forward from the chariot, they are dragged along, and their extended bodies strike the horses across the shoulders, leaving the back unoccupied.

You could not quickly discern whether the drivers, bent forward, were supporting the poles or the axles; already their voices seemed to fly from their eyes.

[Col. 0740B]

When the wider open space had been consumed, a narrow field, artificially constructed, had closed it off:

through this, the Euripus, long, low, and double-walled, held back its own structure.

[Note: The turning-post was double. The farther one stood at the lower end of the Circus; Statius called it the inner one, and Sophocles the “furthest pillar.” The other was nearer, at the front of the Circus, not far from the gates; Tertullian calls these the “first turning-posts.” Between the two extended the wall dividing the sides of the Circus. At the first turning-post the distance of the race began and ended; at the last the chariots turned. For this reason the Greeks called it the kampter, from the turn, and Pacuvius called it the campter in Atalanta. Sidonius therefore sets out the whole scene of Consentius’ contest in this way: “At the first turn, Consentius’ colleague was ahead of everyone; closest behind him were both opponents; Consentius himself was fourth and last, restraining his horses by deliberate effort and keeping them fresh through the seventh circuit. In this order they completed the second, third, and fourth circuits. On the fifth, his colleague, with exhausted horses, turned his chariot and yielded first place to the opponents. After they had completed the sixth circuit and seemed close to victory, Consentius suddenly urged on his horses, passed both of them, and emerged victorious in the seventh circuit.”]

When the farther turning-post released them all,

[Col. 0741A]

your colleague became first, ahead of the two who had passed you; thus, by the arrangement of the circuit, you were fourth.

[Note: Since in the Circus they began the race on its right side, or the right-hand row of stalls, it followed that, as the charioteers ran, the turning-posts were always on their left, toward which and alongside which they raced; on their right were the podium and the spectators’ wedges. Therefore the left-hand course was inner and shorter, while the right-hand course was outer and had a longer bend. In this sense poets consistently condemn the right side in these games. Virgil writes: “Why do you go so far to my right?” Statius: “Arion is scattered into circuits and strays to the right.” And Sidonius has Consentius’ opponent say: “He ran too far to the right beneath the wedges.” Thus, if the racer in front, when turning toward the podium and wedges—that is, toward the right—should open the way, it is the concern of the pursuing rival, Sidonius says, to pass inward on the left and overtake him. So Consentius, although behind his opponents, eventually passed both—just as Homer’s Antilochus passed Menelaus, and Maro’s Cleanthus passed Gyas. The same is intended by the words “He followed and won” in Diocles’ inscription.]

It is the duty of the middle racer, when the first, pressed by the faster outer course, opens up the left-hand side, carrying all his reins toward the podium, to pass him by driving his chariot inward.

You, doubling your effort at the very attempt, rein in your four-horse team, and with consummate skill reserve it for the seventh circuit.

The others pressed on with hand and voice; everywhere the sweat of drivers and wing-footed horses fell in drops upon the field.

The hoarse roar of the cheering crowd strikes the heart, and both men and horses alike feel heat from the race and cold from fear.

So they go once, and then a second time; thus comes the third and fourth circuit.

[Col. 0741B]

On the fifth circuit, unable to bear the weight of those behind him, the one ahead turns his axle, because, commanding swift four-horse teams, he had found his horses exhausted.

Now the sixth return had been fully completed, and the crowd was already demanding the prizes. The opposing side, fearing nothing of your strength, was safely wearing down the earlier circuits;

when suddenly, with the wolf-bit reins drawn tight, chest stretched taut, and foot planted forward, you drive your swift team as hard as that charioteer who used to drag Oenomaus while Pisa trembled.

Here [Note: The chief labor and skill of charioteers is to turn properly around the turning-post, which in Homer is εὖ περὶ τέρματ’ ἐλισσέμεν, “to wheel well around the turning-post.” The essence of the art is to turn inward, not in a wide but in a narrower circuit, close to and beside the turning-post; this opponent of Consentius, urged on by him, was unable to do so. Ovid:

> Wretched me! He circles the turning-post in a broad circuit.
>
> What are you doing? Draw near with the axle and approach the post.

Silius Italicus:

> He never allowed the axle, once flung outward, to stray,
>
> but kept the turning-post close on the inner track.

And Seneca, beautifully directing the same thought, *On Tranquillity of Mind* 11:

> We must turn inward not only in the race and contest of the circus, but also in these courses of life, and avoid the turning-post, lest we cling to it or break the chariot upon striking it.

Hence Horace speaks of the turning-post as avoided by the wheels. Theocritus, in *Heracliscus*:

> To drive the horses beneath the chariot, and, turning safely
>
> the signal-post with the wheel, to keep the axle clear.

[Col. 0742D] Homer, in his exhortation from Nestor to Antilochus:

> Avoid the stone and gain upon him,
>
> lest you injure your horses and overturn them beneath the chariots.

And Cicero, likewise alluding to this, in *For Caelius*:

> At this turning-point, as it were, of his life, the young man’s reputation was for a while checked by the new acquaintance with a woman.

[Col. 0742C] the winding shortcuts of the turning-post

While one, pressed hard and urged on by you,

[Col. 0742A] having once raised his four-horse chariot in its rush,

was unable to bend it around in a joined circuit.

Since he passed beyond the mark without observing the rule,

you overtook him, remaining behind and holding back through skill.

While another rejoiced in popular approval,

he ran too far to the right beneath the wedges.

While he made his course oblique and, slow for a long time,

only late urged on the horn-footed horses with the whip,

you yourself passed him on a straight track.

Here an enemy who had followed you too carelessly,

thinking that he had already overtaken the one ahead,

came shamelessly across the axle.

The horses bend inward; the insolent mass of legs

enters the wheels; three times four spokes

are compressed, until, with the spaces filled,

[Col. 0742B] they crack and the revolving rim

breaks the feet. There the fifth man himself,

thrown headlong beneath the crushing chariot,

makes a mountain from the multiplied wreckage,

staining his fallen face with blood.

The renewed crash mingles everything together,

as great as that which the cypress-bearing Lycaeus,

as great as that which wooded Ossa,

raises amid its frequent, restless storms;

as neither Doris nor Trinacris echoes back

the rolling thunder from the south,

nor Propontis, which with its whirlpool-bearing salt

surrounds the Bosporus.

412

Here the fair-minded commander immediately causes

silken palms [Note: The prizes of victory in the circus were palms and crowns; sometimes, as marks of honor, little ribbons or fillets of silk or gold were added to them. Hence crowns or palms were called *lemniscatae*, “adorned with ribbons.” On crowns Pliny, book XXI:

> Fillets were also added; it was an honor to add them to the crowns themselves, especially in the case of the Etruscan crowns, to which nothing but golden fillets might be joined.

On the palm, Ausonius’ Paulinus:

> And the poetic palm which has long flourished for you
>
> is adorned with a fillet, which my palm lacks.

] to be joined with collars and crowns,

and orders merit to be rewarded,

[Col. 0743A] commanding the defeated to depart

with suitably shameful, multicolored woollen coverings. [Note: It was customary to give some prize even to the defeated, as a consolation. Ambrose, *On Repentance* I.3:

> Often in this secular contest of athletes, the common people have been accustomed to crown even those who were defeated, when their contests had been worthy of approval, together with the victors—especially those whom they saw to have been excluded from victory by chance, deceit, or fraud.

Homer, Virgil, Statius, and Silius represent the same practice in their contests. At the theatrical games of Julius Caesar, in which the mime-poets Laberius and Publius Syrus competed, when Laberius had been defeated Caesar gave the palm to Syrus, the victor, and a ring to the defeated man, as Macrobius records in *Saturnalia* II.7.]

Now, when the youthful performances have been completed, [Note: “In the time of youth.” What follows, “in later age,” clearly confirms this interpretation and refutes the error of highly learned men who have suspected that *Juvenales* here refers to the Juvenal Games; they should also have remembered that the Juvenal Games were of a different kind from the circus games. Sidonius therefore uses *juvenalia* to mean youthful pursuits, the activities of youthful age. Ancient copyists wrote both forms indiscriminately: in Sidonius himself, book I, letter 2, the manuscripts mostly read *juvenali rubore*, “with youthful blush,” rather than *juvenili*; book IV.13 has *juvenali sanitate*; and book IX.6 has *facilitate juvenali*.]

what sort of man you showed yourself to be in later life,

when, sought out for the court of my father-in-law Avitus [Note: The emperor Avitus, whose palace Consentius administered, just as Equitius once administered that of Valens, Constantius that of Honorius, and Aetius that of John. Those who held this office were later called *curopalatae* at the Eastern court, with the highest authority, being “entrusted with the guardianship of the palace,” as Evagrius writes in book V.1; in Francia they were the mayors of the palace. Fredegarius: “They appointed Warado mayor of the palace in place of Ebroin. Warado had a son, who administered the palace in his father’s place, named Gislemarus.”]

you moderated the administration of the palace,

we shall speak of these matters in later writings,

if more time remains for the future.

Now, let gracious Thalia attend briefly

to the hospitality we have mentioned.

O sweet house, O dutiful household gods!

Whom difficult circumstances and freedom

alike cultivate, together with modesty.

O banquets, stories, little books,

laughter, seriousness, witticisms,

[Col. 0743B] meetings, and the same single companionship!

Whether we had to visit the temples of God,

or climb the steps to the bishop,

or go to the heights of Marcius Myron,

or see the splendid house of Livius;

or the home of eloquent Leo,

where, while he taught twice six tables of law,

Appius Claudius would willingly remain silent,

more obscure than he in the decemvirate.

But if he should recite an epic and bend

its meter with rhythmic, sharply divided phrases,

with his plectrum resounding,

413 he would make biting Flaccus fall silent;

although, after extending his satire and lyre,

that man strives to fly toward the Pindaric swan.

Or your favor held us, Magnus,

endowed with many virtues of men:

beauty, nobility, intelligence, and wealth.

If I were to recount him through his varied activities,

a hundred iron mouths would be wearied by praise.

Steadfast, talented, and effective,

a prudent judge, the best of relatives,

withholding nothing from his talent or from anyone else’s,

he looked to persons, places, and time.

Or your halls held us,

my Marcellinus, skilled in the law;

[Col. 0744A] excessively truthful and excessively strict,

you are thought harsh by one who does not know you;

but if anyone has come to know you well,

he knows what the man himself wishes to judge.

For you never fear to speak what is just,

even if Sulla oppresses you and savage Carbo;

if the grim Marii and fierce Cinnae,

and, perhaps, the triumvirs’ swords,

surround your head and side.

Or the home of Limpidius held us,

a magnificent citizen and outstanding man,

who faithfully followed the fraternal rule;

or the exceptional courtesy of Marinus

held us together,

whose diligence and companionship

[Col. 0744B] must be honored by me with everlasting praise;

414 or any other brothers whom both our hearts

were glad to see, for whom I think

that having leisure was a praiseworthy occupation.

Although affection desires to recite their names in verse,

the meter refuses.

Hence you summoned us to your own house,

when the fresh morning had gone out,

and the sun, growing warm, gave the second hour.

Here, bringing out polished balls and hoops,

here, dice rattling in noisy dice-boxes,

while we were drawing ourselves up for the blows of the *tractus* game,

you rejoiced to stir up a cheerful quarrel,

as though you were one of the Naupliads,

the discoverer of the art.

From there we would go to baths—not Nero’s,

[Col. 0744C] nor those which Agrippa gave,

nor those of the man whose tomb the Dalmatians

of Salona look upon;

yet we loved to go to the baths,

well suited to private modesty.

After them your cups and the central couch

of your Muses held us:

such works as neither statues nor images,

in bronze, marble, or colors,

were given by Mentor, Praxiteles, or Scopas;

such figures as Polyclitus himself never fashioned,

nor is any form made beneath the Phidian sky.

[Col. 0745A] But now five hundred hendecasyllables

beg your pardon for their loquacity.

It is a long poem, if you wish;

it is already enough, and you yourself are hindered,

reading your friend’s poem at length,

more idle than sleepers.

415

## POEM XXIV

[Note: This is a farewell poem, in which he sends out a book and escorts it through all the homes of his friends as far as Narbo. This is what the Greeks call *propempein*, “to escort on the way.” There was once a farewell poem of Pollio, written by Helvius Cinna, as Charisius testifies; and one of Ampelius, published by Himerius. There was also a farewell poem of Metius Celer, which is read in Statius, book III of the *Silvae*.]

### FAREWELL POEM TO A LITTLE BOOK

When you have gone out from my doors, little book,

remember, I beg you, to keep to this road,

which leads safely to our friends,

whose names I have carefully recorded.

May you not wear away the ancient roadway,

[Col. 0745B] across whose extent the name of a sufficiently ancient

Caesar flourishes on its columns. [Note: In the Theodosian Code, “Concerning the repair of roads,” law 6:

> Let it be far from us to count among sordid duties the construction of a public road and bridges and the work of paved roads, dedicated by inscriptions to great emperors.

The stones or columns that marked the miles on public roads sometimes bore only the number of miles, while others also carried the titles and names of the emperors under whom, or during whose age, the roads had been repaired and restored. Of this kind is the one published by Savaro in the *Claromontane Origins*, excavated from the military road that once led from Augustonemetum of the Arverni to Lugdunum:

> TI. CLAUD. DRUSI F. CAESAR. AUG. GER. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POTEST. V. IMP. XI. P. P. COS. III. DES. IV.
>
> AUG. M. P. XXI.

164 And this other one, at the boundary of the Arverni and Gabali, excavated several years ago, has not yet seen the light of day; but I fear it reached us in a corrupt form:

> IMP. CAES. M. CAS. LAT. POSTUMO P. F. AUG. COS. M. P. GABALL. V.

[Col. 0746B] The former counts the miles from Augustonemetum; the latter from the Gabali, whom a later age, adapting the name to modern usage, called the Gebaldanenses, as can be seen in the letters of John VIII.]

But go slowly, so that by delaying you may renew

your old affection among your friends.

[Note: In his little book he marks out ten stopping-places and lodgings. The first is the home of Domitius Grammaticus, to whom he writes in book II, letter 2. The second is Brivas, now divided into two places: the new town, famous for its distinguished chapter of canons, and the old town, as Sidonius calls it. The third is the city of the Gabali, after crossing a ridge and the river Triobres, now still called Trobris, flowing down from the mountains of the Gabali into the territory of the Rutheni. The fourth is the home of the brothers Sacerdos and Justinus; he does not mention the location of their residence, but writes to both in book V of the letters. The fifth is the home of Ferreolus, a former prefect, and his wife Papianilla, at Trevidum in the territory of the Rutheni. The sixth is the home of Apollinaris, at his estate of Voroangus, about which he writes in book II, letter 9, where he mentions Mount Lesora, once, as Pliny reports in book XI, chapter 42, famous at Rome for the excellence of its cheese; now, with the letters transposed, it is called Loserum. He also mentions the gold-bearing river Tarnis, which rises in the Cebennae, passes through the territories of Aquitania and Narbonensis, and flows into the Garonne. The seventh is Avitus’ home at Cottium, to whom he writes in book III, letter 1. The eighth is Fidulus’, though he does not say where. There is no other mention of this Fidulus, but the name was not unknown among the Gauls. Not long after Sidonius, in the time of King Theodoric, there flourished Saint Fidulus, an Arvernian by birth and abbot among the Tricasses, who hold him in exceptional veneration and call him Saint Falus. The ninth is Thaumastus’ home at Tresvillae. Thaumastus and his brother Apollinaris are mentioned several times in the letters. The tenth is the home of the sons Magnus, Felix, and Probus. We learned from poem 23 that Magnus was from Narbonese family. From this passage we noted that Probus’ wife, Eulalia, was a relative of Sidonius; see book IV, letter 1.]

And first you will enter the severe home

of Domitius, with your Muses trembling:

not even that censorious man,

who is said to have laughed once in his life,

was so censorial.

But you may rejoice in his learned severity:

if he approves you, you will please everyone.

From there kindly Brivas will receive you,

which cherishes the bones of Saint Julian:

although they are thought to be dead among the dead,

the living power shines from the tomb.

From there you will take the fields farther to the right,

and, having crossed the ridge in a single day,

on the next day you will see the yellow Triobres.

Then you will see the sufficiently snowy land

of the Gabali, and, as the natives

wish it to be thought,

416 their city, lofty in a well.

From there you will hasten to the Laconians of my own time,

Justinus and his brother,

whose love is known throughout the world

and surpasses Pirithous and Theseus

and the faithful companion of raging Orestes.

When you have been received into their embrace,

you will go to Trevidum [Note: This passage is discussed in the *Mémoires de l’Académie des Inscriptions*, volume III, page 260, in the *History*.]

and to the ridge—alas, too close

to the slanderous Rutheni.

[Col. 0746B] There you will find the learned father of Tonantius,

the leader and pillar of the Gauls,

Ferreolus, the equal of the ancient Syagrius;

his wife Papianilla, sharing his cares

in chaste labor, supports him,

such as neither Tanaquil was,

nor she whom you, Tricipitinus, fathered,

nor she who was consecrated to the Phrygian Vesta,

who, against the swollen Albulus,

drew a boat with her maiden hair.

From there Lesora will look upon you,

surpassing the Caucasus of the Scythians,

and swift Tarnis, carrying a fish

pressed with a firm flavor [Note: Hadrianus Valesius, in *Notes on Gaul*, page 544, says that these words, “pressed with a firm flavor,” yield no tolerable sense and that one should certainly read “pressed by a dull stupor.” But this correction seems less necessary to us. Why should the fish of that river not be praised for firm, dense flesh, and therefore more agreeable flavor, since in many fish the taste is more diluted because of their softness? Moreover, “dull stupor” does not suit fish very well. —Baunius, editor of Sirmond, preface to volume I, §11.]

[Col. 0747A] and bearing it through transparent water.

May these lend you the wings of Zetes and Calais,

and, swift as you are, beware the stormy ridge,

for it is fertile in continual storms.

But although you may be carried along in rapid flight,

weary Voroangus will hold you [Note: See the passage cited in the *Mémoires*, page 261.]

There you will find our Apollinaris,

whether, against the heat of the raging lion,

417 he clothes the household gods in marble with coolness;

or strolls in secluded gardens,

such as flourish in honey-bearing Hybla,

such as the pitchy liquid of the Gale­sus

made pleasant for the old man of Corycus.

Whether amid violets, thyme, privet,

wild thyme, cassia, saffron, and marigolds,

[Col. 0747B] he scorns narcissi and hyacinthine flowers,

and the incense-bearing clod which the Sabaean,

seeker of a high price, brings.

Or rather, whether he rests in an artificial grotto,

where, bending back the grove at the edge of the hill,

he works to provide a natural colonnade

and makes not a grove from trees but a cave.

Who here could compare the ancient orchards

of the king of India,

or the golden vines, whose leaves are green electrum,

when Porus placed, amid clattering treasure,

a vine of metal made from the golden branch,

with clusters of floating gems?

[Col. 0748A] From there you will go to Cottium, and to our Avitus

you will say “hail,” then “farewell”;

you owe the man perpetual courtesy.

For let my relatives forgive me:

for me a kinsman does not take precedence over a friend.

From there Fidulus, the glory of good men,

and in no respect second to Tetradius

in the virtues of character or the constancy of uprightness,

will receive you with holy hospitality.

Then direct your step to Tresvillae

418 and seek out Thaumastus, whichever of the two:

the younger is my companion

and colleague as well as brother in rank.

But if the elder happens to be found by you,

salute him, bowing, almost as an uncle.

[Col. 0748B] From there come to the spacious house of the consul Magnus,

and to your Felix, little book.

Probus will have you admitted,

once approved, to the paternal library,

such as even stern Philagrius did not possess.

There you will often be read by my Eulalia,

whose character equaled that of Cecropian Minerva;

the stern old men, and even her once-purple

father-in-law, feared her.

But now it is enough: behold, leave the harbor,

lest I press you with too great a weight of ballast.

In these verses raise your anchor.

[Col. 0747]

## SIDONIAN CROWN

On the precedence of position: who is called “inner” and who “outer”; what it means to cover someone’s side; and whether “to occupy the middle” (*μέσον ἔχειν*) is to the right or to the left.

[Col. 0747C] I have postponed until here two verses in which Sidonius says that, during his Gothic embassy, he walked in the middle between King Theodoric and Frideric, the king’s brother:

> With the king held on one side and his brother on the other,
>
> he entered Palladian Toulouse with hands entwined.

It is not that much needs to be demonstrated concerning the fact that this was done as a mark of honor, since no one doubts that, when three are together, the middle is the most honorable position. Rather, I have wished, at the end of the book, to range more freely and to explain somewhat more fully what we formerly discussed concerning the notions of inner and outer position, the protection of one’s side, and the distinction between right and left in precedence of honor—and to add these reflections, at least as a kind of crown, in the form of notes. I admit that this may be an appendix. But the labor will not be regretted if, even outside the main line, I say something that may win the approval of philologists and shed some light on good authors.

Therefore, because, for example, in the circus game—so as not to depart from our author—Sidonius in poem 23 called the chariot driven on the right the “outer” one, while the chariot driven on the inside was driven to the left, it should not immediately be inferred from similar passages, as has strangely deceived learned men, that the inner position is everywhere the left, or that the right-hand position is always the outer. For it is certain that the inner position, according to circumstances, is now on the right and now on the left, and the same is true of the outer position.

In the circus, certainly, the inner side was the left, but this was because the racers turned toward the left at the turning-post. Suppose, on the contrary, that they turned to the right: everything would be reversed. The inner side would then be the right and the left would be the outer, as must have happened with the chariot which Solinus, chapter 46, relates to have leapt toward the Capitol after its charioteer had been thrown out and the contest abandoned, and to have circled the Tarpeian Jupiter with three rightward turns.

Likewise, in the daily motion of the sky and stars, which themselves circle the pole in a rightward circuit, as though in perpetual movement to the right, Cynosura is inner to Helice and yet is on the right. Nor can the verse from Cicero’s *Aratus* be understood otherwise:

> It turns in a short circuit on the inner course.

You may take “inner course” as “right-hand course.”

Why say more? Every day we see in two-horse chariots, when they turn at the ends of streets, and in oxen, when they plow and draw alternating furrows, that, of two oxen or two horses, the inner one in the turn is now on the right and now on the left. What we observe in these cases should likewise be applied to the movement and procession of human beings. The reason is the same, since the relation of the terms is the same.

Just as, in the circus and at the turn around the turning-post, the one is called “inner” who turns closer to the turning-post than to his opponent, so, when two walk together, the inner position belongs to the one who walks in the inner place—that is, in the middle between his outer companion and the buildings, or whatever else closes off his other side.

[Col. 0749A] In my judgment, this is the meaning of the familiar verses of Ovid, *Fasti* V, where he says that the younger men granted this honor to the old man, so that, if there were two companions, he walked in the middle, and if there was one, on the inside:

> And in the midst of the young men, with none of them objecting,
>
> he walked; and inward, if there was a single companion.

The meaning of “outer,” and of the one said to cover the other’s side, is no different in Horace, *Satires* II.5:

> … Yet do not refuse,
>
> if he orders you, to walk as his outer companion,
>
> lest I fail to cover filthy Dama’s side.

Justus Lipsius, a man of the highest ingenuity, thought that the “inner” person was one whose outer companion preceded him slightly and partly as a mark of honor—or, as he later preferred to interpret it, one who himself went ahead of the other. I fear that this has been devised more cleverly and ingeniously than truthfully.

For, to say nothing of how exceedingly strange and almost ridiculous it would seem for three people to walk at an equal pace, and, when one companion withdrew, for the other immediately to leap from his position in order to precede or follow the old man slightly, it is clear that on this interpretation the side is not properly covered by the one called “outer,” nor is there any reason why he should be called “inner” rather than “forward.”

In our interpretation, however, everything is plain, certain, and straightforward. The inner person is truly the one who walks between his companion and the buildings; the outer is plainly the one who occupies the outer position. The outer person is rightly said to cover the inner person’s side, since he closes off that side of the inner person which would otherwise be uncovered and exposed, while the latter’s other side is protected by the buildings.

In this sense Seneca says in Letter 22:

> Will the side be exposed? An unaccompanied litter?

He calls the side “exposed” because no outer companion covers it. Minucius Felix, on the other hand, writes in the *Octavius* that the sides of the person seated between two others are protected by both:

> And when we sat beside him, he said, so that, being in the middle of the three, they protected my sides through their desire to honor me.

Nor should one inquire whether the inner person always holds the right, as Lipsius and others thought, or the left, as Nebrissensis held. It is sufficiently clear that the inner person in walking, as in other matters, is now on the right and now on the left. Neither side belongs intrinsically to the force of the term; it happens accidentally, according as the person called “inner” is nearer to the right or the left of the one beside whom he walks.

“What then,” someone may say, “if the person walking in the inner position happens to be on the left? Will you say that he walks in the more honorable place?”

Certainly, I reply, since the inner position is the place of honor. The other is the outer person, and he covers the inner person’s side because he is the inferior one and the one rendering honor.

Finally, to sum it up briefly, this is my view. Among the ancient Romans, as today among our Gauls and most other peoples, the principal place of honor in walking and sitting was always the inner position, although it was not always the right. Ovidius and Horace state this clearly and without exception, so that those who wish to argue exclusively for the right or for the left are arguing in vain.

Yet I would not remove its own precedence from the right. It is clear that honor was assigned to the right. First, whenever there was nothing nearby such that one person could be called inner in relation to another, or could be said to cover his side, they always preferred the right to the left. Thus, in Suetonius, *Tiberius* 6, Marcellus was undoubtedly given precedence because he rode on the right in the procession of the Actian triumph, while Tiberius rode on the left.

Then, in the very observance of the inner position, they would strive, insofar as possible, to combine the honor of the right with that position, so that the same person would be both right-hand and inner. With this in mind, Helenius Acro explained the outer position in a verse of Horace as the left-hand position. Eutropius likewise says that the person walked on the left when Suetonius had written of the emperor Claudius that, as he went with Plautius to the Capitol, he covered his side—not because these positions were necessarily always joined, but because they were usually joined by custom.

When circumstances did not permit the inner person to be on the right, then they followed precisely the practice customary among us in Gaul: they gave greater weight to the inner position and granted the place of honor on the left rather than giving the right to the outer person. Thus the left sometimes received its own honor, but only when it was the inner position; the right was always preferred, except when it could not be the inner position.

The inner position, however, always possessed the principal and perpetual dignity—not because it was right or left, but because it was superior, prior, and in a certain sense central: central, I say, between the companion and whatever it was that closed off the other side.

Thus the Greeks also use *μέσον ἔχειν*, “to occupy the middle,” and *μέσον λαβεῖν*, “to receive into the middle,” of two people, when one is received into the inner position. Thus Plutarch, in *Cato of Utica*, says that when they were walking together, Philostratus walked on the outside as a mark of honor toward philosophy:

> Φιλόστρατον ἐν Σικελίᾳ μέσον εἶχε περιπατῶν, ἐπὶ τιμῇ φιλοσοφίας  
> “While walking in Sicily, he kept Philostratus in the middle, in honor of philosophy.”

And the old commentator, explaining a verse of Juvenal, satire 3:

> Here the son of a freeborn man covers the side of a wealthy slave,

says:

> “Either he puts the slave in the middle, or he walks on the left.”

These words wonderfully confirm our entire position. The subject is two people, as in Horace, whose passage Juvenal echoes here. Therefore he distinguishes the two possibilities in this way: “to put into the middle” means to grant the inner position, whether on the left or on the right; “to walk on the left” applies when neither position is inner. In that case only the honor of the right remains, and it is given to the more distinguished person.

[Col. 0749]

## SIRMOND’S EXPLANATION OF THE PROPER NAMES OF THE MIDDLE AGES: THEIR USUAL SOURCES AND THEIR DIFFERENCE FROM ANCIENT ROMAN USAGE

[Col. 0749D] We have already spoken, in the discussion of names in the Middle Ages, of Ennodius, and of the custom that prevailed at Rome after the overthrow of the Republic and in the provinces: although noble persons commonly used several names, each person nevertheless had one proper name, which they always placed last. Since Sidonius’ name also reminds us of this matter, and since we remember that we are bound by our promise, we must discuss it somewhat more fully here.

It is not obscure that the name Sidonius was placed after all his other names according to this rule, as his proper name. For the later age always placed the proper name after all the others. In this respect it departed from the usage and custom of the ancient Romans.

Among the Romans, while the Republic stood, the proper name was the first one, that is, the praenomen. By it brothers themselves were distinguished from one another, although they shared the remaining names: for example, Publius Cornelius Scipio and Lucius Cornelius Scipio, brothers; likewise Marcus Tullius Cicero and Quintus Tullius Cicero, brothers.

Later, however, people began to use and distinguish themselves by the last names rather than the first as their proper names: for example, Salvius Otho and Salvius Titianus, and likewise the brothers Flavius Vespasianus and Flavius Sabinus in Suetonius. With this in mind, Suetonius, in the case of the Vitellian brothers, notes as something peculiar that they alone were distinguished by their praenomina. This certainly would not have been new in the time of the Republic, for then, as I have said, brothers were distinguished in no other way.

Hence also Plutarch’s dispute with Posidonius. At the beginning of the life of Marius, Plutarch criticizes Posidonius, who had taught that the first name was the proper Roman name, whereas Plutarch preferred to call the third name the proper one. This must be understood in such a way that Posidonius was speaking in accordance with the period of the flourishing Republic, while Plutarch was speaking in accordance with his own age—that is, the age of the Caesars, when not the first name, as formerly, but the last name was proper to each person.

I say “proper,” and the one name by which a person alone—when it was desired to omit the others—was designated. This was also what we observed concerning Ennodius. It was often the only name entered in calendars, on coins, on monuments, and in the titles of books.

In the calendars, for example, Domitian’s colleague in his ninth consulship was written sometimes merely as Rufus, and sometimes with all his names, as we learned from a Roman inscription: Quintus Petilius Rufus. Likewise Philip’s colleague under Honorius appears sometimes as Bassus and sometimes as Anicius Auchenius Bassus. Some coins of the emperor Postumus display only this name, while others call him Marcus Cassius Latienus Postumus.

The same can be observed in inscriptions on stones and in books, as well as in other ancient monuments. Nevertheless, it must not be concealed that there seems to have been some deviation in certain book titles. We call the author of *On Agriculture* Palladius, as though that were his proper name; more correctly he should be called Aemilianus, as Isidore names him in book XVII of the *Etymologies* [Note: Cassiodorus likewise does so in *Divine Readings* II.], because this is his last name, when all his names are given: Palladius Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus.

Again, Avienus, in the letter prefixed to his Aesopic fables, and Boethius call the man whom we call Macrobius “Theodosius.” There is no doubt that this was his true name, since it is the last one, when the remaining names are added: Macrobius Ambrosius Aurelius Theodosius.

Therefore, just as it is known to have happened with the author of the *Variae*, so that Cassiodorus was called Senator by those who suspected that “Senator” was not a proper name but an epithet, the same must be believed to have happened through the carelessness of copyists in these two cases and several others: when they began, for the sake of brevity, to write only one of those names in their books, they ignorantly chose the name appearing first rather than the last, which was the proper one.

This error in a few cases should not damage the established and certain rule. Let it therefore stand that, among people of the later age, the proper name was the last one; accordingly, writers of the *Historia Augusta* sometimes call it the true name and sometimes the proper name. Sometimes they even call it simply the name, as a letter of the emperor Valerian concerning Probus in Vopiscus makes clear, while the names that preceded it were called indiscriminately either praenomina or cognomina.

It remains for us to investigate where they usually obtained and assigned names, and how in this respect too they differed from the ancients. Here again the names and examples supplied by Sidonius will provide the evidence.

From these we learn that in later centuries the following custom likewise prevailed in assigning names: both the proper name of each person and the accompanying names—whether cognomina or praenomina, for all these varied almost from one person to another—were usually borrowed from parents and relatives: fathers, uncles, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and other loved ones.

This is certainly true. For example, the names of Fulgentius the bishop were Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius; among these, Claudius had been his father’s proper name, and Gordianus his grandfather’s.

The names of Symmachus the orator’s son were [Note: In the posthumous edition edited by Labbe: Quintus Fabius Memmius Symmachus, in which the cognomen Fabius is uncertain, while Memmius came from his grandfather, and so forth. But Juretus, who illustrated Symmachus’ letters with notes, maintains that the orator’s son was named Quintus Flavius Memmius Symmachus.] Quintus Flavianus Memmius Symmachus. Among these, Flavianus was taken from his paternal uncle, and Memmius from his maternal grandfather, Memmius Orfitus.

Likewise, the name Apollinaris, which had been the proper name of Sidonius’ grandfather, was among Sidonius’ other names a praenomen. Similarly, Magnus was a praenomen for Magnus Felix, because it had been the proper name of Magnus’ father; conversely, Tonantius was the name of Tonantius Ferreolus’ father and served as his praenomen.

Again, Majorianus and Anthemius each bore the name of his maternal grandfather, while Himerius bore that of his paternal grandfather. In short, no other rule should be sought for the names of the later age.

For at that time there were no fixed and established names of clan and family, as formerly—names that were shared by brothers and passed down to descendants. Thus all those born from the Cornelian or Julian clan were called Cornelii or Julii; likewise Scipiones or Cicerones were those belonging to the house and family of the Scipiones or Cicerones.

But after the fall of the Republic everything gradually began to change and decline. Although at first some traces of the old practice remained in hereditary names retained by certain families, as the examples we have cited from the Salvii and Flavii show, later even this practice was neglected. In the end there was no fixed name of family or clan, and sons often differed from their fathers and brothers in all, or nearly all, their names.

This can be seen, to infer the general rule from a few examples, in Flavius Avitus Marin­ianus, the colleague of Asclepiodotus in the consulship. His son was called Rufius Praetextatus Postumianus, himself a consul, when Sidonius was a boy, together with Zeno. The same is true of Quintus Clodius Hermogenianus Olybrius and Faltonius Probus Alypius, who were brothers in the time of Theodosius, and likewise of others.

Nevertheless, amid this very diversity in the use of names, they still observed the rule I have mentioned: that almost all, or at least most, of the names were taken from blood relatives and kinsmen; some were also repeated more frequently as customary family names.

In this sense Trebellius Pollio writes that the family of the tyrant Censorinus was marked by the repeated use of the name Censorinus, and Senator Cassiodorus asserts in *Variae* I.2 that the name Cassiodorus was proper to his family—not because no one outside those families was called Censorinus or Cassiodorus, but because these names were used more frequently within those two families.

To conclude the matter briefly, the names of the Middle Ages had, in a certain sense, a twofold rule. One was that they placed each person’s proper name last; the other was that both this proper name and the remaining names were assigned sometimes arbitrarily from elsewhere, but for the most part derived from close relatives and loved ones.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 482. PERPETUUS, BISHOP OF TOURS

[Col. 0751]

## NOTICE FROM CAVE
[Col. 0751D] Perpetuus, a Gaul by nation, born of a very wealthy senatorial father, succeeded Eutochius, to whom he was related by blood, in the see of Tours in the year 461 or the preceding year. In the same year he attended the First Council of Tours; in 465, the Council of Vannes. In the year 482, having built a very splendid and magnificent basilica over the tomb of Saint Martin, he compelled the provincial bishops to assemble for the celebration of its dedication. He died in 490 or 491. His testament and epitaph are preserved in Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, vol. V. For the use of the Church of Tours he established fasts and vigils, specifying how they were to be observed throughout the course of the entire year. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Deeds of the Franks*, book X, chapter 30, presents the order established by him, transcribed from the public registers of the Church of Tours.

[Col. 0753]

## TESTAMENT OF PERPETUUS [Note: “This noble monument of antiquity,” says Acherius, “which the distinguished man Hieronymus Vignerius extracted long ago, requires no commentary. Everything contained in it agrees with imperial and pontifical law; it agrees with the consular Fasti; it agrees with what Gregory of Tours relates about Perpetuus in chapter 6: ‘Perpetuus too was, as they say, of senatorial stock, and a relative of his predecessor; very wealthy, and possessing estates in many cities.’ And, after some intervening material: ‘He drew up his testament and assigned, in each of the cities, what he possessed, namely, to those very churches, contributing no small property to the Church of Tours as well. He sat for thirty years and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.’] BISHOP. (C,G)*

[Col. 0753A] In the name of Jesus Christ, amen. I, Perpetuus, a sinner and priest of the Church of Tours, did not wish to depart without a testament, lest the poor be defrauded of those things which heavenly grace, without any merit of mine, generously and lovingly bestowed upon me; and lest, God forbid, my possessions pass to anyone other than the Church of the priest.

To the priests, deacons, and clerics of my Church I give and bequeath the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Confirm, O Lord, what you have wrought in us; let them know no schisms and remain steadfast in the faith. Whoever follows the rule of the Gospel, let him be blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places through Christ Jesus. Amen. And may the Lord Jesus slay the impious one with the breath of his mouth. Amen, amen.

Peace to the Church, peace to the people, in the city and in the countryside, from God and the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Come, Lord, and do not delay. Amen.

Therefore, with the advice of Count Agilo, I permit you, the priests, deacons, and clerics of my Church, to bury this body of death wherever you may choose. [Col. 0753C] I know that my Redeemer does not die, and that in the flesh I shall see my Liberator. Amen.
