Yet if you should do me, unworthy as I am, the mercy which I humbly entreat, I would wish to rest at the feet of the lord Martin until the day of judgment. You will see, judge, and choose; I desire, determine, and order that whatever pleases you, my lords and brothers, be done.

First, therefore, I, Perpetuus, wish all the male and female slaves whom I possess in the estate of Saponaria, whom I purchased with my own money, to be free, as well as the children whom on the day of my departure I shall not manumit in the Church. They are nevertheless to serve my Church freely for as long as they live, but without servile status being transmissible to heirs and without attachment to the soil.

I also give and bequeath to my Church the field which Aligarius sold to me in the said estate of Saponaria, together with its pond. Likewise, the mills above the Carus, near the said estate; and also the livestock and meadows, I give and bequeath to that same Church of mine.

The estate of Bertiniacum, with its woodland and all its revenue, under the same conditions on which it was sold to me by the deacon Daniel, I likewise give and bequeath to my Church. It is nevertheless my wish that oil be prepared from its revenues for the perpetual illumination of the tomb of the lord Martin. If this is neglected, however, and my wish—something I do not expect—comes to nothing, I wish, determine, and order that the said estate of Bertiniacum with its appurtenances pass to my heirs, to be named below.

Whatever is owed to me, wherever it may be and by whatever person, on the day of my departure I give and bequeath to the debtors themselves. I wish and determine that no one presume to collect what I remit.

To you, my most beloved brother and fellow priest Eufronius, I give and bequeath a silver reliquary containing relics of the saints. I mean the one which I used to carry. The other gilded one, which is in my treasury, together with two golden chalices and a likewise golden cross made by Mabuinus, I give and bequeath to my Church. At the same time, I give and bequeath all my books, except the Gospel book which Hilary, formerly priest of Poitiers, wrote. That book, together with the aforesaid reliquary, I give and bequeath to you, Eufronius, my most beloved brother and fellow priest; I desire and determine this. Remember me. Amen.

To the Church of Saint Dionysius of Rambasciscum, I give and bequeath a silver chalice and likewise a silver cross, in whose handle there is a relic of that same Saint Dionysius.

To the Church of Proillus I likewise give and bequeath a silver chalice and silver vessels. Likewise, to Amalarius, the priest there, I give one ordinary silk casket, also a *peristerium*, and a silver dove for the repository—unless my Church should prefer to transfer to the same Amalarius the one which it uses and retain mine. I leave the choice to my Church; I desire and determine this.

To my sister Fidia Julia Perpetua I give and bequeath a small golden cross of inlaid work (*emblasma*), containing relics of the Lord. I nevertheless earnestly ask her that, if by the Lord’s command she should happen to depart this life before the virgin Dadolena, she leave it to my Church for her possession. I also ask you, sister Dadolena, when you die, to assign it to whichever Church you please, lest it come to the unworthy. But if Dadolena should pass away before you, then you, my dearest sister Fidia Julia Perpetua, shall be free to leave the aforesaid cross to whichever Church you wish. I desire and determine this. Remember me, dearest sister. Amen.

To you, Count Agilo, because of your outstanding services to my Church and to my poor children, and so that you may continue to undertake their protection vigorously, as you have begun, I give and bequeath my serviceable horse and whichever mule you choose. Remember me, my most beloved son. Amen.

To the Church of Saint Peter I give and bequeath outright and unconditionally the hangings which I have often entrusted to it for use at the Nativity of that same saint.

To you, my dearest brother and fellow priest, whom the Lord will provide to govern after my departure the Church which is now mine, then yours—or rather neither mine nor yours, but Christ’s—I give whatever you may wish to choose from my possessions in the chamber and the adjoining treasury for episcopal use. Whatever you do not want shall belong to my heirs, who are to be named.

Never restore the priest of Malleium or the priest of Orbona to the orders from which they were deservedly deposed. Nevertheless, let them receive their allowance for as long as they live from part of my revenues from Preslaium. Whatever remains, together with that portion which I granted them for use and enjoyment, I leave to you for use and enjoyment after they have died; after your departure, I give and bequeath it to my Church.

But you, dearest brother and fellow priest, love my priests, deacons, clerics, and virgins, as well as your own; assist them by your example and anticipate them with goodwill. See that they know themselves to be your sons, not your slaves; and that you are their father, not their master. I ask, desire, and determine this.

But you, my inmost being, dearest brothers, my crown, my joy, my lords, my sons, the poor of Christ, the needy, beggars, the sick, widows, and orphans—you, I say, I write, declare, and establish as my heirs. After the things mentioned above have been deducted, whatever possessions I have, whether fields, pastures, meadows, woods, vineyards, estates, gardens, waters, or mills, or whether gold, silver, clothing, or any other things concerning which it shall not be established that I have made a disposition, I order that you be the heirs.

And so that everything may be administered with prudence, I wish the possessions to be sold as soon as possible after my death, whenever that can be done, and converted into money, of which there shall be three parts. Two parts are to be distributed among needy men, as Agrarius the priest and Count Agilo may decide. The third is to be distributed among widows and poor women, as the virgin Dadolena may decide. I desire, ask, and determine this.

I, Perpetuus, reread and subscribed this testament, written in my own hand, on the Kalends of May after the consulship of Leo the Younger Augustus. You, Delmatius, my son, keep it deposited with you. Together with another similar document, likewise written and subscribed in my own hand, which I deposited with Dadolena, you shall deliver it to Count Agilo, to be opened and read in the presence of my brothers, the priests, deacons, and clerics. In the name of the Lord, I desire, ask, and determine that it be fixed and valid. Bless, O Lord; come, Christ Jesus.

I, Perpetuus, in your name. Amen.

[Col. 0755]

## EPITAPH OF PERPETUUS, BISHOP. (G,S)*

[Col. 0755C]

The structures that raise their crests to a lofty summit

had been given by Perpetuus, distinguished in merits,

to the lord Martin, beneath whose marble

his bones rest, and whom the devout people venerate with prayers.

He named Christ as his heir, and gave many golden vessels, consecrating them with the Lord’s blood.

He sent to heaven the wealth that was distributed in great measure to the needy,

And made his wealth ascend before him.

[Col. 0756C] Illustrious in ancestors and powerful through forebears, he was also a senator;

But he was more illustrious when he distributed his possessions to the poor.

Nor did he build so great a tomb for Martin alone:

He also made the mound his own.

And although he is buried before Martin’s feet,

Both rejoice in a similar place in heaven.

Look down from above upon this fold, good shepherd,

And upon your perpetual homeland, Perpetuus.

[Col. 0755C] See the letter of Sidonius Apollinaris to Perpetuus above, among the works of Sidonius, book VII, letter 9.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 485. CEREALIS, BISHOP OF CASTELLUM.

[Col. 0755]

## NOTICE FROM GENNADIUS

[Col. 0755D] Cerealis, a bishop of African nationality, was asked by Maximian, an African bishop, whether he could, with only a few testimonies from divine Scripture and without any argumentation, merely establish the Catholic faith. [Col. 0756D] With the truth supporting him in the name of the Lord, he established it—not with the few testimonies Maximian had mockingly requested, but with abundant passages from both the Old and the New Testament—and published them in a little book.

[Col. 0757]

## BOOKLET OF CEREALIS, BISHOP, AGAINST MAXIMINUS THE ARIAN. (C,S)

### INTRODUCTION

[Col. 0757A]

When Cerealis, bishop of Castellum and of the holy Catholic faith, came to Carthage, and because he was nearer to those cities which had [the printed reading is uncertain] through the wrath of God, his arrival struck royal ears. When those charged with the matter asked him whether what rumor had broadcast was true, and he began to relate the events in order, Maximinus, bishop of the Ariomani, arrived and said to Bishop Cerealis:

“Do you see what your sins have done? That is why God has abandoned you.”

**CEREALIS.** Why has he abandoned us, and not rather you, who slaughter souls under the guise of the Christian name and do not hold the true faith?

**MAXIMINUS.** If you hold the true faith, I shall propose questions concerning your faith to you. If you have the true faith, I wish you to produce two or three testimonies to refute each proposition.

**CEREALIS.** [Col. 0757B] I shall produce not two or three, but many more testimonies.

**MAXIMINUS.** First, prove:

That the Son is equal to the Father. Concerning unity: that God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one. How the Father sent the Son. How the Father glorifies the Son. That the Son is omnipotent. Why the Son said, “The Father is greater than I.” Or why it was said that the Father delivered up the Son. Concerning the Son’s free authority. Against what they say: “The one who generates is the author”; they assign a beginning to the Father, and so forth. Against what they say: “The Father commanded the Son to make the creation.” That the Holy Spirit is God. That the Holy Spirit is Creator. That the Holy Spirit is life-giver. That he too possesses his own power and will and is omnipotent. Concerning the Trinity and unity. That the Son is invisible. Against what they say: “All things were made from the Father and through the Holy Spirit.” Against what they say: “Why is the Father named first and the Son afterward?” Against what they say: “The Father subjected all things to him.”

## THE BOOKLET BEGINS. CHAPTER ONE

**CEREALIS.** That the Son is equal to the Father, the apostle Paul teaches as follows: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II). He who is in the form of God the Father cannot be lesser; he did not seize what he did not possess, because he was always in the form of the Father.

In the Gospel John says: “For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John V). Again, the Lord himself said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” Likewise in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.” Here he said “one” with respect to equality, because those who are one are equal. But he said “we are” because the Son is another person. Yet the Father and the Son are one. For God is not divided, since the Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

But since the Father and the Son are not alone one, the Holy Spirit having been added, what follows demonstrates this. One refers to the fellowship of the Father and the Son, while one refers to the Lord alone, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.

Again, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Everything that the Father has is mine.” Likewise, the Son himself says to the Father in the Gospel: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine.” And again: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father.” Likewise in the Gospel: “Whoever hates me hates my Father also.” Likewise in John’s Epistle: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; but whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father.”

Likewise in Solomon: “She is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. VII). This is said about the Son.

Likewise in the Gospel: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.” When he says “granted,” this is understood as “begotten.” Or if the Father later gave life to the Son after he had already been begotten, then the begotten Son was without life. And how does he himself say in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life”?

Likewise, concerning the Son the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “He is,” he says, “the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and he sustains all things by the word of his power” (Heb. I). Therefore, as the radiance of glory and the representation of his substance, he possesses the radiance—that is, the truth. The representation of God is called God’s equality.

Likewise the apostle Paul says concerning the Son to the Colossians: “In him,” he says, “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.” If the whole fullness of deity dwells in Christ, how then is the Son lesser?

## CHAPTER II

That God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one is taught as follows. The Lord himself says in the Law: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And the Apostle says: “There is no God except one.” Again he says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV). Likewise the apostle James says: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble” (James II). The demons tremble at this faith, which they refused to acknowledge as true.

The Lord himself says: “I am God, and there is no other besides me.” Likewise in Psalm XXVII: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” And they themselves confess that the Son is also God. Let them show me how he is one, unless it is because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.

## CHAPTER III

How the Father sent the Son is taught as follows. The sending of the Son is the incarnation of the Son. The apostle Paul testifies both who was sent and whether it was the Son of God or the son of man, saying: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV). Therefore the one who was born of a woman is the one who was sent; he was also under the Law, as he said, for God established the Law.

Likewise the Apostle himself says concerning Christ: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II). When he emptied himself, he sent himself; for the Son himself also says: “I came to seek and to save what was lost.” Here he does not say, “I was sent,” but “I came.”

The Holy Spirit also sent him, as it is written, with the prophet Isaiah himself teaching: “And now,” he says, “the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. XLVIII). Likewise the Son himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor,” and so forth.

Therefore the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, if the one who sends is greater, because the Holy Spirit sent the Son of God.

God is certainly everywhere, for he says: “I fill heaven and earth.” Elsewhere he says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.” How, then, is the Son sent? Or how does the Father send, if the one God is everywhere in heaven and on earth?

Now hear how not only equals are sent by equals, but greater beings are also sent by lesser ones, as we read that an angel was sent by Tobias, and that Christ was sent by Pilate to Herod. Did the angel humble himself because he went where Tobias sent him? Or did Christ humble himself because he was sent by Pilate to Herod?

Would you know that the Son is everywhere and that there is nowhere to which he can be sent? Hear what the Son himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” [Col. 0759C] He did not say, “who was in heaven,” but “who is in heaven,” although he was speaking on earth. At that time he was both man and God on earth.

For if God was not on earth, how did the angels minister to him, as it is written: “And the devil departed, and angels came and ministered to him” (John XVII)?

## CHAPTER IV

How the Father glorifies the Son is taught as follows. The Son also glorifies the Father, as it is written in the Gospel, where the Son himself says to the Father: “I have glorified you on earth.” Again the Son himself says: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.”

The Holy Spirit himself also glorifies the Son, because it is written: “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and will announce it to you.” If, therefore, the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son, the Holy Spirit is never greater than the Son.

The Son himself also says in the psalm: “Sacrifice of praise will honor me.” Therefore the sacrifice of praise is understood as the burnt offering of his passion. In the passion, then, the man is glorified, for God is always glorious.

Would you know that the Son was not only always glorious, but was and is also the God of glory? The apostle Paul says concerning the Jews: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Therefore the one who could die could also be glorified—only the man. For hear what the Son himself says, explaining how he sanctifies himself: “In truth,” he says, “I sanctify myself.”

## CHAPTER V

That the Son is omnipotent is taught as follows. In Solomon it is written: “Your omnipotent word, O Lord, leaping from your royal throne, sprang into the midst of a land of destruction” (Wis. XVIII). Therefore he is also king who possesses the royal throne.

Likewise in the Apocalypse: “These things says the Son of God, who is and who was, the omnipotent God.”

In the Gospel: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John V). Likewise in the Gospel: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.”

In Isaiah the Son says: “Behold, I shall stretch out my hand over you, and those who plundered you shall be plundered; and you shall know that I am the omnipotent Lord, and that the Lord who sent me is omnipotent.”

The prophet Jeremiah says: “Great is he, and has no end; exalted and immeasurable is this our God, and there is no other.” And to make it evident that this is said concerning Christ, he continues: “Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.”

Likewise the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Likewise, when he speaks concerning the Jews: “Their fathers,” he says, “and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER VI

Why the Son said, “The Father is greater than I,” or why it was said that the Father delivered up his Son, is taught as follows. It is written in the psalm, with the Son saying to the Father: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. XXI). Therefore, from his mother’s womb, his God is the Father, and for this reason the Father is greater.

Likewise the Son himself says in the psalm: “O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV), that is, of Mary. He is the servant, and for this reason the Father is greater.

Likewise: “God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI). And again: “Save me from the lion’s mouth.” These things pertain to the man. For he himself also says: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again; no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John XX).

In the psalm: “I slept and took my sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me.” And the Apostle, because the Son himself delivered himself up, says: “He loved me,” he says, “and delivered himself up for me.”

Likewise the Apostle himself: “He loved,” he says, “his Church and delivered himself up for her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word.” Likewise Paul says in his Epistle to the Ephesians: “As Christ also loved us and delivered himself up for us.”

Likewise he himself says in the psalm: “To do your will, my God, I have desired.”

The man speaks in the psalm: “My God,” just as he said above: “From my mother’s womb you are my God.” Yet afterward, when he says, “To do your will, my God,” he adds, “I have desired.” Because he desired it, he did it. For he is the one of whom it is said: “He has done all that he desired.”

He desired to be born; he desired to die; he desired to suffer everything; he desired to hunger, thirst, and grow weary—and yet according to his humanity.

Would you know what kind of being the Son of God is? Isaiah says: “The eternal God, who made the everlasting ends of the earth, neither labored nor grew weary,” and so forth. He speaks concerning the Son, of whom it is said: “All things were made through him.”

For God could suffer no evil or labor, to whom it is said in Psalm XX: “Evil shall not approach you, and the scourge shall not draw near your dwelling.”

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the Son’s free authority, it is taught as follows. In the Gospel he says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII). He did not say, “I ask.”

In the Gospel he did not say to the leper, “I ask,” but “I desire; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII).

Likewise in the Gospel, when Peter asked that he might walk upon the water, Jesus said: “Come.” He did not ask, but said, “Come.”

Likewise he said to the Canaanite woman: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). The woman was a Gentile; nevertheless, because he desired it, he granted the benefit and healed her daughter, although he had said that he had not been sent to her.

For Christ had been appointed not for the Gentiles but for the Jews. Then he said: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.

Why did he grant a benefit to the woman to whom he had said he was not sent? Therefore you see that he did what he wished, not what someone else commanded.

Likewise the psalm says concerning Christ: “Whatever the Lord desired, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths.” It does not say, “Whatever he asked.”

## CHAPTER VIII

Against the claim that the one who generates is greater and the one who is generated is lesser: these distinctions belong to temporal conditions. In Christ, however, there are no times, through whom all things were made.

For the eternal one, who is known to have been generated before the ages, does not come into being from time. Thus we read that Adam was begotten by no one, yet he and his son were both alike and equal, because both were human beings.

The greater and the lesser arise through time, because one grows old and the other grows. But with God there have never been times.

Time itself was made through the Son, and nothing temporal exists in God. Remove time, then, and show me the greater and the lesser.

As to how the Son is lesser not only than his Father but also than the angels, the apostle Paul says concerning him in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Now,” he says, “we see Jesus made for a little while lower than the angels.” Why? He continues: “Because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II).

## CHAPTER IX

Against what they say: “The one who generates is the author”; they posit a beginning. There is no causal priority for the Father where there is no will.

For the Father generated neither willingly nor unwillingly, but by nature. If he generated willingly, then the Father’s very will is the Son, as we read. For he is the Word, the Power, and the Wisdom; he is also the Father’s will.

If there was ever a time when the Son did not exist, there was ever a time when the Father did not exist, because he could not be Father if he had not had a Son. But just as the Father is eternal, so the Son is eternal, concerning whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I).

He is not contained by time, has no beginning, and is not enclosed within the ages.

And the Son says to the Father in the psalm: “I am always with you.” If the Son was always with the Father, how is the Father the author, when he was never before the Son?

Likewise it is said concerning him: “Before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are.”

If, therefore, the Son is the Father’s will, let it be explained to me how the Father is the author, without whom the Son never existed, since the Father could not exist without his will.

The Father is called Father because of the Son, and the Son is called God from God. And he is called Son because of the Father.

For “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” does not signify separation; rather, for this reason God is one.

But if the Son is lesser than the Father, why did he say, “The Father is in me”? The lesser can never contain the greater.

## CHAPTER X

Against what they say, that the Father commanded the Son to make the creation, the answer is as follows.

The Father himself certainly also made it, for it is written: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I). This shows that they worked together, in order to demonstrate that God is one.

The Scripture continues: “And God made man according to his image and likeness.” It does not say, “The gods made man,” although it had said, “Let us make man”; instead it says: “God made man according to his image and likeness.”

Likewise, if the Father did not make the creation, how does the Son say: “My Father is working until now, and I am working”?

Likewise, if the Father did not make the creation, how do the apostles say to the Father: “You are the Lord who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who through the mouth of your holy servant David said: ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples devise empty things? The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ’” (Ps. II)?

“For truly they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and all the people of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had predestined” (Acts IV).

Therefore they were speaking about Christ to the Father when they said: “You are the Lord who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.” Read this in the Acts of the Apostles, and you will find that this statement concerning the Son is addressed to the Father.

## CHAPTER XI

That the Holy Spirit is God is taught as follows. Peter said to the man who had withheld part of the price of the estate: “Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” And afterward he added: “You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts V).

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, while Peter was thinking and hesitating about the vision, the Holy Spirit says: “Behold, men are seeking you; rise, descend, and go with them without hesitation, because I have sent them to you.”

And when Peter came to Cornelius, he said: “In truth I understand that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts X). He had been sent to a Gentile by the Holy Spirit, since the Gospel was not yet being preached to the Gentiles but only to the Jews.

Likewise in the Gospel: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.” Is he not God who fills God? Therefore God was in Christ, who returned full from the Jordan.

Likewise the Apostle: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” He continued: “Therefore glorify God in your body.”

Likewise in Solomon: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world.”

Likewise the prophet Isaiah: “And the Lord said to me: Go, tell this people, ‘You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand,’” and so forth. The one whom Isaiah calls God, the Apostle calls the Holy Spirit.

If God is spirit, how is the Holy Spirit not God? If the Holy Spirit is not God, how does the apostle Paul say: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of activities, but one God, who works all things in all people, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Cor. XII)?

He is the Holy Spirit of whom the prophet Isaiah says: “The Spirit, I mean, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XII

That the Holy Spirit is also Creator is taught as follows. In Job we read: “The divine Spirit is the one who made me.”

In the psalm: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Ps. CIII).

In the Gospel: “Mary was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.” To her it had been said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Matt. I).

In the psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII).

If the Holy Spirit made the Son of God in the womb of the virgin, what did God lack that he did not create?

In the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Regenerating is greater than creating: behold, the Holy Spirit regenerates when we are reborn through him in baptism.

## CHAPTER XIII

That the Holy Spirit is life-giver is taught as follows. The Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (1 Cor. III).

Likewise in the Gospel: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all” (John VI).

In Ezekiel, concerning the dry bones of the children of Israel, the prophet is commanded and told: “I shall put my Spirit in you, and you shall live.”

Likewise the Apostle says: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII, 11).

Therefore mortal bodies are given life by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIV

That the Spirit also possesses his own power and will and is omnipotent is taught as follows. The Apostle says: “To one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good; to another is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another workings of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. XII).

Behold: one and the same Spirit works as he wills, not according to what is commanded him.

The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The Spirit blows where he wills” (John III).

In the Acts of the Apostles, the Spirit commands Philip to join the eunuch of Queen Candace.

Likewise the Spirit says: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the holy work to which I have called them.” Behold, the Holy Spirit sets apart the apostles and calls them.

Likewise concerning the apostles: “They attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Holy Spirit did not permit them.” Behold, he gives commands to the apostles.

Likewise in Solomon he says: “The Holy Spirit is Wisdom to me,” that is, in Christ.

The Holy Spirit is one, manifold, subtle, immovable, undefiled, certain, secure, loving what is good, all-powerful, all-knowing, and capable of comprehending all intellectual spirits; pure and subtle. Behold what kind of being the Holy Spirit is.

Likewise in the Gospel: “And Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit.” Christ walks in the power of the Spirit.

Likewise we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The apostles were speaking as the utterance was given to them.” The Spirit gave the apostles the manner in which they were to speak.

Likewise the apostle Paul shows what the Holy Spirit bestows, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (1 John IV).

And we read in the apostle John: “God is love.” If God is love, what sort of being is the Holy Spirit, whose very nature is love? For above you have this: “The fruit of the Holy Spirit is love” (1 John IV).

## CHAPTER XV
## On the Trinity and the Divinity of the Word

If the Trinity does not exist, why was it said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? If there is no unity, why was it said “in one name,” and not “in names”? If the Trinity does not exist, why does the Lord say: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”? If there is no unity, why does he say “God” three times, and did not likewise call them “gods”? If the Trinity does not exist, why do the Seraphim in Isaiah say in praise: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah VI)? Here they show both Trinity and unity, because they say “God,” not “gods.”

If the Trinity does not exist, why does the Apostle say: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things”? Or, if there is neither Trinity nor unity, why does he continue, “to him be glory,” and not “to them be glory,” if there are several gods? But if some wish to understand this as referring to the Father, then let them not slander the Son, since just as all things were made by the Father, so they were made through the Son.

Therefore God is not counted, increased, or in need, because he is not diminished. If the Son is indeed God, these things do not apply to him, for he himself says to the tempting devil: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew IV). And the Apostle Thomas says, when he touched the places of his wounds: “My Lord and my God.”

The Trinity is inseparable. For he did not speak where he is not present. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are everywhere together, and are not separated by places, because God is not corporeal. God is not counted, because he is not subject to numbers. Our God, therefore, is one.

Although there are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, no Christian can say that there are three gods, because the divine nature differs from itself in nothing. Number is sufficient for order, while equality is not lost: one follows first, and another is added as third. But since degrees cannot arise from equals that could be subordinated—how could they be counted?—there will therefore be one, because he has no second. The second occupies the rank of the lesser, the lesser makes another, another indicates what is later, and what is later signals inequality. Remove difference, and you will have nothing to count.

The Prophet says: “There is no number of his wisdom.” If his wisdom is not counted, how is the Son counted, who is the Wisdom of the Father, as the Apostle says? Why is the Son called second after the Father, when wisdom is not counted? Because he is the Wisdom of the Father.

## CHAPTER XVI

That the Son is invisible is taught as follows: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” In the Apostle it is written concerning Christ: “He is the invisible firstborn of all creation.”

Again: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, the first, Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life; but to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever.”

The Son, therefore, is invisible, although he came to save sinners. If the Son is seen, the Father also is seen, since it is written: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

## CHAPTER XVII

Against what they say: that all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.

Hear that you will find it said that all things were made not only from the Father, but also from the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Apostle says this concerning the Son in his letter to the Ephesians: “But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body is joined and compacted.”

Behold: from the Son. Hear also concerning the Holy Spirit: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” And again it is read in the Gospel: “So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Against what they say: that the Father bears witness to the Son.

Christ himself says in the Gospel: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself.” Therefore he himself bears witness concerning himself. The prophets bore witness to the Son: are the prophets therefore greater than the Son? The apostles bore witness to the Son: are the apostles therefore greater than the Son of God? But since I have shown that he himself bore witness concerning himself, there will be nothing for the adversaries to answer: “I am,” says the Son, “the one who bears witness concerning myself.”

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0765D]

Against what they say: “Why is the Father named first, and then the Son?”

Hear that the Son is also named first by the Father. The Apostle says to the Galatians: “Not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” Again, in the letter to the Thessalonians he himself says: “But our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation,” and so forth.

Behold: the Son is named first. Hear also that the Holy Spirit is named in the first place. The Apostle says: “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.” Behold: he named the Spirit first, and the Father afterward.

But I ask: because we read in Leviticus that Jacob was named in his proper place under one statement, Isaac second, and Abraham third, must it therefore be said that Jacob was better than Isaac, or that Isaac was greater than Abraham his father? For it is written: “And I will remember the covenant of Jacob,” says the Lord, “and the covenant of Isaac, and the covenant of Abraham.”

When men are not prejudged, why does a designation bring prejudice against God, if perhaps somewhere the Father is designated first by the Son, or the Son by the Holy Spirit, after the Father has been designated in the first place?

## CHAPTER XX

Against what they say: “The Father subjected all things to him.”

The Apostle says concerning the Son to the Corinthians: “He must reign,” he says, “until he has placed all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians XV). And to the Philippians: “From there also we await the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, who will transform the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is able to subject all things to himself” (Philippians I).

The Apostle also says that the Son will hand over the kingdom to God his Father; for it is written concerning Christ: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father.” Is the Son therefore greater than the Father, because he himself will hand over the kingdom to his Father?

These are the matters that I have been able, for the moment, to recall and select. Many others have been omitted because of the need for haste, which the reader will be able to find when reading.

Let the reader hold only this: the Lord God is in no way subject to number and in no way separated. For whatever is lesser is not God; but whatever is God—the Son and the Holy Spirit—is each perfect [the text reads *professus*, “confessed,” but the sense appears to require “perfect”].

This is true perfection, which is not subjected to comparison with another and has nothing remaining that could increase. God is spirit, not flesh; he is intellect, not a compact mass; he is inward light, not matter spread around. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not divided, because he is not something that can be cut apart. Yet the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit; and they are nowhere without one another, because there is one who can be understood but cannot be separated.

They are not compacted together, because they are not like things made of air; they are not divided, because they are not without one another.

This is the true and catholic faith, which Christ taught and handed down, which the apostles taught, and which all the holy patriarchs and prophets faithfully proclaimed.

With the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit assisting, I have answered your propositions from the New and Old Testament. Now, on behalf of the catholic faith, which exists everywhere, I have put forward other testimonies to which you ought to respond.

In the Book of Wisdom: God is Wisdom, which is the Son of God; likewise the Holy Spirit knows the counsels of the Father.

In the same book: the Son is omnipotent, through whom all things were made.

In the same book: the Holy Spirit is also the Son, who is called the power of God.

In the same book it is said concerning the Holy Spirit that he is incorruptible.

In the same book, Christ is said to be visible according to the form of the humility he assumed, but according to the form of divinity he is declared not visible but invisible. What is seen is recognized as human; what is not seen is recognized as God.

In the same book it is said that the Son of God is from the substance of the Father.

In the Song of Songs, Christ is called King when the Church speaks to him.

In Ecclesiasticus: the greatness of God is innumerable. From this it is taught that those who, by separating the Trinity, believe that it must be established by degrees and numbers are blasphemers.

In Psalm 117, likewise concerning Wisdom, which is the Son of God, and concerning the Holy Spirit, who knows the counsels of the Father, it says: “Who can know your counsel unless you give Wisdom and send your Spirit from on high?”

In the same book, that the Son is omnipotent, through whom all things were made: “For your almighty hand,” he says, “which created all things and the world from unformed matter, was not incapable.”

In the same book, that the Holy Spirit is also the Son: “Scattered by the Spirit of your power, they suffered persecution from the very works they had made.”

In the same book, concerning the Holy Spirit, that he is incorruptible: “For your incorruptible Spirit is in all things.”

In the same book, where Christ is said to be visible according to the form of the humility he assumed, but according to the form of divinity not visible but invisible, it says: “Seeing him whom they had formerly denied, they acknowledged him to be the true God.”

In the same book, that the Son of God is from the substance of the Father: “In place of these things you fed your people with the food of angels, and supplied them bread from heaven, prepared without labor, containing every delight in itself and the sweetness of every taste; for you were showing the substance and sweetness which you have in the Son.”

In the Gospel according to John, that the Holy Spirit is invisible: “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because the world does not see him, nor know him; but you know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

In the Song of Songs, he says that Christ is King when he speaks of the Church: “The king brought me into his chamber; let us rejoice and be glad in you.” Again: “We shall make likenesses of gold for you, with ornamentation of silver, until the king is at his couch.”

In Ecclesiasticus, that the greatness of God is innumerable: “And who has investigated the extent of his power, and who has numbered his greatness?” From this it is taught how blasphemous are those against the Trinity of God who believe that it must be established by separation, degrees, and numbers.

In Psalm XXVII, likewise concerning Wisdom, which is the Son of God, it is said that there is no number of his wisdom: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no number of his wisdom.”

Maximinus the Arian, unable to answer anything to these propositions, kept postponing from day to day. But Cerealis said to the person who was present and had been assigned the task:

“I answered the questions he put forward with God’s help. Why does he not answer my propositions?”

When the aforementioned Maximinus, to whom the task had been assigned, was summoned, he remained silent. Cerealis then said to him:

“Go to your own church. Since Maximinus, summoned by me, has refused to answer, it is understood that he was unable to do so, since he remained silent and refused to answer your propositions. Now God is judging between you.”

## At the Same Time. [Note: [Col. 0767], that is, 485.]

## Saint Eugenius, Bishop of Carthage

[Col. 0767]

## Notice from Cave

[Col. 0767C]

Eugenius, an African by nationality, was appointed bishop of Carthage in the year 480 by the Catholics, to whom Huneric, king of the Vandals, had granted permission to elect a bishop after being entreated by the prayers of the emperor Zeno and Placidia. The see had been vacant for twenty-four years because of the violence of the Arians.

In the year 484, when Huneric had gathered at Carthage a crowd of Arian bishops to engage in disputation with the Catholics, Eugenius presented the king with a lucid confession of faith, fortified by such force of reasoning that it drove the heretics equally into silence and rage.

Shortly afterward Huneric exiled him to the city of Tamallum, situated on the border of Tripolitania, and handed him over to Antonius, the bishop of that place, an exceedingly savage heretic, to be tortured.

Later, if Gregory of Tours is to be believed (*History of the Franks* II.3), he was carried to Albi, a city of Gaul, where he appears to have ended his life around the year 495 or shortly afterward. For Gennadius speaks of him as still living in his *Catalogue of Writers* (chapter 97), which he composed in that year.

There exists a booklet, or extended Confession of Faith, presented in the name of the African bishops to King Huneric, preserved in Victor of Vita’s *On the Vandal Persecution*, Book III, page 33; Victor’s entire third book consists of it. Although Victor does not say that it is Eugenius’s work, Gennadius, in the place cited, places its authorship beyond all controversy.

It is found in the fourth volume of the Councils, page 1128, and in volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 683.

According to the same Gennadius, he also wrote works that have perished: letters sent shortly before his exile to the people entrusted to his care; disputations conducted through intermediaries with the Arian bishops, addressed to King Huneric; and, finally, prayers for the peace of the Catholics, in the form of apologies, presented to the same king.

[Col. 0769]

## Confession of Faith of the Catholic Bishops of Africa, Composed by Eugenius of Carthage

(S)

(For this Confession of Faith, which constitutes Book III of the history of the Vandal Persecution, see above, column 219.)

[Col. 0769]

## Excerpt from Gregory of Tours Concerning Saint Eugenius of Carthage and the Other Confessors Who Suffered under King Huneric

### I

The Vandals, having departed from their own territory, rushed into Gaul with King Gunderic; after devastating it severely, they turned toward Spain. The Suebi, that is, the Alemanni, followed them and seized Galicia. Not long afterward a dispute arose between the two peoples, because they were related to one another . . . [lacuna]. After this, with the Alemanni pursuing them as far as Traducta, the Vandals crossed the sea and were scattered throughout Africa and Mauretania.

### II

But since persecution against Christians grew strong in their time, it seems appropriate that I should recall some of the things they inflicted upon the churches of God, or how they were expelled from the kingdom.

After Trasamund died [Note: [Col. 0769C] Read “Genseric.”], following the crimes he had committed against God’s saints, Honoric, more cruel in mind, seized the African kingdom and was placed over the Vandals by their election. During his reign, how many Christian peoples were slain for the most sacred name of Christ cannot be comprehended by human beings. Africa, however, which sent them forth, and the right hand of Christ, which crowned them with unfading jewels, bear witness.

Nevertheless, we read of the sufferings of certain martyrs among them; some of these must be retold so that we may come to what we have promised.

### III

Cirola, falsely called a bishop, was then regarded as the chief champion of the heretics. When the king was sending men in different directions to persecute the Christians, the persecutor found the holy Bishop Eugenius, a man of indescribable holiness who was reputed at that time to possess great wisdom, in the suburb of his city.

He seized him so violently that he did not even allow him a place from which to exhort Christ’s flock [Note: [Col. 0769C] Thus the Colbertine manuscript. The printed edition reads: “to exhort Christ’s flock, he allowed him to depart.” Perhaps the reading should be, “he allowed him to depart,” etc. The Royal manuscript reads: “he allowed the Christian to depart.”].

But when Eugenius saw that he was being led away, he sent this letter to his fellow citizens for the preservation of the catholic faith:

## Letter of Saint Eugenius of Carthage to His Fellow Citizens, for the Preservation of the Catholic Faith

[Col. 0769C]

To the most beloved sons and daughters, most dear in the love of Christ, of the Church entrusted to me by God, Eugenius, bishop.

Royal authority has issued an order and commanded us to come to Carthage for the exercise of the catholic faith. Therefore, lest in departing from you I leave the Church of God in uncertainty—that is, in suspense—or leave Christ’s sheep in silence without a true shepherd, I have thought it necessary to send these substitutes for me to your holiness.

In them, not without tears, I ask, exhort, admonish, and sufficiently and abundantly entreat you, by the majesty of God, by the dreadful day of judgment, and by the terrible splendor of Christ’s coming, to hold the catholic faith more firmly, affirming that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Holy Spirit possesses the same divinity as the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0770C] Manuscript 1 reads: “affirming that the Father and the Holy Spirit possess the same divinity as the Son.”].

Therefore preserve the grace of the one baptism, guarding the anointing of chrism [Note: [Col. 0770C] Salvianus, a writer of the same period, in Book III of *The Governance of God*, when listing the good things God assigns to Christians, mentions the grace of holy baptism and the anointing of divine chrism, which he shortly afterward calls ecclesiastical chrism.].

Let no one return to the water after the water, having been born again of water [Note: [Col. 0770C] The Colbertine manuscript adds “and the Holy Spirit.”]. For by God’s command salt is made in water; but if it is reduced into water, all its character is immediately dissolved.

Hence the Lord says not without reason in the Gospel: “If the salt has become insipid, with what will it be salted?” [Note: [Col. 0771D] In Matthew V.13 and Luke XIV.34 the reading is *evanuerit*, “has lost its savor”; and in Mark IX.50, *insulsum*, “insipid.” But the Africans read *infatuatum*, “made foolish,” as is evident from Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.]

And surely this is what it means to become insipid: to wish to be seasoned a second time, when one seasoning is sufficient.

Have you not heard Christ saying: “He who has been washed once has no need to wash again” (John XIII)?

Therefore, brothers, and my sons and daughters in the Lord, do not let my absence grieve you. For if you adhere to catholic discipline, I shall neither forget you through any distance nor be separated from you by death [Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus we have restored the text from a manuscript. The printed editions, together with the Colbertine manuscript, read: “But if you adhere to catholic discipline, I neither . . . forget you . . . nor am I separated . . .” The Royal manuscript has *quasi*, “as if,” etc.].

Know that whatever separates me from you, the palm of victory is with me [Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus the same Colbertine manuscript. The printed edition and the Royal manuscript read: “Wherever they cause me to be separated, the contest is with me.” Baron reads *agone*, “in the contest.”].

If I go into exile, I have the example of the blessed John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0771D] Thus Baron. The Colbertine manuscript has *profero*, “I bring forth.” Another manuscript has “I possess the example.”]. If I go to the destruction of death, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians I.21). If I return, brothers, God will fulfill your desire.

Nevertheless, what I have not kept silent from you, what I have warned and instructed you as best I could, is sufficient for now. Therefore I am free from the blood of all who perish. I know that these letters will be read against them before the tribunal of Christ, when he comes to repay each according to his works.

If I return, brothers, I shall see you in this life; if I do not return, I shall see you in the life to come.

Yet I say to you: farewell, pray for us, and fast, because fasting and almsgiving have always turned the Lord toward mercy.

Remember that it is written in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who, after killing the body, has power to destroy the soul also and to cast it into Gehenna” (Matthew X.28).

The letter of Eugenius ends; Gregory returns to his subject.

### IV

Thus the holy Eugenius was led to the king and contended with that Arian bishop for the catholic faith. When he had defeated him most powerfully concerning the mystery of the holy Trinity, and Christ had moreover displayed many miracles through him, the same bishop, inflamed by envy, was kindled to still greater madness.

At that time there were with the holy Eugenius men of great wisdom and holiness, the bishops Vindemialis and Longinus, equal in rank and not unequal in virtue. For Saint Vindemialis was then said to have raised a dead man, while Longinus granted health to many sick people. Eugenius likewise drove away not only blindness of the bodily eyes but also blindness of the mind.

### V

When that wicked Arian bishop saw this, he summoned a certain man who had been deceived by the error in which the bishop himself lived and said:

“I cannot tolerate the fact that these bishops perform many signs among the people, and that everyone follows them while neglecting me. Now obey what I command. Take fifty gold pieces, sit in the street through which we must pass, and, placing your hand over your closed eyes, shout loudly as I pass with the others, with great force, saying:

“‘Most blessed Cirola, chief priest of our religion, I beseech you, look upon me and display your glory and power, so that by opening my eyes I may deserve to see the light I have lost.’”

The man fulfilled the command and sat in the street. When the heretic was passing with the saints of God, the man who had planned to mock God cried out with a loud voice and great force [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “he had planned it”; then: “he cried out with a loud voice, with all his strength: Hear me, holy one,” etc.]:

“Hear me, most blessed Cirola; hear me, holy priest of God. Look upon my blindness. I shall experience the remedies that the other blind have often received from you [Note: [Col. 0772D] The Colbertine manuscript adds “to receive,”]—remedies that lepers have experienced, which even the dead themselves have felt. I adjure you by the very power that you possess to restore to me the light I desire, because I have been struck by severe blindness.”

Not knowing the truth, he was nevertheless speaking truthfully: desire had blinded him, and for money he thought he could mock the power of almighty God.

### VI

Then the bishop of the heretics turned aside for a little while, as though he were about to triumph through his power. Elated by vanity and pride, he placed his hand over the man’s eyes and said:

“According to our faith, by which we rightly believe in God, let your eyes be opened.”

As soon as this impious act had burst forth, laughter was changed into lamentation, and the bishop’s deceit was exposed in public [Note: [Col. 0772D] Something similar happened in Spain during the time of Leovigild, as the same Gregory of Tours records in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 13. When the king complained that the bishops of his sect performed no miracles of the sort customarily seen among the Catholics, one of them pretended to cure a man who had been bribed to feign blindness; but by God’s will the man actually became blind, exposing the deception.].

For such pain invaded the eyes of that wretched man that he could scarcely press them with his fingers to prevent them from bursting. At last the miserable man began to cry out and say:

“Woe to me, wretched man that I am, for I have been deceived by an enemy of the divine law! Woe to me, because I wished to mock God for money, and I accepted fifty gold pieces to commit this crime.”

To the bishop he said:

“Here is your gold; restore my sight, which I lost through your deceit.”

And to the glorious Christians he said:

“I beg you not to despise a wretched man, but quickly help one who is perishing. For I have truly learned that God is not mocked” (Galatians VI.7).

### VII

Then the saints of God, moved by compassion, said:

“If you believe, all things are possible for one who believes.”

But he cried out in a loud voice:

“Whoever does not believe that Christ the Son of God and the Holy Spirit possess equal substance and divinity with God the Father, let him suffer today what I am suffering.”

And he added:

“I believe in God the almighty Father. I believe in the Son of God, Christ Jesus, equal to the Father. I believe in the Holy Spirit, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.”

When the saints heard this, and each outdid the other in mutual honor, a holy contest arose among them as to which of them should place the sign of the blessed cross upon his eyes. Vindemialis and Longinus, however, urged Eugenius; but Eugenius, in turn, begged them to lay their hands upon the blind man.

When they had done so and held their hands over his head, Saint Eugenius made the sign of the cross over the blind man’s eyes and said:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, the true God, whom we confess as three in one equality and omnipotence, let your eyes be opened.”

Immediately the pain was removed, and he returned to his former health [Note: [Col. 0773D] Hermanuus Contractus mentions this story of the blind man in his *Chronicle* under the year 483, where Bishop Longinus is called Longwinus.].

It was made perfectly clear through this man’s blindness how the bishop of the heretics veiled the eyes of men’s hearts with the miserable covering of his false assertion, so that they could not contemplate the true light with the eyes of faith.

O miserable man, who did not enter through the door—that is, through Christ, who is the true door—but became more a wolf to the flock than its guardian, and who attempted through the perversity of his heart to extinguish the peace of faith that he ought to have kindled in the hearts of believers.

The saints of God also performed many other signs among the people, and there was one voice among the people saying:

“The Father is true God, the Son is true God, and the Holy Spirit is true God; they are to be worshiped in one faith, feared with one fear, and revered with the same honor.”

For it was evident to all that what Cirola asserted was false.

### VIII

When King Honoric saw that his assertions had been utterly stripped bare by the glorious faith of the saints [Note: [Col. 0773D] Thus manuscript 1. The printed edition reads *taliter*, “thus,” and the Colbertine manuscript reads “stripped bare”], and that his sect of error was not being raised up but rather destroyed, and that the fraud of his bishop had been exposed in this crime, he ordered the saints of God to be killed after many tortures, after the racks [Note: [Col. 0773D] Baron reads “and the hooks”], after the flames, and after the claws.

He ordered blessed Eugenius to be beheaded, but under such a pretext that, if at the hour when the sword rested upon his neck he did not return to the sect of the heretics, he would not be killed, lest Christians honor him as a martyr; instead, he was to be condemned to exile. It is clear that this is what happened.

For when, with death impending, he was asked whether he intended to die for the catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Colbertine manuscript reads “was prepared”], he replied:

“For this is eternal life: to die for righteousness.”

Then, with the sword suspended, he was assigned to exile in Albi, a city of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0773D] The Royal manuscript reads “the city of Albi”], where he also ended his present life. Many miracles, and very frequent ones, are now displayed at his tomb.

He ordered Saint Vindemialis to be struck with the sword, and this was fulfilled in the contest [Note: [Col. 0773D] Two manuscripts read: “This was fulfilled in the contest. Octavianus, however,” etc.].

Octavianus the archdeacon, and many thousands of men and women who asserted this faith, were killed and maimed [Note: [Col. 0774D] Manuscript 1 reads “were slain”]. But for the love of glory these punishments were nothing to the holy confessors, who, although troubled amid peace, knew that in many things they were being well prepared, according to the Apostle’s saying (Romans VIII.18):

“For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0774D] The printed edition reads “in the saints.”].

### IX

Many who had been wandering from the faith, when they acquired riches, entangled themselves in many pains [Note: [Col. 0774D] Pope Felix laments the same devastation of the African Church, as we shall say below, chapter 10.].

An unfortunate bishop named Revocatus was at that time recalled from the catholic faith. Then the sun also appeared darkened with a dreadful darkness, so that scarcely a third or even a part of it shone, as I believe, because of such crimes and the shedding of innocent blood.

After so great a crime, Honoric was seized by a demon that had long been nourished by the blood of the saints; he tore himself with his own bites, and amid this torment he ended his unworthy life by a just death.

Childeric succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Colbertine manuscript reads “Hilderic.”]. After Childeric died, Gelisimiris assumed the kingdom. He too was overcome by the state and ended his life and rule, and thus the kingdom of the Vandals fell.

### X

That martyr of the persecution of Honoric [Huneric], Eugenius, is also joined to this crypt in which the body of Saint Amarandus was preserved. He was the greatest adornment of the priestly island; his suffering, or that of his companions, tells how he was thrust into exile in this city.

Since he flourished in the world with great virtues and had already emerged victorious from the torments of martyrdom, he learned through the Lord’s revelation the time of his calling, when he would be summoned to glory. In particular, he came to know what was hidden from the people: that he would become the companion of the martyr Amarandus.

He went to Amarandus’s tomb and, prostrating himself on the ground, poured out a long prayer to the Lord. Then, stretching out his arms upon the pavement, he directed his spirit toward heaven. The Christians gathered it, and it was buried in the very crypt we have mentioned.

[Then all who were standing around him, beating their breasts and uttering groans, cried out:

“O dreadful death, why do you kill so many today, while taking from us the presence of our saint? It would take too long to recount individually how many and what great things we have continued to see shining there without interruption through the holy bishop Eugenius.

“O how many miracles and how great a dignity the Lord displays at his tomb! The sick come and are healed; the possessed come and are freed; lepers come and are cleansed; the tongueless come and speak; those suffering from fever come and are healed.”]

### XI

When countless people had gathered at his feast on a certain occasion, they displayed much merchandise in the forecourt. One girl from the inhabitants of the place approached a stall, as though she intended to buy something. She looked at an item suitable for herself and received it from the merchant. Immediately, more quickly than words can tell, she denied that she had received the article proffered to her.

The merchant insisted:

“I brought it to you with my own hand, and you carefully examined it before accepting it.”

When she continued to deny this, the merchant said:

“If you are so obstinate, urged on by greed, in denying it, let blessed martyr Eugenius judge the matter. If at his tomb you swear, with an oath, that you did not receive it, I will consider that I have suffered no loss.”

She promised that she could free herself from this oath and hurried to the tomb. But when she raised her hands to swear, her limbs suddenly became paralyzed and she became rigid [Note: [Col. 0774D] The Colbertine manuscript reads “became rigid with her limbs loosened”]. Her feet were fixed to the pavement [Col. 0774D], and her voice stuck in her throat; only her open mouth gaped, stripped of speech.

When the merchant saw this with the rest of the people, he said:

“May this article which you took from me benefit you, maiden. The vengeance given through this bishop Eugenius is sufficient for you.”

With these words he withdrew from the place.

She remained held in this torment for a very long time. At last, when the martyr commanded it, she spoke and openly confessed what she had wished to keep hidden.

### XII

What are you doing, unhappy greed? Why do you, a woman’s mind rather than a man’s, succumb to seeking what belongs to another? Why do you pierce the firm breastplate of the mind with the small arrow of desire? Why do you gather, O man, talents of rusting gold, when you will burn with them in Gehenna? What use are perishable profits to you, when they produce the loss of eternal life, according to the Lord’s saying:

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?”

### XIII

[O most beloved brothers, fix your hope in the Redeemer alone, and pass over in mind to the eternal homeland. For if you possess nothing in this world by loving it, then even while possessing everything you have left it all behind. May he himself grant us eternal joys, he who has brought us the remedies of eternal peace, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.]

# In the Year of Our Lord 485. Saint Faustus, Bishop of Riez

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0775]

## Notices

(From Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*)

[Col. 0775B]

Faustus, formerly a monk of Lérins, became bishop of Riez in Gaul. He lived in the period between Saint Prosper and Saint Fulgentius. He wrote works on the Holy Spirit, against the Arians, and against the Macedonians, but these do not survive. He also wrote two books on Grace and Free Will, which do survive and which Gennadius, in his *On Illustrious Men*, praises extravagantly. But Pope Gelasius, in his decree on apocryphal books, rejects them altogether; they are likewise rejected and refuted by Saint Fulgentius, Peter the Deacon, Alcimus Avitus, and others.

Ado of Vienne speaks as follows in his *Chronicle* under the year 422:

“Faustus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lérins, was made bishop in the kingdom of Gaul. Having attempted to destroy the doctrine of the Pelagians, he fell into error. Therefore those who proclaim his views on this point to be catholic, as Gennadius altogether errs in doing when writing in *On Illustrious Men*, are entirely mistaken.

“For both Augustine and the other Catholics in the Church of God teach free will in such a way that illumination, power, and salvation are from Christ, through Christ, and in Christ. But this Faustus attempts to teach the free will of Christians in such a way that illumination, power, and salvation come not from Christ but from nature.

“Against him the blessed Avitus, bishop of Vienne, writes with the clearest faith, refuting his error; likewise John, a most learned man and presbyter of Antioch.”

Isidore, in *On Illustrious Men*, says that Fulgentius wrote seven books against Faustus, who wanted to appear Catholic through remarkable cunning, although he was a Pelagian. The author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter [Col. 0775D] 28, likewise testifies that two books of Faustus, *On Grace and Free Will*, were refuted by Saint Fulgentius. And Peter the Deacon, in his book *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*, in the final chapter, pronounces an anathema against the books of Faustus. I wished to point this out [Col. 0776B] on account of certain people who in our own time maintain that Faustus was Catholic.

*(From the expurgatory index of the Palatine manuscript.)*

Gennadius—who is known to have been very favorable to the Semi-Pelagians and, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, to have generally praised them highly—calls this work of Faustus, *On Grace and Free Will*, excellent; and Saint Sidonius Apollinaris is also found to have praised it extraordinarily in Book IX, Letter 9. But it seems that the snares and deceptions of Faustus were not yet known to that holy and sincere man. For it is absolutely certain that Faustus was a leading figure among the Semi-Pelagians, and that this writing of his, placed here, is filled with many errors of the Pelagians. This was expressly noted by Saint Isidore in Chapter 14 of *On Illustrious Men*, and by Saint Ado, bishop of Vienne, [Col. 0776C] in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 492.

Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles; Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; Saint Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne; and Peter the Deacon wrote expressly against this work of Faustus, *On the Grace of God*. Among the heretics, John Maxentius also wrote against it. Moreover, Saint Gelasius I, in his decree on sacred books, rejects all the works of Faustus among the apocrypha.

Saint Hormisdas, Roman pontiff, also says the following in a letter to Possessor, an African bishop:

> “As for what you have indicated in your letter—that you consulted us concerning a certain Faustus, a Gallic bishop—let this be the answer given to you: neither he nor anyone whom the examination of the Catholic faith or of ecclesiastical discipline does not admit into the authority of the Fathers can generate uncertainty or bring prejudice upon religious men.”

So much for him.

From these matters you may fully perceive how cautiously you ought to read these writings of Faustus, in which you will generally encounter many errors of Pelagian doctrine. If you wish to examine them collected together, consult John Maxentius in his response to Pope Hormisdas’s letter [Col. 0777A] to Possessor.

It should nevertheless be known that this letter of Faustus to the presbyter Lucidus, approved by the subscription of so many bishops at the Council of Arles, and the letter of the presbyter Lucidus to the bishops assembled in the Synod of Lyons—both of which are prefixed to the work of Faustus—are sound and Catholic, confirmed by the judgment of the two synods. Nevertheless, no one should on that account suppose that the three books of Faustus *On Grace* were approved by both councils, as he himself seems deceitfully to imply in the prefatory letter to Bishop Leontius of Fréjus, which follows here. Consult Baronius, who discusses all these matters more fully in volume VI of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year of Christ 490.

*(From Canisius.)*

[Col. 0777B] Whoever wishes to know who Faustus was, who Ruricius was, and who the others were to whom these letters were written, or who wrote to others, should consult Sidonius Apollinaris and Venantius Fortunatus, whom Christophorus Browerus of the Society of Jesus published complete and carefully furnished with notes. He should also consult the illustrious Baronius. We do not wish to append here an account of each individual.

Only concerning Faustus of Riez, who is called “saint” in the manuscript, the following observations from Baronius in the appendix to volume X, concerning volume VI, under the year 490 (Col. 1122), seem worth noting:

> “Moreover, when Faustus himself, after his deceptions had been exposed—the deceptions by which he had attempted to rescue the Pelagian pits from collapse upon the simple-minded—had alienated the minds of the bishops from himself and died ingloriously, we are astonished that some should imprudently call him **SAINT**. Add the following to this: In the earlier edition, it was not improper to have asserted these things on the basis of the writings of various authors that had been cited. But in view of what was subsequently learned and cited, we do not think it unworthy to call the matter itself back for renewed judgment, while the Fathers’ opinions concerning his writings nevertheless remain unchanged.

> “For the fact that the Gallican martyrology has continued down to our own time to place the same Faustus among the saints—until Molanus first removed him; and the fact that, as we have learned, the Church of Riez in Gaul, where he sat as bishop, always honored him as a saint, celebrating his natal day on 17 January; and that there a basilica was erected in his memory in ancient times, marked with the title of his name, and has continued to be frequented by the faithful in observance of his cult; and the fact that, after so many centuries, while the Christian world looked on, the Roman Church remained silent, and no one at all, so far as is known, contradicted it—all these things may be understood as showing that such honors were offered to Faustus. We may therefore hold that what is asserted concerning many holy men could also have happened in the case of Faustus: that while he was committing an error, he nevertheless fell into error; that when the matter had been defined by the authority of the Apostolic See and his opinion condemned by the judgment of other Fathers, he detested his own error in contrary writings, which, like many other works, may have perished; or that he died before the Church’s condemnation of his writings had been issued—indeed, the year of his death is uncertain—while intending in these matters to follow what the Church would teach ought to be followed.

> “That he was indeed disposed in this way in his mind, and that others knew it, may easily be understood from the fact that he always maintained communion—as the acts of the Councils of Arles and Lyons indicate—with the most holy orthodox bishops of Gaul.

> “Let Faustus therefore retain his rights intact, and let him suffer no prejudice from our writings. Nor should novelty, on the basis of a private judgment, be permitted to overthrow antiquity.”

This is Baronius.

[Editorial note: The passage in volume VI which Baronius here retracts reads: “Moreover, when Faustus himself, after his deceptions had been exposed—the deceptions by which he had attempted to rescue the Pelagian pits from collapse upon the simple-minded—had alienated the minds of the bishops from himself and died ingloriously, we are astonished that some should imprudently call him SAINT.”]

[Col. 0777]

# JACOB BASNAGE’S CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS ON SAINT FAUSTUS OF RIEZ: WHETHER HE WAS A SEMI-PELAGIAN AND TAUGHT THAT SOULS ARE MATERIAL; WHETHER HE WAS A CUNNING DECEIVER AND FORGED THE LETTERS TO LUCIDUS AND THE TWO COUNCILS, ETC.

[Col. 0777C] **I.** Faustus of Riez enjoys—and suffers from—a divided reputation, since many number him among the saints, with the support of the Church of which he was bishop. For that Church still celebrates a feast day in his honor. Baronius once wavered, calling him a crafty little fox. But, moved by the prayers of the Church of Riez—whose authority the celebrated annalist had greatly disparaged—he changed his former opinion, as may be read in the Canisian preface, which we have transcribed here in full. (See above on this same page.)

Both the ancient and the more recent writers diverge in their judgments. Sidonius Apollinaris appears to praise him in letters written to him; but whether he intended to jest and mock Faustus’s excessive devotion to philosophy and eloquence, which Faustus tried to pursue, or to praise him, I will not say. At least, many passages occur that absolutely require a favorable interpretation.

Sidonius feared the very sharp intellect of Faustus, who expected letters from him and subjected those he received to criticism:

> “And it was greatly wished and most welcome to me that the letter entrusted to you should neither refuse to be written in friendship nor, once read, submit itself to criticism.”

Let interpreters determine what those words mean.

> “Rather, you might, skilled in the prayers of the islanders, count a soul badly conscious of itself and trembling hour by hour at the obligations of a punishable life among your frequent and powerful suffrages of prayer—prayers which you transferred into the city as well, from the training ground of the community of hermits and from the senate of the little cells of Lérins, while you oversee the sacred affairs of the church, unchanged as an abbot.”

Sidonius seems to be mocking [Col. 0779A] both the senate of the little cells and the monastic discipline that Faustus, promoted to episcopal dignity and thereafter overseeing sacred affairs, observed with an excessively inflated spirit, in order more easily to impose upon the common people and others. He professed a most abstinent life and, instead of a hidden cross, magnified a public vanity through the boastfulness of a windy pride, introducing, as far as he could, a poisoned disputation as though he were the unshakable guardian of the virtues. So Avitus says in Letter 4.

This conjecture is strengthened by the dispute, however trivial, that arose between Sidonius and Faustus. Faustus had sent the monk and bishop Riochatus to the Britons, his fellow countrymen, and had entrusted him with two little books to be concealed in Aquitaine and read only by the Britons. Riochatus remained with Sidonius for two months because of the disturbances then stirred up in Gaul. Although he often spoke about Faustus, he remained completely silent about the writings entrusted to him.
