But later, on the journey, Sidonius says that when certain travelers revealed that Riochatus was secretly carrying treasures of mystical wealth wrapped in closed containers, he pursued the departing man on swift horses, which could easily outstrip the distance covered on the previous day; he embraced the knees of his captured guest, stopped the pack animals, tied the bridles, untied the bundles, found the volume he was seeking, brought it out, and read it, stripping away the principal points from great works.

From this there flowed Sidonius’s most bitter complaints to Faustus himself:

> “Were you afraid of my brow as though I were a stern censor? Or did you therefore take care to regard me with contempt and neglect because you despised me as younger? I scarcely believe that. Or because I was unlearned? That I can more readily endure,”

and so forth.

These things do not suggest the closest friendship. If Faustus was a very close friend, he ought not to have concealed from his friend the writings he was sending to Britain; nor should Sidonius have followed the tracks of the hastening monk in order to appropriate those writings for himself. Most people believe that these writings were the two books *On Grace and Free Will*. But President Mauguin could not cite Sirmond as supporting him, since Sirmond maintains in his notes that these works of Faustus perished, chiefly for the reason that Sidonius, who had read this very elaborate work, says that it was divided in two according to the form of a dialogue and divided into four according to the subject matter; and these features do not fit the books *On Grace*.

Among the ancient writers who opposed Faustus must be counted Avitus, bishop of Vienne, and Ado, bishop of the same city (*Chronicle*, under the year 492). Ado writes that Faustus, while attempting to destroy Pelagian doctrine, fell into error, and therefore taught free will in such a way that its illumination and salvation came not from Christ but from nature. Finally, Isidore of Seville calls him a man of profound cunning.

**II.** More recent writers diverge sharply according to the way they are carried away by partisan zeal.

> “Who could bear with an even temper that Faustus should be attacked everywhere by many and branded as a heretic?” says Sirmond.

He places the blame for the charge upon Maxentius, a Scythian monk who engaged in lengthy controversies concerning grace; these will be discussed elsewhere. He then introduces men who were extremely celebrated at that time: Hilary of Arles, Gennadius, Maximus, and Pope Hilary.

Nevertheless, he does not deny that Avitus of Vienne and Fulgentius noted several things in Faustus’s writings [Col. 0780A], and that Faustus seems to have attributed somewhat more than was proper to our nature in regard to the beginning of faith and other matters (*Sirmond, History of Predestination*, chapter 8). But he calls the Greek Fathers, and even Augustine himself before he changed his mind, defenders of this opinion—to omit the rest.

On the other side stands President Mauguin, a very learned man and refuter of the Predestinarian fable. He not only lowers Faustus but attacks him as a crafty little fox and impostor who forged Lucidus’s letter and the councils’ subscriptions so that he might more easily deceive others.

**III.** We hold the middle path of the blessed. Sirmond errs, however learned he may be, when he praises Faustus’s patrons—Hilary, Gennadius, and others—as Semi-Pelagians. He then attempts, by a frivolous method, to evade the objections of Fulgentius and Avitus of Vienne. Mauguin errs by attributing many things to Faustus as though they were fictitious. Nevertheless, we are astonished that Faustus is counted among Catholics and saints.

First, Faustus published two books *On Free Will and Grace*, which Fulgentius praised and Pope Gelasius condemned. He began with the Pelagians, whom he appeared initially to refute; but afterward, while keeping Augustine’s name unmentioned, he attacked the defenders of prevenient grace and gratuitous predestination with greater vehemence. According to Baronius, the heresy lay hidden, as a snake lies hidden beneath prominent flowers.

Faustus himself actually says:

> “Just as God gave every human being a hand and an eye, so likewise he granted every human being a will, so that he might exercise it in justice. Therefore, in a human being it is not a personal but a general and public gift. The entrance to attaining salvation, like a certain fountain set out in the midst of this world and granted for common use, lies open for all to draw from, so that the one who neglects to draw will be all the more deserving of condemnation.”

Nevertheless, Sirmond denies that Faustus attributed more than was proper to nature.

A second opinion concerning the materiality of souls is found in Letter 16, which Canisius published for general circulation. Faustus proves, evidently, that nothing besides God is infinite or spiritual, and that the soul is corporeal because it occupies a place:

> “Although,” he says, “we may not declare that certain substances are spiritual, such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, as well as our own soul—or indeed this subtle air—nevertheless they are in no way to be regarded as incorporeal. For they have a body according to their own nature, although incomparably more subtle than our bodies.”

Whoever wishes may use authority to diminish the force of this passage by appealing to Origen and the other Fathers who taught such things. Yet let Letter 17 also be read, in which he vehemently maintains that both souls and angels are local and material.

We therefore, serving truth alone, elucidate the author’s genuine meaning and follow Mamertus of Vienne, who, without mentioning Faustus’s name, refuted his opinion concerning souls in a work published soon afterward, using the same method whose inventor is nevertheless said to have been Descartes.

**IV.** Faustus was therefore a most vigorous defender of Semi-Pelagianism, taught that souls are material, and engaged in more vehement disputes with the bishop of Fréjus, whose abbot claimed the bishop’s rights for himself. For this reason he was condemned [Col. 0781A] by the Council of Arles, as will be shown below.

He had the same homeland as Pelagius—Britain—and from there both crossed over to the Gauls. He had devoted himself greatly to philosophical studies, since Sidonius Apollinaris called philosophy his attendant and inseparable companion at his side. He then practiced forensic advocacy; for, according to Sidonius himself, he exercised himself in the urban schools of rhetoric. Later he professed the monastic life and was made abbot of the monastery of Lérins, then extremely famous, in the year 433.

Baronius’s chronology should not be followed here, for he went badly astray concerning the dates of Faustus’s life. Honoratus, the abbot who was promoted to the see of Arles, was succeeded by Maximus in 426. Maximus governed the abbey for seven years; after these had passed, he was transferred to the see of Riez in 433. It remains, therefore, that Faustus, who succeeded Maximus, was made abbot in that same year, 433.

For approximately twenty-two years he governed the monastery of Lérins, and during that period he was appointed bishop of Riez in place of the deceased Maximus. Baronius assigns his episcopate to the year 472, but he is mistaken, as follows from the calculation given above. Faustus must have been ordained bishop in 455, since when disputes concerning jurisdiction arose between Leontius of Arles and Mamertus of Vienne in 463, Pope Hilary appointed Faustus and Auxanius, fellow bishops and our brothers, as judges and presidents of the council. The sentence issued by them was confirmed by the same pope in the same year and ratified by the bishops. From this it follows that Faustus was bishop considerably earlier than Baronius conjectured.

But our calculation must also be confirmed by the fact that Maximus was present at the Council of Arles at which the major dispute between Faustus, abbot of Lérins, and Theodorus, bishop of Fréjus, was adjudicated. The Fathers urged the prelate to hasten to receive the remedies of satisfaction, and, with pardon granted for his fault, to receive the abbot Faustus back into his former peace with the whole affection of charity, and, in the grace and charity of God, to send him back to the island and community entrusted to him.

Both Maximus and Faustus were therefore present at the Third Council of Arles. Faustus had attempted to usurp the rights of the bishop of Fréjus and was consequently separated from the community entrusted to him. Scholars dispute when that council was assembled, but Binius and Pagi differ by only two years: Binius conjectures that it was held in 453, while Pagi assigns it to 455. But Maximus may have died in the following year, and then, after several months had elapsed, Faustus may have taken his place.

Whatever the case, everyone is opposed to Baronius, who is not to be heeded when he makes Prosper of Aquitaine—who was never a bishop—the successor of Maximus, and Faustus the successor of Prosper.

It may be conjectured that Faustus held the episcopal see for thirty-five years or more, not only because everyone was astonished that Faustus neither grew old nor died, but also because Gennadius, who wrote in 490, reported that Faustus was still alive:

> “The distinguished teacher Faustus,” he says, “is believed and acknowledged through living speech.”

And in fact it is clear that he prolonged his life down to this time, because he was present at the Councils of Arles and Lyons, or at least, at their command, still defended their canons and decrees in writing [Col. 0782A], as we shall prove against Gaulmin, who rejects those councils as having been fabricated by Faustus.

**V.** The celebrated scholar argues with great effort that the letters of Faustus and Lucidus, as though written by fictitious persons, together with the subscriptions of twelve bishops that Faustus appended to his letter to Lucidus, and indeed the Councils of Arles and Lyons, whose judgment he had been ordered to interpret, are fictitious and were inserted by a heretical man—or, as Baronius puts it, by a crafty little fox. President Mauguin maintains that by this means the Augustinian cause he defends could more easily be vindicated, if it was in no way abjured by Lucidus or condemned by the votes of the Gallic bishops.

Let others depend as much as they wish on human authority and make faith itself depend upon it. We do not permit historical faith to be violated in order to deceive posterity and our contemporaries. Nor does the faith that depends upon divine authority suffer any damage from this.

**VI.** These are Mauguin’s principal arguments:

1. Gennadius himself, a Semi-Pelagian, neither Avitus, who was hostile to the error, nor anyone except Faustus mentions the supposed Lucidus’s abjuration and the two councils.

2. It is not plausible that so many highly celebrated prelates of the Gallic Church condemned Augustine’s doctrines and approved Semi-Pelagianism by their formal decision.

3. From the manuscript codex transcribed by Canisius it is clear that those subscriptions were added to Faustus’s letter to Lucidus, and that the names of the subscribing prelates vary frequently.

4. Moreover, the name of Leontius, who ought to have presided over the Council of Arles, is absent [Col. 0782C] from Hincmar’s codex, where Leucadius is substituted.

Finally, it is not true that Lucidus wrote the letter that is being produced. We pass over in silence the arguments that most people consider less probative, lest we turn the book into a volume of observations.

**VII.** We cannot condemn Faustus as guilty of so great a fraud. He could be called a man of profound cunning by Isidore and a little fox by Baronius, and he could defend Semi-Pelagianism with the utmost cunning. But what need would he have had to bring Lucidus, a private person recalled from error, onto the stage, or to invent new councils?

1. Faustus’s letter and Lucidus’s renunciation exist, and they cannot be rejected by any argument. Can such a conjecture be proved by a mere suspicion of cunning? Who could believe that a highly celebrated bishop, already advanced in age, would have invented this fraud to no purpose?

2. The bishops’ seals were not initially attached to Faustus’s letter, for he alone subscribed it. But the prelates could have been asked thereafter to countersign it, as frequently happened at that time. This much is true: all the bishops mentioned here lived in that period and were very well known. Their names may vary in different manuscripts; but this too often happens elsewhere through the carelessness or negligence of copyists.

3. A greater difficulty arises concerning the two councils mentioned, because of the silence both of Gennadius and of Avitus. Yet historians do not record everything, and the bishop of Vienne could have kept silent about arguments adverse to the cause defended by Avitus—namely, two gatherings of a few bishops by which the truth had been wounded.

Whatever the case, there exists Faustus’s letter to Leontius, the president of the Council of Arles. Who could believe that he would have dared to write such things while Leontius was alive, while the other bishops were alive as well, bishops by whom the mark of fraud and falsehood could so easily have been placed upon him?

The following is read in Faustus’s letter to Leontius of Arles:

> “Since, in your pastoral concern, blessed Father Leontius, you assembled a council of the highest prelates to condemn the error of predestination and consulted all the bishops of Gaul, but entrusted to weak shoulders the work and responsibility of arranging what you had set forth with such great learning in a public conference, you showed little regard for holy reputation and burdened yourselves, by the judgment of charity, with the danger of choice.”

The letter closes with these words:

> “In this little work, after the subscription of the Council of Arles, the Synod of Lyons required that certain matters be added, since new errors had been discovered.” [Col. 0783B]

Thus Faustus speaks to Leontius, an eyewitness, the president of the Council of Arles, and one acquainted with the Council of Lyons. I would not wish to deny credibility to such a document. Nor is it plausible that this bishop—at that time highly celebrated for his philosophical studies, age, and learning, however erroneous that learning may have been—would have written with such confidence and said to Leontius, his contemporary, that “he had assembled a council of the highest prelates so that the error of predestination might be condemned.”

For this was the origin of the controversies: the Semi-Pelagians contended that predestination, although gratuitous, imposed necessity upon human actions and the human will. Nor is it surprising that the bishops of the Gallic Church embraced that opinion, which most people defend today.

[Col. 0783C] **VIII.** So much concerning the councils held while Faustus was reaching the age of ninety. We now turn to Lucidus, whom many maintain renounced his former faith, while others deny it.

At least the following points seem plausible to us:

1. At that time, in Aquitaine, the prelates who were drawn from the monastery of Lérins tended toward Semi-Pelagianism. Hence it does not seem surprising that councils—not ecumenical councils, certainly, but provincial councils of the Gallic Church—lent authority to this error, and that Faustus, who lived for so many years and possessed the subtlety for which he was renowned, approved the decrees of the councils not only by his vote but also by his arguments, as is clear from the letter to Leontius, which cannot be denied. Anyone who indulges the spirit of synods will prove this truth by many examples.

2. The presbyter Lucidus, who defended Augustine’s position, was under the gravest suspicion both in the eyes of Faustus, the crafty man, and among the others devoted to that party, as commonly happens. Therefore, struck by fear and prompted by Faustus’s letter, while his terrified mind remained uncertain which side to embrace, he was compelled to obey Faustus and subscribe to the anathemas offered to him [Col. 0784B]. We are not permitted to pass judgment on the freedom or coercion imposed upon him. We conjecture only that the renunciation to which Lucidus subscribed was written in Faustus’s hand, as is customary among those who wish to celebrate triumphs over the defenders of their former faith.

3. Hincmar was mistaken in assigning these councils to the year 431; they must be moved to later years. Some assign them to 475, while Pagi assigned them to the year 490.

These are the names of the prelates who ought to have subscribed: Leontius of Arles—but others read Auxanius—Faustus, Paulus, Eutropius, Pragmatius, Patiens, Megetius, Claudius, Leucadius, and Julianus. All of them say that they have reread the document, except Eufranius, who adds: “And I marveled at the holy fullness.” Lucidus, however, subscribed as one who had renounced his position.

Faustus’s letter to Lucidus is immediately appended [Col. 0784C]. Canisius had omitted it, but it is restored from Sirmond (see below, col. 837), so that readers may perceive the entire sequence of events. Faustus’s admonition, however, should precede these documents. (We published it among the sermons below, col. 887.)

If you wish, compare chapter 8 of the *History of Predestination*, in volume LIII of our *Patrology*, col. 685.

[Col. 0783]

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT FAUSTUS, *ON THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE WILL*. (C, S)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

That the opinion of Pelagius, who denied grace, must first of all be destroyed.

[Col. 0783D]

## On the Grace of God and the Frailty of Free Choice

With the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and in accordance with the teachings of the Gospels and the rules of the apostles, we are going to discuss the grace of God and the frailty of free choice. We have thought it necessary first of all to touch briefly and necessarily upon the blasphemies of Pelagius—blasphemies long since exposed by the faith of the Catholic Church, confuted by learning, and trampled under authority. For, among the other abominations of his teaching, he also attempted, with damnable arrogance, to affirm that human effort can have value without grace [Col. 0784D].

Therefore we shall bring forward at least some of his impious opinions, so that anyone who is attentive may recognize that it is one thing to join human effort to the assistance of saving grace, and quite another to assert, with a single act of presumption, bare effort without the protection of grace.

Thus, while he exalts human frailty to an even greater height, forgetful of divine fear, he has lost sound judgment. In another respect, he has fallen because he proclaims the freedom of choice to be entire and unimpaired, just as those who assert that it has been wholly abolished have fallen. At this point, therefore, two errors contend against one another [Col. 0785A]. One suggests grace alone; the other, effort alone, abandoning the path and measure of truth. They differ in the kind of their sects, but resemble one another in impiety. Their aims are different, but they hiss with the spirit of one serpent.

One of them—that is, the advocate of grace alone—at first sight conceals his poison beneath the appearance of piety. The other—that is, the defender of human effort—immediately reveals his conspicuous swelling through shameless arrogance. The latter’s profession is detestable by its very title, since it suggests effort alone; the former is more to be feared beneath its religious coloring. The one betrays its sacrilege to its own ears; the other pours its poison into the innermost organs almost before it can be perceived.

You might think that two reefs occupy a narrow strait: one sinks down into the depths [Col. 0785B], while the other threatens heaven. One is seen to menace sailors; the other, unforeseen, causes hidden shipwrecks. The one speaks of grace, the other of effort. Divine utterances confirm both. If you remove their disagreements and join their statements together, the complete sincerity of the faith will appear.

But because, like rash rowers without a pilot, they entrust their sails to an unexplored sea, unable to regulate the controls and ignorant of how to handle the helm, one is carried, as it were, toward the danger on Scylla’s right, while the other moves toward the precipice of Charybdis on the left. And if you ask what they ought to do amid these dangers, let them entrust the ship to a prepared pilot, keep to the middle course, and both, with a favorable wind, will be brought into harbor.

Let us see to what impiety this twofold error may be compared or likened. In the same way, those stumble upon the rock of offense who, having lost the light of discernment, presume to assert either that Christ the Lord is God alone or that he is man alone [Col. 0785C]. Almost every excess, because it does not know how to maintain distinction and discrimination, incurs an equal crime.

Accordingly, whoever says that Christ is man alone denies the power of the Creator; whoever says that he is God alone destroys the mercy of the Redeemer. Thus those who confess only one substance in the Lord and Savior will be forced into this necessity: either to say that only a man fell from heaven, or that only God was crucified.

But this is not so. Death could have been experienced neither by God alone nor overcome by man alone. Therefore, according to the twofold reality of his substance, man received death and God conquered it. If, then, you assign to each part its proper characteristics and believe and affirm Christ to be both God and man, it is just as though you join grace to effort and do not exclude human striving from the assistance of God [Col. 0785D]. Yet you must do so in such a way that you do not mingle the fault of arrogance at all with devoted endeavor.

For just as failure to labor brings harm, so presumption on the basis of labor brings danger.

Pelagius therefore says that human nature by itself is sufficient for obtaining salvation. This pestilential teacher speaks as though the original condition of our creation still remained unimpaired in its own state. I judge that free choice could not suffice by itself without the aid of grace even before its privilege was violated by transgression. How, then, can it now suffice by itself, when it is said to its arrogance [Col. 0786A]: “For without me you can do nothing” (John 15)? To its presumption the divine word is also addressed: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126).

This work is denied to arrogance without grace, but is granted to humility together with grace.

Pelagius continues by saying that Adam was made mortal and that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. But when the Apostle says, “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death” (Romans 5), you understand that if sin had not preceded, death would not have followed, and the immortality that had been granted would have endured. It is clear that this immortality was bestowed under a stated condition: if the proud man had not departed from obedience, he would have remained eternal [Col. 0786B] in glory.

For when the heavenly prohibition was enacted in these words, “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die” (Genesis 2), the ill-advised presumption of that forbidden tasting became the occasion of death. “You shall surely die.” If grace, which gives so generously, conferred nothing, what is it that the offense of condemnation took away?

Death, therefore—that is, an alien and adventitious evil—is not the order of nature but the penalty of a sentence. For, as it is written, “The Lord did not make death” (Wisdom 1). That immortality had been entrusted to man is itself testified by the envy of the enemy. Because the fallen one begrudged him immortality, he introduced the cause of death by saying: “On whatever day you eat from this tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Genesis 3).

If he had said only, “When you eat, you will be satisfied by the sweetness of the food [Col. 0786C],” the transgression would have extended only to the enticement of carnal desire. But when he proposed this as the end of the transgression—“You will be like gods”—the fault of gluttony advanced to an attempt upon divinity and to the crime of majesty.

Thus they became like gods, stripped of the gift of heavenly grace and driven from the summit of their blessed station. And so the crafty serpent, expelled from heaven because of the evil of pride, devised his schemes for overthrowing man from his own fall and collapse; and just as he had fallen, so he deceived.

What else, indeed, should be understood by the image of God itself in which man was created, except the mark of perpetuity? You recognize that this perpetuity was not only not taken away from the soul but was also restored to the body through the power of the resurrection. Therefore do not doubt that immortality was entrusted to man before his fault, since you see it restored even after his fall [Col. 0786D].

Pelagius asserts, then, that whether Adam had sinned or had not sinned, he would in every case have died. This follows from his own perversity, because he denies original sin. While he insists that mortality was a condition of creation rather than a consequence of transgression, he wants the origin of this debt to appear to have begun not with the servant but with the Lord, not with the contemptuous subject but with the Creator, so that the law of death may be believed to belong to the order of creation rather than to guilt.

He would have it believed that this grievous destruction inflicted upon the human race was transmitted not by the transgressor but by the Creator. And where, then, is the statement: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2)?

By denying the sin of our origin [Col. 0787A], he removes altogether the reason for which the Redeemer came. Let us see whether this unhappy and lamentable condition began through the will of God or through human perversity. Hear what the trumpet of truth proclaims: “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5).

By saying that Adam was made mortal, Pelagius placed death in the first order of creation, although it is clear that it was imposed at the third stage as punishment for the offense of transgression. Man is the work of God; sin is the work of the devil; death is the punishment of sin. For the Apostle did not say, “The will of God is death,” but “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6).

Let us therefore examine more carefully his deceptions hidden in the depths. He attributes death to the Creator [Col. 0787B] so that its true origin in the supreme evil may not be recognized; and thus he more freely asserts that infants are not held by the bond of their origin. In saying this, he blasphemes with a twofold impiety: he attributes death to the discredit of the Creator, and, by denying the original bond, he nullifies the grace of the Restorer.

Thus, in order to assert that little children do not need baptism, he denied universal sin. Once this was denied, the course of his error was that he could not know from what death had arisen. What wonder if he does not recognize that tree in its fruits, when he refused to acknowledge it in its root? He suppresses the cause of the wound and conceals the sword by which the wound was inflicted.

“The wages of sin is death.” Because he failed to understand the author of so great an evil, he did not recognize that the condition of death, imposed as a consequence of sin, followed after it [Col. 0787C]. We have already said: “The wages of sin is death.” He received a reward worthy of such a deed; he earned such wages who served the devil.

Therefore the chosen vessel most clearly sets forth and proclaims the reason for redemption, saying: “For while we were still weak, Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely will anyone die for a just person” (Romans 5). This means: if righteousness had abounded on earth, medicine would not have been sent down from heaven. But for the one and only salvation to come, universal sickness demanded it.

Since Pelagius is bound by such great chains of sacrilege, it is no wonder that, through a reprobate mind, he is handed over to manifold error, since he thinks that people can be saved through effort alone.

Against the presumption of this arrogance, the divine word rightly exercised the force of its authority and rebuke: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6). And again: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9).

He rightly considered this to have been said against himself, since, together with Pelagius, he placed his salvation in his own will and strength. This objection need not be directed against someone who does not presume upon effort alone, but recognizes that God’s daily mercy and continual grace must be implored for his endeavors and that the Lord’s help must be sought through unremitting supplication.

## CHAPTER II. Against Pelagius’s assertion that little children do not need baptism

Pelagius should also consider this: “If original sin is removed through the gift of baptism [Col. 0788A],” he says, “those born from two baptized persons ought to be free from this sin. How,” he asks, “do they transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all?”

They are easily answered: there are two births. Through one of them sin is transmitted from the pleasure of the one who generates; through the other, sanctification is bestowed from the adoption of the one who regenerates.

“How,” he asks, “do they transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all?” What an irrational and thoroughly unjust objection! You do not want them to transmit to their descendants what belongs to nature, yet you want them to be able, as though giving from their own resources, to confer upon them what belongs to grace? Of this nature the Apostle says: “You were by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2).

They rightly cannot give as their own what they received from above and from outside themselves. Pelagius most foolishly believes [Col. 0788B] that the purity of innocence can be given to children through their parents. The second birth does not belong to the parents’ ministry. He wants what is God’s gift to be a human function, so that something demonstrably outside the human substance might run through the succession of humankind as though by a kind of hereditary order.

There is no doubt, however, that original sin passes from parents—even baptized parents—to their children through the origin of the flesh, as we say daily with the Prophet: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50). The Apostle likewise confirms that this incurable offense passed from one person into all human beings.

But Pelagius says that there is no original sin because the very desire of generation is from God. If you ask from where, then, comes this bond that is dragged along through descendants [Col. 0788C], the answer is undoubtedly: through the stimulus of the heat of accursed generation and through the seductive embrace of both parents.

For when you see that only he is free from original contamination who was conceived not through flesh but through spirit, not through a shameful passion but through a wondrous blessing, recognize that the cause of original evil arose from the pleasure of conception and from the vice of desire.

For this reason that condition did not hold Adam and Eve liable in their origin, since their birth too was independent of the ministry of the two of them; their own birth and creation knew no enticement.

But perhaps you will ask why original sin has been placed in conception. The beginning of the whole fall was obedience. The human being was first exalted, and afterward humbled and confounded. And because, when he was in honor, he did not understand [Col. 0788D], “he was compared with the senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48).

As long, therefore, as humility maintained reverence in obedience to the Creator, an undefiled conscience did not perceive nakedness. But when, with the intention of being like God, he desired the taste of deadly food and extended a condemned desire toward the ambition of majesty, he was punished for forgetting the law and the commandments of the law through the rebellion of his members.

And while he presumed equality with his Lord, he lost mastery over his own body. For lack of self-control was born from pride. What had been struck in him was shown when he covered himself in shame. Exaltation came first; confusion followed. Ambitious for divinity, he became captive to lust.

But perhaps you will say [Col. 0789A]: “While asserting these things, you are found to condemn marriage.” It is not so. The institution of marriage began from blessing; the generation of corruption began from transgression. Meanwhile, the gift of marriage was granted by the Creator while they were still in paradise, but its use took its beginning outside paradise.

Sin stood between generation and desire. Whatever divine command established, I praise; whatever human transgression added, I condemn. It is as though someone were to splash dark filth upon the whiteness of a snowy garment: it is not the workmanship that displeases, but the stain. The garment has not lost its use, even though it has lost its dignity.

Generation would unquestionably have been chaste and pure had hostile transgression not intervened. But flesh subjected to the curse stained the undefiled marriage-bed [Col. 0789B], and the spirit of pride corrupted the simple affection. It lost the gift of purity just as it lost the privilege of immortality.

It is not the grace of marriage that is summoned to judgment, but the injury of obscene passion. Gold is not blamed, but whatever fraud and iniquity mixed adulterously into refined gold—just as the author of wickedness infected Pelagius’s spirit, created by God for better pursuits, with the pestilential corruption of evil.

## CHAPTER III. Against what they say: that every person is saved by grace alone, without any effort

We must now turn to those who, while asserting that grace is given to some and denied to others, have lost the gift of grace together with Pelagius.

They say that, for the worship and service of God, even after the saving gift of baptism [Col. 0789C], the obedience of devoted service is not required, but that grace by itself produces the effect of human salvation. “Everything,” they say, “belongs to grace alone.”

We could say this better ourselves, and it might more suitably be applied to our position: we confess that the benefits of grace extend not to one part but to the whole human race, yet in such a way that we judge the diligence of human vigilance must be joined to it in every respect.

For whoever denies that the effort of devoted service must be associated with grace removes from human beings the duty of servitude. I do not know where or when the one who is commanded to work even in paradise should be granted a holiday from work or abandoned to idleness. In it, as we read, he was placed “to work it and to guard it” (Genesis 2).

## CHAPTER IV. Against the view which, by saying “One has been foreordained to death, another predestined to life,” shuts out hope from prayer itself

[Col. 0789D]

When they say, “Everything belongs to the grace of God,” who would not incline the affection of his whole heart toward such a revered name? But when we answer, “Everything certainly belongs to grace, but the Creator and Redeemer offers and presents it to all for the salvation of all,” they, departing far from the path of piety, presume to reply: “The Savior did not give it to all, because he did not die for all.”

At once the opponent of grace appears in the second statement, though he had initially seemed its advocate. They put forward the name of grace in order to conceal beneath it an abominable blasphemous idea.

Thus, in either direction [Col. 0790A], they exclude the assistance of prayer. What more can the one whom grace has already made its own hope for? Conversely, why should the one whom a violent predetermination has condemned not despair? In the one there is no place for guilt; in the other there is no place for grace. Justice will be endangered in both. The one who is taken up will be rewarded without the merit of faith; the one who is abandoned will be condemned without personal crime. Salvation must be thrust upon the one who does not seek it; it must be taken away from the other who labors.

But you say: “He ought to pray because he does not know to which side he belongs.” Who would not think that this was answered reasonably and wisely? Yet what will prayer profit a person who has been established in one of these two conditions in every respect? Even if he does not know to which side he has been assigned, he does know that both sides have been fixed and are unchangeable [Col. 0790B].

What does it matter if he does not yet know his place, when he knows with absolute certainty that neither danger on the right nor progress on the left is now open to him? If this still-confused persuasion thinks prayer necessary, let it unquestionably acknowledge that, contrary to its own definition, a person can pass from salvation to destruction and from destruction to salvation.

If, then, it does not think the practice of prayer should be abandoned, let it not exclude the practice of working. What is this? You judge that I ought to knock, yet despair that it will be opened to me. Let it therefore choose one of two alternatives: either deny the fruit of prayer or exclude the law of fixed destruction.

We see, then, that this assertion, full of error, begins by shutting out the reason for prayer from the light of grace, but its conclusion runs into and expires in the darkness of sacrilege.

So the devil, through the craft of his ancient art and manifold ingenuity, prepares the allurements of sin [Col. 0790C]. So sorcerers too are accustomed to mix deadly herbal juices into a seasoning, or to offer them unknowingly in some sweet drink, disguising the bitter poison by the deceit of sweetness. The first smell of the cup invites, but the hidden taste of poison suffocates. Honey is what rises to the lips; gall is what descends into the inward parts.

They say that, in one or the other condition of things, death claims these people for itself and life protects those. In saying this, the person who affirms that one was lost in origin and the other elected in predestination—see how he turns aside through wicked persuasion. For what else does he say except that neither needs the assistance of prayer?

Prayer will already be unnecessary [Col. 0790D] for those predestined to life, and it will be unable to benefit those assigned to death. For the former it will be judged superfluous; for the latter, ineffective. The one who is in the process of acquiring predestination does not need the benefits of supplication; the one who is on the side of destruction does not receive them.

But if he thinks care must be devoted to reasoning, let him unquestionably understand that what threatens can be changed, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Mark 15). Again: “Watch, therefore, at every time, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 12). And again: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17).

If prayer is not necessary, why did the one who is to be entreated himself establish a form of prayer and pray? In the case of the man who flatters unlearned ears with an assertion of grace alone [Col. 0791A], the prophetic saying will be fulfilled: “The wicked harms when he mingles with the righteous.”

Gold is displayed by its first color, but the baseness of lead is discovered to lie hidden within. It is as if, beneath the assumed appearance of a disguised citizen, an enemy suddenly appeared, or as if the deceitful subtlety of an enemy transformed itself into an angel of light. So, beneath the face of piety, the evil of paganism will be hidden, and within the name of grace, a fatal decree.

If, then, one has been assigned to life and another to destruction, as they assert—as one of the saints said—we are born not to be judged but already judged. Nor can any equity of judgment remain consistent on this account. For if God gave nothing to the servant, what does he demand from the servant?

## CHAPTER V. The works of the law are destroyed and grace commended; or, against the exceedingly ignorant way in which they put forward testimonies in support of grace alone

[Col. 0791B]

“We read,” they say, “in the Epistle to the Romans: ‘For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God’ (Romans 4). Likewise: ‘To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt’ (ibid.). But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. They also add: ‘But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace’ (Romans 11).”

They must be answered that there are two kinds of works, one of which is removed after the Lord’s coming, while the other is approved. For when he says, “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness,” he plainly places faith before the works of the law [Col. 0791C].

Nor shall we say that the testimonies of the apostles conflict and contradict one another, when another apostle says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2). And again: “Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that there is one God; you do well. The demons also believe and tremble.” Likewise: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.”

Nor will Paul himself, the teacher of the Gentiles, appear different from or contrary to himself when he says: “In everything let us present ourselves as ministers of God, in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors” (2 Corinthians 6). And again: “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3).

These things will seem contradictory to the inexperienced and unlearned, and to those who resist the truth with an obstinate spirit. But according to the catholic rule, the works of the law that belong to the letter are emptied, while those that are to be performed after grace, with grace accompanying them, are affirmed.

Let us see whether we can establish this by the facts themselves. We read that the works of the law are destroyed when he suppresses the Jews’ boasting, saying: “Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. Through what law? Of works? No, but through the law of faith. For we reckon that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law” (Romans 3).

Likewise, he says to the Galatians: “Knowing that a person is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law. For by the works of the law no flesh will be justified before him” (Galatians 2).

Thus the impious errorist said that works are emptied, but through deceitful cunning he suppressed which works they were. You will now have difficulty understanding this if you do not understand the distinction between persons and works.

To the Jews it is said: “No flesh will be justified by the works of the law.” But to Christians, already reborn in Christ, the word of instruction is directed in this way: “Let us do good to all, but especially to the household of faith” (Galatians 6).

And again: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15). To Christians, I say, it is said: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5)—that is, so that we may not be dissolved in idleness, but may glory in good works not in ourselves but in the Lord.

To Christians it is said: “I have truly learned that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

## CHAPTER VI. On the saying, “By the grace of God I am what I am”

Hear the Apostle combining labor with grace in humble confession: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15).

See how he always adds the service of labor to the gift of grace: “Not I, however.” Because he had mentioned labor alone, he quickly returned, as though to the embrace of his mother, grace, saying: “But the grace of God with me.”

“By the grace of God,” he says, “I am what I am.” Subjecting himself piously to grace alone, he assigned the first parts to it; he assigned all that followed in the middle to labor, as the teacher of obedience. Moderating both in the completion, he joined grace and labor. He did not say, “I without grace,” or “grace without me,” but “the grace of God with me.”

What he had first set forth separately, how well he joined together at the end of his discourse! Thus, among those who have been reborn, whenever grace without labor, or labor without grace, is mentioned in Scripture, the other is suppressed but not separated. When one is spoken of without the other, the other is kept silent, not denied, according to the rule which Bishop Augustine expresses: “Not everything that is kept silent is denied” [Col. 0792D].

But in another place the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Corinthians 9). Behold the blessed Apostle, already acquired by Christ, already made the chosen vessel: under the name of predestination and grace he does not relax his hands into idleness, but joins his efforts to God’s benefits and says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude.”

Behold, he is already a soldier on the right-hand side; and see how one already proved worthy deserved to be in danger, how the elect feared being rejected. He already holds victory in his hands, yet does not lay down his weapons. He has already been led to triumph, yet still fears the outcome of military service.

Since these things are so, understand that you are not rising in arms against some weak person, but against the teaching of the supreme Apostle (Ephesians 2) with the weapons of impious error, and that you are contradicting Christ who speaks within him.

And while you remove the service of labor and the reasons for prayer, recognize that you are shutting the door of salvation against the human race. And while you do not know how to reject Pelagius’s impiety, understand that you are turning toward the pestilential doctrine of the Manichaeans, who entirely deny free choice.

## CHAPTER VII. How the saying “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” is to be understood; where faith too is counted among works, and the food of the law is described as perishing while the food of grace remains

Just as, being a friend of sloth and ignorant of discernment, you strayed from the path of understanding between the works of the law and the inactivity of faith, so, following your worst guide of persuasion between the two periods of grace, you lost the shining rule of catholic faith [Col. 0793B].

The period of grace in which we were redeemed did not await human merits and did not seek works at all; God was content with the devotion of our faith alone, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Galatians 3). As he says elsewhere: “The righteous person will live by my faith; but if he withdraws himself, my soul will not be pleased with him” (Hebrews 10).

He asserted that the righteous person lives by faith because he remembers that he conferred faith and righteousness upon the one who sought them. But when he says, “If he withdraws himself,” since he voluntarily turned aside into byways, he did not perish as one abandoned; rather, as an ungrateful person, he withdrew himself from the mercy that was offering itself to him.

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “It is necessary that the one who approaches God believe that he exists and that he becomes a rewarder of those who seek him” [Col. 0793C]. How well he joins the Lord’s function with that of the servant, saying, “he becomes a rewarder of those who seek him.” For just as the giving of reward belongs to God, so the devotion of seeking belongs to the human being.

But you say that faith itself can belong to everyone. It is no wonder that, for the person to whom you deny that works belong, you also strive to diminish faith, which is plainly counted among works, as we have in the Gospel: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains unto eternal life” (John 6).

There food—that is, understanding of the letter—is described as perishing, while the food of grace—that is, faith—is described as remaining. The connected discourse follows: “The Jews said to him, ‘What shall we do, so that we may work the works of God?’ Jesus answered and said to them, ‘This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent’” [Col. 0793D].

You perceive that nothing is done in God’s service without work, since even the one who seems to believe is working.

Likewise, the Apostle says: “Neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision, but faith that works through love” (Galatians 5). Similarly, in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians: “May God deem you worthy of his calling and fulfill every desire for goodness and the work of faith in you” (2 Thessalonians 1).

And concerning Abraham, in the Epistle of the Apostle James: “You see that faith cooperated with his works, and by works faith was made complete” (James 2).

Recognize here a twofold duty: both of working and of faith. “By grace,” he says, “you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2).

The first calling, therefore, asks faith’s brief response from us; but the grace of the subsequent period, after we have been redeemed, washed, and renewed, imposes the diligence of work and the care of laborious service, so that what we received without labor we may preserve with labor, with the assisting help of grace, as the Apostle admonishes: “See,” he says, “that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6).

Recognize that the stages of calling and completion are distinct. He expects faith from beginners; from those who have been strengthened he also requires works together with faith—yet in such a way that he increases the affection of belief in those who are making progress and, as they labor, the helper stands beside them daily.

## CHAPTER VIII. Against what they say: that free choice was entirely removed

The advocate of this wicked persuasion considers a human being, enriched with understanding, endowed with reason, and adorned with the honor of the divine image, comparable to brute animals and senseless beasts, so that the person is dragged along the right path not by any guidance of his own but solely by the violent command of the Creator [Col. 0794B].

By the same reasoning he also tries to assimilate the human being to insensible elements: just as from the nature of the earth—which produces nothing fertile by its own choice and is ignorant of its own fruitfulness, which has neither perception nor freedom nor will—crops are nevertheless obtained when the cultivator works, so that from a human being idle in every exercise of virtue, the fruits of righteousness and the desire and progress toward good things are obtained through God alone acting upon him; and, as though he neither perceives nor consents in anything, whenever he desires or does something, it is judged in no way to belong to his effort or diligence.

And just as the great sea [Col. 0794C] is rolled here and there by the driving winds, so the human mind is turned toward any good or crime without any affection of its own, solely by the impulse of divine power.

If these things are so, and understanding does not recall a person from the left side of evil, while ambition does not stir him toward the right side of good, he will no longer be held by the condition of a human being but of a beast.

Behold the heretic’s conception, under the pretext of grace, of what he wants a human being to be after grace. Therefore, if free choice has entirely perished—which consists, in any event, in the love of innocence, the practice of righteousness, and the sanctification of the body—and if it was wholly removed by the transgression of the first human being, how do we read: “Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth” (Isaiah 26)?

And again: “The righteous person will live by my faith” (Hebrews 10); and: “The righteous will possess the earth as an inheritance” (Psalm [Col. 0794D] 35:11); and: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Psalm 33)?

Has innocence entirely perished because its possessor neglected to remain at its first stage? I do not think so, because it is written: “The innocent and upright have adhered to me” (Psalm 24). And again: “Who will stand in his holy place? The one innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Psalm 23). And again: “The Lord will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things” (Psalm 83).

Is the sanctification of the body to be believed entirely lost because, when the members of the rebellious servant did not preserve their proper servitude, the dignity of the first purity was shaken? Certainly not, because we read: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.” And again: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 19).

Thus, in this kind of good things [Col. 0795A]—the things which the inhabitant of paradise, when he pursued them wrongly, had received from his benevolent Creator—action has not perished, even though perfection has been lost. I do not say that the chastity of these virtues has perished, even though virginal integrity has been violated.

## CHAPTER IX. How the weakness of free choice is to be understood

[The supplied source ends here.]

But you ask and say: How is the weakening of the human will to be understood? Its freedom, having been diminished, requires the supports of grace all the more, just as a person exhausted by a long illness needs more assistance and comfort when walking unsteadily. Thus, just as after an entrenched habit of sexual indulgence, the restoration of continence is achieved only with much labor; and just as sobriety, once taken captive by prolonged drunkenness, is scarcely recovered amid the violence of a harsh cross—although, when it was still unharmed, it was preserved with little difficulty [Col. 0795B] (since it is possessed with a certain pleasure when the conscience is inviolate); and just as, after the various blandishments of carnal vices—which an early age, while retaining its proper condition, could easily have trampled underfoot—one returns to the path of virtue only with a great struggle, as though climbing an arduous mountain, so the freedom of the human will, granted by God, has lost the bloom and vigor of its grace. Yet it has not itself perished, so that it recognizes that divine gifts have not so much been forbidden to it as that they must be reclaimed for itself, with the greatest labor and sweat, through the protection of assistance.

Hear the lawgiver disputing about the freedom of the will when he says: “I have set before you life and death, good and evil; choose life, so that you may live” (Deut. 30). And again: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments” [Col. 0795C] (Ps. 118). You see that here no one is oppressed by fate or by the necessity of an imposed destruction, where the power of choosing is granted. For predestination does not draw toward one side when the choice of both sides is offered.

Likewise: “Let your hand be with me to save me, because I have chosen your commandments” (Ps. 118)—that is to say: “The destructive pleasure of the world was indeed troubling me on the left, but the usefulness of your commandments drew me to the right.” Therefore, since the nations themselves are directed toward judgment of good or evil by the will implanted in them, how much more can the humble Christian regulate himself toward the good by the freedom of his will, he who establishes his ability in the power of God his helper.

To him it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess” (Matt. 19). And again: “Do you wish to be healed?” (John 5:6) [Col. 0795D]. Conscious of how great a capacity the powerful Maker has placed in the human heart, he asks the will of the very person whom he is about to heal.

Elsewhere too, he rebukes the people walking about in the freedom granted to their will, saying: “Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf person who has ears” (Isa. 43). Here, the fact that he is deaf and blind is understood to be a matter of obstinacy, not of nature.

And in the Gospel he plainly shows that an inclination toward good will has been implanted in the human being. “If anyone,” he says, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). This means: It is a matter of my mercy that you are called, but it has been entrusted to your will that you should follow.

Let us see whether God invites a person to himself in idleness. “Let him deny himself,” he says—that is, let the one who is evil [Col. 0796A] strive to become good, and let him pray and say: “And by my will I will confess to him.” Each person is commanded to turn by his own will, lest perhaps the sinner despair of being able to change for the better.

“If anyone,” he says, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” that is, let him become another person in place of the former. Let patience conquer anger, temperance restrain desire, humility drive out pride, and the cross crush pleasure. Who would think that these things could be bestowed upon a sleeping person by grace alone, without labor of heart, without affliction of the flesh, and without the great struggle of the whole human being?

“Let him deny himself”—that is to say: O human being, do not think that you were created by your Maker in such a way that you cannot become just instead of unjust, chaste instead of lustful, and benevolent instead of malicious. In order that you may attain this, what must be changed in you is not your constitution, but [Col. 0796B] your life.

In saying these things, we are not equating labor with grace; rather, we place grace altogether above it, without comparison.

## CHAPTER X. How the statement “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” or the other statement, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,” is to be understood

But you say: Human beings are nothing to such an extent, and everything is only of the grace of God, that the Apostle says: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs”—as the Jew claims for himself from the law, or Pelagius from presumption concerning free will—“but, even though it involves human servitude, everything is nevertheless of the one who shows mercy,” namely, God, “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs” (Rom. 9).

Here he plainly marks and rebukes the one who thinks that he is sufficient for himself, without the hand of one who assists him. [Col. 0796C] But to the person who joins his efforts to the help of the merciful one, he does not say, “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs”; rather, he speaks to him quite differently: “Run in such a way that you may obtain.” And again: “You were running so well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?”

If the will of the one who runs is not also to be awaited, why does he say: “I therefore run, not as though uncertainly”; and again: “I have finished the race; I have kept the faith”? “Not of the one who wills or of the one who runs”—the person who does not know how to distinguish either the persons being addressed or the reasons in the holy Scriptures has himself covered his error in darkness.

Here the Apostle of the nations, affirming faith, restrains and suppresses the pride of the Jews, who claimed righteousness for themselves from works of the law and rejected the mercy and grace of God. They were, as the Apostle says, “seeking to establish their own righteousness” and “were not subject to the righteousness of God” [Col. 0796D] (Rom. 10).

Elsewhere too, he condemns them by a pretended justification and an indirect, ironic expression, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9)—the righteous, that is, those who flatter themselves because of their presumption of righteousness. Likewise, elsewhere he rejects the Pharisee who justifies himself and accepts the tax collector who accuses himself.

“I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance”—that is, “I have not come to call the Jews who claim for themselves, on the basis of the law, privileges of righteousness; rather, I seek the nations, who by faith profess repentance for their sins.”

Because of their pride he also says elsewhere: “The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” The Jews, however, boasted that they were righteous and healthy, but they were not. Who would dare to call anyone healthy in a healthy [Col. 0797A] heart, when the whole human race lay languishing, struck by a single bite of the serpent?

There is therefore one hope of healing for the sick person: that he acknowledge himself to be sick before the physician. It is right that the person who pretends not to know his illness should be deprived of a remedy.

And therefore there will be more joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance (Luke 15). Who would not at this point believe that these are truly righteous, since they do not need repentance? Yet no one needs salvation more than the person who does not understand that he needs it.

And for this reason the true shepherd rejoices more over the one sheep that has been called back from error than over the ninety-nine sheep that did not go astray. And who could be free from the evil of that deadly error, when the prophet testifies: [Col. 0797B] “All of us have gone astray like sheep; each one has turned aside into his own way” (Isa. 53)?

What lamentable blindness: the Jews had lost the way by denying the Savior and did not wish to know their error. Therefore this divine statement, under the designation “the righteous,” without prejudicing another meaning, more particularly marks and rebukes the arrogance of the Jews.

For since the number ten and the number one hundred signify the righteous and the perfect, the ninth and the ninety-ninth signify the unjust and sinners by the very structure of the incomplete number. Thus, in this passage the Apostle’s teaching chastises the arrogance of the Jews, who justified themselves from the law and rejected the mercy of the Redeemer, by saying: “Not of the one who wills.” For in the humble Christian, obedience and submission themselves constitute running and ascent; in the pride of the Jew, they constitute falling and descent.

“Not,” he says, [Col. 0797C] “of the one who wills or of the one who runs.” How can this statement apply to the faithful person subject to the laws of Christ, of whom it is said: “His delight was in the law of the Lord”; and to whom belong the statements we cited earlier: “If anyone wishes to come after me”; “I will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord”; “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it”?

See how great and arduous a work he understands to be involved in both losing and finding the soul, and how he places it also in the human will. And for that reason he concluded in this way: “For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each one according to his works.”

Observe that, when he says “his works,” the giver of grace places human salvation not in the predestination of the maker but in the activity of the servant. Therefore, what is designated here is not the human condition but [Col. 0797D] the manner of life; and for that reason he says elsewhere: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may give an account of the things done in his body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14).

Recognize here that it is not the evils belonging to another’s race or origin, but the deeds done in one’s own body, that will be examined at the final judgment. Therefore, in the human being who has been reborn in Christ, what matters is not what he was born as, but what he has done.

If human action does not also belong to the will, how does he say: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1:19)?

Therefore God, the creator of both—that is, of the outer human being—as he arranged the members of the human body by his power, so by his ordering he permitted the human being to perform and administer the service and use of those members. And just as he himself formed the right hand in every [Col. 0798A] human being, yet placed it within human power so that one might extend it wherever one wished and apply it to different purposes, so likewise he inserted, breathed into, and poured into each soul the faculty of reason and the freedom of the will, but left it to be directed and exercised under the authority of human deliberation. He entrusted its functions to human jurisdiction and mastery, so that, if a person in his corruption desired evil, he would know that this had been permitted to him within the freedom of his will, but would not know that it was lawful.

If, however, he desired the good, he would ask the Creator for its performance and perfection, while the reward for it would belong to his dutiful devotion. And therefore the one who formed and governs the human being assigned the use of good will to the human being, but reserved its result for himself.

He did not therefore grant willing to one person and deny it to another, as though this were just and equitable. Rather, just as he gave every human being a hand, an eye, [Col. 0798B] and a step, so likewise he granted every human being a will, so that he might turn it in whichever direction he wished.

Righteousness in the human being is therefore not a personal but a universal and public gift of God, the entranceway to attaining salvation. It is like a certain spring set out in the midst of this world and granted for common use, open for all to draw from it; and the person who neglects to draw is rightly liable to the giver.

What has been offered to all is therefore required from all. For if, as they say, there is a special dispensation concerning human salvation, I do not know how the examination can be universal. But since it says: “We must all be revealed before the tribunal of God,” he would not demand it terrifyingly from all unless he had offered it mercifully to all.

Therefore, having been placed on active military service, the Apostle exhorts the person in this way: “Labor like a good soldier of Christ. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And the person who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed according to the rules” (1 Cor. 9) [Col. 0798C]. And again: “The laboring farmer must be the first to receive a share of the fruits” (2 Tim. 2).

Hear the Apostle elsewhere too, where he does not preach idleness: “Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the world-governors of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand firm.

“Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, [Col. 0798D] clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Eph. 6).

When he says, “so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil”; and again, “so that you may be able to resist on the evil day”; and thereafter, “taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one,” he shows most plainly that the capacity of free will was granted by God to every human being, so that it would be possible for him not only to resist his own flesh but also to fight against the devil.

Of this adversary he says elsewhere too: “Be watchful,” he says, “because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5). If, as you claim, [Col. 0799A] the necessity of origin had already assigned certain people to this adversary, how could he be seeking those whom he might deceive? And vigilance would be of no benefit to those already assigned to him.

But this is not so. For just as the enemy is brought against all, so the right hand of protection and assistance is denied to none, and mercy in its kindness comes to the aid of those who pray and keep watch. This assistance is certainly offered to those who knock more because of devotion than because of predestination.

In the midst of these matters, then, does not the person who says that grace alone, without the exercise of work and labor, can suffice seem to you, with his mind deranged, to break out into this blasphemous proclamation?

Let no one keep watch; let no one fast; let no one chastise the assault of lust by the discipline of abstinence; let no one declare war on vices through the mortification of external things; let no one strive to heal the wounds of his inner care through saving affliction; let no one oppose desire; let no one seek remedies for crimes through the labor of a flesh [Col. 0799B] worn down; let no one strike back with the power of the cross against the enemy armed with the allurements of obscene pleasure, but let him expose his naked breast to the flaming darts of the enemy; let no one redeem what is owed and subject to eternal death through the sacrifices of almsgiving; let no one bring care through works of mercy and righteousness to his wounds, but let him carry them intact to the day of judgment.

Behold: the person who shortly before was thought to be a defender of grace is found, by blocking the way of human salvation, to be an opponent of the grace through which salvation itself was bestowed, and is shown to have passed over into the counsels of the devil as an ally of destruction.

## CHAPTER XI. Against the claim that free will is ready for evil alone and is altogether incapable of good

[Col. 0799C]

Where is the prophet’s statement: “Hear me, you who pursue what is just and seek the Lord” (Isa. 51)? Or the Apostle’s: “Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey, whether of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (Rom. 6).

Therefore, when the Apostle demands better pursuits from a human being, he shows that the capacity for good will exists in him. When we give this capacity precedence, we plainly proclaim the ordering and wondrous arrangement of its creator, which the same Apostle demonstrates to have been prepared for righteous duties, saying: “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; and do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God” (Rom. 6).

Likewise: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness leading to sanctification” (ibid.) [Col. 0799D].

Does he not here summon the very same human being to the pursuit of good works whom he previously showed to have been devoted to evil?

Therefore, when the destroyer of free will declares that everything in either direction has been established and determined by predestination, he also empties the supreme remedies of repentance by a sense of abrupt impiety. And how does the person who denies mercy preach grace? How does he appear to assert the gift of God when he removes his help? How does he dare to presume upon testimonies from the Scriptures when he attempts to exclude the benefits of the Scriptures?

How is it said to me, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36), if I am no longer [Col. 0800A] able to turn away from evil? Why does the Apostle say: “Put to death,” he says, “your members” (Col. 3); and again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. 5)?

How does the preacher of the law propose a change in me, if the maker has imposed an unchangeable law? “Strip off,” he says, “the old human being with his actions, and put on the new.”

If you insist that the ingrained stain of sin belongs inseparably to origin and constitution, although you know that it can be laid aside and removed, understand that you are speaking with a spirit opposed to the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit gave the mysteries of the law and the prophets, the declarations of evangelical truth, to the world for its assistance, and promised the heavenly kingdom to those who, with grace cooperating, observe the divine commandments [Col. 0800B] through the duties of laborious service.

Therefore measure the honor of holy work and labor by the greatness and dignity of its reward. You certainly judge its prize and crown to be worthless if you affirm that they can be grasped without laborious contrition.

Can that commandment of divine instruction be fulfilled without great application to the work? “Do not be overcome by evil,” it says, “but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12). Or this: “Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15).

And how can you maintain among these things that the gift received by grace cannot in any way be endangered, when you read that the good implanted in one’s character can be corrupted by evil?

Who could teach that what the Apostle says is to be attained: “In everything we suffer affliction, but we are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not despairing; we suffer persecution, but are not abandoned; we are struck down, but do not perish” (2 Cor. 4) [Col. 0800C]? And what he says elsewhere: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

If these things and others like them, with which the holy Scriptures are filled, are acquired through idleness, why are they not attained by everyone? Much will be taken away from the glory of the one who rewards and from the justice of the one who rewards, if eminent and illustrious men are crowned through rest and laziness.

And where is the prophetic statement: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult paths” (Ps. 16)? If the pursuit of salvation is an idle undertaking, then the path of virtue is common, universal, and broad. Therefore the Gospels lie when they say: “How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and [Col. 0800D] few are those who find it.”

If works cease, merits will have no honor. If nothing in labor is arduous, nothing in virtue will be precious. But this arduous way exposes the slothful, and labor deters the idle.

Therefore the cause is not the violence of foreknowledge but the disobedience of the sinner, as we read: “They perished because of their iniquities, like a dream when one awakens” (Ps. 72). And again: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Ps. 6). And elsewhere: “They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law” (Ps. 77).

It is therefore not inability that holds a human being back from the work of righteousness, but iniquity and will.

But when the Apostle says: “Rebuke the one who sins in the presence of all” (1 Tim. 5), there is no reason why a person who transgresses unwillingly should either be rebuked or condemned [Col. 0801A]. But this is not so. For through his prophet the Lord says: “I will judge each one according to his ways, O house of Israel.” Whoever has succumbed to passion has not been overcome by foreknowledge pressing upon him, but has been led astray by sin’s seduction.

Still denying human effort and labor, they put forward this testimony: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126).

Those who foolishly bring this forward and think that everything must be denied to the human being cannot, first of all, work out the meaning of their position according to the sound of the letter. Does the Lord, then, administer the salvation of the human race entirely by himself, as though by an isolated undertaking? Certainly not.

Rather, just as a body arranged through its members carries out the command of the head, so the Lord builds his house through the leaders and shepherds of the Church, through [Col. 0801B] those who say: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3:9). Whoever undertakes responsibility for saving a human being is an assistant to the Redeemer.

The Lord therefore builds this house through his saints, and the saints through their Lord. The Church is built through the one who said: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation” (ibid. 10).

Does he build and know the Church in any other way than through the labors and duties of priests, through the ministries and examples of the saints, through the virtues of the apostles and the deaths of the martyrs?

Yet amid all this, although the servant must labor even to the endurance of every evil and the loss of life, the result of the labor must always be referred to the Lord. But to the person who presumes to claim either the beginning or the end of the work for himself, it is rightly said: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” [Col. 0801C].
