For just as indefatigable devotion in service is to be expected from the human being, so the perfection of the completed work must be attributed to the Lord, whose gifts were lacking only to the person who neglected to preserve them.

That servant too recognized that he had received something, yet he scorned to double the talent entrusted to him through the business of salvation, and instead committed it to the torpor of the earth’s idleness (Matt. 25).

Saul too (1 Sam. 9) received the grace of God when he was anointed by Samuel, and obtained a special munificence and royal power, under this condition: that he should not turn aside from God’s commandments. He who had overthrown the sacred groves and shrines together with their python-spirits under the guidance of the priest his master lost faith when that master died and afterward hastened to the deceitful answers of a sorceress, though by overthrowing idols he had shown that he could belong to God.

## CHAPTER XII. Against the interpretation that a vessel made for dishonor cannot rise to become a vessel made for honor

[Col. 0801D]

They say that a vessel of dishonor cannot pass into a vessel of honor, because the Apostle said: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

Here he suppressed, by a concluding statement, the preceding causes by which a human being passes either into honor or into dishonor. For when a human being has begun to be a vessel of honor through grace, he must keep watch so that the honor he has received may be preserved through divine cooperation, lest the person who has been acquired should afterward, when guilt arises, be changed into a vessel of dishonor.

As for what they say—that a state of a human being determined from the beginning [Col. 0802A] of life cannot be changed for the better—this is believed to occur there, after the departure from this life, where there will no longer be either correction or change among the dead.

But up to the end, the worst can pass over to righteousness, and the perfect can fear danger. As we read: “Those who glorify me I will glorify; but those who despise me will be dishonored” (1 Sam. 2).

Why is this one honored and that one despised? Certainly because the one who inflicted dishonor could have glorified God, and the one who bestowed glory could have despised him. For the one who wished to please the Lord his God could have refused, and the one who refused could have wished to please him.

Do not think that there is here a difference of nature: it is the same person who wills and who does not will.

Therefore, unless each person reborn in Christ has first been a vessel of malice through his own fault, he cannot be a vessel of offense and wrath [Col. 0802B]. Conversely, in order to become a vessel of mercy, he must first become a vessel of obedience, so that the sentence of the just Judge may follow upon the preceding causes.

Let us show that a vessel of dishonor can pass into a vessel of honor through the help of God and its own effort.

“If I say to the wicked,” he says, “‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die.”

What is a wicked person except a vessel of dishonor? Behold: through the remedy of repentance he is suddenly honored with the brightness of grace and clothed with the beauty of righteousness, so that, with the filth of his sins washed away, he can confidently say with the prophet: “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.”

Hear the Apostle declare how the stains of conscience can be whitened, so that from a vessel of iniquity a vessel of sanctification may appear. [Col. 0802C] “In a great house,” he says, “there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware” (Rom. 9).

For what else does it mean that some vessels are for honor and others for dishonor? Raise your heart, human condition, freed from unchangeable necessity, and recognize the unspeakable goodness of your Lord concerning human salvation.

When he had said, “some for honor and others for dishonor,” he opened and enlarged the hand of hope for the faithful by saying: “If anyone purifies himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified” (2 Tim. 2).

The power of the heart is therefore capable of both alternatives. What it previously allowed to be poured into itself can easily be emptied out through a change of its former purpose, so that the very same vessel may remain in and with itself once the iniquity poured into it has been poured out.

Thus the vessel refers to the substance of the human being, while what is contained in the vessel refers to the kind and diversity [Col. 0802D] of the will.

Elsewhere too the Lord shows that what has been lost can be restored when he says: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

And again: “It was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”

The loss, therefore, did not occur in his nature; rather, the one who had died by withdrawing from the sight of his loving father in contempt came to life through the desire to return. For just as it is a matter of his own guilt that he fled far from the eyes of his pious father, so it is a matter of his own devotion that, deliberating through the good implanted in him and rising up, he hastened back to his father’s embrace.

But the grace that had summoned the wanderer itself received the returning one. Let the original or fatalistic definition withdraw from here. Behold: the dead person is brought to life, and the lost person is found.

So too with the woman in the Gospel (Luke 15) [Col. 0803A], who searches through the house with a lit lamp for the drachma she had lost—that is, for something belonging either to any gift or to salvation—and applies her own effort to the oil of grace, joining the intention of the seeker to the help of God. Thus what she had lost within, she found within.

Whenever, therefore, a human being strives by the judgment of his mind to become evil from good or good from evil, the will—which is free—is corrected by God’s gift; it is not the force of predestination that operates.

And as often as you read in the sacred pages: “On whatever day the wicked person turns and groans, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33); and again: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn back from your evil ways”; and again: “The wickedness of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns from his injustice”; and this: “Remove the old [Col. 0803B] leaven, so that you may be a new mixture” (1 Cor. 5)—as often as a human being turns toward better things, rejecting what is worse, with grace assisting, so often a vessel of dishonor becomes a vessel of honor.

But for good people to become evil, human weakness more readily admits this into itself, so that a vessel of honor may pass into a vessel of dishonor. As we read in Habakkuk: “And his chosen foods.” Of these it is also said: “He will regard gold as straw.” Jeremiah likewise says: “How the gold has been darkened; how the finest color has been changed” (Lam. 4).

As the Apostle also says: “Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (1 Cor. 6).

Therefore the judgment is clear: through his own fault a human being can be changed from the body of Christ into the portion of the devil.

Elsewhere too he teaches with complete clarity that what is best can become what is worst and that the temple of God can be violated, saying: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (2 Cor. 8) [Col. 0803C].

Behold: he is already recognized as the temple of God; he is already possessed by the Holy Spirit; and yet it is said that through negligence he can be violated and corrupted and occupied by an unworthy guest.

Likewise the prophet rebukes the soul voluntarily emptied of God’s grace: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2).

Behold: a vine planted for God from a noble root and chosen through the cultivator’s care is shown to have been corrupted by its own crime.

And therefore he speaks of it in Isaiah’s song: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” The expectation of the rebuking farmer shows that this vine could [Col. 0803D] have yielded fruits of righteousness.

And when he testifies that the one who stands can fall, saying: “Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall,” he speaks conversely to the one who lies fallen: “Will the one who falls not rise again? For God is able to establish him” (1 Cor. 10).

He plainly shows that the human condition can be turned in different directions, not according to God’s constitution, but according to the freedom of the will.

Isaiah also clearly affirms that what has been corrupted can be corrected and that what is spotless can be washed clean, when he speaks to sinners, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.”

## CHAPTER XII. Likewise, willing and not willing were entrusted to human choice for the good as well as for the evil side

[Col. 0804A]

In the meantime, among the heretics we must carefully inquire whether a human being cannot do good, or is unwilling to do so, given that the seeds of a good will have been implanted in him. Scripture clearly establishes this when it says: “If you will, the commandments will preserve you”; and, “Do not fall away from the discipline of the Lord”; “Do not refrain from doing good to the needy”; “Do not contrive evil against your friend”; “Do not become like a horse or a mule, in which there is no understanding”; “Do not reject the counsels of your mother”; “Do not fix your attention on a deceitful woman”; “He was unwilling to understand, so as to act well”; and, “They were unwilling to accept discipline.” When unwillingness is reproved, it is plainly shown that willingness was readily available.

There are many similar passages in the utterances of the Old Testament, all of which specifically constrain and [Col. 0804B] convict the will. In the new evangelical and apostolic books as well, what else is displayed but freedom of will, where it is said: “Do not store up treasures on earth”; and, “Do not fear those who kill the body.” “Be sober, be righteous, and do not sin.” And to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you,” nor let “your good deed” be as though it were done from necessity, but from willingness. And elsewhere: “Do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality.” “Do not slander one another”; and, “Do not be deceived. God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” And, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.”

We therefore see that the assent of the human mind can move both toward the good and toward the contrary. And for this reason he says elsewhere: “In doing good, let us not grow weary; [Col. 0804C] for in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary. Therefore let us do good to everyone, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith.” He says, “Do not love the world”: unless he had bestowed upon it an inclination toward what is good and better, he would not forbid its desire for evil. [Col. 0804C] Thus the one who is called by his Lord to the right is dragged toward the left by his own crime. And therefore he says again: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” Clearly, the person to whom victory is promised through the choice of good is not oppressed by the necessity of evil.

For the law of origin does not draw into byways the one whom the Creator has placed at a crossroads. And so, since a will has been implanted in him by which he can conquer evil, if he should call for adversaries, and if his spirit should not lack the will to fight, he will not lack the outcome of victory.

We read in Hebrews: “For if we sin deliberately after receiving knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” [Col. 0804D] Accordingly, if we do not possess freedom of choice, how do we sin willingly? If you ask why he is guilty, the answer is that, after receiving knowledge of the truth, he turned aside toward the spirit of error. “After receiving,” he says, “knowledge”—understand that he received grace and lost it through negligence.

And again: “If anyone who has violated the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses, how much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” Why is he accused on the testimony of two or three witnesses and dies as guilty of his own crime, if he is already crushed beneath an inevitable law of nature toward sin? [Col. 0805A] Without doubt, therefore, he deserves punishment because he was able, but unwilling, to preserve righteousness.

If you ask for what reason he was stripped of so great a good, the answer is: because “he insulted the Spirit of grace.” Recognize here that grace was not so much withheld from the human being as that the kindness of the giver, having first been abandoned and despised by the human being, withdrew from him. With a certain grief he reproves the insult of the one who rejects it; and so, when he voluntarily turned aside into the byways, the one who was abandoned did not perish, since he had withdrawn ungratefully from the mercy that pressed itself upon him.

The same result is found in those concerning whom the Psalmist declares: “And he blessed them, and they multiplied exceedingly” (Ps. CVI). In what follows, he sets forth the causes of the lost blessing: “And they were led astray,” he says, “by their own vanities, and they led them astray in a trackless place and not on the way.” Here the transgressor of the commandment [Col. 0805B] appeared guilty because he was led astray toward evil rather than compelled.

Similarly, in Galatians he attributes the guilt of transgression to human offense, saying: “But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. IV). According to this nature, Christ is God, and we are commanded to serve him. He continues: “But now, since you have come to know God—or rather, since you have been known by God—how can you turn again to weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew?”

He did not say, “You cannot be good,” but, “You wish to be evil.” If, once corrected, they had not been able to remain in goodness, they would not be reproved for having fallen into what was worse. To them he says again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Here he asserts that those who had been begotten from faith but had become abortive can still be reformed into the image of Christ; [Col. 0805C] and, by still calling them lost sons, he condemns their transgression without despair, teaching both that what has been lost can be restored and that what has been bestowed can be taken away.

When elsewhere a heretic interprets the Apostle’s statement as meaning God’s predestination or foreordination, where we read, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy” (Rom. IX), he must be asked whether what God wills is ordered or disordered, just or unjust. When he replies that what is necessary is just, we must say: “I think these are words of justice, because the divine will is justice.” Thus this expression is to be understood as follows: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy”—that is, on the one whom I recognize as just, whose ready faith I see, whom I perceive to obey my commands, whom I have proved to do my will. [Col. 0805D]

“And I will show mercy,” he says, “to whom I show mercy”: this is to be understood as follows: Whoever preserves the mercy bestowed by God with a submissive and watchful mind will obtain greater mercy. Thus he says elsewhere: “For to the one who has, it will be given, and he will abound”—that is, because he guards the gift received from God with vigilance and fear of heart, he will receive an ever greater increase of that grace, so that his very progress will produce further advances in him. As he says elsewhere: “And let the holy person still be made holy.”

They also think that the following statement should be referred to God’s foreordination: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. You will say to me then: Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” [Col. 0806A] Here the Apostle plainly introduces an opposing meaning in the person of one asking or objecting; and in the rebuke that follows he chastises the position advanced against him, saying: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

Here, by arguments grounded in authority, he restrains the curiosity of the unbeliever; and when he says, “Does he not have authority?”, he brings against the slanderer only God’s authority, convicting by reason the one who ignorantly and faithlessly ascribed all human actions to divine determination.

“Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” In saying “from the same lump,” recognize from sacred reading, whoever thought that there were two masses of the human race, [Col. 0806B] that there is one. Two masses, however, are produced by the perversity of pursuits and the diversity of wills. Thus, according to their qualities, and not through any compulsion from God, each person becomes either a vessel of dishonor or a vessel of honor.

## CHAPTER XIV  
**Where the grace of God and human will are joined by the testimony of scriptural assertions, and the empty calumny concerning infants is briefly touched upon in passing**

If you direct your attention carefully, you will plainly and abundantly understand how, throughout the pages of the holy Scriptures, now the power of grace is asserted and now the ascent of human will. We demonstrate the frailty of free choice when we say to God: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CVI).

Likewise, the divine word commands that the power of free choice is able to accomplish something [Col. 0806C] when it says to a human being: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit” (Ps. XXXIII). The word of Wisdom commends free choice when it says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV). But the Apostle makes clear that this cannot be done without divine help when he says: “May the Lord guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Phil. IV).

Through the prophet he asserts the capacity of one’s own will, speaking of himself: “I inclined my heart to perform your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet he understands that nothing should be presumed upon from his own powers alone, when he cries out to God: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice.”

Because of free choice, we are commanded: “Make straight courses for your feet, and direct your ways.” But, fleeing to grace in awareness of our weakness, [Col. 0806D] we plead: “Direct my way in your sight, and perfect my steps in your paths” (Ps. V).

He commands us—he who, in the general ordering of things, has granted authority to our own will—to illuminate for us the light of knowledge. But because everything must be referred to the author of grace, we read: “He commands us—having granted this right to our own will in the general ordering of things—to kindle for yourselves the light of knowledge.” Because everything must be referred to the author of grace, we also read: “He who teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. XCIII), or, “The Lord gives light to the blind” (Ps. CXLV); and again: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. XII); and, “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law.”

The Apostle, the proclaimer of free choice, urges its freedom by saying: “Guard your souls.” But he bears witness to God’s mercy when he says: “May the Lord guard your coming in and your going out” (Ps. XC). Through these passages, then, [Col. 0807A] in which at one time the freedom of choice is asserted and at another heavenly generosity is displayed, a human being is now reminded of the powers granted to him, lest he idly hope in grace alone; now he is commanded to hope in grace, lest he be secure in labor alone.

But you say: “If there is no predestination, why are some infants baptized while others are seized without the sanctification of baptism?” It is the fraud of the serpent to abandon the light and flee into dark caverns when, throughout all the volumes of sacred Scripture, free choice speaks plainly. What reason is there for you to wish to question hidden things when you see that the manifest things fully answer your concern? What advantage is there in neglecting certainties and consulting uncertainties, concerning which you find nothing written in the Catholic reading?

Do you not understand that, to the injury of truth, you are investigating whatever truth did not wish you to know? You introduce a subject concerning the nature of free choice, and then, through a destructive error, you slip into a discussion of the condition of infancy, in which no trace of free choice and no sign of personal will can appear at all. [Col. 0807B]

## CHAPTER XV  
**Against what they say: that those who perish after baptism had no faith at all in baptism**

Here you must answer: In what author do you read this, and on the authority of what teacher do you presume to assert it? And since you do not deny that original sin is abolished in baptism, and baptism is proved to be valid when the undivided Trinity is invoked, on what grounds can you say that one who has been baptized still remains under the debt of original sin? [Col. 0807C]

“And they themselves,” you say, “perish in Adam because they did not believe in baptism.” Did you not say shortly before that human effort is not required for receiving the gifts of God? Behold, you yourself most plainly confess that, without the devotion of the recipient, the generosity of the giver is ineffective. You yourself, I say, confirm that without the merit of faith—that is, without the cooperation of human will—grace is of no benefit. How then do you say that God reserved everything for himself concerning the condition of the human being and gave nothing to the human being?

Behold, according to your own position, even the mystery of regeneration cannot stand on its own unless the human being, in accordance with the gift of blessing, supplies the disposition of belief. To the one whom you deny any striving, why do you demand assent?

When the prophet says, “Living waters shall go out from Jerusalem” (Zech. XIV), thereby designating the sacraments of the life-giving flood, how can it happen that a renewed human being [Col. 0807D] retains with himself the bond of the old human being after it has been erased? How can it happen that, having been absolved in Christ from Adam’s debt, he rises again still bearing it? How can it happen that from the irrigation of the sacred font life still gives birth to death together with the adopted child of God, when the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III)? Certainly no one can put him on unless he has removed the garments of his first birth.

And how can you demonstrate that baptism was of no benefit to one who comes voluntarily to baptism, when even for a heretic regenerated in the name of the Trinity the power of the mystery itself confers so much that, if he afterward passes to the faith of Christ, he does not need baptism to be repeated? Rather, through the operation of grace, he is judged cleansed, so that he is clothed only with the blessing of chrism. [Col. 0808A]

The Catholic Church detests this reprobate meaning of your persuasion. “For this reason,” you say, “those who have been washed in whatever birth-water do not receive the gift of baptism: because they come to baptism without faith.”

That is not so. Observe that the very act of coming to baptism and desiring salvation is already an act of faith.

“You say that whoever perishes after baptism perishes in Adam because he did not believe in baptism.” You would more correctly say that they perished after baptism because they did not wish to join the duty of labor to the gift of grace, because negligence born of habit and sloth of heart turned them away from watchfulness in their work and from the diligence of conscientious service.

But if the fault of unbelief is the cause of destruction, what shall we think about infants? In the devotion of their parents and in the simplicity of nursing infancy, [Col. 0808B] they are credited with the vigilance of complete faith; without any danger of unbelief, they obtain the undefiled gifts of regeneration, and many of them, as they grow older, plunge headlong into death. What explanation accounts for this, except that they allow themselves to be conquered by the enervating force of indolence?

He explained the reason why they appeared to have been broken: “Because of unbelief,” he says, “they were broken,” certainly not because of foreknowledge. He shows that God’s generosity is not directed exclusively toward believers, since he demonstrates that even those whom he accuses of unbelief could have believed. In this way he also makes clear that unbelievers received the opportunity for faith; and when he says that they were broken from the natural branches, he restrained the presumptuous with a life-giving correction: “If,” he says, “he did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.”

And he added: “And they, if they do not remain [Col. 0808C] in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.” Here, then, he addresses greatness of spirit and humility of heart: humility, so that the one who is uncertain may fear being broken; greatness of spirit, so that the one who has been broken may not abandon hope of reward.

Thus the diligent shepherd sought the lost sheep, and, when he found it, carried it back to the fold on his shoulders. How could he abandon the one who followed him, when he also follows the one who abandons him?

## CHAPTER XVI  
**Against what they say: that Christ did not die for everyone**

They say that our Lord Jesus Christ did not assume human flesh for the salvation of all and did not die for everyone. The Catholic Church utterly rejects this [Col. 0808D]. For if it were so, how could the Apostle say: “As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV)?

Here the whole cannot be said to refer only to a part. For just as the first part of the statement, “All die in Adam,” plainly shows this, so the Apostle likewise indicated that what follows—“all will be made alive in Christ”—refers generally to all who are to be made alive in Christ, not merely to a portion.

Those same wicked people are also believed to be raised by the power of Christ’s resurrection, although they rise not to be judged but to be punished. When the Apostle says, “Who is the savior of all human beings, especially of believers” (I Tim. IV), by saying “of all human beings” he had in view the purpose of divine goodness. [Col. 0809A] By saying “especially of believers,” he pronounced upon and distinguished those who, through faith, obedience, and submissive will, received the gifts of the Redeemer.

That Christ came for all the Apostle himself declares: “The love of Christ urges us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them” (II Cor. V).

Since, therefore, the general resurrection belongs to the power of redemption, if redemption does not pertain to all, neither will the resurrection pertain to all. And therefore, just as we shall all rise, although we shall not all be changed, so we testify that the Lord the Redeemer came with the benefit of general mercy; [Col. 0809B] and if someone did not receive it, that was because of unbelief, because he was unwilling.

Whoever sought God at any time found him; and whoever did not appear to have found him did not seek him. But if, as impious blasphemy rashly asserts, some appear to have been foreordained to death and others predestined to life, Christ had no necessity to come or to die such as his compassion found.

Thus the new remedy could accomplish nothing if an ancient decree had fixed human affairs before the ages. But because the fatal doctrine that introduces the force of a compelling foreknowledge must be rejected in every way, he therefore both gave the law and raised up prophets in the intervening ages, because he knew that the freedom of human will had been weakened, not removed.

And if its power had entirely perished, how would we read: “And his will was in the law of the Lord” [Col. 0809C] (Ps. I)? And again: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily, Lord.” And to Philemon: “So that your good deed might not be from necessity, but voluntary.”

And when he says in the Gospel, “My flesh is for the life of the world, which I will give” (John VI), we must have no doubt that he gave himself for the whole world, since he gave more than the whole world was worth. As blessed John the Evangelist also testifies: “For he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (I John V).

But you say: “How did he redeem the whole world?” Behold, we see people living in their sins. How can we consider those redeemed whom we see remaining captive?

Let us gather the meaning here from the comparison that has been proposed. For example, if some ambassador or priest, intending to intercede for a captive city, [Col. 0809D] should pay an abundant price and receive back from the one who held the rights of war the entire population of the captivity, and if the whole law and necessity of servitude were completely abolished, but meanwhile some of the captives were enticed by the pleasure of habit or by an evil and flattering captor, and each one should refuse the free gift as a slave of his own will, did the contempt of the ungrateful diminish the grace of the price? Did the one who rejected freedom bring any diminution to the goodwill of the redeemer?

It is not so. Rather, just as the one who returned may be grateful to the redeemer, so the one who remained is guilty for his contempt. For he redeemed those who were willing—the rewarder of wills. God, the just judge, desires the willing person to return, whom he remembers as having fallen unwillingly. [Col. 0810A]

Since these things are so, tell me: whom did he exclude from the grace of redemption, when he erased the universal written bond of the ancient condemnation?

## CHAPTER XVII  
**Against what they say: that they interpret the evangelical statement with ignorant and wicked meaning**

“No one,” he says, “comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI). Who could be so forgetful of his salvation as to dare deny the mercy of the one who draws? But he is truly impious who does not testify that this mercy is extended to all and bestowed upon all.

Here he thinks that the salvation of those who are drawn is a form of violence on the part of the one who draws. He evidently knows only the chains of enslaving bondage, since he does not understand the bonds of devoted love.

But this divine statement specifically reproves the human being [Col. 0810B] who arrogates everything to his own powers and impiously presumes upon his own labor. Since one person judges that everything must be assigned to labor, while another judges that everything must be assigned to grace, the Greek saying is fulfilled in both: “Excesses and inequalities are a similar wickedness.” It is proved to be equally impious whether everything is ascribed to grace alone or everything to labor alone.

What ought we to think between these alternatives except that we should always subject labor to grace and always join grace to labor? Above all, however, let us avoid pride in labor and claim nothing for ourselves from its merits, lest we seem to imitate the Pharisee through the deadly presumption of boasting.

For although, when he prayed, he undoubtedly spoke the truth: “I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke XVIII), he emptied the truth of its credibility because he mixed vanity with truth. [Col. 0810C] Therefore it is not the action but the pride of heart that must be avoided.

“No one,” he says, “comes to me unless the Father draws him.” Is a person to be moved and dragged from place to place like insensible and useless material? No. When the Lord stands beside him and calls, the servant extends the hand of faith by which he may be drawn, and says: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX).

Thus these two things are joined together: the power of the one who draws and the disposition of the one who obeys. It is like a sick person attempting to rise, while his strength does not follow his intention, and therefore asking that a right hand be offered to him. The will cries out, because weakness cannot be raised by itself.

Thus the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, and raises the one who strives. But what is it to draw except to preach; to stir up through the consolations of Scripture [Col. 0810D]; to deter through its rebukes; to set before us what is desirable; to threaten what is fearful; to announce judgment; and to promise a reward?

Hear the Lord drawing not with harsh bonds but with hands, inviting with the arms of love, as the prophet says: “I drew them with the bonds of love” (Hos. XI). And again: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I).

And therefore he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI), so that no one may be able to excuse himself as excluded, when he is convicted of having been invited. Although he foreknew that not all would offer obedience, he nevertheless had granted to all both the will and the ability.

Here we must inquire carefully whether each person wishes to be drawn or is unwilling. If he is unwilling, he does not deserve the customary goodwill of the one who draws. [Col. 0811A] But if he is willing, behold, there is already cooperation between grace and human consent.

“No one,” he says, “comes to me unless the Father draws him.” When you see the one who draws, why do you pretend not to see the one who comes? And therefore, just as being drawn is proved to belong to grace, so following is proved to belong to obedience.

If this mercy of the drawing God is given to the worthy, you perceive that it is already being offered, in some measure, in response to human effort and service. But if it is given to the unworthy, it follows that it is not denied even to the reprobate, and that the goodness of God is evidently offered indiscriminately to both the righteous and sinners.

Yet the one whom you see drawing requires that the commandments be kept in every respect, so that the one who is called may be grasped and drawn by a kind of hook of the will. If you think that he draws those who are unwilling, you impose the weight of injustice upon heavenly justice. [Col. 0811B] But if he is found to draw the unwilling, how much more does he embrace those who desire him!

For even the one who appears to be drawn without labor will have to labor in order to cling to the one who draws him. How many have come and gone away because, after being drawn, they did not wish to persevere in grace when the one who desired them was calling?

As it is written in the Gospel: “Many of his disciples, when they heard this, went back and no longer walked with him” (John VI). Likewise: “Then Jesus said to the Twelve, ‘Do you also wish to depart?’ Peter answered him, ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of God’” (ibid.).

In both groups the will was free: in the first, to depart with an ungrateful mind; in the second, to remain with the freedom of faith.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
**Against what they say: that God’s violence hardens a person so that he cannot come to salvation**

[Col. 0811C]

If he hardens, as the blasphemer wishes, how does the psalm say: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV)? And again: “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II).

Likewise in Jeremiah: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline; they hardened their faces more than a rock, and they were unwilling to return” (Jer. V).

Observe further the cause of hardening according to the judgment of the wisest Solomon, who says: “When the wicked has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII)—that is, despair arises from persistent sinning, and hardening [Col. 0811D] is born from despair.

When Jeremiah says, “They were unwilling to return,” you see that hardness of heart is the crime of one’s own will: the dishonorable, greedy, and bloodstained person, and the slave of every kind of crime, if he does not resist his sins.

Let us see from where this hardening arises. It is not the violence of one who compels, but the kindness of one who relaxes that provides the occasion for hardening. While tireless goodness tolerates the sinner for the sake of repentance, the arrogant security that abuses the goodwill of the one who forgives takes advantage of it.

Therefore blessed Paul says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God” [Col. 0812A] (Rom. II).

You perceive that, by saying “according to your hardness and impenitent heart,” the Apostle attributes the blame for hardness of heart not to God but to the human being. “Do you not know,” he says, “that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God.”

Recognize that it is not God’s severity that hardens the hearts of the wicked, but his goodness. Because they are not afflicted by the labor of trials and scourges on account of God’s patience, they are corrupted by pride. The prophet also clearly recalls that this is so, saying: “They are not in the labor of human beings, and they will not be scourged with human beings; therefore pride has seized them” (Ps. LXXII).

And so, while punishment is reserved for judgment and the Lord’s long-suffering calls them to correction, impunity nourishes contempt [Col. 0812B] in the servant.

“He repays,” he says, “each person according to his works” (Rom. II). Certainly God does not impose upon a human being, on the basis of foreknowledge, a necessity to sin, when he is read to demand an account from him according to his works.

“I have sinned,” says the prophet, “and what sad thing has happened to me?” (Ecclus. V). This means: It is certain that God does not know sins, since he does not hasten to impose punishment in vengeance.

And again: “For he says in his heart: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned his face away, so that he may not see to the end.’” When he says, “God has forgotten” (Ps. IX), he judges the patience of the one who postpones punishment as the negligence of one who does not know, and he considers forgotten what the magnanimous steward reserves for the future.

In this way, God’s warning, as he chastises, corrects the one who fears; but the gentleness of the one who governs hardens the one who despises, so that the wicked person thinks of God that, because ignorance obscures his sight to the end, [Col. 0812C] he does not see whatever the benevolence of the one who tolerates presently refrains from punishing.

And although contempt by the one who insults is proved, God is thought to have produced the hardening. For while he suspends wrath amid ever-increasing sins, he permits the sinner to insult him.

## CHAPTER XIX  
**Against what they say: that human beings are driven by God’s will**

But if, as the heretic says, human beings are dragged into destruction by God’s will, how does a woman speak to David in the Book of Kings? “God does not wish,” she says, “the soul to perish, but he devises a means so that the rejected one may not perish completely” (II Kings XIV).

Likewise Ezekiel explains under God’s words: “Much labor was expended, [Col. 0812D] yet its great rust did not come out of it, nor was your detestable impurity removed by fire; because I wished to cleanse you, and you were not cleansed from your filth” (Ezek. XXIV).

Behold, God not only desires the human being to be saved, but sweats through great labor for his purification. Yet, in accordance with the rule of justice, the care of the healer does not by itself bring the process to completion, because it awaits the will of the one who is to be purified.

Likewise: “The bellows failed; the smelter blew in vain; for your wickednesses have not been consumed.” When you hear “bellows,” or the work of the smelter, understand that pure metal has been corrupted by an adulterating mixture and spoiled in its natural integrity.

If a human being is driven to death by his own impulse and by God’s will, why does he also speak through Ezekiel, reproving them and speaking as if in grief: “Why [Col. 0813A] will you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord. Turn back and live” (Ezek. XXXIII)?

And how does he drive to death, as you blaspheme, those whom he invites to life not only by the command of one who gives a sign, but also by the feeling of one who pleads? Likewise: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Num. XIV).

Let the one who is urged by the Lord to return recognize that returning lies within his power. “As I live, says the Lord.” So that no one may doubt indulgence, the judge confirms his clemency even by the insertion of an oath.

The will of the most benevolent author is also conveyed through the statement of the Apostle Peter: [Col. 0813B] “The Lord is not delaying his promise, but he acts patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish but all to return to repentance” (II Pet. III).

Repentance is urged upon the sinner so that justice may have a place in the granting of mercy. “But he acts patiently,” he says, regarding the human being’s correction, because he desires it impatiently but awaits it patiently.

Likewise, according to Luke: “And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘They will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation’” (Luke XIX).

Here the heretics must be constrained. If the Lord had closed the way of salvation to those destined to perish, then he had falsely wept over their destruction. But if, as is evident, he grieved over their destruction with genuine sorrow, he showed that it was not his will that was lacking in the human being, [Col. 0814A] but the human being’s consent that was lacking in relation to his will.

What is surprising if he shed tears for the salvation of the human being, when he was soon to pour out his blood?

Likewise in Matthew: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.”

Here the divine statement does two things. When it says, “How often I wanted, and you were unwilling,” it expresses the goodness of purpose in God and the freedom of choice in the human being. By saying, “Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you,” it declares that he wished to save them, while clearly presenting the reasons for which he ought to have denied them salvation.

Here, by a twofold means, the wickedness of a murderous mind is shown in the servant; in the Lord, the indulgence of a most benevolent will is revealed. [Col. 0814B]

If God wishes the human being to perish, how does the prophet Micah also say: “I will show you, O human being, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God” (Mic. VI)?

When he says, “What the Lord requires of you,” namely, “to do justice,” he would not demand a ready will to perform a good work if he had not given it. You see that, just as it belongs to God to summon and exhort, so it has been reserved for human obedience to follow.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0813]

## CHAPTER ONE  
**Against what they impiously assert: that the heart of Pharaoh was hardened by God**

[Col. 0813C]

Let us examine more carefully the meaning of Holy Scripture and confound the mind of the objector: was Pharaoh hardened by the Lord willingly or unwillingly? If willingly, you assign the guilt of hardening to Pharaoh himself; but if unwillingly, you accuse God, who hardened him, of injustice. For what justice would there be if he himself punished one whom he himself had hardened? Yet when the Lord himself addresses him and says, “Why are you unwilling to release my people? Or how long will you be unwilling to submit to me?” (Exod. VII), behold how, by divine testimonies, we recognize that Pharaoh possessed free will. In this sense the Lord says, “I will harden Pharaoh,” when I permit him to insult me through the ten plagues that, entreated by Moses, I remove. “I,” he says, “will harden Pharaoh’s heart.”

So at times, even among human beings, we adopt the force of this expression familiarly; so at times we reproach stubborn servants for our gentleness, saying: “By my patience I made you utterly bad; by my leniency I nourished your wickedness and pride; by my indulgence I made you obstinate; by my concealment I stirred up your heart to become hardened against me.” In this way, what in the Lord’s goodness is a testimony to virtue becomes a vice in the servant’s wickedness.

The divine word says: “And when Pharaoh saw that relief had been granted, he hardened his heart” (Exod. VIII). Here it is stated most plainly that the relief granted hardened Pharaoh’s heart. For the expression “he hardened his heart” is not passive but active. Do you wish to know that God acts in his divine governance on account of the hardened mind? Pharaoh himself, placed amid the ten plagues, was softened when he was struck, but when he was relieved, he became hardened. As though divine severity bent the impious man, while goodness hardened him; and, to demonstrate that he possessed free will, when God chastised him he released the people, but when God spared him he recalled them.

Observe how heavenly gentleness hardens a rebellious spirit. When milder treatment and the recent blows approach, he grows insolent. Recognize the reason for hardening and the force of his own will. The Hebrew people, whom he now commands to depart because of the affliction imposed upon him, and now forbids to depart because the plagues have been moderated, he finally urges on and compels to leave when the plagues press upon him. Therefore he is not hardened by the abundance of God’s power, but becomes a despiser through the abundance of God’s patience.

Finally, through the alternating changes of chastisement and remission, when struck he is humbled, when heard he is lifted up, when freed he insults, and when afflicted he obeys. His release of the children of Israel after the tenth plague is known; yet his final willingness testifies that he could have released them at the first. And when, amid the intervening corrections, he declares, “You are just, Lord, but I and my people are impious” (Exod. IX), he shows himself, as a witness to his own conscience, to have been corrupted not by God but by his own will. And do you presume to assert that God was harsh or unjust toward Pharaoh, when the sacrilegious man himself could not deny that God was just and merciful toward him? It follows that Christ is a cruel God, whom even the impious confess to be merciful.

Thus the dispensation of heavenly mercy acts among human beings like the infusion of rain descending upon the earth: when abundant rain falls upon cultivated soil, the tilled and subdued ground multiplies its crops; but uncultivated and raw land is filled with useless weeds and thorns. Thus one and the same rain produces two different and contrary results according to cultivation or neglect.

As we read: “For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives blessing from God. But when it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning” (Hebr. VI). Recognize the earth which, under one and the same rain, sometimes produces thorns and thistles, and sometimes brings forth fruits suitable for blessing. In the same way, while God’s mercy waits and spares, the obedient is corrected, but the unrepentant is hardened.

## CHAPTER II. That God’s foreknowledge does not violently compel human wills either toward what is right or toward what is contrary.

They misunderstand God’s foreknowledge and predestination when they assert that the cause of human actions arises from them. First, we must clearly discern what depends upon what and what proceeds from what. A person does not do whatever he is going to do because the authority of foreknowledge is going to compel him; rather, the freedom and will of the foreknown person impart to God the character of his foreknowledge. Therefore the cause of sin is not imposed upon a person by the violence of foreseeing; rather, the order of foreknowing arises from the merits that human beings will acquire.

General foreknowledge, then, which remains with God concerning the condition of the whole world, arises from power; but in foreknowing the conditions and forms of the human state, it borrows its knowledge from the observation of human action.

But in the midst of these matters you answer God and say: “O Lord, how was I able to apprehend the good, when you foreknew that I would be evil?” It is not so. One thing is what God wills, another what God permits. He wills the good and permits the evil; he foreknows both. By his just goodness he assists what is just; what is unjust he permits in accordance with freedom of will. The fact that he gives grace is from him; the fact that he foreknows offense is from you. Hence, concerning the wicked, he is continually found to prohibit what he has foreseen.

He would never command human depraved desires to be converted to better things if he knew that they could not be changed. Therefore divine providence will answer you accordingly: “O human being, I did not make you such as I foreknew you would be. I formed you good according to the law of my justice, and I warned you not to pursue evil. I foresaw you as evil because of the iniquity of your wills that would follow.” In this complaint, compulsion to sin is not discovered, but consent; the guilty party is not the author but the transgressor.

“If you look,” he says, “to the maker, O human being, you could have been good. But if you look to the foreknower, you compelled me, according to the order of your deeds, to foreknow evil concerning you.”

But you turn back and say: “Foreknowledge and predestination establish and arouse the causes of human actions and merits.” It is not so. Rather, the kind of foreknowledge is derived from the origin of the human will. If some are led by the perversity of their thoughts and suppose that their actions begin in foreknowledge, this proceeds from the vice of their own mind and from incurable obstinacy: they pretend to struggle against their passions and think that they cannot do what they do not wish to do. They call the habit of sinning the law of immutable evil.

But you still say that human works and wills begin at the nod and impulse of heavenly foreknowledge. It is not so. Recognize instead that God’s foreknowledge takes its beginning from the material of human actions. What God ought to foreknow and preordain concerning us, insofar as it pertains to the future, consists in human progress and decline.

Consider the example in which God’s foreknowledge changes in response to human action. When King Hezekiah lay ill, death was announced to him in a grievous word through the truthful prophet’s message: “Set your house in order, for tomorrow you will die” (I Reg. XIX). But he turned to weeping and set his house in order, because he humbled his soul. The prophet, indeed, recognizes a holiness tested and approved, but despair is driven away by hope. Prayer prohibits the oracle; supplication dissolves the decree; full faith surpasses the truth of the declaration. The weakness of one who weeps at the end overcomes the unavoidable cause of the announced death. Human frailty humbles itself, and the divine sentence undergoes a certain force. As it says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. XI).

He would certainly have died in every respect, unless, terrified, he had pleaded. Choose which you prefer: either confess that the fixed necessity was changed, or prove that the truth lied.

## CHAPTER III. That to foreknow is one thing and to predestine another.

The Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII). To foreknow is one thing; to predestine is another. Foreknowledge therefore foreknows what is to be done; afterward predestination describes what is to be repaid. The former foresees merits; the latter preordains rewards. Foreknowledge pertains to power; predestination to justice. Foreknowledge subsists on another’s action, but predestination on its own judgment. The former reveals the deed; the latter condemns it. The former is a witness; the latter a judge. When the former has pronounced the case, the latter then pronounces the sentence.

By foreknowledge what belongs to us is disclosed; by predestination what belongs to us is prepared. Thus, unless foreknowledge has examined the matter, predestination decrees nothing.

The power of sight performs the function of foreknowledge, and whatever presents itself to the gaze, it sees. Is a person believed to have done what he is known to have detected? Since the eyes see not what they themselves work inwardly but what is presented to them from without, if they happen to observe someone committing a crime, I do not think the crime will be judged to belong to the one who sees rather than to the one who commits it. So every offense belongs not to the guilt of the one who foreknows but to that of the one foreknown.

In the same way, God foresees before the day of a person what is to be done not by him but by the person. And just as the material existence of a thing causes the eye’s sight to contemplate it, while the eye does not cause the thing to be born in order to be seen, so God’s foreknowledge does not demand that what will follow from human merits should occur; it precedes what is going to occur.

Since it is customary in sacred writings, through any assumed comparison, to disclose the truth of what is being asserted—for we sometimes read that the kingdom of heaven is compared with a mustard seed, or with the leaven of the woman in the Gospel, or with a net cast into the sea, and with many other such things—we too, wishing to distinguish future events, gather an appropriate kind of comparison for foreknowledge.

But if foreknowledge is compulsion, then is the one who foresees the sinner himself the cause of sin? God foresees adultery: does he himself inflame the adulterer’s bones and marrow with the fires of obscene passion? God foresees a murderer: does he himself suggest bestial impulses to disordered senses? Does he himself sharpen the sword of a bloody mind for carrying out the crime? He foresees the impious person: does he himself incite the spirit of the madman to profane sacrifices? Should he therefore be believed to be the author of the things of which he is the avenger? And in these matters should he be judged to drive a captive will toward evil, when he did not even permit the devil to compel one who was unwilling?

It is the will that commits sin; it is the will that merits assistance.

But you say: “I find an instance in which grace alone operates without the participation of human will. For at Bethlehem the entire population of the innocent obtains such blessed death solely through God’s predestination.” It is not so. For the operation would perhaps then belong solely to grace if the shedding of innocent blood had not intervened. But if there was then one common cause of the innocents, why is not all infancy there saved? For every age of the other sex is excluded from the glory of that time.

If the force of predestination makes a special condition for each individual, why do all the boys born at different times of days or months obtain the same happiness? But if a common principle of election is at work in the human race, why is the entire female condition excluded from this gift?

Here, therefore, when the lot of the decree is set aside, death is inflicted upon the boys through the devil’s fury, while the most blessed death is granted for God’s honor. Predestination did not therefore consign them to death; rather, the occasion of the cause consecrated them. The slaughter of these little ones was therefore ordained not by God’s disposition but by the impiety of the enemy. God, however, who makes good use even of human evils, brings about the glory of the slain through the crime of the slayer. The inventor of evil devises contrary things, but the author of goodness arranges hostile plans for the better.

## CHAPTER IV. Against what they say: “He is merciful toward those whom he acquires, and just toward those whom he abandons,” although he appears merciful toward the wicked and just even toward the good.

If God disposes the condition of human beings, as impiety blasphemously claims, not by equity but by power, then perhaps the one who knocked is excluded, while the one who did not seek is drawn in. Thus he will not appear to have been merciful toward those who are saved, since he did not grant them the opportunity to merit mercy through their conduct; nor can he be considered just toward those who perish, if they are driven away from mercy without any personal crime.

If both are guilty by nature, justice will be endangered in the one who is chosen as unworthy without merit, and mercy in the one who is assigned to destruction without judgment concerning sin. For by what mercy is the idle person honored? By what justice is the innocent condemned? Thus, while he foolishly removes freedom from the human being, he impiously denies justice to God.

If you say that he is merciful only toward the one acquired and just only toward the one lost, you will abruptly deny both virtues in each person. For there will be no equity in the former if he chooses one who has not been approved, nor goodness in the latter if he destroys one who is undeserving.

We, however, confess that these two goods in God’s works are joined in an inseparable embrace, as we read: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psal. C). And again: “The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy” (Psal. XIV). And again: “Merciful and compassionate is the Lord, and just” (Psal. CXL).

For he is merciful even toward the lost, whom he seeks and invites when they have gone astray, and whom he patiently endures when they sin. “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. III). Thus he has filled both indiscriminately with the light of reason, clothed them with the honor of his image, and generally called them to the grace of redemption.

Was he not merciful toward the one upon whom he heaped so many gifts, whom he judged for having neglected and lost mercy? It is now a lesser task to show that toward those whom he acquires he is not only merciful but also just.

He is just, I say, toward those whom he receives when they return, whom he does not abandon when they labor, whom he makes worthy of freedom when they serve faithfully. The heretic denies that he is merciful toward the wicked because he does not believe that the opportunity for salvation was offered to those who fall into death. He does not affirm that he is just toward the good because he thinks that nothing was bestowed upon them for their humble devotion.

He is therefore merciful because he gives even the wicked an understanding of reason and an inclination toward goodness. He is just because he sets a reward before the obedient; just because he saves no one against his will.

Thus the Apostle magnificently joins the duty of labor to the gift of grace, saying: “The laboring farmer ought to receive from the fruits” (I Tim. II). Behold how, through an admirable exchange, divine and human things are joined together. Labor belongs to obedience; the fruit of labor belongs to grace.

And again: “Each one will receive his own reward according to his labor” (I Cor. II); just as he says in the Gospel: “When you have done these things, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII).

Observe that he does not exclude devotion to the work, but requires the obedience of the worker; nor does he reject the labor of servitude, but indicates humility of mind. The fault, therefore, by which you foolishly think labor ought to be avoided lies not in the work but in the heart.

I therefore labor with all my strength, but whatever I receive from heavenly generosity I will attribute to grace, not to industry. I will call it a benefit, not a price; I will testify that it is a gift, not a debt; a reward, not a repayment. Thus, when we do something as a duty, we can by no means charge it to God, because we are paying what we owe.

But do not begrudge the divine goodness if the work that I performed well with his assistance—or even the gifts I received—should be lost. By this argument they allow neither conversion from their preceding evils nor healing.

## CHAPTER V. Against what they say: “The one who perished did not so much wish to be saved as fail to be able to be saved,” according to what we read: “And they could not believe.”

In this connection, when the evangelist John records: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart’” (John XII; Isa. VI), the completed expression sounds as though a necessity of not believing had been imposed upon them against their will.

But the order of the reading makes clear in what follows that the cause or guilt of unbelief arose from them, saying: “Nevertheless, many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John XII).

Here he plainly indicates, as we also read concerning Simon, that the power of believing was granted even to unbelievers: just as the ability to believe was present in them, so the will to confess was absent. That they believe is the generosity of grace; that they do not offer the profession of faith is the wickedness of the mind. And this is fulfilled in them: “But from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. IV).

Behold how the goodness of will and faith, mixed with wickedness, was corrupted. As the Lord himself says elsewhere in the same Gospel: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John V).

You see, therefore, that just as truth is hidden when causes are suppressed, so obscurity is removed when they are made manifest. In Isaiah’s testimony, a somewhat denser mist seems to be drawn over the matter, since it asserts that those whom their own wickedness had made deaf and blind were blinded by God, lest perhaps, turning their hearts to God, they might be healed.

Therefore, setting aside for a moment what Matthew expressed more openly according to the force of the very speech—which, in accordance with the prophet’s words, strikes the reader’s hearing more severely—let us inquire more deeply why in this passage the Lord seems to be unwilling that they should be healed. The reason is that, having received a momentary conversion, they might abuse the benefits bestowed, and, once tested, neglect the wrath they had incurred and reject the remedy through relapsing weakness, like the man to whom the Lord himself says: “You have become well; do not sin, lest something worse happen to you.”

Observe how the impious man is burdened by the goodness of healing. Thus Pharaoh is found to have insulted God’s mercy: when, subdued by the plagues, he repented, converted, and humbled himself, the more often God wished to heal him, the more often he was found, after the kindness of clemency, to have become worse.

Why, I ask, does he delay healing these people? So that they would not become like the one whose seed was sown upon rocky ground—that is, one who receives the word with joy for a moment, believes for a time, and departs at the time of temptation (Matt. IV).

What does it mean to receive momentary healing? It means to believe for a time, then, at the time of temptation, to depart because of the soul’s unbelief and, at the slight heat of temptation, to fail because one’s root is weak.

Let us see whom he attempted to heal, and for whom healing was of little benefit because of the unbelief that followed. Behold that servant in the Gospel, oppressed by great debts and illnesses of the soul: the ten thousand talents that had seemed to be remitted to him are demanded, together with added torments, because of the crime of his own wickedness. Here too we must observe how acquired things are lost and benefits already bestowed are recalled.

We also read that another man, after an unclean spirit had been driven out from him, was healed for a time. The divine word says concerning him: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places, seeking rest and not finding it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it vacant, swept, and decorated” (Luke XII)—that is, emptied of virtues and filled with vanities.

“Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and entering in, they dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” Behold the one for whom the healing bestowed was of no benefit: a harmful illness, multiplied by evils, settled upon him and increased.

In another passage, the person who, after receiving knowledge of the truth—that is, after receiving the care of salvation—had regarded as polluted the blood of the covenant by which he had been sanctified, that is, by which he had been healed, is said by the Apostle’s testimony to deserve more severe punishments. Thus grace is turned into guilt unless preservation follows.

Matthew the evangelist, however, while referring the fattened heart, heavy ears, and closed eyes to human guilt, taught more openly and explained with greater clarity why they would not be healed. He says: “The heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.”

Does it not seem to you that, as though people were asking why those who see do not see and those who hear do not understand, he immediately gives an evident explanation of the causes for which they do not see or understand? It is because they did not wish to hear and see—that is, to understand and obey.

“For,” he says, “not all obey the Gospel”; and again: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted me.” As the Lord himself also says: “I nourished and exalted children, but they despised me.” And again: “Because they abandoned the Lord, the fountain of living waters.”

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Jews saw this,” he says, “they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was spoken by Paul, blaspheming the way of the Lord” (Acts XIII). And again: “Paul,” he says, “was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. But when they contradicted and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said: ‘Your blood be upon your own head; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles’” (Acts XVIII). “When they contradicted,” he says, “and blasphemed.”

See how the physician offers remedies while the sick person refuses them. Blessed Stephen also rebukes their hardness with equal authority, saying: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII).

Behold why they cannot see: because they resist the Holy Spirit and, by closing their eyes of their own accord, exclude the light of truth from themselves.

Therefore, what follows in the Gospel—“lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart; and be converted, and I should heal them” (John XII)—means that the vice of their hardened heart and the punishment of sin prevent them from being converted and healed. “Lest,” he says, “they be converted and I heal them.” Here he does not say that he denies healing to those who wish it; rather, he declares that he does not wish—or, in other words, that he ought not—to heal those who contradict.

The physician’s goodness is most ready to provide a remedy, but the sick person’s intemperance resists it. For whoever thinks that the passage must be understood to mean that he did not wish to heal them acquits the human being and condemns the author.

No one, therefore, is excluded from God’s benefits without first being judged for having neglected those benefits.

## CHAPTER VI. What is meant by the statement: “For when they had not yet done anything good or evil.”

They attempt to confine the Apostle’s meaning within the narrow limits of a Gentile decree, in the passage that says: “This is the word of promise: ‘At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.’ And not only this, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father. For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from the one who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. IX; Mal. I).

The impiety of the Gentile persuasion wants these words to be understood as meaning that God, without any examination by a moderator between evil and good, without the order of one who governs but by the right of one who dominates, makes one worthy of affection and another worthy of hatred; that he receives one by preference and excludes the other by command. And among two lost persons, no consideration is given to labor or devotion: one is chosen without reason and without any service rendered; the other is condemned without discrimination. Thus, since neither merit nor offense exists in either of them, the cause of future judgment is completely removed.

But if such an unworthy confusion of things is alien even to the understanding of the human mind, let us inquire more carefully what is fitting for the divine mind. The Apostle, established as a teacher of the Jews and the Gentiles and discussing justice between two peoples, says: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV). In the elder, the arrogance of the Jews is rejected; in the younger, the faith of the Gentiles is chosen.

He therefore draws clouds of ignorance over himself who does not accommodate himself to the Holy Scriptures with a responsive understanding, but violently and presumptuously attempts to draw and apply the Holy Scriptures to his own interpretation. He persuades himself of something according to his own capacity while disregarding what precedes and follows, although the Apostle never intended to speak that way.

If you return to the beginning of the very chapter under discussion, you will avoid every ambiguity without difficulty. If the teacher of the Gentiles had begun to discuss the origin of human beings and had said that the entire course of a person’s life was determined by his origin and entrusted more to necessity than to free will—because the Lord of all, by a violent exercise of power, had decreed to leave some to destruction and choose others for salvation—then perhaps an impious persuasion could assert this interpretation as though it were running along the lines of the text.

But since the Apostle, by recalling examples from a deeper past, weaves together God’s promises and the calling of the Gentiles, and strives in every way to suppress the presumption of the Jews, who wickedly puffed themselves up over the works of the Law, he does not establish a fatal decree in the origin of the elders, Ishmael or Esau. Rather, in the blessing of Isaac and Jacob he displays the election of the younger people, and therefore placed the younger before the elder not as a manifestation of God’s power but because of justice.

For he foreknew the impiety of the Jews in the same way as the obedience of the Gentiles. Therefore, since he says, “For when they had not yet done anything good or evil, it was said—not from works but from the one who calls—‘The elder shall serve the younger,’” it is clear that the saying came from the one who calls, but was not spoken to compel or repel them; it was spoken concerning those who would believe and those who would not believe. Thus, with divine justice remaining constant, it belongs to human will either to reject or to observe the commandments.

When, therefore, you hear, “It was said by the one who calls,” understand that he invites, not compels.

Likewise, when he says, “not from works,” he asserts that what was operative in them was not the works of the Law—for the Law had not yet come—but the gifts of divine mercy and generosity that existed even before the Law.

“Not from works,” he says. You hear that the works of the Law are being overthrown, and for that reason, with foolish understanding, you also believe that those living under the law of grace can be saved without the works of grace, while others, even with works, are excluded from the gate of salvation by a natural bond and a fatal law.

“Jacob I loved, Esau I hated.” How, according to the interpreter of this perverse understanding, is a heavenly sentence exercised here concerning those not yet born? One who has not yet been born can be neither guilty nor beloved; one not yet brought into the light earns nothing. But just as their manner of life was still reserved for the future, so the foreknower’s future displeasure and the future election are foretold.

For just as divine providence knows how to judge deeds already performed, so it knows how to prejudge deeds that are still to be performed. Let no one therefore suppose that a necessity of different merits was fixed for the brothers before they were born, since the prophet Malachi mentions them only after the course of their life had been completed and pronounces a judgment on their past condition with evident equity:

“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

What is surprising if justice loves innocence and rejects iniquity, when even future deeds are already present to it?

But the fact that the younger is placed before the elder according to the Law, and that Jacob is loved while his brother is disregarded, gives rise to obscurity for those who are somewhat slower to understand. They think that the testimony of love or hatred was pronounced concerning brothers not yet born, while the evident causes for which one displeased and the other pleased are suppressed.

In these two figures, therefore, the laws of nature are not imposed upon human beings; rather, the decrees of justice concerning the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief of the Jews are narrated. For in this passage, according to the letter, the individual persons of the brothers are not specifically described; rather, the causes and mysteries of the matter are set forth, when the Lord says: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. XXV).

If the discussion concerned a law predetermined by origin, why would it have been necessary to insert the ages of the elder and the younger, which had nothing to do with the matter, unless because in the lineage of the Jews, whenever the two peoples are called, the younger is always preferred to the elder?

Yet amid this difference between the two groups, many are chosen even from the rejected Jews, and many are rejected from the chosen Gentiles, so that you may understand that in both peoples the just Judge observes not decrees but merits.

But you say: “Although they had not yet done anything good or evil, they were already assigned to predetermined roles.”

What is surprising if he foreshadowed the outcome of those whose actions he foreknew? Thus, just as it was clear that they would arrange the course of their lives according to their own will, so they are foreknown according to God’s power and preordained according to justice. All this is foretold concerning them; it is not predetermined for them.

In Jacob, therefore, the faithful people are described; in Esau, the unbelieving people are represented. Concerning both, he says:

“What then shall we say? The Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that is from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (Rom. IX).

When he says, “not from works,” do you see that the works of the Law are overthrown, and that obedience opened the way to mercy for the Gentiles, while preceding iniquity and unbelief prepared an offense for the Jews?

“Not from works,” he says, “but from the one who calls.” He does not say that they were empty of their own works; he denies that they were saved by the works of the Law.

Far be it from us to think that the condemnation of origin is being proposed here, where the kindness of the one who calls and the humility of the one who obeys are praised, and where a general teaching impresses upon us the riches of faith and conveys the light of belief. Let not the assertion of iniquity, which spoke of part of the human race as condemned in its very creation, insert itself into this passage.
