The reasons why God loved Jacob and hated Esau are clearly expressed in the history of Genesis, so that you may understand that it was divinely pronounced that Esau should be considered worthy of God’s hatred and Jacob of his love neither without an examination of works nor without a manifest reason.

The evident causes that wholly affirm the rightness of the Lord’s judgment appeared plainly in Jacob’s life, just as it is said to Cain: “Its desire shall be toward you, and you shall rule over it” (Gen. IV).

He did not place sin above the human being under this law of his ordering; rather, he subjected it. Behold the most merciful governor, desiring his creation to be noble even after its fall: although he allowed the human will to experience every passion and desire, he commanded it not to be their servant but their master. He placed the seducer’s friendship or rejection in the human being’s hand and assigned judgment over it to him.

He seems to have permitted the desire for either work to the person’s own choice, but for this purpose: so that the glory of the good might arise from the permission of evil.

“But its desire shall be toward you, and you shall rule over it.” He is not confined by any necessity of sinning when it is entrusted to his discretion to rule over sin by superior freedom. Yet a degenerate mind, which by God’s gift can gain victory over sin, prefers, in offense against God, to be sin’s servant.

Since these things are so, after the transgression of the first human being there followed not the death of free will but weakness; not impossibility but difficulty in the labor undertaken.

Abel too merited pleasing the divine gaze through the good implanted generally by God—that is, through the affection of his own will. This man, whose perfection of blameless life gave him the surname “righteous,” by whose instruction could he have become a follower of justice, unless the law inscribed in his inward parts had taught him?

Or how would he have known to choose sacrifices pleasing to God, to be consumed by heavenly fire, from the fats and firstfruits, unless faith—which had made him a lover of virtues—had inspired him? As we read: “By faith Abel offered a greater sacrifice than Cain, God bearing witness to his gifts” (Hebr. XI).

He could by no means have obtained this unless the servant’s obedience had accompanied the Lord’s gift. And do you judge that he possessed nothing of his own by God’s ordering, when God himself bears witness to his devotion?

You see that the goodness of belief is not a new privilege but an ancient one, and that, from the very beginnings of the world as it came together, the human mind was endowed by the supreme Creator with faith as well as understanding and reason.

Thus, even then, he gave the soul knowledge of himself, when he graciously entrusted his image to it.

## CHAPTER VII. In whose image and likeness the first human being was created.

But you say: “Why do you join the image of God to freedom of the will, when that exalted Creator and future Redeemer, in the ages to come, made man more according to that image which he was to assume from a human being through a virgin?” This opinion is advanced by many, but is stripped of all reason, because the beginnings of an earlier reality can in no way assume the image of one much later. Or how could the one who was first being created receive the likeness of one not yet created?

Among these alternatives, it is easier to believe that the first Adam, in accordance with the order and sequence of time, transmitted his image to the second Adam. [Col. 0824C] It could not possibly be that the one who was fashioned so many ages earlier should be called the image of a substance not yet existing; nor could it be proved a sensible assertion that, as they say, the person of the most ancient progenitor preceded the author of the likeness who was to be born from a virgin.

Furthermore, that view would greatly diminish the dignity of humanity’s first innocence, if the immaculate man had been fashioned as the model of one who was going to heal the stains of those destined to sin—so that, when transgression did not yet exist, the form of the future mediator would already bear the guilt of transgression. It therefore did not follow that he was perfected and completed according to the image of the one through whom what had been lost necessarily had to be restored. Otherwise, under the name of the coming physician, would not ruin have seemed to be foretold at the very moment [Col. 0824D] of a happy beginning—that is, the ruin of the one who was to be supplanted?

It is therefore more consistent with reason that, in man—who receives from God, in the very likeness itself, a reality belonging to grace rather than to nature—this image should rather be called that which he receives from the earlier and higher one. And the likeness should be judged to have been bestowed from the truth more fully, although a father rightly shares that truth with his natural son.

Next, we must observe more carefully that our Lord Jesus Christ, at the first stage, conferred better things from what was his own; but at the second, he assumed worse things from what was ours. Therefore, when he fashioned us from nothing, the Maker added his own image; but when he restored us after we had been lost, the Restorer assumed the form of a servant, as the Apostle says: “Taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness [Col. 0825A] of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II).

But if we were fashioned according to that outward appearance of the human being in whose members are sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, what honor or grace will there be in our sharing that image which we know to be, for the most part, common to us with the beast?

Great, therefore, is the error of those who think that the first man was composed by the incorporeal Trinity according to the one who was to be taken from Mary. For neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was going to be clothed in a garment of flesh and a human appearance, so that he might arrange the features and fashion the limbs of the first man according to the appearance and form of that supposed image of his, and say: “Let us make man according to the image and likeness which we are going to assume from the Virgin.”

Consequently, whatever the Trinity bestows collectively upon man is derived from the likeness of the Godhead. [Col. 0825B] Nor could the first man be said to have received the image of the second Adam even if the Son of God alone had created man. But since the united Trinity says, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. VIII), mingling the singular with the plural and the plural with the singular, and again, “And God made man according to his likeness; according to the image of God he made him,” how often do you read that man was created according to the image of God? And by what authority do you presume to assert, contrary to the divine utterances, that he was composed according to the form of a servant?

Since, then, this image is bestowed by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, without doubt the one Godhead of the three persons grants the first man the dignity of its image.

Since these things are so, you will not doubt that a diminished freedom of his own will exists in man [Col. 0825C] if you examine the first grace with which he was honored by God. He is called the image of God because truth, in gracious and dignified fashion, implanted righteousness in him; reason, wisdom; and eternity, immortality.

It belongs to the image of God that he understands, that he has a right judgment, and that by discriminating judgment he distinguishes between evil and good. And since God’s attributes are goodness, mercy, patience, and justice, the more just and patient someone is found to be, the more he is proved to resemble God. This likeness is possessed not in facial features but in virtues.

Therefore God is called subtle, simple, and sincere. He is simple because nothing extraneous is added to him, nothing is conferred upon him from elsewhere; rather, in him there are virtue, essence, and substance. [Col. 0825D] Thus God is what he possesses; but man does not possess these gifts unless he has received them.

Since, then, God is just and justice, merciful and mercy, devout and devotion, man can be just but cannot be justice; he can be merciful but cannot be mercy; he can be devout but cannot be devotion, because he does not possess these things naturally but receives them as gifts.

By way of example, God is gold, whereas man may appear to be a gilded vessel. In man there is grace, while in God there is nature; in man there is something created, while in God it is shown to be unbegotten. For this reason, in accordance with this principle, man’s condition appears to be twofold: these qualities are implanted in him in such a way that they are often separated from him and taken away.

Those who think that righteousness and the other virtues are the substance [Col. 0826A] of the soul are therefore mistaken. Without these virtues, the soul can nevertheless subsist, to some extent, by the vital strength of its own nature; without them, even the devil is recognized to remain in his own nature. For they are plainly shown to be added qualities, since they are stripped away when guilt takes possession.

Only free will and immortality—which is also implanted in the wicked—are not taken away, although the dignity and blessedness of immortality can be removed. Thus, insofar as freedom of will and immortality are concerned, even the wicked can possess the image of God, though discolored in itself and by itself; but they cannot possess the likeness unless they are good.

Since these things are so, and since human beings adorned with the image and likeness of God deserved to be called angels or sons of God, we must briefly touch upon a few further examples showing how many entered the vestibules of salvation before the written law, instructed by the law of nature—which, as we have said, is the first grace of God [Col. 0826B]—and were to be led through Christ to the very inner chambers of life.

But even here, Abel—made the counterpart of his brother in character and merits, and therefore rejecting his brother’s profane practices—could have chosen better things only if understanding and reason had directed him along the right path. Under their guidance he transmitted holy traditions and praiseworthy disciplines as an inherited gift to later generations, so that they might be reckoned by the name of angels or sons of God throughout many ages.

Who could doubt that innumerable families pleasing to God, endowed with freedom of will, were saved from among the nations, of whom only a very few, but illustrious and perfect ones, are presented in the sacred writings for the enlightenment of the world?

How could Enoch have walked with God or pleased God unless the law infused into his inmost being [Col. 0826C] had illuminated him by a hidden instruction, so that, possessing no taste for anything earthly, he was wondrously taken from the earth while God assumed him? Since by the merit of faith he surpassed the others at the beginning of that age, he demonstrates that faith itself had been handed down to him together with the law of nature.

As we read: “By faith Enoch was transferred, so that he would not see death. For before his transfer he received the testimony that he had pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God. Whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is the rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. XI).

If God did not seek voluntary devotion and intention, he would not grant a reward to man; nor would he have first granted him something by which he could please God. When the text says, “For before his transfer he received the testimony that he had pleased God,” there is no doubt [Col. 0826D] that his life was examined first and that the choice followed afterward.

The error introduced by the doctrine of predestination will easily be avoided if the preceding cause is investigated. God is “the rewarder of those who seek him,” while great guilt does not fail to attach to the one who does not seek him, because God gave him the means by which he could seek him.

What kind and how great a law man received from God at his first creation was also declared by the perfect righteousness of Noah, because he cultivated within himself, through particular zeal for virtue, the general gifts of faith. In his time, when all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, condemnation would not have followed unless transgression had first proceeded from human choice.

Just as guilt therefore deserves punishment, so guilt testifies to punishment, which is inflicted in accordance with the equity of the Ruler. When the divine word [Col. 0827A] says, “All flesh had corrupted its way” (Gen. VI), it attributes the iniquities of that age not to an imposed decree but to voluntary depravity.

Without doubt, then, the heavenly dispensation would not have given the written law unless transgression, advancing as far as the wrath of the Flood, had violated the law of nature. Therefore this law of Moses, which is thought to be the first, is already the second.

That the work of the natural law was written in human hearts is also discussed by the most blessed bishop Augustine in a learned discourse, as follows:

“Both run together in this channel and torrent of the human race: the evil drawn from the parent, and the good bestowed by the Creator. Moreover, no one’s fault is so contrary to nature that it erases even the last traces of nature. Hence it is that even the impious conceive thoughts of eternal things, establish laws that are to be proclaimed even in the present age, and rightly censure many things in human conduct and rightly praise them in human conduct. [Col. 0827B] By what rules do they judge these matters, if not by natural ones? In those rules they see how each person ought to live, even if they themselves do not live in the same way.”

The Apostle also clearly confirms this in his Letter to the Romans, saying:

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest among them. For God has manifested it to them: his invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, as are his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning [Col. 0827C], and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. I).

If the will had not departed from the law of God, ungodliness would not have felt the wrath of God. And when the Apostle says, “Because what can be known of God is manifest among them; for God has manifested it to them,” he clearly explains that, through an inward instruction inscribed on the pages of the mind, knowledge of God ought to have been manifest to them, and that the Creator could have been known through the magnificence of creation.

They would not have been without excuse before God unless they had received an opportunity to perceive the truth both externally and internally, as the Apostle adds: “For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God [Col. 0827D].”

He therefore condemns the impious even for the understanding they abused, and accuses their unrighteousness of contempt for the Godhead. What else did the vast overflow of the famous Flood assert but that the human race had been condemned through the guilt of its own will?

Thus Noah’s perfect righteousness both exposed and condemned the voluntary errors of that age, as we read:

“By faith Noah, having received a revelation concerning things not yet seen, in reverent fear prepared an ark for the salvation of his household; through it he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that is according to faith” (Heb. XI).

Why did he condemn the world? Because the wickedness of the world neglected to follow the example of righteousness. Thus he accuses the guilt of disobedience, and he pleased God through obedience; yet he also demonstrates that another could likewise [Col. 0828A] have pleased him through devotion.

Certainly, no decree of fate had a place in that age. For because universal transgression had preceded, universal condemnation followed. How can you say that one is taken and another left? See how, except for the household of the righteous man, the whole world is destroyed under the pressure of iniquity. The special decree you assert is therefore excluded by a general judgment. And the one who is condemned for wickedness is thereby proved to have been able to do good.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the claim that they say the law of nature perished in the first man and did not remain operative through his descendants until the coming of the Savior

But you say that natural goods ought not to be mentioned, because it is clear that before Christ’s coming the nations did not in any way belong to salvation. [Col. 0828B] Whoever denies that nature should be praised for its goods certainly does not know that the very author of nature is the author of grace. Whoever most foolishly denies this denies the goodness of nature apart from God’s creative work, and instead accepts either the divinity he imagines to exist or fate.

But since the one who is himself the Creator is also the Restorer, one and the same person is celebrated in the proclamation of both works. I therefore rightly assert the gift of both realities, because I know that I owe to him that I was born, just as I owe to him that I was reborn.

For this reason I will not deny the gifts of the Creator merely because I lost them; but neither will I equate the earlier gifts with the later ones, because I received them restored in many ways for the better. I will exalt the benefits of the Creator, but I will place those of the Redeemer immeasurably above them.

Nor will I seem rash if I profess that at certain points in the ordering [Col. 0828C] of our lives—not indeed at the beginnings of our life, but only in its intermediate stages—our will, by God’s ordering, precedes special graces and graces arising from an additional generosity.

Let us ask the sacred writings whether this is so. We read in the Gospel that the Lord says: “What do you want me to do for you?” and again: “Do you want to become well?” You see that the gift of salvation is not bestowed until the desire of the will has first been questioned.

Likewise, when one comes to baptism, the will of the person approaching is first examined, so that the grace of the one regenerating may follow. And in the case of the centurion Cornelius, because his will preceded grace, grace also preceded regeneration.

Here, as I think, there is no presumption, since I continually maintain that I owe even this very will to God—especially since, in all its movements [Col. 0828D], I refer it to the work of grace, whether to the beginnings of its initiation or to the final stages of its completion.

Abraham, too, proceeding from the midst of pagan society, is not only called to salvation together with his entire household, but is also made, by the testimony of Truth itself, the father of many nations. It is God’s goodness that calls him; it is his own will that makes him obey promptly.

Job likewise could not have resisted the enemy pressing upon him without freedom of spirit; yet he joins greatness of heart to the help of his protector. Thus the justice of the one who rewards reveals the devotion of the one who struggles. In spiritual warfare, the conflict appears to belong to human labor, just as the outcome is referred to God.

The fact that Job’s friends also came from the nations, before the law had been promulgated, is shown by this: while Job [Col. 0829A] is said, at the Lord’s command, to have prayed for them and to have been heard, salvation is unquestionably granted even to those who were still living among the nations.

Rahab, too, belonged so fully to a pagan nation that she prefigured the Church to be gathered from the nations. She is received into salvation together with her entire household, with faith actively at work. Of her we read: “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers.”

Why are those who were outside the law accused of unbelief, if not because they did not wish to keep the law of nature, to which faith is joined? Why is unbelief charged against them, if not because the ability to believe was readily available? The principle of free will therefore makes the believer receive a reward and the unbeliever be condemned.

We read in the book of Genesis: “For the sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed.” The Lord foretells that the children of Israel will be humbled in the land [Col. 0829B] of Egypt and will be led out from there through signs and miracles to destroy the impious nations and receive the promised settlements. But he testifies that this cannot happen before the nations whom he was going to hand over to them, by the increasing magnitude of their sins, make room through their deserved scourges and, by the weight of their completed [Col. 0829C] iniquity, compel the hand of extreme affliction to be stretched out against them.

Where an increase of sins is awaited, the perversity of the will is being indicted. He who imposes a sentence in accordance with justice upon a pagan absolved from the law of commandments proves that the law of nature had been trampled underfoot; at the same time, the longsuffering of the one who delays is shown to reveal the justice of the one who condemns.

No one postpones punishment out of moderation if he has decided to punish by predestination. “The sins of the Amorites,” he says, “have not yet been completed.” When the cause of destruction is identified with the fullness of sins, suspicion of a predetermined necessity is removed.

Recognize here the power of divine patience. The people of Israel, who were to be liberated and the impious nations overthrown, are meanwhile held in slavery until the iniquity of the nations is completed. The anger of judgment brings vengeance for as long as the measure of sin grows into a heap, so that, with goodness and severity operating together at one and the same time, the son may be released on one side and the enemy crushed on the other.

## CHAPTER IX. Against the claim that they say the knowledge of the one God was not granted to the nations before the time of grace

Those who say that the nations could not possess knowledge of the one God before the Savior’s coming [Col. 0829D] are wallowing in a great abyss of ignorance. The Apostle asserts that the Maker of the world could have been known through the magnificence of his creation, saying:

“What can be known of God is manifest among them; for his invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, as are his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Rom. I).

How can you call excusable those who were strangers to heavenly gifts, when God declares them inexcusable precisely because they are proved to have abused what they received, and because they could easily have known the sublimity of the Maker if they had questioned his work?

It is far from all reason and piety to think that a human being was only recently instructed to know God, when the whole world, from the beginning of things, bears witness to him. For this reason [Col. 0830A] the Apostle says in the same Letter: “For when the nations, which do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law” (Rom. II).

Let no one therefore believe that the person who grasped what he naturally possesses—having received it, certainly, at the creation of the first man—was imbued with the law of God by some recent instruction.

“They exchanged,” the Apostle says, “the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of serpents” (Rom. I). While foolishly venerating what was base and unworthy, they confessed in every way that they ought to have worshiped beings more worthy of worship.

And while he worshiped wood and stone, he had at hand the capacity to understand that he should worship the Creator of earthly and heavenly things. For when a human being proves that something ought to be worshiped, the very understanding of worship reveals the crime against the Creator. [Col. 0830B]

How, then, did he possess the standard of religion? He would undoubtedly have found God if he had wished to apply the affection of seeking, as the Lord says: “Seek, and you will find.” For when the human mind opens its eyes to see, the light it desires immediately presents itself to the one who seeks it.

Thus the law implanted within taught reverence; [Col. 0830C] but through negligence and stubbornness it did not deserve to find the truth. And therefore, while humanity prostrated the heavenly creation before dead images and lifeless representations, it inflicted an injury not only upon the Maker but also upon itself as a created work. Forgetful of its own nobility, it afflicted itself with shameful insults and, from the error itself, received the punishment of error, as the Apostle says: “Receiving in themselves the recompense that was due for their error. And since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind” (Rom. V).

This rebellious mind was corrupted willingly; it was not forcibly taken away. “Since,” he says, “they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind.” The one who is abandoned because of preceding causes is not oppressed by fate but rejected by judgment.

And if you ask where sin came from among unlearned nations in that inborn savagery, where did it come from except through the movement of the spirit and the consent of the mind? In the end, cattle and dumb animals are entirely free from sin because they do not know discrimination and are ignorant of reason.

You make man worse than the beast. Why do you leave him sin when you take away his freedom of choice? Or, if you subject him to sin, do not deprive him of judgment. Let unrighteousness therefore not deceive itself: the Knower of hidden things knows what he gave to man in secret.

For this reason, whenever someone is reproved and condemned by him [Col. 0830D] for an evil deed, he is proved to have been able to do good. Great, therefore, is the power of the spirit in both directions: it is established upon honesty and is confounded upon dishonesty.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “His eyelids examine the children of men; the Lord examines the righteous and the impious” (Ps. X). Why does the Judge question me about sin, if what I do wrong is determined by his own decree?

Thus the one who individually fashioned human hearts, the secret examiner, questions the ways of human beings and the merits of their consciences. But if you examine yourself as well, whenever you wished to turn toward the left, did not a trembling conscience warn you lest you sin? Did not a sorrowful thought chastise you like a hidden censor?

Thus human beings cannot be hidden [Col. 0831A] from themselves, since conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even defend one another. If amid all this you ask where freedom of will is placed, where the human will is established, where else is it to be found but in understanding, reason, and wisdom?

Since these things are so, you will first have to deny wisdom to man and take away reason before you can deprive him of free will.

Therefore, whenever the soul meditates upon some offense as a captive within its own dwelling, the hidden recesses of its thoughts cry out against it and its inward faculties forbid it; but the habit of sinning withdraws the strength to resist.

Yet you turn back and say that the wicked, and those who are being dragged toward destruction, did not receive freedom of choice. First, we must know that freedom of choice is equipped [Col. 0831B] for a twofold service: it is ready now for salvation, now for its own destruction.

But you object that freedom of the will belongs only to those being liberated and to those established in the benefit of redemption. That is not so. [Col. 0831C] Liberation belongs to the gift of grace and to the purpose of the consenting person’s life; freedom of choice, however, is not a matter of an additional generosity but of nature.

To those who seek it, liberation is either granted or preserved; even to those who do not seek it, freedom is bestowed. Liberation is ministered to those being reborn, while freedom is given to those being born.

Freedom belongs solely to the operation of God; liberation also belongs to the servitude of the subjected human being. Liberation is confirmed in the good, while freedom is implanted even in the wicked. Liberation belongs to those who have acquired it and persevere, while freedom is available even to the lost. Liberation belongs to the Creator; freedom also belongs to the obedient. Liberation belongs to power; freedom belongs to mercy. Liberation belongs to origin and descent; freedom belongs to gift and virtue.

## CHAPTER X. That the nations possessed knowledge of God naturally
Filled with the Holy Spirit, the prophet Daniel, knowing that God had placed the desire for good or evil within the human mind, addresses Nebuchadnezzar as follows: “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor” (Dan. 4). “Redeem your sins,” he says, “by almsgiving.” Whatever can be redeemed cannot be regarded as predetermined. Therefore the one to whom a remedy is recommended is not excluded from healing. Nor is freedom of choice denied to the one whose consent is required. He has not lost the function of a free mind who is shown to have been able to accept counsel. Nor is he found alienated from salvation to whom the [Col. 0831D] means of salvation is offered. And to the one to whom the prophet offers an opportunity for obtaining pardon, he asserts that the power of willing is present.

Likewise, consider the case of the pagan Belshazzar, whom the prophet reproves, saying: “You praised the gods of silver, and gold, and wood, and stone, but the God in whose hand is your breath you did not praise” (Dan. 5). You see that this foreigner could both know God and praise him, but did not wish to do so. The prophet therefore mentioned that human beings possess both knowledge of God and his worship, because he knew that the law of nature operates indiscriminately within the understanding of every human being.

For this reason, when Daniel had revealed the power of the dream to the aforementioned king Nebuchadnezzar, the profane man nevertheless showed that he did not ignore God, saying: “Truly your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings.” And [Col. 0832A] who taught Darius to think and speak in this way about God, unless it was the force of reason and of the law, when Daniel taught that God could be appeased by conversion? Hence he recognized that God became angry conditionally.

For that great city did not come to its senses through Jonah’s instruction, nor did it receive from his admonitions an understanding of the salvation it should seek. The prophet did not teach the people but terrified them; he did not promise mercy but announced an unchangeable sentence. Nevertheless, that city, as it is written, “believed against hope in hope” (Rom. 4), and in a certain way promised itself remedies that had been forbidden, remedies that would greatly please God even if it had sought what had been promised.

These remedies are sometimes withheld by the Lord so that, once obtained with greater violence, they may be preserved more firmly. At the same time, by placing difficulty in the way of attainment, while generosity is concealed, faith is tested, [Col. 0832B] eagerness is exercised, affection is revealed, and all this is brought about by the inner fire that God has implanted in the human being and that the human being nourishes with God’s grace.

That people therefore showed that, by the very ordering of creation, God had placed within the human being those things that pertain to human salvation, and that even before the gifts of the Redeemer, the Creator’s gifts had always been active in rational creation: foreknown by the supreme Creator through nature, but to be confirmed through grace. Through grace, I say, in whose time the salvation of past ages was to be brought to completion, since neither the law, nor written revelation, nor nature brought anything to perfection.

Thus the Lord’s voice, full of clemency and goodness, was plainly manifested to the Ninevites, saying: “Suddenly I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to uproot, destroy, and eradicate it. If that nation [Col. 0832C] repents of its sin, I too shall repent of the evil that I have spoken of doing to it” (Jer. 18). The merciful heavenly Judge desires, by a pious “falsehood,” to alter the decrees of his counsel, if the guilty person hastens to apply medicine to his sin. Against his will he imposes upon the human being the burden of condemnation, when he points out the remedy of satisfaction and awaits the dutiful service of persistent obedience.

Therefore that perfect providence, which delights in the exercise of virtues in this age, judged it most orderly and most worthy of its wisdom that the human being, created for the dignity of the sacred image, should first be tested here by struggles and conditions, but there be perfected by gifts and recompense. Thus, when the servant has displayed obedience through labor, the Lord may show justice in rewarding him; and when human weakness has offered humble devotion, divine power [Col. 0832D] may exercise its ineffable generosity.

We must therefore labor continually, but not depart from grace, and we must say: “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. 69). The very word “help” requires the laborer’s activity. The language of help therefore indicates two persons: the one who works and the one who works with him; the one who asks and the one who promises; the one who knocks and the one who opens; the one who seeks and the one who rewards.

This alone is ours: that, since we are not capable of acting because of our weakness, we may at least please God by our persistence in seeking and knocking. Where would the diligence of the merciful God be, if a person who is unworthy deserves nothing, and idle desires approach him for this purpose? Therefore, unless an unwearied zeal for obedience takes precedence, justice will have no place [Col. 0833A] to remain.

For this reason divine speech depicts the farmer as sustained by the hope of his labor, saying: “Behold, the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the earth, until he receives the early and the late [fruit]” (Jas. 5). What is the early fruit? What is the late fruit?

The early fruits are those that we acquire through the wages of our present service. The late fruits are those that we shall receive after our service has been completed, in the recompense of that age. The early fruits are faith and sincerity of heart, goodwill, bodily self-control, contempt for evil, desire for good, the tranquility of gentleness, and purity of chastity. The late fruits are the acquisition of immortal things, the inheritance of heavenly things, and possession of eternal things.

Of these it is said: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who [Col. 0833B] love him” (1 Cor. 2). Of these it is said through the apostles and martyrs: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

The early fruits therefore consist in virtues; the late fruits in the rewarding of virtues. The early fruits are those which works obtain here through the commandments; the late fruits are those which desires will attain there through rewards.

How greatly, then, God delights in someone becoming a wall—that is, a very strong barrier of supplication against God’s offense—is shown by the man of whom we read: “For a blameless man hastened to pray for the people, bringing forward the shield of his service; he stood against the wrath and brought necessity to an end” (Wis. 18). “He who would stand,” he says, “opposed before me, so that I might not destroy it” (Ezek. 22). This shows how God’s anger is turned aside: in a certain sense, once appeased, [Col. 0833C] he becomes angry.

In view of these things, whoever says that the all-powerful and most just Creator made human beings in such a way that one is assigned to the left without personal guilt, solely by the impulse of foreknowledge, while another is drawn to the right without his merits being examined, is plainly found to assert that the arrangements of both Maker and Judge are disorderly or unjust.

But here let the attentive hearer place before the supreme Author, when he was preparing to fashion the human being—before the supreme Author, I say, for the work and counsel of making humanity—four virtues standing at his side. Which four? Power, goodness, wisdom, and justice.

Consider which of these four you presume to say was lacking in God. Therefore, so that the understanding may gather the matter more clearly, let each of these virtues, as if delivering its own discourse and address, [Col. 0833D] speak in turn.

Power says:

“Let us, after the kingdom of heaven, create a wondrous creature in the second rank, so that in the possession of our dominion, those things which are first may not also appear to be the last. Let us complete this beautiful structure of the world, so that within it we may make the human being and set him over it, through whom the world may be ordered, possessed, and adorned.”

Goodness says:

“It is not right that heavenly beings alone should enjoy our benefits. Let us also make a human being on earth, toward whom we may exercise the abundance of our grace; toward whom we may extend the gifts of our goodwill; into whom we may pour out the riches of our innate benevolence.”

Wisdom says:

“Let us not merely make him, but also honor him with the sense of reason and discernment; let us fill him with the light of prudence; let us make him simple, [Col. 0834A] and make him shrewd. Simple, so that the crafty may not inflict evil; shrewd, so that the unwary may not fall into it. Let us implant in him affection for good and understanding of evil, and, in accordance with our governance, let us permit him to be in the hand of his own counsel and in the freedom of his own judgment.”

Meanwhile Wisdom, which also possesses foreknowledge, deliberates with itself:

“What shall we do, since we leave him free under his own choice? We foresee that he will pass along the byways of sin, and we perceive in advance that he will turn the gifts of the precious creation into instruments of wickedness. Therefore, if we want our work in him to be everlasting, let us remove sin from his power.”

Justice says:

“That is not so. It is not compatible with our laws that the one who ought to be tested by opposites should not be able to be known through his own strength. It is not compatible, I say, with our laws that we should deny the one whom we wish to glorify [Col. 0834B] even through his own service the material and cause of glory; that, when we desire to reward him by sheer grace, we should make him merit nothing through his own labor.

“Rather, let these allied and kindred virtues each exercise themselves in him and perform their respective parts. It belongs to power to create him sublime among all visible things, especially among the enemies among whom he will dwell; to wisdom, to order him prudently; to goodness, to assist him as he struggles; and to justice, to crown him when he conquers.

“Let us therefore make such a human being, for his own usefulness and for the dignity of our work, whom necessity will not draw to the right-hand side, but will;  one who understands evil through reason and accomplishes good through virtue. Let us make one whose goodness belongs to nature, but whose wickedness lies outside nature; who has good in his will and evil in his power; who naturally [Col. 0834C] wills good but can actually do evil; who voluntarily keeps our commandments and cannot be exposed to danger against his will; one whose first occasion for praise is that he both can sin and does not wish to sin.

“It is enough that we have already made among the four-footed and irrational creatures, which are to be subjected to the human being, an animal that, since it is not liable to guilt, cannot possess the fruit of justice. But this being, to whom we are to entrust the dignity of our image, must not be like an animal.

“Let us ask those creatures that we formed without knowledge of sin and without understanding of reason, without any honor of prudence. Will the simplicity of a sheep benefit it, or the fertility of a tree? We cannot confer the palm of praise upon our human being if we want nature to serve necessity.

“Let us therefore order him, subject in condition, free in discernment, and perfected in reason, [Col. 0834D] under an authority that is permitted and a law that is proposed, so that the keeping of the commandment may be both the way and the cause of reward. For if he has had neither opportunity nor permission to do evil, he will not possess the glory of doing good.

“If, in accordance with our goodwill, he has not also maintained a praiseworthy state of health through his own zeal and labor, it will not be innocence but inertia. Moreover, reward disappears where merit does not precede it. The one who does not know how to acquire our good things cannot preserve them.”

Unless devotion to obedience has come first, the offering of grace becomes cheap. At the same time, it is shameful for the one who rewards if an idle person is honored and a slothful person rewarded. Rather, with help cooperating with him, let him become worthy through his own work as well, and let him be blessed with a good conscience.

For unless [Col. 0835A] the generosity of the giver is just, the happiness of the receiver will not be perfect; and unless the eagerness of the seeker has first been tested, in what will the kindness of the giver rejoice?

Still, Foreknowledge argues with Justice, and says:

“It is better that the human race should not be made than that it should appear destined to perish.”

Goodness and Justice reply:

“Shall pious Abel be held guilty because of impious Cain? Shall the world of Noah fail to see justice because wickedness is increasing? Shall we have no Peter because of Judas? Because of those who will be conquered by the seductive power of vice, shall those who, through the stern greatness of austere virtue, are to be crowned by a just judgment not enter into life? Because of the multitude of transgressors, shall the ages of the just, the thousands of martyrs, and the kingdom of the saints be passed over into nothingness? Because we foreknow as sinners those whom we foresee sinning by their own crime, shall we not make those whom we foresee will also [Col. 0835B] please us by their own merit?

“If this is so, foreknown wickedness will defraud our power more than completed wickedness. Will the foreknown generation of the wicked harm the good? Will it harm the good that those should not be created because, once created, they might eventually have been able to harm only themselves?”

But Goodness may say:

“Let us make the human race in such a way that it cannot sin.”

To this discerning Justice replies:

“How shall we give earthly beings what we have granted to heavenly beings? How shall human frailty possess what the nature of angels did not obtain?”

[Col. 0836A]

Since these things are so, let no creature dare to dispute the work of the Creator.

It belonged to Power to create an immortal human being from nothing; to Wisdom, to make him capable of reason; to Goodness, to prepare him for blessedness; to Justice, not to choose him before testing him.

But someone persists and says:

“If it is certain that sinners in that age will be consigned to punishment and handed over to eternal fires, the human being ought to have been made in such a way that he could not sin at all.”

Why do you anticipate the dispensations of your Creator, O human being? Why do you seek the substance of immortality in the realm of death? Why do you seek in wickedness what is prepared in glory? Why do you demand before your labor has been completed what is prepared after labor?

This will be given, but to one already justified eternally, when what has been bestowed cannot perish. This will be given, but in the time of blessedness, where it will no longer be necessary either to conquer sin or even to know it; where there will be neither the will nor the possibility [Col. 0836B] of sinning; where living holily, blamelessly, and piously will be not diligence or effort but nature.

Divine mercy and justice administer this in such a way that the one who has striven for integrity here can no longer be corrupted there by any stain. For he judged it worthy that the weak human being who did not wish to sin should, once eternal, be unable to sin. Thus, as the ages pass endlessly, there may be joy without fear, reward without envy, and a kingdom without an enemy.

[Col. 0835]

# Letters of Saint Faustus of Riez (C, G, S)

## First Letter, or Faustus’s Profession of Faith, against Those Who, While Saying That Some Are Drawn to Life and Others Driven into Death Solely by the Will of God, Assert Fate with the Pagans and Deny Free Choice with the Manichaeans

[Col. 0835C]

To the most blessed and most reverend Lord Leontius, pope: Faustus.

Blessed Pope Leontius, by your pastoral concern you have served all the churches of Gaul by convening a council of the highest bishops for the purpose of rejecting the error of predestination. But in assigning to weak shoulders the task and care of arranging those matters that you had presented with such great learning in a public conference, you have, as I think, given too little consideration to so great an undertaking and too little regard to your holy reputation; and, through a judgment of charity, you have burdened me with the danger of your choice.

Since, therefore, you recognize that your own person is laboring under the burden imposed upon us, you are acting here for our common cause if you extend the hand of support to one whom you see to be unequal to your opinion. The one who appropriately and profitably undertakes the task of asserting grace, while joining to it the obedience of a servant’s labor, resembles a minister who clings inseparably to his patron or master as an attendant.

But if one exists without the other, either the master will appear dishonored without his servant, or the servant, forgetting his condition, will occupy the place of the master. It is therefore right that this order be maintained between the one who assists and the one who strives, so that the former may retain complete dominion and the latter render service with total submission.

The dignity of the ruler will increase if the diligence of the obedient is always present to him. Let the lowly be joined to the highest, and let them be joined in such a way that they are subordinated, certainly, but not made equal.

Just as it is unfitting for a helmsman to be without his rower, a priest without his minister, or an emperor without his soldier, so grace must be bound through inseparable service to obedience nurtured by grace.

But because Pelagius, excessively exalting naked labor, foolishly believed and impiously preached that human weakness could suffice for itself without grace, and is attempting to raise a tower of pride toward heaven, we have judged it necessary briefly to touch upon and refute his blasphemies.

Otherwise, the person who excludes the gift of labor—that is, the commandment of the one who gives orders—might, when we assert that God’s mercy must be merited by faith and works, apply the Catholic voice to the meaning of Pelagius, unaware of the distinction. Falling from the royal road to the right, he might think that we had turned toward the left; and while we speak of labor as serving grace, we might appear to have placed a stumbling-block before the feet of the blind.

When we mention work and labor, we shall use both the words and the meanings of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists. If anyone presumptuously interprets them in the opposite sense, he will undoubtedly attempt not to destroy inventions of ours but to dissolve heavenly things by right and overthrow the foundations of faith.

We have extended our discussion of foreknowledge and predestination to some length so that matters thought obscure might be made clearer for slower minds. But let no one who delights in the ornament of words be offended that, content with the force of the testimonies, we have brought forth the light of truth without lofty elegance of speech.

In this little work, after the signing of the Council of Arles, the Synod of Lyons required that certain additions be made because new errors had been detected.

[Col. 0837B]

## Letter II. The Same Faustus to Lucidus the Presbyter

(This letter may be read in volume 53, column 681, where it was long ago reprinted in Jacques Sirmond’s *Predestinarian History*.)

## Copy of the Letter of Lucidus the Presbyter (C)

To the most blessed lords and most reverend fathers in Christ, the bishops Eufronius, Leontius, Fonteius, Viventius, Mamertus, Patientius, Verianus, Auxanius, Faustus, Paulus, Megethius, Graecus, Eutropius, Leontius, Claudius, Marcellus, Crocus, Basilius, Claudius, Ursicinus, Praetextatus, Pragmatius, Theoplastus, Leocadius, Viventius, Julianus, Amicalis, John, Opilio, and Lycinius: Lucidus the presbyter.

[Col. 0837C]

(This letter may also be read in volume 53, column 683.)

## Note on the Following Letter (C)

Gennadius speaks of this letter when he says: “I have read his short work both against the Arians and the Macedonians, in which he proclaims the Trinity consubstantial. And another against those who say that there is something incorporeal among created things. In it, by divine testimonies and the judgments of the Fathers, he confirms that nothing should be believed incorporeal except God.”

This is what Gennadius says. He treats two distinct short works as arising from this single letter of Faustus: the first part is against the Arians, the other against those who say that there is something incorporeal among created things.

It is not surprising that Gennadius separated them. For in the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 4, folio 759, that section of this letter concerning created things—that nothing incorporeal exists in them—has been torn away from the preceding material and published separately, while, so far as I know, the earlier material has never seen the light.

[Col. 0837D]

We publish this letter in its entirety, with the following warning: it is a shameful and serious error on the part of Faustus and of those who supported Faustus—as Gennadius also appears to have done—to deny that any created thing is incorporeal.

This error, or rather this very section of the letter, was refuted by Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne in Gaul, in three books *On the Condition of the Soul*, addressed to Patricius and Sidonius; those books are extant. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 51, a. 1; *On the Power of God*, q. 6, a. 6; and Baronius, volume 6 of the *Annals*, as well as the appendix to volume 10 of volume 6.

## Letter III

[Note: In Canisius this letter is numbered XVI.]

### The Letter of Saint Faustus Begins

[Note: So the manuscript reads; but see Baronius’s appendix to volume 6 in volume 10.]

You ask me, most reverend of priests, how [Col. 0838A] one should respond to the Arians, who attempt with blasphemous lips to assert: “It cannot happen otherwise than that one begotten must be younger than the one who is unbegotten.”

In accordance with this, as though ordered to bring my silence entirely to an end, I shall venture to speak not so much for the instruction of the subject as for the confession of faith. I shall first observe this precaution: I will not envelop matters obscure in themselves with the artifice of polished speech, but will bring forth certain indications of a poor understanding that seem intended not so much for ornament as for comprehension.

I answer, then, as disciples usually answer teachers who ask questions. Thus, in obedience to your blessedness’s command, I speak so that you may examine my ignorance. I appeal to you so that you may teach me. For if I remain silent before one most learned, I can scarcely know what I do not know.

When we are going to speak about the unbegotten, we must understand that the substances [Col. 0838B] of things are one matter and the names of things another, just as, for example, when you say “gold” and “silver,” you have not immediately uttered the metal itself but the names of the metals. Gold is one thing in the property of its kind and another in the designation of speech. It is one thing when we name it and another when we possess it.

“Begotten” and “unbegotten” signify deity; they are not deity itself. “Nature” is an appellation, not nature; “unbegotten” and “begotten” are designations . . . This serves to make you understand from what someone subsists, and to recognize that the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son: origin from origin, and yet one, without beginning.

It is like saying “God from God”: nevertheless, there are not two gods but one. Therefore “begotten,” “unbegotten,” and “proceeding from both” designate persons, not natures.

[Note: Read: “and the unbegotten and the one proceeding from both.”]

For the majesty that is undivided [Col. 0838C] between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be distinguished by names, but cannot be arranged in degrees.

Here you must apply the foreknowledge of your mind attentively.

Perhaps you say: “Since he is from that one, he is later than that one.”

Come, let us nourish our understanding in this matter with certain comparisons. Let us see whether something can exist from another thing and yet not be later in age than that from which it exists.

For example, the very name “son” is believed to be derived from the name “father,” and yet it is not found to be later, because unless this man were born, that man would not be called a father. Here is a name absolutely coeternal with the one from whom it derives; although the son is from the father, the son gives the father the name “father.” He acquires for the begetter the designation of paternal affection [Col. 0838D] through the person who is born. Since this exists from that, neither is this shown to be later nor the other to be more ancient.

And when the son is named “arm” on account of the powers of his works, behold, the arm proceeds from the body, yet the age of the arm does not precede that of the body. The word is produced from the voice, yet, although it is born from the mouth, it is not shown to be later than the voice. Fire and heat are an undivided partnership; although heat is unquestionably understood to be from fire, fire is in no way recognized as prior to its heat.

Here is something that appears to exist from another thing and yet is joined to that from which it exists without any interval of time.

[Col. 0839A]

When we come to God, the one who is begotten is what the Just and Justice are, what the Wise and Wisdom are, and what the Merciful and Mercy are. According to the Apostle, we understand justice and wisdom to arise absolutely from the just and wise God.

And just as there was never a just one without justice, nor a wise one without wisdom, so the Son is from the Father, but it was never possible for the Father to exist without the Son.

Without doubt, the Arians do not dare to deny our Savior. But by calling him lesser, they cannot assert that he is God. For God exists naturally in the dignity of fullness, and their impiety, by its first confession, testifies that they worship one God. But the person who makes the one considered older into two by calling the other younger cuts through the solidity of unity.

For the very name “lesser” indicates another who is greater than he. Who is older [Col. 0839B] than the one who says of himself: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last” (Isa. 44; Rev. 1)? When asked who he was, he answered in this way: “The Beginning, who also speak to you with the Jews” (John 8:25).

Through the prophet’s truthful voice he confirms: “Before me there was no God, and after me there shall not be” (Isa. 43:10). If the Father says this, he confirms that no inferior being began after him; if the Son says it, he declares that no one existed at all before him.

The prophetic word clearly intimates concerning him: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him” (Bar. 3:36). And afterward: “He was seen among human beings and lived among human beings” (ibid., 3:38).

Accordingly, between the begotten and the unbegotten there is neither order, because they are one; nor an interval of time, because he is first; nor anything to be placed after him, because he is alone; nor anything to be called lesser, [Col. 0839C] because he is full.

Therefore he is called perfect and of simple nature, beyond estimation and impassible, although we truthfully and profitably confess that he suffered for us according to the flesh.

After this, in the next place, you ask me how, in accordance with God’s substance, it can have been written in a certain letter: “He felt nothing with the feeling of one suffering, but he felt with the affection of one suffering with another.”

[Note: This saying appears below in the letter to Gratus.]

[Col. 0839D]

First of all, it is most readily understood that this point did not escape even the philosophers. In a human being, various affections—that is, justice, mercy, holiness, goodwill, piety, and similar qualities—are things that accrue from outside, and for this reason they are called affections. God, however, is not affected by these contingently, because they are recognized as dwelling in him continually and naturally.

Thus what in a human being is an affection received by grace is in God a virtue arising from nature.

For when it was said, “He felt nothing with the feeling of one suffering, but he felt with the affection of one suffering with another,” why should anyone hesitate to say this in the sense also recalled by the prophet: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:2; 37:1)? And again: “The Lord has sworn, and he shall not repent” (Ps. 109:4). And again: “The Lord was angry with his people and abhorred his inheritance” (Ps. 105).

Likewise, Jacob [Col. 0840A] is described as having been loved and Esau hated, with a different affection. God is said to be saddened by our sins and to rejoice in his works; and, presenting himself as subject to affections, he says: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6:7). From the highest seat of heaven he declares: “Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4).

He also seems to show the affection of one suffering with another when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:35), together with the other statements of this kind that readily and abundantly come to mind.

How, then, if a priest endowed with knowledge of many languages and situated among diverse peoples were to address a Hebrew in Hebrew, a Greek in Greek, and a Roman in Roman speech, confirming his words according to the understanding of each; [Col. 0840B] if he adapted the speech of his mouth to each person’s understanding and distributed the expected words of one heart—though expressed in different forms—to various hearers, so God, when he deigns to speak with human beings, assumes the language of human beings and, since he is also to assume human form, expresses through our understanding sounds corresponding to our modes of expression.

For while describing the functions of the five human senses, he says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers” (Ps. 33:16). Again: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1:20). Likewise: “He smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Gen. 8:21). And: “My hand made all these things. Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1).

Through the symbolic language of bodily members, he conveys to our hearts the operations of things. Therefore, because of his effective condescension toward the human [Col. 0840C] race, he does not disdain to call and address people as servants, friends, and sons, so that the human being may converse with him in turn with a human mouth and in a human manner.

Furthermore, God’s anger is justice; God’s fury is the force of severity; God’s swearing is the establishment of a decision; God’s repentance is a sentence, though often mute.

[Note: Perhaps “changed.”]

And when he says that he is injured by someone who persecutes him, he reveals the crime of the one who causes the injury. Every ministry of prayer, and every means by which something is said, understood, or proclaimed, is cut off from us if these exchanges of human speech are removed. Why, then, could it not be said amid these things: “He felt with the affection of one suffering with another”?

If, therefore, this simple and open answer has satisfied the teacher who was examining me, let us pass to the third question, in which [Col. 0840D] you command me to reply:

[Note: From the words “in which” onward, what follows exists as a separate short work or letter in volume 4 of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, folio 759. This is certainly a shameful error on Faustus’s part; see the note on this letter.]

“Which things in human affairs are to be understood as corporeal, and which as incorporeal?”

[Note: In the margin of the manuscript some material had been added that seems to convey this meaning—for it cannot be inserted elsewhere except here, and indeed a sign was attached at this point—“in order that I may answer, you command a discussion of this minor question.” Then follow the words: “Which things …”]

To this I shall bring forward certain points, not on the basis of my own presumption, but according to the opinion of holy elders. Especially since these matters cannot injure the soul, but can nourish faith, and can arm and fortify it against Arian perversities, to the point that the Son appears equal to the Father [Margar.: “and may be required to raise up perversities”]. Therefore, when the discussion concerns a higher doctrine, the understanding and the mind must be prepared for a subtler interpretation. Some of the most learned Fathers assert that some things are invisible and others incorporeal. They define everything created as appearing to be material [Margar.: “to appear to be material”], and as comprehensible and corporeal to its maker. For they also assert that the nature of souls and angels is corporeal, because from the beginning they are circumscribed and occupy space. For, as we read in a certain treatise of Saint Jerome, “They consider the spheres of the stars to be embodied spirits” [Margar., corruptly: “compared”]. And again: “If angels are said to be heavenly bodies and unclean in comparison with God, what do you think a human being should be considered?” Yet you deny that the soul is corporeal because, according to the opinion of some, it is neither local nor sustained by quality [Margar.: “nor does it subsist through quality or quantity,” which, he says, ought to be believed only of God’s majesty].

We read in a certain highly authoritative treatise of the Fathers: “To enter into and fill all things is possible only for the Trinity. Since it becomes the penetrator of every intellectual nature, it can not only surround and encompass it, but also enter into it and, as though incorporeal, be infused into a body. Although we declare that some natures are spiritual—such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, as well as our own soul, or at least this subtle air—nevertheless they must in no way be considered incorporeal. For they have a body proper to themselves, by which they subsist, although it is much and incomparably more subtle than our bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement: ‘There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies’ (II Cor. XV, 40).” From this it is clearly inferred that nothing is incorporeal except God alone. Therefore, all intellectual substances are penetrable only by God himself [Margar.: “only he makes all intellectual substances penetrable”].

Since this is so, he objects to me that the soul is not incorporeal because, as has been said, it is neither local nor subsists through quality or quantity. The danger of believing this will depend upon the examination of our present position, so that, if the soul is neither local nor subject to quality, we may plainly concede that it is incorporeal. But if I demonstrate that it is determined by quantity and confined to a place, you will consequently no longer doubt that it is also contained by a body. [Margar.: “How is it local?”]

How is it not local when, inserted into the limbs and bound to the viscera, it is held enclosed by the wandering condition of its substance, occupied solely with its movements [Margar.: “being occupied”]? If you think that the soul must be regarded as nonlocal because it wanders through different things by means of the senses and is carried about by thoughts, you must first understand that the condition of the soul is one thing, and that which arises here from the soul—the affection of thought—is another [Margar.: “the effect”]. Accordingly, this should rather be judged [Margar.: “to be judged”]: whenever it imagines something for itself, it is more occupied within itself with its own movements; and whatever else [Margar.: “other”] it seems to look upon, that is more fully depicted for it in the mirror of inward recollection [Margar.: *magis incordationis*, reading uncertain].

For when it thinks of an absent loved one, has it already satisfied its desire as though by seeing him in person? Or when, for example, it paints the image of Peter or Paul in the hidden recesses of the mind, has it immediately penetrated the innermost seats of paradise, where we know that they are? Or when, in its heart, it sets before itself from its reading the flames of that rich man, has it already descended into the inaccessible depths of hell, to the places of his torments?

Without doubt, it either fashions all these things with itself within the hidden recesses of the breast through various likenesses; or, if unstable thought, driven by slippery motion, runs about outside the soul’s seat, it does this very thing locally. And whether it thinks of a city or of any region, it is fixed there only in sensation, wherever it is carried by the mind’s attention [Margar.: “where it is carried along at the same time”]. It can imagine some things for itself; it cannot embrace everything at once.

Therefore, when the soul has thought of Alexandria or Jerusalem, if—as you suppose—it was present there in its entirety, let it tell us the situation of the places, the faces of the people, and the movements and actions of the populations. But we know that this very exchange of words now taking place between us occurs through the mutual activity of the spirit: I know that I speak with you, and I feel this in my conscience, but I do not feel that I have come to you. For if the soul is truly believed to be carried along with its senses, and to be presented by its own thoughts to those whom it remembers, behold: throughout these moments of the present time I think of you, and in recollection I see you, yet I do not know in the least what you are doing, or whether you are at rest, reading, or engaged in prayer.

But this happens because I reach you through the affection of the heart, not through the actual reality of my substance. For the nature of our souls does not consist in its movements, which we now perceive to be good and now evil. If it is to be believed that the soul subsists through its thoughts, why, when those thoughts sometimes vanish and perish, does the soul itself persist in its strength and liveliness? How many of our most frequent thoughts and anxieties also die, even beneficially, and contribute rather to the freedom of the inner life [Margar.: “produce freedom”]! If the soul consisted in them, it could not survive when they had wholly perished [Margar.: “through the ages”].

Hence reason speaks more convincingly to our consciences that each soul either gives birth within itself to manifold thoughts, conceived from the causes of things [Margar.: “conceives and gives birth to manifold thoughts arising from the causes of things”], or disperses its senses like certain offices or ministries, to be occupied by different necessities [Margar.: “or disperses certain offices or ministries, occupied with different necessities”]; while it itself rests in the chamber of its body, from which it will one day depart.

Therefore, to offer another sufficient example proving that it is local: was not Lazarus’s soul, while life remained, within his body? But when life departed, did it not go out as an exile from the dwelling of the body, and, poured again into the lifeless body, return when called back from the place from which it had withdrawn? Then you see it driven out as though from the habitation of an inn, and restored again to the lodging from which it had departed; yet you contend that it is not local?

But why should I speak of these things concerning corruptible man? When he whose flesh did not see corruption possessed an immaculate yet local soul—which he certainly held within himself when he was fastened to the cross, but plainly sent outside himself when he lay in the tomb—how is that soul not local, which the flesh contains, which life joins together, and which death separates?

And if, as you say, the nature of souls has not received the necessity of locality [Margar.: “does not concern”], then are those souls from the region of paradise not imprisoned in hell? Tell me, I ask, if they are not local, how does that just abyss divide sinners from the assemblies and fellowship of the righteous by a grievous intervening separation, so that they can neither cross from here to there nor from there to here?

It is now most evident that things contained within spaces are bounded by quantity. If you have acknowledged that the soul is local, concede that it is corporeal. Tell me: did the soul of our glorious Redeemer itself leave the world when he ascended into heaven?

I would not even doubt that angels are local, since it is certain that they are now contained in the heavens, now carried through the void of the air, and now sent down to earthly places. Divine Scripture describes them ascending and descending in the patriarch’s vision; plainly, if they were not local and were everywhere, they could not be present and depart by ascending and descending.

The most blessed Gabriel himself, who testifies that he stands before the Lord, when he announced to Mary that the Lord of heaven would be infused into her womb, and when he stood beneath the eyes of the Lord’s mother, was certainly absent from heaven [Margar.: “was absent”]; he did not fly over the seas, nor fill the empty and extended vastness of the air, but occupied only the place in which he was. [Margar.: “This being so, whoever is sent from one place to another, etc.”]

Since this is so, whatever occupies a place is a body. I do not know how one who is sent from place to place, and is carried about like a body by movement and approach, descends by mass, runs about by mobility, goes, returns, withdraws, and descends, can fail to be subject to the law of locality.

Or is he not, I believe, local who not only revealed himself to be local, but, hurled down from on high, dragged away with himself a third of the stars? Tell me: if he has no body, what was it that fell in that casting down? Why do you deny a bodily nature to one whose fall you do not dare to deny? And if, as you say, he has no body, he will not burn. But where, except in a body, will he feel that fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels?

I consider it unnecessary to say that, in his dwelling in this air, he acquired a certain density from the mingling together of the elements. Tell me: if he has no body, where could this mixture adhere? Where could this density—which I scarcely know how to name—gather itself, if he did not carry with him something corporeal from that heavenly citadel? As I see it, you will carry another’s body to punishment. Recognize, then, even on the basis of your own assertion, that it is a body.

A body is that which is infected, which is stained, which is changed by any addition that comes upon it [Margar.: “which is corrupted”]. Thus this one, formerly the firstborn of the angels, has now become the first of darkness, and, once beautiful as though corporeal, is now degenerate. Formerly conspicuous in heavenly splendor, he is now disfigured by the foul horror of infernal sin. A body, I say, is that which is driven away by action, bounded by quantity, changed by quality, and consumed by pain. Since these things are so, why do they not call the soul corporeal? See into what profound guilt they plunge themselves. [The material from this point through the words at the end, “One God therefore,” is absent from Margarini’s printed edition.]

First, since God, the author of the universe, is said to have made all things according to number and weight, the soul is consequently believed to have been excepted from the materiality of creation as a whole. Since it is not corporeal, and is not local if it is not contained in a place, it must therefore be diffused everywhere. It is said to enter all things, fill them, and be present everywhere; and thus a creature would be joined to its creator as his associate, and frailty would no longer be joined to its author as a thing belonging to God, but would be regarded as a part of God. See where this profound error in its descent leads those who maintain it.

Indeed, the things above us are invisible to us; but all those things, being comprehensible, are also corporeal. He who made all things from nothing, just as he established them by his work, also gave them material form; and to all things, among which the soul too is counted, just as he distributed weight and number, so also he assigned qualities.

If, among these considerations, someone should perhaps think that, as has been said, the subtlety of that angelic nature, gathered through a kind of contagion by its admixture with this air, is found subject to flames, then, as he says, if what burns is aerial, it would burn only in the air, and the punishment would rage not in it but outside it. Yet plainly the substance of a body is the only place in which the force of pain can exercise dominion.

See where the thoughtless and ignorant persuasion leads one who speaks of the incorporeal and thereby confesses it to be incomprehensible: it ascribes to the created work what belongs only to the creator; it communicates the privileges of majesty to created things; and it extends an unwarranted power to the creature, even to the injury of the maker.

If we carefully consider the ends toward which you direct your mind, this cruelty above all cast the devil down from the position of that blessed seat, and for this reason the angel lost his dignity: he presumed to possess the nature of God. [Note: Up to this point the manuscript had the material that is absent from the commonly printed text.]

One God, therefore, is incorporeal, because he is both incomprehensible and diffused everywhere; for he did not derive his beginning from the material body of any created work. And therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father, because he was created from no work and is bounded by no beginnings. He is diffused in incorporeal majesty above all things that, within the world’s body, he fashioned as comprehensible and corporeal for their potter. Begotten from the Unbegotten—that is, from the Father—he rules over those whom he brought forth from nothing, in inseparable fellowship with the Holy Spirit, always with the Father. Amen.

## LETTER IV

[Note: In Canisius this letter is numbered XVII.]

Faustus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, to Benedict Paulinus.

[Note: This letter, as well as the following short works of Faustus, should be read with caution, since they are works rejected and condemned by the Roman Church. Read what Faustus argues here with discernment: for although true repentance at the last moment, under extreme necessity, is difficult to attain, no orthodox person has ever doubted that true and legitimate repentance can sometimes occur then. See Dominic Soto, *Sentences* IV, distinction 19, question 2, article 6.]

The page of your letters, which I have always admired, now shines forth even more abundantly with the double light of eloquence and faith, while, reflecting on the condition of the soul [Note: Elsewhere: “asks and fears”], you sigh with anxious fear at the future judgments.

The divine utterance says in one place: “Wisdom will be credited to one who asks rightly.” For it is a portion of knowledge to know what you do not know and prudently to inquire into what you do not understand through ignorance.

First, you thought it necessary to ask whether, when the straits of extreme necessity press upon someone, momentary repentance proves deceptive through the deadly persuasion of the enemy, when he supposes that stains contracted over a long life can be wiped away even by sudden and ineffectual groans. At such a time confession may be possible, but satisfaction is not. For, since God is not mocked, the one who defeated death for many years and rises, already half-alive, to seek a way has deceived himself: he appears dutiful only when all the services of body and soul are being taken away from the service of the Lord.

For the healing of the inner person, not merely the willingness to receive is awaited, but also the usefulness of action. Thus we read: “If,” he says, “the sinner has done repentance for his sins” [the text recalls *egerit*, “has done,” not merely “has said” or “has received”], “he lives in the righteousness which he has practiced.” [Col. 0845C] Do you see that this medicine must be sought with the mouth but completed through works? The person who refused to come to the physician when he could seems to mock God, and begins to wish to come when he cannot.

It is therefore necessary that the devotion shown in healing wounds be as great as the mind’s intention toward evil was abrupt and vigorous when it sinned.

Second, you asked whether the single knowledge of the Trinity alone is sufficient for salvation.
