[Note: Elsewhere: “whether faith alone, from unity of knowledge, is sufficient for salvation … Faith alone does not profit toward salvation.”] In divine matters, not only the reason for believing is required, but also the reason for pleasing God. Faith therefore, stripped of merits, is empty and void, as the Apostle says: “What does it profit if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can it save him?” For he continues: “If faith does not have works, it is dead in itself.” But someone says: “You have faith, and I have works; show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith from my works.”

Accordingly, it is not proved that belief by itself is sufficient. For even the devil is found to know and believe, as the same Apostle says: “You believe that there is one God; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble.” Do you wish to know, empty man, that faith without works is dead? “Was not Abraham our father justified by works?”

And lest we place our hope in faith alone, he concluded in this way: “Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead,” and he declared that without them a person is empty.

I shall omit many similar testimonies for the sake of brevity. The Apostle Paul, from whose breast the Lord spoke as from his own temple, did not judge that faith alone could suffice for him to overcome the evils of the world, when he said: “I discipline my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected.”

Behold: he fears becoming rejected through the vices of the body. Already approved, he fears becoming a vessel of dishonor through the deadly contagion of carnal passions—he who has already become a vessel of election! Let us see whether faith alone can defend one who squanders his life, and whether one who has been baptized, as you say, cannot now perish.

Recognize how carnal evils make a person alienated from God and enslaved to obscene pleasures. The Apostle says to the Galatians: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; those who do such things will not attain the kingdom of God.”

Likewise, to the Ephesians: “Every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—will not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” Without doubt, one excluded from the kingdom is to be handed over to hell and death. Yet it is clear that many baptized people, while preserving faith, perish eternally in different ways.

The divine utterance condemns not those who transgress faith or violate baptism, but those who have neglected to be merciful, saying: “He will be judged without mercy who has not shown mercy.” And again: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me.”

If the number of the flock on the left had been ignorant of the gift of baptism, he would first have charged them with unbelief and impiety. But although baptized, because they were empty of good works, he assigns them to death and abandons them to everlasting flames. He concludes the severity of the sentence in this way: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” And again: “He gathered the wheat into his granary, but he burned the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Likewise, I say: “These will go into eternal life, but those into eternal punishment.”

Among these matters, let each person beware of accusing God of lying concerning the promise of reward because he doubts the eternity of punishment. It is not so, for he who knows how to punish sins— [The sentence is incomplete in the supplied text.]

These, then, are the three capital crimes: sacrilege, adultery, and murder. Unless they are expiated here by the remedies of perfect repentance, they will be burned there in everlasting fires. Thus, by divine authority, you recognize that these unmerciful people did not merely turn away from faith and baptism, but deserved perpetual death.

This also troubles your mind with prudent concern for the future: whether souls stripped of the body also lose the power to sense and understand, and affection.

Let us question that rich man from the Gospel—not wandering through golden lands, as the ravings of poets assert, but in the prison of hell, among those who have been shut in awaiting punishment, amid the flames of conscience before the appointed day of judgment. Concerned for the correction of his brothers who were still in this world, he speaks with Abraham, mingling earnest supplication across the vast intervening chaos, and, struck by the lively remembrance of his brothers, he pleads for the living in this way:

“I beg you, father Abraham, to send Lazarus to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment; and if someone from the dead should go to them, they will repent” (Luke XVI).

Behold: condemned in the anguish of hell, having no remedy remaining for himself, he nevertheless preserves his former affection for his brothers. And while the condemned man prays for sinners, he shows that those resting amid the groves of paradise are greatly concerned for the welfare of their loved ones.

But as for what you ask—what evil is either inflicted upon or taken away from the wicked after the end, concerning whom we read, “The desire of sinners will perish”— [Note: Beware of everything Faustus brings forward in this passage: his effort to show that human souls are corporeal is wholly absurd and erroneous.]

When the desire and ambition for earthly goods have been removed, only the weight of the account to be rendered and the fear of the unbearable examination remain. The senses will not be taken away, but they will make the thought of the other age more free and alert.

As for your request to be instructed whether the soul itself is corporeal or incorporeal, know that only that which is not enclosed by time or restrained by the boundaries of places—which belongs to God alone—is incorporeal.

As one outstanding teacher clearly replied to someone who asked where God was: “God is not somewhere. Whatever is somewhere is contained by a place; whatever is contained by a place is a body.”

Since this is so, all flesh is body, but not every body is flesh. And because not only the soul but also the invisible and heavenly substance of angels is contained within local spaces, it is likewise proved to be corporeal and comprehensible by its creator. [Note: Claudianus Mamertus, a presbyter of Vienne, wrote against this opinion in Book III of *On the State of the Soul*.]

For what is it, unless corporeal, that was disturbed from the heavenly seats and yielded to a place? What is it that experienced a fall? What is it that is made subject to eternal flame and prepared for punishment?

But blessed Lazarus himself, after being received from the tongues of the serving dogs into the hands of angels—of whom we read, “It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom”—taught that his soul was corporeal, since it was carried into Abraham’s bosom, that is, into a remote and blessed retreat, through the service of angels.

Concerning his own soul, the holy prophet declares: “Bring my soul out of prison,” that is, from the narrow confines of its bodily lodging.

Therefore, since his created work is either wounded by the arrows of sins or advanced through qualities until it reaches the beauty of the divine image, it clearly shows that it is corporeal, since it can be grasped and transferred both by God and by the angels.

Meanwhile, we must ask what it means that, although both parts of the human being—that is, soul and body—sinned together in the region of paradise when the devil persuaded them, only the flesh received the penalty of transgression through the condition of death, while a common guilt remained in connection with the punishment of one.

We must therefore understand that death did not reach the soul because the Lord placed his image and likeness in it. For just as God is immortal, merciful, just, and patient, so he infused the gifts of these virtues into our inner face, so that the more just and merciful each person proved to be, the more clearly Christ, endowed with the gift of divine participation, would appear to dwell in the inner person through faith.

You also ask why the soul, together with its flesh, shares something of bodily error, such as original sin, since, because of the unity of the bodily lodging, it embraces both alike, provided that both are bound together in the fellowship of sins. For there is one cause in participation in crimes, just as there is equal glory in the reward of virtues.

The outer person would never fall into the pit of lust unless the inner person granted consent. Let us question ourselves, and among ourselves we shall be able to recognize that the mind exercises lordship while the flesh is subject to service: one provides the ministry, the other the counsel. Obedience would cease from servitude unless the will proceeded from the one giving the command.

Those who share together in retribution must necessarily recognize a similar condition in damnation.

You say further: since the soul is immortal, how is it tortured for mortal vices? Mortal indeed are the evils, but the torment of the evils will be immortal; and the torment of sins will remain even when the vices have ceased.

The inferior matter will thus be handed over to judgment for improvement, just as the admixture of lead compels gold to be melted. Therefore man will die to God because of mortal evils, and will live amid punishment. This will be his death: he will not be permitted to die while in pain.

You extend your concern also to this question: whether soul and spirit are the same, or how they are distinguished. Let us understand that there are only two substances in a human being, soul and body. Spirit, however, is sometimes shown to be natural, sometimes found as something added, and at other times understood as a desire and spiritual affection produced by virtue. In this sense, one and the same person is at times carnal and at times spiritual.

Carnal are those of whom the Lord says: “My spirit will not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Gen. III); and the Apostle: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII, 8).

A person is carnal who serves the belly and throat through excess in eating and drinking, and who places the good of life in the gluttony and greediness of the stomach; who calculates life by excess in eating and drinking; and whose gluttony dominates him.

But a person becomes animal when, while still thinking purely about God, he is moved according to the soul by worldly prudence toward knowledge of certain things; when he takes pleasure in investigating the causes of hidden things or in the studies of philosophy. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 14).

He begins to be spiritual when he desires honorable and spiritual things; when he rises through strength of heart toward the worship of divine fear; when he invites the spirit into himself through bodily purity and the guardianship of chastity, so that the Apostle’s saying may be applied to him: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (II Cor. XVI).

These things are not implanted in human beings by nature, but are added through grace in such a way that, when negligence intervenes through guilt, they can be separated. Hence the same Apostle says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III, 17).

Behold: through faith a person appears not only to have been baptized but also to be the temple of God; nevertheless, through various crimes he will be destroyed by God’s severity. Here we should understand the term “destruction” as the eternal ruin of the lost soul.

They are unquestionably counted among the baptized, and are said to be members of Christ; yet see how they are compared with the lost, how, when crime is at work, they degenerate from the nobility of sons. The Apostle says: “Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (I Cor. XVIII).

Those, too, had most clearly received the gifts of the second birth, and even possessed an abundance of different charisms. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will say to them, ‘I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matt. VII, 22).

Who could fail to understand that those ordered to depart from the Father’s presence have been rejected from salvation? Their own death will unquestionably receive them as its portion—those whom the Life who is Christ will not recognize.

Do you doubt that the baptized are handed over to destruction because of their iniquities, when you know that baptism itself is lost through many crimes?

As for the fact that, as your page relates, your speech borrowed from the prophet regarded the fire of the simple soul, this must be said only of the substance of divinity, to which nothing has been added, nothing bestowed from above, and nothing is known to have been joined.

He is at once just, justice, living, and life; wise, and both virtue and the origin of virtues. In his principal goods—that is, in what he possesses—he is identical with what he possesses.

A human being, however, can be understood as twofold: he can be called living, just, and wise, but he cannot be called life and justice, because he is clothed with these things in such a way that he can sometimes be stripped of them.

What is given to a human being is inherent in God. A human being, for example, is gilded; God is gold. In God, power and glory are the same as nature.

As for what you subtly indicated—if all those whom Lord Marinus threatens are sinners, I do not know what the impious can deserve more. Under everlasting evils, punishments also have their degrees. Those subject to grave sins endure innumerable punishments, though they may somehow be tolerated; but the impious are tortured by unheard-of torments.

Then you have the grace of baptism, and it could not rescue anyone from death unless its integrity and dignity did not perish in some cases. [Note: Elsewhere: “Grace can rescue a person from eternal death if its integrity does not perish in some cases, etc.”]

The crime of the heretic who refused to receive baptism is grave; no less grave is the crime of the Christian who receives it and then loses it. For the person who, trusting in baptism, rashly entered the wedding feast and violated the sacred council, after losing the radiance of purity, is expelled from the illustrious assembly of the righteous and cast into the outer darkness.

For is one to be thought to possess the snow-white radiance of holy regeneration when, among the incestuous, poisoners, and bloodstained, he cuts short his life by a fall or hanging and passes over into the company of the impious?

We read that unquenchable flames have been prepared for capital crimes; but we do not read that a person living in his evils has been saved by baptism alone.

A dangerous security promises itself what is not read in heavenly Scripture; even more dangerous is the refusal to believe what the truth threatens.

As you say, the blessed man Marinus discussed certain matters with threats. But just as what the Lord promised to those who love him has not entered the human heart, even according to the Apostle’s testimony, because of the greatness of the matter, so the immensity of future torments will exceed the narrow limits of the human mind. These are evils which the fleeting shadow of repentance does not remove; faith without works will not ward them off; nor will the course of passing ages be able to establish an end to them in unquenchable flames. Amid those inexhaustible vapors, the corporeal soul will slowly both feel and see itself.

And therefore let us anticipate the last day with just, chaste, and pious works. Here, by fearing what it will profit nothing to fear there, let us turn away from those things.

Here let us put an end to endless disputes, and, by salutarily contemplating the unbearable fires now, let us obtain eternal refreshment for ourselves from those very flames. [Note: Elsewhere: “contritions.” “From the thought of the eternal fires, eternal refreshment prepared for itself.”]

[Note: These words are not found in the editions printed hitherto, but have now been added from the manuscript of Henry Canisius.]

I am certain of your faith: that the saving testimonies of sincere truth will be more pleasing to you than the artificially ornamented, contrived brilliance of speech.

We greet my son Eminentius, our dear honor, with paternal affection. May our Lord fill his admirable magnificence toward me with present blessings and make him worthy of eternal ones.

## LETTER V

Faustus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, on repentance, to Felix the pope and Patricius.

To Felix, my most devout lord and, as I trust, brother forever, honored by special services and in every respect my lord, Faustus.

A great testimony of piety and faith: across such vast distances of regions and through so many intervening obstacles, you extend the breadth of your charity all the way to us. In this exile of ours, the mercy of our God, the Craftsman, performs a twofold service: with paternal diligence it scrapes away our rust, and it makes your faith toward us shine forth and approves your piety. It polishes us through kindly care; it brings you forward. It constricts us beneficially; it expands you. We are reproved; you make progress. Our losses pass over into your advantages. Since you are our lenders, you begin to be our debtors, for I am the cause of your devotion and the material of your reward. Your works derive profit from us; your merits borrow increase from our scourges. The fruit of your solicitude for us, of your affection toward God, reaches God; and thus, in two ways, through both our chastisement and your recompense, we are bound to divine benefits.

Indeed, the perfection of your consolation had almost imposed silence upon me in replying. For that very solicitude in questioning seems to be a pattern of life, which you daily draw sufficiently from the effective teachings and present examples of my lord, your father, the holy bishop Leontius [Note: Alternatively, Leontius.]. Yet I do not wonder that you also seek my instruction—even if superfluously—since you know my singular affection toward you. You believe, to assist your faith, that my teaching is as perfect as your desire; but although my speech—which the present weakness of my body makes still slower—can scarcely suffice for your ardor, nevertheless, in a few words I shall not so much instruct your way of life as review it.

The acknowledgment of sin, fear of judgment, and dread of eternal fire provide great protection for the anxious. Therefore, for offering the sacrifices of prayers, the night silences are friendly to those who delight in them; let measured reading follow them until the third hour, so that spiritual exercise may not cease to be desired and may always be increased. Would that the Lord provide you with one or two faithful companions, with whom you may perform your daily and nightly duties, and that on two days of the week you might enjoy the services of those who visit you.

The matters we discuss in response to your fervor are difficult; but may that kindly helper of those who labor make his yoke as light for you as his reward will be joyful. Therefore, if your trembling beginnings permit a little more, let the winter days be spent in fasting on alternate days. Just as fasting ought to be moderated, so it must be doubled—doubled, I say, because there are two kinds of abstinence.

The first is to restrain the appetite of incontinence from food and drink and from the various allurements of bodily pleasures; to tame, with the plow of the cross, the soil of the subjected exterior person; and to serve necessity rather than pleasure with measured moderation—receiving a little, if weakness permits, even on alternate days, until the strength of long habit is gradually unlearned. As for the use of clothing, let seriousness gradually submit itself to lower things [i.e. let one gradually adopt humbler clothing], lest the very novelty of sudden moderation cause offense.

It must also be observed that pride does not arise from excessive humility, and that vice is not born from virtue. Yet this will easily be overcome if that shameful history of one’s former way of life is brought before one’s eyes and the guilty conscience is presented to trembling senses. Thus, while presumption instilled by the devil is chastised through remembrance of past evils, and while boasting is driven back after being defeated by the strong weapons of guilt, the crimes that had produced death may begin to serve salvation; offenses may advance toward remedy; medicine may be produced from wounds; and, as the Apostle said, we may labor to condemn sin through sin.

The second kind of abstinence is far more exalted and far more precious: to govern the movements of the soul; to subject to the rule of the mind irrational disturbances and the rebellious tumults of thoughts struggling among themselves; to spit out from the inner chambers of the heart the venom of malice, like some deadly sorcery; to steer the soul amid the waves of various temptations through the discipline of steadfastness; to engage, through the authority of faith, in a kind of conflict against hidden passions as against domestic enemies; to drive far away empty cares; to abstain from harmful conversations and desires by which the devil is nourished; and through gentleness, patience, and tranquility to cultivate in the outward face the man who thinks spiritual and divine thoughts, so that sadness may not break him, joy may not dissolve him, and the equality of magnanimity may display a breast established in the fear of God.

Thus the notable opening of that little book may be fitted to us: “There was one man abstaining from every evil thing” (Job 1). It says “one man,” that is, always the same: for there was nothing doubtful in him, nothing double, nothing accidental, nothing variable or diverse. Remaining permanently in the state of his virtues in an equal order, he was not changed by the passage of time, nor—as is usual with the greatest waves—turned in opposite directions by different blasts of wind.

So also the anxious servant of God, founded upon the unshaken mass of faith, should be changed in this one respect—Christ working within him—that he may always be clothed with new virtues. Above all, insofar as we can with God’s help, let us conquer within ourselves the allurements of the five senses. For whatever becomes beautiful to the sight, whatever entices the sense of smell, whatever softens through touch, whatever becomes sweet to taste, and whatever charms hearing—all these, if we abuse them, drag our attention down from spiritual things to earthly ones.

Therefore, just as Abraham, the father of faith, conquered those five kings with three hundred and eighteen, with a mystery hidden within the letter, so let us also fight against the principal leaders of vices, in the name of Jesus and under the sign of the cross—for both express this [Note: Alternatively, “represent”]—so that we may deserve to hear from the Lord: “To the one who conquers I will give the crown of life, and the one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death” (Revelation 2:11); and because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

The soul must do violence to itself so that it may subject carnal affections to the spirit; prefer the cross to pleasures; place vigils before sweet sleep; conquer the adversary in its members; and find a man, transformed from one kind of person into another, fit for that command of the Lord: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24). If someone becomes patient from being angry, continent from being lustful, peaceful from being bloodthirsty, kind from being envious, and generous from being greedy, then we deny ourselves as often as we turn ourselves toward better things. Therefore, to rise to what we ought to be, let us first strive to hate what we were. The person who wishes to be transformed there into glory must first be transformed here into life.

## LETTER VI. OF THE SAME FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF RIEZ IN GAUL, AGAINST NESTORIUS, TO G., A DEACON

[Col. 0853A]

To Gratus, a holy brother and one most devoted to me in Christ [Note: Alternatively, Gregorius; and in Greek, Gratus], deacon, Faustus.

Honored by your office, honored by your judgment, and summoned by your affection, I shall speak with you in sincere humility, benevolent freedom, and unfaked charity—in the word of truth. Although you could have imposed silence upon me by giving me a reason to remain silent, since in your kind and excessively trusting spirit you grant me as much punishment as you grant yourself knowledge and learning, nevertheless, through your anxious questioning, you have imposed upon me the necessity of replying. In this I judge that I must converse with you while absent, not without trembling, because in matters so profound and exceeding both your strength and mine, it is no less dangerous to answer than to entrust immense mysteries to an unformed style. Therefore, concerning the things my dear brother rashly put forward, I ought rather to have chastised him by silence.

In consulting about so great a matter, in which you have departed far from the royal road, you ought to have questioned men of tested knowledge, senior in learning and age, whom you could more easily trust, according to the prophetic saying: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32:7) [Note: An alternative version adds: “But whoever seeks a guide of any sort must avoid error.” Then, etc.].

Next, in what we do or say, and finally in what we dare to commit to writing, we ought to look for the fruit and progress of the work. But in this little writing that you have kindly directed to me, there appears neither eloquence, nor knowledge, nor reasoning, nor any edification of ordered or compunctionate speech. Rather, testimonies piled together in utter confusion for the convenience of memory accuse the rashness of an unwary heart.

The Lord knows that I speak these things in amazement, out of zeal for your salvation. May it profit the common good both that you have asked and that I have answered. In the writings of the holy bishop Augustine, even if something is thought by the most learned men to be suspect, you should know that nothing has been condemned from the matters you judged worthy of condemnation. Rather, know that the sense of the faith—especially concerning the two substances or natures of God and man in our Lord and Redeemer—has been received in the Catholic Church not only by the authority of the Fathers but also consecrated by apostolic declarations.

Accordingly, this statement which you say was addressed to you in prophetic fashion—since it is certainly not from the Spirit of God—is highly condemnable both before God and before men, unless you first condemn it yourself. Therefore, leaving other matters aside, I shall briefly—so far as I can while absent—restrain this twofold error, born from heresy and dragging one into the dangers of heresy, although your holy sincerity would require the presence of many teachers—not such a one as I am.

In the first place, ignorantly and quite dangerously, it is not merely written but thought that one ought not to accept that a human being is the mother of God. This descends from the impiety of the Nestorian heresy, whose adherent did not fear, in profane audacity, to argue that blessed Mary was only the mother of a man and not also of God. For this reason he was condemned by the strict judgment of the Catholic Church throughout the world.

“He ought not,” he says, “to accept that a human being is the mother of God!” But where is that prophetic or evangelical passage: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14)? And again in the Gospel: “The holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Matthew 1:23). Where also is that statement, marked by the authority of the Fathers, received throughout all the islands and churches, speaking against Nestorius: “Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son of God, true God, was recently born from Mary for our salvation”?

It followed that you said that the nature of God and man is one, in this way: “There is one substance of God.” You would have spoken rightly if you had said this only of the Trinity, where there is one and the same nature under the distinction of three persons. But when one comes to the incarnation of the assumed man, just as we confess that there is one person of man and God, so we know that there is a twofold substance.

But whoever asserts one nature in God the Redeemer has either denied man in the divinity or denied God in the body, since our redemption was perfected not from one or the other separately but from both. Yet at this point it is perilous, without the other, to say that the nature belongs to our God alone [Note: Alternatively, “to our God alone”].

Thus, in the substance of his majesty, was divinity crucified? If you say that there is one nature belonging only to God, then in its own substance majesty died or was buried! All these things God underwent not in himself but in the nature of the man he assumed. For God felt nothing with the sensation of one suffering, but he felt with the effect of the one suffering [Note: Manuscript: “he perceived through the feeling of the sufferer, but he felt through fellow-feeling”]; he felt nothing on account of a difference of substance, but he felt on account of the unity of person.

He united them in unity, and consequently added: we understand him to be one and the same true man and true God. He repeated this: we have no doubt that he must be confessed as true God and true man.

Receive also the words of the hymn of the holy bishop and confessor Ambrose, which the Catholic Church sings throughout all the regions of Italy and Gaul on the Lord’s birthday: “Come forth from your bridal chamber, giant of twofold substance.”

Therefore, holy brother, take refuge amid these truths from the error of either side. If you say that he has only the nature of God, you impose upon God the condition of suffering and death. But if you say that he has only the nature of man, you deprive God of the glory of redemption and the Author of the power of the Restorer.

Hear how the sacred utterances explain both substances through one person. According to the divine nature he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). According to the human nature he confesses: “The Father is greater than I.” According to the heavenly nature he declares: “All that the Father has is mine.” According to the weakness of earthly nature he says: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” As man he indicated: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” As God he testified: “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

According to the nature of the flesh he hung upon the cross; according to the substance of divinity he granted paradise and the heavenly kingdom. The Arians, with their hearts darkened and unable entirely to see this—for presumption and pride cloud the mind’s vision—referred to God what belonged to man, believing that the divinity spoke as the lesser one where only human weakness was being shown.

Establishing no rational distinction between heavenly and earthly things, while refusing to admit two natures in God and man, they divided the substance of God. And while they looked only at the words of the man, they lost through the light of understanding the God who is the fullness of glory. Thus, whoever denies that God the Son of Man must be believed is stained with the impiety of Nestorius; whoever does not believe in two substances in the Redeemer is entangled, deceived by the snare of Arius.

But we, my dearest brother, should believe in Christ God with such a perfect and inseparable distinction that we know him to be one simple person of God and man, yet of two substances. Just as soul and body make a human being, so divinity and humanity are one Christ.

But as for what you, forestalled by a twofold error, thought should be written—that under the union of two natures one ought not to accept that God is the Father of man and that man is the Mother of God—we, confidently and beneficially asserting one person of God and man, testify under the unity of person that God is the Father of man, just as under the embrace of that same unity we confess man to be the Mother of God, according to the authority of the Creed, leaving other matters aside, because we say: “And I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was conceived from the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary.”

If it is an error to have believed in the Lord and Savior one simple substance, what kind of error is it to assert two persons? For if, in the fellowship of the assumed flesh, God put on the form of a servant, there were not two substances. Therefore God was not in man, and the person of man was separate from God. And if you observe this interpretation, you will suddenly see a fourth person arising from I know not where; and you will be driven into the following consequence of this perverse understanding, so that it will no longer be necessary to confess the Trinity.

Listen instead to how the holy Isaiah sets forth the birth of our Lord and Redeemer, arranging it in a distinct order and joined contrast: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6). Receive the Son of God, begotten at the end of the ages from an unwedded mother—nature not knowing, but faith marrying—when the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin; a man wondrously filled with God, and God mercifully changed into man. He did not empty the greatness of his glory, but through assuming the condition of a servant he displayed the Lord’s compassion.

“A child is born to us; a son is given to us!” He was born for us who existed for himself. He was given from divinity, born from the Virgin; born as one who would know death, given as one who knew no beginning. Born as one younger than his mother; given as one whom no father could precede in age. Born as one who would die; given as the one through whom life would be reborn. There he rules; here he is humbled. He reigns for himself and serves as a soldier for me.

“A child is born to us; a son is given to us”—and sovereignty was made upon his shoulder. The shoulder plainly shows the man; sovereignty speaks of the hidden God. Recognize the twofold substance under the unity of person. What he grasped is from us; what he gave is from himself. From us he had that by which he might fall; from himself, that by which he might rise. From us he had that by which he might pay for us; from himself, that by which he might appear in no way a debtor. From us he had that by which he might be crucified; from himself, that by which he might be glorified.

From us he offered the sacrifice for sin; from himself he bestowed the grace of forgiveness. From us, therefore, his humiliation is shown to be; from himself, his ascent. From us he offered the sacrifice; from himself he conferred the reward. Thus, capable of two natures, he is recognized as man by his weaknesses and proved to be God by his powers.

I am reluctant to prolong my speech in asserting so manifest a matter. I know that by recalling these things briefly and tersely I expose myself rashly either in my letters or in your thoughts. Yet while you submit yourself with anxious humility to the salutary practice of questioning, you give me great hope concerning the remedy for this error.

Withdraw your foot, I beg you, from this danger before you are swept into the irrevocable depth by the torrent of pride. Chastise the sound judgment of your soul—which cannot bear the weight of great pride and does not know how to distribute the treasury of knowledge—rather through the occupation of labor. Moderate the immoderate severity of abstinence, which also produces weakness in the mind; I think that this weakness is born from the same source as the presumption of writing.

Return to the royal road. Flee the anxious care that nourishes pride. Since we read, “It is not good to eat much honey” (Proverbs 25:27) (for knowledge inflates a poorly grounded understanding more than it builds it up), beware of excessive reading, so that you may recognize it as a dangerous drunkenness for a heart of little capacity, like wine taken in immoderate quantity.

Never trust your own thoughts. Rather, read what should be imitated than write what should be read. And speak to the Lord in your mind: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 118).

And if you desire to escape dangers that do not assail you from without but have been conceived within, know that nothing is more useful to you than to fortify your life under some other approved abbot and submit your wills to the rules of an elder. And so that you may overcome the ambushes of the adversary, I have thought that this little writing should be retained—or rather suppressed—lest it come into the hands and conscience of some other Catholic who might love you less.

From this you will be able to recognize that the innermost parts of your heart are sound if you continue, like a free man, to listen attentively and willingly to me, your humble and affectionate admonisher. Before your question, your persuasion will appear rash; after my answer, your intention will appear inexcusable. But if amid these matters you believe that something must be charged against me, who desire to heal your soul through austerities rather than sweetness, remember that the wounds of charity are to be preferred to the kisses of one who flatters deceitfully.

## LETTER VII [Note: This letter is numbered V in Canisius.]

To Ruricius, a most pious son and one singularly worthy of my highest honor in Christ, Faustus.

Although it is pleasant for me, through any person whatsoever, to converse with the individual heart itself in the words of charity and to embrace you with diligent eagerness in acts of service, yet now, the more opportune the occasion, the more eagerly I have received the pledge of your spirit through the service of a household bearer. In his merit, report assigned less than recognition proved.

Therefore I rejoiced that your benefit had increased, because in him a better life abolished the condition of his first birth; in him emancipation wiped away the stain of his lineage; and faith emancipated and transferred the person of the slave into the adoption of Christ.

As for how we ought to conduct ourselves toward his sincerity, and toward that of the remaining brothers, you have set forth the Apostle’s very broad dispensation (Philemon 1) in a ready address; and, though less learned, you affirm it with their most learned page. We nevertheless admired in their purified conduct, through the gift of gentleness and humility, the fullness of learning. For the generosity of grace conquers the established forms of teaching.

Although within a short time the bright purity of character and splendid simplicity had entered their luminous hearts and transparent inner chambers—through which the mirror of the divine image shines brightly in the purity of the inner person—this is indeed the divine image. For thus we read of the Lord: “Pure, simple, subtle.” But that divine simplicity indicates something quite different.

In us there is a twofold substance, in spirit and flesh. What we possess, we have received; different gifts of virtue have been added to us, not born within us. What can be taken away is undoubtedly added. To be good, we have borrowed from the goodness of the Author. From him we live, but we are not life as he is. We can be just, but we cannot be justice.

He is therefore simple because nothing has been conferred upon him from an added generosity. He who subsists from himself has taken nothing from elsewhere. God is both living and life; good and goodness; merciful and mercy. In the glory of his virtues, he is himself what man possesses only in name, as though gilded. God is gold; what is grace in man is nature in God.

And therefore, because nothing external has been added to him, nothing can be taken from him. He suffers no loss because he knows no increase. He is author both of himself and of the Son, because the origin of the fountain and of the stream is one. Among those things that possess being without beginning there is communion, not transfusion.

And because we read of the Son, “He is the splendor of God’s glory,” just as God was never without splendor, so the Father was never without the majesty of the Son. And just as their names are coeternal—for unless this one were born, the other would not be called Father—so the antiquity of one fatherhood joins them without separation. He is from him, but he is not later than him, just as a face is born from a head and yet is not found younger than its head.

Thus our God is neither mingled in his individual persons nor divided: one power, neither divided in authority nor in time. Just as subsistence is threefold, because each subsists for himself, so substance is simple, because the one who cannot precede himself neither admits a later nor an earlier.

From this simplicity we too have received our likeness, if there is nothing discordant, variable, or different within us; if we strive, through commendable pursuits and thoughts founded in Christ, always to be the same, so that, immutable in goodness, we may be changed only by new advances each day.

Concerning what someone, out of a desire to challenge, consulted, there is a salutary and perfect deliberation: to relieve the cares of the mind by distributing among several persons the administration of earthly affairs, and afterward, through a threefold consideration, to examine what is better—to place, administer, or dispose of one’s own portion.

The first and truly good course would be for Christ’s servant to strive to walk wholly as the poor Christ’s poor servant, if he were permitted to seek the school of some great monastery, or at least the military service of an island community of angels. For to profess the eremitical life in the midst of the world requires as much magnanimity as it does difficulty.

To impose upon one’s own vices the weight of one’s own [alternative: “elders’”] burdens, according to the abbreviated rule revealed for the soul. But it must be considered whether any of the sons might be capable of such arduous service. [Note: Corrupt passage.] Perhaps his paternal authority, by its sounds [alternative: “by its elders”], toward the father . . . . . It is best, at the second level, to remain under an administrator whose benefits are not harmful, if either the will is sufficient or the means have fulfilled the necessity of an annual payment.

The third is, through the chosen assistance of faithful servants and the duties of the administration entrusted to them, to govern under one’s own and lesser anxiety the amount of property retained, and to direct it along the royal road with complete moderation. When I advise this, I seem to be considering either our own advantage or that of the poor. In this arrangement there is no small profit if ownership is disposed of while use is retained.

Therefore, briefly indicating what is first, what second, and what third, we have left the choice to the judgment or ability of the one seeking advice. May he deign to indicate what is more suitable and can be fulfilled more readily—the one for whose fear and love this consolation itself is being considered. May the Lord our God multiply his benefits in us through a happy and pleasing longevity, most pious lord and son singularly worthy of my highest honor in Christ.

## LETTER VIII [Note: This letter is numbered VI in Canisius.]

To Ruricius, a most devoted brother and one singularly worthy of honor through every virtue of piety, Faustus.

By the favor of divinity, established in the secrecy of religion and in fitting, most tranquil silence, we are in a place where the Lord has admonished us, through the salutary file of chastisement, concerning the rust contracted by long security.

Here, I say, having been granted a great leisure—if we recognize it—as we acquire new citizens through the commerce of charity and rejoice in the salvation of those acquired, set amid these blessings we mock our present exile and recognize that we have not lost our father but exchanged him.

For while the faithful servants of God exercise the goodness of their devotion in our necessities, we are possessors without a home of our own and rich without possessions. Indeed, we enrich those who receive fruit from our consolation. In a wondrous manner our comforters trade with the poor and gain perpetual profits from the needy.

As for me, by the Lord’s generosity I received this first munificence: my most pious Ruricius, after the storms of this life, turned toward the harbor of religion and the prow of salvation, with the hand of the Most High guiding him. After the shadows of seductive vanities and the illusions of fleeting dreams, he desired what endures and is solid. Finally despising the wretched world, he seized its great art, acquired happiness and profit for himself from the perishing world, and, passing beyond the flight of collapsing things by faithful skill, transferred through his contempt the wealth that could no longer benefit anyone through its use.

Therefore, with as much eagerness as we once served secular pursuits, let us now serve the Lord with equal devotion. And because your piety compels me to speak more austerely with you for the healing of sins, it does not heed the offensiveness of that statement which says: “The just man is first of all his own accuser” (Proverbs 18:17).

Above all, therefore, let us avoid the fall of mouth and heart. But if you take care to guard the heart concerning what we have called the mouth, you will not labor to impose discipline upon the mouth. “He can easily place a door of restraint before his lips” (Psalm 140:3). For what is brought forth in the voice is first fashioned in the workshop of conscience. The exterior gives back what the interior dictates. The mind exercises authority; the tongue performs service. And therefore we are taught by heavenly discourse: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). What seems to arise from speech is first conceived in thought. Let the mind command what is just, so that the sound of the mouth may utter nothing unworthy.

And because there are two kinds of fasting, one is to restrain the appetite of incontinence from the dangerously enticing sweetness of pleasures, so that the exterior and earthly man, subdued by the plow of the cross, may grow lean through a beneficial weakness. The other kind of abstinence is far more exalted and far more precious, against which no weakness can prevail: to govern the movements of the soul; to restrain, by the judgment of the inner person, irrational disturbances and the tumult of thoughts struggling among themselves; to crush, by the authority of faith, a kind of angry conflict against hidden assaults or domestic enemies; and through benevolence, gentleness, patience, and tranquility to cultivate the image of God in the face of the inner person. The craftsman’s skill impressed its beauty not upon the form of the body but upon the form of the soul.

Let the man who thinks spiritual and divine thoughts not be broken by sadness or dissolved by joy. Let the magnanimity of constancy display a breast established in the fear of God, so that the notable opening of that little book may also be fitted to us, where the magnificent Elkanah, whose name is interpreted “possession of God,” is called “one man” in mystical speech.

“There was,” it says, “one man”—that is, always the same. For nothing doubtful, nothing double, nothing variable, nothing different appeared in him. Remaining in the steadfast state of his virtues in an unshaken order, he was not disturbed by things that turned against him; changeable times did not change him; nor, as is customary with great virtues, did light blasts of wind turn him in opposite directions.

So also the anxious servant of God, founded upon the vast mass of faith, is changed in this one respect—Christ working within him—that he may always be clothed with new graces. Let useful things be planted in the field of the heart; let harmful things be cut down.

And because divine Scripture gave this command to its soldiers: “When you go forth to war, and among the remaining spoils you seek a virgin, you shall cut off her nails and hair, and then join her to yourself in marriage” (Deuteronomy 21:12), so let us, girded by the fear of Christ, subject to spiritual wisdom the worldly prudence that is simple, incorrupt, sincere, and made by God, taking it captive; let us cut off its superfluities by removing its vices and join it to our breast in a chaste union.

Above all, insofar as we can with God’s help, let us strive to conquer within ourselves the passions of the five senses. For whatever becomes beautiful to the sight, whatever charms the sense of smell, whatever entices touch, whatever becomes sweet to taste, and whatever corrupts hearing—all these, if we abuse them, will drag the mind’s attention down from spiritual things to earthly ones.

Therefore, just as the father of faith (Genesis 14:14) conquered those five kings with three hundred and eighteen, with a mystery hidden in [lacuna], so, through the Lord’s help and through his cross, let us strive to conquer these allurements of the five chief vices. For through the sign of the cross and through the sacred name of Jesus, among the Greeks “Hera” [reading uncertain] is expressed in each of the two reckonings. With these weapons, those who overcome carnal delights will deserve to hear: “To the one who conquers I will give the crown of life.” And: “The one who conquers is not harmed by the second death” (Revelation 2).

Hence you easily despise earthly things, or distribute them as a lender does, while you contemplate the time when sinners will burn like hay, when they will be consumed by the heat of Gehenna in perpetual fury, whose smoke rises forever and ever (Revelation 8:7). Those who neglected what was offered will be punished by such a death that they will not be permitted to die in their pain: destined to die to life and to live forever for death.

While, I say, you arrange before your eyes with provident thought the time to come, concerning which we read: “I will enter your house with burnt offerings” (Psalm 65:13)—that is, when, laden with the fruit of good works and crowned with the insignia of righteousness, you enter the gate of life in triumph over conquered flesh—we read of that time: “The daughters of Tyre will worship him with gifts” (Psalm 45:13). That is, souls acquired for Christ from the nations will offer gifts not from their own resources, saying with thanksgiving: “Behold, I have multiplied the talent that you gave me. Receive your loan with interest, Lord.”

For then there will be a kind of commerce of giving and receiving between man and God. Man will bring what he has labored for, and God will restore what he promised. At that time, when one saint is to be rewarded for another and adorned with a double crown for mutual salvation, you will deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

Then you will marvel that the use of present things has passed into the possession of eternal things, and, to be glorified on behalf of your donors, you will rejoice that through a joyful change of circumstances you have become their debtor.

We greet our inseparable son Leontius and his entire household, together with its elders, with pious service. May the Lord our God multiply his benefits in you through a happy longevity pleasing to him, most devoted and singularly honored brother through the sole virtue of piety.

## LETTER IX [Note: This letter is numbered VII in Canisius.]

[Col. 0861B]

To the most devoted lord Ruricius, a son specially worthy of distinguished honor, Faustus.

Thanks be to the Lord, who in his general dispensation has granted that, among those whom distances of place separate, the free spirit may travel, confined by no laws of absence, and that nothing should be so impenetrable that it would not lie open to the eyes of the mind; so that through the vision of the heart the dear may behold one another from afar, with grace passing between them, where charity itself dwells.

Our inner self also has its eyes, by which it looks within itself as a witness to its conscience; by which, turned inward upon itself, it considers what ought either to cause shame or to bring joy; by which it sees the final day; by which, with prudent forethought for the future, it lays out before its soul the entire history of its life—whether bringing confusion or, by God’s grant, praise—and brings into the present the time of anxious concern when an account must be rendered; and by which it paints, on the secret page of its breast, through hope’s imagining, the things God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9). I think that you too continually raise these eyes to the throne of the awesome Judge, so that the prophetic saying may rightly be applied to you: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

This is why—for there, from him, “son, mother … [lacuna] … your …ditores.” [The text is corrupt.] This, I say, is why you entrust the supports of present things, which must be abandoned, like an eager moneylender, through the prices of captives, into the bosom of the one who repays, after the manner of one sowing; you turn use into possession and transform perishable things into everlasting treasures. This is why, together with your most faithful Sara, under the one yoke of Christ and striving toward a common crown, despising earthly things and seeking heavenly ones, a pilgrim of the age and a candidate for Paradise, you mock this world—which now has no means by which to deceive or seduce—as a soldier secretly serving Christ; and, as the companion of an unending kingdom, you knock at the gate of life with fasts, prayers, and, as it were, the hand of faith, in a pious conspiracy, so that you may receive a double palm for your mutual salvation.

Yet amid all this, whatever is being done here is little: here incurable causes must be healed; here unquenchable fire must be extinguished; here irresistible necessities must be overcome; here the arrows of sins must be torn from the inner parts of the soul; here wounds deeply impressed upon the very marrow must be healed; here invisible stains must be washed away; here eternal joys must be obtained through the labor of faithful devotion. There, indeed, life will be the reward of this; but it is necessary that this life be the price of that one.

Having therefore discharged the services mentioned above, I ask that, whenever opportunity fittingly presents itself, you make us rejoice in your welfare and prosperity. I offer abundant thanks for my sons and deacons. I respectfully greet my lady daughter, a mirror of religion and an example of piety, with the honor due to her. May our Lord God, who is to magnify your goodness toward me, both fill you with present blessings and make you worthy of eternal ones, most devoted lord and son specially distinguished by exceptional honor.

## LETTER X

[Note: In Canisius this letter is numbered VIII.]

[Col. 0862B]

To the most blessed lord, uniquely distinguished above all others by the highest honor in my eyes, my brother Bishop Ruricius, Faustus.

I have such confidence in the kindness of your spirit that I am no longer content to drink alone from its purest spring, but invite others also to refresh themselves with me by using it. Especially since the extension of this generosity becomes a gain for the giver, and the recipient is so enriched by its goodness that the one who imparts it is not diminished; indeed, according to the nature of interest, it grows through expenditure, most blessed lord, uniquely distinguished above all others by the highest honor in my eyes.

Accordingly, I render this unfailing payment of charity—by which the resources of the payer are increased the more they are extended—and presume, by commending the distressed, to present an occasion for a good work. For although I trust that my appeal concerns your benefit, and therefore could not refuse the bearer of this letter—who endured captivity at Lyon—the mercy that ecclesiastical humanity is accustomed to extend to the afflicted, would that the generosity of the faithful could be as ready as his need is plainly great! And because, although in some measure freed himself, he remains captive through the servitude of his wife or children, I ask that, in the exercise of your customary kindness, you show it also in comforting this man; and that you follow him with letters to those in authority, wherever he may ask.

My fellow servant and especially devoted admirer of yours, my brother the presbyter Memorius, joins me in sending you the most reverent greetings. May our Lord God preserve your pious blessedness, mindful of me, for the advancement of his Church, through a prosperous longevity, most blessed lord and brother uniquely distinguished above all others by the highest honor in my eyes.

## LETTER XI

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered IX.]

To the most blessed lord, to be received with the piety due to him and most worthy of the apostolic see, my brother Bishop Ruricius, Faustus.

We give thanks to you when we write to you from our homeland, because you have made our homeland present to us in our exile; through tireless generosity you have softened our longing for home, bringing a certain force of divine justice to bear through benefits succeeding one another: so that what he had inflicted for chastisement he might turn toward honor, confer for consolation, and change into rest for the mind; so that, overlooking our affairs, he might heap up yours; forgetting what was owed, and multiplying your gains; exercising the greatness of his goodness toward both parties, enriching us through your service and enriching you through our exile. Hence it came about that, even in the present, he distributed a blessing while we were impatient for the future, and, with mercy, justice, sincerity, self-restraint, and kindness cooperating—that is, with these household assistants—raised his most faithful servant high upon the lampstand of his house. Behold at what price my Ruricius purchased the supreme priesthood. What he bought is itself what he spent; and while his own witnesses acclaim him, he has displayed in himself the grounds of honor and the safeguards of honor. Only one who knew how to acquire such a great gift knows how to preserve it in Christ’s name.

I commend to you the holy presbyter Florentius, the bearer of this letter, known to me for a long time and adorned both by his teacher’s examples and by the flowers of his character; he is traveling for the release of his sister and has offered himself to me as a timely mediator. [Note: Perhaps “your.”] I greet all our household, elders together with juniors, with paternal affection. My fellow servants, your debtors and admirers, join me in sending you the most reverent greetings. May our Lord preserve your blessedness, which is to be magnified by me, for the advancement of his Church and for our joys, through a fulfilled longevity, most blessed lord, brother to be received with the piety due to him and most worthy of the apostolic see.

## PSEUDONYMOUS LETTERS

Written by Faustus to Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, under various names.

## LETTER XII

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered X.]

To Ruricius, a son to be magnified for the sublime honor of religion and the merits of faith, Graecus.

Thanks be to the Lord, because just as the merit of your faith advances through devotion, so it also grows through action. You anticipate the needs of those who labor through your concern, cherish them through kindness, and support them through humanity. By these means, in accordance with the Apostle—“fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12:11)—you acquire for yourselves the divine rewards of eternity. But these qualities are not new in your exalted position; for just as your spirit is full of the fear of God, so it is full of charity—charity, I say, which advances only through use, grows through giving, knows its due, and feels no loss. For while it is paid out, it is not spent; rather, while it is extended, it increases; and its grace so rewards the one who receives it, while the one who imparts it is not diminished, that, in the likeness of the Divinity, it gives what it has and has what it has given.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered XI.]

To the most blessed and most reverend lord, and in Christ my patron, Bishop Ruricius, uniquely observed by me with the honor due to him, Victorinus.

Although I was granted the opportunity to see your blessedness for only a very brief time and on only one occasion, nevertheless, at the first meeting of acquaintance and contemplation of you, you entered my senses through the purest spring of your kindly heart, so that, even if I cannot receive the precious gifts of your conversation, I nevertheless possess your presence in the depths of my mind; and, even if I receive no external causes for nourishing my longing, I find them within me whenever I remember your grace. For it is not right that the good which is established as infused into the marrow should require growth solely from aids arriving from outside. Hence the charity which, renewed by constant recollection of you in my innermost being, grows sweet, promises me a return of your charity. Thus my affection for you comes to me as a guarantor of your mind, and, in a certain way, the inner consciousness of myself stands by me as a witness to your mutual love. I ask my mind, which burns with the whole ardor of love for you, how much I ought to presume upon you.

Therefore, bringing greetings and seeking your intercession for the bearer of this letter, I offer inadequate thanks. Since his unhappy labor—by which he was driven through exiles in various regions for the release of his wife—was immediately rendered fruitless by the death of the woman who had been redeemed, and since paternal anxiety is now stretched taut once more for the redemption of his daughter, may you order that he be assisted by your letters, thereby increasing the abundance of your reward.

May the pious Lord deign to preserve your revered blessedness, precious to me, for the advancement and adornment of his Church, increasing you both in years and in merits, most blessed and most reverend lord, and in Christ my patron, uniquely observed by me with the honor due to you.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered XII.] (C)

To the holy and most blessed lord, my father, revered by me with every mark of respect and honor, and patron in Christ the Lord, Bishop Ruricius, Turentius.

[Note: Elsewhere, Turitius, Tureitius, Taurentius.]

The letters of your holiness, having nourished me with spiritual food, stirred me toward hope of the future; and your words, radiant with prophetic clarity, shone with the purest light to disperse the darkness of error. I recognize a disposition full of charity and the sincerity of pious correction. I embrace eloquence in your words, perfection in your examples, grace in your counsel, indulgence in your service, steadfastness in truth, and truth and knowledge in your admonition. In doctrine you approve the ancient interpreters of Scripture and expositors of the divine volumes—names revered by me: Cyprian, Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose—as well as other illustrious men blooming with the flower of eloquence; some spiritual in revealing more hidden things, some soothing the minds of the unlearned, and others fighting in defense of the faith. We reproach the former age because it did not produce men so worthy of admiration; those who taught before would certainly have sought the teaching of a younger man.

For my part, I do not recognize age from the husk of whitening hair, nor—as your blessedness borrowed from a secular author—from the color of a whitening beard. Even if I did not belong in the reckoning of old age, I would still feel the years of decrepitude through the increasing illness of my limbs. But with all humility of prayer I beg that, for the correction of my conduct, for inspiring in me the desire to repent, and for the propitiation of our Lord, you may plead for me in your holy prayers; so that you, who show the straight path—one to be walked with labor—to avoid the easy road sloping toward destruction, may obtain for me the effect of entering upon good work and pious amendment, not through the fervor of discipline, but through the medicine of indulgence and the gentleness of mercy. Grant me this reward also: you owe interest to the Lord from the treasury entrusted to your faith and received by you at his command.

Win over those who despair; rebuke the negligent; shake awake those devoted to the sleep of sluggish security; rouse the indolent. It is fitting for a good shepherd to carry the lost sheep back upon his shoulders and to enclose it in safer folds, into which the wolf lies in wait [the printed text is corrupt].

As you had ordered, I found Saint Augustine, whom I had thought to be with our common son, the presbyter Rusticus. You should admire my diligence: although I truly did not know until now what little works it contained, I have inspected the book section by section and am now about to return it. [Note: Perhaps “the book of chapters.”] It is a paper book, and not very strong in resisting damage, since, as you know, paper is quickly consumed by age. Read it, if you wish, and transcribe it. I hope that, once it has become well known to you, it will be returned to me, to whom it is unknown, because I intend to correct my negligence by repeated reading of the manuscript itself. Pray for me.

## LETTER XV

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered XIII.] (C)

To the holy and most blessed lord, to be received with apostolic reverence, Pope Ruricius, Sedatus.

I was sufficiently aware both of how arduous the journey would be for you and of how earnestly I wished you to come, even by some opportunity, to the necessity that brought us here: that I might receive your blessing, and that our common longing might be mutually satisfied by seeing one another. Indeed, after hope of your presence had disappointed me, as though I had been cast down from the summit of my prayers, the labor that fell upon me, the absence from home, and everything by which the distress of disappointed hope and anxiety are heaped upon the mind all came together in me. And the Lord knows that, if I had the strength, or if the weakness of my age permitted me to comply with my desires, or if there were animals by which so much traveling could be accomplished at such a time, I would not have returned from Toulouse before earning the most longed-for blessing of your blessedness and of that singular charity.

But because the matters mentioned above stand in the way of my desires, I ask—and adjure you by Christ—that your piety always present me to you. Do not allow love to diminish through delay in acts of service, or oblivion to obscure it; but, as I am certain you do, pray for me without ceasing, and whenever it is opportune, deign to visit your servant through the conversations of letters.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered XIV.] (C)

To the holy and most blessed lord, to be received with apostolic reverence, Pope Ruricius, and my special patron before the Lord, Sedatus.

Our son refreshed me by bringing news of your greeting. Through him, what letters have I received that I did not deserve? By this means I satisfied my longing, if at least a page of service might reach you. I therefore send you my warmest greetings and ask, by that charity which announces your affection and favor toward me, that you not be reluctant, whenever opportunity permits, to visit your servant through the gift of letters. For I testify before the Lord that, after your presence, nothing is sweeter to me than to have earned either a conversation expressing your most longed-for kindness or the favor of your letters. I also ask and entreat with every prayer that, as I am certain you do, you may deign to intercede and pray for me without ceasing. I greet our sons with both reverence and longing.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: In Canisius it is numbered XV.] (C)

To the holy lord, most blessed in merits, to be received with the honor due to his rank, and apostolic father, Lord Bishop Ruricius, Eufrasius.

I have learned through a slight rumor that your kindness is unwell; but I have sent the bearer of this letter so that you may quickly relieve my anxiety concerning the grievous report. For divine kindness knows that I share both your sadness and your illness—not the pain of one who merely sympathizes, but the pain of one who endures it with you. May divine mercy grant that, for many years, it may preserve for me the vigor of your outward appearance and the liveliness of complete health. For I truly feel myself restored when I learn quickly the good news I desire concerning your welfare.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: In Canisius likewise XVIII.] (C)

To the holy lord, most worthy to be set forth as a luminary in Christ and greatly desired in Christ, the most pious Lord Bishop Ruricius, Caesarius the bishop.

While my mind was greatly troubled that we had not been worthy to obtain your presence at the synod, my holy lord Bishop Verus deigned to tell me that, through his deacon Agate, he had sent me your letters. [Note: Perhaps “from your affection.”] I do not know by what chance or through what negligence I failed to retain them after receiving them. Nevertheless, I most certainly believe my holy lord and brother; and I prefer to attribute this to the negligence of the bearer. Although you sent your holy and desirable letters, nevertheless, as you yourself know very well, it would have been most fitting for you to send someone who could sign in your place, so that what your holy brothers had decided might be confirmed in your person.

But because I know with what holy, frequent, and pious desire you wished to be present among all your brothers, I explained your wish and holy intention; for this reason, we could neither have nor ought to have imputed anything to your kindness. Although we did not have the presence we desired, we nevertheless perceive that we were granted the assistance of your prayers. Therefore, with these words, I offer you greetings with the affection and honor that are your due, and I ask that you commend me to the Lord through your holy and illustrious prayers and merits. I also inform your kindness that your son Eudomius desires, if he can bring it about, that next year we should have a synod at Toulouse, with Christ’s favor, at which he also wishes the bishops of Spain to assemble, if possible. And therefore I pray [Note: Perhaps “pray.”] that the Lord may deign to grant effect to so holy a desire.

I commend to your holiness, with as much insistence as I can, my holy and sweetest brother, the presbyter Capillutus, your admirer and preacher. I offer you great and abundant thanks for him, because, as he himself has reported, your pious and sincere kindness has done so much for him that no human being could adequately express it. Now, since he came to seek your kindness, burning with desire for you, I judged it fitting to send through him this humble letter, so that, when he returns, if Christ permits, I may earn your letters as a heavenly gift. Pray for me.

## LETTER XIX (C)

[Note: The letter to which Sedatus replies is found in Ruricius, *Letters*, Book II, Letter 34, above, col. 110.]

[Col. 0867C]

To the holy and most blessed lord, to be received with apostolic reverence, lord and Pope Bishop Ruricius, Sedatus the bishop.

I received the horse you sent through our brother the presbyter, honored by the magnificent trappings of your words: worthless on the road, precious in the letter; moving when spurred or driven by blows, yet making absolutely no progress; most dreadful in form, cheapest in color, softer than feathers, slower than statues, fearful of solid bodies, but, as I believe, not accustomed to fear shadows alone; fleeing when released, motionless when beaten; standing on level ground, collapsing on rough ground; unable to be held, unable to walk. Before I had seen it, while rereading your letters, I believed it belonged to that race which Daedalian Circe—

> Having stolen bastards from a substituted mother, she created them.

I thought it spirited, swift in its running; when brought out, I expected it to breathe fire through its raised nostrils and to shake the fields with its solid horn; to outrun winds and rivers in speed. Such a creature had the splendid language of your letter promised me. I also believed that, while it was eating its bridle and grinding the iron with its teeth, two stronger men would hold it back lest it escape. Nor was I deceived; for several were dragging it, others were pushing it forward, and more were beating it. When I saw it presented in this condition, I wished that you would always send gifts to your friends as they actually were, not as my letter describes them.

Yet because you left me nothing to say in praise of the gift you sent, so that I might not altogether … [lacuna]

[Note: The manuscript joins what follows without any distinction. I separate it and indicate a lacuna. For, from this word, “which also,” to the end of this letter, everything is taken word for word from Sidonius, *Letters* II.1, which begins: “Your Arverni now suffer two evils at once. Which two, you ask? The presence of Seronatus and your absence. Seronatus, I say, concerning whose very name I shall first speak: fortune seems to me to have played, as though foreseeing the future, just as our ancestors, on the contrary, called battles—than which nothing is more shameful—wars; and, with equal contrariety, called the Fates Parcae because they did not spare. He returned,” and so forth, continuing to the end in the manuscript. I do not readily understand how this error occurred, so that part of Sedatus’s letter to Ruricius and part of Sidonius’s letter to Hecdicius were improperly joined here by the copyist, unless the scribe encountered a codex in which certain pages had fallen out. That such an error occurred here is clear from the index of letters at the front of the book, where, after this letter of Sedatus to Ruricius, various letters of Sidonius are listed, none of which is written in the manuscript codex. The index reads as follows:

“Letter of Sedatus to Ruricius. Letter of Sidonius to Constantius. Another of Sidonius to Eucerius. Another of Sidonius to Tetradius. Another of Sidonius to Asper. Another of Sidonius to Proculus. Another of Sidonius to Domnolus. Another of Sidonius to Nymphidius. Another of Sidonius to Simplicius. Another of Sidonius to Taumastus. Another of Sidonius to Ruricius. Another of Sidonius to Papianilla. Another of Sidonius to Patient. Another of Sidonius to Lupus, bishop of V. Another of Sidonius to Censor. Another of Sidonius to Mamertus. Another of Sidonius to Agraecius the bishop. Another of Sidonius to Sulpicius. Another of Sidonius to Ruricius. Another of Sidonius to Gothus. Another of Sidonius to Principius the bishop. Another of Sidonius to Remigius the bishop. Another of Sidonius to Faustus the bishop. Another of Sidonius to Heresius. The following contains two books of letters of our lord Bishop Ruricius. Then one book of letters of our lord Bishop Desiderius. Also letters of various persons to the same lord Desiderius.”

None of these letters of Sidonius is in the manuscript codex, except that a fragment of Sidonius’s letter to Hecdicius has been improperly joined, without any distinction, to a fragment of Sedatus’s letter to Ruricius. Immediately afterward the two books of Ruricius’s letters follow. I wished to call attention to this, for this passage had long tormented me. Canisius.]

[Col. 0868C]

[Note: What follows is from Sidonius’s letter to Hecdicius, Book II, Letter 1, above, col. 471.]

And likewise, by an equal contrariety, they called the Fates *Parcae* because they did not spare. This Catiline of our age himself recently returned to the Aturrians,

[Col. 0869A]

in order wholly to mingle the blood and fortunes of the wretched, which he had partly dealt out to them.

[Note: The manuscript reads these letters exactly. Savaro therefore correctly emended and marked it in Letter 1, Book II of Sidonius. The Aturrians are the people of Novempopulania, named from the river Aturrus—Aturres, just as from Astura come Astures, as Florus has it in Book IV near the end. Concerning the Aturrus and the Aturric fish, see Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 12. The city of the Aturrians appears in the *Notice of the Provinces* under the province of Novempopulania, which the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, in its account of Narbonensian Gaul, calls Adturrem; and what especially supports this ancient reading and Sidonius’s meaning is that at that time it belonged to the Gothic faction. *Timothy’s Memorandum*: “Anianus, a man of rank, at the command of Our Lord the most glorious emperor, edited and subscribed this codex from the Theodosian laws and legal opinions and various books at Aduris in the twenty-second year of his reign.” Commonly Aire. Canisius.]

Know that in him, day by day, the spirit of a long-concealed madness is being revealed. He openly envies, shamefully pretends, and arrogantly behaves like a slave; he imposes as a master, exacts as a tyrant, assigns as a judge, and slanders as a barbarian; armed all day by fear, starved of avarice, terrifying through greed, cruel through vanity. [Note: Sidonius, Book V, Letter 13, concerning the same Seronatus: “Now he drains them through unheard-of kinds of levies.”] [Note: The printed edition reads: “he does not cease at once either to commit or to punish thefts, openly and with laughing persons summoned.”] He never ceases either to commit thefts or to punish them, summoning people openly and amid laughter; he belches out battles among citizens and letters among barbarians. Though scarcely initiated even into the first letters, he dictates letters publicly out of boastfulness and corrects them out of shamelessness; he treats everything he covets as though he were buying it, neither respecting prices paid nor despairing of receiving documents.
