In council he gives orders; in deliberation he is silent; in church he jokes; at banquets he preaches; in his bedroom he condemns; during an inquiry he dozes. Every day he fills the forests with fugitives, the estates with enemies, [Note: The manuscript reads “with guests.”] the altars with accused persons, [Note: The manuscript likewise reads *reis*, although *rifis* is written in the margin.] and the prisons with clerics; exulting in the Goths and insulting the Romans, mocking prefects, [Note: The manuscript reads corruptly, “and shutting up the accountants.” The word has been erased in the middle and afterward joined by a mark from some other hand. See Savaro’s comments here concerning the accountants.] colluding with the accountants; trampling Theodosian laws and proposing Theodoric’s laws; seeking out old faults and new taxes. Therefore explain your delays more quickly. [Note: The printed edition reads “swiftly.”] And whatever it is that holds you back, cut it off. [Note: The manuscript reads “cut off.”] The last remnant of the freedom of trembling citizens awaits you. Whatever should be hoped for, whatever should be despaired of, let it be accomplished through you, under your leadership. If the republic has no strength, no defenses, if there are no resources of the emperor Anthemius—as rumor has it [Note: Thus I read with Savaro; the manuscript is defective here, reading “Ante.”]—then, with you as author, the nobility has resolved either to abandon the homeland or to cut their hair. Farewell.

# SERMONS OF BISHOP FAUSTUS

(C, G)*

## SERMON I. To the monks

(From the manuscript of Monsieur Chauvelin, keeper of the royal seals.)

[Col. 0869C]

1. Dearest brothers, we have come together in this place not for rest, not for security, but for battle and combat; we have advanced here for the contest, and have climbed up to wage war against vices. For our vices are our enemies, concerning whom Scripture declares: “Take care never to sit with them.” We need, brothers, vigilant care and unwearied watchfulness, because this conflict is without end and this enemy knows no peace. This enemy can be conquered, but cannot be received into friendship. And therefore the battle we have undertaken is sufficiently harsh and sufficiently dangerous, because it is waged between man and himself, and ends only with the man himself.

For this reason we have withdrawn to these tranquil and spiritual camps, so that, crushed each day, we may fight our passions through tireless engagement; so that each day, as though they were servants, we may subject our wills to our conduct; so that we may circumcise the wickedness of the heart or blunt the sword of the tongue. Let us not inflict injuries upon one another, nor even suffer injuries inflicted by others.

2. These matters belong especially to our profession: to seek no consolation and no honor in this life; to reject the comforts of present things and prepare the mind for the rewards promised by eternal recompense; to rejoice in submission and humiliation; to seek poverty deliberately; and to uproot from our hearts not only possessions but even our desires. For sometimes necessity requires having nothing as one’s own, whereas virtue requires desiring nothing.

3. We must also know that those of us who have decided to live this life are either diligent or negligent at great peril. Hence blessed is that soul which, while conducting itself well in the community, is a joy to many, and through which very many are either built up or enlightened. For good things, when shared with many, increase. To this the saying of that most wise man also refers: “My son, if you are wise, you are wise for yourself and for your neighbors” (Prov. 23:15).

Therefore, if someone placed in the community offers humility or patience to those who follow him, to the extent that he lends goodness to his neighbors from himself, to that extent he turns the gains of others into his own. But if, on the contrary, through disobedience or pride he seeks what is worse—and such a thing is usually found more easily—and attracts others to the example of evil or injustice, then, as many as he has destroyed, so great a danger of condemnation he incurs; as many as he has harmed, so many losses he has brought upon himself; and the sin that once departed from him will return to him multiplied.

Therefore, just as he is greatly to be admired and praised whose good course is the advancement of many, so he is not undeservedly to be mourned whose life is the ruin of many. For this reason, dearest brothers, let us strive, placed among others, to do those things that contribute to edification, lest our way harm the virtues of others; lest our sluggishness weaken the fervor of others; lest our anger violate the patience of others; lest our pride corrupt the humility of others; lest our ugliness contaminate the beauty of others; lest we extinguish the burning lamps of others if we cannot light our own.

Indeed, those foolish virgins, however foolish they were, did not wish to extinguish the lamps of others, but to light their own. Therefore, in imitation of them, if any one of us lacks the richest grace of humility, or lacks the fire of faith, the flame of fervor, the oil of charity, or the light of discernment, let him approach those whom he sees to possess these things more abundantly; let him transfer grace into himself from his neighbors, not by taking it away from them but by imitating them; and let him seize the good belonging to another, not only without the owner’s loss but even with the owner’s gain.

For a fire lit among many never suffers loss of light; nor does the multitude of those who behold it diminish the sun’s light. However many look upon it, to that many it lends its gifts, while it itself always remains whole.

4. Blessed by God is that soul whose humility confounds another’s pride; whose patience extinguishes another’s anger; whose obedience silently reproves another’s laziness; whose fervor rouses the inertia of another’s sluggishness; and which, through the grace of consolation and edification, illuminates the eye of the heart of a neighbor troubled by anger.

Better is such a person than the one who, when a brother has been somewhat saddened by someone, does not lift him up by extending a hand of consolation, but, like a leaning wall, helps him toward ruin by pushing him with evil speech; and, when he has been corrected salutarily according to the demands of discipline, so spurs him on through sinister counsels that he dashes him to pieces, and so arms him that he destroys him.

5. Therefore, brothers, the one whose own evils are not enough acts in such a way that he also incurs judgment for another’s destruction. We are certain, dearest brothers, that unless we take care, unless we daily cut away and circumcise our passions, we shall become much worse than we were when we lived in this world, so that our last state will become worse than the first.

Indeed, dearest brothers, as long as we were serving the things belonging to the world, in those actions and occupations of which we are now ashamed, our adversary did not oppose us; rather, he consented, because, concerning our wretched and ruined life, he found nothing in which to exercise his envy. Our deeds delighted him, and our crimes and sins were sufficient for him by themselves. For who would undertake war against his own soldier, and who would wish to attack his own subject? Yet the life of the one whom the enemy disdained to harm was beyond all misery.

But now, after we have renounced his pleasures, he has seen his worshipers return to the service of their former master; he has seen in us, in a certain sense, his idols changed into God’s temple. Gnashing his teeth and roaring like a lion, the ever-watchful ambusher searches out every avenue of harm. The Apostle gives fitting testimony concerning this lion: “Be watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

Blessed are those whom this lion judges worthy to seek and pursue, following the tracks of their virtues and the scent of their merits. For he seeks only the good, since the wicked thrust themselves upon him voluntarily. He runs violently after the former; he attacks the latter even negligently. Blessed, therefore, are those whom this lion is compelled by envy to seek, but whom his malice is not permitted to find.

“Like a roaring lion” certainly sounds terrible in our ears when we hear it. But since it is said, “His prey is choice,” what he seeks is a matter of election, while what he roars is a matter of despair. As we read elsewhere: “He will gnash with his teeth and waste away.” Thus the divine word speaks in such a way that consolation is joined to terror. “He will gnash” is indeed bloody; but the defeated creature is the one that wastes away. Thus, amid how great are the things God has prepared for humanity, the enemy’s envy is made manifest.

## 6

Therefore, dearest brothers, considering these things and laboring in this contest, let us remember that we are disciples and sons of our glorious and distinguished father [Note: There can be no doubt that this was Saint Honoratus, who founded and governed the monastery of Lérins; Saint Faustus was speaking to its monks, and he too had previously been a monk of that place before becoming its bishop.] Let each of us seize whatever we can from the goods of a parent who died intestate. Let one take from the inheritance the precious, all-silk fabric of faith’s varied deeds. Let another take possession of the talent of gentleness and simplicity. Let another claim for himself the ornament of his heart, the necklace of benevolence and wisdom. Let another seize the pearl of compunction and the treasure of chastity. For although that most wealthy friend of God carried away with him all that he possessed intact, he nevertheless left everything to us, if only we desire it. Let us therefore pursue his good deeds, so that he who will be raised up and restored to eternal glory at the end of the ages may now already rise again in his children, through their merits, as the divine offspring of the Church.

# SERMON II. To the Monks

### 1

That, with God supplying and, in a certain sense, commanding it with love through your brotherhood, I bring forth whatever sort of sermon I can, I do not do from any presumption, but from true and complete charity. And although, by God’s favor, you are so perfect that you have no need at all of our admonition, nevertheless, since charity—which knows no fear—commands it, we presume, with true humility and perfect love, to suggest and admonish you even about what we know you fulfill exceedingly well. We do so not without embarrassment, since we know ourselves not yet to be competent disciples, while we seem to be rousing masters to holy work.

Though we are lukewarm, we are compelled to admonish the fervent; though we are sinners, we rebuke the just; though we are unlearned, we instruct teachers; though we are tossed about on the sea of this world by excessive waves, we speak words of exhortation to those who have reached the harbor so happily.

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, because ships, even after overcoming and conquering the waves of the sea, often labor in the safest harbor and, unless there is great caution, are almost submerged, we admonish you with the greatest humility and immense reverence: since Christ has freed you from capital crimes as from dangerous waves and has established you in the harbor of peace and blessedness, hasten continually, with all vigilance and with Christ’s help, to drain away the small negligences and, as it were, trivial sins that flow together in the soul just as drops gather through the tiniest cracks in a ship into the bilge.

For just as a ship, after escaping the waves of the sea, is filled and sunk by tiny drops if its bilge is not pumped out in the harbor, so also a monk, after conquering and overcoming the crimes of this world as dangerous waves, when he has reached the harbor of the monastery, will encounter the danger of shipwreck in that very harbor if he neglects to drain from the bilge of his soul the creeping vices and small, daily sins.

But someone may say: How can the soul be pumped out? Certainly, by praying, fasting, keeping vigil, and showing true charity, true humility, and true obedience. Consider, brothers, how a ship is pumped out by a bucket; so the soul is freed from evil works by the Lord’s Prayer, if one says—and says truly: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). For whoever has mercifully forgiven all who sin against him will leave no trace of any sin in his soul.

Attend, brothers, and consider what I said. I said “whoever has forgiven one who sinned against him”; I did not say “whoever sinned against God,” to whom you ought to grant pardon—which is worse. Sometimes we grant forgiveness late or with difficulty to one who has sinned against us; we forgive quickly one who has offended against God. But if we wish to act justly, we ought not to forgive one who has sinned against God without the strictest discipline, lest, while he is pardoned through indiscriminate compassion, he be offered as an example of destruction to others.

Let each person therefore show himself merciful in matters concerning himself, because the Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (ibid., 14).

### 2

When someone presumes to commit a sin against God, he ought to endure monastic discipline. This should be done with a pious intention, so that by spiritual correction he may be amended in this world and not perish in the next; for every sin that is not corrected in this world will be punished in the world to come.

Thus divine Scripture speaks concerning a son and a servant: “You will beat him with the rod,” it says, “and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Prov. XXIII, 14). Therefore, as I suggested above, let us beware not only of capital crimes but also of the small negligences that we breathe in daily, as it were, the poisons of the devil.

There are some who, after professing religion—by which they appear to have left the world—are relaxed by excessive security, and in them is fulfilled the Lord’s sentence: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III, 15). What does he mean by saying, “Would that you were hot or cold”? Now, because you have withdrawn from the world but have refused through your negligence to embrace spiritual fervor, you have become lukewarm; you will scarcely be vomited out again from the Lord’s mouth so as to be received.

### 3

Therefore, dearest brothers, heed carefully the sentence of divine Scripture: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23). Just as we ought to rejoice over a monk who chooses to display gentleness, obedience, and patient meekness and humility in the monastery, so, conversely, we ought to mourn over one who appears to have left this world only in body but is known either unfaithfully to have remained in the world in his heart or unhappily to have returned to it; who puts forward pride instead of humility, anger instead of patience, contempt instead of obedience, and pours out the poison of malice instead of the medicine of charity.

To such people applies that true and greatly feared sentence of blessed Peter: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Pet. II, 20). And again: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (ibid., 21).

But even concerning such people we must not despair, brothers, because God is able, through your prayers, to kindle the spark of compunction and to consume every pleasure of the world, like thorns and thistles of wickedness, in a saving fire—that fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XXI, 49).

### 4

Pray, therefore, dearest brothers, not only that God may deem you worthy to grant you good perseverance, but also that those who are negligent may at last lift themselves from the pit of pride and escape its snares. If, through your prayers and the counsel you give with charity, any who are lukewarm and negligent are corrected, the Lord will graciously repay you with a doubled reward, both for your own correction and for theirs.

Neither should those who are good exalt themselves as though on account of their own merits, nor should those who are negligent despair of God’s mercy. Rather, let the former preserve God’s blessings with humility, and let the latter, with great compunction, flee quickly to repentance or to the medicine of correction. For if one who is good begins to grow proud, he will be humbled; and if one who is proud humbles himself, he will be raised up through God’s mercy.

Only let him not allow himself to be pressed any longer beneath an exceedingly hard yoke, nor, by persevering in sins through excessive and dangerous concealment, become hardened for too long. Let him flee to God’s mercy so quickly that no trace of sin remains in him. A poultice or bandage is best applied while wounds are still hot, because if the intention of rising again turns swiftly to the heavenly physician, the trace of sin cannot remain with the fallen person: beneath the hand of the almighty physician, the disease quickly perishes and the sick person is rapidly healed.

### 5

Again and again I ask and admonish you, brothers, to strive continually to show obedience, humility, and charity not only toward elders and equals but also toward juniors. For whatever good a servant of God strives to possess, he loses everything with great speed if true humility and charity are not found in him.

Do not murmur, brothers, for it is written that those who murmured perished by serpents. Do not speak evil of others, brothers, for it is written: “The one who speaks evil of his brother will be uprooted.” Do not retain anger in your heart, for it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James II, 20). Do not hate one another, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 15).

But there is no need for us to teach your holy charity at greater length in words, since we both know and rejoice that you fulfill it in deeds, to the glory of Christ. We ask only this in particular: since God has graciously placed you in a dwelling of rest and tranquility, pray more abundantly to the Lord for us, whom the storms and countless waves of this world afflict, so that, if glory is not granted to us who do not deserve it, at least, through your prayers, forgiveness of sins may be granted to us. Amen.

# SERMON III. To the Monks. On Penance

Let public penance be assigned to the worldly person whose neck still hangs beneath the yoke of the world, and let a period be fixed for him according to the enormity of his offense, since time still serves him. But if someone renounces the world and its service and promises that he will serve God all his days, why should he deserve penance once he has been made free and, like a wild ass, pursues the desolation of the wilderness, as Job says: “Who has released the wild ass to freedom in the desert?” (Job XXXIX, 8).

Let him guard himself courageously from the lion, and let him be nourished in the desert on parched grasses and a scant drink. Let him raise his head into the air, and let the breeze of the Holy Spirit extinguish the excessive burning of thirst, lest, while he greatly desires pleasant green places, he be hindered by excessive delights and incur the danger of salvation.

Therefore public penance is not necessary for one who renounces the world, because he has turned back with lamentation and entered into an eternal covenant with God. From that day, therefore, the offenses he committed in the world are no longer remembered—the day on which he promised God that henceforth he would practice righteousness. [Note: From this it is evident that religious profession is a second baptism, by which all sins committed in the world are washed away; other holy Fathers also teach this explicitly.]

Therefore, after the written pledge [Note: The covenant by which monks devoted themselves to serving God perpetually was committed to writing; Saint Benedict later prescribed the same in the Rule, chapter 58.] in which the monk has promised in complete faith that he will fulfill his obligation, even if, after becoming a believer, he has sinned in the world, after making his renunciation anew he should not hesitate to receive the Lord’s body, lest, under the pretext of excessive humility, he be kept away from the body and blood to which he has joined himself in order to become one body.

Therefore, let the one who has ceased from sinning not stop receiving Communion; only let him not sin thereafter. For just as this visible fire has two powers within itself—namely, to burn what is frail and to illuminate what is dark—so that fiery body of the Lord, when it has been received with fear and great reverence, consumes the sins of the body but illuminates the understanding of the soul. And for this reason he ought to receive Communion especially and more frequently.

But if, as it is written, there is leprosy on the skin, it will be unclean—that is, if there is sin in the monk, because Scripture declares that the monk is the skin, mortifying his members upon the earth. Flesh clings to his bones; it is changed because of oil, weakened by fasting, and, fasting, withers like hay. Therefore, if leprosy appears on this skin, it will be unclean, and unless it is hyacinth-colored or pure red, it will not be suitable for the adornment of the tabernacle.

# SERMON IV, OR A NECESSARY EXHORTATION ON THE DAY OF JUDGMENT, THE PUNISHMENT OF THE WICKED, AND THE GLORY OF THE GOOD; AND THAT EVEN LAYPEOPLE CAN AND OUGHT TO DO PENANCE DAILY WITHOUT CHANGING THEIR CLOTHING. To the Monks

*(From a Corbie manuscript written in Merovingian script a thousand years ago.)*

I ask you, dearest brothers, that, as I have often admonished you, we continually strive to consider the day of our death and the terrible and fearsome judgment. For I admonish you that wounds of sin can find no more useful remedies than for each person to consider that hour when he will depart from this world. How can someone presume to commit any sin if he believes that at every moment he may depart from this life?

Thus Scripture says: “Remember, son, that death does not delay” (Eccli. XIV, 12). And again: “Remember the last things, and you will cease from enmity” (Eccli. XXVIII, 6). Whoever carefully considers how harsh the examination will be before Christ’s tribunal, where each person will receive according to his work, cannot find his own sins or crimes pleasing.

When all nations have been gathered before that dreadful judge, what will then befall the unjust, adulterers, and rapacious? The weeping of eyes and the gnashing of teeth, while they see themselves separated from the multitude and glory of the saints at the right hand of the eternal King, and the people of sin plunged into the depths of Tartarus without any end to compassion or forgiveness; excluded in their darkness from the blessed light of the saints and descending without end into the depths of hell, where eternal punishments and everlasting death—which does not die—will press their mouths into the pit.

In vain he asks for the tip of Lazarus’s finger, begging that it be placed upon his burning, parched lips to cool them. Therefore, dearest brothers, while it is still permitted, let us examine our consciences. And if we recognize that any crimes or capital sins not yet cleansed by almsgiving and prayers still rule within us, let us hasten, with Christ as our guide, to enter the harbor of penance after conquering the waves of sin. If we recognize that anything in the little boat of our soul has been damaged by the many storms of sin—through greed, pride, or wrongful desire—let us hasten to repair or restore it by good works.

Past sins do not harm us if they no longer please us. Just as the righteousness of no just person is sufficient if he does not persevere to the end, so the wickedness of no sinner can harm him if, before departing from this body, he flees to the remedies of almsgiving or the medicine of penance.

But because we cannot know when or at what hour we shall be snatched from this world, let us flee without any delay or hesitation from the left to the right. For one must not trust health or age as a lasting remedy for salvation . . . [the intervening text is corrupt or lacunose] . . . he delays, because he is extremely uncertain of his life. For the one who made us secure by saying to the sinner, “On whatever day he turns back, all his iniquities will be consigned to oblivion” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12), also wished us to be cautious, saying: “Do not delay turning back to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Eccli. V, 8).

But perhaps, when all are generally summoned to penance, someone thinks within himself: “I am a young man with a wife; how can I either cut my hair or assume religious clothing?” We are not saying this, dearest brothers; we are not preaching that young men who appear to have lawful marriages ought to change their clothing rather than their morals.

What harm does it do a married man if he refuses to retain corrupt morals and turns to good and honorable works, restoring the wounds of his sins to their former health through almsgiving and prayers? True conversion is sufficient without a change of clothing. Religious clothing, however, without good works, will not only be unable to provide a remedy but will also endure God’s just judgment.

Let us therefore turn to better things while remedies remain in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins. Here let us acquire life through the merits of life, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON V

[Note: This sermon and the following one were transcribed at my request by the learned Dom Remigius Seiller of the Congregation of Saint Vannes, from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Morbach, which bears the name of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, along with other sermons commonly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa, but which learned men restore to Faustus, bishop of Riez.]

To the Monks. On Holy Easter Day

*(From a Morbach manuscript.)*

### 1

Appropriately and fittingly, on this distinguished day of today’s solemnity, we rise with a voice of rejoicing and say with the Apostle: “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). Today, the Egyptians having been slain, the people of God are freed from mud and straw—that is, from the vilest and most empty works. Today that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is offered for the redemption of human salvation; when we are commanded to inscribe the doorposts of our houses with his blood—that is, to have our foreheads marked with the sign of the cross—so that the destroying angel may find no place.

At this time Pharaoh and his army are cast down in the Red Sea, while sins perish in the sacred font, as the Egyptians are plunged into the Red Waves—that is, waves consecrated by Christ’s blood. At this time, upon the return of the younger son who had been lost and was found—that is, for the salvation of the Gentiles—the fattened calf was sacrificed. We are the younger son; while the elder brother, that is, the Jews, delay and refuse to enter, we return to our Creator in repentance for our sins.

For we had overturned and squandered the substance received from God our Father. Let us see what substance this was: the goods of the whole of nature. Everything by which we live, understand, and think is God’s substance. Understanding and reason for distinguishing good from evil are God’s substance. So too is the freedom of choice that we had received, whether for avoiding the allurements of sin, for stirring the inclination of free will toward obedience to the Creator, or for preserving the image and likeness of God.

These riches, therefore, given to us and implanted within us by the Creator, we had transferred to corrupt uses and consumed in the practice of vices. We had abandoned the fountain of virtues and traveled far away from our Father—not departing from him in places and regions, but in hearts and deeds. Whoever follows his own desires and is carried away by his passions becomes an exile from God.

When, having acknowledged our sins, we return to him—and return not by the movement of the body but by the inclination of the mind—he comes to meet us with immense mercy, ineffable joy, and consolation. He enters the celebration of the feast; he arranges dances and harmonies, that is, the exultations of heavenly joys with which the angels rejoice in heaven over one sinner who repents.

When, therefore, we return to amendment, this feast is celebrated daily. Daily the Father receives his children; Christ is continually sacrificed for believers. This, then, is the fattened calf that we are taught to offer in the Old Testament: a bull-calf from the herd, that is, one descending from the patriarchs and prophets, from the seed of Abraham; a male without blemish.

“Male” means strong and powerful against every sin. For it is the mark of a masculine and manly spirit to break the allurements of sin, just as it is the weakness of a feminine spirit to accept the wantonness of vice. Hence Pharaoh, who represented the devil, pressing upon the people of God—hostile to the spirit and friendly to the flesh—was strangling strength and nourishing desires.

### 2

Christ therefore died for our iniquities, and “as a sheep he was led to the slaughter; and as a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7). This is the Lamb whom the law commands us to eat in one house, with our loins girded. What does it mean to eat the head with the feet in one house? It means that we are commanded to receive his flesh within the unity of the Church.

The Arians, therefore, and the various perversities of heretics do not eat him in one house. Therefore, just as in the Flood no one was saved except the one found inside Noah’s ark, so people of various faiths, if they are outside the house of the Church, do not possess the Lamb, who is Christ.

That Scripture says we ought to eat the head of this Lamb together with the feet means that we should venerate God and man with an equal confession. The head is the divine substance; the feet are the human substance. Let us understand the head from what blessed John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). Let us understand the feet from what the Apostle Paul writes: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II, 7); and, “Made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV, 4).

It was therefore necessary that we feed on the flesh of such a Lamb with our loins girded—that is, with our carnal passions put to death—with the greatest purity of heart and body. Let us believe that he was begotten from God and produced from man.

When I said “begotten from God,” perhaps some of the less learned may say in their hearts: “How did God beget a son?” Let us imagine nothing bodily here. For what is “God begot God” except that fire appeared from fire and light proceeded from light?

Therefore, for the sake of some who are slow to understand, let us now take some image or comparison from earthly and visible things. For example, if one lamp is lit from another, if one is illuminated from another, does it not seem to you that flame, in a certain way, gives birth to flame and splendor to splendor? Does it not seem to you that light was born from light by an immeasurable process?

And when fire is transferred from lamp to lamp, although two lamps burn, nevertheless the very same fire shines in the second as in the first. Was that fire made from nothing or from some new beginning? Rather, it was poured forth from the nature of its own splendor. Therefore, the illumination that appears to have been kindled from the first lamp did not begin to exist in the second as if from nothing; it proceeded from a related splendor that already remained in the origin of the first light.

And although in both lamps a twin and double flame appears to flicker, both are nevertheless one substance. So too, in the only-begotten Son of God, although the form of the person is proper to the genus, the nature is nevertheless common: he does not begin from the Father but subsists from the Father and with the Father.

### 3

Everything was created from nothing; he alone is God from God. Therefore, when he was in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant for the salvation of servants. Though he was life, he was hung upon the wood of the cross, as though he were weighing himself out as the price of the lost. He was struck with blows and crowned with thorns.

That he was clothed in a scarlet cloak signifies that the merits of the saints are Christ’s garments; likewise, at that time he is drenched in the blood of the martyrs in that scarlet color. When the Jews, whether they wished it or not, adore him clothed in a purple cloak with bent knee, they confess him as King and Lord.

When he said on the cross, “I thirst,” he was seeking faith from his own people. But because he came to his own and his own refused to receive him, they offered him the vinegar of unbelief instead of the sweetness of faith. They extend the vinegar of malice because, by sinning, they had lost the wine of wisdom that they had received from Christ. He drinks the bitterness of our evils, while he will give the sweetness of his blessings.

Even now, whenever he is saddened and embittered by sins, a kind of vinegar, a drink and food of gall, is poured into him daily. The veil of the Temple is torn. The veil is the adornment of the dwelling place. When grace therefore flashes forth, the Church is built and the Synagogue destroyed; the Temple is stripped of the honor of the veil, the veil of the letter being removed through Christ’s coming, so that, with unveiled face, the inner things of the law may be disclosed with the Apostle.

When the tombs are opened, the barriers of death are unfastened; when the abode of Tartarus is opened, the saints rise with Christ; and he whom the heavenly realms do not receive is recognized as God by the lower realms.

Therefore, recognizing the profound mysteries of the divine benefits bestowed upon us, let us respond to the mercy of the Redeemer as we are able. Let us offer him compunction through the amendment of our sins in place of his thorns; let us offer him a heart pierced by its own fear in place of his nails; let us return to him the palm of perseverance in place of his blows.

# SERMON VI. To the Monks. On the Feast of Saint Peter

*(From a Morbach manuscript.)*

### 1

Honoring the most glorious leaders of the Christian faith with yearly solemnities, dearest brothers, we venerate with due devotion God and our Lord himself, who is the author of this faith. For apostles are called *missi*—“sent ones”—in Latin. Therefore, whoever honors those who were sent plainly honors the one who sent them, since the dignity shown to ministers is undoubtedly offered to the one whose ministers they are, as the Savior himself says to his disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever receives you receives me” (Luke X, 16).

Truly blessed are the merits of the apostles, in whom Christ declares that he is both received and heard; no less blessed are those whose devotion, offered to the apostles, returns to Christ.

Holding fast, therefore, brothers, to the faith of so great a promise, let us rejoice with faithful joy over the sufferings endured by our fathers in confession of Christ, since whoever rejoices in the death of martyrs does not doubt that the martyrs reign with Christ after death.

Let us honor with the most devout zeal the most revered fathers of all the Churches, Peter and Paul, through whose death, by Christ’s gracious gift, a birthday has come about today. For them the end of life gave a beginning to living; for them, as the Apostle Paul says, “to live was Christ, and to die gain.”

Christ was their life, since life was not life for them without Christ. Christ was their life because everything that they lived benefited Christ’s Churches. And to die was gain for them because by such a death they earned eternal life; to die was gain for them because corruption was followed by incorruption, and the losses of present times were followed by everlasting gains.

But now, dearest brothers, I think it necessary to speak of their individual and particular virtues, insofar as the dryness of our tongue and the weakness of our talent permit—or rather, insofar as merciful God grants it.

### 2

This, then, is that Peter who, by confessing Christ the Lord to be the Son of the living God, established for us foundations of faith that are most strong and unconquerable. When the Lord asked who people said he was, he replied: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16).

That is: You, Lord, made from the flesh of the Virgin, are Christ, who are eternally the Son of the living God. You, Lord, born as a human being among human beings, are God with God in an incomprehensible majesty. You are the Christ who, coming to passion for our redemption, remain impassible with the Father.

Who, then, could ever have lifted the gaze of human understanding to so great and incomprehensible a mystery of the Godhead, unless the truth of this saving faith had shone forth from Peter’s mouth? Who could match the glory of his merits, however great his eloquence, from whom the faith in the divinity we must adore both began for us and continues?

What could be more glorious than such a man, who proclaimed the faith of an inscrutable mystery by speaking, taught it by living, and confirmed it by suffering?

To show how great the confession was, the Savior said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” And: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 17).

Who, therefore, could have understood that Christ, born through flesh and in the flesh, was the Son of the almighty Father, unless that Father himself, in his favor, had revealed this to us from heaven through Peter?

This confession granted him the keys of the heavenly kingdom before he entered the gates of heaven. But, brothers, lest any thought of Peter’s keys of the kingdom lead you to think of them as ordinary keys, the tongue of Peter is the key of heaven, because the apostle, judging the merits of individuals, either closes or opens the kingdom of heaven to each person.

This key, therefore, was not fashioned by the hand of a mortal craftsman; it was the power of judgment given by Christ. Finally, he says to him: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 23).

This is Peter, whose most confident belonging to Christ was proved by the seas subjected beneath his footsteps. He asked his Lord to give him new steps upon the waves, as a faithful servant, and he earned them as one beloved. He seemed to tremble for this reason alone: so that human frailty might recognize how great the distance is between Lord and servant, since flesh weighed down by sins is submerged, while the foot of the immaculate does not know how to sink. It also happened so that, if Peter had reached Christ with an unafraid foot while walking upon the waters, he might perhaps have seemed equal to the powers of his Lord.

But why do we say that he trembled so greatly, when his devout trembling made him advance all the more in faith? For just as Peter believed that, at his Lord’s command, he could be sustained upon the waves, so likewise, while he was sinking, he believed that he would be saved by the power of that same Lord.

Truly blessed Peter’s faith was wondrous even while he trembled; fear of pressing danger could not disturb it. For when he cried out as he was sinking, “Lord, save me!” (Matt. VIII, 25), he distrusted himself, not the Lord.

Let no one therefore count this fear of the most glorious Peter as a fault. Although this fear disturbed his faith at first, it nevertheless adorned the confidence of faith restored in him.

This is Peter, to whom Christ willingly granted a share in his own name. For just as the Apostle Paul teaches that Christ was the rock, so through Christ Peter was made a rock, when the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18).

For just as water flowed from the rock in the desert for the Lord’s thirsty people, so, for the whole world exhausted by the dryness of unbelief, a fountain of saving confession emerged from Peter’s mouth.

This is Peter, to whom Christ, when he was about to ascend to the Father, entrusted his little sheep and lambs to feed, so that the ones whom Christ had redeemed through the compassion of his mercy Peter might preserve through the power of his faith.

And rightly indeed the Judge of God’s hidden things entrusted his sheep to be fed and guarded to the one in whom he knew there was neither lack of zeal nor lack of faith in nourishing the Lord’s flock.

This is Peter, who, when he was being led to the cross like a disciple of the crucified one, requested that he be crucified with his body turned upside down. He did not reject the passion, but avoided equality with the Lord’s cross, so that he might show to all the virtue of admirable humility and preserve, even amid torments, the discipline of a new mystery.

How confidently, dearest brothers, Peter went to the cross—he who, having cast away fear of death, sought such an order of dying amid so bitter a passion.

### 3.

What, moreover, shall I say of the most glorious Paul, in whom the Lord chose faith in his name even while Paul himself was persecuting it? While, like the fiercest persecutor, he was laying waste the Christian Church, Christ found in his still-hostile breast a heart that would become his friend. While he was seizing Christians for temporal punishments, he himself was taken captive forever for grace; suddenly he became a shepherd from a wolf, a guardian from a bandit, a defender from an enemy. Thus it became clear both that Paul did not persecute the Lord’s people with a purpose rooted in evil intent, and that Christ was not unaware of whom he would choose in Paul.

This is Paul, who, summoned from heaven by the voice of Christ, with the eyes of his Jewish unbelief blinded, did not lose his power of sight but changed it. He lost his eyes and received them again, so that at one and the same time the punishment of blindness might proceed against the persecutor, and the grace of the God who was calling might enlighten the Church. For the Lord said to him from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4)—that is, “Why are you persecuting me, Saul? What wickedness of mine has aroused your hatred against me? Is it because I have given sight to the blind, because I have healed the sick, because I have driven out demons, because I fed hungry crowds with five loaves? Or [Col. 0882D] because I raised the dead from their tombs? Or perhaps rather because I promised my faithful the kingdom of heaven? But if you doubt that I can grant what I promise, look—if indeed you can—at the one from whom, as though addressing you, I speak. But why are you persecuting me, Saul, or what do you gain by persecuting me? Will your persecution have any effect against one who reigns in heaven? Will you be able to harm me in any way, whom you are unable to see? For I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 22:8)—I who have exchanged earth for heaven, the cross for a kingdom, and death for eternity. Concerning all these things, you should have no doubt; the sight that has now been taken from you and shortly afterward restored to you will convince you.

But blessed Paul, restrained by sudden blindness, nevertheless understood the majesty of the one speaking from heaven. He immediately became faithful, abandoned persecution, and acquired new eyes with which to see Christ. This is Paul who, as a reward for his virtues, was caught up beyond human merit to the third heaven and came to know heavenly secrets, so that, destined to become a teacher of the Churches, he might learn among the angels what he would preach among human beings. Who, then, would thereafter refuse to believe him with impunity, since he speaks not only of what he has heard concerning the Lord’s mysteries, but also bears witness to what he has seen?

How great, brothers, was this act of the grace of our God: that he was called from heavenly places to the apostolate, so that his apostleship might be consecrated in heaven! And after all this, this is Paul who submitted his neck—once proudly raised against the name of Christ—to be struck by the sword of the ungodly, in the deepest humility for Christ’s honor. Nor was he reluctant to die for him whom he had often proved to live and reign after death.

And so it came to pass that glorious Paul, who in various nations had fought for the faith of Christ through arduous struggle and waged countless battles, was received by Rome in triumph as the conqueror of the world. These, therefore, are the most blessed Peter and Paul. Proclaiming with one spirit the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, they consecrated their teaching with devoted blood and most courageous death on the same day of suffering. Having also been made, by heavenly dispensation, as it were the princes of all the Churches, they went to Rome and buried their most sacred bodies in the citadel of that city, which had held sovereignty over the whole world, so that Christ, displaying the power of his might, might place the princes of his kingdom where the world had its imperial capital.

## SERMON VII. To the Monks

[Col. 0883C]

Divine discourse instructs and urges us concerning how we ought to gird ourselves to seek its promises and obtain those goods which cannot be grasped by sight, perceived by hearing, or comprehended by thought. “Ask,” it says, “and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you”—that is, let us ask by praying, seek by laboring, and knock by persevering; and let us be urged toward hope of heavenly things with such zeal and burn with such desire that the greatness of our desires may correspond to the dignity of the rewards.

For our God does not wish his goods to be cheapened by excessive ease of discovery. A precious and desirable commodity requires an eager lover and an avid merchant. Therefore that promiser of such great gifts does not want you lukewarm in your work; he despises the disdainful, rejects the compelled and ungrateful, and spurns the undevoted. To seek the grace of the divine gift sluggishly and with little gratitude is the greatest insult to the Rewarder.

Therefore, even if we sweat through every labor of soul and body, even if we exercise ourselves with all the strength of obedience, still we possess nothing worthy that we could rightly weigh out and offer in exchange for heavenly goods. The services of temporal life cannot equal the joys of eternal life. Let limbs grow weary through vigils, let faces grow pale through fasts; nevertheless the sufferings of this present time will not be worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us. Let us therefore knock as much as we can, because we cannot knock as much as we ought.

Future blessedness can be acquired but cannot be measured. Unless we perform God’s works with eagerness, unless with good will and joy, let us know that we perish before God. Do we suppose that a soul seeks worthily, and knocks so that it may be opened to it, if it dares to answer an elder’s mild command by saying: “Are we your servants? I have already done my share; let him do his”? How can he say this when he has been commanded: “Do not seek what is your own”? And again: “Let each person desire not what is his own”—when what is required of him is not that he fulfill his own reward, but that he invade, anticipate, and seize what belongs to others?

Do we suppose that he asks so as to receive, seeks so as to find, and knocks so that it may be opened to him, who, when corrected for some negligence and disciplined according to the order of discipline, does not turn toward amendment or satisfaction, but instead toward that insolence by which he says: “I am leaving and departing; I cannot endure this; I am a free man”?

First, whoever boasts before a superior or abbot that he is a free man, I think he does not yet know that he has been purchased. Whoever, enrolled in the Christian service, presumes to say that he is free, almost denies that he was purchased by Christ’s blood. What else is this than to cry out to the Lord himself: “I am free; I owe you nothing”? Of such people the Apostle said: “When you were slaves of disobedience, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6:20). He is not rightly called free who is crushed beneath the wretched slavery of vices.

In contempt of discipline and in the sin of his soul he cries out: “I would rather leave than be corrected, than make satisfaction, than fulfill what you command.” What else is this than to shake off Christ’s yoke with a rebellious neck? Such people do not know what they vowed; they have forgotten why they came here. Such people do not ask rightly: if they are wrongly driven by vices, they do not knock in faith but are battered by unbelief.

What does your departure accomplish, when you are bound on every side by chains of passions, and your vices surround you on all sides? Someone would rightly depart if he could go somewhere the devil could not find him. Let no one deceive himself: let him not flee the adversary from place to place, but from vice to virtue, from passion to amendment. If he flees from the devil in this way, the devil follows him; amend yourself, and he will flee from you, as the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7).

But not to obey and to wish to depart is to do the devil’s will twice over; it is voluntarily to bring condemnation for sin upon oneself, even in the present life. For those who commit serious offenses among us, we can find no sadder or harsher sentence than that they should be cut off from the body of the congregation and depart without peace. And is it not a kind of madness for anyone to seek as a remedy what cannot be imposed even by a superior except for the gravest crime?

Let us understand, therefore, that these indignities and contradictions arise through the cooperation and plotting of the enemy. For he who cannot openly drive someone from the place of salvation first introduces occasions and causes; he introduces the passion of disobedience, which unbelief always accompanies. When this has taken the mind captive, it immediately makes even small things intolerable and impossible.

There is no doubt that divine strength is withdrawn from the disobedient. Just as from one who does not possess the necessary devotion of faith, “even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. 13:12), so disobedience hardens the mind it has once seized, so that it cannot be bent to receive commands either by authority or by reason. Worse still, the person believes only himself, follows his own opinions in place of every reason, and thinks the only commandment is the one he has conceived with his heart closed. He becomes like the one concerning whom divine Scripture declares: “The ways of fools are right in their own eyes” (Prov. 12:15). And again: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end leads down into the depths of hell” (Prov. 16:25).

Finally, what happened to the house built upon sand will happen to souls of this kind; for this parable applies especially to the disobedient. For we read: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand,” and so forth (Matt. 7:26). That is, when the drops of passions have poured in, when rivers and torrents and the assaults of tribulations have come because of the multitude of negligences; when the winds blow—those, certainly, that fly through this air, ready to fan Christ’s ark whenever they find straw to snatch away and scatter for their sport—then they will rush upon that house which is found without the foundation of obedience, and its ruin will be great.

But perhaps someone will say: “Is departing immediately from this place really to be called ruin?” I say, dear ones, that it is not a great hope if a ship caught amid the waves, although it does not itself perish, nevertheless suffers the greatest loss of its honor and cargo and reaches the harbor empty. So it is no great joy if someone, returning to the waves of the world, appears to preserve the name and habit of his profession, while his soul wastes away and drains away through negligence.

And what is more grievous than when someone suddenly, like an unexpected uprooted plant, leaves the place to which your Lord had called you, where he had first brought you after the evils of the world as though from a storm into harbor; when you suddenly forget the fellowship and consolation of the brothers, and forget that place where you first put off the sweetest change—the habit and name of the secular world?

Birds themselves love their nests; wild animals love the places in which they were raised; they love their lairs and pastures. Though natural freedom carries them off to various regions, they nevertheless return more often, through a kind of longing, to places dear to them. And you, endowed with understanding and fortified by reason, have sometimes become so estranged from your senses that you prefer your own wishes or opinions to God’s benefits and follow the devil’s insinuations! Though these drag you toward harsh labors, toward shipwreck of salvation and the ruin of your soul, you fail to perceive any of it because of your heart’s excessive resentment.

At the time of departure, the enemy promises many things: that in the place toward which you are heading you will find greater progress, abundant grace, and plenty in all things, and that you will be received like an angel. But afterward, when filled with anxiety and stripped of peace, you have abandoned the pursuit of your progress and the sacred sheepfold, then you recognize—as though the storm of that time had subsided—what harm you have done to yourself. Then you recognize what danger you incurred when you departed without peace and with scandal from the place to which you had come with joy. Then late repentance repents and weeps over its ruins, like certain birds that are said in their grief to weep over those whom they have killed. All these injuries to the soul arise from the evil of disobedience.

Obedient and humble souls, however, overthrow many tribulations and every labor, and reduce them to a manageable measure. For we must know that the more humble and obedient we are toward our superiors and fathers, the more the Lord will obey our prayers.

Let us see how acceptable to the Lord are the works and fasts of those who obey their own wishes rather than those of their elders. They cry out: “Because we fasted, you did not look upon us; we humbled our souls, and you did not know.” And he replies: “Because on the days of your fasting your own will is found.” We therefore see that through disobedience the works of souls are not regarded, fasts are not heard, and vows are not received.

For this reason let us follow his commands all the more closely, because he descended to us from heaven not only to redeem us at the price of death, but also to build us up by the example of his life. With him let us say: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.”

To follow one’s own wishes is so destructive that God, afterward angered, imposes this upon the disobedient as a condemnation for their sin, saying: “And I let them go according to the desires of their hearts.” [Col. 0886C]

Therefore, whoever wishes his works to be right in God’s sight must place nothing before obedience or before the commandments. Whether he is young or old, he ought to strive all the more for edification and perfection. Let no one set an end to his progress or establish a limit to his acquisition, when he hears it said to him: “Prepare your works for the end.” And again: “Do not fear to be justified even unto death.” And again: “Wisdom is sung at the end.”

The more we progress, therefore, the more let us humble ourselves; for the more we have been humbled, the more we shall progress. Let no elder appear so unlearned to anyone that he thinks obedience unbecoming—obedience that was becoming to God. Humility and obedience are still necessities in the young, but in the old they are already an honor.

He progresses well, he completes his course well, who acts each day as though he were always beginning. Therefore Scripture declares that increases in merit are incentives for the perfect. But concerning those who, while neglecting their first negligences, continually fall into others and others, it says: “The sinner adds to his sin.” Of the perfect, however, it is said: “And let the holy person be sanctified still more.”

Let us first examine what “the sinner adds to his sin” means. For example, if the passion of slander—or any other passion—begins to attack me, and I do not immediately begin to repent of this vice, tomorrow such ease in this vice, and a certain—so to speak—sweetness, will come upon me that I will be unable to withdraw from it or restrain myself. Thus it happens that one who does not wish to amend himself at the first moment begins later neither to wish nor to be able to do so.

For example, I began to yield to pride, violated the rule, injured an elder, and undermined a younger brother. If I did not immediately repent that I had been gravely overtaken, then from day to day the very violence of habit and the impulse of passion will gladly sweep me along, so that I will no longer understand that I am doing wrong or feel that I am sinning. For the constant practice of wrongdoing darkens and overwhelms the understanding of wrongdoing.

Indeed, the heart of the negligent person becomes so hardened that, if he does not humble himself and make satisfaction, he thinks he has done harm to his superior; moreover, he insults him and says: “How firmly I resisted him! How well I refused to obey! With what authority I answered him! Did he think I would always humble myself before him?”

Whoever does this has plainly handed himself over to the devil, who rejoices in human vices, passions, and destruction. To a soul of this kind will come that sentence: “The sinner adds to his sin.”

Let us flee from this and instead hold fast to the saying: “And let the holy person be sanctified still more,” so that each day we may add to our merits and presume nothing about ourselves, because everything that we are belongs to God.

Let us therefore be unceasing in God’s work for the sake of eternal recompense, and let us strive daily toward better things. May the very eagerness to attain, and the very habit of progressing, always urge us toward greater things. When God sees the soul’s devotion, he will inspire a more ardent desire; the more ardently we burn for the pursuit, the more assistance he will add; the more diligently we apply ourselves, the more he will add to our glory.

“To the one who has, it will be given, and he will abound” (Matt. 13:12). And elsewhere he says: “I have placed help upon the mighty.” Grace, therefore, is born from grace, and progress serves progress; gains make room for gains, and merits for merits. The more a person begins to acquire, the more he should strive to acquire; and the more eagerly he drinks from the goods of wisdom, the more he should desire to drink, as Wisdom herself says of herself: “Those who eat me will hunger still” (Ecclus. 24:29).

Let us press on with our course, so that our life may increase at its end. Let us seek to the very end what may make us worthy to rejoice without end. But suppose that we cannot undertake bodily labors: let us devote ourselves to the desire for spiritual goods, and to an increase of compunction and charity. If we arrange ascents in our hearts each day, our minds cannot be wearied by any weakness or age, so that we may be worthy to ascend by spiritual steps to the promises of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor, strength and glory, power and splendor, majesty and dominion, now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII

*(From Henry Canisius.)*

Now, dearest brothers, when the divine reading was being read, we heard the blessed Apostle warning us solemnly and beneficially. For he says: “We must all be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). Therefore the Lord also announces in the Gospel, saying: “The Son of Man will come in his glory, with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works” (Matt. 16:27).

Pay close attention, I ask you, dearest brothers, and tremble together with me, because he does not say that he will repay each person according to his mercy, but according to his works. Here he is merciful; there he is just. For the fact that at once he does not bring punishment upon sinners [Note: [Col. 0887D] Perhaps “vindicta descendit,” “punishment comes down,” or “he takes vengeance,” or something similar.]—the surviving text reads: “vin . . . . .”—is patience, not negligence. He does not destroy by his power; rather, he has reserved us for repentance. Therefore we must fear all the more lest, the longer he waits for us to cease from sin, the more severely he condemn us if we refuse to amend.

Since these things are so, brothers, we must know and understand that nothing is more salutary for us than, having condemned the pleasures of all present things, to think instead about when we shall depart from this world, or when, with the last day arriving, we shall lay aside the tabernacle of our body and receive it again at the time of the resurrection, so that together with it we may receive what we have done, whether good or evil.

And therefore I ask you, brothers, to consider what we shall be like when we are offered to the purest sight of the angels on the day of judgment and give an account to the eternal Judge from the books of our consciences. For when all other proofs have been removed, it is certain that on that day the human being himself will be set before himself, and his own soul will be shown to him in the mirror of his heart. Witnesses against it will be produced not from outside but from within, from the soul itself. Not foreign but exceedingly familiar testimonies will be brought forward—that is, its own works. Its sins and crimes will be set before the unhappy soul, so that proof may confound it and recognition may confound it, according to what is written: “I will rebuke you and set them before your face” (Ps. 49:21).

Whoever now, while it is permitted, neglects to amend himself will first receive punishment in the form of confusion before that heavenly assembly. The soul that now dissimulates and refuses, through repentance—a brief settlement—to heal the rottenness of its sins will remain eternally wounded before that fearful tribunal, without any remedy.

If only it were already possible to look upon the face of the sinful soul with the eyes of the heart or of the body, and if we allowed the appearance of our conscience to be brought before our eyes! If this were permitted—and it cannot be expressed with words—with what zeal and fear would we hasten to set in order what has been defiled, wipe clean what has been stained, and heal what has been wounded.

Therefore, since we cannot inspect it with the eyes of the body, let us inspect it with the eyes of the heart insofar as we can. Let each of us set our consciences before the sight of the inner person, and let us ourselves chastise ourselves; let us ourselves provide healing for ourselves from our daily conduct.

Let each soul address itself in secret and say: “Let us see whether I have passed this day without sin, without envy, without slander, without murmuring. Let us see whether today I have done anything that contributes to the soul’s progress. I think that today I lied, that I was overcome by anger or desire, that I did no one any good, and that I did not groan from fear of eternal death. Who will give me back this day, which I lost in empty matters and consumed in harmful and most wicked thoughts?”

And so, brothers, let us be moved to compunction over all our negligences. In our beds—that is, in our hearts—let us condemn ourselves, accuse ourselves daily before our Judge, and while we are in this flesh let us speak daily against the flesh itself. Let us overcome our wishes and opinions while that most longed-for and blessed time comes to us through the happy transformation of eternal life.

Then will be fulfilled what the Lord said: “They will be like the angels” (Luke 20:36); and again: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). Imagine what the splendor of souls will then be, when the light of their bodies possesses the brightness of the sun.

For when we have come to this blessedness, there will be no sadness, no fear, no weakness, no death; nothing will hinder us from serving our God. No weakness will then stand in our way, no adversity of wretched flesh will oppose us, and no need to struggle will remain any longer.

The time will come, I say, when no food or any refreshment will be desired; no weariness of fasting will be felt, and no disturbance from the flesh or temptation from the enemy will be feared. But when the adversary has been thrust down into the depths of hell, we shall first enjoy this happiness: that we shall begin neither to wish nor to be able to sin any longer. When all iniquity, all misery, and all grief have ceased, innocence will possess everything, and happiness will possess everything.

No inferior person will suffer misery, and no happier person will fear envy, because misery, emptied out and utterly extinguished, will have passed away. In human breasts the charity of angels will shine, and human beings, joined to them and now received with heavenly bodies [Note: [Col. 0889B] Manuscript: “if heavenly,” or possibly “of heaven.”], will shine without the weakness of the flesh.

Therefore they will suffer no further weariness from the everlasting power of their Lord, and no failing amid the perpetual exultation of their praises. We shall possess complete blessedness amid those immense benefits of our God, so that we shall never cease giving thanks, made co-heirs of the one who will say: “Come, blessed ones; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

Granted by him who lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 483–492. SAINT FELIX III

[Col. 0889]

## PROLEGOMENA

*(From William Cave.)*

[Col. 0889D]

Felix, a Roman by nationality and the son of the priest Felix, obtained the pontificate of the Roman See on 13 February 483. Once he became bishop, he immediately and openly rejected the Henoticon of the emperor Zeno, issued in the preceding year. He harassed Acacius of Constantinople, who refused to renounce communion with Peter Mongus, by sending letters in every direction; indeed, he finally struck him with anathema in 484.

In the same year, at a synod of forty-two bishops held at Rome, he condemned Peter the Fuller, an intruder into the see of Antioch who taught that God had been crucified. For a clearer understanding of this matter, it should be noted that Peter, by trade a fuller and a monk of the monastery of the Sleepless Ones, was expelled from it because of his adherence to Eutychianism. Soon afterward he became a presbyter of Saint Bassa at Chalcedon. In 471, supported by the favor of Zeno, he stirred up great disturbances at Antioch and, joining himself to the sect of the Theopaschites, taught that God had been crucified, adding this clause to the solemn formula of the Trisagion: “Who wast crucified for us.”

Exhausted by the disturbances, Martyrius, bishop of Antioch, renounced his see in 472, and Peter the Fuller soon tyrannically invaded it. He was immediately expelled by an edict of the emperor Leo and exiled to Oasi, with Julian substituted in his place.

In 476 he was restored to the Antiochene see by Basiliscus, while Julian was overcome by grief. In the following year he was deposed by John, whom he had ordained bishop of Apamea, and he was condemned by a clandestine synod.

In 478 he was condemned by the lawful council of the Eastern bishops at Antioch, by Acacius at Constantinople, and by Simplicius at Rome; Zeno also ordered him to be deported to Pityus. In 484 he was restored to his see by the emperor, at Acacius’s instigation, although at the same time he was condemned by Felix. He held the see until 486, when he died.

But to return to Felix: he died on 30 January 492.

*(From the Liber Pontificalis.)*
Felix [Note: [Col. 0891A] After an interregnum of six days—during which Basil, the praetorian prefect acting at Rome in place of King Odoacer, attempted to meddle with the election of the Roman pontiff by secular authority, as the acts of the fourth Roman synod under Symmachus relate—Felix was created pontiff in the year of the Lord 483, on the eighth day of March. He was Roman by birth, the great-great-grandfather of Gregory the Great, as Gregory himself testifies in Homily 38 on the Gospels and in Book IV, chapter 16 of the Dialogues. At the beginning of his pontificate he rejected, proscribed, and cursed the impious Henoticon of Zeno—that is, the unitive edict of peace and reconciliation—by which a layman had pronounced an anathema against the Council of Chalcedon, against the bishops and other orthodox persons, had sanctioned new decrees of faith, prescribed laws for the Church, attempted to teach the teachers of the Church and to propose to them a new confession of faith, and finally, stealing the keys of ecclesiastical power, hurled an anathema against those who did not obey him—an unspeakable crime! The pontiff not only proscribed this most impious edict of the sacrilegious emperor, this seedbed of impiety, which Evagrius reproduces word for word in Book III, chapter 14, but also condemned those who subscribed to it by a sentence of anathema. Theodoret the Reader, in Book II, called it the Henoticon, that is, the “unitive” document, because through its profession and subscription the heretics might be united with the Catholics at least in some outward appearance.

In his time the Vandal persecution, foreshadowed two years before its outbreak by many signs, was aroused in Africa by Huneric. In it, besides other cruelties, four thousand nine hundred and sixty-six bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other clergy of the Church were sent into exile in the desert. Victor, Book II, On the Vandal Persecution. The same Huneric, by a most savage edict, turned against the Catholics all the laws enacted by Catholic emperors against heretics. The persecutor mentioned above ordered certain Catholics to have their tongues and right hands cut off; nevertheless, by the power of the Holy Spirit, they spoke and still speak just as they had spoken before. “But if anyone wishes to be incredulous,” says Victor, “let him now go to Constantinople, where he will find one of those subdeacons, Reparatus, speaking polished discourse without any impediment. For this reason he is held in especially high honor in Zeno’s palace, and the queen venerates him with extraordinary reverence.” As a testimony to this fact, stronger than any objection, the emperor Justinian says in a constitution issued by him concerning the office of the praetorian prefect of Africa: “We have seen venerable men who, with their tongues cut out by the roots, were speaking of their pitiable sufferings.” But so that the tyrant, the Arian ruler, might not escape this cruelty with impunity, it happened by the just judgment of God the avenger that, when he madly supposed he should celebrate a triumph over the prostrate Catholic faith, he was extinguished with worms boiling throughout his body and thus experienced divine vengeance. Victor, in the place cited above. Gregory of Tours, History, Book II, chapter 3.

When the Eutychian heresy was growing strong at Alexandria and Antioch through the pseudo-bishops of those Churches and the violent usurpers Fullon and Moggos, the body of the holy apostle Barnabas was miraculously discovered together with the Gospel of Saint Matthew—which he had written with his own hand and which most powerfully confirms the true humanity of Christ, to the disgrace of the heresy then gaining strength. Theodoret the Reader, Book II of the Collections; Nicephorus; Cedrenus; Sigebertus; and others.

Xenaias, a Persian by origin and a slave by fortune, who had not yet been baptized but pretended to be a cleric, was the first author of the Iconoclasts. In these times he taught that the venerable images of Christ and the saints ought not to be venerated. Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 27.

Cyrola, the bishop of the Arians, had persuaded one of his followers to pretend to be blind and, at Cyrola’s nod, to look again. But, by God’s cooperation and to the confusion of his perfidy, it happened that he truly made blind the man whom he pretended to enlighten.

During this pontificate Peter the Fuller died, having been condemned by synodal judgment from the see of Antioch because of his heresy and blasphemies; and he was subjected anew to the judgment of God, the most good and great.

In the sixth year of Felix’s pontificate, Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, persevering in anathema, a most ambitious and arrogant man who had allowed images of himself, while still alive, to be dedicated in a church—as is related by Suidas—was summoned from the judgment of the Church to the tribunal of the supreme God. In his place, through the greatest wickedness and fraud, succeeded Flavius, or Flavianus, a heretic polluted by communion with heretics. Since he had not received the letters of communion which, under a feigned profession of Catholic faith, he had requested from the Roman pontiff, he was taken away by sudden death after four months.

Euphemius was appointed in his place. As soon as he had been installed in the see of Constantinople, he approved the Council of Chalcedon; renounced communion with Peter of Alexandria and erased his name from the diptychs; and restored the name of Pope Felix, which Acacius had expunged. But because he had not yet removed the name of Acacius from the diptychs, he obtained not the peaceful letters of communion which he had requested through a synodal letter, but merely letters of notification. Liberatus the deacon, chapter 18; Evagrius, Book III, chapter 23; Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 19.

Peter Moggos, the devastator and plunderer of the Church of Alexandria, died in the thirteenth year of his occupation of the episcopate, which was the ninth year of Pope Felix, in the year of Christ the Redeemer 491. Athanasius Herniosus was appointed as his successor in perfidy and morals, plainly unworthy of so great a see and so great a name. Evagrius, Nicephorus, and Liberatus, in the places cited above. More concerning these matters will be found below in the notes on the letters and councils.

That this Felix was the great-great-grandfather of Saint Pope Gregory, and that he appeared to his niece Saint Tarsilla and called her to the heavenly kingdom, is attested by the Roman Martyrology, corrected from the errors that had crept into it, in these words:

“At Rome, on the twenty-fifth day of February, the feast of Saint Felix III, pope, who was the great-great-grandfather of Saint Pope Gregory. Gregory relates of him that, appearing to his niece Saint Tarsilla, he called her to the heavenly kingdom.”

The words of Gregory, who relates this in Homily 3 on the Gospels and in Book IV, chapter 16 of the Dialogues, are these:

“My father had three sisters, all three of whom were holy virgins. One was called Tarsilla, another Gordiana, and the third Aemiliana.”

And a little farther on:

“One night, as Tarsilla—who among her sisters had grown distinguished through her constant practice of prayer, her devotion to disciplined affliction, her exceptional abstinence, the venerable gravity of her life, and the dignity and height of her holiness—herself related, my great-great-grandfather Felix, bishop of this Roman Church, appeared to her in a vision and showed her a dwelling of perpetual brightness, saying: ‘Come, for in this dwelling of light I receive you.’ Soon afterward she was seized by a fever and reached her final day, and so forth.”

SEV. BINIUS.]

Roman by birth, son of Felix, a presbyter of the title of Fasciola, [Note: [Col. 0893C] Codex Lucensis: 490, XVII.] [Note: [Col. 0893B] Namely, nine years less twelve days. For he died on the fifth day before the Kalends of March in the year of our Redeemer 492. Therefore, if the beginning and this end of his pontificate are taken into account, the stated number of years will be found. SEV. BINIUS.] he held office for eight years, eleven months, and eighteen days. He lived [Note: [Col. 0893B] King Odoacer of the Heruli, summoned into Italy by the Nepotians out of hatred for Orestes, who had proclaimed his son Augustulus emperor, killed Orestes and his brother Paulus, banished Augustulus to Campania, and abolished the Western Empire. He became king of Italy in the year of the Lord 476, as Saint Severinus, the apostle of Noricum, illustrious for holiness and miracles, had foretold to him when Odoacer visited him dressed in the meanest skins.

He reigned in Italy, in accordance with the prophecy of the same Saint Severinus, for thirteen complete and unbroken years, and abstained from the purple, from royal clothing, and from the name of emperor. Thus the Roman Empire, begun in Augustus, came to an end in the West in another Augustus, who, by way of contempt, was called Augustulus.

Although this Odoacer was an Arian, he did nothing concerning sacred affairs that is worthy of remembrance. But when he afterward attempted to introduce Arianism into the City, Pope Gelasius resisted him with great courage, as we shall relate below.

“Moreover,” says Evagrius in the Life of Saint Severinus, “after he had gained possession of Italy, he sent a friendly letter to Saint Severinus, asking him to request whatever he wished, remembering that prophecy by which he had once foretold that Odoacer would reign.” Invited by these holy words, Odoacer ordered a certain Ambrose, condemned to exile—the man who freed Britain when it was oppressed by the barbarians—to be released.

Ennodius, the deacon of Ticinum, testifies in the Life of Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, that Epiphanius asked Odoacer on behalf of his fellow citizens for a five-year remission of the taxes which Orestes had imposed by tyrannical power, and that he obtained from Odoacer what he had requested.

But in the fourteenth year of his Italian reign Odoacer was driven out and defeated at Verona by Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths.
