In a third battle he was overcome at Ravenna and treacherously killed there, in the year of the Lord 493. After this period Italy obeyed the kings of the Ostrogoths, as we shall relate below. SEV. BINIUS.]

He was pope during the time of King Odoacer, down to the time of King Theodoric. He built the basilica of Saint Agapetus beside the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr.

During his episcopate a report again came from Greece [read: from the Greek regions] that Peter of Alexandria had been restored [supply: to communion] by Acacius of Constantinople. Then the venerable Felix, archbishop of the apostolic see of the city of Rome, sent a defender with a council of his see [read: in accordance with a decree of the synod of his see]; after holding a council, he condemned Acacius together with Peter. [Note: [Col. 0894C] It is clear below, from Felix’s sixth letter, which contains the sentence issued against Acacius, and from the notes on the first and second Roman councils under Felix, that these men were appointed and sent away before Acacius’s condemnation. It is therefore false that the account here says that they were sent to Constantinople three years after Acacius had been condemned. SEV. BINIUS.]

After three years a report again came from the emperor Zeno that Acacius should return as a penitent. Then Pope Felix [supply: held a council and, with its consent] sent two bishops, Misenus [Col. 0893B] and Vitalis, so that, if they found Acacius an accomplice of Peter, they should condemn them again; but, if not, should offer him a penitential document.

When they had entered the city of Heraclea [Col. 0894A] [Note: [Col. 0893C] The same manuscript reads: Constantinople.] [read: Constantinople], the aforesaid bishops were corrupted by a bribe and did not act according to the command of the apostolic see.

When they came to Rome, to the apostolic see, [Note: [Col. 0894C] The same manuscript reads: “Pope Felix held a council, and after an examination had been conducted, he discovered …”] Pope Felix the venerable held a synod. After an investigation [read: “a council, and after an examination had been conducted in the council”], he found both bishops—that is, Misenus and Vitalis—guilty and excluded them from communion.

Then Bishop Misenus did not conceal that he had been corrupted by money, and the council granted him a period for repentance. This happened in the time of King Odoacer.

Felix held two ordination sessions in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-eight presbyters, five deacons, and thirty-one bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul. The episcopate then remained vacant for five days. After his death, the presbyters and deacons issued a decree concerning the whole Church.

[Col. 0893]

# LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE FELIX III. (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0893D] This is the synodal letter which the Fathers of the Roman council judged should be sent by Pope Felix to Acacius. Concerning this matter, see below in the notes on the same council. Until now it had nowhere been published; it is now being brought to light for the first time from the recesses of Baronianus’s library and his Annals. It survives in a very ancient manuscript of the Cresconian Collection. Evagrius, Book III, chapters 18, 19, and 25, mentions this and the following letters written by Felix. Liberatus likewise mentions them in chapter 18 of his Breviary. SEV. BINIUS.]

## FIRST LETTER. [Note: [Col. 0894D] In the attached manuscript this inscription is prefixed in these words. SEV. BINIUS.]

### OF POPE FELIX III TO ACACIUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE

The holy Roman synod desires that the emperor Zeno be induced, by diligent effort, to correct the things he has so wrongly done up to this point against the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0893D]

[Col. 0894D] Felix to Acacius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0894D] It is nowhere expressly stated by any historian of which cities these legate-bishops were bishops. Concerning Misenus alone, Baronius says: “In the decree of Vigilius, Roman pontiff, concerning the Three Chapters, we find him named as bishop of Cumae.” But in a very ancient manuscript of our library, entitled Concordance of the Canons, there is, among other materials, a brief summary of history extending from the rise of the Nestorian heresy to the Roman council under Pope Felix at which Acacius was condemned. Although it is found published without the name of its author, it appears to be the work of someone who lived in this century and was devoted to the truth. In this work, among other matters, the following is said concerning these legates sent to Constantinople:

“Therefore, after Pope Felix learned that the letters of his predecessor had achieved nothing and that Acacius was committing certain mockeries for the overthrow of the faith, he sent Vitalis, bishop of Droentinus from the Picene region, and Misenus, bishop of the Church of Cumae from the Campanian region, and so forth.”

But instead of Droentinus one should read Truentinus. For at that time there was a city by the river of that name, called Truentum, today commonly known as the Tronto. Pliny, Ptolemy, and others mention the same city.

This concerns the legates sent to Constantinople. Baronius, year 483, number 19. SEV. BINIUS.] through the bishops Vitalis and Misenus.

After my predecessor of holy memory, Pope Simplicius, had departed from the course of this life at the heavenly command, and the administration of the ministry which he governed had come to the control of my humility, I was immediately seized by the greatest anxiety concerning the various general concerns of the universal Church which the blessed apostle Peter, by the voice of the supreme Shepherd delegating them, dispenses with vigilant governance among all Christian peoples throughout the world—especially concerning the city of Alexandria and the condition of the faith throughout the whole Eastern region, matters which had likewise incessantly pressed upon my predecessor.

As these concerns troubled us day and night, they compelled us to send an embassy through our brothers and fellow bishops Vitalis and Misenus to our lord son, the most Christian prince. This embassy, in our place, was to present to his piety the services that were his due and to petition him for the preservation of the constitutions of our forefathers [Col. 0895B] and for the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] That is, by this embassy. HARDUIN.]

Since he was therefore proceeding on this mission, it was fitting that I should greet your Dilection through beloved and equally affectionate words, and then exhort you to extend at last your patronage to the cause of our common Lord. Do not think that the true confession of Christ and the definition of his universal Church should be despised … or that peace should not be established in concord … if you desire to be renowned both for his honor and in name.

For, in accordance with the apostolic word, we confess that there is great sadness and continual sorrow in our heart (Romans 9) because of the thoughts which we endure amid affairs that are daily advancing (procedentibus) [or pressing us onward (propellentibus)].

Above all, this matter that has long been before the eyes of almost everyone comes to mind: tell us, namely, for what reason this has occurred—that your Dilection, not only when such great opportunities continually arose [Col. 0895C], but also when repeatedly invited [read: urged] by letters from my predecessors, should, as though in stubborn silence, never have wished either to consult or to report anything concerning this matter.

Although we are inclined to form some rashly unfavorable opinion of your mind—God forbid that this should be so—nevertheless, since you have abandoned the custom and pattern of the venerable men who previously governed the Church over which you preside, you cannot in any way avoid being viewed with suspicion.

Certainly, if—which we do not believe—you disdain to show reverence to the victories of the blessed apostle through your proud sentiments [Note: [Col. 0896D] Perhaps: “through your proud utterances.” HARDUIN.], you ought at least, remembering your duty, to have risen steadfastly on behalf of the integrity of the Catholic faith, the preservation of the sanctions of our fathers, the observance of the constitution of the Council of Chalcedon—which thoroughly approves the articles of the Nicene assembly—and the suppression everywhere of its enemies, as an imitator of the orthodox bishops of that city.

For you cannot show yourself otherwise among the members of Christ’s body unless you cease in no way to take precautions against those contagions which you see to have crept throughout the world.

Therefore you ought frequently to approach the Christian-minded Augustus, both to render him an account of his salvation and even of his empire, and often to place before him the means by which his enemies fell and by which he himself rose again; you should likewise make these matters known to him.

You ought to present to him those writings in which he extolled my predecessor with exceptional praise because, by asserting the truth, he had crushed the heretical tyranny opposed to Catholic faith. Likewise, you should present those writings in which he expelled Peter of Alexandria from the neck of the Alexandrian Church and recalled Timothy of holy memory, the orthodox bishop.

Nor should you omit those writings in which, addressing the bishops, clergy, and laity established throughout Egypt, he declared, as a Catholic emperor, that because they had deviated from the divine Christian confession, they would be deprived of their honors, churches, and everything else in that region unless within two months they returned to the communion of Timothy.

Likewise, you should include the writings in which he so revoked the ordinations of Peter—who, as he declared, had unlawfully thrust himself into the Alexandrian Church—and of the now-deceased heretic Timothy, as well as the things which they were secretly saying by various devices.

You should also append the fact that when Timothy of holy memory, the Catholic bishop, was approaching the end of his life, under the impulse of divine inspiration he gave careful instructions—both by replying to the consultations of that pontiff and by writing to the clergy of the city of Alexandria—that, if the Lord should command the aforesaid priest to depart, no one should succeed him except someone from the body of the Catholic clergy who was proved to be a disciple of the orthodox faith, who was in communion with all the Churches, and who had been ordained by Catholics.

He was wisely taking care that Peter—who was either claimed by no one or was vaunted by heretics as possessing this falsely named dignity—should never be able to preside fully upon the rock [whence Peter], that is, upon the Catholic Church, from which he had been expelled by his rash presumption.

It would have been appropriate to communicate these and similar events repeatedly, especially since, when these matters were being promulgated to the most Christian prince as he returned, with God’s assistance, to royal power, you did not remain silent in letters sent here but declared that you had contributed your efforts vigorously and in a manner worthy of a Catholic pontiff.

You boasted that all who had attempted to act against your [read: our] see, against the Council of Chalcedon, and against the preaching of the apostolic see had been overthrown. For this very reason, on behalf of your salvation and your confession, you ought to have alleged such matters more fervently and pleaded them earnestly before the ears of his clemency, so that he would not allow the judgment which he had expressed with a Catholic mind to be violated in any way by anyone’s deception; nor would he permit those outbreaks of heretics, which his piety had destroyed under divine inspiration, to sprout up again against the sanction of the universal Church.

You should have seen this most clearly and, through your preaching in every way, risen again against those things which had opposed him, and without hesitation confirmed the same things, so that, as they had long ago been overthrown, the opposing forces might lie prostrate; lest you should be called either—God forbid—a deserter of your faith or a supporter of another’s perfidy.

For an error that is not resisted is approved, and truth that is not defended is suppressed.

Moreover, since we know that, by the Lord’s favor, you have familiarity with our lord son, the religious prince, no one could ever have been persuaded that your Dilection was unable to act; rather, it must be judged that you were unwilling. And because what was kept silent was not impossible, you yourself do not doubt what the universal Church can judge concerning this matter.

Where is, brother Acacius, the labor with which you toiled during the time of the heretical tyranny? Will you allow such a reward to perish to the detriment of your conscience? Consider the words of the Apostle, who testifies: “You were running well; who bewitched you?” (Galatians 5).

Why, brother, do you now abandon the ancient paths that you used to seek? When wolves rush upon the Lord’s fold, why do you not oppose them with any pastoral vigilance, but calmly and securely watch the flock entrusted to you being either torn apart or killed?

Do you not remember the Lord saying that a good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, while a hireling, who has no real concern for them, as soon as he sees the beast, immediately flees, as though without any consideration? Yet since you have no cause for flight—for there is no danger—I fear that you may appear to have abandoned the Lord’s enclosure not so much through fear as, what is more detestable, to have willingly cast it before savage teeth [read: thrown it down before them].

Listen to the voice of that same Lord, who gives this warning: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11).

Attend carefully to the fact that to fail to care for the things that belong to Christ is nothing other than to profess oneself openly his enemy.

Let us not despair of fulfilling the true saying of our Savior, by which he promised that he would not be absent from his Church until the end of the age (Matthew 28), and declared that the gates of hell would never overcome it (Matthew 16); nor let us despair of those things which, by the decrees of apostolic teaching, are bound on earth and which he said would not be loosed in heaven (Matthew 16:18).

Nor should we think that, however many dangers surround it, either the weight of its strength, the judgment of the most blessed Peter, or the authority of the universal Church could ever be lost. The more carefully it guards against growing lukewarm amid the prosperity of the world, the less it is broken; rather, divinely instructed, it grows stronger against adversity [Note: [Col. 0897D] Perhaps: “against adversities.” HARDUIN.].

Therefore [or “where”] it must be understood that whoever attempts to submerge it in the very sea of this surging world—which no movements [or “masses”] of storms can overwhelm—will himself rather be cast from safe governance into the depths and drowned, while the Church prevails.

And therefore, since this is so, I warn, exhort, and advise you to correct what has been done, and by your subsequent efforts to cause better things to be thought of you: [Note: [Col. 0897D] This passage is cited in the letter of Victor of Carthage in the Lateran Council under Pope Martin, in Secretariat 2. Gratian, XIII, question 1, attributes it to Pope Anastasius II. HARDUIN.]

“For to neglect, when you are able to overthrow the perverse, is nothing other than to encourage them. Whoever ceases to oppose an evident crime is not free from the scruple of secret complicity.” [The variants are Non/Nec, “does not/neither does”; and evidenter/evidenti, “an evidently criminal/evident crime.”]

Therefore, if you see hostile hearts striving against the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and remain silent, believe me, I do not know how you can claim to share in the whole Church.

Furthermore, you do not turn your eyes back upon yourself, because not only is the unity of all Catholic teaching attacked in this matter, but a broad field is also opened to all the heresies that claim to think more correctly than we do: they are given strength to recover and to rise again amid their former practices if what was handed down by our forefathers is once struck, under any pretext.

Therefore, again and again we protest that the statutes of the whole Church must not be allowed to be dragged headlong through the audacity of those who attempt to rise against the Catholic synod.

In this struggle God will establish a firm foundation, as we are permitted to hope concerning him; and “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

Nevertheless, without prejudice to the fact that at the day of judgment it is certain that such a Church will be required from us as we received from the Fathers, even in this life let the person recognize that he does not belong to it who not only attempts to inflict harm upon its fullness, but also fails to provide for those things that are fitting for it.

God forbid that we should believe anything of this kind concerning your Dilection. We remember that you once stood courageously for the Catholic faith, and we do not wish you to be separated from the body of the whole Church.

Therefore, since we love you with sincere affection, we urge you more earnestly through repeated exhortations to avoid hereafter those things which would show you to be separated from the entire household of Christ, and not to pursue those things which would make you divided from it.

Because it was not necessary to gather everything into this letter, we have entrusted many matters demanded by the usefulness of the present affair to our brothers and fellow bishops who are carrying out the embassy of the apostolic see, so that they may discuss them either with our most merciful lord son, the prince, or with your Dilection.

It is right to receive this with a ready mind for the preservation of the Catholic faith and, for the sake of your reputation, to be assisted by petitions before the goodwill of the august mind.

## SECOND LETTER. [Note: [Col. 0899D] This is the synodal letter of Pope Felix which, on the advice of the Roman synod, he sent to the emperor Zeno. The occasion will be discussed below in the notes on that synod. It has recently been transferred into this edition of the Councils from the aforementioned manuscript of the Cresconian Collection. SEV. BINIUS.]

### TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

He pleads on behalf of the Alexandrian Church. He recalls whatever he had previously said or done in defense of that Church, in order to criticize the later expulsion of John, bishop of Alexandria, and the restoration of Peter Moggos.

[Col. 0899A]

The copy of the letter of the most blessed Pope Felix of the city of Rome to Zeno Augustus, sent through the bishops Vitalis and Misenus, begins.

It was certainly fitting, venerable emperor, that after the death of my predecessor of holy memory, and after divine grace had appointed me in his place, I should offer to your Clemency the gift of a letter: either to announce those things which the circumstances required, or to present the first fruits of my service.

When these duties had been properly discharged, matters concerning the protection of your empire and the support of its prosperity should likewise be joined to them; and matters requiring greater care should be entrusted to messengers proportionately more worthy.

Therefore it was appropriate that I should send to you Vitalis and Misenus, my brothers and fellow bishops, together with Felix, the servant of your Church and its defender, on a necessary embassy. They should not convey these matters merely as bearers, but, acting in my place, should in a certain way make me present to you.

Through them, therefore, as though joined face to face with your honor in conversation, I beg you, as a Christian prince, to receive my petition with kind ears. Let not your piety suppose that anyone loves you with a more sincere mind than the one who desires you to possess perpetual peace in God, since you cannot doubt, with a mind devoted to faith, that both the power of temporal majesty and the commerce of eternal life depend upon heavenly favor.

Behold, it has now been a long time since the see of the blessed apostle, after letters had been sent to your serenity by my predecessor of blessed memory, has been waiting and has received no reply concerning the Catholic faith or the tranquility of the Westerners [Note: [Col. 0899D] Or: “of the Westerners, who are concerned for the salvation of the Easterners.” HARDUIN.] [read: of the Easterners], especially since those fearful oaths have bound your conscience, most glorious prince, so that you would not permit the see of the blessed evangelist Mark to be separated from the teaching or communion of his master.

But because the efforts of my aforesaid predecessor, owing to a long illness, were unable to repeat these matters frequently, the duty of my humility now does not cease to repeat them with greater urgency.

Therefore once again the venerable confession of the apostle Peter, through maternal voices, urges you and, refusing above all to cease addressing the confidence of his own sons, cries out:

“Christian prince, why do you permit me to be cut off from the course of charity by which the universal Church is bound together? Why do you break in me the consent of the whole world?”

[Col. 0900A] I beg you, most dutiful son, do not allow the Lord’s seamless tunic, woven from above throughout, by which the Church was shown to be one undivided body, with the Holy Spirit governing everywhere, to be torn by any circumstance. Do not allow what remained intact even among the very men who crucified the Savior to appear divided in your times.

Is it not my faith which the Lord himself showed to be one alone and unconquerable by any adversity, when he promised that the gates of hell would never prevail against his Church, founded upon my confession?

This faith raised you, reborn, to royal dignity; and after power had been driven from its attackers, it opened the way for you to prevail again through the defense of that same faith.

But, I beg you, set before yourself also the examples of what was done, and repay my services in return, so that, having learned through the tests of events, you may both guard against dangers and seek the supports of the dignity you recovered.

I ask these things, which God willed to be spoken through the bishop of the aforesaid see or through the lowliness of my rank, and which, out of regard for your serenity [the text reads “security”], I judged ought to be brought forward: so that you might not appear—God forbid!—ungrateful to the author of the happiness bestowed upon you, as though merely admonished by some vicar, but might, as though warned by the authority of the apostle himself present, look more deeply upon the ways both of divine reverence and of the human condition.

Let it return before the complete deliberation of your mind: what deeds cast down your enemies, what deeds, with God accompanying you, restored you to the imperial height; how they fell together with the wicked acceptance of their doctrine; and how your glory was restored through the expulsion of the heretics.

They, by advancing against the venerable decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and the writings of the most blessed Pope Leo, collapsed through the very undertaking by which they had attempted to act; and it should also be recalled by what means their reversal restored your imperial authority to its former state [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 0900D] The Codex Lucensis reads: “might restore”; Harduin suggests: “restored you.”] [Note: [Col. 0900D] Harduin suggests: “with your reverence”; the Regius manuscript reads: “your.”]

Permit me, I beg, to state confidently what it is fitting not to leave unsaid [read: to pursue]. Only the name of the ancient emperor remains in you. Do not, I beg you, begrudge us your salvation, pious emperor; do not diminish our confidence in pleading on your behalf.

The causes by which the Lord may be appeased must be sought, not those by which his indignation may be provoked.

I appeal, I testify, I entreat, because I fear, I tremble, and I dread that, when the causes change, the outcome may also change—God forbid!

Look favorably upon your predecessors of august memory, namely Marcian and Leo, and, as their lawful successor, upon the faith of such great princes. You ought to embrace their agreement in religion, whose memory you ought to revere.

Far be it from your devotion, far from your power, to be believed to have rejected the judgment of such men.

Finally, I bring before the understanding of your piety your profession and your conscience, which ought to be recalled.

Have the archives of your palace reviewed, and diligently investigate those writings which your piety, as you returned to the height of supreme power, sent to my predecessor in common congratulation. In them you always followed him with great praise because you had crushed the heretical tyranny by the force of Catholic preaching.

By that very preaching of the truth, you certainly labored for nothing other than the complete abolition of the Eutychian error and the exclusion of its followers.

The entire text of these writings spoke piously in defense of preserving the definition of the Council of Chalcedon and of restoring Timothy of holy memory, the priest of the right faith.

Your gentleness certainly knew these things; your clemency could not have proclaimed matters unknown, and you openly and clearly professed what you confirmed by testimony to your own praises.

[Col. 0901B] Let those writings also be sought which your pages of serene authority addressed to Timothy of holy memory, the orthodox bishop of Alexandria; and from the very acts observe that the aforesaid Timothy was not recalled unless Peter had first been excluded from that famous city, Peter who at that time oppressed its Church.

You soon sent sacred and venerable letters to the same pontiff, now restored, in which you proudly proclaimed with a faithful heart that our Lord and Savior, taking thought for the orthodox faith of the holy Church of the great city of Alexandria, had restored the true priest.

Here it is clear that, when you say what is true, you show that the man who was expelled had been false; and when, in the venerable orthodox Timothy, you testify that the Lord restored the faith, you declare that he rejected in every respect the perverse teaching found in Peter.

This was for no other reason than that the man who was pronounced orthodox and true agreed with the Council of Chalcedon, as his profession sent at that time maintains; whereas the man who was expelled as false and perverse differed from the path of that same council.

Finally, you rebuked all the bishops of Egypt and all the clergy [perhaps “clerics”], decreeing in your general letters that unless within two months they abandoned what from the beginning they had devised against the canons, against the churches of God, and against the orthodox faith, and returned through worthy penitential satisfaction to the communion of blessed Timothy, which they had impiously abandoned, they would be deprived not only of their honors but also of the city of Alexandria and of the whole Egyptian region [Col. 0901D]. For, as the Christian emperor affirmed, it seemed unjust that those who had separated themselves from the Church existing throughout the world should possess priests or be reckoned under any sacred title of ministry. [Note: [Col. 0901D] Perhaps “from the Church” or “against the Church.” HARDUIN.] You, indignant that seditions had been stirred up by the Alexandrians, judged those who were held by a similar deception because of their clerical rank worthy of such punishment unless they obeyed salutary admonitions.

You singled out Peter with a particular indictment, because he had unlawfully thrust himself upon the Alexandrian Church, and commanded that all who had been ordained either by him or by the heretical Timothy, now deceased, should be received into the communion of the Catholic Timothy if they came to their senses within the appointed period [Col. 0902A]—though you did not decree that they should be admitted to the privileges of the ranks they had wrongly usurped—adding consequently that the others would suffer worse things if they did not choose the better course. After these various grounds for satisfaction, you entirely removed from everyone whatever, in your enumeration, you had judged those who had withdrawn from the fellowship of unity to have incurred. With wise consideration, you said nothing further about Peter’s person that might renew the matter against him: for you saw that he had been cast down from the citadel of the Church and at the same time stripped of the honor he had seized in the pontificate; nor could it in any way happen that one who had been instituted either by no one or by heretics should ever preside over the orthodox, or that one who had so often, with renewed audacity, violently and deceitfully, as an enemy, entered the Lord’s fold should again enter it.

[Col. 0902B] And therefore what you declared should be inflicted on his followers for the correction of their conduct, you reasonably judged had already been inflicted on him as the teacher of crime: so that he through whom he had plunged his brothers into ruin might himself become an example of fearful condemnation. This is so true that you carefully ordered a legion to stand guard over the venerable Timothy if anything human should happen to him. You were willing to see no shepherd except one from the college of Catholic clergy and consecrated by Catholics, because under the gaze of your serenity that chief of the Eutychian madness could nowhere, by any rite, be or be called the successor of an orthodox bishop. With what spirit, then, do you now allow the beast whom you declared must be driven away from Christ’s flocks to rage again for their destruction? Certainly, by the laws you impose on all, you wish rather to be overcome than to promulgate contrary laws; how much better it would be to let remain inviolate what yesterday you set forth for the preservation of the integrity of the whole Church, so that both the authority of your Catholic empire may remain unshaken and nothing may be added that could obstruct your prosperity in the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 0902C] For you see, venerable emperor, that just as the unequivocal defense of the Council of Chalcedon is the destruction of its enemies, so, conversely, its manifest assault proves the advancement of the enemies of that venerable knowledge [perhaps “protection”]. You remember how the divine words instruct us not to go beyond the boundary of right ordering either to the right or to the left, but, walking along the royal and middle way—as it is written (Deut. XXV)—to condemn and detest on either side the sacrileges of Nestorius and Eutyches. Thus they proclaim the mystery of great piety: that the consubstantial and eternal Word of almighty God the Father, who in his unchangeable divinity was both made flesh and, from the beginning of that ineffable conception which he powerfully prepared for himself in the womb of the Virgin Mother, remained one and the same Jesus Christ our Lord, one and the same Son of God and of man, one and the same truly remaining, without confusion and without division, God and man, brought forth under the inviolate law of the Father—this one, they professed, appeared in this world and performed both divine and human acts; died, and rising from the dead [Col. 0903A], sits at the right hand of the Father; and will likewise come from there, as he was seen to go into heaven. They professed this insofar as the tradition of the divine Books, the rule of the Council of Nicaea, and all the bishops who had preached in earlier times had handed it down.

This is attested by the chapters suitably inserted into the first Council of Ephesus, where the Nestorian plague was destroyed in the time of blessed Pope Celestine, and by the letters sent to Leo of august memory, holy Pope Leo, in which the chapters were included. That man, taking counsel also with the bishops of the whole East [Note: [Col. 0903D] Perhaps “the bishops.” HARDUIN.] and receiving their replies and signatures concerning the approval of the Council of Chalcedon, suffered none of these things to be changed. He judged all the more carefully, with a Christian mind, that this too was true: namely, that what was consonant with the divine affirmations had everywhere been proclaimed in harmony by the Catholic teachers throughout the world long before such a question arose. Therefore what was rightly condemned should not be dug up again by any repetition, lest not only the present cause extend destruction to the Catholic name everywhere, but also an opportunity be opened to all who remained for the resumption of public wars if, in any way, what the ancients had once universally decided were reopened. Thus you now clearly see that the corrupter of the Alexandrian Church, who has long been raging under a disastrous impunity, must nevertheless be driven away by your commands, by which he was rightly proved long ago to have been expelled.

Is he not himself the deserter of the Catholic Church for thirty years, and its enemies’ follower and teacher, always swift and ready to shed blood? Are we perhaps, through some connivance, subject to this dissimulation of the preceptor? No subtle investigation is needed here, because his crimes are manifest. Your piety is certainly grieved that, through the long and serious conflicts of the opposing party, many seem to have been taken from this world without baptism or communion. Therefore, under such a bishop, let them not be baptized and become heretics, and let them pass without communion lest they perish in the perversity of the lost—so that, as it is written [Col. 0904A], “The blind leading the blind, both will fall into the pit” (Matt. XV).

I beg you, is it not the most dangerous of decisions to determine this, when firm treatment is not applied to the wounded and pitiable contagion is inflicted upon the healthy? For how, they ask, can matters be calmed if they are allowed to continue their madness in the future? What does it mean to say that no cause for conflict remains, unless victory is granted to the heretics? Therefore, just as a kindly father, you shrink from inflicting even some bodily chastisement upon them; much more mercifully, do not allow their souls to be destroyed, but through a pious deposition bring them, once restrained, at last under a Catholic priest, so that they may obtain the effect of true rebirth and the secure aid of communion that will benefit them.

[Col. 0904B] Divine providence has placed in your hands the power by which you may likewise break the works of the treacherous. He drove away the devastator of our religion; drive the invasion of the plunderers from the necks of his Church. He pacified the commonwealth—as your own statement also attests—from heretical tyranny; restore freedom to Christians by rescuing the peoples from the very teachers of heresy. He restored you to the lawful imperial court, supported by the right of the emperor; restore the disciple to his teacher. Bring the see of blessed Mark the Evangelist back into communion with blessed Peter, with devotion grounded in the merits of their lives. Thus, when he who began the good work completes it in you, may you safely deserve to hear: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 24). And, for the increase of your glory, may you preside as God’s representative, truly worthy and an imitator of the Divinity, and, although you are still established in temporal affairs, may you already experience the gift prepared for you in eternal blessedness.

What the nature of the affair does not permit to be passed over could not all be included in letters. Certain matters have therefore been entrusted for personal discussion with our venerable brothers and fellow bishops, to whom the charge of the embassy has been assigned. I ask that you deign to hear them kindly and readily assent to them, both for the observance of Catholic truth and for the safety of your reign.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] This is the synodal letter sent by the Roman council to Peter the Fuller, in which, after his blasphemous errors had been refuted in the first session, he was admonished to come to his senses. See what we said there in the notes on that council.]

## LETTER III. TO PETER THE FULLER, FROM THE ROMAN SYNOD

[Note: [Col. 0903] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

It shows that Peter the Fuller, also called Cnapheus, fell not only into the heresies of Valentinus, Manichaeus, Arius, Sabellius, Apollinaris, and Eutyches, but also into the errors of paganism, which asserts many gods. It then urges him to repent and explains that one ought not to add to the Trisagion “Crucified for us”: “For it is not right to add in the Trisagion, ‘The one crucified for us’” (Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ προσθῆναι ἐν τῷ τρισαγίῳ· Ὁ σταυρωθεὶς δι’ ἡμᾶς).

[Col. 0903]

[Note: [Col. 0903D] This and the following letter are not Felix’s but Simplicius’s. Valesius considers them spurious in book I of his *Sacred Observations on Evagrius*, but Pagius defends them as genuine at the year of Christ 478, no. 9 and following, and at the year 485, no. 23. See the learned Maffei’s preface to the *Supplement to Acacius*, printed below.]

Felix, bishop, to Peter, bishop of Antioch.

[Col. 0903D] “Who will give water to my head and a spring of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. IX.) What kind of weeping, and what worthy lamentation, shall I bring to my soul, grieving with the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of the Lord our Savior Christ? For she has wept and wept over her sons and daughters, and there is no one among all who love her to comfort her (Lam. I). All the tyrants and heresiarchs who persecuted her have seized her through you, most honored brother; and, afflicting her, have become her head. All her beauty, insofar as it depends on you, has been reduced to nothing. Her enemies, seeing this, rejoiced over the destruction of her children. Those whom she had cherished, whom she had nourished, whom she had brought to maturity and fed with the milk of prophetic and apostolic teaching—you killed with poison in a single instant.

For just as those who practice fishing cover the hook with bait and catch fish unexpectedly, so you introduced an addition into the angels’ hymn and, under the pretext of piety, devised a dreadful impiety in the Trisagion prayer. For we have received letters from many eastern provinces informing us that your Reverence has revived the doctrine of Valentinus, long silenced, and that among you the saving incarnation of the Savior is being rejected, and that you have fallen into the doctrines of Manichaeus, Arius, Apollinaris, and Paul of Samosata.

To say that the only-begotten Son and our Lord Jesus Christ is not perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, and that he himself did not undergo the passion of the cross, but that there is one incarnate nature of the Word of God, and that the Lord’s body is without soul and mind, strengthens the heresy of Apollinaris. For he did not know that, from the very beginning of the world’s creation, first the soul of our first parent died, or was cast into death, and only thereafter the body. For God said to him: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die the death” (Gen. II). Therefore, according to the sentence imposed on him by God, he died in his soul on that very day. The death of his body occurred only after nine hundred and thirty years.

Therefore God did not make the gift incomplete, but took the whole Adam at once from the Virgin’s womb, so that he might save the whole of what had been lost. For this reason the Lord himself also said: “I lay down my soul for the sheep” (John X). You wish likewise to renew the doctrines of Valentinus, Marcion, the Manichaeans, and the pagans. [Note: [Col. 0905D] The Greek version adds “the Basilidians.”]

For if it is God who died in a divisible and substantial manner, then likewise the Holy Spirit, who is God, will also be found to have died in a divisible and substantial manner. Thus, according to your reasoning and theirs, there will be three gods; and consequently the error of polytheism will prevail. Insofar as you are concerned, the words “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. IV) will be emptied of meaning. Likewise, what Jeremiah said: “This is our God; no other will be reckoned beside him” (Baruch III). And likewise the Lord: “That they may know you, the only true God” (John XVII).

Although Scripture proclaims one God, the holy and undivided Trinity, you and the heresiarchs who preceded you have dared to teach three gods: saying that God the Father is one God apart from the Son, and God the Son another apart from the Father, and again that the Holy Spirit is another God apart from the Father and the Son; one mortal and newly born, the other eternal and immortal.

In these harmful opinions of yours, you wish to think contrary to the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, Constantinople, and Chalcedon, who strengthened the doctrine of consubstantiality and proclaimed one divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and confounded the madness of Arius. But you dared to say in church that one of the uncreated and undivided Trinity underwent the passion. By this you also attempt to dissolve consubstantiality and subject God to number.

For if one of the holy Trinity—the uncreated and coeternal God who was crucified—is the Son, while the other two of the Trinity are the Father and the Holy Spirit, and they are called gods rather than, as right reason teaches, God, as those who saw for themselves and became ministers of the word handed down to us (Acts I), you will also be found to dissolve consubstantiality. For what is mortal and what is immortal can no longer be consubstantial. Thus the plurality of gods will be strengthened, as three gods are thrust upon Christian ears.

Since it is written, “The Word became flesh, and the Word was God” (John I), the Word will not be found to be another God apart from the Father: the Word not merely as a word, but as a substantial Word; and he is found to be God the Son, so that from our lowliness we may recognize the identity of substance of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. For neither will we be found to be other than our own word.

Since, therefore, the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as he is the Word, could not suffer in his own substance, lest the passion be referred to the substance of God the almighty Father—for the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one—his own animated body suffers. The substantial Word of God himself joined this body to himself from the womb of the holy and undefiled Virgin and came forth from a woman, concerning whom the prophets, inspired by the Holy Spirit, sang:

“God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine; and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself” (Ps. LXXIX).

He called the vine and the son of man, whom the Word strengthened, the saving incarnation of the Word, so that he might crush the bars of hell and give life to those who had been dead from the beginning of the ages. For this reason the Lord also said to his disciples: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the husbandman” (John XV); and, “The Son of man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matt. XXVI).

For the Father’s substantial and personal Word, God, entering through the ears of the holy Virgin, brought about the conception ineffably. Therefore, insofar as the only-begotten Son is consubstantial with the Father and one of the undivided Trinity, uncreated and invisible, he remained impassible and immortal. Do not therefore apply what is uncreated and immortal to creation, nor continue to strengthen the argument for a plurality of gods by saying that one of the Trinity died.

But insofar as he was born from a woman and, without sin, shares our substance and our generation, he endured the passion. Moreover, that the Son of God is not only consubstantial with us but also our kinsman according to the flesh, the Lord himself teaches: in the Gospels he says to those who believed in him, “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John XV); and in the Psalms, “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI).

From where could such wicked pride have crept into you that you considered yourself more intelligent and wiser even than the holy angels? Over these things I groan; over these things I lament the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. III).

Did you not consider how great a punishment it brings upon one who scandalizes even a single person among those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ? Yet heedlessly, like the serpent with Eve, you too poured the poison of error into the multitude of the faithful and into their ears, and corrupted the most holy hymn of praise delivered to us by the angels by inserting into it: “The one crucified for us.”

Did you not realize that you surpass Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Artemas in impiety? They posited two Sons of God, one before the ages and the other newly born, whereas you have also introduced plurality into the Trinity by speaking of two Sons of God, one the mighty one and the other the crucified one.

Moreover, you strive to plunge Christ’s most faithful flock into the opinion of Manichaeus, who asserts that the Holy Spirit was crucified. For after “Holy immortal”—which refers to the Holy Spirit—you then add, “The one crucified for us, have mercy on us,” and you seem to teach the people a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

If this hymn had arisen from human tradition, you would not have inserted the cross into the praise so carelessly, in which the designation of the Son—namely, “mighty”—is placed. But since this hymn of praise was given to us by the angels, who before the cross said, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. VI), as Isaiah was deemed worthy to see, while after the cross they cried in praise, “Holy God, holy mighty, holy immortal”—

[Note: [Col. 0909D] The story of the earthquake and the miraculous institution of the Trisagion occurred in the year of Christ 446. Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* and Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 46, mention it. Almost all the bishops, in their letters sent from the Council of Constantinople held under Pope Felix III to Peter the Fuller, confirmed this event, so great and wholly beyond human comprehension, with the most magnificent testimonies. This Trisagion was sung at the end of the first session of the Council of Chalcedon. The Greeks publicly read the entire story in church from their ancient menologion on the day when they commemorate the anniversary of this event. The words of the menologion, as edited, appear above in the notes on the Council of Chalcedon, at the end of session 1, under the word “Trisagion.”]

Finally, when Constantinople was shaken by an earthquake and the people were praying in the field, a very young child was caught up into the heavens for an hour, while the whole people and Proclus, the bishop of the city, watched. There he learned this hymn. Then, descending again, he announced what he had heard in the air, saying that from heaven, as though from a multitude singing psalms, such praises had sounded in his ears, and that he had been told to make that hymn of praise known to the people. When the people began it, they recovered the city; and, having won God’s favor through such praise, they were delivered from the impending wrath.

But you have dared, as recklessly as you pervert the rest of the divine Scriptures, to corrupt the angels’ hymn. Who, then, would not groan at such things? Who would not lament? What sorrow could be found like the sorrow of the Church of the Lord and our Savior Christ?

Behold yourself appointed to be a light to those who are in darkness and an instructor of the foolish (Rom. II, 5); indeed, you are a teacher of foolishness, turning light into darkness. See the peoples, once enlightened, who tasted the good word of God, God’s commandments, God’s prophetic declarations, God’s apostolic and evangelical teachings, being perverted by you and taught not only to crucify the Son of God and expose him to public shame, but also to think contrary to the divine Scriptures and to deny the covenants they made when they approached holy baptism.

For when, in the presence of all the heavenly powers and of the apostolic and evangelical orders, they promised at the time of holy baptism to believe in one God almighty, you have now taught them to believe in three gods. Again, when they promised to believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, incarnate and made man from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, you teach them not to say that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, endured the cross: that he is God according to his eternal and impassible generation from the Father, and the same man according to the generation by which he came forth from his mother in the last days, according to which he also endured the passion; but rather that one of the Trinity died, namely the very Word of God.

Again, they confessed the Holy Spirit to be life-giving and immortal, saying that they believed in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life; but you make the Holy Spirit mortal when you say: “Holy immortal, the one crucified for us.” Flee, I beg you, from this error. You have fallen; do not remain in your ruin. You have sinned; do not sin any longer.

The holy Church of God awaits you and longs to embrace you when you repent of your vain propositions, and to have you proclaim the divine teaching about Christ with her, without denying his animated incarnation, according to which he is also said to have suffered. Through us she cries to you: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

God does not desire the death of a sinner, most dear brother, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII). Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead (2 Tim. II), according to the Gospel. Remember blessed Matthew, who wrote: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I). Recall what Paul writes: “Set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God” (Rom. I).

Remember also John crying out: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, as he is, and the Word was God” (John I); and that he became flesh, having assumed humanity, and that no one has ever seen God (John I, 18).

I have written these things to you together with the holy synod assembled with me, charging you before God and the holy angels to teach these things and to think these things with us, so that our faith may remain undefiled to the glory of God.

[Col. 0904D] “Who will give water to my head and a spring of tears to my eyelids?” (Jer. IX.) What kind of worthy lamentation shall I bring to my own soul, grieving together with the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of the Lord and Savior Christ? She has wept and wept over her sons and daughters, and there is no one among all who love her to comfort her (Lam. I). All the tyrants and heresiarchs who persecuted her have seized her through you, most honored brother; and those who afflicted her have become her head. All her beauty, insofar as it depends on you, has been reduced to nothing. Her enemies, seeing this, rejoiced over the destruction of her children. For those whom she raised, nursed, brought to maturity, and fed with prophetic and apostolic teachings, you killed with poison in a single instant.

For just as those who practice fishing cover the hook with bait and catch fish unexpectedly, so you added something to the angels’ hymn and, as though under the appearance of piety, devised a dreadful impiety in the Trisagion prayer.

[Col. 0906B] For we received letters from many provinces in the East informing us that your God-loving Reverence has taken up again the doctrine of Valentinus, formerly silenced, that among you the saving incarnation is being rejected, and that you have been driven into the Manichaean doctrine and that of Arius, Apollinaris, and Paul of Samosata.

For not saying that the only-begotten Son and our Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, that he himself endured the passion of the cross, but instead asserting one incarnate nature of the Word of God and the Lord’s body without soul and mind, strengthens the heresy of Apollinaris. For he did not know that at the very beginning of the creation of the world the soul of the first-formed man and our forefather was first put to death, and only afterward the body. For God said to him: “On whatever day you eat from the tree, you shall surely die” (Gen. II). Therefore, according to the sentence inflicted upon him by God, on the day when he ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he died in his soul; the death of his body occurred after nine hundred and thirty years.

God, therefore, did not make his gift incomplete, but took the whole Adam at once from the Virgin’s womb, so that he might save the whole of what had been lost. Therefore the Lord said: “I lay down my soul for the sheep” (John X). But you wish to strengthen the religious doctrines of Valentinus, Marcion, the Manichaeans, the Basilidians, and also the Greeks.

For if God died divisibly and substantially, and likewise the Holy Spirit is God and is also found to have died divisibly and substantially, then, according to your reasoning and theirs, three gods will be found, and the error of polytheism will thereby be strengthened. Insofar as you are concerned, the words “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” will have been scattered (Deut. IV); likewise what Jeremiah said: “The Lord our God; no other will be reckoned beside him” (Baruch III); and likewise the Lord: “That they may know you, the only true God” (John XVII).

While divine Scripture proclaims one God, the holy and undivided Trinity, you and the heresiarchs before you have taught three gods: saying that the Father is one God apart from the Son, another God is the Son apart from the Father, and again another God is the Holy Spirit apart from the Father and the Son; one mortal and newly born, the other without beginning and immortal.

In these harmful opinions of yours, you wish to think contrary to the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, Constantinople, and Chalcedon, who strengthened the doctrine of consubstantiality and proclaimed one divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, crying out against the derangement of Arius. Yet you dared to say in church that one of the uncreated and undivided Trinity underwent the passion; and therefore you attempted to dissolve consubstantiality also and to subject the divine nature to number.

For if one of the holy Trinity, the uncreated and coeternal God the Word who was crucified, is the Son—that is, one—and the other two of the Trinity are the Father and the Holy Spirit, and they are called gods rather than, in the proper sense, God, as those who saw for themselves and became ministers of the word handed down to us (Acts I), then consubstantiality is also dissolved: for the mortal and the immortal can no longer be consubstantial. Thus the argument for polytheism will be strengthened by proclaiming three gods in Christianity.

Since it is written that “the Word became flesh, and the Word was God” (John I), the Word will not be found to be another God apart from the Father: the Word not merely in a general sense, but the Word personally subsisting. And he is called the Son so that, from our lowliness, we may know the sameness of substance of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. For we too will not be found to be other than our own word.

Since, therefore, the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as he is the Word, could not suffer in his own substance, lest the passion be reckoned against the substance of God the almighty Father—for the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one—the living body belonging to the Word suffers. The personal Word of God himself united it to himself from the womb of the holy and undefiled Virgin and came forth from a woman. Concerning her, the divinely inspired men, foreseeing the matter, said:

“God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine, and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself” (Ps. LXXIX).

He calls the vine and the son of man whom the Word strengthened so that he might crush the bars of Hades and give life to those who had died from the ages the saving incarnation of the Word. Therefore God also said to his disciples: “I am the vine, you are the branches,” and “My Father is the husbandman” (John XV); and, “The Son of man is about to be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matt. XXVI).

For the personal Word of the Father, God, entered through the hearing of the holy Virgin and mysteriously brought about the gestation. Therefore, insofar as the only-begotten Son is consubstantial with the Father and one of the undivided Trinity, uncreated and unseen, he remained impassible and immortal.

Do not, then, join what is uncreated and immortal to creation, and do not strengthen the argument for polytheism by saying that one of the Trinity died. But insofar as he was born from a woman and is our fellow-born, of the same race and substance as we are, without sin, he endured the passion.

That the Son, according to the flesh, is not only consubstantial with us but also our kinsman, the Lord himself teaches when he says, at one time in the Gospels to those who believe in him: “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John XV); and at another time in the Psalms: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI).

From where did such a wicked conception enter you that you should consider yourself more intelligent and wiser even than the holy angels? Over these things I weep; over these things I lament the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. III).

Did you not understand that to scandalize even one of those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ incurs intolerable indignation? Yet without caution, like the serpent with Eve, you too poured the poison of deception into the multitude of the faithful and into their ears, and adulterated the Trisagion hymn delivered to us by the angels by inserting into it: “The one crucified for us.”

Did you not realize that you have defined yourself as more impious than Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Artemas, who defined two Sons of God, one eternal and one newly born? You too have introduced excess into the Trinity by speaking of two Sons of God, one mighty and one crucified.

Moreover, you think to lead Christ’s most faithful flock into the opinion of Manes, according to whose teaching the Holy Spirit was crucified. For after saying, “Holy immortal”—which is the Holy Spirit—you then add, “The one crucified for us, have mercy on us,” and you teach the people to find a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

If the hymn had existed by human tradition, you might still have placed the cross in the Trisagion with such caution, where the designation of the Son, “mighty,” is spoken. But since this Trisagion hymn was delivered to us by angels—who before the cross said, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. VI), as Isaiah was deemed worthy to see, and after the cross sang, “Holy God, holy mighty, holy immortal”—a very young child, while Constantinople was being shaken and the people were praying in the field, was carried up into the air for about an hour before the entire multitude and Proclus, the city’s bishop. There he learned the hymn; then, having been brought down again, he reported what he had been taught in the air, saying that from heaven, as though from a multitude, this hymn had sounded in his ears, and that he had been told to proclaim it to the people. When the people began it, they recovered the city; and, having appeased God through such a hymn, they were delivered from the impending wrath.

[lacuna]

But you have recklessly dared to distort the angels’ hymn, just as you have distorted the other divine Scriptures.

Who, then, will not mourn at such things? Who will not sigh? What sorrow could be found like the sorrow of the Church of the Lord and our Savior? To see the one appointed to be a light to those in darkness and an instructor of the foolish (Rom. II, 5) instead becoming a teacher of folly and turning light into darkness; to see the peoples once enlightened and having tasted the good word of God, God’s commandments, God’s prophetic revelations, and God’s apostolic and evangelical teachings, being further perverted by you and taught not only to crucify the Son of God and expose him to public shame, but also to think contrary to the divine Scriptures and to deny the covenants they made when they approached holy baptism.

For when, in the presence of all the cherubic powers and the prophetic and apostolic orders, they promised at the time of holy baptism to believe in one God, the almighty Father, you have now taught them to believe in three gods. Again, when they promised to believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was incarnate and became man from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, you teach them not to say that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, endured the cross: that he is God according to his eternal and impassible generation from God the Father, and the same man according to his generation in the last days, according to which he also endured the passion; but instead that one of the Trinity died, namely the very Word of God.

Again, they confessed the Holy Spirit to be life-giving and immortal, saying that they believed in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life; but you suppose the Holy Spirit to be mortal by saying: “Holy immortal, the one crucified for us.” Flee, I beg you, from this error. You have fallen; do not remain in your fall. You have sinned; sin no more.

The holy Church of God awaits you, longing to embrace you when you repent of your futile propositions, and to have you theologize with her about Christ, without denying his living incarnation, according to which he is also said to have endured the passion. Through us she cries out to you: “Come to me, all you who labor,” and what follows (Matt. XI).

God does not desire the death of a sinner, most honored brother, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII). Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead (2 Tim. II), according to the Gospel. Remember blessed Matthew writing: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I). Remember Paul writing: “Set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand in the holy Scriptures,” speaking of his Son, “who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was appointed the Son of God” (Rom. I).

Remember also John crying out: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God—as he also is—and the Word was God” (John I); and that he became flesh by becoming man, and that no one has ever seen God (John I, 18).

I have written these things to you together with the holy synod assembled with me, charging you before God and the holy angels to teach these things and to think these things with us, so that our faith may remain undefiled to the glory of God.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME

Peter the Fuller is deposed and anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 0911] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0911]

Since you have impiously babbled with unbearable words and have not judged it right to yield to the holy Fathers mentioned above, who adorned the see of the blessed and greatly triumphant martyr Ignatius—although you are unworthy of him, I do not know how you have leapt forward to introduce novelty into the Catholic Church by your profane laws and impious doctrines—and since you judged that one ought not to say “Christ crucified for us,” but instead impiously imposed passion upon the impassible and death upon the immortal Father, and did not shudder to twist what you had not received from the divine Gospels, the apostles, and the most approved and glorious Fathers, sophistically distorting these things and imposing the corruption of your own judgment upon the simple, thereby making the scandal of such a heresy not merely equal to the earlier heresies but surpassing them many times over; and since you did not resolve to believe the truth or to heed the two letters we wrote to you, I now begin to pronounce sentence against you—or rather, he does so who is the summit of all pastoral sees, flourishing in holy praises, truly the foremost of the apostles, Peter, whose name you share but not his mind or faith, since you have greatly departed from his right intention and undefiled faith.

And I pronounce sentence not only against you but also against those who were not ashamed of the characters of the venerable evangelists, the words of the apostles who followed them, and those of perfect teachers, and who have been established by an unstable judgment on your wicked exposition, as though they were sweetly pursuing what is truly most bitter, namely an evil doctrine, and have not turned away from such impiety.

We shall therefore say to you, as also against them: “Because you loved wickedness more than speaking righteousness, you loved above all the tongue of hasty speech and deceit” [according to the Greek: “all the words of destruction, a deceitful tongue”]; “therefore God will destroy you forever” (Ps. LI). He will depose you not only from the Church of Antioch but from every city. Let this deposition of yours be confirmed by me and by those who govern the apostolic throne together with me, and by Acacius, pastor of the Church of Constantinople, and by the venerable bishops subject to him, because you did not endure their memorials.

For at one time you say that the Trinity was crucified for us, not Christ; at another, while acting like a Manichaean, you say that the immortal Spirit suffered; at another, fleeing from these positions after being refuted by my arguments and words, you say that Christ suffered after the immortal Spirit, like the Samosatan and Nestorius, dividing the one Son into a duality of sons.

At another time, without rejecting these positions, you yielded to them and came to something worse: not glorifying the cherubic hymn by referring the Trinity, with reverent trembling and without hesitation, to the Son, but wishing to establish the gangrene of the disease that you inflicted upon the innocent by referring the whole hymn to the Son. Thus, caught in the snares of every kind of heresy and departing from the truth, you neither proclaim Christ crucified for us nor devoutly glorify the only-begotten Son of God, who is glorified in the midst of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For what is more forbidden than this: that the Father and the Holy Spirit are not glorified by you? You bring an accusation against the seraphim, saying that they do not glorify the Trinity with “Holy, holy, holy,” but only the Son personally. What precipitous confusion of heresies has acted so shamelessly as you have?

Nevertheless, even in this you have gone farther in your novelty and added God-forbidden and strangling slanders, saying that the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are to be joined together in the manner of Sabellius. You deny the Trinity in which we are baptized, in which we believe, and which we confess.

Who, then, would not weep when you speak thus about the undefiled Trisagion? It is especially fitting for me to reject this and to shed a worthy tear over those who have been plundered through it—the simple souls deceived by you, who fabricate an impious deed as though it were pious. We have judged them alien both from the orthodox faith and the Catholic Church and from communion with our glorious leader and predecessor Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom from our Savior.

But those who wish to be participants with the apostle are guided also by his teaching: he says and believes that Christ was crucified for us and does not deny this, as does Peter, recently deposed because he innovated unlawfully and hostilely in the Trisagion by adding, “The one who was crucified for us.” For you know that you did not receive from the apostles a crucified Trinity—not the Father, not the Holy Spirit—but only the one and only-begotten Son of God according to the flesh.

Flee, therefore, from this hostile communion, and I shall be in communion with you insofar as you are with me, once deceitful fraud has been driven far from our orthodoxy. Preserve, disciples of Christ, and my sons, the traditions that you received from the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0912D] Since you have unfortunately been bewitched by the impiety of your words and did not judge it right to yield to the holy men mentioned above, who adorned the throne of the blessed and much-suffering martyr Ignatius—although you are unworthy of him, I do not know how you have stumbled into beginning, and have approved innovation in the Catholic Church through your profane laws and impious doctrines—not saying that Christ was crucified for us, but lawlessly imposing passion upon the impassible God and death upon the immortal Spirit.

And you did not shudder to twist, through the worst sophistry, what you had not received from the divine Gospels, the apostles, and the renowned Fathers who performed great deeds, and to set before the simpler people the corruption of your own mind, making the scandal of such a heresy something that not only flourishes equally with the earlier heresies but surpasses them in many ways. You did not hasten toward the truth or heed our letters written to you twice.

Now I begin to pronounce sentence against you—or rather, the foremost of pastoral thrones does so: he who adorns himself with holy praises, truly the best of the apostles, Peter, whose name you equally bear, but not his mind or faith, since you have deviated exceedingly from his right aim and undefiled faith.

And not only against you, but also against those who were not ashamed of the writings of the venerable evangelists, the words of the apostles who followed them, and those of perfect teachers, relying with unstable judgment on the exposition falsified by you [perhaps “made unlawful by you”], as though they were most sweetly pursuing what is truly most bitter, namely evil doctrine, and did not turn away from such impiety.

We shall therefore say to you, as also against them: “Because you loved wickedness more than speaking righteousness, you loved all the words of destruction, a deceitful tongue; therefore God will cast you down forever” (Ps. LI), not only from the Church of Antioch but also from every city. Let this deposition be firmly established by me, by those who govern the apostolic throne with me, by Acacius, pastor of the Church of Constantinople, and by the honorable bishops subject to him within his jurisdiction, because you did not endure their records.

For at one time you said that the Trinity was crucified for us and not Christ; at another, acting like a Manichaean, you said that the immortal Spirit suffered; at another, fleeing from these positions and being thoroughly refuted by my admonitions and words, you said that Christ endured the passion after the immortal Spirit, like the Samosatan and Nestorius, dividing the one Son into a duality of sons.

When you yielded even on this point and did not reject it, you came to something worse: you did not glorify the cherubic hymn by reverently and without hesitation referring the Trinity to the Son, but wished to direct the whole hymn to the Son and to establish the gangrene of the disease that you had brought against the innocent.

From that point, being caught in every kind of great heresy’s noose and turning away from the truth, you ceased to proclaim Christ crucified for us, the only-begotten Son of God, who is devoutly glorified in the midst of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For what is more prohibited than this, when the Father and the Holy Spirit are dishonored by you? And when you introduce slander against the seraphim, saying that they do not glorify the Trinity with “Holy, holy, holy,” but only the Son as a single person? What ravine of heresies has acted so shamelessly as you?

Yet, while proceeding through these matters, you have advanced still more innovatively, adding strangling calumnies forbidden by God, saying that the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are to be joined together in the manner of Sabellius. You have openly denied the Trinity, in which we were baptized, in which we believe, and which we confess.

Who, then, would not lament those who rave in this way about the undefiled Trisagion? It is entirely fitting for me to reject this and to shed a worthy lament over those who are being despoiled through it—simple souls whom you deceive and who stage an impious deed as though it were pious.

We have regarded them as strangers to the orthodox faith, to the Catholic Church, and to communion with our glorious leader, the chief bishop Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom from our Savior.

Those who wish to be companions of the apostle are led also by his teaching: they say and believe that Christ was crucified for us and do not deny this, as does Peter, recently deposed because he introduced into the Trisagion, in a strange and hostile manner, the words “The one crucified for us.” For you know that you did not receive from the apostles a crucified Trinity—not the Father, not the Holy Spirit—but only the only-begotten Son of God according to the flesh.

Flee, therefore, from this hostile communion, and I shall be in communion with you insofar as you are with me, once deceitful pretense has leapt far away from your orthodoxy. Preserve, disciples of Christ, my sons, the traditions that you received from the divine Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] The Ballerini brothers, in the dissertation prefixed to volume III of the works of Saint Leo, noted that in the collection called the Avellana, preserved in Vatican codex 4961, there exists an old version of this letter of Felix to Peter, different from that read in the collections of the councils; they assert that it is printed by the compilers of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, volume I, page 326. I have judged that it should be reproduced here, both because it is extremely ancient and because it is contained in the highly esteemed Avellana edition. They further add that in the same Avellana codex there is likewise a different version of the following Greek letters from that which is read here in the councils. I would gladly have had these versions copied for my present use when I was in Rome, if time had permitted. —This is the third letter of Pope Felix which he sent from the Roman synod to Peter the Fuller; in it, after two salutary admonitions, he condemned him, rightly and deservedly, by a sentence of anathema and deposition. That this was the third letter written to him is indicated by these words of the letter, according to the edition found in volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*: “You have been unwilling either to walk in the truth or to incline your ear to our two letters; therefore now I have begun to pronounce sentence against you,” etc. Hence it is clear that the second admonitory letter of Pope Felix sent to Peter has perished. —SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## LETTER OF THE SAME POPE FELIX III TO PETER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH: AN ANCIENT VERSION

### Peter of Antioch is deposed and anathematized

Since you are imbued with pestilential doctrines and impiety of speech, and have not cared to follow the holy Fathers appointed beforehand, who established the see of the blessed Ignatius, the glorious martyr—though, unworthy as you are, I do not know how you obtained its primacy—and since, through your profane crimes and impious doctrines, you have thought to introduce novelty into the Catholic Church, so that you do not say that Christ was crucified for us, but have most wickedly inflicted suffering upon the impassible God and dared to impose death upon the immortal Spirit;

and since you have not been terrified by what was not handed down to you by the holy Gospels, the apostles, and the most blessed and approved men among the Fathers, but have supported these things by crafty inventions and impressed upon simpler people the opinion of your own sickness and the scandal of this heresy, so that it seems not merely similar to the earlier heresies but rather surpasses them in many ways;

and since you have been unwilling either to walk in the truth or to lend an ear to our two letters, I have now begun to pronounce sentence against you—more truly, the supreme prince of the apostles, Peter, who is truthful among the proclamations of the holy apostles—and not only against you, since you are known to be the equal of the man’s name but neither of his judgment nor of his faith, having strayed far beyond measure from his upright purpose and inviolable faith, but also against those who, not blushing before the venerable characters of the Gospels, nor before the discourses of the apostles, their followers, leaders, and learned men, in an inconstant judgment cling to your wicked traditions.

Thus, in truth, they willingly follow the bitterness of an evil sect and do not recoil from such execrable impiety. We therefore say to you, as also to them: “Because you loved wickedness more than goodness, and iniquity rather than speaking righteousness; you loved every word of destruction and a deceitful tongue; therefore God will destroy you forever”—not only from the see of the Church of Antioch, but also from every city.

Let this condemnation therefore be fixed upon you by me and by those who are known to govern episcopal sees under me, and by Acacius, pastor of the Church of Constantinople, and by the venerable bishops subject to his jurisdiction, as men who likewise in no way consent to your inventions.

For at one time you said, “The Trinity was crucified for us,” and not Christ; at another, following the error of the Manichaeans, you said that the immortal Spirit suffered; and at another, fleeing these positions after being rebuked by the testimony of our words, you said that Christ suffered after the immortal Spirit, like Paul of Samosata.
