And, dividing the one Son into a duality of sons, like Nestorius, when you thought you should not remain at this point, you proceeded to worse things, so that the hymns which the Cherubim continually utter with trembling would not be referred to the glorification of the Trinity, but that the entire hymn might be dedicated to the Son.

Seeking to confirm, like a creeping cancer, the opinion which you had put forward against the simple, you were thereby plunged into the snares of all heresies, turning away from the truth and failing to proclaim Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, crucified for us, who is in the midst of the Father and the Holy Spirit and is glorified.

For what could be more condemnable than for the Father and the Holy Spirit to be made inglorious by you, and for blasphemy to be brought against the Seraphim, when it is believed that they do not glorify the Trinity as they say, “Holy, holy, holy,” but only one Person? What infernal heresy was ever so shameless and cruel as yours?

Nevertheless, while you continue to run about in this novelty, you reach even the foundations of blasphemies against God, saying that the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are one; you follow Sabellius, introduce confusion, and at the same time deny the confession of the Trinity, in which we were baptized, and which we believe and confess.

Who, then, would not mourn those who say such things about the holy and inviolable Trinity? It is very fitting for me to lament this and pour out an adequate wail, since the souls of simple people have been taken captive in this matter, and have proclaimed an impious thing as though it were pious.

We also judge such people to be strangers to the orthodox faith, to the Catholic Church, and to communion with our glorious prince Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from our Savior.

Those, therefore, who wish to be companions of the apostle must also follow his teaching, saying and believing that Christ was crucified for us and not denying him, as Peter—who was recently condemned—did, because he wickedly and impiously introduced into the *Trisagion* the novelty “who was crucified for us,” knowing that you did not receive from the apostles a Trinity crucified, nor the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but only the flesh of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God.

Therefore flee from this sacrilegious communion, and I shall be your companion and communicant, and you likewise mine, once the deceitful pestilence has been driven far from your uprightness. Guard, disciples of Christ—and my sons—the traditions which you received from the sacred books.

> “Here ends the letter of Pope Felix to Peter of Antioch, condemning him. As the text of the letter indicates, it was written before the condemnation of Acacius; but because we found it translated from Latin together with other letters addressed to the same Peter in a Greek volume, we have now, compelled by necessity, copied it again in translation from Greek into Latin, because of the plots of the heretics, and have joined it to the aforesaid letters of the same pope.”

## LETTER V: TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

[Note: [Col. 0917] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel by Migne.]

He announces to the emperor that Peter the Fuller has been condemned by synodal judgment with a sentence of anathema, and that therefore communion with him must be avoided. He urges the same emperor to expel the deposed Peter from the Church of Antioch.

[Col. 0917]

[Note: [Col. 0917D] This was sent to Zeno after the Roman synod, in the year 485.]

To the most glorious and serene son, Zeno Augustus, Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

It is fitting to report to Your Clemency the order of the events that have occurred for the tranquillity of your imperial serenity. I ask you to receive my petition with your gracious ears as though I myself were present, as a most Christian emperor; and let Your Piety by no means suppose that anyone loves us with a pure heart who does not wish you to have peace with God.

Since you have believed with a faithful mind, and do not doubt that both the power of the temporal throne and the reward of eternal life depend upon a decree from above, deign also, through our lowliness, to receive the venerable and divine confession of the most blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, to whom the keys of the kingdom were entrusted by the Savior. He will also prepare for your most Christian empire a place in heaven with the holy angels. He was the first to set forth the immutable and undefiled faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, and was called blessed by the Savior himself.

For when he said to the Lord, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), he deserved to hear from him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven; and upon this confession I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (ibid.).

Since, then, the Savior said that the gates of hell would not prevail against his Church, Peter—the firstborn son of the devil—who most unworthily thrust himself into the holy Church of Antioch and polluted the holy see of the pontificate of Ignatius the martyr, who was ordained bishop by the right hand of Peter, and of Eustathius the confessor and president of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, dared to say that Christ must not also be called the Son of God, according to the divine ordinance of the Savior, the tradition of the divine Scriptures, and the exposition of the Fathers, but that one Person of the Trinity endured suffering for us in the substance of deity, in accordance with the blasphemy of Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius.

By this expression he sought to nullify the saving incarnation of the Lord, according to which Christ also underwent suffering. He is also called one of us, since he assumed the seed of Abraham (Hebrews 2). He further attempts to increase the plurality of gods. For the meaning of his statement introduces three gods: one dead and two living.

He also dissolves the term “consubstantial” and rejects the holy councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, and Chalcedon. He is also found not to admit holy Mary the Virgin. For if the Word did not become incarnate and become human from her, what need was there for the Virgin? And why would Gabriel have said to her, “The holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 2)?

After all these impious and blasphemous presumptions of his, and wishing to corrupt the *Trisagion* prayer by adding to it the words “who was crucified for us,” he produced countless absurdities. Though admonished many times by us, by our brothers beloved in Christ who are in the East, and by the venerable Acacius, archbishop of your royal and God-beloved city, he refused to turn back.

Therefore the holy Church of God now does not cease to address you in a mother’s voice, as her distinguished son:

“O emperor beloved by Christ, bond of my dignity, in which the multitudes of the faithful are bound together, do not permit it to be broken. Do not permit the praise of the Lord Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be transgressed, nor that which saved your city when it was in danger; preserve it undefiled, as an angelic tradition.

Expel from the Church of Antioch Peter, the follower of Arian superstition. For what reason does Peter tear my seamless garment woven from above (Matthew 16)? God the Father commanded the prince of the apostles what the Son should be called. His only-begotten Son founded me upon the confession of the chief of the apostles. The Holy Spirit testifies to me daily, saying: ‘Do not judge yourself to know anything except Jesus Christ, and him crucified’ (John 19).

But if enemies, unbelievers, and plotters, who are outside the vine and who slaughtered and stoned the only-begotten Son of God, did not divide his garment, is Peter to tear apart the garment of my faith? The gates of hell did not prevail against me (Matthew 19), and Peter attempts to demolish my walls?

I, most devout emperor, restored you to the empire after you had been expelled from it. I gave the wicked and disobedient, who opposed my divine doctrines, over to your burial; I opened the way of power before you; I struck down your enemies together with their wicked doctrine; I sought out for you the ancient power from God who reigns in the heights, from whom you also received your reign.

Look to your predecessor, the most devout emperor Marcian, and gladly embrace his faith. Root out Peter’s heretical tyranny as quickly as possible. Expel from the city and from ecclesiastical government the disciple of Valentinus and Eutyches, and decree that he has been cast down from hierarchical dignity.

Look, most holy son and unconquered emperor, at what indisputable defense was made at the Council of Chalcedon, and by what means it overcame Aeschinus [according to the Greek: ‘what vengeance was taken upon your enemy’—he means Basiliscus, the enemy of the Council of Chalcedon]. Disperse the publications of Peter’s heretical doctrine.

Let the holy apostolic and Catholic Church of God read this, so that you may not receive into communion the man deposed by it for the reasons stated above; but by the divine letters of your serenity drive him from the territory of Antioch. In his place appoint a man who adorns the priesthood by his works and is a diligent guardian of the holy Council of Chalcedon and of the things confirmed in it.

May almighty God always preserve your power in peace.”

[Col. 0918C]

It befits your benevolence that these events be reported in their proper order, as is fitting, for the benefit of the power of your serenity. And, as though I were present nearby, I entreat you to receive my supplication with your kindly ears, as a most Christian emperor. Let Your Piety by no means suppose that anyone loves us with a pure mind except the one who wishes you to have peace with God.

Since, proceeding from a faithful mind, you do not doubt that the authority of the temporal throne and the recompense of eternal life are suspended from the stream from above, deign, through our lowliness, to receive the venerable and God-inspired confession of the most blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, who, entrusted by the Savior with the keys of the kingdom, will prepare for your Christ-loving empire life in the heights with the angels. He was the first to set forth the unaltered and blameless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, and was blessed by the Savior himself.

For when he said to the Lord, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), he heard from him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in the heavens; and upon this confession of yours I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it” (ibid.).

Since, then, the Savior said that the gates of Hades would not prevail against his Church, so as to remove from it his own name, which is called Christ Jesus and Son of almighty God, Peter—the firstborn son of the devil—who unworthily thrust himself into the holy Church of God at Antioch and polluted the archiepiscopal throne of Ignatius the martyr, who received the archpriesthood from Peter’s right hand, and of Eustathius the confessor and president of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, dared to say that Christ must not be called the Son of God, according to the divine legislation of the Savior, the tradition of the divine Scriptures, and the exposition of the Fathers, but that one of the Trinity endured the suffering for us in the substance of the Godhead, according to the tradition of Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius.

By such a statement he wished to abolish the saving incarnation, according to which Christ also endured suffering. He is also called one of us, since he took hold of the seed of Abraham (Hebrews 2), and he attempts to increase polytheism. For the meaning of his statement introduces three gods: one dead and two living.

He also dissolves the term “consubstantial” and drives out the holy councils: that at Nicaea, that at Constantinople, and that at Chalcedon. He will also be found not to accept the holy Virgin Mary. For if the Word did not become incarnate and become human from her, what need was there for the Virgin? And why did Gabriel say to her, “The holy one who is born from you shall be called the Son of God, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1)?

In addition to all these impious and blasphemous presumptions of his, wishing also to adulterate the *Trisagion* hymn by inserting into it the words “who was crucified for us,” he committed countless absurdities. Though admonished many times by us, by our brotherhood in Christ, by those in the East, and by the most God-fearing archbishop Acacius of your royal and Christ-loving city, he did not wish to turn back.

Therefore the holy Church of God, addressing you in her motherly voice as her distinguished son, does not cease to say:

“O emperor beloved by Christ, bond of my honor, in which the multitudes of the faithful are tightly bound, do not permit it to be dissolved. Do not permit the name of the Lord and Master Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be violated. Preserve undefiled the *Trisagion* hymn, which also saved your city when it was in danger, as an angelic tradition.

Expel from the Church of Antioch Peter, who followed the Arian religion. For what reason does Peter, having denied my faith, tear apart the understanding of the world? For what reason does Peter tear my garment woven from above (Matthew 16)? God the Father commanded the chief apostle what his Son should be called. The only-begotten Son founded me upon the confession of the chief of the apostles. The Holy Spirit testifies to me at every moment, saying: ‘Do not judge yourself to know anything except Jesus Christ, and him crucified’ (John 19).

The hostile, disobedient plotters outside the vineyard slaughtered the only-begotten Son of God, stoned him, and fastened him to the wood of the cross, yet they did not divide his garment. Shall Peter tear apart the garment of my faith? The gates of Hades did not prevail against me (Matthew 19), and Peter attempts to overthrow my wall?

I, most devout emperor, brought you back after you had been driven from this kingdom. I gave the wicked and disobedient, who opposed the divine doctrines in me, as your burial; I opened the way of power before you; I cast down your enemies together with their unlawful doctrine. I sought for you the ancient power from God who reigns in the heights, from whom you also received your reign.

Look to your predecessor, the most devout emperor Marcian, and gladly embrace his faith. Uproot Peter’s heretical tyranny quickly. Expel from the citadel and from ecclesiastical administration the disciple of Valentinus and Eutyches, and decree that he be cast down together with his priestly dignity.

Consider, most genuine son and unconquered emperor, what indisputable vengeance was exacted at the Council of Chalcedon, and what vengeance was exacted upon your enemy; deliver the peoples from Peter’s heretical teaching.

The holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God petitions these things, so that you may no longer receive into communion the man deposed by it for the reasons stated, but by your divine letters arrange for him to be expelled from the territory of the city of Antioch. In his place appoint a man who adorns the priesthood by his works and is a careful guardian of the holy Council of Chalcedon and of the things confirmed in it.

May almighty God preserve your power in peace forever.”

[Note: [Col. 0921D] This is a synodical letter, written from the second Roman council; it contains the sentence of anathema and deposition that, after careful investigation of the case, was issued by the decision of all against Acacius of Constantinople. It was sent to him at Constantinople, but he rejected it, and through the agency of a certain monk it was suspended from Acacius’s pallium while he was proceeding to perform the sacred rites. Thereupon he burst into such madness that, imitating Dioscorus of Alexandria, he removed the name of Pope Felix from the sacred diptychs and expelled Catholic bishops from their sees, substituting heretics and infamous men in their places. Yet he eventually learned to his own loss that the apostolic see does not rest upon a kingdom or empire but upon Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, when the name of that most ambitious and arrogant man—who had allowed images of himself, while still alive, to be dedicated in the church—was completely erased from the sacred tablets, as we shall say below. See Liberatus, below, chapter 18; Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 17; Baronius, year 484. —SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## LETTER VI: TO ACACIUS

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Liberatus cites this letter, chapter 18. —HARDUIN.]

He deprives Acacius of priestly office and communion with the faithful.

[Col. 0921C]

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Valesius thinks that this sentence of Felix against Acacius was issued at the second Roman synod against Acacius; but Pagius proves at length that it was issued at the first, in his notes on the year of Christ 485, no. 9 and following.]

Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Acacius.

You are found guilty of many transgressions and have often been involved in contempt for the venerable Council of Nicaea. You have rashly claimed the rights of foreign provinces. You thought that heretics [supply: and] usurpers, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and had sought to have condemned by the apostolic see, should not merely be received into your communion, but also made to preside over other Churches—something that could not be done even with Catholics—and you even increased their honors, which they did not deserve.

John bears witness to this: though he was not received by the Catholics at Apamea and was driven from Antioch, you appointed him over Tyre [perhaps read: “placed him in charge”]. And Humerius [perhaps “Himerius”], then cast down from the diaconate and deprived of the name of Christian, was by you advanced to the office of presbyter.

And as though these things seemed small to you, in the arrogance of your audacity you stretched out your hand against the very truth of apostolic doctrine, so that Peter—whom you yourself had reported to have been condemned by my predecessor of holy memory, as the accompanying documents testify—should, with your connivance [read: “by your command”], again invade the see of the blessed evangelist Mark; and, after orthodox bishops and clergy had been driven out, should undoubtedly ordain men like himself. After the man who had been regularly appointed there had been expelled, he held the Church captive.

His person is so pleasing to you, and his ministry so acceptable [read: “his ministry was acceptable to you”], that you are now discovered to have afflicted many orthodox bishops and clergy who were coming to Constantinople, to have supported his representatives, and to have believed that the same Peter—who anathematized the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and violated the burial of Timothy of holy memory, as messengers have recently reported to us with greater certainty—should be excused through Misenus and Vitalis. You did not cease to praise him and exalt him with many commendations, so that you claimed that his condemnation, which you had previously reported, was not true [read: “claimed that it had not been true”].

You persist so greatly in defending this perverse man that you allowed Vitalis and Misenus—once bishops but now deprived of honor and communion, whom we had specifically sent for his expulsion—to be imprisoned after their documents had been seized. You then had them brought out to the procession that you held with the heretics and, as was revealed by their statements [read: “statements”], dragged them into communion with the heretics and with yourself, despising the embassy which ought to have been preserved even by the law of nations, and corrupted them with rewards. Thus, to the injury of the blessed apostle Peter, from whose see they had departed, you not only caused them to return ineffective but also showed them to be opponents of everything that had been commanded.

In deceiving them you revealed your wickedness. And, because you did not dare to answer at the apostolic see according to the canons to the petition [read: “from the petition”] of my brother and fellow bishop John, who attacked you with the gravest objections, you confirmed the accusations. You also judged Felix, our most faithful defender, who followed later because necessity delayed him, unworthy of your sight.

In your letters you also testified that you were in communion with those who are plainly heretics. For what else are those who, after the death of Timothy of holy memory, return to the Church under Peter, or those who handed themselves over to him from among the Catholics, than what Peter had been judged to be by the universal Church—and by you?

Therefore, with those whom you willingly embrace, receive a share in the present sentence, which we have sent to you through the defender of your Church. Separated from priestly honor and Catholic communion, and also from the number of the faithful, acknowledge that your name and office of priestly ministry have been taken away. You are condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority [supply: “through us”], and you are never [read: “no longer ever”] to be released from the bonds of anathema.

I, Caelius Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of Christ 484, under the consulship of Venantius, a man of illustrious rank. Sixty-seven bishops subscribed at the same time, without the pope.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] This is the synodical letter sent from the third Roman council under Felix to all the bishops. It was held for a long time at Rome and was marked with the consular date of the year 488, in which it was sent to Africa. It was read in the assembly of the Fathers, and their sentence was approved. I have summarized below in the notes to the aforementioned council what synodical constitutions it contains.]

## LETTER VII: TO ALL THE BISHOPS

It establishes how those who have been rebaptized are to be admitted to the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] The ancient titles of this letter, from the ancient Lucena codex, 490: “From the letter of Pope Felix to the bishops of Sicily.”]

1. The rebaptized person is to be received through penance.  
2. If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been rebaptized, he is to receive lay communion until death.  
3. If a cleric, monk, consecrated maiden, or layperson has been rebaptized, the decree of the Council of Nicaea is to be observed.  
4. Persons of either sex who are of more advanced age are to pass through the laying on of hands. [Col. 0924B]  
5. A person who has been rebaptized is not to be received into the clergy.  
6. No bishop is to absolve or receive the penitent of another bishop.

To our most beloved brothers in Christ Jesus, all the bishops established throughout the various provinces [Note: [Col. 0923D] In Justellus’s codex: “through Sicily.”]—[Note: [Col. 0923D] The Lucena codex adds: “Felix, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.”]

No part of the world has failed to groan, and no land has remained unaware, of how the devil’s cunning has raged among the peoples of the African regions and burst forth into manifold deception, so that it plunged not only the careless common people but even priests themselves into the depths of death.

Therefore, placed in profound grief, we cannot conceal the peril of souls that are perishing and that will be required at our hands. Consequently, suitable medicine [read: “remedy”] must be applied to such wounds, lest premature ease in treatment benefit nothing those seized by the deadly plague, but rather the more slowly treated destruction involve both the wounded and those who treat them in the guilt of an illegitimate cure.

First, then, the confession and person of the deceived individual who comes to you seeking a remedy must be carefully examined, so that an appropriate treatment may be provided. If someone, wishing to satisfy God through penance, legitimately grieves that he has been rebaptized, it must be investigated whether he ran to this crime [read: “hastened to it” or “came upon it”], or approached it under compulsion.

He must know that the person who deceives himself deceives [1 Peter 5], and that nothing is taken away through our leniency from the judgment of the lofty tribunal, before which those things are valid [read: “right”] that are devout, true, and just. The circumstances of necessity must be handled in one way, and the intention of the will in another.

The case of one who was perhaps enticed by money to perish is worse. For the enemy leaves nothing unattempted. Since those ensnared must be rescued lest he be allowed to rejoice in his capture, the hunter’s snare must be broken [read: “crushed”], so that the one who has fallen may, with unfeigned lamentation, return to the fold [perhaps read: “enclosure”] he had abandoned through both the moderation of justice and the compassion of contrition.

Nor should such a person perhaps be ashamed or reluctant to obey during the appointed periods of fasting and lamentation, or to submit to other commands of salutary discipline, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud.

Let anyone who seeks to be raised upright in Christ therefore be cast down by grief for his fall. Through the ministry of our arrangement [Note: [Col. 0925D] Dionysius: “dispensation.” HARDUIN.—The Lucena codex also reads this.]—which it is fitting for your charity to follow, and which no one is permitted or able to overstep—let us deal with the causes of the one who, contrary to apostolic doctrine, surrendered himself to the exceedingly ill-fated repetition of baptism, or of the one who has cunningly thought that his own consent should be excused by certain arguments, with priestly firmness and humaneness.

Thus, with the help of the Lord Judge, the faith—which, unless it is one, is no faith at all—may be restored to salvation in them without offense from our intervention [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Lucena codex: “without the hindrance of haste.”]. For when the sinner’s satisfaction is delayed by us, his mind is found more purified for forgiveness, not without praise and joy for us.

Therefore remember that we hold this judgment concerning these matters: while maintaining discrimination among sinners, not all who have fallen are to be weighed in the same balance, because a greater penalty [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Lucena codex has the same reading; but an ancient hand corrects it to: “interest must be exacted.”] must be exacted from the one to whom the discipline of the Lord’s house has been entrusted.

To begin, then, from the highest offices of the Church: those who are shown to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, whether voluntarily, perhaps, or under compulsion, and who are known to have suffered the loss of that one and saving washing, and to have put off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of the honor they had received—since it is clear that no one could come to a second washing unless he had openly denied himself to be a Christian and professed himself a pagan—

Although this is universally to be execrated, it is much more horrifying to hear or say it of bishops, presbyters, and deacons. But because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wishes no one to perish, it will be fitting for them, if they repent, to lie in penance until the day of their death. They are not to take part in prayer—not merely with the faithful, but in no way even with the catechumens—and only lay communion is to be given to them at death [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Lucena codex: “lay communion.”] [Note: [Col. 0925D] The same codex: “to be restored.”]. The care of the most approved priest must investigate and administer this matter more diligently.

Concerning clerics and monks, consecrated maidens, or secular persons, we command that the following rule be observed, which the Council of Nicaea established concerning those who have fallen or will fall: namely, that those who, without any necessity, fear, or danger, impiously surrendered themselves to heretics to be rebaptized, if they nevertheless repent from the heart, are to remain for three years among the hearers; for seven years they are to submit among the penitents to the hands of the priests; and for two years they are not to be permitted in any way to offer oblations, but are only to join the secular people [Note: [Col. 0925D] The same codex: “among the people.”] [read: “the people”] in prayer.

Let him not be ashamed to submit his neck to God who did not fear to deny him. But if, as happens to mortals, the end of life begins to press upon someone within the limits of the prescribed time, help must be given to the one who implores it. Whether from the bishop who imposed the penance or from another who can establish that it was imposed, or likewise from a presbyter, viaticum must not be denied to one departing from this world.

But to children who are still called from puberty because they are not yet mature [Note: [Col. 0926D] The same codex: “beardless.”] [read: “beardless”], whether clerics or laypersons, or to similar girls, whose ignorance is supported by their age, communion is to be restored after they have been detained for a time under the laying on of hands. Their penance is not to be awaited, since the severity of discipline exempts them from it.

This has been prudently established by us, lest those in whom more or less of the contagion of earthly corruption remains for life, while they are still in penance, commit things for which they must repent [Note: [Col. 0926D] The same codex adds: “perhaps.”] [supply perhaps].

But if, before the fixed time of penance [Note: [Col. 0926D] The same codex: “despised.”] someone, having been given up as hopeless by physicians [read: “despised”], or oppressed by evident signs of death, recovers after receiving the grace of communion, let us observe what the canons of Nicaea ordained: he is to be counted among those who communicate only in prayer until the period of time assigned to him has been completed.

Nor do we overlook our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, because the case is not different, as the same holy canons have ordained, from that of one who, having once confessed Christ, has renounced him in any manner. Let them remain for three years among the hearers and afterward, with the catechumens, receive through the laying on of hands the grace of Catholic communion [Note: [Col. 0926D] After “with the catechumens,” the Lucena codex reads: “let them be permitted to pray through the laying on of hands, to receive the grace of communion.”], except only bishops, presbyters, and deacons, whom we have already said are to be reconciled only at the time of their death.

As for the others—that is, clerics, monks, or laypersons of either sex—who are shown to have undergone a repetition of baptism under compulsion from violence or danger [Note: [Col. 0926D] The Lucena codex: “through violence and dangers”], or who by some artifice [Note: [Col. 0926D] The same codex: “of this.”] say that they are not bound by the guilt of this crime, we decree that their penance is to last three years, and that they are to be received into fellowship in the sacrament through the laying on of hands.

[Col. 0926D] In every respect let this be observed: none of them, at any age, who were baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church is ever to be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical service. It must be enough for them that they have been received among the number of Catholics, since anyone who violates this regulation, or who does not remove one of them whom he knows to have insinuated himself into clerical ministry, will be seen to bear judgment concerning his order and communion [Col. 0927A] [Note: [Col. 0927C] The Lucena codex: “of the bishops.”].

Above all, care must be taken and every precaution exercised lest any of our brother bishops or fellow bishops, or even presbyters, receive in another’s city or diocese a penitent, someone placed under a priest’s hand, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter to whose parish he belongs [Note: [Col. 0927C] The same codex: “or lest a presbyter in the parish, or a bishop in the city, receive him.”] [read: “and letters, or lest a presbyter in the parish or a bishop in the city receive him.”].

If this is neglected through some dissimulation, the fault also touches the clergy [read: “the cleric”] who resides in the places where this matter has been less carefully observed [Note: [Col. 0927C] The same codex: “which, through some neglect, also touches the fault of the clergy.”].

These matters having thus been duly arranged and communicated by our deliberation to the knowledge of your Churches, it is fitting [read: “it was fitting”] that you obey them. Although nothing seems to be lacking for the restoration of souls, nevertheless, if something new should be revealed to anyone, something that escaped us, let him faithfully [read: “confidently”] make it known, according to the blessed apostle Paul, while the one before him is silent.

For the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills, especially when his own cause is being treated. Nor shall we be reluctant to listen and, if anything has been omitted, arrogantly reject it; rather, we shall order it rationally.

May God keep you, most beloved brothers.

Given on the Ides of March, in the year of Christ 488, under the consulship of Dynamus and Siphidius, men of illustrious rank [Note: [Col. 0927C] Dionysius: “Sibilius.” HARDUIN.—The Lucena codex: “Simidius.”].

## LETTER VIII: TO ZENO, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0927C] The Justellus codex adds “of Spalato.”]

He commends Terentianus.

[Col. 0927C]

To his most beloved brother Zeno, Felix, bishop.

My son, the illustrious Terentianus, when he came to Italy some time ago, proved himself an outstanding herald of your affection and proclaimed you to be a man so overflowing with the grace of Christ that amid the storms of the world you appeared as a distinguished governor of the Church.

Therefore, dearest brother, when he was traveling to the province and earnestly requested that a letter from us be sent to your affection, we gladly consented. We desired both to embrace a bishop worthy of God in speech and, especially through him, to accomplish what we had been informed of by his praises.

Although the aforesaid man has in every respect confirmed your brotherhood through holy works and already possessed great confidence in your benevolence, it is nevertheless right that he should obtain what he greatly desired: so that he who was once pleasing to your mind may, through consideration of us, be made still more acceptable; that he may likewise be cherished with maternal and priestly consolation; and that in pastoral piety he may find the support of his journey.

Thus, through the affection of your dignity, it may appear to your sincerity that our greeting also has not been without effect.

May God preserve you safe and sound, dearest brother.

[Note: [Col. 0927C] A certain letter of Felix to Caesarius of Arles is found in Baronius under the year of Our Lord 488, no. 7, under Felix III. In the appendix to volume X, Baronius acknowledged that it had been written by Felix IV, precisely because he recognized that the Second Council of Orange and several other councils over which Caesarius of Arles presided or at which he was present were held long after these times, and because the same Caesarius lived until the year of Our Lord 554—an age he could not have reached had he been bishop of Arles during the time of Felix III. An objection to this view is that Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 86, mentions this Caesarius and the letter addressed to him approving his book on grace. That could not have happened if he had held the bishopric of Arles during the time of Felix IV. For Gennadius submitted what he wrote *On Ecclesiastical Writers* to the scrutiny of Pope Gelasius, as is clear from chapters 99 and 110 of the same work; consequently, the letter mentioned in that book sent to Gelasius cannot belong to Felix IV. This difficulty is insoluble unless we say what Suffridius Petrus says: that Caesarius was inserted into Gennadius’s text in the same way as Avitus, Pomerius, and Honoratus of Marseilles are said by Honorius, in his catalogue *On Illustrious Men*, to have been fraudulently—or at least unknowingly—inserted into that work. See Possevinus, *Apparatus sacer*, under “Gennadius.” SEV. BINIUS.]

## PHILIPPE LABBE’S NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING *BREVICULUS*

In the year 1631, through the work and scholarship of the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond, of holy memory, there appeared an appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, augmented with new constitutions and with several letters of the ancient councils, which we presented in volume II from page 1194 to page 1186, as well as with the letters of three Roman pontiffs: Felix III, preceded by a *Breviculus of the Eutychianists*, or *Acts concerning the Case of Acacius*, together with the edict of that same pope’s sentence; Gelasius; and Vigilius. So that nothing may be lacking from this most extensive collection of ours, we shall, with auspicious beginnings, insert and arrange in their proper places all these materials omitted in the Luparean edition, each according to its position and in the customary manner.

[Note: [Col. 0928C] There are three editions of this *Narration*, and each claims its own manuscript witnesses. Quesnellus gave the shortest in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church*. It begins with the words “A certain Timothy” and ends approximately with “he should foresee for the Church.” Although it extends somewhat farther after this, it adds nothing historical. Here we see a second version, fuller at the beginning and the end, derived from Sirmond. A third has an addition at the end beyond the second. Moreover, what Pagius says—that the author of this little work took it from Liberatus—is refuted by the Ballerini, who found this narrative, in the form in which Sirmond published it, in the Vatican Codex Regina 1977, which they prove to be older than Liberatus. MANSI.]

## BRIEF HISTORY OF THE EUTYCHIANISTS

[Note: [Col. 0928D] Sirmond had published it with the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*. To Valesius, the author seems to be Pope Gelasius; but Tillemont, vol. XVI, p. 659, observes that it is more precise in narrating history than Gelasius usually is. Pagius, under the year 496, no. 4, shows that the earlier part of this little book is excerpted word for word from Liberatus, who wrote under Justinian, while the latter part is compiled from Gelasius’s letters.]

Or, *Acts concerning the Case of Acacius*.

In the cause of the Christian faith, which from its beginning is demonstrably never without enemies, Nestorius and Eutyches, in our own age but at different intervals of time, disclosed not new doctrines of their perversity but names. For Nestorius, about fifty-eight years ago, following the error of Photinus and Paul of Samosata, deserved to be banished into exile at Oasis, saying, as he had learned from his teachers, that Christ our Lord had been born from the Virgin Mary as man only.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Peter was deported into the solitude of Oasis in the year 436.]

Against him Eutyches, after not many years, thinking that he ought to argue the matter, stumbled because he did not know how to keep to the straight path, and was swept into the madness of Apollinaris. He burst out with these words, asserting that Christ had not been a true man and that two natures were not to be believed to exist in him, but only one nature of God the Word, yet incarnate. He declared that this nature was not that of a man but human, so that the resemblance of a human body rather than its actual reality might be inferred. The Catholic faith, however, confesses Christ the Son of God to be true God and true man—not of one nature, but of one essence and one person.

When Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, discovered that this Eutyches, a presbyter and abbot of the city of Constantinople, was teaching such things, he reported him to Bishop Flavianus and appealed for judgment, out of zeal for the faith—a zeal that he had also displayed when he was an *agens in rebus*. For he himself had earlier reproved Nestorius when the latter was preaching sacrilegious things in the church.

The case was heard. When Eutyches saw that his side was being pressed, he sought the protection of the emperor Theodosius through Chrysaphius the *spatarius*. By the emperor’s command, Florentius, an illustrious former consul, could not remain absent from the examination of Eutyches; and in his very presence Eutyches was convicted and condemned.

The emperor was angered and ordered a synod to be assembled in the city of Ephesus. Nearly 360 [140] bishops were present, with Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria; Juvenal of Jerusalem; Thalassius of Caesarea; Eustathius of Berytus; Eusebius of Ancyra; and Basil of Isauria presiding.

Representatives sent from the Apostolic See were also present: Julius, bishop of Puteoli, and Hilary the archdeacon, since Renatus the presbyter had been overtaken by death on the island of Delos.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Accordingly, after the synod, Theodoret did not send a letter to him but to Hilary.]

The notary Dulcitius was also present. At this assembly the dogmatic letter of Pope Leo, addressed to the synod and to Flavianus, was rejected and was absolutely not permitted to be read.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] It was received by Dioscorus, but not read.]

All day long—that is, on the sixth day before the Ides of August—nothing was read except the acts concerning the formerly condemned Nestorius, that is, those of the First Council of Ephesus. At the same time, after all the documents had been read, the judgment concerning Eutyches by Flavianus, of holy memory, was examined.

Meanwhile, when the blasphemies of Eutyches were being reread,

[Note: [Col. 0929D] For his profession was deceitful, and by concealing the heresy he covered it up.]

all acclaimed that this was the true faith, this the orthodox faith. Flavianus was deposed, despite the opposition of the Roman representatives,

[Note: [Col. 0929D] In the year 449, on August 2.]

and Eutyches was restored. Eusebius, the bishop who had accused that presbyter, was also condemned as a Nestorian, although earlier, while still a layman, he had been an accuser of Nestorius.

These Eutychianists are so unwilling that there should be anything between themselves and Nestorius that anyone among them who is not an Eutychianist is regarded as wholly Nestorian, whereas Catholic doctrine unites the two natures in Christ and does not divide them as Nestorius did. Yet these men are found to utter even worse things. For they boldly say something absurd, something even abhorrent to the foolish: that before the union—that is, the incarnation—two natures must be spoken of, but afterward only one nature, that of God the Word, incarnate; just as if we were to say that something had been coated with wax, or pitched, or *stagnatum* [read: *stannatum*, “tinned”],

or colored by any other process.

After the third day of the synod in which Flavianus, of holy memory, had been deposed, Domnus of Antioch was also deposed. Dioscorus suddenly withdrew, and the assembly was dissolved.

Flavianus was led into exile at Epipa, a city of Lydia, and died there, whether because death overtook him or because it was inflicted upon him.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] See the *Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes*.]

[Note: [Col. 0929D] February 18, 410.]

At that time a certain Alexandrian presbyter named Anatolius was staying in Constantinople. For it is the custom of those people that clerics be sent by turns to the imperial court, lest some matter of business or necessity should arise. Thus this Anatolius became bishop of Constantinople, a partisan of Dioscorus.

After a year Theodosius the emperor died,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] July 28, 450.]

Chrysaphius was punished,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] At the Melanthias Gate.]

and Marcian became emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] On August 24, before the fourteenth day of that same month.]

Grievously distressed by the violation of the faith, he convoked a synod at Nicaea, at which he himself and Pulcheria sat,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] This is false, as is clear from the acts.]

together with the entire senate and the authorities. He later transferred the synod to Chalcedon because of its proximity to the palace.

More than five hundred—[630]—bishops of the entire East and Egypt assembled. Dioscorus was brought forward so that he might defend his conduct in the council. The emperor himself was also present at the assembly, as were the senate, all the judges, and all the officials of the court.

That Eusebius of Dorylaeum, who had fled from exile and come to Rome the previous year, also hastened to attend the Council of Chalcedon. He himself accused Dioscorus, as did other Alexandrians.

What more need be said? Dioscorus was condemned. The body of Flavianus, of holy memory,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] In August of the year 450, before the condemnation of Dioscorus, which occurred only in the following year together with the ordination of Proterius.]

was brought back to Constantinople with the utmost honor, and at Alexandria Proterius, a Catholic, was made priest.

A certain Timothy,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] This comes from Liberatus, chapter 15.]

whose surname was Aelurus, a presbyter, and Peter, a deacon,

[Note: [Col. 0930D] Mongus or Moggus, that is, “the stammerer.”]

who now occupies the episcopal office of the Alexandrian Church, followers of Dioscorus, separated themselves from the Alexandrian Church. When Bishop Proterius could not recall them to their ministries by his admonitions, he condemned both of them.

After the emperor Marcian died,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] January 26, 457.]

Timothy and Peter came to Alexandria with crowds of heretics gathered together, and Timothy was ordained bishop by the heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] By only two bishops, according to Evagrius, book XI, chapter 8.]

Thus there began to be two bishops at Alexandria.

Three days before Easter, on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated, a multitude of wicked men assembled and seized the church to which Proterius, of holy memory, had gone as usual. There, on the aforesaid day,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] March 28, 457.]

he was killed in the baptistery, torn to pieces, thrown out, and his corpse was burned, while his ashes were scattered to the winds.

Leo assumed the imperial power,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] On February 7 of the same year.]

and the complaint of the Catholics concerning so great a crime reached him. The heretics petitioned against them, asking that the Council of Chalcedon be abolished; the Catholics, however, were looking for vengeance for so great a crime.

The emperor, considering it excessively burdensome to harass so many bishops again—many of whom were prevented from undertaking this labor either by age, infirmity, or even poverty—sent *magistriani* throughout the East. Bishop Anatolius of Constantinople also sent his deacon Asclepiades.

Through them all those bishops who had been assembled at Chalcedon learned what had happened at Alexandria; and when they had been questioned, they replied, together with the bishops of their provinces, that the Council of Chalcedon must be defended even unto blood, because it had established no other faith than the Council of Nicaea. They declared that Timothy was not merely not to be regarded as a bishop but was also to be deprived of the name Christian.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Thus far Liberatus.]

After Timothy was deposed, another Timothy,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Called Salophaciolus or “the White,” in the year 458.]

a Catholic, became bishop of Alexandria.

Scarcely had Timothy the heretic been expelled

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Aelurus.]

when Peter fled, and Timothy was sent into exile at Cherson, a secluded place in Pontus.

As long as the emperor Leo lived,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] He died in January of the year 474, while his son Leo the Younger died in November.]

Timothy lived peacefully as bishop of Alexandria. But when Basiliscus had seized the imperial power,

[Note: [Col. 0931D] In the year 476.]

he began to condemn the Council of Chalcedon and persecute the Catholics.

Then at last that condemned Timothy, having received his freedom, came to Constantinople and restored the condemned heretics to their own places. He went to Alexandria; the Catholic Timothy fled,

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Liberatus, chapter 16.]

and hid in a monastery. That Peter again joined himself to Timothy, with whom he had previously been condemned.

The emperor Zeno returned to the throne, and Basiliscus was overthrown. Timothy was sent to Alexandria so that, after the usurper had been expelled, the Catholic Timothy might be restored to the Church. But since the condemned Timothy had been overtaken by death, Peter,

[Col. 0931D] [Note: [Col. 0932D] Mongus, mentioned above.]

his associate, was ordained bishop of the Alexandrians by a single heretic.

The most Christian emperor nevertheless ordered him to be deposed and the Catholic Timothy to be brought back, as is contained in the letters of Acacius of Constantinople.

When very many—whether clerics, monks, or men living secular lives—absolutely refused to attend the communion of the Catholic bishop Timothy, the most merciful emperor terrified them all with various sacred sanctions.

Timothy wrote to Pope Simplicius—saying that Peter, once condemned in the diaconate, was now also excluded from Christian fellowship—and sent instructions through Isaiah the bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Perhaps of the city of Naucratis, mentioned in chapter 22 of the third part of the Council of Chalcedon.]

asking that the emperor be written to concerning Peter, who was hiding in the city of Alexandria and plotting against the Church, so that he might be deported into a distant exile.

For nearly three years Pope Simplicius, of holy memory, did not cease writing to Bishop Acacius, asking him to act with the emperor so that what Bishop Timothy requested concerning Peter might be done. The emperor was also written to, but no reply was ever received from him.

After all this, Timothy sent his presbyter and steward John

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Surnamed Taben[n]esiotes, or Talaja.]

to the emperor, asking that, if anything should happen to him, His Piety would order a Catholic to be ordained by Catholics.

A reply was given to his requests, and a letter was written both to him and to the clergy. In those same sacred documents the steward John is praised at length, so that by then almost everyone regarded him as a candidate for the Alexandrian episcopate.

When this Bishop Timothy died,

[Note: [Col. 0932D] In the year 482.]

the Catholic John was ordained bishop by Catholics.

When, according to the custom of the elders, he sent a synodical letter to the Apostolic See through the presbyter Isidore and the deacon Peter, the arrival of Uranias, a subdeacon, bearing an imperial document against John the bishop, caused the pope to suspend confirmation of his episcopate.

And because in the same sacred documents he had mentioned the restoration of Peter, whom he himself had condemned, this portion was entirely repudiated. Hence the most merciful emperor appears to have been offended.

Since the letters of Pope Simplicius, of holy memory, repeatedly sent to Acacius for the peace of the Alexandrian Church and the integrity of the Catholic faith, accomplished nothing, that same holy bishop John arrived and was received by the Apostolic See, as was proper. For his predecessors likewise had sought refuge with the Roman Church during the persecution.

His arrival disclosed everything more fully. When we were reading the letters Acacius had sent concerning Peter

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Cnapheus, or “the Fuller.”]

and John

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Otherwise called Apamenus, who was not received; more about him shortly.]

of Antioch, he discovered that Acacius’s excesses in this matter too were extremely grave.

At the time when he had reported the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria, not long afterward he had also written about Peter and John. He said that Peter had governed a monastery at Constantinople,

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Liberatus, chapter 18.]

but that after abandoning it because of his crimes he had fled to Antioch. There, after the Catholic bishop Martyrius had been expelled, he had occupied his see through the agency of the heretics; and immediately afterward he had been condemned and sent into exile at Oasis by the emperor Leo, who was then ruling.

He further stated that Peter had fallen, returned to Constantinople, and given a pledge that he would absolutely dare to cause no further disturbances.

But, as was said above, during the reign of Basiliscus he had been sent back to Antioch by that condemned Timothy,

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Aelurus, in the year 476.]

who had come to Constantinople, so that he might again hold the episcopate there.

After this, that same Peter ordained as bishop of Apamea a certain John, the presbyter concerning whom we said that Acacius had reported him. Since he was not received by the people of Apamea, he came to Antioch, expelled Peter, the author of his episcopate, from his see, and seized his Church.

Acacius says that both men were again condemned, asking the Apostolic See that, if they should happen to flee to it, it should not consider them worthy even of being seen; and that, if they had perhaps already obtained some indulgence, it ought to be invalid and their repentance ought not to be accepted.

When the aforesaid John, bishop of Alexandria, had reread this, he could not remain silent: Acacius had condemned that John together with Peter, and without hope of a remedy through repentance had caused him to be condemned by the Apostolic See, yet, after so many condemnations of the Tyrians, had sent him to preside over the Church.

After the holy Pope Felix learned that the letters of his predecessor had accomplished nothing and that Acacius was perpetrating certain mockeries to the overthrow of the entire ecclesiastical discipline, he selected Vitalis, bishop of Truentum from the region of Picenum, and Misenus, bishop of the Church of Cumae from the region of Campania, and sent them with these instructions: that Peter was to be expelled from the Alexandrian Church; that Acacius was to answer the petition of the holy John, bishop of Alexandria; and that Acacius himself was to be ordered to anathematize Peter.

Although, in the hostile manner in which they had been thrust into custody, they lost the documents, they nevertheless ought not to have granted to perfidious and condemned heretics what could only be denied—their will.

Thus they not only failed to do what they had been ordered to do, or what they could have accomplished, but also entered into communion with the heretics, carrying confirmation of Peter’s episcopate—the very episcopate from which they had been sent to expel him—and bringing insults against Bishop John, which Acacius had directed.

Moved by these actions, the most blessed pope, after holding a synod, suspended Vitalis and Misenus from office and communion

[Note: [Col. 0933D] On July 28, 484.]

and condemned Acacius.

In his audacity he committed still worse acts: after expelling the Catholic Calendion,

[Note: [Col. 0934D] He had conspired with Patricius and others in the year 483.]

he sent Peter of Antioch

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Cnapheus, or “the Fuller.”]

to the Church of Antioch.

## ADDITION TAKEN FROM THE THIRD EDITION

After John arrived as bishop, and the Roman Church received him, holy Pope Felix organized a legation, as stated above, in the proper manner. It suffered every kind of hostility at the hands of all those men mentioned above. For, after being thrust into custody—together with the aforesaid documents (*praedictis chartis*; the printed phrase is syntactically incomplete)—it barely returned with great disgrace, bringing back confirmation of Peter’s episcopate, although the Roman Church had anathematized him.

[Col. 0934A] Thus Pope Felix wrote to the bishops established throughout Egypt, the Thebaid, Libya, and Pentapolis, among other things:

“But Peter, who separated himself from the unity of the Church under Proterius, of blessed memory, and joined himself to Timothy, the murderer of Proterius, to persecute the orthodox, we do not permit him to rejoice in any fellowship of such a name or honor, since what he considers enduring is found to be as fleeting in its very origin as its creators, who are not unlike himself. Therefore let the aforesaid man be anathema to all, nor let him ever be believed to be received by the Catholic Church: for after very frequent exhortation and persevering in his perversity through so many years, he has forfeited the place of satisfaction.”

## EDICT OF THE SENTENCE OF POPE FELIX CONCERNING THE CONDEMNATION OF ACACIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0934B] “Acacius, who, after being admonished by us for the second time, did not cease to be a despiser of salutary statutes and believed that I should be imprisoned in my own person, God, by a sentence issued from heaven, has made an exile from the priesthood. Therefore, if any bishop, cleric, monk, or layman communicates with him after this denunciation, let him be anathema, with the Holy Spirit carrying out the sentence.”

## LETTER IX OF POPE FELIX III TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

He complains that the envoys sent by him were violated and urges him to submit to the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius.

**Felix to Zeno Augustus.**

Although Your Piety replied to my letters in a more expansive document, it regarded the truth, more carefully explained to its ears, as worthy of contempt. I therefore had to bring briefly to a conclusion matters that you do not wish to have published at greater length.

Accordingly, after first expressing my official respect, I confess that I fear both for your reign and for your salvation. For it will be shown to be contrary to divine reverence that the legation sent by the blessed Apostle Peter—as its own report made clear—was held as though in captivity and, after the documents it was carrying had been violently taken away, was brought out of custody for the purpose of communicating with heretics, namely, the agents of Peter of Alexandria, against whom it had gone.

Therefore, as Pope Nicholas I, Letter 9, records, apostolic censure deprived Vitalis and Misenus of both their honor and apostolic communion for consenting to these acts, even if they had been driven to do so.

But since, even among barbarian nations ignorant of the Divinity itself, the sacred freedom of any legation is protected by the law of nations for the execution of even human business, it is known to all how much more it ought to have been preserved inviolate by a Roman emperor and Christian ruler, especially in divine matters.

Then, once the legation had been dismissed—although, as stated, it could no longer remain inviolate among you—let Your Tranquillity at least learn from the tenor of this letter that the see of the blessed Apostle Peter has never given, nor will ever give, its consent to communion with Peter of Alexandria, who was once justly condemned and was recently struck down by synodal sentence as well.

For, to omit the rest for now, one instituted by heretics cannot lawfully preside over the Catholic Church. Therefore, since you have considered my exhortation burdensome, I leave it to your own deliberation to decide whether communion should be chosen with the blessed Apostle Peter or with Peter of Alexandria.

What kind of man Peter of Alexandria was, how rashly he usurped a priesthood bearing a false name through one scarcely even an accomplice of his perversity, and how he had long been counted among the condemned even in your presence, you may establish from the letters of his supporter Acacius, addressed to my predecessor of holy memory, copies of which you see appended.

With devout readiness toward God, consider whether he can even be called a bishop—for even if he had received that name from several bishops, he could not possess it—or whether he deserves to be imposed upon orthodox peoples contrary to the Council of Nicaea and contrary to its distinctive observance.

There too it is clearly evident that Acacius, who preferred to conceal his own excesses under your name rather than to suggest what would benefit you, possessed as much sincere devotion toward your salvation as he possessed a faithful conscience regarding the rules of the Fathers and the Catholic doctrine itself.

For this reason, since he had perpetrated many wicked acts against the decrees of the ancients, had emerged as the praiser of one whom he himself declared condemned and had caused to be condemned by the Apostolic See, and had once again built what he had previously destroyed, he made himself a transgressor. The legitimate authority assigned him to the portion of those subject to apostolic discipline through Tutus, the defender of the Roman Church, and separated him with lawful severity from apostolic communion and dignity, of which he had shown himself unworthy by associating with that man’s outsiders.

I think that Your Piety, which prefers even to be overcome by its own laws rather than resist them, ought to obey heavenly decrees. Let it recognize that the summit of human affairs has been entrusted to it in such a way that it nevertheless does not doubt that divine things must be received through stewards appointed by God.

I think it is without any doubt useful for you if, during your imperial rule, you allow the Catholic Church to use her own laws and permit no one to oppose her freedom—the freedom that restored to you the power of the kingdom.

For it is certain that this is salutary for your affairs: when the causes of God are at issue, and in accordance with his ordinance, you should strive to subject the imperial will to the priests of Christ, not to place it above them; to learn sacred matters through their leaders rather than to teach them; to follow the pattern of the Church, not to prescribe humanly the laws that she must follow; and not to seek to dominate her sanctions, to whom God willed Your Clemency to bow your neck in devout submission—lest, while the measure of the heavenly ordering is exceeded, one proceed to insult the One who orders all things.

By this statement, then, I acquit my conscience concerning all these matters, since I shall plead my case before the tribunal of Christ. It will be for your mind to consider ever more carefully that, in the present condition of affairs, we stand under divine examination and that, after the course of this life, we shall consequently come to divine judgment.

And in another hand:

Given on the Kalends of August, in the year of Christ 484, during the consulship of Venantius, an illustrious man.

## LETTER X OF POPE FELIX III TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CONSTANTINOPLE

That they should not be disturbed by the treachery of the envoys and should avoid communion with Acacius, condemned by the Apostolic See.

**Felix to the most beloved sons, the orthodox clergy and people established at Constantinople, greetings.**

We reasonably suppose that the firmness of your faith, approved by all, has been disturbed by the treachery of Vitalis and Misenus. By neglecting—and even opposing—everything entrusted to them, they caused it to be believed that the Roman Church consented to communion with condemned heretics.

For, contrary to the prohibition, they were convicted of communicating, without first making the declaration that your holy devotion was to hear, with those who had been sent by that heretic Peter [Mongus], once justly deposed and repeatedly anathematized, the associate of murderers, and who had been received by Acacius, forgetting our instructions. Thus, as we foretold, their excesses were taken for our consent.

We have deprived them both of their orders and of the venerable reception of the divine mystery. Therefore let none of you, because of such an act, be forgetful of his own duty, nor suppose that we fail in the defense of apostolic tradition, when you see that we have punished those who betrayed and destroyed the faith.

You should also have known that the fickleness and inconstancy of Acacius, once a bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Deposed on July 28, 488.]

have been exposed. Although, as is proved by the attached documents, he reported things concerning this Peter that could not be tolerated and once said that Peter had been condemned, he nevertheless pursued him with many praises through our envoys. Those who place the fear of God before their eyes will judge whether anything should be believed from him, since he acted against his conscience.

He also attempted to overturn, in defense of the rights of foreign provinces, the canons of the 318 holy Fathers, as an usurper of unlawful ordinations. For this too he lies under punishment, and he no longer enjoys the communion of the Roman—that is, Apostolic—See, of which he himself deprived himself, since by appearing as the associate and receiver of Peter the Eutychianist, he showed himself a participant in Peter’s condemnation.

Our own sentence has likewise judged him, as is found in the attached documents, to be excluded from the office of episcopal ministry, from holy communion, and from your number—that is, from the Christian community.

As for our son, the presbyter Solomon, whom Acacius thought to deprive of his rank in order to please the heretics, let your sentence preserve his proper rank; or let it declare that all those who may have been expelled by the aforesaid man should remain in their own places and in our communion.

Although we know the zeal of your faith, we nevertheless admonish you: let all who wish to share in the Catholic faith abstain from communion with that man, lest, God forbid, they suffer a similar punishment.

## LETTER XI OF POPE FELIX III TO THE MONKS OF CONSTANTINOPLE AND BITHYNIA

He condemns Tutus, the defender of the Church, for treachery, and explains how they ought to act against those among their own people who have adhered to Acacius.

[Col. 0937A]

**Felix to Rufinus and Thalassius, presbyters and archimandrites, and to the other monks established around Constantinople and in Bithynia.**

We frequently experience the cunning of the devil’s craft, but with God’s help we do not yield to his malignity. For when his deceit seeks to empty of force the measures so often established for the steadfastness of the faith, it is necessary for us also, with the strength supplied by divine grace, to eradicate his efforts.

Having received your letter, carried by Basilius,

[Col. 0937B] [Note: Concerning him, see above, letter 9.]

we learned, among other things, that Tutus—whom we had appointed defender of the Church from among the more senior clerics within the Church, so that he himself might carry to Acacius the sentence that could not be sent directly—had, through a kind of madness, or rather through greed for money, sold himself to the enemies of the faith after our regulations had been satisfied. He was convicted and confessed this.

For his letter was read in the assembly of the brothers, showing how, after an agreement had been inserted through an intermediary, he was believed to have adhered to the man against whom he had carried the sentence, after Maro had been condemned. Recognizing the letter as his own, he could not deny it.

Accordingly, we stripped him, as a traitor to the faith and to the Apostolic See, of the office of defender that we had granted him for a time; and we ordered that he be deprived of communion in the sacred mystery and cast down from his position. We admonish Your Devotion, as you have always done, to keep watch with perpetual vigilance for the preservation of the truth.

And since there is no doubt that some from your monasteries have been deceived and have passed over to the enemies of God, whether voluntarily or under compulsion, we command you to observe the following concerning such men: whoever among you, from any place, has either voluntarily surrendered himself or been corrupted by payment is to be entirely excluded from your fellowship.

For unless the perfidious are removed from the faithful, while all distinction between things is abolished, the innocent will labor under suspicion, just as the path to vices is easy for human beings. Contagion from the lost must be driven away from the fellowship of the approved, since, as it is written, evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15:33).

But the case of those who are shown to have been afflicted with severe punishments in order to be transferred elsewhere must be handled differently. Toward them you ought to be more humane, so that they may return to their cells under the discipline of repentance, and so that their fall may be expiated by more faithful tears, until, after the enemies and their perverters have been excluded, the Catholic Church is cleansed.

## ACACIAN SUPPLEMENT

Containing never-before-published documents, which the Marquis Scipione Maffei extracted and elucidated from the most ancient codices of the Chapter of Verona.

## PREFACE TO THE LETTER OF FELIX REFUTING THE DEFENDERS OF ACACIUS

From the manuscript Veronese library, which for no slight reasons I still keep within domestic enclosures, I am issuing this Supplement to the Acacian case, removing another fragment and once again diminishing it, as it were, by one of its limbs.

A few years ago learned and most congenial fellow citizens compelled me to detach Cassiodorus’s *Complexiones* from that body. The insistence of Nicolaus Coletus has now obtained my consent to allow these letters to be separated from the same source: he repeatedly requested from me a notable monument of ecclesiastical antiquity to enlarge and adorn the highly equipped collection of councils that he is preparing.

To comply with his wishes, I selected this particular treatise, which I had set aside in 1713 after discovering, copying, and elucidating it in whatever way I could. How highly this exceptional document should be valued, and what place it should occupy, I believe will immediately be apparent to all learned men once they understand that it came from Felix III, whose other letters, written in precisely the same style, are customarily counted among the most eloquent issued by Roman pontiffs; and that it concerns a case of which few are found to be more distinguished in ecclesiastical history or to have been pursued and defended with greater exertion.

For it deals with the condemnation of Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and defends and supports the sentence of the Apostolic See, from which so sharp and long-lasting a dispute arose with the Eastern bishops. I do not think it worthwhile to weave together and place here beforehand the entire history of that controversy and of all the events, since this would be wholly superfluous: the celebrated father of the *Annals*, and many learned men after him, have treated the whole matter most fully in works composed specifically for that purpose.

An acephalous book preserves the letter in the most ancient library of the Veronese canons. It is not marked with the larger Roman letter, as are many other capitular manuscripts; only the letter N retains that form. The characters partly resemble typographical letters, or those now in use, and partly the swift writing of antiquity, a style of writing that is usually attributed to a nearer age.

Nevertheless, I have no doubt that this codex is extremely ancient, as I shall establish elsewhere. Its shape is nearer to a perfect square than that of the others; its ink is yellowish; its orthography is older; and the fragment of the papal catalogue that it contains ends with Vigilius, who sat in the middle of the sixth century.

It is written entirely in the same hand. A wooden board, of which part still remains on one side, is covered on the other by the parchment of another codex, painted with very large letters.

Besides many other letters and documents relating to the case of Acacius, this book contains the same collection that appears in the Code of Canons published by Paschasius Quesnellus in the appendix to the works of St. Leo; the same writer calls it, and considers it to be, the Code of the Roman Church. The order of the Narrative precedes it, which the Labbe edition of the Councils does not present, although the Crabb edition did; for the most part, however, it corresponds to the *Brief Account of the History of the Eutychianists* which we owe to Sirmond. The remaining pieces follow in the same order, agreeing for the most part with the printed edition and the manuscript, except for certain readings of no great importance or transpositions of words [Col. 0938D].

A notable difference, however, occurs in the letter that appears as the fifteenth of Gelasius in the Councils and is numbered chapter 51 in the Code of Canons. In Labbe, volume IV, column 1222, where one reads: “And you may seem to have separated yourselves from the same man by your own judgment,” all the editions continue: “and you still say,” or, “You also say, that the synod, in the person of one man,” etc. But our manuscript, after the word “may seem,” inserts the following two pages:

“Behold, they acknowledged, in the profession of those who persevered most steadfastly, what was owed to the faith and to Catholic communion. Behold, they acknowledged how, by withdrawing from such men—indeed, by contriving measures opposed to such men—Acacius deviated from the faith and Catholic communion, and how they likewise subjected themselves to error along with him. Behold, they acknowledged for what just reasons Acacius was removed by the authority of the Apostolic See on behalf of the faith and Catholic and apostolic communion [Col. 0939A], to which those who had remained faithful conformed, while those who opposed the steadfast were taught by it to be estranged from that communion; and likewise all who became his accomplices were removed. He was deservedly separated from communion with it, along with them, from that communion from which he himself is known first to have separated, together with his associates, by differing from the Catholic bishops. He rightly received the sentence of condemnation, to be published against his other associates, since he alone, on behalf of all his associates, confessed in letters sent to the Apostolic See that he had fallen back into communion with perfidy.

“If the Eastern bishops had communicated with him before they brought the matter here, they would unquestionably have been proved involved in the same guilt; and rightly they received through him the sentence of transgression, as men who had shared with him in an external communion of fact. They ought no longer to have been consulted as men of our communion, but rejected as placed in the opposing fellowship. If, however, they had not communicated with him before Acacius brought the matter here, they ought both to have censured the one who was communicating and themselves to have brought the case concerning him here [Col. 0939B]; they ought rightly to have approved him as struck down by the vigor of the Apostolic See, and to have maintained concord more firmly with the Apostolic See and with those great Catholic bishops. But because they had withdrawn from the fellowship of those men and had chosen to communicate with their successors, they did not agree with the Apostolic See, since they had fallen into the lot of the transgressor Acacius and undoubtedly foresaw that they would consequently be bound by his sentence.

“For this reason they did not wish him to appear condemned, because they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they persist to this day. But just as these men, bound by a similar condition, cannot judge their accomplice not to have been justly condemned, nor can the guilty suitably absolve the guilty, so, once that transgressor had been justly condemned, these men too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation, and they will be able to be completely absolved from it only if they repent.

“And you also say that the synod, in the person of one man,” etc.

In the aforementioned edition, this letter brings the Acacian acts to an end. But in the Veronese manuscript there follows a new piece, never before seen, which we now publish [Col. 0939C]. After it, the letter to Euphemius closes the series; this letter is usually placed before the others of Gelasius, so that here it appears, in a certain sense, as a completion of the documents relating to that celebrated case.

As for our letter, it shines in many places with the lights of eloquence, although no one can deny that the author sometimes luxuriates and diligently pursues a pointed and subtle style of expression. Some reader may wonder at the order he uses—or rather, at the order he lacks—as well as at the occasionally disconnected members and the frequently repeated sentences. Yet, besides the possibility that he is perhaps pressing close upon his opponent *καταπόδας* (“at the heels”), I suspect that this is partly attributable to the mutilated manuscript. It is truly remarkable how many scribal errors, and how much corruption and dislocation of the sentences, as it seems, affect it in more than one place. If one adds to these the somewhat intricate style in certain passages, and the difficulty common to ancient writings arising from the lack of punctuation and distinction, such tangled passages were produced that, when I thought they could scarcely be disentangled, I more than once regretted having put my hand to so troublesome a task [Col. 0939D], and more than once was already about to abandon the undertaking.

I was especially deterred by transposed and dislocated passages, because, whenever I detected this fault somewhere, I was forced to suspect it elsewhere as well. But at last it confirmed me and kept me to my purpose when I noticed that precisely the same misfortune, as if by some fate, had befallen the other writings both of this pontiff and of his successor Gelasius. Many of their documents, if I am not mistaken, have reached us so disturbed and intermingled that they seem to me at times to have flown about like the Sibylline verses committed to leaves, the playthings of swift winds.

Our letter begins in the manuscript with a false title: “A copy of the account rendered by blessed Pope Gelasius concerning avoidance of communion with Acacius, sent to the Eastern bishops.” It also has at the end: “Here ends the account of blessed Gelasius concerning avoidance of communion with Acacius.” From this title it is obvious that the letter is wrongly attributed.
