Since it was written while Acacius was alive—or at least before news of his death had certainly reached Rome—it cannot be attributed to Gelasius, who was inaugurated three years after Acacius’s death [Col. 0940A]. Nevertheless, Nicholas I cited the opening lines of this treatise under the name of Gelasius in his letter to all the bishops of Gaul.

Nor was this the only letter of Felix’s to bear the name of Gelasius in manuscripts. Another was found by Sirmond among others, and is number 43 in the Labbe edition; nor, in my opinion, is this error entirely absent from the printed editions. It was easy for copyists to fall into it, both because of the similarity of style and proximity in time, and because the two pontiffs treated the same matters and arguments. We likewise see several of their documents lacking both beginning and end. Our letter plainly does not depart from this practice, since we find it acephalous, even though it begins in the manuscript with a capital letter and without any indication of mutilation.

As for the corruptions and dislocations that I detect in our text, and the fact that I find certain other passages likewise hideously deformed, this must be attributed chiefly to the fact that, even after the labor and diligence of excellent editors [Col. 0940B], they remain squalid and monstrous. Yet it will not, I think, be the least fruit of our labor to have examined them somewhat more attentively and uncovered considerable disorder in certain passages. Let us therefore briefly examine the context and some of the sentences.

It might be proposed that, from the very first period of Gelasius’s letter to Euphemius, riddles are already foreshadowed and dislocations already threatened by the end of the first page. The third sentence of the preceding letter is likewise enigmatic; it is restored, however, if one reads *temporum* (“of the times”) instead of *pro temporibus* (“according to the times”); Cardinal Baronius had already corrected it in this way. He also correctly wrote *Domini sacerdotes* (“the priests of the Lord”). On the same page, where it reads *deitate non prorsus assumpta* (“the divinity not entirely assumed”), read *deitate non prorsus absumpta* (“the divinity not entirely consumed”).

When I noticed that Letter 13 of Gelasius, which is more closely related to ours, diverged greatly from the manuscript in the collection of the Councils, I devoted much labor both to removing interpolations and to recording all the differences. Nevertheless, when it occurred to me to collate the Quesnellian edition as well [Col. 0940C], I was amazed to find that it agreed entirely with our manuscript, which also displays at the end of the letter the same title found in the Thuaneus manuscript: “Here ends the account proving that Acacius was competently condemned by the Apostolic See and that no one can become a participant in his communion without danger to his soul.”

From the material with which the Labbe edition is overburdened, I think it is sufficiently clear that the following passage is not Gelasius’s—even though, through a repeated interpolation, Pope Felix of holy memory is mentioned in it:

“Behold, recently Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, a great and distinguished priest, and many Catholic priests with him, steadfastly resisted Horonicus, king of the Vandal nation, who was raging, enduring every extremity; and even today they do not cease to resist their persecutors. We too, it is manifest, by God’s favor, in no way obeyed the barbarian heretic Odoacer, then ruling the kingdom of Italy, when he ordered things that ought not to be done.”

For if the letter had been written in the year it gives, 495, I do not see how events [Col. 0940D] that had occurred at least eleven years earlier could be called “recent.” Huneric had died in 484, in the second year of Felix. Nor do the words “even today they do not cease to resist” seem to fit that year, since in the preceding year, 494, Gundabundus, Huneric’s successor, had recalled all the bishops from exile and restored them to their churches, as may be gathered from the Augustan fragment preserved by Heinrich Canisius.

Similarly, the final statements concerning Odoacer fit Gelasius rather poorly. Gelasius’s first year was Odoacer’s last; at that time Odoacer was besieged at Ravenna and reduced to extremity by the victorious Theodoric, so that he seemed not only unable to harass the Roman pontiff with his orders, but scarcely able even to retain the kingdom.

This too must not be concealed: many things relating to the defense of the sentence pronounced against Acacius cannot indeed be said to be incompatible with Gelasius, but they suit Felix much better, when the complaints of the Greeks were still recent and burning [Col. 0941A]. The suspicion is strengthened by the fact that several passages of that same letter are as similar as possible to ours, which the entire context asserts to be Felix’s.

Let us pursue greater matters, then, and turn to the treatise *On the Anathema*. In this all the editions agree, as does our manuscript. I attach little importance to the various readings Quesnellus recorded in the margin, in which the manuscript comes closer to the Labbe edition, since matters much more important required attention. The writing is, unless I am mistaken, scarcely anything other than a cento assembled from various fragments through the error of copyists.

Let us begin by observing that this treatise is directed toward explaining and purging the words pronounced in Acacius’s condemnation, according to which he was never to be released from the bonds of the anathema. But this task suited Felix far more, since the words were his, than Gelasius many years later. Indeed, Gelasius’s effort would have been wholly superfluous after Felix himself had already accomplished it fully in the letter we now publish.

Who, however [Col. 0941B], would believe that Gelasius prepared this defense without ever adducing the strongest argument—that it could not be called into question that such was the true meaning of those words, since Felix himself, who had pronounced them, had taught precisely this? Who would believe that Gelasius employed the same passages of Sacred Scripture for the same purpose without ever mentioning Felix? If one adds the nearly identical formulas of speech, wherever the matter concerns a sentence that does not affect the repentant, and the entirely identical tenor of the discourse and style, one will reasonably conjecture that these passages too came from Felix.

But what deserves greater attention is that the abrupt beginning of this treatise has nothing to do with its subject. It is a fragment of another writing, dealing with the bishops of Constantinople, who arrogated to themselves the honor of the second see on the basis of a decree of certain Chalcedonians concerning Peter. As I consider and prepare this material, a new book by Aloysius Andruccius has been sent to me, which discusses these words.

The first column continues this subject [Col. 0941C] up to the words “To sinful man,” etc. Then, although the following words are presented as if continuous, the text suddenly leaps into the intended subject, namely, the removal of the mark of perpetual condemnation. The same matter is treated for three columns, with the division that we see in column 1229 inserted at an inappropriate point.

In column 1231, ten verses are wrongly inserted, beginning “Since the Apostolic See”; they belong to the writing whose beginning they also form. With the word “nevertheless,” the text returns to the subject and adds a period reserved for the Sphinx, which is not adequately restored even with the help of the manuscripts. It proceeds to the words “But if they fear to attempt these things,” where once again we seem to go astray and suddenly enter a fragment of another treatise, in which it was shown that Peter of Alexandria could not be absolved by the emperor. It continues to the end, except for the final periods, which refer elsewhere and are themselves disconnected.

It is astonishing that all this was not noticed by so many most learned men who worked on these documents, whether to publish, examine, or cite them [Col. 0941D]. The editor of St. Leo believed that he had discovered the beginning of this treatise and had restored and rearranged it through certain new readings and a new division; yet the beginning remains abrupt, the ending mutilated, and the sequence confused and intermixed. This will become clear, I think, as soon as it is established that the work contains fragments relating to distinct matters.

That such a dislocation occurred long ago may readily be learned both from the manuscript before us and from Anastasius the Librarian. In the letter prefixed to the *Collectanea* and addressed to the deacon John, Anastasius cites a sentence found on the preceding page of his copy, which apparently belongs elsewhere, and says that it was taken from Gelasius’s volume *On the Bond of the Anathema*.

There may perhaps be some to whom this statement seems harsh, namely, that a cento, so to speak, was received into the canonical Code of the Roman Church. But although I have said that this document was dislocated in antiquity and badly treated by copyists, it is not necessary to understand that this occurred before it was inserted into that code [Col. 0942A]. It must also be observed that the editor of St. Leo bestowed this title on the collection of canons by his own judgment; and if this judgment is examined, he will certainly not carry the vote of all learned men. For there are many things that suggest, and almost prove, the contrary.

What shall we say about the three Greek letters of Felix, which Valesius, Dupin, and others reject, but Cave, Pagius, and others approve? Anastasius certainly seems to have praised the second in the letter mentioned shortly before. From this we should observe that some works published in Latin would have had their Latinity utterly buried beneath the mass of oblivion, had it not recovered them from the later source of the Greek books and taken them up again with a thirsty heart—such as the letter of blessed Pope Felix pronouncing sentence against Peter of Antioch.

But who does not see that they have at least been interpolated? This is especially true of the third, which is not self-consistent, agrees neither with its title nor with its beginning. In the Latin version of the first, the omission of a syllable creates a heresy: “the divisible Trinity.” As I recall [Col. 0942B], another error likewise creates a heresy concerning the Trinity, where the text reads of the Son: “nor was he begotten, but proceeding.” By examining the Greek text, several errors can very easily be removed. I mention them for this reason, so that they may be taken into account in a new collection of the Councils. Many errors of every kind have crept into the earlier editions; quite a few of those contaminating the Acacian documents I shall correct incidentally in this preface and in the notes.

We must now concentrate on the matters concerning Acacius. The fourth letter of Gelasius, or the *Commonitorium* to Faustus, in which the manuscript likewise agrees with the printed editions, is not much cleaner: at the beginning of the second page the connection falters, and at the end it disappears. From “By these things, however, this is too shameless,” up to “might draw him into his depravity,” a different letter seems to begin, and indeed one belonging to Felix, by whom Andromachus had been instructed to exhort Acacius.

The following period returns to the earlier matter, while the next, up to the words “It is not surprising,” must again be attributed to Felix. Nor is the interpretation of the most learned Baronius sufficient [Col. 0942C]—namely, that Gelasius is speaking in the person of the Apostolic See. The words “that he says, if necessary, that he will ask pardon” plainly show that Acacius was still alive, thinking, no doubt, that he would then necessarily have to seek forgiveness for sin if we allowed him not to cease sinning.

Then the matter again concerns the Greeks, although confusedly. But the final words—“nor is any contest to be entered into with these uncorrecting men,” and “we have no right to undertake any contest with men outside communion”—refer back to what was said above. Our manuscript sheds no light on these matters, agreeing remarkably with the printed editions, except at the place where the meaning of the final printed page, column 1168, is completely absent. The manuscript reads: “nor does he know, or pretends not to know, through the numerous judgment of priests,” etc. If one removes the word *constat* (“is established”) from this sentence, or adds the particle *ut* (“so that”), the passage can be restored in full with the smallest possible alteration. But enough on this.

The manuscript gives no date for when Felix III [Col. 0942D]—called Felix II by some, who exclude the other as an intruder while Liberius was still alive in exile—wrote this letter. It can, however, be deduced from the context: namely, after the synod concerning the lapsed held in Africa and convened at Rome in 487, which is mentioned here, and before the death of Acacius, which occurred in 489, during the consulship of Eusebius, as we learn from Victor of Tunnuna.

In the Labbe edition of the Councils, this letter should be placed before Letter 12 of Felix, that is, before the first letter issued after Acacius’s death. It was not sent to specific persons, for it responds to an anonymous writing published in defense of Acacius and Peter of Alexandria; Felix seems not even to have known whether that work had been composed by one person or by several.

From this refutation of that writing, one may gather many things: some are new arguments introduced here and there; others provide further knowledge of certain matters; and still others greatly strengthen what was uncertain or illuminate what was obscure. Yet, in my judgment [Col. 0943A], the individual events that took place in connection with this controversy have not yet been suitably distinguished and securely established, nor can everything that we read about this case in ancient writers be adequately reconciled. I think this must be attributed chiefly to the corruption of the documents of that age.

Nevertheless, the central point in this matter is abundantly clear here: how greatly Acacius sinned, and how justly Gelasius consequently attacked him, even in his memory. I do not understand how Dupin could at one point have let it slip that Acacius’s entire error seemed to consist in displeasing the Roman bishop and adhering too closely to his own prince.

For what Felix and Gelasius decreed against Acacius was upheld by their successors with such constancy that, after the fiercest disputes, peace and concord between the Eastern and Western Churches were neither sealed nor restored until, at last, in the year 519, under Hormisdas, the name of Acacius was erased from the diptychs, as is recorded in the *Supplication of the Deacon Dioscorus*.

The Greeks finally acknowledged the justice of the Roman demand [Col. 0943B] when John, bishop of Constantinople, after anathematizing the heretics Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy the Parricide, and Peter of Alexandria, likewise anathematized Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, as their accomplice and follower.

Let the letter of the Greek bishops cited by Bessarion be examined. They confess that they are **κινδυνεύοντας** (“in danger”) **διὰ τὴν παρέκβασιν τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀκακίου**, “because of the transgression of our father Acacius.”

Moreover, Acacius is listed after the heretics in the decree concerning apocryphal Scriptures. Felix is said to have attacked the very truth of apostolic doctrine. In the printed editions Gelasius declares that Acacius deviated from Catholic communion; in the Veronese manuscript he is said to have deviated from Catholic truth. Hormisdas calls him polluted by the doctrine and communion of Dioscorus and Eutyches. In the second confession of faith, which the emperor Justinian presented to Pope Agapetus, Justinian says: “After Eutyches and the others, we also reject Acacius, a fellow-heretic and follower.”

Liberatus writes that he was fully exposed as a heretic [Col. 0943C], and Nicholas I likewise brands him with this description more than once. Basil the Cilician also reports that Acacius had acquired among many the reputation of a heretic, as we read in Photius: **αἱρετικοῦ δόξαν** (“the reputation of a heretic”).

I do not therefore wish to quarrel with those learned men who, even in dissertations devoted to this question, maintain that although that bishop was justly condemned, he was nevertheless orthodox as far as the faith is concerned. The indications are certainly not very striking—apart from the communion about which Symmachus said in the *Apologetic*: “Is communicating with such men not consenting with them?” Acacius expelled orthodox bishops and installed heretics in their sees; and when the impious Mongus, **αἱρετικὴν συστησάμενος σύνοδον**, “having convened a heretical synod,” marked the Council of Chalcedon with an anathema, he had Acacius as his **συμπράκτωρ**, his accomplice, as the synodal libellus says.

But for clearing the Apostolic See of all doubt, it is more than sufficient that John of Constantinople declared: “Whoever embraces the communion of those men also receives a similar judgment in condemnation” [Col. 0944A]. Nor should the following matters be treated as insignificant: that Acacius led the emperor over to the side of the heretics; that he was the author of composing and promulgating the *Henoticon*; that he overcame the legates of the Apostolic See by taking away their letters and by imprisonment and money; that he so rashly invaded jurisdictions belonging to others; and that, after violently excluding Catholic priests throughout the East, he substituted corrupt and criminal men whom he himself had previously condemned.

He profaned and polluted the sees—Alexandria with Peter Mongus, an associate in parricide; Tyre with John, rejected by the Apameans and Antiochenes; and Antioch with Peter the Fuller, who had been deposed by synodal judgment—by every lawful and unlawful means. What more is needed? Does Theophanes not also show that Acacius erased the name of Felix from the sacred records? **τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐξῆρεν τῶν διπτύχων**, “he removed his name from the diptychs.” Nicephorus and Cedrenus likewise report this. All these acts certainly signify something greater than merely having displeased the Roman bishop.

I shall briefly explain the plan and method by which I prepared this edition [Col. 0944B]. I endeavored to cleanse the text, but I did not wish to transform it. Therefore, even when the parts sometimes seemed poorly connected, I did not exercise editorial discretion; to do so would have been rash, especially since it is clear that the author himself sometimes leaps forward and repeatedly returns to the same matters.

Only once did I restore certain transposed sentences to their proper place, when the rearrangement was obvious and the disorder plain. I did not fill in lacunae, if any exist, of which the manuscript gives us no indication. For when we are not certain what should be restored, I see no reason to attach our own words to the authors.

I was also sparing in emendations and, if I am not mistaken, sufficiently cautious in making them. Consequently, I left untouched sentences that were sometimes less complete and expressions that were less correct. Whenever a notable or somewhat freer emendation has occurred, I shall give the manuscript reading in the notes, so that anyone may exercise his own judgment.

But when we restore the sense by changing the inflection of a word, adding a particle, or removing a syllable [Col. 0944C], why was it necessary to call attention to the change? Or why repeatedly mention minor errors that occur so frequently and from which nothing useful can be extracted? I have not composed notes for show. I do not at all approve of accumulations heaped up whenever an opportunity is afforded by some word, bringing forward nothing but what we have heard a thousand times.

It remains only for the humane and learned reader to forgive errors attributable not to the manuscript but solely to me.

## LETTER OR TREATISE OF FELIX III, POPE

He refutes the arguments advanced on behalf of Acacius and shows that, just as Acacius was justly and duly condemned, so he may be restored only canonically.

[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The first two verses are the same as those with which Gratian introduced his first decree, cited after Gelasius’s treatises in the collection of Councils. There was no apparent source from which it had been extracted, since those words occur neither in the letter cited there, from which the second decree was excerpted, nor in any other work of Gelasius. Nevertheless, Nicholas I quoted the same authority at much greater length, as we have noted, extending to the words “that he be condemned.” When the editors of the Councils reviewed his letter to all the bishops of Gaul, they marked in italics only the opening verses, which they had seen in Gratian; from this document we learn that the following six verses likewise contain words belonging to the same text and should henceforth be written in the same way. It is remarkable that we likewise learn that, from the time of Nicholas I onward, this letter appeared in the archives even of the Roman Church only in an abridged and headless form, as we have just discovered also in the Verona manuscript.

At this point Felix was replying to the defenders of Acacius that they were wrongly attacking the custom and authority of the Apostolic See, which had grown with the Christian Church and had now flourished for nearly five centuries. Just as the first period appears acephalous, so the second, which proves the matter by examples, seems mutilated in the manuscript. It is excellently illuminated, however, by the letter called the thirteenth of Gelasius:

“But we do not pass over this either: that the Apostolic See has frequently, as has been said, according to the custom of our ancestors, even without a preceding synod, possessed the power both of absolving those whom a synod had unjustly condemned and of condemning, when no synod existed, those whom it was right to condemn. For the synod of the East had condemned Athanasius of holy memory; nevertheless, because the Apostolic See did not consent to the Greeks’ condemnation, it received him and absolved him. The synod of Catholic bishops certainly also condemned John of Constantinople, of holy memory; in the same way the Apostolic See alone, because it did not consent, absolved him. Likewise, Flavian of holy memory, condemned by an assembly of bishops, was absolved in the same manner, because the Apostolic See alone did not consent.”

I think that in both our letter and that of Nicholas the sequence of the text could in some fashion be repaired merely by adding a particle, as follows: “That St. Athanasius was therefore not condemned by the synod of the East because this See did not consent; or St. John of Constantinople, or St. Flavian.” SCIPIO MAFFEII.]

They wish to overturn what Christ established five hundred years ago, although the bond of thirty years cannot be broken. Saint Athanasius therefore was not condemned by the synod of the East, because this See did not consent; Saint John of Constantinople, Saint Flavian [lacuna]. If, then, those who were condemned by the synod of the East could not have been condemned when this See alone did not consent, it follows [Note: [Col. 0945B] You should understand this as referring to a universal synod. To understand it in this way, and to believe that Acacius was not examined and condemned without a synod of Italian bishops, we are driven and compelled by the comparison of several documents, by the custom of the Apostolic See in that age, and by arguments that are almost irresistible. If, on the other hand, we attend to the words and to several passages, one may not unreasonably suspect that no synod at all preceded it, and that, in accordance with the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon, the sentence was pronounced by the supreme pontiff alone with his private gathering of presbyters, although it was subsequently presented also to a synod.

For in answer to the bitter complaints of the Greeks, Felix never says that the condemnation was carried out without any synod and by one man alone; nor does Gelasius ever say that it was decreed in a provincial council that Acacius should be condemned, as he shortly afterward says regarding the lapsed in Africa. In the letter we are publishing, Felix repeatedly presses this point: “The reproach of my levity is at issue: why do you wish him to be absolved in such a way that in everything you expose both our conscience and our reputation? Our conscience, if I absolve one who has himself professed to be the author of the entire betrayal; our reputation, [because of] the entire change of judgment.” Perhaps one should read: “our reputation because of the levity of the entire matter,” or something similar.

To show that Acacius had done the very thing of which the Roman Pontiff was accused, Gelasius asks: “Did he expel John and receive Peter after any synod had been held there, at least?” And then: “Why did it not occur to him at that time that, in such cases, the emperor should at least be asked to convene some kind of synod?” Here he seems to concede that Felix convened no synod at all when he first condemned Acacius.

When Theophanes reports Acacius’s condemnation, he mentions only Felix, who wrote the sentence: Φήλιξ δὲ καθῆρεν αὐτοὺς (his legates), γράψας Ἀκακίῳ καθαίρεσιν—“But Felix deposed them, writing to Acacius a deposition.” The same pontiff consequently alludes to a sentence subsequently approved by a synod in these words: “A gathering of very many Catholic priests in Italy rightly recognized that a sentence had been pronounced against Acacius.”

Whatever the case may be, it is entirely clear that, because certain documents have been interpolated and dislocated, the history of the synods under Felix is surrounded by much darkness. I am therefore more astonished than anything else that individual learned men who have dealt with these matters have congratulated themselves as though they had completely disentangled them, and, rejecting earlier writers, have presented their own conclusions as indisputable. That Acacius was not condemned by two synods, as Valesius argues against Evagrius and Pagi holds as certain, will be plainly evident below. SCIPIO MAFFEII.]

that, even without a synod, whoever was condemned by that single See condemning him was nevertheless condemned. [Note: [Col. 0945D] It may be inferred that many things preceded this. In what follows we recognize a lacuna, and scarcely grasp the complete context. A letter from Acacius to Simplicius is indicated, in which he announces the death of the heretic Timothy the Cat and the flight of Peter the Hoarse; these are the words of that letter: “so that for this reason he might be subjected to greater punishments.”

From the words that follow, obscure and scarcely meaningful as they are, it is nevertheless possible to extract either an emendation or even the sense of the difficult wording. For in the letter to Simplicius mentioned above one reads: “from the Alexandrian bishop to Rome, to one or the other, these things were reported.” Here one must either restore the reading found in this passage, “to both Romes, the new and the old,” or understand *alteruter* as meaning “both,” just as in Columella (Book XII, chapter 1) one reads: “it was necessary that one of the two should be outside, etc., and one inside, etc.” In the Vulgate (James 4:11; 5:16), *alterutrum* translates ἀλλήλων, “one another.” Below Felix likewise says that he was reported both here and at Constantinople. SCIPIO MAFFEII.]

Finally, if there is no sentence of his alone, why are they so eager to have this dissolved [lacuna]—on the testimony of Acacius, where he confirms that Timothy the Catholic reported to both Romes that Peter had been condemned; that he had been ordained by a heretic, that is, an accomplice in his madness; where he says, “so that for this reason he might be subjected to greater punishments.” [Col. 0946A]

[Note: [Col. 0946B] Among the arguments brought forward on behalf of Peter of Alexandria, it had not been heard that, while Timothy the Catholic was sitting in office, he had a successor designated in reserve. Nor, unless I am mistaken, had the term *in sequestris*, or *in sequestri*, been heard in this matter; here it is used four times to signify a future succession. It has been transferred from the law, in which a *sequester* was something handed over for safekeeping and return, as a deposit. See *Digest*, title “On Deposits,” law “Properly.”

It should be observed that although these claims were falsely made on behalf of Peter of Alexandria, Felix nevertheless does not reject or refute them on account of their novelty and extraordinary character. Indeed, he seems to add that Timothy the Catholic had been permitted to choose his successor; this also contributes to the historical evidence supplied by the present letter. Shortly afterward he confirms it when he says that the emperor promised Timothy that whatever he had determined would remain in force.

We know, however, that in the Alexandrian Church successors were more than once designated by the bishops through their vote, especially when the bishops were lying in the final illness. Alexander ordered that no successor should be given to him after his death except Athanasius, as Saint Epiphanius testifies (*Heresy* 58): Ἀλεξάνδρου δὲ ἐντειλαμένου μηδένα κατασταθῆναι εἰ μὴ Ἀθανάσιον etc.—“Alexander having ordered that no one be appointed except Athanasius,” etc.

I also once noted these words of Liberatus (chapter 20): “It is indeed the custom at Alexandria that the man who succeeds the deceased keep vigil over the body of the deceased, place his right hand upon the deceased’s head, and, after burial, receive with his own hands the pallium of blessed Mark around his neck, and then sit lawfully in office.” Since the successor was required to keep vigil over the body of the deceased, it may appear that he had been elected before the bishop’s death.

The synod of Antioch disapproved this practice, and it had already been decreed in the Roman council under Pope Hilary, canon 5, that no bishop should choose a successor for himself. Felix says below, again citing this same Timothy: “nor could he ordain a priest over himself while he survived”; and again: “nor could he ordain a pontiff while he was still in existence,” although ordaining and designating are different things.

As far as the matter at hand is concerned, the holy pontiff here shows how incredible it is that he was designated by Timothy, with whom he did not communicate and whom, as we shall see, he requested should be exiled farther away. SCIPIO MAFFEII.]

Therefore he was not designated to be substituted for the holy Timothy after his death, as is now alleged, as though he were being kept in reserve; rather, he was subjected to punishments for his crimes, which Acacius reported. Yet no one maintains that a person reserved for honor is worthy of punishments. The emperor left everything to the choice of Timothy the Catholic. It is therefore necessary that what he determined should stand, and he said that a Catholic had been ordained by Catholics. It is consequently false that he was appointed in reserve to be substituted for the man with whom he had never communicated and by whom it had been requested that he be exiled farther away.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] The supporters of Peter of Alexandria were insisting that John Talaia be expelled from the Alexandrian see, as though he had seized it contrary to the oath he had sworn [Col. 0947C] in the imperial city. Evagrius also reports this, but from Zachariah the Rhetor. Felix shows how incongruously they made this charge: for if John had bound himself by this oath, Acacius would never afterward have written of him in such a way as to suggest that he was worthy of promotion to the episcopate. [Col. 0947D] “How did you declare him worthy,” etc.: the verb *mandare* (“to declare” or “to commend”) is used in this sense today in the French language. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

If John had sworn that he would not become a bishop, [Col. 0947A] how did you declare him worthy of having greater responsibilities entrusted to him, responsibilities pertaining to the governance of the Church? What is greater than the presbyterate for the governance of the Church, except the episcopate? If he had sworn it, how could you commend this? And if he had sworn it, why did you expose him to doing what he had sworn not to do? Or, if what you commended was done, why are you angry? Why do you say that he perjured himself, when what he had sworn he would not do was done—when you commanded that he ought to be made this, [Note: [Col. 0947D] Several men were advanced to the episcopate from the office of *apocrisarius*, or legate. He himself attended to all the Church’s affairs, either because he was also an administrator, as appears from Liberatus and the *Breviculum*, or because the *apocrisarius* was the representative of ecclesiastical business, as Hincmar of Reims says, using the Greek name explicitly, in Letter 3. There he also reports that this office began under Constantine: “Since the emperor resided at Constantinople, representatives both of the Roman see and of the other principal sees kept watch in the palace over ecclesiastical business; for they also had responsibility for every matter of ecclesiastical religion or order, and likewise for canonical or monastic disputes.” SCIPIO MAFFEI.] when he was an *apocrisarius*? Everything belonged to him; he himself managed all the affairs of the Church; no one among the Alexandrian clergy was regarded as his superior. In honor he was a presbyter; what could be added above that for the governance of the Church? What more could be conferred upon him except the episcopate? You therefore wanted him to be a bishop, [Col. 0947B] when you commanded that he ought to be something greater than he was—although nothing else remained except that he should be a bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0948C] It was alleged on behalf of the emperor that he had suffered violence from the people; Felix turns this into an excuse for John, who could all the more easily have suffered violence. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

I am astonished that, if the emperor is under constraint and therefore cannot expel Peter, you insist that one man could not endure constraint so as to be compelled against his will to do what he did not want. For the emperor himself, when he pleads constraint, defines as evil what he does under constraint, declaring that he does not do it willingly and testifying that he suffers it against his will. If you think Peter’s position ought to be excused, we prove it to be criminal, heretical, and condemned. If you claim that he was held in reserve [Note: [Col. 0948C] “To be avoided.” Below, in the passage concerning the diaconate, the manuscripts read: “he was in the diaconate under condemnation by St. Proterius.” I have corrected this from the *Breviculum*, where we read: “Peter was formerly condemned while in the diaconate.” Liberatus, chapter 16: “Timothy writes to Simplicius that Peter Mongus was condemned while in the diaconate.” The parts of this sentence are somewhat awkwardly connected. SCIPIO MAFFEI.] because of the scandal, to be substituted for the Catholic Timothy, neither the writings of Acacius support this—for he clearly states why Peter was excluded—nor those of the emperor, who promised the Catholic Timothy that what he had decreed would remain in force. Peter had been separated from Timothy’s communion, and Timothy had requested that Peter be sent into more distant exile; and Peter was reported both here and at Constantinople in this condition.

Acacius also testifies that Peter had been condemned by the holy Proterius while in the diaconate—not that Peter, who was a heretic, was placed in reserve so that he might be substituted for him. Those whom Peter ordained were ordered to be condemned without delay if they did not return to communion with the holy Timothy. If it is said that Peter was afterward corrected, this nevertheless shows that up to that point he had lain in error; and after his error he ought not to have been placed over Catholics, by whom he had been corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Felix is consistent with himself. In Letter 12 to Zeno: “He ought to have merited pardon, not honor.” For the passage where you read what the emperor said, see Felix’s Letter 2 to Zeno: “Finally, all the bishops,” etc. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Therefore he had been worthy of pardon, not of honor; and, having been ordained especially by heretics, he possessed absolutely none of the substance of episcopal dignity. If this is denied, it will be established both by the testimony of Acacius and by the logic of the matter. For when the heretic Timothy was condemned together with his accomplices, Peter was his companion and remained with him until Timothy’s death; and Peter was instituted by Timothy’s followers.

Finally, it must be asked whether Peter communicated with the holy Timothy up to the day of Timothy’s death. If he did not, he will undoubtedly belong among those whom the emperor declared to be separated from the communion of the Catholic Timothy and permanently condemned unless they returned to his communion and favor within two months.

It is laughable that some assert that Peter was ordained by that same Catholic Timothy. [Col. 0948B] While Timothy was alive, he certainly did not ordain Peter, since Peter never at all entered into Timothy’s communion. Timothy requested that Peter be sent into more distant exile, as has been said; nor could he have ordained a priest over himself while he was still alive. Let them see for themselves, then, if the dead Timothy ordained him.

At the time when Peter invaded the Church, the holy Timothy was not in Alexandria; and while Timothy was still alive, he could not, as has been said, ordain Peter as bishop. Rather, Peter, acting wickedly in everything, dared to assume for himself the name of bishop while Timothy, the legitimate priest, was still alive.

Nor did any of the Catholics at that time do this. They all, of course, shared Timothy’s position and communicated with him. Only one man, Peter’s partner in madness, did so, as Acacius already testifies.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Namely, in the letter to Simplicius: “with one and only one person present, and with him who persisted as his partner in madness.” How far this departed from ecclesiastical practice in that age—that bishops should be ordained by only one bishop, even if he were Catholic—can be seen in the Council of Arles, canon 20; the Council of Nicaea, canon 4; the Council of Régens, canon 2; and the Council of Orange, canon 21. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

For the Catholics who had not communicated with the heretic Timothy, but who did communicate with the Catholic Timothy while he was alive—and with that Catholic whom they knew to be the legitimate priest—could neither introduce another in his place nor consecrate a heretic. Hence it is clear that Peter was ordained by heretics and therefore cannot preside over the Catholic Church, since it must be judged utterly abominable and criminal that one who had long wallowed in perfidy should be imposed upon the necks of the faithful.

If this is admitted, the same thing could likewise be permitted everywhere in the case of other heresies; yet no examples, rules, or ecclesiastical laws ever allow such a thing to be imposed. But, you say, he was corrected. In the meantime, as has already been said above, you thereby show that he was a heretic: even if he is said to have turned from a condemned heresy to the Catholic faith, he ought to have been subject to the Catholics by whom he was corrected, not to preside over them. For the disciple is not above his teacher. It was enough for him to offer himself as an example by submitting to his correction, not, after prolonged error and lengthy perfidy, to rule over those by whom he had been reformed and corrected.

Moreover, I ask what error he condemned, what correct confession he chose, and which faith he declares false and which true. If he follows the faith defined at Chalcedon and the Catholic faith, why does he communicate with those who in no way accept the truth of the two natures in Christ? Why does he cause Dioscorus and the heretic Timothy to be commemorated? Why does he allow all who come from that party to defend positions opposed to the Council of Chalcedon? Peter unquestionably communicates with these people. But if he declares the faith of such men to be the true faith, it is sufficiently clear how far he has turned from his own error.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] We see with what effort the supporters of Acacius defended Peter of Alexandria as well, although he was a heretical and utterly corrupt man. “Yet that Alexandrian bishop,” etc. Thus Gelasius later writes in Letter 15, at the words: “Since it is always clear.” It appears that the Eastern patriarchs themselves were not accustomed to reconcile heretics before the assent of the Apostolic See and without the decision of the Roman pontiff. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

But I am not surprised that he is called corrected while he remains in his perversity, since it is not established either by whom he was corrected or by whom he was received. For if the Church’s rule and ancient tradition are known to everyone, he ought to have been examined or received by the bishop of his province—that is, by the bishop of the second see. Yet that Alexandrian bishop, even if he judged that Peter ought to be received after his condemned depravity, would not have done so before referring the matter to the Apostolic See.

The Catholic records concerning Timothy and the examples of many others demonstrate this. When they received the written confessions of heretics, in which the heretics professed that they condemned their former error, they did not confirm their reception and communion until they had sent the records of those who offered satisfaction to this see and had requested that their reception be ratified here, as was done.

I ask, then, who examined Peter, who received him, who truly reconciled him, and who permitted him to enter Catholic communion. For the moment I say nothing about the fact that all these things belong to a penitent, since he was both a heretic and ordained by heretics. He plainly—and it is established—had erred, yet is now said to have been corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Peter had sinned not through fear but by a voluntary choice of depravity. “Of the pontiff himself,” that is, of his own bishop. “Rather, to whom,” etc., namely, to the Alexandrian bishop. MAFFEI.]

For pardon after a fall caused by fear is one thing; choosing voluntary depravity is another. If Acacius receives Peter, by what right and according to what rule does he do so? It was not even the pontiff’s right to do this, and Acacius was unwilling to refer the matter to me. Rather, he had been repeatedly warned not to do it and had been expressly ordered, at our urging, to drive Peter farther from Alexandria, away from the priesthood and from Catholic right.

Why did he presume to do what I had forbidden and trample upon what had been commanded? Did the emperor examine and receive Peter? It is established, meanwhile, [Col. 0950A] that he was not received according to the ecclesiastical rules. His reception, therefore, is wholly alien to ecclesiastical rule.

If you say, “But the emperor is Catholic,” then, with due respect to him, we shall say that he is a son, not a bishop of the Church. In matters pertaining to religion, he ought to learn, not teach.

He possesses the privileges of his own authority, which he has obtained from God for administering public affairs; and, not ungrateful for God’s benefits, he must not usurp anything contrary to the ordering of the heavenly hierarchy. For God willed that matters requiring the disposition of the Church should belong to priests, not to the powers of this world. If these powers are faithful, God has willed them to be subject to his Church and to its priests.

Let him not claim another’s right or a ministry assigned to someone else, lest he abruptly oppose the one by whom everything has been established and appear to fight against his benefits, from whom he received his own authority. The almighty God willed that the masters and priests of the Christian religion should be appointed, examined, and that those returning from error should be received not by public laws or by the powers of this world, but by pontiffs and priests.

Christian emperors ought to subject their enforcement of authority to ecclesiastical bishops, not place it above them. Therefore there is neither a valid examination nor can this reception remain in force: the Church, according to its laws and proper procedure, did not examine or receive Peter at all, nor restore him to communion. Acacius consequently shared in his error and prostituted the Catholic faith to him, rather than bringing him back to Catholic communion. For where reception has not been properly carried out, it follows that the person has remained in error.

We have also removed Acacius from our communion, lest through him we too should be judged to have communicated with Peter, whom no ecclesiastical rule had examined or received and who therefore remained in his former error.

How, then, is Acacius not summoned as guilty for communicating with one whom he had reported as condemned? “Can fresh water and bitter water flow from the same opening?” (James 3:11). For when the Apostle says, “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor” (Galatians 2:18), you must judge whether Acacius is not a transgressor, since what he had formerly condemned he afterward praised with his own mouth.

“By your words,” he says, “you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” “Peace, peace,” and there is no peace.

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Felix used these words in Letter 13 to Flavita. In the Labbe edition, at the margin of the preceding Letter 12, “Euphemius” has been added; it should be restored to “Flavita,” to whom the following letter is addressed. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

For peace is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1:5). What of these things is found in Peter? What of them is shown to be found in Acacius? Peter, neither examined nor received according to legitimate ecclesiastical rule, remains in his perversity; Acacius becomes the companion of one who remains in perversity, even after he himself had declared Peter condemned.

“But Acacius communicated with Peter under imperial compulsion,” you say. This alone is enough, since what is said to have been done under compulsion is thereby shown to be perverse. Let Acacius—or whoever makes this claim—consider whether he is declaring the Catholic emperor to be the author of this perversity.

We do not believe this of a Catholic emperor, since we retain his sacred letters in which he professes that he holds the Catholic faith and the definition of the Council of Chalcedon. For that reason we also ask him to expel the heretics. The man who says that the emperor either does not wish or is unable to do what he believes shows the worst opinion of him. Nothing may be preferred to the divinity, and it is impious not to carry out willingly what pertains to God.

We do not, I say, believe this of the emperor. Far be it from us to say that, contrary to what he openly professes and contrary to the dignity of the empire, he attacks the Catholic faith. Yet he would attack it—God forbid—if he compelled anyone by force to do what is hostile to the Catholic Church. As has been said, the very fact that something is said to be done under compulsion establishes that it is perverse.

But those who make these claims may see to the matter concerning the emperor. For our part, in this matter too [Note: [Col. 0951D] In the letter to the bishops of Dardania, the emperor Zeno himself professes in his own letters that he had done everything on the advice of Acacius. SCIPIO MAFFEI.] we cite the emperor’s sacred letters, in which the emperor promises that he did everything with Acacius’s counsel; and we also produce Acacius’s writings, which praise the emperor for doing these things.

No one praises what he suffers under compulsion; no one, on his own advice, asks that compulsion be imposed upon him. If he acted under compulsion, let him admit that what he did was evil. For he acts unwillingly, not willingly; what he does under compulsion he does not do by his will. He acknowledges as evil what he would not want done if he were not under compulsion.

If what he does under compulsion is evil, why does he pursue it with praise? Why does he become, for the destruction of others, the herald of a deed that he supposedly commits unwillingly? It is therefore evident that what he does arises not from compulsion but from his will, since he approves it, praises it, and proclaims it superior to the conduct of earlier pontiffs.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] These words come from Acacius’s lost letter on behalf of Peter of Alexandria. As Liberatus, chapter 18, reports, Acacius praised him extravagantly, although he remembered having previously reported such serious crimes against him. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

For Acacius says that the Alexandrian Church now breathes again and is filled with the abundance of spiritual nourishment. Yet earlier he had said that, after Peter had been expelled, the hearts of the faithful—that is, of his people—rejoiced with the Father, that is, with the Catholic Timothy.

Finally, let Acacius himself consider whether he is saying that the emperor does everything that is evil, since the emperor claims that he tolerates under compulsion what he calls evil, and declares that he does not do it willingly. These things are so evil that he would not do them if compulsion did not press him. Yet, according to us, what he makes a great point of praising he demonstrates that he does not do under compulsion but willingly.

If they admit that Peter erred and are seeking a remedy, let them seek a remedy in its proper order. Let them consent to have their wounds treated. No sick person imposes the conditions of his treatment upon the physician. Therefore let them patiently allow their wounds—or rather, the wounds they have inflicted upon the whole Church by all their excesses—to be treated, so that they may receive true healing: those very wounds whose wrongful infliction they themselves do not deny.

“But the Alexandrian people,” you say, “demanded this with great desire and will not tolerate Peter’s removal by any means.” What if the Alexandrian people demanded that idolatry be prepared? What difference would there be between permitting a heretic and permitting a profane person to be imposed upon the Catholic Church? What if they asked that a man from some other heresy be appointed as their bishop? He who has done this with one heresy can also do it with another, if he takes pleasure in making such requests.

If an attempt were made to perpetrate something among human beings contrary to the public laws, no good emperor would approve it. Will he yield to those who demand things contrary to God? If one must yield to those who desire what is perverse, where are imperial authority, moderation, and the governance of the laws? If, contrary to the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical rule, what people demand is to be granted, how can a Catholic emperor permit something not to be done against human will while it is done against God? How can he permit those conceiving wickedness—indeed, deadly things—not to be corrected, and those plotting madness to perish forever?

It is neither the conduct of a good emperor nor of a Catholic ruler to grant people what they demand to their own harm. Rather, it is salutary for the men concerned, for the whole state, for its safety, and for its government not to yield to what is contrary to God.

“But these things,” you say, “are contrary neither to good morals nor to the true faith.” How are they not harmful to good morals, when they demand as administrator of divine affairs a partner in Proterius’s murder, an associate of heretics, and a condemned man—one whom it would be sacrilegious, or at least unbecoming, to place in authority? [Col. 0952C] How is it not contrary to religion to want a condemned heretic, who received from heretics a false title of priesthood, to preside over the Catholic faith?

“But he has been corrected,” you say, “and all those by whom he was corrected wanted this; it has been approved by those who recognize him.” Let us carefully examine who these people are. They are certainly those whom you likewise testify to have been corrected from the same error. It remains beyond doubt that they are his accomplices. By what laws, then, should the testimony of those involved in the same crime be admitted on behalf of any one of them?

“But,” you say, “those who also seemed to communicate with the Catholic Timothy, now communicating with Peter, have asked similar things concerning him.” These people, then, are marked by their betrayal of Catholic communion. As is said, they maintained communion with the Catholic Timothy until his death, but after Timothy’s passing they fell into association with this man, with whom the Catholic Timothy is shown never to have communicated. Thus they have fallen away from the Catholic Timothy—or rather, from Catholic communion.

See how Peter has been corrected and approved: he is said to have been requested as bishop either by his accomplices or by betrayers of Catholic communion.

“But the Catholic Timothy did not communicate with Peter,” you say, “because Peter had usurped the episcopate while Timothy was alive.” If it had been sufficient for Timothy to remove Peter because of the episcopate, then Timothy’s refusal to communicate with him would not have been caused by the episcopate but by heresy. Communion pertains to the faith. For if the reason had been honor, Timothy could at least have communicated with Peter as a layman, provided that Peter had retained the true faith.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Felix promises in Letter 13 that he will see to it that, for the restoration of the Church’s charity, nothing should be lost, while preserving the Catholic confession, from those whom Acacius ordained or baptized. He argues in such a way that, if those ordained by Acacius needed a special dispensation in order to be received, it is clear that the ordainer himself was not in Catholic communion. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Why, then, were those ordained by Peter ordered to be regularly received into the Catholic faith? This shows that Peter himself was not in Catholic communion.

Furthermore, if Peter has been corrected, why did all the Catholics—whether in Alexandria or throughout Egypt—remain separated from him? Why do those Catholics who communicated with the Catholic Timothy until the day of their death not communicate with Peter? They are truly Catholics for this very reason: they continue in the same communion without violating it in any way.

It therefore clearly appears that only those communicate with Peter and have requested him as their bishop who, as has been said, are either ancient accomplices in his depravity or have deviated from Catholic communion and passed into his company. For that reason they also ceaselessly persecute the Catholics.

We have repeatedly heard and learned through reliable reports who are said to communicate with Peter and who are separated from his communion. They are seen daily to act against the Catholic faith, against the preaching of the Apostolic See, and against the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Thus he calls the celebrated letter of Leo the Great to Flavian, which became a kind of standard for the council and thereafter was regarded as a touchstone for those who held a correct view of the mystery of the Incarnation. In the collection of the councils, we read that the testimonies of the holy Fathers appended to this letter were added by St. Leo himself to the letter addressed to the emperor Leo. It may be inferred that there were many more such testimonies: if excerpts had been taken from only nine or ten bishops, Felix would not have used the hyperbole “from all the pontiffs who have ever existed throughout the whole world from the time of the Lord and Savior.” You can see here the weight and use of tradition. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

This is so true that we can produce as witnesses of his ancestral madness the sons whom we have here. Finally, all the Egyptians who are detained in this city on various commercial business and who communicate with Peter cannot even listen to the Council of Chalcedon and its definitions to such an extent that they dare to accuse us of holding them.

The teaching of the master is therefore apparent from the disciples, and the impious father is recognized from his offspring. They openly declare that, if they hear Peter preaching the Council of Chalcedon, they will not hesitate to anathematize him. From this it is sufficiently clear what sort of doctrine they testify that he proclaims.

We ask you plainly whether you think the Council of Chalcedon ought to be followed or not. If it should not be followed, how do you profess in your letters that you hold to it? It is therefore apparent that none of you stands firm not only in the Catholic definition but even in your own profession. How, then, shall we believe you when you boast that you hold the Catholic faith, when you do not even hold what you publicly declare in writing?

[Col. 0953D] If, bound by your own profession, you firmly assert that you will preserve the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon in every respect, then you also say that you will accept the preaching of the Apostolic See, which was reread, examined, and accepted in that council. The blessed pope Leo approved all these definitions by the testimonies of all the pontiffs who had existed throughout the whole world from the time of the Lord and Savior, which he appended to his letter to the emperor Leo of blessed memory.

If, therefore, you follow the ancient faith transmitted to us by the holy Fathers; if, concerning the Incarnation of the Lord and Savior, you hold with us what they held and in no respect deviate from the teaching of the whole Church—for we are neither wiser than our predecessors nor permitted to arrogate to ourselves a new position different from what our ancestors both learned and taught there; and we are no more learned interpreters and explainers of the Council of Nicaea itself than were those many and venerable bishops, who either wisely understood it or faithfully proclaimed it—[Note: [Col. 0954D] It is known that the Eutychians, in order to assert their impious doctrine by which they denied that Christ was human, foolishly cited the Council of Nicaea, where those who denied that the Son was God had been condemned. SCIPIO MAFFEI.] then let us all hold this faith together with sincere mind and true heart, and there is peace.

Let us also preserve inviolate the rules that the Church received from those same Fathers, and there is peace. Let these matters therefore be certain and fixed among you, and there will be no disagreement. But if you claim that they remain inviolate among you, allow us for a little while to examine them in our concern; for the more genuine a peace we desire to have, the more certain a basis for peace we wish to recognize.

If these things remain inviolate among you, why do you say that Peter of Alexandria has been corrected and received into the Catholic faith? He must therefore have cast aside everything that conflicts with these definitions and have passed with his whole heart into this form of Catholic doctrine.

What, then, do those people want, whom we recognize shouting among us every day, raging and gnashing their teeth against the Council of Chalcedon and against the preaching of the Apostolic See? If they have been corrected, they therefore hold the matters mentioned above. If they hold them, why do they vehemently attack them? If they profess them, why do they withdraw from the Catholics who steadfastly maintain the same profession? Or why do those who profess the true faith dissent from the company of these people?

If they know that these people retain one faith with them, it follows that those who do not hesitate openly to attack the matters belonging to the Catholic faith, and who dissent from the profession of the Catholics, are not Catholics at all and have therefore not been corrected.

What, then, why does Peter communicate with such men? If, while these people remained in error, Peter was examined and received according to the true faith, then, if he was corrected, he was transferred to those things that agree with the Catholic faith; he did not remain in those things that are shown to be hostile to it. Why, then, does he communicate with such people? If he openly professes the matters to which he is known to have passed after abandoning his error, why does he communicate with the enemies of that profession?

It is therefore proved more clearly than daylight that he was not corrected but remains in the same pestilence, since he communicates with its followers and professors. Thus even this very claim—that you want him to have been corrected—appears false and is most plainly refuted.

Accordingly, even if Peter had been corrected, he ought to have been subject to those who corrected him, not placed above them. Since he had been ordained by heretics, he could not in any respect preside over them. In this respect too the man whom you claim to have been corrected is convicted, since he is plainly found to communicate with those who persist in depravity. He is therefore rightly and justly excluded in every way from our communion.

See, then, how just a cause we have for separating even Acacius from our communion: he had rightly reported Peter as previously condemned, yet afterward wickedly received him into his own communion.

We had ancient communion with Acacius. To preserve it unharmed, [Note: [Col. 0955D] “We warned”: namely, the Roman pontiffs. We read “for five years” also in Liberatus, chapter 18; but Gelasius says “for three years” in Letters 8 and 13. The accounts can be reconciled by supposing that Simplicius warned him for three years and Felix for two. Hence the *Breviculum*: “For nearly three years the pope of holy memory, Simplicius, did not cease writing.” The five years may be reckoned before the dispatch of the legates, since the text adds, “finally, after the legates had been sent,” etc. This deserves consideration by those who think that Felix sent legates immediately after his inauguration. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

we warned him for five years. Although he did not deign even to reply, we nevertheless never ceased exhorting him to retain the Catholic faith. Finally, after sending legates, we terrified him, appealed to him with kindness, issued warnings and threats, persuaded, entreated, and held out the threat of condemnation, so that he would not yield to the communion of the corrupt. We instructed him to remember the labors he had first undertaken for the Catholic faith, stirring him to glory and deterring him from danger.

Disregarding all these things, he deceived the legates, pretending that he was in agreement with us, and joined himself in communion to a heretic and a condemned man whom he himself had especially reported as such.

Until I learned these things, my former communion with him could have continued. But once I discovered them, if I had not immediately separated him from my communion, it would have seemed to me that I was continuing to share communion with a transgressor, and that the communion I had had with a Catholic was also being maintained with one who had preferred to enter into the company of heretics.

To prevent this, it was necessary for me to break off his communion and separate him from my fellowship. This had to be done because it did not belong to the Catholic faith to fail entirely to do so.

“But,” you say, “the emperor imposes upon Acacius the necessity of communicating with Peter.” Much has already been said above about this necessity, and much more will be said, so that it may become clear that, even if the necessity were real, a priest ought to have despised it for the Catholic faith and endured whatever adversity arose, provided that he deviated in no respect from the integrity of the Catholic faith. Furthermore, clear reasoning will show that the emperor imposed no necessity whatsoever upon Acacius; rather, it is sufficiently evident that the emperor did everything on Acacius’s advice.

“But,” you say, “the emperor himself is under the necessity of doing these things.” For the moment I do not inquire into the cause of this necessity. Yet no necessity is greater than being subject to divine worship and religion, from which all things prosper, by which every necessity is most fully resolved, and by which all adversity is removed. Nothing must be preferred to this, since we have been commanded not to prefer even our own souls to God.

When God is despised, no necessity can be resolved and no human affair can stand. It is therefore clear that the greatest necessity and the greatest cause above all others is to postpone everything to God.

Add to this that there is no necessity, but it is alleged; there is now no one [lacuna].

A foolish sedition is being alleged concerning Peter’s exclusion, especially since, when the heretic Timothy was expelled, no one attempted to resist, and, when Peter was consequently expelled, no one opposed it.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] In the sense of resisting: Gelasius used it this way in Letter 15: “Heretics are substituted” [read: “were being substituted”]; “no one resisted.” In Letter 13: “Behold, the emperor did not persist against the one who resisted,” where the erroneous correction—or variant reading—is *restitit*, “resisted.” For Acacius did resist the emperor at that time, and the emperor did not persist against one who resisted. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

It is therefore falsely pretended that what has already been accomplished without disturbance in cases of the same kind could not be done here. Let it not be for the sake of money, and there is no necessity.

The disturbance at the killing of the holy Proterius was provoked by the incursion of heretics; no disturbance has ever been stirred up by Catholics. It is fitting that the seditions of any people whatsoever be suppressed by public authority.

Thus, in order to indulge the fury of wicked people who could have been quieted by a slight fear, divine religion is overturned and the Church of Christ is torn apart.

Finally, by claiming that there is a necessity, he declares by that very claim that what he does is evil. Therefore, if he has a necessity to strive against divine things, I have no necessity to perform that act. I must beware of the evil that you yourself admit to be evil when you testify that you do it under compulsion and against your will. Rather, I have the greater necessity of fearing God and the future judgment, so that I may avoid evil.

Why do you try to draw me into your wickedness, which you undertake under compulsion, when there is no necessity for me to submit to it? Rather, as has been said, the greater and better reason is that there is a necessity not to do it.

“But correct me,” you say, “and do not separate me from your fellowship.” Abandon evil, turn to good, return to me, and you are corrected, freed from evil, and in no way separated from me.

“But I cannot,” you say, “and you ought not to abandon me.” You are grieved, as I see, because I will not perish with you; I grieve that you will not be saved with me. If Peter’s person has such power over you that you despise God, that is your concern. It is neither right nor pleasing for me to do the same.

“Demand what can be done,” you say. And I tell you: ask me to do what can be done. For it can more easily be done that a human being be placed below God, that a human being be rejected rather than God. If that cannot be done, it is much less possible for us to choose a human being after rejecting God. We have a greater reason why we cannot do this than you have for refusing to do the other.

We can say: “All of you, say ‘Anathema to Peter.’ As long as he lives, do not communicate with him, and we will communicate with you.” What account shall we render to God if he takes the souls whom Peter destroys and, with our permission in some sense, takes them in order to destroy them?

Where are you trying to drag me—to yourself? Why do you not instead return to me? There is destruction there; here is salvation. There is a precipice there; here is faithful security. There is deception there; here is admonition. You do not wish to return to these saving things, yet you want me to descend to what is dangerous.

I do not know whether, even in your judgment, I ought to...
to entrust it. But Acacius, you say, was overcome by force, and is being coerced, so that either he has reached this position or does not correct it. That he did not suffer force is proved by many arguments, indeed is even demonstrated: for if he had been unwilling, he would not have reached this point; moreover, he is refuted by his own letters, [Col. 0957B] in which he praises all that was done on his advice, as though divinely inspired. But even if he suffered force from the emperor . . . . . not through the emperor to plot against the legates—a statement already made in the profession of our own legates. If this is true, he is guilty; if false, we burden these men with this additional charge: besides their treachery, they have added a lie. But since this too is demonstrated from Acacius’s letters, they did not say it falsely; thus the blame falls upon his person, since he was unwilling to cooperate with our legates, but rather plotted against ours . . . . Certainly he should at least have reported this before entering into communion, and should have warned them not to enter into communion.

Finally, even if he is being coerced, he ought to have endured the force, not, by trampling upon faith and communion, to betray himself to the faithless and mingle with the condemned; just as the blessed Flavian of holy memory did, and others under persecuting emperors, whether heretics or pagans, and as recently happened in Africa. [Note: [Col. 0957D] The Vandal persecution, which raged under Huneric, did not abate even in the early years of Gundobad, as is evident from Procopius, On the Vandal War, Book I. See Cardinal Noris, History of Pelagianism, Book II. SCIPIO MAFFEI.] [Col. 0957C] What then? Did they not suffer the greatest force from those men? And for that very reason they conquered by suffering force, not by yielding to violence. Were they not rightly condemned by Catholics and Christians under those persecutors who denied Christ or passed over into heresy? Was it an excuse that, having suffered force, they were unable to persevere?

“Why, then,” you ask, “were remedies for the lapsed provided?” Very well: I shall therefore receive him, if you wish, practicing the penitence of the lapsed throughout his whole life and receiving it at the end; as it is written that provision was made for the lapsed, let us recall him to the Church according to the formula of that decree. [Note: [Col. 0957D] What was established concerning the lapsed in Africa, or concerning those rebaptized, at the Roman council is found in Felix’s seventh letter: “If they repent, it is fitting that they should lie in penitence until the day of their death.” SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

But now, if the healing of the whole Church is brought into consideration, it will be of such importance—for this belongs to the pontiff of the Apostolic See, and the universal need for healing seems to demand it—that Acacius’s person may be restored to priestly honor. By this very fact he shows that he did not succumb willingly and that he possessed a Catholic mind, while he properly applies himself to the work of healing. But if he wishes to do this and cannot, why does he oppress the others through the imperial person? If the emperor, as is reported, obeys Acacius, he can do so; if the emperor does not obey him, although he ought, and ought still, to deal with him firmly and manfully, then by this very fact he admits that he is succumbing against the Catholic truth.

Therefore it is clear that, in the present state of affairs, I must not enter into communion with him. For if he is being pressed and cannot come to his own aid, I ought not already to become an accomplice in his oppression and transgression. Rather, because by God’s gift I am free, I preserve myself at least unharmed, so that, if he can do so now, or when God commands it, there may be someone able, for the sake of the integrity of communion and faith, to assist those who have lost the integrity of communion and faith. Otherwise, if we all lose it—God forbid—from where will it later be restored? Especially if, God never allowing it, it should be violated at the height of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0958A]

Therefore, if Acacius is enduring human force so that he may not correct his errors, I have a greater necessity—the fear of God and the preservation of Catholic communion and faith—not to become, in any manner or under any condition, an associate of those placed in error, but to keep myself entirely free from their contagion. For if he has the excuse of force, I, by the Lord’s favor, who am secure, can no longer have even that excuse, since, by the Lord’s favor, I am not oppressed by force, as has been said.

Let these matters be left to divine judgment until God himself, as we have very often experienced, restores freedom to Catholic communion and the Christian faith. Then we shall deal with those who are in his error. For Acacius’s person cannot be released without the healing of the whole Church, through whose wound the whole Church has been wounded. [Col. 0958C]

“But even then,” he says, “Acacius was in communion with you, when the heretic Timothy, or this Peter, held the Church of Alexandria under the tyrant Basiliscus.”

You speak truly, but at that time Acacius was by no means in communion with them and remained in my communion. Hence, if Acacius is suffering force now, he ought to show himself such as he showed himself under Basiliscus, the heretical tyrant and his persecutor.

“But now,” you say, “the welfare of the state is at stake.”

The priest ought rather to have argued that the public welfare required divine communion and faith to be preserved intact. Is the overthrow of religion useful to the state, while the integrity of religion is not useful to the state? I do not know whether those who make such claims belong to the same religion, or whether people of the same religion ought to make such claims. [Note: [Col. 0958D] The sentence is incomplete, and the context itself testifies to a lacuna and dislocation. Perhaps it read: “It could be tolerated if he wished some one of his own …,” etc. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Perhaps he wished one of his own men and faithful to remain as priest, with John excluded, provided that he allowed a Catholic bishop of our communion to preside over places suspected of belonging to our communion. [Col. 0958D] Does this matter not plainly make John’s case the better, since, when he is excluded and a heretic substituted, it is shown that this was not earned by the person himself, but that the destruction of the Catholic faith is being brought about?

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Here begins the clearing of that clause of his, “and never to be released from the bonds of anathema,” about which we spoke in the preface. Moreover, Felix’s mind, his policy, and his inclination toward reconciliation are also revealed in Letter 15: “Therefore, a thing which must be said not without dread of divine judgment, even though we wished it, if he had asked us, he was not permitted to be absolved”; and in Letter 13: “even though we were striving.” In Letter 6, which contains the clause mentioned above, where it reads respondere dissidens, it should perhaps read diffidens; and where it reads “and Humerius, then removed from the diaconate,” the manuscript has “and deservedly removed from the diaconate,” with “deprived” and “promoted” following. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

We did not pronounce sentence against Acacius because he is a human being, or because he is called Acacius, as could be said of any heretic; rather, we did so because he is a treacherous person. Therefore, what was punished in him by the imposition of a sentence was his evil deed. If this treachery, this evil deed, departs, that person against whom I seemed to have issued an irrevocable sentence will no longer exist. The man and Acacius will remain—the one whom the sentence does not condemn insofar as he is a human being and is reckoned by the name of man, but insofar as he is treacherous and an evildoer.

To the one against whom my sentence is irrevocable, this sentence of mine is now irrevocable only while that person remains in him. Once the one against whom it was imposed has been removed, the sentence will have no place at all. For he will be another person from the one against whom the sentence was imposed, once he begins not to be what he was, or not to be the one against whom the sentence was imposed. But when he begins to be what he was not, or when this alone begins to be true of him, although the sentence was not imposed against that state, there will be nowhere at all for the sentence issued to stand.

For as long as he remains the one against whom the sentence was imposed, that sentence is truly irrevocable, together with the one against whom it was irrevocably imposed. But when he is no longer that person, even if the sentence does not remain in him, it will undoubtedly pass away with that evil deed against which it was irrevocably imposed. In this person, therefore, it will be dissolvable—or rather, it will not belong to one against whom it was not imposed; rather, it will be foreign and alien to the one against whom it is not established to have been imposed. For in Acacius it was the evil deed and the treachery that received that irrevocable sentence, not the fact that he is a man or is called Acacius. Once the evil deed is removed from him, the sentence itself is removed with all its force and cause.

[Note: [Col. 0959C] He confirms this with several examples drawn from Holy Scripture, showing that the Bible often pronounces matters as though they were definitively concluded, so that all hope seemed entirely cut off, and nevertheless afterward opens an avenue to repentance and, through repentance, to grace. But at this point the manuscripts contain dark complications and an inextricable [Col. 0959D] error. After the words “the sentence having been removed,” there followed abruptly: “lest at any time,” he says, etc. The passage beginning “But in the Scriptures,” which strengthens the structure and prepares the way for the testimonies that follow, lay after all those passages uselessly and out of place.
