The passage beginning “The three days, and Nineveh,” through the word “consequently,” I found inserted three pages after the sentence, where it could not belong, and mixed in among other material. Since the whole matter was so confused and entangled, the passages seemed plainly incurable, all composed of words heaped together at random. Nevertheless, I think I have restored both passages with no little success, doing only this: returning each item to its proper place. I made no emendation except that, where the codex reads “Did they not, with him inspiring, come from the same Jews,” I substituted “Did they not, with God inspiring, come from the same Jews?” This may serve as evidence of how miserably disfigured and torn apart many monuments of antiquity have reached our hands—whether the confusion arose from leaves that had been separated, torn out, and scattered, which scribes later copied; or from the fact that, through negligence, they sometimes omitted passages as they flowed along, and afterward, noticing them, did not hesitate to place them at the point they had then reached, as though it were enough that they should not be missing.

As for the meaning of what Felix presents here, everything becomes clear both from the contexts of the biblical passages from which these words were extracted and from the similar reasoning that we can follow in the treatise On the Bond of Anathema, beginning with: “Thus Tyre and Berytus,” etc. There too the meaning of Holy Scripture is opened and illuminated: “lest they turn,” that is, lest they be saved by their own works, in which they certainly trusted, etc.; “and I heal them,” namely, lest saving grace be granted to them as though it came through their own ability and merits, etc.

At the passage “The three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” the author follows the Greek version, which Symmachus and Theodotion corrected from the Hebrew text. Saint Prosper follows the same version, or perhaps the author of the poem On Providence. See Saint Augustine, City of God, Book XVIII, chapter 44. In “seeing, they saw,” etc., he is referring to the sense of the eighth and thirty-first verses of Romans, chapter II, although he changes the wording. Likewise, the passage of Isaiah VI, 10: “lest they perhaps see with their eyes and hear with their ears,” which in the ancient version was rendered: “and seeing, let them not see; and hearing, let them not hear,” etc., as I learn from the treatise On the Bond of Anathema, where that verse is cited. The phrase “if by imperial force” returns to what was said several times above. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

But in the Scriptures we find an interminable sentence imposed upon many sinners, yet remitted to those who depart from sin; and some are said to be killed and brought to life—since in them what they were is killed, and they begin to be what they were not—or to be uprooted and planted, and similar things: “In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III, 4); likewise, in the case of King Hezekiah, fifteen years were added to his life after death had been announced; likewise, concerning branches that were broken off and grafted in; and concerning those same branches, that if they do not remain in unbelief, they will obtain mercy.

“Lest at any time,” he says, “they should turn and I should heal them.” This was said of those who had a hardened heart and, seeing, did not see, and hearing, did not hear. Did they not, with God inspiring, come from the same Jews of whom it was said, “Seeing, they saw; hearing, they heard; and they believed with the heart”—such as the apostles and so many thousands, whom the Apostle testifies to have been preserved as a remnant? He treats this meaning in this way when he says: “For I also am an Israelite” (Rom. XI, 7).

If Acacius is pressed by imperial force to do the things he is doing, he himself first professes that the emperor is acting against the Catholic faith and therefore is not Catholic. There is no reason, then, for him to persuade us to say what he himself produces, or what he himself attests. Further, by claiming that he is suffering force, he declares that what he is doing is evil and demonstrates that he is acting against the Catholic faith. Why, then, does he urge and ask me to become an accomplice in an action which he admits to be perverse?

But if he contends that it is not evil, it remains that he should no longer persuade us that he is suffering force from the emperor, since he voluntarily does what he affirms to be good. For when he says that what he is doing is good, he undoubtedly indicates that he is doing it voluntarily, as something he considers good. Acacius therefore does not do this under compulsion, as something evil that he does unwillingly, but voluntarily, as something good. For if he is compelled, he is certainly unwilling; if unwilling, it is certainly evil. Therefore he does it not voluntarily as something good, but unwillingly as something evil. If he is not unwilling to do it as something evil, it follows that he does it voluntarily as something good. Thus, with zeal, desire, will, and his own judgment—not under compulsion—he acts; therefore he does not suffer force, but sins voluntarily.

“But by your obstinacy,” you say, “you are bringing the cause of the whole Church into danger.”

If Catholic faith and communion are preserved, does religion come into danger, or is religion endangered? And if—God forbid—Catholic faith and communion are violated, is religion not brought into danger, or does religion remain safe? Let no Catholic and son of the apostolic faith say this.

“But by this obstinacy you diminish the dignity of the Apostolic See.”

If Catholic faith and communion are preserved, is the dignity of the Apostolic See diminished? If they are violated, does the dignity of the Apostolic See remain? Let no Christian and Catholic utter this.

If Catholic faith and communion are harmed, is the state helped? And if they are safe, is the state harmed? Let no Christian and Catholic profess this.

If Catholic faith and communion are preserved, is the emperor harmed? And when they are violated, is the emperor not harmed? Let no Christian and Catholic emperor say this, nor let any Catholic Christian say that it ought to be done: namely, that the Catholic faith and communion ought to be harmed so that the emperor may not be harmed, because, if Catholic faith and communion are preserved, the emperor would be harmed.

We love the emperor so much that we wish him to do what is for his own salvation, what is for his soul and conscience. [Col. 0961B]

Let any offense against Catholic bishops, if it is substantiated, be forgiven; it is for him to do what he knows benefits his conscience, his soul, and his salvation. If he does not wish to do what is useful in these matters, let him see to it himself. We are acquitted both before God and before men. For if it is fitting that bishops intercede with God even on behalf of criminals, how much more fitting is it that bishops intercede with God on behalf of priests? If he himself intercedes for sacrilegious persons, how much more fitting is it that we intercede for those who, as he says, have injured him.

[Note: [Col. 0961C] The offenses attributed to the Catholic bishops are explained in the letter to the bishops of Dardania. But suppose that Calendion removed the emperor’s name; let John be accused of having lied to the emperor. The interrogative mark that follows in the edition of Labbe at this point reverses the meaning. The holy pontiff does not deny, but affirms, that a new investigation ought to have been instituted because of new circumstances. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Why do you wish to exaggerate Acacius’s treachery and confirm his condemnation, so that I may appear increasingly inconsistent and opposed to my own judgment? If—God forbid—I had become an accomplice in evil, I would now need a remedy, not provide one; and the See of blessed Peter—God forbid that this should happen—would seek a remedy elsewhere, not itself supply one.

Why are you indignant that we pronounced sentence against Acacius? Unless we had done so, we could in no way have separated Catholic communion from the heretical and condemned communion with which he had here mingled, nor protected and preserved it inviolate.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] He takes up what he had begun to touch upon shortly before in the words “Why do you wish to exaggerate,” etc.; but he immediately abandoned it through the familiar dislocation of the text when certain intervening passages were inserted. The Greeks were pressing for the absolution of the legates Vitalis and Misenus as well. Felix replies that their absolution cannot be decreed without renewing Acacius’s condemnation, and he shows that their requests contradict one another. For if Acacius, once condemned, is considered seriously condemned, will he not be seriously condemned after being condemned twice? Here it is plainly evident—and it will become even clearer below—that the distinguished Henri Valois was unquestionably mistaken when, in his observations on Evagrius, Book II, he tried to prove that Acacius had been condemned by two synods; the distinguished Pagi likewise praises him and considers Acacius twice condemned (under the years 484 and 485). Their arguments rest chiefly on two foundations. One is the synodical letter to the Eastern clergy and monks, which certainly contains several incongruities and does not appear in our codex among the documents dealing with the principal points of Acacius’s case; and, if carefully examined, it does not present any renewed condemnation of Acacius. The other is taken from the words in the letter to Vetranio, “he was expelled by repeated excommunication.” These words, however, are very easily explained. After Felix had said that the Eutychians had been condemned by the Council of Chalcedon, and consequently Acacius, he adds: “Therefore the aforesaid Acacius was deservedly expelled by repeated excommunication from the Apostolic See, which, as executor, certainly did not fail at that time to uphold the repeatedly mentioned Council of Chalcedon, approved for the Catholic faith.” At Rome, therefore, the sentence of Chalcedon was repeated. In the words that follow, read reddamur [“let us be restored”] in place of reddamus [“let us restore”], and add nunc [“now”] to the marginal note in the Councils; that particle is of considerable importance here. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

How, then, do you compel us, by a constitution repeated in a certain sense, to confirm and duplicate—along with an exaggeration of Acacius’s treachery—the undoubtedly just sentence?

Will Misenus and Vitalis be able to be received unless they pronounce anathema against Peter of Alexandria and all who entered or enter into communion with him after the anathema? They will therefore, by our definition, condemn Acacius again. How, then, do you wish to absolve him? Does it seem serious that Acacius was condemned once, but not serious that he was condemned twice? Or do you wish it to appear or be said, whether by you or by us, that the Apostolic See was deceived?

[Note: [Col. 0962D] I suspect that these words have been wrongly inserted, since they concern another matter. Certain Eastern bishops, apparently prompted by the supreme Pontiff, seem to have admonished Acacius by letter. Where the text reads “neither to you nor to me,” the manuscript has “neither to you nor to the king.” I can find no non-absurd interpretation capable of preserving that reading. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Behold, we asked you; behold, you wrote; behold, he did not deign to reply either to you or to me. You see the obstinate ruin of perversity. Ought you not, both for the sake of religion and because of the injury done to you, to be united with us?

“Tell us,” they say, “whether you intend to absolve Vitalis and Misenus or not.”

We reply and ask you in turn whether you wish them to be absolved with faith, Catholic communion, and reverence for the Apostolic See intact, or not. If you do not wish this, we shall not save them in this manner or by such a procedure.

“But you promised,” they say.

What I promised is recorded; I am now striving to fulfill it. For I promised to deliberate how they might justly appear to be absolved; this too I now promise without hesitation.

Know, then, that our deliberation has reached this conclusion: we cannot absolve these men unless our sentence seems to have been justly relaxed before its appointed time; unless we remove from them the burden of treachery and make them more amenable to healing; and unless it is worthy to anticipate our sentence against them, once we have found them guilty of a lesser fault. We may say that they have been sufficiently corrected by the very fact that they sinned through some negligence of their own and have, up to this point, been removed from sacred communion.

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Since his intention is to join the absolution of the legates to the peace of the universal Church, the holy pontiff declares that he will not separate or advance their sentence in any other way than if some just reason for this anticipation should appear, based upon the proven lesser gravity of their offense. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

But if, in order to release them, we say that they were deceived and misled, it follows that, to the extent that we lighten their burden, we oppress Acacius. For you will no longer wish to say anything else, nor may we judge anything else, than that he is the author of the entire treachery—if indeed the records show that this is what their confession stated in the synod.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Apparently the synod at which the author of the Breviary completed his work. In it the legates had exposed Acacius as the author of all the evils. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Therefore, if by repeated assertions, a reiterated profession, a recent investigation, and a decree we confirm as just the sentence pronounced against Acacius, with the entire treachery duly magnified, you must find how afterward he can be absolved—the man whom by a repeated declaration we condemn, so to speak.

How, I ask, are we attempting to absolve him when we bind him with all the bonds of treachery, and when we bury beneath the entire weight of condemnation the man whom we strive to raise up? Therefore either let these men wait to be freed through the healing of the whole Church, according to the sentence; or swear to us that nothing concerning Acacius’s absolution will ever be requested.

Why do you wish him to be absolved in such a way that you expose in every respect both our conscience and our reputation? Our conscience, if I absolve one who has himself professed to be the author of the entire betrayal; our reputation, because the sentence would thereby be entirely changed.

Nor can it be said that, when the sentence was issued against these men as the authors of the evil deed until a fixed time, it was withdrawn from them as though they were innocent, while the same reasoning should be applied to Acacius until the time prescribed for them, because he is the author of all the evil. For I said that my sentence against Acacius, as the author, would be irrevocable and would not be relaxed at a fixed time. If I confirm it again, it will remain according to the force of its definition, so that he cannot be absolved. For it was not said there, “until that time”; it was said that he was never to be released.

“But although you have already said this,” you reply, “you are now attempting to absolve him.”

It is enough to provide for the release of a sentence once pronounced. Why do you wish me to repeat it by my decree? If you are indignant that it was pronounced once, why do you insist on doubling it? If it seems difficult to absolve him from a sentence pronounced once, what shall we do with a duplicated sentence? Perhaps, in the case of a sentence pronounced once, I may discuss its dissolution and discover that I understood something less than what was said. But once I have confirmed it by a repeated declaration, what remedy do you wish me to have—especially if I demonstrate that I confirm it even at the very time when I am striving to absolve him?

“But the emperor used force against Acacius.”

I shall not say this, because it is not true, and I cannot openly accuse the emperor at all. Certainly, you be the authors of this accusation.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] After this the codex continues: “If the one who is proved to have sinned against God is thought to be absolved, how much more ought the one who is said to have sinned against a man to be absolved?” This sentence is plainly intrusive and belongs to the passage where John Talaia is excused. I have removed it so that the context would not become still more entangled. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

[Note: [Col. 0964D] So too in the Roman council under Gelasius, when Misenus was absolved. It was said that these men would remain suspended until, with God as author and through the efforts of Catholic princes or the Christian people, etc. By the words “through their obstinacy,” and below “they were made obstinate,” certain people seem to be indicated who had fallen into error through the legates’ mistake; other material must have preceded concerning them, but it is not extant. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Through what was said in the tenor of the sentence issued—namely, that the matter was to be healed with the assistance of the Christian prince or the people—this result comes less from their obstinacy. If we wish to deal with the case of Misenus and Vitalis, through whose communion and agreement those men were made obstinate, we both burden these men whom we think should be absolved and, by magnifying their sin, make our sentence irrevocable from the appointed time.

[Col. 0964B] Their reception must therefore be handled in such a way that our conscience and the reputation of those chiefly concerned may be secured by the revocation of their sentence, and that we may show that we justly revoked or remitted it before the appointed time. We must also console those who persevere in the Catholic faith by demonstrating, concerning communion with these men, that they did not then enter into communion at our command, nor give their consent to their communion, and that we remain steadfast with them in the Catholic faith.

For this reason they too strive to remain steadfast with us. But if they hear that the sentence against these men has been relaxed before the appointed time without any appearance of justice, they will believe that they entered into communion by our will. They will perhaps judge that what we seemed to suspend was merely a pretense, a shadow of an excuse, and that we are rightly transgressors. Then either they will fail and surrender themselves to the communion of those men, or they will justly condemn us as violators of an alien communion or of Catholic communion.

How, then, are these matters to be healed? A just method must be sought. There is no other than this: the men whom we wish to absolve before the appointed time must be relieved and excused, and our remission must appear just. This can happen if the entire transgression is transferred to Acacius. The very men who persevere in the Catholic faith eagerly and ardently await this, for they rage more fiercely against him than against these men; they will consider it of great importance that these men be released, provided that they hear every evil deed transferred to him as the author of the treachery.

Once this has happened, it follows without doubt that the punishment, that is, the condemnation, inflicted upon him for these matters will appear just. That condemnation is shown, by the terms in which it stands, to be irrevocable. Thus Acacius’s person becomes beyond remedy through the exaggeration of the crime and the agreement concerning vengeance. For if Acacius’s person is freed through the healing of the whole Church, [Col. 0965A] these men too will in every respect be absolved according to our sentence.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Supply “of absolution.” We clearly see Felix’s excellent intention, moved neither by hatred of Acacius nor by any other affection, since he insists here that Acacius’s absolution be treated first. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Since, as we said above, this course cannot be brought to completion because neither the emperor nor the people lend their assistance, it can only burden one side or the other rather than resolve the matter. Therefore a remedy must be provided in the affairs by this one means alone: first, Acacius must be dealt with for absolution, with the health of the whole Church alone in view, and then these men must be released in due order.

But if Acacius absolutely refuses to be absolved, the burden imposed upon him will lighten the case of these men. All the more because Acacius is shown to have rejected what was offered to him, our sentence will be excused—both the absolution of these men granted before the appointed time and the condemnation of Acacius, confirmed with an exaggeration of his crime.

For this reason those who remain in the East persevere in the Catholic faith: they see that I defend it and are encouraged by me. Otherwise either they too will fall because of me, or, if I should fall—God forbid—they will persevere and justly condemn me before God and men. They did not abandon me even when placed under persecution; shall I abandon them without persecution? What shall I say about this to God, what to men?

Can I say to them: “I could not have confirmed the condemnation of Acacius in any other way than by absolving Vitalis and Misenus through the exaggeration of his sin”? But if afterward I am compelled to absolve Acacius, once his evil has been magnified, what account or defense shall I render to him?

“But if the whole Church is healed through Acacius,” you say, “is the absolution of one man worth so much? Is the absolution of one man worth so much at any time, whenever it may occur?”

It concerns my conscience, and the charge of levity against me is at stake. For if the Church is healed through Acacius, this very fact teaches that the Church, which could be healed through him—that is, through his correction—also appears to have been wounded through him, since it could have remained unwounded had he not sinned.

“But if you cast the burden of these men upon Acacius,” you say, “you rightly absolve them; and when Acacius likewise acts so that the Church may be healed, you will fittingly absolve Acacius.”

If this is the hope, why do you compel me to press him beneath the weight of condemnation, whom you testify can or ought to be absolved? Granted that these men can be absolved through Acacius’s burden: why do you wish me to burden him whom I am striving to absolve? “Because otherwise,” you say, “these men cannot be helped.” But by this you either wish him to be crushed, or you expose me.

“But you diminish your privileges by this obstinacy.”

[Note: [Col. 0965D] These words indicate that the Easterners also brought forward this argument to overcome the pontiff: that their own cause was at stake; for once Acacius and his followers were cut off from his communion, his jurisdiction would be greatly diminished and confined within narrower limits. From this it seems confirmed that, even in that age, when the Church’s government remained uncorrupted, more learned men even among the heterodox acknowledged that the Roman bishop presided over the Christian world not merely by dignity but by right and power. Felix himself certainly spoke of the Apostolic See to which Flavita had sent legates in these terms: “through which, by Christ’s gift, the dignity of all priests is made solid.” The holy pontiff shows, however, in Letter 13, that these privileges must be defended only insofar as they serve the Christian faith. It is indeed in the interest of the Christian state that it should have a head, since the greater part of ecclesiastical government has been gathered into one, so that, once a head has been established, the occasion for schism may be removed, as Saint Jerome taught (Against Jovinian, Book I, chapter 14). Near the end of the letter, in place of “therefore concerning the absolution,” etc., I think one should read: “Therefore the obligation of the just sentence must be absolved.” SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

Then, lest we have less authority and become heretics, and lest we lose the privileges of ecclesiastical power, shall we lose religion itself? Lest the dignity of the Apostolic See be diminished among the few, shall it err among the many?

I do not know whether anyone would say that falsehood ought to be followed with the majority rather than truth preserved and defended with the few. Will falsehood therefore not be falsehood because it is held by a multitude? Will truth therefore not be truth because it is possessed by a few?

Since truth consists not in the multitude but in whatever part or portion of itself it may possess, while religion is fixed nowhere except in truth, and its privileges consist nowhere except where religion itself is firm: will truth, if it is found among the few, not be truth, and falsehood, if it is found among the many, not be falsehood?

Falsehood is a greater error when it spreads among many; truth suffers no loss when it is found in a small number, because truth remains fixed in whatever portion of itself it possesses. Just as a multitude does not make falsehood cease to be falsehood, so a small number does not make truth cease to be truth.

There are countless examples showing that, while falsehood raged among the many, truth remained among the few. [Col. 0966B]

“But we abhor this,” you say.

What, then, shall we do? Shall we refuse to hold truth among the few and err among the many?

“God forbid,” you say.

Let us therefore reject falsehood even with the many, provided that we hold truth even among the very few. Did not the Church stand among the Apostles while the whole world held falsehood, just as truth commanded? Did not the Church remain among the seven thousand Israelites while the whole people had gone astray? And if we review everything, we find countless examples. Is it not written that narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, while broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matt. VII, 13–14)?

“But they say,” you will reply, “that they hold what is more correct.”

In the meantime, what they admit they hold will already be false. For if they hold it better, they hold something else; and it follows that they must prove that they hold it better than we do.

If they hold it better, let them keep away from me, who hold it badly. The wish to be corrected in faith and to follow what is better ought to arise from the will, not from force.

I am not troublesome to him; why is he troublesome to me? I do not ask him to correct me. Why does he thrust himself upon one who does not ask, why does he intrude upon one who is unwilling?

If he thinks that my opinion has no value, let him disregard it. Why does he so insist on being absolved? If he asks to be absolved and does not doubt that the sentence has some force, he confirms that it is a just condemnation and does not deny that he is held bound by it.

Let him therefore confess the error against which the sentence was imposed; let him lay aside the error, and the sentence is void. If it is unjust, he ought no more to be concerned about it, since before God and his Church no one can be burdened by an unjust sentence.

Thus, let him not desire to be absolved from a sentence by which he plainly sees that he is in no way bound. But if he judges himself bound by it and asks to be absolved, he certainly does not claim that it is unjust—the sentence that could bind him—and he asks to be absolved from it because it could bind him only if it were just.

But if it is just, it can be recognized as just only when the error has been condemned. Therefore, to dissolve the obligation of a just sentence, let him confess the error; let him lay aside the error by which he—
A just judgment holds him bound; once that is removed, the basis of the obligation is dissolved.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] In the catalogue of the bishops who assembled at Carthage by order of King Huneric, Sacconius of Uzalis is listed among the foremost, from the proconsular province. I think this letter was addressed to him, extracted from the same manuscript, as was the following one. Whether, however, “Succonius” should be read, as it appears here, or “Sacconius,” as in the printed editions, others may judge. Of the 484 African bishops then compelled to assemble, we now learn that he was among the twenty-eight who withdrew by flight. But since that flight occurred in 484, and since the letter appears to have been written not long afterward, I believe it should be attributed to Felix, who occupied the see until 492, although it is inscribed under the name of Gelasius. Felix also cited the passage from Jeremiah, “Who will give water to my head,” etc., in Letter 3 to Peter, bishop of Antioch. Nevertheless, I spoke with some hesitation [Col. 0968D], since it does not seem wholly implausible that it could have been composed by Gelasius before the Catholic bishops were restored: for Gundobad’s actions remain obscure down to that restoration, Victor of Vita’s History not proceeding beyond Huneric, while Procopius and Isidore contradict one another. Thus it is not inconsistent with probability that Succonius endured exile until the time of Gelasius. Here the author calls the Arians raging in Africa and the Eutychians in the East the two horns of Antichrist; by my reckoning, this author should be considered Felix. Perhaps Succonius imprudently communicated at Constantinople with Acacius. In the summary it is said, “so that he may correct”; likewise in the Roman council of the same period: even if he perhaps did correct them, this use of the verb occurs elsewhere too. SCIPIO MAFFEI.]

## The Same Felix’s Letter, Prefixed in the Same Manuscript under This Title

*A letter of Pope Gelasius to Succonius, an African bishop residing at Constantinople, who, fleeing the persecution of the Arians in Africa to Constantinople, is charged with having fallen into violation of the Council of Chalcedon by communicating imprudently: so that he may correct himself.*

Although widespread opinion spoke of your steadfastness in Christ and your fervent teaching, it cannot be expressed how greatly we rejoiced in the Lord that divine grace had prepared such an outstanding vessel, especially useful in time of war; and, embracing you with all our prayers and accompanying you in the whole affection of our heart as though you were standing close before us, we attended you in your absence. But, suddenly struck by a grievous report, we confess that, our minds thrown into confusion, we collapsed; and for a long time we hesitated whether to send your Charity a letter concerning these matters, for grief prevented speech, while affection for Christ did not permit silence.

While we were wavering amid these circumstances, divine knowledge prevailed—through which, throughout the entire body of Scripture, we are fully taught to admonish freely those who have been overtaken by some stealthy temptation, with charity. First, rumor brought word that your Beloved had communicated in the regions of the East with the adversary of truth [Col. 0967C]; then the report of many, which could not be dismissed, made the matter clear. Lest you accuse us of having believed rashly—if what we wish is false—forgive the pious concern we feel for you; but if it is true, I ask you patiently to accept the salutary wounds inflicted by friends who rebuke you, since you have undergone the destructive kisses of friends [read: enemies] who flatter you.

Could you, most loving and beloved one, have accepted associations opposed to the Catholic rule? Could such an enormous sin have taken effect in you, when it is not believed that it could even have crept into your thoughts? Could you have chosen to endure the pleasure of the present time rather than to suffer with the people of God? The mind is stunned, the wounded spirit succumbs, grieving hearts fail, and yet no lamentation is found equal to so great a sorrow.

Are you not the one who, scorning the threats of kings and despising the savage laws of raging barbarians, laid aside at once your homeland, your possessions, and the privileges of priestly honor [Col. 0967D] [Col. 0968A], so that you might deserve to receive them eternally in Christ? What, then, are we doing now? You have discolored your glory, violated your confession, intercepted your victory; and the greater the confidence and favor in your name that had been growing at the Apostolic See, the more grievous the present confusion.

Had you not perceived that Antichrist, by displaying two horns, was striving at one and the same time to undo Jesus no less in the East than in Africa? For the former confess God in such a way that he is not God, while the latter preach a human being in such a way that they strive to nullify the human being. Amid these deadly dangers, what benefit is there in escaping a precipice if one withdraws into an abyss? Did it not come before your eyes that not only those who commit such acts, but also those who consent to their perpetrators, are judged to the same condemnation?

Woe if this crime remained hidden from your learning [Col. 0968B]! Woe still more if it did not remain hidden, and yet was carried out! For if nothing else, this alone ought to have been sufficient for your Beloved to take precautions: that you should not mingle with the communion of those whom you knew blessed Peter had denied his communion.

But when we see you filled with the Scriptures and endowed with Catholic instruction, we have no way out to such consolation, since we perceive that, knowingly, you sought alliances with the lost. Who, then, will give water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes (Jeremiah 9:1)? Now indeed there has been departure from the companionship of one’s homeland; now true exile is felt. The former is for the sake of salvation; this is for ruin.

Nor do we cast all these things upon you alone without reason. For, according to the Apostle, just as all the members rejoice with the glory of any one member [Col. 0968C], so, when any part of the body is convulsed, the whole structure suffers. For our part, out of the affection we owe you, we have considered it necessary to disclose to you the anguish of our inmost being. It will be for your conscience to determine how you do not refuse to free yourself from these snares.

For us, in either event, the fruit will not be empty: either we shall rejoice in the restoration of your salvation and reputation, which we implore with all our desires; or, if—God forbid—you despise our letters, we shall at least appear not to have failed to assist a brother.

## Here Begins the Letter of Blessed Pope Gelasius to Natalis the Abbot

Gelasius, bishop, to his most beloved son Natalis, abbot.

Although, in accordance with the divinely instituted governance of blessed Peter the Apostle, by which the vicars of his see, etc.

(This letter may be read among the works of Gelasius.)

# LETTER XII. OF POPE FELIX III TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

After praising his zeal in the ordination of the new bishop, he urges him to agree with the Roman Church in condemning the names of Acacius and Peter, concerning which the envoys of the clergy replied that they had received no instruction.

[Col. 0969A]

Felix to the Emperor Zeno.

I confess that the human mind is not sufficient to offer worthy thanks to our God for the fact that divine mercy has established such concern for religion in the heart of Your Piety that you judge it deserving both to be preferred to all affairs and to be upheld by the stability of the state—an assessment as truly Christian as it is august—for in truth the whole order of things subsists through heavenly favor.

I recognize that everything expressed in your tranquil discourse concerning reverence for divine worship has proceeded from this marvelous devotion of Your Clemency [Col. 0969B]. In particular, desiring to strengthen the unity of the Catholic faith and to reinforce the peace of the Churches with the greatest care, you sought to place over the Constantinopolitans a bishop who, with heavenly grace attending him, would shine in uprightness of character and excel above all in devotion to orthodox truth.

Therefore, excellent prince, I receive great joy from both matters: first, because the Church, with God as its maker, has received in the soul of Your Serenity—just as it has received you at the summit of the world—an outstanding son; and second, because I rejoice that the very man whose episcopate you glory in, while tracing the beginning of his dignity back to the See of blessed Peter the Apostle, has already given evidence of his own moderation.

Here your magnanimity likewise shines forth, since you desire the cause of the Church to be settled, as divinely instituted, by the ordination of bishops; and since the man who is said to have been advanced to the priestly office wishes to be supported from the source whence, with Christ’s will, the grace of all bishops flows in fullness.

The intention of his letter also refreshes me. As befits one striving to please Christ, it did not remain silent about blessed Peter, the chief of the Apostles, and the rock of faith (Matthew 16); it wisely set forth that the keys of the heavenly mysteries had been entrusted to him; and, in order that it might have with us an assent agreeing in orthodox faith, by which unity would be increased, it sought this agreement.

When these professions and wishes of his had been disclosed by extensive reading, and when I saw that my sons, the monks of holy purpose, had likewise arrived, I believed that all the difficulties which had initially obstructed us had been removed by this arrangement [Col. 0969C]. For this reason, when the clergy arrived, persons were associated with them—contrary to custom—who appeared not to communicate with Peter or Acacius, so that, once the names of those through whom scandal had come upon the Churches had been set aside, sincere charity might thereafter arise.

After duly considering these matters, nothing remained for me, in my joy, except to grant the communion of the Apostolic See to those who had been sent. But when I carefully admonished them, for the sake of the Catholic faith, that those who received this communion should withdraw from association with the condemned, they declared that no such instruction had been given to them. I confess that, disturbed by this difference in the facts, I remained anxious and perplexed, since the letter and the actual circumstances indicated one thing, while the statement of the persons mentioned contained another [Col. 0969D].

Desiring to enter into pure concord with the man who is said to have been made bishop, I hastened to bring the matter to the attention of Your Glory, so that you might not allow anything to remain from which disagreement could again arise.

Since it is established that, by the Council of Chalcedon—which Your Clemency has long declared in writing that you venerate—Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned; and since Timothy and Peter are shown by many documents from those regions to have been their followers; and since Acacius followed their communion, although it was forbidden, even though in his own letters he had called them heretics and condemned them: they are convicted of being bound by the sentence of that council and of having deservedly fallen under the punishment of those whose association they chose. For, as with all other heresies, once a synod has been held, all followers of any rejected error are consequently involved in its condemnation [Col. 0970A].

I therefore ask you, most glorious prince, that we not be judged to be fostering in the successors what is manifestly shown to have been condemned in the founders; and that no one suppose Peter to have received a legitimate purification when the Apostolic See, which bound him, did not absolve him according to the custom of the ancients.

For your Christian mind knows, venerable emperor, that heavenly dispensation has granted the bishops, each in his proper order, the power to release the sins of mortals according to conscience. Yet this Peter, if he had truly been received, ought to have obtained pardon, not honor; for, having received from condemned heretics the false name of priesthood, he could not preside over the Catholic Church.

These things I, most reverent prince, as the imperfect vicar of blessed Peter, do not extort by the authority of apostolic power [Col. 0970C], but faithfully implore as an anxious father, desiring that the salvation and prosperity of my most merciful son may endure.

Behold, we desire, wish, and seek that the Church of Constantinople remain joined to us, as always. I beg that it be stripped away from those who are not ours, and we likewise wish it to be with us.

You graciously hear in public the petitions of barbarian nations for the peace of the earthly kingdom, venerable emperor. How much more nobly, I ask, will you, once appeased, admit the prayers of the Apostolic See for the tranquility of sacred affairs?

For this is expedient: if each Rome is now called by the pledge of mutual kinship, let there be one faith in both Romes—that faith of the Romans which blessed Paul the Apostle testifies was proclaimed throughout the whole world (Romans 1:8), just as it flourished among our ancestors without distinction [Col. 0970D]. Let what agrees in origin and name not be divided in religion, through which even things that differ are joined together.

Do you suppose, venerable emperor, that I do not pour out these words with tears and, as though present, throw myself at the feet of Your Piety? Nor am I ashamed to bow before imperial offices in such a cause, since the Apostle says that he became the refuse of all (1 Corinthians 4:13).

I kept silent about these matters for a long time, lest, when others were making contrary suggestions, my letters should instead provoke irreverence. But now that the opportunity has been granted, I make known how strongly the affection of Your Piety lives in my heart: I desire that the success of the power divinely entrusted to you may stand firm through divine favor.

Nor, venerable son, reject one who supplicates you, nor wish to disregard my person. For in me, however imperfect a vicar, blessed Peter the Apostle—and in him Christ himself, who does not permit his Church to be torn apart—pleads with you [Col. 0971A].

Far be it from your Christian mind either to be able or to deem it right to prefer anyone to the one whom you desire to have entreated for you with all your prayers. Especially since your deeds—those you performed and continue to perform after tyranny was destroyed for the sake of the Catholic faith—are so great and of such a kind that we recognize in full the proofs of your conscience before God.

If something has perhaps been omitted in these matters, it concerns only the poison of the perfidious Acacius, who, while striving to increase himself by illicit additions, ceased to inform you, occupied as you were with public affairs, of what agreed with true religion. For how could Your Piety not have considered it necessary to follow what you saw a priest had done? Therefore, by divine judgment, he could in no way be absolved, even when we wished it [Col. 0971B].

For this reason I do not cease to supplicate you ever more earnestly: once that deadly cause, with its names and persons, has passed away, may we, with the assent of our Lord, be joined in certain and complete joy with the bishop now created, in the words of the blessed Apostle: “If, therefore, anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (1 Corinthians 5:17).

Your letters proclaim the unity of the Catholic faith and, through royal piety, declare the peace of the Churches. When they were read with the honor due to them, the whole order of the Roman presbytery, ready to pray continually for your life and lasting prosperity, repeatedly acclaimed you with its voices; those who had been sent heard this, and everywhere the embassy of so glorious a message was thought to be hastening toward us [Col. 0971C].

The needs of the people of the city of Alexandria must be especially provided for in this respect: that they be withdrawn from the snares of a pestilential ruler. Let everything converge; let us all take action, so that, as the Apostle teaches (Galatians 1:12), “the one who troubles us” may be removed from our midst.

May the faithful peace of the Churches, which Leo of august memory, your father and teacher, continually guarded, and which you have resolved magnanimously to preserve, be true unity. For the paternal faith and the communion of blessed Peter must be preferred to any person.

And let it be shown to belong to Your Glory, as does the prosperity of your empire, that, after God, the integrity of the heavenly kingdom also pertains to you; so that Christ, accepting Your Serenity’s goodwill in preserving the laws of his Church, may both multiply temporal gifts for you and grant eternal ones.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The manuscript of Verdun attributes this letter to Gelasius; but Gelasius was not pope at this time; Felix was. Liberatus, *Breviarium*, chapter 18: “Acacius dies,” he says, “and Flavitas the presbyter is ordained after him, who was from Saint Thecla. He did not consent to be enthroned without the Roman pontiff, but sent the synodical letter to the Roman pope Felix. He died after living for a short time, without receiving the latter’s letter.” See Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 19. JACQUES SIRMOND.]

# LETTER XIII. OF POPE FELIX III TO FLAVITAS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Because he suspended his envoys from communion on the ground that they had replied that they had received no instruction concerning the names of Acacius and Peter. He urges Flavitas himself to refrain from reciting these names and to persuade Zeno to do the same.

Felix to Flavitas, bishop of Constantinople.

There are many things that give us joy concerning the ordination of Your Beloved and encourage us to hope, by divine favor, for the restoration of ecclesiastical peace.

First, that heavenly grace has chosen you as one whose life is said to have been commendable from childhood and whose devotion to the Catholic faith—what we desire above all—is proclaimed. Next, because amid these gifts the Lord has joined to your Charity the wish and favor of our lord son, the most glorious prince, so that, supported by the power of his aid, with God’s assistance you may more easily seek wisely what you have pursued according to the truth.

Finally, because nearly everything that follows the beginning of your honor displays both the benevolence of the imperial clemency toward us and the character of your own will. For these things are regularly sent to the Apostolic See, through which, by Christ’s grace, the dignity of all priests is made firm [Col. 0972B].

Your own letter of affection confesses blessed Peter the Apostle to be the chief of the Apostles and the rock of faith, and acknowledges that he is the dispenser of the heavenly mystery, to whom the keys were entrusted. Finally, it testifies that, so that we may be more fully unanimous, Your Beloved wishes to have with us an assent in the orthodox faith.

Since these appeared to be no small indications, leading us to believe that your wishes proceeded from your mind, a further and greater testimony was added: that our sons, the religious monks, distinguished by their confession of the true faith, should come here as well.

When we saw them, we judged that they had been sent only because the names of the condemned—whose communion these men avoided—had already been expelled from the Church of Constantinople. Thus we saw that nothing remained except for those carrying the synodical letter of Your Beloved to enjoy participation in apostolic communion [Col. 0972C].

But when we dealt with them more carefully, asking that, if they wished faithfully to receive the communion of blessed Peter the Apostle, they should state that both they and Your Beloved would henceforth be wholly separate from the recitation of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius, they replied that no such instruction had been given to them and refused to consent to the salutary grace we offered.

Disturbed by their hesitation, while the incoming letters and the arrangement of the circumstances themselves seemed to promise one thing, and the report of those mentioned conveyed something quite different from what had been hoped, we sorrowfully postponed our communion—though we desired it, once all uncertainty had been removed, to be full in the Catholic faith. We judge that this assent concerning orthodox faith, which Your Beloved promised to share with us, will come.

Otherwise, we shall not be chargeable with anything if the society of Peter of Alexandria is preferred to the fellowship of blessed Peter the Apostle, who embraces those bound together by the alliances of charity. It will be manifest before God and human beings that those who commit such acts are separated, not through our fault, but entirely by their own choice; and the same will be judged with every terror before the tribunal of Christ.

We are not obstinate, but defend the teachings of our fathers. Your Beloved’s letter itself indicated that we ought to display zeal for the orthodox [Col. 0973A]. Is it not established that Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned by the Council of Chalcedon, which the universal Church sanctioned and preserves? Are Timothy and Peter, their accomplices, not shown by many consistent documents to have been their followers, as the men sent by Your Beloved also perceived?

Did Acacius not follow their communion, although we had frequently and regularly forbidden it—men whom he himself had called heretics and formerly condemned in his letters? By rebuilding again what he had previously destroyed well, he appeared, according to the Apostle (Galatians 2:18), as a transgressor.

Therefore, in accordance with the course of the aforementioned synod, all who chose to share in that condemned perfidy deservedly underwent an equal punishment [Col. 0973B]. Just as a synod established against any particular heresy binds all who share in the similar wickedness of the rejected error, so that what is rightly shown to have been overthrown in the founders should not have to be restored in their successors.

Peter could not in any way be absolved without the assent of the Apostolic See, by whose command he had been excluded, as the rule of the ancient bishops concerning the reception of such persons testifies. Even that Peter, if he had been healed by legitimate correction, ought to have been received for pardon, not for priestly dignity: having been instituted by condemned heretics, he could in no way be placed over Catholic congregations.

You too, together with us, have recognized that what we say is salutary. Hence, in your own letter, when you speak of the faith of blessed Peter—which we read with complete joy—you expressed yourself with a Catholic mind:

“And may we, who with him glory in a harmonious voice, as you believe, be able to gather together the scattered.”

I therefore ask what those scattered things are, or by what disturbance they have been scattered. Nothing else now occurs to us except what has been devised by the madness of the followers of that same Eutychian plague.

Let Your Beloved labor with us, so that what you yourself confess to have been scattered may be gathered together. I use the Apostle’s words: “I beseech you, you have done me no wrong” (Galatians 4:12). I do not impose this as one exercising authority, but so that I may appropriately free my conscience.

I exhort you lest the rational sheep divinely entrusted to you, perish—God forbid—without danger to yourselves. Think together, all of you who are reckoned among the pastoral dignity, that for the Christian faith—which is Christ’s if it is true—we must live, and, if necessary, die for love of the most holy religion [Col. 0973D].

Consider, therefore, that the time of this life is always uncertain, lest, suddenly snatched away, we be dragged before the judgment of him whose knowledge inspires fear.

For this reason, as though you were present, we bind Your Beloved more earnestly by the law of charity: shuddering at the fate of the unhappy Acacius, who, as Scripture says, was not permitted to be absolved, despite our efforts, so that he might go to his own place, strive by whatever means you can to show yourself more truly an imitator of the Catholic bishops of that city.

And, joining my prayer to yours, do not cease humbly to entreat our lord son, the most glorious prince, and his wife, so that, as devoted children of the Church, they may both graciously receive our supplications and decide, with consideration for the security of their kingdom and their own perpetual salvation, to bring the matter to completion.

Nor should Your Beloved complain about the delay of apostolic communion. We would not wish it to be suspended by any difficulty, unless regard for Catholic truth stood in the way. To that truth I both desire and exhort Your Beloved to cling with all your strength.

Let the name of Peter and Acacius be removed from our midst; let us not be joined either in letters or in association with the envoys of the condemned Peter. And, as the Apostle says: “Let those who trouble us be cut off” (Galatians 5:12).

Again, as he himself declares: “Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough” (1 Corinthians 5:7), once the past cause has been erased together with its names and persons.

With God’s inspiration, we shall provide reasonably, as we have written, that if everything comes together, nothing may be lost—while the Catholic confession remains safe—from those whom Acacius ordained or baptized, for the restoration of the Church’s charity [Col. 0974B]. Thus may that peace come which “made both one” (Ephesians 2), not the peace condemned by the prophet: “Peace, peace, and there was no peace” (Ezekiel 13:10).

And may pure charity succeed, the charity for which Your Beloved has often asked in your letters, of which it is said: “Charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

Let light have nothing in common with darkness, because we cannot and must not participate both in the table of the Lord and in the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10). Thus, once the sheep entrusted to you have been cleansed by the removal of the past congregation, there may be one flock and one shepherd (John 10).

You remember that it is written: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4:7); and the prophet cries out: “You did not distinguish between the clean and the unclean” (Ezekiel 22:26).

We have touched on all these matters in summary, with such vigilance that, once hearts have been salutarily cleansed, we may be able to maintain a concord that is as firm without hesitation as it is true, as perpetual as it is united.

Therefore, let Your Beloved make us certain about these matters as quickly as possible, so that, with God bringing to completion what he has begun, we may be able to agree in full reconciliation within the structure of Christ’s body.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The title prefixed to the following letter in an old manuscript is as follows: “A copy of the letter carried on an embassy by the monks sent to Rufinus, Hilarus, and Thalasius, archimandrites at Constantinople.” JACQUES SIRMOND.]

# LETTER XIV. OF POPE FELIX III TO THALASIUS, ARCHIMANDRITE OF CONSTANTINOPLE

That neither he nor his monks should communicate with the Church of Constantinople or its bishop before the Apostolic See has given instructions.

[Col. 0974D]

Felix to Thalasius [Thalassius].

After sending through our sons, men of religious purpose, the letter which we instructed them to deliver to Your Beloved, we judged it necessary to admonish you, lest more diligent care should overlook anything concerning the protection of the Catholic faith.

Even if, by the assistance of our God, the names of the condemned—that is, Peter of Alexandria and the unhappy Acacius—have been removed from ecclesiastical recitation, so that persons similar to them in perdition may not be permitted to usurp priestly dignity, let neither Your Beloved nor the congregation you govern, nor any future bishop of the Church of Constantinople, decide to communicate before everything has been reported to the Apostolic See—either by the letter of the bishop who has been created or through an address from Your Beloved.

For just as, by your Catholic profession, you followed the rule of the Apostolic See by suspending yourself from condemned communion, so you must follow the example of blessed Peter: when communion has been restored by his authority, then know that your fellowship too is to be joined with them.

Let no one persuade Your Beloved at all that our communion has already been granted to those regions, since you see that matters remain in doubt and that, among us, everything concerning the bishop created there is altogether uncertain.

Communion could not be joined to one whose honor we have not yet approved as received, and whose faith and intention have not yet been confirmed [Col. 0975B].

Let Your Beloved therefore await the command of the Apostolic See, and then join the Church of Constantinople in sacred communion, if you desire to remain in participation with blessed Peter and in Catholic truth.

Given on the Kalends of May, [Note: [Col. 0975D] It should read “under Longinus and Faustus,” in the year 490.] under Probus and Faustus, illustrious men, in the thirteenth indiction.

# LETTER XV. OF POPE FELIX III TO VETRANIO, BISHOP

Explaining the causes of the dissension of the Church of Constantinople, he urges him to move Zeno to restore union with the Roman Church.

Felix to Vetranio, bishop.

We have learned from the report of many that Your Beloved desires to be strengthened by the complete restoration of the Church’s unity and is both distinguished by excellent character through the gift of divine grace and supported by the familiarity of our lord son, the most Christian prince. Your fraternity, if the matter were made clearer, is ready freely and prudently to defend the cause of the Catholic faith.

From these indications concerning your mind, we have judged you to be such an advocate [read: agent] of the truth as we desired to find there. We therefore rejoice that the Lord has not wholly rejected his inheritance, but has preserved hidden in the hearts of these men a flame of true confession—whether they completely abstained from confused communion or had fallen back into it through ignorance—since they nevertheless preferred both to have what is right declared and to follow what had been approved according to the tradition of the ancients.

For this reason we have taken care to address Your Beloved at length and to instruct you appropriately concerning the matters that caused the Church of Christ to fall into dissension.

In the Council of Chalcedon, therefore, which proceeded according to the standard of the Council of Nicaea and was celebrated for preserving the integrity of Christian confession, both by the authority of the Apostolic See and with the agreement of the universal Church, Eutyches and Dioscorus are known to have been condemned.

Timothy and Peter are unquestionably shown to have been their followers; and Acacius is shown to have mingled himself in their impious communion, even when forbidden by us [in the year 483] [Col. 0976A]. For this reason, according to the form of the aforesaid synod, all who chose to share in that wickedness incurred the same sentence of condemnation that had been imposed upon it.

Hence the aforesaid Acacius was deservedly expelled by renewed excommunication [on July 28, 484] from the Apostolic See, which, as executor of the often-mentioned Council of Chalcedon, approved at that time for the Catholic faith, did not fail in its duty—lest, through him, we too should, God forbid, be made accomplices of the lost.

Nor should anyone believe that Peter was legitimately purified, since he was not received by the See of blessed Peter the Apostle, by whose command he had been cast out. I do not doubt that Your Beloved knows well that a person of this kind, whenever reason required it, could or should be appropriately absolved only according to the proper order of ecclesiastical law, as divinely established [Col. 0976B].

Since this was not done, it is clear that Peter remains in the same perversity and condemnation in which he formerly was. Even if he had wished to be legitimately corrected, he ought to have obtained pardon, not ecclesiastical dignity: having assumed from heretics and condemned men the name of a false priesthood, he could not, by any rule, preside over the Catholic Church.

These events concerning the persons mentioned above are confirmed by documents arriving from that region, as the Constantinopolitan clergy who were sent have acknowledged. It was openly shown that Acacius had made himself a participant with those whom he himself had called heretics and reported as condemned in his letters.

Having therefore learned in summary what appears to have caused the dissension of the Churches, and recognizing that we were not without reason anxious for the Catholic faith, Your Beloved should henceforth not only take care to keep away from communion with the condemned, but should not cease, with whatever diligence you can, to withdraw Christ’s flock from it.

You must also continually urge our lord son, the Augustus of Christian mind, not to omit restoring, in tranquil order, the full peace of his times and the sincere truth of Christ—as a foremost son of sacred religion and distinguished by pious devotion—remembering the deed which, with the inspiration of our Lord, he is said graciously to have carried out for the Catholic faith.

After the name of Peter of Alexandria and that of Acacius have been removed from the Church of Constantinople—the cause from which the whole storm arose—may he, after God, graciously bring about the unimpaired unity of the faith of the fathers’ tradition.

That unity would never have been violated if Acacius had wished faithfully to disclose it to the most Christian emperor. But while he strove to move the boundaries of the Fathers and shamelessly sought an opportunity for transgression through his ambitions, he did not hesitate to trample upon venerable decrees. And, while the revered prince was occupied with public affairs, he concealed from him what he knew to be true and ought to have disclosed, thereby showing that he bore toward the salvation and imperial power the same kind of conscience that he displayed in the matter of religion itself.

Thus, as must be said not without fear of divine judgment, even if he had sought it from us when we desired it, he was not permitted to be absolved [Col. 0977A].

How, then, could our venerable lord son, the emperor, fail to judge that he ought to do what he saw a priest either doing or teaching?

Therefore, joining my prayer to yours, let Your Beloved entreat our often-mentioned lord son with every possible supplication and profession of tears, asking him patiently to permit those who trouble us to be cut off, lest we appear to have restored in the successors of the heretics what is certainly shown to have been condemned in their founders.

Let him not permit men similar to the former ones to oppress ecclesiastical dignity, so that we may say with the Apostle: “If, therefore, anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (1 Corinthians 5:17).

May he grant, through his peaceful disposition after God, that the Church of Constantinople be united with us, as always. For this is desired both by the increase of his present happiness and by the fruit of the eternity he is to attain.

But I specially admonish and charge Your Beloved that, at the fearful judgment of our Savior, you will in every way have to render me an account if you carry out less diligently—something we do not believe of your mind—the tasks I have entrusted to you for the integrity of human salvation, for the orthodox and canonical constitution of the Fathers, and for restoring the true and sincere peace of the whole Church.

*(From the manuscript of Verdun.)*

Felix to Andrew, bishop of Thessalonica.

We gladly embrace the concern of Your Beloved, by which you desire to come to the communion of the See of blessed Peter, since we desire the Church to be firmly strengthened by the complete restoration of the Catholic faith. But we would wish your desire to become, as the caution of orthodox truth requires, steadfast in every respect.

# Decree of Pope Felix III

*(Taken from Gratian.)*

In ecclesiastical affairs, the will of the ruler is to be placed after the priests.

It is certain that it is salutary for your affairs that, when matters concerning God are at issue, you strive, in accordance with his own constitution, to subject—not place above—the royal will to the priests of Christ; and that you learn sacred matters from their prelates rather than teach them; that you follow the ecclesiastical order, rather than, by human compliance with it, prescribe laws for it; and that you do not wish to exercise dominion over its decrees, [Col. 0977D] [Note: [Col. 0977] To whom God willed that your Clemency should bow the neck of pious devotion. See above, letter 9, whence this decree was excerpted by Gratian or someone else. LABB.] whose clemency God willed your neck of pious devotion to submit to: lest, while the measure of the heavenly dispensation is exceeded, one proceed to insult the disposer.

## A BOOKLET TRANSMITTED BY POPE FELIX CONCERNING THE DECREE OF THE COUNCIL TO THE EMPEROR ZENO

[Col. 0978A]

When the universal Church rejoiced that peace had been restored to it, after the heretics whom you had perceived to be rising up had been suppressed; when the empire of your piety had also carried off victory over its enemies; when throughout the whole world the prayer of all the priests was praying to the Lord for the salvation of your Serenity; and when your piety, guardian of the faith and defender of orthodoxy, was reigning under the favor of the eternal King—at that time, in the midst of the joys of the recovered empire, the venerable letters of your Highness and the authority frequently proceeding from your sacred breast, running close to God, had overthrown, by an ordinance most acceptable to God, Peter, who had associated with heretics and adhered to that parricide Timothy, who had been ordained bishop of the Alexandrian Church by profane men—for no one else could do so—to the extent that he had supposed;” and had annulled, for the commendation of his reign, the tyrant’s letters which an insane mind had dictated for the overthrow of, contrary to law, the definitions of the sacred Council of Chalcedon. Thus he rendered his unlawful ordinations, and likewise those of Timothy, as belonging to heretics, invalid; and he judged [Read: indicated] them to be outside the Church to whatever extent they had been.

But now we have learned that he presides over the Alexandrian Church, turning all our joys into mourning. If this is true—as it must confidently be brought before God by a most Christian ruler—we suggest that it should not be considered lightly in the divine judgment, unless what is said to have been done as an insult to God has been expiated by certain remedies. And because, as it is written, “the whole body suffers the pains of one member” (II Cor. III), the Churches of the East are shaken in his person. This concerns my brother and fellow bishop, the priest of Constantinople, against whom a petition was presented to me by the man who is said to occupy the aforesaid see; I have appended it to the lamentations of my humility, so that my same brother and fellow bishop Acacius may obediently undertake to clear himself before the blessed apostle Peter of the matters which he sees reported against him—as ecclesiastical necessity requires and as it is fitting that this should be done under your laws—and may not in any way consider delay permissible. If, as we trust, his conscience is clear, he ought not to reject the apostolic judgment and the moderation exercised with his fellow priests, so that, approved by priestly actions and faithful examination, he may first enjoy glory before Christ our Lord and all the priests, and thereafter the favor of your piety.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 492. GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES, PRESBYTER

[Col. 0979]

## PREFATORY MATERIAL

(From William Cave.)

[Col. 0979A]

Gennadius, a Gaul by nation, a presbyter of Marseilles—not, as Jacobus Gaddius wrongly says (*On Non-Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 222), nor, as do Sigebert (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 30) and Platina (*Life of Symmachus*), who are much older than Gaddius, a presbyter and then bishop of Marseilles—flourished in the year 495, when he completed his *Catalogue* and sent his book *On the Faith* to Pope Gelasius. The judgments of both ancient and recent writers differ concerning his zeal for the Catholic faith. Pope Hadrian numbers him among the most holy men (*Letter to Charlemagne*); the Church of Lyons places him among the Pelagians (*Book against John Scotus*), eight hundred years ago. It is certainly established that he was an enemy of predestination, and for this reason he also seems to have held Augustine and Prosper in less esteem (see *Catalogue*, chaps. 38, 84), since he wrongly judged that they defended the doctrine of the Predestinarians. Yet the books he wrote against Pelagius free him from the charge of Pelagianism; nor is it evident that he removed the necessity of prevenient grace—which was characteristic of Semi-Pelagianism—in such a way that he may rightly be counted among Catholic writers.

[Col. 0979]

## TESTIMONIES CONCERNING GENNADIUS

### WALAFRID STRABO

(*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chap. 20.)

[Col. 0979B]

Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, standing, as it were, midway between the ancients and the younger writers in ecclesiastical doctrine, moderates his judgment with such balance that he says he neither praises nor condemns daily reception of the Eucharist.

### ALGERUS

(*On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book I, chap. 22.)

It is found in Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “I neither praise nor condemn receiving communion of the Eucharist every day,” and so forth.

### PETER LOMBARD

(*Sentences*, book II, distinction 20.)

[Col. 0979C] Gennadius says in his definitions of ecclesiastical dogmas: “We do not believe that demons, through their activity, enter the soul substantially,” and so forth.

### THOMAS AQUINAS

(*Quodlibet* 12, art. 11.)

[Col. 0980B]

The book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is not Augustine’s, but Gennadius’s, who flourished under the emperor Anastasius in the year of our Lord 490 (Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, fol. 236).

### PLATINA

(*On Pope Symmachus*, 1.)

In his time Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, greatly helped the Church of God. He was a diligent imitator of Augustine, composed a book *On Dogmas*, and explained what was necessary for each person’s salvation.

### CAESAR BARONIUS

(Vol. II of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year of Christ 263.)

Gennadius of Marseilles left behind a commentary *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which is sometimes wrongly cited under the name of Saint Augustine. In it he wrote: “Nothing created or serving,” and so forth.

# [BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL DOGMAS]

[Col. 0979]

## THE BOOK OF GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES ON ECCLESIASTICAL DOGMAS

(From the edition of Elmenhorst.) [Note: [Col. 0979] Notes to this document may be found in columns 999–1054.] (C, S)

### 1. CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0979C]

We believe that there is one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father is so called because he has a Son; the Son, because he has a Father; the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and is coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Father, therefore, is the source of the Godhead: just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds—not born, because he is not a son; not unbegotten, because he is not the Father; and not made, because he is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son. The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is.

2. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says; nor is the Godhead separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes; but the Father is one in person, the Son another in person, and the Holy Spirit another in person. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in nature in the holy Trinity.

### CHAPTER II

The Father did not assume flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone: so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity might himself become, in humanity, the son of a human mother; lest the name “son” pass to another who was not a son by eternal birth. Thus the Son of God became the son of man, born according to the truth of nature from God the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from man the Son of man. Thus the truth of what was begotten possessed the name of son by birth in both births—not by adoption or appellation—and there was one Son, true God and true man.

Therefore we confess not two Christs or two sons, but one Son, God and man. For this reason we also call him the only-begotten, remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature has conferred upon him, 3 not with the natures confused or mixed, as the Timothians wish, but united by fellowship. God therefore assumed man, and man passed into God—not by the mutability of nature, as the Apollinarists say, [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript of Florence, Tertullian, and the Apollinarists say this.] but by God’s gracious condescension: so that God was not changed into human substance [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript reads “sufficiency.”] by assuming man, nor man, glorified, into the divine by becoming God. For change or mutability of nature produces both diminution and abolition of substance.

We believe that the holy Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation. Therefore the Son of God was born from a human being, and not through a human being—that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says—but drawing flesh from the body of a virgin, and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches affirm. Nor was he born in appearance, that is, without flesh, as Valentinus asserts, [Note: [Col. 0981D] Thus the manuscript of the Florentine library of Saint Mark.] nor from a thesis, that is, putatively imagined, but with a real body. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript reads: “not unequal, as Eunomius; nothing through grace, but the heart flesh; with no perception”—an evidently corrupt passage.] He is not merely flesh from flesh, as Marcianus says, [Col. 0981D] but true God from divinity and true man from flesh, one Son of God: in divinity, the Word of the Father and God; in humanity, soul and flesh. The soul was not without perception and reason, as Apollinaris held, nor the flesh without a soul, as Eunomius held; rather, the soul had its reason, and the flesh its senses. Through these true senses he endured the pains of his flesh in the Passion and before the Passion.

### 4. CHAPTER III

Nor was he born [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript deletes “from a virgin.”] from a virgin in such a way that, by being born, the man also received the beginning of divinity—as though, before being born from the virgin, he had not been God—as Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus taught. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The word “Marcellus” is absent from the manuscript.] Rather, eternal God and man was born from the virgin, [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript reads: “but eternal God before the ages, man,” and so forth.] not losing what he was, but graciously consenting to be what he was not. [Note: [Col. 0982D] “Not losing what he was, graciously consenting to be what he was not”: I have restored this here from the manuscript, where it properly belongs.]

### CHAPTER IV

Let us believe that there is nothing created or servile in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the fountain of Arius, wishes; [Note: [Col. 0982D] The manuscript reads “to be believed.”] nothing unequal, as Eunomius wishes; nothing unequal in grace, as Aetius wishes; nothing earlier or later, or lesser, as Arius holds; nothing external or performing service for another, as Macedonius holds; [Note: [Col. 0982D] The manuscript reads “difficult.”] nothing inserted by invasion or stealth, as Mani holds; nothing bodily, as Melito and Tertullian hold; nothing formed corporeally, as the Anthropomorphite and Vadianus hold; [Note: [Col. 0982D] The manuscript has “Nadicinus,” incorrectly. Danaeus, in Augustine, *On Heresies*, chap. 50, reads “Audians.”] nothing invisible to creatures, as Origen holds; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus holds; nothing differing in morals or will, as Marcion holds; nothing drawn down from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian hold; nothing singular in function or incommunicable to another, as Origen holds; nothing confused, as Sabellius holds; but everything perfect, because everything is from the One and the One is from everything—not, however, solitary, as Praxeas and Sylvanus presume, that condemnable doctrine of Pentapolis. [Note: [Col. 0982D] The manuscript introduces: “nothing unequal in grace.”]

### CHAPTER V

[Col. 0982C]

Ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*), that is, coessential, is the Son in divinity with the Father; ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit; ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*) with God and man is the one Son, remaining God in his humanity in the glory of the Father, desirable to be seen by angels. As the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshiped by angels and by every creature, so he is worshiped; he is not a man made apart from God, [Note: [Col. 0982D] The manuscript reads “but.”] or Christ with God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but man in God and God in man.

### CHAPTER VI

There will be a resurrection of all the dead, but one resurrection, together and at one time. There will not be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as the dreamers’ fable has it, but one resurrection of all. And if that is said to rise which falls, then our flesh truly rises, just as it truly falls. Nor, according to Origen, will there be a change of bodies—that is, another new body in place of the flesh. Rather, the same corruptible flesh that falls, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous, will rise incorruptible; and it will be able either to suffer punishment for sins or to remain in eternal glory according to its merits.

### 6. CHAPTER VII

The resurrection will belong to all human beings.
