[Note: [Col. 0983D] The manuscript reads: “Rather, because it will belong to all.”] If it will belong to all, then all die, so that death, derived from Adam, may rule over all his children; and that privilege may remain in the Lord which is said specifically of him: “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm XVI, 10). [Note: [Col. 0983D] In the printed editions there follows: “for his flesh did not see corruption”; I deleted this because it is absent from the manuscript.] We have accepted this reasoning as handed down by a very great multitude of the Fathers.

Yet because there are also other men, equally Catholic and learned, who believe that those who are found alive at the Lord’s coming will, while their souls remain in their bodies, be changed to incorruption and immortality, and that this will be reckoned to them as resurrection from the dead because they lay aside the mortality of the present life [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Of the present life”: added from the manuscript.] by a change, not by death, whoever accepts either position is not a heretic, unless he becomes a heretic through contentiousness. For it is enough, according to the law of the Church, to believe that the resurrection of the flesh will take place from death.

### CHAPTER VIII

When we say in the Creed that at the Lord’s coming the living and the dead will be judged, this does not signify only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks. We also believe that “the living” means those who will be found in the flesh and who are still believed destined to die—or, as others wish, destined to be changed—so that, raised or transformed immediately, they may be judged together with those who died earlier.

### CHAPTER IX

After the resurrection and judgment, let us not believe that there will be a restoration, as Origen dreams: that demons or impious men, after torments, as though cleansed by punishments, might either return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or that the unjust [Note: [Col. 0983D] Thus the manuscript; other editions read “these,” incorrectly.] might be granted association with the righteous, on the grounds that this would accord with divine mercy, so that nothing rational might perish among creatures, but everything might somehow be saved.

Rather, let us believe in the judge of all, the just retributor of the righteous, who said: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life, so that they may receive the fruit of their works” (Matt. XXV, 46). [Note: [Col. 0983D] And again: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” Thus the manuscript of the Florentine library.] And again: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

### CHAPTER X

In the beginning God created heaven, earth, and water from nothing. While darkness still concealed the water itself and the water hid the earth, the angels and all the heavenly powers came into being, so that God’s goodness would not be idle, 8 but would have beings in whom to display his goodness through many ages beforehand. Thus this visible world was both made and adorned from the matter that had been made by God.

### CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0984A]

Nothing incorporeal and invisible in nature is to be believed in [Note: [Col. 0984D] The manuscript omits “in.”] except God alone—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He is rightly believed incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and holds together all things. He is therefore invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal.

### CHAPTER XII

Every creature is corporeal. The angels and all the heavenly powers are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual creatures to be corporeal for the reason that they are circumscribed locally, as is the soul, which is enclosed in flesh, and demons, who are of the substance of the angelic nature.

### CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0984B] We believe intellectual natures to be immortal because they lack flesh and have nothing by which they might fall, so that after a ruin they would require a necessary resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0984D] The manuscript deletes “necessary.”]

### 9. CHAPTER XIV

Human souls were not among the other intellectual natures from the beginning, nor were they created simultaneously with them, as Origen imagines; nor were they sown [Note: [Col. 0984D] The printed editions read “are sown.”] together with bodies through intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latins assert, as though preserving the succession of nature. Rather, we say that only the Creator of all knows the creation of the soul; that only the body is sown through the union of marriage; and that, by God’s judgment, it is joined together, compacted, and formed in the womb. Once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being composed of soul and body may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance.

### CHAPTER XV

Nor do we say that there are two souls in one human being, as James and other Syrian disputants write: one animal soul by which the body is animated and which is mixed with the blood, and another spiritual soul which supplies reason. Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in a human being, which both gives life to the body by its association with it and orders itself by its reason, possessing freedom of choice, so that in the thought of its substance it may choose what it wishes.

### 10. CHAPTER XVI

We believe that only the human being has a substantial soul, which lives after being stripped of the body and vigorously retains its senses and faculties. It does not die with the body, as Aratus or Epicurean vanity asserts; [Note: [Col. 0984D] I added this passage, which is either Epicurean vanity, from the manuscript.] nor does it perish after a short interval, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially and retains its reason. [Note: [Col. 0984D] Thus the Florentine manuscript.]

### CHAPTER XVII

The souls of animals, however, are not substantial. They are born together with the flesh itself at the flesh’s birth, and with the death of the flesh they reach their end and die. Therefore they are governed neither by reason [Note: [Col. 0985D] The words “nor do they live” are taken from the manuscript.] nor do they live, as Plato and Alexander hold, [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript reads “discuss.”] but are driven by every impulse of nature.

### CHAPTER XVIII

The human soul does not die with the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript reads “because it is not the flesh’s.”] because, as we said above, it is not sown with the flesh. Rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, it is created and infused by God’s judgment, so that the human being may live within the womb and thus proceed through birth into the world.

### CHAPTER XIX

The human being consists of only two substances: soul and body. The soul has its reason, and the body its senses. [Note: [Col. 0985D] Here and below the manuscript has “flesh” in place of “body.”] [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript adds: “that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch.”] Yet the body does not move these senses without the soul’s association with it. [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript reads “the flesh.”] The soul, even without the body, retains its rational faculty. [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript reads: “Even without the flesh it retains its reason intact.”]

### CHAPTER XX

There is no third spirit in the substance of the human being, as Didymus contends, [Note: [Col. 0985D] The manuscript reads “a spirit.”] but the spirit is the soul itself, either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes in the body and is therefore called spirit. The soul, however, is so called because it animates the body for living or for giving life.

The third element introduced by the Apostle together with soul and body (I Thess. I, 22) is to be understood as the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle prays that it may remain whole in us, lest through our fault it be diminished or driven away from us, because “the Holy Spirit will flee deceit” (Wis. I, 4).

### CHAPTER XXI

From the first creation of the world, the human being was entrusted to the freedom of his own choice, so that, if he wished to remain in the condition in which he had been created, he might persevere in guarding the commandment, with the vigilance of his mind also striving toward this. [Note: [Col. 0985D] The word “of the world” is added from the manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0985D] Thus the manuscript; others read “with salvation preserved.”] [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus the manuscript; others read “admitting,” incorrectly.] [Note: [Col. 0986D] Others read “of the commandment.”]

But after he fell through the serpent’s deception by means of Eve (Gen. III, 6), he lost the good of nature and likewise the strength of free choice, though not choice itself. Otherwise it would not be his own act to avoid sin, nor would what he had not cleansed by his own choice rightly be forgiven. [Note: [Col. 0986D] The manuscript reads “would correct.”]

Freedom of choice therefore remains for seeking salvation—that is, rational will—but only after God has first admonished and invited the person to salvation, so that he may choose, follow, or act when the opportunity for salvation arises, that is, through God’s inspiration. But that he obtains what he chooses, follows, or undertakes when the opportunity arises, we freely confess to be God’s doing.

Thus we have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy. To consent to the saving inspiration lies within our power; to obtain what we desire by consenting to the admonition is a divine gift; not to fall away from the gift of salvation already obtained belongs to our diligence and equally to heavenly assistance; to fall belongs to our power and negligence. [Note: [Col. 0986D] The manuscript adds: “that is, of rational will.”] Yet we cannot obtain salvation without him who makes those who seek find, who opens to those who knock, and who gives to those who ask (Matt. VII, 7).

Therefore, just as we believe that we have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy and inspiration, so we freely confess that the choice of our nature follows divine inspiration.

[Note: [Col. 0986D] This seems to be superfluous and should be removed as spurious.] Accordingly, not to fall away from the good either of nature or of merit belongs to our diligence and equally to heavenly assistance; to fall belongs to our power and negligence.

### 13. CHAPTER XXII

It must be believed with the utmost firmness that, in Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence; and that no one can rise by free choice from the depth of that ruin unless the grace of the merciful God has raised him up. For free choice itself suffered this: while using its own goods [Note: [Col. 0986D] In Isidore’s collection of councils: “gifts.”] without due care, it fell and was submerged in the depths of transgression. It found nothing by which it could rise thereafter, and, deceived in its freedom forever, would have remained hidden beneath the oppression of this ruin unless the coming of Christ had raised it up afterward by his grace. Through the purification of new birth he cleansed every past sin by the washing of his baptism.

### CHAPTER XXIII

No one is good by himself unless he who alone is good grants him participation in himself. [Note: [Col. 0986D] Isidore reads “grants.”]

### CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0986C] No one who has been renewed by the grace of baptism is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through daily assistance from God, he receives perseverance in a good way of life. [Note: [Col. 0986D] Isidore likewise reads “overcoming.”]

### 14. CHAPTER XXV

That no one makes good use of free choice except through Christ is proclaimed by the same teacher in the letter sent to the Council of Milevis, where he says:

“Understand at last, O perverse doctrine of minds most depraved, that the first human being was so deceived by freedom itself that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from this unless the providence of regeneration, through the coming of Christ the Lord, restored him to the state of his former freedom.” [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Through the grace of Christ”: Isidore adds this.] [Note: [Col. 0986D] Thus correctly Isidore.]

### CHAPTER XXVI

All the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, [Note: [Col. 0986D] Isidore reads “are.”] [Col. 0987A] because no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has granted. In this judgment the authoritative rule of the blessed Pope Zosimus directs us, when, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“But we, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—reported everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops venerated this statement, radiant with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows: [Note: [Col. 0987D] Isidore reads “they wrote in reply.”]

### 15

“Now, what you included in the letters which you arranged to have sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Yet we act at God’s prompting,’ and so forth, we understand to have been said in such a way that, as you passed swiftly through, you cut down with the strict sword of truth those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance.

“For what have you done with such free choice as the fact that you referred everything to the awareness of our humility? [Note: [Col. 0987D] Isidore reads “you have done.”] And yet you wisely and faithfully saw, and truthfully and confidently declared, that this was done at God’s prompting. [Note: [Col. 0987D] Isidore reads “you referred.”]

“This is so, certainly, because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord.’ And so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations. ‘All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God’ (Rom. VIII, 15), so that we may neither perceive our own choice to be absent nor doubt that, in every individual movement of human will toward good, his assistance is more powerful.” [Note: [Col. 0987D] Isidore reads “of the faithful.”]

### CHAPTER XXVII

Thus God works in the hearts of human beings and in free choice itself, so that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, without whom we can do nothing. [Note: [Col. 0988D] Isidore adds “in.”]

### CHAPTER XXVIII

If anyone says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins that have already been committed, and not also for the assistance of grace by which they are not committed, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXIX

If anyone says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin only because through him the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled to love and be able to do what we have recognized ought to be done, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXX

Let us also consider the sacramental prayers of the priests, which, handed down from the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church, so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing. For when the prelates of the holy peoples, carrying out an embassy entrusted to them, act as advocates for the human race before the divine clemency, and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; 17 that the light of truth appear to the Jews when the veil of their heart has been removed; that heretics may recover their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the Spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally that, once catechumens have been led to the sacraments of rebirth, the court of heavenly mercy may be opened to them— [Note: [Col. 0988D] Isidore reads “by the report.”]

the effect of these very matters shows that they are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love, and making vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. The whole of this is perceived to be so entirely the work of God that thanksgiving and confession of praise are continually offered to him for the illumination or correction of such people.

### CHAPTER XXXI

We also contemplate with attentive regard what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young people come to the sacrament of rebirth, they do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven away from them through the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy. Then it truly becomes evident how “the prince of this world is cast out” (John XII, 31), and how the strong man is first bound and afterward his vessels are plundered (Matt. XII, 29), transferred into the possession of the victor, who “led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV, 8).

### CHAPTER XXXII

We profess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and of every virtue by which, from the beginning of faith, one strives toward God. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

By this assistance and gift of God, free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked straight, what was weak sound, and what was imprudent provident. God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes the merits that are his gifts to be ours, and for the things he has bestowed he is going to bestow eternal rewards.

For he works in us so that we may both will and do what he wills. He does not permit what he has granted for exercise, not neglect, to lie idle in us. Thus we too are cooperators with God’s grace; and if we see anything in us growing weak through our own negligence, let us hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our weaknesses and redeems our life from destruction (Psalm CIII, 3–4), and to whom we say daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 2).

### CHAPTER XXXIII

If anyone says that the first human being, Adam, was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die—that is, leave this body—not on account of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

If anyone denies that infants newly born from their mothers’ wombs are to be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing from Adam of original sin that is cleansed through the washing of regeneration, with the consequence that in them the form of baptism for the remission of sins must be understood to be not true but false, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle’s statement must not be understood in any other way: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12), except in the manner in which the Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, has always understood it.

For this reason, infants also, 20 who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves, [Note: [Col. 0989D] Isidore reads “in themselves.”] are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them.

### CHAPTER XXXV

The holy apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). If anyone thinks this should be understood to mean that, out of humility, one ought not to say that we have no sin, rather than because it is true, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.” Here it is sufficiently clear that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully. The Apostle could have said: “If we say, ‘We have no sin,’ we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he clearly shows that whoever says he has no sin is not speaking the truth but falsehood.

### CHAPTER XXXVI
Whoever says that the saints therefore say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 2), not on their own behalf—because this petition is no longer necessary for them—but on behalf of others in their community who are sinners; and therefore says that each saint does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us [Col. 0989D] our sins,” so that the just person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself—let him be anathema. For the apostle James was holy and just when he said: “For in many things we all offend” (James III, 2). Why else was “all” added, unless this statement corresponded to the psalm where we read: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLIII, 3)? And in the prayer of the wisest Solomon: “There is no one who does not sin” (Eccl. VII, 21). And in the Book of holy Job: “In the hand of every human being he marks it, so that every human being may know his weakness” (Job XXXVII, 7). Hence Daniel too, holy and just, when in his prayer he said in the plural, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly” (Dan. IX, 5), and the other things that he there truthfully and humbly confesses—lest it be thought, as some hold, that he said this not of his own sins but of those of his people—later said: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (ibid., 20). He did not say “our sins,” but spoke of his people’s and his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would understand these matters so perversely. [Col. 0990D: Isidore, “understand.”] [Col. 0990A]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Whoever wants the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, where we say, “Forgive us our debts,” to be said by the saints in humility but not truthfully—let him be anathema. For who could tolerate someone praying, and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself, who with his lips says that he wishes to be forgiven, while in his heart he says that he has no debts to be forgiven? [Col. 0990B]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

If anyone says that, through the offense of Adam’s transgression, the human being was not wholly changed for the worse—that is, in body and soul—but, while the soul’s freedom remained unharmed, believes that only the body became subject to corruption, deceived by the error of Pelagius, he opposes the Scripture that says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4), and: “Do you not know that to whoever you obey, and by whom anyone is overcome, to that one he is made a slave?” (Rom. VI, 16). [Col. 0990B]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression harmed Adam alone and not also his offspring, or at least testifies that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, and not also sin—which is the death of the soul—passed through one human being into the whole human race, he makes God unjust, contradicting the Apostle who says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all human beings sinned” (Rom. V, 12). [Col. 0990C]

## CHAPTER XL

If anyone says that God’s grace can be bestowed through human invocation, but not that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah—or the Apostle, who says the same thing: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me” (Isa. LXV, 1; Rom. X, 20). [Col. 0990C]

## CHAPTER XLI

If anyone maintains that God awaits our will in order that we may be cleansed from sin, but does not confess that, so that we may also desire to be cleansed, this comes about in us through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit, he resists the Holy Spirit himself, who says through Solomon: “The will is prepared by the Lord”; and the Apostle, who salutarily proclaims: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13). [Col. 0990D]

## CHAPTER XLII

If anyone says that both the increase of faith and its beginning itself, together with the inclination to believe by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5) and arrive at the regeneration of holy baptism, is naturally present in us, rather than being a gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who turns our will from unbelief to faith and from ungodliness to piety—he is shown to be an adversary of apostolic teachings, since blessed Paul the Apostle says: “We are confident that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. I, 6). And: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (ibid.). And: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves: for it is God’s gift” (Eph. II, 5). For those who say that the faith by which we believe in God is natural make all who are alien to the Church of Christ, in a certain sense, believers. [Col. 0991A–B]

## CHAPTER XLIII

If anyone says that, without God’s grace, mercy is divinely bestowed upon us who believe, will, desire, strive, study, ask, seek, and knock, but does not confess that, so that we may believe, will, and be able to do all these things as we ought, this occurs in us through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit; and if he adds the assistance of grace to human humility or obedience, but does not agree that it is itself a gift of grace that we should be obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7), and: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10). [Col. 0991C]

## CHAPTER XLIV

If anyone affirms that by the power of nature one can appropriately think of, or choose, some good belonging to the salvation of eternal life, or consent to salvation—that is, to evangelical preaching—without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who gives everyone sweetness in consenting and believing the truth, he is deceived by a heretical spirit, not understanding the voice of God in the Gospel, which says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 6). And: “Not that we are competent of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our competence is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

## CHAPTER XLV

If anyone contends that some can come to the grace of baptism through mercy, but others through free will—which is acknowledged to have been corrupted in all who were born from the transgression of the first human being—he is proved alien to the right faith. For he either does not assert that everyone’s free will was weakened by the sin of the first human being, or else considers it so injured that some are nevertheless able, by themselves and without God’s revelation, to seek out the ministry of eternal salvation. How contrary this is, the Lord himself proves (John VI, 44), for he testifies that not some but no one can come to him unless the Father draws him. Thus also he says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17). And the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3). [Col. 0991D]

## CHAPTER XLVI

The free choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism. What was lost cannot be restored except by the one from whom it could have been given. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII, 30). [Col. 0992A]

## CHAPTER XLVII

Even if human nature had remained in the integrity in which it was created, it could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since it could not preserve without God’s grace the salvation it had received, how will it be able without God’s grace to restore what it lost?

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Just as the Apostle says most truthfully to those who wish to be justified in the law and have fallen away from grace: “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21), so it is said most truthfully to those who think that the grace commended and received by the faith of Christ is nature: “If righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.” For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature already existed here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: so that the law might be fulfilled through him who said: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17), and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished (Luke XIX, 7). [Col. 0992B]

## CHAPTER XLIX

According to the foregoing statements of the holy Scriptures and the definitions of the ancient Fathers, we ought, God being propitious, both to preach and to believe this: that through the sin of the first human being the human race was so bent downward that afterward no one could either love God as was fitting, or believe in God, or do what is good for God, unless the grace of divine mercy had first preceded him.

Hence we believe that the illustrious faith of righteous Abel and Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of the whole multitude of the saints of old—which the Apostle Paul praises in them (Heb. XI, 4, 7, 8)—was bestowed not through the good of nature, which had first been given in Adam, but through the grace of God. After the Lord’s coming, we likewise know and believe that this grace is bestowed on all who desire to be baptized, not as something possessed in free will, but by the generosity of Christ, according to what has already often been said and what the Apostle Paul proclaims: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. I, 29). And: “God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord” (ibid., 6). And: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift” (Eph. II, 8). And what the Apostle says about himself: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (I Cor. VII, 25). He did not say, “because I was,” but “so that I might be.” And: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7). And: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 16). And: “No one has anything unless it has been given to him from above” (John III, 27). [Col. 0992C–D]

## CHAPTER L

We also believe, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that after receiving the grace of baptism, all the baptized, with Christ helping and cooperating, can and ought to fulfill the things that pertain to the salvation of the soul, if they are willing to labor faithfully. We not only do not believe that some have been predestined by divine power to evil, but, if there are people who are willing to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence. [Col. 0993A]

## CHAPTER LI

In every good work, we do not begin and are afterward helped by God’s mercy; rather, he himself, with no preceding good merits on our part, first inspires in us both faith and love of himself, so that we may faithfully seek the sacrament of baptism and, after baptism, with his assistance, be able to fulfill what pleases him.

Therefore it must be believed most clearly that the extraordinary faith of the thief whom the Lord restored to the homeland of paradise (Luke XXIII, 43), of the centurion Cornelius to whom the angel of the Lord was sent (Acts X, 3), and of Zacchaeus, who was deemed worthy to receive the Lord himself (Luke XIX, 2), was not from nature but was bestowed through the generosity of divine grace. [Col. 0993B]

## CHAPTER LII

There is one baptism, but it is in the Church, where there is one faith and where baptism is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if some have been baptized among heretics who baptize in confession of the holy Trinity and come to us, they are indeed to be received as baptized, lest the invocation or confession of the holy Trinity be annulled; but they are to be taught and fully instructed in the sense in which the mystery of the holy Trinity is held in the Church. If they agree to believe, or consent to confess it, they are to be strengthened, already cleansed by the integrity of faith, through the laying on of hands.

If they are children or simple-minded people who cannot understand the teaching, those who present them should answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism. [Col. 0993D: Thus the manuscript; others, “name.”] Thus fortified by the laying on of hands and chrism, they are to be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.

But those who have been baptized among heretics without invocation of the holy Trinity and come to us, we declare ought to be baptized, not rebaptized. For we must not believe that those have been baptized who have not been immersed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, according to the rule established by the Lord. Such are the Pauliani, Procliani, Borboritae, [Manuscript: Symphori, Fortuniani, Montanists, who are also called Priscillians or Maximianists, and Manichaeans.] Siphori, who are now called Bonosians; the Photinians; the Montanists, who are also called Priscillians; the Manichaeans; and various other shoots of impiety; or the other plagues of their origin or order, who introduce two principles unknown to themselves, such as Cerdon and Marcion; or contrary principles, such as the Manichaean; or three and barbarous principles [Manuscript: “tetra, as Baida,” incorrectly.], such as the Sethian and [Manuscript: Theodotus.] Theodosian; or many principles [Manuscript: “hiulca,” incorrectly.], such as Valentinus; or those who say that Christ was a human being without God, such as Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon, and Photinus.

If any of these, I say, come to us, they are not to be asked whether they have been baptized or not, but only whether they believe the faith of the Church; and they are to be baptized with ecclesiastical baptism. [Manuscript: that is, Catholic baptism.] [Col. 0993D–0994A]

## CHAPTER LIII

I neither praise [Others have “the Eucharist” in place of “communion of the Eucharist.”] nor condemn [Others: “I censure.”] receiving communion of the Eucharist every day. Nevertheless, I advise and urge that communion be received every Sunday, provided that the mind is free from the desire to sin. [Manuscript has “not” instead of “without.”] For I say that one who still has the will to sin is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified. [Manuscript: “purified.”]

Therefore, even if someone is troubled by sin but thereafter has no will to sin, let him make satisfaction through tears and prayers before receiving communion; and, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, who is accustomed to forgive sins upon pious confession, let him approach the Eucharist without fear and in confidence.

But I say this concerning one who is not weighed down by capital and mortal sins. [Manuscript: “does not have capital and mortal sins.”] As for one who is oppressed by mortal crimes committed after baptism, I urge him first to make satisfaction through public penance and then, reconciled by the priest’s judgment, to be joined to communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for his own judgment and condemnation. We do not deny, however, that mortal crimes may be absolved through private satisfaction [Manuscript: “namely.”], provided that he first changes his secular clothing, professes devotion to the religious life through correction of his conduct, and, grieving continually—or rather perpetually—[Manuscript: “with fasting.”] with God’s mercy, obtains pardon. [These words, “may obtain pardon,” have been supplied from the manuscript.] This is to be done only in such a way that he performs actions contrary to those for which he repents, [Manuscript: “those” instead of “these.”] and receives the Eucharist every Sunday, suppliant and submissive, until death. [Col. 0994B–C]

## CHAPTER LIV

True penance is not to admit sins for which one must repent, and to mourn those that have been admitted. The satisfaction of penance is to cut away the causes of sins [Manuscript: “erase”] and not to give access to their suggestions.

## CHAPTER LV

In the divine promises, let us expect nothing earthly or transitory, as the Melitans hope. Let us not expect the union of marriage, as Cerinthus and Marcion rave. Let us not expect what pertains to food or drink, as Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Lactantius, following Papias, accept. [I have corrected this passage in this way. The manuscript has “Papias”; others have “of Papias,” incorrectly.]

Nor should we hope that, after a thousand years, Christ’s kingdom will be on earth and that the saints will reign with him in delights, as Nepos taught, inventing a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of the ungodly. Between these two resurrections of the dead, he held that nations ignorant of God would be preserved in the flesh in the corners of the earth. After the thousand-year reign of the righteous on earth, these nations are to be stirred up by the devil to battle against the righteous who are reigning [Manuscript: “resisting”]; and, while the Lord fights for the righteous, they are to be restrained by a fiery rain and, thus killed, together with the others who previously died in ungodliness [Manuscript: “the dead,” in place of “previously dead”], raised in incorruptible flesh for eternal punishments. [The manuscript adds: “We greatly avoid this superstition.”] [Col. 0994C–0995A]

## CHAPTER LVI

We believe that no one comes to salvation unless invited by God; that no one who has been invited works out his salvation unless God assists him; that no one merits assistance unless he prays; and that no one perishes by God’s will, but by himself, according to the choice of his free will, lest the freedom and power of natural nobility once attributed to the human being be compelled into servile necessity. [Col. 0995B]

## CHAPTER LVII

Evil or wickedness was not created by God but invented by the devil, since he too was created good by God. But because, as a rational creature, he had been entrusted to free will by God and had received the capacity for thought, he turned his knowledge of good toward evil. Through thinking many things, he became the inventor of evil; and what he had lost in himself he begrudged others. Not content to perish alone, he persuaded others, so that, being the inventor of his own wickedness, he might also become the author of wickedness in others. From this, evil or wickedness spread among the other rational creatures. [Col. 0995B]

## CHAPTER LVIII

From this we know that nothing is immutable by nature except God alone—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who cannot be changed from the good, because he possesses the good by nature and cannot be anything other than good. [Manuscript: “everlasting.”] [Col. 0995C]

## CHAPTER LIX

The angels, however, who persevere in the blessedness in which they were created, do not possess the good by nature so that they would not be changed along with the others. Rather, they preserve a good will by choice and repay their Lord with the goodness of their condition and with faith. For this reason the Lord himself rightly calls the holy angels holy: they held fast to holiness by choice and did not deviate from the good by the example of their companions.

## CHAPTER LX

The true faith, which is Catholic, confesses the good substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, and that evil has no nature, because God, who is the Creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good. Thus the devil too would have been good if he had remained in what he was made. But because he used his natural excellence badly and did not remain in the truth, he did not pass into an opposite substance; rather, he departed from the highest good, to which he ought to have adhered. [Col. 0995D]

## CHAPTER LXI

The angelic powers that remained steadfast, fixed in divine love, after the proud angels fell, received this gift of recompense: that they should no longer be gnawed by any rust of encroaching guilt, but should remain without end in the contemplation of the Creator’s blessedness and endure in this condition, as they were created, with eternal stability. [Col. 0996A]

## CHAPTER LXII

The angels were created such that, if they wished, they could persist in the light of blessedness, but, if they wished, they could also fall. Thus Satan fell with the legions that followed him. But after his fall, the angels who stood firm were so confirmed that they could not fall at all, because they received the power of immutability so that they might not fall at all thereafter.

## CHAPTER LXIII

Marriage is good, but for the sake of children and for the purpose of restraining fornication. [Col. 0996B]

## CHAPTER LXIV

Continence is better, but it is not sufficient by itself for blessedness [Manuscript of Florence: “It is sufficient for itself alone”] if it is considered solely out of love of chastity [Manuscript: “is retained”]. Rather, it must be chosen together with the corresponding purpose of devoting oneself to the Lord [Manuscript: “with such an inclination”]. Otherwise it will seem more a repudiation of marriage than a desire for chastity. [Manuscript: “chastity” instead of “desire for chastity.”] [Col. 0996D]

## CHAPTER LXV

Virginity is superior to both goods, because it conquers both nature and struggle: nature through bodily integrity, and struggle through the peace of chastity, which exists in peace for the sole love of purity.

## CHAPTER LXVI

It is good to take food with thanksgiving, and whatever God has commanded is to be eaten. To abstain from certain things, not as though they were evil but as though they were unnecessary, is not evil. To regulate their use according to necessity and time is properly Christian. [Col. 0996C]

## CHAPTER LXVII

To call marriages evil, or to compare them with fornication or adultery; and likewise to believe foods evil, or to think that they cause wickedness in those who receive them [Manuscript: “create causes of evil”]—this is not Christian, but properly Hieracite and Manichaean.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

To equate marriages with consecrated virginity, or to believe that those who abstain from wine or meat out of love for disciplining the body gain no merit, is not Christian but Jovinianist. [Thus the manuscript; others: “Consecrated virginity, however.”]

## CHAPTER LXIX

With complete faith we must believe that blessed Mary, the mother of God Christ, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin after childbirth. Nor should we accept the blasphemy of Helvidius, who said: “She was a virgin before childbirth, but not a virgin after childbirth.”

## CHAPTER LXX

We should not believe that the elements—that is, heaven and earth—will be destroyed by fire, but that they will be changed for the better; nor that the form of the world—that is, its appearance, not its substance—will pass away. [Col. 0997A]

## CHAPTER LXXI

It is good to distribute one’s resources to the poor with wise administration. It is better to give them all at once for the purpose of following the Lord [Manuscript: “once”] and, freed from anxiety, to suffer want with Christ.

## CHAPTER LXXII

A man who has been the husband of two married women after baptism is not to be ordained a cleric. Nor is one who had one woman but a concubine rather than a married woman [Manuscript: “not,” instead of “but”]. Nor is one who took a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute in marriage. Nor is one who, overcome by anger or by a reasonable or unreasonable fear, mutilated any member of his own body. Nor is one who is convicted of having accepted interest, or is known to have performed on the stage [Manuscript: “is proved”]. Nor is one who publicly mourns mortal crimes. Nor is one who at some time became insane in a frenzy [The word is unusually used for “driven into a frenzy.” Vincent of Lérins likewise says in *On Heresies*, chapter 5: “to hurl himself into frenzies”], or was afflicted by the oppression of the devil. Nor is one who, through ambition, offers money in imitation of Simon Magus.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

We believe that the bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed martyrs, are to be honored with the greatest sincerity as though they were members of Christ, and that the basilicas called by their names, as holy places dedicated to divine worship, are to be visited with the deepest affection and the most faithful devotion. If anyone acts against this judgment, he is considered not a Christian but an Eunomian and a Vigilantian. [Manuscript: “is to be considered.”] [Col. 0997D]

## CHAPTER LXXIV

We believe that the only path of salvation is for the baptized. We do not believe that any catechumen, even one who has died in good works, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, in which all the sacraments of baptism are completed.

The person to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest and, when questioned, responds; the martyr does the same before the persecutor: he confesses his faith and responds when questioned. After confession, the former is either sprinkled with water or immersed; the martyr is either sprinkled with blood or touched by fire. The former receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; the latter becomes a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in him. [Manuscript: “a place of habitation.”] The former shares in the Eucharist in commemoration of the Lord’s death; the latter dies together with Christ himself. The former confesses that he will renounce the world’s activities; the latter renounces life itself. All sins are forgiven the former; in the latter they are extinguished. [Col. 0997C–0998A]

## CHAPTER LXXV

In the Eucharist, pure water ought not to be offered, as some are deceived by an appearance of sobriety, but wine mixed with water. For wine was part of the mystery of our redemption, when he said: “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on” (Matt. XXVI, 29); and wine mixed with water—not the water given after the meal, but the water that flowed with blood from his side pierced by the spear (John XIX, 30, 31)—shows wine expressed from the vine of his true flesh together with water. [Col. 0998A]

## CHAPTER LXXVI

Our flesh is good, and very good, since it was created by the one good God. It is not evil, as the Sethian, Ophian, and Patrician maintain [Manuscript: “Thimoteans and Priscillians”]; nor is it the cause of evil, as Florianus taught; nor is it compounded from evil and good, as the Manichaean blasphemes. But although it is good by creation, it becomes good or evil for us through the choice of the soul [Manuscript: “of the mind”], not through a change of substance but through the reward of its actions. For it is the flesh itself that will stand before the tribunal of Christ, where the soul may bear what belongs to its own body according to what it has done, whether good or evil (Cor. V, 10). [Col. 0998B]

## CHAPTER LXXVII

At the resurrection from the dead, the form of the sexes will not be changed. A dead man will rise in the form of a man, and a woman in the form of a woman, although lacking the condition of the sexes that exists in this life—not their natural appearance—lest the resurrection be unreal if what rises is not what falls.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

Before the Lord’s passion and resurrection, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the obligation arising from Adam’s transgression, until, by the authority of the Lord, they were freed from servile bondage through his undeserved death. [Thus the manuscript.] [Col. 0998D]

## CHAPTER LXXIX

After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the souls of all the saints are with Christ, and when they leave the body they go to Christ [The manuscript adds: “as it is written: The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God”], awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with him they may be changed into complete and everlasting blessedness.

The souls of sinners likewise, placed under fear in hell, await the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with the devil himself they may be thrust into eternal punishment. [Manuscript: “may be converted.”] [Col. 0998C]

## CHAPTER LXXX

We unhesitatingly believe that penance abolishes sins, even if someone repents of his offenses in the final breath of life and his sins are disclosed through public lamentation. For God’s purpose, by which he determined to save what had perished (Luke XIX, 7), remains immovable. Therefore, because his will does not change, whether through amendment of life, if time is granted, or through humble confession, if life is immediately ended [Manuscript: “public confession”], forgiveness of sins is to be confidently expected from him who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn from perdition through repentance and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live (Ezek. XIX, 23; XXXIII, 11). [Col. 0999A] If anyone thinks otherwise about God’s most just mercy, he is not a Christian but a Novatian.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

We are certain that the devil does not see the inward thoughts of the soul, but through experience we have learned that he infers them from bodily movements and the indications of emotions. The secrets of the heart, however, are known only to the one of whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of human beings” (I Kings VIII, 40).

## CHAPTER LXXXII

Not all our evil thoughts are always aroused by the devil’s instigation; sometimes they emerge from a movement of our own free will. Good thoughts, however, are always from God.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

[“Demons through *energeia*.” Thus the manuscript; others have “through energetic operation,” incorrectly.] [Col. 0999B]

We do not believe that demons, through *ἐνέργεια* (*energeia*, “operation” or “activity”), enter the soul substantially, but that they are united to it through application and oppression. To enter the mind belongs only to the one who created it: subsisting incorporeally by nature, he is capable of entering his own creation. [Manuscript: “induces.”] [Col. 0999B]

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

We have learned from God himself that even sinners can perform signs, wonders, and healings in the Lord’s name. When they help others through this presumption, they harm themselves through ambition for human glory, because they glory in a gift falsely attributed to them rather than one owed to their merits.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

We rightly believe that a Christian can become renowned through signs and wonders and yet not holy, if he lives with intemperate and harsh conduct; but that through temperate and peaceful conduct, even without the efficacy of signs, he can become holy, perfect, and a man of God. [Col. 1000A]

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

No holy and just person is without sin, yet because of this he does not cease to be just or holy, provided that he holds holiness with sincere devotion. For we acquire holiness not through the powers of human nature but through the assistance of our purpose, by God’s grace. Therefore all the saints truthfully declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to mourn—if not a reproach of conscience, then certainly the instability and mutability of their transgressive nature. [Col. 1000B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

Easter, that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, cannot be celebrated in the same month before the passage of the spring equinox and before the completion of the fourteenth moon. [Manuscript: “of the sixteenth”; “beginning.”] [Col. 1000B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

Against the novel legislators who say that only the soul was created in the image of God, so that, since God is rightly believed to be incorporeal, the soul too might be believed incorporeal, we freely confess that the image is found in eternity and the likeness in conduct.

[Col. 0999]

# ELMENHORST’S NOTES TO THE BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL DOGMAS

[Col. 0999C] 97 [Gennadius] Walafrid Strabo, Algerus, Peter Lombard, Thomas Aquinas, Platina, and the Florentine manuscript codex most correctly identify the author of this little book in this way, as the most learned man Fridericus Lindenbrogius, an eyewitness to the matter, informed us.

[On Ecclesiastical Dogmas] That is, “on ecclesiastical opinions.” Augustine, vol. IV, book I of *Questions on the Gospels*, question 11: “Dogmas are the opinions of sects.” Diogenes Laertius, book III, on Plato, p. 217: “*Dogma* is called this in two senses: both what is believed and belief itself. Of these, what is believed is a proposition, while belief is an apprehension.”

Greek: Δόγμα δὲ ἑκατέρως καλεῖται, τό τε δοξαζόμενον καὶ ἡ δόξα αὐτή· τούτων δὲ τὸ μὲν δοξαζόμενον, πρότασις ἐστὶν, ἡ δὲ δόξα, ὑπόληψις.

Before Gennadius, Musanus and Didymus of Alexandria also wrote on ecclesiastical dogmas, but their brief works perished along with them. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.

## CHAPTER ONE

“We believe that there is one God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0999D]

He begins with the common rule of faith, which he sets against all heresies as a foundation. Gregory Nazianzen, *On Faith*, Oration 49. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 25. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1. Guitmund, *On the Trinity*, vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*. Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo, vol. III, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 1; *On Time*, sermons 195 and 125. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 8. Pope Gregory, *Decretals*, part I, title 1. Athanasius, *Exposition of the Faith*, fol. 394 and following. Second Council of Constantinople, chapter 7. First Council of Toledo, chapter 21. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 1. Lateran Council, chapter 1. Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 23. The author of *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 1, in Augustine, vol. III. Victor, *Exposition of the Faith*, vol. V of the *Library of the Fathers*, fol. 457. Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book III, fol. 54. Ferrandus the deacon, *Exhortation to Reginus*, fol. 1893, in the appendix to the *Library of the Fathers*. Edict of the emperor Justinian on the faith, vol. I of the *Greek-Roman Law*, fol. 521. Third Council of Arles, chapter 1. Council of Worms, chapter 1. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Institution of Clerics*, book II, chapter 57. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 1. [Col. 1000C]

[One God] He says that there is one God so that no one may accept three gods with the Tritheists, or several gods with the polytheistic pagans. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, *Responses to the Arians*, fols. 30 and 33; *To Donatus*, fol. 91. Deuteronomy VI, 4. Isaiah XLII, 10; XLIV, 8. II Corinthians VIII, 6; Ephesians IV, 5; I Timothy II, 5. Ignatius, *To the Philadelphians*, epistle 5, p. 23. Justin Martyr, *Exposition of the Faith*, fol. 292. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 5. Cyril, *Exposition of the Nicene Creed*, fol. 204.

Peter Chrysologus, *On the Apostles’ Creed*, sermon 60: “The Christian faith believes in one God in the Trinity: it knows the Father, it knows the Son, it knows the Holy Spirit; it knows no gods. The Godhead is threefold in persons, but the Godhead is one in the Trinity; the Trinity is distinct in persons, not divided in substances. God is one, but in Trinity; God is alone, but not solitary. The Godhead is neither divided by the Trinity nor confused by unity.”

Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 3: “The Father is one God, the Son is one God, the Holy Spirit is one God; not three gods, but one God, threefold in names, one in the deity of the substance.”

[The Father, because he has a Son] Against the Muslims, who say that God has no son. Qurʾān, sūra XI, fol. 37; sūra XX, fol. 70; sūra XXVIII, fol. 94; sūra XXXI, fol. 140; sūra XXXIII, fol. 111; sūra XXXV, fol. 114; sūra XLVII, fol. 104; sūra XLIX, fol. 143; sūra CXXII, fol. 788. John VI Cantacuzenus, emperor of Constantinople, *Oration 3 against Muhammad*. *Saracenica* of Commelinus, p. 2. St Clement, *First Epistle to James, the brother of the Lord*, vol. I of the Councils, fol. 30: “When you hear ‘Father,’ recognize that he truly has a Son begotten, just as someone is called a possessor who possesses something.” [Col. 1001B] Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 7 for the Enlightened*, fol. 85. Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 99, sermon 38. Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, fol. 158. Chrysostom, vol. III, *On the Holy Trinity*. Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, in Jerome, vol. IX, fol. 74. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 23, In Praise of the Philosopher Heron*. Hilary, book III, *On the Trinity*. Phoebadius, *Against the Arians*. Ambrose, *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, chapter 5, fol. 91. Chrysologus, sermons 57, 58, 59, 60. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 10. Baeticus, *On the Faith*.

[The Son, because he has the Father] Bede, *Exposition of Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews*, chapter 1, fol. 1056: “The Son of God is called this inasmuch as he has the Father, inasmuch as he has one from whom he is; not inasmuch as the Father existed first and the Son afterward.” Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 11 for the Enlightened*, fol. 79. Gregory Baeticus, *On the Faith*. Fulgentius, *Against the Objections of the Arians*, fol. 27. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 4, On Theology*. Jerome, on Psalm XVII.

[The Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son] [Col. 1001C] The mission of the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, as the Roman Church rightly approves and believes, against the common error of the Greeks, who affirm that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. Psellus, *On the Theological Chapters*, p. 157, chapter 10: “The holy and catholic Church teaches dogmatically that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten from the Father, and the Spirit proceeding from the Father alone, but not also from the Son?” And Cyril, *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 10. *Graeco-Roman Law*, vol. I, fol. 440. Council of Nicaea. First Council of Constantinople, chapter 7. Epiphanius, at the end of the *Ancoratus*. Anastasius, *On the Dogmas of the Faith*, fol. 674. Gregory of Nazianzus, *On the Holy Lights*, oration 39. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 9. Theophylact of Bulgaria, archbishop, on John, chapter 3. See the Council of Florence, vol. III of the Councils, session 18 and following; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 11; Durandus, book I, distinction 11, question 1; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part I, question 36, article 1; Bonaventure, *On Peter Lombard’s Sentences*, book I, distinction 11, question 1. Marcialis, bishop, *Epistle to the People of Bordeaux*, chapter 10: “The Spirit of the Lord is neither begotten, nor made, nor created, but proceeds from the Father and the Word.” The author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 11: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son. For the Son says, ‘When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father.’ There he taught that it is his own Spirit, because he himself is the truth.” [100] Our prophetic and apostolic teaching also commends to us that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. For Isaiah says of the Son, “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the Spirit of his lips he will slay the wicked.” Of this the Apostle also says, “Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the Spirit of his mouth.” The only-begotten Son of God himself, likewise indicating that the Spirit is the Spirit of his mouth, after the resurrection breathed upon the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Isidore of Seville, *Epistle to Claudius*, fol. 694. Cyprian, *On the Holy Spirit*, fol. 437. Hilary, book VIII, *On the Trinity*. [Col. 1002A] Gregory the Great, vol. II, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 26. Bede, *Summer Homilies on Time*, fol. 46. *On the Philosophical Elements*, book I, fol. 313. Jerome, *On Isaiah*, book XVI, chapter 57, and vol. III, *To Hedibia*, question 9. First Council of Toledo, chapter 21. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 1. *Canonical Corpus*, part III, distinction 5, *On Consecration*. Fourth Lateran Council, chapter 1. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book II, chapter 57. Author of *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 54. Author of *The Mirror*, chapter 18, in Augustine, vol. IX. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapter 26 and following; vol. V, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapter 19; *On the Faith and the Creed*, chapter 1. Author of *On the Trinity and the Unity of God*, chapter 1, in Augustine, vol. IV, fol. 673.

[The Father is the principle of the Godhead] The ancient Greek and Latin theologians establish the Father as the principle of the Son and the source of “the river of righteousness” (τοῦ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ποταμοῦ), according to causality (κατὰ τὸ αἴτιον), not because the Father is prior to the Son either in time or in nature. For the Son is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, light from light, true God from true God, “maker of the ages, not subject to time” (ποιητὴς χρόνων οὐχ ὑπὸ χρόνον). [Col. 1002B] “But if we say that the Father is the beginning and the greater of the Son, we do not imply that he is prior to the Son in time or in nature—for through him he made the ages—nor in anything else, except according to causality; that is, because the Son was begotten from the Father, and the Father was not begotten from the Son, and because the Father is naturally the cause of the Son, just as we do not say that fire proceeds from light, but light from fire. Therefore, when we hear that the Father is the beginning and greater of the Son, let us understand it according to causality. And just as we do not say that fire is of one substance and light of another, so it is impossible to say that the Father and the Son are of different substances, but they are of one and the same substance.” Since, however, the Son exists from the Father by generation, these properties are not attributed to him: that he is without beginning (ἄναρχος), without cause (ἀναίτιος), or unbegotten (ἀγέννητος). Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 11*, p. 237. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, *Dialogue 2*, pp. 107 and 111. Hilary, book IX, *On the Holy Trinity*. Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 8, p. 37 and following. Basil the Great, book I, *Against Eunomius*. [Col. 1002C] John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 9. Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *On Ecclesiastes*, book VI, chapter 2: “The Father is the origin of the Godhead.” Author of *On the Spirit and the Soul*, in Augustine, vol. III, fol. 635: “The Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit is simultaneously from the Father and the Son.” John Theophilus, *Exposition of the Nicene Creed*, vol. [Thus the Father was never not Father] These are the words of Arius: “God was not always Father, but there was a time when God alone existed and was not yet Father; afterward, when he came into being, he became Father” (Athanasius, *Disputation 2 against the Arians*). A most evident testimony against the blasphemies of Arius, who, seized by impiety, dared to assert that the Father had not always been Father. Athanasius, vol. I, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, fol. 144 and following; vol. II, fol. 33. Damascene, *Against the Manichaeans*, p. 239; *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 8. [101] Epiphanius, *Against the Sabellians*, heresy 62, in the *Ancoratus*, fol. 326. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 4, On Theology*. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 8. Socrates Scholasticus, book I, chapter 3. *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 13. Gennadius, in *Syagrius*.

[From whom the Son was born] Caesarius, *Dialogue 1*. Gregory of Nazianzus, *On the Nicene Faith*, *On the Holy Lights*, oration 39. Augustine, *Questions on the Trinity*, vol. III, fol. 739. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 9; book IV, chapter 7.

[The Holy Spirit was not born] Ambrose, *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, chapter 3, fol. 89: “What is neither born nor made is the Father, for he is from no one. What is born and not made is the Son, who was begotten from the Father. But what is neither born nor made is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Alcuin, *On the Doctrine of the Faith*, in the appendix to the *Library of the Fathers*, fol. 1924. Question: Why should the Holy Spirit not be called unbegotten or begotten? Answer: Because if he were called unbegotten like the Father, two fathers could be supposed; if begotten, two sons.
