Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 18; book IV, chapter 7.

[The Father is unbegotten] The Greek and Latin Fathers commonly call God the Father causeless (ἀναίτιον), without beginning (ἄναρχον), unbegotten (ἀγέννητον)—devoid of cause and principle, not born, unbegotten. Justin Martyr, *Exposition of the Faith*, fol. 292. Basil the Great, *Against Eunomius*. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, *Dialogue 2*, pp. 106, 111. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 11*, fol. 237. Cyril of Alexandria, [Col. 1003B] *Questions and Answers*, p. 122; *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 9. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 9, and *Questions*, p. 138. Psellus, *Theological Chapters*, chapters 1 and 10. These words, however, are not found in Holy Scripture but are gathered from it, as Gregory of Nazianzus says, *Oration 5, On Theology*. Nicetas, on Nazianzenus, vol. II, fol. 927. Augustine, *To Pascentius*, epistle 174. Epiphanius, *Against Aetius*, heresy 76. Athanasius, *Disputation against Arius*, vol. II, fol. 374, writes: “When the Sabellian heresy wished to assert that the Father had been begotten from a virgin, the Church, in confessing ‘unbegotten’ against this, handed down the Father.” In book II of the *Dialogue on the Holy Trinity*, fols. 160, 161, 162, and 164, together with Epiphanius, *Against the Semi-Arians*, heresy 73, and Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, chapters 8 and 9, he plainly rejects the word ἀγέννητον (by which Aetius and Arius strove to prove that the Father was of one substance and the Son of another, since the one was called unbegotten and the other begotten), and affirms that the Father should be called not “unbegotten” but “Father,” in accordance with Holy Scripture. [Col. 1003C]

[The Son is coeternal with the Father] Fulgentius, *Against the Objections of the Arians*, fol. 27: “What the Father is, the Son also is, because God is from God, perfect from perfect, immense from immense, omnipotent from omnipotent; the Son, born from the eternal Father, is coeternal.” See Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 5; Augustine, vol. VI, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, fol. 454. Author of *The Five Heresies*, fol. 30. Author of *On the Trinity and the Unity*, chapter 5.

[The Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son] Augustine, *On the Faith and the Creed*, vol. III, fol. 102, chapter 9: “The Holy Spirit is not of a lesser nature than the Father and the Son, but, so to speak, consubstantial and coeternal, because this Trinity is one God.” See John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapters 10 and 18.

[The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says] Honorius, *On Heresies*: “The Sabellians assert one person of the Father, [102] Son, and Holy Spirit.” Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heretics*, chapter 34. Didymus of Alexandria, on the First Epistle of John, chapter 5. Victor, *On the Catholic Faith*. Cassian, *On the Incarnation of Christ*, book I. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book I. [Col. 1003D] Epiphanius, heresies 62, 69. Leontius, *On the Sects*, p. 437. Caesarius, brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, *Dialogue 1*. Harmenopulus, *On the Sects*, p. 589. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5. Philastrius, heresy 54. John the Monk, *Canon against All Heresies*, vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*. Theodoret, book II, *Fables of Heretics*. Fulgentius, *On the Orthodox Faith to Donatus*, fol. 94. Faustinus, *On the Faith against the Arians*, fol. 770. Baeticus, *On the Faith*. Nicephorus Callistus, book VI, chapter 25. Pope Leo, *Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord*, p. 37. Ambrose, *On the Apostles’ Creed*, chapter 2.

[The Godhead is neither separated nor divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes] Proclus, *On the Faith to the Armenians*, fol. 413: “Let us flee the madness of Arius, who divides the Trinity, inseparable in substance.” Cyril, on John, book VII, chapter 10. Athanasius, vol. I, fol. 444; *On the Incarnation of [Col. 1004A] Christ*, fol. 490; *Oration 5 against the Arians*, fol. 323. Honorius, *Catalogue of Heresies*. Caesarius, *Dialogue*. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5. Emperor Manuel’s *Embassy to the Armenians*, pp. 57 and 89. Epiphanius, heresy 69. Augustine, heresy 49.

[The Son is another in person] Against the heretics called the followers of Aeschines (κατὰ Αἰσχίνην). Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 52: “Those who are called followers of Aeschines have this private blasphemy: they say that Christ himself is both Son and Father.” See Augustine, *On the Faith and the Creed*, chapter 9.

[But the Father is another in person, and the Son another in person] Lombard, book I, distinction 2: “Let us hold that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Yet the Father is not himself the Son, nor is the Son himself the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the Father or the Son. For the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, which the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον, ‘consubstantial’; in it the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.” [Col. 1004B] Augustine, *To Maximus the Physician*, epistle 66; *On Time*, sermon 38. Anastasius, *On the Dogmas of the Faith* [103], fol. 676. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2. Hilary, book I, *On the Holy Trinity*. Vincent of Lérins, *On Heresies*, chapter 19.

[The Holy Spirit is another in person] Against Urbicus of Potentia, who said that the Holy Spirit was either the Father or the Son, or certainly a creature. Athanasius of Alexandria, vol. II, fol. 417.

[The Father is one God by nature in the Holy Trinity] Author of *The Faith to Peter the Deacon*, in Augustine, vol. III, chapter 1, fol. 149: “Above all, and without doubt, retain with your whole heart that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and ineffable Trinity—are naturally one God, and so forth.” Athanasius, *Rescript to Pope Liberius*, fol. 398. Jerome, *On Those Things Attributed to God in Holy Scripture*, vol. IX, fol. 67. Gregory of Nazianzus, *In Praise of Heron*, oration 23; *On [Col. 1004C] the Faith*, oration 49. Caesarius, *Dialogue 1*. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book I, chapter 11. Cerealis, bishop, *Against Maximinus the Arian*, chapter 2. Psellus, *Theological Chapters*, chapter 1. Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 38.

## CHAPTER II

[The Father did not assume flesh] Against the Patripassians and the madness of Praxeas, who said that the Father descended into the Virgin, was born from her himself, and himself suffered. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 1; *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 53. Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, in Jerome, vol. IX, fol. 75. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Trinity*, chapter 4. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, p. 270 and following. Author of *The Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, fol. 150, in Augustine, vol. III. Marius Victorinus, *Against Arius*, book I, fol. 305. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book I. John Damascene, *On the Two Wills of Christ*, fol. 488; *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 4. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 45. Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, [Col. 1004D] *Sentences*, book III, distinction 1. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book I: “The dispensation of the assumed flesh pertains neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Son alone; for it was the Son, not the Father, who was properly born from the Virgin.”

[He himself would become in man the Son of man] Ferrandus the deacon, *Exhortation to Count Reginus*: “The Father, who was never the Son, was not born from a human being according to the flesh; nor was the Holy Spirit, who was never at any time either Father or Son. But the Son was born, so that he himself might become the son of the virgin mother, who is the Son of God the Father.”

[104 The Son of God became the son of man] See John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 4.

[Not by adoption, not by appellation] Against Felix of Urgel and Elipandus, bishops of Toledo, who asserted that Christ, insofar as concerns his humanity, should be called the adopted Son of God, not his proper and natural Son. Caesar Baronius, vol. IX of the *Annals*, [Col. 1005A] under the year of Christ 783, fol. 357. Adelmus Benedictine, *Annals of the Frankish Kingdom*, under the year of the Lord 792, fol. 399. Hilary of Poitiers, bishop, *On the Trinity*, book V: “The Son of God is not a false God, nor an adopted God, nor a so-called God, but true God.” See Paulinus of Aquileia, bishop, *Against Felix of Urgel*, fol. 435, vol. V of the *Library of the Fathers*. Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, book III, fol. 26; *To King Thrasamund*, book III, fol. 54. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 11*, fol. 80.

[Therefore, not two Christs nor two sons] He attacks the abominable error of Nestorius and Paul of Samosata, who say that there are two Christs and two sons: one servant, the other lord; one capable of suffering, the other incapable of suffering. Theodotus, bishop of Ancyra, *Sermon against Nestorius*, in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 260. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book II. Emperor Manuel’s *Embassy to the Armenians*, pp. 39, 45, 51, 59, 163, 179. Harmenopulus, *On the Sects*, p. 165. Cyril of Alexandria, [Col. 1005B] *Argument against the Nestorians*, p. 2; *On the Right Faith to the Emperor Theodosius*, in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 14; *Epistle to Bishop Succensus*, fols. 262, 270, and vol. IV, *To Bishop Acacius*; epistle 29 to John of Antioch, in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, vol. V, chapter 9. Theodore the presbyter, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, p. 233. Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapters 17 and 18. Elias of Crete, on Gregory of Nazianzus, fol. 1011. Gregory of Nazianzus, oration 31, and epistle 1 to Cledonius, fol. 739: “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, the second from the mother, and not one and the same Son, let him also fall away from that adoption as sons which has been promised to those who rightly believe. For although God and man are two natures, just as soul and body are, there are not two sons, nor two gods; for here too there are not two men, even though Paul called the inner and outer parts of man by these names.” [Col. 1005C] That is: “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, the other from the mother, and not one and the same, let him be excluded also from that adoption as sons which has been promised to believers. Although God and man are two natures, just as soul and body are, there are nevertheless not two sons or gods; just as here too there are not two men, although Paul called the inner and outer part of man in this way.”

Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book I: “We confess one God, and the same one the Son of God and the son of man, not two; and in this way the Word consecrated for himself the beginnings of flesh within the hidden recesses of the virgin womb, yet the nature of the Word was not changed into flesh. Likewise, through the union of the flesh with the one who assumed it, the nature of the flesh passed into the person of the Word, yet was not consumed in the Word. For both remain—that is, the nature of the Word and of the flesh—and from these two natures, which still remain, there is one Christ and one person.” See Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Right Faith to the Emperor Theodosius*, in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 17; *That Jesus Christ Is One Son of God and Lord*, fol. 59; *On the Right Faith to the Queens*, fol. 70. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, vol. XI, fol. 219, sermon 14.

[We call him the Only-Begotten] Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, [Col. 1005D] book I, chapter 9: “He is called only-begotten (μονογενής) because he alone was uniquely begotten from the Father alone. For no other generation resembles the generation of the Son of God; nor is there another Son of God.” Book IV, chapter 8. Chrysostom, *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*, vol. V, fol. 988. Theodoret, *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, fol. 393. Augustine, *On the Faith and the Creed*, vol. III, fol. 166; *On Time*, sermon 38. Theophylact, on Matthew, chapter 1. Pope Damasus, *Epistle to Paulinus of Antioch*, vol. I of the Councils, fol. 381. Hilary, *On the Holy Trinity*, books III and IV. Gregory Baeticus, *On the Faith*. Fulgentius, *Response against the Arians*, fol. 30; *To King Thrasamund*, book III, fol. 54. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Properties of Sermons*, book IV, chapter 10.

[With the natures unconfused] Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book III, fol. 58: “In one and the same Christ the true nature of divinity and the true nature of humanity remained, while God, not confused with man but united to him, displayed in one person [Col. 1006A] the signs of both natures as they remained, so that the true God, full of true and divine powers, might shine forth in the man assumed, and the reality of human weakness might show the true and complete man in God. —When the transaction of our redemption was being accomplished, it was fitting that the complete and true God should be united to a complete and true man, yet in such a way that, in the unity of the person, neither God in man nor man in God could be confused.”

John Damascene, *Oration against the Acephali*, fol. 573: “From perfect divinity and perfect humanity there came to be one Christ, one Son, the same one of God and man, one Lord, the same perfect God and perfect man, wholly God and wholly man, with the natures united to one another without confusion, without alteration, and without separation. Without confusion, indeed, because each nature retains its own distinction: divinity retains the uncreated, humanity the created; divinity the impassible, humanity the passible, and the like. Without alteration, because each nature remained unaltered, not changed into the other, nor did one composite nature come into existence [Col. 1006B] from them; rather, there are two natures, existing and enduring forever. Without separation, finally, because they are united to one another hypostatically, possessing one hypostasis—the one that was eternal, incorporeal, and simple, but in the last times was immutably embodied from the holy and ever-virgin.” The same passage: “From perfect Godhead and perfect humanity one Christ was made, one Son, the same Son of God and of man, one Lord, the same perfect God and perfect man, wholly God and wholly man, the natures being united to one another without confusion, without change, and without separation. Without confusion, because each nature retains its own proper distinction: Godhead, its uncreated and impassible character; humanity, its created and passible character, and the like. Without change, because each nature remained unaltered, not transformed into the other, nor was one composite nature fashioned from them; rather, the two true natures are and will remain forever. Without separation, finally, because they are united to one another hypostatically, having one hypostasis, which, though eternal, incorporeal, and simple, was in the last times immutably incarnate from the holy and ever-Virgin.” [Col. 1006C] And *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 3; book IV, chapter 9. Peter the deacon, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 2.

[The Timotheans] Danaeus, on Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 90, from the Gembloux manuscript: “The Timotheans say that the Son of God was indeed born a true man from the Virgin Mary, but that he made one person in such a way that he was reduced to one nature. They wished the interior of the Virgin to have been a kind of furnace, through which the two natures—that is, God and man—were dissolved and compacted into one mass, producing one form of God and man, with the property of the natures unchanged but their operations joined. And to confirm this impiety, which asserts that God was changed from his own nature, they compel the testimony of the Evangelist who says, ‘And the Word became flesh,’ interpreting it in this way: the divine nature was changed into the human. O abolition that assails that inviolable substance! The originator of this impiety, Timothy, now exiled at Byza in Bithynia, deceives many under the appearance of an honorable and religious life. Samuel, formerly presbyter of the Church of Edessa, [Col. 1006D] opposed his madness, showing that the Word became flesh while the Word remained in its own substance and man in his own nature, and that by association, not commixture, they produced one person of the Son of God.” Gennadius of Marseille, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, under Samuel.

[God assumed man] That is, as Augustine says, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 2: “God the Word took the nature of man, not a person.” For to say the contrary—namely, that a person remaining in its own personhood was assumed—is the error of Nestorius, who posited two persons or two supposita in Christ; whereas “the one who clings to God is one spirit.” This error was condemned at the Council of Chalcedon. See Durandus, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 5, question 1. Peter Lombard, book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 5. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 1. Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book III. Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 14. Augustine, *To Maximus the Physician*, [Col. 1007A] epistle 66. Sophronius, *On the Assumption of Saint Mary*, in Jerome, vol. IX, fol. 49. Peter the deacon, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 5. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book II, chapter 31. Thomas Aquinas, part III, question 4, article 2 and following.

[Man passed into God] A harsh expression, like that of Augustine to Volusianus, vol. II, epistle 3, fol. 7: “God was mingled with man”; and that of Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 27: “The Son, arbiter and minister of the Father, mingling man and God in himself.”

[Not by a changeability of nature, as the Apollinarists say] The Apollinarists said that the Word (Λόγος) was changed into flesh through transmutation. Theodore the presbyter, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, books I and II. Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, fol. 386. Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 3. Athanasius, vol. I, fols. 479 and 249. Cyril of Alexandria, vol. IV, *Epistle to Nestorius*, fol. 29. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XII, chapter 4.

[108 So that God was not changed into human substance] [Col. 1007B] Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund of the Vandals*, book III, fol. 58: “From the very beginning of the virginal conception, personal unity remained in Christ, and the unconfused truth of both natures endured in such a way that neither could man be torn away from God nor God separated from the man he had assumed; yet God did not consume man, nor did man change God in any respect. A little later: ‘Thus the true God assumed true man, so that in the reality of the human assumption he did not lose the truth of his divinity. Thus he deigned to become what he had not previously been, without ceasing to be what he had always been. Thus God also willed to have one person with man; and although Christ God was not one person and Christ man another, true God nevertheless remained in man, and true man remained in God. Thus in one Christ there was the perfection of the divine and human nature, equally unconfused and undivided.’” See Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 28. Pope Hormisdas, *Decrees*, chapter 3.

[Not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says] The Ebionites thought that Christ [Col. 1007C] was merely a man and had been produced by ordinary birth from a man and a woman. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 27. Theodoret, book II, *Fables of Heretics*, in the *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, fol. 402. Philastrius, heresy 37. Epiphanius, heresy 30. Saint Ignatius, epistle 9. Origen, on Luke, chapter 11, homily 17.

[Drawing flesh from the body of the Virgin] See Bede, on Job, chapter 26.

[Not bringing flesh with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches assert] Marcion, Eutyches, Origen, Apollinaris, and Valentinus fell into this impious error: they believed not only that the Word and flesh had one nature, but also impiously asserted that Christ’s flesh had not been assumed from the body of the holy virgin Mary, but had descended from heaven into the Virgin. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book III. Theophilus of Alexandria, *Paschal Epistle*, vol. I of the *Library of the Fathers*, fol. 371. Athanasius, *On Heresies*, fol. 852. Theodore the presbyter, *On the Incarnation of [Col. 1007D] the Lord*, p. 235. Theophylact of Bulgaria, on John, chapter 3. Suidas, under “Eutyches.” Sedulius, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1. Gennadius of Marseille, presbyter, under Leo, bishop of Rome. Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 49. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis for the Enlightened at Jerusalem*, p. 77: “Believe that this only-begotten Son of God, because of our sins, descended from heaven to earth, assuming the humanity that shares our affections, and was born from the holy Virgin and the Holy Spirit—not in appearance and imagination was the incarnation accomplished, but in truth; nor did he pass through the Virgin as through a tube, but was truly made flesh from her, truly eating as we do and truly drinking as we do. For if the incarnation was a phantom, salvation too was a phantom.” [Col. 1008A] “Believe that this only-begotten Son of God, for our sins, descended from heaven to earth and assumed a humanity subject to the same affections as ours; and he was born from the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit. He assumed humanity neither by opinion nor by fantasy, nor as though passing through the Virgin like a channel, but was truly incarnate from her, truly nourished with milk, and truly eating as we do. For if that incarnation was a phantom, salvation too was a phantom.” Ignatius, epistle 2 to the Trallians and epistle 5 to the Philippians.

[Not in appearance, as Valentinus asserts] Valentinus, Eutyches, Saturninus, Marcion, Basilides, Cerdo, and Manichaeus, preachers of illusion, say that the Son of God, although God, did not substantially exist as a human person, but merely pretended, through some supposed action and manner of life, to be human. Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 20. Vigilius the martyr, *Against Eutyches*, book I. Gennadius of Marseille, presbyter, *On Illustrious Men*, under Bishop Sabbatius. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 17; *Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 49; *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 8. Epiphanius, heresy 30. Arethas of Caesarea in Cappadocia, bishop, on the Apocalypse, chapter 8. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, [Col. 1008B] book VI, chapter 31. Socrates, book I, chapter 17. Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book I. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, *Dialogue 2*. *Against the Fables of Heretics*, book IV, at the end. Emperor Manuel’s *Embassy to the Armenians*, p. 181. Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenian*, book IV. Damascene, *On Heresies*, fol. 584. Bede, on Luke, book VI, chapter 23. Basil the Great, *To the Sozopolitans*, epistle 65.

[The soul was not without sensation and reason, as the Apollinarists say] Honorius, *On Heresies*: “The Apollinarists say that Christ assumed only a body without a soul and had the Godhead in place of a soul.” Theodoret, book IV, *Fables of Heretics*, in the *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, fol. 402. Vincent of Lérins, [110] *Against Heresies*, chapters 17 and 22. Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 4. Socrates, book II, chapter 36. Augustine, *On Eighty-Three Questions*, vol. IV, question 80; *On the Christian Contest*, chapter 19. Theodoret, *Dialogue 2*. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 20. Cyril, on John, book VI, chapter 7. Cassian, book I, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*. Leontius, *On the Sects*, p. 447. Harmenopulus, [Col. 1008C] p. 559. Paulinus, epistle 25. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Epistle to Cledonius*. Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, vol. I. Suidas, under “Apollinaris.” Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 5, article 3. Emperor Manuel’s *Embassy to the Armenians*, pp. 179 and 183. Theodore the presbyter, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, p. 231. Theophylact, on John, chapter 1, and on Matthew, chapter 2.

[Flesh without a soul, as Eunomius says] Eunomius preached that the flesh had been changed into divinity. Honorius of Autun, bishop, *On Heresies*.

[He truly endured the pains of his flesh in the Passion and before the Passion]

Against the followers of Muhammad, the Simonian, Basilidian, Marcite, Cerdonian, Marcionite, Apellite, Docetic, and Manichaean heresies, who assert that Christ suffered only fictitiously and apparently, not truly. Philastrius, *On Heresies* 32, 42, 44, 45, 61. Augustine, *On Heresies* 1, 4, 14, 20, 23, 46. The Saracen materials published by Commelinus in the year 1595. Qur’an, surah XI, fol. 37. John Cantacuzenus, *Apology 2 against the Muslims*. Cyril of Alexandria, *Anathema 12*:

> If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, let him be accursed.

He interprets this anathema in his booklet to Evoptius, vol. IV, fol. 219:

> No one should foolishly doubt or fear that the sacramental expression declares the nature of the Son to be passible when it says that he suffered in the flesh. For the sufferings of his own body truly became his own. Holy Peter appears to hold this view also when he says: “Since Christ therefore suffered for us in the flesh.” It is one thing to say “to suffer in the flesh,” and another simply to say “the nature of the deity suffers.” Since the same person is both God and man, he is impassible with respect to the nature of his deity, but passible according to his humanity. What absurdity is there in saying that he suffered in that which can suffer, while he remained impassible in that which cannot suffer?

In the acts of the Council of Ephesus, vol. I, chapter 5, fol. 57:

> Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh. For since Christ is God, the disciple wisely and prudently says that he suffered in the flesh, thereby excluding from suffering the ineffable nature, to which suffering is foreign. The Word from God therefore suffered in his own flesh, although he is accustomed to be free from suffering. Christ, then, is God: divine in nature he is impassible, but passible according to the flesh.

“Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh.” Since Christ is true God, the disciple rightly and wisely affirms that he suffered in the flesh. By this expression he exempted that immeasurable nature, upon which no suffering falls, from every form of suffering. He therefore suffered in his own flesh. For the Word of God, considered in himself, is incapable of any suffering. Christ, accordingly, is God: according to his divine nature he cannot suffer at all, but according to his human nature he can.

*Letter 10 to Nestorius*, fol. 30:

> We confess that the very same person who is the Son begotten from God the Father, the only-begotten God, although impassible according to his own nature, nevertheless suffered in the flesh for us according to the Scriptures, so that he appropriated to himself the sufferings of his own flesh in the crucified body, and by the grace of God tasted death for all in the body given to him as his own, although according to his own nature he himself is life and resurrection.

In the *Exposition of the Nicene Creed*, fol. 229, vol. IV:

> Without any controversy, the Word of God is impassible insofar as his own nature is concerned; and no one is so bewildered as to think that the nature which is above all things is capable of suffering. But because he became man, he made the flesh that was from the holy Virgin his own. Therefore, following the language of the economy, we affirm that he who is beyond all suffering, as God, suffered in his own flesh in human fashion.

In the acts of the Council of Ephesus, vol. I, chapter 12:

> We say that Christ suffered and rose again, not because God the Word suffered in his own nature, or endured blows, the wounds of nails, or any other injuries—for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering—but because that body which was made his own is said to have suffered all these things for us. God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered. We understand his death in the same way. For God the Word is naturally immortal and incorruptible, life and giver of life. But because his own body, by the grace of God, according to Paul’s saying, tasted death for all, he himself is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because he himself experienced death insofar as his own nature is concerned. To think or say this is madness.

*On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*, chapter 26:

> Christ suffers and does not suffer, in different respects. He suffers in human flesh, because he is man; but as God he remains impassible in his deity.

I have cited these passages of Cyril to refute those men who recklessly assert that he attributed suffering to the deity itself; from that error he was entirely removed. For the one statement—“the Word suffered impassibly”—which they produce from chapter 27 of his work *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, fol. 261, in order to establish their novel doctrine, is so suitably explained by Cyril himself that it gives them no assistance and clearly demonstrates that he did not hold the doctrine of which he is accused. They therefore wrong this wholly innocent man by burdening him with a heresy from which he openly defended himself and which was not his at all, but plainly belonged to the Apollinarians, Theopaschites, Arians, Armenians, Eutyches, Dioscorus, and Severus, as appears from Athanasius, *To Epictetus, against all heresies*, fol. 454; Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* XVI.33 and XVIII.52; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Letter 1 to Cledonius*, fol. 740; John Cantacuzenus, *Apology 2 against the Muslims*; and Saint Nikon, *On the Evil Religion of the Armenians*, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, fol. 456.

The martyr Vigilius likewise improperly refers the suffering proper to Christ’s flesh to the property of the nature of the Word. For in *Against Eutyches* II, fols. 555, 556, and 558, vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, he says:

> The deity also endured the injuries of the Passion.
>
> The deity was pierced with nails, but could not itself be penetrated.
>
> It is evident that God the Word suffered impassibly.
>
> The deity was struck by the injuries of the Passion.

Yet Vigilius subsequently appears to have corrected this error salutarily when he says in book IV:

> The one and same Son of God died according to the form of a servant, and did not die according to the form of God;

and in book II:

> In the form of a servant he endured all the injuries of the Passion. The Word is immortal, and the Passion is according to the flesh. Hence the apostle Peter also says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh.” The Passion therefore belongs properly to the flesh according to nature, but to the Word according to person, because the Word and the flesh have one and the same person.

Eastern and Western bishops vigorously defend the divine nature’s *impassibility* (*apatheia*) in their writings, referring sufferings specifically to the flesh. Junilius, *On the Parts of the Divine Law* I.16. Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus II.28. Acacius, bishop of Melitene, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus VI.11. Nicephorus, bishop of Constantinople, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus V.22. Theodoret, *Dialogues* III, at length. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas* 29. Proclus, *On the Faith, to the Armenians*, fol. 412. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical Preparation* IV.13. Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters* IV, letters 166 and 179. Pope Leo, letter 10 to Flavian. Fulgentius, *To Thrasamund* III, fols. 54, 56, 58, 59, and 60. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith* III.4, 6, 18, and 26. Theophylact of Bulgaria, archbishop, on John 3 and 8. Augustine, *Sermon on the Time* 191. Gregory of Nazianzus, letter to Cledonius; *On the Faith*, oration 49. Philastrius, *On Heresies* 91. Paulinus of Aquileia, *Against Felix of Urgel*, fol. 439. John, bishop of Rome, *On the Two Natures, against Eutyches*. Second Council of Seville, chapter 13. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, in his letter to Deodatus, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. John Cantacuzenus, *Oration 3 against Muhammad*. Pope Gelasius, *Against Nestorius*, fol. 475, vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Paul of Emesa, bishop, *On the Incarnation of Christ*, in Cyril, vol. IV, homily 7, fols. 104–105. Epiphanius, *Against the Ariomaniacs* 69; *Against Aëtius* 76; *Against the Dimaerites* 77. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospel* 25. The author of *On the Faith to Peter* 2.

Paul of Emesa, homily 2 on the Nativity of the Savior, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 278:

> Holy Mary therefore gave birth to Emmanuel, impassible according to his deity, but passible according to his humanity. For although God the Word makes the sufferings of his own body his own and refers them to himself, he nevertheless remains within the bounds of impassibility. Even if you hear him saying, “I gave my back to scourges, my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting,” do not suppose that he suffered anything in his own nature; rather, understand that he appropriated the scourges of his own body. For God the Word remained impassible.

Ambrose, on Luke VI.7, fol. 103:

> Separated from death, the deity did not undergo participation in bodily sufferings.

Book X, chapter 23, fol. 220:

> As Christ was about to ascend the cross, he laid aside his royal garments, so that you might know that he suffered as man, not as God; and although Christ is both, it was as man, not as God, that he was nailed to the cross.

And in *On the Faith to the Emperor Gratian* II.3–4, fol. 136:

> Christ is troubled as man, weeps as man, and is crucified as man. For the apostle Paul also said that they crucified Christ’s flesh. And Peter: “Since Christ suffered according to the flesh.” The flesh therefore suffered, while the deity was free from death; the body, according to the law of human nature, submitted to suffering. Hence, when we read that the Lord of majesty was crucified, we should not think that he was crucified in his own majesty, but because the same person is both God and man—God through his deity and man through the assumption of flesh. Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, is said to have been crucified because, sharing both natures, human and divine, he endured human suffering on earth. Thus, without distinction, the one who suffered is called both the Lord of majesty and the Son of Man, who, as it is written, descended from heaven.

Eranistes, in Theodoret, *Dialogue* III, p. 273:

> We say that God the Word himself suffered impassibly.

Orthodoxus:

> What sane person could tolerate these laughable verbal tricks? No one has ever heard of an impassible suffering or an immortal death. For the impassible does not suffer, and what has suffered cannot remain impassible.

And on p. 287:

> Just as you said that the divine nature descended from heaven, and that it was called Son of Man because of the union, so it is proper to say that the flesh was nailed to the wood, while we confess that the divine nature was not separated from it, whether on the cross or in the tomb; nevertheless, it did not receive suffering from that source, since it is not by nature capable of suffering or death, but possesses an immortal and impassible essence. Thus he also called the crucified one the Lord of glory, assigning the name of the impassible nature to the passible nature, because the latter was his body. Let us also examine this argument. The divine apostle said: “If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” They therefore crucified the nature that they knew, not the nature that they were entirely ignorant of. If they had known the nature of which they were ignorant, they would not have crucified the nature that they knew. Since they were ignorant of the divine nature, they crucified the human nature. Or have you not heard them say: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because, although you are a man, you make yourself God”? By these words they show that they recognized the nature visible to their eyes, but were entirely ignorant of the invisible nature. If they had recognized that nature also, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

Irenaeus says that the divine nature rested during the Passion.

Irenaeus, in Theodoret, *Dialogue* III, p. 293:

> For just as he was man in order to be tempted, so also he was the Word in order to be glorified: the Word remaining at rest while he was tempted, crucified, and dying, but being united with the man when he conquered, endured, showed kindness, rose again, and was taken up.

Damasus, pope, in Theodoret, *Dialogue* III, p. 307:

> If anyone should say: “In the suffering of the cross the Son of God and God himself endured pain, and not the flesh together with the soul which he assumed, nor the form of a servant which he took for himself, as Scripture says,” let him be accursed.

[He truly endured pains in the Passion]

By this the error of Hilary is refuted, since he asserts that Christ felt no pain in the Passion. Hilary, *On the Holy Trinity* X, p. 150:

> Jesus Christ, man and the only-begotten God, through the flesh and the Word, both Son of Man and Son of God, assumed a true man according to the likeness of our humanity, without ceasing to be God. In him, although a blow might fall, a wound descend, bonds be fastened, or suspension raise him up, these things certainly brought the force of suffering, but did not inflict the pain of suffering—just as a weapon might pierce water, prick fire, or wound air. All these sufferings are indeed imposed upon their respective natures, in order to pierce, prick, and wound them, but the nature of the thing does not retain the suffering imposed upon it, since it is not in the nature of water to be pierced, of fire to be pricked, or of air to be wounded, although it is the nature of the weapon to wound, prick, and pierce. The Lord Jesus Christ did suffer when he was struck, suspended, crucified, and died; but when suffering rushed upon the body, it was indeed suffering, yet did not exercise the nature of suffering, while it raged through the ministry of punishment and the body’s power, without sensation of pain, received into itself the force of the pain raging against it.

Claudian Mamertus, bishop, *On the State of the Soul* II.10. Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, *Sentences* III, distinction 17. Cyprian also speaks improperly in his book *On the Vanity of Idols*, fol. 264, concerning Christ’s death, and must be read cautiously:

> The testimony of all the prophets had gone before in this way: Christ had to suffer, not in order to feel death, but in order to conquer it.

Fulgentius speaks more correctly in *To King Thrasamund* III, fol. 54:

> The impassible God experienced true suffering in true flesh;

and on fol. 61:

> Christ possessed sufferings and infirmities that were voluntary, indeed, but real, because he assumed the nature of human flesh not in appearance but in truth.

## CHAPTER III

[That man received the beginning of deity by being born]

The author of *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, in Augustine, vol. III.

[Artemon]

He maintains that Christ was a mere man, that is, a savior existing without God. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.28, in the *Apology for the Origin*, fol. 486. Nicephorus Callistus IV.21. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, *Heretical Fables* II. The imperial embassy of Manuel to the Armenians, p. 181. Augustine, *On Heresies* 44. This is also the doctrine of Carpocrates. Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics* 48.

[Berillus]

He began to teach certain foreign doctrines, alien to the truth, asserting that our Lord and Savior neither existed before the birth of the flesh nor possessed a proper substance of deity, but only that the paternal deity dwelt in him. Nicephorus Callistus V.22. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.24.

[Marcellus]

He ventured to say that the Lord Christ was merely a man. *Tripartite History* III.9. Nicephorus V.22. Marius Victorinus, *Against Arius* I, fol. 294. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* I.24. Sozomen II.31. Basil the Great, letter 78 to Eustathius.

[Born from the Virgin both God and man]

Augustine, vol. X, sermon 1, *On the Assumption of Mary*, fol. 880:

> Christ assumed flesh from the most sacred body of Mary and united the divine nature to the human, without losing what he was but assuming what he was not, so that the Word might become flesh—that is, so that God might become man.

## CHAPTER IV

[Nothing created or servile is to be believed in the Trinity]

Nicetas, on Gregory of Nazianzus, *On Holy Baptism*, fol. 881:

> Nothing in the Trinity is servile, created, or adventitious—that is, something that previously did not exist and then arrived. Therefore the Son was never lacking to the Father, nor the Holy Spirit to the Son; rather, the Holy Trinity is always immutable and free from alteration.

Cyril, vol. II, *That the Holy Spirit is God and not a creature*. Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.25. Harmenopulus, *On the Sects*, p. 559. Athanasius, vol. I, *To Serapion*. Augustine, *To Boniface*, letter 50; *On Heresies* 52. Nicephorus Callistus XI.42. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Properties of Speech* IV.10.

[Dionysius, the source of Arius]

Athanasius demonstrates at length that this Dionysius was falsely accused of Arianism, vol. I, fol. 428 and following. Rufinus, *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, in Jerome, vol. IX, fol. 153. See Caesar Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals* II, under the year of Christ 263, fol. 600.

[Nothing unequal to grace, as with Aëtius]

He likewise held, as Arius did, that the Son was created, made from things that did not exist, and unequal to the Father. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* 36; XI.11. Basil the Great, *Against the Apology of Eunomius* I.

[Nothing unequal, as Eunomius holds]

He asserted that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son. Augustine, *On Heresies* 54. Nicephorus Callistus XI.11. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* X.25. Basil the Great, *Against the Apology of Eunomius*.

[Nothing earlier or later, greater or less, as with Arius]

Athanasius, vol. II, fol. 14; and *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, vol. I, fol. 681. Caesarius, *Dialogue* 1:

> Nothing greater or less was born, nothing prior existed, and nothing adventitious in the divine Trinity existed before the ages, exists today, or will exist hereafter. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the Trinity, understood and worshiped by those who do not worship in pretense or blasphemy, as Arius did, but truly—those who do not divide the nature of God and imagine something greater and something less in the divine Trinity.

[Nothing foreign, as with Macedonius]

The Macedonians entirely distinguish the Holy Spirit from the substance of the Father and the Son, as though he were a minister of wholly inferior rank. Fulgentius, *To Donatus*, fol. 94. Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* X.2. Nicephorus Callistus IX.47. Gregory the Great, *Letters* IV.32, fol. 793. John of Damascus, *On the Two Natures of Christ*, fol. 499. Theophylact, archbishop of Bulgaria, on John 3, 14, and 16.

[Nothing inserted by invasion or stealth, as with Manichaeus]

See Augustine, *On Heresies* 46. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.31. Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, *Heresy* 66.

[Nothing corporeal, as with Tertullian]

Augustine, *On Heresies* 86: Tertullian says that God is corporeal. *To Optatus*, letter 157; *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* X.25. Thomas Aquinas, on Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians, chapter 4, lecture 5. Tertullian, *On Repentance* 3; *On the Flesh of Christ* 2; *Against Marcion* II.16; *Against Praxeas* 7.

[Nothing bodily represented, as with the Anthropomorphite]

Honorius of Autun, church presbyter:

> The Anthropomorphites assert that God has human limbs and human form, although God is spirit and incorporeal.

Jerome, on Psalm 93, fol. 120. Origen, on Paul’s Letter to the Romans I.1. Cassian, *Conferences* X.5. Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII.5. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* X.25; letter 3 to Fortunatianus; letter 157 to Optatus. Rufinus, *Invective 1 against Jerome*, fol. 164.

[Vadianus]

Augustine, *On Heresies* 50:

> Those whom they call Vadians—and Epiphanius wishes them to appear schismatics rather than heretics—are called Anthropomorphites by others, because in their carnal imagination they fashion God in the likeness of the image of corruptible man. Epiphanius attributes this to their rusticity, sparing them the name of heretics.

[Nothing invisible to itself is visible to creatures, as with Origen]

Origen taught that God the Father, being invisible by nature, is not seen even by the Son. See his *On First Principles* II.4. Jerome, *Against the Errors of the Jerusalemites*; letter 61.3; letter 59 to Avitus, fol. 204. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 54, and his letter to John of Jerusalem, and *Ancoratus*, fol. 381. Papias, under “Origenists.” Honorius, *On Heresies*. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies* VIII.5. Athanasius, *On the Blasphemies of Arius*, vol. I, fol. 681; and *Tripartite History* I.13 attribute this opinion to Arius.

In the time of Servus Dei there also arose heretics who said that Christ, while living in this life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes, but only after rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, when he had been transferred into the glory of God the Father—God the Father evidently granting him this advancement as a reward for his martyrdom. Against them the aforementioned bishop sharply directed his pen, demonstrating in a sound disputation and in a treatise adequately supported by scriptural evidence that the man who had become God had always seen the Father with his bodily eyes, and the Holy Spirit through the special and united fellowship of God and man. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, under Servus Dei.

[Nothing different in morals and will, as with Marcion]

See Epiphanius, *Heresy* 44. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.28.

[Nothing from the essence of the Trinity reduced to the nature of creatures, as with Plato]

See Plato, *Timaeus*. Bede, *On the Elements of Philosophy* I, fol. 313. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, vol. III, chapter 1, fol. 341:

> Every intellectual or bodily creature was made by God from nothing, not from God’s nature, and nothing in it belongs to the Trinity except that the Trinity created it and it was created.

[And Tertullian]

Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV.38:

> He commands man to be restored to the Creator, in whose image, likeness, name, and material he was formed.

[Nothing singular in office]

See Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*. Photius, *Bibliotheca*, fol. 5.

[Yet not solitary, as with Praxeas]

Praxeas and Sylvanus believed in one God in such a way that they refused to reckon either the Son or the Holy Spirit with him. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas* 21. Gregory of Nazianzus, *On the Nicene Faith*:

> We do not confess one God in such a way that he is solitary, nor the same person who is Father to himself and himself also Son.

First Council of Braga, chapter 1:

> If anyone does not confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons of one substance, power, and authority, as the catholic and apostolic Church teaches, but says that there is only one solitary person, so that he himself is the Father who is the Son and himself also the Paraclete Spirit, as Sabellius and Priscillianus said, let him be accursed.

## CHAPTER V

[The Son is of the same substance as the Father]

Against the blasphemies of Arius, who asserted:

> This Lord is foreign and alien to the substance of the Father; he is called Word only by conception, and is not by nature and truly the Son of God, but is called Son by appointment, like a creature.

Athanasius, vol. I, *On the Opinion of Dionysius against the Arians*, fol. 441.

Athanasius defines *homoousios* in *On the Holy Trinity* I, fol. 149, as that which receives the same account of essence: just as one human differs in nothing from another insofar as each is human, and one angel from another insofar as each is an angel, so God differs in nothing from God insofar as he is God.

Concerning this word there was formerly an extremely bitter dispute between the Arians and the Catholics. The Arians said that *homoousios* was a new word and was not found in Holy Scripture, since it had been entirely unknown to the ancients and had only recently been introduced by the Catholics at the Council of Nicaea. For this reason they also called the Catholics, together with the Macedonians, *homoousiasts*. The Catholics, by contrast, maintained that the word was very ancient, drawn from Holy Scripture, and used by many holy men before the Council of Nicaea.

Athanasius, *On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea against the Arian Heresy*, fols. 400, 415, and following; *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, fols. 429, 695, and following; *On the Holy Trinity*, dialogue 1, fols. 146, 155, and 158; dialogue 3, fol. 191; *On the Nicene Faith*, fol. 49 and following. Hilary, *On the Synods against the Arians*, fol. 241. Gelasius, *On the Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, p. 241. Phoebadius, *Against the Arians*, fol. 264. Marius Victorinus, *Against Arius* I, fol. 293 and following, and *On Accepting the Homoousion*, fol. 361. Psellus, *Theological Chapters* 2 and 5. Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Trinity* I. Fulgentius, *Response to the Arians*, fol. 33. *Tripartite History* II.7. Epiphanius, *Against the Ariomaniacs*, heresy 69. Ambrose, *On the Faith to the Emperor Gratian* III.7. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.31.

[Not a man made apart from God, as Nestorius blasphemously teaches]

For he said that it was not the Son of God who, having dwelt in the Virgin’s womb, became incarnate, but a mere man born from Mary who afterward had God accompanying him. Theophylact, archbishop of Bulgaria, on Luke 2, fol. 213; on John 1, fol. 388. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.32. Nicephorus Callistus XVIII.49. *Greek-Roman Law*, vol. I, fol. 439.

[The Son is worshiped by angels and every creature, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are]

A notable testimony against those fanatics who deprive Christ of the worship of *latria*. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catecheses for the Enlightened in Jerusalem*, catechesis 4, p. 12:

> Christ, having been crucified, is worshiped by the whole inhabited world.

Theophylact, on Luke 24, fol. 377:

> The Savior ascended into heaven himself as the forerunner of all, in order to display the holy flesh before the Father’s sight and to sit in heaven with the Father.
>
> And now our nature in Christ is worshiped by every angelic power.

John Cantacuzenus, emperor of Constantinople, *Apology 2 against the Muslims*, fol. 26:

> The Son and Word of God, being God before the ages, was worshiped together with his Father, God, by the angels. And now, having become man, he is again worshiped by those same angels, and together with the body. Therefore the man whom the Son and Word of God assumed together with his person is also worshiped, just as he was worshiped in the beginning by the angels.

Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, *Dialogue* II:

> The Lord’s body rose incorruptible, impassible, immortal, and glorified with divine glory, and it is worshiped by the heavenly powers.

The Lord’s body rose incorruptible, impassible, immortal, and glorified with divine glory, and it is worshiped by the heavenly powers.

Fulgentius, *Response to the Arians*, fol. 34:

> Although placed in the form of a servant and made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, the Son is nevertheless always worshiped in heaven by all powers and angels.

Cyril of Alexandria, vol. IV, letter to Nestorius, fol. 30:

> Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son, is worshiped with one worship proper to him together with the flesh.

John of Damascus, *On the Two Wills of Christ*, fol. 474:

> Together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, I venerate and worship Christ, the incarnate Son of God.

And *On the Orthodox Faith* IV.3 and 2:

> Christ is worshiped by every creature with one worship together with his flesh.

Gregory the Great, vol. II, *Homily on the Gospels* 8, fol. 343:

> After the angels saw our nature, which they had previously despised, assumed above them, they venerate and worship it in the heavenly King, the man who is God.

See Cyril in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 24.

[There will be a resurrection of all the dead]

Gennadius, on Tichonius:

> Tichonius the African says that there will not be two resurrections in the flesh, one of the righteous and another of the unrighteous, but one resurrection, once and for all, of everyone; in it even those miscarried and malformed will rise.

Augustine, the presbyter Philip, and Bede support Tichonius concerning the resurrection of miscarried infants.

Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius* 185:

> A question arises concerning miscarried fetuses, which have already lived in their mothers’ wombs but were not yet born in such a way that they could be born again. If we say that those who were already formed will rise, what is said may somehow be tolerated. But who would not more readily judge unformed miscarriages to perish, like seeds that were never conceived? Yet who would dare deny—and, even if he does not dare affirm it, who would deny that the resurrection will bring about this—that whatever form was lacking will be supplied? Thus there will be no lack of the perfection that would have come with time, just as there will be none of the defects that came with time. Nature will not be deprived of what the days would have brought in a fitting and appropriate way, nor disfigured by what they brought in an adverse and contrary way; rather, what was not yet complete will be completed, just as what had been corrupted will be restored.

And *City of God* XXII.13:

> I dare neither affirm nor deny that miscarried fetuses, which had already lived in the womb but died there, will rise again, although I do not see how the resurrection of the dead would not pertain to them if they are not excluded from the number of the dead.

Philip the presbyter, on Job I.3; and Bede, *Exposition on Job* I.3, fol. 614:

> Job says: “Why did I not die in the womb? For now I would be sleeping in silence and resting in my sleep with kings and consuls.” Perhaps this is an example against those who say that only those will rise who were born according to the order of nature. If those who are conceived die in the womb, they must therefore live; or, whatever dies will undoubtedly rise again. Thus, whatever was in the limbs and lived, or whatever nature gave less than it should, will be restored whole in the resurrection. For in this way the restoration of the human race for the better will restore everything that nature had withheld.

The scholastic theologians disagree, saying that miscarried fetuses will not rise because they did not live. Bonaventure, *Sentences* IV, distinction 49.

[Not a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners]

This excludes the error of those who say that the resurrection will not take place for all at once, but that the first resurrection will be that of the righteous and the second that of sinners. This was also the opinion of Lactantius and Stephen Gobarus. Thomas Aquinas, on Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, chapter 16, lecture 8. Lactantius VII.20 and 26; *Epitome* 8. Photius, *Bibliotheca*, fol. 471.

[The bodies will not be transformed according to Origen]

Origen thought that bodily substances would completely dissolve at the resurrection, and that the bodies of the future would be what the ether and heaven now are, or whatever other body might be conceived as more ethereal and purer. Jerome, letter 59 to Avitus, fol. 205, *Against the Errors*; *Against John of Jerusalem*, to Pammachius, chapter 9, fol. 219; *Commentary on Isaiah* VIII.14; *Commentary on Ezekiel* XII.40; *Commentary on Amos* 5. Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, fol. 390. Julian, bishop of Toledo, *Prognosticon* III.17.

Eutychius also held this error. Ado, bishop of Vienne, *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 575. Bede, on Luke VI.23, fol. 510. Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote that our body in the glory of that resurrection would be intangible, subtler than winds and air.

Rufinus, in the preface to Macarius in the *Apology of Eusebius for Origen*, and Eusebius, *Apology for Origen*, fol. 489, say that Origen’s critics falsely attributed this error to that excellent man. Origen himself, vol. I, on Matthew 25, homily 9, fol. 291, appears to reject the opinion of those who introduce after the resurrection an airy body that is gradually dissolved into thin airs.

Gregory the Great, *Moral Exposition on Job* XIV.30:

> We confess that our flesh after the resurrection will be both the same and different: the same by nature, different by glory; the same by truth, different by power. It will therefore be spiritual because incorruptible, and tangible because it will not lose the essence of its true nature.

## CHAPTER VII

[There will be a resurrection of all human beings]

Cyril of Jerusalem, *Fourth Catechesis for the Enlightened*, p. 97:

> The resurrection belongs to all human beings, but the resurrection is not the same for all. For we all receive eternal bodies, but not all receive bodies alike. The righteous receive them so that, living forever, they may join the angels in their chorus; sinners receive them so that for endless ages they may endure the punishment of their sins.

See John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith* IV.28.

[You will not give your holy one to see corruption]

Isidore of Seville, *On the Resurrection of the Lord* 53. Chrysostom, on Psalm 37. Athanasius of Alexandria, *Treatise on Definitions*, fol. 58, vol. II. Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund* III, fol. 63. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith* III.28.

[Those who are found alive at the Lord’s coming will be changed into incorruption]

See Jerome, letter 152 to Miner(i)us and Alexander. Oecumenius, on Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, chapter 15. Thomas Aquinas, on Paul’s First Letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, lecture 2. Peter Lombard, *Sentences* IV, distinction 43. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis for the Enlightened* 14, fol. 138. Augustine, *City of God* XX.19. Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta* VI, annotation 265. John Gerson, *On the Articles of Faith* II, fol. 25.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Diodorus]

Diodorus of Tarsus thought that incorruption at the future judgment would be common to all, but that transformation would belong properly to the righteous. Jerome, letter 152 to Miner(i)us and Alexander. The author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, in Augustine, vol. III, fol. 153.

[We believe that those who are found in the flesh are alive]

Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, vol. III, chapter 8; *Enchiridion to Laurentius* 55; *On Twelve Questions of Dulcitius*, vol. IV, question 3. Chrysostom, vol. V, *Exposition of the Creed*:

> The living are understood to be those who will be in the body at the Lord’s coming; the dead are those who have departed from this light.

## CHAPTER IX
[We must not believe that a restoration will take place, as Origen raves]

Bede, *Exposition on the Proverbs of Solomon*, book I, chapter 2, folio 881: The Origenists promise heretics, prostitutes, and every class of the utterly wicked—and even the devil himself [Col. 1017B] and his angels—forgiveness of their crimes, life, and a kingdom in heaven after innumerable ages, although the universal judgment has been completed. They wrongly understand Isaiah’s words: “And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited.” They interpret this as saying that, after the judgment has ended after many ages, the wicked will be released and saved, whereas Isaiah, on the contrary, grants them no salvation. Rather, he indicates only that those who, because of the enormity of their crimes, have deserved to be shut up in the prison of punishments during this present age will be visited for a short time at the resurrection, so that, once they have received their bodies, they may be condemned more severely at the judgment and immediately thereafter be confined forever in more dreadful punishments.

Thus the most accursed Muhammad says that even the demons can be saved through the Qur’an: “καὶ τοὺς δαίμονας δύνασθαι σωθῆναι διὰ τοῦ Ἀλκοράνου” (“that the demons too can be saved through the Qur’an”). Richard the monk of Florence, *Refutation of the Saracen Law*, chapter 1, folio 88; chapter 9, folio 124. John Cantacuzenus, *Oration IV against Muhammad*, folio 106. Qur’an, sura LXI. Athanasius, *On the Common Essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*, folio 391; *Questions to Antiochus*, question 101. John the monk, *Canon against All Heretics*. Caesarius, *Dialogue* 3. Yet if that letter is genuine rather than fabricated—the letter which Rufinus, in *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, folio 494, says that Origen himself published against those who, while he was still alive, corrupted his books—then it must be believed that Origen never thought or wrote what Gennadius and the other teachers of the Church wished to attribute to him here. Among other things, while addressing his Alexandrians, he says:

“Some of those who gladly accuse their neighbors charge us and our teaching with the crime of blasphemy, which they have never heard from us. Let them look to it themselves, unwilling as they are to observe that commandment which says that slanderers shall not possess the kingdom of God. They say that I call the father of wickedness and destruction, and of those who are cast out of the kingdom of God—that is, the devil—one who is to be saved; a thing which not even someone mentally deranged and manifestly insane can say.”

*Commentary on Job*, book I, folio 237: “The devil, who is the author of every iniquity and the father and inventor of every crime, will never again ascend to the heavenly court from which he freely fell; he will never return again.” And in *Homily 9 on Matthew*, chapter 25, folio 291: “We believe that the devil and the impious will suffer eternal torments.” [Col. 1018A] Let those, therefore, be ashamed who did not hesitate to concoct this fiction about so learned a man.

[That demons or impious human beings after torments]

Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau*, around the year of the Lord 1315, records that heretics arose in the city of Cremona who asserted that Lucifer, unjustly cast from heaven with his demons, would at last be restored to blessedness together with all his followers.

Nevertheless, nothing definite about these matters is set forth in the Church’s preaching. Origen, in the preface to *On First Principles*, folio 421: “For this is contained in the Church’s preaching: that there are certain angels of God and good powers who minister to him for the completion of the salvation of human beings. But when these were created, and what they are like, is not sufficiently distinguished in clear terms.” Eusebius, *Apology for Origen*, volume IX, in Jerome, folio 137. Hence the worthless apostate Julian the emperor, in the three books which he spewed forth against the holy Gospels and the Christian name, accused Moses, the greatest and most ancient of the prophets, of ignorance because he had said nothing about the origin of the angels, their creation, or how they were produced. Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, book II, folio 32; book III, folio 64.

[So that God’s goodness might not be idle]

John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 14:

“The good, all-good, and supremely good God, who is goodness in his entirety, because of the surpassing riches of his goodness, did not endure that goodness alone—that is, his own nature—should exist without being participated in by anything. For this reason he first made the intellectual and heavenly powers, then the visible and sensible world, and then the human being from the intellectual and sensible realms. Therefore, all things made by him participate in his goodness according to their being; for he himself is being to all things, since beings exist in him—not only because he brought them from non-being into being, but also because his activity preserves and holds together the things made by him.”

John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 14:

“The good, all-good, and supremely good God, who is goodness in his entirety, because of the surpassing riches of his goodness, did not endure that goodness alone—that is, his own nature—should exist without being participated in by anything. For this reason he first made the intellectual and heavenly powers, then the visible and sensible world, and shortly thereafter the human being from intellectual and sensible nature. Therefore, all things made by him participate in his goodness according to their being, because all things are from him and in him: not only because he himself brought them from nothing into being, but because they are his activity, which preserves and holds together the things made by him.”

See Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 4. Origen, *On First Principles*, book II, chapter 9. John Cantacuzenus, *Apology II against the Muslim Sect*.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Athanasius, *Questions to Antiochus*, question 17:

“From what, then, is it evident that at the time of death the soul does not die together with the body? For some think so. Answer: The Son and Word of God, Jesus Christ, plainly teaches us that the body is mortal and that our soul is immortal, saying: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.’ It is therefore clear that it is immortal and impassible.”

That is: “How can it be shown that at the time of death the soul also does not die together with the body? For some hold this opinion. Response: The Word of Christ and our God teaches us most clearly that our body is mortal and that our soul is immortal. For Christ says: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.’ Hence it is established that the human soul is immortal and exists from God.”

Lactantius, book VII, chapter 12:

## CHAPTER LII

[There is one baptism]

Against the Valentinians, who say that there are two baptisms. Jerome, *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians*, book II, chapter 4, folio 178. Sedulius Scotus, *Collection on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians*, chapter 4, folio 80. Cyprian, *Letter to Quintus*, letter 71; *Letter to Jubaianus*, letter 73. There is one baptism, and it is found in the Catholic Church. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 15. Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, book I, chapter 3. Epiphanius, *Against the Cathari*, heresy 59. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Properties of Speech*, book IV, chapter 10. Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenianus*, book V. Ambrose, *On Penance*, book II, chapter 2. [Col. 1026B] Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis 1*. Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 14.

[Where it is administered in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit]

Fulgentius, *To King Trasimund*, book II, folio 57:

“In this above all the truth of the Catholic faith is recognized: that it rightly customarily baptizes in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, because it believes that the whole Trinity is equally present everywhere.”

And book III, folio 66. Gregory the Great, book I, letter 24. Alcuin, *On Divine Offices*, folio 1969. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis II*, page 198. Bernard, abbot, letter 339 to Baldwin. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 10. *Apostolic Canons*, chapter 49. Pope Vigilius, letter to Eleutherius, chapter 3. Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 12. Cyprian, letters 23 and 73. Clement, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VII, chapter 22. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 24. Athanasius, *Against the Arians*, oration 3, folio 118 and following. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 6. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 3. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

Let the fury of Menander the Samaritan be spat upon: he denied that anyone could have salvation unless he had received his baptism. Tertullian, *Prescription against the Heretics*, chapter 46; *On the Soul*, chapter 50.

[Where it is administered in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit]

This condemns the error of Eunomius, who, contrary to the tradition of the apostles, attempted to establish that divine baptism should be performed by a single immersion. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 11. Sozomen, book VI, chapter 26.

[If they have been baptized among heretics in the confession of the Holy Trinity, they are received] Council of Carthage I, canon 1. Pope Nicholas I, *To the Consultations of the Bulgarians*, canon 15. *Capitularies of the Emperors Charlemagne and Louis*, book VII, canon 319. *Corpus of Canon Law*, part III, distinction 4. African Council, canon 15. Ursinus the monk, in Gennadius, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, book VI, at length. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 26 [Col. 1026D]:

> One true baptism is celebrated, only in the name of the supreme Trinity, as the Lord himself demonstrated and the apostolic canons teach. Therefore, whoever has been baptized either by heretics baptizing in the Trinity, or by any other person whatsoever, under the legitimate invocation of that same Holy Trinity, ought not to be rebaptized, lest the invocation of the supreme Divinity appear to be annulled; but by chrism and the imposition of hands what was incomplete must be perfected.

Bede, volume XII, in the summer homilies on the saints, folio 128, and on John, chapter 3, folio 554:

> Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any evildoer baptizes in the confession of the Holy Trinity, one who has thus been baptized may not be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession and invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

The author of *On the Faith, to the Deacon Peter*, chapter 3:

> Whether in the Catholic faith, or in any heresy or schism, someone has received the sacrament of baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he has received the complete sacrament.

Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, therefore erred—or rather, went mad [Col. 1027A]. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 7, incorrectly makes Cyprian the first author of this error. Agrippinus was the first of all mortals to judge, contrary to the divine canon and the rule of the universal Church, that rebaptism must be administered. His presumption provided not only all heretics with a model of sacrilege, but also certain Catholics with an occasion for error. For in the time of Pope Cornelius, Cyprian, together with nearly eighty bishops of his African churches, judged that everyone who had been baptized outside the communion of the Catholic Church ought, on coming to the Church, to be baptized again.

Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 9. Augustine, *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, book I, chapter 18; book III, chapter 12; to Vincent, letter 48; *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book I, chapter 32; book II, chapter 38; book III, chapter 1. Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 8. Cyprian, to Quintus, letter 71; to Jubaianus, letter 73; to Magnus, letter 77.

But that a bishop of such merit and such [Col. 1027B] virtue should have thought differently about baptism from what a more diligently investigated truth would establish was compensated by the abundance of his charity and cleansed by the pruning-hook of his martyrdom, as Augustine says in the place cited above, and Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 6.

[Let them be confirmed by the imposition of hands] Pope Eusebius I, decretal letter 1 to the bishops of Gaul, volume I of the Councils, folio 209:

> Concerning what you have indicated should be done with converts from heresy, know that we receive those who have been baptized in the faith of the Holy Trinity through the imposition of hands.

See Justin Martyr, *Questions to the Orthodox*, question 13, folio 312.

[If they are infants, let those who present them answer on their behalf] Augustine, *Sermon 14 on the Words of the Apostle*; *On the Merits and Remission of Sins, against the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 34; to Boniface, letter 23; to Vitalis, letter 107. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book I, chapter 26. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 6 [Col. 1027C]:

> All who come to baptism ought to profess their faith and explain what they have come to the church to request. If the person is an adult, he answers for himself that he believes in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But if he is an infant, unable either to believe or to speak, another answers on his behalf.

[By the imposition of hands] Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 8. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book I, chapter 30.

144 [Strengthened with chrism] Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, letter 70:

> It is necessary that the baptized person be anointed, so that, having received chrism, he may be anointed as one of God and may have within him the grace of Christ.

Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 7. Origen, on Ezekiel, chapter 16, homily 6. *Corpus of Canon Law*, distinction 4, *On Consecration*. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 10.

[Let them be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist] For ecclesiastical custom does not give the body of Christ to those who have not been reborn from water and the Spirit. Bede, *On Luke*, book IV, chapter 15; *Questions on the Book of Kings*, chapter 16; *On John*, book I, chapter 2. Cyprian, letter 63. Augustine, *On John*, tractate 2; *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, book II, chapter [Col. 1027D] 14; *Against the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 15.

Cyril of Alexandria, *On John*, book XII, chapter 50:

> We exclude catechumens from the sacraments, even though they have already come to know the truth and loudly confess the faith, because they have not yet been enriched with the Holy Spirit, who dwells in those who have been perfected through baptism. Therefore, when they have received baptism, since the Holy Spirit is believed to dwell in them, they are not excluded from touching and receiving the communion of Christ’s saving body. For this reason, when those approaching the mystical blessing come forward, the ministers of the mystery loudly proclaim, “Holy things for the holy,” signifying that the touch and sanctification of Christ’s body are fitting only for those sanctified by the Spirit.

Indeed, the ancients held this sacrament in such high regard that they would admit no one even to its viewing except the faithful and the baptized. Thus, before the consecration, catechumens, the possessed, and penitents were ordered to leave. Micrologus, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 51, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*. Maximus the monk, *Exposition of the Liturgy*, chapters [Col. 1028A] 15 and 16. Nicholas Cabasilas, *Commentary on the Divine Sacrifice*, chapter 23. Germanus, archbishop of Constantinople, *Theoria of Ecclesiastical Matters*, folios 678–679. William Durandus, bishop of the Church of Mende, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book IV, folio 37; book VI, folio 129. Albert the Great, bishop of Regensburg, *On the Office of the Mass*, treatise 3, chapter 23. Albinus Alcuin, tutor of Charlemagne, *On the Divine Offices*, folios 1994 and 2015. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 80, article 4.

Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, pages 133, 221, and 141:

> Κατηχουμένους ἐνεργουμένους τε, καὶ τοὺς ἐν μετανοίᾳ ὄντας, ὁ τῆς ἁγίας ἱεραρχίας θεσμὸς ἐφίησι μὲν ἐπακοῦσαι τῆς ψαλμικῆς ἱερολογίας, καὶ τῆς ἐνθέου τῶν πανιέρων Γραφῶν ἀναγνώσεως· εἰς δὲ τὰς ἐξῆς ἱερουργίας καὶ θεωρίας, οὐ συγκαλεῖται τούτους, ἀλλὰ τοὺς τελείους τῶν τελεσιουργῶν ὀφθαλμούς.

> The custom of the holy hierarchy permits catechumens, the possessed, and those who are in penitence to hear the sacred chanting of the psalms and the divinely inspired reading of the most sacred Scriptures; but for the sacred acts and contemplations that [Col. 1028B] follow, it does not summon them, but rather the perfected eyes of those worthy to behold the sacred rites.

It should be noted here that in former times the Eucharist was given to newly baptized children. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, to Severus, letter 12. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catecheses*, folio 23. Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, folio 222. Augustine, volume X, sermon 8, *On the Words of the Apostle*, folio 197; to Boniface, letter 23; to Vitalis, letter 106; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 22; book IV, chapter 4; *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book I, chapter 20.

The author of *Hypognosticon*, in Augustine, volume VII, on article 5, folio 956:

> How can you promise the kingdom of heaven to infants who have not been reborn from water and the Spirit, who have not been fed with the flesh and have not drunk the blood of Christ, which was poured out for the remission of sins? Behold: one who is not baptized, and is deprived even of the life-giving food and drink, is excluded from the kingdom of heaven, where Christ, the fountain of the living, remains.

This custom continued [Col. 1028C] until the age of Charlemagne. For in his *Capitulary*, book I, chapter 161, the following ordinance is found:

> Let the presbyter always have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever someone falls ill, or an infant becomes ill, he may immediately give him communion, lest he die without communion.

His tutor, Albinus Alcuin, likewise says in *On the Divine Offices*, folio 1971:

> Care must be taken, he says, that newly baptized infants receive no food and are not nursed before they communicate.

The same was prescribed in the Roman Order published by Melchior Hittorp; and it is still observed by the Bohemians and Moravians, as Joachim Vadianus notes, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book I, folio 14; book II, folio 40. Jacobus Pamelius, in his notes on Tertullian, *On Baptism*, folio 470, thinks that this custom was abolished when the baptism of adults ceased and the fixed times for baptizing were no longer observed, because of the danger of irreverence.
