Whatever the case may be, since, according to the admonition of Saint Paul in 1 Corinthians 11, self-examination and the proclamation of the Lord’s death are required for this mystery, I do not [Col. 1028D] see how the institution of this sacrament can apply to infants, who, being without reason, can perform none of these things. John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, therefore judges correctly that the Eucharist should be given to children when they have reached the years of full use of reason and discernment. Thus, in *On the Communion of the Laity under Both Kinds*, part 1, folio 17, and in *Moral Rules*, part II, folio 75, he writes:

> Those children are fit to receive the Eucharist, and appear to be bound to receive it once a year, who according to the laws are judged capable of marrying.

[But those who are not baptized in the invocation of the Holy Trinity] For there is no baptism if it is not administered in faith in the Holy Trinity. Jerome, *On Joel*, chapter 2, folio 86. Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*, book II, folio 224. Cyril of Jerusalem, *First Mystagogical Catechesis*. Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, in Cyprian, letter 75. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, [Col. 1029A] chapter 10. Fulgentius, *To Donatus, on the Orthodox Faith*, folio 94.

The mystery of the redemption of humanity is in no way completed if in baptism the name either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit is omitted.

[Paulianists] Council of Nicaea, canon 19:

> Concerning the Paulianists who flee to the Catholic Church, a definition was issued that they must be baptized in every respect.

*Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 47. Council of Carthage VI, canon 19. Council of Arles II, canon 16. Gelasius, *On the Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, page 168. *Greek-Roman Law*, volume I, folio 378.

These people were called after Paul of Samosata, who says that Christ, God and the substantial, personal, and eternal Son of God, was not always with the Father, but asserts that he had his beginning when he was born of Mary; nor does he think him anything more than a human being. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 44. John of Damascus, *On Heresies*, folio 580. Philaster, heresy 64.

[Proclians] They taught that Christ did not come in the flesh. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 60.

[Borborites] That is, “muddy ones,” because of the disgracefulness [Col. 1029B] they display in their mysteries. See Epiphanius, heresy 26. Augustine, heresy 6. Philaster, heresy 72. Oecumenius, *On the Epistle of Jude*, chapter 1. The Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, book 16, title 5, calls them Borborians.

147 [Bonosians, Montanists] Syricius, Pope I, in his letter to Bishop Victoricius, volume I of the Councils, folio 456, and the Council of Arles II, canon 17, teach that Bonosians and Montanists are not to be rebaptized, but, after rejection of their false doctrine and confession of the true doctrine, are to be cleansed solely by the imposition of hands. The presbyter Timothy, however, *Greek-Roman Law*, volume I, folio 378, and Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 66, article 9, place Bonosians and Montanists among those who are rebaptized.

Gregory the Great agrees with their opinion, *Letters*, book IX, letter 61 to Bishop Quirinus, folio 1087:

> Heretics who are not baptized at all in the name of the Trinity, such as the Bonosians, Cataphrygians, and others of this sort, are baptized when they come to the Holy Church, because what they received while in error, not at all in the name of the Holy Trinity [Col. 1029C], was not baptism.

[Bonosians] They deny that Christ, God, existed from the substance of the Father before the ages, asserting that he was an adopted Son of God, not a true one. Honorius, heresy 68. Pope Innocent I, letter 20 to Bishop Laurentius, volume I of the Councils, folio 464. Gregory the Great, *Letters*, book IX, letter 61.

[Montanists] They say that the Holy Spirit, whom Christ promised his disciples in the Gospel, was given through Montanus and Priscilla. They prohibit marriage and prepare a funeral Eucharist from the blood of a one-year-old infant. Augustine, *On the Christian Contest*, chapter 28; *On Heresies*, chapter 26. Harmenopulus, *On Sects*. Epiphanius, heresy 48.

[Manichaeans] See Epiphanius, heresy 66. Philaster, heresy 61. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 46.

[Manichaeans and Marcion] Theodore the Studite, letter to Naucratius his son, volume I of the *Library of the Fathers:

> The Marcionites, Tascodrugites, Manichaeans, and those [Col. 1029D] of the same order are baptized.

The presbyter Timothy, *On the Difference among Those Who Approach the Holy Faith*, folio 931. *Greek-Roman Law*, volume I, folio 378.

[Who introduce two mutually unknown principles] Honorius, *On Heresies*: “Marcion and the Cerdonians assert two contrary principles.” Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book I. Epiphanius, heresies 41 and 42. John of Damascus, *On Heresies*, folio 578. Philaster, heresies 44 and 45. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5. Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 51; *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 2.

[Contrary principles, as Manichaeus] Epiphanius, heresy 66. Philaster, heresy 61. Augustine, heresy 46.

[Three and barbarous principles, as Sethianus and Theodosius] Theodoret, book I of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*.

[Or many, as Valentinus] Tertullian treats this at length in *Against the Valentinians*, and in *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 5; *Prescription against Heretics*, chapters 33 and 49. Epiphanius, heresy 31. Philaster, heresy 38. The presbyter Timothy, folio 931. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 11.

[Cerinthus] The presbyter Timothy, folio [Col. 1030A] 931:

> The Sabellians, Cerinthians, Menandrians, and Ebionites are baptized.

Cerinthus, however, presents Christ as born from the seed of Joseph, maintaining that he was merely a human being, without divinity. Irenaeus, book I, chapter 25. Augustine, heresy 8. Epiphanius, heresy 28. Tertullian, *Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 48.

[Photinus] He asserts that Christ was merely an isolated human being, to whom he attributes his beginning from Mary. Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 16. Marius Victorinus Afer, *Against Arius*, book I, folios 288, 294. Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book I, folio 37. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 44. Pope Leo I, *Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord*, page 37. Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, folio 87. Vigilius the Martyr, book I, *Against Eutyches*. Epiphanius, heresy 71. Nicephorus Callistus, book IX, chapter 31. Sozomen, book IV, chapter 5. *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 5. Philaster, heresy 65. Theodotus [Col. 1030B], bishop of Ancyra, in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, volume VI, chapter 10.

## CHAPTER LIII

[To receive communion of the Eucharist daily] In the primitive Church, when great devotion to the faith still flourished, it is known from the Acts of the Apostles and from the decretal letter of Pope Anacletus, volume I of the Councils, folio 56, that the faithful communicated daily. This custom continued in Africa until the time of Cyprian and Augustine, and in Milan, Rome, and Spain until the times of Ambrose and Jerome. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, folio 244. Augustine, to Boniface, letter 23; to Januarius, letter 118. Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 4. Jerome, to Lucinius, letter 28, folio 38; to Hedibia, letter 150, question 2, folio 416; *Apology to Pammachius for the Book against Jovinian*, chapter 6, folio 184.

Later, when the fervor of faith diminished and charity grew cold, that custom gradually fell into disuse. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 80, article 10. [Col. 1030C]

It was therefore decreed by the Roman pontiffs that, if not more frequently, the laity should receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at least three times a year—at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—or at minimum once a year, on the Lord’s Supper, unless they wished, while alive, to be entirely barred from entering the Church and, when dead, to be deprived of Christian burial. Council of the Lateran, canon 21. Council of Tours III, canon 50. Council of Agde, canon 63. *Corpus of Canon Law*, distinction 2, canon 16. Burchard, bishop of Worms, book V, chapter 18. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, part II, chapter 27. *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, book II, chapter 45. Bonaventure, bishop of Albano, on Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 12, question 2, no. 82 and following. Emperor Louis, addition 3 to Charlemagne’s *Capitulary*, canon 38. Durandus, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 12, question 5. Albert the Great, *On the Office of the Mass*, treatise 3, chapter 21.

In the eastern regions, the Greeks communicated not daily but only on feast days and Sundays. Athanasius, volume I, *Apology 2*, folios 569–570. Augustine, [Col. 1030D] *On the Words of the Lord according to Luke*, volume X, sermon 28, folio 76; and *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book II, folio 815:

> Many in the eastern regions do not communicate daily at the Lord’s Supper.

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 4:

> If it is daily bread, why do you take it after a year, as the Greeks in the East have been accustomed to do?

The holy Fathers themselves also emphasize not so much daily and frequent communion as worthy reception of the sacraments. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 20:

> Gennadius of Marseille, a presbyter, in his *Ecclesiastical Dogma*, standing as it were midway between the ancients and the younger generation—for while some still communicated only on Sundays, certain others were already communicating daily—balances his judgment in such a way that he says he neither praises nor censures daily reception of the Eucharist. He does, however, exhort everyone to communicate every Sunday, provided that capital sins do not forbid it and the mind is not fixed upon the pleasure of sinning.

Among the Greeks, those who have passed two or three Sundays without communion are likewise said to be excommunicated [Col. 1031A].

Augustine, letter 118 to Januarius, folio 360:

> Someone may say that the Eucharist ought not to be received daily. You ask why? “Because,” he says, “the days should be chosen on which a person lives more purely and more continently, so that he may approach so great a sacrament worthily. For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.”
>
> Another, on the contrary, says: “Rather, if the wound of sin and the force of the disease are so great that such medicines must be postponed, each person should be removed from the altar by the authority of the bishop in order to perform penance, and by that same authority be reconciled. For this is to receive unworthily: to receive at a time when one ought to be doing penance, not to withdraw from communion or return to it arbitrarily, according to one’s own decision.
>
> “But if the sins are not so great that a person ought to be judged excommunicable, he should not separate himself from the daily medicine of the Lord’s body. Perhaps the dispute between them is more rightly settled by the one who urges them above all to remain in the peace of Christ.
>
> “Let each person do what he devoutly believes should be [Col. 1031B] done according to his faith. Neither of them dishonors the body and blood of the Lord, if both strive zealously to honor the saving sacrament. For Zacchaeus and the centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either set himself above the other: one received the Lord joyfully into his house, while the other said, ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.’ Both honored the Savior in different, indeed apparently contrary, ways; both were wretched because of their sins, and both obtained mercy.
>
> “This comparison is also applicable to the fact that among the first people manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own desire. Thus that sacrament should be judged in the mouth of each Christian according to how it is received. One, by honoring it, does not dare to receive it daily; another, by honoring it, does not dare to omit it on any day. That food desires only not to be despised, just as manna was rejected with loathing. For this reason the Apostle says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods with the special reverence due to it.”

Chrysostom, on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews [Col. 1031C], chapter 9, homily 17, and *On Not Despising the Church of God and the Mysteries*:

> Many partake of the mysteries once a year, others twice, and others frequently. Which of these, then, shall we approve—the ones who do so once, those who do so frequently, or those who do so rarely? Neither those who do so once, nor those who do so frequently, nor those who do so rarely, but those who approach with a pure conscience, with a pure heart, and with a blameless life. Let such persons always approach; but let those who are not such persons not approach even once, for they receive judgment and condemnation for themselves.

And *On Saint Philogonius*, volume III, folio 835:

> Many Christians have fallen into such senselessness and such contempt that, although they teem with countless evils, they nevertheless take no care for their life but negligently and rashly approach the Lord’s table on feast days, not understanding that the time for communion is not a feast or celebration, but a pure conscience and a life cleansed of sins. Just as one who is conscious of no evil ought to approach every day, so one who is occupied with sins and does not repent is not safe to approach even on feast days. Nor does approaching once a year [Col. 1031D] free us from sins if we approach unworthily; rather, this very fact increases our condemnation, that although we approach only once, even then we do not approach purely.

And homily 61 to the people of Antioch, on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 10; homily 24 on Ephesians, chapter 2; homily 3 in the sermon on the baptism of Christ. Anastasius, *Questions on the Holy Scriptures*, question 7, folio 135. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 18. Basil the Great, *On Baptism*, book I, chapter 3; book II, question 3. The author of the homily on the Lord’s Supper, in Jerome, volume IX. Jerome, on 1 Corinthians, chapter 11. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book I, chapter 11; *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, chapter 57. Origen, on Psalm 38, homily 2; on Leviticus, chapter 23, homily 13. Martial, bishop, to the people of Bordeaux, chapter 4. Eligius, bishop of Noyon, *Homily 8 on the Lord’s Supper*. Augustine, volume X, sermon 252, *On Time*. Ambrose, on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11. Bonaventure, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 9, [Col. 1032A] no. 42. Algerus, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book I, chapter 22.

[Let the person who is about to communicate make satisfaction with tears] Thomas Aquinas cites these words in his commentary on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11, lecture 7.

[Who is not burdened by mortal sins] He calls adultery, homicide, sacrilege, theft, and perjury mortal sins. Jerome, *On Ezekiel*, book XI, chapter 34; *On Zechariah*, book I, chapter 5. Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*, folio 288. The author of *On the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct*, in Augustine, volume IX, folio 793. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 9.

[Whom mortal crimes oppress after baptism] Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 17:

> Sacraments are so called from sanctification or from a hidden power. Accordingly, those who depart from the members of Christ through the foulness of capital crimes are also suspended from the sacraments by ecclesiastical authority. It should be understood that the holy Fathers established this above all for the purpose of keeping those who commit mortal sins away from the Lord’s sacraments, lest, receiving them unworthily [Col. 1032B], they become involved in a greater guilt, like Judas, whom, after rashly receiving bread from his master, the devil is said to have invaded more completely, so that the crime he had previously conceived through wicked premeditation might be consummated by an even more wicked resolve.
>
> Or, as the Apostle says concerning the Corinthians, lest those who presume should incur bodily weakness and infirmity, and even death itself.

Ambrose, sermon 6, folio 9:

> It is your duty to forbid a murderer to receive the Eucharist before he performs penance.

Council of Tours I, canon 7:

> Murderers are absolutely not to receive communion until their crimes have been washed away through confession and penance.

Martial, bishop, in his letter to the people of Bordeaux, chapter 4:

> One who has killed a human being is unworthy of the Lord’s table. For if he presumes to receive the Eucharist, he is guilty of the death of his soul and body.

Thus the patriarch Photius refused to admit Basil, the emperor and murderer of Michael, to the sacred supper. Zonaras, volume III of the *Annals*, folio 151. Communion is also denied to public prostitutes, usurers, mime actors, and performers. Nicephorus [Col. 1032C] the Confessor, volume I of the *Greek-Roman Law*, folio 196. John Gerson, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, part 2, folio 27. Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, on Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 4, question 5. Pope Gregory, *Decretals*, book V, title 19, chapter 3.

[I first urge public penance.] Public penance is mentioned by Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 9. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 28. Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 9. Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book II, chapter 10. Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 28. *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 35. Sozomen, book VII, chapter 16.

Jerome, to Oceanus, letter 30, folio 85—speaking of Fabiola’s public confession:

> Who would have believed it? After the death of her second husband she came to her senses—at a time when negligent widows usually cast off the yoke of servitude, claim to act more freely, visit the baths, fly about the streets, and display the faces of prostitutes—and put on sackcloth and publicly confessed her error. With the entire city of Rome looking on, before Easter, in the basilica of Lateran, who was cut down by Caesar’s sword, she stood in the order of penitents [Col. 1032D]; while the bishop, the presbyters, and all the people wept with her, she bowed her disheveled hair, sallow face, filthy hands, and dirty neck.

Gratian treats the rite of that solemn act at length, *Decretum*, distinction 50. Bonaventure, book IV, distinction 14, no. 39. Durandus, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 14, question 4. Beatus Rhenanus, on Tertullian’s book *On Repentance* and in his *Admonition on Tertullian’s Dogmatic Teaching*, folio 557.

It was imposed for the gravest and most notorious crimes, which had disturbed an entire city or an entire neighborhood, so that one who had destroyed himself through the destruction of many might redeem himself through the edification of many. Emperor Louis, addition 2 to Charlemagne’s *Capitulary*, chapter 23. Durandus, in the place cited above. The author of *On the Usefulness of Penance*, in Augustine, volume IX, folio 706, chapter 3. John Gerson, part II of *On the Visitation of Prelates*, folio 43; *On the Power of Absolution*, page 33. Augustine, volume IX, book I of *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, chapter 6; *On the Souls of the Dead* [Col. 1033A], volume X, sermon 4, folio 894. Martin of Braga, bishop, in the *Excerpts from the Greek Canons*, volume II of the Councils, chapter 23, folio 224. Bonaventure, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 17, no. 79.

[By secret satisfaction] Albinus Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, in the appendix to the *Library of the Fathers*, folio 1952:

> We do not deny that mortal crimes are absolved by secret satisfaction; but daily and lighter sins, without which human life is not lived, are cleansed by the Lord’s Prayer.

See Martin Chemnitz, a most learned theologian, *Examination of the Council of Trent*, part 2, pages 381 and following.

[To receive communion of the Eucharist daily] Rabanus Maurus, *On the Meaning of Preaching*, book IV, chapter 10; *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book I, chapter 31. *Corpus of Canon Law*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter 12. Pope Innocent III, *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, book IV, chapter 42, folio 394. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 20. Algerus, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book I, chapter 22. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 12.

## CHAPTER LIV

[True penance is] Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 34, folio 482; and *Letters*, book IX, letter 39, folio 1069:

> To do true penance is to mourn over what one has committed and to avoid again what must be mourned.

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, homily 16. Ambrose, sermon 34, folio 47. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 14. John Gerson, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, part 2, folio 27.

154 [Satisfaction of penance] Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 15:

> The satisfaction of penance is to cut away the causes of sins and not to grant access to their suggestions.

Rabanus, *On the Meaning of Preaching*, book IV, chapter 10; *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book II, chapter 31. Bernard, *On the Interior House*, folio 1063. Bachiarius, *On Receiving Back the Lapsed*. Bonaventure, book III, distinction 20; book IV, distinction 15, question 3. See Martin Chemnitz, part 2 of the *Examination of the Council of Trent*, pages [Col. 1033C] 378 and following.

## CHAPTER LV

[In the divine promises there is nothing earthly] See Augustine, *On John*, tractate 32, chapter 7.

[Not the marital union, as Cerinthus taught] The heresy of Cerinthus was that he asserted Christ’s kingdom would be earthly; and because he was devoted to the belly, gluttony, and lust, he determined that those things would be future which his own desire dictated. He preached that the impulses of the belly and of the things below the belly were to be satisfied with foods, drinks, and marriages. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 28; book VII, chapter 23. Theodoret, book II of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5. Epiphanius, heresy 28. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 14; book VI, chapter 22.

Thus the impure Muhammad, so that he might please his most degraded slaves, the Saracens, who were great lovers of women, promised them after death a delightful paradise, and in it the most beautiful women and long, secure sexual pleasures. The Qur’an [Col. 1033D], surahs II, LXV, and LXVI. John Cantacuzenus, *Oration 2 on Muhammad*, *Muhammad’s Doctrine to the Saracens*, folio 197. Anastasius the Librarian, under the year of Christ 622.

[Not what pertains to food and drink, as Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Lactantius agree, according to Papias] Jerome, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, to Dexter, folio 123:

> Papias, a hearer of John, is said to have published a Jewish thousand-year tradition (*deuterosīs*, δευτέρωσιν). Irenaeus and Apollinarius followed him, as did the others who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh with the saints. Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, as well as Victorinus of Pettau and Lactantius, are guided by this opinion.

And in the preface to Isaiah, book XVIII, folio 213; on Ezekiel, book IX, chapter 36. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 39. Nicephorus Callistus, book III, chapter 20.

[Irenaeus] See him, book V, chapter 32 and following, in the edition of Francis Feu-Ardent.

[Col. 1034A] [Tertullian] In the fragment of the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 25; *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 29; book III, chapter 24; book IV, chapter 29.

[Lactantius] Book VII, chapters 24 and 26; in the *Epitome*, chapter 8.

[As Nepos taught] Nepos understood the future promises in a Judaic sense and taught that they would be presented bodily, and that for a thousand years the saints would reign with Christ on this earth amid bodily delights. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 22. Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book III. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria.

## CHAPTER LVI

[We believe that no one comes to salvation unless God invites him] Against the Pelagians, who taught that the beginning of a good work is in us, but its completion comes from God. Augustine, to Vitalis, letter 107; to the presbyter Sixtus, letter 105; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book [Col. 1034B] II, chapter 5; *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34. Origen, *On First Principles*, book III, chapter 1. The author of *Hypognosticon*, in Augustine, volume VII, article 3, folio 932. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, to Galla, letter 2; to Proba, letter 4; *On Predestination to Monimus*, book I. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, letter 224. *On the Manner of Living Well*, sermon 3. Thomas Aquinas, on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 1, lecture 1, and in *Quodlibet* 1, article 7.

[No one perishes by God’s will, but by himself] Eusebius, *Apology for Origen*, in Origen, volume I, folio 482:

> It must be held among ecclesiastical teachings that no human being has been handed over by God to perdition; rather, each of those who perish perishes through his own negligence and fault, since, having freedom of choice, he both could and ought to choose what is good.

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, book II, chapter 2, folio 309:

> It must be observed that nowhere is God said to have destroyed anyone, but each person suffers from himself [Col. 1034C] what destroys him.

Council of Orange II, canon 25:

> We not only do not believe that some have been predestined by divine power to evil, but if there are those who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

Augustine, *On the Third Article Falsely Imposed upon Him*, volume VIII, folio 922:

> God is the creator of all human beings, but no one was created for the purpose of perishing, because the cause of being born is one thing and the cause of perishing another. For that human beings should be born is a benefit; that they should perish is the fault of the transgressor.

*On the Merits and Remission of Sins, against the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 17. *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 103. Ambrose, *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 7. Chrysostom, *On Compunction of Heart*, folio 495. Faustus, *On Free Choice*, book I, chapter 19; book II, chapter 1 and following. Fulgentius, *On Double Predestination, to Monimus*, book I, folios 7, 8, 9 and following. Jerome, *On Ezekiel*, book I, chapter 3. The author of *Hypognosticon*, article 6, folio 959 and following. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, chapter 30; book IV, chapters 20 and 22.

The heresy must therefore be detested in many ways which, in impious novelty, presumes [Col. 1034D] to assert that God creates the greater part of the human race for the purpose of destroying it eternally.

## CHAPTER LVII
### [Evil or evilness was not created by God]

Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 8, folio 12: “Evilness arose from us; it was not established by God the Creator. It is generated by frivolity of conduct; it possesses no prerogative of a creature, nor any authority belonging to natural substance, but is a fault of mutability and an error of falling away. For life does not generate death, nor light darkness.” See Justin Martyr, *Questions to the Orthodox*, question 73; Jerome, *Against the Errors of Jovinian*, book I, chapter 17; Epiphanius, *Against the Basilidians*, heresy 24; Gregory of Nyssa, *Treatise 2 on Psalm 56*; *Catechetical Oration*, chapter 5; Faustus, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 1; Damascene, *Against the Manichaeans*, page 751; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Properties of Speech*, book IV, chapter 10; Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I [Col. 1035A], chapter 3; *Questions to Orosius*, volume IV, chapter 16; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, chapter 35.

### [The devil was created good by God]

Against the Priscillianists, who said that the devil had never been good, and that his nature was not God’s workmanship, but that he had emerged from chaos and darkness—since, they claimed, he had no author of his being and was himself the beginning and substance of every evil—[p. 157] Pope Leo I, letter 91 to Turbius, bishop of Astorga, volume I of the Councils, chapter 13.

Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 10: “God established the devil as good according to the form of good works; indeed, formerly he was blameless from the day of his creation, created good by God, the good Creator of blameless beings; cultivated with every angelic glory and placed with God, as one good beside the Good. Afterwards, however, he was transferred by himself into evil.”

Papias, under the heading “Evil”; Damascene, *Against the Manichaeans*, folio 543; *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, chapters 4 and 27; Cyril of Alexandria, *Commentary on John*, book VI, chapter 6; Didymus of Alexandria, *Commentary on the Epistle of Saint Jude*, chapter 1; Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book IV, chapter 4; [Col. 1035B] book VII, chapter 17; Elias of Crete, *Commentary on the Third Oration of Gregory Nazianzen*, folio 210; Theodoret, *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, folio 599; Chrysostom, *On Repentance*, volume V, folio 563; Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 21; *City of God*, book V, chapter 9.

## CHAPTER LVIII

### [Nothing by nature is immutable except God the Father alone]

Gregory Nazianzen, *On the Faith*, oration 49: “We believe the Son of God and the Holy Spirit to be immutable and unchangeable, just as the Father is.” Theodoret, on Psalm 150; Athanasius, *On the Divinity of Christ*, folio 339; *On the Incarnation of the Word*, folio 480; the author of *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 17; Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*, folio 122; Jerome, *On Those Things Attributed to God in the Holy Scriptures*, volume IX, folio 67; Isidore of Seville, *On the Highest Good*, book I, chapter 10; *Sentences*, book I, chapter 1; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Properties of Speech*, book IV, chapter 10; Durandus, *Sentences*, book I, distinction 8, question 3.

### [And the Son]

Against the fury of Arius, who said that the Son was not unchangeable like the Father, but changeable in the manner of creatures. Athanasius, volume I, *Disputation 2 against the Arians*, folio 141, and *Oration against the Arians*, volume II, folio 30; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 3; *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 13; Origen, *Commentary on Numbers*, homily 16, chapter 23; *On First Principles* (*Περὶ ἀρχῶν*), book I, chapter 8; Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book III, folio 56; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 4; Sozomen, book I, chapter 14; Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, [p. 158] chapter 5: “The catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes those who say that the Son of God is changeable or mutable.”

## CHAPTER LIX

### [Angels do not possess goodness by nature]

Angels are not holy by nature; rather, they came to be called holy through faith, through a manner of life pleasing to God, and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit himself. Faustinus, *On the Faith*, chapter 7; Cyril of Alexandria, *The Treasury*, book IV, chapter 1; Baeticus, *On the Faith*; Didymus of Alexandria, *Commentary on the First Epistle of John*, chapter 3; [Col. 1035D] *On the Holy Spirit*, book I; Origen, *On First Principles* (*Περὶ ἀρχῶν*), book I, chapters 5 and 8; Basil the Great, homily 8 on Psalm 32; *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 19; Athanasius, *Dialogue 1*; Nazianzen, oration 44.

### [They are called holy angels]

They are called holy angels because of the exceedingly beautiful and blameless ministry that they offer to God. Philo, *On the Giants*.

## CHAPTER LX

### [He confesses the substance of all creatures to be good]

Against the fury of Mani, who, following other ancient heretics, held that there are two natures and substances, namely, one good and one evil. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 45; *On Christian Religion*, chapters 9, 19, and 23; *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, book II, chapter 8; *Soliloquies*, book I, chapter 1; *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book VI, chapter 2; *Against Julian*, book I, chapter 3; Papias, under “Manichaean”; Epiphanius, heresies 24, 36, and 66; [Col. 1036A] the author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 21; Athanasius, *Against the Pagans*, folio 2; Damascene, *Dialogue against the Manichaeans*, page 251; *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 21; Jerome, *Commentary on Jeremiah*, book I, chapter 3; *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book IV, chapter 28; *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 4; Basil the Great, homily 2 on the *Hexaemeron*, and sermon *That God Is Not the Author of Evils*.

Gregory Nazianzen, oration 40, *On Holy Baptism*, folio 671:

“Believe that evil has no substance, nor kingdom, nor that it is without beginning, nor that it arose by itself, nor that it was generated by God; rather, believe that this is our work and the work of the Evil One, which entered into us through our lack of vigilance, but not through the work of the Creator.” [p. 159]

The learned Hierotheus, in Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names* (*Περὶ θείων Ὀνομάτων*), pages 313 and following.

## CHAPTER LXI

### [The angelic powers that remained fixed in divine love]

Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 28; *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 10; the author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 23; Isidore of Seville, [Col. 1036B] *Sentences*, book I, chapter 10; Bede, *Commentary on Job*, chapter 4; Philip the Presbyter, *Commentary on Job*, book I, chapter 6; book II, chapter 25; Caesarius, *Dialogue 1*; Nazianzen, oration 2, *On Holy Easter*.

## CHAPTER LXII

### [The angels were created such that, if they willed, they could remain in the light of blessedness]

Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, chapter 3:

“They are therefore a rational and intellectual nature, endowed with free power, mutable according to purpose, or changeable according to will; for everything created is mutable, whereas only the uncreated is immutable, and everything rational possesses free power. Thus, insofar as it is rational and intellectual, it possesses free power; but insofar as it is created, it is mutable, possessing the power both to remain and to advance in the good, and to turn toward what is worse.”

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, book I, folio 186; Origen, *On First Principles* (*Περὶ ἀρχῶν*), book II, chapter 8; Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 29; the author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 3; Peter Lombard, book II, distinction 5; Beaticus, *On the Faith*; Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 2; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Second Catechetical Lecture for the Enlightened*, folio 12.

### [After the fall, the angels were so confirmed]

Bede, in the *Questions on Genesis*, folio 122, from Gregory: “The angels were created such that, if they willed, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but if they did not will it, they could also fall. Hence Satan fell with the legions that followed him. But after his fall, the angels who remained were so confirmed that they cannot fall at all.” [p. 160] Philip the Presbyter, *Commentary on Job*, chapter 4, folio 13.

## CHAPTER LXIII

### [Marriage is good]

By God’s institution, since he joined it together at the beginning of creation with the bond of faith, enriched it with the gift of blessing, and increased it through the growth of offspring. Fulgentius, *To Proba on Virginity*, letter 3, folio 77; Genesis I; Martial, bishop of Limoges, *Letter to the People of Toulouse*, chapter 9; Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book I, chapter 1; Arethas, *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, chapter 39; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture to the Enlightened at Jerusalem* (*Κατήχησις δʹ φωτιζομένων ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις*), page 22; the author of *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 3, in Augustine, volume III; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 29; Jerome, *To Salvina*, letter 9; *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 1; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 25; Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 23; Maximus, bishop of Turin, homily 1, *On the Lord’s Epiphany*; Junilius, bishop, *On Genesis*, folios 36 and 39; Theodoret, *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, folio 413; Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chapter 12; *To Celestine on Original Sin*, book II, chapter 23 and following; Athanasius, [Col. 1037A] *Against All Heresies*, volume I, folio 853; Epiphanius, heresies 62 and 67; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 26.

That marriage is a good thing is proved not only by the fact that the Lord is read to have instituted marriage between the first parents, but also by the fact that Christ attended a wedding at Cana of Galilee and commended it by a miracle, changing water into wine.

And in distinction 30: “The final cause of contracting marriage is the procreation of offspring; for this reason God instituted marriage between the first parents, to whom he said: ‘Increase and multiply.’ The second reason, after Adam’s sin, is the avoidance of fornication; hence the Apostle says: ‘Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.’”

## CHAPTER LXIV

### [Continence is better]

Bernard, *On the Way of Living Well*, sermon 22, folio 1268: “Conjugal chastity is good, but widowed continence is better, while virginal integrity is best.” See the author of *On Continence*, [Col. 1037B] in Augustine, volume IV, folio 703 and following; Jerome, *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians*, book IV, chapter 5; Bede, volume VII, *Winter Homilies for the Season*, folio 285.

## CHAPTER LXV

### [Virginity is superior to both forms of goodness]

Saint Paul and all the Fathers, by unanimous agreement, prefer virginity to marriage. Paul, *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter 7; Chrysostom, volume I, *On the Words of Isaiah, “I Saw the Lord,”* homily 3, folio 1294: “Marriage is good, but virginity is better; yet because virginity is better, marriage is not therefore evil, but it is inferior, though it too is good.” Also *On Virginity*, volume V, chapter 11; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 25; Cyprian, *On the Nativity of Christ*, folio 405; Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 1; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 15; Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapters 18 and 40; Fulgentius, *On Virginity, to Proba*, letter 3; Gaudentius, treatise 8, folio 70; Nazianzen, *On Praise of Virginity*, and oration 20, *In Praise of Basil the Great*; [Col. 1037C] Athanasius, *To Ammon the Monk*, volume II, folio 43; Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters*, book II, letter 133; book III, letter 353; book IV, letter 115; Sulpicius Severus, book II, *Life of Martin*; *Reply of the Bishops of Teles to Pope Siricius*, volume I of the Councils, folio 422; Ambrose, letter 7, folio 185 and following; Junilius, bishop of Africa, *On Genesis*, folio 39; Epiphanius, *Against the Origenists*, heresy 63.

## CHAPTER LXVI

### [It is good to take food with thanksgiving]

Maximus, bishop of Turin, wrote a homily on giving thanks to God after eating, as Gennadius notes in *On Illustrious Men*. Origen also relates that ancient Christians invoked the Lord’s name before eating and marked food and drink with the sign of the cross, [Col. 1037D] *Commentary on Job*, book III, folio 270:

“If, when we eat and drink, we remember the faith and invoke the terrible name of the Lord; if we mark ourselves and our food or drink with the sign of the venerable cross of Christ; if, lifting our eyes to heaven, we say, ‘You who give food to all flesh, grant also that we may partake of this food with your blessing,’ and so forth.” [p. 162]

I also observe that, according to Clement, baptized persons did not eat with unbelievers. Thus, in book I of the *Recognitions*, folio 10, he says:

“When he had said this, he withdrew in order to take food with his companions; but he ordered me to eat separately. After the meal, when he had praised God and given thanks, he also explained this very action to me, adding: ‘May the Lord grant that you may become our equal in all things, so that, once you have received baptism, you may come to the same table with us.’”

And in book VII, folio 113:

“We also observe that we do not share a table with Gentiles unless they have believed, received the truth, been baptized, and been consecrated through a threefold invocation of the blessed Name; then we eat with them. Otherwise, even if they are father or mother, wife or children, or brothers, we cannot share a table with them.”

### [To abstain from certain things, not as though they were evil]

Christians sometimes abstain from meat and wine, not because they hate these things as *abominations* (*βδελύγματα*), “but so that the flesh may not grow vigorous with regard to sexual pleasures” (*ἀλλὰ τοῦ μὴ σφριγᾶν περὶ τὰ ἀφροδίσια τὴν σάρκα*), as Clement of Alexandria says, *Stromata*, book VII, folio 315.

The author of *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 3: “The servants of God, in abstaining from meat and wine, do not avoid them as unclean things, but follow the practices of a purer life.” And chapter 42: “Hold most firmly that the servants of God who abstain from meat and wine do not reject as unclean things those things made by God, but abstain from stronger food and drink solely for the disciplining of the body.” [Col. 1038A]

See Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, book VII, folio 167 and following; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture to the Enlightened at Jerusalem* (*Κατήχησις δʹ φωτιζομένων ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις*), page 23; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 18; Bernard, *On the Way of Living Well*, sermon 24; Peter Damian, letter 1; notes to Minucius Felix, folio 54.

## CHAPTER LXVII

### [To say that marriage is evil is characteristic of the Hieracites and Manichaeans]

For they reject marriage as evil and as an affair of indecency, asserting most foolishly that every sexual union is filthy and that married people cannot possess the kingdom of heaven. Epiphanius, heresy 67; Athanasius, *Against All Heresies*, folio 852; Jerome, *To Celantia*, letter 14, chapter 8; *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 1; [p. 163] Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapter 30 and following; John Damascene, *On Heresies*, folio 581; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 29; Augustine, *Against Secundinus the Manichaean*, chapter 21, and *On Heresies*, chapter 46; Pope Vigilius, in the decrees, volume II of the Councils.

Council of Gangra, chapter 1; First Council of Braga, chapter 11: “If anyone condemns human marriages and abhors the procreation of children, as Mani and Priscillian taught, let him be anathema.”

Ignatius, archbishop of Antioch, letter 6 to the Philadelphians, page 34:

“If anyone calls lawful intercourse and the birth of children corruption and defilement, or calls any of the foods abominable, such a person has the apostate dragon dwelling within him.” [Col. 1038B]

### [They also believe foods to be evil]

Tatian, the Encratites, Jovinian, Mani, and Priscillian reject the foods that God created for use. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 1; Epiphanius, heresies 47 and 56; Theodoret, *Epitome of the Divine Decrees*, folio 416, and *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book I; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 46, and *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book VI, chapter 6; Clement, *Constitutions*, book VI, chapters 10 and 25; Pope Nicholas, *To the Questions of the Bulgarians*, chapter 43; Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 116, folio 761; the author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 41.

First Council of Braga, chapter 14: “If anyone considers the foods of meat unclean which God gave for human use, and abstains from them not for the affliction of his body but as though they were unclean, so that he does not even taste cooked vegetables prepared with meat, as Mani and Priscillian taught, let him be anathema.” [Col. 1038C]

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### [To make marriage equal to consecrated virginity]

The heretic Jovinian, and the empty talkers Sarmatio and Barbatianus, asserted that virgins, widows, and married women who had once been washed in Christ, if they did not differ from others in their works, possessed equal merit, and that there was no difference between those who abstained and those who simply feasted. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 2; Isidore of Seville, *Origins*, book VIII, chapter 5; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 82; *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book III, chapter 7; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, volume VII, chapter 2; Ambrose, letter 25, folio 238; Jerome, *To Celantia*, letter 14, [p. 164] chapter 8: “The rule of apostolic teaching neither makes the works of continence equal to marriage with Jovinian, nor condemns marriage with Mani.” See Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue 2 on the Life of Martin*.

## CHAPTER LXIX

### [It must be believed with complete faith that the blessed Virgin Mary conceived and remained a virgin after childbirth]

This refutes the arguments of the Antidicomarianites, the Claudians, and the heretic Helvidius, who said that Saint Mary the Virgin, after the Savior’s birth, had children through her association with Joseph, who were called the Lord’s brothers. Jerome, volume II, folio 133 and following; Bonaventure, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 30, number 5; Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, under Helvidius; Epiphanius, heresy 78.

### [She gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin after childbirth]

Origen, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 1, homily 1: “The holy Virgin gave birth to God, yet remained undefiled; she became a mother, but did not lose her virginity. Therefore she gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin.” Also *Commentary on Leviticus*, homily 8, chapter 13; Chrysostom, homily *On John the Baptist*, volume III, folio 359; Alfonso of Toledo, *On the Unblemished Virginity of Mary*, volume VIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; Augustine, *Against Julian*, book I, chapter 2, folio 637; *Tractate 120 on John*; Jerome, *On the Assumption of the Virgin Mary*, part 2, treatise 4, letter 56; Cyril of Alexandria, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, folio 63.

[Col. 1039B]

### [She was a virgin before childbirth, but not a virgin after childbirth]

Heretics of the city of Cremona dared to defend this ungodly blasphemy of the heretic Helvidius, saying: “If Mary remained a virgin after childbirth, she gave birth not to a human being but to an angel; therefore she was not a virgin after childbirth.” John Trithemius, *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle*, folio 212, around the year of Our Lord 1315.

## CHAPTER LXX

### [We should not believe that the elements will be destroyed by fire, but changed for the better]

See Oecumenius, *Commentary on the Second Epistle of Saint Peter*, chapter 4; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, chapter 6; Bede, *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, chapter 21; Chrysostom, *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, chapter VIII, homily 14; Proclus, in Epiphanius, heresy 64; Philip the Presbyter, *Commentary on Job*, book I, chapter 14; Julian, bishop of Toledo, *Prognosticum*, book III, chapter 43; Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book XIV, chapter 51; Sixtus of Siena, *Holy Library*, book VI, note 340; Thomas Aquinas, *Supplement to the Summa*, part III, question 74, article 5 and following. [p. 165]

## CHAPTER LXXI

### [It is good to distribute one’s possessions to the poor]

Thomas Aquinas, *Commentary on Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter IX, lesson 1; Bernard, *Sentences*, folio 486; Ambrose, *On Naboth*, chapter 7, folios 554–555; Jerome, *To Hedibia*, letter 150, question 1.

## CHAPTER LXXII

### [A cleric who has married two women must not be ordained]

Because of the excellence of the celebration of sacred rites, and “because of the surpassing honor of the priesthood” (*καὶ διὰ τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τῆς τιμῆς τῆς ἱερωσύνης*), the Church does not admit to the priesthood a man who, after the death of his first wife, has entered upon a second marriage. Epiphanius, *Against the Phrygists*, heresy 48; *Against the Cathari*, heresy 59, folio 215; *Apostolic Canons*, chapter 16; Pope Innocent I, in the decrees, chapter 6; Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 23; Jerome, book II, *Against Jovinian*, chapter 2; *On Monogamy, to Ageruchia*, letter 2, [Col. 1039D] chapter 2; Chrysostom, *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to Titus*, chapter I, homily 2; Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 18; Council of Epaon, chapter 2; First Council of Orange, chapter 25; Justinian, emperor, novella 6; Origen, *Commentary on Luke*, chapter XI, homily 17; Ambrose, letter 25, folios 246 and 282; Gregory the Great, book II, letter 25; notes to Minucius Felix, folio 57.

### [Nor a man who has had a concubine]

Third Council of Orléans, chapter 9: “Concerning those who have publicly taken concubines as partners, we have judged that this must be observed: they are not to be ordained thereafter.” *Apostolic Canons*, chapter 16; Jerome, *To Oceanus on the Life of Clerics*, volume IX, folio 255.

### [Nor a man who has taken a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute]

Apostolic Canon 17:

“He who has taken a widow, or a divorced woman, or a prostitute, or a slave, or one of those who perform on the stage, cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor belong at all to the priestly order” (*Ὁ χήραν λαβών, ἢ ἐκβεβλημένην ἢ ἑταίραν, ἢ οἰκέτιν, ἢ τῶν ἐπὶ σκηνῆς, οὐ δύναται εἶναι ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὅλως τοῦ καταλόγου τοῦ ἱερατικοῦ*).

That is: “He who has married a widow, or a woman separated from her husband by divorce, or a prostitute, or a maidservant, or any woman devoted to public spectacles, cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor, in short, belong to the priestly order.” *Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 17; Council of Telese, chapter 4; Council of Gerunda, chapter 8; Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 5; Roman Council, chapter 2; *Corpus of Canon Law*, part I, distinction 34; Martin of Braga, *Extracts from the Greek Synods*, volume II of the Councils, chapter 26; Gregory the Great, *Letters*, book II, letter 25. [p. 166]

### [Nor a man who has mutilated any member of his own body]

Apostolic Canon 21:

“He who has mutilated himself must not become a cleric, for he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation” (*Ὁ ἀκρωτηριάσας ἑαυτόν, μὴ γινέσθω κληρικος, αὐτοφονευτὴς γάρ ἐστιν ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δημιουργίας ἐχθρός*).

That is: “He who has cut off his own sexual organs must not become a cleric; for he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation.” See Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 14; Martin of Braga, *Extracts of Greek Chapters*, chapter 21, volume II of the Councils; Pope Gelasius, *Decrees*, chapter 20; Gelasius, *On the Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, page 157; *Corpus of Canon Law*, part I, distinction 55. [Col. 1040A]

### [Nor a man convicted of having taken interest]

Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 67: “Usurers are never to be ordained as clerics.” Martin of Braga, *Extracts of Greek Chapters*, volume II of the Councils, chapter 63, folio 226; Gelasius, *On the Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, page 167; Justinian, emperor, novella 123; Council of Elvira, chapter 20.

Basil the Great, however, states in the *Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 18, that one who has taken interest may be admitted to the priesthood if he spends the unjust profit on the poor and thereafter ceases to take interest:

“He who receives interest, if he spends the unjust profit on the poor and thereafter ceases to receive interest, is admissible to the priesthood” (*Ὁ τόκους λαμβάνων, εἰ τὸ ἄδικον κέρδος εἰς πτωχοὺς ἀναλώσει, καὶ τοῦ λοιποῦ παύσαιτο τόκους λαμβάνων, δεκτὸς εἰς ἱερωσύνην*).

### [Nor a man known to have performed on the stage]

Apostolic Canon 41: “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to dice or drunkenness must either cease or be deposed” (*Ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος κύβοις σχολάζων καὶ μέθαις, ἢ παυσάσθω, ἢ καθαιρέσθω*).

That is: “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who indulges either in gambling or drunkenness must either desist from it or be deposed.” See Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 9, chapter 27; Peter Damian, letter 2, folio 358. [p. 167] [Col. 1040C]

### [Nor a man who publicly laments mortal sins through penance]

Council of Epaon, chapter 4: “Those who have professed penance are in no way to be admitted to the clerical state.” Pope Stephen I, letter to Hilary, volume I of the Councils, folio 156; Council of Agde, chapter 43; Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 53; Third Council of Arles, chapter 3; First Council of Orange, chapter 16; Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 5; Pope Innocent I, volume I of the Councils, chapter 6; *Corpus of Canon Law*, distinction 50; Louis the Emperor, addition 4 to the *Capitulary of Charlemagne*, chapter 4; Durandus, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 14, question 5.

### [Nor a man who has at some time become insane]

The canons of the Arabic Council of Nicaea, translated by Francisco Turrianus, chapter 1: “We command that an insane man not become a cleric.” Pope Stephen, letter to Hilary, volume I of the Councils, folio 156.

### [Or one afflicted by the devil]

*Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 31:

“Let one possessed by a demon neither be ordained nor pray with the faithful; once cleansed, however, let him be admitted if he is worthy” (*Ὁ δαιμονῶν μήητε κληρούσθω, μήτε πιστοῖς συνευχέσθω, καθαρισθεὶς δὲ, εἰ ἄξιος, προσδεχθήτω*).

That is: “He who is afflicted by a demon must neither become a cleric nor pray with the faithful. Once cleansed, however, let him be admitted if he is worthy.” Pope Gelasius, *Decrees*, volume I of the Councils, chapter 21; Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 15; First Council of Orange, chapter 16; Council of Elvira, chapter 29. [Col. 1040D]

### [Nor a man who offers money out of ambition]

Apostolic Canon 30:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon obtains this dignity through money, let both he and the one who ordained him be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off from communion, as Simon Magus was by me, Peter” (*Εἴ τις ἐπίσκοπος διὰ χρημάτων τῆς ἀξίας ταύτης ἐγκρατὴς γένηται, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, καθαιρείσθω καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ ὁ χειροτονήσας, καὶ ἐκκοπτέσθω τῆς κοινωνίας παντάπασιν, ὡς Σίμων ὁ μάγος ὑπὸ ἐμοῦ Πέτρου*).

That is: “If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both he and his ordainer be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off from communion, as Simon Magus was by Peter.” Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 1, chapter 24; Gregory the Great, *Letters*, book IX, letter 55; Gennadius of Constantinople, letter to P. R., volume of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; T[.....]ra[.....]ius, patriarch of Constantinople, to Pope Adrian, [Col. 1041A] letter concerning ordinations not performed for money; Council of Chalcedon, act 15, chapter 2; Council of Chalon, chapter 16; Pope Symmachus, *Decrees*, volume I of the Councils, chapters 2 and 5; Louis the Emperor, *To the Capitularies of Charlemagne*, chapter 14, folio 1200; *Corpus of Canon Law*, part II, cause 1, question 1; *Greek-Roman Law*, volume I, folio 187 and following. [p. 168]

## CHAPTER LXXIII

### [The relics of the blessed martyrs are to be honored as Christ’s members]

Jerome, letter 53, folio 188, to Riparius: “We do not worship or adore the relics of martyrs, lest we serve the creature rather than the Creator. We honor the relics of martyrs so that we may adore him whose martyrs they are. We honor servants so that the honor shown to servants may redound to the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever receives you receives me.’”

See Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, *On the Honor of the Martyrs* (*Περὶ τῆς τῶν μαρτύρων Τιμῆς*), oration 8, *Against the Greeks*; Isidore of Pelusium, book I, letter 55; Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 34; Cyril of Alexandria, [Col. 1041B] *Against Julian*, book VI, folio 140; book X, folio 234; Chrysostom, *To the People of Antioch*, homily 66; Ambrose, sermon *On the Apostles Peter and Paul*, folio 142; *On the Feast of the Martyrs Nazarius and Celsus*, folio 246; John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 16.

### [Eunomianus and Vigilantius are held to have done this]

For they did not frequent the basilicas of the martyrs, nor venerate the relics of the saints; they called those Christians who received the bones of dead men “ash-worshippers” and idolaters. Jerome, *To Riparius the Presbyter*, letter 53, folio 188; *Against Vigilantius*, book I, chapter 3, folio 191; *Commentary on Isaiah*, book XVIII, chapter 65; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 16.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

### [We believe that the way of salvation belongs only to the baptized]

The holy Fathers entirely exclude from the company of the blessed those who have not received the sacrament of regeneration, relying especially on Christ’s declaration in John III, verse [Col. 1041C] 5:

“Truly, truly, I say to you: unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (*Ἀμὴν, ἀμὴν, λέγω σοι, ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ Πνεύματος, οὐ δύναται εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ*).

They apply this also to unbaptized infants.

Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins against the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 24: “The Christians of Africa most suitably call baptism itself nothing other than salvation, and the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing other than life; without these no one can attain eternal life.”

The author of the book *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 27, in Augustine, volume III, folio 164: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not only human beings who already possess the use of reason, but also infants—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or, having been born from their mothers, depart from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is given in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—are to be punished with the everlasting torment of eternal fire. For although they had no sin arising from their own action, they nevertheless contracted the condemnation of original sin through carnal conception and birth.”

Clement, *Recognitions*, book VI, folio [Col. 1041D] 102; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Third Catechetical Lecture to the Enlightened at Jerusalem*, folio 20; Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, folio 342; *To Demetrianus*, folio 258; *On Mortality*, folio 272; Caesarius, bishop of Arles, sermon 5, *On Easter*, folio 137; Primasius of Africa, *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 5, page 48; Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 24; *Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 13; *Sentences*, book I, chapter 22; Augustine, letters 28 to Jerome, 43 to Valentine, 102 to Evodius, 105 to the presbyter Sixtus, and 106 to Boniface, and letter 157 to Optatus; *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 8; *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book VI, folio 750 and following; *On Baptism against the Pelagians*, volume X, sermon 14; *On the Soul and Its Origin, to Renatus*, book I, chapter 9; *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapter 20; *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book X, chapter 15; *On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians*, chapter 8.

The author of *Hypognosticon*, in Augustine, [Col. 1042A] volume VII, on article 5, folio 953 and following; Origen, *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 2, homily 14; Gregory of Nyssa, *Against Those Who Delay Baptism*, folio 470; Ambrose, *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 8; *On Abraham*, book II, chapter 11; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapters 1, 12, and 13; Bede, *Commentary on Genesis*, folio 199; *Commentary on John*, book I, chapter 2; Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, folio 1975.

The scholastic theologians, and Augustine himself, as well as Nazianzen, Nicetas, and Athanasius, say that the punishment of unregenerate infants will be exceedingly mild—namely, that they will experience neither the punishment of material fire nor the worm of conscience, except that they will lack the vision of God forever.

Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book II, distinction 33, number 43 and following; book IV, distinction 4, number 43; Durandus, book II, distinction 33, question 3; Augustine, *Against Julian*, book V, chapter 8; *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 93; *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book I, chapter 16.

Gregory Nazianzen, oration 40, *On Holy Baptism*, folio 653:

“Unbaptized infants will neither be glorified nor punished by the just Judge, since they are unsealed but not evil; rather, they have suffered the loss than committed the offense. For no one who is not already worthy of punishment is thereby already worthy of honor, just as no one who is not worthy of honor is thereby already worthy of punishment” (*μήτε δοξασθήσεσθαι, μήτε κολασθήσεσθαι περὶ τοῦ δικαίου κριτοῦ, ὡς ἀσφραγίστους μὲν, ἀπονήρους δέ, ἀλλὰ παθόντας μᾶλλον τὴν ζημίαν ἢ δράσαντας· οὐ γὰρ ὅστις οὐ κολάσεως ἄξιος ἥδη, καὶ τιμῆς, ὥσπερ οὐδέ ὅστις οὐ τιμῆς, ἤδη καὶ κολάσεως*).

Nicetas the Greek scholiast: “There are three grades: one consisting of those who enjoy the delights above; another of those who are tormented by eternal punishments; and a middle one of those who experience neither the pleasures of the heavenly kingdom nor any punishments. The infants who have not been washed in baptism will be placed in this middle state, as will those who desired baptism but were prevented from receiving it by some violent circumstance.”

Athanasius, *Questions to Antiochus*, question 114, folio 309:

“Where do dying infants go—to punishment or to the kingdom? And where are the infants of unbelievers? And where are unbaptized infants of the faithful who die placed—with the faithful or with the unbelievers?”

**Response:** “Since the Lord says, ‘Let the children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven,’ and since the Apostle likewise says, ‘But now your children are holy,’ it is evident that the baptized infants of the faithful enter the kingdom as undefiled and believing. But the unbaptized and the children of the Gentiles enter neither the kingdom nor punishment, for they have committed no sin.” [Col. 1042B–C]

The Roman Catholics also follow and approve this opinion of the Fathers concerning unbaptized infants, as is evident from Gregory of Valencia, volume IV, folio 815, and Robert Bellarmine, *On the Sacraments of Baptism*, book I, chapter 4.

We, however, assert that the infants of the faithful who die without the sacred washing are not condemned, because the necessity of baptism is not absolute but ordained; it by no means excludes God’s extraordinary action and his mercy in salvation. God has not so bound this mercy by the ordinary laws of Christian tradition and by the sacraments themselves that, without prejudice to that law, in a case of necessity or deprivation, he could not sanctify children not yet born, while still within the womb, by the baptism of his grace or through the power of the Holy Spirit, as John Gerson says, *Sermon on the Nativity of the Virgin Mary*, part 3, consideration 2, folio 59.

Albert the Great, bishop of Regensburg, therefore truly writes, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, distinction 6, treatise 2, chapter 1:

“One in whom baptism is excluded not through contempt for religion but through the circumstance of necessity does not lose the fruit of baptism; rather, he is regarded as baptized with the baptism of the Spirit in the Holy Spirit. For then baptism is invisibly fulfilled, when the mystery of baptism is excluded not through contempt for religion but by the circumstance of necessity.”

Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, [Col. 1043A] distinction 4; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, letter 77 to Hugh of Saint Victor; Durandus, book IV, distinction 4, question 1; George Cassander, *On the Baptism of Infants*, in his consultation to Emperor Ferdinand, article 9, page 61; John Calvin, *Institutes*, book IV, *On Baptism*, chapter 15, section 20, and chapter 16, section 28.

[We believe that no catechumen possesses eternal life] The author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 3, folio 159:

“From the time when our Savior said, ‘Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,’ no one can receive the kingdom of heaven or eternal life without the sacrament of baptism—except those who, in the Catholic Church, shed their blood for Christ without baptism.”

Cyril of Jerusalem, *Third Catechetical Lecture for the Enlightened of Jerusalem*, page 61:

> Εἴ τις μὴ λάβῃ τὸ βάπτισμα, σωτηρίαν οὐκ ἔχει, πλὴν μόνον μαρτύρων, οἲ καὶ χωρὶς τοῦ ὕδατος λαμβάνουσι τὴν βασιλείαν.

“If anyone does not receive baptism, he has no salvation, except for martyrs alone, who obtain the kingdom even without water.”

Bernard’s opinion is more lenient, for it inclines more toward humane treatment. In his longer letter 77 to Hugh, folio 1483, he says:

“Whoever, at an advanced age, after the remedy of baptism has been proclaimed everywhere, refuses to be baptized, adds to the general and original stain the deliberate crime of pride, carrying with him a double and most just cause of condemnation, if he should happen to depart from the body in such a state. Yet if, before death, he should repent, and wish and ask to be baptized, but, overtaken by the crisis of death, should perhaps be unable to obtain it, provided that right faith, devout hope, and sincere charity are not lacking, may God be merciful to me, for if water alone is lacking to this man, I cannot by any means despair of his salvation, or consider his faith vain, or confound his hope, or extinguish his charity—provided only that water is prevented not by contempt but solely by the impossibility I have mentioned.”

Ambrose, *On the Death of the Emperor Valentinian*, who was still a catechumen, volume V, folio 112:

“I hear that you grieve because he did not receive the sacraments of baptism. Tell me, what else is there in us but will, but petition? Indeed, he had long possessed this desire: to be initiated. Does he therefore not possess the grace he desired? Does he not possess what he requested? Certainly, because he requested it, he received it. Hence the saying: ‘The just man, by whatever death he is overtaken, is in a place of refreshment.’ Therefore, holy father, grant your servant the gift which, while sound, strong, and unharmed, he requested. If illness had caused him to delay, he would nevertheless not have been wholly estranged from your mercy, since he would have been deprived by the swiftness of time, not by his will. Since he possessed your Spirit, how did he not receive your grace? Or if it is the fact that the mysteries were not solemnly celebrated that troubles you, then martyrs too, if they are catechumens, should not be crowned. For they are not crowned if they are not initiated. But if they are washed in their own blood, then this man too is washed by his devotion and his will.”

Zwingli promises eternal life not only to catechumens who died in good works, but also to Gentiles who had no knowledge of Christ at all. Thus, in his *Exposition of the Christian Faith*, folio 559, he addresses the king of France:

“You will see in the eternal fellowship all holy, devout, wise, brave, and honorable men: Adam, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Peter, Paul, Hercules, Theseus, Socrates, Aristides, Antigonus, Numa, Camillus, the Catos, and the Scipios.”

“These things are extraordinary, these things are new, these things are false. We are astonished at what is extraordinary, we are wary of what is new, and we reject what is false.”

Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book III, chapter 3, folio 676. Peter, in Clement, as cited by Origen in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 26, tractate 35, folio 110:

“The good works performed by unbelievers benefit them in this age, but not in the age to come, for the attainment of eternal life.”

See also Athanasius, *To Antiochus*, question 100, folio 303, volume II; Augustine on Psalms XXXI and LXVII; *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book IV, chapter 3; *On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius and Coelestius*, book I, chapter 26; and George Cassander, *Consultation*, article 5, page 38, *On the Works of the Ungodly*.

173 [Except in martyrdom, where the entire sacrament of baptism is completed]

The doctrine of baptism by blood is ancient. Clement also mentions it in *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 5; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 16, and *Scorpiace against the Gnostics*, chapter 6; Primasius, bishop of Africa, in his commentary on Paul’s *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 6; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Thirteenth Catechetical Lecture for the Enlightened of Jerusalem*, folio 110; Cyprian, *To Fortunatus*, letter 73, and *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, folio 399; *On the Star of the [lacuna] Magi,* folio 409; Athanasius, *Questions on Holy Scripture*, question 103, and *To Antiochus the Prince*, question 72; Origen, *Commentary on John*, tractate 8, folio 194, and *Commentary on Matthew*, tractate 12, chapter 20; Ambrose on Psalm CXVIII, folio 891; Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, on Paul’s *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 6; Nicetas in his discourse on Gregory Nazianzen’s *Holy Lights*, folio 842; Augustine, *To Seleucia*, letter 108; and Gennadius.

At this place Gennadius, together with Origen and Prosper, equates baptism by blood with true baptism. Origen, *Commentary on Judges*, chapter 6, homily 7, folio 218:

“Baptism by blood alone is that which makes us purer than baptism by water has made us.”

Prosper of Aquitaine, *Epigram* 88:

> If he dies to the world, reborn through the divine fountain,  
> he becomes new in life, who is buried in water.  
> They are not deprived of Christ’s sacred baptism, for whom he himself was the fountain, a wave of his own blood.  
> Whatever the mystical form of the sacred washing conveys,  
> all of it has been fulfilled by the glory of martyrdom.

But this is false. Martyrdom is not properly and simply called baptism, but only by attribution. Consequently, its efficacy does not reach the efficacy of true baptism, which is one, properly and simply; which possesses its power from Christ’s passion; which takes place in water with a determinate form of words; and which is the sacrament of which the apostle Paul says in Ephesians 4:5: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.” See Christopher Pelargus, a theologian of no ordinary learning, *New Jesuitism, On Baptism*, page 90.

[Baptism’s recipient confesses his faith]

Among the ancients, those preparing to receive the grace of baptism publicly recited the creed in the hearing of the people of the faithful. Ruffinus, *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, folio 74; Jerome, volume IX; Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book VIII, chapter 18; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 20; Gregory Nazianzen, *On Holy Baptism*, and *Oration 18 on Cyprian*; the Council of Laodicea, canon 46; Martin of Braga, bishop, *Excerpts from the Greek Canons*, volume II of the Councils, canon 49, folio 226; Cyril of Alexandria, *Against the Emperor Julian*, book VII, folio 172; Severus of Alexandria, *On the Rites of Baptism*, folio 54; Bede, *Commentary on Mark*, book I, chapter 1.

Thus the rhetorician Victorinus, about to enter baptism, memorably professed his faith from an elevated place, in the presence of the holy multitude at Rome. Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 2, folio 99.

# CHAPTER LXXV

[Pure water ought not to be offered in the Eucharist]

In the Eucharistic sacrifice, the Hydropathists—Ὑδροπαραστάται, “water-offerers”—used water alone. Cyprian condemns them in his letter 63 to Caecilius, folio 131 and following; so too Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 46 and 47; Philastrius, *Against Heresies*, 77; *Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 18; and Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, *On the Meaning of Expressions*, book IV, chapter 10.

[But wine mixed with water]

The ancient writers mention the tempered and mixed cup: Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*, folios 76–77; Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, *Against Heresies*, book IV, chapter 57, and book V, chapter 1; Clement, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 12; the *Liturgy* attributed to Saint James, folio 24; the author of the homily *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, in Jerome, volume IX, folio 248; Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 1; the author of the commentary on Mark, chapter 14; Pope Julius I, *Decretals*, volume I of the Councils, chapter 7; Martin of Braga, bishop, *Excerpts from the Greek Canons*, volume II of the Councils, chapter 55; John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 14; Caesarius of Arles, homily 5, *On Easter*, folio 147; the fathers of the Council in Trullo, canon 32; the African Council, chapter 4; the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 24; the Council of Worms, chapter 4; the Council of Tribur, chapter 24; Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 16; Paschasius, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, chapter 11; Bede, *Commentary on Luke*, book VI, chapter 22; Micrologus, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 10; Algerus, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book II, chapter 4; Pope Eugenius IV, *Decretals*, volume III of the Councils, folio 506; *Corpus of Canon Law*, distinction 2, *On Consecration*; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 74, article 6.

Theophylact, in his commentary on John, chapter 19, folio 567, curses the Armenians, who do not mix water with wine in the mysteries:

> Αἰσχυνέσθωσαν Ἀρμένιοι, οἱ μὴ παρακιρνῶντες ὕδωρ τῷ οἴνῳ ἐν τοῖς μυστηρίοις.

“Let the Armenians be ashamed, who do not mix water with wine in the mysteries.”

In the *Epitome of the Sacred Canons*, folio 17, a priest who does not mix wine with water is deposed:

> Εἴ τις ὕδωρ μόνον, ὡς οἱ Ὑδροπαραστάται, ἢ οἶνον, ὡς οἱ Ἀρμένιοι, ἀλλὰ μὴ οἴνῳ ὕδωρ μιγνὺς, οὕτω τὴν ἄχραντον προσάγει θυσίαν, καθαιρείσθω.

“If anyone offers the immaculate sacrifice in this manner—water alone, like the Hydropathists, or wine, like the Armenians, but without mixing water with wine—let him be deposed.”

The Roman Catholics even now vigorously insist on this admixture. William Durandus, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, book V, folio 70:

“Just as water cannot be consecrated without wine, so wine cannot be transubstantiated without water. Therefore, if he omits it through forgetfulness, he sins venially; through negligence, mortally; and he is to be severely punished.”

Robert Bellarmine, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book IV, chapter 10:

“The Catholic Church has always believed that it is so necessary to mix water with wine in the chalice that this cannot be omitted without grave sin. Therefore, the Fathers of the Council of Trent, chapter 8, canon 9, strike with the sword of anathema all who deny that water must be mixed with the wine when it is offered in the chalice.”

The Greeks did not observe this custom of mixing. Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XVIII, chapter 53; Pope Innocent III, *On the Mystery of the Mass*, book IV, chapter 32, folio 390; William Durandus, bishop of Mende, *Rationale*, book IV, folio 70; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 11; Bonaventure, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 11, number 36.

Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, *On Peter Lombard’s Sentences*, book IV, distinction 12, question 5:

“It is said that the Greeks do not add water, and yet they truly consecrate; for it is not necessary to the sacrament.”

Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 74, article 7; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, letter 69 to Guido, since it is not read that Christ, at the institution of the chalice, handed his disciples wine mixed with water; Paschasius, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, chapter 11; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Eucharist*, chapter 11.

“Therefore, this sacrament can rightly be consecrated with wine alone because of Christ’s institution, since Christ, the author of all things, celebrated this sacrament with the wine of the vine.”

Bonaventure, book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 11, number 58; Albert the Great, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, distinction 3, treatise 2, chapter 1; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 74, article 6; Durandus, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 12, question 5; John Gerson, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, part 2, folio 26.

# CHAPTER LXXVI

[Our flesh is not evil, as the Sethians, Ophites, and Patricians maintain]

Here Gennadius wrongly conflates the Sethians, Ophites, and Patricians, since each group has its own doctrines and distinctive errors. The Sethians honor Seth, Adam’s son, and believe that he himself is Christ. The Ophites nourish and venerate the serpent, believing that it first brought us knowledge of good and evil. The Patricians and Venustians say that the devil made the human body from the loins down to the feet. Papias on Seth; Philastrius, *Against Heresies*, 1 and 3; Honorius, *Against Heresies*, 31; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 37 and 39; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book I; Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5; John of Damascus, *On Heresies*, folio 578; Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 47; Augustine, *Against Heresies*, 61, and *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book V, chapter 5.

[Florianus]

Papias: “The heretics called Florians derive their name from a certain Florianus. They teach that the Lord created evil, contrary to what is written: ‘The Lord made all things good.’”

[By the soul’s free choice, good or evil is produced in us]

See Ambrose, bishop of Milan, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 5; Theophylact, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 7, folio 29:

> Ἡ φύσις ἡμῶν ἀγαθή ἐστιν, ὡς Θεοῦ δημιούργημα, κατὰ δὲ προαίρεσιν πονηρευόμεθα.

“Our nature is good, as God’s creation; but by our choice we become evil.”

Augustine, *Commentary on John*, tractate 42, chapter 8, folio 214:

“Every nature is good, but human nature has been corrupted by an evil will. What God made cannot be evil, unless the human being is evil to himself.”

# CHAPTER LXXVII

[At the resurrection from the dead, the form of sex will not be changed]

This is directed against Origen, who asserts that in the future age women will be changed into men. Jerome, *Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*, letter 61, chapter 3.

Julian, bishop of Toledo, *Prognostic*, book III, chapter 24:

“Many believe that what the Apostle says, ‘Until we all attain to a perfect man,’ and so forth, means that all women will rise in the male sex, because man was made from clay, whereas woman was made from the side of man.
