But we, instructed by the opinions of Catholic teachers, believe and hold that the omnipotent God, who created, established, and redeemed both sexes, will restore both in the resurrection.”

Justin Martyr, *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox*, question 60; Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 17; Athanasius, *Questions to Antiochus*, question 24; Bonaventure, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 44, article 2; Clement, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 6; Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 23; the author of *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 3; Jerome, *Epitaph for Paula to Eustochium*, letter 27, folio 79, and *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 21, folio 156; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Meaning of Expressions*, book IV, chapter 10; Thomas Aquinas, *Supplement to the Third Part of the Summa*, question 81, article 3.

# CHAPTER LXXVIII

[Before the Lord’s passion and resurrection, all the souls of the saints were in hell]

Gennadius holds that, from the time Adam sinned and paradise was closed to him, no saint’s soul ascended to heaven, but that all were detained in hell—later writers called it the limbo of the fathers—for whom Christ also descended into hell, to free them and make them possessors of himself.

This was the common opinion of many Fathers: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Fourth Catechetical Lecture of the Enlightened in Jerusalem*, page 11; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapters 7 and 55; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI; John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, chapter 29; Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 181; Gregentius, *Disputation with the Jew Herbanus*, page 178; Jerome on Psalms XXIII, folio 28, Psalm XV, folio 15, and Psalm CXVIII, folio 159, and on Daniel, book I, chapter 3; Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 27, book XII, chapter 7, and book XIII, chapter 16, and *Homilies on the Holy Gospels*, homily 19, folio 391, and homily 22, folio 401; Fulgentius, *To King Thrasamund*, book III, folio 54; the author of the commentary on Matthew, chapter 3, homily 5, folio 557, in Chrysostom, volume II; Gaudentius on Exodus, tractate 10, volume VII of the *Library of the Fathers*; Nicephorus Callistus, book I, chapter 31; Philip the presbyter on Job, book III, chapter 38; Procopius the Sophist on Isaiah, folio 154; Athanasius, *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, folio 506, and *On the Passion and Cross of the Lord*, folio 802; Jerome, volume III, letter 129, folio 370, on Paul’s First Letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, and on the Letter to the Ephesians, book II, chapter 4; Julian, bishop of Toledo, *Prognostic*, book II, chapter 12; Theodore Abu Qurrah, *Disputation with the Emesan*, chapter 7; Remigius of Auxerre, bishop, on Psalm LXXXV and on Zechariah, chapter 9; Bede on Job, book I, chapter 10; Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, *Allegories on John*, folio 191, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*; Ambrose on Paul’s Letter to the Romans, chapter 5; Epiphanius, *Against the Tatianists*, heresy 46; Sedulius on Paul’s Letter to the Romans, chapter 5; Dionysius the Carthusian on the First Letter of Peter, chapter 3, and on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 2; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part III, question 53, article 5 and following.

In confirmation of this they produce the following scriptural testimonies:

- Genesis 37:35: “I shall go down to my son mourning into hell.”
- Ecclesiasticus 24:45: “I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth, and I will look upon all who sleep, and I will enlighten all who hope in the Lord.”
- Zechariah 9:11: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”
- Job 38:17: “Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?”
- 1 Peter 3:19: “And coming, he preached to the spirits who were in prison.”

Bullinger, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 25; John Calvin, *Institutes*, book II, chapter 16, section 9; and Beza, on Acts 2, on the First Letter of Peter, chapter 3, and on the Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 4, say that the passages mentioned above were wrongly twisted by the ancients into a penal prison for pious souls. They maintain that those souls, even before Christ’s coming and passion, were in the bosom of tranquility, free from punishment, awaiting the consolations of the resurrection.

Augustine does not seem to contradict their assertion when he confesses that he still does not know what benefit Christ’s descent into hell brought to those righteous people who were in Abraham’s bosom, from whom Christ never withdrew according to the blessed presence of his divinity.

But we shall bring Augustine’s own passages forward, from his letter 99 to Evodius, volume II, folio 284:

“Almost the entire Church agrees that Christ freed the first man, the father of the human race, from hell; and we must believe that the Church did not believe this without reason, even if no explicit authority from the canonical Scriptures is brought forward concerning it.

Some add that this benefit was also granted to the ancient saints—Abel, Seth, Noah and his household, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the other patriarchs and prophets—so that when the Lord came into hell they might be released from those sufferings. But how Abraham, in whose bosom the pious poor man was also received, could have been in those sufferings, I do not see; perhaps those who can explain it do so.

As for the claim that only two persons, namely Abraham and Lazarus, were in that bosom of memorable rest before the Lord descended into hell, and that only of these two it was said to the rich man, ‘Between you and us a great chasm has been fixed,’ I do not know whether anyone would not regard it as absurd. Moreover, if more than two were there, who would dare say that the patriarchs and prophets were not there, to whom Scripture bears such distinguished testimony to God’s justice and piety?

What benefit, then, did he provide for these people, who released the sufferings of hell, when they were not in those sufferings? I do not yet understand—especially since I have nowhere been able to find the lower world called good in the passages of Scripture. If it is never read in the divine authorities, then certainly Abraham’s bosom—that is, the dwelling of a certain secret rest—is not to be believed a part of hell, although in the very words of that great teacher it sufficiently appears, as I think, that this bosom of such great blessedness is not some part or member of hell. For what is the great chasm except a certain gap separating things widely, between which there is not merely a separation but a firmly established one?

Therefore, if Holy Scripture had said that Christ, having died, came into Abraham’s bosom, without mentioning hell and its sufferings, I wonder whether anyone would dare assert that he descended into hell. But because clear testimonies mention both hell and sufferings, there is no reason why we should believe that the Savior came there except to save people from its sufferings. Yet I am still asking whether he found all those in them, or only certain ones whom he judged worthy of that benefit.

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that he was in hell and granted this benefit to those situated amid its sufferings. Hence I have not yet discovered what he conferred, when he descended into hell, upon those righteous people who were in Abraham’s bosom, from whom I do not see that he ever withdrew according to the blessed presence of his divinity.”

And in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, volume III, folio 498, book XII, chapter 33:

“I confess that I have not yet discovered that the place where the souls of the righteous rest is called hell. It is reasonably believed that Christ’s soul came as far as those places in which sinners are tormented, in order to release from their torments those whom, by his hidden justice, he judged should be released.

For I do not see how else what is said—‘whom God raised from the dead,’ and so forth—can be understood, except that we should take him to have released the sufferings of certain people in hell, by that power by which he is Lord, before whom every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. By this power he could not himself be held by the sufferings he released.

For neither Abraham nor the poor man in his bosom—that is, in the secrecy of his rest—was in sufferings. Between their rest and the other torments of hell, we read that a great chasm had been fixed; nor are they said to have been in hell. For, it says, ‘The poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man also died and was buried, and when he was in hell in torments,’ and so forth.

We therefore see that hell is not mentioned in connection with the poor man’s rest, but with the rich man’s punishment. Consequently, as I said, I have not yet found, and I am still seeking, any place where canonical Scripture has set hell in a good sense. I do not know whether anyone can hear that Abraham’s bosom and that rest to which the pious poor man was carried by angels are not to be understood in a good sense; and therefore I do not see how we can believe that he was in hell.”

Thus far Augustine, learnedly and truly.

But this deserves notice: the same holy man, in his commentary on Psalm LXXXV, volume VIII, folio 652, posits two hells, a lower and an upper: in one the souls of the righteous rested, while in the other the souls of the ungodly were tormented. Yet he seems to have advanced this not by affirming but by conjecturing. For he says:

“Brothers, whether this or that is the case, hold me here as an investigator of the word of God, not as a rash assertor.”

Certainly Origen, *On First Principles*, book IV, chapter 2, and Ambrose, in chapter 5 of Paul’s Letter to the Romans, proposed this doctrine in their writings before Augustine; so too Gregory the Great, *On Job*, book XII, chapter 9; Bede on Psalm LXXXV; Bernard, sermon 2, *On the Assumption of Mary*, folio 149; and others who are found to have approved their opinion.

Jerome refutes them in his commentary on Psalm LXXXV, folio 108:

“You have rescued my soul from the lower hell,” and so forth. “Not because there are two hells, but because this man called sin the upper hell, while he called the lower one the true hell, in which sinners are condemned. He therefore praises the Lord’s mercy because he has been rescued from the punishment of the lower hell.”

This fiction was greatly pleasing to the scholastics. Not content with what their predecessors had deliriously imagined about a double hell, they carved out two further hells and thus produced a fourfold hell:

1. The hell of the damned;
2. The limbo of infants;
3. Purgatory;
4. The limbo of the fathers.

Bonaventure, bishop of Albano, book IV, distinction 45, numbers 12 and 15. Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 22, question 4:

“It must be known that hell is fourfold, according to the fourfold kind of punishment. For some receive the punishment of loss, that is, perpetual deprivation of the vision of God, and perpetual punishment of sense, on account of actual mortal sin in which they died. These are said to be in the hell of the damned.

Others are subject to perpetual punishment of loss without punishment of sense, namely those who die in original sin alone; these are said to be in the limbo of infants.

Others are subject to punishment both of sense and of loss, not perpetually but temporarily: namely, those who died in grace while owing some punishment because in the present life they had not fully made satisfaction for their sins. These are said to be in purgatory.

Others are subject only to punishment of loss, without any punishment of sense; these were said to be in the limbo of the fathers. Before Christ’s passion they were prohibited from the vision of God, because satisfaction had not been made for the sin of the whole human nature, although they were not liable to any punishment for their personal sins.”

Let the Roman Catholics see how they may defend these fabrications. We—who approve nothing except what is ecclesiastical and accords with the authentic prophetic and apostolic provision brought forth in that very age—prefer to be uncertain about hidden things rather than quarrel over doubtful matters. We consider it better to remain within the bounds of unknowing and ignorance—“For it is better not to know than to err,” as Augustine says in his commentary on John, tractate 21—and simply to confess our lack of knowledge than, with unlearned rashness and without the authority of the divine Scriptures, to introduce childish nonsense and the fabulous doctrines of the nations into the Church of God under the Christian name.

Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapters 1 and 2; Jerome, *To Hedibia*, letter 150, question 10, folio 420; Augustine, *To Optatus*, letter 157, and *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VIII, chapter 5.

# CHAPTER LXXIX

[After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the souls of all the saints go to Christ]

Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 14:

“From the time of Christ’s resurrection, the saints, as soon as they depart from the body, immediately ascend to their heavenly dwelling—something not granted to the ancient fathers. For before the Savior’s coming, although the souls of the saints were without the punishment of torment, they were nevertheless held not in heaven but in hell, on whose account the Lord descended into hell to release them.”

Gregory Nazianzen, funeral oration in praise of his brother Caesarius, folio 173:

> Πείθομαι σοφῶν λόγοις ὅτι ψυχὴ πᾶσα, καλήτε καὶ θεοφιλὴς, ἐπειδὰν τοῦ συνδεδεμένου λυθεῖσα σώματος ἐνθένδε ἀπαλλαγῇ, εὐθὺς μὲν ἐν συναισθήσει καὶ θεωρίᾳ τοῦ μένοντος αὐτὴν καλοῦ γενομένη, ἅτε τοῦ ἐπισκοτοῦντος ἀνακαθαρθέντος ἢ ἀποτεθέντος, ἢ οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅτι καὶ λέγειν χρὴ, θαυμασίαν τινὰ ἡδονὴν ἥδεται, καὶ ἀγάλλεται, καὶ ἵλεως χωρεῖ πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτῆς δεσπότην, ὥσπερ τι δεσμωτήριον χαλεπὸν τὸν ἐνταῦθα βίον ἀποφυγοῦσα, καὶ τὰς περικειμένας ἀποσεισαμένη πέδας, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὸ τῆς διανοίας πτερὸν καθείλκετο· καὶ οἷον ἤδη τῇ φαντασίᾳ καρποῦται τὴν ἀποκειμένην μακαριότητα· μικρὸν δ᾽ ὕστερον καὶ τὸ συγγενὲς σαρκίον ἀπολαβοῦσα, ᾧ τὰ ἐκεῖθεν συνεφιλοσόφησε, παρὰ τῆς καὶ δούσης καὶ πιστευθείσης γῆς, τρόπον ὃν οἶδεν ὁ ταῦτα συνδήσας καὶ διαλύσας Θεὸς, τούτῳ συγκληρονομεῖ τῆς ἐκεῖθεν δόξης· καὶ καθάπερ τῶν μοχθηρῶν αὐτοῦ μετέσχε διὰ τὴν συμφυΐαν, οὕτω καὶ τῶν τερπνῶν ἑαυτῆς μεταδίδωσιν, ὅλον εἰς ἑαυτὴν ἀναλώσασα, καὶ γενομένη σὺν τούτῳ ἓν καὶ πνεῦμα, καὶ νοῦς, καὶ Θεός, καταποθέντος ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ θνητοῦ τε καὶ ῥέοντος.

That is:

“I am persuaded by the words of the wise that every beautiful and God-loving soul, once released from the body with which it was bound and having departed from this world, immediately—becoming conscious of and contemplating the good that awaits it, since what cast darkness upon it has been cleansed or removed, or whatever term should be used for the matter, I do not know—experiences a certain marvelous pleasure, rejoices, and proceeds graciously toward its own Lord. It has escaped this life as from a harsh prison and shaken off the fetters that surrounded it, by which the wing of the mind was dragged downward. It already enjoys, as it were through imagination, the blessedness laid up for it.

A little later, when it has recovered its kindred flesh from the earth, which both gave it and received it in trust—how this will happen is known to him who joined and separated these things—then it will admit that flesh with itself as a co-heir of heavenly glory. Just as, because of their natural conjunction, it shared in the flesh’s sufferings, so it will also share its own joys with it, consuming the whole body into itself and becoming with it one thing—spirit, mind, and God—when what was mortal and transient has been swallowed up by life.”

It is exceedingly cold and frivolous that Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 25, and Bede, volume VIII, *Book of Questions*, folio 402, say that this benefit is granted not to all the righteous but only to the perfectly righteous. For who can be perfectly righteous in this mortality, where the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh?

Macarius, homily 8, page 106; Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins against the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 13, and *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book II, chapter 7; Lactantius, book VI, chapter 15; Jerome on Psalm CXIV, folio 150:

“In the present age no one can be perfectly righteous—not David, not an apostle, nor any of the saints.”

[The souls of sinners are in hell]

Here Gennadius completely overturns the fable of purgatory—πυρκαθαρτήριον, “purifying fire”—which the brainy sophists vigorously press in their writings. He asserts only two dwellings, excluding every intermediate and third place, to which souls stripped of their human bodies migrate: heaven and hell.

Jerome supports Gennadius in his commentary on Amos, chapter 19, folio 123:

“When the soul, released from bodily bonds, has obtained the freedom to fly wherever it wishes or wherever it is compelled to go, it will either be led to the lower regions or lifted to the heavenly regions.”

Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 28:

“There is no intermediate place for anyone, so that he may exist anywhere except with the devil, if he is not with Christ.”

The author of the *Hypognosticon*, article 5, in Augustine, volume VII, folio 957:

“The first place, by divine authority, the faith of Catholics believes to be the kingdom of heaven; the second, Gehenna. We utterly know nothing of a third; indeed, we do not find that one exists in the sacred Scriptures.”

The author of *On Right Conduct in Catholic Life*, in Augustine, volume IX, folio 797:

“Know that when the soul is torn from the body, it is immediately cast into paradise for good works, or certainly into hell for evil ones.”

Much earlier than these was Justin Martyr, *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox*, question 75, folio 339:

> Ἐνταῦθα μὲν τὰ τῆς ἑνώσεως πάντα κοινὰ ὑπάρχει δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων, καὶ οὐδεμία ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς διαφορὰ κατὰ τοῦτο, οἷον τὸ γενέσθαι καὶ τὸ ἀποθνήσκειν, καὶ τὸ νοσεῖν, καὶ τὸ πλουτεῖν, καὶ τὸ πένεσθαι, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τὰ τούτοις ὅμοια· μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ σώματος ἔξοδον, εὐθὺς γίνεται τῶν δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων ἡ διαστολή· ἄγονται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων εἰς ἀξίους αὐτῶν τόπους· αἱ μὲν τῶν δικαίων ψυχαὶ, εἰς τὸν παράδεισον, ἔνθα συντυχία τε καὶ θέα ἀγγέλων τε καὶ ἀρχαγγέλων, κατ᾽ ὀπτασίαν δὲ καὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον «Ἐκδημοῦντες ἐκ τοῦ σώματος, καὶ ἐνδημοῦντες πρὸς τὸν Κύριον·» αἱ δὲ τῶν ἀδίκων ψυχαὶ, εἰς τοὺς ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ τόπους, κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον περὶ τοῦ Ναβουχοδονόσορ βασιλέως Βαβυλῶνος «Ὁ ᾅδης κάτωθεν ἐπικράνθη συναντήσας σοι» καὶ τὰ ἐξῆς· καὶ εἰσὶν ἐν τοῖς ἀξίοις αὐτῶν τόποις φυλαττόμεναι ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναστάσεως καὶ ἀνταποδόσεως.

That is:

“In this life, all the things that belong to the union of body and soul are common to the righteous and the unrighteous, and in this respect there is no difference between them: being born and dying, being healthy and being sick, becoming rich and becoming poor, and other things similar to these.

But after the souls’ departure from the body, the distinction between the righteous and the unrighteous immediately takes place. For they are led by angels to places appropriate to them. The souls of the righteous go to paradise, where they enjoy the companionship and sight of angels and archangels, and by vision also of the Savior Christ, in accordance with the saying: ‘While we are away from the body, we are present with the Lord.’

The souls of the unrighteous go to the places in Hades, in accordance with what is said concerning Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon: ‘Hades beneath was embittered, meeting your arrival,’ and what follows. Each is kept in the places appropriate to it until the day of resurrection and recompense.”

# CHAPTER LXXXII

[Not all evil thoughts always arise from the devil’s prompting]

Bede imitated this passage in his commentary on Mark, book II, chapter 7, volume VII; in his Lenten homily, folio 338; and in his *Book of Questions*, volume VIII, folio 403:

“Those must be refuted who think that thoughts are introduced by the devil and do not wish them to arise from their own will. The devil can be the helper and kindler of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. If, however, he is always lying in ambush and kindles a slight spark of our thoughts with his fuel, we must not suppose that he also searches out the hidden things of the heart. Rather, he judges what we are turning over inwardly from the body’s posture and gestures. For example, if he often sees us gazing at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the arrow of love.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.

**[Easter before the passage of the vernal equinox]**

The month and day on which the celebration of Holy Easter ought to be held were debated in various ways among the ancients. The holy apostles, Anatolius, and the Westerners as far as the Ocean held that it should be after the vernal equinox. The Gauls observed it on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, and the Syrians, Cilicians, Mesopotamians, and Asians, together with the Jews, maintained that Easter must be observed on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it might be.

Since such observances were therefore maintained in the individual provinces, the priests were deeply saddened because those who professed one faith disagreed in their fasts. Accordingly, Pius I and Victor, bishops of the city of Rome, wishing to remedy this public evil, established that the paschal festival should be celebrated on a Sunday between the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month and the twenty-first day of that same month. Later, at the plenary Council of Nicaea, the entire Christian world was persuaded that Easter should rightly be celebrated by all Catholic Churches on one and the same day and at one and the same time.

# GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES, BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

*(From the edition of J. Albert Fabricius.)*

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 1053]

### TESTIMONIES CONCERNING GENNADIUS AND HIS BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

### CASSIODORUS

*(Book on Divine Readings, chapter 17.)*

[Col. 1053C]

“Here is the book of Saint Jerome *On Illustrious Men*, in which he briefly both honored and touched upon various Fathers and their little works; then there is another by Gennadius of Marseilles, who made a most reliable judgment concerning the writers of divine law whom he had diligently investigated. I have left these works joined in one body, so that the slowness involved in learning the matter through separate books might not arise.”

### ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

*(Book VI of the *Origins*, chapter 6.)*

“Jerome and Gennadius likewise searched throughout the whole world for ecclesiastical writers and treated them in order; they included their studies in a single little volume.”

### ROBERT BELLARMINE

*(Book on Ecclesiastical Writers.)*

[Col. 1054C]

Gennadius of Marseilles lived in the time of Pope Gelasius, around the year of the Lord 490. For Gennadius himself testifies, in the final chapter of his book *On Illustrious Men*, that he sent his book *On the Faith* to Gelasius, although Gennadius’s book is not found complete in every manuscript.

He wrote a book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which exists among the works of Saint Augustine; and this is believed to be the book that he sent to Gelasius. He also wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, in which he left considerable suspicion concerning the correctness of his faith. For he praised Cassian and Faustus, who were Semi-Pelagians, and disparaged Saint Prosper, who fought most vigorously for the grace of God against Pelagius.

He also wrote many other works, which he himself mentions in the final chapter of his book *On Illustrious Men*; but they do not exist, or at least they have not come into my hands.

[Col. 1055]

## Preface of Suffridus Petrus of Leeuwarden

[Col. 1055A]

Sigebert of Gembloux, below, in chapter 30 of his *Catalogue*, calls this Gennadius a bishop, as does Platina, who calls him Bishop of Marseilles in his account of Symmachus. Walafrid, however, in chapter 20 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, calls him a presbyter of Marseilles, as does John Trithemius. Indeed, Gennadius himself, in the conclusion of this work, when listing his writings, calls himself a presbyter of Marseilles. Therefore we too shall assign him this title as genuine until we are convinced by stronger arguments of the contrary; for those who write that he was a bishop appear to have been deceived by the similarity of the name to that of the bishop of Constantinople, who was also named Gennadius and about whom our Gennadius treats in chapter 90.

This Gennadius of ours must plainly be read with discernment—not only because he approves here certain writers whom the Church rejected, but also because some things have been added to him by certain Catholics, out of zeal, as a remedy, which do not belong to Gennadius himself. Therefore, so that the candid reader may read him with greater caution, we shall append here, concerning both matters, the judgment of the outstanding and most weighty theologian, Master M. N. John Molanus, censor of pontifical and royal books at Louvain, which he graciously shared with us out of his zeal for the Catholic Church.

“That this Gennadius belonged to the party of the Gauls,” he says, “of whom Prosper and Hilary speak in the letters prefixed to the book *On the Predestination of the Saints and the Gift of Perseverance*, is clear from his *Catalogue*. For, to omit the fact that he prefers Rufinus to Jerome in chapter 17, and praises the dialogue of Severus in chapter 19, which Jerome rejects in chapter 36 of Ezekiel and Gelasius subsequently rejects, he expressly condemns Prosper’s book against the *Collationer* and praises Cassian; likewise, he praises Faustus in the matter of grace and free choice, although Gelasius condemns both of them while praising Prosper.

“John Maxentius demonstrates Faustus’s heresy at the end of his book against the letter of Possessor, as do Peter the deacon and his companions in the little book sent to Fulgentius, which Fulgentius approves. Against this Faustus, as one secretly agreeing with the Pelagians, Fulgentius wrote, as Vincent testifies in his *Historical Mirror*, book XX, chapter 106.

“Certainly, the Second Council of Orange, convened at the command of Leo I, appears to have been directed against Cassian, Faustus, and their associates. Isidore says in his *Catalogue*: ‘Fulgentius wrote seven books of *Responses on Grace and Free Choice*. In them he endeavors to destroy the profound subtlety of Faustus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, who agreed with Pelagian depravity.’

“Indeed, Gennadius praises Pelagius’s book *Eulogies*, which Jerome rejects as heretical in book I *Against the Pelagians*. For it teaches that all people are governed by their own will, that a human being can be without sin, and that, if he wishes, he can easily keep the commandments of God. Augustine demonstrates that this is heretical in Letter 89 to Hilary.

“We pass over the fact that Gennadius praises Evagrius’s *Apatheia* [freedom from passions], whom Jerome says was condemned by the bishops as an Origenist in his letter to Ctesiphon, and he condemns Evagrius’s apatheia.”

[Note: [Col. 1055D] That is, the books of *Sentences*, in which the soul’s ἀπάθεια, or freedom from passions, is defended. **Editor.**]

Thus far he concerning Gennadius’s error.

Concerning the things inserted into Gennadius by others, he says the following:

“A manuscript in the Parco collection concludes Gennadius’s *Catalogue* in this way, omitting Honoratus, whom we place last among Jerome’s works:

> ‘I, Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, wrote eight books against all heresies, six books against Nestorius, and three books against Pelagius, as well as treatises on the Thousand Years and on the Apocalypse of Blessed John; and I sent this work on my faith to Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome.’

“Here it should be noted that the book against Nestorius, which is placed in the *Antidote against Heresies*, belongs to Gennadius, not to Gelasius. The names could easily have been altered, because Gennadius wrote to Gelasius. I believe that in our book the final Gennadius was omitted and Honoratus inserted, because Gelasius approved the faith of Honoratus, not that of Gennadius—so that Honoratus was placed as a remedy, just as the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* contains remedies.

“Indeed, a manuscript in the Parco collection contains many remedies in Gennadius’s *Catalogue*. For where Gennadius says this about Augustine:

> ‘Although he might cause doubt concerning the aborted among those capable of understanding, nevertheless his error, as I said above, was contracted through much speech and intensified by the struggle of his enemies, and it had not yet given rise to the question of heresy,’

the manuscript of the Parco collection reads as follows, omitting these words:

> ‘Serving the Church with outstanding talent and exceptional zeal, he replied to the books of the heretic Julian amid the assault of the besieging Vandals at the very end of his days; and, persevering in the defense of Christian wisdom, he died while Theodosius and Valentinian were ruling.’

“And concerning Prosper, the written book gives the following after saying that Cassian and Prosper held contrary opinions about grace and free choice:

> ‘Prosper also, after the death of Blessed Augustine, became his defender against the enemies of Christ’s grace.’

“After Faustus, the written book of the Parco and Bethlehem manuscripts adds, in chapter 86:

> ‘Caesarius, bishop of Arles, a man renowned for holiness and virtue, wrote excellent and very welcome little works, necessary also for monks. He also published testimonies of Scripture, supported by the judgments of the holy Fathers, concerning grace and free choice, in which he teaches that a human being does nothing good from himself unless divine grace has preceded him. Pope Felix also strengthened this work through his letter and published it among the Latins. He flourished at the same time as Faustus, while Anastasius was governing the empire.’

“This is what the written manuscript contains. These additions do not appear to belong to Gennadius, but to a Catholic wishing to provide a remedy for Gennadius.

“Caesarius was the first to sign the acts of the Second Council of Orange, and Pope Felix III is mentioned here. Although Gennadius lists Pomerius in his *Catalogue* and says that Pomerius discussed original sin, Gennadius should not for that reason be thought to approve him. For this Pomerius, according to Isidore in chapter 12 of his *Catalogue*, ‘in the second book of his work, agreeing with Tertullian’s errors, said that the soul was corporeal, attempting to establish this with certain deceptive arguments.’ This is what Isidore says. It is certain that Gennadius did not approve this.

“This is his judgment, and most of our manuscript copies support it, as we shall indicate in their proper places. There is no more immediate proof of this matter than that the older the manuscripts are, the fewer remedies they are found to have added to Gennadius.

“Honorius, at any rate, who seems to have wished to omit no one—for he even preserved Dionysius the Areopagite alongside Jerome, whom all the manuscripts in Jerome’s own *Catalogue* lack—does not recognize Avitus, in chapter 47, Pomerius, in chapter 98, or Honoratus of Marseilles, in chapter 99 of Gennadius’s *Catalogue*, as genuinely Gennadian.

“Furthermore, in a fairly recent manuscript in the Martinian collection, which we used among the others, we found this prologue placed before Gennadius. We have therefore decided to reproduce it here word for word. Since it has nothing to do with Gennadius, it appears to have been added as a remedy, suitably mitigating Gennadius’s unfavorable judgment of Jerome, mentioned above. The prologue reads as follows:

> ‘Our Jerome, learned above all in Greek and Latin letters at Rome…’”

[Col. 1057]

## EXCERPT FROM THE *VINDICATIONS OF ALARDUS GAZAEUS IN DEFENSE OF CASSIAN*

[Col. 1057B]

“Lest the reader wonder that we could say of the men of Marseilles that they once dissented from Augustine, Prosper, Fulgentius, and others who thought correctly without the stigma of schism or injury to Catholic unity, until the Church issued a definitive judgment, he should know that the Second Council of Orange, which was composed from the opinions of Augustine and Prosper against the Semi-Pelagians, was celebrated in the year 529 under Pope Felix IV. Many people wrongly confuse it with the First Council of Orange, which was convened under Leo and issued no canons on faith, but only on the morals and freedom of the Church.

“It is sufficiently clear that, up to that time, the teachers and pontiffs tolerated the men of Marseilles—who were later called Semi-Pelagians—as Catholics and holy men, even though they were entangled in a particular error. Otherwise the Church of God would have judged very differently concerning those who denied the absolute predestination most vigorously defended by Augustine but nevertheless acknowledged prevenient grace; differently concerning the Semi-Pelagians, who removed the necessity of prevenient grace but confessed the necessity of grace considered simply; and differently, finally, concerning the Pelagians, who admitted that grace was useful but denied that it was necessary.

“For the Pelagians were expelled from the number of Catholics, barred from ecclesiastical offices, and condemned by imperial decrees. The Semi-Pelagians were formerly regarded as Catholics and were permitted to remain in the ecclesiastical orders. Nevertheless, their opinion was eventually condemned by synodal decree and by the authority of the Roman Church, but in such a way that the men of Marseilles who had held it before the Second Council of Orange were not condemned.

“Those, however, who denied the absolute decree of predestination against Augustine were not only not condemned as heretics, as the Pelagians were, but not even condemned as erring, as the Semi-Pelagians were. They were permitted to follow their own understanding, although Prosper and other defenders of Augustine strongly refuted them.

“There is no need to demonstrate that the Pelagians were then subjected to an anathema as heretics; no one doubts it. But it is sufficiently clear that the men of Marseilles and the teachers of Gaul who agreed with them were not deprived of Catholic communion on account of their error, but were counted among the holy brethren. This is evident from Augustine himself, who, in the books written to Prosper and Hilary against them, repeatedly calls them brothers, and in book II, chapter 17, excuses them from heretical depravity, saying:

> ‘For they are not Pelagians, so that they contend against this manifest truth with harsh and heretical perversity; but, they say, faith commands that these things be given to us by God, although faith begins from us.’

“And in the same work, chapter 24:

> ‘We wish that the Pelagians may have this gift—the gift of boasting in the Lord—but that these, our own people, may have it more fully. Let us therefore not be ready in disputations and sluggish in prayers. Let us pray, beloved; let us pray that God may grant our enemies—he means the Pelagians—and especially our brothers and beloved ones, to understand and confess that, after the great and ineffable ruin in which we all fell in one person, no one is liberated except by the grace of God; and that this grace is not bestowed according to merits, as though it were weakened, but as true grace, without preceding merits.’

“Here he calls those who denied the necessity of prevenient grace and thought that the gift of regeneration was given according to merit of suitability sometimes ‘our own people’ and sometimes ‘his brothers.’ When he calls them ‘beloved,’ he indicates what Prosper had said to him in the letter to which he was responding: namely, that, apart from their doctrine concerning prevenient grace and absolute predestination, the men of Marseilles loved, followed, and admired Augustine in all other respects.

“For Prosper writes:

> ‘Let your Blessedness know that one of them, a man of the highest authority and spiritual learning, the holy Hilary of Arles, is in all other matters an admirer and follower of your teaching.’

“This Hilary, inscribed in the catalogue of the saints and then living in the highest authority, disagreed with Augustine. Thus Augustine, judging more modestly concerning himself, calls those whom Prosper said were otherwise admirers of Augustine ‘his beloved ones.’

“Therefore, although Augustine rightly resisted their error, he nevertheless recognized them as Catholic brothers. Prosper likewise, although he attacks them more vehemently, nevertheless calls them, in his letter to Augustine, ‘men distinguished by merits and honors, outstanding in every pursuit of virtue, and conspicuous among the simpler people for the great reverence inspired by their observed goodness’; indeed, he calls them holy men. In his book against the *Collationer*, chapter 33, he calls them Catholics, saying:

> ‘Who would believe that these things are proclaimed by Catholics among Catholics?’

“And in the epilogue of that writing:

> ‘Nevertheless, since they have not yet been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should be endured rather than their correction despaired of, until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the lawful ministers of his judgments, sets in order these matters which have been disturbed by the pride of a few and the ignorance of certain others.’

“Prosper therefore also holds that Cassian and the others, although in his judgment and in reality gravely mistaken, could dissent from him without the loss of Catholic unity until the question was settled by a decree of the Church. Let these statements stand without prejudice to ecclesiastical judgment.”

Thus speaks, more or less, the writer of the *Vindications in Defense of Cassian*.

[Col. 1059]

[Col. 1059]

# BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS (C, S)

[Col. 1059B]

[Note: [Col. 1059C] Trithemius does not include this chapter in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 188, nor does it appear to have been known to Honorius of Autun, who excerpted the second book *On the Luminaries of the Church* from Gennadius. It is not found in editions before Marcianaeus, nor in manuscript books, except only in the very ancient Corbie or Saint-Germain manuscript, which, as they say, is more than a thousand years old and was written in ancient Merovingian characters. See Mabillon, volume II of the *Analecta*, page 42. It is also found in the Martinian manuscript, from which Suffridus Petrus published it under the name of a prologue in his letter to the reader prefixed to Gennadius’s book.]

Our Jerome, thoroughly learned in Greek and Latin letters at Rome, was also ordained a presbyter there. As a young man he came to the town of Bethlehem, where, like a prudent animal, he presented himself at the Lord’s manger, intending to remain there.

Among the other little works of his writings, beginning with blessed Peter and continuing up to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius’s reign, he wrote *On Illustrious Men* down to himself. In addition, having published innumerable books composed from the writings of the apostles and prophets, he completed the immovable tower of the Catholic Church against the arrows of the faithless.

He was also so well instructed in Hebrew and Chaldean letters that he translated all the books of the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew manuscripts. He likewise translated the prophet Daniel, who spoke in the Chaldean style, and the righteous Job, who spoke in Arabic, both authors into the Roman language through a complete interpretation.

He also made Matthew’s Gospel Roman—that is, Latin—from the Hebrew. For, preaching and preserving virginity of mind and body and repentance for sins, he alone among all the Romans commented on all sixteen books of the prophets.

Moreover, in the holy prologues to his books, he presents himself to Catholic readers as a most eloquent interpreter, and in the immense volumes of his letters as vigorous, so that he appears never to have spared the faithless or yielded to the envious.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Suffridus Petrus does not have *books*.]

As they report, he later rested in the Lord at nearly ninety years of age. Stridon gave him birth, illustrious Rome educated him, nourishing Bethlehem holds him—

[Note: [Col. 1059D] The reading *held* is intended; understand “but holds him” from the tomb.]

—and the heavenly court received his spirit. He flourished especially under the emperor Theodosius and his sons Arcadius and Honorius.

## CHAPTER ONE.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Saint James of Nisibis, or the Nisibene, bishop of the city of Nisibis, distinguished for miracles and learning, was one of the confessors during the persecution of Maximinus, who at the Council of Nicaea condemned the perversity of Arius by opposing homoousios (“of the same substance”). Through the prayers of this James and of Bishop Alexander, Arius received at Constantinople the fitting reward for his wickedness, with his entrails poured out—to use the words of the Roman Martyrology. He is also commemorated in the Greek Menologion on 21 October. Theodoret also mentions him in Book II, chapter 30, of his Ecclesiastical History, and in Book I, chapter 7, where he says that James was present at the Council of Nicaea and raised the dead. For those wishing to know more about this miracle and the others, he refers the reader to his book entitled Philotheus, or Theophilus, which is Book Nine of the Lives of the Fathers in the Plantinian edition. Nicephorus also discusses this Nisibene in Book VIII, chapter 14, and Book IX, chapter 28. He was present not only at Nicaea but also at the Council of Antioch, as is recorded in the acts of Saint Alexander, bishop of Constantinople. MIRAEUS.—When I was publishing Jerome’s book On Ecclesiastical Writers, I said that in the Corbie manuscript Jerome’s life, written by Gennadius, appeared immediately in first place; I did not think it necessary to repeat it. Our manuscripts, omitting Jerome, begin with the life of James of Nisibis. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

## CHAPTER I

JAMES, surnamed the Wise, bishop of the noble city of Nisibis, now a city of the Persians, was one of the number of the confessors under the persecutor Maximinus, and of those who at the Council of Nicaea condemned the Arian perversity by opposing homoousios, “of the same substance.”

[Note: [Col. 1060D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “bishop of the noble city of Nisibis, now indeed a city of the Persians,” and so forth.—The Corbie codex has: “bishop of the noble city of Nisibis, now indeed a city of the Persians.” Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume II, p. 44. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

[Note: [Col. 1061B] The Nuremberg and Wolfenbüttel manuscripts read “under Maximianus.” But the earlier reading should be retained, as Tenzelius proves in *Selected Exercises*, part 1, exercise 6. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

Saint Jerome, in his *Chronicle*, names this man as one of great virtues; and his omission from the *Catalogue* can readily be excused if we consider that he testifies that he had read the three or four Syrians whom he included—Bardesanes, Ephraem, and Archelaus—in Greek translation.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] The Corbie manuscript has “homousia,” that is, “of the same substance.”]

It is therefore clear that at that time he was ignorant of the Syriac language or script and consequently did not know this writer, who had not yet been translated into another language.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] W. E. Tenzelius, the blessed one, denies this. See volume I of his *Selected Dissertations*, p. 254, where he attacks Garnerius for attempting to deprive Gennadius of credibility concerning the writings published by James, although Garnerius himself did not hesitate to accept them.]

He comprised his entire work in twenty-six books, namely: *On Faith*; *Against All Heresies*; *On Universal Charity*; *On Fasting*; *On Prayer*; *On Special Love of Neighbor*; *On the Resurrection*; *On Life after Death*; *On Humility*; *On Patience*; *On Repentance*; *On Satisfaction*;

[Note: [Col. 1061D] The Cortrei manuscript reads: “On repentance; on satisfaction; on the census of the soul; on virgins; on the circumcised; on the blessed grape-seed.”]

*On Virginity*; *On the Sense of the Soul*; *On Circumcision*; *On the Blessed Grape-Berry* (*acinus*), for which Isaiah 65:8 reads, “The cluster must not be destroyed”;

[Note: [Col. 1061C] Suffridus Petri makes the following note here. The printed codex states that this writer comprised his whole work in twenty-five books, and the Gembloux manuscript supports it. Our other codices have twenty-six books—the Corbie manuscript, according to Marcianus, has twenty-seven—but they list only twenty-four. Trithemius likewise has twenty-five, which he enumerates, but he was misled by an error in his manuscript and made two books out of one. For the book that he attributes to Isaiah is plainly identical with the one he attributes to the blessing of the unleavened substance. Anyone can readily recognize this as true who notices that *azymi* (“of the unleavened”) should be read *acini* (“of the grape-berry”). Thus it is expressly read in the manuscripts of Gembloux, Affligem, Groenendael, and Sigeberg. Isaiah 65 contains these words concerning the blessing of the grape-seed, and the mention of a cluster sufficiently clearly shows that *acini* ought to be read here: the Greek text is as follows, “As when the grape-berry is found in the cluster, and they say, ‘Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it.’” Here *ho rhōx* signifies a grape-berry, in which the blessing is said to reside. A little farther on, concerning Christ’s coming, the Sigeberg manuscript reads “of Antichrist.” All the codices have twenty-six books, though they do not list them. In the Nuremberg manuscript *On Faith against All Heresies* is one book. Even if one counts two books and includes the chronicle, there are still no more than twenty-four. From this agreement among so many codices, I seem able to conclude that Gennadius himself saw no more than twenty-four, although he reports that James wrote twenty-six. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

*On Christ, that he is the Son of God and consubstantial with the Father*; *On Chastity*; *Against the Gentiles*; *On the Construction of the Tabernacle*; *On the Conduct of the Gentiles*; *On the Kingdom of the Persians*; *On the Persecution of Christians*.

He also composed a chronicle, less concerned with the Greeks’ curiosity but more trustworthy, because it was constructed solely on the authority of the divine Scriptures and silences the mouths of those who, with presumptuous suspicion,

[Note: [Col. 1062B] The Corbie manuscript reads “presumptuous conjecture.”]

speak idly and philosophically about the coming of Antichrist,

[Note: [Col. 1062B] The Miræus edition has “of Christ.” ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

or of our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1062B] The words “or of our Lord” are absent from the Corbie manuscript.]

This man died during the reign of Constantius and, according to the command of his father Constantine,

[Note: [Col. 1062B] The same manuscript reads: “within the walls of Nisibis, by the command of his father Constantine.”]

was buried near the walls of Nisibis, evidently to protect the city.

[Note: [Col. 1062B] So read our codices. Miræus has “within the walls.” ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

This happened in accordance with Constantine’s faith. For many years later, Julian entered Nisibis and—whether out of envy for the glory of the buried man or out of hostility to Constantine’s faith, whose house he was therefore persecuting—ordered the sacred remains to be carried out of the city. A few months later the emperor Jovian, who had succeeded Julian, handed the city over to the barbarians, admittedly for reasons of state; and to this day it remains subject, together with its inhabitants, to Persian rule.

## CHAPTER II

JULIUS, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote one letter to a certain Dionysius concerning the Lord’s incarnation. At that time it seemed useful against those who asserted that, through the incarnation, there were two persons in Christ in the same way as there were two natures; but now it is judged harmful.

[Note: [Col. 1062C] The Acephali attributed a letter to Dionysius to Pope Julius; Gennadius believed it truly belonged to Pope Julius. Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, suspects that it was spurious in Book I of his work, as does Eulogius of Alexandria in Oration 3, preserved by Photius. Leontius of Byzantium, however, who quotes the words of the letter that the Eutychians abused, teaches in chapter 8 of *On the Sects* that it belonged not to Julius but to the heretic Apollinaris. Anastasius likewise asserts this in the *Eclogue of Quotations*, and before both of them Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, stated it in the disputation held at Constantinople with the Acephali: “We have clearly shown that the famous letter of blessed Julius, written to Dionysius, was Apollinaris’s.” He also maintains that another letter to Prosdocimus, or Docimus—the testimony of which was used by the Council of Ephesus—was not Julius’s either, but belonged to Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris. Others, however, and among them Ephraem, patriarch of Antioch, in Book III of *Sacred Laws* preserved by Photius, likewise attribute this letter to Julius without controversy. Thus, approximately, Sirmondus in his notes on Facundus of Hermiane. Saint Julius was the first pope of that name and is listed in the Roman Martyrology on 12 April. He became pope in 336 and died in 352, being succeeded by Liberius. MIRAEUS.]

For it is fuel for Eutychian and Timothean impiety.

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The words “against those” through “and natures” are absent from the Corbie manuscript.]

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The Corbie manuscript and Honorius call this writer Paulona, and, as Suffridus Petri says, they are supported by our manuscripts of Groenendael, Gembloux, and Sigeberg. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

PAULINUS, a presbyter and disciple of blessed Ephraem the deacon, a man of exceedingly keen intellect and learned in the divine Scriptures,

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The Corbie manuscript adds: “learned in divine Scripture.”]

was, while his teacher was alive, distinguished among ecclesiastical teachers and was especially an extemporaneous speaker. After Ephraem’s death, however, out of love for primacy and reputation, he separated himself from the Church and wrote many things contrary to the faith.

As blessed Ephraem was about to die, he is said to have said to Paulinus, who stood beside him: “See, Paulinus, that you do not submit yourself to your thoughts and become exalted.”

[Note: [Col. 1063C] The Corbie manuscript reads: “and that you do not exalt yourself; but when you think that you have comprehended God, believe that you have understood nothing.”]

“But when you think that you have comprehended God completely, believe that you have not understood him.”

[Note: [Col. 1063C] The Corbie manuscript has: “For he had perceived that, through his studies or conversations, Paulinus was investigating new things and stretching toward boundless understanding.”]

For he had perceived that, through his studies or conversations, Paulinus was investigating new things and reaching toward boundless understanding.

[Note: [Col. 1063C] I consider the reading of the Nuremberg codex better than Miræus’s: “reaching toward an understanding of heresies.” ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

[Note: [Col. 1063C] The Corbie and Nuremberg manuscripts have “And therefore.” ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

For this reason he frequently called him “a new Bardesanes.”

[Note: [Col. 1063C] See what is said about Bardesanes in Jerome, chapter 33 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]

## CHAPTER IV

VITELLIUS AFRICANUS, defending the schism of the Donatists,

[Note: [Col. 1063C] The Corbie manuscript has “Vitilinus Africanus, the schism of Donatus.”]

wrote *On the Fact that the Servants of God Are Hated by the World*.

[Note: [Col. 1063C] The Gembloux manuscript reads: “that the servants of God are hated by the world.”]

In this work, if he had remained silent about our designation as persecutors,

[Note: [Col. 1063D] “As though he had published the name of an eminent and learned persecutor.” Corbie manuscript.]

he would have produced an outstanding work of doctrine. He also wrote against the Gentiles and against us, whom he described as traitors during the persecution, concerning the divine Scriptures; and he discussed many matters belonging to ecclesiastical discipline. He flourished under Constans,

[Note: [Col. 1063D] The manuscript has “Constantine.”]

the son of the emperor Constantine.

## CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 1063D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “Macrobius the presbyter, who, as we learn from the writing of Optatus, was himself later a Donatist and a secret bishop of his own party in Rome.”]

MACROBIUS, also a presbyter, was, as we learn from the writings of Optatus, a Donatist and later a secret bishop of his party in the city of Rome. While he was still a presbyter in the Church of God, he wrote one book to confessors and virgins. It was a moral work, but its teaching was very necessary, and it was especially fortified with highly suitable maxims for preserving chastity. He first became distinguished among our people in Africa and afterward in Rome among his own, that is, the Donatists or Montenses.

## CHAPTER VI

HELIODORUS the presbyter wrote a book *On the Natures of First Things*. In it he showed that there is one principle and that nothing is coeternal with God; that God is not the creator of evil, but the creator of all good in such a way that the matter which was turned toward evil after wickedness had been discovered was made by God; and that no material thing should be believed to have been created apart from God, nor that there was any other creator of things besides God, who, foreseeing by his foreknowledge that nature would be given over to death, gave warning concerning the punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] The Gembloux and Groenendael manuscripts, as also the Sigeberg manuscript according to Suffridus Petri, and the Wolfenbüttel manuscript examined by Ernest Cyprian, read “to be changed” instead of “to be given over to death.”]

## CHAPTER VII

[Note: [Col. 1063D] Honorius and Trithemius incorrectly have “Bachomius.” In a booklet printed at Cologne in 1513, *On the Office of the Rector of a Church*, the sayings of Abbot Pachomius are cited, as Suffridus Petri notes.—Saint Pachomius, abbot of Tabennesis in Egypt, wrote a Rule for Monks, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome; it appears at the end of Cassian’s works in the Roman, Lyons, and Arras editions. A summary of the same Rule is quoted by Palladius in the *Lausiac History*. He flourished in the year 340 and is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 14 May. Several other ascetic writings of the same Pachomius are still extant at Trier, in the Benedictine monastery of Saint Maximin, and at Cologne, in the house of the Canons Regular at Corpus Christi, in handwritten codices preceded by this title: *Rule of the Fathers*. MIRAEUS.]

PACHOMIUS the monk, a man endowed with apostolic grace both in teaching and in working signs, and the founder of the Egyptian monasteries, wrote a Rule suitable for both classes of monks, which he had received under the dictation of an angel. He also wrote letters to the associates in his office of leadership. In these he enclosed an alphabet veiled in mystical sacraments, surpassing, as it were, human understanding,

[Note: [Col. 1064C] Thus the manuscripts more correctly read, instead of “exceeding”; the reference is to the alphabet.]

and, I believe, disclosed only to those who possessed the necessary grace or merits: one letter to Abbot Syrus and one to Abbot Cornelius; and, in the meantime, one letter to the superiors of all the monasteries, so that, gathered together in the one most ancient monastery called *Baum* in the Egyptian language,

[Note: [Col. 1064C] The manuscript has “Baun.” The Gembloux and Groenendael manuscripts have “Bauai.”]

[Note: [Col. 1064D] “Baum” is also read in the codex of the Rules of Benedict of Aniane published by Holstenius.]

they might celebrate the day of Easter as an eternal law. Similarly, he wrote one letter concerning the Day of Remission, which is observed in August,

[Note: [Col. 1064D] The words “which is observed in August” are absent from the Corbie manuscript. It reads immediately afterward: “so that the brothers might be gathered together in one place.” All these writings of Pachomius mentioned by Gennadius still exist and were published in Latin by Luca Holstenius in the *Code of Rules*, Rome 1661 and Paris 1663, quarto.]

so that the superiors might assemble in one place; and one letter to the brothers who had been sent outside the monastery to work.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Note: [Col. 1064D] Saint Theodore the monk, praised by Gennadius in this chapter, is listed in the Roman Martyrology on 28 December. Concerning him, see the writer of the Life of Saint Pachomius, Book I, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, and Saint Nilus in *On Prayer*. Another Saint Theodore, likewise a monk and a disciple of Saint Antony, praised by Saint Athanasius in Antony’s Life, is listed in the same martyrology on 7 January. MIRAEUS.]

THEODORUS the presbyter, successor in the grace and office of leadership of the aforementioned Abbot Pachomius, wrote letters to the other monasteries,

[Note: [Col. 1064D] In the same Holstenian *Code of Rules* there is only one brief letter of this Theodore, entitled “To All the Monasteries Concerning Easter.”]

arranged in the language of the Holy Scriptures. In them he frequently mentions his teacher and instructor Pachomius and presents examples of his doctrine and life, which Pachomius had learned through an angel’s ministry in order to teach them. Theodore also urges perseverance in the purpose of the heart and in devotion, and calls back to concord and unity those who, after the abbot’s death, had separated themselves from the assembly of unity by withdrawing. There are three letters of this exhortation.

## CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 1065B] In the Corbie manuscript this chapter on Oresiesis follows the chapter on Macarius. Honorius and Trithemius call him Oriesiesis; some manuscripts have Orestesis; in the Holstenian *Code of Rules*, where his teaching likewise appears in Latin, he is called Orsiesius.]

ORESIESIS the monk, associate of both Pachomius and Theodore, a man perfectly instructed in the Holy Scriptures, composed a book formed with divine salt and constructed from all the instruments of monastic discipline. To put it simply, nearly the whole Old and New Testament is expounded in it through concise discussions, according only to the needs of monks. Shortly before his death, he offered this book to the fathers in place of a testament.

[Note: [Col. 1065B] Oresiesis, or Oriesius’s, book *On the Formation of Monks* is found in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. To prevent confusion, I point out that this man is quite different from Orientius, or Orentius, praised by Sigebert in chapter 34. The latter wrote, in elegiac verse, an admonition which Martinus Antonius Delrius first published at Antwerp in 1600 with notes; it was later published in volume V of the final Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1065B]

[Note: [Col. 1065B] Before beginning to speak about the Macarii, it is useful to set out the very words of Suidas: “There were two Macarii of the same name, celebrated on account of their exercises, life, conduct, and discipline. One was Egyptian. He worked miracles and, with religious caution, was severe toward those who visited him. The other was Alexandrian, in every respect like the Egyptian, but humane. He was so humane toward those who visited him that, by employing graceful kindness, he encouraged young men to undertake their exercises.” Thus Suidas. Palladius, *History*, chapters 19 and 20; Nicephorus, Book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14; Baronius, in his note on the Roman Martyrology for 2 January; and others likewise testify that there were two Macarii. The elder, surnamed the Egyptian and a disciple of Saint Antony, wrote homilies in Greek, which John Pico, president of the class of examiners in the Paris Senate, translated into Latin in 1559. They were published together in Greek and Latin at Paris in 1622, with the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus and Basil of Seleucia. The same Macarius the Egyptian wrote to the younger monks of his profession a letter or rule beginning: “Therefore, soldiers of Christ.” It survives in manuscript at Bruges in the college of the Society of Jesus, among the rest of the Pamelian library. This Macarius, abbot in Egypt, is listed in the Roman Martyrology on 15 January; the other Macarius, surnamed the Alexandrian, abbot in the Thebaid and a disciple of Saint Pachomius, on 2 January. The Greeks also commemorate them, but on one and the same day, namely 19 January. The rule already mentioned of Saint Macarius the Egyptian is entirely different from the Rule of Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, the other Macarius, and thirty-four others. This Rule was published from the Affligem manuscript at the end of Cassian’s works, in the Plantinian press, under the direction of Henri Cucquius, later bishop of Roermond. Of these men, Serapion, surnamed Scholasticus and beloved by Saint Antony, was ordained bishop of Thmuis in Egypt by Saint Athanasius. Jerome also praises him in chapter 99 among ecclesiastical writers, and he is listed in the Roman Martyrology on 21 March. MIRAEUS.]

MACARIUS, that Egyptian monk, famous for signs and virtues, wrote only one letter to the younger members of his profession. In it he teaches that a person can serve God perfectly if, recognizing the condition of his creation, he bends himself to every kind of labor and, struggling and imploring God’s help against everything pleasant in this life, reaches natural purity and thereby obtains continence as a gift owed by nature.

[Note: [Col. 1066B] The Corbie manuscript reads: “continence as a natural gift.”]

## CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 1066B] This is a different Evagrius from Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, concerning whom see Jerome, chapter 125.—In the preceding chapter I showed from Suidas that there were two holy abbots named Macarius, one surnamed Egyptian and the other Alexandrian. Evagrius became the disciple of these men and practiced philosophy, having previously philosophized only in words, to use Suidas’s expression. At Constantinople he was admitted by Gregory the Theologian to the order of deacons; then, having gone to Egypt, he encountered the men mentioned above and imitated their life. He wrote very serious and weighty books, one entitled *The Monk*, or *On the Active Life*, and another *The Gnostic*, or *On Those Who Have Been Granted Knowledge*. This latter book contains fifty chapters. The third, *Antirrheticus*, is directed against demons who tempt people and is divided into eight parts, according to the number of the eight thoughts. He also wrote six hundred prognostic problems and two elementary works: one for monks living in monasteries or communities, the other for the heaven of virgins (*virginum coelum*). Thus far Suidas. Saint Jerome has much to say about this Evagrius—whom he calls “the Pontic Hyperborean” because he was born near the Euxine Pontus—in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians. At the end of the year 388 Baronius, following Saint Jerome, teaches that Evagrius was an Origenist and that Gennadius falsely attributes signs and wonders to him in this chapter and elsewhere. MIRAEUS.]

EVAGRIUS the monk, the familiar disciple of the aforementioned Macarius, distinguished in divine and human literature—whose book entitled *Lives of the Fathers* also mentions him as an exceedingly continent and learned man—

[Note: [Col. 1066C] This parenthesis, misunderstood by Honorius of Autun in his catalogue, Baronius, Bellarmine, Possevinus, and other eminent men, led them into the error of believing that Evagrius Ponticus was the author of the book called *Lives of the Fathers*. Heribert Rosweid was the first to observe this in the fourth and fifth prolegomena to the *Lives of the Fathers*, published by Moretus in 1628. In Moretus’s edition, the author or translator of Books II and III was the presbyter Ruffinus of Aquileia, as Rosweid teaches in prolegomenon 10. In Book II, chapter 27, there is a life of Evagrius Ponticus, who is praised there beyond measure for his knowledge of spiritual matters and his incredible abstinence. It is not likely that Evagrius himself wove such praises about himself.]

[Note: [Col. 1066D] Gennadius does not mention these *Lives of the Fathers* below, in chapter 17, among Rufinus’s writings; he seems to have read them without the name of either author or translator.]

wrote many things necessary for monks. Among them are the following: against the suggestions of the eight principal vices, which he either first observed or learned among the first, he composed eight books from testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, following the example of the Lord, who always opposed his tempter with Scriptural testimonies, so that each kind of suggestion, whether from the devil or from corrupted nature,

[Note: [Col. 1067C] Or: “the suggestion of the devil’s corrupted nature,” with a testimony directed against it.]

might have a testimony opposed to it. I translated this work into Latin, as I was ordered, with the same simplicity in which I found it in Greek.

He also composed for anchorites living a simple life a book of one hundred maxims arranged by chapters, and for learned and studious men a book of fifty maxims, which I was the first to render into Latin. Since I saw that the former translation had become corrupted and disordered through the passage of time, I restored it to the author’s truth, partly by retranslating and partly by correcting it.

[Note: [Col. 1067C] Miræus has “he opposed.” Our codices, in my opinion more correctly, have “he composed.” These words, from “He also composed for anchorites” through “I restored it to the author’s truth,” are absent from both the Wolfenbüttel and Nuremberg codices. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

He also composed for cenobites and synodites a *Doctrine Suitable for the Common Life*,

[Note: [Col. 1067C] “Cenobite,” or “synodite,” denotes a class of monks living in common, distinguished from the anchorites mentioned shortly before.]

and for virgins consecrated to God a small book suitable to their religious state and sex.

[Note: [Col. 1067C] Miræus has “synodites,” contrary to the evidence of the codices. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

He also published a few very obscure maxims, which, as he himself says in them, are intelligible only to the hearts of monks; these likewise I published in Latin. He lived to an advanced age, endowed with signs and virtues.

[Note: [Col. 1067C] Some copies have “signs and wonders”; “wonders” is a gloss.]

## CHAPTER XII

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The Corbie manuscript erroneously has “Theodoretus.”—The man whom Gennadius here calls the presbyter Theodore is said by others to have been a presbyter in the monastery of Raithu. In volume V of the final Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* there is a commentary by this writer, entitled *On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Nestorius and Eutyches*. Bellarmine also mentions it in his *Catalogue*. MIRAEUS.]

THEODORUS, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, a man careful in knowledge and eloquent in speech,

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The manuscript has “most eloquent.”]

wrote fifteen books against the Apollinarians and Eunomians concerning the Lord’s incarnation, containing fifteen thousand lines. In them, by the purest reasoning and by testimonies of Scripture, he showed that the Lord Jesus possessed the fullness of divinity just as he possessed the fullness of humanity.

He also teaches that a human being consists of only two substances,

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The manuscript has “of two substances.”]

namely, soul and body; and that sense and spirit are not another substance but innate functions of the soul, by which it breathes, by which it is rational, and by which it makes the body capable of sensation.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The manuscript adds: “in the fourteenth book.”]

In the fourteenth book of this work, discussing specifically the uncreated, only incorporeal, and sovereign nature of the Holy Trinity, which is mistress of all things, and the nature of creatures, he explained the subject in accordance with his understanding and the authority of the Holy Scriptures. In the fifteenth volume he confirmed and fortified the whole structure of his work by citing also the traditions of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Prudentius himself disclosed his age and the year in which he wrote his sacred poems by naming the consul under whom he was born in the preface to the *Cathemerinon*, which ancient manuscript copies rightly place at the beginning as the prologue to the whole work: “Suddenly gray hairs have invaded the old man, accusing me of having forgotten the ancient Salia, under whom my first day dawned.” Salia was consul with Philip in the year of Christ 348. Add the fifty-seven years he had completed, and it follows that he wrote these works in the year of Christ 405. Plantinus published all the works of Prudentius in 1564, corrected on the basis of ten manuscripts by the work of Theodore Pulmannus and Victor Giselinus. MIRAEUS.]

PRUDENTIUS, a man educated in secular literature,

[Note: [Col. 1068C] The word “man” is absent from the Corbie manuscript.]

composed the *Dittochaeon* (*διττοχαῖον*), concerning selected persons from the whole Old and New Testament.

[Note: [Col. 1068C] The Corbie manuscript has *trocleum*, corruptly; but *δίπτυχον* (“diptych”) should be read, following Gisanius’s emendation.]

[Note: [Col. 1068C] All the manuscript codices have *exceptis* (“selected”); Miræus reads *excerptis* (“excerpted”). ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

He also commented, in the Greek manner, on the *Hexaemeron*, from the creation of the world to the creation of the first man and his transgression.

[Note: [Col. 1068C] The Corbie manuscript has “Hexaemeron … from the creation of the first man.”]

He also composed small books to which he gave Greek titles: *Apotheosis*, *Psychomachia*, and *Hamartigenia*, that is, *On Divinity*,

[Note: [Col. 1068C] Miræus has “books which he prefixed with Greek titles.”]

*On the Conflict of the Soul*,

[Note: [Col. 1068C] Miræus incorrectly has “on the conflict of the mind”; the codices have “of the soul.” ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

and *On the Origin of Sins*.

[Note: [Col. 1068C] Miræus has “on various matters,” incorrectly.]

He also wrote one book in praise of the martyrs, under the names of others, inviting people to martyrdom,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] The words “under the names of others, an invitation to martyrdom” are omitted from our manuscripts, and rightly so. ERNEST CYPRIAN.]

and another book of hymns, with a particular intention directed against Symmachus, who defended idolatry. From reading these works it is recognized that he had been a soldier of the Palatine guard.

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Prudentius does not mention this in the books against Symmachus but in the preface to the *Cathemerinon*: “At last, when I had advanced through the ranks of military service, the piety of the emperor raised me up, ordering me to stand nearer him in the next rank.”]

## CHAPTER XIV

AUDENTIUS, a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans, the Sabellians, and the Arians, and especially, with particular intention, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] The Corbie manuscript has “Fontinians.”]

a book entitled *On Faith against Heretics*. In it he showed that the antiquity of the Son of God was coeternal with the Father,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] The manuscript has: “that he had been coeternal, not that his divinity had a beginning.”]

and that he did not receive the beginning of his divinity from God the Father when, as a human being, he was conceived and born from the Virgin Mary, with God as the maker.

[Note: [Col. 1068D] The manuscript has: “when he received humanity from Mary his mother.”]

## CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Trithemius also discusses Audentius and Commodianus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. MIRAEUS.]

COMMODIANUS, while reading both secular literature and our own, found an occasion for faith. Having therefore become a Christian and wishing to offer Christ, the author of his salvation, some gift from his studies, he wrote in mediocre language, almost in verse,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Thus Suffridus Petri correctly reads it. Although the Corbie manuscript has “almost a book.”]

a book against the pagans. Since he had touched only slightly upon our literature,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Some copies have “our writings.” Rigaltius published Commodianus’s book with notes, as did Heinrich Leonard Schurzfleisch at Wittenberg in 1705, quarto.]

he was better able to destroy their doctrines than to strengthen ours. Accordingly, he discussed the divine promises against them in a rather base and coarse understanding, so to speak, causing them astonishment and us despair, while following Tertullian, Lactantius, and Papias as authorities. He did, however, impress upon his students moral teaching, and especially the love of voluntary poverty, with excellent effect.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 1069B] This Faustinus lived during the time of Pope Damasus I and was twice a schismatic: once in the schism of Ursicinus against Damasus, and again in the schism of the Luciferians, as Gennadius testifies in this chapter and Baronius in volume IX of his *Annals*, under the first year of Damasus and the fourth of Siricius. Nevertheless, Bellarmine thought it appropriate to place him in this catalogue because he wrote seven quite learned books against the Arians to Flaccilla, the wife of the emperor Theodosius and mother of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius; these books exist in the *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*. Thus Bellarmine speaks in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*. This book, *On the Trinity*, or *On Faith against the Arians*, was also published entirely under the name of Gregory of Baetica, mentioned by Jerome in chapter 100, except that the letter to Flaccilla was mutilated. MIRAEUS.]

FAUSTINUS the presbyter wrote to Queen Flaccilla against the Arians and Macedonians seven books.

[Note: [Col. 1069C] The Corbie manuscript has “against Arius and Macedonius.” Instead of “seven books,” it would be more correct to say “seven chapters.” Sirmondus published the minor works of Faustinus. See Paschasius Quesnel’s Dissertation 14 on Leo the Great.]

In these works he especially reproved and convicted them through testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, which they misuse with perverse interpretation for blasphemy.

He also wrote a book which he presented to the emperors Valentinian and Arcadius, on behalf of his own party, together with a certain presbyter Marcellinus.

[Note: [Col. 1069C] The Corbie manuscript adds: “formerly a presbyter.”]

From this it is shown that he agreed with the Luciferian schism,

[Note: [Col. 1069C] The manuscript has “wrote about the Luciferian schism.”]

because in the same book he censures Hilary of Poitiers and Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, as though they had given poor counsel to the Church by receiving into communion and the priesthood, for the sake of restoring peace, bishops who had become traitors.

The admission of bishops who had communicated with the Arians at the Council of Ariminum displeased the Luciferians just as the admission of repentant apostates displeased the Novatians.

## CHAPTER XVII
[Note: [Col. 1069C] Rufinus, presbyter and monk of Aquileia, initially distinguished by his friendship with St. Jerome and later more notably by their estrangement, died shortly after Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths—that is, shortly after the year of Christ 410, as Baronius believes. Sonnius printed Rufinus’s works in two volumes [Col. 1069D] at Paris in 1580; concerning them, see Bellarmine’s judgment in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, and Rosweyde’s fourth and fifth prolegomena to the Lives of the Fathers. MIRAEUS.]

## RUFINUS

Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, was no insignificant part of the teachers [Note: [Col. 1069D] Corbei.: “of the churches.”] of the Church and possessed an elegant talent for translating from Greek into Latin. In the end, he made the greater part of the Greek library available to Latin readers: namely, the works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Gregory of Nazianzus, a most eloquent man; the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; the ecclesiastical *History* of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine [Note: [Col. 1069D] Corb.: “and the history of Eusebius, bishop of the Church of Caesarea in Palestine.”]; the *Sentences of Xystus*; and the *Sentences of Evagrius*.

[Note: [Col. 1069D] Rufinus falsely published the book of Xystus the Pythagorean under the title of Xystus, pope and martyr. This is established by various passages of St. Jerome, as in his commentary on Jeremiah 22, where he attacks him under the name of Grunnius, and on Ezekiel 18; likewise by Augustine, *Retractations* II.40 (who, previously deceived, had cited it under the name of Pope Xystus in *On Nature and Grace* 64), and by Rufinus’s own letter [Col. 1070B] to Apronianus, which he prefixed to his translation of the *Enchiridion of Xystus*. Let us hear Jerome himself thundering against Rufinus in his letter to Ctesiphon: “Who could describe in worthy language that audacity—indeed, madness—of his, by which he gave the book of Xystus, a Pythagorean, a pagan and without Christ, a new title, [Col. 1070C] naming it after Xystus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church?” MIRAEUS.]

He also translated the *Sentences of the martyr Pamphilus Against the Mathematicians*.

[Note: [Col. 1070C] Honorius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers* II.17, usually copying Gennadius, corrupted this passage by writing *six*, expressing it as: “the sentences of Xystus the philosopher against the mathematicians.” For Xystus did not write against the mathematicians, but Pamphilus the martyr did, as Gennadius states distinctly here. Moreover, besides the works mentioned here by Gennadius, Rufinus also wrote, or translated from Greek into Latin, the *Lives of the Fathers*, contained in books two and three of the Plantinian edition, as Heribert Rosweyde proves at length in the fourth prolegomenon, §10. MIRAEUS.]

Whatever of all these works is read in Latin with the prologues prefixed was translated by Rufinus; [Note: [Col. 1070C] The words beginning “But those without a prologue” and ending “and Jerome also some,” are absent from Corbei.] but whatever lacks a prologue was translated by another, who did not wish to compose a prologue. Of Origen’s works he did not translate everything, since Jerome also translated some portions; these are distinguished by their prologue.
