By his own labor—or rather, by the grace and gift of God—the same [Col. 1070B] Rufinus expounded the Creed [Note: [Col. 1070C] In the same Corb. it reads: “Rufinus discussed the Creed and the blessings of Jacob upon the patriarchs . . . in mystical language. He also wrote letters urging the fear of God, among which those addressed to Proba are especially notable.”], so that, by comparison with him, others might scarcely be thought to have expounded it at all. He also discussed Jacob’s blessing upon the patriarchs in three senses: historical, moral, and mystical.

He wrote many letters exhorting people to the fear of God, among which those he addressed to Proba are especially distinguished. To the ecclesiastical history which, as we have said, was written by Eusebius and translated by Rufinus, he added a tenth and an eleventh book.

[Note: [Col. 1070C] In translating the History of Eusebius, Rufinus used excessive freedom, adding, omitting, and changing much. He omitted half of the eighth book and scarcely touched the tenth. Thus, from Eusebius’s ten books he made nine, to which he added two of his own—the two mentioned here by Gennadius. Gelasius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, translated these two books into Greek and prefixed his own preface. He had Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, as his maternal uncle; he was not the Gelasius of Cyzicus who wrote about the events of the Council of Nicaea. We discussed these two Gelasiuses above, in the note on Jerome, chapter 130. MIRAEUS.]

He also answered the detractor of his little works in two volumes, arguing and proving that, with the [Col. 1071A] Lord’s help, he had applied his talent with God’s regard and the Church’s usefulness in view; but that the other, driven by the spur of rivalry [Note: [Col. 1071B] Corb.: “a rival.”], had turned his pen [Note: [Col. 1071B] Same manuscript: “had applied his pen.”] to slander.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 1071C] Tichonius the African, a Donatist in certain doctrines, wrote a volume of rules, which St. Augustine discusses and examines in *On Christian Doctrine* III.30 and *Retractations* II.18, as do Cassiodorus in the preface to the Psalms and Isidore in *On the Supreme Good* I. He lived around the year 390. Thus Molanus in his manuscript *Sacred Library*. Andreas Schottus published these seven books of Rules, collated with manuscripts, in volume XV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. MIRAEUS.]

TICHONIUS, an African by birth, was learned in the divine Scriptures, adequately versed in history, and not ignorant of secular studies; he was also diligent in ecclesiastical affairs. He wrote three books *On the Civil War* and *Expositions of Various Cases*, in which, in defense of his own people, he mentions ancient synods. From all these works it is recognized that he belonged to the Donatist party [Note: [Col. 1071C] Corb. manuscript: “of the Donatist party.”].

He also composed seven *Rules for Investigating* [Note: [Col. 1071C] The words “and finding” are absent from Corbei.] *and Finding the Meaning of the Scriptures*, which he enclosed in one volume.

He also expounded the Apocalypse of John in its entirety [Note: [Col. 1071C] Same manuscript: “in full . . . understanding only the spiritual meaning. In this exposition he said.”], finding nothing carnal in it [Col. 1071B] but understanding everything spiritually. In this exposition he said that the angelic station is a body.

He also held the opinion that the kingdom of the righteous on earth would last a thousand years after the resurrection; nor did he assert two future resurrections of those dead in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1071C] Corbei. manuscript: “He entertained the opinion of the thousand-year kingdom; nor did he hold that there would be two future resurrections in the flesh, one among the righteous and one among the unrighteous, but that there would be one resurrection of all at the same time, in which the prematurely born and deformed would rise” (below, chapter 38). “The distinction between the two resurrections, however, he makes as follows.”], one of the righteous and another of the unrighteous, but one resurrection of all at once, in which even those prematurely born and deformed would rise [Note: [Col. 1071C] Another reading: “restored”; and shortly afterward: “so that nothing deformed and endowed with the substance of the human race should perish, or the endowed substance should perish.”], so that no part of the human race possessing animate substance should perish.

He makes the distinction between the two resurrections as follows: “The first, which the Apocalypse calls the resurrection of the righteous, we believe is now being enacted in the growth of the Church, where those justified by faith are raised from the death of their sins through baptism to the reward of eternal life” [Col. 1072A] [Note: [Col. 1071D] Corb. manuscript: “human beings are raised. There are, however, two classes of all human beings, the righteous and sinners. He flourished, etc.”]; “but the second is the resurrection of all human flesh in general.”

This man flourished in the same period as the already mentioned Rufinus, during the reign of Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1071D] “Theodosius with his sons.”] and his son.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Severus, surnamed Sulpitius, and by others Sulpitius Severus, is called simply Severus by Paulinus of Nola, Gregory of Tours, and others. He was an Aquitanian by birth, as he himself admits in *Dialogue* I.20. Indeed, he came from the Nitiobrigi, since in book II of his *Sacred History* he calls Phoebadius—who was bishop of Agen in Gaul and is mentioned by Jerome in the *Catalogue*, chapter 108—his bishop. Agen is known to have been among the Nitiobrigi.

He lived chiefly at Elusotte, as Paulinus states in letter 6, or at Primuliacum, as the same writer relates in letters 11 and 12. It may also be inferred from Severus’s own letter to his mother-in-law Bassula that he lived at Toulouse. Elusio, or Eluso—now Lausun—was formerly a city situated between Narbonne and Toulouse in Narbonese Gaul, as is clear from the Bordeaux Itinerary published by Pithoeus. It must be distinguished from Elusa, formerly situated between Bordeaux and Toulouse in Aquitaine and Novempopulania. Primuliacum [Col. 1072C] was not far from Eluson, where Severus lived chiefly. Paulinus, letter 12, mentions a basilica founded by Severus at Primuliacum.

This Sulpitius of ours was not bishop of Bourges, as Sigonius, Galesinius, Giselinus, and many other learned men thought, but only a presbyter, as Gennadius testifies in this chapter. He lived now at Primuliacum, now at Eluson, as the various letters of Paulinus of Nola indicate.

Very different from our Sulpitius, and later in age, was St. Sulpitius Severus, bishop of Bourges and martyr, listed in the Roman Martyrology on January 29. He took part in the Second Council of Mâcon, and Gregory of Tours dedicated to him his history of the Seven Sleepers.

As for the writings of our Severus, he composed a *Sacred History* in an elegant style, beginning with the creation of the world and carrying it down to the consulship of Stilicho and Aurelian, that is, to the year of Christ 400. He also wrote the *Life of St. Martin*, bishop of Tours, with whom he was intimate, and three letters concerning the praise of that same bishop.

Three dialogues of his also survive. The first recounts the virtues of the Eastern monks; the two later ones explain the virtues of St. Martin omitted in book I. In the *Dialogues*, Sulpitius follows the error of the millenarians, as Jerome notes in his commentary on Ezekiel 36. Hence Pope Gelasius calls the little works of Postumianus and Gallus apocryphal. MIRAEUS.]

SEVERUS, the presbyter surnamed Sulpitius, from the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and learning and distinguished by his love of poverty and humility, also renowned for his acquaintance with the holy men Martin, bishop of Tours, and Paulinus of Nola, wrote some works of no little worth.

He wrote many letters to his sister exhorting her to love of God and contempt of the world [Note: [Col. 1072D] Another reading: “exhortatory.”], which are well known. He wrote two letters to the aforementioned Paulinus [Col. 1072B] and others to other persons.

But because some also contain matters of private and personal concern, they are not arranged [Note: [Col. 1072D] Same manuscript: “He wrote three others to the aforementioned Paulinus of Nola. But because…”].

He also composed a *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 1072D] Same manuscript: “Chronicle.”].

He also wrote, for the benefit of many, the life of the blessed Martin, monk and bishop, a man illustrious for signs, wonders, and virtues [Note: [Col. 1072D] The Corbei manuscripts add: “which Postumianus and Gallus later developed in a remarkable manner. But the conversation of Postumianus, etc.”]. He presented the conversation of Postumianus and Gallus—held with himself as mediator and judge—concerning the conduct of the Eastern monks and of Martin himself in the form of a dialogue, in three divisions [Note: [Col. 1072D] Same manuscript: “comprised in the form of a dialogue and in three sections.”].

In the first of these he reports that, in his own time, a synod [Col. 1073A] of bishops at Alexandria decreed that Origen should be read more cautiously by the wise as beneficial, but rejected as harmful by those of lesser understanding [Note: [Col. 1073B] That is, “to be cast aside.”].

[Note: [Col. 1073B] Joan. Clericus, volume XX of the *Bibliothèque choisie*, p. 330, thinks that this final passage was stitched on by another hand. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts recognize it. MIRAEUS.]

In his old age this man was deceived by the Pelagians; recognizing the fault of his loquacity, he maintained silence until death, so that he might correct by penitential silence the sin he had contracted by speaking [Note: [Col. 1073C] Thus I restored the reading from the Corbei manuscript in place of “completely.”].

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 1073C] Corbei. manuscript: “Antiochus . . . composed one large volume against avarice and a homily on the healing of the blind man who was healed by the Savior.” Another Antiochus was the monk in the Laura of St. Sabas; his works include a homily of confession and a book to Eustathius *On Vicious Thoughts*, translated from Greek into Latin by Peter Pantinus and printed in volume VII of the last Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* (volume XII, Lyons). Baronius may be consulted concerning him in volume VIII. If I am not mistaken, the book preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library under the title “St. Antiochus to Eustathius: Various Chapters” is also by this Antiochus. Gonzalo Ponce de León discusses his date at length in his notes to St. Epiphanius’s *Physiologus*, chapter 22. MIRAEUS.]

ANTIOCHUS, bishop, wrote one long volume *Against Avarice*. He also composed a homily on the healing of the blind man who was enlightened by the Savior, full of the compunction of the fear of God and of humility.

[Note: [Col. 1073C] Same manuscript: “He died during the reign of Marcian.”]

He died during the reign of the emperor Arcadius.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 1073C] Concerning Severianus of Gabala, or Gavalus (Suffridus Petri: “of Gavello”; the Gembloux manuscript: “of the Church of Gavilla”), Molanus writes in his manuscript *Sacred Library*: “Severianus, bishop of Gavalus, to whom Chrysostom entrusted his church when he was sent into exile, wrote various sermons, some of which survive among the works of Chrysostom and Chrysologus, while fragments of many others occur in the books of the ancients.” Petavius says in his *Chronological Calculations* that, because of rivalry with Chrysostom, he earned less favorable fame among posterity. MIRAEUS.]

SEVERIANUS, bishop of the Church of Gabala [Note: [Col. 1073D] Corb.: “of Gabala”], was learned [Col. 1073B] in the divine Scriptures and an astonishing declaimer in homilies. Therefore he was frequently summoned to Constantinople by Bishop John and by the emperor Arcadius [Note: [Col. 1073D] “By the emperor Arcadius.”] to deliver sermons.

I have read his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians and a very pleasing little work on baptism and the solemnity of Epiphany [Note: [Col. 1073D] Same manuscript: “an exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, and a work on baptism and Epiphany.”].

He died during the reign of the younger Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1073D] Same manuscript: “during the reign of Theodosius the younger, his son, at his baptism.” The Nuremberg codex, like the Wolfenbüttel codex: “during the reign of Theodosius, his son, at baptism.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

## CHAPTER XXII

NICEAS, bishop of the city of Romaciana [Note: [Col. 1073D] “Of Rome,” incorrectly. In other manuscripts Suffridus Petri testifies that he found “of Romaciana.”], composed, in simple and polished language, six little books of instruction for candidates preparing for baptism [Col. 1074A].

In the first he explains how candidates who desire to attain the grace of baptism ought to conduct themselves. The second concerns the errors of paganism [Note: [Col. 1074B] Corbei. manuscript: “in which he says that, almost in his own time, a certain Melgidius, a householder . . . and Gadarius, a rustic, etc.”]. In it he says that, almost in his own time, a certain Melodius [Note: [Col. 1074B] “Melodius” in the Nuremberg manuscript; “Meladius” in the Wolfenbüttel manuscript; Miraeus has “Melchidius.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.], a householder, was transferred among the gods by the pagans because of his generosity, and Gadarius, a rustic, because of his courage [Note: [Col. 1074B] The Nuremberg manuscript reads: “because of fornication.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

The third book is on the one faith of the one majesty; the fourth is against genethliology [Note: [Col. 1074C] Another reading: “genethlogy”; in Corb. corruptly, “genocly.” Miraeus has the same reading. N.: “genealogy.” Gu.: “genelogy.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.]; the fifth is on the Creed; the sixth is on the victim of the Paschal Lamb.

He also published a little book *To the Fallen Virgin* [Note: [Col. 1074C] Same manuscript: “a book for human beings who have fallen, and an incentive [to repentance].”], an incentive to amendment for almost all who fall.

## CHAPTER XXIII

OLYMPIUS, a Spaniard by birth [Note: [Col. 1074C] Another reading: “Olympus.” The Gembloux codex, according to Suffridus Petri, reads “Opilius.” Augustine, *Against Julian* I, calls him Olympius and gives a fragment from one of his ecclesiastical sermons, dealing with original sin. Thus Gennadius and Cave do not list all his writings; the latter thinks that he flourished around the year 430. But since Augustine, writing against Julian, called him a man of great glory in the Church and in Christ, he seems to have flourished considerably earlier. Augustine died in 430. ERN. CYPRIANUS.], a bishop, wrote a book of faith against those who attribute guilt to nature rather than to free choice [Col. 1074B], showing that evil was implanted in nature not by creation but by disobedience.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 1074C] Suffridus Petri has “Bacciarius.” The Martini and Corbei manuscripts have “Bacharius.” Gembloux and Green Valley have “Bachiarius.” Honorius has “Bachianus,” corruptly. The letter of this Bachiarius to Januarius concerning the reception of the fallen survives in the *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*. It was also published by Plantin with the little works of Pope Sixtus III, edited by Jacobus Salvator Solanius of Murgi, who calls him St. Bracharius. See below, chapter 56. MIRAEUS.]

BACHIARIUS, a man of Christian [Note: [Col. 1074D] Corbei.: “a man accomplished in Christian discipline.” In place of “naked,” Ludovico Antonio Muratori would prefer “polished.” But I think “naked” is correct, and that it should not be referred, with Honorius, to the preceding words, but to what follows; it has precisely the same meaning as “unencumbered.” It signifies that he had left his homeland and family.] philosophy, intending, stripped and unencumbered, to devote himself to God, also chose exile in order to preserve the integrity of his life [Note: [Col. 1074D] Another reading: “to preserve the integrity of his way of life,” or, as Corbei. has it, “the integrity of his purpose.”].

He is said to have published pleasing little works; but of them I have read only one, a little book *On Faith*, in which he gives satisfaction to the bishop of the city against those who complain about and defame his exile [Note: [Col. 1074D] Corbei.: “complainers.” The Green Valley codex: “against Cerelli.” But “complainers” is correct. So below, chapter 39, concerning Orosius: “he wrote against the complainers and defamers of the Christian name.”], and declares that he undertook his exile not from fear of human beings but of God, so that, going out [Col. 1075A] from his land [Note: [Col. 1075B] Corbei.: “from his land or kindred,” from Genesis 12:1. The learned Ludovico Antonio Muratori first published this little work of Bachiarius, with notes, in volume II of the *Anecdota of the Ambrosian Library*, Milan, 1698, quarto. At the very beginning it reads: “Although we knew our homeland according to the flesh, now we no longer know it; and desiring to become children of Abraham, we rejected our land and our kindred.”], he might become a fellow-heir of the patriarch Abraham.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Note: [Col. 1075C] This chapter is absent from Corbei. The learned Latinus Latinius is mistaken in identifying this Sabbatius with Phoebadius, whom Jerome discusses in chapter 108. The Gembloux codex has “Sapatius.”]

SABBATIUS, bishop of a Gallican church, was asked by a certain chaste virgin dedicated to Christ, named Secunda, to compose a book of faith against Marcion and his author Valentinus [Note: [Col. 1075C] Thus the manuscripts and the old editions of Honorius; in place of this, some have “hearer,” incorrectly. He calls him “author” in the sense of teacher and founder of the heresy.], and against Eunomius and his teacher Aetius.

He demonstrated to them by reasoning and by testimonies from Scripture that there is one principle of the Godhead, one God who is the author of eternity and creator of the world from nothing [Note: [Col. 1075C] The Sigeberg codex, examined by Suffridus Petri: “that there is one Lord, author of eternity.” “That there is one principle of the Godhead, one God, author of eternity.” Thus, as I think, I have happily restored the passage from the Nuremberg codex. Miraeus has the incongruous reading: “one author of the Godhead and of the world from nothing.” Gu. likewise has: “principles of the Godhead.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

He also showed concerning Christ that he did not appear as a man in mere appearance, but possessed true flesh, through which—by eating, drinking, becoming weary, weeping, dying, and rising again—he was proved to be truly human. For Marcion and Valentinus opposed these teachings, asserting [Col. 1075B] that there were two principles of the Godhead and that Christ came in mere appearance [Note: [Col. 1075D] Our manuscripts do not contain the word “of the Godhead.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

Against Aetius and his disciple Eunomius he showed that the Father and the Son are not of two natures, nor equal in divinity [Note: [Col. 1075D] Thus we have supplied the text from the Nuremberg manuscript. Miraeus’s reading does not fit: “and equal in divinity.”], but are of one essence (*ὁμοιουσίων*, “of like essence”), one from the other—that is, the Son from the Father—and one coeternal with the other. Aetius and Eunomius contradict this belief.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Note: [Col. 1075D] This chapter too is absent from Corbei, nor is there any trace of it in Trithemius. This Isaac was a Christian converted from Judaism, for his little book is titled in the Pithoean codex, according to Sirmondus: “The Faith of Isaac, Converted from Judaism.” Cave assigns him to the year 430; Suffridus Petri to 450; Sirmondus, whom I follow, thinks that he flourished somewhat before the year 400.

Jacobus Sirmondus, S.J., a theologian, first published Isaac’s book of faith—by Isaac, converted from Judaism to Christ—treating of the Holy Trinity and the Lord’s incarnation, together with little works by the presbyter Leporius, Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, and Victorinus the African, at Paris in 1630. MIRAEUS.]

ISAAC wrote a book on the three persons of the Holy Trinity and the incarnation of the Lord, a work of exceedingly obscure disputation and involved language. He affirmed that in [Col. 1076A] one Godhead there are three persons, in such a way that each possesses something proper to itself which the others do not.

The Father has this as his proper attribute: that he himself is the origin without origin of the others. The Son has this as his proper attribute: that, although begotten, he is not later than the begetter. The Holy Spirit has this as his proper attribute: that he is neither made nor begotten, and yet is from another.

Concerning the incarnation he writes in such a way that, while the two natures remain in it, one person of the Son of God is believed to exist.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 1076B] In a Vatican codex this Ursinus is named as the author of the little book *On the Rebaptizing of Heretics*, which was published anonymously by Rigaltus and by John Fell, bishop of Oxford, at the end of the works of St. Cyprian. See Labbe, volume I of the *Councils*, p. 770.]

URSINUS, a monk, wrote against those who decree that heretics must be rebaptized. He taught that it is neither lawful nor worthy of God to rebaptize those who have been baptized in the name of Christ, or in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, even if with an erroneous understanding; but that, after a simple confession of the Trinity and of Christ, the laying on of the hands of a Catholic priest is sufficient for salvation.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1076C] Different from the person mentioned above in chapter 10. Rufinus of Aquileia dedicated his apology for Origen to this Macarius the Roman. Jerome writes in his second apology against Rufinus: “Therefore, unless you had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the mathematicians”—clearly referring to this Macarius the Roman, whom Rufinus held in very close friendship, whom he drew away from the mathematicians, and infected with Origen’s soot. Consult Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 317.

This Macarius is different from another Macarius the Roman, whom the Greeks celebrate in their menology on October 23 and whose life appears in volume I of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Baronius had confused these two Macariuses in the Roman Martyrology on January 2, as Rosweyde noted in his notes to Paulinus of Nola’s letter 36. MIRAEUS.]

MACARIUS, another monk, wrote in the city of Rome a book against the mathematicians [Note: [Col. 1076C] “Astrologers, genethliacs.” Rufinus mentions this Macarius’s little works against fate and *mathesis* in his first invective against Jerome.], in which labor he sought the consolations of the Eastern Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1076D] Rufinus implies that Macarius was assisted by his writings. See Baronius on the January 2 entry in the Martyrology, and Tillemont, volume XII of the *Memoirs*, p. 203 and following.].

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 1076D] This Heliodorus is different from the other Heliodorus, also a presbyter, whom Gennadius himself mentioned above in chapter 6. MIRAEUS.]

HELIODORUS, another presbyter of Antioch, published an excellent volume on virginity, furnished with material from the sacred Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Note: [Col. 1076D] John, bishop of Jerusalem, lived in the time of St. Jerome. A book addressed to Caprasius, *On the Instruction of a Monk*, is attributed to John; it survives in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and elsewhere. But it appears to have been written by someone much later. Thus Bellarmine, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Baronius under the year 444 believe. The Carmelites, however—especially Thomas of Jesus of Bragança and Peter Wastelius—try to defend the earlier view.

John of Jerusalem, Rufinus of Aquileia, and Palladius of Galatia were among the greatest supporters of Origen in that age; for this reason St. Epiphanius and St. Jerome attacked them in their writings. MIRAEUS.]

JOHN, bishop of Jerusalem, wrote a book against the detractors of his scholarly pursuits [Col. 1077A] [Note: [Col. 1077C] “Addressed to Theophilus of Alexandria.” See Peter Wastelius’s *Vindication of John of Jerusalem*, p. 530 and following, and Tillemont, volume XII of the *Memoirs*, p. 186 and 197.], in which he showed that he had followed Origen’s intellect, not his faith.

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Note: [Col. 1077C] The Gembloux and Green Valley codices call him Paulinus, according to Suffridus Petri.]

PAUL, a bishop, wrote a little book on repentance, in which he lays down a rule for penitents: they ought to grieve over their sins in such a way that they are not overwhelmed by excessive sadness and the enormity of despair.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Note: [Col. 1077C] Corbei. manuscript: “Helvidius the heretic.” By Auxentius they understand the Arian bishop of Milan, and by Symmachus the man whom our author earlier, in chapter 13, said defended idolatry.]

HELVIDIUS, a disciple of Auxentius and an imitator of Symmachus, wrote out of zeal for religion, but not according to knowledge, a book supported neither by polished language nor by sound reasoning. In this work [Note: [Col. 1077C] Corbei.: “little work.”] he tried so to bend the meaning of the sacred Scriptures to his own perversity that he wished to assert from their testimonies [Col. 1077B] that St. Mary, who bore the Lord as a virgin, after the Lord’s birth was joined to her husband Joseph and had children by him [Note: [Col. 1077C] Same manuscript: “conceived children.”], who were called the Lord’s brothers [Note: [Col. 1077C] After this the Corbei codex reads: “Against whose impiety the most blessed Jerome published an excellent and welcome little book, in which he showed that the most blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, remained a virgin after giving birth just as she had been a virgin before giving birth.”].

Jerome, refuting his perversity, published against him a little book adequately supported by the evidence of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, wrote three Paschal letters to St. Jerome, his friend; Jerome himself translated them from Greek into Latin, and they survive in the *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*. The prologue addressed to the emperor Theodosius concerning Holy Pascha was written in the year 380. The works that he wrote against Origen and the other writings mentioned here by Gennadius no longer survive.

The same Theophilus appointed Synesius of Cyrene—a pagan philosopher converted to Christianity—bishop of Ptolemais around the year 410. He fiercely persecuted St. John Chrysostom; concerning this, consult Baronius in the *Annals*. Jerome discusses Theophilus of Antioch and Theophilus of Caesarea in the *Catalogue*, chapters 25 and 43. MIRAEUS.]

THEOPHILUS, bishop of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1077D] From the year 385 to 412.], wrote one large volume against Origen, in which he condemns almost all his statements [Note: [Col. 1077D] The words “and him himself as well” are absent from Corbei.] and Origen himself alike. At the same time he taught that Origen was not first expelled from the presbyterate and driven from the Church by him, but by the ancient Fathers, especially Heraclas, and that he was expelled from the city as well [Note: [Col. 1078C] The words “and driven from the city” are absent from Corbei.].

He also refuted at great length the heretics called anthropomorphites, who say that God consists of human form and limbs, and convicted them by testimonies from the divine Scriptures [Col. 1077C–1078A]. He showed that God, according to the faith of the Fathers, must be believed incorruptible [Note: [Col. 1078C] The word “incorruptible” is absent from Corbei.] and incorporeal, composed in no way whatsoever of the outlines of limbs. For this reason nothing in created things is similar to him in substance, nor has he given his own incorruptibility to any being; rather, all intellectual natures are corporeal, all are corruptible, and all are mutable, so that only he is not subject to corruption and mutability who alone possesses immortality (1 Timothy 6:16).

He also presented to Theodosius the Paschal cycle which the great synod at Nicaea had determined should recur after ninety-five years according to its proper season, day, and lunar date, adding certain calculations and explanations of the feast itself [Note: [Col. 1078C] The entire period is extremely obscure. N. reads: “with the festival calculations”; Gu.: “with the festival explanations.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

I have also read three books *On Faith* bearing his name; but because the language is discordant [Col. 1078B], I did not place much trust in them.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note: [Col. 1078C] Perhaps Eusebius, bishop of Milan, is meant.]

EUSEBIUS wrote on the mystery of the Lord’s cross and on the apostles, especially Peter’s steadfastness [Col. 1078C] [Note: [Col. 1078C] Corbei. manuscript: “Peter’s steadfastness, and the virtue acquired through the cross.”], through the virtue obtained by the cross [Note: [Col. 1078C] “Acquired through the virtue of the cross of faith.” Thus the Nuremberg manuscript. ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

## CHAPTER XXXV

VIGILANTIUS, a presbyter and a Gaul by nationality, held the church of the Spanish parish of Barcelona [Note: [Col. 1078C] The Gembloux and Green Valley codices read: “of Barcelona.”].

He too wrote certain things out of zeal for religion; but, misled by human praise and presuming beyond his powers, a man polished in language but untrained in the meaning of Scripture, he interpreted the second vision of Daniel with perverse ingenuity and said other frivolous things [Note: [Col. 1078C] The Gembloux and Green Valley codices have “superfluous.”], which necessarily place him in the catalogue of heretics.

The blessed presbyter Jerome also answered him [Note: [Col. 1078C] Corbei.: “answered him most eloquently.”].

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Col. 1078C]

[Note: [Col. 1078C] St. Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, is listed in the Roman Martyrology on August 16. Several letters of St. Ambrose survive addressed to him; Simplicianus had first been Ambrose’s assistant and later succeeded him in the episcopate. St. Augustine dedicated to him two books *On Various Questions*, mentioned in *Retractations* II.1 and *On the Predestination of the Saints* I.4. St. Vigilius, bishop of Trent, wrote him a little book on the martyrdom of St. Sisinnius and his companions.

An epigram of Ennodius of Ticinum concerning him survives as number 78, beginning:

> Ambrose, leaving the duties of the widowed flock,  
> Transferred them, Simplicianus, to your care.

He fell asleep in the Lord in the third year of his episcopate, while Pope Siricius was seated, and rests at Milan in the church dedicated to his name, as Joseph Ripamontius recounts at length in book VI of his *History of Milan*. MIRAEUS.]

SIMPLICIANUS, bishop of Milan, urged Augustine, while he was still a presbyter [Note: [Col. 1079B] Another reading: “still a presbyter.”], in many [Col. 1079A] letters to exercise his intellect and devote himself to expositions of the Scriptures, so that he might even appear to be a new Ambrose, an *ἑργοδιώκτης* of Origen—that is, a persecutor of Origen’s work [Note: [Col. 1079B] See the note on Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 56.].

Therefore he composed many answers to Scriptural questions addressed to Augustine. He also has a letter consisting of propositions, in which, by asking questions, he teaches as though he were learning from a teacher [Note: [Col. 1079B] Corbei.: “he teaches the teacher by showing what should be asked.”].

## CHAPTER XXXVII
[Note: [Col. 1079B] Saint Vigilius, bishop of Trent, suffered martyrdom during the consulship of Stilicho (as Usuardus records under 6 July), that is, in the year of Christ 400 or 405, as may be inferred from the consular fasti, which record Stilicho’s two consulships. Saint Ambrose’s Book III, Letter 24, is extant to him. Saint Vigilius himself wrote to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, mentioned in the preceding chapter, a short work on the martyrdom of Saint Sisinius and his companions, published by Surius under 23 May. Another Vigilius, later in date, wrote five books against Nestorius and Eutyches in defense of the Council of Chalcedon; they appear in volume V of the Library of the Fathers. He lived in the time of the emperors Zeno and Anastasius and also wrote, under the name of Anastasius, a short work against Sabellius and Photinus, published in the same volume. Andreas Schottus restored, in volume XV of the latest Cologne edition of the Library of the Fathers, a gathering of Vigilius’s works that had hitherto been missing. Moreover, the history of the life of Saint Vigilius published by Surius requires correction. For it falsely relates that Saint Vigilius wrote against Eutyches, who was later in date, and that he was crowned with martyrdom around the year 700, whereas it is clear from the foregoing that Saint Vigilius lived in the age of Saints Ambrose and Simplicianus. Philip Ferrarius also noted this against the error of Galesinius in his Catalogue of the Saints of Italy. MIRAEUS.]

VIGILIUS, a bishop, wrote to a certain Simplicianus, in praise of the martyrs, a short work and a letter containing an account of the martyrdoms of his own time among the barbarians.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1079C] Saint Augustine. He was born in Africa during the consulship of Arbetio and Mavortius Lollianus—as he himself states in Book I of *The Happy Life* and Book I of *On Order*—that is, in the ordinary year of Christ 355. He died on 28 August, at the age of seventy-six, in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate and the forty-third year after his conversion, at a time when the Vandals had already been besieging Hippo for three months, as Possidius relates in his *Life*. His works, revised by the theologians of Louvain, were first published by Plantin in 1577, and afterward in ten volumes by the Paris and Cologne presses. Bellarmine clearly explains, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, which books in each volume are genuine, suspect, or spurious. In more recent years, Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* was discovered in the abbey of Saint Bartholomew at Fiesole and first published at Augsburg through the care of Cardinal Scipione Cobelluzzi and Marcus Welser. Following their example, Claudius Menard published at Paris in 1616 two later books of Saint Augustine against Julian the Pelagian, from manuscript copies; and Jacques Sirmond, in the same city in 1631, first published forty new sermons of Augustine, collected from various ancient exemplars and supplied with notes. Indeed, no one who remembers that Augustine himself, Possidius, Victor of Utica, and others praised the immeasurable multitude of his treatises and homilies will be surprised that new sermons of Augustine, which had hitherto lain concealed, could still be found. Whoever wishes to know more should consult the latest Paris and Cologne editions of Saint Augustine’s works. [The most recent and splendid edition after Miraeus is the one for which we are indebted to the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, Paris, 1688 and following years, reprinted with an appendix at Amsterdam in 1700, in twelve volumes, under the direction of the distinguished John Clericus.]] 

AUGUSTINE, an African and bishop of the town of Hippo, a man renowned throughout the world for divine and human learning, [Col. 1079B] sound in faith and pure in life, wrote as much as could scarcely be found elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 1080B] Thus the same codex reads *for who, then*.] For who could boast that he possessed all of his writings? Or who could read with as much diligence as he wrote? [Note: [Col. 1080B] In the Corbie manuscript the words from *and therefore many things* through *you will not escape sin* are absent.] Hence, in speaking at such length, he experienced what the Holy Spirit said through Solomon: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10:19). [Note: [Col. 1080C] The same manuscript reads *he, already an old man*.] Nevertheless, as an old man he published the fifteen books on the Trinity which he had begun as a young man. In them, as Scripture says, having been brought into the king’s chamber (Esther 2:16), and adorned with the many-colored garment [Note: [Col. 1080C] The Corbie manuscript reads *of manifold wisdom*.] of God’s wisdom, he displayed the Church as having neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), or anything of that kind. He also published a suitable pious work on the Incarnation of God. On the resurrection of the dead as well he proceeded with comparable sincerity, although he left those of lesser understanding in doubt concerning miscarried infants. [Note: [Col. 1080C] Augustine neither dares affirm nor deny that miscarried infants will rise again: *City of God* XXII.13.] Yet his error, contracted—as I said—by his extensive speech and magnified by the struggle with his enemies, did not yet give rise to a question of heresy? [Note: [Col. 1080C] Some copies incorrectly read *settles the question*.] [Note: [Col. 1080C] At the end of this chapter Miraeus’s edition contains much that is absent from our copies and ought not to be missed. It appears to have been written in the margin by some reader of Gennadius and subsequently inserted into the text by the scribes. It reads as follows in Miraeus: “Nevertheless he remained Catholic, and his error, contracted—as I said—by his extensive speech and magnified by the struggle with his enemies, did not yet give rise to a question of heresy. Serving the Church with excellent intelligence and outstanding zeal, he answered the books of the heretic Julian amid the attack of the besieging Vandals, at the very end of his days; and persevering in the defense of Christian wisdom, he died while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning.” Suffridus Petri testifies that he also found these words in the Martinian manuscript, correctly observing that they are not Gennadius’s, but belong to someone wishing to “heal” Gennadius.]]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1080D] Corbie: Orosius. Paulus Orosius, a presbyter of Tarragona, wrote seven books of history down to the year of Christ 416, at the urging of Saint Augustine. Sent by Augustine to the East, he brought the relics of Saint Stephen from there to Africa around the year 416. He also wrote an *Apology against Pelagius on Free Choice*, published through the work of John Costerus at Louvain in 1558 and afterward at Cologne in 1572, edited by Francis Fabricius. A foreign patch has been sewn onto this *Apology*—that is, more than fourteen chapters have been added from Saint Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace*. Andreas Schottus separated these chapters and published them independently in volume XV of the *Library of the Fathers*. The same thing happened long ago with the Pisan Pandects, the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, Censorinus, and other ancient writers. MIRAEUS.]

OROSIUS, a presbyter, [Note: [Col. 1080D] Some copies read *of Spanish origin*.] a Spaniard by birth, an eloquent man [Col. 1081A] and a student of history, wrote seven books against those who complain and defame the Christian name, saying that the decline of the Roman state had been brought about by the teaching of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1081C] Thus above, chapter 24, *against those who complain and defame his journey*.] In these books, reviewing the calamities and miseries of almost the whole world’s history, and the disturbances of wars, he shows that it is rather a consequence of Christian observance that the Roman state, despite its deserts, still endured, and that the empire, pacified by the peace of the worship of God, retained its dominion. In the first book he carefully describes the configuration of the world, divided by the intervening Ocean and bounded by the Tanais; the situation of places; the names, number, and customs of peoples; the characteristics of regions; the beginnings of wars; and the origins of tyrannies, consecrated by the blood of neighboring peoples. [Note: [Col. 1081C] Another reading is *were present*; it is erroneous.] This is the Orosius who was sent by Augustine to Jerome to learn the nature of the soul and, on his return, brought back the relics [Note: [Col. 1081C] Below, chapters 46 and 47.] of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, newly discovered at that time, and was the first to convey them to the West. He flourished [Note: [Col. 1081C] The Corbie manuscript reads *in the final year of the emperor Honorius*.] almost at the end of the reign of the emperor Honorius.

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 1081C] Saint Maximus, bishop of Augusta Taurinorum, now in the territory of Piedmont, is entered in the Roman Martyrology under 25 June. He took part in the synod of Milan held by Eusebius, bishop of that city, and in the Roman synod celebrated under Pope Hilary, during the consulship of Basiliscus and Herminericus—that is, in the year 465. Therefore those who write that he died while Honorius and the younger Theodosius were reigning are mistaken. [Col. 1081D] For the younger Theodosius died during the consulship of Valentinian VII and Gennadius Avienus—that is, in the year of Christ 450—as Cassiodorus testifies in his *Chronicle*. Moreover, the homilies of Saint Maximus of Turin were published at Rome in 1335. Quite a few of them were falsely published under the name of Saint Ambrose, as Costerus and Bellarmine observed. MIRAEUS.]

MAXIMUS, bishop of the Church of Turin, a man sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures and capable of teaching the people extemporaneously, composed treatises in praise of the Apostles, one on the nativity of John the Baptist, and a general homily on all the martyrs. [Col. 1082A] He also wisely expounded many passages from the Gospel chapters and the Acts of the Apostles. He composed two treatises on the life of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor of Vercelli; and on the martyrdom of Saints Cyprian and Laurence; and he published a book on the spiritual grace of Baptism. He wrote on avarice, hospitality, the waning of the moon, almsgiving, and the passage written in Isaiah 1:22, “Your tavern-keepers have mixed wine with water”; on the Lord’s Passion, the general fast of the servants of God, the special fast of Lent and the fact that one must not jest during it; on Judas the betrayer, the Lord’s cross, the Lord’s tomb, his resurrection, the Lord accused and judged before Pilate, and the Kalends of January. I have read many homilies of his on the Nativity of the Lord, on the Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost; on not fearing carnal enemies, giving thanks to God after meals, the repentance of the Ninevites, and many others on various subjects, which I do not retain. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Thus the manuscript copies and printed editions before Miraeus; likewise the Marcian edition. But Miraeus, following Baronius, wrote *he flourished*.] He died while Honorius and the younger Theodosius were reigning.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Saint Petronius, bishop of Bologna in Italy, obtained that see after Saint Felix, the successor of Saint Eusebius. Eusebius took part in the Council of Aquileia against the Arians during the consulship of Merobaudes II and Saturninus—that is, in the year of Christ 383. Saint Petronius, however, lived in the time of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, namely around the year of the Lord 441. Eucherius himself writes in his paraenetic letter *On Contempt of the World* to his kinsman Valerian: “Hilary was recently, and Petronius is now, a bishop in Italy. Both rose from that fullest seat, as they say, of worldly power—one to the religious life, the other to the priesthood.” From these words Baronius plausibly concludes, in his notes on the martyrology under 4 October, that Saint Petronius once administered the prefecture of the Praetorium, just as his father, Sextus Anicius Petronius Probus, had done; the latter had also held the consulship with the emperor Arcadius in the year 406. The deeds of Saint Petronius published by Surius were recorded not by Sigonius but by Galesinius, although the name of Sigonius appears before them in Surius. MIRAEUS.]

PETRONIUS, bishop of the Church of Bologna, a man of holy life and trained from adolescence in the pursuits of monks, is thought to have written the *Lives of the Fathers*, [Note: [Col. 1082D] Gennadius seems to praise these above, chapter II.] the lives of the monks of Egypt, which monks embrace as a mirror and rule of their profession. [Note: [Col. 1082C] He is thought to have written the *Lives of the Fathers*. Similar statements are made by Honorius of Autun in his catalogue, no. 41; Vincent of Beauvais in *Historical Mirror*, Book XX, chapter 25; Mombritius in volume II of *Lives of the Saints*; and Trithemius in his *Catalogue*. This led some to believe that the *Lives of the Fathers* now in everyone’s hands were written by Saint Petronius. But since Gennadius says “is thought to have written,” it is not entirely certain that he wrote the *Lives of the Fathers*. And even if he wrote some such lives, Rosweyde sufficiently demonstrated in Prolegomenon 4, §7, that he certainly did not write those that we possess. Alfonso Chacón, however, in his treatise *On Saint Jerome’s Cardinalate*, cites the following from a manuscript treatise by Saint Petronius, *On Selected Sayings of the Holy Fathers*: “Jerome, a man most complete in every kind of learning, when accused by his rivals of having transferred countless things from Origen’s volumes into his own works, said: ‘The praise that ought to be offered to Origen is very great. And when I imitated him in my works, I intended to imitate one whom I have no fear will displease us or any prudent person.’ Since these words are not found in the *Lives of the Fathers* cited by me above in the notes on the final chapter of Saint Jerome, it may be concluded that Saint Petronius wrote some other book of the *Lives and Sayings of the Fathers*. Would that someone would bring it forth. MIRAEUS.]

I have read, under his name, a treatise *On the Ordination of a Bishop*, full of reason and [Note: [Col. 1083B] Some copies add *and humanity*.] humility. Its more elegant language shows that it is not his, but, according to some, belongs to his father, Petronius, a very eloquent man and highly learned in secular literature. For in the treatise itself he indicates that he had been prefect of the Praetorium. He died while Theodosius, the son of Arcadius, and Valentinian were reigning.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 1083B] The Corbie manuscript: “Pelagius the Briton, arch-heresiarch.” Pelagius, a Scot by nation and originating from Britain—whence he is also called “the Briton”—while he was a monk in Palestine, conceived, together with his disciple Coelestius, in his mind a most destructive doctrine against the grace of Christ. Coelestius, [Col. 1083C] who first openly proclaimed the heresy in Africa, was condemned at Carthage in the year 412. Pelagius, first attacked in writing by Saint Jerome and afterward by Augustine, was finally deprived of ecclesiastical communion, together with Coelestius, by Innocent I, the holy pope, in January 417. In the same year, 418, Zosimus, Innocent’s successor in the pontificate, condemned him, and the emperor Honorius struck him with his edict. The African bishops, having received Zosimus’s decree—in a plenary synod, as Prosper writes, of 213 bishops assembled at Carthage—formulated eight canons against the Pelagian heresy. These are commonly, but mistakenly, attributed to the second synod of Milevis in Numidia. MIRAEUS.]

PELAGIUS, the arch-heretic, before he was exposed as a heretic, wrote for devout men [Note: [Col. 1083C] Some copies read *useful*.] three necessary books *On the Faith of the Trinity*; and, for practical conduct, one book of *Eulogies*—that is, selected or choice sayings—from the divine Scriptures, marked out by an index of chapters [Note: [Col. 1083C] He is referring to the three books of *Testimonies* of Saint Cyprian the martyr addressed to Quirinus.] in the manner of Saint Cyprian the martyr. After he had been publicly declared a heretic, he wrote works favorable to his heresy.

## CHAPTER XLIII

[Note: [Col. 1083D] Saint Innocent, the first pope of that name, who is entered in the Roman Martyrology under 28 July, was the first of the pontiffs to deprive Pelagius and his companion Coelestius of ecclesiastical communion, in the year 417. Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, condemned them in 418. The letters of both pontiffs are extant in the volumes of the Councils and elsewhere. Baronius arranged the deeds of Innocent by year and defended him against the calumnies of the pagan writer Zosimus, who was extremely hostile to Christians. MIRAEUS.]

INNOCENT, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree issued against the Pelagians by the Western and Eastern Churches [Note: [Col. 1083D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “issued against Pelagius, after whom his successor…”], which afterward his successor, Pope Zosimus, [Note: [Col. 1083D] Suffridus Petri reads *in Latin*.] promulgated more widely.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 1083D] We said in the preceding chapter that this Coelestius, together with his teacher Pelagius, was condemned by the pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus. MIRAEUS.]

COELESTIUS, before he fell into the Pelagian doctrine, indeed while still a young man, wrote to his parents [Col. 1084A] three letters on the monastery, in the form of short books, necessary for all who desire God. [Note: [Col. 1084B] The Corbie manuscript omits what follows and has these words in its place: “Afterward, when he had been publicly declared a heretic, he was condemned by Pope Zosimus.”] His moral discourse in them contains nothing of the vice later revealed, but was wholly directed toward encouraging virtue.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Note: [Col. 1084B] Julian, son and successor of Memorius, bishop of Capua, foolishly undertook the defense of the Pelagian heresy, which had been condemned and nearly overthrown by the pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus. Driven from his see because of this heresy, he afterward entered into a great contest with Saint Augustine. He was a man quick of tongue, but insolent and rash. MIRAEUS.]

JULIAN, bishop [Note: [Col. 1084C] Sigebert’s manuscript reads *of Campania*. This reading is supported by Bede’s preface to his book on the *Song of Songs*, where he mentions Julian of Celan in Campania. The Corbie manuscript contains no mention of an episcopate, but merely reads: “Julian, a man keen in intellect.” In place of *Celanensis* in Bede, some, following Marius Mercator, read *Eclanensis*. See what the Benedictines noted in the preface to part II of volume X of Saint Augustine.] of Capua, a man of keen intellect, learned in the divine Scriptures and schooled in Greek and Latin, was distinguished among the teachers of the Church before he revealed Pelagius’s impiety in himself. But afterward, when he attempted to defend Pelagius’s heresy, he wrote four books against Augustine, its opponent, and then seven more books. There is also a book [Note: [Col. 1084C] The same copy reads *of the dispute*. This does not seem to have been a work different from the preceding one. See Garnerius on Mercator, volume I, p. 387.] of the dispute between the two men, each defending his own side. This Julian, during a time of famine and hardship, distributed all his possessions in alms to the needy and, under the appearance of compassion, attracted many—especially nobles and religious persons—to join his heresy. He died while Valentinian and his son Constantine were reigning.

## CHAPTER XLVI

[Note: [Col. 1084C] Lucian, a presbyter of Jerusalem, described in Greek the revelation made to him concerning the body of Saint Stephen, the proto-martyr. Avitus, a Spanish presbyter, whom Gennadius praises in the following chapter—different from Alcimus Avitus, a Gaul by nation—translated it into Latin. It is extant in the appendix to volume X of Saint Augustine’s works. Besides Gennadius, Bede, Usuardus, and others also mention this work. Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in Africa, whom Sigebert will praise below in chapter 15, and Severus of Balcaris, bishop of an island, whose work Baronius found in the Vatican Library and published under the year 418 in his *Annals*, wrote about the miracles of Saint Stephen’s relics at almost the same time. MIRAEUS.]

LUCIAN, a presbyter, a holy man to whom God revealed, in the time of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, the place of the tomb and [Note: [Col. 1084D] The Corbie manuscript reads *the relics*.] relics of the body of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, wrote the Revelation itself, [Note: [Col. 1084D] The same source reads *to all the persons of the Church*. This account of the revelation of the relics of Saint Stephen, the proto-martyr, by Lucian, presbyter of Jerusalem, begins: “To the most holy persons in every city and country” (*Τοῖς κατὰ πᾶσαν πόλιν καὶ χώραν ἁγιωτάτοις*). It is extant in Latin in Baronius under the year 415, no. 3 and following, and in Surius under 2 August, as well as in the appendix to volume VII of Augustine’s works in the Benedictine edition, from the translation of Avitus, a Spanish presbyter. Gennadius also mentions the relics of Saint Stephen discovered at that time above, in chapter 39, in the entry on Orosius.] in Greek, for the persons of all the Churches.

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 1085A] Concerning Avitus and other Spanish writers of this age, Mariana writes as follows in Book IV, chapter 20: “Pontius Paulinus, a native of Bordeaux, spent time in Nearer Spain, together with his wife Tarasia. Having become a presbyter at Barcelona, he was attached to the ministry of no Church, an example both new and almost unique. From there he advanced to the episcopate of Nola after he had migrated from Spain to Italy. Abundius Avitus, a presbyter born at Tarragona, gave Lucian’s book on the discovery of Saint Stephen’s body a Latin form. Licinius Baeticus, celebrated in memory for his friendship with Jerome and his exceptional generosity toward the poor of Jerusalem. Desiderius and Riparius, Spanish presbyters, attacked in writing Vigilantius, a presbyter of Barcelona born at Pamplona, who assailed the honor and worship of the saints reigning with Christ in heaven.” Thus Mariana. MIRAEUS.]

AVITUS, a presbyter, a Spaniard by birth, translated into Latin the writing of the presbyter Lucian mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1085B] Mentioned in the preceding chapter.] and, adding his own letter, [Note: [Col. 1085B] Avitus’s letter to Falconius, bishop of Braga, prefixed to Lucian’s account: “Therefore I sent you, through my holy son and fellow presbyter Orosius, the relics…”] published it for the Westerners.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 1085B] Saint Paulinus, an Aquitanian by country and Roman by origin and lineage, a man most distinguished for the nobility of his family and his learning, and wonderfully celebrated by the writings and friendship of Ambrose, Martin, Jerome, Augustine, Sulpicius Severus, and others, passed to the better life in the year 431. Having become bishop of Nola in Campania, he offered to all ages a memorable example of charity and self-contempt when he gave himself into slavery to the Vandals in order to ransom the son of a certain widow, as Gregory the Great relates in Book III, chapter 1 of the *Dialogues*. We possess, in proportion to the greatness of the man, only modest monuments of Paulinus’s learning, because many were destroyed by the injury of time. All his works that could be found were published at Antwerp by the Plantin press in 1622, in octavo, with notes by the Jesuit theologians Fronto Ducaeus and Heribert Rosweyde. [A more recent and fuller edition was produced by John Baptist Le Brun, Paris, 1685, in quarto. See also Peter Francis Chifflet’s *Paulinus Illustrated*, Dijon, 1622, in quarto, and the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori’s *Latin Anecdotes*, volume I, Milan, 1697, in quarto. Moreover, Meropius Pontius Anicius Paulinus—this was his full name—was born in Aquitaine, or at Bordeaux, as the presbyter Uranius relates in Surius, volume III, who committed to writing a summary of his life, or rather his death; or at Ebromagus, which Paulinus himself calls his homeland. This was a paternal town not far from Bordeaux, on the bank of the Garonne River. There is now a village named Embrau in that place, below Bourg and below Blaye, as Elias Vinetus writes. He was born around the year of Christ 353. As he grew to adulthood, he advanced under Decius Magnus Ausonius, his teacher at Bordeaux, so far that in oratory and poetry he either equaled or even surpassed his teacher’s renown. He then happily entered marriage, and Terasia, a wealthy, wise, and deeply religious wife, was given to Paulinus. While they were living in Spain, after long prayers they finally obtained a male child, but he was not viable. Thus, carried away on the eighth day after his birth at Complutum, he made a way for his parents to seek and find a posterity of merits that would not be subject to decay. As devotion gradually entered his mind, Paulinus was baptized at Bordeaux by Saint Delphinus, the bishop, and two years later was ordained a priest at Barcelona by Bishop Lampius; from there he finally moved to Nola. Terasia, as Hydatius puts it in his *Chronicle*, became his sister rather than his wife. Venantius Fortunatus says the same of Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus and wife of Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of the Arverni: before his priesthood she was his wife, afterward his sister, in accordance with the prescriptions of the sacred canons and the perpetual custom of the ancient Church. In that custom, those who were taken from marriage into the priesthood, separated from their wives’ bed, afterward lived with them no otherwise than with sisters. [Col. 1086B] After God, the first glory of Paulinus’s conversion seems to have been owed to Saint Felix the confessor, or rather martyr. Great and plainly evident miracles were taking place at that time through his sacred bodily relics. For this reason people flocked from everywhere to Nola, to his tomb. Paulinus also went there, all the more readily because he owned estates in the vicinity from his father; indeed, weary from the turmoil of the world, he resolved to rest in that retreat as in a harbor. Each year, therefore, he was accustomed to honor the feast of Saint Felix, celebrated on 14 January, with a new poem for the feast, as though paying an annual tribute. Of these poems only ten had come down to our age, and there was no mention that Paulinus had composed more, until Dungal’s short work was published separately at Paris in 1608 and afterward in 1610 in the *Library of the Fathers*. In it he counts fifteen and produces no small fragments from those that do not survive. Dungal, moreover, lived under Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, to whom he dedicated his book in defense of the veneration of sacred images, against Claudius of Turin. [Muratori, praised above, was the first to publish Natal Poems 11, 12, and 13 from the Milan manuscript and to illuminate them with learned notes in volume I of his *Latin Anecdotes*.] MIRAEUS.]

PAULINUS, bishop of Nola in Campania, composed brief poems, though many of them, and also [Note: [Col. 1086C] Gennadius would have put it more suitably: “He composed an epitaph for the boy Celsus.” It is extant as number 15 among Paulinus’s poems, under the title *A Panegyric on the Death of the Boy Celsus, Addressed to His Parents Pneumatius and Fidelis*. MIRAEUS.] a consolatory short work in the form of an epitaph for a certain Celsus, on the death of a Christian and baptized infant, fortified by Christian hope; and he wrote several letters to Severus. [Note: [Col. 1086C] Saint Paulinus wrote many letters to Sulpicius Severus, mentioned above by Gennadius in chapter 19, which are found among his works.] He also wrote, before becoming a bishop, a prose panegyric [Col. 1087A] to the emperor Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1087B] This panegyric on Theodosius the Great, victor over Eugenius and Arbogastes in 394, like many other works mentioned here by Gennadius, is unfortunately lost. On 17 January 395 the senior emperor Theodosius died. Since pagan writers bitterly assailed him, Paulinus, at the prompting of Endelechius, a man most closely bound to him in friendship, undertook to defend and celebrate him according to his merits. His chief purpose was to proclaim in Theodosius not so much an emperor as a servant of Christ: powerful not through the arrogance of dominion but through the humility of service, and a ruler not by his kingdom but by faith, as Paulinus himself says in Letter 9. Paulinus sent that encomium to Saint Jerome in Palestine through Vigilantius, then a monk commendable in appearance but afterward a most foul heretic. In replying to that letter Jerome says: “I gladly read your book, which you sent, wisely and elegantly composed in praise of the emperor Theodosius; and I was especially pleased by its division. While in its earlier parts you surpass others, in the next-to-last you surpass yourself.” Cassiodorus also mentions the same panegyric in Book I, chapter 21, of the *Sacred Readings*, but everyone laments its loss. As for the holy Endelechius Severus, at whose urging Paulinus wrote this panegyric, he was an outstanding orator and poet, and a Christian. His short poem *On the Deaths of Cattle* survives. Moreover, besides Paulinus of Nola, several others known also from their writings lived in the age of Sidonius: Paulinus, bishop of Béziers, whose letter Hydatius mentions around the year of Christ 420; Paulinus, author of the *Eucharistic Poem*, whom from his verses I have inferred to have been a grandson of Ausonius through his son Hesperius; and finally Paulinus, author of six books on the *Life of Saint Martin*, likewise written in verse. Since the ancient Vatican and Corbie copies call him Paulinus Petricordius, it may perhaps be supposed that he was a Petrocorian—that is, from Vesunna. Thus, in substance, Sirmond in his learned notes on Sidonius. MIRAEUS.] on the victory over the tyrants, chiefly because he had conquered more by faith and prayer than by arms. He also composed a Sacramentary and a Hymnary. [Note: [Col. 1087C] The Corbie manuscript reads *and of hymns*.] He sent many letters to his sister on contempt of the world. He also published [Note: [Col. 1087C] The words from *He also published* through *treatises* are absent from most printed editions and have been restored from the Corbie manuscript.] treatises on various subjects, discussed in various ways. The chief of all his short works, however, is the book *On Penance* and *On the General Praise of All the Martyrs*. He flourished in the time of Honorius [Note: [Col. 1087C] The same source reads *of Theodosius and Valentinian*.] and Valentinian, distinguished not only for learning and holiness of life but also for power [Note: [Col. 1087C] The same source reads *authority*.] against demons.

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Note: [Col. 1087C] This Eutropius, a disciple of Saint Augustine, is incorrectly confused by Ptolemy, Volaterranus, Gesner, Eisengrenius, Zwinger, and Possevinus with the Eutropius who wrote a brief history of Roman affairs from the founding of the City to the emperor Flavius Valens and dedicated it to him. For the author of the brief history was not younger than Augustine. MIRAEUS.]

EUTROPIUS, a presbyter, wrote two letters to his two sisters, handmaids of Christ, who, because of their devotion to chastity and love of religion, [Note: [Col. 1087C] The same source reads *disinherited*.] were disinherited by their parents. They were consolatory in the form of books, written in elegant and clear language, and supported not only by reasoning but also by testimonies from Scripture.

## CHAPTER L

[Note: [Col. 1087C] This man is different from Evagrius of Pontus, whom Gennadius mentioned above in chapter 11. See what we said above in the notes on chapter 125 of Jerome concerning the various Evagriuses. MIRAEUS.]

EVAGRIUS, another man, wrote the *Dispute between Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian*, which is known to almost everyone.

## CHAPTER LI

VIGILIUS, a deacon, compiled from the tradition of the Fathers a Rule for Monks, [Note: [Col. 1087D] It does not survive, any more than the writings of Eugenius and Eutropius mentioned in the preceding chapters.] which is read in the assembly at the monastery for the advancement of the brothers and which contains, in brief and clear language, the discipline of the entire monastic profession.

## CHAPTER LII

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Atticus’s book addressed to Flaccilla and Pulcheria has also perished. Trithemius likewise discusses the deacon Vigilius and Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. MIRAEUS.]

ATTICUS, bishop of Constantinople, wrote for the empresses, the daughters of the emperor Arcadius, a highly distinguished book *On Faith and Virginity*, in which, anticipating the Nestorian doctrine, he attacks it.

## CHAPTER LIII

[Col. 1088B]

[Note: [Col. 1087D] Corb., Nestor. — Nestorius, an Antiochene monk, was appointed to replace Sisinnius, bishop of Constantinople. Shortly afterward he published a new heresy, asserting that Christ consisted of two persons and that Blessed Mary was not the Mother of God but only the mother of Christ as man. Among others, Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, hastened to extinguish this conflagration, encouraged by letters from Pope Celestine. Accordingly, a synod was convened at Ephesus in 431; Pope Celestine’s legates attended it, and more than two hundred bishops were present. The Eastern bishops, who had been summoned together with John, bishop of Antioch, arrived late. Thus, although the synod had begun on 22 June and Nestorius had been deposed from his see, John arrived with his party five days later; among them Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, was prominent. Having hastily convened a small assembly, they annulled the legitimate acts of the synod and condemned Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus. When the emperor was inflamed against them by slander, Cyril himself was thrown into prison. At last the emperor was informed of everything by a trustworthy man who, traveling to Constantinople in the guise of a beggar, carried the Catholics’ letters concealed in a reed; and when the monks pressed the matter and Pulcheria, Theodosius’ sister, exerted herself, the acts of the synod were approved by imperial authority. Nestorius was expelled, and Maximian was appointed in his place. After the synod ended—which, Prosper reports, also condemned the Pelagian heresy—hostility between John and Cyril, and between the bishops attached to each side, continued for some time. It was settled through Theodosius’ efforts and the intervention of Simeon Stylites. Nestorius was first exiled to his former monastery of Saint Euprepius, which was in Antioch; then, because he was infecting many with his contagion, he was sent away to the Oasis in 436. There, later, with his tongue putrefying, he met a miserable end. His books were consigned to the flames by an edict of the Emperor Theodosius. The Gallican monk Leporius, to be mentioned by Gennadius below in chapter 59, had previously foreshadowed the Nestorian heresy. Later, after being dissuaded by Augustine, he sought pardon for his error in 419 or 420 by submitting a written statement.

Thus far concerning Nestorius. It will not be out of place to append a few remarks, drawn from the manuscript commentaries or “reports,” as they are called, of Leonardo Abel, bishop of Sidon, who was sent to the East as apostolic nuncio by Gregory XIII in 1583, concerning the Nestorians who still live in Asia today.

The nation of the Nestorians is now divided under two patriarchs. Of these, some are called by us Latins Chaldeans, Assyrians, or Easterners; the others are simply called Nestorians. The patriarchs of the Eastern Assyrians—Simon Sulaca, Abdisu, and Donha Simon—were confirmed by the Apostolic See. Although they held the title of the church of Musal, or Mosul, in Babylonia, neither they nor their successors have so far been able to possess it, because of another opposing patriarch who occupied and retained it. Consequently, those patriarchs have been compelled to reside in different places: now at Caramit, now at Seeri, now at Zeinalbach, on the borders of Persia.

Simon Sulaca, a monk of the Order of Saint Basil, rendered obedience to the Holy Roman Church during the pontificate of Pope Julius III. After being confirmed by him and returning home, he ordained certain archbishops and bishops and ordered the Nestorian invocation—which at that time was customarily performed by a deacon—to be rejected. But at last he was captured by the deceit of his opposing patriarch and killed by the Turks. Andreas Masius of Brussels translated Sulaca’s profession of faith from Syriac into Latin and published it in Plantin’s press.

Sulaca was succeeded by Abdesu, or Abdisu, of the same Order of Saint Basil. He came to the Council of Trent and rendered obedience in Rome to Pius IV; after returning home, he ordained a great many priests, bishops, and archbishops. After his death a few years later, he was succeeded by Aatalla, of the same order, who did not receive apostolic confirmation because he did not request it in Rome. After Aatalla’s death, Donha Simon, archbishop of Celu, was appointed in his place. During the pontificate of Gregory XIII, he sent his procurator, Hermete Helias, archbishop, to Rome. In the name of his patriarch, Helias rendered the required obedience to the Apostolic See and, having obtained confirmation together with the patriarchal pallium, departed from the city in 1582.

Among these Eastern Chaldeans, the richest and most powerful reside in the city of Amit. Together with their prelates, they strive above all to preserve and increase obedience to the Roman See. The more powerful and wealthier members of the Nestorian nation, subject to the opposing patriarch, inhabit the fortress of Musalet, in Gezire in Babylonia. Their patriarch has a great number of peoples under him and usually resides in the patriarchal monastery of Saint Hermetes, near the same city of Musal in Babylonia, formerly called Assur. Andreas Masius thinks that Musal was formerly called Seleucia of the Parthians, on the Tigris River.

The principal heresies and errors found in our own times among the schismatic Nestorians are these. First, they believe that human nature in Christ our Lord is not perfect without a human person; consequently, they confess that there are two persons in Christ, although they do not deny that Christ, perfect God from the first moment of his conception, became man. Nor do they call the Blessed Virgin the Mother of God. For they say that the word “God” contains within itself the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and consequently that she would have to be called the mother of all three divine persons. Nevertheless, they affirm that she is the mother of God the Word and of the Son. They venerate Nestorius and condemn Cyril of Alexandria. They do not accept the First Council of Ephesus, much less the other universal councils held afterward. They also contract marriages within prohibited degrees without their patriarch’s permission. They do not create their patriarch by election, but by resignation, from parent to parent. Nor do they confess their sins to a priest privately. They administer the sacrament of the Eucharist into their own hands to both clergy and laity, and they have no scruple about conferring orders simoniacally.

We have taken this almost word for word from Leonardo Abel and inserted it in our *Information concerning the Bishoprics of the Christian World*, published by Plantin in 1613, book I, chapter 16. Jacobus Vitriacus also discusses the Nestorians in chapter 77 of his *Eastern History*, as does Thomas of Brabant in his book *On the Conversion of All Nations. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER LIV

[Note: [Col. 1090B] Saint Celestine I, pope—whose name is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 6 April—ordered the ecumenical Council of Ephesus to be held against Nestorius in 431. He finally died on 11 April 432 and was succeeded by Xystus, who, while still a presbyter, had vigorously opposed the Pelagian heresy. The letters of Pope Celestine survive in the volumes of the Councils. Certain statements concerning the grace of God and free choice of the will are customarily appended to these letters. Although these statements are not Celestine’s, they were nevertheless attributed to Celestine by ancient writers, whoever their author may have been: by Peter the Deacon in his book *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ* addressed to Fulgentius; by Florus the Master in his book against John Scotus, which circulates under the name of the Church of Lyon; by Hincmar of Reims against Gottschalk; and by Gresconius, Ivo, and others, as Sirmond noted in his annotations on volume I of the Councils of Gaul. ## CHAPTER LVI

[Note: [Col. 1091A] Fastidius is called bishop of London by John Pitseus, a theological doctor and dean of Liverdun in Lorraine, in his book *On the Illustrious Writers of Britain*. Besides Gennadius, Honorius of Autun and Trithemius also mention Fastidius in their catalogues and state that he flourished in the year 420. Nothing from Fastidius’ works has so far been published.

In the same cited book, Pitseus reports the following concerning Bacharius, or Bachiarius, whom Gennadius mentioned above in chapter 24:

“Bacharius Maccaeus, a Briton by nation and a disciple of Saint Patrick, seeing his homeland afflicted by continual calamities, undertook very long sacred pilgrimages in order to implore divine assistance. But there were not lacking detractors who accused him of fickleness and inconstancy. Therefore he cleared himself in writing and wrote to Leo I, Roman pontiff—as I infer from Gennadius, Honorius, John Capgrave, and others—an apology for his pilgrimage; also a work *On the Restoration of Those Who Have Fallen*, or *On the Fruits of Repentance*, addressed to Januarius; and another *On Persevering Faith*, together with other works. He was famous as an old man in the year 460.”

Such, approximately, is Pitseus’ account. If conjecture is permissible, Bacharius seems to have withdrawn from Britain because of the invasions of various peoples, by which it was then especially afflicted. For around the year 441 the Angles, Saxons, Jutes, and Frisians—peoples of Germany mentioned by Procopius, Bede, and other ancient writers—crossed into Britain. Tiro Prosper, published by Pithoeus and Canisius in volume I at the eighteenth year of Theodosius, writes:

“Britain, torn up to this time by various disasters and misfortunes, is reduced under the dominion of the Saxons.”

Nor had the Scots perhaps arrived much earlier from their Ireland. Their name, like that of the Picts, was unknown in the age of Julius Caesar. Certainly the first writer whose works now survive to name the Scots and Picts is the panegyrist of the Emperor Constantius. The Picts seem originally to have been designated by the common epithet of the Britons and eventually to have been called by the Romans by their proper name as the peoples of the northern parts of the island—peoples who retained the ancient Britons’ marks, as Tertullian calls them, and the designs impressed on their bodies with iron. Herodian also mentions this custom in book III.

I know that Gildas and other writers of British history think differently about the Picts. But anyone who remembers that the name “Picts” arose in the time of Diocletian, and that the Caledonians and Vecturiones, ancient inhabitants of that region, are counted among the Picts by the same panegyrist and by Ammianus Marcellinus, will not reject this conjecture. Thus the Pictish people appear ancient, but the name seems new and imposed.

Finally, Claudian, in *On the Gothic War*, plainly agrees with us that the Picts were so called because of their body-painting:

> A legion came, drawn up before the farthest Britons,  
> which turns its back upon the savage Scot and scans the bloodless figures marked by iron,  
> while the Pict is dying.

Sirmond gives much the same account in his notes on Sidonius’ panegyric of Avitus. Ammianus, book XXVII, may also be consulted concerning the Scots and Picts. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER LVII

[Note: [Col. 1092B] Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria in Egypt, began to occupy the see after his uncle Theophilus, in the consulships of Honorius IX and Theodosius V—that is, in the year 412—as Socrates reports in book VII, chapter 7. He presided at the First Council of Ephesus, in the name of Pope Celestine, mentioned above in chapter 54, and condemned Nestorius the arch-heresiarch, first by books that he published and then also by his own authority. At last, as an old man, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year 444, on 9 June. On that day the Greeks celebrate his memory in the *Menologion*, while the Latins celebrate it on 28 January, according to the Roman calendars.

Many eulogies of this most holy man survive among ancient writers. I would nevertheless warn the reader not to trust Socrates in book VII, chapters 13–15, where he speaks abusively of Cyril and disparages him. For, as a member of the Novatian sect, Socrates was less fair toward Cyril because, immediately upon becoming bishop, Cyril declared fierce war on the Novatians, who had until that day been tolerated, as Socrates himself complains in book VII, chapter 7.

All the works of this Cyril that could be found, after various editions, were published in seven Greek-Latin volumes at Paris in 1638. Bellarmine, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and others have explained which of these works are genuinely his. *Moral Apologies* attributed to this Cyril—or to another Cyril?—were printed at Vienna in Austria in 1631. That little book had earlier been published at Paris by Jean Petit under the title *The Mirror of Wisdom*. Jerome treats Saint Cyril of Jerusalem in chapter 112 of his catalogue. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER LIX

[Note: [Col. 1092D] The presbyter Leporius, around the year 420, wrote the *Book of Correction*, or *Book of Satisfaction*, which contains a confession of the Catholic faith concerning the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, together with a repudiation of his former error. Jacobus Sirmond was the first to publish this book in full at Paris in 1630, together with short dogmatic works by Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, Victorinus the African, and others.

Besides Gennadius, Cassian and Facundus of Hermiane mention where and for what reason it was written.
