## CHAPTER LXI

[Note: [Col. 1093C] John Cassian, a disciple of Saint John Chrysostom and a presbyter of Massilia, wrote in Latin twelve books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, twenty-four *Conferences of the Fathers*, and seven books *On the Incarnation of Christ*. All these works were published with notes and censures by Henri de Cuyck at Antwerp; by Pietro Chacon at Rome and Lyon; and also by Alard Gazaeus at Arras in 1628. I say “with censures” because Cassian must be read cautiously in many places, as those same commentators, Bellarmine in his catalogue, and others teach. See also the prolegomena that I prefixed to Gennadius.

Of the *Conferences*, the final seven were written to monks who were on the Stoechades Islands; an equal number were addressed to Honoratus of Arles and Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. One of these men was the founder and the other an alumnus of the monastery of Lérins. The Stoechades lie off the coast of Massilia; Lérins, or Lirinus, and Lerus, likewise islands, lie opposite Antibes. In former times they were all filled with monasteries and monks’ cells, as Cassian’s *Conferences* abundantly testify.

It is often debated by the curious whether Cassian should be numbered among the saints. In Gazaeus’ latest edition at Arras, an apologetic defense of John Cassian’s sanctity is prefixed. From it I extract the following:

“Certain members of the Society of Jesus, men highly commended for virtue, prudence, and learning and therefore entirely worthy of belief, went to Massilia and discovered that the abbey over which Cassian presided is now called the Monastery of Saint Victor, built near Massilia. They found that Cassian’s head is preserved there intact in a reliquary decorated with gilded silver and gems; that his body lies buried in the same place in a crypt among the sacred relics of many other saints, in a marble tomb supported by four columns; and that 23 July is dedicated to his festive commemoration, with a solemn octave of nine lessons, its own office, and its own Mass. These things appear in the supplement of the saints of the Victorian monastery, published at Lyon in 1600.

In the office itself it is said: ‘Today Cassian was carried by angels into heaven.’ The substance of the lessons read at Matins is as follows: Saint Cassian, by birth a Scythian, was born at Athens, where he also founded a certain fellowship. From boyhood he was a Bethlehemite coenobite, and later established another fellowship in Bethlehem itself. Then he withdrew into the cave of the three elders, Chaeremon, Nestor, and Joseph. After traveling through Egypt, he arrived at Constantinople with the abbot Germanus and was ordained deacon by Saint John Chrysostom; at Rome he was ordained to the priesthood.

At length, after accomplishing many distinguished deeds in the East, he went to Massilia. There, having founded a celebrated monastery, he became the instructor of five thousand monks; in another sacred monastery he governed a large flock of holy virgins. After writing the twelve books of the *Institutes*, the *Conferences of the Fathers*, and a treatise *On the Incarnation*, he died peacefully in the ninety-seventh year of his age, famous for many virtues, under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, on 23 July.

Nor should the reader wonder if, after twelve centuries, Cassian’s sanctity—unknown to most people—has only now emerged from darkness into the light. Divine providence has permitted the same thing in the case of other saints, whose judgments are inscrutable. Certainly many revered Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, who died in schism, and among them, as the foremost of all, Baronius, the compiler of the *Annals*, in his account of the year 368.

Antiochus Bronchus of Cagliari, writing in chapter II of the *Apocalypse*, disputation 11, question 2, vigorously attempts to prove that Lucifer repented and died in the holy peace of the Church. These are the words of Cornelius à Lapide, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, on chapter III of the *Apocalypse*. He argues this especially from the fact that Saints Jerome, Hilary, and other Fathers call Lucifer blessed and celebrate him with great praises. He also argues that the people of Sardinia and Vercelli publicly honor and invoke him as a saint and have erected a basilica in his honor near Cagliari, which still exists.

Again, when Baronius revised what he had written in volume VI under the year 490 concerning Faustus, bishop of Riez, he speaks approximately as follows in volume X, in the additions under the year 490:

‘As we have learned, the Church of Riez in Gaul, where Faustus served as bishop, has always honored him as a saint, celebrating his feast on 17 January. A basilica was anciently erected there in his memory and marked with his name; it is still frequented by the faithful for his worship, and so forth. Let Faustus therefore retain undiminished what is his. Let him suffer no prejudice from our writings, nor let private judgment be allowed to overthrow antiquity by novelty.’

So much, approximately, from the defense mentioned above. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER LXIII
[Note: [Col. 1095C] Saint Eucherius, formerly a monk of Lérins and later bishop of Lyon, wrote, as he himself testifies, in the year 1085 from the foundation of the City (that is, in the year of Christ 432), while he was still a monk, a hortatory letter to his kinsman Valerian, On Contempt of the World. Moretus published it in 1620 from the Plantinian press, with brief notes by Heribert Rosweyde. In the latest Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, however, this little book is incorrectly entitled *On the Solitary Life*. For there exists another little work by the same Saint Eucherius, addressed not to Valerian but to Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, under the title *On the Solitary Life*, or *On the Praise of the Desert*, likewise published from Moretus’s press in 1621 and collated with manuscripts by Nicolas Faber of Paris. Concerning it Isidore says the following in chapter 15 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Blessed Eucherius, bishop of Gaul, elegant in his thoughts and adorned in his words, composed for Hilary, bishop of Arles, who was seeking the desert wastes, one little work on the praise of that same desert, written with great brilliance and in a sweet style.” Eucherius wrote this little book at the time when Hilary, having left the bishopric of Arles, returned to Lérins, seized by his former love of the desert, as may be gathered from Hilary’s own homily on Saint Honoratus. Moreover, by his lawful wife before the priesthood, named Galla, Eucherius had two sons, Salonius and Veranus, and as many daughters, Consortia and Tullia. From Salvian of Marseille’s letter to Eucherius it is clear that Eucherius’s sons, while their father was still alive, began to become heads of churches and bishops. Among the letters of Pope Leo the Great there is a letter written to Leo by the bishops Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus. The *Bibliotheca Patrum* also contains Salonius’s commentaries on Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Concerning Eucherius’s two daughters and his advancement to the episcopate, Ado says the following in his *Martyrology*, on 16 November: “The feast of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, a man of admirable faith, life, [Col. 1096C] and teaching. He was converted from the most noble senatorial order to the religious life and habit, and for a long time, in his own estate beside the river Durance, voluntarily shut within the enclosure of a cave, he served Christ, devoting himself to fasts and prayers. When the bishop of Lyon died, the clergy and people, with equal purpose and unanimous agreement, chose him as their priest and solemnly placed him in the episcopal chair. His wife Galla, living in holiness and serving God, entered his cave and spent all the remaining time of her life there in the practice of religion. Their two daughters, one named Consortia and the other Tullia, became renowned for the glory of their virginity and miracles.” Thus far Ado. As for Saint Eucherius’s other works, Claudianus Mamertus, presbyter of the church of Vienne and brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, testifies in his books *On the Condition of the Soul* that Eucherius wrote extremely eloquent sermons or homilies; perhaps these are the works circulated under the name of Eusebius of Emesa. Various writings of Saint Eucherius are found in volume V of the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, as well as in the *Lérins Chronicle* and elsewhere; Bellarmine explains his opinion of them in his own book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. John Molanus, in his manuscript *Sacred Library*, notes that the Roman edition of Saint Eucherius’s works, published by Galesinius in 1564, contains many spurious writings. Peter Steuartius, doctor of theology, published at Ingolstadt in 1617, with notes, the history of the passion of Saint Maurice and his Theban companions, supposedly written by Saint Eucherius to Silvius, bishop. Furthermore, our Saint Eucherius subscribed to the First Council of Orange in the year 441. There was another Eucherius who attended the Second Synod of Orange in 529; Cyprian mentions this later Eucherius in his *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles*, as printed by Surius. MIRAEUS.]

EUCHERIUS, presbyter of the Church of Lyon [Note: [Col. 1096D] The Corbie manuscript has “pontiff”; the editions of Gennadius in Jerome’s works have “bishop.”], [Col. 1097A] wrote to Valerian, his kinsman, one letter, *On Contempt of the World and Secular Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 1097B] The manuscript Codex Martinianus, according to Suffridus Petri, reads “to Uranus.”], in a scholastic and reasoned style [Note: [Col. 1097B] The Corbie manuscript has “in a rational and eloquent style.”]. He also explained, for the benefit of his sons Salonius and Veranus, later bishops [Note: [Col. 1097B] As above, chapter 60, addressed to his son Etherius.], the more obscure passages of the sacred Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 1097B] Baronius, in his account of the year 433, judges the statement of this Gennadius as follows: “This is what Gennadius says, of the same sort as Cassian: lest he should have to say that, after refuting errors, Eucherius had purged Cassian by abridging his works, he pretended that he had merely curtailed an extensive discourse.” Thus Baronius. But because the fourth book *On the Lives of the Fathers* in the Plantinian edition has been assembled from Severus Sulpicius and John Cassian—for it consists only of certain excerpts from their books, almost in the same words—learned men dispute who assembled it. Some think it was Eucherius of Lyon; others, Victor of Martyritana, a bishop in Africa, whom Cassiodorus mentions in *Divine Institutes*, chapter 29. On this subject consult Rosweyde, *Prolegomenon* 6 to the *Lives of the Fathers*. MIRAEUS.]

He also brought together into one volume certain little works of Cassian [Note: [Col. 1097C] The Corbie manuscript has “of Saint Cassian.”], stretched out in a diffuse style [Note: [Col. 1097C] The same manuscript has “holding to an expansive eloquence.”], reducing them to a narrow compass of expression, and other things necessary both for ecclesiastical and monastic studies [Note: [Col. 1097C] The word “studies” is absent from the Corbie manuscript.]. [Note: [Col. 1097C] The final words, beginning with “he died,” are absent from the same manuscript; in their place it has: “He flourished in the age of blessed Caesarius.”] He died under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

## CHAPTER LXIV

[Note: [Col. 1097C] Saint Vincent of Lérins, a monk in Gaul, wrote his golden little book against heresies three years after the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus—that is, in the year of Christ 434—as he himself testifies. John Costerius and Bartholomeus Petrus Lintrensis, doctor of theology at Douai, illustrated this little book with brief notes. Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, was Vincent’s brother; he was famous for his embassy to Britain and for the glory he won by making peace among his fellow citizens against Attila. It is established from Sidonius’s letter 1 of book VI and letter 14 of book VIII, as well as from Eucherius of Lyon’s little work *On the Praise of the Desert*, that Lupus had lived on that same island of Lérins, which at that time was a common training ground for those renouncing the world. The letter of Lupus and Saint Euphronius, bishop of Autun, on bigamous clergy and those who had taken wives is found in Sirmond, volume I of the Councils, and in Claudius Robertus’s *Gallia Christiana*. Lérins is a very well-known island in the Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Gaul, opposite Antibes, a town in the second province of Narbonensis; today it bears the name of Saint Honoratus, founder of the monastery of Lérins and later bishop of Arles. Near Lérins lies another island called Lerus, now named after Saint Margaret. MIRAEUS.]

VINCENTIUS, a Gaul by birth [Note: [Col. 1098B] The Corbie manuscript has: “a presbyter at the island of Lérins, a man very well versed in the holy Scriptures and in knowledge of doctrine,” etc.], a presbyter at the monastery on the island of Lérins, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures and sufficiently [Col. 1097B] instructed in knowledge of ecclesiastical doctrines, composed, in a sufficiently polished and clear style, a most powerful disputation for avoiding the company of heretics, which he entitled, under his concealed name [Note: [Col. 1098B] The same manuscript reads “entitled it.” This is the famous *Commonitorium* of Vincent, which, after Costerius and others, was illuminated by the distinguished scholar Stephen Baluzius.], *Peregrinus against the Heretics*. Because he lost, through the theft of certain persons, most of the second book that he had written in notebooks, he reconstructed its original meaning in a few words by way of summary and published it as a single book [Col. 1098A]. He died while Theodosius and Valentinian [Note: [Col. 1098B] The Corbie manuscript has “were reigning.”] were reigning.

## CHAPTER LXV

[Note: [Col. 1098B] Gennadius alone mentions Syagrius. Cave, *History of Literature*, part I, p. 240, presents the subject of the earlier book somewhat more obscurely as follows: “He wrote a little book on the faith against certain heretics who did not wish the persons of the Holy Trinity to be expressed by names indicating mutual relation.” It seems to me that the heretics refuted by Syagrius held that the first person of the Godhead should not be called Father, nor the second Son, lest the unity of the divine nature be shaken; for they maintained that Father and Son could not fail to possess numerically distinct natures. If, therefore, there were in the Godhead a Son who was not the Father, and a Father who was not the Son, it would be necessary to admit two—or even three—divine natures. For they reasoned as follows: “Whoever is a person outside the Father is a nature outside the Father.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

SYAGRIUS wrote *On the Faith, against the Presumptuous Names of the Heretics*, which were used to destroy or alter the names of the Holy Trinity. They said that the Father ought not to be called Father, lest the name “Father” contain an allusion to a son [Note: [Col. 1098C] The Corbie manuscript has “sound,” that is, “resonate.”], but that he should be called unbegotten, unmade, and solitary, so that whatever is a person outside him should be a nature outside him [Note: [Col. 1098C] Miraeus wrongly has “should be outside him in nature.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.]. Syagrius showed that the Father, who is of the same nature, can also be called unbegotten, and that Scripture said that he himself begot the Son as a person, not made him, and brought forth from himself the Holy Spirit as a person, neither begotten nor made him [Note: [Col. 1098C] These words are absent from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]. Under Syagrius’s name I found seven books entitled *On the Faith* [Note: [Col. 1098C] Some copies read “or on the Rules.”] and *On the Rules of Faith*, but because their style differs, I did not believe that all of them were his.

## CHAPTER LXVI

[Note: [Col. 1098D] The Gembloux manuscript has “Isaiah.” I find two Isaacs, Syrians by birth and monks by profession. The elder, mentioned here by Gennadius, died under the emperors Marcian and Leo, that is, around the year 454. Gregory testifies in book III of the *Dialogues* that the other survived until the final period of the Goths. It is uncertain to which of the two belongs the book *On Contempt of the World*, which is found in volume VI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Possevinus attributes it to the elder Isaac, but neither Gennadius nor Trithemius, who enumerate the writings of that Isaac, mentions this book. Thus it may seem no less probable that the book belongs to the younger Isaac. MIRAEUS.]

ISAAC, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, wrote much in the Syriac language over a long period [Note: [Col. 1098D] The Corbie manuscript has “especially against Nestorius and the Eutychians.”], but with particular care against the Nestorians and Eutychians. He also lamented the destruction of Antioch in an elegant poem [Note: [Col. 1098D] The same manuscript has this reading, which seems to me preferable to “in a long poem,” which Suffridus Petri claims to have restored from Honorius in place of a corrupt reading. The Corbie manuscript has *Antiochene city* instead of *Antioch*.], [Col. 1099A] imbuing his hearers with the same sound with which Ephrem the deacon had lamented the fall of Nicomedia [Note: [Col. 1099B] This is how it stands in all copies, and nothing is missing, contrary to the view of Suffridus Petri.]. He died while Leo and [Note: [Col. 1099B] The Sigeberg manuscript has “Marinus”; the Corbie manuscript, “Majorian.”] Marcian were reigning.

## CHAPTER LXVII

[Note: [Col. 1099B] Salvian, a presbyter of Marseille, not a bishop, wrote around the year 440 to Salonius, bishop and son of Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, eight books *On the Providence and Government of God* and on his just and present judgment. In them he chastises the vices of the Christians of his time and vividly portrays the condition and causes of Gaul’s devastation by the barbarians. I say that he wrote under the year 440 of Christ, for he calls the war waged by Litorius against the Goths recent. Among other things, Salvian fiercely attacks circus games and spectacles of that kind, then familiar to the Belgians and other Gauls. He also wrote one book of Letters and four books under the name of Timothy, addressed to the Catholic Church. Peter Pithoeus compared all these works with manuscript copies and published them at Paris in 1579 and 1608. His other works, listed by Gennadius in this chapter, by Ado of Vienne in the *Brief Chronicle*, and by Trithemius, have perished. Salvian is believed to have been born at Cologne Agrippina or nearby, and he lived for a long time at Trier. He witnessed with his own eyes the destruction of that city, devastated by the Franks, Burgundians, and other barbarians, around the year 433; afterward he moved to Marseille, when the seat of imperial government was transferred from Trier to Arles. If you wish to know more about these matters, read our *Chronicle* in the account of the year mentioned and those that follow. MIRAEUS.]

SALVIANUS, a presbyter of the Church of Marseille [Note: [Col. 1099D] The Corbie manuscript has “a presbyter at Marseille.”], instructed in human and divine literature and, to speak without envy, the teacher of bishops [Note: [Col. 1099D] The same manuscript has “the teacher of the holy bishops Salonius and Veranus.” The Martinian manuscript has the same, according to Suffridus Petri.], wrote much in a scholastic and clear style. Among his works I have read these: three books *On the Good of Virginity*, addressed to the presbyter Marcellus [Note: [Col. 1099D] “Presbyter” is absent from the Corbie manuscript]; four books *Against Avarice*; five books *On the Present Judgment*; one book addressed to Bishop Salonius, concerning satisfaction for the merit of those things [Note: [Col. 1099D] The same manuscript has “for satisfying their reward.”]; one book, an exposition of the final part of Ecclesiastes, addressed to Claudius, bishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 1099D] Some copies read “to Claudianus,” below, chapter 83. The Corbie manuscript also has “Claudius.”]; and one book of Letters [Note: [Col. 1099D] The words “one book” are absent from the Corbie manuscript]. Following the custom of the Greeks, he composed in verse one book of a *Hexaemeron*, from the beginning of Genesis to the creation [Col. 1099B] of humanity [Note: [Col. 1099D] The same manuscript has “as a kind of *Hexaemeron*.”]; many homilies addressed to bishops [Note: [Col. 1099D] The same manuscript has “many homilies delivered to bishops.”]; and as for sacramental works, I do not even remember how many. He remains alive to this day in a good old age.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1099D] It is uncertain who this Paulinus was, and, so far as I know, nothing of his survives.] PAULINUS composed treatises *On the Beginning of Lent*, of which I have read two; *On Easter Sunday*; *On Obedience*; *On Repentance*; and *On the Newly Baptized*.

## CHAPTER LXIX

[Note: [Col. 1100B] Saint Hilary, formerly a monk of Lérins and later bishop of Arles, took part in the Council of Riez in 439 and the First Council of Orange in 441. He wrote to Pope Leo I, in heroic verse, a *History of Genesis* extending to the seventh chapter; and in prose a *Life of Saint Honoratus*, his predecessor, first published in Paris through the efforts of Gilbert Genebrard in 1578 and later edited by Surius. Some attribute to him a letter to Saint Augustine *On Predestination*; on its occasion Saint Augustine wrote his books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. Bellarmine in his catalogue, however, and others judge that the letter was not written by Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, but by some presbyter named Hilary. After spending several years in the episcopate, Saint Hilary, touched by his former longing for the solitary life, returned to Lérins, as Hilary himself testifies in his homily on Saint Honoratus and as Sidonius says in his *Eucharisticus* addressed to Faustus, bishop of Riez, where among other things he mentions Eucherius’s journey when he came and Hilary’s when he returned. At that time Saint Eucherius wrote to Hilary his elegant little work *On the Praise of the Desert*, as I explained above in chapter 63. The *Life of Saint Hilary of Arles*—who died in the tenth year of Pope Leo I, that is, in the year of Christ 446—is preserved in Barralis’s *Lérins Chronicle*, together with Saint Hilary’s epitaph. We shall discuss below, in chapter 99, who wrote that life. Another Saint Hilary was Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, whose works are commonly accompanied by several little works of Saint Hilary of Arles. MIRAEUS.]

HILARY, bishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 1100C] The Corbie manuscript adds “of the city.”], learned in the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1100D] The same manuscript adds “learned, and a lover also of poverty.”], a lover of poverty, and concerned for the provision of the needy not only through the compassion of his mind but also through the labor and exertion of his body [Note: [Col. 1100D] The same manuscript reads: “he, a man of noble birth and distinguished, undertook farming with his own strength.”]. For the sake of restoring the poor, this man, noble by birth and brought up in a very different manner, even undertook agricultural labor beyond his strength; yet he did not neglect spiritual matters. In teaching he possessed great grace [Note: [Col. 1100D] The same manuscript has “the greatest grace.”], and without respect of persons he imposed upon all the discipline of preaching [Note: [Col. 1100D] The same manuscript has: “without partiality, he brought correction to all. With a zealous intellect he published a few small works, which are evidence to the learned and faithful.” These words close the chapter in the Corbie manuscript.]. With an immortal talent he also produced a few small works, which testify to an educated mind and a faithful tongue. Among them, chiefly and for the benefit of many, he necessarily composed the *Life of Saint Honoratus*, his predecessor. He died while Valentinian and Marcian were reigning.

## CHAPTER LXX

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Saint Leo I held the Roman see for nearly twenty-one years, from 440 to 461, and died on 11 April. He was outstanding in piety, learning, and eloquence, so that the surname “the Great” deservedly clung to him. The Parisians published all his works together with those of Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, who died around the year 450. A book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* is usually placed among Saint Leo’s works; but it cannot be his, since it mentions the rule of Saint Benedict. Likewise, among his letters, number 96 incorrectly includes a letter of Leo, bishop of Bourges, who wrote it together with Victurius of Le Mans and Eustochius of Tours to the bishops and presbyters of the province—not of Thrace, as is commonly printed among Leo’s letters, but of the third province, by which the Touraine is meant, the third province of Lyon, as Sirmond observed in his notes to volume I of the Councils of Gaul. MIRAEUS.]

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote to Flavian, [Col. 1101A] bishop of the Church of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1101C] The Corbie manuscript has “pontiff.”], against the presbyter Eutyches, who at that time was attempting through ambition for the episcopate to introduce innovations into the Church. In this letter he warned him that, if he confessed his error and promised correction, he would receive him; but if he persisted in his undertaking [Note: [Col. 1101C] The same manuscript has “if he persists,” instead of “if he persisted.”], he would be condemned together with his heresy. In the same letter he also teaches, and confirms by divine testimonies, that our Lord Jesus Christ, just as he is the true Son of the Father’s divinity, must likewise be believed to be truly human according to human nature [Note: [Col. 1101C] The same manuscript reads “to be the man of human nature.”], that is, to have drawn flesh from the flesh of the Virgin Mary and not to have received a body for himself from heaven, as Eutyches asserted. He died while Leo and Majorian were emperors [Note: [Col. 1101C] The same manuscript has “while Valentinian and Majorian were reigning.” But Suffridus Petri says that all our manuscript copies read “he died while Leo and Marcian were emperors.” Since historical truth supports it, we have restored that reading. Yet historical truth confirms that Leo the Great died in the same year in which Majorian was killed.].

## CHAPTER LXXI

[Col. 1101B] [Note: [Col. 1101D] The Corbie manuscript has “Mozymus”; others, “Moschimus.” The Gembloux manuscript has “Mochomeus”; others, “the Mesopotamian presbyter.” Nothing by this writer has come down to us.] MOCHIMUS, a Mesopotamian presbyter, wrote at Antioch an excellent little book against Eutyches; he is also said to have written other works that I have not yet read.

## CHAPTER LXXII

[Note: [Col. 1101D] In the year 451 a general synod of 630 Fathers was held at Chalcedon. Paschasinus of Lilybaeum attended it with three other legates of the Roman pontiff. Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned there. In place of Dioscorus, who had been deposed, Proterius was ordained bishop of Alexandria. After Proterius was finally butchered in 455 by the enraged populace or by soldiers, Timothy, a crafty and impure man, seized that see. At the insistence of Pope Leo I, he was subsequently deported first to Gangra and then to Cherson, as Theodoret, Evagrius, and Baronius relate at length. A different man was Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, who lived in the time of the emperor Theodosius and whose canonical answers, together with the commentaries of Balsamon, are found in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. MIRAEUS.]

TIMOTHY, after Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, had been killed by the Alexandrians, while the populace was still in turmoil, either wished or allowed himself to be made bishop in place of the murdered man by a single bishop [Note: [Col. 1102C] The Corbie manuscript has “before he wished, before he suffered … until the synodal decrees were enacted.”]. And lest he deservedly be deposed as having been made contrary to law, he declared all those with whom Proterius had communicated to be Nestorians, seeking rashly to wash away the stain on his conscience [Note: [Col. 1102C] The same manuscript reads “declaring them Nestorians … presuming rashly to cleanse his conscience.”], in order to gain the favor of the populace, which had hated Proterius. He wrote to the emperor Leo a highly persuasive little book, which he attempted to reinforce with testimonies of the Fathers interpreted in a perverse sense, to such an extent that, in order to deceive the emperor and establish his own heresy [Col. 1101C] [Note: [Col. 1102C] The same manuscript has “to refute”; others, “to strengthen.”], he almost made Leo, pontiff of the city of Rome, and the Council of Chalcedon, as well as all the bishops of the West [Note: [Col. 1102C] The Corbie manuscript has “the bishops of the whole West”; others, erroneously, “of the East.”], appear, through the support of others, to be Nestorians. But, by God’s favor, the enemy of the Church was exposed and refuted by the Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 1102C] The Corbie manuscript has “was constrained and confuted by the Council of Chalcedon.”]. The heresiarch is said and held still to be living in exile. At the request of the brethren, I translated this very book into Latin, for the purpose of knowing it, and entitled it *A Book to Be Avoided* [Note: [Col. 1102C] This book of Timothy the Eutychian exists neither in Greek nor in Gennadius’s Latin translation.].

## CHAPTER LXXIII

ASCLEPIUS the African, bishop of a small village in the territory of Baiae [Note: [Col. 1102C] Instead of “Baian,” certain manuscripts, such as the Corbie manuscript, have “Gabais”; others, such as the Nuremberg manuscript and Trithemius, have “Vaga.”] [Note: [Col. 1102C] The Corbie manuscript has “bishop of a large neighboring city.”], wrote against the Arians, and is now said to be writing against the Donatists. In extemporaneous teaching he was highly esteemed [Note: [Col. 1102C] The same manuscript has “he enjoys a great reputation.”]. Nothing of Asclepius’s writings has come down to us.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

[Col. 1102B] PETER, a presbyter of the Church of Edessa and a distinguished declaimer, wrote *A Treatise on Various Causes* [Note: [Col. 1102D] The subject was various, as he says elsewhere: “treatises on various hypotheses,” for example in chapters 57 and 53. These writings of Peter of Edessa have perished. Like Mochimus, praised above in chapter 71, he wrote in Syriac and composed psalms in Syriac meter.], and, following the custom of Saint Ephrem the deacon, composed psalms in meter.

## CHAPTER LXXV

[Note: [Col. 1102D] This chapter is absent from the Corbie manuscript. Trithemius also discusses Asclepius the African, Peter of Edessa, and Paul of Pannonia. The reader should note, however, that Honorius and Trithemius call this Paul “Peter.” The same is true in the Martinian and Nuremberg manuscripts. MIRAEUS.]

PAUL, a presbyter and, as I learned from his writings, a Pannonian by birth, wrote two books, in an ordinary style but seasoned with divine salt, *On Maintaining Virginity and Contempt of the World, and on the Formation of Life or Correction of Morals* [Note: [Col. 1102D] These two books of Paul, or Peter, the Pannonian, are now lost.], addressed to a certain noble virgin consecrated to Christ, named Constantia. In them he mentions the heretic Jovinian, a preacher of pleasures and lusts. The discipline of a continent and chaste life was so contrary to him [Note: [Col. 1102D] This reading seems more probable to me. Miraeus absurdly has: “so that among letters of lust he might belch out his soul.” The Nuremberg manuscript has: “so that among luxurious banquets he might count the happiness of the soul.” The Wolfenbüttel manuscript has the same. ERN. CYPRIANUS.], that he “vomited out his soul among luxurious [Col. 1102C] [Note: [Col. 1102D] The manuscripts consulted by Suffridus Petri have “that he might reject the blessedness of the soul.” But the same man wrongly reads “letters” for “banquets.” [Col. 1103C] ] banquets.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI

[Col. 1103A]

PASTOR, a bishop, composed a small book in the form of a creed [Note: [Col. 1103C] This little book of Pastor is nowhere extant today.], containing almost the whole of ecclesiastical belief in a series of propositions. Among the other perverse dissensions that he anathematizes while omitting the names of their authors, he condemns the Priscillians together with the name of their founder [Note: [Col. 1103C] Suffridus Petri published “with the bishop.” Miraeus’s reading is not satisfactory. We have followed the Nuremberg manuscript: “with him.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.].

## CHAPTER LXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1103C] Around the year 530 Victor, an African bishop, wrote *On the Reason of the Catholic Faith* to Huneric, king of the Vandals. This book is found in volume IV of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Thus Bellarmine in his catalogue. MIRAEUS.]

VICTOR, bishop of the Mauritanian city of Cartenna [Note: [Col. 1103C] The Corbie manuscript has “Maurus.”], wrote one long book against the Arians [Note: [Col. 1103C] This book has perished. See Tillemont, volume XVI of the *Memoirs*, p. 611.] and presented it to King Genseric for reading through his attendants, as I learned from the preface of the book itself [Note: [Col. 1103C] The same manuscript has “to the king of the Vandals.”]. He also wrote one book *On the Publican’s Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1103C] The same manuscript has “on public penance,” incorrectly. The work still survives among the works of Saint Ambrose, having been published several times, and is attributed to Victor of Tunnuna in a manuscript of Reims.], in which he established for penitents a rule of life according to the authority of Scripture; and for a certain Basil, concerning the death of his son, a consolatory book [Col. 1103B] [Note: [Col. 1103D] The same manuscript has “a little book fortified by the hope of resurrection.” This work too is found among the writings of Saint Basil and Eucherius. The homilies, so far as I know, never saw the light.], fully furnished with instruction and hope of resurrection. He also composed many homilies, which I learned were preserved, arranged in books by brethren anxious for their own salvation.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1103D] The Corbie manuscript has “Vogonius, bishop of Castellana, a city of Mauritania.” In the Wolfenbüttel manuscript he is called “Buconius”; nor is he called otherwise by Honorius and Trithemius. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

VOCONIUS, bishop of the Mauritanian town of Castellum, wrote against the enemies of the Church, the Jews, Arians, and other heretics. [Note: [Col. 1103D] The Corbie manuscript adds “a book.” But neither this book of Voconius nor his other work *On the Sacraments* exists anywhere today. Trithemius, chapter 171 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, calls Voconius “Victorianus Buconius.”] He also composed an excellent volume *On the Sacraments*.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1103D] The bishops who successively governed the see of Marseille were Venrius, Eustathius, and Graecus. At the urging of Venrius, Musaeus, also called Mussaeus, a presbyter of Marseille, excerpted readings from the divine Scriptures for the entire year; this is mentioned by Bernard Guidonis. Sidonius, in book VII, letter 2, mentions Eustathius and Graecus, bishop of Marseille, and says that Graecus succeeded Eustathius. Sirmond noted this in his annotations to Sidonius, contrary to the opinion of Claudius Robertus in *Gallia Christiana*, where he lists the bishops of Marseille. MIRAEUS.]

MUSAEUS, a presbyter of the Church of Marseille, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and refined by a certain exceptionally subtle practice in understanding their meanings, and also scholastic in speech, at the urging of Saint Venrius, bishop, excerpted from the sacred Scriptures readings suitable for the feast days of the whole year [Col. 1104A]; he also excerpted sections of the Psalms for responses [Note: [Col. 1104C] The Corbie manuscript has “responsories,”] appropriate to the seasons and readings. This work is so necessary that it is approved by the readers in the Church, so that, being desired and readily available [Note: [Col. 1104C] The same manuscript has: “It is approved by the reader in the Church as something convenient.”], it removes both anxiety and delay, imparts knowledge to the people, and brings dignity to the celebration [Note: [Col. 1104C] The same manuscript adds “and the splendor of beauty.”]. He also composed for Saint Eustachius, bishop and successor of the aforementioned man of God, an excellent and substantial volume *On the Sacraments* [Note: [Col. 1104C] The Corbie manuscript has “a not small and excellent volume.” It is not implausible that I have read some of this work of Musaeus, or of the Voconius mentioned in the preceding chapter, in the sacramentary of Gregory the Great.], divided according to the needs of the offices and seasons, the text of the readings, and the sequence and singing of the psalms [Note: [Col. 1104C] The words from “and seasons” to “he is also said to have delivered homilies” are absent from the Corbie manuscript.], but harmonious in the substance of its petitions to God and its declarations of his benefits. [Col. 1104B] From this work we recognized the man’s profound thought and disciplined eloquence. He is also said to have delivered homilies, which I learned were possessed by faithful men, though I myself have not read them. He died while Leo [Note: [Col. 1104C] Suffridus Petri’s manuscripts have “and Marcian,” but the Corbie manuscript has “while Leo and Majorian were reigning.” The latter is more correct, for Majorian, not Marcian, ruled after Leo.] and Majorian were reigning.

## CHAPTER LXXX

[Note: [Col. 1104C] Those are mistaken who think that the so-called “Vincentian” objections against Saint Prosper, defending the writings of Saint Augustine, were written by Vincent of Lérins, praised above by Gennadius in chapter 64. Vincent not only did not attack the defenders of Saint Augustine; in chapter 43 of his book against heresies he highly praised them. It should therefore be known that another Vincent lived in Gaul in the same century; Gennadius writes about him in chapter 80. I would rather attribute that work to him. Whatever the case, it is certain that those efforts were the work of a Pelagian and are unworthy of attribution to Vincent of Lérins, who in his plainly golden little work attacks all heresies, and especially the Pelagian heresy together with its authors, as is clear from chapters 2 and 14. Baronius says nearly the same in his notes to the martyrology for 24 May. See, however, Vossius, book I of *The History of Pelagianism*, chapter 9. MIRAEUS.]

VINCENTIUS, a presbyter and himself a Gaul by birth, trained in the divine Scriptures and possessing a tongue polished by habitual speaking and extensive reading, commented on the Psalms. He read some of this work to a holy man named Cannata [Note: [Col. 1104D] Some copies have “Cannati.” Nothing of this Vincent’s commentaries on the Psalms has survived.], in my hearing, while promising at the same time that, if the Lord granted him life and strength, he would labor with the same diligence over the entire Psalter.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

[Col. 1105A]

[Note: [Col. 1105B] Honorius and Trithemius, as well as the manuscript copies, have “Cyrus”; others have “Cyrillus.” Consult Trithemius concerning Cyrus, or Syrus, of Alexandria, and likewise concerning Samuel of Edessa, who will be mentioned shortly. MIRAEUS.]

CYRUS, an Alexandrian by birth [Note: [Col. 1105B] Some copies have “by race.” The Corbie manuscript has only “Cyrus the Alexandrian.” Suffridus Petri, from the Martinian manuscript, has “Syrus” instead of “Cyrus.” But he also testifies that “Cyrus” is read in the Green Valley and Sigeberg manuscripts, while the Gembloux manuscript has “Cyrillus.” Nothing of this Cyrus’s writings has come down to us.], a physician by profession, a monk formerly a philosopher, and a man skilled in eloquence, first wrote elegantly and forcefully against Nestorius [Note: [Col. 1105B] The Corbie manuscript has “against Nestor,” instead of “Nestorius”;] but later, while he attacks him excessively [Note: [Col. 1105B] The Corbie manuscript has: “While he attacks him more vigorously, Timothy’s doctrine is shaken by syllogisms more than by Scriptures.” Others have “while he is found to be excessive in attacking that man.” Concerning Timothy the Eutychian, see above, chapter 72. For the difference between the Timotheans and the other Eutychians, see chapter 82. “In him he is found to be excessive” is the reading of the Nuremberg manuscript. The Wolfenbüttel manuscript differs in one word, reading “in him he is found to be less excessive.” Miraeus’s reading cannot be accepted: “he attacks him excessively.” For Cyrus measured the mystery of the Incarnation by the ten-foot rule of human reason and, excessively devoted to philosophy and the art of speaking, embraced the Eutychian error. ERN. CYPRIANUS.], and, proceeding more by syllogisms than by the Scriptures, began to support the Timothean doctrine. Finally, uncertain even of his own position, he suspended his judgment regarding assent to the decree of Chalcedon and did not think that the Son of God, after the Incarnation, consisted of two natures.

## CHAPTER LXXXII
SAMUEL, presbyter of the Church of Edessa [Note: [Col. 1105C] Corbei., “of Edessa.”], is said to have composed many works in the Syriac language against the enemies of the Church, chiefly, however, against the Nestorians, Eutychians, and the recent followers of Timothy [Note: [Col. 1105C] So also Corbei.; others read, “or against various heretics.” What follows is read very corruptly in the same manuscript, and the greater part is plainly missing.], but [Col. 1105B] against various heretics. Hence, frequently, by ecclesiastical judgment together with the authority of the holy Scriptures, he summarily strikes down the threefold beast, showing [Col. 1106A] to the Nestorians that God was in the man, not a mere man born of a virgin; to the Eutychians, that the true flesh of the human race was assumed by God, and was not brought down from heaven, nor did the substance of thick air enter into and take shape in the flesh; and to the Timothians, that the Word became flesh in such a way that, while the Word remained in its own substance and the man in his own nature, the one person of the Son of God was produced by association, not by mixture. He is said still to be living at Constantinople. For at the beginning of the reign conferred upon Anthemius [i.e., in A.D. 465], I learned both that his writings existed and that he himself was alive.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1105C] The Gembloux manuscript calls this writer Claudius. Above also, in Salvian, chapter 67, all the manuscripts call him Claudius; “we change nothing,” says Suffridus Petri. Trithemius, chapter 178, calls him Claudius and names him a bishop. By others he is called by his full name, Claudianus Ecdicius Mamertus, presbyter of the Church of Vienne, as he is styled on the title page of the three books *On the State of the Soul*, first published at Basel in 1520 by Petrus Mosellanus from a manuscript of the Old Cell of Meissen, now preserved at Leipzig in the Paulina Library, as Daumius notes, p. 336, in his remarks on Paulinus of Périgueux. With the notes of Caspar Barthius, we possess the same books which Claudian opposed to Faustus of Riez, printed at Zwickau in 1655, in octavo. On Claudian himself, see Sirmondus, note to Sidonius, vol. I of the works, p. 929, etc.; Tillemont, vol. XVI of the *Memoirs*, and vol. II of the *Acts of the Saints*, May, p. 629.

Claudianus Mamertus—or rather Mamertus Claudianus—presbyter of the Church of Vienne and full brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, wrote to Sidonius before the latter became bishop three books *On the State of the Soul*, published in the *Library of the Fathers* and elsewhere. The letter prefixed to the work bears this title: “To Praefectorius, Patricius, a most learned and excellent man, C. Sollius Sidonius, Claudianus sends greetings.” Claudian himself mentions these books in his letter to Sidonius, which is read among the Sidonian letters, book IV, number 2. A poem by the same Claudian against various errors, or against vain poets, is extant among the works of the Christian poets and in the cited *Library*. Claudianus Mamertus flourished in the year 443; and after his death Sidonius wrote him an epitaph in verse, which he himself recites in book IV of his letters, number 11.

Moreover, Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, first instituted the Rogation processions held before the Lord’s Ascension, as is clear from the homily on those same Rogations by Alcimus Avitus, bishop of the same church; all the ancient writers agree with him. [Col. 1106C] Thus those labor in vain who, because they read that litanies and supplications existed in the Church before Mamertus, wish to call him not the first author but merely the restorer of the Rogations. In vain, I say; for the question is not whether he first introduced the use of litanies into the Church—for it is clear that this practice was much older—but whether he instituted those celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension, which are now specifically called Rogations. On this point, as I have said, all agree, and the words of Sidonius in book V, letter 14—“he found, instituted, introduced”—leave no room for doubt.

Mamertus, therefore, was the first author of the Rogations. Nor did he merely institute fixed and solemn supplications for those days; he also prescribed a form of prayer holier and more august than the customary form. Following Mamertus’s example, not only the neighboring peoples of Gaul—as may be understood from the letters of Sidonius himself and from the First Council of Orléans—but also other nations, and at length Rome itself by the authority of Leo III, adopted them, as the authors of the liturgical books teach. They therefore called it the Gallican Litany, [Col. 1106D] because its institution came from Gaul, and the Lesser Litany, to distinguish it from the Greater Litany, which is celebrated on 25 April. Thus, in substance, Sirmondus in his notes on books V and VII of the letters of Sidonius. MIRAEUS.]

CLAUDIANUS, presbyter of the Church of Vienne, a man skilled in speech and subtle in disputation, composed three books, as it were, *On the State* or *On the Substance of the Soul*, in which his entire purpose is to show that something incorporeal exists besides God. [ [Note: [Col. 1106D] These words and what follows to the end of the chapter are absent from the commonly circulated copies of Gennadius. They are, however, read in a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael of Tumba in Brittany, as Sirmondus notes in his remarks on Sidonius (vol. I of the works, fol. 933). The same manuscript also contains certain previously unknown material on the poet Sedulius, as Sirmondus likewise explains in his notes on Ennodius. Sedulius died while Theodosius the Younger—to whom he had dedicated his work—and Valentinian were reigning. His verses, collected after his death from his archives, are said to have been edited by Turcius Rufius Asterius, who was Roman consul with Protogenes in 449. MIRAEUS.] He also wrote several other works, including a hymn on the Passion of the Lord, whose beginning is: [Note: [Col. 1107A] Ancient writers and manuscripts also attribute this hymn to Venantius Fortunatus, but its style has a greater refinement than is usual for Fortunatus. Sirmondus believes that it was written by Claudianus Mamertus himself and praised by Sidonius in book IV, letter 3, to Claudian. “Everything praised by Sidonius,” he says, “fits him aptly.” It is written in trochaic verse, with occasional pyrrhic rhythms inserted; it is arranged in cola, cut into frequent and appropriate clauses, with thoughts not broken off but falling gently with the verse. Finally, this poem is claimed for Claudian not only by the ancient scholiast but also by Gennadius—not as it has been edited, indeed, but as it appears in the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael of Tumba, which contains a fuller text in its notice of Claudian. MIRAEUS.] “Sing, tongue, of the glorious…” (*Pange, lingua, gloriosi*). He was the brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne.]

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 1107B] Prosper of Aquitaine was a presbyter, not a bishop—if we believe Victor of Aquitaine, Gennadius, Gelasius, Marcellinus Comes, and Bede. Following the arrangement of Eusebius, he composed a chronicle with remarkable brevity, to use Victor’s own words, beginning from the origin of the world and extending in its third edition to the eighth consulship of the Emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius—that is, to the commonly reckoned year A.D. 455.

He seems to have completed the first edition under the fourteenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Maximus, that is, in A.D. 433, since in that year he gathers the epochs and totals of all the years before it; this is ordinarily done only at the end of a work, unless some special circumstance intervenes, and none is apparent here. Prosper seems to have enlarged the second edition by twelve years and brought it to the sixth consulship of Valentinian and the consulship of Nonius—that is, to the commonly reckoned year A.D. 445—where the version of his chronicle ordinarily attached to the Eusebian and Hieronymian chronicles ends.

Finally, the third and last edition was the one extended to the capture of the City by Gaiseric, or to the eighth consulship of Valentinian Augustus and the consulship of Anthemius—that is, to A.D. 455. Peter Francis Chiffletius, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, will, I hope, soon publish it from a manuscript of the cathedral basilica of Speyer. Arnoldus Pontacus once possessed a similar manuscript, which he calls the Lodunensis; and we saw a third similar manuscript at Antwerp among the papers of Heribert Rosweyde, though it was mutilated.

This third edition is not only fuller than the first two but also much more illuminating, since it records events from the creation of the world with vigorous brevity and additionally brings the consular fasti from the fifteenth year of Tiberius down to the year 455. [Col. 1107D] The latter part of this third edition, ordinarily appended to the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, corrected and enlarged according to the manuscripts of Jacques Sirmondus and Peter Francis Chiffletius, is extant in André Duchesne, vol. I of the *Contemporary Writers of the History of the Franks*.

Bucherius, in his commentary on Victor’s canon, chapters 6 and 12, and Sirmondus, in his notes on Sidonius, book VIII, letter 15, discuss at length the three or four Prospers of this century: the men of Orléans and Riez, the chronicler, and the “Tyro.” As for Tyro Prosper, Bede says at the end of his short work *On Metrics* that he was married.

Moreover, from the time at which Prosper ends, Marius of Avenches, or of Lausanne, bishop, extended his own chronicle to the year 581 of the common era. Duchesne published it in the cited volume from a very ancient manuscript belonging to the same Chiffletius. MIRAEUS.]

PROSPER, a man of the region of Aquitaine, [Note: [Col. 1107D] Corbei. adds, “counselor of Pope Leo.”] scholastic in language and vigorous in argument, is said to have composed many works. Among them I read a chronicle bearing his name as its title [Note: [Col. 1108A] Corbei., “a chronicle entitled with his name.”], containing, according to the faith of the divine Scriptures, the history from the creation of the first man down to [Note: [Col. 1108A] Corbei., “down to the end.”] the death of the Emperor Valentinian and the capture of the city of Rome by Gaiseric, king of the Vandals.

I also read a book against the works published under the name of Cassianus, which the Church of God approves as beneficial, while he condemns them as harmful. [Note: [Col. 1108A] Gennadius is wrong to condemn Prosper here, and speaks as though sprinkled with the soot of the Semi-Pelagians, or Massilians. Elsewhere also he prefers Rufinus to Saint Jerome, accuses Augustine of excessive verbosity, praises the *Eulogies* of Pelagius, commends the books of Faustus of Riez, and writes other things of the same sort in favor of the Semi-Pelagians. MIRAEUS.] For the opinions truly held by Cassianus and Prosper concerning grace and free will are found in certain respects to be contradictory to one another. [Note: [Col. 1108B] Corbei. reads: “He denounces him. For the new and true [writings] of Cassianus . . . are found to be contrary to one another. Here also Prosper, after the death of blessed Augustine, stood forth as the defender of his books against heretics, enemies of the grace of Christ. There are also letters, etc.” Suffridus Petri found the same material in other manuscripts and does not doubt that it was added to Gennadius by some Catholic as a corrective.]

[Note: [Col. 1108B] The words inserted by Miraeus after “are found to be contradictory” come from another hand: “Here also Prosper, after the death of blessed Augustine, stood forth as the defender of his books against heretics, enemies of the grace of Christ.” They are found in none of our manuscripts and are not placed in a suitable position. Compare Vossius, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 18. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

There are also said to be letters of Pope Leo against Eutyches, concerning the true incarnation of Christ, addressed to various persons and dictated by Prosper himself. [Note: [Col. 1108C] If any letter is Saint Leo’s, this one certainly is, whether one considers Leo’s style or doctrine; it is not Prosper’s, contrary to Gennadius’s statement. Conversely, the books *On the Calling of the Nations* are genuinely Prosper’s, not Saint Ambrose’s. The book *On the Providence of God*, however, does not appear to be Prosper’s, but rather that of someone from the Semi-Pelagian faction. See Bellarmine in the *Catalogue*. Consult Bucherius and Sirmondus at the cited places.

As for the three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which are usually published among Prosper’s works and are frequently cited under his name by Gratian, the compiler of the canons, and by others, they do not appear genuinely to be Prosper’s. First, because Gennadius, listing Prosper’s works in this chapter, does not mention them. Second, because their author, in book II, chapter 9, speaks of Hilary of Arles—Prosper’s contemporary—in a way that indicates that Hilary was older than himself. Finally, to pass over other arguments, in an ancient collection of canons in the manuscript of Angers they are attributed to Pomerius as author, at the place that appears in Prosper, book II, chapter 6. In a manuscript of Saint Salvator, the author assigned to these books is Julianus Pomerius. Isidore likewise explicitly attributes them to Pomerius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 12: “He also published three other books on the contemplation of the future life, or on active conduct, and likewise on vices and virtues.” These words clearly describe the subject matter of the individual books of that work.

The same Julianus Pomerius had also published eight other books, whose titles Isidore explains individually in the same place; Julianus the younger, bishop of Toledo, frequently used them as sources in his *Prognostics of the Future Age*. This Pomerius was an African, a Moor by birth, but flourished at Arles in Gaul, first as a rhetorician and later as a presbyter and abbot, as may be gathered from the life of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and from a letter of Ruricius to Pomerius. Thus, approximately, Sirmondus in his notes on volume II of the Councils of Gaul. MIRAEUS.]

## CHAPTER LXXXV

[Col. 1109A]

[Note: [Col. 1109B] Faustus was a Gaul-Briton by birth—that is, one of those Britons of Gaul who live north of the Loire River—first abbot of Lérins and later bishop of Riez, or Réii, in Gaul. He wrote on the Holy Spirit and against the Arians and Macedonians; these books are no longer extant.

He also wrote two books *On the Grace of God and the Free Will of the Human Mind*. They do exist and are praised by Gennadius in this chapter, but they are rejected by Pope Gelasius in his decree on apocryphal books and are likewise refuted by Saint Fulgentius, the deacon Peter, Alcimus Avitus, and others. Faustus was certainly a Semi-Pelagian, but he lived and died before the Second Council of Orange, held in 529, at which the Semi-Pelagian position was first condemned. He is nevertheless honored as a saint in his Church of Riez. See what we said above in the prolegomena and in the scholia on chapter 61 of Gennadius. MIRAEUS.]

FAUSTUS, having become bishop at Riez in Gaul after being abbot of the monastery of Lérins [Note: [Col. 1109B] Corbei., “of Riez, a city of Gaul.” There is no doubt that this reading should be retained. Erasmus and others, influenced by Vossius, book I, chapter 8 of the *History of the Pelagians*, wrongly read “at the kingdom of Gaul.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.], a man [Note: [Col. 1109C] Corbei., “devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures.”] sufficiently intent upon the divine Scriptures, taking occasion from the tradition of the Creed, composed a book on the Holy Spirit, in which he showed that, according to the faith of the Fathers, the Spirit is both consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son, and possesses the fullness [Note: [Col. 1109C] The manuscript of Wolfenbüttel reads, “of divinity.”] of the Trinity.

He also published an excellent work *On the Grace of God, by Which We Are Saved*, [Note: [Col. 1109C] The words “and the free will of the human mind” are absent from various editions and from the Corbie manuscript.] and on the free will of the human mind. In this work he teaches that the grace of God always both invites, precedes, and assists our will, and that whatever free will itself acquires through pious labor as a reward [Note: [Col. 1109C] Corbei. reads, “has acquired as the reward of pious labor.” The two books of Faustus *On Grace and Free Will* were written in A.D. 475 and were first published by Heinrich Canisius and subsequently many times. See the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII, Lyons edition, p. 525.] is not its own merit but a gift of grace.

I also read his short book against the Arians and Macedonians, in which he proclaims the Trinity coessential [Note: [Col. 1109C] Corbei. reads “essential,” a faulty form.], and another [Note: [Col. 1109D] Faustus wrote a short work against those who say that something incorporeal exists among created things, affirming that nothing of this kind should be believed to exist except God. Claudius Mamertus, praised above by Gennadius in chapter 83, refutes this error in his books *On the State of the Soul*. For this reason Faustus’s short work is usually prefixed to them, but without the author’s name. Faustus also inserted this opinion of his into his letter to Paulinus. It was once the error of many, including Tertullian, who in his book *On the Soul* assigns a body to the soul, though an exceedingly subtle one: “Indeed,” he says, “because of its very extreme subtlety, it is in danger of being regarded as corporeal.” MIRAEUS.] against those who say that something incorporeal exists among created things. In it, both by divine testimonies [Col. 1110A] and by the judgments of the Fathers, he confirms that nothing incorporeal should be believed to exist except God.

There is also a letter of his, in the form of a short treatise, addressed to a certain deacon named Gratus [Note: [Col. 1109D] Corbei. reads “given to a certain deacon named Greek”; others read “Gregory.” The latter is erroneous; compare Tillemont, vol. XVI of the *Memoirs*. I read “Gratus” with Vossius and Cave. The Nuremberg manuscript has “Graecus,” a reading also mentioned by Vossius. Others have “Gregory.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.], who, abandoning the Catholic faith, had gone over to the Nestorian impiety. In this letter he admonishes him to believe that the holy Virgin Mary did not give birth to a mere man who afterward received divinity [Note: [Col. 1110B] Corbei., “the holy Mary.”], but to the true God in a true man.

There are also other writings of his, which, since I have not yet read them, I have chosen not to name. Nevertheless, he is both believed and acknowledged to be an excellent teacher by his living voice. [Note: [Col. 1110B] Corbei. adds: “He also wrote to Felix, a man of prefectural and patrician rank.” This letter to Felix is extant in volume VIII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 552. Moreover, Lupus of Ferrières distinguishes two Faustuses in letter 112: “I ask that Fausta be addressed, not the one whom Augustine refutes” [Faustus the Manichaean], “but the one whom Gelasius mentions in his decrees.” Compare letter 121.]

Later he wrote to Felix, prefect of the praetorium and a man of patrician rank, the son of the consul Magnus, [Note: [Col. 1110B] Corbei., “already religious,” and “a letter suited to one who was wholeheartedly preparing to do penance.”] who was already devoted to religion, an exhortatory letter concerning the fear of the Lord, suited to persons who were preparing with their whole heart to do penance.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

[Col. 1110B]

[Note: [Col. 1110B] This chapter is absent from most manuscripts and editions of Gennadius and was added to Gennadius by another hand. It is nevertheless also read by Honorius in a manuscript of Gennadius. But, as Suffridus Petri correctly notes, the manuscripts had already been corrupted in the time of Honorius. Certainly Caesarius was not yet a bishop in A.D. 494, when Gennadius compiled this catalogue.

Saint Caesarius, after being abbot of Lérins, became bishop of Arles. He wrote one rule for monks and another for religious women; both are extant in the *Library of the Fathers* and in the edition of Stellartius. Caesarius’s rule is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, book IX, chapters 39–41, and also by Venantius Fortunatus, book V, chapter 2: “And may the beneficent rule of the pious bishop Caesarius, adopted from the city of Genoa, be observed for it.”

Caesarius attended the Council of Agde in 506 and the Fourth Council of Arles in 524, and died at a very advanced age. In 567, Saint Radegund, abbess of Poitiers, wrote a letter to the bishops assembled at the Second Council of Tours, for the protection and stability of her recently established community. Among other things she says: “Through the generosity of King Chlothar, I established a monastery for girls in the city of Poitiers; moreover, for the community gathered by me, I adopted the rule under which Saint Caesaria lived, which the solicitude of blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, collected from the institution of the holy Fathers.”

Sirmondus notes that there were two women named Caesaria who held the same office. One was the full sister of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles; Caesarius appointed her abbess of the monastery he had founded and gave her a rule under which she and her companions were to live. The other, who came later, succeeded the first in the office of abbess after the latter’s death, while Caesarius was still alive, as Cyprian relates in the *Life of Saint Caesarius*, which he composed at the request of this Caesaria. This same abbess Radegund requested the rule of Caesarius for transmission to her monastery.

Moreover, Ennodius calls this Caesarius the most distinguished of the bishops of his age, outstanding in learning, eloquence, and holiness of life. Brought before King Theoderic on a fabricated charge and taken under guard to Ravenna, he so moved the king by the sight of his angelic bearing and the confidence of his innocence that the king not only received him peacefully and humanely but also honored him with gifts. A few years earlier, when Arles was still subject to the Visigoths and he had been accused of treason before Alaric, he had likewise been released with honor. Cyprian has included both events in book I of the *Life of Caesarius*. His second book, absent from the edition of Surius, is extant in the monastery of Saint-Martin in Paris; it concerns the miracles of Saint Caesarius.

Various letters of Roman pontiffs to Caesarius are also read in volume I of the Councils of Gaul. Among them is the letter of Pope Felix IV, which exercised Baronius and other learned men in vain because of suspicion about a corrupted subscription, as though it were said to have been written “after the consulship of Baetius”; the Arles manuscript clearly has “after the consulship of Mavortius,” which was the year A.D. 528—the second consulship of Pope Felix IV, as Sirmondus first observed in his notes on Ennodius and the councils of Gaul. MIRAEUS.

Although Vossius acknowledges this chapter of Gennadius as genuine in book I, chapter 14 of his *History of the Pelagians*, and consequently confuses the highest with the lowest in chapter 53, it is certain that the life of Caesarius of Arles was inserted into this catalogue long after Gennadius. This is learnedly demonstrated by the highly esteemed cardinal of the Roman Church, Henri de Noris, book II, chapter 16 of the *History of the Pelagians*. Add the words of Cave, part I, p. 271: “I am not unaware that the published manuscripts of Gennadius’s catalogue, written in A.D. 495, speak of Caesarius as though he were then governing the see of Arles and as though the author were one whose many books had been approved by Pope Felix. But the chronology wholly contradicts this; nor is the little catalogue of Gennadius, having suffered the worst interpolations at its end, authoritative enough in this matter to secure credence.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

CAESARIUS, bishop of the city of Arles, a man renowned for holiness [Col. 1111A] and virtues, composed excellent, welcome, and highly necessary little works for monks. [Note: [Col. 1111D] This book of Caesarius of Arles is lost.] He also published testimonies *On Grace and Free Will*, supported by the judgments of the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, in which he teaches [Note: [Col. 1111D] Miraeus reads: “that man can do nothing good from his own resources.” Those versed in Pelagian matters cannot accept this reading. ERN. CYPRIANUS.] that a human being can do nothing good on his own unless divine grace has first gone before him.

Pope Felix also strengthened this work by his letter [Note: [Col. 1111D] A letter of Felix IV, written in A.D. 528. See the note of Miraeus below.] and promulgated it more broadly [Note: [Col. 1111D] The Wolfenbüttel manuscript reads “in Latin.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.]. He flourished at the time when Faustus also did, while Anastasius was administering the empire. [Note: [Col. 1111D] Rather, several years afterward.]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1111D] This chapter is absent from Corbie. The book of this writer mentioned by Gennadius is itself lost.] SERVUSDEI, a bishop, wrote against those who say that Christ, while living in this present life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes, but only after rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, when he was transferred into the glory of God the Father, as though that glory were granted him as a reward for martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1111D] Augustine calls this opinion madness; he attacks it without naming its author in letters 92, or 6 in the new edition, and 146, or 112, chapter 22. Gennadius does not seem to disapprove of it in quite the same way. Compare the *Acts of the Erudite*, A.D. 1714, p. 115.]

In this work he shows through his own discussion and through testimonies of the holy Scriptures that the Lord Jesus, from the moment of his conception by the Holy Spirit and his birth from the Virgin—since the true God himself, born as a true man, also became Man-God—always saw both the Father and the Holy Spirit with the eyes of his flesh, through the special and united fellowship of God and man.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1111D] The Green Valley manuscript, Honorius, and Trithemius call him Victorinus. But the manuscripts of Sigebert also call him Victorius in chapter 20.

Victorius—called Victorinus by others and Victor by some—was an Aquitanian from Limoges. He wrote a Paschal canon under the consulship of Constantine and Rufus, as he himself states in the preface, that is, in the commonly reckoned year A.D. 457, for Hilary, then archdeacon of the Roman Church and later successor of Saint Leo the Great in the chair of Peter. Aegidius Bucherius, an Atrebatian theologian of the Society of Jesus and our friend, first published the canon in print in the Plantin edition of 1633 and illustrated it with a highly learned commentary. Folio. MIRAEUS.]

VICTORIUS, [Note: [Col. 1112B] Corbei., “an Aquitanian man, a most painstaking calculator”; others, “a calculator of the Scriptures.”] an Aquitanian by birth, a meticulous calculator, invited by Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome, composed a Paschal Cycle with the most careful investigation, after the four earlier authors who composed such works—namely, Hippolytus, Eusebius, Theophilus, and Prosper [Note: [Col. 1112B] We discussed Hippolytus of Porto above, in Jerome, chapter 61; Eusebius of Caesarea in chapter 81; and Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, in chapter 33 of Gennadius. Which Prosper Gennadius means here is discussed at length by Bucherius in the commentary cited above, chapter 6. I think Saint Prosper, bishop of Riez in Emilia, is intended. MIRAEUS.]; [Note: [Col. 1112C] Corbei., “and extended the sequence of years to 532.”] and extended the sequence of years to the five-hundred-and-thirty-second year, so that in the five-hundred-and-thirty-third year the solemnity of Easter would begin again in the same month and on the same day, and under the same [Col. 1112B] [Note: [Col. 1112C] Corbei., “moon under which the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord first took place.” He flourished under the Emperor Leo.] moon under which the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord first took place.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1112C] Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus in Syria and pastor of eight hundred churches, was a contemporary of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and at times even his opponent, as is clear from the Council of Ephesus. Although at the beginning of the controversy he favored Nestorius, he later repented and listed Nestorius among the heretics in book IV of *The Fables of the Heretics*, and was received among the Catholics at the Council of Chalcedon.

He began to preside over his church around A.D. 423, according to Baronius in the *Annals*. In 449, at the Ephesian assembly commonly called the Robber Synod, presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria, he was deposed by the heretics and reduced to the rank of a layman. Note this against Trithemius in his catalogue and against Franciscus Horantius, *Commonplaces*, book III, chapter 18, who write that he flourished in A.D. 390.

Birckmannus published Theodoret’s works in Latin at Cologne in 1567 and 1573; Sirmondus recently undertook to publish them in Greek and Latin at Paris. What he wrote against Saint Cyril was condemned at the Fifth General Council, together with the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom Theodoret also praises excessively in book V of his *History*. The letter attributed to Theodoret in the same Fifth Council, act 5, addressed to John of Antioch concerning Cyril’s death, is entirely false, fabricated, and unworthy of Theodoret, especially since it is established that John of Antioch died before Cyril. MIRAEUS.]

THEODORITUS, bishop of the city of Cyrus—for Cyrus, founded by the Persian king Cyrus, [Col. 1113A] still preserves the author’s name in Syria today [Note: [Col. 1113B] Corbei., “and to this day preserves the author’s name.”]—is said to have written many works. The following, however, have come to my knowledge: a work *On the Incarnation of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1113B] This work of Theodoret is lost apart from a few fragments.] against the presbyter Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1113B] Some manuscripts incorrectly have “Dionysius.”], who deny that Christ possessed human flesh. He wrote forcefully, confirming by reasoning and [Note: [Col. 1113B] Corbei., “by titles,” i.e. headings or citations.] by testimonies of the Scriptures that Christ possessed true flesh of his mother’s substance, which he took from his Virgin Mother, just as he possessed true divinity, which he received by being born from God the Father, who eternally begets.

There are also ten books of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 1113B] Only five books of Theodoret’s *Ecclesiastical History* survive, ending in A.D. 429. Nor does Theodoret appear to have written more, since at the end of book V he expressly declares that he is closing his history with the deaths of Theodore of Mopsuestia and Theodotus of Antioch, and in the preface declares that he has covered events over a period of 105 years. Thus either Gennadius was mistaken, as Valesius thinks, or he encountered a work of Theodoret continued by someone else.

Five books of the *Ecclesiastical History* survive today. Beginning with the rise of the Arian heresy, Theodoret carries the narrative down to the time of Theodosius the Younger. In them he recounts the proceedings of the Second General Council more fully than the other historians. Gennadius says in this chapter that Theodoret continued his history with five additional books to the time of the Emperor Leo, but these have not appeared. Concerning Theodoret’s style, Photius, codex 31, judges that it is more suited to history than the style used by Socrates, Sozomen, or Evagrius Ponticus. MIRAEUS.

The five later books Vossius, *On Greek History*, book XI, chapter 20, believes to have perished. Valesius, however, in the preface to his edition denies that Theodoret wrote more than five, since, expressly refuting Gennadius’s opinion at the end of book V, he testifies that he is closing his history with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and no ancient writer except Gennadius attributes ten books of *Ecclesiastical History* to him. It is therefore probable that Gennadius was mistaken here. For all the manuscripts read “ten.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.] which, following Eusebius of Caesarea, he wrote, beginning where Eusebius’s books end and continuing to his own time—that is, from the Vicennalia of Constantine to the reign of Leo the Elder, under whom he also died.

## CHAPTER XC

[Col. 1113B]

GENNADIUS, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, a man polished in language and keen in intellect, was so richly furnished by reading the ancients that he expounded the prophet Daniel in its entirety, word for word, [Note: [Col. 1113D] Probably from memory, dictating to a scribe. Otherwise it would be surprising for him to have expounded Daniel word for word. He was so devoted to the cultivation of memory that, according to Theodore the Reader, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, p. 554, he ordained no one who did not know the Psalter by heart. ERN. CYPRIANUS.] as a commentary. He also composed many homilies. [Note: [Col. 1113D] These writings of Gennadius of Constantinople have perished. For others, see Tillemont, vol. XVI of the *Memoirs*.] He died while Leo the Elder held the empire.

## CHAPTER XCI
[Note: The Codex Viridis Vallis (as Suffridus Petri notes), the Gembloux manuscript, and also Honorius call him Theodorus. Theodulus, or Theodolus in some copies, whom Honorius calls Theodorus, was a presbyter in Coelesyria and later a bishop. He wrote various works which Gennadius lists here; I have not yet learned whether any of them survive. Under the name of Theodulus there are commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul in volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. [But it is established that those works belong to Oecumenius.] MIRAeus.]

THEODULUS, a presbyter in Coelesyria, is said to have written many works. A book of his reached me, which he composed on the Harmony of Sacred Scripture—that is, of the Old and New Testaments—[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “against the heresies of the ancients.”] against the ancient heretics who, because of the difference between the commandments or ceremonies, said that the God of the Old Testament was one and the God of the New Testament another. In this work he showed that it was the dispensation of one and the same God, the author of both Scriptures, that one law should be given to the ancients through Moses in the ceremonies of sacrifices and the penalties of judgments, and another to us through Christ’s presence in the sacred mysteries and future promises. These things should not be believed different, [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “so that they were not dictated by one Christ and one author.” Other editions read: “or not dictated by one Spirit and one author.”] but dictated by one Spirit and one author, [Col. 1114B] since that law which, if observed only according to the letter, kills, is the very same law which, according to its spiritual meaning, gives life. This writer died three years ago, while Zeno was reigning. [Note: Zeno the Isaurian ruled from A.D. 474 to 491; hence it is clear that Gennadius’s catalogue was written no later than A.D. 494. MIRAeus.]

## CHAPTER XCII

[Note: This chapter is missing from most printed editions and manuscript copies. Honorius nevertheless read it in his copy of Gennadius.]

SIDONIUS, [Note: Some copies read “of the Arverni.”] bishop of the Arverni, wrote various agreeable little works [Note: Some copies read “volumes.” The works of Caius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, were revised in our time and published at Paris with explanatory notes by Jacobus Sirmondus and Joannes Savaro, both Arvernians. It is established that he was born to a father and grandfather who had been prefects of the Gauls. Although others hold different opinions about his birthplace, he himself indicates more than once that he was from Lyons. Thus born at Lyons on the Rhône, and instructed by the best teachers of the liberal arts—among them he mentions Haenius in poetry and Eusebius in philosophy—he attained through nature and study such distinction in every field that he was regarded as the most accomplished and eloquent of the learned men of his age, as the praises of Mamertus Claudianus concerning him show. Especially famous for poetry, he was esteemed not only by his contemporary friends but also by the emperors themselves. The first is demonstrated by the poems of every kind that he wrote at the request of friends; the second by the three panegyrics in which, in A.D. 457, he publicly praised his father-in-law Avitus, as well as the emperors Majorian and Anthemius, and received from each the rewards of favor. At Rome, under Avitus, he earned a statue among the poets in the Library of Trajan’s Forum; and when Majorian gave the circenses at Arles, Sidonius was admitted among the honored guests at the emperor’s ceremonial banquet. Finally, after Anthemius had granted him the office of *comes* and other dignities, he was made prefect of the City; Anthemius also rendered patrician his family, which he had received from his ancestors as a prefectorial family.
