Not long afterward, when Eparchius, bishop of the Arverni, had died, Sidonius was appointed his successor in A.D. 472, although unwilling and not yet a cleric. He undertook this office with the utmost modesty and administered it with equal holiness and vigilance during the most turbulent times. First, when Clermont was besieged by the Goths, he endured the hardships of a long and violent assault. Then, after the city had been reduced to the power of the enemy through the treaty made with Nepos, the emperor, he was banished by them under the pretext of an embassy and forced to live in exile for some time. At length restored to his people, he devoted himself to the care of his office and omitted none of the duties of an excellent shepherd among the barbarians, yet he aroused the hatred of his rivals. After these enemies had finally been defeated, he did not long survive; having designated Aprunculus as his successor, he departed to the rewards of heaven in A.D. 482, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, while Zeno was emperor. By his wife Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus, he had children before becoming bishop: a son, Apollinaris, and daughters, Roscia and Severiana. He is honored among the Arverni and elsewhere on a fixed day and according to the rite of the saints, and his sacred bones are reverently preserved in the Basilica of Genesius; they report that they were transferred there long ago from the ancient shrine of St. Saturnus, where he had first been buried. Thus, approximately, Sirmondus. See also the Roman Martyrology, 23 August. MIRAeus.] and works of sound doctrine. For, being thoroughly instructed in both divine and human subjects, and sharp of intellect, he wrote for various people a distinguished volume of letters, composed in different meters or in prose, in which he showed what he could accomplish in literature. Yet, strong in Christian courage even amid the harshness of barbarian savagery, which at that time oppressed the Gauls, he is regarded as an eminent Catholic father and teacher. He flourished at the time when Leo and Zeno ruled the Romans. [Note: He died in A.D. 482.]

## CHAPTER XCIII

[Note: As I suppose, some writings of this John of Antioch survive in the acts of the Council of Ephesus and in volume V of Cyril’s works.]

JOHN, formerly a grammarian and presbyter of the Antiochene parish, wrote against those [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “who assert that Christ, in one substance only, is to be worshiped.”] who assert that Christ is to be worshiped in one substance alone and refuse to confess two natures in Christ. He taught, according to the [Note: The same manuscript reads “reason.”] relation of the Scriptures, that there is in him one person of God and man, not one nature of flesh and the Word. At the same time, he attacks certain statements of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, saying that they were rashly directed against [Note: Some copies read “Nestorius.”] Nestorius and that they give encouragement and strength to the followers of Timothy—an entirely groundless claim. He is said still to be alive and to declaim publicly from time to time.

## CHAPTER XCIV

[Note: This chapter too, although recognized by Honorius and most manuscripts, is absent from some printed editions and manuscript copies. St. Gelasius I, pope, was an African by birth and occupied the see from A.D. 492 to 496. He wrote various letters, which are found in the volumes of the Councils, as well as other works listed by Bellarmine in his catalogue. Bellarmine in the cited passage and Baronius under the year 496 judge that the book *On the Two Natures of Christ against Eutyches*, which is found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, does not belong to Pope Gelasius but to Gelasius of Cyzicus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. Yet Henricus Spondanus, discussing this book in his abridgment of Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 496, added the following note in the margin: “Thus, indeed, most others have hitherto thought, namely, that this little book is not the work of Pope Gelasius. But St. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, who lived at the same time and was likewise African by birth, attributes it to Pope Gelasius without any hesitation, citing much from it in his second reply to the deacon Ferrandus. Many have already shown that the words of this same little book, which heretics twist to their own meaning, do not damage Catholic truth.” Thus Spondanus. We leave the whole matter to be examined more precisely by others. The same Pope Gelasius, after summoning to himself the most learned bishops, issued a distinguished decree concerning canonical and apocryphal books. It survives in full in volume I of the Councils, book III, chapter 217, in Burchard of Worms. Gratian, omitting its first part, quotes the same decree in Distinction 15; and Didacus Covarruvias, bishop of Segovia, explains it with notes in volume II of his *Various Resolutions*, book IV. MIRAeus.]

GELASIUS, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a substantial and distinguished volume against Eutyches and Nestorius, as well as treatises on various Scriptures and sacraments, in polished language. He also wrote letters against Peter and Acacius, which are still held in the Catholic Church. He composed hymns after the manner of Ambrose, the bishop. He died while Anastasius was emperor.

## CHAPTER XCV

HONORATUS, [Note: The Nuremberg manuscript reads “of Constantia.” That letter to Arcadius survives in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and in Baronius under the year 437. But its author is not called Honoratus, but Antonius, bishop of the city of Constantia.] bishop of Constantia, a city of Africa, wrote to a certain Arcadius, who had been sent into exile by King Genseric in the regions of Africa because of his confession of the Catholic faith. The letter encouraged him to endure hardships for Christ and was strengthened both by contemporary examples and by references to Scripture. It taught that perseverance in confessing the faith not only cleanses past sins but also procures the merit of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XCVI

[Note: Cerealis, bishop of Castala in Africa, wrote a book *On the Faith* against Maximinus or Maximianus, which is found in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*. MIRAeus.]

CEREALIS, an African by birth, was asked by Maximinus, an Arian bishop, whether he could establish the Catholic faith briefly and solely by testimonies from divine Scripture, without argumentative assertion. He, in the name of the Lord and with truth supporting him, established it not with the few testimonies which Maximinus had enviously and mockingly demanded [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “from Maximus”; but below the same manuscript has “Maximinus, envious.”] but with abundant evidence from both the Old and New Testaments, and published it in a little book. [Note: The same manuscript reads “the book.”]

## CHAPTER XCVII

[Note: The bishop of Carthage in Africa is called Eusebius by Honorius of Autun, but Eugenius by Trithemius and others. In the commonly circulated copies of Gennadius, Pomerius Maurus and Honoratus of Marseille are added after Eugenius; yet Honorius does not include these two in his catalogue, and therefore they seem not to belong to Gennadius’s catalogue. Isidore, however, in chapter 12, and Sigebert, in chapter 54, mention Pomerius; neither mentions Honoratus of Marseille. In brief—and it will be enough to note this once—the older manuscript copies of Gennadius differ among themselves: in some only Honoratus is omitted, while in others Pomerius, Caesarius of Arles, Sidonius, and Pope Gelasius are also omitted. Nevertheless, so that nothing may be lacking to the curious reader, I shall give the complete century of writers as Suffridus Petrus published it under Gennadius’s title at Cologne in 1580. MIRAeus.]

EUGENIUS, bishop of Carthage, a city of Africa, and a public confessor, was instructed by Huneric, king of the Vandals, to explain the Catholic faith and especially the propriety of the term *homousios*—“of the same substance.” With the agreement of all the bishops and confessors of Africa, Mauretania, Sardinia, and Corsica who remained in the Catholic faith, he composed a *Book of the Faith*, supported not only by statements from the sacred Scriptures but also by the testimonies of the Fathers, and delivered it through his fellow confessors. [Note: It survives, preserved by Victor of Vita in book III of *On the Vandal Persecution*. The rest of Eugenius’s works have perished.]

Now, when he was about to be carried into exile as recompense for his faithful speech, he left letters with his sheep, like reminders of the faith and of the one holy baptism that must be preserved, as a vigilant shepherd. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “He left them for exile in place of a written reminder of the faith.”] He also wrote down the disputations which he had conducted through intermediaries with the Arian bishops and sent them to Huneric through the master of the household. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “He sent them to Huneric.” The Nuremberg manuscript likewise has “Huneric.”] In the same way, he offered the same king prayers for the peace of Christians, as defenses. He is said still to be alive for the strengthening of the Church.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

[Note: This chapter too seems to have been added to Gennadius, since Isidore, chapter 12, and Sigebert, who had not seen Isidore’s book, chapter 54, speak of Julian Pomerius as someone whom Gennadius had omitted. Julian Pomerius is called an African or Moor by Gennadius or his continuator; by Cyprian in the *Life of St. Caesarius of Arles* he is called an inhabitant of Arles, and Isidore of Seville agrees, making him a Gaul. According to the same Isidore, he wrote a book *On Instructing Virgins*, and also three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which, as we showed above in chapter 84, have wrongly been attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine until now. He also wrote, in dialogue form, eight books *On the Nature of the Soul*. These seem to have been excerpted from St. Gregory of Nyssa’s books *On Philosophy*, or rather from the philosopher Nemesius’s books *On the Soul*. He also wrote a *Prognosticon* in three books, entirely different from the work later written by St. Julian, bishop of Toledo, as Baronius observed in his notes on the Martyrology for 8 March and Bellarmine in his catalogue. Isidore of Seville, chapter 12, further accuses Pomerius of a Tertullianic error, because in the books he wrote *On the Nature of the Soul* he attempted to make the soul corporeal. MIRAeus.]

POMERIUS, a Moor by birth, [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “in Gaul.”] ordained a presbyter in Gaul, answered the questions of Bishop Julian and the presbyter Verus according to the method of the dialecticians, using dialectical skill and language suited to his intellect. He composed eight books *On the Nature of the Soul* [Note: The words “and its quality” are absent from the Corbie manuscript.] and its quality, *On the Resurrection*, and *On the Particularity of the Faithful in This Life and the Universality of All Human Beings*. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Eight books on the Resurrection or after the Resurrection.”]

The first of these explains what the soul is and how it is believed to have been made in the image of God. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “How it is fashioned in the image of God.”] The second asks whether the soul should be believed corporeal or incorporeal. The third asks from what the soul of the first human being was made. The fourth asks whether the soul that is to be infused into a body at birth is newly made and without sin, or whether it is drawn from the substance of the soul of the first human being like a shoot from a root and therefore carries with it, by origin, the sin of the first soul. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Whether it is drawn from the substance of the first human soul like a shoot from a root and carries with it even the sin.”] The fifth is a recapitulation of the fourth book, its disputation and distinctions, and explains what the soul’s faculty—that is, its possibility—is, and that it obtains it from one undivided will. [Note: Some copies read “disputations and distinctions.”] The sixth asks, according to the Apostle’s statement, from where the opposition between flesh and spirit comes. The seventh concerns the difference between the lives, deaths, and resurrections of flesh and soul. The eighth concerns the things foretold as future at the end of the world and the solutions to the questions customarily raised about the resurrection. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “On the Resurrection or after the Resurrection.”]

I remember having once read a work of his addressed to someone named Principius, an exhortation *On Contempt for the World and Transitory Things*, and another entitled *On Vices and Virtues*. [Note: “On vices that mock those who are less cautious under the guise of virtues.” He is also said to have written other works. Thus the Corbie manuscript.] He is said to have written other works as well, and still to be writing works that have not come to my knowledge. He lives to this day in a manner worthy of God, with a profession and rank appropriate to his calling. [Note: Some copies read “with a confession.”]

## CHAPTER XCIX

[Note: This chapter is absent from Honorius and from some printed editions and manuscripts. It seems to have been added as a kind of remedy; certainly, according to Suffridus Petri, its style does not resemble Gennadius. While I was obtaining manuscript copies of Gennadius from various places, Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, a theologian of Besançon and a distinguished man, brother of Joannes Jacobus Chiffletius, wrote to me from Besançon on 11 May 1638 as follows: “I possess a very old book of Gennadius of Marseille, not fuller than the printed editions but rather more abbreviated toward the end. It lists Pomerius in its ninety-fifth and final chapter and omits Honoratus of Marseille. Certainly, relying only on the testimony of the commonly published Gennadius, Petrus Saxius in the *Pontifical Register of Arles* attributes the life of St. Hilary of Arles, which the author of the *Lérins Chronicle* assigns to this Honoratus, to Reverentius, or Ravennus, bishop of Arles and Hilary’s successor, on the basis of a manuscript copy. There are other matters as well that make me suspect Gennadius’s mention of Honoratus of Marseille.” MIRAeus.]

[Note: Some utterly incompetent little fellow inserted this account of Honoratus’s life under Gennadius’s name. Its style is plainly different from the manner of writing of our Gennadius. Nor is it found in our manuscripts. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

HONORATUS, bishop of the Church of Marseille, was an eloquent man who, without any impediment of speech, declaimed extemporaneously in church. Because he had grown from childhood in the fear of God and had also been trained in ecclesiastical affairs, he opened his mouth like a treasury and composed many works in the manner of homilies for the benefit of readers, especially for cultivating the rule of faith and refuting the perversity of heretics. [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “composed.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads “for inculcating.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads “of heresies.”]

In his frank steadfastness in preaching, not only the priests and peoples of neighboring cities take delight, but also those who live far away. Whenever he must go to them, they earnestly ask him to teach in their churches. The holy Pope Gelasius, pontiff of the city of Rome, recognizing through written testimony the integrity of his faith, judged it approved in his reply. [Note: Some copies read “judged it proved.”]

He himself also adapts the Lives of the holy Fathers for reading, for the edification of posterity, especially the life of his foster father Hilary, bishop of Arles. With the people entrusted to him, he performs litanies, as far as he is able, to implore God’s mercy. [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “to incline.”]

## CHAPTER C

[Note: This chapter too is absent from many printed editions and manuscripts.]

I, [Note: Gennadius of Marseille was a presbyter, not a bishop, as Sigebert and Platina judged. He lived during the reigns of the emperor Anastasius and Pope Gelasius I. Besides the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, mentioned by Cassiodorus in *On Divine Readings*, chapter 17, and now reproduced by me, various writings of Gennadius survive, including a book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which he dedicated to Pope Gelasius. More than eight hundred years ago, the clergy of Lyons, writing against John Scotus Eriugena in the case of Gottschalk, warned that this book had falsely been attributed to St. Augustine. We have already noted above in the prolegomena and elsewhere that Gennadius was a semi-Pelagian and therefore must be read cautiously in many passages. MIRAeus.]

[Note: Vossius discusses Gennadius in *Latin History*, book XI, chapter 18, p. 235, and in *Pelagian History*, book I, chapter 10. Henricus de Noris, in book XI of his *Pelagian History*, chapter 16, discusses learnedly the date when this catalogue was written; Cavius, part I, p. 266, disagrees, since he wants the book to have been written in the year A.D. 495. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

GENNADIUS, a presbyter of Marseille, wrote eight books *Against All Heresies*, six books *Against Nestorius*, [Note: Some copies add: “And eleven books against Eutyches.” The Nuremberg manuscript instead reads: “And six books against Eutyches.” ERN. CYPRIANUS.] three books *Against Pelagius*, and treatises *On the Thousand Years* and *On the Apocalypse of Blessed John*. He also wrote this work and sent a letter *On My Faith* to blessed Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome. [Note: I do not know whether this reading of the Wolfenbüttel manuscript will satisfy learned readers. It is nevertheless plainly evident that Miraeus’s reading—“and this work *On My Faith*”—is inept. This passage scarcely seems capable of being corrected in any other way. ERN. CYPRIANUS.]

## CHRONOLOGICAL INDEX OF THE VANDAL PERSECUTION

**A.D. 406.** While Innocent I was pope, Arcadius emperor in the East and Honorius in the West, and Arcadius Augustus and Anicius Probus were consuls for the sixth time, toward the end of the year of the common era, the Vandals, abandoning their own settlements and invading Gaul, were defeated by the Franks. Shortly afterward, with the help of the Alans, they put the Franks to flight; and when their king Godegisel was killed amid these disturbances, they substituted his son Gunderic and thus entered Gaul with the other barbarians.

**A.D. 407.** Various martyrs were crowned throughout Gaul by the Vandals during this year and the next.

**A.D. 408.** Paulus Orosius and other authors assign the Vandal invasion of Gaul to this year. Theodosius the Younger succeeded his father Arcadius. Stilicho was killed by the army at Ravenna, and his son Eucherius at Rome, although, despite being a pagan, he had been designated for the imperial power.

**A.D. 409.** Alaric besieged Rome. In the same year, according to Prosper and Hydatius, the Vandals, Suebi, and other barbarians migrated from Gaul into Spain.

**A.D. 410.** Attalus, an Arian, was made emperor by Alaric and shortly afterward deposed by him. Rome was captured and plundered by the Goths under their king Alaric.

**A.D. 411.** Alaric died. The Goths buried him in the middle of the bed of the Busento River near Consentia, together with immense riches, after temporarily diverting the waters and later restoring them to their course. A conference was held at Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists before the count and notary Marcellinus, by order of the emperor Honorius.

**A.D. 412.** The errors of Caelestius were condemned at the Council of Carthage.

**A.D. 413.** Marcellinus the tribune, who had acted as the representative of the emperor at the conference, was killed by Count Marinus at the instigation of the Donatists. For this reason he was listed among the martyrs in the Roman Martyrology on 6 April.

**A.D. 415.** Athaulf, whom Placidia, the sister of Honorius, had married after being captured during the sack of Rome, was killed by a certain Goth because he seemed to favor the Romans.

**A.D. 416.** The Council of Carthage was held against the errors of Pelagius, and another council was held at Milevis in Numidia against the same heretics. After Athaulf’s death Placidia was returned to the Romans and married Constantius. The relics of St. Stephen were brought from Palestine to Africa by the presbyter Orosius.

**A.D. 417.** Zosimus was appointed to the Roman Church in place of Innocent.

**A.D. 418.** Valentinian, later emperor, was born to Constantius and Placidia. Pelagius was condemned at Rome and again at Carthage. Boniface became Roman pontiff after the death of Zosimus, although the schismatic Eulalius opposed him.

**A.D. 419.** The Romans and Africans disputed the question of appeals to the apostolic see.

**A.D. 420.** Constantius, the father of Valentinian III, was declared Augustus by Honorius. St. Jerome died.

**A.D. 421.** The temple of the goddess Caelestis at Carthage was destroyed at the request of Bishop Aurelius. The emperor Constantius died.

**A.D. 422.** Castinus, master of the soldiers, undertook an expedition against the Vandals in Spain, but with an unsuccessful outcome. Augustine disputed in Africa against Maximinus, an Arian bishop of the Goths.

**A.D. 423.** Pope Caelestine succeeded Boniface. Honorius sent his sister Placidia and her son Valentinian to Constantinople because he suspected that she had summoned the barbarians into Italy. Shortly afterward Honorius died, and Joannes, chief of the notaries, seized the imperial power.

**A.D. 424.** Valentinian III, son of Constantius and Placidia, was made Caesar at Constantinople by Theodosius the Younger. The tyrant Joannes was killed at Ravenna, although Cassiodorus assigns his death to the following year.

**A.D. 425.** Valentinian was proclaimed Augustus at Ravenna.

**A.D. 426.** In this year or the next, Gunderic, son of Godegisel and king of the Vandals in Spain, died. His brother Genseric succeeded him, born, however, of a concubine; according to Gregory of Tours, he began a persecution in Spain.

**A.D. 427.** War was publicly declared against Boniface, who had refused to come from Africa to Rome. He, however, summoned the Vandals into Africa after making a treaty with them. Hierius and Ardabur were consuls.

**A.D. 428.** Some writers say that the Vandals arrived in Africa in this year. Theodosius the Younger renewed the edicts issued against the heretics.

**A.D. 429.** Around this time Count Darius was sent to Africa to end the war. He recalled Boniface to obedience to the emperor.

**A.D. 430.** Hippo was besieged by the Vandals, and in the third month of the siege Augustine, its bishop and an outstanding teacher of the entire Catholic Church, died.

**A.D. 431.** The general Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, at which no one from Africa was present except Bessula, deacon of Capreolus, bishop of Carthage. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, a most holy man, died at the age of seventy-eight. Sixtus III was appointed Roman pontiff in place of the deceased Caelestine.

**A.D. 432.** Count Boniface returned from Africa to Italy. Shortly afterward he was made master of the soldiers but died from a wound received in battle against Aetius.

**A.D. 435.** Peace was made with the Vandals through Trigetius; Prosper, in Canisius’s edition, gives a period of three years, with a portion of Africa itself left to them for habitation.

**A.D. 437.** The persecution begun by Genseric commenced; in it Arcadius and his companions were crowned with martyrdom. Valentinian went to Constantinople to marry Eudoxia, daughter of Theodosius.

**A.D. 438.** Barbarian pirates harassed Sicily and the neighboring islands with repeated invasions.

**A.D. 439.** Genseric invaded Carthage and drove Bishop Quodvultdeus into exile aboard an old ship with most of the clergy. In a single stroke he stripped Carthage of its shepherd, clergy, sacred places, and senate. Salvianus, a presbyter of Marseille, wrote books *On Divine Providence*, in which there is much concerning the Vandals raging in Gaul, Spain, and Africa.

**A.D. 440.** St. Leo, surnamed the Great, was appointed to the Roman Church after the death of Pope Sixtus. Genseric invaded Sicily, but later, fearing Count Sebastian, abandoned Sicily and returned to Carthage.

**A.D. 441.** Theodosius prepared an army against Genseric, but without success.

**A.D. 442.** When the Huns were devastating the eastern provinces, Theodosius was forced to recall the army he had sent against the Vandals. Peace between Valentinian and Genseric was renewed. Around this time, apparently, St. Leo sent the legate Potentius to Mauretania to restore ecclesiastical discipline. Genseric persecuted the Catholics in his dominions and even treated harshly those of his own people who had conspired against him.

**A.D. 443.** The Manichaeans were discovered at Rome by St. Leo. Most of them, after Africa had been devastated by Genseric, had withdrawn to the City.

**A.D. 444.** After killing his brother Bleda, Attila ruled the Huns alone. A council was held at Rome against the Manichaeans.

**A.D. 445.** A constitution of Valentinian III was issued against the Manichaeans.

**A.D. 450.** Marcian became emperor in the East after Theodosius the Younger died without sons. Placidia, mother of Valentinian, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

**A.D. 451.** Attila, king of the Huns, entered Gaul and devastated various cities. Finally, after a battle was fought in the Catalaunian Plains, he was put to flight by Aetius and the other allied forces. Meroveus, king of the Franks, and Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, were killed there. A general synod was held at Chalcedon against Eutyches.

**A.D. 452.** Attila invaded Italy and devastated Aquileia. Overcome by the entreaties of Pope Leo, he withdrew to Pannonia.

**A.D. 453.** Attila died in Pannonia, although Count Marcellinus records his death under the following year. Pulcheria Augusta, wife of Marcian, died; she earned a place in the sacred calendar.

**A.D. 454.** Deogratias was ordained bishop of Carthage. Aetius was killed by Valentinian.

**A.D. 455.** After Valentinian was killed, Petronius Maximus seized the imperial power; shortly afterward he too was killed. Genseric plundered Rome, transported the empresses with an immense multitude of captives to Carthage, then devastated all Africa, the neighboring islands, and various regions and subjected them to his rule. Eparchius Avitus became emperor.

**A.D. 456.** Avitus was forced by Ricimer to lay down the imperial purple and became bishop of Piacenza.

**A.D. 457.** Deogratias, bishop of Carthage, died. Genseric ordered the Catholic churches closed and the clergy driven into exile. After the death of the emperor Marcian, Leo the Great, or Marcelles, became emperor of the East, and Julius Majorian was appointed to the Western empire, a man worthy of better times.

**A.D. 458.** Majorian prepared an army against the Vandals, but his efforts failed because Genseric seized the ships on the coast of Spain.

**A.D. 461.** The emperor Majorian was killed by Ricimer, who caused Libius Severus to be created Augustus at Ravenna. Hilary succeeded Pope Leo.

**A.D. 465.** The emperor Severus was killed at Rome by poison through Ricimer’s agency.

**A.D. 466.** The Romans were completely expelled from Spain by Euric, king of the Visigoths.

**A.D. 467.** After an interregnum of two years, Flavius Anthemius was proclaimed Augustus. Leo Augustus sent him into Italy with an army for this purpose. Pope Simplicius succeeded the deceased Hilary. Through the treachery of Basiliscus, Leo’s expedition against the Vandals failed.

**A.D. 468.** The patrician Marcellinus was treacherously stabbed by Romans fighting against the Vandals, at the very time when he was bringing them aid. Fulgentius was born at Telepte in Byzacena.

**A.D. 469.** Patriciolus, the Arian son of Aspar, was made Caesar, despite the protests of the Catholics, who demanded an orthodox Caesar.

**A.D. 471.** Aspar and his sons Ardabur and Patriciolus Caesar, supporters of the Arian sect, were killed in the palace by Leo’s order, although some assign this event to the preceding year.

**A.D. 472.** The emperor Anthemius was killed at Rome through Ricimer’s treachery. Through Ricimer’s agency Anicius Olybrius ascended the throne; but, according to Cassiodorus, Ricimer died on the fortieth day after these crimes had been committed.

**A.D. 473.** After Olybrius died, Flavius Glycerius assumed the imperial power at Ravenna. Leo the Younger was proclaimed Augustus in the East by his grandfather.

**A.D. 474.** After Glycerius was expelled, Julius Nepos was proclaimed Augustus. After Leo, emperor of the East, died, Zeno administered the empire on behalf of his son Leo the Younger, whom he had fathered by Ariadne, daughter of the emperor Leo. Soon afterward he was crowned by that same son and proclaimed Augustus. Leo the Younger died immediately afterward.

**A.D. 475.** The patrician Orestes, having expelled Nepos, transferred the imperial power to his son Romulus Augustus, or Augustulus.

**A.D. 476.** Peace was made between the emperor Zeno and Genseric. Basiliscus, after expelling Zeno, occupied the imperial power for twenty months. Odoacer, king of the Heruli, killed Orestes, expelled Augustulus, and captured Rome. Rejecting the title of emperor together with the purple and imperial insignia, and content with the name of king alone, he established a new kingdom in Italy, and thus the Western empire was extinguished.

**A.D. 477.** Genseric, king of the Vandals and conqueror of the two most powerful cities in the world, died at the beginning of this year. His son Huneric succeeded him, more cruel toward the Catholics than his father. Zeno drove out Basiliscus and forced him, after his capture, into exile in Cappadocia, where he died of starvation.

**A.D. 480.** Nepos, long before expelled from the imperial power by Orestes, was killed at his own villa not far from the city of Salona.

**A.D. 481.** Eugenius was ordained bishop of Carthage, and shortly afterward persecution against the Catholics began.

**A.D. 482.** Zeno promulgated the edict of Henoticon, or Union.

**A.D. 483.** Pope Felix II succeeded Simplicius. Persecution against the orthodox in Africa grew worse. Among others, Liberatus the abbot completed a glorious martyrdom at Carthage with six other monks. Huneric issued an edict for a conference to be held at Carthage the following year.

**A.D. 484.** A conference between the Catholic bishops and the Arians was held at Carthage by Huneric’s command. A severe famine raged in Africa. Huneric, with the eighth year of his reign almost completed, departed this life, and Guntabundus, son of Gento, succeeded him.

**A.D. 486.** Around this time St. Fulgentius assumed the monastic habit.

**A.D. 487.** Peace was granted to the African Church to some extent, with Eugenius restored to his see. A Roman council was held under Pope Felix concerning the reception into penance of those who had fallen in Africa. Victor of Vita wrote his *History of the Vandal Persecution*.

**A.D. 488.** Pope Felix wrote to the African bishops prescribing the manner in which those who had fallen were to be received into penance.

**A.D. 489.** King Theodoric first entered Italy after defeating Odoacer twice. Theodoric besieged Odoacer, who was shut up at Ravenna.

**A.D. 490.** After the Vandals requested peace from King Theodoric, they ceased their customary plundering of Sicily.

**A.D. 491.** Anastasius succeeded the emperor Zeno.

**A.D. 492.** Gelasius succeeded Pope Felix.

**A.D. 493.** Odoacer was killed by King Theodoric. From this point the beginnings of the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy are to be reckoned. Theodoric established his royal residence at Ravenna.

In the year 494. Guntabundus permitted the churches of Africa to be reopened and the exiled bishops to return to their own churches.

In the year 495. Baronius writes that in this year Eugenius of Carthage died after being driven into exile, but incorrectly.—Pope Gelasius, in a letter to the bishops of Dardania, praises the steadfastness of Eugenius and the other African bishops.

In the year 496. Guntabundus, king of the Vandals, died; his brother Trasamundus succeeded him. [Col. 1123]—Pope Anastasius II was elected after the death of Gelasius.—Clovis, the first Christian king of the Franks, was baptized at Reims by Saint Remigius, together with most of the leading men of that nation. Hence Remigius was rightly called the apostle of the Frankish nation, and especially of our kings.

In the year 499. Symmachus became Roman pontiff in place of Pope Anastasius, who had died; against him Laurentius raised a serious schism, later suppressed by the authority of King Theodoric.—A conference between Catholic bishops and Arians took place at Sarbiniacum, and then at Lyon in the presence of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians; there the Arians were defeated, chiefly through the efforts of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne.

In the year 500. King Theodoric came to Rome; at that time Saint Fulgentius heard him delivering an oration.

In the year 505. Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, died in exile at Albi in Gaul.

In the year 507. In this year, apparently, the Byzacene Fathers assembled and resolved, contrary to the king’s command, to appoint bishops to the sees of deceased bishops.

In the year 508. Fulgentius became bishop of Ruspe. He built a monastery in his city and shortly afterward was led away into exile.

In the year 514. Hormisdas succeeded Pope Symmachus.

In the year 517. Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, renounced the Arian heresy and, at the urging of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, became a Catholic.

In the year 518. Justin succeeded Anastasius as emperor; he was a most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith.

In the year 519. Peace was made between the Eastern and Western Churches.—That celebrated controversy began to be stirred up concerning the proposition, “One of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh,” which the Scythian monks defended.

In the year 521. Fulgentius and the other Byzacene bishops held a council in Sardinia against the errors of Faustus; the synodal letter of this council is preserved among the works of Saint Fulgentius.

In the year 523. Trasamundus died and was succeeded by Hilderic, the son of Huneric. He restored peace to the African Church by recalling the bishops from exile.—Boniface was ordained bishop of Carthage. [Col. 1124]—John I became Roman pontiff after the death of Hormisdas.

In the year 524. The Council of Junca was held in Byzacena under Liberatus the primate, and shortly afterward the Council of Sufes in the same province.

In the year 525. The Council of Carthage was held under Boniface.—Pope John was sent by Theodoric to Constantinople. He was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to be honorably received by Justin Augustus, and he diligently attended to the affairs of the Church; on the holy day of Easter he celebrated in the Roman manner and in the Latin language. On his return to Ravenna, he was thrown into prison by the king and subjected to many hardships.

In the year 526. When Pope John died in prison at Ravenna, Felix III was substituted for him.—Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, died.

In the year 527. After the death of Justin, Justinian was proclaimed Augustus.

In the year 529. Saint Benedict moved from Subiaco to Mount Cassino, where the most celebrated monastery in the whole world was built.

In the year 530. Boniface II succeeded Felix as Roman pontiff; against him Dioscorus, aspiring to the pontificate, stirred up a schism.

In the year 531. Gelimer, having expelled Hilderic and held him in chains, seized the Vandal kingdom in Africa.

In the year 532. John, surnamed Mercury, was raised to the see of the deceased Boniface.

In the year 533. On the first day of this year Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, died.—Gelimer also killed many of his own nobles.

In the year 534. After Carthage had been captured by Belisarius, and Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals, who shortly before had killed Hilderic, had been defeated and sent in triumph to Constantinople, Africa was restored to imperial rule.

In the year 535. Boniface, bishop of Carthage, died; Reparatus was immediately substituted for him and held a general council of all Africa at Carthage in the basilica of Faustus.

After the death of John, Agapetus was placed over the Roman Church. He congratulated Reparatus and the bishops of Africa on the restoration of the Church’s liberty. Justinian also enacted many measures for the benefit of the Church and the peoples of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 1199] These indexes refer only to the works of Gennadius of Marseille in columns 979–1054 of this volume. In these indexes, Arabic numerals refer to column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

[Col. 1199]

# INDEX OF MEMORABLE SUBJECTS AND WORDS

## A

They think that even malformed aborted fetuses will rise again: Tichonius the African, Augustine, Philip the presbyter, and Bede, 122, 123. Scholastic theologians deny this, ibid. Abraham’s bosom, 179, 180. Abstinence from meat and wine is praiseworthy, 36, 162. If Adam had not sinned, he would have been immortal, 19. When he fell, we all fell, and in both body and soul we were changed for the worse, 22, 139, 140. Nor can we do anything good unless the grace of divine mercy has gone before us, 27. Adam was in hell before Christ’s birth and resurrection, 177, 179.

Aetius the heretic, 4. He asserts that the Son is unlike the Father in every respect, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son, 117.

Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, the first author of rebaptizing, 143.

Angels were created before the sensible world, 127. They do not know the secrets of the heart, 184. They are bounded by place, 130. Their nature is mutable, 34, 159. They are holy by participation, not by nature, 158. After Satan’s fall they were so established that they can no longer fall at all, 35, 160. They are called holy because of the most beautiful and blameless ministry they offer to God, 158. Many of the ancients attribute bodies to them; yet the truer opinion declares their nature to be ἀσώματον (*asōmaton*, incorporeal), 8, 128. Scripture gives no certain account of their creation, 127. Hence the apostate Julian also accuses Moses of ignorance because he did not explicitly mention their creation, ibid. Angelic dignity does not suffer death, 8, 130.

The soul is so called because it animates the body in order to give it life, 11, 135. It is incorporeal, 44, 132. There is one soul, not two, in one human being, 9, 132. It comes into this world without sin and now sins by its own will, 131. Through baptism it comes back to life, 61. It was not from the beginning among the intellectual creatures, as heretics invent, 9, 130, 131. Nor is it generated through intercourse with bodies, ibid. Its creation is known to God alone, 9, 10, 131, 132. It is immortal and does not die with the body, as Epicurus and Aratus foolishly assert, 132, 133. Before Christ’s passion and resurrection, the souls of the saints were held in hell, 41, 177, 178, 179. The souls of the devout, once released from their bodies, go immediately to God in paradise; those of the impious go to the devil, εἰς τοὺς ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ τόπους (*eis tous en tō hadē topous*, “to the places in Hades”), 102, 183.

The souls of animals are born with the birth of the flesh itself and end with the death of the flesh, 10, 133. They are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, 133. Rather, nature leads them toward every form of impulse, ibid.

The Antidicomarianites deny that Mary remained a virgin after giving birth, 146.

The Anthropomorphites imagine God as corporeal and fashion him for themselves with human limbs and appearance, 118.

The Apellites think that Christ suffered only fictitiously, 110.

The Apollinarists say that the Λόγος (*Logos*, Word) was changed by conversion into the Godhead, 3, 107. They strive to separate the rational soul from Christ, 109. They attribute the passion to the Godhead, 112. They affirm that Christ assumed flesh not truly but only δοκήσει (*dokēsei*, “in appearance”) and putatively, and that he possessed the Godhead in place of a rational soul, 108, 109.

The water of sanctification, 62. The use of water in the sacrament of the Eucharist, 173, 174. It is not necessary to the sacrament, 175. The Aquarians, heretics, offer only water in the sacramental cup, 174.

The Arabians say that the soul is mortal, 132. Aratus foolishly believes that the soul perishes with the body, 10, 132. The Armenians assign the passion to the Godhead, 112. They do not use water in the sacred rites, 175.

Those who think that thoughts are inserted into human beings by the devil must be refuted, 185.

Arius tears apart the Holy Trinity by profane division, 2, 102. He imagines in it a greater and a lesser, 118. He asserts that the Father was not always Father, 110. He subjects the divinity to suffering, 112. He denies that the Son is ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, of the same substance) with the Father, 120. He calls Catholics ὁμοουσιασταί (*homoousiastai*, “homoousians”), ibid. He blasphemously says that Christ is the Son of God only by μετοχή (*metochē*, participation) and κατὰ θέσιν (*kata thesis*, by designation), 120. He presents him as changeable, after the manner of creatures, 157. He sacrilegiously dared to proclaim that the Father, invisible by nature, is not seen even by the Son, 119.

[Col. 1200]

Artemon the heretic, 4. He maintains that our Savior was a mere human being, 116.

## B

There is one baptism in the Catholic Church, administered in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 29, 139, 141, 142. Punic Christians call baptism salvation, 169. The baptism of blood, 137. Yet Gennadius wrongly equates it with baptism, ibid. Baptism is invisibly completed when a necessity prevents its administration, 171. It is no baptism if it is not given in the faith of the Holy Trinity, 142. Those baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should not be rebaptized, 142. Those not baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be baptized, 146 and following. The baptized must live chastely, 103. The person to be baptized confesses his faith, 173, 174. Only the baptized have the way of salvation, 39, 158, 171. Infants must be baptized, so that through regeneration what they acquired through generation may be cleansed, 20. The baptized did not eat with idolaters, 162. The fruit of baptism is denied to one who refuses baptism, not to one who was unable to receive it, 171.

Barbatianus equates marriage with virginity consecrated to God, 163.

The basilicas of the holy martyrs should be visited with most devout affection, 39, 168.

Basilides the heretic says that Christ appeared to human beings in fantasy, 109. He says that souls sinned in heaven before they were born, 131.

Bellarminus falsely writes that the Eucharist was given to children under at least one species, 145.

Berillus blasphemously confessed that Christ did not exist before the birth of the flesh, 4, 116.

Bimariti: men twice married are not to be ordained clerics, 38, 165.

It is blasphemy to say that God suffered in that condition in which he is God, 112 and following.

The Bohemians also offer the Eucharist to newly born children, 145.

It is good to distribute one’s resources to the poor, 146.

It is good to receive food with thanksgiving, 161.

Marriage is good, but virginity is better, 161.

The Bonosians, 30. They contend that Christ is God’s adoptive son, not his proper Son, 447.

The Borborites, impure heretics, 30, 146.

## C
To be free from every sin belongs to God alone, 187. Our flesh is good, created by God, 40, 176. By the will of the soul it becomes good or evil in us, ibid. Our flesh will rise incorruptible, yet it will not lose the essence of true nature, 124. In it the soul will undergo what properly belongs to the body, according as it has acted, whether well or badly, 40. Christ’s flesh did not experience corruption, 6, 124. It is truly human, 109. And endowed with a rational soul, ibid. It was not confused with the Godhead, 108. It was not merely apparent or phantom-like, 109. It was assumed from the Virgin Mary alone, not from a man, 9. It is adored by angels and every creature, 121, 122.

Carpocrates blasphemously said that Christ was merely a human being (ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον), 116. The holy Fathers prefer chastity to the works of marriage, 164. Catechumens, the possessed, and penitents do not participate in the sacred mysteries, 144. When they were present, the offering (πρόσφορα) was not made, ibid. They are condemned if they depart this world without holy baptism, 171.

Cerdo, the heretic, introduces two mutually contrary principles, 147. He impiously asserts that Christ was not a true human being, 109. He affirms that Christ suffered only according to appearance (κατὰ φαντασίαν), 110. Cerinthus, in a delirious error, invents a fable of a thousand years in which marriage, food, and earthly pleasures are again promised, 154. He impiously believes that Christ was at least merely a human being, 148.

Chrism in baptism, 30, 144. Christians sometimes abstain from meat and wine as bodily discipline, 162.

Christ is the eternal Son of God by nature, not by adoption, 104. He was not born of a virgin in such a way that, by being born, a human being received the beginning of divinity, 4, 116, 117. Rather, the eternal God before the ages was born as a human being from the Virgin, ibid. He appeared to human beings not in a phantom [Col. 1201] but in true flesh, 109. In that flesh, both before the Passion and during the Passion, he endured real sufferings, 3, 115. His flesh did not experience corruption, 6, 124. He is adored by angels and every creature, 5, 121. With his fleshly eyes he always beholds the Father, 119. He is the same God who is human, and the same human being who is God—not by confusion of nature but by unity of person, 108. He is not God by position (θέσει) or by participation (μετοχῇ), as Arius blasphemes, 120. In him two natures are united without confusion, without change, and inseparably, 106, 108. In his humanity he experienced what belongs to humanity; in his divinity he remained impassible, 110, 111, 112. Christ, God and human being, is not two persons but one person (πρόσωπον), 105. Christ is eternal in divinity and temporal in the flesh, 4, 103. He was born not from intercourse with a man but from the Holy Spirit, 108. He did not bring flesh with him from heaven but assumed it from the Virgin Mary, 108, 117. He possessed a true body and an intellectual soul (ψυχὴν νοεράν), with their proper attributes, 109. He was perfect human being and perfect God, 106. By his coming he redeemed human beings from eternal destruction, 13. He will judge the living and the dead, 6. He descended into hell so that he might make all the saints who were held there share in himself, 178, 179. In wine from the vine he instituted the sacrament of his body, 175. It is good to take food with thanksgiving, 36, 161. Ancient Christians marked it with the sign of the cross, 161.

The Encratites, Tatian, Jovinian, Manichaeus, and Priscillian reject the foods that God created for use, 163. The Claudinians deny that Mary remained a virgin after childbirth, 164.

A cleric cannot be twice-married, 30. Nor can one who has had a concubine, a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute in marriage, 165, 166. Nor one who has castrated himself, 38, 166. Nor one convicted of having taken interest or acted on the stage, ibid. Nor one who has performed public penance, 167. Nor one who has gone insane or has been afflicted by the devil, 167. Nor one who offers money, ibid.

The devil does not know the inward thoughts of the soul, 42, 184. Not all evil thoughts are stirred up by the devil, 42, 185. Both good and evil thoughts come forth from the heart, 186.

Daily communion in the primitive Church, 148. It was abolished when charity grew cold, 149. Gennadius neither praises nor condemns it, 150. It is not given to parricides, performers of mime, actors, prostitutes, or public usurers, 152.

Confession in baptism, 143. The goodness of continence, 36, 160. God alone knows the secrets of the heart, 42, 185.

Many Greek and Latin Fathers attribute bodies to angels, 129. Yet the opinion of those who assert that angels are incorporeal is more correct, 130. The resurrected bodies will be free from corruption, yet they will not lose the essence of true nature, 124.

All creatures, bodily and intellectual, were made by God from nothing, not from the nature of God, 119. Nothing in them belongs to the essence of the Trinity, ibid. All creatures are good, 35, 158. All are bodily, 130. All are mutable, 159. Ancient Christians marked food with the cross, 167.

Cyprian’s error concerning the rebaptism of heretics, 143. He is excused, ibid. Cyril says that souls are transmitted through generation, 9. Cyril of Alexandria is falsely accused of attributing suffering to the Godhead, 112.

## D

Demons are, in substance, of angelic nature, 8. They have bodies, but bodies so subtle that they cannot be perceived by the senses, 129. They do not know the thoughts of the heart, 185. They infer them from a person’s outward movements, ibid. They cannot substantially fill the human mind, 186. They hide in statues, 76. Their torments will be eternal, 125, 126.

The possessed are not admitted to the clerical order, 167. We are debtors to God, 189. Christ’s descent into hell, 178 and following. The Godhead did not experience suffering on the cross, 110, 112.

There is one God, 97, 98. He is called Father because he truly has a Son born from him, ibid., 98. He is alone, but not solitary, 98. He is wholly good and goodness itself, 128. From nothing, not from pre-existing matter, he created all things, 7, 126. He is one and triune, 98. He is incorporeal, 8, 128. He is immutable, 34, 156. He is invisible to all creatures, 119. He is everywhere and fills all things, 8. Nothing in creatures is substantially like him, 119. He alone knows the secrets of the heart, 24, 185. He does not will the death of the sinner, 42, 156. He did not create evil, 156. Nor is he the author of evils, 158. Nor did he predestine any human being to evil, 155, 156.

God is not confused with a human being but united to one, 105. How God assumed a human being is to be understood, 107. [Col. 1202]

The devil was created good by God, 33, 157. He discovered evil and became evil by thinking evil thoughts, 33, 35, 156. He does not know the thoughts of the heart, 42, 185. From human actions he gathers the secrets of the mind, ibid. He was conquered through Christ’s cross, 71. He will be tormented forever, 126. Muhammad deliriously claims that he was formed from a flame of fire, 127.

Didymus introduces a third spirit into the substance of the human being, 11, 134. Diodorus, the heretic, 124. Dionysius is falsely accused of Arianism, 117. Dioscorus improperly maintains that the Godhead suffered on the cross, 112. The error of the Docetists concerning Christ’s Passion, 110.

Dogmas are the opinions of sects, 97. Before Gennadius, Musanus and Didymus of Alexandria wrote about ecclesiastical dogmas, ibid.

On Sundays all whose minds are free from the inclination to sin should frequently receive communion in the churches, 31, 149. A human being consists of only two substances, 10, 134.

## E

Ebion, the heresiarch, says that Christ was born from intercourse with a man, 3, 108. The Church of God, because of the excellence of its celebration of sacred rites, does not admit a twice-married man to the priesthood, 165.

The elements—that is, heaven and earth—will not perish completely but will be changed for the better, 164. Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, writes that Christ is the Son of God by adoption, not by nature, 104. The Encratites reject the eating of meat as unclean, 163. Epicurus says that death has nothing to do with us, since when death is present, we are not, 132.

In the primitive Church the faithful were accustomed to receive the Eucharist daily, 31, 148, 149. Gennadius neither praises nor condemns this, ibid. Nevertheless, he advises communion every Sunday if the mind is free from the inclination to sin, ibid. In former times it was also given to newly baptized children, 145. It must be received with a pure mind and sincere heart, 150, 151. It should first be given to children when they have reached the years of discernment and the age of understanding, 146. It is the medicine of immortality, 203. Punic Christians call it “life,” 169.

Eunomius does not enter the basilicas of the martyrs, 168. Nor does he honor their relics, ibid. He says that Christ had flesh without a soul, 3. He asserts that the Trinity is unequal, 4, 117. He teaches that the Godhead was changed into flesh, 110. Against the tradition of the apostles, he established that holy baptism should be performed with a single immersion, 142.

Eutyches, the heretic, 3. He says that the Lord’s body descended from heaven and passed through the Virgin as through a channel, 108. He invented the claim that the Savior appeared “in mere imagination and in the empty outline of a human body” (Φαντασίᾳ ψιλῇ καὶ σχήματι διακένῳ σώματος ἀνθρωπίνου), 109. He attributes suffering to the Godhead, 112. After the resurrection he asserts that our bodies will become intangible, 123.

Exorcism before baptism, 17, 138. Its rite is very ancient, ibid. Nevertheless, no command concerning it exists in Holy Scripture, ibid. Nor do Justin Martyr and Tertullian mention it in their writings, ibid.

From nothing God created heaven and earth, 7, 126.

## F

No creature can see the face of God according to the property of his nature, 67, 119.

Felix of Urgell, in sacrilegious audacity, said that Christ is God’s adopted Son, not his proper and natural Son, 104.

The form of the world, not its substance, will pass away, 37.

The Son of God is eternal, 2, 58. He became the Son of a human being, 103, 114. His body was animated by a rational soul, 3, 109. He is not God’s adopted Son but his natural Son, 104. Nor is he so by position (κατὰ θέσιν), as Arius blasphemes, but truly so, 3, 120. He is consubstantial (ὁμοούσιος) and coessential with the Father, 101, 102. He alone assumed flesh, not the Father and the Holy Spirit, 103. He is called Only-begotten, 105. He is one alone, not two, 2, 104. He is immutable like the Father, 157. He is adored by angels and every creature together with his flesh, 5, 121, 122. He did not become a human being apart from God; rather, the human being is in God and God in the human being, 5, 103. He was not confused with flesh but united to it, 3, 106, 108. He is called Son because he has the Father, 99. Before he was born from the Virgin, he was God, 4, 68. On the third day he rose from the dead, 58. No one will be able to escape his eyes, ibid. The Holy Spirit also proceeds from him as from the Father, 99, 100.

Florianus, the heretic, teaches that our flesh, which is evil, was created by God, 40, 176.

## G

Gennadius rejects the fable of purgatorial fire (πυρκαθαρτήριον), 183. He wrongly equates baptism of blood with true baptism, 173. He believes that before Christ’s Passion and resurrection all the souls of the saints were in hell, 177.

God’s grace helps us not to sin, 15, 137. It is freely granted to us, 23, 24. Thanksgiving after taking food, 161.

The Greeks do not communicate daily but on feast days and Sundays, 119. In the mysteries they do not mix water with wine, 174. Nevertheless, they truly consecrate the sacrament, ibid. If any of them pass two or three Sundays without communion, they are excommunicated, 150.

## H

Specific names of heretics: Aetius, 4. Alexander, 10. Antidicomarites, 164. Aratus, 10. Arabians, 132. Arius, 2, 4. Actemon, 4, 31. Barbatianus, 163. Basilides, 130. Berillus, 4. Bonosians, 30, 147. Borborites, 30, 146. Cerdon, 30. Cerinthus, 31, 3. Claudinians, 164. Diodorus, 6. Ebion, 3, 31. Encratites, 163. Epicurus, 10. Eunomius, 3, 4, 39. Eutyches, 3. Florianus, 40, 176. Fortunatus, 4. Helvidius, 37. Hermogenes, 126. Hieracites, 37. Hydroparastates, 174. Jacobus Syrus, 9, 132. Jovinianus, 37, 136. Luciferians, 9, 131. Macedonians, 4. Muhammadans, 125, 127. Manichaeans, 30, 37, 40. Marcellus, 4. Marcianus, 3. Marcion, 3, 4, 30, 32. Melito, 4, 32. Menander, 142. Montanists, 30, 147. Nestorius, 5. Novatus, 24. Ophites, 40, 176. Patricians, 40, 176. Paulinians, 30. Pelagius, 22. Philolaus, 131. Photinians, 30, 31. Plato, 10, 131. Praxeas, 5. Priscillians, 30, 131. Proclians, 30. Sabellius, 24. Sarmatio, 163. Seleucus, 126. Sethians, 30. Siphorites, 30. Sylvanus, 5. Tatianus, 163. Theodosius, 148. Timothians, 3. Vadians, 4. Valentinus, 30, 139. Venustians, 176. Vigilantius, 39, 168. Zeno, 10.

Heretics who have not been baptized among heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are baptized by Catholics, 147. The heretics called “according to Aeschines” say that Christ himself is both Son and Father, 102. Heretics say that Christ did not see the Father with his fleshly eyes, 119. The heretics of the city of Cremona promise Lucifer, after innumerable torments, a restoration of his former blessedness, 126. They say that Mary was no longer a virgin after childbirth, 164.

Helvidius, the heretic, most perversely supposes that Saint Mary had other sons through her union with Joseph, who were called the Lord’s brothers, 164. He says that Mary was a virgin before childbirth but not after childbirth, 37, 164.

Hermogenes foolishly asserts that God created all things from uncreated matter, 126. The Hieracites condemn marriage and consider every sexual union filthy, 37, 162. Hilary, the bishop, falsely thinks that Christ felt no pain during the Passion, 115.

Actors are not permitted to receive the Eucharist, 152. The Eucharist is not given to murderers, 152.

A human being consists of soul and body, 10, 134. He was created in the image of God, 189. He has free will, 11, 12, 135. Through the serpent’s deception by means of Eve he fell, 11, 155. Thus he lost the good of nature, not his choice, 136. With God’s prior warning he does something good, 12, 136, 152. By divine power he was not predestined to evil, 156.

“To pass into God” is an improper expression concerning a human being, 107. Muhammad deliriously claims that God created human beings from a shadow, 127.

## I

The properties (Ἰδιώματα) remain intact in the natures united in Christ, 105, 108, 177. God alone is immutable, 157. There will be transformation at the future judgment, 6. The torments of ungodly human beings will be eternal, 7, 126.

The laying on of hands in baptism, 30, 144. In the Trinity there is unity, and in unity there is Trinity, 50, 102, 103. In the Trinity there is no rank, and nothing that can be called lower or higher, 4, 117. In the Eucharist pure water must not be offered, but wine mixed with water, 174.

At the resurrection the form of sex will not change, 176. In Christ the two natures are united without confusion, without change, and inseparably, 106. In every good work God goes before us, 29. In Adam’s transgression all human beings lost innocence, 13. In the divine promises let us expect nothing earthly or transitory, 32, 154. In the inner human being there is the image of the Creator, 189.

To be unbounded is proper to God alone and is found in no other nature whatsoever, 8, 128. Infants are baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them, [Col. 1204] 20, 134. In the primitive Church the Eucharist was given to them up to the time of the emperor Charlemagne, 145. Unblemished infants were used in magic, 159.

Many of the ancient theologians think that the unbaptized children of the faithful are condemned, 168, 169. The contrary is demonstrated in the notes, 171. Origen, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Bede, and Bernard posit two hells, 180. Scholastic theologians foolishly suppose that hell is fourfold, 180. Scripture never placed hell among good things, 108.

We have the beginning of salvation through God’s mercy, 12. An insane person should not become a cleric, 38, 167. The triple interrogation in baptism: “Do you believe in God?” etc., 30. The Holy Spirit abandons the minds of the envious, 64. Irenaeus wrongly asserts that after the resurrection the saints will reign with Christ on earth for a thousand years, 154, 155.

## J

Jacobus Syrus, the heresiarch, posits two souls in one human being, 9, 132. Jovinianus says that there is no difference between virginity and marriage, 37, 163. He rejects the eating of meat as unclean, ibid.

The Jews, out of envy, removed Christ from the earth, 60, 73. Judges who hear cases ought to judge rightly, 52. The emperor Julian brands Moses, the greatest of the prophets, with the charge of ignorance because he did not explicitly mention the birth and creation of the angels, 127. The souls of the just, once released from human bodies, go immediately to God; those of the unjust go to the regions of hell itself, 183.

## L

Lactantius, 32. He falsely believes that there will be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, 123. In his writings he foolishly imagines that after the resurrection Christ will reign with the saints on earth for a thousand years, 154, 155. He is wrongly accused of saying that the soul is propagated with bodies through the transmission of human seed, 131.

The human being was created with free will, 11, 12, 135. This is shown to have been impaired in Adam’s transgression, 13, 14, 35. And it cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism, 26, 27.

The superstition of bindings was very common among pagans and Christians, 61. It is condemned, ibid. The Limbo of the Fathers, 181. The Limbo of children, 181.

Improper expressions of the ancient theologians concerning Christ, 107: of Augustine, Gennadius, and Tertullian, ibid.; of Hilary, 115; of Cyprian, 116; of Vigilius the martyr, 112.

To say that the Word suffered impassibly (Λόγον dicere passum impassibiliter) is a jest, 113. The Word (Λόγος) assumed a human and animated body, 109. He united it to himself in an economy (οἰκονομίᾳ), 3, 109. The Word suffered and died not in himself, but by appropriating the suffering and death of his body to himself through the economy of union (ἐνώσεως οἰκονομίᾳ), 110, 111. The Word is eternal and coeternal with the Father, 101. He is not God by position or participation, 120. He is consubstantial (ὁμοούσιος) with the Father, ibid. He is unchangeable (ἄτρεπτος), 157. The Word received human nature, not a human person, 107.

The Luciferians say that the soul is transmitted by generation, 131. The heretics of the city of Cremona promise Lucifer, together with all his demons, restoration of his former blessedness after countless torments, 126.

## M

The Macedonians call the orthodox “consubstantialists” (ὁμοουσιαστάς), 120. With abrupt impiety they declare the Holy Spirit to be God’s servant, 118.

Muhammad promises the devil eternal salvation through the Qur’an, 125. With sacrilegious audacity he invents that God created human beings from a shadow and the devil from a flame of fire, 127. He denies that God has a Son, 98. To his gluttonous Saracens he promises after death a delightful paradise containing beautiful women and prolonged, secure sexual pleasure, 154. With blasphemous mouth he asserts that the Savior suffered only fictitiously and supposedly, 110.

Evil or malice was not created by God but devised by the devil, 33, 156. It has no nature of its own, 158.

Manichaeus, the heretic, 4. He condemns marriage and the foods that God created for use, 37, 162, 163. He holds that there are two principles and two substances, namely good and evil, 148, 158. He falsely imagines that our flesh is compounded from evil and good, 37. In Christ he preferred to believe in a phantom of flesh rather than in flesh’s nature, 110.

Marcellus presumed to call the Lord Jesus merely a human being, 117. Marcion says that Christ brought a body with him from heaven, 3, 108. He says that Christ did not exist substantially but merely simulated a human being through some supposed action, 109. He most foolishly asserts two mutually contrary principles [Col. 1205]. He wickedly attempted to preach that Christ suffered at least in appearance, 110.

Mary was a virgin before marriage, during marriage, and after marriage, 37, 164. Martyrs who shed their blood for Christ are saved even if they depart without the sacrament of baptism, 171. Martyrdom, 173. The relics of the martyrs are to be honored with complete sincerity, not adored, 168.

The materialist heretics Seleucus and Hermogenes wrongly presume that God made heaven and earth not from nothing but from pre-existing and uncreated matter, 126. The ultimate purpose of marriage is the procreation of offspring, 130. It is better not to know than to err, 181.

Menander, the heretic, dared with impure mouth to say that no one could possess salvation unless he received Menander’s baptism, 142. Falsehood is from the devil, 14. A pure mind is a most welcome dwelling for God, 62. Only the Trinity can substantially fill the human mind, 43, 186. Public prostitutes are not given communion, 152.

All the merits of the saints are gifts of God, 14, 18. Mass, 50. The Montanists, 30. They say that the Holy Spirit was restored in Montanus and Priscilla, 147. The Moravians give the Eucharist to children under both kinds, 145.

Bodily death is the punishment of sin, 22. Mortal sins, 151. The emperor Julian accuses Moses of ignorance because he did not explicitly mention the birth of the angels, 127. Change and mutability of nature produce diminution of substance, 3.

## N

Human nature cannot preserve itself without its Creator, 26. It was created good by God but was corrupted through an evil will, 176. Two natures are united in Christ, 108. No one is good by himself, 13. No one is without sin, 183, 187. No one is saved without God’s mercy, 155.

Nepos likewise invented a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of the ungodly, 32. He asserts in his writings a bodily reign of a thousand years, 155.

Nestorius says that Christ became a human being apart from God, 5, 121. In Christ he attempted to preach two persons, 104. He furiously believes that Christ assumed a person, a person, 107.

Nothing from the essence of the Trinity was brought into the nature of creatures, 4, 119. An unbaptized person cannot possess eternal life, 39, 168. That this is not absolutely true is demonstrated in the notes, 169. The Eucharist is not given to the unbaptized, 144. There is not a third spirit in the substance of the human being, as Didymus maintains, 11, 134. It is not deprivation but contempt for the sacrament that condemns, 171, 172.

There are not three gods but one God, triune in names and one in the divinity of substance, 98. There are not two Sons, nor two gods, nor two Christs, 104, 105. Novatus, the heretic, says that sinners cannot be restored completely through penance, 184. No sin is unforgivable before God, 184. No saint is perfect; rather, each is a sinner in some respect, 182. No one has been predestined by God to evil, 29, 33, 155, 156. No one can come to salvation unless God invites him, 33, 155.

There is no baptism if it is not given in faith in the Holy Trinity, 146. Marriage is good, 36. Christ sanctified it by his present majesty, 79, 160. It is an error to make it equal to holy virginity, 163, 164. Those who condemn marriage have the ancient dragon dwelling within them, 163.

## O

Offerings of the altar, 52. Priestly supplications, 16, 137. God is the author of every good work, 18.

All the souls of the saints were in hell before Christ’s resurrection, 41, 177, 178. All the saints declare themselves sinners, 43, 139. All human beings are mortal, 6. Everyone sins and must necessarily say every day, “Forgive us our debts,” 20, 31, 139.

The Son is consubstantial (Ὁμοούσιος) with the Father, 5, 120. The Arians deny this, ibid. Among the ancients there was varied discussion of this term, ibid. It was approved at the Council of Nicaea, ibid. What “consubstantial” (Ὁμοούσιον) means, 120. The Arians and Macedonians call Catholics “consubstantialists” (Ὁμοουσιαστάς), ibid.

The works of unbelievers benefit them at least in this life, 172. The Ophites venerate the serpent, 176.

Origen’s error concerning Christ, 3, 4, 108, 119; concerning the Holy Trinity, 4; concerning the resurrection of the flesh, 5, 123, 176, 177; concerning the salvation of demons and ungodly human beings, 7, 125; concerning the pre-existence of souls, 9, 130. His opponents falsely attributed many things to him, 123, 125.

## P

Pagans worship many gods, 98. Papias vainly dreams that after the resurrection Jerusalem will be restored in gold and jewels and that the saints will reign there with Christ for a thousand years, 32, 154. Irenaeus, Apollinaris, Nepos, Tertullian, Victorinus, and Lactantius also held this opinion, 154, 155.

Easter cannot be celebrated before the passing of the spring equinox, 44, 188. At the Council of Nicaea it was decreed that all Christians should celebrate it at one and the same time, ibid.

Christ’s Passion was real, not phantastic (φαντασιώδης) or mythical (μυθώδης), 116. The eternal Father has an eternal Son, 1, 98. He did not assume flesh, 2. He was always Father, 100. From him the Son was born, 3. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God, 102, 120.

The holy Fathers insist not so much on daily and frequent communion as on worthy reception of the sacraments, 150, 151. The Patripassians are heretics, 103. The Patricians are heretics, 40, 176. The Paulinians are heretics, 30. They say that Christ is a mere human being, 146.

Paul of Samosata introduces two Christs and two sons, one servant and the other lord, 104. Sin is the death of the soul, 22. Mortal sins, 31. Pelagius, the heretic, says that human beings can be without sin if they wish, 187. The Photinians acknowledge that Christ began from the Virgin, 148.

Photius, the patriarch, refused to admit the emperor Basil, a homicide, to the sacred meal, 152. Philolaus’s error concerning the pre-existence of souls, 132. Plato says that something from the essence of the Trinity was brought into the nature of creatures, 4. He says that souls had previously sinned in their heavenly dwelling and for this reason had been cast down into bodies on earth, 133. He attributes reason to brute animals, 133.

The punishment of unregenerated children will be extremely mild, 169. Public penance, 31, 41, 152, 153. Those who have professed penance are not to be ordained clerics, 167. It must certainly be believed that sins are abolished through penance, 41, 184. True penance is to eradicate the causes of sins, 32, 153.

The Pontificians condemn children who have not been regenerated, 170. They posit a fourfold hell, 180, 181. They say that those who do not mix water with wine in the sacramental cup commit mortal sin, 175.

Praxeas introduces a solitary God, 5, 120. He affirms that the Father descended into the Virgin and took flesh from her, 103. Prayer before meals, 161. Christians and pagans did not taste first-fruits before they had been offered by a priest, 179. Rulers have authority from God, 78.

The Priscillianists are heretics, 30. They condemn marriage, 162. In the spirit of folly they believe that the soul sinned before it existed in this world, 131. They reject the eating of meat as unclean, 163. In a heretical spirit they assert that the devil was never good, 156, 157.

The procession of the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, 1. The Proclians, heretics, taught that Christ came to us in the flesh, 146. We should pray for the ungodly, that they may rise from the night of ignorance, 84. Prosper Tiro wrongly equates baptism of blood with true baptism, 173.

Public penance, 31, 152. It was imposed on people because of the gravest sins, 153. Children before the years of discernment should not receive communion, 146. Punic Christians call baptism “salvation” and the Eucharist “life,” 169. The Pythagoreans think that souls sinned in heaven before birth and were therefore sent into bodies to undergo punishment, 131.

## Q

Whoever has committed mortal sins should in no way presume to receive communion, 150, 151. Those who were baptized among heretics without invocation of the Holy Trinity are baptized by Catholics, 30, 142. Whoever has taken a concubine, two married women, a repudiated widow, or a prostitute in marriage cannot be a cleric, 38, 165, 166. Nor can one who has castrated himself, ibid. Nor one who has taken interest, ibid. Nor one convicted of having acted on the stage, ibid.

Whoever has not been baptized cannot have eternal life, 168. This is not absolutely true, 171, 172. “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another,” 50.

The faithful received the Eucharist daily in the primitive Church, 31, 148. This custom continued until the time of Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, ibid. Later, when charity grew cold, it began to waste away, 149. Therefore the Roman Fathers decreed that, if not more frequently, the laity should communicate at least three times, or at minimum once, each year, unless they wished to be entirely barred from entering the church, ibid.

## R

The rule of faith concerning the Holy Trinity, 1, 97. The relics of the martyrs are to be honored with complete sincerity, not adored, 39, 168. Renunciation of Satan in baptism, 39.

There will be a resurrection of all the dead, 5, 122, 124. It will be one, simultaneous, and once for all, ibid. It will not be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as Lactantius and Stephen Gobarus maintain, 123. In it the truth of the body will not be emptied, 124. Nor will the form of sex change, 40, 176. Rather, a dead man will rise in the form of a man and a woman in the form of a woman, 177. Even miscarried and deformed infants will rise, 122. The resurrected bodies will be free from corruption and death, but they will not lose their own nature, 124.

## S

Sabellius, the heretic, 1, 4. He compresses the Trinity into the narrow limits of a single person, 101.

A priest who does not mix wine with water in the mysteries is deposed, 175. Those known not yet to have been regenerated cannot participate in the sacraments of the altar, 144. Priests are to be honored, 102. Punic Christians call the sacrament of Christ’s body “life,” 169. Sacraments are so called from sanctification, 151.

Sarmatio, the heretic, says that virgins and married women have equal merit before God, 163. What satisfaction is, 32, 153. Saturninus says that Christ appeared in a phantom and not truly, 109. Sethianus sacrilegiously dared to preach that our evil flesh was created by God, 40, 176. He honors Seth, Adam’s son, ibid.

Severus, the heretic, wrongly believes that God suffered in his own nature, 112. Sinners too can perform signs, 43, 187. A Christian may become renowned through signs, but not holy, 43, 187. Ancient Christians marked foods with the sign of the cross, 161. The Simonians maintain that Christ suffered in appearance, 110.

Without God we can do nothing good, 15, 25. Nor can we obtain the ministry of eternal salvation, 26. “Spirit” in place of “soul,” 11, 134.

The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, 1, 99, 100. He was neither begotten nor made, 101. Therefore he should not be called begotten or unbegotten, ibid. He is equal and coeternal with the Father and the Son, ibid. He did not assume flesh; only the Son did, 103. The Arians and Macedonians blasphemously say that he is less than the Father and the Son, 118. [Col. 1208]

Stephen Gobarus says that there will be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, 123. A human being consists at least of two substances, 134. Suidas wrongly makes angels unbounded, 139. Sylvanus posits a solitary God without the Son, 120. No one should be ignorant of the Apostles’ Creed, 149.

## T

Tatianus considers foods made from meat unclean, 163. Tertullian posits a corporeal God, 118. He thinks that something from the essence of the Trinity was brought into a creature, 120. He asserts that the soul is transmitted by generation, 131. He most foolishly imagined that the saints would reign with Christ on earth for a thousand years, 155.

Scholastic theologians say that miscarried fetuses will not rise because they did not live, 123. They posit a fourfold hell, 180. They deprive unregenerated children of eternal blessedness, 169. The Theopaschites attribute suffering to the Godhead, 112. The Timothians say that the two natures in Christ were resolved into one mass, 106. The Tnetopsychites say that the soul dies with the body, 132.

Nothing in the essence of the Trinity is divided or distinguished, 2, 3, 101, 102. There is nothing servile or created, 117. Nothing is unequal, nothing earlier or later, 4, 118. Nothing from it was brought into the nature of creatures, 119. The Holy Trinity is called consubstantial (ὁμοούσιος) because all three persons are of the same substance, 102, 103. The Tritheists worship three gods, 98.

## U

The Hydroparastates (Ὑδροπαράσταται), heretics, use only water in the Eucharist, 174. There is one person and two natures in Christ, the Only-begotten Son of God, 105. Christ is called Only-begotten, 2, 105. In the Holy Trinity there is one God by nature: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 2, 98, 103. Urbicus of Potentia says that the Holy Spirit is the Father, or the Son, or a creature, 208.

A usurer cannot be a cleric, 38, 166. Communion is not given to him, 152.

## V

Vadianus says that God consists of human form and bodily members, 119. Valentinus, the heretic, says that Christ was not a true human being but merely an empty apparition, 3, 109. He believed that the Word and flesh had one nature, 108. With impious mouth he babbles that Christ brought a body with him from heaven and did not assume it from Mary, 108. He introduces two principles and two baptisms, 141, 148.

The Venustians, heretics, say that the devil created the human body, 176. “The Word became flesh,” while the Word remained in its own substance and the human being in his own nature, 107. Victorinus the rhetor publicly professes his faith at Rome, 174. Vigilantius, the heretic, despises the relics of the martyrs and calls Christians who venerate them “ash-worshipers” and idolaters, 168. Vigilius the martyr wrongly refers the Passion to the property of the Word’s nature, 112.

The use of wine in the sacrifice of the Mass, 175. Virginity is preferred to marriage, 36, 161, 164. The Virgin Mary gave birth to the Savior with her genital integrity preserved, 164. Those who will be in the body at the Lord’s coming are called “the living,” 127.

## Z

Zeno says that the soul continues after death but is nevertheless subject to corruption, 10, 133. Zwingli also promises eternal life to those who are alienated from the Church of Christ, 177.

## Saint Hilary, Pope
