### Letters

11. Letter of Hilary the deacon of the Roman Church to Pulcheria Augusta. Same place.

**Letter I (of Pope Hilary).** — To the bishops of Tarragona concerning the synodal decree, 12.

Letter of the bishops of Tarragona to Pope Hilary, 14.

Another letter of the same bishops to the same recipient, 16.

**Letter II.** —

1. That no one is to be ordained bishop without the consent of the metropolitan.
2. That no bishop, after abandoning his own church, is to transfer to another.
3. That Irenaeus, removed from the Church of Barcelona, is to return to his own.
4. Concerning the removal of bishops who have been illicitly ordained, and concerning the prohibition of having two bishops in one church.
5. Concerning the condemnation of Irenaeus if he does not return to his own church, 17.

**Letter III.** — On the same subject, 19.

**Letter IV.** — Hilary delegates to the bishops Veranus and Victurus the dispute between the bishops Ingenuus and Auxanius, and decrees that the city of Cemelenum and the fortress of Nicea be returned to the administration of a single bishop, 20.

**Letter V.** — Hilary to Leontius of Arles, concerning the beginnings of his episcopate, 22.

Letter of Leontius of Arles to Pope Hilary, congratulating him on his pontificate and asking him to protect the rights of the Church of Arles. Same place.

**Letter VI.** — Hilary replies to Leontius’s letter, which had been written before Leontius had received Hilary’s preceding letter, 23.

**Letter VII.** — Hilary warns Leontius to send a report concerning Herme, who was said rashly to have usurped the episcopate of the Church of Narbonne, 24.

**Letter VIII (to the bishops of Gaul).** —

1. He permits Herme to preside over the Church of Narbonne, but without the power to ordain bishops.
2. That councils be held annually, with attendance from whatever provinces is possible, and be convened by Leontius.
3. That bishops not travel to another province without letters from the metropolitan.
4. He refers to the bishops the judgment concerning the parishes of the Church of Arles claimed by Leontius.
5. That ecclesiastical estates not be alienated unless the reason for the alienation has first been demonstrated before a council.

Same place.

**Letter IX (to Lontius).** — Concerning Mamertus, a bishop who had ordained a bishop outside his own boundaries; his case is to be examined in council, 27.

**Letter X (to certain bishops of Gaul).** — That no one transgress his own boundaries, and that councils be convened annually by Bishop Leontius. Same place.

**Letter XI.** — Pope Hilary’s order concerning the Church of Dea, where a bishop had been improperly ordained by the bishop of Vienne, 28.

**Decrees of Pope Hilary**, 31.

## Saint Simplicius, Pope

Life of Saint Simplicius, pope, from the *Pontifical Book*, 31.

### Letters

35. **Letter I (to Zeno of Seville).** — Concerning the authority entrusted to him in place of the see over all the churches of Spain. He appoints the bishop of Seville, an excellent man, as vicar of the apostolic see. Same place.

**Letter II.** — Simplicius rebukes John of Ravenna because, by force, he had ordained Gregory bishop; he orders Gregory to govern the Church of Modena, without having any dispute with John, same place.

**Letter III (to the bishops Florentius, Equitius, and Severus).** — Gaudentius, bishop of Rufina, is deprived of his priestly office and of a threefold portion of the Church’s revenues because of illicit ordinations, 37.

**Letter IV.** — He asks Zeno to restrain by royal authority Timothy the Cat, who was attempting once again to occupy the see of Alexandria and to disseminate his heresies at Constantinople, 38.

[Col. 1214] **Letter V.** — Simplicius writes to Acacius that he should resist Timothy with every effort, so that the universal council which Timothy was arranging with the emperor might not take place, 41.

**Letter VI.** — He commends Acacius because no church at Constantinople had been open to Timothy the Cat, and urges him to warn the emperor not to permit the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon to be violated, 42.

**Letter VII.** — He commends the steadfastness of the clergy and monks living at Constantinople, since they had not admitted Timothy to communion; he demonstrates that Timothy, having often been condemned, ought not to be heard, 43.

**Letter VIII.** — Simplicius congratulates the Emperor Zeno on the recovery of his empire and urges him to restore the bishop of Alexandria to his see and to ensure that the decrees of Leo and of the Council of Chalcedon are observed, 44.

Letter of Acacius to Pope Simplicius, 46.

**Letter IX.** — Simplicius congratulates Acacius that Timothy, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, has been restored to his Church, 47.

**Letter X.** — He gives thanks to the Emperor Zeno that Timothy has been restored to the Church of Alexandria, and asks him to order Peter, the disturber of that Church, to be expelled, 48.

**Letter XI.** — Simplicius writes to Acacius that Timothy had asked him for pardon because, out of fear, he had recited the name of Dioscorus at the altars, and that he had written to the emperor so that the emperor might keep Peter at a distance, 49.

**Letter XII.** — Simplicius urges the Emperor Zeno to protect Timothy, restored to his see, and to order Peter to be expelled, 50.

**Letter XIII (to Acacius).** — On the same subject as the preceding letter, 51.

**Letter XIV.** — Simplicius praises the concern of the Emperor Zeno in punishing those who had conspired at Antioch to murder bishops. He regrets that his letters to Acacius had not been carried out, and approves the election of the head of the Church of Antioch, made without observing the decree of the Council of Nicaea. Same place.

**Letter XV (to Acacius).** — On the same subject, 53.

Observation of Antonius Pagi, 54.

**Letter XVI (to Acacius).** — He confirms the election of Calendion as bishop of Antioch, 55.

**Letter XVII.** — He complains that he did not receive Acacius’s letters together with the emperor’s letters, and that the emperor was asking for the heretic Peter to be made bishop of Alexandria, while Simplicius himself was prepared to confirm John; finally, he begs Acacius to warn the emperor not to wish to favor an already condemned heretic, 56.

**Fragment of a letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno**, 58.

**Letter XVIII.** — He writes to Acacius that he is astonished that Acacius had not at all informed him about the afflictions of the Church of Alexandria; he urges him to suggest to the emperor that peace be restored to that Church, 59.

Letter of Simplicius to the same recipient, published at Rome by Luca Holstenius. Same place.

Observation of Antonius Pagi, 61.

## Saint Faustus of Riez

Preliminary material, 775.

### On Grace and Free Choice

**Book I**, 783.

**Chapter I.** — That the Pelagian view, which denied grace, must first be refuted. Same place.

**Chapter II.** — Against the Pelagian teaching that infants have no need of baptism, 788.

**Chapter III.** — Against the claim that, through grace alone, every person is saved without any effort, 789.

**Chapter IV.** — Against the view which, by saying, “One has been predestined to death, another predestined to life,” shuts out hope from prayer. Same place.

**Chapter V.** — The works of the law are overthrown and grace is commended; or, against the extremely ignorant way in which they put forward testimonies in support of grace alone, 791.

**Chapter VI.** — On the statement: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” 792.

**Chapter VII.** — How the statement is to be understood: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast”; here faith too is counted among works, and the food of the law is described as passing away while the food of grace remains, 793.

**Chapter VIII.** — Against the claim that free choice has been entirely taken away, 794.

**Chapter IX.** — How the weakness of free choice is to be understood, 795.

**Chapter X.** — How the statements are to be understood: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” and, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,” 796.

**Chapter XI.** — Against the claim that free choice is inclined only toward evil in human beings and is wholly absent with respect to good, 799.

**Chapter XII.** — Against the view that a vessel destined for dishonor cannot rise to become a vessel for honor, 801.

[Col. 1218] **Chapter XIII.** — Likewise, willing and refusing were entrusted to human choice with respect to the good as well as the evil side, 803.

**Chapter XIV.** — The grace of God and the human will are joined together by the testimony of Scripture, and the empty slander concerning infants is briefly passed over, 806.

**Chapter XV.** — Against the claim that those who perish after baptism never truly believed in baptism, 807.

**Chapter XVI.** — Against the claim that Christ did not die for all, 808.

**Chapter XVII.** — Against their ignorant and wicked interpretation of the Gospel saying, 810.

**Chapter XVIII.** — Against the claim that God’s violence hardens a person so that he cannot come to salvation, 811.

**Chapter XIX.** — Against the statement: “Human beings are driven by the will of God,” 812.

813. **Chapter I.** — Against the impious assertion that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened by God. Same place.

**Chapter III.** — That foreknowing is one thing and predestining another, 816.

**Chapter IV.** — Against the claim, “He is merciful toward those whom he acquires and just toward those whom he abandons,” since he appears merciful even toward the wicked and also just toward the good, 817.

**Chapter V.** — Against the claim, “The one who perished did not so much wish to be saved as fail to be able to be saved,” in accordance with what we read: “And they were not able to believe,” 819.

**Chapter VI.** — What is meant by the statement: “When they had not yet done anything good or evil,” 821.

**Chapter VII.** — In whose image and likeness the first human being was created, 824.

## Saint Felix III
## Prolegomena

889 **LETTERS.** Ibid.

**FIRST LETTER** (To Acacius).—The Roman synod urges the emperor Zeno, with diligent effort, to correct the things he has hitherto wrongly done against the Catholic faith. 893

**LETTER II.**—He pleads with the emperor Zeno on behalf of the Church of Alexandria. He recalls whatever he had previously said or done in its defense, in order to criticize the subsequent expulsion of John, bishop of Alexandria, and the restoration of Peter Noggus. 899

**LETTER III** (To Peter the Fuller).—He shows that Peter the Fuller, otherwise called the Felt-worker, had fallen not only into the heresies of Valentinus, Mani, Arius, Sabellius, Apollinaris, and Eutyches, but also into several errors of paganism, which asserts many gods. He then admonishes him to come to his senses, and says that the words “Crucified for us” ought not to be added to the *Trisagion*. 903

**LETTER IV** (To the same).—He deposes and anathematizes Peter the Fuller. 911

Letter of the same Pope Felix to Peter the Fuller. An ancient translation. 915

**LETTER V.**—He announces to the emperor Zeno that Peter the Fuller has been condemned by synodal judgment with the sentence of anathema, and that therefore communion with him must be avoided. He urges the same emperor to expel the deposed Peter from the Church of Antioch. 917

**LETTER VI.**—He deprives Acacius of priestly office and of communion with the faithful. 921

**LETTER VII** (To all the bishops).—He determines how those who have been rebaptized ought to be admitted into the Catholic Church. 924

**[Column 1219] LETTER VIII.**—He commends Terentianus to Zeno, bishop. 927

**A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE EUTYCHIANISTS.** 928

**ADDITION** taken from the third edition. 933

**DECREE OF THE SENTENCE OF POPE FELIX** concerning the condemnation of Bishop Acacius. 934

**LETTER IX.**—Felix complains to Zeno about the violation of his legates by him, and advises him to submit to the condemnation of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius. Ibid.

**LETTER X** (To the clergy and people of Constantinople).—He urges them not to be disturbed by the treachery of the legates and to avoid communion with Acacius, who has been condemned by the Apostolic See. 936

**LETTER XI** (To the monks of the city of Constantinople and of Bithynia).—He explains that Tutus, defender of the Church, was condemned on account of treachery, and how they themselves ought to proceed against those among their own number who have adhered to Acacius. 937

**TREATISE OF POPE FELIX.**—He refutes the arguments advanced on behalf of Acacius and shows that, since Acacius was justly and lawfully condemned, he could be restored only canonically. 941

Letter of Pope Felix, elsewhere attributed to Pope Gelasius. 967

**LETTER XII.**—Having praised the emperor Zeno’s care in the ordination of the new bishop, he urges him to agree with the Roman Church concerning the condemnation of the names of Acacius and Peter, about which the legates of the clergy had replied that they had received no instructions. 969

**[Column 1220] LETTER XIII** (To Flavitas, bishop of Constantinople).—He explains that he suspended his legates from communion because, concerning the names of Acacius and Peter, they had replied that they had received no instructions. He urges Flavitas himself to abstain from those who recite these names and to persuade Zeno to do the same. 971

**LETTER XIV** (To Thalassius).—Neither he nor his monks are to communicate beforehand with the Church of Constantinople or with its bishop, until this has been ordered by the Apostolic See. 974

**LETTER XV** (To Vetranio, bishop).—He dissents from the Church of Constantinople, explaining the reasons, and urges Vetranio to move Zeno to renew union with the Roman Church. 975

**DECREE OF POPE FELIX.**—In ecclesiastical cases, royal will must be subordinated to the priests. 977
